The Śrī Svacchanda Tantra,
accompanied by the commentary titled Udyota composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Kṣemarāja.
The First Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
[Salutation to] Him who is the singular form of the universe, the soul of the universe, and the cause of the creation and other processes of the universe.
We praise Svacchandabhairava, whose very body is the light of others.
Salutation to the ocean Bhairava, the storehouse of all perfections, who sports with the world as a playful wave amidst the surging tides of his creative power.
Victorious is this single oyster-shell of the power of the ocean of awakening,
within which this entire world shines forth as consisting of nothing but pearls.
Those whose every stain of ignorance has been utterly shaken off by mere remembrance,
and who are expansive through the excellent words of their Guru, are triumphant throughout the three worlds.
Kṣemarāja, whose vision of the Great Mahāśaiva doctrine has become pure and manifest through service to that [teacher], elucidates the system of the venerable Svacchanda to a small degree.

O connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, for the sake of pacifying the latent impressions of this worthless saṃsāra, savor the fragrance from my heart-lotus, which has blossomed through the radiance of the sun of ever-new awakening.

Here, a certain disciple of the Goddess, whose heart is moistened by the essence of the desire to bestow grace and who has been brought face-to-face with supreme consciousness, speaks in order to introduce the treatise:
"Bhairava, free from all affliction, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa..."
[He was accompanied] by Caṇḍa, Nandi, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha, and Bhṛṅgin. || 1-1 ||
The Great Lord (Maheśāna) was being praised by Kumāra, Indra, Yama, Āditya, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, who stood at their head, and was attended by the Gaṇas and the Mothers.
To the God who is the agent of creation and dissolution, the cause of preservation and withdrawal, the bestower of grace, and the destroyer of the distress of those who bow before him; || 1-3 ||
Seeing Bhairava delighted, the Goddess spoke these words:

"In this [system], the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the self-manifesting radiance of Svacchandabhairava, which belongs to the Supreme Lord who is a mass of consciousness and bliss and who transcends the principles taught in the *Brahmadarśana*. Thus [is the teaching] of the Blessed One’s scripture."
And this is its very designation. With the intention that He performs the fivefold activity whose sole nature is His own self,
the Goddess, having beheld the joyful Lord Bhairava who performs the fivefold activity beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*), [spoke].

It has been stated, "He spoke these words. In this context, the Lord is intent upon the play of the entire creation, from Śiva down to the earth; furthermore, because He is non-different from the universe, He desires to conquer through His absolute pre-eminence, even in the form of worldly activity.

He is radiant, being praised by Śiva, Mantra-Maheśvara, and the others; he is the goal and the refuge of all who have no other resort, and his essence is non-dual consciousness. As it is said: "The root *div* [is used] in the sense of playing (*krīḍā*) and so forth. He is Bhairava, whose nature consists of supporting (*bharaṇa*), sounding (*ravaṇa*), and vomiting out (*vamana*) the universe; and according to the etymology, he is the fearlessness (*abhaya*) for those who are afraid (*bhīrūṇām*).

He is the bestower of fearlessness to those wandering in *saṃsāra*. "Fear" (*bhaya*) means terror or dread of *saṃsāra*; the "cry" (*rava*) produced by that is a wailing, and from that arises the "terrified one" (*bhīrava*). He is the one who causes this very "terrified one"—who is characterized by such wailing—to arise through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), by means of reflecting upon the fear of *saṃsāra*.

*Bhera* is Time (*kāla*), so called because it sets the lunar mansions (*bhāni*) in motion; *bheravāḥ* are the yogins who "blow" toward that [Time], being those who take delight in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that devours time. This is their internal nature.

For the sake of fear—that is, for the terror of the ignorant masses—there is a "roar" (*rava*), which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the digits (*kalā*) such as form (*ākāra*) arising from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).
He is Bhairava, the Lord of those goddesses of consciousness (saṃviddevī) who take the form of the circles of the Khecarīs, Gocarīs, Dikcarīs, and Bhūcarīs; he is Bhairava, the Terrifying One,
intent on shattering the cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), as it is etymologically explained in the scriptures by the venerable Bṛhaspati.
And because its essential nature has been explained etymologically as "the abode of Śiva" (śivatanu),
for this very reason, he who is joyful, endowed with the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti) which is a mass of eternal bliss—
that alone is what is designated by the name Bhairava, and not the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, or Śiva.
According to the principle established in the eleventh chapter, because this [reality] is devoid of intrinsic nature, or because it is that which causes these [phenomena] to manifest and dissolve;
for this very reason, he is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the sovereign of all these. For this very reason, he resides in the crown of the head.

In the *brahmabila*, the flickering *elā* is the *śakti*; he whose seat (*āsana*) is situated upon that is the one seated on the peak of the pervasive *samanātman*—the station situated above all paths—which is that peak of Kailāsa. There he sits, transcending that [peak], a single mass of pure light.
And by its pervasive extension everywhere, it is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*). Thence, it measures (*mimīte*) from all sides (*ā*), thus it is *āmaya*;
Māyā is known as the nature of power (*śakti*), which is the coiled power (*śaktikuṇḍalī*) below that. (10-1263)
Thus, [He is] free from that Great Māyā, which consists of the aforementioned nescience (akhyāti), and from whom disease has departed for those who take refuge in Him.
By means of Caṇḍa and the others, ending with Kumāra— who are pervaded by the expansion of the Lord’s powers and are themselves graced by Him— ...

Of the Blessed Lord Umāpati, whose nature is the pervasive expansion of that very proliferation (prapañca), who has assumed the form of Bhairava through the immersion into the expansive state of Bhairava as explained [in the scriptures], and who is known by that name while seated upon the peak of the Himavat mountain called Kailāsa, which will be described later in the section on the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
By the world-protectors such as Indra and others who are his internal retinue; by all the destroyers such as Rudra and others characterized by Yama;
by all those consisting of splendor characterized by the Ādityas; and by those characterized by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
He is praised by all, beginning with the venerable Ananta-bhaṭṭāraka, who effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe],
as well as by others led by him who have been made vessels for the independent descent of power (nirapekṣa-śaktipāta);
he is thus praised as being supreme due to the submergence of the state of being a constructed subject (kalpita-pramātṛtā).
Being embraced by the Gaṇa— the eight Bhairavas beginning with Kapālīśa,
whose retinue will be described later— by the Mothers— the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī— and by Umā-devī, who is the measure of the Gaṇas through her pervasion of the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Being served by her who is the foremost among the internal retinue already mentioned,
being entered [into the heart] precisely through the descent of His power (*śaktipāta*) by way of the pacification of nescience (*akhyāti*),
and habitually performing both emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), He is the very self of the manifold expansion of emission and withdrawal.

And [he is] one who effects dissolution and maintenance as the fruit of specific transgressions, and who always performs the fivefold activity by way of his inherent nature of bestowing grace through such qualities as being habitually gracious and being designated as such;
and [he is so] by fulfilling the desires of practitioners and others who have bowed down to him.
The destroyer of all afflictions.

Having thus beheld— that is, directly realized— the god Bhairava who is joyful and possesses the form of the deity as described, the Goddess, who is the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), spoke these words.
He perceives [the universe] through the nature of full self-identity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*).

For that very perception is the Lord himself, whose essence is the contraction of the vowels and consonants (*akāra-hakāra-pratyāhāra*), and who takes the form of the first sprout of the entire expansion of all scriptures, within which the whole universe is contained.

The aggregate of sounds. As he will say: "From the supreme cause, Śiva, who is tranquil and whose form is unperceived, the scripture—which is in the form of resonance (dhvani)—has emerged; it is exceedingly difficult to attain. (8.27)
And so forth. The Lord Bhairava, whose nature is consciousness alone, having first assumed the forms of Sadāśiva and the others,
[manifests] the form of Umāpati, which consists primarily in pervading the entire expansion of his own substratum, by means of his entry into his own existence.

Having established himself in the state of bliss that is essentially Bhairava, and likewise having assumed the form of the venerable Umā-bhaṭṭārikā through the adoption of the roles of teacher and disciple, he promulgates the scripture—
consisting of questions and answers— for the sake of favoring the world. As he will say:

"Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself [revealed] the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and subsequent words, according to the distinction of supports. (8.31).
Thus, because it strings together the meaning of the scripture by means of both internal and external sequences, it is "sūtra-like" (sūtrabhūta).
This introductory statement of the Tantra, consisting of three and a half verses, should be understood as such;
and herein, it should be understood as a single sentence. This is intended to clarify the meaning implicitly contained within the terms *deva* and *bhairava*, as previously explained.

Other qualifiers beginning with "Kailāsa" have been employed. To explain: the two purposes of heaven—namely, play (*krīḍā*) and worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)—have been made manifest by the section beginning with "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with "bestowing grace" (*anugrahakara*). Among those, [the purpose of play] is [treated] in the first five chapters and the chapter on mudrās (*mudrāpaṭala*).

The favor [bestowed] by means of the fourteenth [chapter], which constitutes a limb of this [work], has been established; the nature of creation and so forth was stated by the eleventh; and the purpose of the self desiring victory was manifested by the word "Kailāsa," which is intent on the internal meaning, and by the term "Maheśāna" through the tenth chapter.
It has been determined; its meaning of illumination is revealed by the two words *anāmaya* and *mudita*, and it is manifested from time to time in the middle [of the text]:
"Situated therein, one manifests that splendor which is the supreme, ultimate cause" (4.397).
In such passages of the text, the purpose of the praise— from the words "Caṇḍa," etc., up to "practiced"—
is made clear as being for the sake of the accomplishment of the gods and demons, by means of the method of worship.

This meaning— characterized as "the refuge for those without refuge"— which was established in the introductory sections beginning with "Commanded by the God of Gods," is also made explicit by the concluding phrase "the destroyer of the distress of those who bow down."
It has been brought forth by the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, twelfth, thirteenth, and fifteenth chapters;

in this same manner, the meaning of the term *bhairava* should also be applied. For therein, just as the meaning of *ravaṇa* (shouting) was indicated by the words ending with "he spoke" (*abravīt*) and demonstrated by the chapter on the introduction of the Tantra (*tantrāvatāra*), [so too is the meaning of *bhairava*].

Likewise, other meanings should also be applied as appropriate, by virtue of being synonymous with the term "deity" (*deva*). Furthermore, by the word *kailāsa* in its second sense, [the Lord] is praised through the sequence of locations by means of terms such as "Deva-Bhairava," and through the sequence of states by means of the passage beginning with "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with "being praised."

The introduction of this treatise preceded by praise is revealed by this very introductory statement; by the word "delighted" (*muditam*), the disciple's knowledge of the appropriate occasion for inquiry is revealed; and by the term "Bhairava," its origin from the Southern Current (*dakṣiṇasrotas*) is indicated.
The teaching of the scripture has been indicated; we shall demonstrate the division of its streams in the ninth chapter. || 3 ||
In response to the inquiry, "What did she say?", he says:
The Goddess said: "O Supreme Lord, that which was spoken by you to me concerning the *Svacchanda*... (1.4).
The great tantra of the Four Seats, which extends over a hundred crores [of verses], spreading through infinite divisions, brings about the arising of the fourfold fruit. (1.5)
O Śaṅkara, human beings who possess little vigor and prowess, short lifespans, meager wealth, and weak resolve are not capable [of this]. (1.6)
For that purpose, please graciously relate a compendium of its contents, which expands upon the meaning of this concise treatise and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

O Śaṅkara! O benefactor whose sole intent is grace! O Supreme Lord whose own nature is the Self! Since you, by your very will—being one whose desire is directed toward me alone—bear the name of the unrestrained Bhairava;

*Svacchanda*—expanded by hundreds of millions [of verses] according to the perspective to be described in the chapter on the introduction to the tantra, spread out through an infinity of divisions such as *Koṭarākṣa*, *Vyādhi*, *Bhakṣa*, *Aghoreśvara*, *Svacchanda*, and so forth; [it consists of] the four: the *vidyās*, mantras, maṇḍalas, and mudrās.
The *pīṭha* is the support by virtue of its mere existence.
"The *mudrā*-pīṭha, the maṇḍala-pīṭha, and likewise the mantra-pīṭha;
and similarly here the *vidyā*-pīṭha—thus the *Saṃhitā* consists of four *pīṭhas*. So it is said.
Likewise: "Svacchandabhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava—
these are the four other texts, O fair-faced one, [known as] the Mantrapīṭha."

Because it is stated in the *Śrīsarvavīra*: therein, Vidyā is the radiance (*sphurattā*) whose nature is Svacchanda-Śiva, the ultimate Mātṛkā; the Mantras are those beginning with Catuṣkala; the Maṇḍala is that beginning with Navanābha;
and the Mudrās are those imitating the skull-bowl (*kapāla*) and so forth.

That [teaching] has been described as that from which arises the fruit— consisting of the bestowal of enjoyment, liberation, and so forth— of the fourfold group comprising the *samayin*, *putraka*, *sādhaka*, and *ācārya*, which is divided by the distinctions to be explained hereafter.

Human beings are subject to the laws of birth and death; they are endowed with only slight vigor, enthusiasm, prowess, and capability, and for that very reason are incapable of heroic accomplishments (*vīrasiddhi*). Due to their short lifespan and meager wealth, they are unable to perform great undertakings, and because of their limited fortitude, [they are likewise constrained].

Devoid of the consolation of the instructions on the knowledge of the great purpose, they are unable even to hear or study [the extensive treatise], let alone practice it; for their sake, therefore, there is a compendium— a summary— of that scripture, such that the expansion of the scriptural meaning is small, which [treatise] possesses both worldly enjoyment and liberation by its very nature.
O Giver, speak with favor—that is, with grace consisting in the manifestation of inner purity. || 7 ||
Now he sets forth the subjects to be determined by way of questions:
"O Maheśvara, what kind of guru and practitioner should one know?
What kind of one bestows fear and fearlessness, and what kind of disciple and ground? (1.8)
The mantras in brief, as well as the time in brief;
the sacrifice, the oblation, the consecration, and the colored powders.
The five products of the cow, the sacrificial pap, the tooth-stick, the mandala,
initiation, the paths, consecrations, the pledges, and the means of accomplishment.
O Maheśvara, tell me likewise how things are accomplished in the Kali age;
what kind of ground, beginning with the Guru and ending with the earth, should one know how to accept or reject;
and how the fifteen subjects, from the Mantras down to the means of accomplishment (sādhana), are perfected in the Kali age.

Speak! In that regard, a *samayin* who has heard the scriptures and desires to attain the status of a *putraka* and so forth must examine the Guru, or be examined by the Guru himself; the Gurus and others are to be appointed here, as they are indicated in sequence according to their relative importance: namely, the disciple (*śiṣya*), the *putraka*, and the *samayin*.

The true guru, whose nature will be described, bestows fearlessness upon the group of disciples consisting of the four categories beginning with the guru; the false guru, however, bestows fear. The group of true disciples and the group of false disciples bestow fearlessness and fear, respectively, upon their own selves. Fear...

"From the obstacle to success and liberation"— because of the absence of that [obstacle], there is fearlessness; "the bestower of fear and fearlessness"— this should be applied, by changing the gender and other grammatical markers as appropriate, even to the ground, mantras, tooth-sticks, and so forth, according to the method to be explained below.

The ground is the site for the layout of the mantra-sacrifice; the mantras are those such as the proximate (āsanna), the manifest (mūrti), the with-parts (sakala), and the partless (niṣkala); the time is the solar and the internal, which is manifold;
in brief, regarding the sacrifice and the oblation common to all who are initiated, [this concerns] all the materials required for initiation.

Consecration (*adhivāsa*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the induction of fitness; "dusts" (*rajāṃsi*) refers to rice flour and so forth to be mentioned later, which are used for mandalas such as the nine-naved one;
initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the destruction of bonds and the bestowing of the state of Śiva; and the path (*adhvan*) has many divisions.

The sixfold [initiation] consists of the aspects of phoneme, mantra, word, ritual portion (kalā), principle (tattva), and world-sphere (bhuvana). Consecration (abhiṣeka) is the sprinkling with water from the mantra-pitcher at the conclusion of the sacrifice for the preceptors and others.

The rules (samayas) are the prescribed injunctions and prohibitions for those who have been initiated, which must be observed as a remainder [of the initiation]. The means of accomplishment (sādhanas) [are also included].

The means for the accomplishment of practitioners—such as ritual placement (nyāsa), recitation (japa), the consecration of clarified butter (ājya-saṃskāra), and so forth—are not mentioned separately here, because everything else is included within this very [system]. || 10 ||
Now, beginning the determination of the questions, the opening statement— which expresses the purpose for the sake of engaging the disciple through encouragement— is as follows:
The illustrious Bhairava said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, that which has been requested by you!"
"For the sake of favoring mortals, I shall now speak to you.

By repeating "Excellent! Excellent! (*sādhu sādhu*), the Lord praises those people who have shown compassion by asking for the opportunity at the right time; thus, in order to establish their fitness for receiving the instruction, He stimulates the intellect of the disciple.

By the term "O highly fortunate one," her readiness to bestow grace is praised; [it is said] by you for the sake of favoring all mortals subject to death in general— not just certain restricted qualified individuals— for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation, that entire collection of objects of knowledge...

That which was prompted by the sequence and asked is for the sake of favoring them alone. Now, at this opportune moment of the great expansion awakened by entering into the reality of Supreme Bhairava,
it is appropriate to proceed through the sequence beginning with the demonstration of initiation suitable for children, the ignorant, the learned, and others.
Having done so, I shall explain it to you.
And here, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the knowledge of the sequence of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) previously indicated and subsequently referred to by the word "this" (*atra*).

The purpose of that [treatise] is grace, consisting of enjoyment and liberation; and therein lies the relationship, consisting of the nature of the means and the end. It concerns the eligibility of mortals, and the stimulation of the fitness of a disciple who, being oriented toward the supreme desire to favor others, has turned away from the longing for worldly enjoyment.

In the ninth chapter, the Supreme Lord has defined the sixfold relationship, which establishes the authoritativeness of the Self and its essence as the connection with the Other, by virtue of being the occasion for the emergence of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the expansion of Supreme Bhairava.
Even though the opening statement is intent upon demonstrating the primary purpose that has come into being. || 11 ||
Now, in order to determine [the requirements] according to their enumeration, he says:
First of all, one should examine a teacher who possesses auspicious characteristics. (1.12)
"Auspiciousness"—

this is the definition, consisting of the realization of a nature non-different from Śiva, which will be stated right here [in this very work] in the verse: "Because he moves together with Śiva, the Teacher is praised by him" (4.409).
He is the teacher (ācārya) who must be approached and served by practitioners (sādhaka) and others.

"In the beginning" refers to the disciple whose true nature has been revealed by the words of a friend awakened by the descent of power (śaktipāta); such a one, desiring to receive initiation as a *putraka* and so forth, and having heard the scriptures of the *Saṃhitās*, is a *samayin*.

Alternatively, the guru himself should first examine the disciple in order to appoint him as an ācārya, as it will be said: "One should appoint those who possess learning, good conduct, and proper behavior to the office of a teacher. (4.454)
By the word "tāvat" (at least/firstly), this is implied:
according to the principle that "even if devoid of all auspicious marks, a teacher who possesses knowledge is supreme," the very fact of his being perceived [as such] is his auspicious mark.

For, according to the principle that will be stated in the verse, "I alone am the supreme Haṃsa, Śiva" (4-399), she herself is the liberator; furthermore, it will be shown that even the ritual act of initiation has as its essence the pervasion by non-difference from Śiva. || 12 ||
Birth in a noble land and so forth are the causes of accumulation that constitute a limb of accomplishment for disciples; for this very reason, he points this out later:
"Born in a noble land, adorned with all its limbs."
One who knows the rules of the Śiva scriptures and is proficient in both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Devoted to the service of the gods, tranquil, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows;
endowed with strength of character and vigor, and possessed of compassion and courtesy. || 1.14 ||
Having obtained such a guru— one who is self-sacrificing, free from hypocrisy, and purified by the scriptures of Śiva— perfection and liberation are not far off.
The Ārya country is that in which the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya) is well-differentiated. As Viṣṇu says:
"That country in which the establishment of the fourfold social order does not exist should be known as the land of the Mlecchas; beyond that is Āryāvarta."

One who is proficient in the ritual procedures such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, in knowledge according to the Śiva scriptures, and in that which is to be known—the reality of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivatattva*)—as well as in the pervasion of the respective paths (*adhvan*) and other matters; who is stainless, tranquil, and has conquered the senses;
who is truthful and firm in his vows, meaning one who carries out what he has undertaken; and who is possessed of strength of character (*sattvavān*).

He is unwavering in his vigor, perfected and fulfilled through the ultimate meaning of the supreme mudrā; he possesses compassion for those wandering in saṃsāra, a desire to favor them, and courtesy—meaning freedom from envy and agreeableness; he regards wealth as mere straw, is free from hypocrisy, and conducts himself without crookedness.

Having attained— that is, having reached as its cause— a Guru who is the instructor, one who has found rest and confidence in the Śiva-scriptures alone even while possessing mastery over all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), and whose essence consists of such a self-realization as was just described— namely, non-different from Śiva— the two, namely accomplishment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*), act [to bring about their respective results].

The meaning is that these qualities do not come from afar, but arise instantaneously. It has already been largely explained that the possession of auspicious marks as previously described, as well as being born in a noble land and so forth, are the causes for the disciple’s attainment of liberation. || 15 ||
Having thus described the true nature of the Guru who bestows fearlessness, he states the opposite:
"One who is wrathful, fickle, mean, devoid of compassion and courtesy, squint-eyed, protruding-toothed, one-eyed, most sinful, and devoid of knowledge of the scriptures. (1.16)
One who is excessively tall, as well as short, emaciated, obese, or afflicted by consumption; one who is deceitful, full of hypocrisy, and devoid of truthfulness and purity. (1-17)
He who is devoted to other scriptures does not bestow the fruit of liberation.
One who is prone to anger is full of wrath; one who is fickle is ill-behaved and unsteady in his duties;
one who is base is intent on achieving petty accomplishments; one who is squint-eyed has a restless gaze; and one who is afflicted by consumption [is likewise unfit].

"Tākīka" refers to one who is afflicted by *yakṣman* (consumption), being solely devoted to the treatises of fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*). However, reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of *ūha* (inference) is indeed praised in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, as it is said:
"Reasoning is the supreme limb of yoga" (17.18).

One who is devoid of purity, lacking in the purification of wealth and so forth—the rest is clear. Such a guru does not bestow upon the practitioner the fruit characterized by spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*); on the contrary, he grants nothing but fear in the manner that will be described below. Furthermore, one who is devoted elsewhere to other scriptures, such as those of the Vaiṣṇavas, and then—

Furthermore, having studied the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara-śāstra) through the practice of magnetism and other such means, he remained unconvinced by them, as it is said therein: "Even if one performs initiation and other rites, a most sinful teacher does not bestow liberation;
however, one who is devoted to the Śiva-scriptures indeed bestows the fruit of liberation upon all those who are established in their respective partial teachings."
Because it stands above all [levels], as it will be stated:
"The supreme state of the Śaivas has emerged from the entire path" (10.74).

Having applied [the principle] that "it bestows liberation and the fruit in the form of accomplishment," one should explain it as stated: "In the *Krodhana* [mudrā], one should know [it bestows] the cessation of distress," and so forth. (1-22)

The statement ending with, "The mantras do not succeed for him who is devoid of truth and so forth" (1.27), is consistent with the fact that [practices] such as the wrathful rites yield results contrary to what is intended, as will be explained later.
For this very reason, the fact that they yield contrary results for one who is devoted to other scriptures has not been mentioned subsequently.
That too is indeed appropriate; for,

although [the verse] beginning with "One should recognize affliction in one who is angry" (1.22) follows here according to the sequence, it is not recited there, but is instead recited immediately after the determination of the disciples.
This suggests that, for the most part, such a teacher is a source of fear for the disciple alone. || 17 ||
Now, he describes the nature of the disciple who bestows fearlessness upon himself:
"The disciple is compassionate, steadfast, and free from hypocrisy and deceit. (1.18)
Devoted to the gods, the sacred fire, and his guru; devoted to the scriptures and firm in his vows; intent on service to the guru and endowed with perfectly tranquil senses. (1.19)
Such indeed should be the disciple; he is the vessel for grace in this matter.

Compassion (*dayā*) is sympathy toward those who are miserable and the like; fortitude (*dhairya*) is enthusiasm in all circumstances; hypocrisy (*dambha*) is a lack of clarity in the heart; deceit (*māyā*) is trickery; and one of firm vows (*dṛḍhavrata*) is one whose mind is resolute.
This concerns the subject of the practitioner; for that very disciple of the teacher Vajrīta, who possesses a resolute intellect, is the qualified candidate for the practice,
since the distinction between the Śiva-dharma and the worldly dharma will be determined on its own occasion.

Devotion to the fourfold group beginning with the gods is the primary characteristic of the disciple. Devotion occurs when the guru is at a distance, whereas service consists of constant attendance upon him; by the statement "he is here the recipient of grace," his capacity to bestow fearlessness within one's own self is expressed. This is the second [point].
The word *śiṣya* ends in the suffix *arha*. The rest is clear. || 19 ||
He states the opposite of this:
"Endowed with deceit, dishonest, cruel, devoid of truth, and fond of quarreling. (1-20)
One who is lustful, possessed by greed, devoid of devotion to Śiva, and a defamer of the Guru and the scriptures—though initiated, such a person does not partake in liberation. (1.21)

He is deceitful, having an impure heart; cruel, of a fierce nature; fond of quarreling, and given to caviling; possessed of greed, he practices financial dishonesty even regarding offerings and honors despite his capacity for them. By the phrase "devotion to Śiva" and so forth, it is stated that he is permeated by the power of dissolution (*vilaya-śakti*).
By the phrase "not partaking of liberation," it is stated that this [ignorance] produces fear within one's very own self, because all beings are its disciples. || 21 ||
Now he describes how the teacher is a source of fear for the disciples: "One should know that an angry teacher causes distress; in a fickle teacher, fortunes are fickle;
and a base teacher, O fair-faced one, takes away the accomplishment of the mantra. (1.22)
One devoid of compassion suffers misfortune; one who is unskilled brings oppression by robbers; one with squinting eyes suffers disease; and one with protruding teeth causes strife. (1.23)
One who is one-eyed produces enmity, and one who is bald causes the destruction of wealth;
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, there can be no success in initiation and other rites for one devoid of the scriptures. (1.24)
A long [tooth] should be known as causing enmity with kings; a short one brings about the destruction of sons.
A thin one should be known as causing decline, while a thick one brings about calamities. (1-25)
Through that which is associated with decay, there shall be death; in Tākīka, there is slaughter and imprisonment.
O fair-faced one, he should be known as a hypocrite and a producer of evil. (1–26)
The mantras of one who has abandoned truth and so forth do not succeed;
O Goddess, all those [actions] are inauspicious both in this world and in the next. (1.27)
One should know that [the mantras] are not obtained; they do not succeed and do not perform functions such as bestowing grace (*anugraha*).

This is stated from the perspective of teachers for whom ritual action (*karma*) is primary. However, a teacher who is established in the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) incurs no fault even when possessed of defects such as being one-eyed, as it has been said:
"Even if devoid of all auspicious marks, a teacher who possesses knowledge is supreme.

The rest is clear. Furthermore, regarding this matter, which has the word of the Lord as its sole authority, the arguments written here are mostly like a web of straw; they are truly laughable. || 27 ||
Now, he indicates the ground appropriate for the *mātṛkā* array as well as for subsequent rites such as sacrifice:
"The ground— white, red, yellow, or black— is purified by sprinkling."
Viśalyā, endowed with auspicious marks, who accomplishes all desires and aims. || 1-28 ||

The word “having resorted to” (śritvā) is to be supplied as the ellipsis, because it will be explained later that through initiation there occurs the elevation of caste (*jātyuddhāra*) and the attainment of the *bhairavīya* caste. [Regarding the verse: “For the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, white clay, gold, and white [are the substances].”

Thus, unlike the perception of distinct divisions, no such partition is mentioned here; rather, the earth, whose colors are intermingled, is demarcated— cleansed by means of a float through the pouring of water on top—
and its slope toward the east, north, or northeast is examined, or it is made level and even, as it has been stated:
"Excellent is the boat that has risen from the water...

Thus, [the physician should choose] a *viśalyā* (thorn-remover) that is free of bone, charcoal, and other such debris, endowed with characteristics such as smoothness and beauty; this same statement is also intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*).
It is injunctive, because there is no other injunctive sentence [to which it could refer]. || 28 ||
Having taken recourse to such a ground— endowed with fragrant scents, adorned with heaps of flowers,
thick with the aroma of excellent incense, and beautified by canopies above— (1.29)

The word "having done" (kṛtvā) is to be understood as the ellipsis; the meaning is that one should first worship the Earth, which is the power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī) and His sustaining power (dhartṛśakti). || 29 ||
Now, preceded by the presentation of the appropriate teacher, he describes the procedure for the extraction of the mantra:
"The teacher, having become pure, anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, well-perfumed with incense, serene in soul, and provided with chalk and water... (1.30)
Facing either east or north, with a single-pointed mind and well-composed,
one should spread out the Mātṛkā there in sequence from 'a' to 'kṣa'.

Pure, having performed his bath as desired, and having completed the daily obligatory rites prescribed by the words beginning with "sandalwood" (*candana*), he is therefore serene; that is, one whose self has emerged from the immersion in the body and so forth into the state of Śiva.
Since the faces of Tatpuruṣa and Sadyojāta are the causes of worldly attainment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*) respectively, the teacher [should act] according to his intention.
It has been stated that one should face either the east or the north. With a single-pointed mind intent on contemplating the emergence of the mantra,

and thus being concentrated (*samāhita*) and having attained the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra, one [should contemplate] *Mātṛkā*— the Mother of the Universe, the progenitor of all mantras and tantras for those bound by ignorance (*paśu*), consisting of the letters from *A* to *Kṣa*.
Having issued forth by means of the sequence of powers such as *icchā* (will) and *ānanda* (bliss), headed by the *kalā* that is the essence of the pervasion of the *anuttara-kula*,

one should "spread out" (*prastaret*) the *piṇḍa-mantra*— which consists of the letters from *ka* to *sa* through the process of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal)— as the essence of the ultimate pervasion demonstrated therein.

One should spread [the mandala], preceded by the contemplation of the pervasion of the entire alphabet, consisting of the fourfold power (śakticatuṣṭaya) as taught in the *Śrīsarvavīrabhargaśikhā*— namely, the anusvāra and the powers of the emanation, withdrawal, and awareness of the fifty natural Rudras who abide within the power of one's own means of knowledge (*svapramāṇaśakti*). The word "prastaret" (one should spread) is an archaic Vedic form (*ārṣaḥ*).

The reading is as follows: In this way, other words of the Supreme Lord are also indeed correct, because the statements of the Blessed One cannot be subject to doubt by those of limited vision. || 31 ||

Thus, having first demonstrated the Mātṛkā— which serves as the foundational wall for this treatise— with the desire to establish it as the seat of the taught sciences, he now defines its nature as Śiva and Śakti:
"The primordial [Mātṛkā], through its sixteenfold division, is indeed directly remembered as Bhairava."
The *ka*-group, the *ca*- and *ṭa*-groups, as well as *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*. || 1.32 ||
Endowed with reabsorption (saṃhāra), she is indeed known as Bhairavī, the Source (yoni).

The first group is the beginning; it consists of the sixteen [phonemes] that nourish the universe, starting from the Goddess Anuttarā and ending with the Emission (sarga), which shines by itself through its inherent nature of sounding.

Because it causes differentiation and affliction through its universal projection, and because it serves as the substratum for the expansion of the reality of the phonemes— the source of all denotata and denotators— which are subsumed within that which is expressed by the word *svara*,
and because it brings that [expansion] forth, it is designated as the "seed" (*bīja*), whose true nature is the expansion of supreme consciousness.
Bhairava is directly present through differentiation and manifoldness because he consists of the entire universe without exception,

and because of the non-difference between the signifier and the signified. However, because the letters beginning with *ka* possess density in the form of the solidification of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), they are manifested by that seed.

She is the *yoni* because, through the conjunction with the aforementioned seeds (*bīja*), she is the cause of the universe for those things designated by the sounds of the consonants (*vyañjana*). Likewise, she is Bhairavī by means of the letter *kṣa*, which is the withdrawal of the entire series of letters (*varṇa*).
Having demonstrated the *prastāra* (expansion) of the *mātṛkā*, which is the form of the previously mentioned Bhairava-śakti,

and showing the worship of this [mātṛkā] as an ancillary to the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*)— which is the essential expansion of all mantra-deities— he also indicates its specific nature as a ritual practice: "The Mātṛkā-Bhairava."
One should worship the deity with the [mantra] group beginning with "pra. || 33 ||
Bhairavī is to be worshipped with the *kādi* [vowels];

[she is] Bhairava, the presiding deity of the *mātṛkā*, whose supreme reality consists of filling (*bharaṇa*), sustaining (*vaṇa*), and withdrawing (*avamana*) by way of his very nature as the expansion (*sphāra*) of that [mātṛkā], the form of the partless (*niṣkala*) venerable Lord, [to be worshipped] with the *a*-group.
One should worship with the sixteen [vowels] whose essential nature has been manifested. Bhairavī as well,

whose essential nature is indeed non-different from the Lord Niṣkala, is Umā in the form of Yogīśvarī, the presiding deity of that [group], by means of the unpartitioned collection of the group of matrices (yoni) beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*.
She is to be worshipped. || 33 ||
...one should worship the Mothers with their respective groups [of consonants].
In the *ava* group is Mahālakṣmī; in the *ka* group is Kamalodbhavā. (1.34)
In the *ca*-group is Maheśānī; in the *ṭa*-group is Kumārikā;
in the *ta*-group is Nārāyaṇī; and in the *pa*-group is Vārāhī.
Indrī, Yavargasthā, and Cāmuṇḍā Śavagīkā—
these are the seven great Mothers (Mahāmātṛs) established throughout the seven worlds.
The seven Bhairavīs— Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā— are forms of the Mothers who have the appearance of rays of light,
situated in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Soma, Yama, Varuṇa, Indra, and Nirṛti.

Since it will be stated [later] that "the Mātṛkā-vidyā is indeed divided into eight groups," and because the 'a'-group has already been utilized, one should worship by dividing [the letters] into the seven groups beginning with 'ka'; if this is so, then this other mode of practice is also entirely appropriate, and thus:

On the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), among the worlds of the intellect (*buddhibhuvana*), after the eightfold yoga, the world of Umā is to be explained. In the world named Svacchanda, there exists indeed the essential nature of the meditation and other practices for Umāpati— the Lord of Umā— who consists of the pervasion of the manifestation of Supreme Bhairava and is accompanied by a retinue of seven Mothers.
For example,
beginning with: "Umāpati, the Lord of the World, supreme in bestowing grace upon all" (10.1008),
and having described his meditation, [it continues:]
Having established the meditative visualization and arrangement of the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and the others, through the passage starting with “The Mothers are seven-formed” (10.1017),
[it is said that] they attend upon Śvacchanda according to the division of the supreme and the non-supreme (10.1029).
Having said this,

by the passage beginning with, "Umā indeed, having become sevenfold through various transformations of form" (10.1029), the very distinction of the modes of practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) is established; therein, however, [the teaching] of the Lord is further...

Form has been mentioned previously, but here the distinction is that it is the "supreme form" (*paraṃ rūpam*), as he will state: "The *Svacchanda* [Tantras], however, are other supreme [scriptures] established in the supreme void;
they attend upon the *Svacchanda* according to the division of the supreme and the non-supreme. (10.1028)

Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that the worship of Mātṛkā-Bhairava, which is an ancillary part of the extraction of the mantra, takes the form of a separate ritual performance. || 36 ||
And this is logical, as it has been said:
"One obtains all desires; thus Bhairava spoke regarding the Goddess.

However, in the context of being a subsidiary part of the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), the principle applies that "that which is fruitless is a subsidiary when in proximity to that which possesses fruit."
According to the established rule, this statement regarding the worship of Mātṛkā-Bhairava would be false,
because it is impossible to point out a fruit for a ritual action that has not been completed.
And having done so, one should extract the mantras from this [text] at the end, according to the application of their proper sequence. (1.37)

Regarding this worship of the Mātṛkās, by means of that application which follows the sequence of the seat-mantra (āsana-mantra), the form-mantra (mūrti-mantra), and so forth, and which consists in being intent upon the contemplation of the deities expressed by those respective mantras—
that sequential yoga is useful on the occasion of the ritual placement (nyāsa) occurring in the second and subsequent chapters. Thus [ends verse 37].
Here, the extraction of the mantra is also stated according to the sequence of the forthcoming installation (*nyāsa*); therein:
"The thirteenth [vowel] joined with the *bindu* is the supreme seat of Ananta.
With this, one should join everything situated between the Moon, Sun, and Fire. (1.38)
One should conceive of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna as ending with the corpse (Śava).
The thirteenth [syllable] is the letter *O*, joined with the *bindu* and having the form of the *praṇava*;
it is the designator of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), yet it is currently employed by Īśvara to denote the seat (*āsana*).

The meaning is that the mantra is the seat extending from the lower station (adhaḥsthāna) up to Ananta, from the root-vidyeśas up to the middle vyāpinī-pada, and ending at the seat of Ananta. This will be so because the pervasive expansion of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which consists of the forms of the earth and Ananta, belongs solely to the venerable Lord Ananta who pervades the entire vertical path (sarvādhvordhvavatī). That is what will come to pass.

The pervasion of the seat (*āsana-vyāpti*) here extends as far as the infinite, being established in the state of the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*); therefore, he says "supreme" (*uttama*), meaning that by which [the consciousness] has risen up and stands at the summit of all paths (*adhvan*). He clarifies this very point with the following: "by this..."
With the *āsana-mantra*, one should join everything as being possessed of a foundation (*adharavatī*), connecting it through the state of a single foundational power (*ekādhāraśaktitayā*).
Thus, having placed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna within the midst of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—this is the meaning:
in the true nature of the pervasion of the Śākta-lotus, within the divisions of the petals, filaments, and pericarp of the Vidyā-lotus.

Having placed within— the interior of— the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, which are the essence of the pervasion of all objects of knowledge, means of knowledge, and knowers, the entire collection of causes beginning with Brahmā,
and having contemplated them through the pervasion of differentiation, [one perceives] the venerable Lord Anāśrita who resides above that.

One should contemplate that seat, at the end of which is the pervasion of the corpse (śava) as will be shown in the second chapter, being itself pervaded by the Praṇava through the pervasive application of the specific qualifications well-known from the mouth of the Guru. || 38 ||
In this way, by this very ritual placement (nyāsa), duality is dissolved. To effect the dissolution of the state of being an atom (aṇutva), he says:
"One should fashion the form with the syllable *haṃsa* itself, as divided by the nasal drop (*bindu*). (1.39)
With the syllable *haṃ*, which assumes the majesty of a half-moon, possesses its own sound, and has the luster of snow; which,
by virtue of the upcoming reference to the Self in the passage "The Self is indeed *haṃsa*...", constantly traverses the path of the *haṃsa*.

By means of the letter *ha* in its moving form, which is also the nature of the friction-stick (*araṇi*) for all mantras and is joined with the *bindu* that consists in the knowledge of the divisions of all vidyās— therefore, by means of that which is to be uttered,
because it has acquired the status of mantra according to the direction to be explained in the section on the five praṇavas; by means of the *ha* with its *bindu* thus divided.

One should conceive—that is, reflect upon—the state of the Self designated as "mūrti" (form), due to the delusion regarding the pervasive differentiation ending at the *muṇḍa* [crown] and because of the elevation of the state of the pure Self. Of what kind? It is that by which an intensity (*āṭopa*) is produced, like the form of a *bindu* within the half-moon, for the purpose of piercing the knot of the forehead.

The meaning is: "established in enthusiasm. Precisely because of that differentiation, she is in the form of the Mother of Sound (*dhvanimātṛ*), whose nature is the self-reflexive awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*) of her own respective names;
likewise, she is of the luster of snow, whose nature is the light of consciousness in the form of a *kadamba* bud. As it is said in the *Śrītrikahṛdaya*:
"In the infinite height of Bhairava, this is the supreme-non-supreme (parāparā) form;
by the mere placement (nyāsa) of which, the state of being an individual soul (aṇutva) dissolves. Thus [ends verse 39].
Beyond that—as well as above that—one should visualize the complete deity Svacchanda. || 1.40 ||

The word "that" (tad) refers to having submerged that contraction above the form of consciousness; one should conceive of—that is, meditate upon—the Lord as Svacchanda, who possesses the entire body of all denotations and denotata whose nature was previously explained, and who has emerged as if piercing through the wall of the form of consciousness for the sake of bestowing grace upon those to be graced. || 40 ||
The distinction between the Mūrti-, Bhairava-, and Niṣkala-mantras is made solely through conceptual construction; he states this as follows:
One should first utter the syllable *Oṃ*, immediately followed by *aghorebhyaḥ*.
Then, having written *ghorebhyaḥ*, one should thereafter write the rest. (1.41)
And from all those that are most terrible and even more terrible than the terrible, one should utter "Śarva" from every side;
and for all others, another word, namely: "Obeisance to you, O Rudra. (1.42)
Having written [the syllables] from the forms (rūpa) and ending with the salutation, this is declared to be the King of Mantras, Aghora, who is worshipped by the gods. (1.43)
In this context, the rules of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) have not been shown for the sake of preserving the original form of the mantra words.

Excluding the *praṇava* at the beginning and the salutation (*namaskāra*) at the end, this thirty-two-syllable great mantra is indicated by the verse. Its secret meaning is as follows: "O Supreme Lord!"

O Rudra, cause of the dissolution of all fetters through the obstruction of the mind by entering into the expansion of supreme consciousness! O Ghorasadbhava, who brings forth the states of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the rest, which consist of both difference and non-difference!
O Śarva, because you manifest the nature of Māyā, which is composed of duality!

By means of these three forms of address— “O You who take the form of seeking refuge through the bringing about of mere creation, maintenance, dissolution, and withdrawal”— which are employed for their suitability to the three forms that will be explained,
[the author] pays homage to the Blessed Lord Parabhairava, whose entire body manifests all states.
Having brought [the subject] face to face, he says: "Those" refers to yours, belonging to your kinsmen—

the various Rudras who consist of the manifestation of the triad of powers known as Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā, and who are composed of the circles of their respective powers (*śakticakra*), which in other *Saṃhitās* are etymologically designated by the names Aparā, Parāparā, and Parā.
To those [gurus] who, in due order, are free from the nature of bonds— which consist of difference, or a mixture of difference and non-difference,
and which are of a terrible form— and who cause the recognition of one's own true nature as the Great Bhairava, which is a mass of supreme consciousness and bliss.
To the *aghora*s; likewise, to those who bestow the state of the Self through the distinctions of the forms of Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and so forth;

furthermore, by the word "atha" (now), because they manifest immediately following the aforementioned foundational ground (*bhitti*), and therefore, due to their terrifying nature in relation to the primordial form, as the emergence of the *daṃta* (the "tooth" or "point") occurs while being veiled by the *ahantā* (I-consciousness).
"From the terrible ones"— from those forms or natures which, by means of the manifestation of the Supreme Consciousness,

project the appearance of "I-ness" and "this-ness," and which, carved upon the mirror of one's own power (*svaśakti*), provide the expansion of differentiation beginning with *māyā* and ending with the earth;
and from those even more terrible forms, because of their extreme horror— of each one.

Salutation to those who, because form (*rūpa*) consists of the foundational ground of Supreme Bhairava, are full; who flash forth everywhere, in every way, as all forms, from all, at all times, and in all places, as the self-nature of everything; and who consist of the reflective awareness of the supreme *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), which is the vital potency (*vīrya*) of the Great Mantra.

The meaning is: "I enter into a state of prostration before the plane of the constructed subject—the mass of fetters and the body, which have become helpless through the expansion of the three powers of the Great Rudra, having turned toward the contemplation of the words of address. And it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:

Those others who are known as even more terrible (ghoratara) are said to be those who, having embraced the rudra-aṇus, cause the individual souls (aṇu) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower.
Those [energies] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma and obstruct the path to liberation, are the terrible *parāpara*s.
"As before, the supreme Aghora Śiva-powers, which bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the multitude of living beings, have been revealed by those who know that [reality]. (3-31-33).
However, in the *Śrīpañcārthapramāṇa*—

"Aghora" refers to that which is not possessed of the terrible (*ghora*)—namely, the fearsome net of bonds (*pāśajāla*) joined with evil; those in whom this does not exist are proclaimed to be Aghoras.
The Rudras, beginning with Vāmeśvara, reside above Jālamūla;
they are indeed declared to be the Aghoras. Now hear, in brief, about the Ghoras.
Those Rudras who begin with Gopati and dwell within the depths of the forest are declared to be the Ghoras; they are said to reside in various worlds.
Those who are Mahāmāheśvaras, beginning with the Vidyeśvaras and ending with Ananta,
as well as others who are Ghoras and Ghorataras, should be known as residing below [them].
These are the non-terrible (aghora), the terrible (ghora), and likewise the most terrible (ghoraghoratara);
within these, the supreme powers of the Lord (pārameśvarī-śaktayaḥ) are eternally established.
In the acts of maintenance, dissolution, and creation, as well as in the operations of bondage and liberation,
these powers exist within these forms by virtue of being the impellers of all objects.
"The subtle self (aṇu) offers salutation to all these forms;
salutation is renunciation, characterized by the relation of cause and effect.
Thus [ends verse 43].

Having thus described the essential nature of this great mantra— which consists of the reality of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) who is the self of all things in every way, which is difficult to attain yet is constantly obtained by those possessed of devotion—
the [author] now reveals its majesty:
O Goddess, when uttered even once, it destroys all sins accumulated by wandering through thousands of millions of births. (1.44)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "employed by the Guru at the time of initiation for the disciples. || 44 ||
Likewise:

"O Goddess, by remembering [the Lord], one destroys darkness, just as the rising sun destroys darkness. Here, "darkness" refers to the *āṇava* and *māyīya* impurities (*mala*). Just as the rising sun destroys the darkness of night, so too [does remembrance destroy these impurities].

Through initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the teacher] indeed destroys ignorance (*ajñāna*)— which consists of the identification with the body and so forth— in the form of darkness; and by means of the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the deity Bhairava, who is his own referent, he likewise destroys for the disciples the stain consisting of the failure to perform the rules (*samaya*) through negligence, as well as for the practitioners (*sādhakas*) the obstacle in the form of impediments.

Even darkness is surely destroyed by the mere recollection consisting of the continuous application of the supreme reality of vigor as already explained; therefore, one should not be deluded by any suspicion that this great mantra— which bestows all enjoyments and liberation— is merely a figurative exaggeration (arthavāda).
And likewise, it is stated in the venerable Mataṅgaśāstra:
"His word is the sole authority; it is the truth spoken by the Lord" (1.3.18).
Our own teachers as well, who consist of the expansion of Supreme Bhairava, have declared this in the Tantrāloka:
"And this very sentence is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), never an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
There can be no character of being an explanatory passage in a sentence belonging to Maheśvara.

In order to delineate the form whose pervasion will be demonstrated within the very embodiment of consciousness for the sake of bestowing grace upon those possessed of devotion to this Supreme Lord, he states the mantras of the faces:
"The letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *va*, conjoined with [the process of] withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). (1.45)
The faces of Bhairava, which are conjoined with the Bindu at their crowns,

are perfectly (samyaṅ) joined (āyutāḥ) from the beginning with the letter *kṣa*— the end of the Mātṛkā— by way of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); they have as their essence the pervasion of the Bindu, whose nature is sensation (*vedanā*).

Because these mantras denote the upper, eastern, southern, western, and northern faces of Bhairava— which have as their essence the powers of the Supreme Sky (*paramavyoman*), Wind, Fire, Water, and Earth— and because they serve as the means for entering the essential nature of Bhairava, they are called the "faces" and so forth of Bhairava.
And these [mantras] are to be applied in the manner of Brahmā, from the head down to the feet. (46)

Because Brahmā is vast (*bṛhat*) and because he is the nourisher (*bṛṃhaka*) of the universal self in the form of power (*śaktimūrti*), and because of the five lords of the Brahmas, such as Īśāna and the others, by way of their distinct divisions (*bhaṅgyā vibhāgena*); therefore, it is filled with the *praṇava*: "kṣaṃ" for the head of Īśāna, and "yaṃ" [for Tatpuruṣa].
"To the face of Tatpuruṣa: *raṃ*; to the heart of Aghora: *vaṃ*; to the secret place of Vāmadeva:

*laṃ*; to the form of Sadyojāta: *laṃ*. Thus, because of the oneness of the forms, the forms of the Lord—shaped like staffs and with undivided limbs—should be conceived by means of a single mantra. || 46 ||
To demonstrate the division of this [face], he shows the arrangement of the door-panels, which serve as the foundation for the future division of the clear face within the field of the face:
"Furthermore, the face should be conceived above, first to the south, and then to the north."
Furthermore,
by changing the case and number of the word *mukhāni*, it should be applied here as the third-case plural;
thus, by means of the "face-mantras" *kṣaṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ*, [one should worship] again.
Regarding the placement [of the mantras] upon the *nyāsa* in the manner of Brahmā: the word "mouth" (*mukha*) is for the purpose of providing space for the mouth;

the meaning is that one should place them on the upper, eastern, and other doors. And in this regard, the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed separately for each, as in: "Oṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to the face of Īśāna," and so forth for the faces.
Because of their being distinct.
Furthermore:
...having performed [the visualization], one should then perform the placement according to the division of the parts (kalā). || 1-47 ||
The letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Īśvara, is joined with the east, the south, the north, the west, as well as the zenith above. (1.48)
In this regard:
"Śiva has one great power, and Śiva is indeed one and without beginning; that power is further divided by powers into manifold distinctions... (11.271).

Thus, according to the method to be explained, just as there is the assumption of a formal body for the Blessed One— who consists essentially of the power of absolute freedom— so too does he consist of the expansion of those respective powers in a manner corresponding to that [form],
and not of a quiescent nature; this is how the true reality of the vision is disclosed through the various arrangements such as the door-panels.

The deposition (*nyāsa*) of the powers (*śakti*), which are synonyms for the *kalās*, is now described. In this regard, according to the established principle that "the sequence based on meaning is stronger than the sequence of recitation," the forms situated one above the other are first [deposited] in the order: south, north, west, and east;
thus, because it delivers one from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it is appropriately named [the "Deliverer"].
"Tārā, Sutārā, Taraṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāriṇī—
these are the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna.
This division of digits, which will be described [later], [is applied] to that by which "the letter *kṣa* is the mantra whose form is that of Īśa."

One should place the faces starting from the east and so on, consisting of the expansion (*sphāra*) of the deity who is the denotable object (*vācyadevatā*) known as the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka (*Īśāna*). The statement "the letter *kṣa* is first," and so forth, is to be applied through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
furthermore, the division of the *kalās* is to be contemplated in reverse order—this is the tradition of the Gurus. Thus:

The summary meaning is that the ritual placement of the *kalās* (*kalānyāsa*) should be performed to demonstrate the pervasion of Īśāna: "kṣaṃ sutāriṇyai namaḥ" on the upper door-panel, "kṣaṃ tārayantyai namaḥ" on the eastern one, and so on up to "kṣaṃ tārāyai namaḥ" on the western door-panel. || 48 ||
Now, in order to clarify the faces, he says: "In this way, one should apply the fourfold face to the very faces.

The phrase "by means of the division of *kalās*" is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. And "in this way" (*evam*) refers specifically to the principle of the division of the *kalās* of Īśāna.
One should apply the mantra of the eastern face—the letter *ya*—fourfold upon the faces;
specifically, for the sake of manifesting the characteristics of the eastern and other faces, one should join it fourfold according to the division of the *kalās*.
And the *kalās* here are as follows:

"Niṣṭhā, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śāntā—these are the four *kalās* of the Puruṣa... (1.55), as will be stated hereafter. Here too, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed in reverse order according to the sequence of emanation; therefore:
One should connect [the mantras] starting with "Yaṃ śāntāyai tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ" up to "Yaṃ nivṛttaye sadyojātavaktrāya namaḥ," and one should meditate upon the clarity of the four faces.
Because [the faces] beginning with the Puruṣa clearly manifest distinct divisions, he states the limit regarding the upper face, where the distinction of form has not yet emerged:
"That which is the fifth face should be indicated by the phoneme *kṣa* alone. (1.49)

It is called "mouth" (*vaktra*) because it manifests the nature of the other [the Supreme] and because it protects from *saṃsāra*. By the use of the particle *eva* ("only/precisely"), one should here contemplate its state of having a manifest form; this is what is suggested by the word "resounds" (*dhvanati*). || 49 ||

Having thus described the arrangement of the door-panels (*kavāṭa*) and the faces of the *kalā* in the upper and lower fields, he now describes the arrangement of the *kalā*s of Aghora in the heart-field and so forth:
"In the heart, the neck, the shoulders, the back, as well as in the navel and the abdomen."
One should place [the hand] on the back and the chest with the Aghora mantra in due order.
"Darkness, delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age—these eight indeed are the beautiful powers (*kalā*) of Aghora. (1.56).
This is because of the distinction of the powers (*kalā*) that will be described; [the phrase] "by Aghora" refers to the *Aghoravaktra* mantra, [to be applied] in due order.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). By means of that, the *nyāsa* beginning with "Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Tamā at the heart" and ending with "Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Jarā in the belly" should be performed, because the venerable Aghora is primarily characterized by withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). The *kalās* likewise have names appropriate [to their functions]. (50)
He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the digits of Śrī Vāmadeva in the secret and other fields (*kṣetra*):
"In the secret place, as well as in the anus, likewise in the thighs, the knees, the shanks, the buttocks, the waist, and on both sides. (1.51)
And one should indeed place them on the left side of the body in due order:
Rajā, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālyā, Kāmyā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā,
Ṛddhi, Māyā, Rātri, Bhrāmaṇī, and likewise Mohanī.
"These are indeed the Manonmanī and Kalā [energies]; in Vāmadeva there are thirteen.
(1.57.58)—thus, the division of the energies (*kalā*) of Śrī Vāmadeva, who is primarily characterized by emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), is described;
this passage is intended to reveal the thirteen locations beginning with the "Secret" (*guhya*), using names appropriate for his primary function of emanation.

"In order [one should place] with the left" means one should place [the seed-syllable] with the venerable Vāmadeva face; by that, it should be understood that "vaṃ, obeisance to Rajā" is to be applied to the secret organ. || 51 ||
He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the venerable Sadyojāta-kalā located in the sacred fields beginning with the feet of the Blessed One:
"The two feet, the two hands, likewise the nose, the head, and then the two arms. (1.52)
"O Goddess, one should fashion all this in due order by means of Sadya.
By "Sadya," [it means] by the *śrīsadyojāta* mantra; one should fashion the feet and so forth in due order, that is to say, by the very digits (*kalā*) of Sadyojāta, which will be described below.
"Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Sudhā, and Sthiti—these eight are proclaimed as the kalās of Sadyojāta. (1.58.59).
Thus, because the venerable Sadyojāta causes sustenance (*sthiti*) and nourishment (*āpyāyaka*), these are his kalās, beginning with Siddhi.

Therefore, one should apply the formula: "Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to Siddhi, on the right foot. Although the opening of the faces was already performed by means of the mantra of the eastern face, nevertheless, the visualization of the field of the head and the field of the nose must again be performed according to this procedure.

Because it is stated explicitly [as a specific rule]. In this way, by declaring that the digits (*kalā*) of Sadyojāta located in the feet pervade as far as the field of the nose and head, he instructs one through the method [of saying] "everything exists everywhere," [expressed as] "one should fashion the hands. This is like the statement, "One wipes the cup."
Since the number [of hands] is not intended to be significant for this primary injunction, and because the state of having eighteen arms will be mentioned later,
[this is understood] through the tantric principle of anticipation (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*), as in the case of the statement: "There are nine *graha* offerings dedicated to Prajāpati."
It should be understood that there is the conceptualization of two pairs of arms located on the right and left sides, [accompanied] by Splendor (Dyuti) and Fortune (Lakṣmī). || 52 ||
To point out the arts (kalā), he says:
"I shall state their names correctly and in their proper sequence. (1.53)
Tārā, Sutārā, Taraṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāraṇī—
these five are the digits (kalās) of Īśāna, following the state of the stainless (nirañjana).
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti—these four are indeed declared to be the kalās of Puruṣa. (1.55)
Delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age—these eight indeed are the powers (kalās) of Aghora, O fair-complexioned ones. (1.56)
Raja, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālyā, Kāmyā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā, Ṛddhi, Māyā, Rātri, Bhrāmiṇī, and likewise Mohanī. (1.57)
These are indeed the thirteen *kalās* of Vāmadeva, beginning with Manonmanī:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Sudhā, and Sthiti.

Thus, the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta have been fully described. "Properly" means according to their respective pervasions (*vyāpti*). "In successive order" means by way of the sequence of the faces: upward, east, south, north, and west. And here—
"The other body is the gross one, composed of thirty-six principles" (4-407).

According to the method that will be explained, because the thirty-sixth principle has three divisions— as stated in [the verse] "The Pure Self, Unmanā, and the Supreme"— the deposition of Bhairava’s body must be performed precisely through the pervasion of these principles.

Others maintain that it is for the purpose of attaining the state of consisting of the three abodes (tridhāman) through the pervasion of the sixteen, twelve, and ten digits (kalās) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire respectively. 58.

Now, regarding this body composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), he demonstrates the deposition of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) through both subtle pervasion (*sūkṣmavyāpti*) and supreme pervasion (*paravyāpti*):
"Furthermore, O Goddess, the practitioner [should perform it] in all the limbs in due order. (1.59)
One should contemplate the nine principles (navatattva) and the three principles (tritattva) with the *dhruva* mantra.

The word "again" (*punar*) refers to the period following the placement of the body complete in its constituent parts (*kalārūpa*), upon all the limbs as they have been described according to their respective divisions.
"Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as Niyati and Kāla,
Māyā, Vidyā, likewise Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva"—
(5.11) thus the nine principles (tattvas) to be described hereafter are [pervaded] by the expansion of the powers beginning with Vāmā.

And by the pervasion of the Bhairavas beginning with Kapāleśa and ending with Svacchanda; and by the pervasion of the three principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, which are the pure Self, Unmanā, and the Supreme Principle. By the *dhruva*—that is, by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) which possesses an unswerving pervasion throughout all mantras: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Self of the nine principles, from Śiva down to Prakṛti."

By means of this application, one should perform the visualization in the sequence beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to the Śiva-principle," following the aforementioned locations— on the head, the face, the throat, and the heart—
and one should visualize [the principles] at the crest-lock, the space between the eyebrows, and the heart, according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

Thus, when the manifestation of the Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka has been brought about by this placement (*nyāsa*) up to this point, one should again perform the placement of the limbs of the Vidyā; hear their mantras, O Dear One. (1.60)
The limbs of the Blessed One, who possesses many forms and whose nature is the form of knowledge through the state of having perfected all sensations, are as follows.
He states their mantras:
having written "aghorebhyaḥ," the second [syllable] is "tha ghorebhyaḥ."
And one should arrange the third [syllable] for those who are most terrible and even more terrible than the terrible. || 1-61 ||
O Śarva, one should assign the fourth [mantra] to all [directions] from every side;
and the fifth, according to the rule, with "Salutation to you, O you who possess the forms of Rudra. (1.62)
O beautiful lady, one should first utter the syllable Oṃ, and immediately thereafter the syllable Juṃ; thus one should fashion the three eyes of the Vidyā-body. (1.63)
One should know the ancillaries of the Vidyā:

they are the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon, which constitute the five mantras for the five limbs of the Blessed One whose body is the thirty-two-syllable Vidyā; however, the three-syllable [mantra] is...
Of the three eyes— the upper, the right, and the left— and here, as before, the rules of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) have not been applied to the words.
Now, learn from me their names as well:
Sarvātman, Brahmaśiras, Jvālinī, and likewise Piṅgala. || 1.64 ||
The *Durbhedya*, the *Pāśupatya*, and likewise the *Jyotīrūpa* [mantras]:

here, according to the method of the *Anāgatāvekṣaṇa-tantra*, the generic suffixes such as *namaḥ* and *svāhā* should be applied at the end; therefore, the practical application should be performed as "aghorebhyaḥ sarvātmane hṛdayāya namaḥ," and so forth.

The two words "durbhedyam" and "pāśupatyam" are to be applied to the weapon (*astra*); and herein [are found] omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, undiminished power, and infinite power—
these qualities of the Lord are traditionally taught to have emanated as the limbs [of the mantras], beginning with the heart and ending with the eye.
Immediately after the placement of the armor (*kavaca-nyāsa*), the placement of the eyes (*netra-nyāsa*) is to be performed, and thereafter the placement of the weapon (*astra-nyāsa*).
Because the weapon constitutes an external limb (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the mantra of the eyes lacks the status of being a constituent part of the body of knowledge (*vidyā-deha*),
its assignment was made later.
After the placement (*nyāsa*) of the faces, seats, the forms of consciousness, and the various facial expressions of Brahmakavāṭa,

he described the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās* through five sections by means of their pervasion of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) consisting of the five *kalās* and so forth; then, [he described it] through the pervasion of the ninefold Bhairava.
Having described the placement of the nine principles (*navatattvanyāsa*) through the pervasion of the pure self (*śuddhātma*), the supreme mind (*unmanā*), and the supreme principle (*paratattva*),
as well as the placement of the three principles (*tritattvanyāsa*), the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is taught through the pervasion of attributes such as omniscience.
In this way, the Blessed Lady possesses manifold forms (*bahurūpatva*) because she is the body of the entire universe, consisting of both the presiding subjects and the objects presided over.
Thus it has been explained.

And in order to demonstrate that all this, although resting upon the triad, consists essentially of the expansion of the three powers (*śaktitraya*), he speaks of the following for the purpose of the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the mantras of power (*śakti*):
Action, knowledge, and likewise will—learn from me the mantras pertaining to them.
Since rest occurs only through the withdrawal of the powers of universal expansion, the sequence consists of action, knowledge, and will. || 65 ||
He states their mantras in sequence:
"The letter at the end of 'ha' (kṣa), joined with the fourth vowel (ī) and adorned with the bindu, is declared to be Kriyāśakti, who illumines all creation. (1.66)
The fourth vowel is the letter *ī*; the end of *ha* is the letter *kṣa*. || 66 ||
The third letter after Śa, joined with the sixth vowel and accompanied by the bindu—this is known as Jñānaśakti, the auspicious progenitor of awakening. (1.67)
The third letter after Śa is Sa; it is joined with the sixth vowel, Ū. || 67 ||

The letter *kṣa* and so forth, combined with two vowels and conjoined with the third and fifth [vowels], is declared to be the power of will (*icchāśakti*) of Bhairava, whose nature is immeasurable. (1.68)
The first letter of the syllable *kṣa* is "ha"; the vowel with two morae (*dvisvara*) is "ā"; and the fifteenth vowel, which is three times five, is "aṅ". || 68 ||

Now, he states the mantra for the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*) upon all the aforementioned mantras, for that Lord Svacchandabhaṭṭāraka—who, though being the self of all, is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)—in whom all these powers that produce the entire universe find their rest: [The mantra follows: *oṃ namaḥ sakalaguṇātmaka-vigrahāya... svacchandabhairavāya...* etc.

The syllable called *haṃsa*, conjoined with the *bindu* and differentiated by the sixth vowel, ending with the crescent moon (*bālacandra*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the power (*śakti*), is known as the partless (*niṣkala*) *Svacchanda*. (1.69)

The one called Haṃsa, by virtue of performing the emission and withdrawal of all things, possesses the qualities of abandoning and taking up; as will be stated in the passage, "Both Prakṛti and Vikṛti are joined with the sixth" (6.20),
he is the primordial source (prakṛti) of the entire universe from A to KṢa.
"The supreme seed-syllable known as Ṅa," as stated in [Kālacakratantra] 1.5 and other passages,
refers to that which is described in the scriptures as the form of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*); "there is no one to utter it, nor is there anyone to obstruct it."

"The God utters [it] himself... (7-59). Thus, the expansion to be described hereafter is the vowel-less letter *ha*, whose sole essence is a constant, unceasing, and ever-shining vibration; it is conjoined with the sixth vowel *ū*, which is the nature of the unfolding of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) characterized by the act of opening (*unmeṣa*).

By bearing the entire universe as having the form of upper and lower [extremities], through the appearance of a slight deficiency in the expansion of consciousness, and by means of the sequence of writing— which consists in the outlining of the power of action—
the two tips of the powers extending upward and downward are manifested, delineating the entirety of the pure and impure.
By means of its constant expansion, which consists of the creation and dissolution of the universe;

as it will be stated according to the principle set forth in [Tantrāloka 6.17], "O Goddess, its qualities are known to be the sixth and the fifth," it exists as a subordinate attribute in the form of the power of the Lord Nāda.
And by moving upwards and downwards, it is differentiated and then conjoined in the form of the *caraṇa* (foot). Furthermore,

having slightly moved from the plane of supreme non-differentiation (*parābheda-bhūmi*), it becomes oriented toward bestowing grace upon those to be graced by assuming the form of the mantra being uttered, [accompanied] by the *bindu*.

By means of the Self that consists in the realization of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) of the entire universe without exception, it is "perfectly" (samyak) joined through the attainment of non-duality;
