[this state] contains within it the moon, sound, and power (*nāda-śakti*), which are the true nature of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) to be described hereafter,
and which encompass the expansion of the reality of the objects of knowledge— beginning with *nirodhikā*, *anāhata*, *nādānta*, *vyāpinī*, *samanā*, and *unmanā*.
He in whom all things find rest is indeed the Supreme Lord, the autonomous (svacchanda), partless (niṣkala),

and the very essence of the potency of the Great Mantra consisting of the unstruck sound (anāhatadhvani); yet, by means of the sixth letter *sa*, which takes the form of the head and represents the wheel of the most terrible power (*ghoratara-śakti-cakra*), he [projects] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

It manifests the world consisting of differentiation— merely the creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and dissolution of the cosmic eggs of Brahmā, Prakṛti, and Māyā, as well as the objects of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the subjects of knowledge— by way of its true nature which is about to be explained.
And through the sequence of objects of knowledge beginning with the *bindu*, [one perceives] those who possess the nature of Ghorarūpa,
such as Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Anāśrita, and others, who abide within the Egg of Power (*śaktyaṇḍa*),
who are established in the state of the Fourth (*turya*), and who are progressively more excellent.
He causes [the world] to appear by means of the power of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal; but by the power of *unmanā*,
through the ultimate reality of the wheel of powers in the form of Aghora, and by ascending to the entire state that transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*),
he makes it identical with his own self and thus liberates it— such is the Lord of many forms (*bahurūpa*) by way of the meaning of the words.

Whatever extent has been explained as the expansion [of the universe], all of that resides within this Blessed One without any distinction; thus, this Blessed One, Śrī Svacchanda, who eternally performs the fivefold act, is inseparable from the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti) which consists of the entire wheel of powers (śakti-cakra), and is partless (niṣkala).
Thus, the meaning is that from whom all the *kalās* (parts) and *śaktis* (powers) have emerged— that form of manifestation— and who himself has emerged as the immeasurable; furthermore,
although he is designated by the term "four-fold" (*catuṣkala*) due to his connection with the *kalās* such as *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and so forth, in reality [he is beyond them].
He is "partless" (*niṣkala*) because his ultimate reality is the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*) which is devoid of parts. As he will state:

"Śiva with qualities (*saguṇa*) is to be known as 'with parts' (*sakala*), while Śiva without qualities (*nirguṇa*) is 'partless' (*niṣkala*). Enough, then, with revealing the secrets of the mantras; let me not violate the tradition (*sampradāya*).

It has been slightly unveiled. It is remembered that the *praṇava* consisting of four parts—whose own nature was obtained through the grace of the Supreme Lord by the Blessed One Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord, and also by Sadāśiva through the lineage—is [expressed as]: "Obeisance to Svacchandabhairava."
The application: || 69 ||
And he reveals the majesty of the first member [of the name]:
"By the mere utterance of this, those who are burdened by all sins, becoming like pure crystal, go to the state free from affliction. (1.70)
This has already been explained by the preceding commentary. || 70 ||
He describes the limbs (*aṅga*), which consist of the expansion of his own essential nature as the Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*) and take the form of omniscience and so forth:
"One should fashion the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, Eyes, and Weapon, differentiated by the six long vowels and distinguished by their respective classes [of consonants]. (1.71)

The letter *ha* with the *anta* (anusvāra) is the *śānta*; the six long vowels are *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *au*, and *aḥ*. These, by implication, are joined with the *bindu* except for the *visarga*. The "classes" (*jātayaḥ*) are those to be mentioned later, such as *ṅ*, *maḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth. These six are, respectively, the mantras for the heart and the other limbs. || 71 ||
He states the procedure for the ritual application:
"The syllable Oṃ is the illuminator of these; at their end, one should append the caste-designation (jāti).
Then, in sequence: Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vauṣaṭ, Huṃ, Vaṣaṭ, and Phaṭ. (1.72)
(In this regard, the reading "namah svāhā vaṣaṭ caiva huṃ vauṣaṭ phaṭ krameṇa tu" should be considered the correct one.
Therefore, their application follows the sequence beginning with "Oṃ hāṃ to the heart, namah," and so forth. || 72 ||
He states the fruit of this placement (nyāsa) along with its ancillaries (sāṅga):
"This Bhairavarāja is the accomplisher of all desires and aims; he is the bestower of all enjoyments and liberation"—this is the meaning. By speaking thus, [the author]...
This indicates that even for this [rite], which consists of the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) of all venerable deities (*sakalabhaṭṭāraka*),
there is also the state of being a separate ritual procedure for each individual person who is its recipient.
And for this reason, the mantras of the faces will appear in the thirteenth chapter, while here [they are presented] in this [chapter].
Since these [mantras] are exactly as previously described, they lack the status of being denotable by words like the complete Lord (sakalabhaṭṭāraka) and its limbs;

rather, they possess only the nature of seed-syllables (bījākṣara). Thus, unlike the case of the partless Lord (niṣkalabhaṭṭāraka) and its limbs, no further "partlessness" (nīṣkalīkaraṇa) is performed through other face-mantras, because this [state] consists of the expansion of Śakti.
Of this method.
He states the mantra of the Bhagavatī: "Haraīma," which consists of the letter 'a' joined with the vowel following 'ṅ'. (1.73)
The letter *ya* joined with *e*, preceded by *ṣa* and distinguished by the final *la*;
the letter *la* preceded by the three vowels and conjoined with *haṃsa* [the letter *ha*] together with the *bindu*. (1.74)
Endowed with the sixth vowel and terminated by the syllable *phaṭ*,
she is renowned as Aghoreśvarī, who moves upon the lap of Svacchanda.

The letters *ha* and *ra* are without vowel (*anackau*), because the letter *a* serves as their means of pronunciation. Therefore, *ha*, *ra*, *ī*, and *ma*—when combined as *haraīmo*—constitute one seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The letter *a*; the first of the *ṅ*-group, which is *gha*; joined with the vowel *o*, it becomes *gho*; the letter *ra* ending in *y* (i.e., *rya*); and [the letter *m*] with the vowel *e*.
The letter *re* joined with the initial of *ṣā* (the letter *ś*), differentiated by the letter *va* ending in *la* (i.e., *śva*),

the initial of *las* (the letter *ra*) mixed with the vowel *i* consisting of three sounds (*ri*), and joined with *haṃsa* and so forth to form the nature of the four *kalās*: this Goddess is the essence of the expansion of the unity of the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*).

It expands [the meaning]. *Haṃsa* consists of the letter *ha*, which is a vowelless consonant (*anac*), joined with the *bindu* and endowed with the sixth vowel *ū*, forming *hūṃ*. It is specifically fashioned at the end with the syllable *phaṭ*, and is eternally associated with a fierce nature; for this very reason, its essence is the burning away of all dualistic distinctions, and it is solely intent upon bestowing grace. For this very reason...

She is the mistress of the wheel of powers (śakticakra) known as Aghora, whose essential nature has been explained; she is especially renowned for being the essence of the *Khecarī* [tradition], shining brightly, seated upon the lap of the venerable Svacchandabhairava, and eternally inseparable from him.
The meaning is that she is the essence of the expansion of the connection with the Transmental (unmanā) at its limit, and she is inclined toward its manifestation.
Now, in order to join the limbs and faces of the Goddess who is seated upon the lap of the embodied Lord, he says:
"Endowed with the limbs of Bhairava and joined with five faces."
By the word *bhairava*, the primary, partless (*niṣkala*) [Bhairava] just explained is intended here;

therefore, the limbs of the Goddess—who is essentially non-different from him—are indeed the limbs of the partless [Bhairava]. By the general statement "endowed with the five faces," she is shown to have a single form consisting of both the mantra with parts (*sakala*) and the mantra without parts (*niṣkala*).
The faces of the Śrīdevī, fashioned from the previously mentioned seed-syllables, are indeed inseparable [from her], just like the Bhaṭṭāraka who is both with and without parts (sakala-niṣkala).
Now he states the mantras of the eight Bhairavas, who consist of the mass of rays of the venerable Svacchandabhairava:
"The letter ending with *ha* (i.e., *kṣa*), beginning with *ya* and ending with *ya* (i.e., *ya*), beginning with *ra* and joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*). (1.76)
Through the union of the *bindu* and the *nāda*, Kapāleśa is proclaimed.
The letter *kṣa* is at the end of *ha*; *anac* is *kṣ*. Its beginning is *m*; the end of *ya* is *r*; the beginning of *r* is *y*.
Having thus mixed them in the sequence "kṣmry," it is joined with the sixth *kalā*, the vowel *ū*.
Because the half-moon and other stages are also accepted as being included within the *bindu* and *nāda*,

according to the sequence beginning with the *bindu*, the half-moon, and so forth— as will be explained in the forthcoming commentary— this [deity] is called Kapāleśa, due to his yoga (*yoga*), which consists of the complete (*ā*) attainment of identity with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*).
Because the mantras and the deity of the mantra are of one and the same essence, so it is elsewhere as well.
The tranquil *bindu* is below, and fire is joined with the sixth; thus it is proclaimed. (1.77)
O fair-faced one, he who is known as Śikhivāhana (the Peacock-vehicled) should be understood as follows:
the letter *h* with a nasal stop (*sāntaḥ*), below which is fire (*r*), and the sixth vowel *ū*; this is intended as an indication of the Bindu, Nāda, and so forth. (77)
The withdrawal [mantra] is joined with the sixth [vowel] and endowed with the end of the sixth. || 1.78 ||
The King of Wrath is thus proclaimed: [the letter] *kṣ*,

which is the [letter of] withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), joined with the sixth vowel, the letter *ū*, and likewise with the final [letter] of the six classes— *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*— which is the letter *ma*, by way of the pronunciation of the *anusvāra*.
"Endowed," meaning even endowed with the *bindu* and so forth.
...so I shall tell you another:
the letter beginning with *ña*, joined with the sixth vowel and combined with three feet. (1.79)

O fair-faced one, [the letter] beginning with *ña*— namely *jha*— is pierced at its head by the *bindu*, appearing formidable; it is joined with the vowel *au*, which elsewhere is designated by the term "trident" (*triśūla*), as it consists of the pervasion of will, knowledge, and action through three parts, and with the sixth [vowel].
It is endowed with the letter *u*, and is joined with the pronunciation according to the method of following the letter *au*. || 79 ||
The letter *sa* joined with the letter *śa*, and below it also joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*). || 1-80 ||
Overwhelmed by the fourteen vowels and adorned with the Bindu and the end of the Nāda, this is indeed declared to be Manmatha, who is saluted by gods and Siddhas. (1.81)
By which this entire world, both moving and stationary, has been conquered:

*sāntaḥ* (the end of *sa*, i.e., *ha*), the first of the palatal *śa*s (i.e., *v*), the sixth vowel (*ū*), and the fourteenth vowel (*au*). This mantra, consisting of a collection of these syllables, is joined with the *bindu* and so forth. || 81 ||
Joined with *ha*, *ra*, and so forth, it is the letter *ū* with a bindu beneath it. || 1.82 ||
For this Bhairava is celebrated as Meghanādeśvara;

because it serves as the basis for the pronunciation of the letter *a*, he is joined with the letter *y*—which is without a vowel (*anacka*)—preceded by *h* and *r*, and is accompanied by the nasal bindu (m). || 82 ||
Joined with the letter *kṣa*, the nasal bindu, and the fifth [vowel], it is divided by the fifth [consonant]. || 1-83 ||
Someśvara is proclaimed as the destroyer of birth and death.

Between the two letters *kṣa*— namely, the letter *kṣa* [composed of] *k* and *s*— the letter *h*, differentiated by the fifth vowel *u*, is brought to the state of being uttered as the form of the mantra.
That which begins with *kṣa* and ends with *ya*, joined below by one ending in *ha*. || 1-84 ||

The radiant one, ending in the letter *la*, beginning with *ra* and joined with the lower Rudra, is endowed with the point (*bindu*), the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and possessed of the power of resonance (*nāda*). (1.85)
This is declared to be the King of Vidyās, the destroyer of great sins.

It begins with *kṣ* and ends with *h*; the end of *ha* is *r*; the end of *ra* is *ṣ*; the end of *ṣ* is *m*; the beginning of *va* is *l*; the end of *la* is *v*; the seed-syllable that is the beginning of *ra* is *y*; and below it is Rudra, the vowel *ū*.
Thus, there are eight syllables ending in the vowel *ū*, and the ninth is the *bindu* which has grasped the pervasion of the *nāda* and so forth;

this is the ninefold self (*navātmā*), which—as before—is the destroyer of great sins. And these have been described in this manner because they will be explained in the ninth chapter as the means for accomplishing their respective supernatural powers (*siddhi*). || 85 ||
And thus, this group of eight Bhairavas is proclaimed as the retinue. || 1.86 ||

This group of eight Bhairavas, which serves as a mass of rays for Parabhairava who has assumed a form for the sake of favoring transmigrating beings, possesses the nature of meditation that will be demonstrated in the second chapter. 86.

In order to state the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapālas), who are the presiding deities of the universe, who are presided over by Kapāleśa and others as forms of the Blessed One’s power, and who are worshipful due to their supramundane nature precisely because of that pervasion, he says:

Likewise, having extracted the guardians of the world (lokapālas), one should fully arrange them along with their respective names preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), ending with the words "namas" and "svāhā," together with their weapons.

The analysis of the compound is: those whose beginning is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) together with their own names. By the term "along with weapons" (*sāstrān*), one should not conceive of the weapons as separate coverings; rather, one should [invoke] Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna in the sequence beginning with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand."

"One should visualize [the deities] as having a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*), with their hands holding a spear, staff, sword, noose, banner, mace, and trident, ending in the fourth case and beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*; thus he instructs.
'[They] are to be meditated upon in the form of the eight Bhairavas' (2-125)."

Because it will be stated thus [later], here there are only the eight world-protectors (*lokapālāṣṭaka*), and not their ten-fold group as found elsewhere. Although the mantras of the lords of the cremation grounds (*śmaśānādhipa*) are yet to be described, they have not been extracted here; for, since they pertain to the same subject matter, they are [to be understood] by the method of expression: "having extracted them, one should arrange them."

Introducing the method for the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) and worship that occurs immediately following the preceding chapter, the Blessed One demonstrates the thematic connection (*pāṭalikī saṃgati*).
Having immersed the entire path and emerged as the pure white form of Consciousness,
and having made that [form] assume the nature of Bhairava— that whole form consisting of the three principles (tritattva),
composed of the three powers (śakti), and dissolved within the supreme abode of Svacchanda, which is manifested by its throbbing power— [The wise one attains liberation.]
"We praise that Self which pervades everything in the world, up to the Lord of the World.

"The darkness of the distinctions of commentaries proclaimed by those who follow the path of the followers has been dispelled; the self-manifesting radiance has arisen, overflowing with the essence of supreme non-duality."

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Extraction of Mantras," in the illustrious *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. || 1 ||
The second chapter, *Svacchandodyota*:
the wretchedness of worldly existence dissolves, the glory of liberation takes refuge in the heart-lotus, and it shines forth.
Victorious is that worship of Īśa wherein supreme bliss flows forth.

Following the sequence of the questions, the nature of Time (kāla), which has reached its proper occasion, is not yet discussed— since it is generally of little utility in the context of obligatory injunctions (*nityavidhi*) like optional ones (*kāmya*), and because there is much to be said about it— but rather that wherein these mantras possess their most effective power (*sādhakatamatva*) and by what means the mantras become bestowers of fruit.

The commencement of the second chapter is for the purpose of elucidating the rules for worship, recitation, fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth, which have obtained the opportunity for exposition through their logical connection with that subject matter. Therein, in order to first demonstrate the rule for what is constant (*nitya*)— according to the principle that "the occasional (*naimittika*) follows what is not previously established"— [the author] proceeds.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now I shall explain the ritual of worship (arcana) correctly and in its proper sequence.

The word "atha" (now) means immediately after the manifestation of the mantra, and following the rites of bathing, ritual placement (nyāsa), invocation (āvāhana), and so forth, as well as recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and the like.

Since it is a constituent part of worship, it is worship itself that constitutes the primary act; I shall explain this "exceedingly," meaning in its full extent, "properly," meaning with the reality of the pervasive principle internalized, and "in due order," meaning according to the sequence of bathing, purification, and so forth, because this ritual of worship is like the process of cooking.

Since it is purified by the initiation of actions involving many constituent parts, its presentation is preceded by the performance of constituent actions such as bathing; and since one who has not performed purification has no entitlement to bathe, he demonstrates that bathing must indeed be preceded by ritual purity.
Having performed purification, one should then perform a bath with earth and water.
First, having taken earth from a pure place and purified it with the Astra-mantra, one should wash the riverbank and place that [earth] there, O fair-faced one. (2-2)

Regarding the phrase "with the weapon [mantra]," since one who is partless (*niṣkala*) lacks the authority for gross ritual action, one should extract [the impurity] from grass, hair, leaves, wood, and so forth, using the *sakala* [form] and the weapon-mantra. || 2 ||
"Then, O slender-waisted one, the two portions [of the earth] must be divided by means of the Astra-mantra.
The word "then" (tataḥ) refers to the purified clay.
The hips, the thighs, the shanks, and likewise the feet, [should each be] half a part.
One should wash it according to the rule three times with an interval [between applications],
using half a portion— that is, by means of half belonging to one portion—
according to the method previously stated beginning with "Śrī."

According to the meaning of the word *yathānyāya* (in due order), one should first wash the feet by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), and then wash the shanks, thighs, and hips; this is the proper method. Having washed the feet and the hands three times—since the connection between the washings was interrupted in the middle by your hand-washing—[one should proceed].

One should wash the shanks, then the hands, then the thighs, then the hands, then the hips, and again the hands; thus, there are three instances of hand-washing in the middle—this is the meaning of the phrase "by means of the three intervening applications. And it is said in the Śrī Mṛtyujit:

"One should purify the feet, shanks, hands, and thighs with three applications of clay respectively, using a method of triple intervals; then again, one should wash the hands with seven [applications]. The meaning is that subsequently, one should wash the hands with seven [applications]; it does not mean...

It should be explained that "with three [repetitions] for the hands," because when a substance is repeated, the *suj* suffix is applied. As for the explanation given by someone who reads and interprets it as "since the conjunction is separated by three measures (*mātrā*) or parts of clay (*mṛdbhāga*)," that should be disregarded due to its utter lack of logical consistency. || 3 ||
Then, taking half of the remaining portion, one should empower it with the mantra of the weapon.
O beautiful woman, one should cause it to be illuminated by the sun seven times.
"The remainder" refers to from one portion. "Illuminated by the sun" means having rubbed it with both hands;
or, when the sun is not visible, having touched it with the breath. 4.
With that very [liquid], having enveloped [the body] from the head down to the feet, one should perform the bath. (2.5)
This is for the purpose of pervading the emanation of the pure reality (śuddhatattva). "Having enveloped" means having smeared [it]. || 5 ||
Having emerged from the midst of the water and performed the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) in due order,
one should perform the salutation to the twilight (saṃdhyā) according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.

"Upasparśana" means sipping water (ācamana); therein, for the purpose of purifying the subtle body internally, one drinks water three times with the *praṇava*, wipes the corners of the mouth twice, and touches the sense-entrances such as the eyes, according to the sequence of the words' meaning, as seen in the scriptures and established in the Vedas and other texts. || 6 ||
Thus is the impurity-bath; now we shall explain the ritual bath.
From that which was previously situated as half a portion, divide it into three portions. (2.7)
On the east, south, and north of the left hand, respectively:

"impurity-bath" (*malasnāna*) refers to the purification of the mind and body. Regarding the phrase "half a portion": since one entire portion has been utilized, the second portion remains whole; however, in relation to the clay, it is half. || 7 ||
Then, one should consecrate the eastern part with the Astra-mantra seven times.
O fair-faced one, having thus consecrated the one situated on the south with mantras through its faces, and likewise having consecrated the northern one together with the deity and its limbs; 2-9.
Having taken the eastern portion, one should cast it in the ten directions;
with the northern portion, one should consecrate the water.
O lady of excellent vows, remembering Bhairaveśa with an extent of only one arm's length, one should veil oneself on the right side.
One should bathe with royal honors using fragrant *āmalaka* and other such substances.

Right here, Lord Bhairava is to be understood according to his manifestation, whether as *sakala* (with parts) or *niṣkala* (partless); in the same way, his limbs and so forth are also to be known. "With the measure of only an arm" means facing toward the *Śivatīrtha*.

The meaning is that one should prepare [the paste] measuring only a hand's span. Regarding the phrase "due to the king's neglect," the sense is that for householders, when possible, bathing with fragrant myrobalan (*āmalaka*) and the like after an oil massage is indeed prescribed; it is not prohibited as it is for those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*). || 11 ||
Furthermore, breath control (prāṇāyāma) and consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed by means of Bhairava.
Prāṇāyāma is remaining in the state of the kumbhaka function; abhiṣeka is the pouring of water upon the head with the kalaśa-mudrā immediately after emerging [from the water]. || 12 ||
Having emerged from the midst of the water, one should change that garment;
having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should recollect the root mantra. (2.13)
O Goddess of the gods, having gathered the *tīrtha* water, one should place it before oneself;
the performance of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is done briefly by means of the eleven mantras. "Having gathered the *tīrtha*" means having drawn it forth with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. || 13 ||
Staying there, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), beginning with the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) and following the proper sequence.
The *aghamarṣaṇa* rite should be performed, followed by the worship of the Sun;
having performed the recitation (*japa*) and offered it thus, one should prostrate, O fair-faced one. (2.15)
Having performed the libation for the mantras together with the gods and the sages,
as well as for all the hosts of beings, one should then withdraw the sacred water (tīrtha).

Having recollected the root mantra... through the recollection of the root mantra, which culminates in resting at the heart, the palate, and the dvādaśānta, this twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) is performed according to the sequence of the Supreme Lord’s mantra; whereas previously, however—

This [rite] should be performed with Vedic mantras by those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from their previous birth have not yet ceased; however, for others, it should be done immediately after the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*) using Śaiva mantras, as it has been stated:
"One may perform the Brāhma rite or not, but one must certainly perform the Śaiva rite."

In this same manner, the two-fold *saṃdhyāvandana* should also be applied to the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*). The sprinkling downward with drops from the left hand using the fingers of the right hand while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and the sprinkling upward with the mantras of the faces and limbs, constitutes the *mārjana*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is implied that water from the right hand, consecrated by the recitation of the *mantrasaṃhitā*, is poured upon the head.

The casting out (kṣepa) follows this sequence; the sequence being that after the *aghamarṣaṇa*, there is the sprinkling (*mārjana*) and so forth, followed by the worship (*upasthāna*). Such is the traditional authority (*āgama*) regarding that: the water held in the right hand, white in appearance and inflamed by the splendor of the *praṇava*, [is to be expelled] through the right nostril alone.

Having meditated on the black form [of impurity] that has entered within and which has emerged from the left nostril due to the cleansing of the stains of speech, mind, and body, one should cast it downward;
such is the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) performed facing the Sun, who is the self of the power of the Supreme Lord.

The casting of the joined palms with the *mantra-saṃhitā*, then performing recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, offering it to the Blessed Lord residing in the heart by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), and performing prostration (*praṇāma*) consisting of the entry into the supreme nature that emerges from the state of total surrender of the body and so forth.

Having performed the libation with water for the mantras of one's own ritual cycle, and having performed the libation for the assemblies of gods, sages, and spirits in the sequence beginning with "Homage to the Gods," one should,
while recollecting the root mantra, withdraw the Śiva-water into oneself by means of the withdrawal mudrā.
One should meditate upon that which has entered [into it]. || 16 ||

Having thus described the ritual bath with water, he speaks next regarding the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), which is mandatory for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and optional for the householder (*gṛhastha*):
"The ash-bath follows after this."
The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having prepared ashes consecrated with the *astra-mantra* according to the procedure taught in another tantra,
one should apply the ashes by smearing them (*samuddhūlya*) starting from the heart down to the feet, or from the head down to the heart, following the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
One should perform the ritual bath for removing impurity with a purified inner self.
With a serene mind. || 17 ||
Then, having changed one's garment, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) as before,
using water alone.
Then, one should perform the ritual bath while recollecting Bhairaveśa.
Contemplating the pervasive presence of Bhairava within oneself.
One should sprinkle the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the ends of the feet, part by part, in due order with the Bhairava mantra accompanied by its ancillary limbs (aṅgas).

Having consecrated the ashes with the root mantra together with its ancillaries, one should smear them from the head down to the feet for the purpose of creating the pure principle (śuddhatattva). || 19 ||
Then, moreover—
one should perform the consecration while recollecting the supreme reality,
entering into the power of the partless (*niṣkala*).
O fair-faced one, one should perform the salutation at the twilight hour just as before.
The phrase "as before" means that the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* and other rites should be performed with water alone.

Consecration (*abhiṣeka*) consists of casting a handful of ashes upon the head while reciting the root mantra and employing the *kalaśa-mudrā*. In this manner, even a householder may perform the ash-bath (*bhasma-snāna*) at will, according to the method prescribed in another Tantra.
Or a householder should perform at least the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) alone.
Having thus performed the ritual bath, one should proceed to perform the rite of worship (arcāvidhi).
Then, having gone to the sacrificial hall (yāgagṛha), one should wash both hands and feet.
Since the feet are smeared with the dust of the road, one should also wash the hands due to that contact.
Having tied the topknot and meditated upon the topknot, he should perform the ritual sipping of water according to the prescribed rule.

Having touched water and sipped it according to the rule with one-pointed mind, having remembered the *śikhā* and the *śikhā-mantra*, and having bound—that is, firmly grasped—the *śikhā*, which is the central power (*madhya-śakti*). || 21 ||
In order to generate within oneself the qualification for external worship, one should briefly perform the recollection of the eleven mantras; thus,
O lady of excellent vows, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the body, one should take up a flower.
Having paid homage to the Mothers of the Directions, one should carefully sprinkle the entrance with water.
By means of the water of Śiva and the Astra-mantra, the expulsion of obstacles shall occur.
By saying "by the water of Śiva," he indicates that one should first prepare the general arghya-vessel for the purpose of the external worship. || 22 ||
Then—above the doorposts, one should likewise [worship] the god Gaṇeśa and Śrī. || 2-23 ||
Having worshipped them in due order with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense and the like,
and with offerings of water for the guest (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya),
one should cast a flower while reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Mothers of the Directions," outside the sanctuary or the sacrificial hall.
Or, in the sky, [one should visualize] the orb of light, the bull, the trident, and the sun; then,
in the upper display that culminates in the external retinue, from the right side of the door to the left,
one should worship Gaṇeśa, as well as Vāgīśī and Śrī, who are conjoined with the word "tathā," using the mantra beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
The sequence is that one should worship with the mantra ending in the word "śabda. || 23 ||
...then, to the north of the door. || 2-24 ||
Having worshipped Nandigaṅgā and Mahākāla to the south, and having fully honored Kālindī as well, according to the proper sequence; || 2-25 ||

The Kālindī, that is, the Yamunā— because of the predominance of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) in the southern current, Mahākāla and Yamunā are to be worshipped specifically on the right of the door; whereas Nandin and Gaṅgā are on the left,
because this principle is the essence of the expansion of power (*śaktisphāra*), and thus [they are worshipped] in secret places such as one's own home on the left of the door.

The Gurus state that one should worship starting from the left hand. This sequence of deities of the door is seen in the venerable *Triśirobhairava-srotas*; however, in that [text], it is stated that Dīṇḍimaha and Udaro are to be worshipped as the presiding deities of the left and right sides of the door, respectively. In the division of the Left Current (*vāmasrotas*),...

Furthermore, in systems where creation is primary, the sequence is that Nandin, Gaṅgā, and Meṣāsyā are on the right of the door, while Mahākāla, Yamunā, and Chāgalāsyā are on the left; however, in the Siddhāntas, Nandin and Gaṅgā are on the right of the door, while Mahākāla and Yamunā are on the left. And generally, one who is fond of the Siddhāntas...

The world relies upon the sequence of established tenets (*siddhānta*); therefore, in this supramundane stream of Bhairava (*bhairavasrotas*), one must rely solely on the sequence taught by the Lord and not otherwise wander into error.

Thus, those who are deluded regarding the philosophical systems (*darśana*) [of the Siddhānta] interpret what was taught by the Lord according to the distinction between the eastern and western doors.
Those who cause others to fall into error are themselves indeed mistaken. || 25 ||
Then—
having recited the Bhairava-weapon mantra, having taken up a flower while remaining in meditative absorption,
and having consecrated it seven times so that it is filled with blazing crests of fire— 2.26.
One should enter into the middle of the house by means of the application of the *nārāca* weapon.

Here, first one should perform the worship of the threshold (*dehalī*); [this involves] the extremely radiant *bhairava* weapon, which is indeed the *niṣkala* weapon, with a visualization such as "blazing," and so forth.

The discharge of the iron arrow (*nārāca*) occurs by the impelling of the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb; "from the middle of the house" is said, with the word "discharging" understood as the ellipsis. || 26 ||
By him, the entire infinite web of obstacles was warded off.
The word "should meditate" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 27 ||
Then, for the sake of protection, one should cast forth the weapon-mantra in the ten directions,
in order to destroy any opportunity for obstacles to enter.
Then, having worshipped Brahmā in the center with perfumes and flowers in due order— || 2-28 ||
Then, seated upon the seat established on the *praṇava* within the southern image, he should assume the posture that has been well-practiced before him.
"Brahmā" refers to the presiding deity of the site (*vāstu*). "In the south" means in the engagement with the practice of the southern current (*dakṣiṇasrotas*),
because it is appropriate for facing the Aghora face, which consumes all dualities.

Since the performance of the ritual has not yet commenced at the beginning of the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), it is stated that one should face either the east or the north. Seated upon the *praṇava*-throne, which is pervaded by the phonemes (*varṇa*), one should remain firmly established in the sense of identity with Bhairava. (29)
He describes the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa):
Having smeared the two hands with fragrant substances, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra; having enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should drench them with nectar.

Having thoroughly agitated the supreme power (parā śakti) with fragrance such as lac-dye and the like, one should smear and anoint it; one should purify it, that is, cause it to attain the state of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). The supreme power is the form of the moonlight of Śiva’s moon situated at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).

Having agitated [the energy] by means of the method of Anaṅgadhenuvīyukti and made it ready to flow forth, one should "drench" (plāvayet)—that is, sprinkle it—with "nectar," the essence of supreme bliss. Afterwards, for the sake of protecting that very form, one should envelop it with the Kavaca mantra. || 30 ||
...Then one should visualize Ananta.
In the procedure for the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the respective mantras must indeed be performed.
By that [means], [one should place] the [deities] residing above the feet of the Vidyā, starting from the *Anāśrita* [Śiva], up to the end of the knot at the tip of the forearm-staff.
One should, by means of the Praṇava, conceive of him as seated upon the infinite throne, whose true nature has already been determined.
Having deposited the Mūrti [mantra], one should assign the secondary faces according to one's own will.

The placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mūrti*, *brahma*, the door-panels (*kavāṭaka*), the *kalā*s, the faces (*vaktra*), and so forth, has already been determined previously. Therefore, wherever [these elements] occur, one must follow the pervasion (*vyāpti*) determined in the first chapter.
Thus, [it is said to be] "according to one's own will" (*svacchanda*).
Thus ends the whole [chapter]. 31.
Immediately thereafter—
one should assign the five limbs from the thumb to the little finger on both hands which have assumed the lotus-mudrā; "the weapon-mantra [is assigned] to the nails," so say the gurus.
Then—having also visualized the Bhairavas—one should recollect the supreme reality. (2.32)

One should recollect—the eight Bhairavas, beginning with Kapālīśa and ending with [Bhīṣaṇa] from the left index finger to the right index finger; the supreme reality, Niṣkalanātha, together with his limbs (aṅgas) and his Goddess—meaning, within the expanded thumbs—one should contemplate them as being followed by the entire universe. Although...
Although the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands is accomplished simply by the future projection of the hand-masses (*piṇḍa*), because they are already constituent parts of those masses,

nevertheless— prior to the placement of the body— in order to recognize the two [hands] as being composed of the Lord’s power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which are like the first sprouts for the engagement in all ritual acts:

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) described in all the scriptures is indeed appropriate; however, the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) is of a different nature, being the domain of a specific, specialized rite.
Having thus explained the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), he states the procedure for the ritual placement on the body (*dehanyāsa*):
"Three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) must be performed as the cause for the purification of the body;
here [the rite] consists of the burning, immersion, and nourishing of the body, preceded by the separation from consciousness."

Having established purity, one must effect the attainment of the nature of Bhairava. And regarding consciousness—according to the principle that "prior consciousness is transformed into breath"—the purification must be performed by means of the breath itself; for it cannot be performed by that [breath] when it is impure.
First, it is possible; that is the purification, the cause of the complete purification of the impure body in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
Demonstrating this, he speaks in order to explain the separation from consciousness:
"The impure [body] should be emptied of its own vital breath and filled with the pure [breath]. (2.33)
Having performed *kumbhaka* (retention) and *recaka* (exhalation), one should cause the self to rest in the void (*vyoman*).

The term "impure" (*aśuddha*) refers to that which exists as a fetter for the individual soul (*jīva*) due to its state of conceptualization, which is intensified by the force of agitation and instability during outward expansion. The term "to be exhaled" (*recya*) refers to the pacification of the natural flow [of the breath].

One should place [the breath] at the *bhoga-dvādaśānta*. By the phrase "with the pure," it means by means of the power of Śakti obtained through resting at the *dvādaśānta*. One should fill [it] completely by obstructing the natural flow [of the breath], and one should permeate it with that touch of Śakti. Having filled it in this manner for some time...

By means of the entry and cessation [of breath], for the sake of attaining power, one should establish [the breath] from the heart to the root-seat (mūlapīṭha) in an immovable state like a full jar. Then,
by that [breath] which has acquired the power of Śakti through the excellence of the kumbhaka [retention].

Having performed the upward *ūrdhvarecaka* in accordance with the method for the divine instrument (*divyakaraṇa*) to be described hereafter, one should cause the Self, which has the vital breath as its support, to rest in the void at the end of the *muṇḍa*.
This *prāṇāyāma* should be performed accompanied by the internal resonance of the *praṇava*. And herein, during the exhalation and so forth—

At the conclusion of the fivefold rest in the void, having contemplated the fivefold concentration (*dhāraṇā*) with the mind through subtle enjoyment, one should dissolve the mind, ego, and intellect into the Supreme Reality by resting in non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*). In this way, the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) occurs.
Thus say the teachers. || 33 ||
He asks, "Of what form is the self? and replies:
"It resembles a firefly, subtle, and devoid of the instruments [of perception]. (2.34)
Devoid of any effect and its sphere of operation destroyed by *māyā*,
it is like a firefly, consisting of the principle of mere luminosity; it is subtle and unknowable by the thirteen instruments— the tenfold organs, both gross and subtle, along with their effects.

"Listen to how that very Self, even when thus brought to a state of purity— wherein the sphere of Māyā, time, necessity, and so forth has been utterly destroyed— becomes Śiva through His own activity. (2.35)
"Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva"—according to this maxim. Listen; reflect within. 35.
"But having grasped the supreme state...

[referring to] the supreme nature that will be described in passages such as, "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause" (4.399), "properly" means by means of the support of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).
Having taken up, that is, having accepted.
Therefore, through immersion into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord who performs creation and withdrawal—...
"therefore, O Dear One, the body is to be dried up;
because the subtle [body] is pure, the gross [body follows]."
How [is it]?
By means of the withdrawal [mantra], which is distinct and joined with the seed-syllable of Rudra. (2.36)

The withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the form of Īśāna, which is expanded; that which is joined with "ya" is the seed-syllable of Rudra, the letter *ū*, with the *bindu* implied by the sense. It is the same elsewhere. Here, having performed the earth-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the body, when that [earth] is dried up, the air-element concentration must be recollected. Of the body...
Emaciation is the attenuation of the essence of the conceit of "I-ness. || 36 ||
By that very [seed-syllable], conjoined with fire above and below, the burning should be performed.

By that same [syllable] now determined as the reality of withdrawal (saṃhāra), conjoined with the fire above and below— that is, with the letter *ra*— by means of the seed-syllable formed into a cluster (*piṇḍīkṛta-bījākṣara*), namely *r kṣ r y ūṂ*, through the fire-element concentration (*āgneyī dhāraṇā*).

By means of the fire of time (kālāgni), there is a burning from the feet up to the crown of the head; thus, the burning away of the bond of the conceit of "I-ness" (ahantābhimāna) must be accomplished.
Below, it is joined with Viṣṇu, has the color of wind, and is accompanied by the bindu.
For this *viṣṇu-ukāra* is indeed the purifier... the letter *y* has the color of wind (*vāyu-varṇa*). Purification (*utpūyana*) means leaping upward (*utplavana*);

even for one whose identification with the body has been scorched away, there remains only the residual impression (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*), which is shaken off by the very practice of the *vāyavya-dhāraṇā*. 37.
In the rite of immersion (*plāvana*), it is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
when the nasal drop (*bindu*) is joined to the top of the letter,
the letter *va* together with the *bindu* belongs to Varuṇa through the meditation (*dhāraṇā*) on Varuṇa.

It is taught that [the practice] which completely drenches [everything] proceeds from the upper *dvādaśānta* with floods of white light-water flowing forth from the drops (*bindu*) shaped like the full moon, directed downwards; the meaning is that it is capable of performing the drenching and the construction of the foundation for the future pure creation.

All these seeds should be contemplated as having become the radiance of the power of one's own nature distinct from that of others. And here, just as with poison, the quality of being lethal is neutralized by the application of mantra;
likewise, day by day, the nature of the body as a bond consisting of the conceit of "I" is consumed by fire.

And through the excellence of that practice, the *ahantā* of Śiva unfolds; however, the body is not directly consumed, because that would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*). For this very reason, since the beginningless *ahaṅkāra* of the body must be removed, there occurs daily the abiding in the pure Self, its grasping, its bringing forth, its immersion in the nectar, and the attainment of the state of Bhairava.
What is being done is indeed appropriate.
Having thus explained the method for the withdrawal of the impure body, he speaks in order to describe the creation of the pure body:
"Then there should be the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa). (2.38)

Then, immediately after the cremation of the body and so forth, there should be the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the power of Manonmanī— the supreme sovereignty— which bears the manifold variety of the universe and serves as the foundational wall for the construction of the future pure body composed of mantra. 38.
Thereafter—

one should bring that [Self] back as it was brought, and indeed flood it with nectar; "as it was brought" means that which was brought by the upward-moving *ūrdhvarecaka* through the middle path, one should [bring it back] by that very same upward-moving *ūrdhvarecaka*.

One should bring [it]—that is, one should cause the center, the heart of Śaktideha—to reach [the supreme state] through mental visualization; one should drench it with nectar, meaning the essence of the firm support of immersion into the supreme state (parabhāva), and thus make it consist of the reflective awareness of non-duality (abhedaparāmarśa). One should bring that very [state] which has been led to such a condition back [to its source].
And of what nature is it? Consciousness (caitanya) that is obscured by impurity (mala), resting upon the categories of limited agency (kalā) and limited knowledge (vidyā). || 2-39 ||
With its self colored by passion (rāga), likewise measured out by time (kāla), further constrained by necessity (niyati), and augmented by the state of being a person (puṃbhāva). (2.40)
Endowed with the primary intention, possessed of the three qualities,
seated upon the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), and enveloped by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).

[The Self] is joined with the mind, the intellect, the organs of action, the sense organs, the subtle elements, and the gross elements—this is the ellipsis. Because it is the locus of bringing [objects] toward itself and taking them away, its consciousness is obscured and rendered subordinate by the impurity (mala) which consists in the appearance of contraction; for this very reason...
It is supported by *kalā* and *vidyā*, which consist of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and limited knowledge (*jñātṛtva*).
The same applies to the others. We shall determine the nature of the remaining principles, beginning with *kalā*, in their proper place later on. || 41 ||
This entire collection of principles, beginning with Māyā and ending with Earth—by means of the Praṇava, all that is the cause for the arising of His body. (2.42)

O Goddess of gods, one should deposit [the mantras] in sequence, numbering thirty-one. The thirty-one principles (tattvas), beginning with Māyā and ending with Earth, which are the cause of the body's origination, should be deposited with the Praṇava, which possesses an expansion equal to that of the venerable Niṣkala Bhaṭṭāraka.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) for the sake of generating a pure body. Through the placement of the *praṇava*, these [powers] become entirely different from their state prior to that. For instance:
his *māyā* consists of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), which, through the boldness of duality, causes delusion; his *kalā*...

Vidyā is that which awakens the sense of agency in performing acts such as worship and meditation, and bestows authentic discernment; Rāga bestows attachment through devotion; Kāla bestows the reckoning of objects such as instruction and the like; Niyati is the regulator in the performance of the Lord’s worship and other rites; and Puṃbhāva is the realization: "I am indeed Śiva."
The sprout of renown; thus is the rest. 42.
"O fair-faced one, among these thirty-one principles, the group of six principles connected with the Self should be known here. (2.43)

The group of six principles, beginning with *māyā* and ending with *niyati*, which constitute the nature of the coverings (*kañcuka*), should be correctly perceived as distinct from the self—the *puṃstattva*—and understood as being bound [to it] like the husk and the grain of rice;
however, one must not grasp at the identity of the self within them. Thus, the body is external to the self. (43)
He speaks of the gross and the subtle simultaneously:
"The body, extending from the primary matter (pradhāna) down to the earth, is fashioned;
it should be known"—here, the change of gender [from neuter to masculine] is due to grammatical adaptation. It is "fashioned" (vinimīta), meaning artificial, and not [natural].
The meaning is "real" (tāttvika).
And here: "The twenty-four principles, moreover, are devoid of consciousness. (2.44)
O lady of excellent hips, they are to be seen... they are to be seen as objects of knowledge, and thus determined. 44.
If these [elements] are insentient, how is it that they are seen [to act]? To this he says:
"But when presided over by the Puruṣa, all of them should always be known as truly sentient. (2.45)
*Adhiṣṭhitatā* (the state of being presided over) is the infusion of one's own agency as intensified by *kalā*.

Those things to be known (*jñātavyāni*) are the objects of cognition (*vedyarūpāṇi*) which must be understood through the casting aside of the sense of "I" (*ahantā*), because even the intellect (*buddhi*) is an object of cognition by way of its modifications (*vṛtti*). Precisely because they are objects of cognition, these [six categories] are external factors (*bahiraṅga*), like the husks of rice. This is the group of six principles (*ṣaṭtattvī*).
But [it is] the state of being an object of cognition for the innermost self, which is the primary subject. || 45 ||
Together with that,
this is proclaimed as the twenty-fivefold *prākṛta*.
*Prākṛta* is simply *prakṛti*, and that which has come from *prakṛti* is also *prākṛta*.

[The sequence] extends from the *guṇas* down to the earth (*kṣiti*). With the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the pure body," one should simultaneously project the Self’s body—which has been drenched in the supreme nectar—as being of three types: the supreme, consisting of the six *tattvas*; the subtle, consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and the gross, consisting of the earth and other [elements]. One should thus perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
In order to clarify that very state of pure form, he says:
"Then, O Goddess, one should deposit the image, well-marked by the root mantra. (2.46)
O Sulocanā, having assigned the entire thirty-two-syllable Bhairava mantra,
one should subsequently fashion the faces from the head down to the feet.
Thereafter, one should fashion the faces—above, in front, to the right, to the north, and to the west—according to their proper divisions. (2.48)
One should arrange the path to be purified according to its divisions of *kalās* as before:
the nine principles (*tattvas*), the three principles, the limbs of *vidyā*, and the three eyes. (2–49)
Transcending the groups, the Kṣurikā is ignited by fire above and below;
situated within the sixteen, she is indeed the protector and the destroyer of obstacles.
Thereafter, one should arrange nine [sections] on the head, the face, and the throat;
at the heart, the region of the navel, the secret place, the thighs, and the knees. (2.51)
Having likewise placed [the syllables] at the end of the feet, conjoined with the qualities of one's own meditation—
namely action (kriyā), knowledge (jñāna), and will (icchā)— on the right, the left, and in the middle.
For this Bhairava, the leader of mantras, is remembered as the King of Knowledge (vidyārāja).
All of this should be understood hereafter exactly as its true nature has been determined in the first chapter;
however, that which is difficult or additional shall now be explained. "Mouths" refers to [the letters] beginning with *kṣ*.

The sequence beginning with the *mūrdhan* (the head) and so forth is indeed appropriate as a sequence accompanied by the "breaking of the staff" (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*), because it has been stated that the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) remains established up until the placement of Bhairava (*bhairavanyāsa*); therefore, it is not otherwise intended for those who have reached the final goal (*naiṣṭhika*).
This must be explained: "according to their proper divisions" means by way of the door-panels (*kavāṭa*) and the facial expressions (*vaktrabhaṅgi*).

"The path to be purified" refers to that which is to be purified during initiation itself—specifically, at the conclusion of the placement of all [mantras], one particular path such as *kalā* and so forth, by virtue of the future application (*bhāviyukti*) and the inclusion (*garbhīkṛta*) of the placement of the other five paths.
One should arrange [them]. As he will say:
"But at the time of initiation, O Goddess, one should arrange the path to be purified" (2.273).
Here, *vidyāṅga* is a substitute for the word *saśa*; the meaning is "the limbs of the Vidyā."
The *kṣurikā* mantra is to be placed on the waist; since it was not mentioned previously, it is stated here.
"Beyond the groups" (*vargātīta*) is *kṣ*; "fire" (*agni*) is *r*; "the end of the sixteen" (*ṣoḍaśānta*) is *aḥ*, the end of the sixteen vowels.
"The group of nine" (*navaka*) refers to [the letters] accompanied by the eight beginning with *īśakapālī* according to the *Śrīsvacchanda*. On its head is *rm*.
The instruction begins with these words. It will follow immediately after [the section on] being established in meditation (*svastha-dhyāna*) and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "action" (*kriyā*), because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more powerful than the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*):
"When Jyeṣṭhā is the Command (*ājñā*), Dakṣā is the Action (*kriyā*), and Vāmā is likewise in the North" (7.152).

Thus, because of the identity of meaning with the subsequent text and due to their predominance, the deposition of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is on the right and that of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is on the left. || 52 ||
He states the placement [of mantras] upon another:
"Having likewise invoked the partless [deity], one should likewise [place] the limbs in due order. (2.53)
"One should install" means this very thing. "Having caused to descend" means having brought down from all around, up to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having thus invoked [the deity], it has already been stated previously that the limbs (*aṅga*) consist of the six qualities such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). Therefore, in this context, the limbs are those whose nature is the protection of the limbs (*aṅgatrāṇa*).

The application of other tantras is incorrect. The teachers maintain that at the occasion of the *aṅganyāsa*, the binding of the six mudrās must be performed. Among these, the fist with the thumbs tucked inside is for the heart;
that same [mudrā] with the thumbs raised is for the head; and with the index fingers raised, it is for the topknot (*śikhā*).
For the armor (*kavaca*), the two hands with fingers interlaced;
for the three eyes (*netra*), the touching of the three eyes with the middle, index, and ring fingers; and for the weapon (*astra*), the snapping of the thumb and index finger.
Immediately after the invocation—
One should worship the Lord of the gods with perfumes, incense, various flowers, and diverse kinds of food and edibles, all mentally conceived. (2.54)
And thus—having meditated upon oneself as Bhairava, one should then perform the ritual (āgama) in the heart;
this procedure has been commenced in order to transform even the body of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka) into Bhairava. || 54 ||
In that regard, having first elaborated upon the placement of the seat (āsana-nyāsa) for one's own self in the form of Bhairava, he now defines it:
"Having established the bulb (kanda) at the navel, the stalk (nāla), however, is twelve finger-breadths long. (2.55)
One should fashion [the space] as far as the end of the heart, and there one should visualize a lotus that is eight-petaled, greatly radiant, possessed of filaments, and complete with a pericarp.

The "kanda" is the root from which the lotus arises; having placed it there—that is, having conceptually established it—one should place and uplift the kanda at the navel, within the region of the navel, by means of the method of pressing the "intoxicated fragrance" (mattagandha).
The "stalk" (nāla) is the form of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), because the distance between the navel and the heart is twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśāṅgula).
It is said to be twelve finger-breadths in length. || 55-56 ||
Regarding this, he states the pervasion:
"The bulb there consists of power; and those thorns upon the stalk are indeed the worlds of the Rudras, O fair-complexioned one. (2.57)
The knot, which consists of illusion (māyā), is situated on the impure path;
[above it is] the lotus of knowledge (vidyā), greatly radiant and adorned with the seed-syllables in its pericarp.
And the Puṣkara lotuses there, O Goddess of gods, are known as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Having thus meditated upon the auspicious Great Lotus, which consists of all the gods.

The word "one should conceive" (*kalpayet*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. Power (*śakti*), whose essence is will, is the supreme lord’s foundational support; it is that in which this entire universe is deposited as a mental object (*ādhi*). As will be stated [later], she is "of the form of space" (*vyomākārā*), and thus she contains within herself the four principles beginning with Earth (*dharā*). As it is said in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:

"First, however, the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) is four finger-breadths below the navel; [then] the earth, the ocean of wine, the ship, and the bulbous root (*kanda*)—these are the fourfold [set]. (8.55).
Among these, by the pervasion of the water-element (*aptattva*), there is the ocean of wine (*surārṇava*); by the pervasion of the fire-element (*tejas*), it is known as the ship (*pota*).

The meaning is that this is the essence (*sāra*) of that whose manifest form is the *prakṛta* power, which has the nature of a bulb (*kanda*) due to the pervasion of the wind (*vāyu*)— the cause for the production of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— and which thus possesses such a manifestation. For this very reason, it is there [in that state] that the entire path (*adhvan*), in the form of sprouts and stalks, becomes manifest.

The pervasion of the stalk extends from the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) up to the principle of *kalā*. "Of the Rudras" refers to those who preside over their respective principles. "Greatly radiant" is because it consists of the splendor of all mantras residing within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). "Lotuses" refers to the seeds.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are those beginning with the venerable Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.

Thus, the well-known sixfold seat (ṣaḍuttham āsana), consisting of the bulb (kanda), the stalk (nāla), the knot (granthi), the petals (dala), the pericarp (karṇikā), and the seed-syllables (bīja), is established.
He states the sequence for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of this seat as follows:
First there should be the placement of the power (śakti), and immediately after that, the bulb (kanda).
One should then conceive of the sprout, the arrangement of the stalk, and Ananta. (2.60)
Having entered the Will-power (*icchā-śakti*), which consists of light, is exceedingly pure, and shines with flickering rays— the very wall upon which the universe is projected—

and having ascended the bulb (*kanda*) whose nature is the support of that [power], [he perceives] everything consisting of the sprout and the stalk, which are the forms of its unfolding and its expansion.
The meaning is that, having established the path ending with Māyā, one should, by mere recollection, conceive of the infinite Vidyeśa above it as consisting of radiant light. || 60 ||

Regarding what was stated—that one should arrange [the lotus] and "imagine it as infinite"—he explains how to sequentially imagine the lion-throne at the location of the knot in its center, and the lotus above that:
"One should place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in sequence. (2.61)
And these—white, red, yellow, and black—are situated in the directions starting from the southeast up to the northeast;
they are the pedestals in the form of lions, three-eyed, and of terrifying prowess. (2.62)
Regarding the term *pādakāḥ*: for those permeated by these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) indeed wander in *saṃsāra*;

thus, all those wandering in *saṃsāra* who are ignorant are "feet" (*pādāḥ*), and they are called *pādakāḥ*. These [beings] are of the form of lions (*siṃharūpāḥ*) by virtue of the greatness of their prowess, because they stride across the entire universe. This occurs through the presiding power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*).
Thus, this applies to them [the Rudras], but not according to the Sāṃkhya system where they are of the nature of attributes of the insentient intellect (*jaḍabuddhi*);
rather, these three-eyed ones are presided over by the power of Īśvara, and because they are the cause of the destruction of terrible saṃsāra, they possess formidable prowess. || 62 ||
And these mantras, consisting of the power of Śiva, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, should be installed by one who seeks liberation;
for in reality they consist solely of the power of the Supreme Lord, though they are not recognized as such [by the uninitiated].
They move through lower levels; however, when they are recognized as they truly are, then—

possessing the nature of *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection)— they manifest the form of mantra by the will of Śiva, the recognizer, and become pure *prasaraṇis* (emanations) belonging to the transmigratory world, being devoted to Him.
This is the ultimate truth; however, these mantras do not possess any other form of mantra-nature, because they are established within the impure path.
Regarding the other limbs on the lion-throne, he says:
non-dharma, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty [are located] in the eastern direction. (2.63)
The northern boundary should be established;
for these indeed have limbs that are white in color.

They have the form of lion-throne plaques. Generally, because they are covered by the illusion (*māyā*) consisting of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), they consist of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and so forth; for this very reason, they long for righteousness (*dharma*) and the like, such that unrighteousness and the rest are their limbs unknown within the sphere of illusion.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *gātra* when the meaning is that of something unknown. || 63 ||
Right here are the junction-pins (saṃdhānakīlaka), which resemble the flax flower (atasīpuṣpa). || 2.64 ||
O beloved, the Vedas and the Yugas must also be known in their proper sequence.

In each corner, starting from the southeast (Āgneyī) and so forth, there are two stakes for the purpose of binding the two limbs along with the foot. The Vedas are the *Ṛg* and the others, and the Yugas are the *Kṛta* and the others; these represent the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of their respective experiences.

Nourishing the causes of bondage in *saṃsāra*, they take the form of various doubt-thorns and are called "connecting pegs" (*saṃdhānakīlaka*). Precisely because they are binding, they should be understood as being black in color; for, in their nature as the previously mentioned power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-śakti*), they are as [they are] when unknown.

They become bondsmen. Now, one might ask: "How have these attributes of the intellect (buddhi) reached such a state? It is said: Māyā is the ground of origin for all attributes beginning with the intellect;
the intellect and the rest are merely the locus of manifestation. However, when they are severed from the fundamental ground, they are eradicated and do not [return].
Since these [impurities] sprout from the state of origination, this sequence has been taught for their eradication. || 64 ||
For this very reason, in order to uproot *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* from their very foundation and to place upon the lion-throne a cushion (*masūraka*) consisting solely of the *guṇas*, he says:
"One should contemplate the covering below as red and the one above as white. (2.65)

One should understand that *tamas* is in the middle; these qualities (*guṇas*) are thus established. Above, because it is close to *śuddhavidyā*, it is white, having the nature of *sattva*. Below, however, because it conforms to *saṃsāra*, it is red, consisting of *rajas*. But in the middle...
Due to the excellence of concealment through manifestation, that which consists of *tamas* is black; the *prādhānika* expansion is unreal within *māyā*,

and so forth, yet it is not non-existent, because the entire effect of *māyā* exists within *māyā* in a subtle form, abiding in the manner that will be described when explaining the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).
By means of the purifications resulting from the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), all of this must be realized as being of the nature of Śiva’s power through the very state of mantra;
as he will say, beginning with "Wherever [it may be]," "since everything consists of Śiva" (4.310).
Thus [it is said].
Then, regarding the placement of the knowledge-lotus (*vidyāpadma*) upon the cushion of the lion-throne, it is said:
"One should know the lotus to be white; one should contemplate its filaments. (2.66)
The root, middle, and tip regions are white, red, and yellow respectively;
the pericarp resembles gold, while the seeds are green.
A white lotus is indeed of such a color. Its whiteness arises from its being composed of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). Regarding the placement of the deities upon its petals, he says:
"Having placed Vāmā on the eastern petal, one should place Jyeṣṭhā resting on the southeastern petal."
One should place Raudrī on the southern petal and Kālī in the domain of Nairṛta.
One should place one Kalavikaraṇī on the western petal,
and another Balavikaraṇī resting upon the northwestern petal.
One should employ the goddess Balapramathanī in the north,
and one should employ Sarvabhūtadamanī in the northeast.
One should place the single Manonmanī in the pericarp in the center;
this is clear. || 70 ||
And this circle of power (śaktimaṇḍala), resembling a rainbow, O Goddess, is to be meditated upon. (2.71)
Even beyond that—one should meditate upon Manonmanī in the center, possessing the radiance of a thousand suns.
These goddesses, situated in the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and so forth, abide within the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva) in their supreme form; in the center—

The distinction is that [the powers] are [manifested] by the supreme-non-supreme (parāpara) form in the state of the feet, but here in the context of the Vidyā, they are by the non-supreme (apara) form. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate their essential nature according to their names in that very place, as everything consists of the three previously mentioned powers.

In order to enjoin the three mandalas—which consist of the forms of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and the knower, and whose true nature is the pervasion of knowledge, action, and will—within the principle of Vidyā, he says:
"Having joined the solar path-mandala on the petal and the lunar [mandala] on the filament... (2.72).
O Goddess, one should place the fire-mandala within the pericarp;
for here, the moon— which is the object of knowledge— possesses the state of being situated in the midst of the mother-measures consisting of fire and sun,
since [the object] cannot exist without the wall of the light of the subject, nor without the permeation by the light of the measure.

There is no object of knowledge (*meyaprakāśa*) whatsoever. For it is by the knower alone (*pramātrā*)—through the solidification of the essence of consciousness—that the object of knowledge is manifested;

and that which is being manifested becomes permeated precisely by the light of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaprakāśa*). Enough of this elaboration; this will be treated in detail in the chapter on emanation and reabsorption (*sṛṣṭisaṃhārapaṭala*).
In order to reveal here the inclusion of the universe within those presiding deities, he defines these three deities who preside over the three abodes:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are traditionally known as the presiding lords of the maṇḍalas. (2.73)
He describes the meditation on these [deities] through the higher and lower pervasion:
Brahmā has four faces and is red; he is adorned with four arms, wears a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and is seated upon a lotus throne. (2.74)
O Goddess, he holds a water-pot and likewise has a staff in his hand;
the god wears a rosary of beads, holds a lotus in his hand, and has beautiful eyes.
Having meditated upon him, who resembles the flax flower and holds the conch, discus, and mace, one should place him upon the leaves; he is the destroyer of all sins.
The god wears yellow garments and is adorned with a forest garland;
his crown-jewel sparkles, and he is embellished by a network of tiny bells.
Having meditated upon the high-souled Viṣṇu, who wears divine earrings and is seated upon the throne of Garuḍa, one should place him within the filaments.

The lotus is indicated by the conch. Because of the state of fusion between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, Viṣṇu—the sustainer—is present within the lunar orb, which is the nature of the object of knowledge and primarily characterized by emanation;
and Brahmā, the presiding deity who effects emanation, is present within the solar orb, which is the nature of sustenance and consists of the means of knowledge. Thus, it is logical.
Thus it is. || 78 ||
White as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon; holding a trident in his hand;
three-eyed; ten-armed; large-eyed; and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
O fair-faced one, having meditated upon Rudra—clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with the moon, blue-throated, and mounted upon a bull—[one should worship]. (2.80)
One should place [the seed-syllable] in the pericarp, which destroys great sins;
thereafter, one should place upon it the Great Preta, laughing and conscious. (2.81)
Red in color, possessing great splendor, and adorned with three eyes;

he has entered into a state of existence where non-egoity (ahantā) is predominant, having thoroughly transcended (prakarseṇa itaḥ) through the immersion of the teeth [of duality]; and he is one for whom the universe is thoroughly transcended (prakarseṇa ca itaṃ), gone beyond, and integrated.

According to this etymology, "preta" here refers to Sadāśiva, and he is the form of Anāśrita-Śiva by means of the word "mahat. Furthermore, the Lord Paramaśiva alone is the single essence of consciousness who exists within the forms of those below him; thus, the [principles] beginning with Anāśrita have him as their sole life-force.

He himself, however, is like a ghost (preta); he is called a "ghost" because he abides here in the lower path in a state of stillness. Furthermore, according to that [threefold] pervasion: by the lower [pervasion], he is Sadāśiva in his gross form; by the middle, he is that very same one in the form of sound (nāda); and by the higher, he is Anāśrita. Accordingly, there is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).

And the lotus is to be joined. That preta is Paramaśiva himself, laughing through the very entry into the sense of "I" (*ahantā*), consisting of the reflective awareness of *nāda* and characterized by great expansion; he is conscious precisely by means of that Paramaśiva in the form of *nāda*. Even so, because he possesses the nature of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the unfolding of the internal [light] (*antaronmeṣa*) to that extent.
Because he delights all beings, he is red in color; because of the predominance of pure consciousness, he is intensely radiant.
And it will be said:
"He possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns. (10.1214)

Thus, in the Bhuvana-paṭala: [He is] adorned and shining with a special upward gaze—the triad of eyes consisting of the powers of will, knowledge, and action—which leads the universe, whose nature consists of that which is to be desired, that which is to be known, and that which is to be accomplished. As it has been said:
"When the three goddesses constantly attend upon him, then he is to be known as Tryambaka... (81)
In this manner, up to this extent,
one should perform the entire placement of the seat for Bhairava with the Praṇava.

With the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the seat," one should perform the placement [of the seat], for it will be stated that "all this seat is pervaded by non-difference from Cidbhairava; everything is composed of Śiva. Thus, it is of the nature of Śakti, and not a separate or other form; one should place it while internalizing it within the Praṇava (Oṃ). And here:

"The mantrin should distribute the seats in sequence with the lotus-gesture (padmamudrā)," because it is stated thus in the venerable *Raurava*; therefore, having joined both hands in the bud-like gesture (mukulīkṛtya), the lotus-gesture should be struck and established. || 82 ||
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers by means of the *praṇava* alone,
one should then fashion the form (*mūrti*).
Having the form of a kadamba flower, with a brilliance like that of the moon amidst frost.
The meaning is: consisting of light and bliss. || 83 ||
Then, above the form, one should visualize the god Bhairava as possessing all parts (sakala),
inlaid with the thirty-two phonemes, blazing like a flash of lightning. (2.84)
Having performed the utterance of the mantra from the heart to the *dvādaśānta*, and having rested there for a moment,
the Gurus maintain that one should deposit the King of Mantras— the *puryaṣṭaka*— right within the heart in order to transform it into Bhairava.
And here, everything beginning with the Brahma-door, the lattice, the digits, and the facial expressions is merely indicated in outline as it will be explained later.
One should contemplate [it] according to the analogy of a mass of light; with this intention, it is said: "blazing like a flashing lightning bolt. || 84 ||
Then,
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should fashion the faces through one's own meditation,
from the head down to the feet, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

One should conceive of the path to be purified as consisting of thirty-eight divisions of *kalās*, as well as the nine principles (*tattvas*) and the three principles known as the group of nine called Bhairava. (2.86)
One should fashion the limbs of knowledge, as well as the eye and the razor;
then one should install the three powers in the right, the front, and the left directions.
O Goddess of the gods, in Madhyapradesh...

this has been recited again for the sake of non-forgetfulness. By means of the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), [the worlds] are created by the Supreme Lord and consist of His power; yet, O Blessed Lady, they are in essence a mass of light and bliss.
For this very reason, it has been stated that by sitting upon the seat [of consciousness], the universe is composed of Śiva. || 87 ||
He speaks of meditative absorption (dhyāna): "Then one should recollect the form [of the deity]:
the god with fifteen eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair. (2.88)
Resembling ten million moons, with the crescent moon as his crest,
five-faced and large-eyed, adorned with snakes and a bull-nose.
He was adorned with a necklace of scorpions glowing like fire,
decorated with a garland of skulls, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The god holds a noose and a goad, carries an arrow in his hand, and wields the Pināka bow;
he grants boons and fearlessness with his hands, and bears a severed head and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
He holds a lute and a hand-drum, with a bell in his hand and a trident;
he displays the majesty of a thunderbolt-staff and holds an axe as a weapon in his hand.
He was resplendent with a variegated, round mallet;
he was clothed in a lion’s skin with an elephant hide as an upper garment.
The Lord, who possesses eighteen arms, a blue throat, and great splendor,

has manifested in such a form upon the plane of the Unmanā-śakti through His own sovereignty, in order to cause those desiring to ascend to enter the stainless abode; for this does not occur anywhere within the worldly realm (bhuvana).

Such is this deity. Precisely because he consists of the expansion of Śakti, he possesses eighteen arms, for Durgā-devī is likewise constituted by that same nature.
