And within this *Kṛtigrantha*, which serves as the locus for the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*), the pervasion of Cid-bhairava remains entirely unbroken. To illustrate: by means of three...

He is the "three-five-eyed one" (tripañcanayana), because he possesses the eyes by which he leads the five [deities] who abide pervading everything up to Māyā, through their divisions into gross, subtle, and supreme forms, along with the Para-śaktis;
[he is so called] by means of his matted locks (*jaṭā*)— which are the powers such as Vāmeśvarī and others situated in the upward direction— and by his crown (*mukuṭa*).
Adorned by the expansion of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), it resembles ten million moons; that is, it is a mass of light and bliss. As it is said in the *Śrīlakṣmīkaulārṇava*:
"O Mistress of the Gods, because of His non-duality, He is celebrated on earth as Bhairava."
"But one should contemplate him as gentle, not because of the fierceness of his fangs.
Thus, "having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament" means he is connected with the digit of nectar called Amā, which effects the nourishment of the universe;
"five-faced" refers to the five [powers] known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.

He whose faces manifest His own supreme nature and serve as protection from saṃsāra—him, the large-eyed one. As it is said: "With the internal object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from the opening and closing of the eyes."

Thus, [it] abides as the expansion of the traditionally taught Supreme Bhairava, and by means of the sequence beginning with "sarpa" and ending with "virājitam," its nature consists in being intent upon the play of joining and separating the three bonds known as māyīya, kārmāṇava, and āṇava, which have been cast outward.
"Released," meaning "adorned with a garland of skulls," refers to the Lord whose body is the entire universe;
the universe is his ornament in the form of an expansion of limbs consisting of a garland of skulls, but not a covering.
For the Blessed One, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss, there are three powers—will, knowledge, and action—which function as instruments.

Each individual power (*śakti*) possesses nine forms due to its threefold nature; therein, each is further divided into two—higher and lower—resulting in eighteen arms. Among these, with the sword, which is the essence of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), there is the severing of bonds (*pāśa*); and with the shield, which is the form of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), [there is the protection] of the devotees.

The avoidance of fear of saṃsāra; sovereignty over the noose that binds all; the drawing [of beings] by means of the hook; the piercing of the garland of knots of causal matter by means of the arrow and the Pināka bow;
the bestowing of enjoyment and liberation through the hands granting boons and fearlessness; and [the attainment of power] through the wearing of the severed head.

The state of being the remover of the skull of Māyā, whose nature is non-apprehension (*akhyāti*); the fact that the entire universe, from *Anāśrita* downwards, which is like a skeleton or a corpse, is fixed upon the wall of one’s own consciousness, symbolized by the carrying of the *khaṭvāṅga*;
and the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of the Sound (*nāda*), which is the locus of the variety of sounds—low, high, and middle—by means of the lute, the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and the bell.
The state of having one's power focused on contemplative observation;

the severing of the three bonds by means of the trident—the staff of the sovereign powers of will, knowledge, and action; and, by means of the thunderbolt—the triad of powers beginning with will situated above and the triad beginning with the object of desire situated below—the realization of one's own power as the essence of the entire universe.

By means of the staff (*daṇḍa*), which is the nature of the power of destiny (*niyati-śakti*), there is the governance of the universe; by means of the axe (*paraśu*) shaped like a plow, which is the nature of the power of resonance (*nāda-śakti*), and by means of the mallet (*mudgara*) which is the form of the power of the point (*bindu-śakti*), there is the tearing asunder and pulverizing of all duality—this is what is suggested. [The lion...]

The five-faced one consists of Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva; he is the expansion of consciousness. His "skin" is his conduct. And the "skin" of the elephant—that is, the conduct or playful manifestation of the elephant whose nature is Māyā, which is extensively spread out and cannot be pierced by the lion whose nature has been described—is his "garment," because it is closely attached to his own essential nature.

[He is] that upon whose own nature— which consists of non-difference from awakening— the Lord (deva), whose nature is play and so forth, the Blue-throated One (Nīlakaṇṭha), who removes the great poison consisting of non-recognition, and the one of great splendor, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss, revolves. Such [descriptions] have been set forth by us in the *Bhairavānukaraṇastotra*.
It has been explained. || 93 ||
He describes the meditation on the face of this Blessed One:
"O Great Goddess, one should contemplate the upper face as having the luster of crystal. (2.94)
One should know that the eastern face is yellow, with the luster of a blue lotus petal; one should likewise contemplate the southern and the northern faces. (2.95)
One should contemplate the western [face] as resembling the pomegranate flower, like water mixed with saffron, and similar in appearance to ten million moons. (2.96)
The diversity of the forms of the directions of the faces arises from the diversity of their respective functions, such as bestowing grace and so forth. || 96 ||
Thus, that man who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon such a god, Svacchandabhairava, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, will quickly attain perfection. (2.97)

One whose self is disciplined and whose mind is one-pointed attains success; he obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Just as it was previously stated that the reciter destroys all sins by uttering [the mantra] even once, so too it is stated that the object of recitation bestows all accomplishments through mere meditation; thus, its great power is proclaimed.
He states the supreme nyāsa:
"Thereafter, by means of the supreme seed-syllable, [one should meditate upon] the Supreme, the ultimate cause, the utterly tranquil, partless, all-pervading, and stainless God. (2.98)
"O Goddess, with a joyful heart I shall tell you how one should invoke [the deity]:

'supreme and unsurpassed'—with a 'joyful heart' means due to an intense longing for immersion into the state of Śambhu; 'one should invoke' means one should cause [the deity] to descend from the *dvādaśānta*."

The meaning is that, by means of the support of the supreme power (paraśakti), one should cause its own nature to emerge and make it the very essence of its own wonder (camatkāra) as far as the heart. || 99 ||
Of what nature is it?—it is situated within the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the end of the sound (nāda), reaching its ultimate limit. (2.99)
"Unwavering, beyond causes...
[means] that which ends with *nāda* and ends with *śakti*; its end, its limit, is the *dvādaśānta*.
By that, it pervades simultaneously from the heart up to the *dvādaśānta*, being unwavering and not moving from its own essential nature.
Thus,
having invoked the Supreme Lord and established the God according to the rule, one should then assign the six limbs.
"Having placed the two palms face upwards with the two thumbs positioned in the middle of the palms— this is the *āvāhanī* [mudrā]...
Thus, the invocation is performed with the *āvāhana-mudrā*.
"With the thumbs bound and the fists positioned facing upward, it shall be the *sthāpanī* [mudrā].
Thus is the installation with the mudrā.
Then— water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering; immediately after that, a welcome, and then the invocation of presence, O Goddess of gods...

The word "should offer" (*kalpayet*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. Water for the feet is *pādya*. "Welcome" (*svāgatam*) means: "May there be a most beautiful arrival for the sake of showing us favor. Through the *yonimudrā*, [one effects] the presence [of the deity].
Having done thus, one should suppress [the breath] with forceful effort. || 2-101 ||

The *niṣṭhurā* mudrā; by means of it, one should restrain [the breath], that is, establish it immovably. It is as follows: "The two fists with the thumbs placed inside... and "...is called *niṣṭhurā* for its restraint. Thus it is said. (101)
Then—
having perfumed him with scents, flowers, and incense, one should worship him;
all of this should be performed mentally.

Then, one should subsequently display the mudrā for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity; it is so called because it bestows joy (*muda*) and delight (*harṣa*) three times during the ritual action of the three periods of time, it seals (*mudrayati*) the wealth of the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava, it gladdens (*modayati*) the devotees through supreme immersion, or it causes the fetters (*pāśas*) to dissolve (*drāvayati*). Thus is its etymological derivation.
The seal (*mudrā*) which consists of the reflection of the supreme nature (*parasvarūpa*), of eighteen kinds as will be described:
"O Great Goddess, one should display these seals of Bhairava during invocation, during the act of restraint, and likewise during dismissal. (14.20)
Thus, regarding the ritual action pertaining to the three times that is about to be described: "Threefold" means—as it is said:

"Born of the mind, residing in the mouth of the Guru, and arising from speech; born of the mantra, and born of the body through the movements of the limbs—this mudrā is traditionally held to be threefold."
Thus it is taught in the sacred tradition. || 102 ||
In order to explain the internal sacrifice in detail, he says:
"Then, O fair-faced one, having performed the rites such as bathing and so forth, and having dressed [the disciple] in fine garments made of silk cloth. (2.103)
Having anointed [the deity] with agallochum and camphor, one should adorn him with the crown and other ornaments;
the sequence is: having anointed, having clothed, one should adorn.
One should worship with various kinds of pure flowers and further adorn [the deity].
O Maheśānī, having offered the *argha*, one should again display the mudrās, having prostrated before the god Bhairava, the independent Lord of the universe. (2-105)
*Arghaṃ* means the special *argha* offering. *Praṇamya* means having resorted to the state of being one with that through total immersion (*samāveśa*).
Therefore, O fair-faced one, having placed the ornaments on the outside,
although the faces, limbs, and so forth— which are the very form of the Supreme Lord’s power— are deposited as non-different from that [central deity],
they nevertheless appear as if separate by His will alone, acting as coverings like a mass of radiance, because they are manifested by Him.
That which is situated should be established [in its true state]. By speaking thus, he teaches this:

although the universe—conceived as the grasped and the grasper—is of the nature of Śiva, it appears as if separate because it is manifested by Śiva in that manner; however, its actual separateness never exists in reality.
Regarding the placement of the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), he states the division: "From the northeast, to the east, to the south, and ending in the north. (2-106)
One should arrange five faces, each endowed with five mouths, together with ten arms and the moon as a crown. (2.107)
Their essential forms should be meditated upon as granting boons and protection;

for each individual Śakti possesses the nature of five Śaktis, and because each one manifests through a differentiation from the essential nature consisting of the expansion of Śakti, they possess the form of five faces. Nevertheless, even so—

Because their essence consists in non-difference [from one another] through the conjunction of mantra and the channels (*nāḍī*), their individual worship has also been taught. "Svarūpāṇi" refers to those whose forms possess the previously mentioned characteristics, such as being like crystal and so forth.
[Their] state of having hands in the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
It is characterized by the sword, shield, noose, goad, arrow, Pināka bow, severed head, and khaṭvāṅga staff;

and because the mantras possess the nature of *para*, *parāpara*, and *apara*, and because each of these— *para* and the others— is threefold, and because they are pervaded by the form of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*), they possess ten forms.
And because it pervades that [body], there is the state of having ten arms. || 107 ||
He states the secondary limbs associated with the face and the veils:
"And one should place that [mantra] in the four directions—namely, those of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu. (2.108)
The heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon are to be assigned according to their respective divisions:

the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon are located in the directions of Agni (southeast), Īśa (northeast), Rakṣas (southwest), and Vāyu (northwest) respectively; thus is the division for the four directions. These very limbs, taken as a whole, constitute the separate protective coverings.
They are to be worshipped, but not as partless limbs; for those [deities] who possess a single form such as omniscience and so forth, have the nature of a single partless unity. || 108 ||
He describes their forms:
"The heart has the luster of red color; the head has the brilliance of yellow orpiment. (2.109)
One should contemplate the crest-lock as resembling a circle of lightning;
one should know the armor to be smoky-grey and the weapon to be tawny-brown.
In order to explain the description of the location of the form of the eye, he says:
"One should place the eye, which resembles the form of light, situated in the center. By the word "in the center," he means in the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*), for he will state later:
"The eye, however, is indeed in the pericarp" (2.171).
And all these are remembered as having five faces, ten arms, and being adorned with the moon. (2.111)
Adorned with various ornaments, anointed with diverse garlands and fragrant unguents, and dressed in various garments, they were radiant with beautiful crowns. || 2.112 ||
Adorned with strings of jewels and decorated with necklaces and armlets, they are sixteen years of age, handsome, and possessed of perpetual youth. (2.113)
The mantras beginning with Bhairava are known as the lords of the *pīṭha* and the destroyers of the *pīṭha*.

The mantras beginning with Bhairava and ending with the *aṅgas* are the lords— the masters— of the fourfold *pīṭha*, which consists of the forms of the *vidyā*, the mantra, the maṇḍala, and the mudrā.
And the *mardakas* [are so called] because they make [the deity] their own.

However, those who explain this as being ultimately about the *pīṭhas*, *kṣetras*, *saṃdohas*, and *pallīs*, while even in the midst of the installation of the deities (*devatānyāsa*) during this internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) they conceive it in such a way—they are truly laughable. (113)
Now, that supreme power Aghorī who was previously described by me— || 2.114 ||
Having worshipped Bhairava, one should place her upon his lap.
Regarding her meditation, it says:
"Indeed, the form of Bhairavī is exactly like the form of Bhairava. (2.115)
And so it is said:
"One should always meditate upon Bhairavī, whose face is slightly terrifying, whose voice is deep and expansive, whose countenance is serene, and whose eyes are wide with wonder. (2.116)

His ferocity arises from imitating Bhairava; his consumption of fetters results from devouring the bonds [of limitation]; his deep and vast resonance stems from the primacy of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); his serene countenance is due to his inclination toward grace (*anugraha*) in accordance with the nature of Supreme Bhairava; and for this very reason, through the entry into the *mudrā* of Bhairava, his gaze is one of wonder.
Then—
O Goddess, one should place the eight Bhairavas in the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
By the word "second," the limbs (*aṅga*) and faces (*vaktra*) are included as a single enclosure, because they possess equal pervasiveness.
And because it is the originator of the Lord’s body, he shows this as follows.
He explains how one should perform the placement:
"One should place Kapālīśa in the east, and Śikhivāhana in the southeast. (2.117)
In the south is the King of Wrath, Vikarāla;
in the southwest is Manmatha; and likewise in the western quarter is Meghanādeśvara.
Having placed the Goddess in the northwest, and likewise the Moon-King in the north,
one who is well-concentrated should place the King of Vidyās in the northeast.
All eight [deities] likewise have five faces, three eyes, ten arms, and the crescent moon as their crest;
they are adorned with garlands of skulls and embellished with shimmering rubies. (2.120)
He describes their meditation according to the sequence of the directions: "O Goddess, the eastern [quarter] is remembered as yellow; in the domain of Agni (southeast) it is red;
in the south it has the luster of a dark blue cloud; and in the southwest (Nairṛtya) it has the brilliance of fire. (2.121)
He is dark-complexioned in the western quarter and smoke-colored in the domain of the northwest;
he has the luster of the moon's orb in the north and the brilliance of crystal in the northeast.
Now, in the third [mandala], one should likewise imagine the Lords of the World (lokeśas) together with their consorts. I shall state their names correctly and in proper sequence. (2-123)
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Samīraṇa; Soma-rāja, Kubera, Īśāna, and Parameśvara. || 2-124 ||
By saying "from the Śāstras," he establishes that the armor and weapons are not to be placed separately, as indicated by the mention of "in the third. || 124 ||
And they, O fair-faced one, should be meditated upon in the form of the eight Bhairavas;
for, as previously stated, they consist of the expansion of the eight Bhairavas whose essence is the mass of powers (*śakti*) of Supreme Bhairava.
They should be visualized precisely in the form of the eight Bhairavas mentioned, beginning with the yellow one.
In this way, he enumerates by name these weapons as well—whose essence consists in the pervasion of the Bhairava weapon and which are intent upon the protection of the sacrifice:
"The Vajra, the Śakti, the Daṇḍa, and likewise the Khaḍga and the Pāśa. (2.125)
The banner, the mace, and the trident are indeed the weapons of the world-protectors.
Regarding meditation, he says:
"The thunderbolt is enriched with many colors, and the spear has a luster equal to gold. (2.126)

One should visualize the staff as having the luster of split collyrium, the sword as having the radiance of a blue lotus, the noose as resembling the *kiṃśuka* flower, and the banner as white. (2.127)
One should meditate upon a mace with the luster of coral and a trident with a brilliance equal to lightning as being held in their hands. (2.127)
Then,
having fully worshipped the entire retinue, one should perform the unification within the leader of the mantra.
The word "must be performed" is to be supplied [from the preceding context]. || 128 ||
In response to the inquiry "How so?", [it is said]:
"The weapons, the world-protectors, the eight Bhairavas, the five Brahmans, and then the limbs—these indeed are the enclosures. (2.129)
One should pronounce everything in sequence until that which is the Lord within the womb;
the method stated in the third chapter beginning with "the weapons" (astrāṇi) is to be followed here. And this is the true essence of worship in this context:
Having transcended the entire web of paths and having taken refuge in the stainless form of Consciousness,
or else having embraced with the intellect that [Consciousness] which assumes many forms as it emerges,
one who has become identical with Her— who consists of the Great Reality (mahātattva) possessing the splendor of the four stages beginning with effort— should offer everything here within that state.
"With the mind, one who is beyond [the senses] should worship the All.
Thus [ends verse 129].
Immediately thereafter, the joining of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) must be performed with the root mantra. || 2-130 ||
In this case as well:
"Having performed the emission of the partless *ātman*, one should deposit it into the *kumbha*.
Then, one should exhale from the left side of that which resides in the *kalaśa* and subsequently fill it."
"Having [inhaled] with the right, one should exhale again with the left. (4.46–47).
According to the procedure to be described in the fourth chapter, one should utter Niṣkalanātha;
having emerged through one's own left [nostril], one should enter through Bhairava’s right, and then proceed in due order.

One should perform exactly the same [process] up to the faces, limbs, Bhairavas, and Lokapālas; thus, by means of the root mantra, there is the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*). For in this way, through the sequences of withdrawal and expansion, the entire wheel of deities arises as consisting solely of the Blessed One, Supreme Bhairava. As for those who...

Having examined this text of the third and fourth chapters, those who explain the joining of mantras (*mantrasandhāna*) and the joining of channels (*nāḍīsandhāna*) in one way and then another are indeed mistaken; for it is the settled conclusion of those learned in grammar that "consideration of what follows" (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*) is a principle of tantric composition (*tantrayukti*). || 130 ||
Then, having meditated [on the deity] as far as the ultimate limit (*parānta*), one should present the food offerings (*naivedya*).
By the phrase "having meditated as far as the ultimate limit," it is meant that one should present the food offerings after having performed the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).
"One should offer," and so forth, he instructs. For he will say in the third chapter:
"This indeed is the conjunction of mantras...
having said this.
Listen now to the process of bringing [the deity] to perfection.
Then, O Lord, one should utter the deity accompanied by short, long, and elided vowels.
"One should recite the mantra until the sphere of Nirvāṇa is reached," and so forth, up to:
"O Goddess, one should place that pervasive [mantra] upon all the coverings."
"And presided over by Him, they all grant the fruits of all desires.

(3.24) Thus, in such passages, one should reflect upon the preceding and following context. Furthermore, having visualized [the space] as far as the furthest limit and meditated upon it as consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), [one offers] the food offerings (*naivedya*).

"One should offer" means one should dedicate it to the Blessed Lord with the perspective of *brahmārpaṇa*; "one should offer" means one should know [all things] to consist of Śiva—this is the meaning.
He specifies the mental food offerings:
"Ghārikā, vaṭakas, śaṣkulīs, and likewise modakas. (2.131)
One should prepare bowls of sugar-candies and laddus, various kinds of edible foods, as well as rice cooked with *śāli* grain, lentil soup, and clarified butter. (2.132)
One should prepare *kauśalyā*, cakes fried in ghee (*maṇḍaja-pūpa*), and honey-topped sweets (*kṣaudraśiras*), as well as *cillaka* fried in clarified butter and salt. (2.133)
Many kinds of appetizers, both pungent and sweet, as well as *rasālā*, curd, milk, and various types of fermented liquors. || 2.134 ||
Free from deceit and hypocrisy, one should fill the foremost vessel of Śambhu with various kinds of fish and meat, as well as those things that are to be licked and drunk. (2.135)

"Whatever brings joy to the mind, having first reflected upon all that through reasoning, one should cause it to dissolve into that very abode of one's own self, which is the singular essence of Bhairava due to the non-difference from the universe; such is the secret of the food offering (*naivedya*). 'One should avoid stinginess regarding wealth'—this is to be applied to the external sacrifice, for indeed..."
In a mental sacrifice, some may experience a sense of meanness.
Having done this, one should subsequently offer the *argha* with well-scented wine, in order to contemplate the state of one's own self as the form of the Blessed One, filled with supreme bliss.

This was stated precisely because liquor (*surā*) is a cause of bliss. However, those who explain the word *surā* as referring even to water within this Bhairava system— even though it is here the opening of the eyes to the nature of the Supreme Bhairava that uproots one's caste— have been seized by the demon of caste-obsession (*jāti-graha*).

"O fair-faced one, one should not despise those who possess proper conduct or those who lack it, nor those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin), even if they consume liquor, meat, fish, or other such things"— according to this [verse], those who transgress the future rules are indeed merely *paśus* (bound souls).
And having done this, one should subsequently display the mudrā three times during the ritual action of the three periods of time. || 2-136 ||
The phrase "in the action pertaining to the three times" is a restatement; this has already been explained previously. || 136 ||
Then, having performed prostration, one should subsequently perform the recitation (*japa*).

Prostration is the immersion (*samāveśa*) of the body and so forth—which remain as mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—into the Supreme Bhairava, who is the conscious Self; otherwise, when the state of Bhairava has been realized both internally and externally, who would be where?
To whom should one prostrate? Here, "japa" (repetition) refers to the repeated contemplation (*vimarśa*) upon the essential nature of Supreme Bhairava.
To the question "How?", he says:
"Having taken up the rosary, which has been honored with perfumes and flowers... (2.137).
With speech restrained and his mind well-composed, seated upon a lotus throne, he should recite the root mantra and contemplate it as dissolved into the *nāda*. (2.138)
Having opened his eyes and reflected [upon this], he should then begin the recitation (*japa*) using the formula:
"Oṃ, salutation to the rosary (*akṣamālā*)," according to the expression *samacītām iti*.
By the phrase "seated upon the lotus-throne" (*rājīvāsanasaṃsthita*), [it is indicated that] he is mounted upon the divine vehicle to be described later.
It is observed as follows: for this very reason, he by whom speech—in its forms such as *paśyantī* and so forth—is restrained and made to consist of the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of mantra;

for this very reason, he whose self possesses such a beautiful and unwavering mind; [he who recites] the "root-mantra," whether with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), "properly" (*samyak*), that is, sequentially, as a continuous flow of both syllables and the non-syllabic.

"Having uttered [the sound] and having caused it to move upward, it is called *nāda*. 'There is no one who utters it'—[this refers to] being dissolved in and becoming one with the self that is the eternally arisen radiance (*sphurattā*), as will be explained. Specifically, [it means] being merged.

One should contemplate by means of entering into that [state]. How? Having "opened" the senses—that is, having directed the sense-faculties upward—and having "contemplated" the mantra-deity, meaning having contemplated it correctly as one's own identity, one should begin the recitation while still contemplating; one should repeatedly reflect upon the mantra.
And it is said:
"That cultivation which is repeatedly cultivated toward the supreme reality—this itself is the recitation here;
the sound whose essence is mantra is what is to be recited in this manner."
Thus, in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava* (verse 145). || 138 ||
And in this regard: "The flow of syllables and non-syllables is neither too fast nor too slow. (2.139)

Japa should be performed as closely as one's own vital breath (prāṇa)... where there is a continuous flow and expansion from one syllable to the next; by that [process], the short, long, and other prosodic measures (mātrās) of the seed-syllables (bījākṣara) become the constituent letters of the garland-mantra (mālāmantra).
One should contemplate [the mantra] as being woven together with the garland of the mantra-deity, whose essence is the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*). As it has been said:
"Relying on the mantra like a jewel, one should perform recitation, meditation, and so forth upon the radiant mantra-deity; one should never do so by remaining indifferent."

Thus: "not hurried" means having avoided the rule of swallowed (grasta) sequence; "not delayed" means devoid of excessive connection at intervals. "Equal to the breath" (prāṇasama) means that the breath flowing through the middle is equal [to the recitation] by way of its nature as both emergence and entry. The breath flows through the middle.
The meaning is that one must endure the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the mantra. Therefore,

one should practice by gradually and increasingly applying the *mālā-mantras*— which consist of parts and sub-parts— to the power of the vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*), until the reflective awareness of the entire *mālā-mantra* is attained.

The power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) endures within; for when that is so, there occurs the attainment of the true nature of consciousness, which consists in the swallowing of the kalās. As for the "lump-syllables" (piṇḍākṣara), such as the four-kalā praṇava and others, they are [to be understood] precisely through the contemplation of the pervasion (vyāpti) to be described in the section on the five praṇavas.
One should recite the mantra while pronouncing it with the equilibrium of the middle breath (*madhyamaprāṇa*). And it has been said:
"One should not employ the mantra in the individual soul (*puṃs*), nor in the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), nor in the power (*śakti*). (139)
Having thus explained the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), he defines the distinction of the fruits:
"The one situated in the day (*dinastha*) is for those desiring liberation;
the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*) from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* is the 'day,' and [the deity] abides therein."

Having entered the mantra-essence (mantragarbha) through the downward movement of the breath (apānavṛtti) into the womb-less [state], one should recite while intent on resting at the end of the upward breath (prāṇa); such is the meaning.
That, however, should be known as the withdrawal (saṃhāra),
because it is the withdrawal of everything without exception.
Therefore, it is precisely this [which] bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva. || 2-140 ||
According to the intention of the practitioner, however:
"When the sound (nāda), having reached the void, turns back once more, that should be known as the night, [lasting] until it has returned to the heart-lotus. (2.141)
This creation has been fully described as that which brings about the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

In the void at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), the mantra—which is subordinate to the *nāda*—comes to rest; thus, by virtue of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) attained through abiding at the end of the twelve, one should enter within via the process of the downward breath (*apāna*).

It is called "emission" (*sṛṣṭi*) because it causes nourishment, and because in it there arises the manifestation of all fruits of accomplishment, from the lowest to the highest. Therefore, for the sake of removing obstacles to liberation, the practitioner, by means of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*),

should resort to the end of the *muṇḍa* while remaining within the womb [of the central channel], and then, by relying on the emerging power of the downward breath (*apānaśakti*), proceed as far as the attainment of the heart.

Recitation (japa) should be performed; however, for those who seek both goals, it should be understood by implication that it may be done in either way. Thus, because this mantra effects the withdrawal of impure principles and the emanation of pure principles, its full potency is singular and bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment; yet, due to the difference in the disposition (āśaya) of the practitioner, [the results differ].
It has been taught by distinguishing them individually. || 141 ||
And while acting in this way, O fair-faced one, one's own form as Bhairava should always be meditated upon. (2.142)
His obstacles perish and his recitation becomes fruitful.

For one who contemplates and reflects upon the Self as being the nature of the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava in all conditions, [the obstacles] specifically destroy the attainments of liberation and supernatural powers; thus, "obstacles" (vighnāḥ) are the fetters (pāśāḥ).

And the obstacles perish; therefore, for these [practitioners], the recitation (japa) shall become fruitful through both worldly enjoyment and liberation, according to their respective desires. || 142 ||
Having recited [the mantra], O Goddess of beautiful countenance, one should offer it to Bhairava.
By means of the practice of *pūraka* (inhalation),

for Bhairava residing in the heart, the seeker of liberation— through the practice of *pūraka* in the form of an entry from the *dvādaśānta* (the point twelve finger-breadths above the head) and by virtue of not being intent upon the fruits [of action]— [should say]: "O Blessed One, this many recitations..."
One should announce, "Please accept [this]. || 143 ||
Of what nature is it?
... abiding in the three and endowed with the triad;
O Goddess, it bestows the attainment of the threefold perfection.

He who abides in the three states consisting of emergence, entry, and both [emergence and entry] is "one who abides in the three" (*tristha*); likewise, he is endowed with and joined to the triad consisting of speech, mind, and vital breath;
and there is the accomplishment for practitioners which is threefold in form due to the distinction between superior, middling, and inferior. Furthermore—

Success for one seeking liberation is of a different nature, consisting of liberation itself; that which bestows this [success] by means of the arguments already stated and those yet to be stated should be explained by connecting it with the terms "the triple success" (*trisiddhi*) and "success" (*siddhi*).
Moreover—.................. this is declared along with its secret [teaching]. (2.144)
According to the method to be explained in the *Yojanikā* and the section on the five *praṇavas*,

for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) and those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), [the breath] is drawn upward as far as the *dvādaśānta* and brought down from above as far as the heart; this, along with its secret [teachings], is known only by a few.
The meaning is that it is to be attained by means of the expanded middle path. || 144 ||
To state the specific distinction for the practitioner according to the particular nature of the accomplishment, he says:

"In rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the recitation is mental; in rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it is said to be whispered (*upāṃśu*); and in rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), it is with sound. [The practitioner should face] east, north, or south. (2.145)
He explains this as follows: "That which the self does not hear is declared to be mental (mānasa); that which is heard by the self is known as the whispered (upāṃśu) recitation. (2-146)

O Goddess, that which others hear is called *saśabda* (with sound). The mental [utterance] occurs in the *madhyamā* speech, while the *upāṃśu* and *saśabda* occur in the *vaikharī*, which possesses both subtle and gross effort.
The fact that this triad is the cause of enjoyment is stated elsewhere as well:

"The middling [recitation] is called that of enjoyment and liberation; the whispered [recitation] bestows supernatural powers (siddhi); the vocal [recitation] conquers spirits and poisons; and the audible [recitation] is for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
Thus it is said.

By speaking thus, he indicates that the recitation (*japa*) should be performed through both the *paśyantī* and *parā* levels of speech for one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) as well as for one who is fully liberated (*mukta*). And it has been said:
"The higher [recitation] is to be known as being for one liberated while living; for one who is fully liberated, it is that which seals all distinctions."
Thus [ends the verse]. 146.
He demonstrates the rosary useful for recitation:
"The rosary together with the central bead consists of exactly one hundred and eight [beads]. (2.147)
[The rosary] may be made of rudrākṣa, conch, lotus seeds, putrajīvaka, or pearls; likewise, it may be made of crystal, precious gems, gold, or coral. (2.148)
And these—O Goddess of gods, these ten rosaries are proclaimed for householders;
by eight [rosaries] plus one hundred as the maximum. By the word "only" (eva), [any] higher number is excluded.
There is an exclusion, because the numbers twenty-seven and fifty-four also exist.
In due order— having meditated upon the Sūtra, then the Supreme Śakti, then the portions of the path, and then the jewels (maṇis)— 2:149.

The path of Śiva is the locus of manifestation; therefore, one should meditate upon its attributes. One should perform [the rite] with twenty-seven [units], or with twice that number, or even four times that number.

The wise man should not transgress that single principle of Śiva-tattva, which consists of all things united together and resides in the mouth [of the Guru], for it is the cause of both creation and dissolution. (2.151)
And here, regarding the nine, eighteen, or thirty-six principles enumerated in the *Mṛtyuñjaya* and other texts during the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*),
their number is exactly such because they are divided into three categories— gross, subtle, and supreme— which consist of Paraśakti and Śiva.
Since it exists, there is pervasion (vyāpti) therein. || 151 ||

Regarding those who have reached the final goal, he says: "For heroes who delight in the posture of the hero (vīrasthāna), O fair-complexioned one, the great conch-shell and the rosary (akṣasūtra) bestow the fruit of all desires. (2.152)
The place of heroes is the cremation ground and so forth; the great conch is human bone; and heroes are those who are unshakable.
But this— [which causes] supreme distress— must not be done by a householder;
for it is thus:
Therefore, that crystal rosary should be recited over by the most excellent practitioners.
By the best of practitioners who are householders. || 153 ||
For she indeed accomplishes various desires— whether inferior, middling, or superior—
consisting of the attainment of diverse siddhis, movement through the air, the vidyās, the tattvas, and so forth; but for one who seeks liberation, [she brings about that end].
The tenfold rosary has already been described.
He concludes:
"In this way, the all-pervading Bhairava, who resides within the lotus of the heart, is to be worshipped. (2.154)
Having made [the sacrifice] both external and internal, one should thereafter begin the worship.

That sacrifice which exists together with both the external and the internal—namely, the attainment of the state of Bhairava through the body and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka)—is indeed one and the same; it is not something distinct in form within the hands, the body, or internally.

This is because the identity with Bhairava alone is what is to be attained and will be taught. Having performed the sacrifice—which, through the unity of the internal and external, is withdrawn into the Bhairava of Consciousness and consists of the offering of the entire universe—and having also directed one's intention toward the external sacrifice, which takes the form of a reflection of the heart-sacrifice; and furthermore...

The meaning of "having made [everything] external and internal" is as follows: "Afterwards"—that is, after the recitation—one offers the elements, the senses, the objects, and so forth, together with the mind, into the fire that is the abode of the Great Void; that is the *homa*, and consciousness is the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*). (149)

Thus, according to the method taught in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*, having performed the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) consisting of the offering of all phenomenal existence preceded by the recollection of the mantra at the *dvādaśānta*, one should begin the external worship, which is the form of a reflection of the internal sacrifice; this is the meaning. || 154 ||

By means of the vision of the offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇadṛṣṭi), one regards the agent, instrument, source, locus, recipient, object, and performer— namely, the self, the mantra, the arghya vessel, the maṇḍala, Bhairava, flowers, and other ritual substances— as being offered to the Absolute.

Through the perfection of the practice of external worship, which consists in the realization of supreme non-duality, the identity of all causal factors with the Consciousness-Bhairava (cid-bhairava) is made manifest in all worldly transactions;
thus, this is the introduction to the true nature of the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga).

Immediately following the internal sacrifice consisting of the purification of the agent and the instruments, he first states the rule for the arghya vessel for the sake of the purificatory rites such as *apādana*, which bestow purification upon the ritual materials and other elements: [The text continues with the specific ritual procedure.]
In that regard, the vessel for the arghya offering should first of all be made of gold or likewise of silver.
Having taken a vessel made of conch, pearl-oyster, mother-of-pearl, copper, or even clay, or one derived from a lotus leaf or palāśa leaf, and having washed it with water; || 2-156 ||
O Goddess of Gods, having smeared [the vessel] with agallochum and sandalwood consecrated by the recitation of the mantra,
and having fumigated it with pure incense, one should then fill it with water.
With water purified by a cloth and rendered pure...

the *argha* vessel is the locus of protection. Therein, when the state of Bhairavī has arisen through the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the word "first" refers to the purpose of consecrating the flowers and other materials. [The vessel] should be made of gold or similar materials as far as possible for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

The *śambūka* is a particular marine creature; the *palāśa* is the sacrificial tree. *Ākṣālana* is the removal of the splinters of differentiation; *āpūraṇa* is the state of being composed of the entirety of the universe.
From that—
One should strike [it] while reciting the Astra mantra;
having performed the veiling with the Varma [mantra],
even that which was not mentioned here— the nourishing [of the deity]— should be performed with this same mantra using the Amṛta-mudrā.
Immediately thereafter—one should install the sacrifice in that very place. (2.158)
The term *ijyate* refers to the collection of sacrificial mantras; by this very [term], worship (*pūjana*) is also indicated here. || 158 ||
How—
by means of the previously stated procedure...
preceded by the seat and other elements mentioned in the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).

The meaning is: by means of the method of the placement (nyāsa) of the eleven mantras, which consist of the totality of forms of throbbing splendor, as well as the partless (niṣkala) [mantra] and its limbs (aṅga).
From that [state] as well...
[he] should briefly sprinkle with that [water] the collection of materials intended for the sacrifice.
"Having looked [at it] by means of the support of the revolution (parāvṛtti)"—this is the ellipsis. "Sprinkling" (prokṣaṇa) here refers to the production of the state of being composed of light.
Then, having worshipped Cidbhairava on the head with flowers and other offerings—
...then one should commence the sacrifice. || 2-159 ||

Here he prepares the preliminary stage: "Then, first of all, having projected the Power (śakti), which is of the form of space, brilliantly blazing, all-pervasive, subtle, and omnipresent as the support of Śiva. (2.160)
She who is illuminated by the syllable *Oṃ*, concluding with the salutation (*namaskāra*),

whose support and refuge is Śiva, whose nature is the first unfolding (*prathamonmeṣa*), who serves as the foundation for all seats and so forth to be arranged, and who has the form of space because her essence is pure consciousness alone.
She blazes brightly with the radiance of the nature of knowledge free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhijñatva*); she pervades all things because she has internalized the entire universe;

she is subtle because she cannot be perceived by anyone; and she is omnipresent as a single deity, for she abides having attained Śiva, who is both her support and seat (*ādhāra-āsana*) and her supported object (*ādheya*).

One should contemplate the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvarī śakti*), which is the substratum manifesting the universal play (*viśvakrīḍā*) and other phenomena; this power, being of the nature of the support, is to be energized by the syllable *Oṃ*—which, through the pervasion already stated and to be stated hereafter, takes the form of the Supreme Bhairava—in order to realize that everything to be conceptualized is identical with Śiva because it arises from that [power]. *Oṃ*.
The meaning is that one should perform the placement (nyāsa) using the formula "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti" and then commence the subsequent rite;
furthermore, this placement of Śakti (śaktinyāsa) should be remembered even in previous contexts such as the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). || 160 ||
And having likewise placed Ananta, as well as Dharma and Jñāna. || 2-161 ||
Likewise, dispassion and sovereignty [arise] in the order beginning with the southeast;
and likewise, non-dharma, ignorance, non-dispassion, and non-sovereignty [arise] in the same sequence. (2-162)
O Goddess, [one should fashion] the joining-pins, the lower covering, and the upper part;
the lotus with its filaments, O Goddess, as well as the pericarp and the petals.
The three mandalas, the deities, and also Śakti ending with Śiva;
the form, the web of Brahma’s kalās, the nine principles, and the three principles.
The eight Bhairavas, the Vidyā-aṅga Lōcana, as well as the Kṣurikā, the three Śaktis, the Supreme Lord accompanied by the six Aṅgas—[these are the deities]. (2.165)
"O Goddess, having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should constantly contemplate [the deity] according to the prescribed rule.

'According to the prescribed rule' means by means of the methods previously mentioned, such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Whatever has not been stated here should be understood from what precedes, and whatever was not stated previously [should be understood from what follows]."

Therefore, this should be understood according to the distinction of qualification (*adhikāra*), because the internal and external sacrifices alternate in the form of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*); and all of this has been previously determined.
Having performed [the sacrifice] according to the rule with a joyful inner self—2.166.
One should perform the welcoming, the offering of water for the feet, and likewise the presentation of the guest-offering;
then, while recollecting the root mantra, one should carry out the confinement with a harsh [mantra]. (2.167)
An extensive worship should be performed with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth;
thereafter, one should display the mudrās three times during the ritual actions of the three periods of the day. (2.168)
Then, O fair-faced one, the enclosure should be established on the outside;
one should arrange it ending with the directions of Īśa (northeast), Pūrva (east), Yāmya (south), Saumya (north), and Varuṇa (west).

O Goddess, the pentad of faces, endowed with the qualities of their respective meditations, [is located] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, as well as in the directions of the south and east. (2-170)
The northern limit should be established, and likewise the five limbs;
the eye, indeed, is situated in the pericarp in the eastern direction.

This too has already been explained previously. "With a delighted inner self" means being permeated by the totality of Bhairava. Here, the previous placement (*nyāsa*) of the venerable Aghoreśvarī should be remembered. Regarding the phrase "from the eastern direction to the end of the north," this refers to the end of the north from the eastern direction.
One should fashion the weapon for the four directions; this is how it should be applied. As was stated previously:
"And one should place that in the four directions—Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu," and so forth. || 171 ||
He states the rule that pervades all cases:
"With one's own mantra, however, one who is composed should offer arghya and pādya to all"—
the word "should give" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
He clarifies the state of being composed:
"The practitioner should never mix the flowers of the mantras. (2-172)
One should not arrange the mantras behind one's back;
they must be given in the proper sequence, and one should never transgress the mantras under any circumstances. (2.173)
Where there is a confusion of mantras, one should not offer such flowers;
the meaning is that one should not worship with one mantra using the deity of another. When this is done, the practitioner becomes a vessel for supreme accomplishment—this is the meaning. || 173 ||
And thus—
one should simultaneously visualize [the deities] as conjoined with their respective mudrās and mantras.
In meditation, worship, and so forth, one should visualize the deities as conjoined with their respective mudrās and mantras.
For those for whom no specific mudrā has been mentioned,
one should recall the forthcoming rule: "In cases where [mudrās] have not been stated, one should display the skull-cup and the khaṭvāṅga staff" (14.20).
It has been stated that worship should be performed on a very extensive scale; however, what should one who lacks the necessary wealth do?
To this he says:
"One should always perform at least the offering of water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and incense (dhūpa). (2.174)
This procedure has been proclaimed for all mantras alike:

one should always worship [the deity], avoiding stinginess regarding wealth; however, in the event of a total lack of wealth, the meaning is that one may worship even with a conch-shell and so forth as prescribed, or even with the mind alone. || 174 ||

Having thus incidentally described worship—which consists of offerings such as water for the feet, water for the guest, and flowers, and which is impossible for one who lacks wealth—he returns to the subject at hand:
"One should fully visualize the eight Bhairavas and the world-protectors together with their weapons. (2.175)
Then,

outside [the mandala], one should arrange the layout of the cremation grounds (śmaśāna), beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namas," according to the prescribed rule, from the east up to the northeast.
And first indeed [he saw] Āmardaka, the powerful lord of the cremation ground,
surrounded by cremation grounds with headless trunks and terrifying impaled corpses.
With blazing funeral pyres and the most terrifying howls of jackals,
there is Agnikam in the southern quarter and likewise Kālākhya in the west.
Likewise, Ekapāda is in the north, Tripurāntaka in the southeast,
Agnijihva in the southwest, and Karālin in the northwest.
In the northeast, Bhīmavaktra is proclaimed as the lord of the cremation ground;
these [lords] reside in Śrīkāmarūpa, Ujjayinī, Kāśmīra, Kāñcī, Karavīra, Devīkoṭṭa, Uḍḍayāna, and Hiraṇya.

"Of the city-dwellers"—by this traditional teaching (āmnāya), the purpose of worshipping these foundational seats (pīṭhas) and so forth is already established. Here, the phrase "with the cremation grounds and the headless trunks," and so on, applies universally to all cremation grounds.
These instrumental case endings (tṛtīyā) are used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe). || 179 ||
And one should satisfy these with fish, meat, and the like, as well as with various kinds of fermented liquors.

One should cause incense, flowers, and likewise incense-smoke to be offered to all. The cremation grounds (śmaśānas) are not mentioned in the Hṛdayāgama, lest there be withering of the body; thus, because of their fierce nature, there is first satiation (tarpaṇa) by means of fish and so forth, followed by worship. These [practices] pertain specifically to ascetics (yatis). And here:
In one alternative, the Lokapālas and the weapons constitute separate enclosures, so that there is worship with five enclosures. || 180 ||
And here:
"Then, having performed prostration and having recited the mantra with well-cultivated concentration... (2.181)
Having offered [the oblation] according to the ritual procedure by means of the practice of exhaling (recaka),
and having performed prostrations with the sound "huḍḍuṅkāra," one should then depart.
Having approached the vicinity of the fire-pit with an *argha* vessel in hand and well-concentrated,
one should recite the mantra— the root mantra together with its limbs— according to the rule by means of the *recaka* breath;
that is, having first ascended to the *dvādaśānta*, rested there, and descended from it, one should mutter the mantra through the tip of the nose.
One should offer it with the formula: "O Blessed One, accept this flower of my speech.
The *huḍuṅkāra*—also known by the synonym *mukhavādya* (mouth-instrument)—is a sound consisting of the awareness (*āmarśa*) of the resonance (*nāda*) arising from the power of devotion. || 182 ||
He states the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
"One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit, endowed with the proper characteristics, with water empowered by the weapon-mantra. (2.183)
Having enveloped this with the Kavaca mantra, one should draw it with a blade of Darbha grass used for weapons;
then, O beautiful lady, having lifted it up, one should sprinkle it with the Astra mantra.
He should perform filling and leveling; he should likewise have the sprinkling, pounding, and plastering carried out by him. (2.185)
One should perform both sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and drying (*śoṣaṇa*) using the *astra-mantra* alone.
[The image] is endowed with the proper characteristics (*lakṣaṇopeta*), its mental nature being determined by the scriptures on installation (*pratiṣṭhā-śāstra*) and other sources.
Following the observation by the vision of another (the Guru), sprinkling is performed for the sake of purification, as is the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*).

The phrase "for the sake of protection" is to be understood as applying everywhere; by means of that very [protection], the striking is included because of the specific nature of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). And these thirteen [rites], beginning with the sprinkling and ending with the drying (*śoṣaṇa*), [should be performed] either at the occasion of the completion of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or even when it has already been completed.

These [rites] should be performed through meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) for the sake of attaining the form of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the power of action (kriyā-śakti). One should delineate and excavate. "Extraction" (uddharaṇa) means the removal of impure earth; "sweeping" (saṃmārjana) means the clearing away of dust.
Immediately thereafter—
The worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth [is performed] by means of the formula:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Kuṇḍa, whose self is the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Now, herein [one should consider] the fitness for the descent of Vāgīśvarī.

To explain the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), the vajrification (*vajrīkaraṇa*), and the grasping (*gṛhīkaraṇa*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), he says: "And the consecration is performed with the *asinā* [mantra]. (2-186)
The vajrīkaraṇa [is performed] with the Astra-mantra;
he explains that very point:
"There are three lines, east-west."
And that which faces both south and north is proclaimed as this *vajra*. (2.187)

The word "three" [in the verse] results from a change in gender; this task is to be performed by means of the act of scratching. Alternatively, having placed a single blade of *darbha* grass oriented north-south in the middle of three *darbha* blades oriented east-west, one should produce the stability of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the form of a thunderbolt (*vajra*). || 187 ||
Furthermore:

"O Goddess, for the purpose of establishing a house, that fire-pit should be covered both inside and out with darbha grass blades spread with their tips pointing eastward, using nothing but the sword. (2.188)
In order to bring about a home free from obstacles. || 188 ||
Now, he describes the seat for Vāgīśī, the Mahattaraka:
"On the southern side of the *kuṇḍa*, one should prepare a seat of dried cow-dung, a *viṣṭara* of *darbha* grass, and a flower, using the *praṇava* [syllable Om]. (2-189)

Inside the sacrificial pit, to the south, upon a seat of cow-dung, one should place a mat of darbha grass and flowers upon it, and offer them with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Brahmā. || 189 ||

Regarding this, he speaks of something even greater: "One should establish Brahmā by means of the vocative case alone, joined with one's own name-word, ending in 'namaḥ', and through meditation on oneself; then one should worship him. (2-190)
With flowers and the like, as well as with excellent incense and so forth, one should proceed according to the fixed sequence.
And here, the ritual application is: "Oṃ Brahman, be present; salutations to you. || 190 ||
Regarding this, he speaks for the sake of obtaining the center of the house:
"One should [draw] a crossroads in the middle of the sacrificial pit with two blades of darbha grass, using the syllable Om. (2.191)
With the two [mantras] for the eastern and northern tips, one should place a seat upon it;
then, with the Heart mantra itself, one should worship a flower upon that.

And having invoked Vāgīśī with the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the heart-mantra (*naiṣkala*)—she who belongs to Vāgīśa is the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) Vāgīśī—the application everywhere is as follows: [the name] followed by the vocative case for invocation, and then "namaste" (salutations to you). || 192 ||
He describes the worship preceded by meditation for her:
"She who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with beautiful eyes like those of a rutting elephant. (2.193)
Having meditated upon the Goddess as being complete with all the primary marks and adorned with all the secondary limbs, one should thus establish her in the center of the sacrificial pit.

Like [a woman] during her fertile period, one should worship her as she lies supine with her head toward the northeast, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, while recollecting the mantra of Bhava. (2.195)

One should place—that is, bind—the radiant power of speech (*vāk-śakti*) within the center of the *kuṇḍa*, which is of the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). It should be placed face upwards, having the form of an expansion that stretches toward the upper abode;
for this very reason, its eye is beautiful, as its light shines forth.

Her dark-blue hue, like that of a blue lotus, is relative to her illusory form (*māyīya-rūpa*). Her "season" is the state of being ready to give birth to Fire and the other elements, whose nature is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). She is established in the northeast, eternally connected to the Lord Īśāna, the Sovereign Lord of Freedom (*svātantryabhaṭṭāraka*), by means of the head, which is the Supreme Form (*parārūpa*).
And [he should meditate on] Niṣṭhaśiras. What is he doing? By means of this or that form, such as the entire Brahmabhaṅgī and so forth, he becomes the partless (niṣkala) Lord;
recollecting His mantra, he becomes permeated by His very existence. || 195 ||
Furthermore:
Then the knower of mantras should display the mudrā for the sake of bringing [the deity] into proximity—
the mudrā known as the Yoni.
Then, taking the vessel of fire, one should sprinkle the auspicious water with the Astra-mantra.
Having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship it with the Praṇava alone,
according to the prescribed rule, [using wood] produced from a forest or similar source, extending from the worlds up to the sacrificial fire.
The word "fire" (agni), situated in the subsequent [verse], is to be connected here as well, like the eye of a crow. 197.
Then—having meditated upon the fire as being luminous (śukravat), one should, by means of the *praṇava*, conceive of its consciousness;
"of this" is the ellipsis. Having caused the fire to enter through the path of the nose, one should effect its unification with one's own consciousness.
"Having led [the breath] upward, one should exhale," so say the teachers.
Even from that,
one should worship with the six limbs alone, for immortality is indeed established through the *dhruva*.

The meaning is that one should perform his worship in the form of the attainment of supreme nectar by means of the *dhruva* mantra, which is the *paracaitanya* mantra, specifically through the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) rite of the venerable *niṣkala*. || 198 ||
Then, having meditated upon oneself as Bhairava and having meditated upon the fire as being like a seed-syllable,
one should cause it to descend by circling it three times outside the sacrificial pit with the *dhruva* mantra. (2-199)
Having cast [the seed] into the womb like a seed with the Bhairava-water of Śiva, the wise one, having recited the Astra-mantra and sprinkled [it], should cover the womb. (2-200)

Having rotated it three times with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the *dhruva-mantra*— that is, having rotated the vessel held in the form of a womb-casket three times by way of the left and right [circumambulations] for the purpose of agitating the womb— one should lower it into the womb.

One should cause [the deity] to arrive by means of the Bhairava mantra, specifically the Śrīniṣkala; and by the Dhruva-mantra, that is, the Praṇava. One should construct the enclosure (akṣavāṭa) with Darbha grass placed upon the high girdle, with the tips pointing eastward and northward, situated at the dwelling of the fire-god. Thus, in the Śrīmantrarāja, it is said: "with [grass] facing upwards."

This should be disregarded as a mere fabrication. [The claim that] the Buddha possesses only the unique absorption (*samāveśa*) of Śiva, while the self possesses causal agency (*hetukartṛtva*) but Śiva possesses primary agency (*mukhyakartṛtva*), and so forth, is incorrect;
for only one who has become Śiva (*śivībhūta*) is authorized in the sacrifice to Śiva (*śivayāga*). What room, then, is there here for any suspicion of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*)?
Or how can there be the power of liberation while in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*)? [The scripture states: "Mantras are indeed the instruments for accomplishing the task of the bound soul;
the teacher is declared to be the instrument, since he is remembered as being of the nature of Śiva. (3.160)
And what is the connection with that which will be stated by the words "ityādi" and so forth? Let this matter rest for now.

Here, the secret meaning—which has remained unopened until today and has come down through the oral lineage of our gurus—is being revealed: the Supreme Speech (parāvāk), belonging to Maheśa, gave birth to the universe through its own non-manifestation.

This [Goddess], whose inner abode is pure and whose body is expanded by the pervasive power of the Jyeṣṭhā-kalā which has seized the manifestation of the transformations of the universe, makes manifest through her fierce gaze that Child who is appropriate for her— that Child who is the essence of non-duality with Śiva.
Therefore, satiated by the tasting of the nectar-essence of fullness,

and having seized everything from fire onwards by his own power through the immersion into Śiva— the speech that is auspicious due to its longing for the flavor of Śiva— the preeminent Guru [attains this].
He brings forth this world, which consists of the radiance of his own self, whose singular essence is Śiva.
Thus [ends the section]. || 200 ||
Furthermore:
"Then one should establish the enclosure for the eyes;
with the weapon-mantra alone, one should arrange it in the four directions using *darbha* grass. (2.201)
For the protection of the Goddess, one should place a fence of *akṣa* plants, serving as a curtain, using *darbha* grasses pointing upwards for the sake of guarding it. || 201 ||
Then, for the pregnant queen,
he should tie a bracelet made of *darbha* grass on her right hand using the Astra-mantra seven times, while recollecting the Astra-mantra. (2.202)

"For the protection of the one containing fire..."—here the modified mantra is: "Oṃ, I bind the bracelet; obeisance. In this manner, modified mantras (ūhamantra) must be employed everywhere according to the suitability of the ritual action. [The bracelet is placed] on the right hand for the sake of the embryo.
The binding of the bracelet. || 202 ||

Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with these thirteen purificatory rites ending with drying— namely, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), scratching (*ullekhana*), lifting up (*uddharaṇa*), sprinkling again (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth— and having worshipped it,
one performs the three self-purifications consisting of the consecration with the *astra* mantra, the transformation into a vajra (*vajrīkaraṇa*), and the covering of the pit.
Having performed the rites for the sake of obtaining a house, having arranged the seat, invocation, and worship for Brahmā,
and having constructed a crossroads for the attainment of the central part of the house,
[one should perform] the invocation of Vāgīśī, her seating, worship, meditation on Śukra, and the infusion of consciousness (*caitanya*). (Amṛtī-)

Having performed the nine purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) consisting of meditation on the specific instruments, three circumambulations, and casting [the seed] into the womb; and having further performed the four purificatory rites of Vāgīśī consisting of sprinkling, covering the womb, constructing the enclosure for the dice, and binding the bracelets;

In order to produce a mantra-body capable of accomplishing the rites beginning with initiation for the fire-god, he describes the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*) starting with conception (*garbhādhāna*) according to the sequence of the mouth and limbs:
"Therefore, conception (*garbhādhāna*) shall take place..."
Furthermore, one should perform worship with three oblations using the Heart-mantra.
Having offered three oblations with the heart-mantra, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) is accomplished.

Having first uttered the syllable *la*, which is the seed-syllable of the western face, preceded by the *praṇava*, and having recited "I perform the rite of conception, svāhā" three times, one should [offer] with the Niṣkala heart-mantra: "May the rite of conception be perfected."

One should offer oblations three times with the mantra "svāhā"; this should be understood accordingly for what follows hereafter. In this context, the intermediate passage—"worship, however, is performed with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]"—is to be applied first; thus, at the beginning, there are three oblations with the limb-mantra (*aṅgamantra*), because such a sequence exists throughout the subsequent sections as well. || 203 ||
He states the *puṃsavana* rite:
"One should cause a drop of water to fall here with the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. (2.204)
Then, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the *śikhā* [mantra];
likewise, one should offer three oblations with the *uttara* [mantra] and three oblations with the *śikhā*.
Indeed, it is merely the imagination of a man that [the child] is born from a woman's womb;

rather, one should cast the *jīva*—in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city)—into the deposited embryo with the ritual application ending in "Become a man, obeisance! (*puṃsān bhava namaḥ*), by means of the *śikhā* [mantra] for the sake of perfection.
"By the following [vowel]" means by the letter *va*. Masculinity is increase, which is the capacity for action; femininity is decrease. || 205 ||
Then,
with the tip of a darbha blade held in his right hand, he should part the hairline.
One should fashion the neck, the shoulders, the hips, the arms, and the shanks;
having thus conceived the various limbs, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) should take place.

In this context, the "parting line" (sīmanta) is merely the division between the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) and the gross body; the mantra of the Aghora face is the southern face, and the "limbs" (*pratyaṅga*) are the hands, chest, feet, fingers, and so forth.
And here—worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and with three oblations offered from the head;
one should designate three portions in the fire for the east, the middle, and the west. (2.208)

The regions of the face, heart, and feet are [purified] by the *homa*, and that consists of the three principles (*tritattvaka*). "Worship" (*pūjā*) is to be performed; "with the head" (*śirasā*) functions like the "crow's eye" (applying to both parts of the sentence). From the *homa* consisting of three oblations—this constitutes a single syntactical unit. And these three parts consist of the nature of the three principles known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Nara. By means of the mouth...
The head and the secret part [the genitals] are projected from the two feet; this indeed is the "breaking of the staff" (daṇḍabhaṅgi) in this context.
Regarding what was stated as "the minor limbs," in order to analyze them and to exclude the door-panels and faces and so forth, he first describes the arrangement of the door-panels (*kavāṭanyāsa*):
Having offered the five heads with the upward-facing [mouth], three by three.

The word "should fashion" (*kalpayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The door-panels are the heads [of the letters], by means of the letter *kṣa* facing upwards. And here, the *kalās* beginning with Sutāriṇī are to be connected as before. || 209 ||
Now, having restated this, he describes the conceptualization of the faces by means of the arts of speech:
"Having conceived the five faces—namely the central, eastern, southern, northern, and the western—one [should worship] with oblations three times through the eastern face. (2.210)
"In the same way, there is the expiation for the faces by means of three oblations.
Since it was stated previously that "the fifth face is indeed [associated] with the syllable *kṣa*" (1.49), one should first [offer] to the middle and upper faces with the syllable *kṣa*.

Having first fashioned [the deity] through the connection with the *śāntyatītā* [kalā], one should subsequently fashion the four faces with the syllable *ya* at the eastern face, by means of the connection with the *śānti* and other *kalās*, using three oblations for each;
since it was stated [in the passage] beginning with "in the middle," the placement of the central face comes first. And this—
This should be connected throughout. || 210 ||
Furthermore:
having mentally assigned an eye to each eye, one should likewise assign a triad [of limbs] to each of the faces. (2.211)
By means of exactly three oblations...
with the eye [mantra], that is, with the mantra of the All-Eye (sakalanetra). || 211 ||

And this—[all] should be performed with sesame seeds. "All" refers to the entire collection of rites for the consecration of the fire; as for the clarified butter (*ājya*), it is for the satiation of the Śiva-fire once it has been fully established.
And its perfection consists precisely in this form of Bhairava.
Then [he perceives] the collection of kalās, namely five and then four.

The placement of the artistic skill of her face and so forth, which is distinct from other tantras, is taught here specifically within the context of the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) rite. || 212 ||
Having thus described the ritual assignment of the limbs (*pratyaṅganyāsa*) by means of the parts (*kalā*) of Īśāna and Puruṣa, he speaks [next] by means of the parts of Aghora:

"Likewise, the eight limbs, as well as the three, ten, and eight, should be assigned in sequence with the remaining faces; having thus fashioned the forms of the parts, one then becomes [the deity]. (2-213)

The limbs (*aṅga*) are those previously mentioned, such as "the heart, the neck," and so forth (Svacchanda Tantra 1.50). "In this way" means for each individual limb; [this is done] by three oblations through the contemplative connection (*anusandhi*) with their respective *kalās*. The term "one whose *kalās* are his forms" (*mūrti*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. || 213 ||
Then, right here—thereafter, one should assign the limbs (*aṅga*) beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*) in due order.
Since the eye has already been mentioned, one should likewise assign all the limbs along with their respective mantras. Thus...
That which was stated as "having conceived the individual limbs," that very point has been analyzed in detail by the preceding six verses beginning with "First [the earth]," and so forth.
Having performed all this in this manner— offering three oblations with the right hand...
[one should offer] with the mantra ending in "I perform the parting of the hair (śīmantonnayana) for the southern face."
Then, with the head [of the mantra], one should offer three oblations. || 2-214 ||

The word *ca* ("and") implies by this very fact that one should perform worship at the beginning; thus it suggests the completion of the introductory context. As for what was previously stated, "Worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and with three oblations from the head" (2.208), that was intended for the purpose of conceiving the three principles (*tritattva*) through the conceptualization of three parts. || 214 ||
He concludes:
"For the *sīmāntonnayana* is thus...
[of] Agni whose parts are thus divided."
...then the birth rite (jātakarma) is prescribed; one should fan the fire with the Astra-mantra and worship it with the Astra-mantra alone. || 2-215 ||

Having offered three oblations with the preceding [mantra] and three oblations with the Astra-mantra itself, the birth rite (jātakarma) is thus accomplished by means of these two mantras alone. (2.216)
Fanning is the act of bringing about the manifestation [of the seed-syllable], by means of the preceding letter "ya. || 216 ||

Having thus performed the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), parting the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and birth (*jātakarma*), one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) for the immediate purification of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
For although the state of Śiva has been attained, the fire is the body [of the ritual], and therefore [this is done] for the sake of the successful completion of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other rites.
Therefore, the assumption of a body by the conscious self— taking the form of birth and being the first sprout of all impurity— is precisely that which must be purified.
After the fire has been produced,
one should subsequently open its mouths with three oblations through the mouth itself.
"Opening" (udghāṭana) means expansion (vikāsa).
As follows:
"The faces are to be purified with the sword by means of the application of three oblations. (2.217)
Having touched each face with its own mantra, one should offer oblations three times while reciting the Astra-mantra at the end of the modification "I purify. || 217 ||
Likewise:
"The pouring [of the oblation] into the mouths; in each mouth, three by three.
Pouring into the mouths means radiance. "Three by three" means one should offer the oblations.
The remainder.

To describe the ritual placement (nyāsa) of deities in the directions for the sake of protecting the fire, he says: "One should sprinkle the sides of the sacrificial pit with the water of Śiva, consecrated by the Weapon-mantra. (2.218)
Having spread out *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, arranged from south to north;
likewise, [he should place] the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*) with their tips pointing northward in the eastern and western directions.

The enclosing sticks (paridhis) are branches one cubit in length. A seat made of Darbha grass with a knot in the middle is called a *viṣṭara*. In this manner, the inner Darbha grass, the enclosing sticks, and the *viṣṭara* are arranged in successive order.
All of them should be deposited there with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
In that regard—
Having established Brahmā on the eastern seat, Rudra on the south, and Viṣṇu on the western seat... || 2.220 ||
Then, O Goddess, one should first meditate upon Sadāśiva in the north, marked by his own name as a word; one should place the syllable *dhruvam* at the beginning and the word *namaḥ* at the end.
They are to be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; one should contemplate their true nature within them.
This is clear.
Furthermore, internally—
One should worship the Lokeshas above the girdle with the Praṇava.
And thus:
"Those deities beginning with Brahmā who were worshipped for the protection of the newborn infant—thereafter, having removed the bracelet situated on the right hand... (2.223)
Having taken up a flower, the deity should assign a name [to the child].

Because the fetus has been born and because protection from the internal [obstacles] has been established, the duty regarding the protection of the fetus is concluded; thus, there is the release of the bracelet. By the deity, that is, by the root mantra together with the *praṇava*.
The naming [of the fire] is performed with the formula: "Obeisance to Śivāgni, become [manifest]. || 223 ||
Then, [one should perform] the ritual service with the armor-mantra (kavaca), using perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth. || 2.224 ||
One should perform the ritual service—that is, worship—with the *naiṣkala* armor-mantra ending with "śivāgnaye namaḥ.
Herein:
one should offer three oblations with the upward-facing [face] and again three with the armor-mantra.
One should perform these as before with the *ūha-mantra*.

Thus, there are eight intermediate consecrations (*avāntara-saṃskāra*): the purification of birth-defilement (*sūtaka-śuddhi*), the opening of the mouth (*vaktrodghāṭana*), the purification of the mouth (*vaktra-śuddhi*), the sprinkling of the mouth (*vaktrābhighāra*), the placement of the seat and other items (*viṣṭarādi-nyāsa*), the installation of the deities (*devatā-sthāpana*), their worship (*tad-arcanā*), and the release of the bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa-mokṣaṇa*).
Having performed this, the final sacrament known as the naming ceremony was completed.
Then, having produced a fire marked with the name of Śiva, [he addressed] the gods thereafter.
