One should dismiss Sāvitrī to her own place with the *praṇava*,
having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, and with three sets of three oblations (*homa*).

The word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and) and is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). Therefore, having worshipped the gods beginning with Brahmā and Sarasvatī by reciting their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), and having gratified each one with three oblations, one should dismiss them after saying, "May you be forgiven. || 226 ||
Then,
with the very same sacred fuel, sacrificial wood measuring one cubit in length and numbering twenty-four, should be offered into the fire for the propitiation of Śiva’s fire.
By means of the partless radiance; the fuel-sticks are unsplit, straight, and possessed of their bark. || 227 ||

Having thus described the consecrations with sesame seeds, he speaks now for the purpose of performing the consecrations involving clarified butter (*ājya*), specifically for the preparation of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles used for pouring the butter:
"Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* over the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water while reciting the Astra-mantra."
Having enveloped these two with the Kavaca mantra, one should cause them to be whirled three times over the Śiva-fire.
One should wipe them with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, then touch them with the tip of a blade of Darbha grass;
having again whirled them over the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water.
Having touched it with the middle of a *darbha* blade and having rotated it again over the fire to heat it,
one should sprinkle it with auspicious water and touch it with the root of a *darbha* blade.
Then, one should place the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles face down upon the *darbha* grass; they should always be worshipped by the wise to the south of the fire.
Wiping is indeed sprinkling, while heating is for the purpose of removing the state of being wood and so forth. As it has been said: "One should heat [the two] three times in the fire;
thereby, once they have arisen and been heated, they turn away from the state of being wood."
Thus [it is said].

In this process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), by touching the tip, middle, and root of the *darbha* grass with its tip, middle, and root, and by rotating [the vessel] three times, these two [the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles] come to consist of the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*).
The phrase "by means of the *sruc* and *sruva*" means "of the *sruc* and *sruva*. This occurs after the twelve purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

"The two to be worshipped are face-down" is said with the intention that they are oriented toward emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). "To the south of Agni, on the left of the Hotṛ"—by this simultaneous connection of these two through illumination (*dīpti*) and nourishment (*āpyāyana*), there arises the state of being composed of both Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomamayatva*). || 231 ||

Then one should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), beginning with its placement upon the fire. "Placement" (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is the setting of the flowing liquid into a vessel that has been consecrated by sprinkling.
In some places, the reading is *adhisravaṇam*. In that case, the meaning is "heating in a vessel which serves as the locus."
He states the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) indicated by the word "etcetera":
"Having sprinkled the clarified butter with the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra. (2.232)
Having heated it over the Śiva-fire with the Astra-mantra and having withdrawn it with the Kavaca-mantra,
O Goddess, one should place it after circling it three times around the sacrificial pit.
The vessel for the clarified butter (ājyapātra) should be placed in its proper position;
heating it in the southeastern direction is for the sake of making it radiant. Lifting the fire and holding it above is for the sake of making the flame clearly manifest. || 233 ||
Furthermore—
..................the overflowing and the submerging;
the remainder [of the sentence] is that one should perform the overflowing of that clarified butter (ājya).
He asks "by what? and says:
"Having taken two tips of darbha grass, one span in length, with a knot tied in the middle. (2-234)
This is prescribed as the purifier, by which one crosses over the flood;
the *prādeśa* is the measure from the extended thumb to the index finger. || 234 ||
He asks "How? and replies:
"Having grasped this purifier with the thumb and the ring finger... (2.235).
Turning away three times and likewise facing forward three times with the Astra-mantra itself—
for the purpose of removing the insubstantial parts by means of *utplava* and for extracting the essence by means of *saṃplava*.
Moreover:
"The manifestation [of the world] occurs through the fire of Śiva. (2.236)
The phrase "by means of the weapon" (astreṇa) must be supplied as the remainder of the sentence, meaning "it should be performed. || 236 ||
He explains that:
"Having grasped a torch of *darbha* grass, one should inspect the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*).
One should illuminate it with that. And at this juncture, by gazing with the splendor of one's own eyes, [one perceives] that which consists of the supreme light."
The meaning is that one should prepare the clarified butter (ājya).
Then one should perform the *nīrājana* ritual:
the complete lustration by waving flaming *darbha* grass all around,
using the *astra-mantra* itself.
...then the circumambulation with fire. || 2-237 ||
How so?— having recited the weapon-mantra with the *dhāman*, one should cast that firebrand into the fire;
with the *dhāman* together with the root-mantra, the "making of fire" (*agnikaraṇa*) on all sides and in every direction is the attainment of the state of being composed of light.
Then—
the practitioner of mantra should sprinkle [the site] with water free from impurities, according to the very same rite as that for the abode.
The ritual procedure is the intention of non-difference from Śiva. || 238 ||
Furthermore:
having consecrated [it] with the six-limbed [mantra], immortality is attained through Śiva;
thus, the consecration is performed with the partless (niṣkala) or the embodied (sāṅga) [form], and immortality is achieved by means of the Amṛta-mudrā.

Having thus performed the twelve purificatory rites (saṃskāras)— namely, sprinkling with clarified butter (ājya), veiling (avaguṇṭhana), heating (tāpana), taking out from the fire (udvāsana), circling (bhrāmaṇa), splashing (utplava), flooding (saṃplava), illuminating (avadyotana), lustration (nīrājana), carrying fire around (paryagnikaraṇa), sprinkling again (prokṣaṇa), and the rite called nectar (amṛta)— one should worship [the deity] with the Bhairava mantra by means of a single utterance.
By means of the partless. || 239 ||

In this way, having effected the unification with the deity Bhairava— who is of the nature of the recipient— through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, the instrument, the means, the locus, and the object (namely, the sacrificer, the arghya-vessel, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the sacrificial ground, the fire, the clarified butter, and so forth), that very [unification]...
In order to strengthen the union of those whose faces are fire, he states the intention by means of the mantras of the Bhairava faces:
"The joining of the faces is performed with the faces by means of three oblations.
He explains this as follows:
One should perform the joining of that face with one's own lower face.
In this way, the joining of the gentle face is accomplished;
by the application of three oblations, this same procedure applies to the southern face as well. (2.241)
Then, in the same manner, the eastern face should likewise be joined with Śiva;
by the application of three oblations, the junction of the faces is proclaimed. (2.242)

"With the other face" means with its mantra; "the joining of that face" means the joining by means of that very other face, which—by implication—is the clearly manifest northern [face] through the seed-syllables and names of the northern face.
As it has been said: "In this way, the joining of the gentle (northern) face shall be accomplished."
And for this reason, the ritual application is as follows: "Oṃ laṃ, with the face of Sadyojāta; Oṃ vaṃ, I join it with the face of Vāmadeva, svāhā.
Likewise: "Oṃ vaṃ, with the face of Vāmadeva; Oṃ raṃ, I join it with the face of Aghora."
The ritual application is "svāhā. The same applies to the others. "Endowed with Śiva" means having the essence of repose in Īśāna.

Here, one should offer oblations for each face with three sesame seeds, but not with clarified butter (ājya), because the purificatory rites for that have not yet been completed. Repose is upward, facing westward.
It should be performed. || 242 ||
He states that this [upper face] alone is primary for those seeking liberation:
"The upper face is remembered as the principal one, while the others are subordinate.
Now, whichever face is principal according to the suitability of one's activity, that should be remembered as being above.
Having thus stated the underlying intention regarding this matter as well, he speaks of the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the different orientations of the mouth, as an incidental point:
"For one desiring liberation, during initiation, the upward-facing [mouth] is primary. (243)
This concerns the subject of occasional rites. || 243 ||

But regarding rites for specific desires, he says by way of distinction: "Indeed, all the various accomplishments (siddhis), beginning with foot-ointment and collyrium and extending up to Sadāśiva, one should offer as oblations at the eastern face. (2-244)
"Various" means superior, middling, and inferior. "One should offer oblations" means one should accomplish [the goal] through the fire sacrifice (homa). || 244 ||
But for killing, eradication, and the like, as well as for inciting enmity and immobilization, supreme success shall arise from the oblation performed at the southern face. (2.245)

One should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the north for rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), the attainment of good fortune, attraction, and the accomplishment of the ascent to good fortune. (2.246)
The summoning of the minds of others and so forth. || 246 ||
He also states that it concerns the eternal [rites]:
"The eternal rites in the Western [tradition] must be performed by all, because they are preceded by [prescribed] injunctions."
This very application has been proclaimed...
And thus, whoever desires to perform an action through whichever face, he should place [the mantra] above that.
But above that position, as he will state:
"Having conceived that which is desired as the primary face by means of whichever action [is intended]... (Svacchandatantra 2.264).
Thus it is said.
Thus, regarding the rite that has been introduced as a daily duty (nityakarman):
"The two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) must indeed be offered into the western [fire] with its opening facing upwards. (2-247)
In the west, in Sadyojāta; that is to say, he has been brought to the position of the upper face, in the place of the upper face.

Thus, having performed for him the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) ending with the attainment of Bhairava, and having brought about his unification with Bhairava through the connection with the mouth of the fire-Bhairava, [the author] now says this in order to bring about the state of the three abodes (*tridhāmatva*) for both the clarified butter and the fire in due order:

O lady of excellent hips, one should indeed place [the vessel] upon a blade of darbha grass in the center of the ghee-vessel with the Bhairava mantra; thereafter, the preparation of the path should be performed.

"Then" (tataḥ) means that, by the offering of two blades of *darbha* grass placed in the middle, the construction of the three paths (*vartman*)—that is, the three tracks—should be performed. The word "darbha" is used in the singular to denote the class [of the grass]. || 248 ||
To explain how this is done, he says:
"Having uttered the Bhairava-mantra, one should cast the *saṃpāta* (the residue) into the vessel by way of the path;
simultaneously through the three channels, one should deposit three portions into the vessel. (2.249)
Having uttered the partless Bhairava through the path consisting of the three channels (*nāḍī*)— that is, by means of the threefold way—

and having performed a simultaneous descent and rest within the three portions residing in the clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of the triple power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*), which consists of will, knowledge, and action, [one attains] that which is composed of the three abodes consisting of fire, moon, and sun.
One should assign and contemplate the three parts. || 249 ||
Here is the division:
one should conceive of Suṣumnā as situated on the central path, and Piṅgalā on the right; however, whatever light is in the portion of Iḍā, one should conceive of that as gentle on the left. (2.250)
Having thus made the clarified butter (*ājya*) consist of the three abodes (*tridhāman*), he says the following in order to make the fire itself consist of that through its oblation:
"Having thus resolved it into three parts and filled the *sruva* ladle, one should offer the oblation with the *bhairava* mantra itself, ending with 'svāhā to Agni'. (2.251)
Having extracted [the essence] from the portion of fire...

the abode consisting of fire and moon, which resides in the central channel and is the essence of light and bliss, manifests its distinctness: it takes on the nature of the moon on the left and the nature of fire on the right; therein—

Because there is no internal kindling within the oblation of the self that is Soma, it does not possess the nature of burning through division like fire; thus, it is described as having the form of the sun merely by virtue of its luminosity. However, due to the appropriateness of the material cause (*upādāna*), it also possesses the nature of fire; therefore, the southern part here is the portion of fire. For this very reason, in this context...
The right channel is designated by the name of the fire as Piṅgalā; however, in the third chapter it is said:
"By means of the central path of Piṅgalā, according to the sequence of the utterance of phonemes" (Svacchandatantra 3.22).

And since it is stated that "Piṅgalā is the middle channel" (Svacchandatantra 3.149), it is indeed appropriate that she is described as the central channel; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever between what precedes and what follows. Therefore, the division here follows the convergence of the channels established on the right, [and] from one's own right...
The human [form] is in the southern part of the fire; likewise, it should be understood to be so in the left as well. || 251 ||
Then, with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter, uttering at the end: "The portion of Soma, svāhā to Soma! (2-252).
By stating "the mantra here begins with the *niṣkala* [form] preceded by the *praṇava*," and so forth,
he reiterates what was previously mentioned:
"One should offer an oblation of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, beginning with the *dhāma-mantras* and the *praṇava*."
This is an adverbial modifier.
From that as well:
"Agniṣoma"—these two names, ending with *svāhā*, and the *dhāman* at the beginning. (2-253)
Having filled the *sruva* ladle from the beginning of the *praṇava* up to the middle of the *ājya*, one should perform the oblation (*homa*).
This is indeed the procedure for the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "Agni-Soma," the actual usage here is "agnīṣomābhyām. This is the rule for the bright fortnight.
But in other cases—................... it would be otherwise during the dark fortnight. || 254 ||
He said to him:
"The sun should be in the lunar portion; however, the designation 'fire' remains as before.
One should offer the oblation from the middle of the fire and the sun. (2-255)
Since, indeed, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) the moon enters into the midst of the sun;

because the moon is full during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), there is an oblation to Soma; but in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), because the waning moon enters the solar orb, there is an oblation to Sūrya. However, in the middle—
"From fire and the sun"—the rest is as before. || 255 ||
Having thus established that the fire also consists of the three abodes, [the author states]:
"Therefore, for the purpose of consumption, the oblation (homa) for the faces is performed by Bhairava. (2.256)

The word "kārya" (should be done) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. For this very reason, immediately after the realization of the three abodes (*tridhāmamayīkaraṇa*), one should utter the *praṇava*, the partless mantra (*niṣkala*), and the face-mantra (*vaktramantra*), and then perform the ritual application ending with: "I perform the consumption of the fire, svāhā. Furthermore, "consumption" (*prāśana*) here refers to the instillation of fitness for the future consumption of the fetters (*pāśa*) and so forth.
He states the true nature of the abundance and perfection of the auspicious fire through another series of ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*) as follows:
"Those ritual preparations beginning with the topknot (*cūḍā*) and ending with the child (*bāla*) belong to the fire."
For the sake of attaining all [goals], one should cause a single full [offering] to be presented.

Having uttered *bhairava*, [one should perform the rites]; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included the initiatory rites (*upanayana*) and so forth for the child student (*brahmacārin*), ending with those which stand at the conclusion, such as marriage (*udvāha*) and others. And here [it is said]: "May all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the tonsure (*cūḍā*) and so forth, belong to Agni."
The ritual application ends with "svāhā. The procedure for the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) will follow. || 257 ||
When this has been performed, the Śiva-fire, having increased, bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The meaning is that, according to the *tantra*, it grants all accomplishments to everyone, beginning with those who have taken the initiatory vows (*samayin*).
Thus, for the sake of the *caru* offering from the consecrated Śiva-fire, as well as for the sake of the daily rites (*nityakarman*) without further consecration—
“The *śrāpa*, *caru*, and *puroḍāśa* [are offered] into the fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*).”
Since it is stated elsewhere, "In the auspicious fire that has not been summoned... and so forth, [the fire] refers precisely to the Unsummoned Supreme Lord (anāhūta-parameśvara).
One should subsequently lift up the fire, place it in a vessel, and preserve it.
One should make it protected by enveloping it with the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 258 ||
Then, on the northern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and outside the seat (viṣṭara),
one should prepare the Praṇītā vessel there...
The word "of the seat" (viṣṭarasya) refers to that which has Rudra as its locus.
He explains the sublime [practice]: ...a cup filled with water. || 2-259 ||
A *camasa* is a wooden vessel. || 259 ||

And there, for the sake of providing a seat for Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the sacrificial rite— one should place a sacred thread (pavitra) provided with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds. And upon that—
Having invoked [the deity] beginning with the syllable Om, one should then offer salutation by the name "Viṣṇu. (2-260)
Having established Viṣṇu by means of the very word of address (*āmantraṇapada*),
one should worship him with welcome, a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and the guest-offering (*argha*)...
here, as before, according to the ritual application.
...then one should inform him. (2-261)

Whether the sacrifice has been commenced for the sake of the sacrificial animal or for the sake of oneself by the practitioners, O Blessed One, may there be freedom from defects in our sacrifice through your grace. (2.262)

It should be applied as follows: "for the sake of the animal sacrifice" in the case of the occasional rite (*naimittika*), "for the sake of the rule of initiation" in the case of the obligatory rite (*nitya*), and "O Blessed One, for the sake of the optional rite" (*kāmya*).
Having thus performed the ritual procedure, one should then perform the sacrifice in the fire and worship Bhairava.
To the question "How? he says:
One should arrange Ananta and the other deities according to the procedure prescribed for the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
Having first explained the division [of the faces] here, he speaks in order to perform the visualization of the faces and tongues of the fire according to the suitability of the ritual action:

"Having first meditated upon the five faces, whichever face is desired for the particular rite that is intended, one should conceive of that as the principal face, with its mouth having the dimensions of the sacrificial pit. (2.264)
One should meditate upon nine tongues established within each face;

the conceptualization of the primary qualities of the faces has already been well-distributed [in the previous section]. Regarding the term "mouth" (*mukha*), which refers to the oral cavity, he explains the directional division of the tongues as follows:
First, there are eight in the east and one in the center;
beginning from the east and ending at the northeast (aiśāna), there are eight.
And of those [goddesses]—....................those who have gone to the directions for the sake of fulfilling desires. (2-265)
The meaning is that those [deities] who are situated in the eight directions beginning with the east are [invoked] in rites performed for specific desires (kāmya-karma). || 265 ||
He designates them by names impelled by their respective functions:

"The one for the sake of sovereignty," "the producer of burning," "the giver of death," "the causer of enmity," "the subjugator," "the expeller," "the giver of wealth," and "the bestower of liberation. (2.266)
He states the name appropriate for the ritual of the ninth [day]:
"Bestower of all siddhis in the center...
because it is thus:
Therefore, one should perform the oblation in the center.
Thus, for those [deities] previously mentioned—for the purpose of arranging the tongues according to Bhairava—the full oblation (pūrṇā) is indeed [to be offered]. || 2-267 ||
Furthermore, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the Bhairava mantra.

In one case, the application is preceded by the root mantra: "I fashion the tongues of fire" (*agnijihvāḥ kalpayāmi*). In the other case, it is: "May there be the presence of the tongues; *svāhā*" (*jihvāsaṃnidhirastu svāhā*). || 267 ||
Now, he carries out what was previously proposed—that one should visualize Ananta and the others after first performing the supreme consecration of the fire—stating:
"Having grasped the tip of the flame with the heart-mantra, it is fashioned as the consciousness of the fire. (2.268)
Having visualized the seat of yoga situated within one's own heart,
one should then conceive of the bulb (kandaka) at the navel of fire, following the path of the central tongue.
Having meditated upon the heart as the limit, one should contemplate a lotus there;

having visualized it as being fashioned from the nature of fire-consciousness, one should seize its flame-tip with the heart-mantra from the heart, take it in through the path of the nose, and [unify it] with the single state of the fire of consciousness residing in the heart.
Having made the external fire *bhairavī* (terrible), in order to make even the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) *bhairava*,
one should [visualize] the Yoga-pīṭha, from Ananta up to Sadāśiva, according to the principle stated in the *Mataṅga*: "His powers, which are his own, flash forth on all sides" (1.5.5).
One should conceive of his seat as being of the nature of power (śakti). || 269 ||
Endowed with eight petals, white in color, and possessing great splendor. || 2-270 ||
One should conceive of the infinite there, beginning with Dharma and ending with Caraṇa; likewise, from Oṃ down to Śiva—this has already been explained. || 270 ||
Then—one should provide protection from fire. (2.271)
As before, by means of the syllable *haṃsa* itself. || 271 ||

Then, moreover—[the practitioner] should again uproot with the *dhruva* [mantra] that crest-lock (*śikhā*) which resides in the heart; by means of exhalation (*recaka*), he should cast it into the fire as the forms whose nature is Bhairava. (2.272)

With the fixed (dhruva) and partless [mantra], one should uproot [the impurity] and extract it as unified with one's own consciousness-Bhairava; then, by way of the right nostril, one should cast it into the external fire-form. In this way, this form becomes identical with Bhairava. || 272 ||
Then,
O fair-faced one, having thus conceived [the soul] as having become embodied and endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, one should deposit the path to be purified at the time of initiation.
The thirty-eight *kalās* mentioned previously are intended as indicators for the contortions of the face and so forth.
"The path to be purified" refers to that path by which the Guru intends to perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Having done this—having worshipped Bhairava according to the ritual prescribed in the scripture—the junction of the faces occurs between the two faces: that of Śiva and that of Agni. (2.274)
"According to the method seen in the Śāstra" means by means of the mental [offering] following the sequence beginning with the *argha* and ending with the aforementioned veils (*āvaraṇa*).
"From the two faces" uses the dual number for a plural sense; therefore, it means "by the mantras of the faces.
In the face of Śiva is the face of Bhairava, and here [the mantra is]: "Oṃ Laṃ, the face of Bhairava known as Sadyojāta..."

The conjunction of the faces should be performed in the sequence beginning with "I join [the offering] into the mouth of the Śiva-fire, Svāhā!", and this conjunction of faces is distinct from the previously mentioned conjunction of faces. || 274 ||
Moreover:
having thus joined the two tongues together...
[one should perform the union] of the internal and external fires of the faces with the faces of the Supreme Lord, preceded by the mantra.
Having performed the connection of the tongue, one should become intent upon the junction of the channels.
Regarding that, it is said:
Having fully uttered the root mantra, [one visualizes it] as having emerged from the nostril of the fire.
One should unite with the one who has the same purpose as Śiva residing on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having recited the root mantra through meditation from the Heart of Fire (agnihṛdaya), one should exit by its southern side, enter the sacrificial mound by its northern side, and exit by its southern side; such is the sequence.

Having connected [the mantra] with all the *sarvāvaraṇa* mantras, one should enter from the left of the fire; "for a single purpose" means that it is non-different, having the nature of Svacchandabhairava as the form of the deity to be expressed. || 275 ||
Having thus made this connection: "O fair-faced one, one hundred and eight oblations of pure clarified butter [should be offered]. (2.276)
One should offer to Bhairava a tenth part for his faces and limbs;
one should perform oblations to the eight Bhairavas and the world-protectors with a tenth part.
The thirty-six principles, through their divisions into gross, subtle, and supreme, amount to one hundred and eight;

[by means of] the twelve purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), they are rendered as clarified butter (*ājya*) by virtue of consisting of the entire universe in its entirety.
By performing one hundred and eight oblations with the *sruva* ladle, one should satisfy the deity of the Bhairava mantra;

the meaning is that one should cause her to become inclined toward bestowing grace (*anugraha*). Regarding the intention behind the [mantras of] the faces and so forth being one-tenth [of the total], this has been determined in the section on recitation (*japa*); others hold that [the mantras of] the Goddess are like those of the [principal] Deity, as if they were its limbs (*aṅga*). || 277 ||
Then,
having recited the root mantra, one should offer a single full oblation for the satisfaction of the entire circle of mantras.
Then, for the sake of satisfying the root mantra which is the most preeminent even among those, one should offer a second full oblation; thus he says:
"Likewise, one should pour out a full oblation for the purpose of nourishing Bhairava. (2.278)
From that [point] as well—[the remaining part of the verse is:

"one should pour the full [offering] with the root mantra for the sake of remedying any deficiency or excess, and for making [the rite] flawless. It is precisely for the purpose of removing deficiency and excess [that this is done].
Making [the mind] free from flaws.
Having thus completed the procedure for the daily fire offering (nityahoma), the subsequent homa should then be performed as desired, O fair-faced one. (2.279)
"According to one's desire" means [a rite] performed on a specific occasion (naimittika) or for the sake of a desired result (kāmya). || 279 ||
Now, he points out the classification of the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) according to the intention of each respective rite:
"The fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter is praised as bestowing all desires;
however, separately—"
For the sake of accomplishing the goal of wealth through grains...
[the phrase] "anointed with clarified butter" (ājyāktaiḥ) is to be supplied everywhere. Wealth (dhana) refers to goats and sheep; purpose (artha) refers to gold and the like.
...from the oblation of ghee and guggulu. || 2-280 ||
Vast accomplishment— whether inferior, middling, or superior— is born [thereby].
Likewise,
with white lotuses smeared with clarified butter...
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed;
by means of bilva fruits, one shall obtain prosperity. || 2-281 ||
O fair-faced one, the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) is performed by offering oblations of sesame seeds soaked in milk;

furthermore, the ritual substances generally exist in four types according to their origin—namely those fit for oblation—which are white, red, yellow, and black, corresponding respectively to the rites of pacifying, attracting, nourishing, and [subjugating]. (282)
And one should perform the rite of killing in due order, O lady of excellent hips.
Furthermore—
for the sake of obtaining a son— with *kunda* flowers...
He becomes a human being.
...through sorrows, there is reunion with the beloved. || 2-283 ||
A maiden of the Gandharvas [is worshipped] with *jātikuḍmala* buds; a Nāga maiden with *bakula* flowers; and a Siddha maiden with *siddhārtha* seeds. (2.284)
And with *caṇyakas*, O lady of beautiful hips, the lord of men [performs the rite]; but with *phalguṣa* smeared with ghee, he does so together with the mantra and the family priest. (2.285)
O fair-faced one, a queen together with her son comes under control;
a yakṣiṇī likewise comes under control by means of flowers from the kadamba tree. (2.286)
The phrase "by them" (*taiḥ*) should be understood as applying to all the desired items. "By *nāgas*" means by male *nāga* trees;
"by *siddhārthas*" refers to a specific kind of flower. In this context, one should perform the worship with the very same flowers used for the *homa*; "phalgu" means human flesh. || 286 ||

In this manner, one should accomplish the Vidyādharī by means of *kuyyakas*; there is no doubt in this matter. *Kuyyakas* are those known as *kuṭakas*. By the phrase "there is no doubt in this matter," he states that through certain conviction, the ritual action becomes fruit-bearing;
for this very reason, in the definition of the disciple's characteristics, the term "one of firm vows" (*dṛḍhavrata*) is used with respect to the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
It has been applied.
Regarding the hand-gesture (hasta-saṃsthāna) for the *mṛgī* [mudrā], he says:
having formed the *mṛgī*, the oblation (*homa*) is performed with sesame seeds;
it consists of the index and little fingers extended, while the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger form a pincer-like grip (*saṃdaṃśa*).
The deer-bond.
...presided over by lotuses and bilva fruits. || 2-287 ||
The ellipsis is that one should perform the oblation using unbroken [grains]. || 287 ||
With foodstuffs in the measure of a morsel, and with grains in the measure of a handful;
and in this matter, the placement of the hands should be understood according to what is appropriate.
He concludes: "In this way, the practitioner, established in the ritual procedure, acts according to the fire-oblation. (2.288)
One who is constantly devoted to worship and fire-offerings (homa) certainly accomplishes whatever desires they may seek, according to the word of Bhairava. (2.289)

When one is properly established in ritual action governed by the scriptures, one attains the desired fruits; for just as Bhairava’s command— being of the nature of scripture— accomplishes everything through its mere authority,
so too does it do so through that very form of true resolve belonging to Bhairava.
This statement belongs to the All-Powerful One, and not to any limited being;

thus, for those who have taken refuge in Him, this rule, when practiced in that manner, certainly accomplishes the desired goal—may my mind be intoxicated by the fragrance of the lotus feet of the Guru. May there be auspiciousness!
Whatever reality has been expounded here in the Śaiva scriptures—
including various rites and secrets— when practiced by those possessing true devotion, leads them day after day to the penetration of the abode of Bhava.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on Worship," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 2 ||
The third chapter, titled *Svacchandodyota*,
wherein, upon its unfolding, the entire outflow of worldly latent impressions dissolves.
This entire abiding conquers all, flowing forth from supreme bliss.
Having thus explained the daily rites (*nityakarman*), which must necessarily be performed and which contain within them the subsequent subjects of inquiry as a secondary topic,
Bhairava spoke in order to determine the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), which is the first of the occasional rites (*naimittika*) whose time for definition has now arrived:
I shall explain the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) correctly and in due order.

*Adhivāsa* consists of the undertaking of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) which constitute the fitness appropriate for the future initiation of the deity, the preceptor, and the disciple, as well as the preparation of the sacrificial hall and its furnishings; and this must be performed by the preceptor.
He describes that very commencement of its refinement:
"With his self thoroughly purified by water, having accomplished what was to be done, and with a serene intellect... (3.1).
With his body smeared with ashes and adorned with the ornaments of mudrās,
he may wear a crooked sacred thread, or be clothed, or be naked.
His limbs were smeared with fragrant perfumes, he was adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers, endowed with divine ornaments, exceedingly serene, and well-purified.
Well-perfumed with incense, well-chewed betel, and cooled by sandalwood and agallochum;

"self" refers to the body and the mind. Having performed his duty—such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*)—he is thus one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*), being completely filled with identity with Supreme Bhairava; consequently, his intellect (*dhīḥ*) is serene, having abandoned all external desires.
Of whom: adorned with ornaments and seals, having the five seals (*pañcamudrā*) placed upon the topknot, the ears, and the forearms; "crooked" refers to a corpse;
"produced from that" means produced from its hair; and this [practice] pertains, as appropriate, to the householder, the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), and the teacher.
This is to be explained. By the words "fragrant" (*sugandhi*) and so forth, he says this:

even one whose nature is not otherwise devoted to the contemplation of Śiva may, by means of external ritual offerings, clarify the mind and, being well-cultivated, become characterized by the unfolding of absorption into Śiva. For:
"And one who shows contempt at the time of the ritual for the sake of uplifting [beings] from saṃsāra,
or who harms a disciple regarding the transmission of mantras or the instruction on vows, shall become a denizen of hell"—
thus it is taught in the tradition.
To the question "What should he do?", he says:
"But having stood at the region of the eastern gate, he should be meditated upon as before. (3-4)
Having worshipped the gatekeepers, one should then perform the scattering of flowers;
having produced the sound of the *tāla* clap by employing the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Indeed, through the conjunction of the heel and the lower hand, for the purpose of expelling obstacles:
one should strike those situated on the ground with the heel, and those in the atmosphere with the palm.
Having thus purified the divine [deities] with mantras, one should then enter the sacrificial hall (*yāgaharmya*).

The construction of the sentence is as follows: one should enter while performing the scattering of flowers, the sound of clapping (*tālāśabda*), and the expulsion of obstacles (*vighnaproccāṭana*) by means of the contact of the heel with the ground below and the contact of the hands.
The intermediate space is the world of the atmosphere (*bhuvoloka*). The rest is clear. || 6 ||
Then, one should arrange protection all around as before by means of the Astra-mantra. || 3-7 ||
Having indeed concealed the sacrificial hall with armor in the form of an illusion,
O lady of beautiful countenance, he then sat down in the southern quarter.

The ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) is performed as before; likewise [are] burning (dahana), purification (utpūyana), immersion (plāvana), nourishment (āpyāyana), and the rite of making the deity complete (sakalīkaraṇa). || 3-9 ||
As before, one should perform the mental sacrifice within the inner body.

"On all sides" means in the form of a protective wall of weapons (*astraprākāra*). "In the form of Māyā" means in the form of that which covers everything from the *kalā* principle down to the end [of the universe] and is difficult to pierce; it is by way of that form. The remainder [is as follows].
This has been determined previously. || 9 ||
He recalls the procedure previously mentioned regarding the internal sacrifice:
"The infinite support of Śakti, extending from Dharma up to the feet. (3-10)
The limbs [of the body] are adharma and the other [qualities], as well as the connecting bolts;
the lower covering and the upper [covering] are the filaments and the pericarp of the lotus.
One should offer the lotuses, the spears, the circles, and the lords of the circles;
one should grant the seat ending with Śiva by means of the Dhruva mantra, which is its primordial form.
The array of the kalās of Mūrtibrahman, the nine principles (navatattva) and the three principles (tritattva), the thirty-two-syllable deity, and indeed the eight Bhairavas. (3-13)
Likewise, one should meditate on the limbs of knowledge, the razor-edged sword, the three eyes,
the three supreme powers, and the Supreme Lord endowed with the six limbs.
And this has been determined: the intention behind the repetition [of the text] is that all of this must be performed even in the case of an occasional rite (naimittika). || 14 ||
Moreover— one should arrange the mudrās, mantras, and ritual substances in their proper places.
The mudrās consist of the forms of invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (saṃnidhāna), and confinement (nirodhana), starting from the seat (āsana).
The mantras ending with Bhairava, and the substances such as water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering;
"in their proper places" means according to the method previously described.
Having thus reflected upon all this, one should arrange it according to the rule and as is appropriate. (3.15)
"According to what is appropriate and in due order" means that whichever principle is to be ascertained, one should follow its pervasion (vyāpti) without deviating from it. || 15 ||

Now he also causes [the practitioner] to recall the deposition of the veils (āvaraṇanyāsa): "One should assign Sadyojāta, Vāma, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśa—the deities previously mentioned—to the portions situated upon the petals of the god. (3-16)

"Then [I] spoke of the five [deities], beginning with Hṛdaya, in the cardinal and intermediate directions"—this is the meaning of "I spoke. The reading "diśāsu" and so forth belongs to the Īśa [recension]. || 16 ||
Furthermore:
"From the east up to the northeast, there is the outer enclosure of Bhairavas. (3.17)
One should visualize the world-protectors and their weapons, starting from the east and ending with the northeast; this is understood as being supplied to the preceding [injunction].
He states the conjunction of mantras:
"The weapons, the world-protectors, and likewise the eight Bhairavas. (3.18)
The five Brahmans and the [five] limbs—these indeed are the enclosures;
one should pronounce them all in sequence until the Īśvara within that womb. (3.19)
This indeed is the conjunction of mantras (*mantrasaṃdhāna*).

The conjunction of mantras is the pronunciation, in reverse order, starting from "Obeisance to Īśāna, the spear-handed one" (*śūlahastāyeśānāya namaḥ*) and ending with *sakala*, by means of the process of successive absorption (*uttarottaralīnatā*).

Regarding the statement, "Then the five Brahmās and the limbs," although the order is in reverse (prātilomya), the reading is given in direct (ānulomya) sequence because the faces and limbs serve as the cause for a single enclosure; thus, this sequence consists of three enclosures. || 19 ||
Now, listen to the supreme perfection;
then, O God, one should utter the deity endowed with the short, long, and protracted vowels. (3.20)

One should recite the mantra as long as it remains within the sphere of Nirvāṇa—the deity who is the true essence of illumination and so forth, the venerable Niṣkala. Regarding the words "short," etc., [it is said]:
"Short, long, protracted, subtle, extremely subtle, and the supreme Śiva" (6.4).

Thus, according to the state that will be explained in the section on the five *praṇavas*, having come to rest— following the expansion to be described— within the phonemes and digits (*kalā*) of the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*, which consist of the short and other measures (*mātrās*), one reaches the *dvādaśānta*, the sphere of *nirvāṇa*.
The meaning is: as long as one should recite the mantra. || 20 ||
Right here he fulfills the procedural requirement (itikartavyatā): "From the lower power up to the upper [power], within the path of the Moon and the Sun. (3-21)
By means of the central path of Piṅgalā, through the sequence of vocalizing the phonemes,
one [attains] the pentad of deities, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
Having gradually differentiated everything up until the very end of dissolution,
one reaches the state that is waveless, called the pathless, all-pervasive, and beyond the mind (unmana).

By means of the sequence of divine instruments to be described hereafter, having brought the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) from the "lower" region— the *kanda*— to the heart, one should [lead] the vowels beginning with *a* and *u* up to the *nāda* through the central path named Piṅgalā, according to the directions previously determined, situated between the left, right, and central channels.
Having differentiated the pentad of deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva through the sequence of pronouncing the phonemes starting with the short vowels,

and having further differentiated [the levels] from Śakti up to Unmanā by means of the extremely subtle mantra-fragments situated above them; then, by means of the method of tearing asunder the state of being a knot, one should perform the reflective awareness of the mantra whose nature is Parāvāk, which remains.

The meaning is that one should recite the mantra until reaching the *dvādaśānta*, which is the state of total tranquility at the end of death (*nidhanāntika*). Of what nature is this end of death? It has emerged from the waves—the surging manifestations of differentiation—and it is itself the emergence, the radiant manifestation.
It is that from which the designations and manifestations of the paths (adhvan) such as phonemes (varṇa), mantras, and so forth arise;
likewise, it is the all-pervasive [reality] of everything without exception. To the question, "How can such a single entity exist?", he says:
it is *unmana*, meaning it exists having transcended all limited cognition (*saṃvedana*).
The meaning is that it is independent. || 23 ||
Then,
having ascended that [state] and having entered for a short time into that partless reality (niṣkala-tattva) with firm concentration...
...one should cause [it] to enter the heart-lotus in direct order;
and from the *dvādaśānta* onwards, the reality (*tattva*) is indeed *śamanā* and *unmanā*. (11.29)
Having descended by means of the sequence of emanation— the object of the mantra— according to the perspective to be described below,
one should meditate upon [the deity] as being all-pervasive, established within the heart-lotus, encompassing all the Bhaṭṭārakas.
Furthermore:
"O Goddess, one should thus place that pervasive [mantra] upon all the veils. (3.24)
"Thus" means by a single effort alone. || 24 ||

And all [mantras] presided over by that [deity] bestow the fruits of all desires, because all mantras, beginning with *sakala*, consist of a mass of its rays; the particle *ca* has the sense of "indeed" (*hy-arthe*).
In this context, he recalls what was previously stated regarding meditation and so forth:
"Just as their essential nature, configuration, and color were described by me [in verse 3.25]."
Thus, they should be employed in the mental [sacrifice] by means of the mind.

Their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the root, consisting of the forms of Brahmā, the limbs [of the deity], and so forth; their configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is their shape; and their color (*varṇa*) is white and so on, as stated in the second chapter. "In the mental [sacrifice]" (*mānase*) refers to the sacrifice; "by the mental" (*mānasena*) refers to the mind (*citta*).
And then— having established Bhairava, who exists in a twofold state, within the pericarp (kaṇīkā)— || 3.26 ||

Resembling pure crystal and adorned with all mantras; whose state exists by its own sovereignty in two ways—through the differentiated (*sakala*) and undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) aspects—for the sake of bestowing grace upon those to be graced; the differentiated being white in form, while the undifferentiated is...
"Adorned with the reality of pure light" means surrounded by rays.

Thus, although the root mantra is partless (*niṣkala*) in view of its thirty-two syllables, it nevertheless possesses a state of being "with parts" (*sakala*) when there is the utterance of the vowels beginning with *a*. || 26 ||
That which is the reality devoid of parts in truth, he points that out:
even there, the object of knowledge is beyond [the senses], indefinable, and free from affliction. (3.27)

In that regard, beyond those two—the differentiated (*sakala*) and the undifferentiated (*niṣkala*)—the nature of Bhairava should be known as the supreme, in its perfectly complete form; the meaning is that it is to be recognized as self-luminous.
For that is indefinable, because it is not an object of "this-ness" (*idantā*), and it is free from affliction (*anāmaya*).
It is empty even of the most subtle affliction, namely the touch of the great illusion (*mahāmāyā*) characterized by non-apprehension (*ākhyāti*). || 27 ||
And thus: "Where there is no duality..."—
because [the reality] consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of all things, such as the partless (*niṣkala*) and the with-parts (*sakala*).
...and there is no conceptualization of mantras and so forth;
one should point out that dissolution as the merging of the syllable Oṃ, the bindu, and the nāda. (3-28)
The meaning is that one should know that to be the state of rest for all that is measurable by mantras. As he will say:
"As long as it is uttered by speech, and as long as it remains even in writing, so long is it to be known in its entirety. (7.239)
Likewise:
"How can there be liberation in syllables? The supreme reality is beyond syllables. (7.238) || 28 ||
And therefore:
"Considering that state to be difficult to attain, one should never give rise [to such thoughts], for it has neither top nor bottom, nor does it have directions or intermediate directions. (3.29)
Neither sound nor even space [is perceived] when one meditates upon that; rather, one is liberated through it.
It is called a "station" (*sthāna*) because everything abides within it. Because it is empty of form, it lacks a base, a tip, and so forth;
because it is empty of the nature of sound and the form of mantra consisting of phonemes, it is said to be "not sound. Even so, it is not...

With the intention that it is empty, he said "not space. Having meditated—meaning, having entered by resting in the unconditioned self-reflection—one is liberated; that is, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is attained.
Thus, in this manner—first the mental sacrifice, and afterwards that accompanied by material substances. (3.30)

The teacher who is devoted to sacrifice should always perform [the ritual] in this manner upon his own hand, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), on a linga, in a mandala, and likewise in the sacrificial oblation (caru). || 3.31 ||
By worshipping [the deity] both in water and in fire, one properly obtains the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Since it has been stated that mental worship comes first— because there is no eligibility for the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) without attaining the state of Śiva— the *deśika* is the teacher (*ācārya*) whose purpose is instruction.
"Constantly" means because of being engaged in daily worship (*nityārcā*). "In one's own hand" refers to the occasion of bestowing the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva).

"On the sacrificial ground" (*sthaṇḍila*) refers to the time of consecration (*adhivāsa*). "In the *liṅga*"—regarding the word *liṅga*, the wise say: "By the word *liṅga*, [they mean] the cause of creation and dissolution."

According to such etymological explanations (*nirukti*), [the term "maṇḍala"] refers metaphorically to the consciousness of the disciple appropriate for the occasion, or externally to the form of the arrow and so forth;

to the "maṇḍala" in its form to be described below; to the *caruka*, which consists of a specific sacrificial oblation; to the water contained in the jar; and to the fire that burns away the fetters (*pāśa*). [All these serve as the locus] for the fruit of initiation for the disciples.

Therein, one attains the recognition of one's own true nature as Bhairava, and thereby acquires the capacity for being the agent who effects the cause. And thus, preceded by the mental sacrifice consisting of the state of becoming Śiva in every respect, one should perform the external sacrifice. || 31 ||
Otherwise—[he who], without having performed the mental sacrifice, should undertake another sacrifice. (3-32)

But he should be known as inauspicious (aśiva); he is not ordained for liberation. "Inauspicious" means that due to the absence of the state of Śiva—which is the goal of the mental sacrifice—he is such a bound soul (paśu) and is therefore not ordained for liberation; the meaning is that he is not qualified for that purpose. || 32 ||
For: "When the sacrifice of the self has been performed, the purification of the body arises. (3.33)
Regarding the word "co" (for/indeed): the particle *eva* (indeed) is to be construed immediately after the word *jāyate* (is born).

Therefore, because from that sacrifice a purification—consisting of the immersion into the state of Śiva—is indeed produced for the body, which is of both external and internal nature, for that reason it must necessarily be performed.
This is the meaning. || 33 ||
For if that were so, one should designate that very teacher as being presided over by Śiva;
for it will be stated that he is called an "ācārya" because of his constant association with Śiva.
Furthermore—both that which he spoke regarding self-immolation and that which pertained to the mind. (3.34)
The meaning of "I" is the self; here, the self is of two kinds: the body and [the inner self]. || 34 ||
Having known [this] correctly, the teacher is remembered as Śiva, the destroyer of bonds.
Correct knowledge consists in the immersion into the state of "I am Śiva" through the pacification of the egoity directed toward the body and other such things.
He describes the power of this sacrifice:
In whatever place one may be situated, whoever should perform this rite in such a manner.
"Even a killer of a Brahmin would be liberated, how much more so one who is devoted to Śiva!

Even one who has committed a prescribed great sin, if he performs this sacrifice and worships the Blessed One with the intention [of following] this rule for the sake of the purpose of the Blessed One's will, he too is liberated. (35)
Furthermore:
"And even when situated in all states, he is not colored by sense objects. (3.36)

"One who worships even once would be liberated, how much more so one who does so day after day," and so forth; thus, even one who enjoys worldly pleasures and is unable to maintain the observances (*samaya*) is liberated by worship through the initiation without seed (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*). Therefore, this worship should be performed constantly.
This statement is intended to mean that the *putraka* (spiritual son) alone is to be initiated from this day forward.
He proclaims the greatness of this ritual of worship and so forth:
"That which has been stated according to the prescribed rule, by means of the procedure taught in this Tantra. (3.37)
Even in another tantra, that very same [rite] such as sacrifice (ijyā) and so forth would be "Kāmika" (desirable).

If, in another Pārameśvara tantra belonging to either the common or uncommon current (srotas), sacrifice and so forth are taught preceded by the rules for initiation (dīkṣā) and the like, then that [is considered Kāmika] because its entire procedure (itikartavyatā) is complete according to what is stated in that tantra.
By means of that [rite] performed according to the prescribed rule (*vidhi*), it becomes "desirable" (*kāmika*), meaning it serves the purpose of the various desired enjoyments and liberation.

By this statement, the meaning is that even when the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) employed elsewhere—such as in initiation—is adopted here, it certainly fulfills the desired goal because it is complete. Regarding the phrase "tadvai," if the reading is *tasya* (of that), [the sense remains the same].
The phrase "to do that" (tasya kartum) is how it should be explained. || 37 ||
For this very reason, this [mantra], when resorted to elsewhere as well—
[described as] "endowed with various supernatural powers and qualities"—
produces even further qualities in the form of accomplishments (*siddhi*) that are taught in the *Kriyāpāda*.
Likewise, ... [it is] the bestower of various fruits of desire. (3-38)
It also brings about, without delay, the fruit described in the Caryāpāda. || 38 ||
He says that [this] also brings about what was taught in the *Yogapāda*:
"And the perfection of yoga shall arise...
Furthermore, even that which was taught in the *Vidyāpāda* follows from this, for it touches upon the supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*).
He also states that by performing the prescribed rite,
the practitioner indeed achieves [the goal] and certainly attains liberation:
"Furthermore, this worship of the performer of the sacrifice..."
Sadāśiva knows it as well, as do the gods, the asuras, and others.
"Even those possessed of devotion to Parabhairava, though they possess great power, still yearn [for this]"—this is the sense.
(39) Having thus spoken incidentally, he states the subject at hand:
"But having performed the mental sacrifice in this manner, one should perform the external [sacrifice]."
Therein, first of all—contemplating the supreme state (parā vṛtti), one should initially examine the substances. (3.40)

The meaning is that one, maintaining a state consisting of the immersion into Bhairava that is perfected through the supreme internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), should first render the sacrificial substances— prior to their consecration through sprinkling and other rites— possessed of great purity, whose essence is unity brought about by supreme non-dual knowledge (*parādvayajñāna*).
He enumerates them:
white sandalwood, camphor, excellent incense, two white garments, flowers of divine fragrance, sesame, rice, ghee, and so forth. (3.41)
Mango sprouts, darbha grass, white mustard seeds, as well as chalk, a ruler, scissors, and a cord for binding with nooses.
The water-vessel, the auspicious jar, as well as the fuel-sticks, the enclosing sticks,
the sacrificial wood, the tooth-stick, the vessel for the oblation, the large ladle, and the small ladle.
Rice grains, milk, and various other such items [are used];

because the purpose of initiation is the purification that brings about the state of Śiva-nature, white is predominant by virtue of its suitability for that purpose. [The initiate wears] two white garments and mango sprouts.

The water-pot (*kalaśa*) is for the purpose of the *vārdhānī* offering; rice (*vrīhi*) is for the purpose of the scattered offerings (*vikira*); white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) are for the purpose of protection on the occasion of the bed and so forth;

chalk and a small basket are for the purpose of the mandala; a pair of scissors is for cutting the noose-thread; the *vārdhānī* vessel is for the sacrifice of weapons (*astra-yāga*); and the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are as previously mentioned.

Twenty-four pieces of fuel, each one cubit (hastamātra) long, are for the satisfaction of the kindled fire; four enclosing sticks (paridhi), each measuring one cubit and provided with leaves, are placed outside the sacrificial pit in the cardinal directions to protect against the entry of obstacles; and the fuel-sticks (samidh) are produced from sacrificial trees, stripped of their bark, and free from blemishes.
"Auspicious [sticks] are those which are a span (prādeśa) in thickness and longer than the little finger.

These have been described for the purpose of producing a flame in the fire; the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) is for the sake of the disciple, and the rice-milk porridge (*taṇḍulakṣīracaru*) is also for the sake of the deity and the teacher. The rest is clear. Such are these items.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that there are powders for the sake of the maṇḍala, as well as the five products of the cow, the eye-cloth, and so forth, for the sake of the disciples. || 43 ||
Having thus examined the ritual substances,
one should then take the argha vessel and wash it with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship with the Praṇava;
O fair-faced one, one should fill [the vessel] with water and the other eight ingredients.

Water, milk, flowers, kuśa grass, mustard seeds, rice, barley, and ghee—these eight constitute the *arghya* offering for the Eightfold Lord (Aṣṭamūrti), intended for the group of eight [primal elements]. 45.
Then, O Dear One, having established the entire seat with the Praṇava, one should thereafter place the form [of the deity].
One should worship her, together with the Bhairava enclosures, in due order, using perfumes, flowers, and incense, preceded by the application of the mantra. (3–47)
One should install [the deity] joined with Bhairava and the enclosures (āvaraṇas), and worship her preceded by the unification of mantras (mantrasandhāna).
Furthermore:
"The supreme reality (parama-tattva) is that which is to be contemplated; through that alone one becomes immortal.
The supreme reality is partless (niṣkala), according to the reasoning previously stated."
The meaning is that while reciting [the mantra], one should consecrate [the substance] as nectar by displaying the Amṛta-mudrā.
And for the purpose of the *argha* vessel—one should likewise arrange a triad of vessels according to the rule for the rite of cessation (*nirodha*). (3.48)
Regarding the *paśvargha* and so forth:

the *vidhyargha* vessel is for the purpose of worship, whereas the *nirodhārgha* vessel, which is to be used on occasions such as the cessation (*nirodha*) and dismissal (*visarjana*), should be prepared with wine (*surā*). As it has been said:
"Afterwards, the *argha* offering should be presented with well-scented wine" (2-136).
For the animal sacrifice, however, there is a vessel for the *argha* of the animal, intended for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites. 48.
Having thus fashioned these three [elements], one should fashion the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) in this worldly rite of initiation by the teacher who acts as an instructor.
Regarding the question of how the rite is performed with the hand when it is not yet distinguished [by initiation],

even for one who has been consecrated by the permanent rites (*nityakarman*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), there is a specific occasional rite (*naimittikakarman*) characterized by the destruction of superior bonds and the bestowing of the state of Śiva.

In order to establish the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatā*), the status of being the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahastatā*)— the essence of which is the firm support of the potency of the agent whose nature is Śiva, who is meditated upon through the identification with one's own self via the placement of the radiant wheel of mantras— must necessarily be attained first.
It must be performed.

As for what will be stated right here later— "Having meditated on the All-pervasive Lord in the hand of Śiva, [one should place] the collection of mantras, blazing brightly" (3.142)— that refers exclusively to those who are to be graced.
The conjunction of mantras as before, and likewise the conjunction of the channels (nāḍī). || 3-49 ||
The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 49 ||
He states the primary method for the internal concentration on mantra (mantrasaṃdhāna):

"Having recollected the root mantra, one should pierce through the heart, throat, and palate, up to the space between the eyebrows—the peak of sound—which is the station of the Fourth State (turya). (3.50)
One should pierce through the left, right, and middle [channels] by means of the breath situated at the equinox (viṣuvat);
having led it to the supreme dvādaśānta, the mantra-body resides within the hand.

The word "should be connected" (*anusaṃdheya*) is the ellipsis. Having recollected the supreme root-mantra— the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) consisting of all expressive sounds, which is the form of the totality of mantras internalized within, and which is the peak-syllable in the form of sound, whose eternal nature consists of the supreme *nāda*— [The practitioner should perform the ritual.]

The teacher, intent on the realization of the mere formation of the instruments (*karaṇabandha*) that will be described hereafter, should pierce the fourth station—consisting of the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows—by his own will. To the question "How?
he replies with the words beginning with "vāma" [the left], by means of the central path (*madhyamārga*).

The meaning is that, by means of the process of "up to the space between the eyebrows," one whose mind is fixed between the eyebrows shall, with the sharp needle-tip of the central breath obtained through the technique of equal expansion of the left and right nostrils, pierce the knot of the *bindu* without effort, and thereby pierce even the knots of the *nāda* and the others.

And this will come to pass: then, having led the mantra to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], the form of the mantra residing in the hand should be contemplated through the attainment of purity, so that the instrument possesses the essence of the agent's vitality. || 51 ||

He also speaks of the joining of the channels: "By this same method, one should enter [the heart] in reverse order; by means of the self's own exhalation (recaka), one should enter the heart through inhalation (pūraka). (3.52)
This indeed is the union of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) proclaimed by Śiva:

having gone from the self upward by means of the upward exhalation (ūrdhvarecaka), and then [having gone] from that [state] of the Lord held in the hand in reverse order, one should enter again from the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta) into the heart; then, having risen up from there, one reaches that same limit of the twelve.

By means of that very inhalation (*pūraka*), one should enter into one's own heart; this "joining of the channels" (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*) has been proclaimed by Śiva as distinct from the previously described joining of the channels through the sequence of the nostrils.
By this [statement], he suggests that this [method] is to be adopted because it demonstrates the pervasive non-duality (*abheda-vyāpti*). || 52 ||
Thus, having entered one's own heart by means of the union of the channels (nāḍī), one should meditate upon Śiva as all-pervasive, presiding over the form of the mantra. (3.53)
One should meditate upon Śiva, the pervasive Lord Niṣkala, who remains presiding over the entire form of the wheel of mantras situated within, without, and in the hand of Śiva. || 53 ||
Then, having thus contemplated the great pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) within the hand of Śiva,
he describes the consecration of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which is useful for the disciple and others:
"Having taken a blade of *darbha* grass and empowered it with the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) seven times..."
One should purify the vessel for the five products of the cow with the water of Śiva.
Cows are pure, purifying, and the embodiments of all deities;
in cow urine resides the chief river of heaven (the Gaṅgā), while the earth on its banks is cow dung.

"That divine milk is nectar; curd is its transformation; ghee is that [curd]; the essence residing therein is that which eternally satisfies the immortals. Thus, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), possessing the excellences described in the venerable Parākhyasaṃhitā, are collected.
In that [vessel], one should purify the five products of the cow with water infused with *kuśa* grass; the meaning is that one should wash it. || 54 ||
One should wash that [seat] with the Astra-mantra and veil it with the Kavaca-mantra.
And for that—
having prepared a seat of Darbha grass with the Dhruva-mantra— one should arrange the mandala.
It should be circular or in the form of a svastika. || 55 ||
One should place a vessel upon it and bring cow-dung and other materials;
having placed them each in separate vessels, one should sprinkle them with the "water of Śiva" while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Then, having addressed the cow dung with the Heart mantra, the cow urine with the Head mantra,
the curd with the Crest mantra, the milk with the Armor mantra, and the clarified butter with the Weapon mantra, [he should mix them] with water from *kuśa* grass. (3.57)
Likewise—
one should subsequently consecrate it with the *dhāman* and then add cow-dung and other ingredients; into the previously prepared vessel, one should [place them] with one's own mantras.
Likewise—....................cow dung and so forth. || 3-58 ||
Having joined them together, one should subsequently consecrate them all simultaneously with those very [mantras], beginning with the heart-mantra.

Thus, for the sake of performing a special consecration (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*) of this conditioned [deity] here, he states the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*), preceded by the preparation of the seat:
"Having first resolved with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) upon Ananta, whose form is a physical body... (3.59)
Having worshipped the limbs and the abodes on the outside, one should perform the stationing of the enclosures,
the unification of the mantras, and likewise the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
Having contemplated that auspicious nectar (śivāmṛta) and worshipped it, one should then install it.
The form (mūrti) is the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa); the body (vigraha) is the Sakalabhaṭṭāraka; the abode (dhāma) is the root mantra.
Now, in order to consecrate the sacrificial ground (yāgabhūmi):
Taking a blade of darbha grass consecrated with mantras, perform the ritual scraping.
As far as the ground extends all around, standing with a gentle face toward the south,
he should then extract the shaft situated down to the water's edge.
One should recite the pure mantra and meditate upon it; one should fill [the vessel] with pearls and other such substances.
Equalizing is done with the Astra-mantra, while sprinkling is performed with the Kavaca-mantra.

Then, having performed these purificatory rites— beginning with striking [the site] with the weapon-mantra and ending with the visualization of the completed sacrificial pit— one should proceed to the sweeping and the smearing.
With the Astra-mantra, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and with scented water, [he should sprinkle] above.
The meaning is that there should be a smearing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and after that, with scented water. || 64 ||
Then,
one should consecrate the scattering materials (*vikirān*) seven times with the *astra* mantra using water from the *śiva-kalaśa* joined with the *astra-mantra*.
Having sprinkled [the area] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), the *vikirāṇi*—namely sesame seeds and so forth—are scattered. As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga-tantra*:
"Sesame seeds, parched rice, barley, dūrvā grass, and auspicious white mustard seeds..."
"And abundant white flowers that are very fragrant;
this auspicious scattering is mixed with a small amount of sandalwood paste. (2-50-23-24). One should consecrate these scattering materials (*vikirāṇi*) with mantras.
Then, having stood in the middle, facing the eastern direction... || 3-65 ||
One should scatter grains upwards and downwards and contemplate them as having become weapons;
the preceptor’s position is in the center, like that of Śiva.
And these—one should withdraw with a very bright chowrie using the weapon-mantra. || 3-66 ||
[The seats] face exactly toward the northeast...
Why [is this so], and up to what limit? To this he says: ...from the southwest (nairṛtya) as far as the northeast (aiśvara).
Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial ground in due order with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with scented water, and with the water of Śiva; || 67 ||
Having invoked Śrī with the Dhruva mantra—she who holds a lotus in her hand, possesses beautiful eyes, sheds white flowers, and is endowed with all auspicious marks. (3.68)
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, gazing upon the sacrificial hall,
she is seated in the Brahma-position, auspicious and facing the door.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should prepare the Śiva-kumbha.
For the disciple or others entering the sacrificial hall facing the door, one should worship the auspicious Goddess of Liberation (mokṣalakṣmī) and then prepare the Śiva-kumbha.
How so? He says:
"Having taken recourse to the northeastern direction, [one should prepare] a mandala with the five products of the cow. (3.70)
Having smeared it with scented water, one should sprinkle it with the *śivāmbhas* and the *astra-mantra*.
Having provided the seat beginning with Ananta by means of the *dhruva-mantra*, [one proceeds] up to the mandala.
Having smeared a jar that is free from all defects with sandalwood paste,
and having adorned it with svastikas and other designs, [one should place] barley, white mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass [within it].
Having wound it with a white thread and filled it with water filtered through cloth,
one should cover it on all sides with the sprouts of the mango, the holy fig tree (aśvattha), and others.

Having sprinkled [the site] with water containing gems, the womb-jewel, and medicinal herbs, along with the groups beginning with Sahadeva, and having grasped it while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should envelop it with the Kavaca-mantra.
While recollecting the root mantra, one should place it upon the seat,

extending as far as the *āmaṇḍala*. This means up to the end of those solar and other mandalas presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, which consist of the powers of the *brahmabila* and the *vyāpinī*, through the pervasive extension of the Supreme (*paravyāpti*).

But it does not end with Śiva, for [it is said]: "Because the body has been dried out by the fierce powers of the mantra through processes such as desiccation and incineration, therefore there is the consecration. (4.450)

Thus, because it is untenable for the seat ending with Śiva—which is primarily intended as a conclusion for the purpose of nourishing according to the future [method]—to be occupied by barley and other grains placed inside; rather, it is characterized by these [grains] being internal, and by the thread acting as its armor, as well as containing gems and medicinal herbs. [It is further characterized] by groups such as the Sahadevas and others.

Because it is stated in the *Sārasaṅgraha*: "In the arrival of Śiva, Sahadevā alone is the best among herbs," the meaning is that [the site] is endowed with a collection of metals, minerals, and seeds, of which Sahadevā is the principal herb.
By the words "the root mantra" and so forth, it is stated that the water-pot consists of the form of supreme consciousness. || 74 ||
Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) there of the paths of the digits (kalā), Bhairava, and so forth, one should prepare the water for libation (argha) and the other offerings. || 3.75 ||
Having formed the mudrās, one should worship the heart and other [limbs] upon the petals starting from the southeast;
one should adorn them with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and so forth, and with a white cloth.

And here, the entire sequence previously mentioned, beginning with the ritual placement (nyāsa), is to be adopted. "The purifier" refers to the water in the vessel of honor (arghapātra) and not to the *pavitraka* thread, because the latter is restricted to specific times for the fulfillment of fixed observances. The same applies to what follows. || 76 ||
Then,
on the left side of the water-pot, having sprinkled a mandala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with auspicious water, one should place the seat with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having sprinkled the auspicious water-vessel (vārdhānī) with the Śiva-water and having worshipped it like the [main] jar, one should place it upon the seat.

"On the left side" means for the sake of accomplishing the pacification of obstacles through the pervasion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), by way of the sequence of pouring forth the future stream [of water]; the meaning is that it is done precisely through its pervasion because, like a water-pot, it is situated upon the seat as a constituent part thereof. "Endowed with auspiciousness" means endowed with excellent characteristics.
Then,
having worshipped the water-vessel (vārdhanī) with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and other offerings,
one should recite the Astra-mantra and lead the vessel before the ritual substances in due order.
Causing an unbroken stream of water to flow in the natural direction,
he should lift it up from that spot as far as the corner of Śaṅkara.

"Having uttered [the mantra]" means like the crow's eye (i.e., moving from one place to another). Having uttered the weapon-mantra from that position— the left side of the *kalaśa*— and having lifted up the *vārdhānī*, one should arrange the substances to be consecrated (*adhivāsya*) in front and behind, in direct order, following the sequence of the directions starting from the east, reaching the corner of Śaṅkara (the southeast) and the corner of Īśāna (the northeast).
"Having uttered the weapon-mantra (*astram*), while pouring down an unbroken stream of water for the destruction of obstacles"— thus [is explained] by the two grammarians (*dvauṇicau*).
And in this rite—the teacher should subsequently raise the jar with the Bhairava mantra;
he should lead it by way of the *vārdhānī* vessel and then place it back within that [jar]. (3.81)
The meaning is that, while the *vārdhānī* vessel is being carried first, one should carry the *śivakumbha* behind it and install it with one's own mantra. || 81 ||
One should place the *vārdhānī* (water-vessel) behind [the deity] while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

Regarding the word "should place": having established the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) by means of the descent of the stream through the pervasion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), one places the weapon in the right hand of the Blessed One.
Then, [one should perform] the special worship of both with perfumes, flowers, and sacred threads. || 3-82 ||
One should perform the conjunction of the mantras and then the conjunction of the channels of both.
Furthermore—
one should first arrange the scattered offerings together below the vessel of water.
And for this very reason:
"There were many unimpaired weapons—arrows, spears, swords, mallets, discuses, axes, thunderbolts, and so forth, ending with tridents, in great numbers. (3.84)
Pervading the entire sacrificial abode, they remain situated horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
all of them are established as rays of the Vārāhyāstra.
And these—
having placed the *astra* weapon joined [with mantras] in the right hand of the disciple,
he should place that *astra* to the south of the *śivakumbha*, upon Śiva who has been installed in His own place.
One should place [it]. As it is also stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"To its south is the Great Weapon" (*Ki. 7.24*), and so forth.
Since this is so, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice, one should place this jar at the beginning of the ritual. (3.86)

Regarding the word "kalaśam," it means the Blessed One, who is the substratum of the *kalaśa* vessel and whose purpose extends from the entire sacrificial rite and its replenishment up to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*). || 86 ||
And having offered that various *naivedya* and having praised him, one should address the Lord:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I shall complete the sacrifice. (3.87)
"I desire constant proximity to you"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Since it is stated that "the mention of the action must also be made," the dative case is employed.
And then:
"Always be present for the purpose of removing obstacles.
Having done this—
