Having been permitted, he should rise and proceed with the *argha* water in hand toward the lords of the directions.
And then:

One should diligently worship those [mantras], which consist of the arrangement of one's own name and begin with *oṃ* and end with *namaḥ*, using perfumes, flowers, purifiers (*pavitra*), and other offerings. (3.89)
One should worship these [deities] preceded by the arrangement of their own names, beginning with: "Oṃ, Indra, be present; salutations to you. || 89 ||
He enumerates them briefly:
one should worship the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with Ananta.
It is said that they "end with Ananta" because Brahmā is above and Ananta is below; in this regard:

Brahmā is to be worshipped above in the northeast direction, and Ananta in the southwestern quarter. Here, during the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), the ten world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped for the sake of protecting the house. However, in the actual sacrifice (yāga), there are only eight, through the pervasion of the previously mentioned group of eight Bhairavas, because it is so heard in the scriptures.
To explain the purpose for which this is done, he says:
"Then, one should arrange a mandala in the center of the sacrificial ground. (3.90)

The meaning is that one should first smear [the ground] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then smear the mandala above it with scented water. As for the powder mandala (rajo-maṇḍalaka), it will come later after the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). || 90 ||
Then, having sprinkled this with the water of Śiva using the Astra-mantra, one should veil it. || 3.91 ||
That is to say, with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra). || 91 ||
And here at the beginning—
having first worshipped the Gurus to the east of the Brahma-position and Vināyaka in the northwest,
O Goddess, one should worship them in sequence with perfumes and flowers. (3.92)

For the sake of removing obstacles, one should first worship Gaṇapati in the northwest; thereafter, one should worship the Guru and others in the eastern direction—this is the meaning of the sequence. || 92 ||
Then, having paid homage to these [deities], one should contemplate the command given by them alone. Having thus received the command—
Then, one should designate the Yogapīṭha located in the Middle Country.
According to the previously mentioned procedure...

the seat (*āsana*) of the Supreme Lord, beginning with the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*) and ending with the *preta*, is the pedestal (*pīṭha*) which is His own power (*sva-śakti*) denoted by the word "union" (*yoga*). As it has been said:
"Yoga is his own inherent powers" (Mataṅga 1.1.4). || 93 ||
And here— O fair-faced one, having worshipped Bhairaveśa together with his threefold enclosure by means of the purificatory rites (pavitra) and other offerings... || 3.94 ||

Endowed with the qualities of self-meditation (*svādhyāna*) and adorned with the ornaments of the *mudrās*, there are three enclosures (*āvaraṇas*): the enclosure of the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*), the enclosure of Bhairava, and the enclosure of the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) together with their weapons. In this meditation, the quality consists of such attributes as being like pure crystal; [this refers to] the *mudrā*.
The arrangement of weapons, and ornaments such as garlands of skulls, etc. || 94 ||
And here: first, the conjunction of mantras, and also the conjunction of the channels. (3.95)
One should perform the act of supreme transformation by means of the supreme pervasive [deity];
having offered various kinds of food offerings, one should display the mudrā. || 3-96 ||
Having performed prostrations and recitation according to the prescribed rule, and having made the offering,
one should afterwards present the bali-offering to the Mothers and the assembly of spirits.
O Goddess of the gods, [this applies] everywhere for the lords of beings (*bhūteśvara*) and the field-protector (*kṣetrapāla*).

By means of the mantra that will appear later, beginning with: "The beings who are of various forms, whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric," [one should offer] even at the conclusion of the sacrifice of the jar (*kalaśa*) and so forth, to these [beings].
Bali should be given to the attendants of the Blessed One. || 97 ||

Having thus offered the bali-oblation, O observer of excellent vows, the preceptor should then bathe, or else perform the ritual smearing with ashes, or alternatively, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then, having gone to the fire-pit, one should perform the purification as before and worship Bhairava there according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.

One should perform bathing and other rites according to the conceptualization of impurity arising from contact with the *bali* offering, which acts as an obstacle to the virtuous ritual; this constitutes the purification and consecration of the fire. || 99 ||
Then, having transformed [the fire] into Śiva and worshipped it,

one should perform its satiation with a thousand or a hundred oblations of sesame seeds and other materials as available; it has already been stated that for the retinue, this should be done with a tenth part [of the quantity].
Then one should cook the caru-oblation... [that is,] one should cook it or cause it to be cooked.
And how is that?
... Having taken a flawless cooking pot. || 3-100 ||
Having washed it with auspicious water, one should veil it with the *kavaca* mantra;
one should smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and fumigate it with refined incense.
O you of excellent vows, one should wrap a thread around the neck as a protective armor;
then, O beloved, one should prepare the mandala with a blade of *darbha* grass that has the nature of the weapon-mantra (*astra*). 3-102.
Having sprinkled [the seat] with auspicious waters, one should veil it with the *kavaca* mantra;
there, one should install the seat beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva.
And there—
having placed the vessel in its embodied form, one should worship Bhairava situated therein,
together with his three enclosures, in due order with perfumes and flowers. (3.104)
O fair-faced one, [this worship is performed] through mental application with flowers of meditative cultivation;
worship is not mentioned here so that the sacrificial offering (caru) may not become tasteless due to being mixed with [ordinary] flowers and the like.
Then,
having sprinkled the hearth with the Astra-mantra, one should thereafter worship it just as one does the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is intended to indicate the other consecrations mentioned regarding the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 105 ||
Having placed the vessel there, one should subsequently set the fire beneath it,
which has been previously consecrated and drawn forth.
Then, having sprinkled the milk and the rice together in the vessel with the auspicious water of Śiva— || 3.106 ||
Having poured [the substances] with the mantra recited one hundred and eight times, O Goddess of Gods, one should cook them slowly, single-minded and composed, while reciting the root mantra. (3.107)
"Slowly," meaning so that the vessel does not break. || 107 ||
And therein—
one should perform the shaking, opening, and so forth with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
The instruction "one should cause [it] to be performed" means by a disciple who has already been initiated previously.
Then, in this sacrificial porridge (caru)—once it is well-cooked—one should provide the sprinkling over the hot [ghee] and likewise arrange the ritual portions (aṅgas). || 3-108 ||
O beloved, one should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle using clarified butter (*ghṛta*) three times each;

this [fire], having been heated through the pervasion of Agni, is the essence of kindling by means of the sprinkling of the nectar of clarified butter (*ājya-amṛta*), according to the meaning of the verbal roots. And this [offering] is performed in the vessel with mantras ending in "Svāhā" while it is ablaze.
For the destruction of the defects of undigested food in human beings. || 108 ||
Then, having drawn a mandala on the ground, one should cause [the deity] to descend with the syllable *praṇava*.
One should offer the oblation of cold clarified butter (śītāghāra) from a vessel smeared with ghee,
using the six-limbed Bhairava mantra accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* exclamation.

The word "śītā" (cool) is for the purpose of destroying the defect of non-cooking through the pervasion of Soma; in this interval, the teachers say that one should offer the oblation while uttering "svā" over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and "hā" over the fire. Thus, the sacrificial porridge, consisting of Agni and Soma, is perfected through the process of refinement. As it is stated in the Śruti:
"Indeed, for one who offers this *ājya* oblation to Agni and Soma, this [offering] of his becomes immortal.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmṛgendrottara*.
"These two libations (āghāra) prescribed for the cooked oblation (caru) have Agni and Soma as their essence;
that [oblation] serves to attain immortality, because it is of the nature of Agni and Soma. || 110 ||
Then—
having prepared a mandala near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should lay down a seat of darbha grass;
having placed a vessel (sthālī) upon it, one should deposit the remnants of the oblation together with the collection of mantras.
One should cause [the substance] to fall into the fire with each individual oblation using the Bhairava mantra;

having first uttered the Niṣkala mantra along with its limbs and faces, one should offer the oblation into the fire by pronouncing "svā" for the fire and "hā" for the sacrificial food (caru)—this is the procedure for the *saṃpāta* oblation. || 111 ||
In this context, for the purpose of manifesting the nature of Agni and Soma, he describes the *saṃpāta-homa* everywhere:
"Recalling the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) with exactly one hundred and eight [repetitions]. (112)

Then, O Goddess, at the beginning of the dust-pile, and likewise upon the knife and the two instruments, one should perform the sprinkling of chalk, sesame seeds, and clarified butter with the root mantra. || 113 ||

The meaning is that, in performing that [rite], one should employ the root mantra by recollecting the supreme nectar whose nature is consciousness and bliss, and by acting in accordance with its power. || 112-113 ||
Then, having divided that *caru*— which is situated in the vessel— into three parts,
one should offer the first portion to Śiva, and the [other] portions to the Śiva-fire and the practitioners (*sādhakas*). || 3.114 ||

Having prepared an extraordinary *caru*— one that consists of three portions for the sake of Śiva, the fire, and the practitioner— one should offer the first portion from the top of the portion set aside for Śiva (which has been divided for the purpose of the vessel, the jar, and so forth) to Śiva, who resides within the mandala. || 114 ||
He states the application of the portions for Agni and the others:
"One should offer the second portion into the fire; the third is for the practitioners (*sādhakas*). The practitioners are those who worship Śiva."
He states the procedure for the offering to Śiva:
"Having taken the sacrificial oblation (caru) in a vessel, one should worship it with the Bhairava mantra. (3.115)
Having brought [the deity] with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should present him to the abode.
Immediately thereafter—one should present a tenth part to those residing in the heart and other locations of the enclosure. (3.116)
It is exactly the same for the water jar as well...
the ritual procedure for the water jar together with its retinue is like that of the mandala. || 116 ||
Then—
in the fire— the sacrificial oblation of cooked rice (caru) is offered with a ladle (sruva).
Here—
One hundred oblations are to be offered to Bhairava, and a tenth part for his limbs.

O Dear One, one should cover and set aside whatever remains for the practitioners (*sādhakas*). "Remains" refers to the portion that has been left over. One should set it aside because the practitioners—the disciples who are as yet uninitiated—lack the qualification to consume the consecrated sacrificial porridge (*caru*). (117)
Now he describes the oblation for the purpose of formal acceptance:
"In the case of Vināyaka, one hundred oblations are to be offered, and likewise during the ritual acquisition of the ground. (3.118)
For the purpose of accepting *bhuvaḥ*, which is presided over by the goal of liberation brought down from above, there is the application: "Oṃ bhuve svāhā, Oṃ śriye svāhā.
One hundred oblations should be offered for each. || 118 ||
Furthermore:

"In the same way, here in the *adhivāsa* [rite], there is an oblation (*huti*) one hundred and eight times; this is for the purpose of the *adhivāsa* previously determined. The meaning is that the oblation should be offered to Bhairava.
Now,
[the following] is the occasion for expiation in cases of both natural (anuloma) and inverse (viloma) unions.
O Goddess of the gods, when there is deficiency or excess, there is an oblation of one hundred and eight [times] with the root mantra.

*Anuloma* refers to the sequence of the ritual procedure; *viloma* is its reverse or otherwise. Regarding that deficiency or excess, *prāyaścitta* means the mental resolve (*citta*) toward austerity (*tapas*) for that purpose, performed with the root mantra.
The oblation is performed with the mantra ending in: "I offer for atonement, svāhā. || 119 ||
In order to purify the disciple, he performs the preparation of the seat:
"Then, O fair-faced one, having worshipped Bhairava and requested his permission," (3.120).
Listen to how the rite for the *śiśu* (the child/initiate) is to be performed.

By "the child" (*śiśu*) is meant one in whom the state of Śiva has sprouted through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). By "rite" (*karma*) is meant that which takes the form of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*);
he explains it as follows:
Having made a small mandala at the door, one should place darbha grass upon it.
Having prepared the seat with the syllable *praṇava*, one should cause the disciple to sit upon it, with feet even, body erect, face serene, and hands joined in *añjali*. (3.122)
At the gate or near the gate, standing with the body erect, facing the auspicious direction, and with a serene countenance. || 122 ||
The Guru, facing east, should sprinkle him with the weapon-mantra using the water of Śiva;
he should strike him on the head with ashes and touch him with the weapon-mantra.
Striking with ashes is for the ascetic; likewise is touching or contact [with them]. || 123 ||
One should perform three repetitions neither above nor below the navel.

These three consecrations are for the purpose of loosening the bonds; the three below are for the removal of the three impurities (mala), while those above are for the stimulation of the three powers (śakti).

Then, for the child whose body and other parts have been purified precisely because the bonds have thus become loosened—one should worship Śiva, together with the constituent parts of the ritual placement (nyāsa), by means of the Bhairava-mantra. || 3.124 ||
Furthermore:
having sprinkled the cloth with the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra;
one should worship it with the Bhairava-mantra itself.
With that very [object], he should likewise cover his face. || 125 ||

The covering of the mouth, which is the locus of the sensory organs, is for the purpose of preventing the outward diffusion of the instruments of action and for turning inward the light of Bhairava that has been placed within. 124.
Regarding the restraint of the sense organs and organs of action,
it is said that one should cause the disciple to enter preceded by the firm support of the principal hand: "Then, having grasped him with both hands, one should enter the interior of the curtain."
Then also—
having turned [it] toward the face of the deity... and of that...
...one should cause the flower to be placed in the hand. || 3-126 ||
Having given a single flower, consecrated at its root, for the purpose of correctly determining the fall of the flower;
And then—
having cast [the flower] with the *dhāman* mantra...
he should employ the command, "Cast the flower," and at the moment of its falling, he should recite the root mantra (*mūla*).
The meaning is "the Guru."
Then,
having opened his mouth,
one should show him the Cause together with Sadāśiva, along with the hosts of Vidyās and Mantras. (3.127)
The "Cause" refers to Niṣkalanātha, who exists together with Sadāśiva, the Lord endowed with all parts (sakala-bhaṭṭāraka). || 127 ||
Then,
liberated from the veil of ignorance and awakened, that bound soul (paśu),
having prostrated like a staff upon the earth, bows down again and again. (3.128)

By the word "ignorance," the pervasion [of the cause] in the removal of the cloth is stated. The bound soul (paśu) who was in a prior state has now become awakened; for this very reason, he is again filled with wonder from beholding the nature of the Lord, unprecedented even after thousands of births.

He gazes again at the Blessed One. By moving like a staff, through the casting aside of the state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) such as the body and so forth, his fitness for following into the immersion (samāveśa) of Śiva is demonstrated. 128.
Therefore,
he— having accomplished his purpose, with a joyful soul... and him—
Raising up the child whose eyes were wide with joy, he should take him by the right hand and lead him forward. (3.129)

"Having raised [him] with eyes wide with joy through contact with one's own nature, which consists of consciousness and bliss"—the meaning is that having first been submerged for a long time in the plane of the body and so forth, he is then caused to emerge by means of a method (*yukti*). "The right-hand [path]" (*dakṣiṇām*) means that which is favorable and identical with Śiva, and not that which belongs to the bonds (*pāśaka*) consisting of the body. (129)
And facing the venerable Lord Aghora— having prepared a small mandala there with a flower as the seat for the *praṇava*,
one should place the child upon it with the upper body erect and facing north. (3.130)
The Guru, standing facing the east, should perform the sprinkling and other rites;

by the word "and others" (ādi), striking and touching are included as before. Regarding the instruction "he should cause [them] to be performed," he should employ the mantras while they are being performed, through the entry of their potency.
Then, having seated [the disciple] upon this seat, one should perform the rite of sakalīkaraṇa.

For the sake of attaining specific fruits, for the seeker of liberation or the practitioner who has undergone the general purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and has even beheld the true form of the Lord—
[it is said]: "In the worship of Śiva, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and so forth, one whose body has been made *sakalīkṛta* (endowed with the limbs of the deity)..."
"Not otherwise than by its prior nature" (3-146),
as will be stated; therefore, for the sake of enjoyment or liberation as appropriate,
and for the sake of accomplishing the specific fruit of being worthy of worshipping Śiva and so forth, [the author sets forth] the procedure for this sakalīkaraṇa.
Having performed [this], the connection is with the distant phrase: "one should subsequently deposit the path of the digits (kalādhvan). || 131 ||
He instructs on the sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual of making complete) in sequence:
"Having smeared the two hands with fragrant substances, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra. (3.132)
Having enveloped these two with the Kavaca mantra, one should drench them with nectar.
For those very two,
one should prepare an infinite seat and perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the limbs of Bhairava.
"Bhairava and the limbs" is a dvandva compound. || 133 ||
He describes the deposition of the body (dehanyāsa):
"O Dear One, having joined the Self with the ether, the body of the disciple should be dried up;
then, having meditated on the fiery concentration (dhāraṇā), one should burn that disciple with the weapon-mantra. (3.134)
One should visualize the body as burnt, free from smoke and flames;
then, once it has been reduced to ashes and become tranquil, one should drench it with nectar.
One should contemplate the body as being like the sky and consciousness as being like gold and fire;
first, one should perform the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa) and then place the lotus with the syllable Om (praṇava).

Above that, one should meditate upon oneself as auspicious and consisting of light; having recited the mūrti-mantra, one should conceive of oneself as having become the very form [of the deity]. (3.137)
All that should be accomplished through meditative cultivation. || 137 ||
He asks, "How so? and says:
"By the mantra previously extracted"—the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*). By that—
"The sequence previously described in its entirety, beginning with [the verse] 'By means of the dissolution which is differentiated' (2.36), must be followed. The same applies hereafter."
Just as before, by the savor of the firm support of the immersion into Śiva—.................... one should indeed flood [the disciple] with nectar.
Now—
The placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) is performed as before, up to the thirty-eight kalās.

Then, right here, for the sake of creating the body consisting of the pure principles (śuddhatattva) both internally and externally, one should subsequently deposit the path of the *kalās* according to the sequence of emanation, following the order beginning with Śāntyatītā:
[the lines] are like crystal, black, red, white, and yellow. (3.139)
The *kalās* beginning with Śāntyatītā should be known as being of the nature of the *tattvas*;

"being of the nature of the *tattvas*" means they have attained the form of the *tattvas* starting from space (*kha*) and ending with earth (*pṛthivī*). For this very reason, meditation upon them in their respective proper forms is appropriate; thus, [this is] for the purpose of the emanation of the pure *tattvas*.

The deposition of the five *kalās* has been taught here for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*). However, for the initiation of the *putrakas* and others, this will be explained differently in a future chapter according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) for the purpose of initiation; one must not fall into the error of thinking that this [present teaching] is irrelevant to the current context. || 139 ||

After performing the placement (nyāsa) of all the aforementioned mantras, one should invoke [the deity] into the abode, perform the placement of the limbs (aṅga), and thus the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) becomes established. || 3-140 ||
Just as one [conceives] the Self within the internal organ, so too should one commence the worship;
having uttered the *dhāman*, one should again establish [the deity] both externally and internally. (3-141)

"Reconnection (saṃdhāna) consists of the channels (nāḍī) and mantras, both external and internal"—this refers to Bhairava as the object residing within the body and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). However, the notion that it is "divided by the interior of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila)" is incorrect;
rather—
Having meditated upon the All-pervading Lord within the hand of Śiva as the brilliantly blazing collection of mantras,
and having uttered the [divine] abode and performed the union, he should place his hand upon the head of the disciple.
With the hand of Śiva facing downward, one should touch the heart and the back;
[one should touch] the pervasive Lord, who is intensely blazing for the sake of burning away the bonds.

Having performed the "aiming" (*saṃdhāna*) as before through the sequence of the channels and mantras, [one should perform it] even at the two abodes of the Blessed One, namely the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and the heart.

Since there is the state of being enveloped by bonds (pāśa) in that foundational ground, there is a touching with the "Hand of Śiva"— which consists of the pervasion of the five powers beginning with consciousness (cid-ādi-śakti) manifested through the five fingers— for the purpose of igniting the innate nature of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-svabhāva) by burning away those bonds.
Having raised [the disciple] and placed a flower in his joined palms (añjali), [he should do so] with the Bhairava mantra. || 143 ||

Having caused [the disciple] to enter, one should worship Śambhu... [and then] "having raised him up. Since the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ud* has the sense of "exertion," the meaning is: having caused him to undertake the exertion of worshipping the Blessed One. The entry [into the maṇḍala] is by means of the command: "Worship Śiva here in the maṇḍala."
It is the induction of one who is oriented toward devotion and faith into a state of total dedication, as in the phrase "having been introduced to grammar.
Regarding the word *arcayet*: it is derived from the root *arca* with the suffix *ṇic*. (143)
The disciple, likewise having been instructed in the mantra by the teacher, should utter "Śivam" and cast the flower. Then—
Having gone out, one should prostrate like a staff before the deity;
the term "maṇḍala" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
Likewise—.................. three times clockwise. || 3-144 ||

One should salute [the Lord] situated within the fire-pot of Śiva and also standing upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). This is done three times—that is, in each of the three modes—prostrating like a staff throughout the entire path of time, while circumambulating and making the Lord stand to one's own right with the desire: "May You, the Right One, be intent on the manifestation of my own true nature."
One should praise. || 144 ||
And thus:
"In the worship of Śiva, the fire-sacrifice, and so forth, one whose body has been made complete (sakalīkṛtavigraha) [should perform the rites]. (3.145)

"Otherwise, he would not be worthy of worship in his original form"—this should be applied to both parts of the sentence. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), recitation, meditation, and so forth are included. (3-145)
Furthermore:
"Having led him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, without letting him out of the hands of his disciple... (3.146)
Then, in the direction to the left of oneself, one should draw a mandala with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having offered a seat with the syllable Om, one should place the disciple upon it.

By means of his own hand—which consists of the expansion of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) through the splendor of the mantras being deposited—he draws forth the powers of knowledge and action from the child (*asya*), who has been immersed [in the fire], by means of the technique of pulling with the hand; this is for the purpose of ensuring the non-separation of the hands.
"In the right" (*savye*) refers to the right [hand]; "the child" (*śiśum*) refers to one whose nature as Śiva has not yet reached full maturity. (147)
Having seated him, he should place a blade of *darbha* grass in his hand with the *Bhairava* mantra.
The root of the *darbha* held in the disciple's hand should be placed between the ankles of the preceptor, while its tip remains in the disciple's hand. (3.148)

It stands between the two hands, which are extended and take the form of the left and right branches; thus it is "situated in the hands. Regarding "of the two shanks," this means at the junction of the thighs and knees, including both the shanks and the lower parts of the shanks (upajaṅgha).
[148] He describes the pervasiveness of the *darbha* grass as follows:
The *piṅgalā*, the central channel, has emerged from the body of the disciple;
it has become the *darbha* grass here and has merged into the channel of the Guru. (3.149)
Then, for the purpose of joining the channels, three oblations are offered by Bhairava;
through that channel, [the deity] should enter the heart of the disciple once. (3-150)

However, for the purpose of seizing and attracting, Bhairava is partless (niṣkala); the application [of this] is found in the mantra: "Oṃ, may the central channel of the disciple merge into my own central channel, svāhā. This occurs precisely preceded by the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*), which consists of the attainment of oneness (*ekātmya*).
Seizing and attracting are applicable [in this context], as it is said in the venerable Spanda:
"This very [state] is the seizing of the Self" (4.2). || 150 ||
Therefore he says:
"Because at the time of initiation one repeatedly grasps and releases [the breath] in this manner, for that purpose there is the collection of channels. (3.151)

"The teacher becomes the very self of the disciple" is the remainder of the end of the preceding quarter-verse. In the initiation of the *samayin*, there is the drawing forth of the disciple's self from the heart to the *dvādaśānta*, and from there, its attainment of a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) within one's own heart; however, in the initiation of the *putraka* and others, it is merely the [severing of] the fetters (*pāśa*).
The additional [instructions] regarding the union with the womb of Vāgīśī and so forth are as follows. || 151 ||

Now, in order to manifest the nature of Agni and Soma simultaneously within the disciple and the fire by means of mantras deposited upon all the substrates, he describes the *saṃpāta-homa* (the oblation of the final residue):
"Then, having performed [the rite] with the Bhairava mantra upon the ground at the head of the disciple..."
One should offer an oblation of clarified butter with all the mantras, using the *dhruva* mantra as the final one.
The word "should offer oblations" (juhuyāt) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 152 ||
To explain how this is done, he says:
"Having recited the root mantra, one should cast 'svā' into the fire;
the syllable 'ha' is the descent upon the head of the disciple, impelled by Śiva. (3.153)
The meaning is clear. || 153 ||
He explains the *saṃpāta*:
"But as for those mantras which reside within the body of the disciple, both externally and internally;
and those which were worshipped in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), beginning from the primary abode (*dhāman*) and extending to the final enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). (3.154)
The simultaneous satiation of these [mantras] is called *sampāta*;
in this rite, it is performed with three oblations for each individual mantra. (3.155)

The meaning is that "convergence" (saṃpāta) refers to the simultaneous manifestation everywhere of one's own essential nature, which consists of Agni and Soma; it is a transformative purification (saṃskāra). || 155 ||
Furthermore—
the meaning is that, having then raised the disciple up, one should perform the satiation of the mantra for that purpose.
Therein—having offered one hundred oblations to Bhairava, there is an offering of ten [oblations] for the heart-mantra and the others. || 3.156 ||
The meaning is that it should be [performed] with a tenth part. || 156 ||
Then, having risen by means of the [mantra] *dhāman*, one should offer the oblation and satisfy [the deity] with the *pūrṇāhuti*.
By the word "having risen," he reminds [the practitioner] of the procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Having thus explained the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) pertaining to the initiation of the initiate (*samayin*) in general, [the author] now speaks in order to establish the specific procedure for the "son" (*putraka*) and others, regarding the ritual of the *pāśasūtra* which will follow; therein,
he states the following in order to activate the mantras for the purpose of binding the fetters (*pāśas*):
One should perform the illumination of the mantras in sequence, beginning with the abode (dhāma) and ending with the weapon (astra). || 157 ||
He explains how this is done:
"Uttering the root mantra between two *huṃ* syllables, one should offer oblations beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *phaṭ*. (3.158)
This very [power] is declared here in the *Dīpanā* to be the "universal class" (*jāti*) of all [mantras], beginning with the Heart-mantra.
It is called "universal class" because by means of it, a specific application of mantra arises in accordance with its respective function.
The word "heart" (hṛd) indicates the mouth and other [organs].
And this is remembered as the kindling of the mantras for the purpose of binding the fetters. (3.159)
And those mantras, being ignited, serve as the instruments for accomplishing the "work of the bound soul" (paśukārya);
the "work of the bound soul" is initiation (dīkṣā).
He who possesses these instruments is of great power—
the teacher is declared to be the instrument;
the meaning is that he is the agent.
How can mantras be the instrument for one who possesses a body and so forth? To this he says: "Because [the teacher] is traditionally remembered as being of the nature of Śiva. (3.160)
The meaning is that even while the body exists, one consists of the state of "I am Śiva," which is the unconditioned light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).

They say this because only such a person is authorized for grace (*anugraha*): "In initiation, Śiva, residing in the teacher (*ācārya*), is the direct agent; however, [Śiva] situated within the mandala is the instrumental cause."

Consequently, [your claim] that "at the time of Sarasvatī’s impregnation, Śiva was the direct agent (sākṣātkartā) and the teacher (ācārya) was the instigator (prayojaka)," and so forth, contradicts what you yourself have stated. Furthermore, since there is no relationship of instigated and instigator (prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva) either here or in the preceding portion of the text, this [claim] is simply false. Therefore:
The preceptor authorized here is one who consists of the very self of Śiva, the mass of consciousness (cidghana), which is the cause of the arising and the manifestation of all mantras;
the meaning is that the awakening of the mantras must necessarily be performed by him. || 160 ||
When a cruel rite is to be performed, one should employ the mantras after having inflamed them;
one should always employ the expressive words in accordance with the nature of the cruel species.

The "cruel action" of the nooses refers to the severing of bonds and so forth; the "kindling" of the mantras consists precisely in their application according to the previously mentioned sequence of cruel classes.
And at this juncture— one should contemplate the objects of expression as having faces made terrifying by frowns;
such is the cruelty of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser, even in other cases involving cruel rites directed toward the practitioner.
It must be considered.
Therefore, during the rites of nourishment and so forth, one should visualize those belonging to the lunar class as being of a gentle nature and gentle form when the moon is present. (3-162)
The gentle class consists of vaṣaṭ and so forth. || 162 ||
He declares that for which the kindling of the mantra is intended:
"Thereafter, I shall explain the ritual of the fetters (pāśakarma)...
And this is for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the future *putraka* initiate. "Thereafter" (*tataḥ*) means immediately following the kindling of the mantra.

The meaning is: I shall now describe that rite of preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), which pertains to the future thread of bonds (*pāśasūtra*) intended for use in the ritual of the bonds (*pāśakarma*) and the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the spiritual sons (*putraka*) and others.
He states that sequence as follows:
"The thread passed through the girl's [finger],
having been tripled and then tripled again..."

"The maiden has assumed a form that imitates the power of another, yet without having produced any transformation [in herself]. Therefore, regarding the fetters (*pāśas*)— consisting of the forms of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārma*— which have proceeded from the fundamental ground (*mūlabhūmi*),
which possess the pervasion of the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) composed of the three groups of qualities such as *sattva*, and so forth:

The cutting of the bonds of existence and so forth is for the purpose of uprooting them along with their roots; such is the intention regarding the state of being performed by a maiden and the tripling of the tripling.
Now, this is the thread for binding the fetters. || 3-163 ||
Having sprinkled it with the Śiva-water using the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra;
then, having worshipped it according to the rule with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Having grasped it from the head down to the thumbs, one should extend it over the disciple whose body is held steady...
[reciting] "Oṃ, obeisance to the thread that binds the fetters"— this is the procedure for worship.
The contemplation of the pervasion of all time [is performed] for the disciple—that is, for the *putraka* and others, but not for the *samayin*.

"Stiffness of the body" arises from the binding of the fetters (*pāśas*) through the pervasive lack of activity in the body, senses, and so forth. The person holds that thread with the right hand, or the woman with the left hand.

To say that one should hold it on the crown of the head is incorrect; since the hands of the initiate are occupied by holding the blades of *darbha* grass, one should therefore hang the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*) upon the topknot (*śikhā*) itself. Thus, the single power of action belonging to the Supreme Lord remains in the form of a bond through the concealment of its own true nature.

Thus, in this [system], there is a single thread for the *pāśasūtra*. However, in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara) and other scriptures, the three powers themselves abide as the three principles (*tritattva*);
with this intention, they speak of "three threads. This is merely a difference in methodological procedure (*prakriyā*). || 164 ||
And he should contemplate that thread of his as having become a channel (nāḍī). || 3-165 ||
And that Suṣumnā, the central channel, is endowed with all the channels;
[it is worshipped] beginning with the syllable Oṃ and ending with a salutation by its own name. (3-166)
One should grasp the channel residing within the body of the disciple and join it to the thread;

"by means of meditative cultivation" (bhāvanayā) is the ellipsis. [This means that] within the channel which has become the thread, all the channels are joined and united through meditative cultivation. || 166 ||
Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should veil her with the *kavaca* [armor-mantra]. || 3-167 ||
Right here, he states the oblation for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity:

"One should offer three proximity-oblations (saṃnidhānāhuti) consisting of one's own name, word, and genus"—this is the ellipsis. The practical application (*prayoga*) in this case is: "Oṃ suṣumnāyai svāhā. || 167 ||
Then, having again sprinkled the disciple’s heart with the Śiva-water weapon-mantra (śivāmbho'stra), || 3-168 ||
One should strike with the weapon-flower... and thus...
the consciousness (cit) becomes withdrawn into the heart.
The meaning is that although she is all-pervasive, she becomes fixed solely within the heart.

Thereafter, either by means of the sequence of yoga or through meditative cultivation—by means of the yoga of uttering the syllable *huṃ* with the exhaling breath—one should enter [the seed-syllable] into the heart. (3.169)
Having entered through the opening of the channel, one should contemplate the consciousness of the disciple as being shaped like a *kadamba* bud and resembling a shimmering star. (3.170)
Having severed that which resides in the heart with the sword-weapon accompanied by the *huṃ phaṭ* ending and the [seed-syllable] of its class,

[one uses] the sword which is indeed the partless weapon; with that, one severs the disciple’s subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) so that it is no longer desirous of separation from the mere rays [of consciousness].
And by means of the power in the form of a goad, one should draw [the object] gradually until the limit of the śakti is reached.
"Aṅkuśa" refers to that which is known as the curved lock of hair at the back; its limit is the *śakti*, the *dvādaśānta*, and that is here [designated] as *nāsikya*.
Then—
having grasped [the breath] at the *dvādaśānta* and encapsulated it with the heart-mantra,
one should join it to the thread conceived as the channel by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. (3.172)
Having meditated upon the pervasive [deity], one should veil it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).

By means of the ritual application—preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava* and the *niṣkala* [mantra]—"I join the consciousness of Devadatta to the thread of bonds; obeisance"—there arises the meditation on the pervasiveness of this [consciousness] which has been joined to the body of the thread. 172.
Then, having performed worship for him—
with three oblations offered by means of Bhairava— for the sake of [his] presence.
The word "should give" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 173 ||
He states the purpose of the procedure for the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra):
"The second [body] is the body of the cord, wherein these bonds reside;
they are to be bound, severed, and likewise burnt in the place of the cord..."

In the Sūtrasthāna, since the vital breath and the body— which are the substratum of all bonds and the cause of their concealment— are imperceptible, it is impossible to directly [address] bondage and so forth; therefore, having fashioned a "thread-body" (*sūtradeha*) as a substitute for them by outlining the future body to be purified, [the text treats] the bonds residing therein.

The meaning is that one should bind, cut, and burn. Regarding the word "these" (*ime*), they refer to those which will be mentioned immediately hereafter in the scripture: "That by which this [world] exists, indeed, through experience (*bhoga*).
Therefore, [this applies] to those whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) after initiation; however, it does not apply to that which is the cause for the worship of the Lord and so forth.
He says that burning and so forth are appropriate: "...... not in the case of a physical body" (174).
He now describes the number, names, and essential natures of the bonds (pāśas) in sequence:
"The bonds are to be understood as threefold: those born of Māyā, those born of Āṇava, and those born of Karma.
These are obstructors of consciousness and consist of both effect and cause. (3-175)

Since the state of arising from *māyā* and the state of existing within *māyā* also exist in other impurities (*mala*), the impurity whose nature is the manifestation of a distinct object of knowledge is called *māyīya* (pertaining to *māyā*) by conventional usage alone. For this very reason, it is said elsewhere: "Now, the impurities of the self known as *māyā*... and so forth.

This is the term "āṇava" (pertaining to the individual soul). It consists of the sense of being incomplete (*apūrṇammanyatā*), which takes the form of restlessness (*lolikā*). "Karma" refers to actions such as sacrifice or the killing of a Brahmin; that which is born from this, or rather that which is mounted upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*) therein, consists of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). And these [three impurities] possess the quality of obstructing consciousness.
The nature of being a bond (pāśatva) consists precisely in the state of being reduced to the condition of a subordinate quality (guṇabhāva). || 175 ||
He clarifies the nature of these as cause and effect: "Impurity (mala) is the cause, while action (karman) is the effect;
beyond that, impurity and action are both the cause, because action is the cause of impurity."

Because the māyīya [impurity] is the cause, that which follows it—the māyīya—is the effect of *mala* and *karman*; this is the meaning. Although the *kārma* [impurity] exists when the *māyīya*, which consists in the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge, is present, nevertheless it is not caused by that [māyīya], because for the knowers (*jñānins*) who possess full expansion [of consciousness], [the *kārma* does not arise].

Since that [object] is not perceived even when its existence is present, it follows that it becomes an object only for those who consider themselves incomplete; therefore, what has been stated is indeed superior.
And therefore:
the causal form consists of the body, the worlds, and so forth. (3.176)
The state of being a support (ādhāratā) is the state of being the basis for enjoyment; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [other] entities (bhāva) are included. || 176 ||
And here, regarding the occasional (naimittika) impurity consisting of illusion (māyīya-mala)—
the "cause" (nimitta) is that which is called desire (abhilāṣa); the meaning is that it is the individual impurity (āṇava-mala) in the form of craving (lolikā).
He asks, "By what alone? and says:
"By various causal forms;
the meaning is that it is joined with auxiliary factors consisting of merit and demerit."
He follows the subject at hand: "And he should observe them in the thread according to the cause of binding and being bound. (3.177)

One should contemplate those nooses by means of the principle of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, which will be explained later; for what purpose? For the sake of binding those who are to be bound, that is to say, because they themselves are the cause of their own bondage. || 177 ||
Now, he describes the sequential application of these [mantras] to the bodies of the disciples, preceded by striking and seizing:
"The striking of the fetters (pāśas) must be performed with the [mantra] ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and [the appropriate] seed-syllable (*jāti*)."
Beginning with the Praṇava of one's own name, in the sequence starting from Śāntyatīta.

Having uttered the *praṇava*, the seed-syllable of the Śāntyatītā level, and the abode, one should recite the mantra: "To the Śāntyatītā who pervades the fetters residing in the self of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ. || 178 ||
One should strike him on the head with a flower; then, having grasped [him],
one should join him with *hūṃ* and the other [syllables].
Having grasped [the essence] by means of the yoga ending with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
One should unite [the soul] with the light (dhāman) by means of the thread,

using the previously mentioned mantra which ends with the salutation (*namaskāra*) and is joined with the root-mantra preceded by the *praṇava*; having grasped the three bonds (*pāśatraya*) with the *saṃhāramudrā* to be described hereafter, one should discard the previously stated birth-status (*jāti*).
With this very mantra, ending with the word "namaskāra" and followed by one's own name, one should join it to the cord of the noose. || 179 ||
He extends this very sequence to the *kalās* of pacification (*śānti*) and so forth by means of the method of joining them with the names of one's own mantras:
"In this way, having grasped the bonds (*pāśas*) of pacification and the rest from their locations, one should join them. (3.180)
The locations here, in sequence, are the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
And one should meditate upon these three kinds of bonds that pervade the path of the five principles (tattvas),
immediately following the initiation into the Kalās.

Since it will be stated later [in 3.140], "But those *kalās* are indeed the *tattvas*," the meaning is that they pervade the entire path (*adhvan*) by means of those five *tattvas* which are of the nature of *kalās* and constitute their very self.
Now, one might ask: how is there the pervasion of the *kalās* by the bonds (*pāśas*), and how can the bonds have existence in the state of the *śāntā* and *śāntyatītā*, which reside above *māyā*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The supreme power of the Lord, called action (kriyā), pervades these three. || 181 ||
This power of the Supreme Lord, which is eternally inseparable from Him and established under five names according to the divisions beginning with Śāntyatītā, is called Kriyā;
having assumed the state of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), it manifests the diversity of objective phenomena (idantā).
Having attained the state of the five elements beginning with Śāntyatītā, she pervades the three impurities (malas).
As it has been said:
"This power of Śiva, whose nature is action, is the one who leads the bound souls (paśus)."
"...the binder" (Spanda-kārikā 4.18).
For this very reason, as long as the manifestation of "this-ness" persists, the fetters remain in accordance with its propriety.

Thus, even in the state beyond peace (śāntyatītāpada), that purification is appropriate. And when the pervader (vyāpaka) is purified, there occurs the complete purification of that which is pervaded (vyāpya), whose life-force is that [pervader]. Therefore, because the impurities (mala) are pervaded by the *kalā* that constitutes their very essence, they are purified by means of designations corresponding to that [essence]; and that [purification]...
It is precisely the emergence [of consciousness] in the form of the power of the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty, which is eternally inseparable [from Him].
As it has been said:
"The knower situated on the path of the dog brings about the attainment of perfection" (Spanda-kārikā 4.18).
Thus,

the purification of these [energies], which appear as if they have attained differentiation because their ultimate non-dual nature is submerged by means of mantras whose essence consists of the determined power and potency of this [reality], is entirely logical. || 181 ||
And thus:
"The perceiver of the object to be contained should cause the container to be grasped by the bound soul. (3.182)
The digits (kalās) are that which is to be supported; the impurities (malas) are the support. || 182 ||
Now, through the pervasion of the Supreme Lord’s power, he states its essence:
"Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should satisfy the fetters within the thread according to the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā."
And that libation consists of three oblations each for [each of the deities]. (3.183)
Therefore, for the sake of bringing the nooses into proximity, one should inflame those very nooses;
by means of the power of the mantra, one should render them simultaneously fully ripened, in accordance with the suitability for attaining all the enjoyments of the process to be realized.
He asks, "How so? and replies:
"And by means of one's own name, the genus-syllable, and the sound *phaṭ*, there are three [syllables] for each. (3.184)
"Having offered the oblations"—this is the ellipsis. Here, "jāti" refers to the syllable *huṃ*. The sequence for the recitation of the mantra is as before. || 184 ||
And this [process] proceeds from the consciousness of the disciple— for the purpose of effecting the separation of the fetters (pāśas), there must be their "kindling" (dīpana).
Precisely because of this:
Then the blazing nooses are to be bound [upon them] by means of striking, seizing, and so forth.

From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [we understand] the giving of the knot (*granthidāna*) so that there may be no further sprouting. For those very fetters whose vigor has been inflamed, "binding" (*bandhana*) consists in the removal of their autonomy regarding the obscuration of the disciple's consciousness.
He states "striking" (*tāḍana*): [185]...
One should strike those [deities] residing in the Sūtra with flowers, as if they were residing within one's own body, in due order.

(Regarding "as if residing within one's own body": it means just as if they were in one's own body. "In due order" means according to the sequence of the previously mentioned mantras, their pervasion, and so forth; one should strike them in that manner once they have been struck.
He states the method for binding: "Having encapsulated [the name] with the *dhāman* and with its own name, once each. (3-186)
But regarding the act of binding, this is the procedure:

immediately after [reciting] the *dhāman*, the *śāntyatītā*, and the seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should utter, "I bind the *śāntyatītā* which pervades the bonds residing in the self of Devadatta," and then [the syllable] *ṅamaḥ* for the *dhāman*.
Uttering the final word, one should tie a knot at the top of the cord of the noose; the same applies to the others.
Thus it says:
"........one should cause knots to be tied in the thread.
Regarding the term "knots," there are five by way of pervasion.
Furthermore:
"In bondage, there is a limitation of both the action and its object. (3.187)
Not only the knots, but also at the time of the bondage of karma— of the object consisting of the pure and so forth,

and of the world and so forth which consists of the impurity of Māyā— one should determine the measure of the impurity of Āṇava (indicated by the word "ca"), as well as its fixed pervasion of the paths (*adhvan*). Likewise, in the [tattva] Nivṛtti, there is one.

The scope [of this work] will consist of the earthly reality (*pārthiva-tattva*) and the one hundred and eight worlds beginning with Kālāgni; for action (*karman*) pervades up to the end of the levels of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vidyā,
whereas impurity (*mala*), by way of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), extends even to the end of Śāntā and Śāntyatītā.

One should reflect upon this: even in its subtle form, existence truly persists; all this is interconnected. And thus, through the conjunction with bonds, the individual soul (jīva)—situated within the thirty-six principles (tattvas)—experiences worldly enjoyment.
It is pure.
Furthermore, he says that it is not otherwise because of the severing of the bonds:
"...and not otherwise."
Not in this sense.
He states the subject at hand: "Having placed the fetters in the vessel, one should offer the *saṃpāta* oblation once. (3-188)
"Pāśān" refers to the *pāśasūtra*; "having established" means having released it from the body of the disciple. "The *sampātahoma* is performed with all the mantras at the point of contact" (3.142).
This has been determined in such passages as the above. || 188 ||
Then one should offer these nooses, situated within the cavity of the vessel, upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila);
for the intention is that these reside in the interval between the object of knowledge (vedya) and the knower (vedaka) located within the middle of the vessel.

And by means of the pervasive application of the armor (*kavaca*) and the veil (*avaguṇṭhana*), [he should act] upon the sacrificial ground (*śthaṇḍila*). When the Blessed One has been thus invoked there, the meaning is that he should make this petition: "The bonds (*pāśāḥ*) of this bound soul (*paśuḥ*) have been bound by you alone; having entered my own body, [O Lord,] please release them. Thus he should perform the request.
And in the same way—
having led [the deity] and offered [him] into the jar...
one should address the Blessed One residing therein as follows:
...protect the nooses, O All-pervading Lord! 3-189 ||

And their protection consists of the consecration (*adhivāsa*) which, for these [substances] that would otherwise be destroyed by the initiation of future sons and others, currently effects the binding of their own functional capacity. || 189 ||
Then—
[the teacher] should release the disciple from the *darbha* grass previously prepared for the purpose of joining the channels (*nāḍī*).
Then, one should cause him to place a flower in his hand; with that,
he [should offer it] to the Blessed One together with the mantra.
One should worship upon the sacrificial ground, in the auspicious water-jar, and in the fire of Śiva.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [it is understood] that this also applies to the form of the Guru. || 190 ||
Then, having performed a circumambulation, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
Then, having raised him up, one should indeed give him the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances with the Bhairava mantra.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the tooth-stick are included; [this is performed] with the entire [mantra] of Bhairava. || 191 ||
Regarding this, he states the procedure:
"On a pure place, one should prepare three small mandalas with cow dung.
Seated upon one mandala, the child should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (3.192)
Having sat down, the wise one should consume the *caru* oblation in the second [mandala];
then, having sipped water and used a tooth-stick, he stands in the third mandala.
And having consumed [the sacrificial food], O Goddess of Gods, one should then discard it.

The *pañcagavya* is for the purpose of making one fit to eat the portion of *caru* prepared and consecrated; the *caru*, however, from this point forward, is for the realization of being both the enjoyer and the enjoyed whose nature is Śiva; and the tooth-stick is for the sake of the Supreme (*parā*).
In order to manifest purity; the word "having sipped water" (ācamya) should also be applied to the preceding [verse]. || 193 ||
And as for its falling: it is auspicious if it falls first to the east, then to the west, then upward, and finally toward the north. (3.194)

Know that for anyone else there is impurity; for them, there should be a hundred oblations with the *astra* mantra for the purpose of pacifying obstacles. And this [prescription] applies primarily to the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Then, for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of this rite up to this point,
the preceptor should subsequently perform the expiatory oblation with the Śiva-mantra.
Regarding the deficiency or excess of the ritual procedure when it results in mental distraction:

the connection [of the text] is that when there is mental distraction due to a deficiency or excess in the ritual procedure, one should offer a burnt oblation (*juhuyāt*) as its expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

And that [is performed] at the conclusion of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), according to the future sequence indicated by the statement, "The fire-rite as before... (4.31), and not immediately now; such is the meaning of the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*).
And in this case—having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one is purified from the transgression. || 3-196 ||
Now, in order to pursue rest in the root itself:
"Afterwards, one should satisfy [the deity] with a thousand or a hundred oblations," which means as long as his rest is accomplished.
The mantras expressing the limbs and faces [should be formed] by a tenth part...
immediately after these very [parts]—
...the offering of the food oblation (naivedya) into the fire. || 3-197 ||
Furthermore:

O fair-faced one, having performed the special worship, the offering of water (argha), the binding of mudrās, the hymn of praise, and the instrumental music, and then having consumed the sacrificial oblation (caru), one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana). || 3.198 ||
[This refers to] the Supreme Lord, by implication. || 198 ||
And having offered the arghya with the mantra of cessation (nirodhārghya), O fair-faced one,
one should withdraw it by means of exhalation (recaka) while recollecting Bhairava.
O fair-faced one, having filled [the vessel] with the fist and brought it forth, one should worship;

"situated in the fire" (agniṣṭha) refers to what was previously mentioned as "that which is situated in the fire," and "filled" means by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), having gathered it from the mandala.
Having caused [the deity] to stand in the fire by means of the *recaka* breath, one should likewise worship there as well. || 199 ||
Having grasped it with inhalation (pūraka), one should establish it once again. || 3-200 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] residing there, one should deposit him into the jar;
having honored Bhairava within the jar itself with flowers and other offerings, one should place him therein. (3.201)
This is out of the intention that the sacrificial hall should not remain unoccupied. || 201 ||
Then, O Dear One, having cast away the *nirmālya* from the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should touch it with cow dung; however,
the garland that has been removed does not belong here due to its connection with Caṇḍīśa.
And in that very place—having sprinkled [it] with the water of Śiva—one should prepare a bed for the disciple. (3.202)

O beloved, for a householder, however, a bed of darbha grass is prescribed, while for an ascetic it is ashes; the householder should be made to lie with his head toward the east, and the ascetic with his head toward the south.
Facing the southern face; the remainder is clear. || 203 ||
Then, with the *śikhā-mantra*—
O fair-faced one, one should perform the binding of the topknot (*śikhā-bandha*) for the disciple stationed there;
likewise—
One should perform the protection ritual while recollecting the sword, using the mantras beginning with Siddhārtha and Rocana.
For both the ascetic and the householder, one should sequentially visualize the protective wall of the weapon-mantra using lines drawn with ash, yellow pigment (rocanā), and so forth.
He concludes this as follows:
Then, having enveloped the disciple with the Kavaca mantra, one should cause him to sleep.
And having emerged from that very place, one should commence the *balikarma* (offering rite).
Regarding this, it is said:
"First, Bali was prepared with reverence toward all beings. (3.206)
Having grasped that, O Goddess of gods, one should cast it starting from the east and ending in the northeast;
it is prepared for the sake of the elemental reality and accomplished. || 206 ||
And here:
"The beings who exist in various forms, whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric," || 3-207 ||
Those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla who are well-disposed toward the sacrifice of Śiva, all beings beginning with Dhruva, and those situated in the directions beginning with the East; || 3-208 ||
One should cast [the offering] while reciting "may they be satisfied" (*tṛpyantu*) in conjunction with the utterance of *svāhā*.

Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and then reciting the mantra beginning with "those beings who" (*bhūtā ye*) and ending with "and those who are situated" (*sthitāśca ca*), one should cast the *bali* offering with the mantra "may they be satisfied, svāhā" (*tṛpyantu svāhā*). Here, in the middle, [the phrase] "beginning with Dhruva" (*dhruvādī*) is used.
For the purpose of reflecting upon the world of Dhruva; moreover, since Dhruva is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), this mantra should be recited beginning with that. || 208 ||
And he says that one should offer the *bali* preceded by worship:
"Having worshipped with prostrations and with perfumes and incenses in due order" (3.209).

From the east to the northeast, and including below and above, on all sides, while concluding the ritual of offerings during the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), he introduces other substances [with the words]:
"And the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*) stationed in the corners, as well as the outcasts (*śvapaca*) who have fallen [therein]. (3.210)
Having offered the bali-oblation to all and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), O fair-faced one,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) in due order.

The meaning is that on this occasion of bestowing grace, one should satisfy the desires of all these [disciples] by honoring them as much as possible. Regarding the term *caru*: it refers to that which remains after [the offering] and what was requested from the presence of the Lord.
"In sequence" means according to the traditional order of the Guru and the practitioner (*sādhaka*). || 211 ||
As it is said:
"Accompanied by his companions, the hero, with a single-pointed mind and concentrated, facing either east or north, stands individually within the mandala. (3-212)
A "hero" (vīra) is one who is unwavering, having abandoned the grasping at caste and other such distinctions; he is thus "composed" (samāhita), his mind fixed on the non-duality of Śiva.
One desiring worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) faces east during initiation, while one desiring liberation (mumukṣu) faces north;
each stands separately within the mandala for their respective assistants.

This is with the intention that there be no suspicion of confusion (*saṅkara*) due to the absence of equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) among the practitioner, the spiritual son (*putraka*), and the others; however, when resting in equal pervasion, there is no loss whatsoever even if they belong to a single mandala. || 212 ||
Therein—first one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the tooth-cleansing twig;
having thus consumed these and performed the ritual identification with the deity (sakalīkṛtya), one should perform protection as before. (3.213)
The word "having performed" (vidhāya) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 213 ||
O fair-faced one, he should afterwards sleep on the sacrificial ground together with his disciples;
for in the sacrificial hall presided over by the Lord, the sleep of the Guru and others is intended for the vision of dreams appropriate to the subject of initiation.
He states another method:
"Or else, while remaining awake in samādhi through the yoga of meditation on Bhairava. (3.214)
The teacher should act for the sake of the disciple—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "In meditative absorption" means for the purpose of achieving composure. Thus all is auspicious. || 214 ||
Having caused the lotus of the heart to blossom like Rāma through the rays of the sun that awakens the sky of the mind,
O noble ones, apply it to the rite of worshipping Śiva and utterly abandon the impurity of the suffering of wandering in saṃsāra.

Thus ends the third chapter, named "The Consecration" (Adhivāsa), in the venerable Svacchandatantra, accompanied by the commentary called Uddyota composed by the illustrious and great teacher of Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja.
The Fourth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
The forest rows of the wicked fetters, scorched by initiation, gnosis, and ritual action.
Victorious is the one great light, the blissful Bhairava, the consumer of the oblation.
In order to introduce the initiation (*dīkṣā*) that occurs immediately after the acceptance [of the disciple], the venerable Bhairava said:

"At dawn, when it is clear, having performed the purification and other rites in the prescribed sequence as before, and having performed the ritual of 'making complete' (*sakalīkaraṇa*) as before, one should enter the house. (4.1)
By way of connection with the chapter, the subject at hand is the preceptor; "purity and so forth" refers to bathing and other such acts, indicated by the word "and so forth.
As before, he should enter: having performed the worship of the deities of the door, the disciple—being pure, having sipped water (ācamana), and holding flowers in his hands—should enter.
And he,
having then bowed his head to the guru...
And having bowed to him, being delighted, he should report his dream to the guru. (4.2)
And I shall describe those auspicious dreams as well as the inauspicious ones, O fair-faced one:
drinking liquor and eating raw meat in dreams. (4.3)
Smearing oneself with worms and excrement, consecration with blood, eating curd-rice, and smearing oneself with white cloth. || 4-4 ||
A white parasol held over his head, adorned with white garlands and wreaths;
a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, and the royal consecration.
Jewels, limbs, ornaments, and the like; betel, as well as fruit; the sight of Śrī and Sarasvatī; and the embrace of an auspicious noble woman. (4–6)
Kṛmirlākṣā; all this is excellent.
Having engaged in conversation with kings, sages, gods, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Gaṇas, and teachers, one attains success in a dream.
Right speech is concordant discourse. || 7 ||
And likewise: "Crossing rivers and the ocean, traveling through the sky, as well as the rising of the sun and a blazing fire. (4.8)
The sighting of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as the moon’s orb;
or likewise, the climbing of a palace tower or even the pinnacle of a mansion. (4.9)
Climbing upon men, horses, bulls, young elephants, trees, and mountain peaks; traveling in celestial chariots; and the sight of one whose mantras have attained perfection.
There is gain, as well as the sight of perfected beings (siddhas), wandering mendicants, gods, and others;
and [the attainment of] pills, tooth-sticks, swords, sandals, and yellow pigment (rocanā). (4.11)
The sacred thread, collyrium, nectar, the pārata herb,
the spear, the water-pot, the lotus, the rosary, and realgar.
Having seen blazing perfected substances and those ending with red ochre (gairika) at the end of a dream, one attains success and likewise the acquisition of land and the healing of wounds.

He whose mantra has been perfected through the sequence of recitation (*japa*) and so forth; "a wound" means one produced by a weapon upon his own body; "at the end of sleep," but not at the beginning or middle of sleep. As it is said elsewhere:
"An omen occurring before [the event] should be grasped during the day, but one occurring after should be grasped at night."
Thus [ends the section]. 13.
Furthermore:
"Victory in battle, crossing the ocean of blood in combat;
the blazing cremation ground, beautiful and frequented by heroes and lords of heroes. (4.14)
And having obtained from the heroes, vetālas, and siddhas the sale of great flesh,
he respectfully offered a portion of that great sacrificial animal to the gods.
Whether worshipping, reciting, meditating, or even praising the deity within himself,
he beholds the blazing fire as well-offered, radiant, and honored.
It was frequented by swans, cranes, ruddy geese, peacocks, and parrots,
and was inhabited by the Mothers, the Bhairavas, and the hosts of Mātṛs and Rudras.
Seeing Bhairava, the *bhairakas* attain accomplishment here; of this there is no doubt.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*) with "by the heroes, vetālas, and siddhas. The *mātṛrudras* are specific classes of deities.
A "great beast" (*mahāpaśu*) is a human beast. A *sārasa* is a particular kind of swan that dwells in a lake (*sarasi*).
"It is accomplished" means that one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*) in the form of the superior (*uttama*) and other grades, corresponding to that dream. Although it is said:
"That which is seen, heard, experienced, desired, or likewise imagined..."
"Sleep is known to be of seven kinds, including that born of mental impressions and that born of physical defects.

Thus, although there is sleep arising from other causes, nevertheless, in this sacrificial hall presided over by the Lord and the Guru, [the dream] occurs solely in accordance with the future fruit due to the majesty of the mantras and so forth.
He is seen in his dwelling. || 17 ||
Thus have the auspicious dreams been described by me; now learn from me the inauspicious ones as well. (4.18)
He said to them: "Anointing with oil, as well as drinking of oil itself..."
...and entering the subterranean realm (rasātala), falling into a blind well, and then sinking into the mud. || 4-19 ||
Falling from trees, vehicles, or carriages, or from a palace or a mountain; or the cutting off of the ears and nose, or else of the hands and feet. (4.20)
The falling out of teeth and hair, the sight of bears and monkeys, as well as of vetālas, cruel creatures, and men of the Hour of Death (kālapuruṣas). 4-21.
A woman with black hair standing upright, who is filthy, dressed in black garlands and garments,
and has red eyes, should embrace a man in a dream.

There is no doubt that he will perish in this world if one does not perform the rite of pacification; there will be the destruction of houses and palaces, as well as of beds, garments, and seats. (4.23)
In battle, there shall be the defeat of oneself and the seizure of one's own property;
and [rebirth] among donkeys, camels, horses, jackals, as well as among herons, vultures, and cranes.
Ascending upon a buffalo, an owl, or a crow;
the consumption of cooked meat; and the wearing of red garlands and unguents. (4.25)
One whose mind is deranged perceives black and red garments in a dream, as well as laughing, leaping, and wearing withered garlands. (4.26)
Having seen in a dream the cutting off of one's own flesh, imprisonment, being devoured by a black serpent, and likewise marriage, one does not attain success at all. (4.27)

A cruel creature refers to a tiger or the like; "in battle" means in combat; one whose mind is distorted by obstacles or who has a terrifying appearance; laughing, marriage, and so forth pertain to oneself; and "leaping" refers to dancing. || 27 ||
He concludes:
"Indeed, the impure (aśubhā) has been thus described; it should be understood by the best of teachers.
Regarding the phrase "should be understood," the consideration of its strength or weakness is to be made precisely according to the time, the essential nature, and the capacity of the practitioner.
The meaning is that it is to be performed.
In that regard—those which are auspicious are to be rejoiced in; however, in the case of those which are inauspicious, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa). || 4-28 ||
One hundred and eight [times] with the [mantra of the] abode...
being thus, there is the pacification of obstacles to initiation. || 28 ||
...one becomes purified through expiation.
Regarding this, he states the procedure:
"Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa as before, [one performs] the expulsion of obstacles and protection. (4.29)

One should perform the encircling as before, [using] the auspicious water and the auspicious hand; then, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), the Śiva-pitcher, and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The fire-ritual is to be performed as before, including the offering of the final oblation;
thereafter follows the expiation which was prescribed for the purpose of [neutralizing] bad dreams. (4.31)

The ellipsis is "one should do that. Enveloping with the *kavaca* [mantra]; "Śivāmbhas" is for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth; the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) is for the sake of the proper pacification of expiation through the radiance and attainment of the ritual action; "the sacrificial ground" (*sthaṇḍila*) refers to Bhairava, who is to be established thereon. || 31 ||
Concluding this and introducing the subject at hand, he says:
"Having thus performed the worship and other rites, and having dismissed Śiva from the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should remove the floral remains (nirmālya), purify the ground as before," [4.32].
Thereafter, one should perform the daily rites, such as worship, fire-oblations, and recitation;
once the daily observance is completed, one should then perform the occasional rites.

The *nityakarman* pertains to the domain of one's own regular practice; since one who is under penance lacks the qualification for it, its description is given at the conclusion of that purification. The *naimittika* arises from a specific occasion (*nimitta*), namely, initiation (*dīkṣā*).
He begins that [process]:
having smeared [the area] with auspicious waters, one should worship the station of Brahmā with devotion,
using perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
With devotion by means of the *praṇava* [the syllable Om], one should then draw the mandala. || 4-34 ||
The procedure for that will follow later. || 34 ||
Then one should worship the ritual instrument and the chalk with Bhairava;
by means of the radiant power (*dhāman*), the dust is cast down.

Bhairava is with parts (sakala); the subsequent falling of the colored powders (rajas), which have been consecrated by the *dhāman*, is indeed without mantra; otherwise, the mention of future defects in the colored powders would be untenable.
And that falling of the dust-particles—[which is] beginningless and proclaimed in the scriptures.
He from whom the primordial white *rajas* is cast down; thus he is declared in the *Āgama*, the *Bṛhattantra*. || 35 ||
Then, once the mandala has been completed, one should bathe and perform the daily rites;
this means on the following day.
But upon the completion of the daily rites, the wise man should perform the occasional rite.
Having restated those daily rites (*nityakarman*), he prescribes the occasional rites (*naimittika*):
"Bathing and so forth as before with mantras; the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and so on;
self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*), the weapon (*astra*), the rampart (*prākāra*), and the worship of the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla*) and others. (4.37)
Having established the expulsion of obstacles and the binding of the directions for those dwelling on earth, in the netherworld,
and in the sky, one should construct a rampart of missiles and veil oneself with the armor-mantra.
Seated facing north, he should perform the purification of the hands and so forth as before;
then [he performs] the auspicious water, the auspicious hand, and the preparation of the threefold *arghya* offering.

The word "having done" (kṛtvā) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The "fence of missiles" (astraprākāra) is for the purpose of self-protection. The connection with "the expulsion of obstacles dwelling on earth, in the netherworld, and in the sky" is mediated by the authority of the scriptures (āgama). The phrase "fence of missiles" refers to the sacrificial enclosure (yāgagṛha). [The term] "facing north" (udaṅmukham) [is used].

This is because even the initiation for one desiring worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu-dīkṣā) culminates in liberation; and because the southern-facing [fire] burns away all fetters (pāśa); furthermore, at the commencement of the initiation, it is specifically stated here that the preceptor (ācārya) faces northward, as indicated by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "purification of the hands, etc. (karaśuddhyādi).

The purification of the body and so forth. "Śivāmbhaḥ" (the water of Śiva) refers to water consecrated by the Śiva-mantra for the purpose of sprinkling and the like; it is set apart from the arghya-vessel, and this is to be understood from the two preceding chapters.
In the three vessels, there is a triad of arghya intended for Vidhi, Nirodha, and Paśu. || 39 ||
Then—
having fully worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should worship the auspicious jar (śivakumbha).
After that also—
Having stood before the mandala, one should sprinkle the mandala with the sword.
Afterwards, one should wrap it with armor (varman) and consecrate it with the Praṇava;
by reciting the Dhāman one hundred and eight times, it is purified from the defects of dust.

By the phrase "in front of the mandala," it is implied that the mandala may also face other directions depending on the specific excellence of the person to be initiated. "With the syllable Om as the abode" means with the partless (niṣkala) mantra preceded by the syllable Om. || 41 ||
And thus, having worshipped the weapons in the four directions at the gate of the consecrated mandala with perfumes and other offerings in due order,
one should visualize the protective wall as the weapon-mantra.
