The word "door" (*dvāra*) is used in the singular to denote a class; thus, the meaning is: "in those eight doors which are located in the four directions of the nine-petaled lotus mandala that is about to be described."
...one should then enter the maṇḍala. || 4-42 ||
The meaning is that one should begin with the worship alone. || 42 ||
Therein—
One should worship as it was stated in the third chapter:
"Having worshipped the Gurus and Vināyaka to the east of the Brahma-sthāna," (3.92),
[and] in the Vāyavya [direction].
Then—
[one should place] the infinite seat (anantamāsana) as before, ending with Śiva, by means of the Praṇava.
One should install the forms and so forth, as before, extending from the heart to the end of the enclosure;
having worshipped according to the previously stated rule, one should present the food offerings.
Having offered the arghya with the mantra of cessation (nirodhārghya), one should indeed effect the cessation;
then, having performed recitation, meditation, and so forth, one should worship Bhairava situated within the fire.
Having established the connection of the channels at the three locations, one should satisfy the All-pervading Lord;
"in the fire" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 45 ||
In that regard, he first describes the joining of the channels: "Having performed the emission of the partless [breath] of the self, one should settle it in the *kumbhaka*. (4.46)
One should exhale through the left [nostril] while [the breath] resides in the *kalaśa*, and then fill it;
for one residing in the *maṇḍala*, one should again exhale through the left with the right [nostril].
One should remember that its light enters through the right side of the one situated at the fire;
then, by means of the waters from the mantra-pitcher, following the sequence of piercing the knots while ascending to the upper *dvādaśānta*,
and then returning from there to the heart, resting there, and circling clockwise, [one proceeds] by way of the moon.

Having emerged, one should enter by the right of the [deity] residing in the jar; there too, having adopted this same sequence, having exited by its left, having entered by the right of the [deity] residing in the mandala,
and having exited by the left as before, one should enter by the right of the [deity] residing in the fire, and rest in the heart just as previously.
Thus, through the unification of the four substrates,

one should abide in the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the fires of Agni, Soma, and Sūrya within the central fire; one must not, however, return from that to one's own heart, for one remains established in the fire itself, since the sacrifice is currently underway.
Because it is logical that [the cause] exists precisely as the predominant factor. || 47 ||
As it says: "Having thus performed the joining, one should then begin the libation (tarpaṇa). (4.48)
"Thus" refers to the point up to the resting of the fire. || 48 ||
And then: "Having offered with a division into ten parts, one should cast the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
This means that after offering according to the previously mentioned root-homa (mūlahoma), one offers with a tenth part of the [offerings] for the faces.
Then, for the sake of purification through expiation, one should perform one hundred and eight [repetitions].
Then, with the formula "by the power" (dhāmnā)—which, like the eye of a crow, applies to both—there is the full oblation for the rite that has been completed or exceeded. || 49 ||
Furthermore:
Then the preceptor, with the arghya water in his hand, should enter the mandala. (4.50)
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord with flowers and other offerings, ending with the arghya water,
and having first formed the mudrās and prostrated while kneeling upon the ground— || 4-51 ||

He should announce for the sake of the sacrificial animal: "This supreme sacrifice has been commenced; whatever was performed in the mandala and at the fire, beginning with the ritual bathing and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), [is completed]. (4.52)
"May that abundant and perfect ritual procedure come about here through your grace;
one should inform the Supreme Lord for the sake of the bound soul (paśu)—such is the connection. (4-52)
Having made a declaration concerning the rites already performed, he also speaks regarding those to be performed:
"Now, however, within the body of the disciple, [the ritual] beginning with the sakalīkaraṇa... (4.53).
"May the purification of the path extending for a *yojana* be accomplished through your grace.

Then, from the commencement of the ritual until its completion, may one— solely by means of the inward-turned process and through firm realization— make manifest the Lord’s presiding presence within oneself."
The intention is that of representation. || 53 ||
Therefore,
having been thus authorized by the Supreme Lord with the words "So be it," the King of Heroes— || 4.54 ||

Having received permission, with a joyful soul, he should exit from the maṇḍala as Vīrarāja, presided over by the Supreme Lord. Thus, through that very immersion, he attains the state of Bhairava, which consists of the total destruction [of all limitations].
With a joyful soul; "outside" means within the sacrificial hall itself, separated by a curtain. || 54 ||
Having taken that argha vessel which was prepared for the sake of the animal sacrifice, || 4-55 ||
The Guru should cause a mandala to be made on the southern side of the abode;
"southern" is said because it faces south, as it burns away the bonds (pāśa). || 4-55 ||
Then, having laid down a seat of the *praṇava* made of *kuśa* grass there, he should cause the pure disciple to sit down. (4.56)
Having struck [the disciple] with the Śiva-water, the weapon-mantra, and sequentially with ashes and kuśa grass,
one should conceive of the disciple as having become an embodiment within the prepared mandala.
"Pure" means one who has bathed. The phrase "with the Astra-mantra" is to be applied to all three [of the preceding items]. "Prepared" refers to its function as a seat;
and here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the forms (*mūrti*) and so forth is exactly as previously described. The same applies to what follows. || 57 ||
Then,
having sat down before him, [the teacher should perform] the placement of the hands (karanyāsa) preceded by the weapon-mantra for the purpose of burning away [impurities],
as well as the internal and external placement (nyāsa) and the application of the mantras.
The Guru should perform [it]. || 58 ||
Then—
the Guru, having meditated upon the God as brilliantly blazing, should bestow the hand of Śiva.
In this way, the Guru should cause his splendor to descend upon the disciple's head, which destroys the sprouts of the fetters.
The destruction of those sprouts of the nooses— the primary manifestations that cause the growth of saṃsāra—
as it is stated elsewhere:
"Śiva, conjoined with the five Brahmans and presided over by Śiva..."
He who severs the bonds is the secure one; he is celebrated as Śivahasta.
"By this, as soon as it is attained, the embodied soul, freed from all bonds,
becomes stainless and free from affliction, and proceeds to union with Śiva. (59)
Having raised [the disciple] from there, one should lead him and cause him to enter the mandala.

He states that it is appropriate for the disciple, whose eyes are bound, to behold the mandala in order to establish one-pointedness upon the Blessed One by means of pacifying the outward diffusion of the sense faculties:
Having sprinkled the garment with water, one should veil it with the *kavaca* mantra.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and consecrate [the disciple] with the Bhairava mantra.
Having bound the eyes with a blindfold,
[one should proceed] with the eyes [consecrated] by the blindfold, preceded by the recitation of the blindfold-mantra (*netramantra*).
Having bound the eyes, which act as the vanguard for the expansion of all the sense faculties.
[The teacher] should cause the disciple to place a flower in his hand. 4-61.
And he— standing facing the deity— should cast the flower even if unwilling;
immediately thereafter, for one desiring enjoyment—
And one should indeed bestow a name upon the practitioner according to the falling of the flower.
For a male, [the sequence] begins with the face, the limbs, and so forth, and ends with Śiva; for a female, however, it ends with Śakti.
But for one who is free from desire— that is, for the seeker of liberation— the teacher may act according to his own will; the meaning is that he may perform [the rites] as he pleases, or he may not.
Of the aforementioned practitioner (*sādhaka*) who has received initiation and is fit for initiation—[whether] it be the name of the [disciple] or indeed the name of the practitioner;
the word "or" (*vā*) signifies certainty. The meaning is that one must certainly perform [the rite].
Then, having opened his mouth, he should cause that disciple to prostrate before Śiva. || 4.63 ||
The Gurus maintain that one should open its mouth with ease by means of the pervasive unfolding of the Śākta path, so that it may blossom according to the principle of a flower in full bloom. 63.
Furthermore:
Having performed a circumambulation clockwise around the mandala and having prostrated before the fire, the preceptor, together with the sacrificial victim, should stand near the fire-pit. (4.64)

The word "should be" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The agency of performing circumambulation and so forth belongs to both [the practitioner and the deity]. And here, the previously mentioned method of drawing the hands together should be kept in mind. || 64 ||
Then, in the direction to one's left, one should prepare a mandala with the syllable Om (praṇava);
the connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) is performed as before, and for that purpose, three oblations (āhuti) are offered.
Having performed the *sampātābhihuti* and the *aṇutarpaṇa*,
one should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti* and perform the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*).
"And by means of the [mantra] consisting of one hundred and eight [repetitions]...

(3-149). According to the previously stated principle, "The *piṅgalā*, the central channel, has emerged from the body of the disciple," this is performed through the method of joining the darbha grass held in the hands of the disciple and the shanks of the guru.
The junction of the channels (nāḍīsandhāna), and the subtle mantras beginning with the root-mantra (mūla). || 66 ||
Having performed this—

[and] subsequently, one should offer three oblations with the *dhruva* mantra for the elevation of caste (*jātyuddhāra*) as well as for the attainment of the state of the twice-born (*dvijatva*). (4.67)

Having uttered the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*), one should offer three oblations for the elevation of the birth associated with the body of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) by means of the formula: "I effect the elevation of the birth of [Name], svāhā.
Thereafter, by means of the formula: "I effect the attainment of the status of the twice-born, svāhā."
With mantras possessing inconceivable power for the purpose of rendering [the soul] fit for the attainment of the status of a future portion of Rudra,

one should offer three oblations (āhutis) for the sake of conferring the state of being twice-born (dvijatva), which consists in fitness for the generation of the stage of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
And therefore, as for what some have said— that this conferral of the state of being twice-born does not concern the present body— [that is incorrect].
In that regard, since the caste of Śūdra and so forth alone resides as inherent to that body, and because the other eternal caste of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) cannot be produced [in that life],
this period of forty-eight years is calculated only with reference to a twice-born body that may be attained through the power of other [past] actions.

The claim that "the task belongs only to the twice-born by virtue of their performance of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)" must be disregarded; for, because they are seized by the demon of caste (*jāti-graha*), their discernment has not awakened, and thus they do not understand the true essence of the meaning of the Supreme Lord’s scriptures. This is because:
Regarding this matter— that it concerns a future body for a twice-born— one has scriptural authority (*śruti*). Just as,
through the power of mantras possessing inconceivable potency, burning and other rites are performed upon the present animal body and its elevation from that birth-class is accomplished,
so too [is] the production of another body consisting of pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) and the induction of the state of being a seed [for such a body], if...

Even for those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), [this practice] is performed; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Indeed, in this matter, the scripture exists in its stated form as a clear *itikartavyatā* (procedure).
For it is heard that even today, through the power of mantras and so forth, yoginīs [assume] the body, caste, and other attributes of themselves and others.

Regarding the term "transforming": according to the system of the Māheśvara [Tantras] and its stated methodology, everything other than Śiva, the individual soul (puruṣa), and Māyā—including the categories of reality (tattva-jāti) and so forth—is entirely impermanent. As for that which occurs on the path of the worlds (bhuvana-adhvan)—namely, the attainment of the status of the twice-born through the application of the forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāra)—[it is likewise impermanent].

It is performed for the sake of purifying the enjoyment of the twice-born (the initiate) amidst the purification of the enjoyments of the elements that are to arise from the various principles, through the method of impregnation and so forth in the womb of Vāgīśī by means of the son of Kriyā.
However, this [purification] pertains to the present body of the *samayin* (initiate bound by rules), because the purification of the principles has not been enjoined for him.

And for this reason, because for those who have been initiated—according to the principle that will be stated [later] as: "That single lineage is remembered as Bhairavīya, auspicious and imperishable" (4.543)—there is no status of belonging to the Śūdra or other castes; on the contrary, [they belong to that lineage].
It has been stated that, according to the established doctrine of the scriptures, the status of being a rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*) exists prior to the proclamation of one's original caste.
Furthermore, even for a twice-born person, this extraordinary attainment of the state of being twice-born must indeed be performed. As for the statement:
"That by which this [is attained] is indeed through experience" (*Kiraṇāvalī*).
Thus, some say that the application of mantra should not be performed in the present body while it remains in existence;
however, the claim that it should not be performed for the sake of purifying the karma that has already initiated this body is incorrect,
because [the practice] is indeed enjoined even for the present body for purposes such as drying, burning, nourishing, and the extraction of the birth-class (*jāti*).
It must certainly be performed; otherwise— "Since the body has been withered by the fierce powers of the mantras, such as drying and burning, therefore there is this consecration. (4.450)
Thus, it would be inconsistent. || 67 ||

Regarding this, he states another duty to be performed for the attainment of the status of the twice-born: "In the purification of the seed, the food, the place, and the disposition, one becomes a twice-born.
[The mantra is: "Oṃ, I perform the purification of the seed, food, place, and disposition of [Name]."
The application [of this] is in the phrase "svāhā. Here— "Brahminhood arises from the purity of the seed, and that is established in women;
yet their minds are fickle and run even after outcastes."

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Mukuṭasaṃhitā*, a real purification of seeds (*bījaśuddhi*) cannot be conceived anywhere; therefore, it must be accomplished by means of mantras alone. Furthermore, impurity exists because food cannot be maintained according to the procedures prescribed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and because even the location may be defiled through contact with barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like.
Because it is separated from the lack of truth and lack of uprightness inherent in existence, purity is indeed something to be acquired.

In this very context, for one who has attained the supramundane state of the twice-born through birth in Śuddhavidyā by means of these mantras—likewise, three oblations with the *praṇava* are performed to bring about his status as a portion of Rudra. (4.68)
Preceded by the *praṇava*, one should perform the rite of making him a portion of Rudra with the formula: "Become a portion of Rudra, svāhā!

This is to be done for the sake of his attaining the stage of the future state of Bhairava, so that he, having mastered the meaning of the scriptures, may become solely intent on the meditation upon Rudra. || 68 ||
In that regard, he speaks in order to show the procedure:
"One should sprinkle the disciple with [water] consecrated by the Astra-mantra and strike him with flowers;
then, having gone out by means of the Recaka breath, one should enter into the disciple's body at the heart. (4.69)
"By a flower" means by a flower consecrated with the Astra-mantra; "by exhalation" means by that which moves upward. || 69 ||
Then, having recited the mantra of Śiva beginning with Oṃ, and the Astra-mantra ending with Phaṭ,
one should perform the rite for the separation of consciousness according to the prescribed rule.
One should sever it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and veil it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having drawn it forth with the hook (aṅkuśa), one should cause it to enter the dvādaśānta.
The person situated there is to be grasped by means of the *dhruva* [mudrā] while [the hands] are joined together;
[he is to be dissolved] correctly by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*...
into Śiva, who is partless, [that is,] of consciousness in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*, according to the prescribed method.

By means of the previously mentioned meditation on non-separation from the mere rays [of light], and by means of the "hook"— that is, by displaying the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* according to the sequence of the curved digit (*kalā*) of the root mantra— the individual (*pudgala*), which is the living soul (*jīva*),
is [drawn forth] "correctly," meaning through the firmness of the realization of its non-difference from oneself. As it is said in the *Spanda*:
"This very [state] is the grasping of the self" (Svacchandatantra 2.7).
Then, with the *ūrdhva* [mudrā] and the inhalation (*pūraka*), one should enter into the heart. (4.72)
In oneself. || 72 ||
Therein—
having thoroughly purified and rendered it into a lake— one should again emit the person (pudgala),
who then abandons the sixfold group of deities and likewise his own station. (4.73)

Equalization (*samarasīkaraṇa*) is the production of non-difference with oneself as will be described hereafter; exhalation (*recana*) occurs by way of upward winding; the deities are those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva.

The [centers] located in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)—the very abandonment of these is the cause for bestowing upon the disciple the fitness for disjunction (*viśleṣa*) on the path presided over by them. This is because when the Lord is conquered, one's own self is also conquered; "one's own station" refers to the space between the eyebrows. As he will state:
"He attains the state of Īśvara. (4.79). According to that system, however, it is through the worship of Him that He bestows upon him the fitness for attaining that state. As it has been said:
In the *Mṛgendrāgama*, beginning with the words: "Thus is the ritual act pertaining to the observance" (*kriyāpāda* 7.70).
"Having attained which, one becomes fit" (Kriyākālaguṇottara 7.70).
Thus [ends verse] 73.
Having grasped that person who stands there and having encircled him with the *bhava* [mudrā], one should draw him out with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and join him to the heart of the disciple. (4.74)
"Having consecrated with Bhairava..."—
they say that the consecration by Bhairava, meaning by the Niṣkala [form], is to be performed seven times.
This much of the text is for the purpose of attaining the status of a portion of Rudra (rudrāṃśāpādana), and not for the purpose of attaining the status of a twice-born (dvijatvāpādana).
One must not be deluded. || 74 ||
Regarding the attainment of the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*), he states the remainder of what was to be said concerning the previously mentioned [rite]:
"In this manner, one should give the sacred thread (*upavīta*) to the child.
By the word "in this manner," it means having consecrated it with the *Bhairava* [mantra], now by the power of the mantra alone...
The state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) arises from the connection with a second birth, whose nature is produced from the plane of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
Regarding the term *upavīta*: it is that which has come (*ita*) specifically near (*upa*) to the self by means of the power of the mantra, and is moreover *vīta* (woven or bound).
This sacred thread is the very image of the thread of power whose nature is pure knowledge, which pervades the deities of infinite mantras and is itself pure.

For once the sacred thread has been bestowed upon him, he becomes consecrated in his status as a twice-born through the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires and ending with the funeral oblation. (4.75)

The forty sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, which will be described hereafter, are for the purpose of the second birth already mentioned, which consists in the emergence of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); and these are accomplished solely through the power of the mantra. || 75 ||
By these forty formative forces (saṃskāra),
the formation of the aggregate of birth occurs;
"it comes to be" is the understood conclusion.
He asks "How? and says:
"By the triad of oblations, however"—the meaning is: by that very [triad] previously determined.

Not only is the production of the individual's birth brought about by these purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), but even the infusion of consciousness [into the body] occurs through the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*). (4.76)
By means of subtle consciousness, one becomes consecrated in the state of the twice-born.

Accompanied by the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) which occurs at the beginning, the forty-first sacrament consists of the final rites (*antyeṣṭi*) that conclude the life; after that, what will be described further on.

By means of the meditation: "The eightfold refinement of personal qualities, consisting of compassion, patience, and so forth, [is achieved] through subtle consciousness," one should thus perform the induction of the portion of Rudra (rudrāṃśāpādana) after having accomplished what was stated for the purpose of attaining the status of the twice-born, according to the aforementioned reality. || 76 ||
At the end of that as well—having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations—one should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 4.77 ||

The word "should give" is to be understood as the ellipsis. It is already established that the fire-oblation for the root mantra is one hundred [times], while for its ancillaries it is one-tenth. || 77 ||
He summarizes this as follows:
"The initiate (samayī) is thus consecrated...

The word "thus" refers to [being consecrated] by means of the extraction of one's birth, the attainment of the status of a twice-born, and the entry into the portion of Rudra. "Samayī" means one who possesses the *samaya* (the initiatory observance).
This is because he transgresses the boundaries of the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara). As it has been said:
"...he would be fit for its recitation, as well as for its hearing, study, fire-oblation (homa), worship, and so forth. (4.78)

Recitation (*vācanam*) is the repetition [of the text] for the purpose of ascending to understanding and so forth; hearing (*śravaṇam*) is the comprehension of the meaning; study (*adhyayanam*) is the constant recitation of the scriptural treatise like the Veda; and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and other such practices are included. || 78 ||
In this way,
this practitioner— whose self is purified through conduct (*caryā*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*)— attains the state of the Lord.
One whose self is purified precisely by means of conduct and meditative absorption, as well as by the practice of the yoga of observing the commitments (*samaya*).
For by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), even without the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) through conjunction, the very fitness for union with Īśvara is instilled in him;

thus, through that very union, his bonds are purified and he attains the state of Īśvara. Consequently, when someone has been conjoined with the principle of Īśvara (*īśvaratattva*), there is no further purification of lower levels required during initiations such as that of a *putraka*.
The claim that the term *īśvara* is not appropriate—

on the grounds of the statement from the *Kiraṇatantra*, "For one who abides in a state of purity, one should place Kālarudra [within him]," or that it refers instead to the abode of the Fire of Time (*kālāgnidhāman*)— is incorrect.
Because the *samayin* is not mentioned in the *Kiraṇa* and other [tantras],
and because this passage from the *Kiraṇa* concerns the initiation into the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*) for the *putraka*. For in the *Kiraṇa*, after the initiation of the *samayin*,
having begun with the words, "Then one should perform the initiation," there follows the initiation into the worlds concerning the *putraka*.
It is sufficient to say that this has been accomplished by means of these leading statements; the attainment of the state of Īśvara is the other form of liberation.

Now, he introduces the determination of the initiation for the "spiritual sons" (*putraka*) and others—which is to be performed either immediately after the initiation involving the stated pledges or at the very outset—for the purpose of purifying the path of initiation and for those who desire the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
"Now, for the sake of purifying the path of initiation for those desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation... (4.79)
The subtle procedure that effects the severance of the bonds is now being described.

For practitioners (sādhakas) who seek worldly enjoyment, and for spiritual sons (putrakas) and teachers (ācāryas) who seek liberation— the initiation intended for them is called "subtle" because it serves the purpose of purifying the paths (adhva-śuddhi) through its future pervasiveness.

The procedure for uprooting the noose along with its roots is said to consist of the form of union with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) and so forth. For the initiate (*samayin*), however, there is merely the fitness for the yoga of worship of the Lord-principle (*īśvaratattva*) preceded by the separation from the presiding cause;
thus, for him, there is neither the subtle procedure, nor the supreme liberation, nor—

The definition of the initiation of the initiate (*samayidīkṣā*) is merely the generation of the fitness for attaining future statuses such as that of a *putraka*, by means of the sequence of propitiating the mantra.
As it has been said:
"The pacifier is like a prince. || 79 ||
Now he provides a summary introduction concerning the distinction between the domains of the initiation for a "little son" (putraka) and that for a practitioner (sādhaka):
"The Guru questions the disciple who desires one of two kinds of fruits. (4.80)
The seeker is of two kinds: one who desires enjoyment (bubhukṣu) or one who desires liberation (mumukṣu); the fruit is either liberation or worldly enjoyment. || 80 ||
Therefore, one should say this to him: "Whatever kind of fruit you desire, begin the corresponding means;
the means is the rite of initiation."
For: "The attainment [of the goal] is impelled by the mantra to be accomplished, according to the distinction of latent impressions (vāsanā). (4.81)
The mantra that is to be accomplished and worshipped is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); it bears fruit according to one's latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
For this very reason, the *Śrīspanda* states: "Having seized that power, the mantras... (Spanda 2.10).
Beginning with these words and ending with "by the mind of the worshiper of Śiva" (Svacchanda Tantra 2.10). || 81 ||
And thus:
"The fire-oblation (homa) of mantras, mudrās, paths, and substances is declared to be common to both enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti)."
But that [knowledge], divided according to the difference in latent impressions (vāsanā), is likewise distinct for disciples and for the teacher. (4.82)

When the disciple relies on his own conviction (*svapratyayī*), then the Guru should offer oblations for the sake of either liberation (*mukti*) or enjoyment (*bhukti*), according to that disciple's latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). But when the disciple relies on the Guru (*gurupratyayī*), then the Guru should offer only for the sake of liberation, because of the absence of any desire for enjoyment in him; this is the sense implied here by the context. || 82 ||
Now, he explains the classification of disciples according to the difference in their latent impressions (vāsanā):
"In this regard, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is of two kinds. One is established solely in the Śiva-dharma;
his path is purified by the Śiva-mantra, and he is engaged with the mantra of the goal (*sādhya*). (4.83)
One who possesses knowledge, has been consecrated, and is intent upon the propitiation of mantras—
he, the practitioner of Śiva, is indeed worthy here for the threefold accomplishment.

He is one for whom the Śivadharma—the practice taught in the Śiva scriptures—exists through constant non-separation; therefore, he is purified by the very mantra to be accomplished (sādhya-mantra) denoted by the word "Śiva," and not like those of worldly dharma whose path is established only partially; and it is precisely within him that the mantra to be accomplished is joined.
Thus he was appointed by the Teacher as a worshipper; "possessed of knowledge" means one who has mastered the secrets of mantra and tantra. || 84 ||
Another says:
"The second stands on the worldly path, devoted to the performance of sacrifices and charitable works;
performing rituals while desiring their fruit, he abides solely in the auspicious and is free from the inauspicious. (4.85)

The worldly path consists of the conduct prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and traditional custom; "iṣṭa" refers to rites such as bathing at sacred fords and the giving of food; "pūrta" refers to the construction of wells, tanks, monasteries, and so forth. Desiring a fruit, he performs only auspicious ritual action, but not the propitiation of mantras.

Because it will be stated [later] that "this initiation is worldly, devoid of the propitiation of mantras" (4.144), this practitioner is one who achieves the fruit through auspicious action alone; however, by means of initiation, only his inauspiciousness is to be pacified—thus he says, "abandoned of the inauspicious. || 85 ||

For this very reason— his task is always the destruction of inauspicious portions by means of mantras. "Always" means throughout whatever he has done or will do, excluding the karma that initiates the body, in the interval between those.
Whatever portion is inauspicious, all of that must be subtracted from this.

Since the statement, "............ one should not purify the *prārabdha* alone" (4-141), applies almost universally to all cases, he says that one must abide by the Śiva-dharma with unadulterated conduct:
Whether he be a householder or an ascetic, remaining in any one of these stages of life (āśramas).

Or one may achieve accomplishment through the very conduct of a cemetery-dweller and so forth; or through the conduct of a householder with such [forbidden] substances, but not with a mixed lifestyle. "This one" refers to a follower of the Śiva-dharma and no other, because others lack the qualification for the propitiation of mantras. However, this does not mean that the [other] stages of life (āśramas) are not applicable.
Because there is no utility here [in that case]. || 86 ||

Having determined the practitioner who is solely intent on liberation, he speaks in order to determine the *putraka* (spiritual son): "The seeker of liberation is said to be of two kinds: the seedless (*nirbīja*) and the seeded (*sabīja*).
He states the distinction between the scope of these two as follows:"
[This applies] to children, the foolish, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual enjoyments, and those who are diseased. || 4.87 ||
For these, there is the seedless initiation (*nirbījikā dīkṣā*), which is devoid of [the usual] rules and so forth.

A child is one who is ignorant; an old man is one incapable of performing [ritual] practice. Even one who enjoys worldly pleasures—one who is solely attached to the pleasures that have arrived—is indeed fit for initiation provided that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred. Others...

They argue that this person, being afflicted by laziness, is not a fit vessel; therefore, he is a consumer of enjoyments and devoted to what is unwholesome, and thus he is "sick. A sick person is difficult to treat. The explanation of the term *nirbījika* (seedless) is "one who is devoid of the *samaya* and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the ritual procedures for the *pavitraka* and other rites are included. And he will say further:
"And one should purify the fetters of the conduct of pacification within the seedless [state]. (4-147) || 87 ||
But for those who are learned and capable of enduring the pairs of opposites, O Dear One, it is said to be "with seed" (sabīja). || 4-88 ||

Because those who are learned, skilled in discerning the scriptures, capable of enduring the pairs of opposites (dvandva), able to withstand the hardships of performing vows and other disciplines, and likewise empowered to observe the rules of conduct (samaya). || 88 ||
The initiation that bestows grace for them is conjoined with the conduct of the rules (samayācāra);
the former concerns those who lack discrimination or capacity, whereas this [latter] concerns those of the opposite nature—this is the intended meaning.
And therefore:
"Those specific conventional practices which are proclaimed in what is called Mantra... (4.89)
"They must be protected here with effort by one who desires the attainment of liberation,
in this Mantra-pīṭha known as Mantra— those who [do not] revile Lord Bhairava nor the scripture originating from him. (5.44)
Thus, the specific rules of conduct (*viśeṣasamayācāra*) to be described hereafter have been stated;
these must be diligently observed in this context of initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*), otherwise there will be the necessity for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
The phrase "in that which is called mantra" is intended as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) and so forth as well. (89)
This initiation which has thus been determined is to be known as "with seed" (sabījā), and it is established for both the spiritual son (putraka) and the teacher (ācārya). || 4.90 ||
The "son" (putraka) is one who has been born from the womb of Vāgīśī and is favored by her through the pacification of saṃsāra.

Although the observance of rules (samaya-pālana) is prescribed for the initiation of the practitioner (sādhaka), nevertheless, that initiation is not called "with seed" (sabīja), because of the technical definition: "the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) is of two kinds. || 90 ||
Thus, in this fourfold rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), first—whether one is a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—one should initiate after forming a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Observe that here the meaning of the sentence functions as the object of the action, as in the expression "the deer runs"; therefore—

Having first determined whether this person belongs to the householder stage of life and thus desires worldly enjoyments, or whether he is a renunciant and the opposite of that, one should perform the initiation according to the appropriate, unmixed procedure for each case.
Therein, he proceeds with the initiation of the "spiritual son" (putraka):
having taken a cord of bonds (pāśasūtra), he should suspend it upon the body of the disciple. (4.91)

At the time of the ritual of formal acceptance (adhivāsa), the support that was previously established and protected in front of the vase of acceptance—from the tip of the crest-lock down to the feet—should be placed as before. || 91 ||
Then,
the wise Guru—
who knows the pervasion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) about to be described— should, primarily within the fire of Śiva alone, unite the path by means of the [mantric] abode (dhāman).
"O burner of all fetters without exception"—here, "the path" refers to the path of the *kalās* under discussion;
however, in initiation concerning the *tattvas* and so forth, one should contemplate it in the form of the *tattvas* and so on.
And it is not only in the fire, but as far as—[the path] which resides in the fire of the jar-mandala, and that which resides within the self of the disciple. (4.92)
Furthermore, the junction of the time-periods (adhvasandhi) is proclaimed by the Guru to be situated within the Self, even though it is described in the Sūtra as being located in one place. 92.
Having stated "in one place," he speaks in order to define the purification of the paths by dividing the locus [of that statement]:
"But of the sixfold path of the way, which is common to all... (4.93)
Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) over the vessel and purified it, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*) at the junctions of the paths (*adhvasandhi*).

This is done for the sixfold path— which consists of the divisions of phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, words (*pada*), aspects (*kalā*), principles (*tattva*), and worlds (*bhuvana*)— which serves as the "way" (*mārga*) because it is the cause for attaining its respective stages within the jars and other vessels.

Among the six topics (*adhikaraṇas*), from that which pertains to the common [category], which remains undifferentiated and is known as such, one must purify; thus, it is desired to primarily purify whichever one among the five internal paths (*adhvan*) is included therein. Having formed the intention (*saṅkalpya*) in the *kuṇḍa*, that is, in the fire of Śiva situated therein—
One should perform a fire oblation for the purpose of connecting the temporal periods. || 93 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of the eight hundred recitations of the root mantra for the purpose of connecting the paths. (4.94)

The teacher, who knows the pervasion of the paths (adhvavyāpti), should offer one hundred and eight oblations using the formula: "May there be the junction of the paths preceded by the utterance of the root-mantra *praṇava*; svāhā!"—this is the meaning. || 94 ||
Subsequently, there is the observation of the time-periods (adhvan) through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader;
the remainder [of the sentence] is that one should perform this observation as a meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
He clarifies the pervasion:
"The pervasion of the worlds exists within the principles (tattvas), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva. (4.95)
The pervasiveness [of these principles] over the worlds, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva, resides within the *tattvas*.
And those principles (tattvas) are all-pervasive, numbering thirty-six;
as for the other three paths (adhvan)—
...consisting of the syllables and words of the mantra.
There are fifty syllables and eighty-one words related to the ninefold self (navātman).
And they—
since all [of them] are included within the principles (tattva) and are considered to include the principles within themselves.
How [is this so]?
... through the connection between the signified and the signifier. (4.96)
The principles (tattvas) are the denotata, while the mantras and so forth are the denoters; how this relationship of denoted and denoter functions will be explained further on. || 96 ||
Since the initiation of *kalā* has been introduced, he first states the inclusion of the five paths (*adhvan*) within it:
"Indeed, those [paths] beginning with Nivṛtti are traditionally held to be included within the *kalās*."
This is the summary of the meaning of this entire book on the paths:
the Supreme Lord, the mass of consciousness and bliss, the independent Bhaṭṭāraka,
according to the state to be described in the eleventh chapter by the name Unmanā.

By its own power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), it simultaneously manifests upon its own ground an infinite range of signifieds and signifiers— from the void (*śūnya*) down to the earth (*kṣiti*)— which, though not distinct from itself, appears as if it were something additional. Among these, the signifier (*vācaka*),
situated within the aspect of the subject (*grāhakabhāga*), consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and words (*pada*), distinguished as supreme (*para*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and gross (*sthūla*).
It is threefold; the denotable [word] as well, being intent upon the aspect of the object to be grasped, consists of the phonemes (*kalā*), the principles (*tattva*), and the worlds (*bhuvana*).

Likewise, the phonemes (*varṇa*), whose essence is non-dual awareness (*abhedavimarśa*), assume the form of mantras characterized by the awareness of both difference and non-difference through a certain degree of grossness, and from that, through further grossness, [they become the denotable].

They appear in the form of words that convey the awareness of differentiation (*bhedavimarśa*). In this way, the supreme power of the Lord called *kalā*, which consists of the nature of the denotable (*vācya*), assumes the state of the *tattvas* and *bhuvanas* through a progressive hierarchy of distinctions;
yet in reality, this power of the Lord flashes forth as entirely free from succession (*akrama*). And even therein—

By its own sovereignty, it displays even succession, like a city in a mirror; and within that succession, each preceding element exists as the pervasive substrate in what follows, just as clay exists in a jar and so forth,
while each succeeding element exists in what precedes it in the form of a latent power (*śakti*), just as a tree exists within its own seed— thus everything [is established].

It is indeed the self of all. For this very reason, in the initiation of the five principles (*pañcatattvadīkṣā*), the pervasion of the elements will extend up to the principle of Anāśrita. And thus, every single cognizer (*pramātṛ*) or objective entity (*bhāva*) is, in reality, grounded in the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*), whose essence consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) ranging from the beginning (*ādi*) to the end (*anta*)—that is, from the expansion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvasphāra*) to the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśaśakti*).

The one who lacks self-awareness (*a-svatattva*) is indeed the very form of Supreme Bhairava; however, due to the lack of full knowledge of that state, he considers himself incomplete because of the power of Māyā. Consequently, his sovereign power is obscured by the *kalās* of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), such that his true nature does not manifest through the phonemes (*varṇa*), the *kalās*, and so forth.

Having developed the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) toward the body and so forth through the process of the arising of conditions, and having conceived the pride of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) regarding mere objects, one becomes a bound soul (*paśu*) who has attained the state of being an object of enjoyment for the four wheels beginning with Khecarī; therefore, for the sake of pacifying this state of being a bound soul, [the teaching] of the Supreme Lord is [necessary].

The grace-bestowing power (*anugrāhikā śakti*), shining in its ultimate essential nature within the heart of the Guru— who is non-different from Śiva— purifies the entire path of the disciple by expanding it through the removal of its contracting tendencies, such that it consists of the essence of one's own uncontracted power.

Through the application of initiation, knowledge, and so forth, the mantras and other factors—whose essence is the expansion of the Ācārya—are the purifiers; those who are identified with the nature of the bound soul (paśu) are the objects of purification. Thus, even within this relationship of the purifier and the purified, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, because each individual path possesses the nature of containing everything, for that very reason:

In the initiation (dīkṣā), according to the predominance of each respective path (adhvan), the purification consisting of the inclusion of the other five paths must be performed, along with the true nature of the previously described pervasion (vyāpti).
And it is said in the venerable Spanda:
"This power of Śiva, whose nature is action, binds those who are like bound souls when it remains within its own path; yet when known, it brings about accomplishment. (3.16).
Enough said. Only—
"As long as one does not indeed understand the pervasiveness of either the sacrificial pit or of the Self,"

"Until he plays like a child with the victim to be sacrificed, with the sacrificial animal itself, and with the fetters of the six paths, how could there be any task for him? (Mṛtyujit, 16.54–55). Since this has been stated therein, it is our primary concern to demonstrate the pervasive presence [of Śiva] in each of those respective instances.
One should not imagine that we are talkative with our minds.
Now, as a digression, he states the mantras that denote the arts:
"The seed-mantras of those [arts], beginning with the Heart, are proclaimed as their denoters. (4.97)

The seed-mantras (bījamantra) are partless; the mantras beginning with the Heart—namely the mantras of the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, and Eye—are, in their respective order, the designators of Nivṛtti and the other kalās.
And thus, in this ritual procedure of initiation by means of the *kalās*, one should contemplate the distinct pervasion (*vyāpti*) of each individual *kalā*;
and that [pervasion] will become manifest before long.
And those [powers]—earth and the rest—are to be known as the kalās; they are Brahmā and the others, who are the causal deities.

Nivṛtti and the other kalās should be understood as having the nature of the powers (śaktis) of earth and the other elements, because it is precisely earth and the others that exist in a subtle state up to the level of Anāśrita.
This will become clear in the ritual procedure for initiation into the five principles (pañcatattva-dīkṣā). These...

Thus, by way of being the presiding forms, [the powers] are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva; and from this, it is also indicated that these [powers] become pure through the purification of their presiding deities. || 98 ||
He summarizes: "Having thus meditated upon the pervasion...
[referring to] the pervasion that will be explained immediately hereafter at every moment. "Thus" means...
Having meditated upon the path according to the determined sequence of the subtle and gross levels of others.
...the re-establishment (*upasthāpana*) would take place.

Re-establishment is the bringing face-to-face (*sammukhīkaraṇa*) of one [of the deities] as the primary [element] for the sake of purification. And here, by the phrase "the abode and so forth" (*dhāmādīti*), [it is referred to] according to Svacchandatantra 4.101.
He will state the mantra.
For one who has thus become present, in order to bring [the deity] into close proximity—
[he] should offer three oblations with the *dhruva* [ladle]; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
from this, purification of the past occurs. (4.99)
How so? He says:

"But when the deity has been worshipped in the fire and the deposition on the path (adhvanyāsa) has been performed, one should perform that very [deposition] starting from the feet in the sequence beginning with earth. (4.100)

"That very [state]" refers to the forms beginning with *nivṛtti*. "From the foot" means according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). In that regard, *nivṛtti* extends to the ankles, *pratiṣṭhā* to the navel, *vidyā* to the palate, *śānti* to the crown of the head, and *śāntyatītā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); thus it will be. And in this way:

Since the purification and other rites performed on the thread— which serves as a representation of the present vital breath and body, and which extends along the path from the heels to the navel and so forth following the contours of the body—

have been accomplished, they are effectively accomplished within the body itself; therefore, there is no need for a separate procedure as there is in the case of the initiation of the rules (*samayadīkṣā*).

The extraction from birth (*jātyuddhāra*), the attainment of the status of a twice-born (*dvijatva*), and so forth, are performed separately because there is no injunction for them [in that specific context].

However, by way of their future state—through their inclusion within the *niṣkṛti* oblations and by virtue of consciousness having a future body as its locus—that which is accomplished [by those rites] results, through the logic of establishing that [future state], even for one whose locus is the present body. Thus...

And in the view that the initiation of the *putraka* is included within the initiation of the *samaya*, the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of initiation concerning the present body is employed once again. || 100 ||
Regarding the previously mentioned re-establishment (*upasthāpana*), he states the mantra:

"Beginning with *dhāma* and beginning with *praṇava*, and again 'salutation to Nivṛtti'—this is the mantra for re-establishment, having meditated upon the pervasion (*vyāpti*) situated within the paths (*adhvan*). (4.101)

The word "should be employed" is the ellipsis. And here, immediately after the two abodes of the *praṇava*, the previously mentioned heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) is to be recited, according to [Tantrāloka] 4.97:
"The designators of those [energies] beginning with the Heart are their seed-mantras."
Because it has been stated thus; in the same way, it should be understood in what follows as well. || 101 ||
To clarify what was stated—that there is a distinct pervasion for each individual *kalā*—it is said:
Within *nivṛtti* is the earth, extending over a hundred million [yojanas];
and within it are one hundred and eight worlds. (4.102)
Twenty-eight words and one syllable are established here;
two mantras alone are to be known...
"A hundred crores" means an extent of a hundred crores of *yojanas*. "One hundred and eight as the limit" means—
Therein, Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Hāṭaka are the three [deities] situated in the lower portion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). In the middle is Śiva, the lord of the earthly realm (bhūloka);
above him is Brahmā, who presides as far as Satyaloka; and above him are Viṣṇu and Rudra.
There are seven [deities] ending with "of his own two worlds"; outside of him, there are one hundred Rudras situated in the ten directions;
above them is Vīrabhadra, the lord of them all—thus, this constitutes one hundred and eight.
The verses (padas), however, are twenty-eight.

The eighty-one syllables consisting of nine groups— which are to be described and are situated within the eighty-one divisions that initiate the circle of the future nine-fold manifestation— are "words" (padāni) because they bestow repose in each respective [state].
From among those, [the syllable] situated in the ninth division located in the direction of Īśa (northeast), presided over by the principle of *prakṛti*...

In reverse order, starting from the north of Īśa and proceeding clockwise up to the central position, there is a group of nine words beginning with Oṃ and ending with A. Likewise, based on the Puruṣa-tattva, there is a group of nine beginning with A and ending with Ya, located in the direction of Kubera (the north).
Similarly, there is a group beginning with Ū and ending with Ma, located in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), situated in the station of Niyati.

There are twenty-seven words; with the letter *ū* situated in the northeast corner, located in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), which is the locus of the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), there are twenty-eight words. To clarify this very point, the following diagrammatic arrangement (*prastāra*) is shown—(to be seen on the previous page)—[showing] that there is one syllable.

The letter *kṣa* is connected to the *mātṛkā* in reverse order (*prātilomyena*). Although this [letter] was previously described through a figurative turn of phrase as the "Supreme Reality beyond Peace" (*śāntyatītā-paramārtha*) as the designator of the Īśāna face, here it is described as the designator of Earth; nevertheless, [this applies] to the entire sequence from *a* to *kṣa*.

Since the entire mass of sounds consists of the reflective awareness of Supreme Bhairava, whose body is the undivided universe, even a single part— “even a single region of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization.”

Thus, by virtue of abiding as the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), they denote the universe; and the denoted aspect (*vācya*) as well—by the principle that "even within each single *tattva*, there is the nature of the thirty-six *tattvas*"—is the denotation of all phonemes because it consists of the universe. And therefore, by the Blessed One...

In order to regulate the *śakti*, there is no inconsistency whatsoever even if one examines, in the various respective scriptures (*āgama*), even the most subtle [principles], such as the established expressive relationship (*vācaka-bhāva*) that is useful for the sequence of diverse initiations (*dīkṣā*) and so forth.
"The two mantras" refers to the partless (*niṣkala*) Sadyojāta.
Thus, within this power of cessation (nivṛttikalā), one should contemplate the sixfold path. || 4.103 ||
Then, having worshipped this Nivṛtti— whose pervasion of the other paths is internalized according to the previously stated sequence— with flowers, incense, and so forth,
[one should worship] her with the aforementioned mantra.
...three oblations in the presence [of the deity].
The ellipsis is that one should offer three oblations for the sake of bringing [the deity] into proximity.
He speaks as follows in order to state that the three impurities (mala) within the paths beginning with Kalā are to be purified:
The impurities consisting of the forms of the worlds belonging to Māyā, as well as karma, are established there.
The word "nooses" (pāśāḥ) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 104 ||
In that regard—those belonging to Māyā are said to have the form of bodies and worlds;
furthermore, action (karman) is the cause of experience, while desire (abhilāṣa) is the impurity (mala) here. (4.105)

The world, beginning with existence and its manifestations, is characterized by that [impurity]; therefore, whatever appears as an object of cognition is the impurity consisting of *māyā*. By means of experience (*bhoga*), the birth projected by that [impurity] is also indicated. And it has been said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"In this very context, the manifestation of a differentiated object of cognition is called *māyā*."
Thus it is said:
"But the *kārma* [karman] bestows birth and experience upon the agent when there is non-awareness" (*Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* 3.2.5).

"Desire" (abhilāṣa) refers to a state characterized by self-perception as incomplete, taking the form of restlessness; it does not mean "may something belong to me," because that is the very nature of the principle of attachment (rāga-tattva). "In this case, however" means that while this [impurity] exists as the foundational wall, the other two impurities [follow]. || 105 ||

For this very reason, since it will be demonstrated that even in the state beyond peace (śāntyatītā) there exists a subtle abiding in the worlds, and because the latent impression of impurity (malasaṃskāra) persists to that extent, [the author],
wishing to demonstrate its state as something to be purified, concludes as follows:
In this way, the three bonds situated within the paths (adhvan) should be meditated upon during initiation.
Having thus meditated upon them, initiation is then performed according to the rule for the sake of their purification. (4.106)

He performed various [rites] for the sake of purifying those fetters specifically by means of their pacification up to the limit of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), and— by the force of the word "and"— for the sake of manifesting the state of Śiva which is accomplished through the rite of union (*yojanikā*).
The initiation (dīkṣā) is performed, consisting of the nature of giving and austerity. || 106 ||
He introduces the procedure for that [initiation]:
"First, O Goddess, one should install Śakti, endowed with the Kalās and Tattvas—
the Śakti of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśī), whose form is the Foundation (Ādhāra) and who is called Kriyā, because of the context of the initiation into the Kalās."
First, she is connected with the five subsequent paths, which are internalized within the reality whose nature is the power of withdrawal (*nivṛttikalā*).
Likewise—
having mentally conceived Vāgīśī, who pervades all wombs, with the heart-mantra (hṛd) [4.107].

One should place [the seed-syllables]. The word "with the heart" (*hṛdā*) should be applied to the preceding [syllables] as well, like the eye of a crow. And it has been said: "The [mantras] beginning with the Heart are the designators of those [deities]" (4.97);
and, "Speech alone gave birth to all the worlds."
Thus, by this established principle, it has already been determined that she pervades the birthplaces of the fourteenfold creation of beings. || 107 ||
He describes the wombs (yoni) according to the process of withdrawal:
"Various wombs exist, beginning with Śatarudra and ending with Ananta;
they are diverse, giving rise to the fourteenfold creation of beings."
And among them—by means of their simultaneous state of menses—one should cause Vāgīśī to be present. (4.108)

For one upon whom the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred, that [power] is already present by virtue of its association with the state of *ārta*— which consists in the fitness for the simultaneous creation of multiple bodies, brought about by the orientation toward pure emission (*śuddhasṛṣṭyaunmukhya*). The teacher, however, through the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka*), which consists in relying on the fundamental strength of that [power], [awakens it].
Having first performed the binding of the *saṃnidhi-mudrā*, one should establish [the deity] within the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*). || 108 ||
Then, one should worship her with flowers, perfumes, and incense in due order;
and here, having uttered the *praṇava* and the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), [one should proceed].

The mantra for the rites of invocation (*saṃnidhāpana*) and worship (*pūjana*) is: "Obeisance to Vāgīśī, who pervades the *nivṛtti* [kalā], and who is the cause of the diverse bodies of the fourteenfold creation of beings residing in the various worlds beginning with Ananta and ending with Vīrabhadra, all situated within the *pṛthivītattva*."
Then,
with the syllable Oṃ, one offers three oblations for the purpose of invoking Vāgīśī.
The word "should give" is the ellipsis. || 109 ||
And having given [the initiation],
one should sprinkle the disciple with the Astra-mantra and strike him while reciting the Astra-mantra;
the sprinkling is performed with the water of Śiva upon the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra) according to the region of the heart, while the striking is—
Or else, with ashes made from those very [materials].
Then, having gone from there as well by means of the exhaling breath (recaka), one should sever his heart with the sword of the self.
"By way of the moon-path, [the power] situated in the sun should enter the heart of the disciples.

According to this principle stated in the *Śrīlakṣmīkaulārṇava*, having emerged through one's own right [nostril] and entered through the left of the disciple, one should— by means of the *astra-mantra* and meditative visualization— [purify] the disciple’s self in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
One should cut that which is situated on the thread. || 110 ||
And having severed it—having drawn that self by means of the [inner] light, one should place it at the *dvādaśānta*.
The method of drawing [it upward] has already been explained previously. And this—
"It should be performed without being separated from even a mere ray [of light]," so it has been said.
Then,
having encapsulated that consciousness situated therein with the Dhruva [mantra], one should seal it within oneself.
One should fill [it] with Bhairava alone...

that which resides there, residing at the *dvādaśānta*. By means of the *mudrā* called *saṃhāra*, performed with the hand of the radiant Śiva; "in oneself" means in one's own heart; "with Bhairava" means with the partless (*niṣkala*) [Bhairava]. || 111 ||
And with that very [wind],
one should fill and then exhale by means of the nose alone.
And for that very reason:
"Having drawn [the breath] from the dvādaśānta, one should join it with the Bhava-mudrā. (4.112)
The *yojana* is within the womb of Vāgīśī; the *bhavamudrā* is the *liṅgamudrā*. || 112 ||
Regarding the procedure for the *yojana* (joining), he says:

"Having meditated upon oneself as the Lord (*Īśvara*) and likewise [upon] Māyā as Vāgīśvarī, and having joined the consciousness (*caitanya*) into her, one should project bodies within the path (*adhvan*). (4.113)

Īśvara is the creator due to the predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); however, Vāgīśvarī, who was previously established [as the source], is now *māyā* because she is the subject (*pramātṛ*) of the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*). But in the production of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), she herself will become the nature of *mahāmāyā*. And of this [Vāgīśvarī] who has the form of *māyā*...

There is no contact with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), because otherwise it would be impossible to create infinite bodies for the sake of simultaneously purifying successive karmic experiences; "of the candidate" refers to consciousness (caitanya) by implication, and "on the path" (adhvani) refers to the present context, namely that which is dominated by the kalā of Nivṛtti. 113.
He states for what purpose [the Lord] creates:
"For the sake of experiencing the remaining fruits of prior karmic impressions.
This refers to those fruits consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience, which are caused by prior karmic impressions and are entirely without remainder.
Their state of being objects of enjoyment is such that the accomplishment of enjoyment may occur.
And these bodies—possessing distinct enjoyments simultaneously by virtue of place, time, and body. (4.114)
They ripen through the power of mantra...

the body here is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Those in whom experience (*bhoga*) is differentiated—bodies that extend up to the three [categories] beginning with space—ripen simultaneously through the power of mantra and become oriented toward the bestowing of their fruit.
Not only do bodies ripen simultaneously with distinct experiences,
but even persons of such a kind—
having cast off their separate bodies— are emitted into the wombs of the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśī). (4.115)
By the term "individuals" (*pudgalāḥ*), he suggests that even for a single person to be initiated, there is a plurality due to their possession of various bodies;

this implies the unreality of the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*). For even in the case of a single self to be initiated, a state of multiplicity arises through the diversity of objects of experience during the purification of the various bodies that serve as the locus for diverse enjoyments.

"Of such a kind" means having distinct enjoyments. "In wombs" refers to the plurality [of births] in view of the fourteen-fold creation of beings; "emission" (visṛṣṭi) is the conjunction for the sake of fixed enjoyment. 115.
Thus, having united the consciousness of the disciple with the [divine] abode (dhāman), one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*).
These consist of the various worlds, beginning with Nivṛtti— which is pervaded by the utterance of the partless (*niṣkala*)— and ending with Vīrabhadra, extending through Ananta and the others.

The mantra is: "I perform the union of Devadatta with the womb of Vāgīśī for the sake of accomplishing the creation of the fourteen kinds of beings that have not yet come into being; obeisance. In the fire-oblation (homa), however, it ends with *svāhā*.
In this manner, the modified mantras for subsequent instances should be inferred by oneself.
Thus, when there is conjunction—simultaneously, in all wombs, bodies of various forms [arise]. (4.116)

The ellipsis is that those who are perfectly endowed with the will of Bhairava extend as far as the hundred Rudras and beyond. Here, by the word "Bhairava," the teacher (ācārya) who possesses the immersion (samāveśa) into Bhairava is meant. || 116 ||
Then, [one should perform] the completion of the embryos within the wombs with three oblations to Bhairava. || 4-117 ||

Having performed the oblation, one should then perform the rite of birth by means of three further oblations. Here, the mantra is modified according to the name of the specific rite; having offered the oblations for the sake of the embryos during those three oblations in which the embryos are brought to completion, "birth" refers to the emergence of the embryo from the womb, and this is performed "by that" [mantra].
By the partless alone. || 117 ||

In the body of the disciple: 1. suspending the thread of bonds (pāśasūtra), 2. the unification of the paths (adhvan) pertaining to the six substrates (ṣaḍadhikaraṇa), 3. the oblation (homa) thereof, 4. the contemplation of the pervasion of the paths, 5. the establishment of the paths, 6. their worship, 7. the oblation, 8. the contemplation of the three internal bonds (pāśa).

9. The placement (nyāsa) of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) endowed with the power of the arts (kalāśakti); 10. The invocation (saṃnidhāpana) of Vāgīśī; 11–12. Her worship and fire-oblation (pūjā-homa); 13–14. The sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) and striking (tāḍana) of the disciple; 15. The extraction of his consciousness (caitanya); 16. Its establishment at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta); 17. Then its grasping (grahaṇa); 18. [The completion thereof].

The rite called "birth" (janma), refined by twenty-one intermediate purificatory rites—namely: 19. joining [the soul] in one's own heart; 20. leading it to one's own dvādaśānta; 21. joining it within the womb of Vāgīśī; and the fire-oblation for the production of various wombs—is performed through oblation.
Having described the *saṃskāra*, he speaks in order to explain the *saṃskāra* called "qualification" (*adhikāra*):
"In all wombs, their bodies simultaneously attain growth. (4.118)
The word "to be cultivated" (bhāvyāḥ) is the ellipsis. || 118 ||

Since only those whose bodies have fully developed possess the entitlement to experience, he describes that experience: "Karma is the auxiliary cause for the accomplishment of experience"—the word "must be" (bhāvyam) is to be understood as the ellipsis. This refers to whatever [karma] of the bound soul (paśu) is past and future.
It is conceivable that all karma— consisting of wholesome impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth— which brings about a succession of infinite enjoyments,
is like a seed burnt by subtle flames; it is "karma pertaining to many births" (*anekabhavikaṃ karma*).

"Even that which is yet to come is restrained by that through which this [world] exists as experience"—according to the principle stated in the *Śrīkiraṇa*, one should contemplate this through the application of mantra for the sake of the simultaneous accomplishment of experience. Of what kind? By means of activities (*vyāpāraiḥ*).
By means of the activities of speech, mind, and body; "with a cooperative cause" (sahakāraṇa) means "with a cause" (sahetuka).
And this must necessarily be so; otherwise,
in the absence of that [karma], there would be no experience,
for it is karma alone that is the cause of experience within the realm of māyā.
"All beings engage in the acquisition of the means for that [enjoyment] solely for the sake of enjoyment"—thus he says:
"For that purpose, purification is prescribed. (4.119)

Since, when the means for enjoyment have not been mastered through the performance of virtuous acts and the like, the enjoyment to be experienced consists of the nature of both suffering and pleasure; having thus determined the nature of enjoyment, he speaks as follows to describe its dissolution— even when that enjoyment has ceased— as being like a state of existence within Māyā, consisting of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*):
There is complete absorption through supreme joy, even amidst pleasure, pain, and the like. (4.120)
The ellipsis implies that the teacher must be one who is to initiate [the disciple]. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"For some time, there is dissolution" (8.90). || 120 ||

Having thus conceptualized through meditation the three purificatory rites known as *adhikāra*, *bhoga*, and *laya*— one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for each of these three by means of the *dhāman* itself with three [recitations] each;
that is to say, with three oblations at the end of the modified mantra (*ūha-mantra*).
Having thus explained birth, authority, enjoyment, and dissolution, he speaks in order to explain the fifth purificatory rite, called *niṣkṛti*:
"Furthermore, one hundred oblations are to be offered with the *dhāman* mantra for the sake of *niṣkṛti*. (4.121)
He will explain its true nature not far from the point of atonement.
Now, why is there a specific oblation (*homa*) in this [rite]? Regarding this, he states the reason:
"But that karma which consists of objects of experience—characterized by birth, lifespan, and enjoyment—is purified at the end of its expiation and remains situated in the world of earth. (4-122)

That form which is to be experienced as the fruit consisting of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment, and which is produced by action (karman) of a pure or impure nature, is purified only through its complete discharge; therefore, a hundred oblations (śatahomam) are appropriate for this [rite]. The worlds of Bhūḥ refer to the realms of existence ending with Vīrabhadra; that which is situated therein has attained the state of being an object of experience.
And this has been stated here as "cessation, purification, and clarity" (*nivṛtti-śuddhi-prasāda*);

furthermore, that is intended as an illustration of the enjoyment of the worlds (*bhuvana-bhoga*) contained within the principles (*tattva*) pervaded by *Pratiṣṭhā* and the others. However, another [author], having read the text as "in the world of earth" (*bhūloke*), has explained it as referring to what was attained in Kanyādvīpa, which is a specific region of the earthly realm (*bhūrloka*).

By the statement, "Experience consists of suffering and pleasure," experience has now been determined; lifespan will be determined in the chapter on creation and dissolution. Thus, he indicates the remaining category, birth, through its various types of manifestation: The text states: "Experience consists of suffering and pleasure. By this statement, experience (*bhoga*) has just now been defined. Lifespan (*āyuḥ*) will be defined in the chapter on creation and dissolution (*sṛṣṭisaṃhārapaṭala*).
Therefore, he points out the remaining category, birth (*jāti*), by means of its various modes of arising:

The fourteen worlds of transmigration... the meaning is that the creation of beings (*bhūtasarga*) itself constitutes the fourteenfold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is divided into the categories of gods, humans, and animals.
In the *bhuvanadīkṣā*, he will state the purification of all castes: "One should purify those of the lowest castes, as well as Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas" (10.384). But here, however—

"In this way, those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring objects of desire, attain the state of going and returning" (Gītā 9.21). According to the principle stated here, because the six duties (*ṣaṭkarman*) are binding actions due to one's eligibility for them, it is only the *brāhmaṇya* caste that constitutes the purification of the human species.

It must certainly be purified by means of the expiatory oblation (*niṣkṛti-homa*) alone; in order to state that this rite is concise, he says: "The forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*), together with the eight, will be described on the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) for the sake of attaining the status of the twice-born. (4.123)
The womb, the seed, as well as disposition, food, and location— O Goddess, the purification of these [is required].
There are forty [rites], beginning with conception and ending with the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), and those beginning with compassion (dayā) and ending with longing (spṛhā).

Regarding the "eight": those forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) which will be clarified further on must be purified separately during the initiation into the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*); whereas the [impurities] beginning with food (*āhāra*) and so forth are included within the expiatory fire-oblations (*niṣkṛtihoma*) during initiations such as that of the *kalās*. This is the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) here, based on the connection with the statements to follow.

Furthermore, this production of the twice-born caste refers to a future body whose existence is caused by karma; however, it was previously determined that for the initiate (*samayin*), there is something entirely different in the present body itself, consisting of the fitness for the class of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). For this very reason, previously, regarding the initiate—

The attainment of the state of Rudra was previously described as consisting of the fitness for attaining the principle of Īśvara; however, this [present case] consists of the contemplation of the fitness for attaining future Rudra-hood by virtue of entering into the womb of Śakti, and not the actual attainment of Rudra-hood itself, because the bonds (*pāśas*) of *nivṛtti* remain impure even now. Thus it has been said:
And in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Rudrāṇī is called Śakti; the attainment of fitness for her womb is the state of being a portion of Rudra, not the state of being Rudra himself.
(*Kriyāpāda* 8.65)
Thus [ends the section]. || 123 ||

He states that this very process of restoring the portion of Rudra, along with the purification of caste, lifespan, and experience, must be accomplished in the midst of the expiatory oblations (*niṣkṛti-homa*) itself:
".........so too the restoration of the portion of Rudra. (4.124)
Having performed the visualization here, one becomes pure through atonement alone.
Not only must purity be established through the atonement for births, lifespans, and experiences,
but even that purity whose nature is described as the attainment of the state of being a portion of Rudra (rudrāṃśāpatti) must be achieved.
The meaning is that it should be deposited in that very place. "Here" refers to the expiation; "contemplation" refers to [the nature of] entities.
He explains the nature of atonement (niṣkṛti): "Whatever objects exist in the form of the worlds, which have the nature of things to be experienced... (4.125).
Because the remainder of the fruits of karma have been consumed by it, that [initiation] is traditionally known as *niṣkṛti* (expiation).
The term *bhuvana* (world) is intended to indicate states such as those of women and so forth. The word "in them" (*teṣu*) is to be supplied within the middle of the verse.
That initiation by which the fruit of karma is consumed entirely and completely—that is what is meant here.

This is an instance of the reversal of the usual word order (*pūrvanipātavyatyaya*). "Expiation" (*niṣkṛti*) is derived from the etymology: that in which there is a complete performance, meaning the total completion of the enjoyment of the fruits of all karma. Regarding the phrase "is remembered," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "in the initiation itself, as that which is to be purified. (125)
Now,
separation [occurs] from experience as a result of expiation...
separation from experience [means] the non-connection with further experiences for the experiencer, due to the absence of the state of being an experiencer.
A purificatory rite must also be performed as an act of expiation.
For that [is] indeed taught to occur in the absence of enjoyments. (4-126)
For it is not possible to purify [the body] without an expiation consisting of the completion of [the allotted] enjoyments. || 126 ||

In order to state the state of separation, which consists in the absence of the nature of being an enjoyer, preceded by a restatement of that very nature of being an enjoyer, he says: "The nature of being an enjoyer is attachment to objects; it is proclaimed to be the effect of impurity (mala). The absence of the nature of being an enjoyer is that which is brought about by the body in that very [state]. (4-127)
By the command of Śiva, the disjunction of that bound soul (paśu) is performed through mantras.

Whatever has been done by means of the body, or whatever remains unexhausted by the bodies, the attachment to those very objects as one's own domain— the clinging [expressed as] "may something be mine"— this is the effect of impurity (mala).
The state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) arises from the *āṇava-mala*, which consists of the sense of incompleteness (*apūrṇamanyatā*).
For such an enjoyer who is a bound soul (*paśu*), a separation from that state of being an enjoyer is effected through the command of a Guru who is non-different from Śiva, by means of the Mantra;
and this is said to be the absence of the aforementioned state of being an enjoyer—such is the logical connection. || 127 ||
And here—three oblations are offered with the [mantra of] the abode for the purpose of effecting separation. (4.128)
"Amukāya nivṛttipāśaviśleṣaṃ karomi svāhā"—this is the mantra here. In the same way, one should apply one's own reasoning for subsequent rites as well, according to their appropriateness. || 128 ||
Then, one should cause three oblations to be offered with the *dhāman* even for the severing of bonds.
Regarding that which is the oblation for the purpose of severing bonds, he speaks of those bonds:
The nooses pertaining to Māyā within the body, however, extend from the kalās down to the elements (bhūtas).

The forms of the body and its instruments exist for the accomplishment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*.
