Within the body, the fetters belonging to *māyā*— beginning with *kalā* and ending with the gross elements (*mahābhūta*)— which serve as the cause of the body, fashion the body and the senses, as well as the worlds, states of being, and so forth, which are indicated by those [two].
They bring about [the means] for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). And it has been said:
"This sphere of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*) extends from *kalā* down to the earth. (11.295).
The word "but" (*tu*)—
"The state of being an enjoyer and attachment to sense objects are the effects of impurity.
(4-127). Likewise, in that same [work]:
"But that which is performed by means of the body" (4-127);
this indicates the distinction from the previously mentioned *āṇava* and *kārmika* bonds. || 129 ||
And thus, due to the absence of experience resulting from the separation caused by atonement, bodies perish in a thousand ways. (4.130)

"Bodies" refers to those in the form of gross, subtle, and so forth. "In thousands" means in the form of various and manifold creations of beings. "Perish" means they are destroyed without the possibility of rebirth. || 130 ||
And for that candidate for initiation for whom these [instruments] fail—
his procedure for the severing of bonds is performed with mantras enjoined by the ritual rules,
for one whose nature consists in the cessation of the pervasive influence of the bonds such as the *āṇava* and others, which reside within the thread of the bonds.
Upon the severing of the noose, the ritual procedure (vidhi) must be performed with mantras enjoined by the scriptural statements consisting of knowledge. And that procedure is as follows:
"This infallible power of Śiva is proclaimed to be the knife."

Thus, according to the pervasion taught in the *Śrīhaṃsapārameśa*, one should sever the bonds by reciting the mantra of Śiva along with his weapon— ending in *huṃ phaṭ*— joined with the *pluta* (protracted) technique, while the weapon-mantra has been consecrated (*japta*) by the *kartarī*.
As it is said in the *Śrīmṛgendra*:
"Then, with the Śiva-weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and accompanied by the proper tone,
he should sever that many bonds with a pair of scissors consecrated with the weapon-mantra. (Kriyākāṇḍa 8.113–114).
He concludes: "In this way, the severance of even the three bonds is said to occur through initiation. (4-131)

"Thus" means preceded by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as previously explained, namely those called birth (janman), qualification (adhikāra), enjoyment (bhoga), abode (laya), and expiation (niṣkṛti). And here, the oblation (homa) of the severed bond (pāśa) must be performed together with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) using the very mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* that has been mentioned. Thus.
The meaning stated in another *saṃhitā* should be accepted. Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra* itself:
"Then, having filled that *sruva* [ladle] with clarified butter, one should offer oblations by means of that very same application of mantras" (*Kriyāpāda* 8.114–115).
Thus [ends the verse]. 131.

Thus, when the sixfold ritual of refinement (saṃskāra) has been performed at the conclusion of the separation— meaning the Guru must effect in the disciple the contemplation of the single consciousness through the total dissolution of the body.
And at this juncture—[one should offer] the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the very word "Śiva," accompanied by the exclamation "vauṣaṭ. || 4.132 ||
The word "should give" is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. || 132 ||
Now, due to the absence of fetters (pāśa)—
that consciousness, which is situated at the summit of the pure principles (śuddhatattva) and possesses a golden luster,
becomes unified with that [divine] consciousness above the pure principle known as Nivṛtti.

Having meditated upon [the deity] as blazing and abiding in a state of perfect non-obscuration, one should again cause three oblations to be offered with the *dhāman* mantra for the purpose of extraction. || 133 ||
And the formal application (prayoga) here is: "I extract Devadatta from the earth-element (pṛthivītattva), which is pervaded by cessation. || 133 ||
Then,

having extracted consciousness together with its impurity from that reality (tattva) by means of the mudrā according to the previously prescribed method, one should fill it within the heart, abiding in the self.
Although it is stainless due to the purity of cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is joined with impurity because the other *kalās* have not been purified.

"By means of the *mudrā*" refers to that called "reabsorption" (*saṃhāra*). The "prior procedure" consists of such forms as being encapsulated by the *praṇava* (OM) and having the *haṃsa*-seed syllable at its beginning. || 134 ||
Then—
having performed *kumbhaka*, having exhaled, and having gathered [the breath] from the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *dhruva* [mantra],
one should deposit this into the body of the disciple through the opening of the channel (*nāḍīrandhra*) as before. (4.135)
Then, for him—namely, for the purpose of making [the disciple] established therein—one should offer three oblations by means of the *dhāman*;
this is the ellipsis. [The mantra is: "I establish the purified consciousness residing in the heart of Devadatta, svāhā."
The application here is as follows.

Thus: the severing of the bonds, the oblation for that, the full oblation (pūrṇāhoma), the contemplation of the unity of consciousness, the oblation for its extraction, the bringing [of the deity] to the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka), the retention (kumbhana), the exhalation (recana) to the limit of twelve finger-breadths, then the grasping [of the deity], the entry into the body of the disciple, and the oblation for that purpose.
Having thus accomplished the separation refined by these eleven intermediate purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), he speaks in order to effect the cessation of what remains:
"But at the conclusion of the purification of the *kalā*, [he should worship] Brahmā, the lord of the instruments. (4.136)
Having performed the invocation and worship using one's own name preceded by the *praṇava*, and having offered libations, one should present [the offering].

The compound "svanāmapraṇavapūrvamāhvānaṃ tubhyaṃ namaḥ iti ca pūjā yasya" is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that which has an invocation preceded by the *praṇava* of one's own name and a worship consisting of 'salutation to you' (*tubhyaṃ namaḥ*). The libation for that is performed in the fire with the mantra "svāhā."
From that [state] comes application, and from that too comes the offering for the sake of offering the *puryaṣṭaka*. || 136 ||
Regarding this, it says:
"In that state, one should abandon sound and touch.
How so?
...the two beginning with Dhruva, joined with their names. || 4-137 ||
By means of the application of the *svāhākāra*, one should offer those two into Brahman.
Through three oblations each, [one should offer] with the formula:
"Oṃ, I offer sound to Brahman, svāhā! Having thus offered three times, (Oṃ, to Brahman...)
One should offer oblations three times with the mantra "I offer contact, svāhā"; this is to be understood from the repetition [indicated by the word *iti*]. || 137 ||
In this manner, he should offer this [oblation] to him—the eightfold constituent of the city (puryaṣṭāṃśa). || 4-138 ||

The eightfold group that initiates the city of the subtle body consists of the subtle elements (tanmātras), the mind (manas), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi); we shall clarify our intention regarding the distribution of their respective portions later on. || 138 ||
Furthermore:
"One should cause the proclamation of that [command] to be made by means of the vocative case.
"Of that" refers to Brahman; "proclamation" (śrāvaṇā) is the command of Śiva. As it has been stated in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"O Lord of the World, by the command of Śiva, you must not place any obstacle in the way of this practitioner who is proceeding to the state free from affliction. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.65)
And having performed the proclamation—having worshipped Brahmā and performed the fire-oblation, one should dismiss him. (4.139)
Furthermore:
Having worshipped Vāgīśī with the *dhruva* [mantra] and having gratified her, one should dismiss her.
"Dismissal" (*visarjana*) is the contemplation (*vimarśana*) of the identity between one's own speech and supreme speech, by means of the *dhruva*, which is partless (*niṣkala*).
Thus, from the joining of the paths (*adhvasandhāna*) until the dismissal of Vāgīśī, having offered oblations, one should behold therein the pure net of fetters (*pāśajāla*). (4.140)

"Having offered" (hutvā) means: the joining of the paths (*adhvasaṃdhāna*), the attendance upon the paths (*adhvopasthāna*), the union with the womb of Vāgīśī, the birth which is the completion of that womb and the attainment of authority (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), dissolution (*laya*), expiation (*niṣkṛti*), separation (*viśleṣa*),
the fire-oblation for severing the fetters (*pāśacchedahoma*), the fire-oblation for the fetters (*pāśahoma*), the full oblation (*pūrṇāhoma*), and the extraction oblation (*uddhārahoma*).
Having performed the nineteen oblations not previously mentioned— namely, *tatsthīkaraṇa*, *brahmatarpaṇa*, the *puryaṣṭakāṃśārpaṇahoma*, the *punarbrahmahoma*, and the *vāgīśīhoma*—
[one should know that] "therein" means in the pure *nivṛttikalā*; and so it is likewise for what follows.
The collection of the formative forces (saṃskāra) and the calculation of the oblation (homa) should be remembered. || 140 ||
And here, at the time of observing the purification of the bonds (pāśa-śuddhi):
"Then one should contemplate the non-existence of that which arises from past karma,
because for one desiring liberation there is no dependence [upon it]..."
The compound *bhāvyeva bhāvikamarthāt karma* refers to the collection of both future karma (*bhāvya*) and past karma (*prākkarma*), provided that it is destined to manifest (*bhāvika*).

This is because, being independent [of other conditions], it lacks the orientation toward a fruit like a productive agent (*sādhaka*). However, some interpret it by connecting the terms as follows: "that which comes into being through past karma is 'past-karma-born' (*prākkarmabhava*)," and the fruit that arises therein is what is meant.

The statement that "it belongs to the state of existence resulting from prior karma" has already been explained; that is incorrect, and it should be disregarded along with the claim that it is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
Regarding the question of what happens to one who is currently engaged in the act of bestowing fruits [of action], he says:
"One should not purify that which has already begun. (4.141)
The meaning is that [it is so] because one passes the time by means of enjoyment alone. || 141 ||
Having described the account of the purification of karma for one seeking liberation (mumukṣu), he speaks of that for the practitioner (sādhaka):
"But for the sake of the prosperity of the practitioner...
The meaning is that even that which has prosperity as its purpose—namely, the future form of propitiating the mantra—one should not purify.
Only...
[he] should purify a single prior karma;
for that which was previously begun by his body for the sake of prosperity, whether auspicious or inauspicious, from that [karma], it is only the inauspicious one [that remains].
One should purify [it], for in this way the accomplishment of enjoyment occurs without obstacle. || 141 ||

However, whatever auspicious or inauspicious karma has been accumulated in other births, and whatever he will perform in this birth—all that must indeed be purified for him like a spiritual son (*putraka*) according to the method already described, with the exception of the propitiation of the mantra.
Thus it is said: "Having contemplated the past karma and the future [karma] as unified in one place, one should initiate him. (142)
The word "sādhakam" (the means of accomplishment) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Ekastham" (situated in one) means cultivated as a single, unified whole.
And thus:
"This initiation belongs to those whose duty is Śiva..."—
the word "for the practitioner" (*sādhake*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
...the worldly dharmas are otherwise than this.
To the question "Of what sort?", he says: "It causes the destruction of unrighteousness belonging both to the past and to the future. (4-143)
"She should be known as one who follows worldly norms (*lokadharminī*), having abandoned the propitiation of mantras.

As for the phrase "one devoted to the rites of sacrifice and public works, performing actions while desiring their fruit" (4.85), the person who follows worldly norms has already been defined. The term "causing the destruction of unrighteousness" (*adharmakṣayakāriṇī*) is used in a relative sense.

This is a summary: [the practitioner] is entirely free from all [practices], such as the propitiation of mantras—which is the cause for the attainment of *piṇḍasiddhi* and the cause for attaining the status of a *mantra* and so forth—because there is no specific injunction [to the contrary]. Furthermore, in the *Śrīmṛgendra*, it is established that the propitiation of mantras, which is the cause for present-day accomplishments (*siddhi*), consists solely of the qualities of Śiva (*śivadharmāṇi*).
And so it is said there:
"The Śiva-dharma is the root of the individual soul (aṇu), the glory of the fruits of the Śiva-dharma;
it is beneficial and other than harmful until the dissolution of the bodies of beings on earth. (Kriyākāṇḍa 8.6)
Thus [it is said].
This is its meaning: initiation into the Śiva-dharma is for the sake of the soul's glorious fortune consisting of the fruits of the Śiva-dharma.

The root [initiation] is the sole cause for the attainment of the fruit of the Supreme Lord, which consists in the state of being a mantra, a lord of mantras, and so forth; the other, however, is beneficial until the time of dissolution— up to the point when the various worlds (*bhuvah*), which are planes of enjoyment, have not yet dissolved— provided there is no destruction of the body.

It is that which accomplishes the attainments (siddhis) such as the desired sword, the power of seeing the netherworld (pātāla), collyrium, and sandals; it is not the other [type], which is characterized by worldly qualities. Thus it should be explained:
"When the portion of one's evil deeds has been destroyed in all the realms of enjoyment..."
"For the sake of attaining another body, the powers such as *aṇimā*, and other worldly goals, these are desired by the learned. (Kriyākālaguṇottara 8.7).

This is because, in that very context, distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) has not been determined. Nor should one be deluded into thinking that the status of a practitioner (*sādhaka*) cannot be achieved without the propitiation of mantras; for it can also be achieved through the means of performing sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*).
Enough with saying "from the attainment of that. || 144 ||
Thus, by virtue of having undergone initiation into the worldly dharmas, he indeed experiences the powers such as *aṇimā* upon the dissolution of the body that was begun [in this life]. (4-144)
The meaning is that, by virtue of his initiation, his enjoyments result in auspicious karma, culminating in the attainment of Īśvara and the other [tattvas].
Then, having eaten, one should proceed upward wherever one has been directed by the Guru,
whether in the Sakala or the Niṣkala state.

According to the principle stated in the verse, "Whoever should desire enjoyments in whatever [place]," a seeker of liberation— whether at the end of the experience of the fruits of auspicious karma, for the sake of *sāyujya* (union) and so forth with a particular Lord of a world (*bhuvaneśvara*) in the *sakala* (manifest) state, or joined to the *niṣkala* (unmanifest) Śiva— shall go to that very station.
As it is stated in the *Śrī Mṛgendra*:

"Having superimposed the worldly attributes upon the Lord of the worlds who is present in the mind, one should effect the attainment of those attributes for Śiva, or [one should do so] for the seeker of liberation. (Kriyāpāda 8.148)
Thus [it is said].
The upward departure and the distance of one *yojana* occur respectively, according to the status of the disciple and the teacher. (4.145)
The meaning is that [the result] arises by virtue of the intention of both the disciple and the guru. And this was stated previously:
"Whatever kind of fruit you desire, I shall begin the sacrifice accordingly," and so forth. (4.81)

Having thus determined the two-fold initiation for worldly enjoyment (*bhoga-dīkṣā*), he speaks in order to determine, in sequence, the initiation for liberation (*mokṣa-dīkṣā*)— both with seed (*sabījā*) and without seed (*nirbījā*), as well as that which grants immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadā*):
"Even in the case of the initiation with seed leading to liberation, one may fall away due to the absence of [the exhaustion of] karma."

"The specific rules of conduct (*viśeṣasamayācāra*) which were previously determined for that initiation (*dīkṣā*) characterized by the seed (*sabījā*) for the sake of *nirvāṇa*— those known as the *mantras* must be observed here with great effort. (4.90)

The meaning is that due to the absence—that is, the non-performance—of the aforementioned action, one perishes; having fallen for some time from one's own Śiva-nature, one attains the state of a flesh-eater (kravyāda). || 146 ||
Therefore, for this reason: "The initiated one should indeed maintain the bond of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra-pāśa). (4.146)
That bond would certainly not be purified...;
therefore, the initiated one should maintain the bond of the conduct of the rules (samayācāra), and for that reason,
one should not purify it, just as in the case of one who has received the seedless initiation (nirbījadīkṣita).
And this initiation is...
[this] is proclaimed as being with seed (sabījā). In the seedless (nirbījā) initiation, however, one should purify the bond of the conduct of the rule (samayācāra-pāśa). (4-147)
The procedure for its purification will be explained further ahead. || 147 ||
And for this one who has been initiated by means of initiation without seed (nirbījadīkṣā)—liberation shall occur through mere initiation, always by virtue of devotion alone toward the Guru.
The meaning is that for him, the sole observance (samaya) is simply devotion to the Guru. || 4-148 ||
He states another division of this [initiation]:
"The initiation that bestows immediate liberation is the seedless (nirbījā); that is the second. (4.148)
At the conclusion of initiation, there shall be purification from the three bonds (pāśa) undertaken in the past and future; upon the casting off of the body, the supreme state is attained.

"Immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) means precisely at the moment following the persistence of the bodily constituents once they have been separated [from the self] by initiation (*dīkṣā*) through the most radiant mantra. For this very reason, it is that which separates even the three bonds (*pāśatraya*) whose effects have already begun; the meaning is: "therein," that is, at the conclusion—the completion—of the initiation at the time of the abandonment of the body. Thus...
The intended meaning is that this [rite] must be performed only for one whose death is certain to be imminent due to signs such as the appearance of *ariṣṭas*.
As it is said in the venerable Guhyasūtra: "Having seen a disciple seized by old age and tormented by disease..."
Then, having caused him to ascend, one should unite him with the Supreme Reality.
Thus [ends verse 149].
He concludes the incidental discussion on the discrimination regarding initiation:
"In this way, according to the disposition of the disciples, the fruit of various forms is always brought forth by the Guru through a well-performed initiation. (4.150)
Because—the power of mantra is indeed inconceivable, having arisen from the mouth of the Supreme Lord.
The "mouth" of the Supreme Lord is the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti); it is inconceivable precisely because it originates from that. By the word "power" (śakti)—
He speaks of the essence of mantras being diligence. || 151 ||
And that [mantra] should be employed by the Guru at the time of the ritual action, preceded by devotion. (4.151)

Ritual action consists of initiation and the like; devotion is that very same [action], consisting of the penetration of its vitality through the process of reflecting upon the true nature of the mantra.
With the words beginning with "inconceivable" (acintya), he says this:

"Just as one might swallow snares with poisons, the Guru who knows the reality of mantra and is possessed by Śiva certainly effects [the swallowing] of the snares in an instant through mantras. (4.152)
The bonds pertaining to the person are to be purified during initiation, but not those residing in the intellect;
therefore, even if that [intellect] is defective, initiation is not fruitless.
Those who have received an extremely intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and are freed from the seeds of defects shine forth;
they are observed [as liberated] even through initiation by means of the scales (*tulādīkṣā*), like the purification of a jar.
If you do not admit the gravity of sin, then what do you say regarding the purification of a jar?
Since that occurs through the power of mantras, the diversity of initiations (*dīkṣā*) is not inconsistent.

"Just as beating and other such acts may befall men when [the name] is written in letters, so too, by the power of the mantra, the severing of the bonds (pāśas) in the thread is manifest. Let this matter rest for now; we shall determine it in detail further on. || 152 ||
Having thus resolved the incidental subject matter, he speaks while returning to the main topic:
"One should perform the conjunction of the *kalās* (energies) as they proceed in two forms, pure and impure;
[this refers to] the conjunction of the *nivṛtti-kalā* in its pure form."
One should perform the rite as pure when it is conjoined with the power of impure consecration; for this very reason, it possesses a twofold nature.
And in this regard:
"One should pronounce the pure [syllable] short, and the impure long. (4.153)
Having meditated upon oneness, one should contemplate that which is dissolved and pure.
Here, the Lord Niṣkala-Bhaṭṭāraka is the purifier of all fetters without exception; however, the eleven Brahma-mantras of the limbs are what is to be purified. And yet:
Because he possesses both pure and impure aspects, Niṣkalanātha is designated as both pure and impure;

and because he denotes the pure state of cessation (*nivṛtti*), one should pronounce him as "pure" and as "short"— that is, with all outward expansion stilled, whose true nature is the pervasion of the Supreme Bindu.

And because it denotes an impure foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), it is "impure" and "long"—that is, its true nature is the pervasion of *nāda* directed toward expansion. One should pronounce [the mantra] after having meditated upon oneness and aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). And here, in order to indicate the pure foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) as being dissolved, one uses the root mantra which denotes that [foundation].
One should visualize it as having become unified with that. || 154 ||
Now follows the purification of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā:
here, neither short nor long measures (*mātrā*) are to be uttered;
rather— "The *nivṛtti* [kalā] consists of the *praṇava* and so forth, and immediately after that is *pratiṣṭhā*. (4.154)
At the end of that, however, the *namaskāra* is known as the "junction of the parts" (*kalā-sandhānaka*).
Having uttered the short, partless (*niṣkala*) *praṇava* which denotes *nivṛtti*, and the heart-mantra (*hṛn-mantra*),
at its end one says the word "for the sake of *nivṛtti*," and after that, the long, partless *praṇava*.
Having uttered the *śiromantra* which expresses "establishment," the application here is "pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ"; however, in the fire-oblation (*homa*), it ends with "svāhā. || 155 ||
And thus:
having invoked [the deity], established [him], and worshipped [him], one should offer three oblations. (4.155)
Regarding *kalāsaṃdhāna* (the conjunction of the *kalās*):
some say that the meditation (*dhyāna*) for the support (*dhāraṇā*) of the *kalās*, beginning with Earth (*pṛthvī*), must be performed.
Now—
...one should observe its pervasion;
that is, of that installation.
Therein—[one should perform] the conceptualization of the path within the body of the disciple, beginning from the ankles up to the navel. (4.156)
The pervasion of the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā] consists of twenty-four principles (tattvas), fifty-six worlds (bhuvanas), and twenty-three phonemes (varṇas). (4.157)
It is prescribed as having twenty-one topics regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and three mantras.
It consists of twenty-four principles (*tattva*), beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*) and ending with primordial matter (*pradhāna*), together with the principle of qualities (*guṇatattva*).

Furthermore, it contains [the chapters] known as the Secret (*guhya*), the Most Secret (*atiguhya*), the Purifying (*pavitra*), the Fixed (*sthāṇu*), the Gross (*sthūla*), the Source of Deities (*devayoni*), and the Application (*yoga*).
In this [state], there are seventy-four forms which will be described in the context of the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*);

these are presided over by fifty-six Lords of Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*), and it is that [state] in which these many worlds— along with the intermediate worlds contained within them— are the primary worlds.

In which [mantra] there are twenty-three syllables beginning with the letter *ha* and ending with the letter *ṭa*. Regarding the "twenty-one": previously, starting from the nine-syllable pada located in the western direction—the abode of the *kalā*-tattva—up to the letter *ū* situated in the northeastern corner, these were employed; thus, in reverse order, one begins from the letter *a* situated within that interval.

There is a group of eight ending with the letter *la*; likewise, there is a group of nine beginning with *mū* and ending with *ma*, located in the nine squares situated in the southwest direction (nairṛtadik) which rests upon the *māyātattva*; and from the center of the nine squares situated in the southern direction (dakṣadik) presided over by the *vidyātattva*, there is a group of four beginning with *ū* and ending with *la*.

In which [mantra] there are twenty-one words, including *ceti*; and in which there are three mantras—*vāmadeva*, *śiras*, and *śikhā*—but not the *hṛdaya*, because the *hṛt-mantra* is included within *nivṛtti*. || 157 ||
And thus, those consisting of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvātmānaḥ) are indeed remembered as the primary fetters (pāśāḥ).
Their primacy is due to their being common to all individual souls (sarvāṇu-sādhāraṇyāt); for even the words, phonemes, and mantras [are included therein].
By the reasoning [stated in] *Svacchanda Tantra* 4.15, "of that which arises from the mass of sounds," it is the *pāśas* (fetters) themselves that assume the form of signifiers; for this very reason,

[anything] other than the *mūlamantra*, whose ultimate reality is the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of the essential nature consisting of the undifferentiated mass of consciousness and bliss, [is a fetter].
Everything here is indeed to be purified. As stated by our gurus in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Whatever is other than the Supreme Śiva—whose nature has been described as beautiful through the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness—that is called a bond (*pāśa*). (8.292)
Thus [it is said].
And right here—.................. one should contemplate the subtle and infinite [forms]. || 4-158 ||
He clarifies this:

"But the purification of the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the sense organs, which is well-known in other systems, is to be included here. Other systems refer to those such as the Lākula and others. And although...

Although it was stated that "the twenty-three principles" include the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth, one should not be deluded into thinking that those [principles] are identical to these; for while those pervade the external arrangement of the world, these are distinct and reside within the gross and subtle bodies. || 159 ||
Furthermore:
One should always cause the six sheaths and the five sense objects to be absorbed within that. (4.159)

The six sheaths known as blood, flesh, hair, marrow, bone, and sinew exist above the subtle body in the form of sheaths. The word "always" (sadā) refers to the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus, even while [the subtle body] exists in this manner, the purification of the body is indeed enjoined; therefore, those who say that it need not be performed therein are simply mistaken.

Therefore, having performed the establishment of the specific [deity] in the form of the contemplation that pervades the aforementioned paths, one should then worship with perfumes and other offerings.
Likewise:

The remainder [of the sentence] is that one should offer three oblations with the Bhairava [mantra]. Regarding the term "with the Bhairava," it is like the eye of a crow [functioning in both directions];
thus, having uttered the Praṇava, the Niṣkala, and the Pratiṣṭhā-bīja, one says: "Salutation to Pratiṣṭhā."
Worship is performed with the mantra, and the fire-oblation (homa) is performed with the mantra ending in *svāhā*; the same applies hereafter.
Then, [the visualization of her as] Vāgīśī is described. 4-160.
For she is capable of internalizing everything within a single drop; and here, one should remember what was previously stated, beginning with "one should first install the Śakti," and so forth.
Furthermore: "The invocation by one's own name and so forth, as well as the *argha* offering, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites are as before;
likewise [there are] the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the striking (*tāḍana*), the cutting (*cheda*), and the drawing in and seizing (*ākarṣagrahaṇa*). (4.161)
Having filled [the vessel] with the light and held it in breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should then sever [the connection] and cause [the disciple] to grasp it again;
then, following the previous sequence, [one performs] the union, the state of being held in the womb, and the birth.
By the extension [of the rule] "as before," he instructs that one should recollect the entire sequence of the ritual procedure as described in the section on cessation. || 162 ||
Now, as an incidental digression, he completes what remains to be said regarding all initiations:
"Having assumed the form of the Goddess, one should perform the striking and other rites.
Thus, the acts of striking, sprinkling, and so forth are to be performed when there is an immersion into the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
They are indeed endowed with the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) as the Lord, in whom the power of action (kriyāśakti) predominates.
Furthermore:
"Empowerment, as well as enjoyment, dissolution, and expiation. (4.163)
These [rites] should be performed in the form of Śiva...

Knowledge of the qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth is to be accomplished through lordship (*prabhutva*). And since the Lord is indeed Śiva everywhere, beginning with Sadāśiva, that [knowledge] is appropriate only through the sense of identity "I am Śiva" (*śivāhaṃbhāva*). In the stage of cessation (*nivṛtti*), there are the rites of expiation (*niṣkṛti*) and the oblation of separation (*viśleṣahoma*).
They are stated by the root [verse] itself.
Here he states the distinction between those two:
"The expiation is performed with the head,
while the separation is to be offered with the heart."
The word "again" (punar) is used everywhere for the sake of specification:
"...so too is the severing of bonds with the sword. (4-164)
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is also [to be done] with the Root-mantra (*mūla*). As was stated previously:
"A triad of oblations [is offered] with the *dhāman* even for the severing of bonds" (4.129).
Thus, the meaning of the word "likewise" is that the cutting, striking, and so forth of the *puryaṣṭaka* are also performed with this very sword.
It has been stated that attraction, grasping, and so forth are performed by means of the abode alone. || 164 ||
Furthermore:
"The extraction of the *pūrṇāhuti* should be performed as before by Bhairava;
that is to say, by the partless (*niṣkala*) one."
Śrī Sadāśiva is preeminent in the power of knowledge; abiding in the body of Sadāśiva, one should perform the rites of separation and so forth. (4.165)

Since [the rites] such as *viśleṣa* (separation) are intended for the pacification of distinctions, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of Sadāśiva, which is primarily concerned with that [pacification], should be understood. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [rites] such as *uddhāra* (extraction), which are permeated by the single consciousness, are included. || 165 ||
Having thus completed the digression, he states the subject at hand:
"By means of inhalation (*pūraka*), [the breath] situated in the self [is brought] to the heart; by means of the process of exhalation (*recaka*), [it is brought] to the heart.
All of this has already been determined previously.
Then, having meditated upon Viṣṇu as the presiding lord of the installation, one should invoke him by uttering his own name and establish him. || 4.166 ||
One should worship with flowers, perfumes, and so forth;
and for this [deity],
one should offer three oblations for the purpose of satiation (tarpaṇa).
One should give.
Furthermore:
"One should always offer the essence, which is a portion of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), to Viṣṇu. (4.167)
The word "in initiations" (dīkṣāsu) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 167 ||
Having performed the proclamation as before,
one should then dismiss Viṣṇu and dismiss Vāgīśī. Then—
The juncture of the *kalās* is as before, through the application of short and long [vowels]. (4.168)
One should contemplate non-existence within that infinite web of bonds; then, liberated from the two *kalās*, the bound soul (*paśu*) becomes eager for the upward path. (4.169)
Now, having joined that [individual soul] to the third Vidyā, one should purify it;
by implication, this refers to consciousness (caitanya). || 169 ||
Having established that vidyā and having worshipped it, one should then offer three oblations. || 4.170 ||
The meaning is that, having thus brought [the path] face-to-face, one should perform the observation of the paths as before. || 170 ||
He states that very point: "The pervasion of Vidyā is held to extend from the principle of the individual soul (puruṣatattva) up to the limit of Māyā. (4.171)
And thus—
the seven principles (tattvas) known as Puruṣa, Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, Kalā, and Māyā.

This hexad of principles belonging to the person (puruṣa) exists in the form of a sheath; because it stands as the cause for internal experience, it is pervaded by the power (kalā) called vidyā. It is termed *pratiṣṭhā* according to the etymological derivation that "it is where the network of principles, which are the causes of experience, is established. [Therein] it ceases.
It should be understood that *nivṛtti* is so called because it is the creation of the principles (*tattva*); *śāntā* is so called because all differentiation has ceased;
and *śāntyatītā* is that which has transcended even that [state], being empty even of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Likewise—

..................and indeed twenty-seven worlds. Although the sequence of principles (tattvas) begins with the Person (puruṣa), Necessity (niyati), and so forth, nevertheless, for the Person who consists of a longing (lolikā)—

There is non-deviation [of the soul] from passion (rāga), which consists in a general attachment; from knowledge (vidyā), which consists in some degree of feeling, by means of necessity (niyati), which consists in restriction; and from limited agency (kalā), which consists in the intensification of the power of agency, by means of time (kāla). This is the method of the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa) yoga in the initiation into the categories (tattva) and the words (pada).

Since this will be explained later, the arrangement of the worlds (*bhuvana*) therein follows that very sequence: in that [level], within the *puruṣa* and *rāga* principles, there are eight worlds presided over by the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), who constitute the primary [principles]; however, as for *niyati* and *vidyā*...
There are nine [worlds] presided over by the nine lords of the worlds beginning with Vāmā and ending with Manonmanā;
there are three [worlds] presided over by the triad beginning with Mahādeva, belonging to Kāla and Kalā. Thus, there are twenty.
Within Māyā, which is the cause of these principles (tattvas), Gopati is in the lower part, Viśva is above, and [Rudra] is in the middle.
The four [deities] are Trikālajña, Īśa, Brahmādhipati, and Śiva; their presiding lord is Ananta—thus there are seven, making twenty-seven worlds.
Likewise—
twenty-four steps are declared...
from the nine steps situated in the direction of Dakṣa (the southeast) up to the letter *la*, there is a group of four.
That which was included previously remains: the group of five beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣā*, as before;
likewise, from the nine fire-squares presided over by the principle of Īśvara, the group of nine beginning with *ū* and ending with *ra*;
and from the nine squares in the eastern direction presided over by the principle of Sadāśiva, [the group] beginning with *ū* and ending with *kṣa*.
The group of six consists of twenty-six words.
Furthermore:
...the seven notes (varṇas) are proclaimed. || 4-172 ||
The vowels beginning with *ñ* and ending with *gh*. 172.
Likewise—
there are two mantras...
Aghora is the armor (kavaca).
Thus here—
having known the sixfold path in this manner, one should perform the conceptualization of Vāgīśikā.
Here, he reminds [the reader] of what was stated previously:
Having invoked the Pervasive One into all wombs with the syllable Om (praṇava), || 4.173 ||
Having meditated upon them as being simultaneously deceased and having worshipped them, one should offer libations.
Furthermore: "Then, having sprinkled the disciple with auspicious water, one should strike him with the Astra-mantra. (4.174)
By means of that very weapon-mantra, joined with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
and by means of one’s own exhalation (*recaka*),
[he] goes— this is the ellipsis.
...should enter into the heart of the disciple’s body. || 4-175 ||
Then, having severed its form as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should draw it out by means of the weapon [mantra].
Having grasped it from the *dvādaśānta*, establish it within oneself as before. (4.176)
Then, having restrained [the breath] by means of inhalation (pūraka) and having exhaled (recayitvā), one should apply it;
having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) as before, [one should place] consciousness within all wombs (sarvayoniṣu).
The meaning is that one should perform [the practice] from the beginning of yoga up to its dissolution, and here, by means of the *dhāman*, as before. || 177 ||
But the specific distinction here is this:
through a hundred oblations with the *śikhā*, the expiation for the *vidyā* is accomplished. (4.178)
Then, immediately after the severing of the bonds of separation, he should effect the state of being situated in the Supreme and the state of being situated in that [Self]. || 178 ||
Then, for the purpose of offering the portions of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka),

one should first invoke Rudra with the Praṇava and other mantras, establish him, and worship him. Then, O Goddess, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of his [mantras] upon the forms of scent and form, followed by the two fixed oblations (dhruvāhutī).
In this manner—
having deposited the portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* and dismissed the deity Rudra,
and likewise having dismissed Vāgīśī— the junction of the *kalās* is performed as before. (4.180)
It should be performed.
How [should one proceed]?
One should employ the Vidyā for pacification according to the distinction between short and long [syllables].
For the purpose of reconnection, however, one should offer three oblations with the Mūla-mantra. (4.181)
Immediately following the *saṃdhi*, for the purpose of establishing the [deities] in their respective positions:
the invocation by their own names, preceded by the peaceful and sovereign rites, and the offering of the objects of cognition (*prameya*). Having performed the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)...
And one should worship her with flowers and other offerings. || 4-182 ||
One should offer three oblations with the root mantra... || 182 ||
He states its pervasion across the intermediate stages:
"From the *vidyā*-tattva [up to] Sadāśiva; the pervasion of the principles (*tattva*) occurs within this triad, and likewise, there is a triad of phonemes. (4.183)
And also in the case of "ka-kha-ga. (183)
The eleven-word [section] is to be known as follows:

since the group of six beginning with *kṣānta* is included within the *vidyā* from the group of nine situated in the eastern direction, there is a triad consisting of the letter *ra*, the *praṇava* (oṃ), and the letter *ha* from the middle [section].
The group of eight beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *ha*, starting from the new [vowels], constitutes the eleven-word unit.
...and seventeen cities.
Among those, in the sphere of Knowledge (vidyātattva), there is one [city] for the Vidyārājñīs beginning with Triguṇī;
however, in the sphere of the Lord (īśvaratattva), there is the world of Īśvara, and eight worlds belonging to the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
There are four worlds for Dharma and the other [qualities]; one world for the triad of powers beginning with Vāmā;
and one world for Knowledge and Action. Within that very world, there is a further internal division of fifty-nine worlds, beginning with the two Vidyās and ending with the twelve Prabhavas.
And he will say:
"Fifty-nine worlds [arise] in sequence from the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) onwards" (10.1185).
Thus, there are fifteen worlds in the principle of Īśvara. As he will further state:
"Five and ten worlds are to be purified in the state of Īśvara" (10.1171).
Thus, in the Sadāśiva-tattva, there is one Sādāśiva world which, like its own [Īśvara],
pervades the infinite worlds contained within the Brahma-aṅga, the group of eight beginning with Sakala, and the coverings consisting of the divisions of Śiva and Rudra.
There are seventeen worlds.
Likewise, here—
there are two mantras,
which have the form of Tatpuruṣa and Astra.
Thus, in this regard—...the sixfold path is considered to be these primary bonds. (4.184)
And as before—
one should always cause many subtle bonds to enter into that;
then—
One should visualize Vāgīśī there and offer oblations according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, worship with the root mantra, followed by sprinkling and striking;
likewise, cutting, attracting, seizing, and the birth resulting from the wearing of the yoga.
Likewise, the empowerment, enjoyment, and dissolution should occur as before;
all these are performed with the root mantra by means of three oblations.
The conjunction [of the soul] within the embryos is consciousness; its state as sustainer is the simultaneous nourishment of the embryos. As it has been said:
"Those embryos in all wombs attain growth simultaneously" (4.118).
"All" refers to the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth. || 4-187 ||
Furthermore:
"In the expiation, one should perform a hundred oblations with the *kavaca* [mantra].
The word "tu" (but/and) is for the purpose of distinguishing this from what precedes it.
The preceptor should effect the separation and the severing of the bonds by means of the Astra-mantra.
By means of the extraction (*uddhāra*), the establishment within oneself (*ātma-sthatā*), and the stabilization therein (*tatsthīkāra*) through Bhava,
one should then invoke the Lord by His own name preceded by the *praṇava* and worship Him. (4.189)
Having worshipped, offered oblations, and performed the libations, one should offer the two portions of intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṅkṛti*).
Here is the ritual application: preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *svāhā*, one should offer the intellect using one's own name. (4.190)
Having likewise offered the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) in this manner, one should then ask for forgiveness; having worshipped Vāgīśī and offered libations, one should dismiss her. || 4-191 ||
Whatever has not been stated here is to be applied from what precedes. || 191 ||
Now— first, one should apply the conjunction of the *kalās* within the *śāntyatītā*;
by means of the division of short and long [vowels]...
The meaning is that one should connect [the mantras] to the Śānta and Śāntyatīta [kalās], as previously described.
And for that purpose—one should offer three oblations. || 4-192 ||
Then, the knower of the ritual procedure must perform the unification with reality (*tattvasaṃdhāna*) by means of the *dhruva* [mantra],
as before, preceded by the utterance of the seed-syllable of Śāntyatītā from the abode of the *praṇava*: "To Śāntyatītā..."

The application "namaḥ" should be remembered here; the reality in this context is the Śāntyatītā [Kalā], which is to be pervaded by one who knows the ritual procedure and understands the universal concomitance (vyāpti).
Furthermore:
"O Dear One, after subsequently establishing the *kala*s, one should perform the oblation with the *dhruva* [vessel]. (4.193)
By performing the offering three times while uttering the word for one's own name,
one should invoke Śāntyatītā, establish her, and worship her again.
Having observed the pervasion residing in the [three] paths,
he clarifies that very [pervasion]:
"And those who have reached the Śiva-principle..."
The meaning is that those categories (padārthas) are to be contemplated here.
He states them: "Bindu, nāda, and likewise śakti are established within the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). (4.195)

In this context, the Śiva-tattva, extending up to the pervasion of Samanā, is precisely that which is to be purified. Here, the Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti constitute the primary coverings (āvaraṇas), within which the sixteen worlds to be described hereafter are contained. || 195 ||
Furthermore:
"One word, one mantra, sixteen syllables are proclaimed;
one should meditate upon the subtle worlds within the Śāntyatīta [kalā]. (4.196)

The *pada* is the syllable *Oṃ* situated in the center of the nine central squares; the *mantra* is the venerable Īśāna, whose form is non-different from the eye-mantra consisting of the three abodes (*dhāma*); the *varṇas* are the sixteen [phonemes] beginning with the visarga and ending with the letter *a*; and the *bhuvanas* are subtle because they consist merely of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) in the form of the planes (*bhūmikā*), and not otherwise.
They possess specific configurations, and these are sixteen. Namely: in the enclosure of the *bindu*, there is one world-sphere of Śāntyatītā, surrounded by the four *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti;
then, two world-spheres of Ardhacandra and Nirodhikā, each adorned by its own respective pentad of *kalās*.
Furthermore, in the enclosure of Nāda, there are five worlds presided over by the powers beginning with Indhikā, who are themselves presided over by their respective possessors of power;
at the end of Nāda (Nādānta), there is one world presided over by Suṣumṇeśa and the Supreme Brahman;
whereas in the enclosure of Śakti, [there is a world] adorned by the quartet of powers beginning with Sūkṣmā.

The world of Parā-Śakti is one; beyond that, in the plane of Vyāpinī, are the five worlds of Vyāpya, Vyomarūpa, Anātha, Ananta, and Anāśrita; and beyond that, in Samanā, which consists of Mahāmāyā, he ascends upon her power.

"Śiva is the performer of the fivefold activity. Now, one might ask: how is it that even the purifying mantras (*śodhaka-mantra*) are here said to be themselves objects of purification (*śodhya*)? If that were the case, what would possess the power of purification? Furthermore, since the Root Mantra (*mūla-mantra*) is also a mantra, it would follow as a logical consequence that it too must be an object of purification, just like [the kalās] Nivṛtti and the others.
Why is the limb-mantra not mentioned even for Śāntyatītā?

For Nivṛtti and Śāntyatītā, the expiatory oblation (niṣkṛti-homa) is performed with the root-mantra; for Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and Śāntā, it is with the head, crest, and armor mantras respectively. In the case of Nivṛtti, there is a separation [of the mantra], while in other cases, it is with the root-mantra.

"What is this sequence—first with the Heart-mantra and then elsewhere with the Weapon-mantra? To this it is replied: Here, for those who have attained immersion in Śiva and know the potency [of mantra], the mantras manifest as purifiers by virtue of being the essence of the Guru’s own power (*sva-śakti*). For bound souls (*paśu*), however, their own potency remains concealed, serving as a veil over their true nature.
"Those who remain [in the state] are indeed to be purified, and they are eleven through the divisions of the limbs and faces; as for the root mantra, however,
according to the principle to be stated later— 'the Lord himself utters it' (7.59)— it vibrates as everything, having as its ultimate reality the reflective awareness of Nāda."

It is not that this [reality] is something to be purified; rather, it is the expansion of the eleven mantras, beginning with *a* and ending with *samanā*, which are here internalized in a subtle form.
This is stated with the intention of one desiring to ascend, by means of the logic of the sequence of differentiation, according to the perspective of the parts and sub-parts.

"How can there be liberation in syllables? How can there be a flower in the sky? (7.238)—this was said with reference to the root mantra. And with the intention of referring to the various portions of the expressed meaning: "O fair lady, the infinite web of fetters extends up to the end of tranquility" (4.432).

Thus it has been said; however, in reality, this Niṣkalanātha consists of the non-duality of the entire universe and is of the nature of the eternally manifest, unutterable Great Contemplation (*mahāvimarśa*).

Whether he is the Niṣkala (undivided) Lord or the Sakala (divided) one whose form is non-different from that [Contemplation], his state of being something to be purified (*śodhya*) is never to be suspected. Furthermore, in the Śāntyatītā [kalā], because of its conformity with its very name, [there is no such suspicion].
A separate mantra for each limb is possible; however, the mantra of the eye, which consists of the three abodes (dhāmatraya),
must necessarily enter into the forms distinct from the Īśāna-mantra, otherwise the group of eleven mantras would not be purified.
Furthermore, the forthcoming statement, "The mantras are to be known as eleven" (4-200), would otherwise be inconsistent; therefore,
the *astra-mantra* is employed only for striking and similar acts, whereas the *netra-mantra* is non-different from the *mūla-mantra*.

Thus, the view of certain authorities—that those two [the *kalās*] are not to be purified within the *kalās*—is incorrect. As for the restriction regarding mantras mentioned in connection with expiatory oblations (*niṣkṛti*) and so forth, there the command of the Lord alone is the regulator; thus, everything is beyond reproach. 196.
All these very bonds,
O Varārohā, must be purified—
she whose *āroha* (ascent) or exultation is *vara*, meaning excellent, consisting of resting at the supreme limit (*ūrdhvadvādaśānta*).
From power.
And these are to be purified until they become the rays of Śiva;
through the complete cessation of all differentiation, they take on the nature of Śiva’s rays, consisting solely of undivided light.
The meaning is that they are accomplished.
Therefore—Śiva is to be known as being above Śiva, where, once joined, one is not born again. (4.197)

The venerable Lord Svacchanda—the mass of consciousness and bliss who transcends the universe yet pervades the universe, standing above the Śiva-tattva that has been transcended—is joined there by means of the sequence of *yojanikā* to be described; he is not born again, which means he is liberated. || 197 ||
Therefore, whatever has been elaborated here up to the end of the five-fold Kalāpa— all that is to be known as the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) in its unity;
it is to be understood as abiding non-differently within the single self of Paramaśiva, having attained identity with Him.
It was conceived in its entirety by the Guru.
To demonstrate how far this path extends—that one who is to be initiated attains identity with Śiva—he says:
"Listen again to its enumeration:
the *kalās* are to be known as five, and the *tattvas* are indeed thirty-six. (4.198)
It should be known that there are two hundred and twenty-four worlds;
herein, there are eighty-one *padas*, and it is remembered as consisting of fifty syllables and a half. (4.199)
The mantras are to be known as eleven; this is the mandala of the paths.
When this has attained purification, the initiated one attains liberation.
It has been stated that its purification is the manifestation of Paramaśiva. || 200 ||
Having thus stated the incidental section on the purity of the time-periods (*adhvaśuddhi*), he speaks of the subject at hand:
"Having invoked Vāgīśī with the *dhruva* [mantra], one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyaset*)...
For that purpose:
...as before, there is the oblation (*huti*). Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should [offer] the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) into that womb as previously described. (4.201)
The word "should apply" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 201 ||
Furthermore:
"Everything from birth until dissolution must be performed with the *dhruva* [mantra].
For the rite of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra. (4.202)
One should perform [the rites] with the *dhruva* mantra as before, by means of both separation and the cutting of bonds.

The term "by means of the two cuttings" (*chedābhyām*) indicates purpose; thus, the meaning is that one should perform the rites of oblation and so forth as before for the sake of separation and the rest. || 202 ||
Furthermore:
"By means of the *graha*, the state of being established in the Self is attained; by means of the *praṇava*, the state of the bound soul (*paśu*) is remembered. (4.203)
The Praṇava is Niṣkalanātha. || 203 ||
Then, having invoked Sadāśiva while reciting the root mantra,
one should establish him with a prostration, worship him with flowers, and satisfy him with libations.
One should deposit the mind, which is a portion of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), into the Lord of Causes.
To the question "How? he says:
having uttered the Praṇava and so forth, [one should utter] the name "mind" (manas) and likewise "salutation" (namaḥ). (4.205)
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should subsequently worship [the deities] ending with the name followed by *svāhā*.

Immediately after the two abodes of the *praṇava*, the application of the mantra is: "I offer the mind of Devadatta, *namaḥ*"; however, in the case of a fire-oblation (*homa*), it ends with *svāhā*. Thus, it is said to end with the name and *svāhā*.
An adverbial modifier. || 205 ||
And here—having offered three oblations, one is purified from the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka). || 4-206 ||
Then one should dismiss the deity and the causal Sadāśiva, after having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings; immediately thereafter, one should worship Vāgīśī.
Having worshipped her and gratified her, she, filled with devotion, should make this request:
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, forgive me for having caused you distress on account of the sacrificial animal."
"Now you must not detain me; go, O Goddess, to your own abode.
The word "tu" (but) is used to highlight the specific point that this request must be carried out at the conclusion of every initiation (*dīkṣā*).
"Fatigue" (*khedana*) refers to the repeated descent [of the deity] from its supreme nature for the sake of the *garbhādhāna* and other rites.

"One should not obstruct" means that you must not now cause obstruction to this initiated one— that is to say, you must not conceal his true nature. Therefore, go to his own celestial realm (*svaviṣṭapa*), which is the substratum consisting of the essential nature of Paramaśiva’s own self, and remain there eternally as one with him.
The meaning is "it vibrates. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrīspanda*:
"Known as being situated on the path of the dog, she brings about the attainment of supernatural powers" (*Spanda-kārikā* 3.18).
As it has been stated: one should offer sound and touch to Brahmā; taste to Viṣṇu; form and smell to Rudra;
intellect and ego to Īśvara; and the mind, as a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka*, to Sadāśiva.
The intention here is this: in this context, Brahmā resides above the end of the *nāda* by means of supreme pervasion.

Brahmā is the form of Brahman presiding over the *brahmabila*; Viṣṇu, moreover, is the essence of the primary power (*pradhānaśakti*) whose nature is the power of expansion (*prasara-rūpa-śakti*) situated above that; Rudra, too, is the form of Anāśritanātha abiding in the station of Vyāpinī; and Īśvara as well—

According to the systematic arrangement stated in the eleventh chapter— that Śiva is the one authorized for creation who has ascended to the level of *samanā*, whereas Sadāśiva is the Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), a mass of pure, autonomous consciousness and bliss— of the Supreme Brahman...
Because it occupies the middle between *nāda* and *antaśakti*, there is a connection with the two most subtle [elements], sound and touch.

Thus, although the power (*śakti*) at the root-ground is primarily characterized by touch, it consists of taste (*rasa*) due to its nature as an expanding form; consequently, Viṣṇu, who is identical with that [power], has a connection with the most subtle taste, and Rudra has [a connection] even more subtle than that.

In the all-pervasive state of Anāśrita, there exists a connection with the most subtle scent— consisting of nothing more than the extremely minute residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the universe that existed prior to its creation and subsequent dissolution— which arises from the non-measurable Self through the threading together of the entire world. However, this is not the case in Śiva, who is the presiding subject of that [Anāśrita] level.

In that state whose essence is mere reflection (*manana*), attachment to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of intellect and ego dissolves; even though the Supreme Śiva is embraced by the *unmanā* power, there occurs the dissolution of even the residual impression of reflection, such that there remains a connection with the most subtle and perfectly tranquil mental impression.

With this intention, the offering of a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* is solely for the sake of pacifying the *puryaṣṭaka* along with all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) without exception. Others, however, say:
"The impairment of hearing and touch belonging to Brahmā is the cause of birth as a consumer of Brahman’s flesh."
The gustatory, the Vaiṣṇavī, the Raudrī, and that which has the nose and eyes as its cause.
"The Goddess is the form of pride, the mental deity Śiva. (Mi.Kri. 8.140-141).

Thus it is stated in the commentary on the *Śrīmṛgendravākya* concerning the subject of initiation without seed (*nirbījadīkṣā*), for the purpose of pacifying those various states of being a flesh-eater that may arise from the corruption of the senses and the transgression of one's own religious observances (*samaya*).

Even in a statement primarily concerned with the purification of bonds (*pāśa*), they have applied here that which was stated by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha regarding the *nirbīja-dīkṣā*: namely, that the offering of sound and touch from the *puryaṣṭaka* into Brahman must be performed, and so forth. In that regard:
In all initiations, whether with seed (*sabīja*) or without seed (*nirbīja*), the offering of a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* is traditionally taught; therefore,

even in the statement from the *Mṛgendra-tantra* concerning the purification of the bonds of the religious observances (*samaya-pāśa*), the offering of a portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* was made specifically regarding the initiation without seed, and its intended meaning was described by him accordingly.
Whether that is appropriate or inappropriate is a matter for those with discernment to judge by means of valid cognition; enough said. || 208 ||
Alternatively, having thus dismissed Vāgīśī, the Kalā Śāntyatītā should be meditated upon as having gone to dissolution. || 4-209 ||
At the limit of the support of one's own power, which abides in an extremely subtle state of non-existence, His own power—whose nature is absolute freedom—is the inherent substratum (*samavāyinī*).
He alone is the "limit" (*paryanta*) because He is the locus where all things find their final rest in *Samanā*; for this very reason, He is "perfectly" (*suṣṭhu*) so.

Wherein is established the configuration— that is, the structural arrangement— of the Great Void (mahāśūnya), which is subtle, of the nature of non-existence, all-pervasive, and serves as the foundational wall for the totality of existents and non-existents from the level of Vyāpinī down to the Earth. || 209 ||

Then, when a transformation has occurred in the actions of body, speech, and mind—one should indeed offer a hundred oblations with the flame through the discernment of the reality of the Self. (4.210)
The word "ātman" indicates both *vidyā* and *Śiva*; therefore, the meaning here is "by means of the division of the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. || 210 ||
Likewise—
one should offer oblations into the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) by means of the employment of the utterance of the word "sa," preceded by the utterance of the partless (niṣkala) Praṇava.

"May there be purification of the defects of deficiency and excess in the ritual procedure for the purification of the paths (adhvan) beginning with Māyā and ending with the pervasion of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) of the one to be initiated— svāhā!"— this is the application here.
And this reality of the Self—extending up to the principle of Māyā—is to be known by the teacher in the great sacrifice. (4.211)
The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) consists in the pervasion of all that is to be known, ending with Māyā;
this occurs in the great sacrifice (mahādhvara), the Śiva-sacrifice which has initiation as its purpose.
For what purpose is this oblation? He says:

for the sake of the rite that remedies deficiencies in the procedure, and for the purification through expiation. "Procedure" refers to worship, oblation, and so forth as enjoined by the scriptures; its "deficiency" is the failure to perform it correctly.

For the sake of that [attainment], there is the performance [of rites] that may be deficient or excessive; for the purpose of removing that [deficiency or excess], there is the purification through expiation (prāyaścitta), and it is for that [purification].
Then, O beloved, one hundred and eight oblations should be offered into the fire-principle (vidyātattva).
And one should offer that into the principle of Vidyā by means of whispering recitation;
this is indeed another [form] of the Vidyā previously mentioned.
To state that for the Blessed One, *vidyā* (knowledge) exists at the end of *māyā* as its instrument (*karaṇa*), he says:
"One should designate the path ending with Sadāśiva as the *vidyā-tattva* (the principle of knowledge). (4.213)

Power (*śakti*), whose nature consists of knowledge and action, is the cause of Śiva, and Sadāśiva has that same form; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) extends up to that point. || 213 ||
And in this regard:

"Whatever atonement may be required due to the reverse recitation of the mantra, that oblation which is performed within the principle of Vidyā (vidyā-tattva) shall serve for its purification. (4.214)

"Vilomatā" means making [the sequence] otherwise. In this context, having uttered the *praṇava* and the *niṣkala*, the ritual application is: "May there be the purification through the reversal of the mantra-utterance during the purification of the path (*adhvan*)—extending from the *vidyātattva* up to Sadāśiva—for the one to be initiated; *svāhā*. || 214 ||
Immediately following—
due to a deficiency in mental consciousness (manovijñāna), whatever atonement (prāyaścitta) may be required,
for the sake of its purification, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) in the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) with the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 4-215 ||
Through mental application...
mental consciousness is cultivation; with respect to the principles of Śiva and Liberation, this here is the nature of the subject—and this—
...situated on the path ending at Śakti;
for it pervades as far as the venerable Lord Śiva, having transcended that which ends at Śakti and extends up to Samanā.

Now, for the sake of pacifying the binding nature of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*)— which flows upward from the interior of the skull and acts as a bond by flowing downward— he prescribes the cutting of the tuft (*śikhā*) located in the gross body, which corresponds to that [upward-flowing energy].
At the conclusion of the purification of the three principles, one should perform the cutting of the topknot.
And how [is she]?—She who stands beyond the darkness of the paths, supreme, tranquil, incomparable, and free from ailment;
all-pervading among all principles (tattvas), the cause of all causes. (4.217)

Having meditated [on her] at the tip of the child's crest-lock, like a drop of water on the tip of a flower, she stands at the end of the path— therefore, in the state where the end of the path no longer exists— as the Supreme (Parā), the Tranquil (Śāntā),
namely the Transcendent Tranquility (Śāntyatītā); she is free from ailment and stainless due to the exhaustion of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) among even the six [energies].
Having meditated upon the cause of causes at the tip of the child's crest-lock—such is the connection. || 217 ||
Furthermore:
having addressed the *kartarī* with the tuft-mantra, one should cut the tuft with the tuft-mantra. (4.218)

"By the *śikhā*" means by the *śikhā-mantra* which is *naiṣkala*. Since no specific distinction is mentioned here, the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā-chedana*) pertains to both types of initiation—the *nirbīja* and the *sabīja*—and not to the *nirbīja* alone. || 218 ||
Then,
having handed over the *śikhā* to another, he should depart along with his disciples;
and there—
The disciple should perform his bath because his topknot has been cut off.
But from touching that, the sipping of water (ācamana) for the guru shall take place. || 4-219 ||
Out of association with his disciples, or in order to perceive the intentions of others, the Guru may perform either ritual bathing or the smearing of ashes according to his own will.
Thereafter—
Having entered and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon oneself,
one should offer the śikhā-oblation with the pūrṇāhuti.

[She] imitates the power that is the life-force of the previously stated pervasion (vyāpti); and here, the mantra for the oblation of the fetters (pāśahoma), as previously authorized, should be employed. || 220 ||
And thus:

having offered the oblation, having gone out, having sipped water and washed the *sruk*, *sruva*, and *kartarī* spoons, having re-entered and performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one performs the worship of the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*). (4.221)
The meaning is that one should perform [it].
Then, within the mandala, one should subsequently worship the Supreme Lord with flowers and all other offerings; thereafter, one should address a petition to Śiva.
O Blessed One, by your grace, having grasped the sacrificial animal situated at the six stages of the path and having purified it, ending with the cutting of the crest-lock (śikhāccheda); || 4-223 ||
I have indeed carried out, even if only in part, the procedure taught by you from your own mouth:
the grasping [of the soul] from the thread of the noose and from one's own body, and the purification from impurities;
it has been accomplished. || 223 ||
Moreover, although it is my desire that you attain the desired abode, you must nevertheless proceed swiftly to the auspicious and eternal state by means of your own power alone. (4.224)
The particle *eva* is independent [of other qualifiers] and suggests that it is the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) alone that prevails here;
this we shall determine at the end of the fifth chapter. The seventh *dhruvapada* is the station of Paramaśiva, and for that very purpose—
Now, the application of the ritual action is commenced by me;
therefore, herein—
"...who follow your command.
O Lord, let your command be given; I shall unite the disciple [with the truth]. (4.225)
"At your command" refers to what was obtained during the occasion of the qualification [for initiation], namely: "The disciples are to be initiated by you."
Then,
having obtained permission for himself through the very means of receiving that command, by virtue of the immersion into the power of Rudra—
...having departed from the city with great joy,
he should go toward the fire with an *argha* offering in hand...
"From the city" means from the site of the mandala.
Then, having summoned the disciple here, one should sprinkle him. || 4-226 ||
For one who has been sprinkled with water and is seated as before, there is the performance of the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making the body complete) and so forth,
followed by the internal placement of mantras (*antaḥkaraṇavinyāsa*) preceded by the joining of the channels (*nāḍīsandhāna*). (4.227)
One should perform worship and libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantras and for Śiva in the fire;
the libation for the faces and limbs is performed with reference to the root mantra.
By means of a tenfold division...
and since there is no fixed restriction regarding the quantity of substances here, he says:
"...according to the [available] substance. (4-228)
As he will say:
"Three, five, ten, or one [offering], either with sesame seeds or with ghee. (4.448) || 228 ||
Now, those who, by immersing themselves in the partless nature [of reality] and emerging as the state of possessing all parts (sakalatā),

are empowered to bring about purification through the conscious self by means of the mantras of the faces and limbs— which are forms of the Lord’s internal power— by dispelling the manifestation of duality; to them—
One should subsequently purify the mantras established in the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa by means of a single offering;
it has been determined that the purification of other mantras occurs through the root mantra alone. Therefore:

Having first uttered the unmanifest (niṣkala) Praṇava, and then having pronounced each [mantra] beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya) and ending with its respective seed-syllable (jāti), one should offer an oblation while contemplating rest in the unmanifest abode (niṣkaladhāma) through the following application: "O Blessed One, become intent upon the manifestation of the pure, unmanifest abode for this disciple; svāhā!"
Then one should cause them to hear this: "......... let the qualification be relinquished. (4-229)
The remainder [of the meaning] is that you must never again perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the bound soul (paśu). || 229 ||

Having thus stated the purification of the eleven mantras of the candidate as the procedure to be performed, the Blessed One said to the Goddess: "Now I shall tell you the application that is to be employed. (4.230)
That which is conducive to union (*yojanā*) is *yojanīya*.

Now that the destruction of all fetters has been accomplished, I shall describe the "union"—the supreme yoga in the form of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—which is capable of being joined by the one Supreme Power, the Blessed Lady, who is solely intent on bestowing grace. I speak of this for you.
The meaning is: "I cause [the disciple] to attain the state of discernment. || 230 ||

And in order to demonstrate that this [teaching] is to be accomplished by the most excellent of teachers—who are difficult to find because they possess the yoga of cultivated knowledge—the Supreme Lord introduces the following by means of an extensive introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*), in order to determine and make clear to the hearts of true gurus the thirteen objects of knowledge (*prameya*) useful for the [textual] arrangement: [The text continues with the verses: "O Goddess, the supreme reality is established through the threefold means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is the object of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). ... [and so forth]. (Note: The provided source text contains only the introductory prose; the subsequent verses are implied by the context of the "thirteen objects of knowledge" and the mention of *pramāṇatraya*.)

Having understood the measure of the movement [of breath], as well as the circulation of the vital breath (prāṇa), and the division of the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidhādhvan) as it resides within the single vital breath; || 4-231 ||

The utterance of *haṃsa* by means of the phonemes, as well as the very abandonment of the causes—this should be known as the void (*śūnya*), the equal flavor (*samarasa*), the renunciation (*tyāga*), the union (*saṃyoga*), and the emergence (*udbhava*). (4.232)

Furthermore, having understood that the differentiation of categories occurs through the attainment of their essential nature, and that there is thus the pervasive extension of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva, one should apply [this realization]. (4.233)
In this regard:
"O Goddess, one who is joined to that supreme reality, endowed with qualities such as omniscience, becomes the one Śiva, undivided from all things. (4.402)

Thus, the unification— consisting of the attainment of identity with Supreme Bhairava according to the method of the future state— must be performed by the Guru solely through the pacification of the egoity of the *puryaṣṭaka*. For it is certain that in the *puryaṣṭaka*,
which rests upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is likewise a resting upon the void (*śūnya*) during both dreaming and deep sleep.

Since both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the state of emptiness (*śūnyapada*) must be pacified, the measure of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*) by way of place and time must necessarily be known; therein, too,
there is a movement consisting of ascent and descent for one who has mastered that movement.
In that state, the thorough knowledge of all the paths to be transcended is useful;

and the transcendence of the paths occurs through the thorough knowledge of the upward-sounding *ha* (the *hasa*) of one's own self. That *uccāra* is twofold: natural (*svābhāvika*) and effortful (*prāyatnika*).
In the effortful type, it consists of the phonemes *a*, *u*, and so forth, which are devoid of parts (*naiṣkala*).
The abandonment of the causal deities, beginning with Brahmā, should also be understood;
by the word "and" (ca), the abandonment of the appropriate time for them—though not explicitly mentioned here—is likewise to be known as it will be explained later.
Furthermore, even the Void (śūnya) must be understood, because like the vital breath (prāṇa), it too is to be pacified.
And the unification with the nature of Supreme Bhairava is preceded by the realization of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) regarding the mantra, the self, the channels (*nāḍī*), and so forth;
since the knowledge of that equilibrium is preceded by the realization of identity (*sāmya*), it will also take the form of the equinox (*viṣuvat*) consisting of identity,
which is to be known as twelvefold, beginning with the letter *A* and ending with *Unmanā*.

It must indeed be known as an auxiliary to the utterance of the mantra; and it is said that this [mantra] is to be known for the sake of renunciation (*tyāga*), which occurs preceded by the conjunction with those respective states (*daśā*). Furthermore, upon the renunciation of those respective states, the emergence of the Self through ascending higher and higher must also be known—this being the case until these knots [are severed].
The piercing has not yet occurred; therefore, its upward emergence through that [piercing] is not possible, for piercing occurs by means of both knowledge and yoga, as he will state:
"One should pierce with the spear of knowledge" (4.335).
Likewise:
"One should pierce with the spear of mantra, joined with the visualization of the mudrā," and so forth (4.357).

And that occurs by virtue of the attainment of the state of being— which consists of a firmly established realization and which consists of the experience of various words and so forth as will be described— within the vital breath (prāṇa) that has become void, preceded by such knowledge. Thus [it is].

Furthermore, even when [the mind] has been stilled, it must necessarily be understood that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the experience of the pure state of the Self (*ātmatattva*) which has transcended this much; the state of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) consisting of rest in the "beyond-mind" (*unmanā*); and even for the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), that which consists of immersion into the Supreme Principle (*paratattva*).

With the intention that such thorough knowledge of the objects of cognition is useful for the process of application both through scripture and through direct experience, the word "having known" (jñātvā) is employed twice in this sentence.
In order to determine what has been indicated, he says:
"I shall declare its division so that it may be known according to reality.
Division (*vibhāga*) means differentiation (*vibhajana*), characterized by the discernment [of things] through their specific, non-common forms.
He explains the classification of its types as they occur, stating in sequence:
"The movement [of the breath] consists of thirty-six finger-breadths, from the heart-lotus up to the Śakti. (4-234)
O Dear One, it is measured by a time consisting of sixteen *tuṭis*.

Regarding the word "yāvat," there is an elision of the suffix *-tal*. By the first half [of the verse], the spatial extent is stated; by the second, the measure of the movement (*cāra*) in terms of time. Here, "power" (*śakti*) is intended as that which extends up to the level of *Samanā*, according to the rule beginning with "bhāvinī."
A *tuṭi* is the thirty-second part of the flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which consists of six parts of a *caṣaka*.
Now, he describes the movement of the *prāṇa*:
Listen to me as I explain, according to their true nature, that which moves about through its various divisions.
