Listen as it is told, and reflect upon it within yourself: that *prāṇa* which moves correctly, witnessed by one's own direct experience, according to its divisions following the locations such as the palate; [know that] it should abandon one part of its course up to the heart-lotus. 235. It should abandon one part of its course up to the heart-lotus.
The second is at the tip of the nose, and the third is at the end of the power (śakti).
Established therein, one may turn back as long as one does not find reality;
but once the supreme reality is known, even while remaining there, one is no longer afflicted.
According to the method of this treatise, starting from the heart-lotus— the locus of the emergence of the mantra— this "course" (ayana) refers,

by virtue of the principle to be stated in the section on time, namely "the rising of the day occurs in the breath," to the location of the palate as the support for the midday position of the sun of the vital breath (prāṇāditya), extending to a distance of eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).

And that station of Rudra, consisting of the knot of *māyā*, is difficult to pierce; however, for one who has not yet mastered its entry, he reaches the tip of the nose or the middle of the eyebrows—the station of Īśvara—by means of the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*), even while the knot of the eyebrows remains unbroken. In that state, too:
At the tip of the nose: one should abandon the second part, which measures six finger-breadths;

having failed to reach its entry, [the breath] resorts to the two lateral channels until the point where its entry has been mastered, reaching as far as the end of power (śakti) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila). Nevertheless, for one who has not yet appropriated the power of Śakti—
At the end of that *śakti*, one should discard the third part, which measures twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*);

there, for one who knows the interior, it should flow downward through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). This very point has been stated in the half-verse beginning with "situated therein" (*tatrastha*); therefore, one who has attained the power of *śakti* is proficient in the movement through all the knots (*granthi*).
When the supreme reality (*paratattva*) is known, as it is said "therein," even while situated in the locations of the knots (*granthisthāna*), one is not afflicted;

that is to say, one does not fall under the power of the limited subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) consisting of the body and so forth. Therefore, the essential meaning is that the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasañcāra*) must be trained until it culminates in the realization of the supreme reality.
In this very context of movement, he reveals the technical designations:
"When one goes downward by means of *śakti*, then one becomes unawakened (*abudha*),
because one has not ascended to the reality (*tattva*) even when the state at the limit of *śakti* has been attained."
But when, for the sake of ascending that [state], he who was situated in the heart rises up again while becoming conscious, he is called "awakened" (budhyamāna). || 4.238 ||
And then— once the wise one has attained power, he is to be known as such...
even beyond that, for one who knows the method of ascending through the principles (*tattva*) by virtue of having obtained the power of Śakti.
...awakening occurs in the aspect of the Pervasive (Vyāpinī).
But when he ascends even further than that, having transcended this path up to the limit of Samanā, he is "well-awakened" (suprabuddha). ...

Some maintain that because the supreme reality has not been attained, there is simply no state of being the Buddha-nature; however, this is incorrect, because even though that [state] is the subject at hand here, it consists solely of the perfectly awakened one, otherwise it would be impossible for it to possess the status of a Guru.
And of this—
At that time, the state of being beyond the mind (unmanastva) occurs. || 4-239 ||
Also because of the exhaustion of the mental formations. || 239 ||
Furthermore:
There is no time, no movement of the digits, no principle, and no cause;
it is the supreme, pure, perfect nirvāṇa, transmitted through the lineage of gurus. (4.240)

Having known that, one is liberated; having gone there, one is not born again. Time begins with the *tuṭi* and ends with the *parārdha*; the *kalās* begin with *nivṛtti* and so forth; the movement is the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the principles (*tattvas*) begin with earth; the causes begin with Brahmā; and [the goal is] perfect liberation (*sunirvāṇa*).
Because it consists of supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*), it is for that very reason supremely pure (*param śuddham*),

being more excellent even than the states of Śuddhāśuddha-Sadāśiva and the rest; "pārampara" refers to the very lineage of the gurus (*gurūṇām paramparā*), consisting of the forms of Supreme Bhairava, His Power, Sadāśiva, Īśāna, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and so forth.
"Having known" means having experienced it as it has come; "is liberated" means he would be liberated even while living;
"having gone" means that at the end of the body, he attains identity with That.
Now he describes the division of the six paths: "I shall tell you how the sixfold path is situated within the vital breath. (4.241)

Indeed, that which is the perception of consciousness from the feet up to the crown of the head should be known as the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and likewise as the path of the principles (tattvādhvan). (4.242)

In this context, based on the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) that "it-ness" (*tattva*) refers to the state of being that [particular], *tattva* is the manifestation of a universal grounded in particulars, which serves as the cause for the construction of bodies, worlds, and states of being. Its full manifestation consists of bodies, worlds, and so forth; for example, the manifestation of solidity in a body, or in clay, wood, stone, and the like.

The earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*), and likewise the others; and the manifestation of the universal (*sāmānyābhāsa*) shines upon the wall of consciousness (*cidbhitti*) and within the ground of supreme consciousness (*paracidbhūmi*). Since everything is of the single flavor of consciousness (*cidekarasa*), there is no division whatsoever therein, according to the principle that "first, consciousness transforms into the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," because of that [consciousness] which contracts the vital breath.

Intending to show that for one who pervades even the body by ascending through the vital breaths (prāṇas), that which consists of the manifestation of the principles (tattvas) alone constitutes the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), [the author] states: "That consciousness of the intellect (citi) from the feet to the top of the head,
which consists of the manifestation of hardness and so forth— that alone is the path of the principles and the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan)."
Thus it has been said. And by the very existence of the *tattvas*, the existence of the worlds (*bhuvanas*) is also inferred through their subtle nature.

The movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) from the heart to the end of Śakti is stated to be thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*). However, the division of the six paths (*adhvan*) occurs within the single locus of the vital breath; thus, it refers solely to the subtle vital breath that pervades the entire body.
Thus, it is correctly stated that this is merely an enumeration [of the principles] and not the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*), beginning from the feet and so forth;

for even at the conclusion of the enumeration of the principles, it is said in the *Śrīmataṅga*: "The principle (*tattva*) is the manifest state of reality, clearly established through the vision of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)."
"Or rather, because that very reality is stretched out (*tatata*) within the continuum of reality," thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"This entire path, which extends from Śiva down to the earth, is to be known as consciousness; for nothing is liberated [from bondage] due to a lack of consciousness.
He describes the persistence of the *kalās* within the vital breath (*prāṇa*):
"The vital breath, its continuity fashioned by the *kalās*, always moves;
it is that whose stream—the flow of the breath—is fashioned, that is, pervaded, by the *kalās*."
For this [state], indeed—nivṛtti (cessation) and pratiṣṭhā (establishment) are on the lower part, at the tip. (4.243)

Vidyā and Śānti are likewise above, while Śāntyatītā is the Adhiṣṭhikā. Having stated, "From the feet up to the top of the head," the vital breath (prāṇa) is indicated as that which pervades the entire body, consisting of the nature of universal animation, and of which [the breaths] prāṇa, apāna, and so forth are the components.
The functions (vṛttis) are distinguished. Therefore, the passage beginning with "flowing toward the lower part" and so forth is entirely consistent.

However, those who maintain that this [channel] is based on the upward-moving vital breath (prāṇa), having read "flowing toward the lower part" with the intention that it refers to that, have offered the following etymological interpretation: "those two in which there is activity or abiding in the lower part," and so on. This is their [interpretation].

Those who explain it thus have forgotten what was stated previously— that "when [the breath] moves downward by means of Śakti" (4.238)— and they have also asserted that Kalā, which consists of Śakti, pervades the insentient (jaḍa), but [they have not]...
Let this matter of "contrariety" rest for now. There are many such interpretations by commentators that are largely inconsistent;
these should be investigated by oneself. For fear of making the work too voluminous, I have not unpacked every word, but have merely shown a small portion.
Thinking, "May the disciples' intellect grow toward that which is to be accepted by means of the abandonment of what is to be rejected," he speaks in order to define the state beyond all parts:
"The supreme reality is beyond that..."
The meaning is that the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is the form of the pure state of the Self, having even transcended the *śāntyatītā* [state].

For this very reason, it consists of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of power and the possessor of power (*śakti-śaktimat*), which is the essence of the supreme reality (*unmanā-paratattva*)—[it is] "the imperishable state above that. (4-244)
For the sake of attaining which, there is such great exertion in this treatise. || 244 ||
Having described the existence of the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he also describes the existence of the *mantra-kalās*:

"In this way, the *bindu-kalā* is to be known, as well as those consisting of the power of *nāda*, and those consisting of *vyāpinī* and the rest, according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader. (4.245)

All [energies] are established solely in the vital breath (*prāṇa*)... all the *kalās*, whose nature consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, are perceived as they are uttered by means of all the vital breaths.
As for those beginning with *bindu* and ending with *samanā*, which exist in a sequential relationship of the pervaded and the pervader—
All of these should be known as abiding within the *prāṇa* and must be experienced through diligent effort.
Among them, the three—*bindu*, *nāda*, and *vyāpinī*—are mentioned here as primary;
the other powers, beginning with the *ardhacandra*, are included within these according to their respective correspondences.
Because of its predominance.
For this very reason—.................. dissolution occurs in the seventh through the abandonment of the six.
All perceivable things consist of the portions of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*; however, those attainable through yoga are the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *vyāpinī*.
By abandoning all six of these, the supreme yogis must effect dissolution and rest within the seventh—the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) which possesses the Supreme Power (*paraśaktimat*).
Having thus concluded this, he introduces another topic:
"The path of the kalās has been fully explained in this way; now learn from me the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan). (4.246)
He said to him:
"All phonemes (varṇa), whose essence is sound, exist in this world of the moving and the unmoving through fifty divisions, [as taught] in the scriptures numbering infinite millions. (4.247)
From sound, the vital breath (prāṇa) is fully described; from that vital breath, the phonemes arise and dissolve, wherein sound itself has gone to dissolution. (4.248)
Within the infinite number of scriptures numbering in the millions, which exist in fifty varieties in the form of *mātṛkā*s,

the phonemes (*varṇa*) reside— whether in the moving, sentient, and vocal, or in the unmoving, internally conscious, and stationary, manifesting their respective unmanifested objects of expression, beginning with the syllables. And these...

Those whose nature is sound (*śabda*) have the form of articulated speech (*śabdana*); and sound itself has the nature of vital breath (*prāṇana*), for the vital breath is the true essence of resonance (*dhvani*). Therefore, from this form of resonance, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are born; and where the vital breath, whose nature is sound, undergoes dissolution, there too the phonemes dissolve. Thus, within that which consists of the vital breath, it is the vital breath alone [that remains].
The path of phonemes is situated [therein]. || 248 ||

And because the dissolution of the phonemes and the vital breath occurs in one place, therefore—O Varārohā—one who has transcended sound is united with the ultimate reality (tattva). O Goddess, being thus united, he is omnipresent and free from both merit and demerit. (4.249)

When one has attained the Śiva-principle, one no longer looks downward; for by means of the reality (tattva), one is joined with Paramaśiva and attains oneness. Therefore, being omnipresent, one is free from merit and demerit, from the out-breath and in-breath, and from the auspicious and the inauspicious.
*Adha* signifies a distinction in the form of "this" (*idam*); *yadā* means "from which" (*yataḥ*).
He establishes this as follows:
"By unrighteousness one indeed goes downward; by righteousness one shall go upward once again. (4.250)
Having abandoned the duality by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*), one becomes all-pervasive here in this world.

By means of unrighteousness and the inauspicious, one goes downward as far as the immobile beings, reaching the level of the body and the earth which are the domain of the *apāna* breath; by means of righteousness and the auspicious, one reaches the birth of the gods and so forth; but by means of the *prāṇa* breath, one proceeds as far as the limit of power (*śakti*). This is the duality.
But by means of that distinguished knowledge, which consists of the self-reflection on identity with Śiva, one abandons [the sense of "here"];
thus, even while remaining in the body, one becomes the omnipresent Śiva.
He summarizes: "Thus the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been fully described...
Now—"
...the path of the feet is now being described. || 4-251 ||
Even the eighty-one syllables that abide as the King of Vidyās are essentially composed of phonemes; here, those phonemes abide as the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore, these words therein follow the sequence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Even within this single sovereign king of knowledge (*vidyārāja*), which consists of ninefold selfhood, there exist eighty-one words according to the previously explained method; and by the logic just established, these too consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), and those phonemes are...
The words have the nature of vital breath (prāṇa), because they consist of that.
Thus has the path of the worlds (padādhvan) been fully described; now, in this regard, learn from me the path of mantras (mantrādhvan). 4-253.
He said to him: "That which is the elevenfold mantra is established in the *haṃsa*;
that which is the elevenfold word moves perpetually within the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (4-254)
Since the elevenfold mantra, whose form consists of the limbs and faces of Niṣkala, resides in the swan— the central vital breath—

that elevenfold state, which is the cause of resting in the form of the partless digit (niṣkalakalā) and eternally uttered, consists of the phonemes beginning with 'A' that denote Brahmā and the other deities.
It has the form of words ending in "sama" and "na"; and this has already been determined previously. || 254 ||
He spoke these words: "The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu*;
the half-moon, the *nirodhin*, the *nāda*, and indeed the end of *nāda*. (4.255)
Śakti and Vyāpinī are indeed remembered as the eleventh, along with Samanā.
What kind of creative power (akārakalā) exists in the Lord Niṣkala, and what the nature of these kalās is, will be determined shortly thereafter. || 255 ||
To demonstrate that this Ekādaśikā has the nature of the *adhva* (the path), he says:
"And beyond that is Unmanā; that which transcends it is the stainless [state]. (4-256)
"Tataḥ" (thence) means having transcended that *samanā*. "Tadatītam" (transcending that) means having gone beyond (*atiśayena itam*) that *unmanā*, having reached it, being non-different from it.

Since it is the cause for attaining the supreme reality (*paratattva*) of *unmanā*, it is the "path" (*adhvan*) of mantras as well—just like the levels (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and so forth; such is the meaning. || 256 ||
He concludes: "The mantras thus abide in the vital breath...
[even] for the expansion of the path (adhvaprapañca) which exists externally in gross form, [this occurs] during the utterance of the phonemic units (mātrākala) of the mantra."

With the intention that, through its subtle form, the desire to utter a mantra results in an experience that is conducive to the mantra itself during the state of resting in the mantra— which is its supreme form— the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) is determined at the conclusion.
Following the sequence,
the utterance of *Haṃsa* is thus described.
He says this regarding it:
The letter *ha*, however, is remembered as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), self-impelled and having the form of a plowshare (*halākṛti*).

"O Goddess, this letter *ha*, which has the form of a plough, is without phonemes (*anacka*), consists of the sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*), and arises by itself"— thus it proceeds spontaneously according to the principle that will be explained later.

According to the perspective stated in another Tantra, "That supreme seed-syllable called Ṅa" (Kāloka 1.5), this very life-force (*prāṇa*)— which is synonymous with the act of breathing (*prāṇana*) and is the individual soul (*jīva*)— shines forth spontaneously as everything; it is "remembered," meaning it has been studied through an uninterrupted lineage of gurus.

And yet, according to the differentiation of the [subtle] dusts (*dhūlibheda*), having internalized the entire universe within the form of a plow (*halākṛti*), it takes the shape of the *kuṇḍalinī*, resembling a sleeping serpent. It is said to be "self-extended" (*svapravṛtaḥ*), meaning that it remains having itself submerged into the nature of the reflective awareness of sound (*nādāmarśarūpatā*) and entered into the form consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For:
The supreme power called Awakening, belonging to the Supreme Lord, having internalized the universe, being the Parā Kuṇḍalikā,
manifests through the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa) as the form of the Kuṇḍalikā of phonemes consisting of sound (nāda);
then, with this very nature withdrawn within, she exists as the Prāṇakuṇḍalikā.
"Thus it shines"—so says the sacred tradition (āmnāya). And in this way, the vital breath (prāṇa), whose nature has been explained, is indeed the *haṃsa*;

for, flowing upwards and downwards by its own inherent force, it manifests as the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the letters *ha* and *sa*, which possess the characteristics of abandoning and taking up [respectively]. || 257 ||
Now, intending to determine the abandonment of the cause by means of the phonemes right here, he first defines the pronunciation of the phonemes:
"When the letter *u* is joined with the letter *a*, together with its foot..."
The pronunciation of the phonemes, when joined with the letter *ma* alone, becomes distinct. (4.258)

This very perpetual utterance of the *haṃsa*, whose nature is *nāda*, becomes a clear articulation of phonemes (*varṇa*); how so? When it is joined with the letter *a*, which serves as the cause for manifesting the vowelless *ha* and functions as its "head," then it becomes the syllable *ukāra*.

Because it moves upwards and downwards, it is of the nature of movement (*caraṇa*); thus, when it is joined with the letter *A*, which consists of a single measure and follows the thread of the objects of knowledge such as the *bindu* and so forth, it is perceived by all as it is being uttered in this manner. || 258 ||
And furthermore—
through the union with the *bindu* at the head, one attains a beautiful tone;
such indeed is the pronunciation of phonemes for yogins as it has been described.

Having resorted to the form of the *bindu*, which consists of non-dual awareness (*avibhāga-vedanā*) that condenses all distinctions once they have been fully assimilated by the three vowels beginning with *a* at the center of the eyebrows, [one attains this] through union with the head; thus, in the head— that is, in the forehead— where the predominance of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is subsiding, there is the *ardhacandra*.

By virtue of the predominance of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) which has become completely tranquil, it exists as a clearly delineated line directed upwards; because it obstructs the entry of the non-yogi into the path of sound (*nāda*), it is designated as *nirodhikā*; and through perfect yoga on all sides—that is, by ascending to those respective levels—it possesses a beautiful resonance (*susvaratva*) in the state of the Lord (*īśvara*), where the distinctions of the objects of knowledge have been subordinated and the state of the Lord is predominant.

The meaning is that it grasps the stage of the end of sound (nādānta) from the state of nāda, which is primarily characterized by the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the non-differentiation of all denotators.
And therefore, for one who has ascended to this state—sound (nāda) is said to be his mouth...
because, according to the aforementioned principle, this *haṃsa* is the ultimate reality of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*). Thus:
Even in the state where the nature [of consciousness] consists of the utterance of phonemes, the *nāda* alone, situated in the center of the forehead, is its primary limb, like a mouth.
And this is logical, because:
"The mouth should emit sound. (4.259)

The mouth, whose form is sound (nāda), should emit the word whose essence is the end of sound; it should impel it from the surface of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and manifest as that very form.
Not only is this vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of sound (*nādātmā*), called "Haṃsa" as it resounds while joined with the head, face, and feet; rather,
by this very yoga, the *haṃsa* is also said to be the *puruṣa*.
Indeed, moving through all living beings by way of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, || 4-260 ||

The *puruṣa*, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), by means of this very yoga consisting of ascending through the middle and upper paths, moving through the channels of the heart, throat, between the eyebrows, and the forehead among all living beings, is called the *haṃsa* because its nature consists of abandoning the lower stages and assuming the higher stations. As he will state:
And in the beginning:
"Śiva is the *haṃsa* by virtue of *dharma*, while the sun is the *haṃsa* endowed with radiance" (7.39),
and so on.
"The Self is indeed called the *haṃsa*; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is endowed with the *haṃsa*. (7.30).
We shall explain this very point in that same place [later]. 260.
Thus,
having assumed the form of the final resonance (nādānta), it dissolves into the principle of power (śaktitattva).
Having stilled the state of the final resonance, it takes refuge in the Cavity of Brahma (brahmabila) as the nature of the touch of bliss.
Then, by means of that consciousness whose nature is the firm resolve to enter the state of Śiva, one should ascend upwards.
How so?
Having abandoned the pervasive *samanā*, one should proceed to Śiva by means of *unmanā*.

Having experienced touch within the *śakti* by means of the method of upward entry, and having attained pervasion in the *vyāpinī* at the level of the skin and hair, one should then abide above that— at the place of the crest-hair (*śikhā-keśa*)— at the level of the *sāmanasī*, in the form of mere contemplation due to the absence of anything to be contemplated; and even further above that is the *haṃsa*.

One whose nature is the pure self, whose essence transcends mental reflection, and who is the light of the non-dual manifestation of the entire universe simultaneously, should, by taking recourse to the power of *unmanā*, proceed toward Śiva and attain the state of supreme Bhairava, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss. || 261 ||
And thus:
"The *haṃsa* situated in the *śiva-tattva* does not move...
[the one] called the *śiva-tattva*, Paramaśiva, does not move; he neither contracts nor expands."
Rather,
it would be all-pervasive by way of its nature as the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, and also by way of that form which transcends it.
The meaning is that it vibrated.
He concludes: "The utterance of Haṃsa has been fully explained, together with its causal factors. (4.262)

It is properly endowed with, or mixed with, the causes such as Brahmā and others— and by virtue of the word "and" (ca), with the phonemes beginning with 'a'— as they exist according to the nature of things.
Now he defines the abandonment of causes by means of the phonemes;
therein—the letter *ha* is the self of the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*).
By its stated state as the self of the power of breath, it is of the nature of life.
The letter 'Kā', which consists of the line of the head of this [syllable], is the designator of Brahman;
its renunciation occurs in the heart.
That is to say, up until the utterance of the designator.
Likewise, further on—..................the syllable *u* denotes Viṣṇu. (4-263)
The letter *ma*, which denotes Rudra, is to be abandoned at the throat;
one should abandon it in the middle of the palate...
[the word] "should abandon" (*tyajet*) contains the agentive suffix and the particle *tu* (but/indeed), indicating that one must pay close attention to the piercing of the Rudra-knot.
It is indicated... and the dot (bindu) itself is Īśvara. || 4-264 ||

By stating their non-difference, [the author] demonstrates that from this point onward, there is no longer a separate relationship between the signified and the signifier, just as in the case of form and so forth.
"Its abandonment is prescribed in the middle of the eyebrows"—this connects with what follows later. Of this very [state], [there is] the half-moon, the obstructress, and the end.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*)... [is] Sadāśiva who is to be expressed through [the phonemes] beginning with *a*;
the meaning is that one should contemplate [him] as non-different from that.
The relinquishing of that [element] is prescribed from the forehead up to the crown of the head. || 4-265 ||
The yogis, with diligent effort, bring about the pervasive rule wherein the end of sound itself is the limit of the end of sound. || 265 ||
Now, as for those [levels] which are accessible through subtle experience—
Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā— their designatum is the imperishable Śiva.
This one is "imperishable" (avyaya) in relation to Sadāśiva, but in relation to Paramaśiva, he is indeed perishable (savyaya).
Therein—one should cast the Śakti into the center of the crown, and above that, one should cast the Vyāpinī. || 4-266 ||
It has been explained thus for the very purpose [of showing] that [it occurs] at the end of the experience of touch. || 266 ||
At the conclusion of the experience whose nature is mere reflection—
[the state] called *samanā*...
one should abandon it above that, in this manner.
Thus, for the yogin who has attained the nature of the pure Self by transcending this much of the path—[the verse states:
"Having abandoned Unmanā through the abandonment of the six, there is dissolution in the seventh";
the ellipsis [is to be supplied]. This occurs by means of entering the power of Unmanā, whose nature has been explained.
The very state of becoming Supreme Śiva (paramaśivībhāva) is the abandonment of Unmanā. Thus, by abandoning the six causal deities known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva—
transcending them preceded by a state of rest— one attains dissolution in the seventh, Supreme Śiva.
There is an attainment.
He concludes by adding this further instruction: "O Dear One, one should renounce the states of being in this very manner, through [levels] increasingly subtle and more subtle. (4.267)
By means of entities that are gross and grosser, which bestow various fruits of accomplishment (*siddhi*),

the entities and categories— which consist of the signified and the signifier as previously described— become gross and grosser in the order of descent (*avaroha-krama*) and grant their respective accomplishments according to the reasoning to be explained hereafter.
They are situated by those very [levels] in the order of ascent, characterized by each being increasingly more subtle than the last.

"In this way" refers to the entire path; one should abandon it "in this way," that is, precisely according to the reasoning already stated—by those [levels] which, as they are being abandoned, are characterized by being increasingly more subtle in the order of ascent.

In this manner, each subsequent stage is indeed [preceded by] those [previous ones]; according to the principle demonstrated by them acting as causes, one should abandon [the lower stages] in the way described. It has been further introduced here that while the gross elements serve as the cause for the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the subtle elements serve as the cause for liberation (*mukti*). || 267 ||
In that regard—The supreme state, which is extremely subtle, is designated as non-existence (abhāva). (4.268)

The supreme state (*paro bhāvaḥ*), supreme existence (*parā sattā*), Paramaśiva, who is exceedingly subtle, is the meaning of that which is to be known as the cause of all; and because he consists of the dissolution of all phenomenal states (*bhāva*), he is non-existence (*abhāva*).
And he is not merely such [as previously described], up until:

"The state of *unmanā* is another condition..."— it is called *unmanā* because, in relation to the supreme state (*parabhāva*), it possesses a slight orientation toward the external due to its nature as the self-reflection of one's own essence.
The other is the state consisting of the Great Being (mahāsattā), which is the subtle state; thus is the synthesis of existence and non-existence.

...the gross [state] is considered its other [aspect]. This "other" is the state called *samanā*, which exists as a relative to that essential nature known as *unmanā* by way of being its correlate, in the form of the pervaded and the pervader; it is not something separate from it.

However, that [subtle body] is also subtle in comparison to the gross [body] and the letters beginning with 'a'; otherwise, the plural form in the phrase "by the subtle, subtler, and most subtle" would not be appropriate.
"Furthermore, its other void..."—the meaning is as follows:

"its" refers to the entity that is the universal self (*samanātman*); "other" refers to its pervasive form, the void which consists of the non-manifestation of all entities, namely the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*).

By the word "again," it is stated that there is first one void (*śūnya*) consisting of *samanā*, which takes the form of a thread that delineates all existence and non-existence without remainder; this [second void], however, is like a wall for the manifestation of all existence and non-existence.
And for this very reason:
...and after that, the contact with [the object]. || 269 ||
This means "the state of power" (śaktipada). || 269 ||
From that too— the sound...
whose nature is the end of resonance and which consists of the form of resonance.
Beyond that also—
light—
the bindu is the state of the half-moon which pervades the obstructive [power].
...Then there are the mantras, the causes, and the worlds.

The mantras are the denoters, consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the phonemes *ma*, *u*, and *a*; their denoted objects are Rudra, Upendra, and Brahmā, who are the causes, as well as the principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*) that serve as their substrates.
And the meaning is that they become extremely gross in succession.
Thus it is said: "The world, consisting of the five elements, is presided over by its causes. (4.270)

The self is the cause of that world which consists of the five elements and so forth, existing in both gross and subtle forms. For even in the realms of Māyā, Vidyā, and the others, there are worlds; yet those [worlds] therein are not composed of gross elements, nor are they composed of subtle elements.
Their grossness exists only in relation to their presiding causes; in reality, however, these worlds and other elements are of the very nature of Śiva.
As it has been stated elsewhere:
"The universe, the body, light, space, sound, and the mantra—Śiva is said to be sixfold when differentiated by the bindu, nāda, and so forth.
For those desiring to ascend [the path], however, it is said that [He is perceived] through forms increasingly grosser and grosser, and so on. (270)

Regarding what was stated, "gross entities bestow accomplishments," he now demonstrates the differentiation of those accomplishments by analyzing them in the reverse order of the sequence previously mentioned:
"He who should contemplate the world as having the single form that is about to be described..."

"He attains the state of a Lord of the World (bhuvaneśatva)... refers to what will be described hereafter; thus, on the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the state of being a Lord of the World consists in having the form of Kālāgni and so forth. However, for the Supreme One, because of his state as a Yogi, this world—as well as the physical body and so forth that will be described—is [perceived] solely as the form of Śiva.
He beholds [it]—having meditated upon Śiva and become absorbed in Him. (4.271)

And the meditation on Śiva is by means of his very nature as a mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*), not by means of a [physical] form. But for others—the causes such as Brahmā and the rest—one who, while meditating on their embodied forms during practice, possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, shall attain identity with them. (272)
The word "previously" was mentioned on the occasion of determining the seat; in the phrase "and he who," the word "he" (saḥ) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The accomplishment of mantras through mantras arises from recitation, fire-offerings, and worship; the word "when propitiated" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

And therefore, those mantras such as the Aṅgas and Brahmās which have already been mastered through recitation (japa) and other means, will undoubtedly be perfected here through the previously described meditation on the forms. || 4-273 ||
For these, meditation has already been explained; the means and the fruit will follow later. || 273 ||
Through meditation on the light, the lord of yogis shall attain the perfection of yoga;
the light is the bindu, and the perfection of yoga is the knowledge of the past and so forth.
But through the excellence of yoga, when he attains identity with that [reality], he becomes a sovereign of yogins. (4.274)
"Adhipa" means the form of the Blessed Lord, Īśvara. || 274 ||
And through meditation on sound, one whose self is sound becomes the filler of the realm of speech;
"sound" here refers to *nāda*.
And from the meditation on touch, the one whose nature is touch would become the cause of the world. || 4-275 ||
Touch, whose nature is bliss, resides within Śakti; because it is the cause of the world below her, it is said to be the cause of the universe. || 275 ||
But in the state of the Pervasive One (vyāpinī), through meditation on the void, one becomes the self of the void, pervasive and omnipresent.
By means of the yoga of meditation on the Equal One (samanā), the yogi shall attain omniscience. (4.276)

Having thus established the accomplishments (*siddhis*) in relation to states that are gross, grosser, and so forth, one should practice meditation on the supreme reality of *unmanā*, which is extremely subtle, according to the perspective set forth in such passages as: "The state that is extremely subtle is the highest" (4.268).
He instructs [the practitioner] regarding that which bestows liberation, beginning with the words "unmanyā tu":
one should always contemplate the supreme, subtle non-existence (*abhāva*) through *unmanī*.
Through *unmanī*, the inherent power (*śakti*), one should contemplate the supreme non-existence, which is of the nature of the previously mentioned Śiva-tattva.
One should meditate.
He explains non-existence (abhāva):
"That which transcends all senses and the mind is called the uncharacterizable non-existence. (4.277)

He has transcended and utterly emerged beyond all the senses and the mind, because for him who stands above the state of "with-mind" (samanā), there is only the singular nature of the Knower; for this very reason, he is unperceivable.

Furthermore, based on the etymological derivation that it is a state where no entities such as the objects of knowledge exist, he is called "non-existence" (abhāva); yet in reality, he is indeed a mass of consciousness and bliss.
Now, one might object: "If this is so, how was it said that 'one should always cultivate non-existence'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Having made existence supportless by means of the cultivation of non-existence through [the power of] existence..."

That state (*pada*) in which no entities exist is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-rūpa*); it is to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), that is, to be meditated upon (*bhāvanīya*), by means of existence—that is, by means of the form consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), which is the supreme being (*parasattā*). Now, one might object: "The nature of consciousness (*citattva*) is the subject that brings about cultivation (*bhāvaka*);
how then can it be said to be 'that which is to be cultivated' (*bhāvya*)?"

"Having made existence supportless" means: that which exists (*bhavati*) is "existence" (*bhāvaḥ*), [the hierarchy] beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the earth; having made that supportless—that is, without a basis—by transforming it into its own nature through entry into the abode of Power (*śaktidhāman*) by way of a state of perfect tranquility.
And thus:
"He attains the state that is freedom from all limiting conditions (upādhi) and is non-existence. (4.278)
He summarizes: "This is your renunciation of the causes...
Regarding the renunciation of the causes, he states the renunciation of the *kalās* (aspects), which is implied by the sense of the context:
.........learn from me the abandonment of time.
And that [time] joined with sixteen *tuṭis* is declared to be a single breath (*prāṇa*). (4.279)
And of that [wheel],
resting upon two *tuṭis*, each one Bhairava is situated,
beginning with Kapālīśabhairava, established in the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*).
And in this [world], by means of the division of day and night, they indeed bring about their arising. (4.280)
Just as eight [breaths] rise during the day in the prāṇa, so too do they rise at night in the apāna. || 280 ||
The pervasive among these is the supreme ninth deity...
"Supreme" means that Śrī Svacchandanātha is the fulfiller and the pervader of the eight [previous deities], as well as the most excellent.
From this pervasive Great Light, which is their very self... they arise from that radiance;
the meaning is that they vibrate precisely upon its foundation. And therefore, in the arising of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is inseparable from it—

Whether it be the cognition of external or internal objects such as blue or pleasure, or even the conceptualization thereof, for the great yogin these consist solely of the expansion of Supreme Bhairava; they are never at any time or place fragmented, but rather are constantly adorned by the expansion of his own Self— this is the secret meaning hinted at here.
This being the case— I shall tell you how one should properly abandon all time within the vital breath (prāṇa). (4.281)
In that regard, sixteen *tuṭis* have been declared; they are the instrument of time (*kālasya karaṇam*).
Time, which is established as beginning with those, pervades the entirety of the realm of speech. (4.282)
"But they are the instrument" means that through them, by means of initiating the vital breath (*prāṇa*), all time is set in motion. Thus it begins with that, as in:
"Two *kṣaṇas* are declared to be a *tuṭi*" (11.201).

Thus, although time consists of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth according to the future [explanatory] rule, nevertheless, by the very statement of the future text— “A moment is one-eighth part of a human blink” (11.201)— it is stated that the object of definition is to be inferred; therefore, it cannot be perceived even by those who are attentive.
It has been stated that everything consisting of speech moves as something clearly perceivable, like a momentary flash (*tuṭi*).

By means of the pervasion of the *mātṛkā* being uttered through the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it pervades the entire collection of signifiers (*vācaka*), and by means of that, it also pervades the signifieds (*vācya*). || 282 ||
He analyzes what was stated as "beginning with that":
"A *tuṭi*, a *lava*, a *nimeṣa*, a *kāṣṭhā*, and likewise a *kalā*;
a *muhūrta*, a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), a fortnight (*pakṣa*), a month (*māsa*), and likewise a season (*ṛtu*). (4.283)
The half-year, the year, the yuga, the manvantara,
as well as the kalpa and the mahākalpa—
these, along with the sixteen beginning with the *tuṭi*, and the two [others] to be mentioned in the eleventh chapter.
"They will be determined [as follows]: 'At the end of a mahākalpa, Brahmā goes to the supreme dissolution' (11.264).
This *mahākalpa* mentioned here is not to be taken [in that sense], because it would be inconsistent; rather, [it refers to something else].
The supreme great kalpa is the self that lasts until the end of Sadāśiva’s life.
As it is said: "......... one should abandon that at the end of Śakti. (4.284)

The meaning is that, at the conclusion of the entry into the inclusion within the *śakti*, time— which effects the withdrawal of the five causes ending with Sadāśiva— is pacified when viewed with subtle insight.
Now—
At the end of the pervasive [cycle], there is the supreme time (*paraḥ kālaḥ*); that is its limb (*aṅga*).
That supreme great aeon (*paramamahākalpa*) is the limb, the constituent part; therefore, it is "possessing the limb" (*aṅgī*), meaning "supreme," which is called "equilibrium" (*sāmya*).
As he will state:
"That time is indeed known as the state of equilibrium. (11.209)
...one should abandon that;
and one should abandon it during the state of experiencing equality.
And with respect to the previous category—
that [state] is to be known as the seventeenth...
even beyond that—
The parārdha is the state beyond that. || 4-285 ||
O Goddess, that eighteenth [state] also should be abandoned at the end of Samanā;
one should abandon it—that is, cause it to subside—at the conclusion of the experience of Samanā, through its absorption into Unmanā. || 285 ||

In this way, by means of a single utterance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the most excellent Guru, having stilled even the time extending externally as far as the end of a *parārdha*, should establish a firm state in the station that is not measured by time. Thus it is said:
"But he who pervades all time is the supreme, imperishable [Lord]. (4.286)
One should be joined to the supreme state at the end of *unmanī*; there, no time exists.
Of time—that which extends to the end of a *parārdha*—he is pervasive because he is eternally arisen at all times; for this very reason, he is supreme and imperishable.
One should be joined to that supreme state at the end of *unmanī*, which is the immersion into the experience of Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti (*śaktimad*).
He is to be recognized through the state of absolute identity (*sāmarasya*). And therein, time, which consists of mental construction (*kalana*), does not exist;
the meaning is that because He alone effects the construction of the universe, no one can construct Him. || 286 ||
Therefore, he is—
eternal, eternally risen, all-pervasive...
"Eternally risen" means that he is not covered by anything.
And because it stands above all, one should not abandon its primordial form. (4.287)
One should resort to that very [state] by means of the method of firm support.
And this being so—
having attained that which is eternally risen, the lord of yogis (yogīndra) becomes forever one with it; this is the ellipsis.
And thus, having determined that the abandonment of time follows immediately upon the abandonment of the cause, he says:
"The abandonment of time would indeed be thus... [and so on], which follows the order of the enumeration.
...the state of emptiness is thus declared. || 4-288 ||
Form is an empty entity or thing; the meaning is that it serves as the means for attaining the supreme state of emptiness. || 288 ||
He said of that:
"The void above, the void below, and the third is the void in the middle;
the fourth is the pervasive void. (4.290)

Because it will be stated thus [later], the "upper void" (*ūrdhvaśūnya*) here is the plane of Power (*śaktipada*), which is the ground for the complete pacification of all bonds (*pāśa*) at the end of the End of Sound (*nādānta*);
the "lower void" (*adhaḥśūnya*) is the field of the heart (*hṛtkṣetra*), in which the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has not yet emerged; and as for the "middle void" (*madhyaśūnya*), however—
In due order, it consists of the pacification of the lower objects of knowledge,
located in the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture at the crown of the head.
And thus:
For these three voids are mobile; they are located below, in the middle, and above. || 4-289 ||
The meaning is that these three voids, situated respectively below, in the middle, and above, are to be abandoned because they are relative. || 289 ||
Furthermore:
the fourth is the pervasive void (vyāpinī-śūnya), the fifth is in the state of Samanā,
and likewise the sixth is in the state of Unmanā.
In this case as well, it should be understood that "this is indeed unstable" because of its relativity.
And therefore:
"These six are established as conventional. (4.290)

In this context, the term *āmaya* (disease) indicates that which is to be abandoned (*heyatva*). Therefore, the meaning is that these [states] are to be abandoned because they are characterized by movement.

Even in the state of *unmanā*, there exists a slight degree of movement when compared to the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*). However, because the Supreme Reality itself is immovable, it is that which is to be accepted (*upādeyatva*). || 290 ||
Therefore, all these—even those belonging to the conventional (sāmaya)—bestow accomplishment when presided over by reality (tattva).
Reality is Paramaśiva; "presiding over" means pervasion. Here, "accomplishment" refers to that of the supreme yogin.
The Self alone is the mass of full bliss; for anything else, however, there is only that which is appropriate to the various states of dream.
Therefore:
"Having abandoned the six voids, bring about dissolution in the seventh. (4.291)
For it is said:
"That [state] is void, supreme, subtle, and devoid of all conditions.
That it is "supreme and subtle" has been determined previously. Regarding Unmanā as well—

According to the principle stated in the *Vijñānabhairava* (20), "The Śaiva [state] is here called the mouth," because it serves as the means for entering the Supreme Reality with the intention of one desiring to penetrate that supreme state, it possesses the status of a "state" (*avasthā*). Thus, considering this, [the following applies].
The supreme reality is devoid of all states and is of a single form throughout the three states.
If this is so, how can it be empty? To this he says:
"That which is non-empty is called 'empty,' and emptiness is said to be non-existence. (4.292)
That is observed as non-existence (abhāva) wherein all entities have come to an end.
That which is called "void" (śūnya) is, in reality, not void; it is the supreme Śiva-tattva, a mass of consciousness and bliss.
The reason for this is the word "void. For the particle "ca" has the sense of "because"; because that which is called "void" is [in fact] non-existence.

And since non-existence does not exist where all existence—the manifold of objects of cognition and so forth—is absent, according to this etymological derivation, it is precisely the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) that is taught here; therefore, it is rightly said that "emptiness is indeed non-empty."
Therefore, that is mere existence (sattāmātra),
which is the nature of Great Existence (mahāsattā); for the existence of all things, whether existent or non-existent, is indeed nothing but Light (prakāśa).
But through the complete pacification of all distinctions, that certain supreme state, which is utterly tranquil, remains. (4.293)
The meaning is "supramundane. || 293 ||

And it is not only that this has a form transcending the universe, but it also consists of the entire universe; thus he says: "Wherever else [the levels] beginning with Nāda, up to the gross, are situated, there the Supreme Void is established, pervading everything. (4.294)

Those things beginning with *nāda*— namely *bindu* and so forth— and those beginning with the power (*śakti*) of *nāda*, such as *vyāpinī* and others, wherever they may be in fields such as the forehead; and also other gross entities denoted by *nāda* and the rest, such as Sadāśiva and others, together with the respective *tattvas*, worlds (*bhuvanas*), and so forth, which are presided over by them, whether internally or externally.

Established therein, throughout all of this, the supreme void—which is of the nature of pure existence alone—pervades everything, even down to the finest particles like the essence of sugar, and remains present in manifold forms;
and it is the pervader itself that manifests as the pervaded, for there is no such thing as a "pervaded" entity other than that. Thus he says:
That very [reality] becomes gross, O Dear One, by virtue of a gross limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Since the venerable Svatantranātha, whose nature is the Great Light, manifests through his own sovereignty as a gross appearance, the meaning is that he is called "gross" by virtue of that adjunct.
And thus:
"That one [reality] is established through its divisions into gross and subtle. (4.295)

Therefore, for that great yogin whose consciousness has ascended to such an intensity, he—having attained that [state] and having achieved identity with it—attains it; there is no doubt in this matter. "Having attained" (prāpya) means having grasped it through firm realization. "There is no doubt" means...
This must be understood as the very truth; one should not entertain the kind of doubt that is easily accessible to the ignorant.
For one who lacks confidence in such a profound matter, it is appropriate to abandon the cause [of worldly attachment] and so forth.

Having withdrawn this [practice] into emptiness according to the appropriate sequence, he introduces the state of equal flavor (samarasa): "The state of emptiness has been fully explained; now learn from me the state of equal flavor. (4.296)
That in which the flavor is equal is "equal-flavored" (samarasa), which is the state of liquefaction (lolībhāva). || 296 ||
He enumerates its divisions:
"One should know the first to be in the self, equally blended; the second in the mantra;
one should place the third in the channel, and the fourth in the power (śakti). (4.297)
The fifth is proclaimed in Vyāpinī, while the sixth is in Samanā;
O Goddess, the seventh is ordained as the tattva of Samarasa.
He defines these according to their enumeration:

"Having first gathered the disciple's self by means of the previously mentioned procedure in due order, and subsequently having joined it to one's own self, one should contemplate it as having become thoroughly blended. (4.299)

Having joined the self— which is consciousness consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*— to the self that is pure consciousness alone, according to the previously mentioned method (beginning with striking, cutting, and so forth), one should contemplate it without conceptualization and, through that very resting in it, bring about a state of aesthetic unification (*samarasīkuryāt*). || 299 ||
Right here, completing the portion concerning the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), he points toward the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with the *nāḍī* and the mantra;
therein, for the purpose of seizing the disciple's self,
one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), and then arrest [the breath] by means of the *samāna* [vital energy].

By means of the *samāna* breath, which has acquired strength through the excellence of *kumbhaka*, one should restrain [the vital energies]; that is to say, by implication, one should pervade all the channels (*nāḍīs*).
As it has been said:
"O Goddess, as many channels as there are, situated horizontally, upwards, and downwards... (4.300).
Drawn together by the equalizing breath, they become unified.
Thus, for one who remains established in the excellence of *kumbhaka*, those winds within them also attain a state of homogeneity with the *prāṇa*. (4.301)
The channels, however, remain unified within the *suṣumnā*; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 301 ||
In this way, preceded by the state of equilibrium of the channels (nāḍīsāmarasya), there arises the state of equilibrium of the mantra (mantrasāmarasya). Regarding this, it is said:
"Then indeed the mantra should be uttered...
[The word] *ud* means upward; for one who is concentrated, [the mantra] should proceed—that is, it should flow forth spontaneously.
And as it is being uttered, one should contemplate it as dissolved into the state called Sādākhyā, which consists of unmanifest sound (avyaktadhvani), [and further] into Nāda. || 4.302 ||
He brings it together:
"The mantra, the self, and likewise the channel—thus they become of one flavor.
In the left, the right, and the middle..."
When the state of perfect identity with the mantra and so forth has thus occurred simultaneously, one should then release the resonance (nāda). || 4.303 ||
And he should release— that is, cause to proceed— the *nāda* along that path called *setubandha*, by going upon which one is not born again;
a path consisting of the *setubandha* in the form of Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā,
a way that leads to the state of Śiva who stands on the further shore of all paths.
And when that [liberation] has occurred, one does not transmigrate; the verb *muc* (to release) is treated as having two objects because the sense of "going" is intended.
And here, he states that the equilibrium of the causal factors is established by the very nature of the matter:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself. (4.304)
These attain equality here when there is repose in the heart,
throat, and other locations through the utterances of the syllables *a*,
*u*, and so forth; otherwise, however, they remain distinct.
He characterizes the intervals of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) situated within the attainment of the bridge (*setu*) just described:
"In that [state], one should emit the resonance (*nāda*) until, having reached dissolution (*laya*), one is absorbed in the power (*śakti*). (4.305)
The resonance situated in the midst of power is indeed established as having the nature of power;
everything there consists of power, and everything becomes of one flavor. (4.306)

"In that" refers to the previously mentioned bridge-construction; "all" refers to the state of becoming one in flavor (*samarasībhūta*) within the *nāda*, which consists of the self, the mantra, the channels (*nāḍī*), and their causes.
Having attained this unity of power, and having reached the Vyāpinī above that, one should attain the state of being identical with all;
everything becomes non-different from the Vyāpinī that has been reached.
Because it pervades everywhere, it is called "pervasive. || 4-307 ||
And then—
having pervaded the level of Samanā above that, one should again attain identity with it.
And there—
And she should be known as all-pervading, abiding in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya). || 4-308 ||
The word "ca" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed); the meaning is that she alone is omnipresent there and is to be understood by all.
Here, the root *gam* has the sense of "knowing. || 308 ||
Thus,
having abandoned the sixth state of *samarasa*, one should then proceed to the seventh;
through the penetration of the power of *unmanā*, one shall attain [the goal].
Having attained that state of identity with it, indeed, no further deliberation is required here.
And he who has thus attained supreme identity with all things—

[he perceives] in all beings, in the elements, in the principles of existence, and in the senses, as well as in the stationary and the moving, and in all that exists as conscious or unconscious. (4.310)
Pervading the entire path, he abides in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).

He is both that which is stationary and insentient, and that which is moving and sentient; in brief, having pervaded the sixfold path existing in two ways, he is present within all things contained therein.

Abiding in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) within the fourteen levels of existence—beginning with the divine wombs (*devayoni*)—as well as within phenomena such as merit (*dharma*), objects such as jars, principles such as earth (*pṛthivī*), and the senses which are the instruments of enjoyment;
he remains, in all states, with his immersion into Supreme Bhairava unimpaired. And this very [state] is...
Its essence is the samādhi of non-emergence; it is the supreme secret.
But even the mind of yogis, though it has ascended into meditative absorptions, forcibly continues to waver. (4.311)
It moves crookedly due to the desire for enjoyments and runs only toward distraction; it does not seize the desired state, because it is thus. || 311 ||
Then—
The mind of one whose state consisting of the knowable is stable, full, and all-pervading does not waver, even when situated in any condition whatsoever. (4.312)
The object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is the supreme reality (*paratattva*) as it has been explained; "state" (*bhāva*) means intention (*āśaya*);
"firm" (*sthira*) means immovable; "full" (*pūrṇa*) means free from desire; "on all sides" (*samantataḥ*) means by perceiving everything;
and "but" (*tu*) is used in the sense of "even though. || 312 ||
For such a great yogi:
"Wherever the mind goes, one should contemplate the object of knowledge right there; for having moved, where could it go? Since everything is composed of Śiva. (4.313)
The mind alone, permeated by the contemplation of its identity with the Supreme Reality, contemplates as described the object of knowledge everywhere. As it has been stated by the Great Teachers:
"When the mind, bound from worldly existence by the medicine of the contemplation of Śiva..."
"Just as [the power of] mercury [brings about] the state of Śiva-gold when applied to wood, walls, and so forth" (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.48). || 313 ||
He confirms this very point:
"Abiding in all objects and in all sense-objects, wherever one may examine it, nothing whatsoever is found that is not Śiva. (4.314)

The sense organs, their objects, the sensory faculties, and the purpose—the enjoyment of those objects—in whatever these may be established, if that best of yogis is scrutinized and investigated, there is no inauspiciousness for him anywhere; for all this exists as manifestation, being of one essence with Śiva, who is the mass of light. || 314 ||
Having thus realized the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), one shall never be deluded;
for it is the intention of the word "never" that limited yogins are indeed deluded during the period of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
And for this reason: "He whose existence is thus in every respect must also be omnipresent. (4.315)

There is no disagreement that Śiva is indeed all-pervasive; however, he whose state of being or disposition is thus one with Śiva as all-pervasive—he too becomes all-pervasive and certainly experiences the Great Pervasion.
Having summarized this, he now defines the nature of the *viṣuvat*, which arises in the stage preceding this and is otherwise unobserved:
"Thus has the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) been declared; now learn from me about the *viṣuvat*."
He analyzes that [as follows]:
"The first is to be known as the *prāṇa-viṣuvat* of the mantra; the second is likewise. (4-316)
The third is the channel-equinox (nāḍiviṣuvat), and the fourth is the tranquil one;
the fifth is the power-equinox (śaktiviṣuvat), and the sixth is indeed called time (kāla). || 4-317 ||
The seventh is the *tattvaviṣuvat*...
it is called *viṣuvat* because poison (*viṣa*) attains a pervasive state (*vyāpti*) in the form of equilibrium (*sāmya*).
Of this [reality] thus divided—
[its] detailed classification is now stated.
That by which a thing is distinguished (*prakarṣeṇa vibhajyate*), that is, established by way of excluding others, is [the classification].
That differentiation is the defining characteristic.
In that regard:
having joined the self and the mind to the vital breath (prāṇa), one becomes equanimous (viṣuvat). (4.318)

Having properly joined oneself along with the six disciples and one's own mind into the central-flowing vital breath (prāṇa) by means of the method of practice already described and to be described hereafter, it becomes the equinox of the vital breath (prāṇaviṣuvat).
Thus—
in the vital breath, that which is called the equinox has been explained...
now...
The mantra is said to be the equinox;
one should recite the mantra until the mind becomes single-pointed. || 4-319 ||
Through the division of the higher and the lower, that which is the essence of mantra is thus described:
the Śrī Niṣkala is the mantra; "the higher and lower" refers to the lower [state] ending with Nādānta, while the higher [state] ends with Unmanā.
The mantra has been described as the *viṣuvat*;
the channel (*nāḍī*) is the substratum for the utterance of the mantra. Therefore, learn from me that which resides within the channel.
Among all the channels, that which is situated in the center is to be known as Suṣumnā; by means of its radiant power, it has gone to Śiva.
Starting from the navel, by means of power— that is, through entering into the experience of power— they have gone to Śiva, having attained the supreme reality.
This being the case:
"there one should cause the *nāda* to flow"—
that is, one should cause the *nāda*, which consists of the form of unmanifest sound, to flow upward with excellence through its conjunction with the letters beginning with *a*.
One should cause [him] to attain.
This very state, consisting of the equilibrium of all the channels (nāḍīs),
is called the "equinox of the channels" (nāḍī-viṣuvat).
It is said— that is, it has been stated— such is the meaning.
Now, in due order,
I shall describe to you the Praśānta and likewise the Viṣuva.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In the solstice (ayana), the movement is six finger-breadths; the causes [of the breath] reside in each finger-breadth.
Having set aside those causes from below, there are indeed only six. (4.323)

In the seventh [finger-breadth], however, it is indeed utterly tranquil, with the range of the senses completely stilled; this refers to the *viṣuvat*. Within the movement of thirty-six finger-breadths, according to the established rule of the authority of time, in each of the solstices (*ayana*) consisting of the transit through the zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn starting from the heart—

The movement is six finger-breadths; and therein, for every group of six, there are six causes at every single finger-breadth—that is, at every sixth [finger-breadth]. Thus, having set aside those six causes situated below which exist through the pervasion of the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), one reaches the seventh, the supreme cause.
The distinction is that it becomes a "tranquil equinox" (praśāntaviṣuvat) due to the state of equilibrium of the causal factors (kāraṇas), which constitutes tranquility (praśama).
He explains "tranquil" (praśānta): "Tranquil is to be known as steady; steady is considered to be motionless. (4.324)
Immovable, waveless, stable, and full in every respect—
through the subsiding of the waves of duality, the very density of consciousness becomes tranquil; such is the intended meaning of the term "the waveless and full state."
Having established oneself in this state of being, the initiations (dīkṣā) should be performed by the teachers (daiśika).
The meaning is: having come to rest in the perfectly tranquil equinox (*praśāntaviṣuvat*). This [is] the perfectly tranquil equinox... Now—
...Learn from me the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of power (śakti): when the resonance (nāda), situated in the midst of power, moves upward beyond the resonance. (4.326)
At that time, however, [he is] the Śakti-viṣuvat...

having entered the center of Śakti, ascended to the central abode; Nāda is the unmanifest sound. When one moves from the state of Sadāśiva, which is above Nāda, into the station of Śakti, when he is situated in the middle, then—
The equinox of power.
Now, learn from me that which is called Time.
To that end, he says:
"The sixteenfold *tuṭi*, however, is situated at the end of the breath. (4.327)
The duration there is said by me to be merely the blink of an eyebrow;
divide that again into three parts according to the distinction between the higher and the lower.

The sixteenth *tuṭi* occurs at the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); within that, at its conclusion in the form of half a *tuṭi*, there is a time consisting of the movement of a very subtle shift of eight-sixtieths of a finger-breadth, which is no larger than the blink of an eye—divide that single unit into three parts: by means of the subsequent, the supreme, and the intermediate (parāpara) portions.
The meaning of the word "again" (punaḥ) is the threefold division of the Tuṭi that has been halved. || 328 ||
In that regard—
another [period] up to the sixteenth...
the sixteenth previously mentioned is called a *mahākalpa*, up to another, which is gross.
The seventeenth [tattva] is Kāla;
it was previously designated by the name Parā.
But that time which is both supreme and non-supreme, O beloved, is the eighteenth Lord.
"Parāpara" means higher than even the "para"; it is the eighteenth [category] called *parārdha*, the Lord who pervades all divisions of time. || 329 ||
Thus, in this manner— the vital breath (prāṇa), having divided time in this way into three parts, should again be abandoned;
first, by means of the phonemes, within the upper half-tuṭi of the [vital] breath.

At the occasion of abandoning the causal [state], the abandonment of the eighteen-fold parts (*kalā*) produced in succession was taught through the method of mantra-recitation. Now, however, by means of the sequence of yoga and through the stability of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
one should diligently abandon the seventeen-fold time and [abide] in the eighteenth, the equinox of time (*kālaviṣuvat*).
The meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is "one must rest."
He recalls the previously mentioned division of locations for time divided into three parts:
"The other [state] resides at the summit of Śakti, and the second is in Vyāpinī. (4.330)
The third is at the position of Samanā; it is known as the equinox of that time (*tatkālaviṣuvat*). The connection is: "that which is the third is the equinox of that time.
For above that—
"It is said: 'Time exists there. (4-287) || 330 ||
Thus,
this sixth [chapter] has been fully explained... now—
...the seventh reality (tattva) is now being described. || 4-331 ||
Regarding this, it is said:
"O Goddess, beyond that is Unmanā; there one should unite the self.
For when the self is joined to that, it becomes identical with it. (4.332)
"From the other" refers to the state of *samanā*; that which is precisely the yoga of *unmanā* for the self. || 332 ||
That very [state],
O Goddess, called the reality (tattva), is the equinox (viṣuvat) situated beyond all;
he concludes:
Having understood the equinox to be of such a nature, who would not be liberated from bondage?
The equinox has thus been explained... Now, he provides an enumeration in order to traverse the five categories that are invariably connected through tradition:
... listen to the classification of the categories.
Abandonment, experience, and indeed application in the supreme state.

The *padās* are the locations beginning with the heart, which will be described according to their measures; they are called *padārthas* because they are sought (*arthyante*) therein through the experience of their respective causes. These consist of eleven [principles] beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *samanā*. Their "piercing" (*bhedana*) is the bringing them under one's own control through the method of experience, as in the phrase: "they have been pierced."
"...the local rulers. In this context, when there is necessarily a relinquishing of each successive lower stage, there occurs the experience of each subsequent higher state;

that very process is first designated as "union" (*saṃyoga*) in the form of a thorough application, and at the culmination of the process of differentiation, union with the supreme state necessarily occurs.
And that has been previously indicated by the word "all," because its nature consists of the cultivation of all that is supreme.
In that regard,
the eleventh category of objects should be understood as that which was previously determined.
But above that,
[the state] ending with Unmanā becomes supreme;
this is the meaning of the term "padārtha" (the reality of the categories).
Therefore, for the sake of abiding therein, one should pierce that eleventh category of reality with the spear of knowledge—
that very knowledge which consists of the expansion of the light of the supreme power, as will be determined immediately hereafter.

It is called a *śūla* (trident/spear) because it pierces through [reality] by means of its extreme sharpness, which is manifested in form and enveloped by the three powers— will and the rest— which have become one in essence (*samarasībhūta*).
Not only is this a differentiator, but furthermore—knowledge is the indicator of the object of knowledge. 4-335.
The supreme reality is that which is to be known here.
Therefore,
its indicator is incomparable awareness— consisting of the manifestation of the supreme power— and not awareness in the form of the experience of objects; such is the established state.
The second [explanation]: the grammatical designation is Vedic (chāndasa).

The reason for this is: "Because it illuminates like a lamp. Clarifying this, he says that the means of knowledge should come to rest within the object of knowledge: The reason for this is: "Because it illuminates like a lamp. Clarifying this, he says that the means of knowledge should come to rest within the object of knowledge: "Since it illuminates like a lamp. Elucidating this, he states: "The means of knowledge should find its repose in the object of knowledge. Thus he says: [the verse follows].
Just as someone with a lamp in hand might see and then take up an object; || 4-336 ||
In this way, by means of knowledge, one should establish the object of knowledge within that [knowledge];
the relationship between the illustration and the illustrated exists merely through a partial correspondence, like that between a lamp and its light.
But knowledge is not distinct from the object of knowledge like a lamp; thus he says:
"Knowledge, O lady of excellent vows, is declared to be the defining characteristic of the reality that is the object of knowledge. (4.337)
Nor is the supreme reality indicated by knowledge in the same way that a student is identified by his water-pot; thus he says:
"The characteristic is declared to be a quality...
For a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is indeed a unique property (*dharma*) that establishes the true nature of a thing.
Therefore,
that— namely, *kalā*— always gives and cuts for the *tattva*, that is, for Paramaśiva who is to be recognized as the *tattva*. It gives everything and it cuts [everything].

By way of etymological derivation, the defining characteristic is indeed the power (*śakti*) known as autonomy (*svātantrya*), which effects the creation and withdrawal of the universe and is eternally inseparable from [the Lord]. And it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
"Just as by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun..."
"Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known, so too, O Dear One, Śiva is resorted to by means of His power. (Vijñānabhairava).
In such a manner, by way of its essential power:
there is no reality (tattva) without the quality (guṇa), and no quality without reality. (4.338)
The meaning is the eternal state of non-dual union between Śiva and Śakti.
Even so—everywhere they grasp the qualities (*guṇa*), but the reality (*tattva*) is not grasped anywhere.
It is specifically through the medium of attributes (*dharma-mukhena*) that Śiva, whose essence is Paramaśiva, manifests as the possessor of attributes (*dharmī*). In him—
Because in the state of universal fullness (*viśvanirbhara*), it is impossible to enter [into that state] by itself without the means of power (*śaktyupāya*).
And this is logical, as he says: "For it is apprehended both by inference and by direct perceptual experience. (4.339)
Furthermore, through the relationship of proponent and opponent,
it is established by scripture that the inference of a creator for the universe is indeed based on its being a specific arrangement;
this occurs primarily by way of [establishing] His omniscience and authorship, and there is also direct perception for yogins.
It occurs precisely through the medium of the power that has been described, as it was said:
"Then his innate nature, characterized by knowledge and agency,
[manifests]" (Svacchandatantra 10).
The seeker is the questioner, and the respondent is the speaker who cuts through doubt;

their relationship consists of the state of being the one to be favored and the one who favors. Through the scripture that proceeds from this [relationship], even though it takes the form of sound, that very reality is attained solely by way of its determined power.
He explains that scripture shares the same status as the aforementioned yogic perception:
"It has been stated that scripture is knowledge; [yet] there are infinite millions of treatises. (4.340)

It has been stated that the infinite millions of scriptures (*śāstra-koṭi*)—which is the scripture of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-āgama*)—is the knowledge whose form is the expansion of the supreme power (*para-śakti*). Because it causes one to go toward (*ā-gamayati*) and, by means of non-duality, to contemplate (*vimṛśati*) the essential nature of the Supreme Lord from all sides (*ā-samantāt*), the supreme power itself is the scripture; that which expounds it, however, [is the scripture].
The composition of words [constitutes the treatise], because it is the means for that [attainment]. || 340 ||
How is it that the scripture has the nature of the supreme power? He says:
"The entire scripture consists of sound; sound is proclaimed to be the *haṃsa*.
Whatever is a teaching anywhere, because it instructs, that is scripture, and it consists of sound."

The true essence of the collection of sounds consisting of the fifty phonemes is the mass of sound (*śabdarāśi*); the mass of sound is essentially the upward movement of *haṃsa*; and the upward movement of *haṃsa* has as its core the expansion of the experience of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*).
He states that this has been determined:
"The Haṃsa-yoga was previously explained...

because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have the power (*śakti*) as their object, that which possesses the power (*śaktimat*), the true form [of reality], is indeed beyond the reach of measurement (*aprameya*)."
It is rightly said that "they grasp the quality everywhere"; this is the connection [of the text],
beginning with "one should pierce with the spear of knowledge" (4.335) and continuing with "one should pierce with the spear of mantra" (4.357).
Thus he will demonstrate. Therefore, he provides a preliminary outline (sūtra) in order to explain the true nature of consciousness at the time of uttering the phonemes and mantras,
as well as the relationship between the signified deity and the signifying phoneme,
and the dimensions of the heart and other locations which serve as the abodes of those deities who are signified.
Now, the enumeration of the measures (mātrās) is being stated.

The application of measure (*mātrā-yoga*) and its extent within the heart and other centers is as follows: "measure" (*mātrā*) refers to the duration of the pronunciation of phonemes such as *a* and so forth; "of this" (*asya*) refers to the differentiator, namely the utterance of the *haṃsa*, which consists of the recitation of mantras; [it describes] how its application is by means of measures, and likewise the locations of that utterance.
The meaning is that all the measurements of the *hṛdāni* (heart-lotuses) are now being stated.
Regarding that, he first states the measurement:
"Above the navel, at a distance of one span (*vitasti*), and below the throat, at six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). (4-342)
The heart is located in the middle region, measuring four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula).

At its end is a span (vitasti) of twelve finger-breadths; at the limit of two regions, six finger-breadths below the throat, in that middle portion, lies the heart-knot (hṛd-granthi), which is four finger-breadths in size.
The connection.
Regarding this, he states the presiding deity: "Brahmā is established there by means of the twenty-four principles. (4.343)
The third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*); the meaning is that Brahmā is situated here, presiding over the end of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Above that—
know the throat to be eight finger-breadths; Viṣṇu is established there,
conjoined with the six principles (tattvas).
From the Puruṣa up to the end of Kalā.
