And four finger-breadths above that. (4.344)
And there—
relying upon the principle of Māyā (māyātattva), Rudra resides at the base of the palate;
above that—
The space between the eyebrows is declared to be the measure of two finger-breadths.
There, O Goddess, Īśvara is situated, endowed with two principles (*tattva*). The two principles are those called Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara.
From that also—
And thus, at eleven finger-breadths above, is the Lord Sadāśiva.
Endowed with the two principles (tattvas), he has gone as far as the aperture of Brahma;
that is, he is joined with the principles of Sadāśiva and Śakti. By speaking thus, he teaches that the venerable Sadāśiva is the presiding deity from the Half-moon up to the end of Nāda.

However, according to the systematic arrangement of the principles (*tattva*), this pervasion by the deities named Īśvara and Sadāśiva is entirely distinct from the pervasion of the principles themselves— according to the method to be explained later— where the principle of Īśvara extends up to *nādānta* and the principle of Sadāśiva extends up to the end of *nirodhya*.
One finger-breadth above that is the Śakti;
the meaning is that the Śakti is located at the site of the knot (granthi). Śiva is established there. (4-347)
The one called Anāśrita (the Unsupported). || 347 ||
And right here, within the finger-breadth (aṅgula)—when only the skin remains—it is said that Vyāpinī and Samanā [reside].
The meaning is that she too, as the ground (bhū), is presided over by Śiva alone. [These are] those known as Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.

The meaning is that the levels of the Śiva-principle (śivatattva-bhūmayaḥ) are presided over by the cause named Śiva. And speaking thus, that which is the location within the *muṇḍa* at ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) when measured from the feet externally, is precisely what is here designated as the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) by way of internal pervasion, extending to that same limit of the *hā* [the letter *ha*].
This implies that [the division] is by way of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Elsewhere,

it is said that the external measurement extends up to one hundred and eight finger-breadths, reaching as far as the upward-moving streak of smoke (*dhūmalekhā*) seen externally, starting from the *muṇḍa* (the cranial aperture).

Regarding "the state of being without obscuration" (*nirāvaraṇatā*), although there are two ways of presenting this, there is no discrepancy whatsoever regarding the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); for the entire series of rungs of the ladder of objects of knowledge, beginning with the *bindu* and ending with *samanā*, is described as being identical in their respective positions throughout.
Having thus explained the measure of the six locations which serve as the basis for the six causes, he states that the seventh state, which is beyond all measure, is presided over by Paramaśiva:
".........thereafter Unmanā."
But that which follows is the supreme reality, which is devoid of all means of valid cognition.
Now, the number of *mātrās* and the *yoga* pertaining to the Haṃsa are being described as auxiliary to the differentiation of its constituent elements.
The term "of the Haṃsa" refers to that which is non-different from it—the partless (*niṣkala*) reality. Even though—
"The enumeration of the measures (*mātrā*) and how their application is for him has already been indicated [in verse 4.342];
nevertheless,
that which is now being determined follows after having stated the measurements of the heart and other centers presided over by Brahmā and the other causal deities."

That is indeed appropriate; for it is precisely through the sequence of resorting to the locus (sthāna) that the differentiation of word-meanings occurs, consisting in the experience of the pervasion of the deity to be expressed, by means of resting upon the phonemes (varṇa), the artistic modulations (kalā), and the time (kāla) which are expressive.
In that regard:
"The letter *a* and the letter *ha*—these two stand as one. (4.349)
There is no distinction between these two, just as there is none between wind and space.
The letter *A* consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the supreme power, and the letter *Ha* has the nature of the Śāmbhava reflective awareness;
and because Śiva and Śakti are non-different, these two abide as one in a single place like ether and air, pervading the entire universe.
This is because the vowel-less *ha*-kāra, when uttered by itself, enters into the *ā*-kalā, which takes the form of a horizontal line at its head.
It should be known as having a single measure; it proceeds forth from the heart.

That letter *ha*, when joined with the vowel *a* (forming *ha*), is thus [manifested]; however, in its isolated state, because it cannot be articulated, it is indeed devoid of temporal duration (*akālakalita*). || 350 ||
The vowel *ū* indeed has two morae and should be articulated in the throat;
the syllable *m*, however, has three morae and should be articulated in the middle of the palate. (4.351)
The state of having three measures (trimātratva) occurs within the syllables and tones of a song, like the utterance of a word that is empty of syllables. || 351 ||
Having described the division of measures (mātrā) through the method of protracted pronunciation in its gross state, he speaks also of its subtle state:
"The bindu is indeed half a measure... [it] has the form of the pronunciation of the anusvāra."
He asks "Why? and says:
"For that is said to be half a *mātrā*.
By the reasoning to be stated, for the yogi whose knots have been severed, its utterance becomes precisely half a *mātrā*."
He states its location: "O Goddess, that utterance is prescribed by him to be in the middle of the eyebrows. (4.352)
By yogis whose knots have been severed. || 352 ||
Then, from that very [sound] whose nature consists of the resonance of dissolving divisions, there arises a form of reverberation (anunirhrāda)—
and from its remainder comes the half-moon (ardhacandra), which shall consist of one quarter-measure (pādamātra).
This is understood to mean "from the measure" (mātrāyāḥ).
The *nirodhin* consists of half a foot;
this very *ardhacandra* is one part of the *nirodhin* mantra. One should utter it at the end of the forehead. (4-353)
The meaning is that two [syllables] are uttered within the two internal [parts], which consist of the forehead-tip and its further portion. || 353 ||
Beyond this—
nāda, which consists of sixteen parts, should rise as far as the crown of the head (mūrdhan).
Since the end of sound (nādānta) is essentially a mere extension of nāda, it is not mentioned separately.
From this point upward—the Śakti, consisting of thirty-two parts, shall emerge at the end of the thirty-six. (4.354)

That which consists of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) should be uttered at the end of its characteristic mark, by way of experiencing the mere touch of the division of perfect tranquility. Here, within this very [body], Śakti is at the end of the aperture of thirty-six finger-breadths; Vyāpinī is at the limit of the skin; and [Samanā] is in the region of the hair.
It brings together; this is stability. || 354 ||
The measurement of Śakti has been stated therein. Regarding Vyāpinī and Samanā, he says:
"Vyāpinī, consisting of sixty-four parts, is situated beyond Śakti;
and Samanā..."
It is indeed a sixty-fourth part; thus, these two sixty-fourth parts, when unified, become a thirty-second part.
That too, when joined with the thirty-second part consisting of Śakti, becomes a sixteenth part. That sixteenth part of Nāda, in turn, becomes an eighth part.
That which has arisen, being the fourth part together with the eighth part of the cessation,
is the *ardhacandra*; the other fourth part is the *bindu*, which is the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*)— this is the *mātrā* ending with the letter *ma*, and these are the six measures (*ṣanmātrā*).

This venerable Niṣkalanātha, who is the very essence of the supreme reality (amanāparatattva), encompasses the seven future goddesses along with their respective durations of seven mātrās; he is himself devoid of measure (amātra). As for that which is stated: "The Parārdha stands beyond [the previous count]..."
It has been stated: "O Goddess, that eighteenth [vowel], however, one should abandon at the end of Samanā" (4.285).

That [passage] is intended for the pacification of gross external time, which serves as the limit for the deity expressed by [the mantra]; this [present passage], however, is intended to indicate the extremely subtle time of pronunciation residing within the constituent parts of the mantra—thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Therefore, it has been established that by the very time of uttering the subtle phonemic units (*kalā*) of mantra, the lord of yogis should pacify even the most extensive path of the *kalās*— which might otherwise be conceived as spreading far and wide within the external reality— just as one splits the leaf of a banyan tree by splitting its seed-cup (*vaṭadhānikā*).

It occurs as follows: here, at the time of reflecting upon the components of the mantra, one should understand that there arises both the experience of each respective deity who is the signified object, and the assimilation of the experience of each lower level into the nature of the experience of each progressively higher state.
Even for the Samanā [state]...
[and] Unmanā is above, beyond measure, supreme, and imperishable. (4.355)

Accompanied by *unmanā*, he possesses supreme power; because he is devoid of expenditure (*vyaya*), he is "without measure" (*amātra*), meaning he is free from contact with time such as measures (*mātrā*) and half-measures (*ardhamātrā*). || 355 ||
He summarizes this as follows:
"The number of measures and the yoga have been fully described;
all of this [is now concluded]."
Having understood this, O lady of excellent limbs, one should then differentiate the categories of objects.
"O fair-limbed one," as before. || 356 ||
How?—
one should pierce [the object] with the spear of mantra, conjoined with the visualization of the mudrā,
and with the spear of mantra whose true nature is the previously determined spear of knowledge, together with the mudrā.

By means of the state (*bhāva*) consisting of the desire to know, the object of inquiry, and the resulting experience— which takes the form of the instrument (*karaṇa*) to be described hereafter— this triad, whose essence is the expansion of the powers of knowledge, action, and will, is therefore composed of those very powers. Thus, he reveals that the Guru, who is one with the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) consisting of these powers, should perform the act of differentiation (*bhedana*).
The mantra is indeed the power of knowledge, and the mudrā is essentially the power of action.
And "being" (bhāva) is said to be the mind; that mind is preceded by the intellect (*buddhi*).

Having determined that the mind is constant reflection and experience preceded by the intellect, one who has set out [on the path] attains those respective experiences. Furthermore, this differentiation is for the purpose of pervading the supreme reality.
And the pervasion of the supreme reality occurs through the full self-awareness that blossoms from the utterance of mantra within the bond of the instruments, of which the desire to know is primary—
thus he says:
And the subsequent [element] is accessible through the mind, being presided over by the power of will.

The meaning is that [the object] is first made the domain [of consciousness], presided over by the mind through self-awareness, by the power of will, and by the desire to know its ultimate reality. || 358 ||
And this is logical, because:
"Wherever there may be desire, knowledge proceeds there,
through the connection of action and instrument..."

The meaning is that through the proper binding (*samyag-bandha*)— that is, the yoga consisting of action, activity, the instrument, and the bodily configuration suitable for that activity— knowledge arises regarding the object sought to be known.
Thus, for the Guru who knows the immersion (āveśa) into Śiva, whose nature consists of the three powers, there occurs the utterance of the reality (tattva). || 4-359 ||
The mantra is the reality whose essence is vigor. || 359 ||
To demonstrate the emphasis on this very point, he states the contrast (vyatireka) which is implied by the sense:
"And for one devoid of the instruments of action, there can be no utterance at all;
therefore, for the sake of achieving the correct recitation of mantras, one must properly understand the distinction between actions according to the distinction of their instruments."
He begins to demonstrate this:
"And that very action is traditionally held to be threefold, according to the distinction of its instruments. (4.360)
Therein,
the wise one should utter the reality with a single instrument by means of the upward expulsion (*ūrdhvarecaka*).
Then, with the second [breath], one should block the channels and the gates.
Having performed the third divine practice by means of *kumbhaka*, one should indeed utter the *tattva*.
By that *kumbhaka*, having blocked the gates, one should utter the partless (*niṣkala*) *tattva* through the divine practice.
Having performed the *bandha*, one should recite the mantra with the upward exhalation (*ūrdhvarecaka*); this is the sequence here.
He begins to clarify that very point:
"Having performed inhalation and retention, one should block all the gates. (4.362)
Precisely at the occasion of the breath-retention (kumbhaka). || 362 ||
For those [channels],
being obstructed by the obstruction of the anus-gate, become blocked elsewhere;
and this obstruction should be effected through contraction and expansion by means of the power of immersion (āveśa).
Having done thus—one should then contemplate that single door flowing upwards. (4.363)
One should contemplate it in the form of the central channel, but one should not cause it to flow at this very moment. || 363 ||
For when that is so—
O Dear One, those channels and lotuses of the knots which are directed downwards become completely unblocked and blossom all around by means of the *kumbhaka* [retention of breath]. (4.364)

The heart and other centers are "knots" (*granthi*) because they are the abodes of the crookedness of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*). They are "lotuses" (*padma*) because their nature is to contract and expand. And these [lotuses] are downward-facing due to the flow of the downward-moving energy (*apāna-śakti*).
"Expanding" means they turn upward with their arms raised. || 364 ||
Thus, immediately after the *kumbhaka*, having performed the *karaṇa* [posture] thereafter...
and here [it says]: "Perform the utterance of the *tattva*" (4.367).
Thus, there is a connection with what precedes; meanwhile, the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is given in the middle.
Regarding that, he says:
"Listen indeed to its characteristic:
the tongue should be joined to the palate, slightly upward, without touching it. (4-365)
Having slightly opened the mouth, one should not touch the lips together; likewise, the rows of teeth should remain apart, and the gaze should be neither downward nor upward. (4.366)
Having held the body erect, it is called the divine posture (*divyāsana*).

Here, when the tongue is joined to the palate, its contraction is obtained by implication; [it follows that] one should not touch the lips at all. "In the same way" means that having extended [the arms], one should not touch them.
The avoidance of looking downward or upward is for the sake of abandoning conceptual construction by means of the steadiness of the pupils.
"Exalted" (*samunnata*) means properly elevated due to being unmodified. It is "divine" (*divya*) because it exists as a means for attaining supreme consciousness in the celestial realm (*divi*).
Therefore, in this manner—having made the divine instrument (karaṇa), perform the utterance of the reality (tattva). (4.367)
By the word "and" (ca), retention (kumbhaka) and upward exhalation (ūrdhvarecaka) are also included; the reality (tattva) is the root mantra. || 367 ||
Regarding this occasion for the divine ordeal, he says that one should also perform the upward *ūrdhvarecaka*:
"The breath which has been retained (*kumbhita*) should be exhaled very slowly;
[it should go] upwards, by implication."
For if that were so:
"The channels and the lotuses of the knots which are situated within the body... (4.368)
"Propelled by the exhaling breath (recaka), they become upward-streaming;
the meaning is that they attain the nature of the central channel (madhyavāha). And here, the emergence of horripilation is the sign of attainment.
Thus, one who is intent upon the binding of the three instruments (karaṇatraya-bandha)..."
Then, indeed, piercing the knots with the spear of knowledge, one should recite [the mantra] completely.

The "spear of knowledge" (*jñānaśūla*) has been previously determined. It is the piercing of the knots (*granthi*) at the locations of the heart and so forth, through the manifestation of the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*), whereby the attainment of those respective experiences occurs. One should utter it perfectly without conceptualization;
thus, it should spontaneously ascend upwards. This refers to the *mantra* by implication. (369)

In this context, he describes the distinction between the experience of determination regarding the cause previously stated— that for the yogin who is practicing through differentiation, there is the attainment of existence— by means of the following:
"But having pierced the knot of the heart-lotus, from that the sound is produced."
When, through union with space—
meaning through a correct and all-pervasive yoga consisting of one-pointedness in the pronunciation of the unstruck (*akala*) sound of the mantra and so forth— the "sound" (śabda),
whose nature consists of the internal subtle parts (*kalā*) such as the letter *a* and so on, is clearly heard in the form of a whispered utterance (*upāṃśu*).
And that [mind] would be like the sound of an echo. || 4-370 ||
"The sound that arises from the conjunction of the ear and the finger,
possessing the full resonance of a blazing fire— that is called *nāda*;
such is the *ghoṣa* characterized [in the verse], which belongs to the blazing fire."
The meaning is that a sound resembling the noise "dhaka-dhaka" is heard as it issues forth. || 370 ||
The sound residing in the throat should cease upon reaching the throat, O fair-faced one;
the meaning is that when the mantra, which is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), reaches the throat and becomes established therein, then the resonance (*ghoṣa*) should be stilled.
In that case, however—when [the vital point] in the region of the throat is pierced, a "dhug-dhug" sound is produced. (4.371)
The meaning is that it arises in the form of that [object]. || 371 ||
Thereafter— O lady of virtuous vows, when the vital breath reaches the center of the palate,
as it pierces the knot of the palate, a sound like *ghumaghum* arises. (4.372)

"Suvratā" means she whose vow (*vrata*) is auspicious, consisting of the discipline (*niyama*) of gazing upon the central abode (*madhyadhāman*); this is her address (*suvrate*). "Ghumaghumāyate" means that she utters an imitation of that [sound], namely the syllable *makāra*; such is the meaning. || 372 ||
Thus, by means of the piercing of the three knots, those experiences have been described to you as the vital breath moves, O lady of good vows;
they have their objects in the words that have been spoken.
These three are said to have eight kalās each, arranged one above the other in sequence.
In this eleventh chapter:
"O Goddess of Gods, that manifest sound is said to be eightfold:
resonance (ghoṣa), roar (rāva), tone (svana), sound (śabda), that which is called the explosion (sphoṭa), and indeed vibration (dhvani)."

By the statement, "The sounds *jhāṅkāra* and *dhvaṅkṛta*—these eight sounds are proclaimed," he will describe the eightfold nature of manifest sound (*vyakta-śabda*). The three [vowels] *a*, *u*, and *m* are manifest; thus, regarding their places of articulation:
Regarding the words whose objects are experienced through the breaking of the knots (*granthibheda*), they possess the eight qualities beginning with resonance (*ghoṣa*).
As for what was stated—that [the state] is "like resonance" (*ghoṣopama*)—it does not mean that it is of the same nature as resonance alone; rather, it means it is similar to resonance.
Even in that case, words such as *ṛ* and so forth certainly exist. || 373 ||
Thus it is:
wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) indeed remains, there the Self attains its state;
for consciousness rests upon the vital breath and reaches each respective location solely through its medium.
In that regard—its form becomes such and such, in accordance with the nature of its respective location. (4.374)
In the appropriate locations such as the heart and so forth, "existence" (bhāva) consists in the inclusion of their respective causes.

Thus, within the heart, throat, and palate— which are presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— the Self assumes the nature of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal according to the sequence of the vital breath's (prāṇa) abidings.
When [the breath] reaches the middle of the eyebrows, the sound *sphoṭa* arises.
Because it is the manifestation of the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*) which were previously unmanifest, this *sphoṭa* is like a soundless [utterance].
And this—
O Goddess, for one who pierces the *bindu*, a sound like "dhuma-dhuma" arises.

Regarding the term "bindu": for one who pierces the *bindu*-knot (*bindugranthi*), there arises an utterance resembling the sound "dhu-dhu," which consists of the awareness of the constituent parts of the mantra known as the *bindu-kalā*. This piercing of the *bindu*-knot is like the first step in ascending to the state of liberation (*apavarga*); therefore, yogis must apply themselves to this, for once it is pierced, [the path] has been transcended.
Thus, saṃsāra consists of differentiation. || 375 ||
Otherwise, however:
"O Dear One, how can there be liberation, both internal and external, for the monkey [the individual soul] together with the coconut [the body], when it is not distinct from the Bindu? (4.376)
The phrase "he resorts to" (*bhajate*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Here, the relationship between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) is obtained through the sense; thus, just as a monkey does not resort to liberation from a coconut that has not been split open—nor indeed does it resort to the coconut itself—[so too is the case here].

Without breaking it for the sake of tasting its flavor, he does not release it; likewise, the teacher, together with the unbroken *bindu*-knot—that is, along with the disciple to be initiated—why? Because, having made [the knot] both external and internal, he partakes in liberation from the external, which is the gross.

The meaning is that one is not liberated from the internal, subtle body consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* and the void-body (*śūnya-śarīra*), but one is indeed liberated through the piercing of the *bindu*. The explicit reading is: "By the coconut [fruit] of Kapi and likewise by the *bindu* of the Ācārya. (376)
And therefore:
"O Goddess, having pierced the *bindu*, one should then pierce the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
As the half-moon is being pierced, a *jhimijhima* sound resonates in the forehead. (4.377)

The meaning is that as one pierces the half-moon knot (*ardhacandragranthi*), right at that spot, a portion of the mantra called the "half-moon" (*ardhacandra*), which imitates the sound *jhi-mi-jhi-mi*, arises. In this same manner, the application [of the method] should be understood for what follows as well.
Then, having indeed pierced the half-moon, one should pierce the obstructing [channel];
as it is being pierced, its sound resounds like *simisima*.
Regarding the pervasion of the *kalās* in the *bindu* and so forth, as before, he says:
"O Goddess, these three locations are endowed with five *kalās* each;
therein, of the *bindu*..."
Beginning with, "Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti," [it continues] up to,
"To the left side of this is Śāntyatītā. (10.1217–1218)
Thus he will describe the pentad of *kalās*. Likewise, for the *ardhacandra*, [the sequence is]:
"Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, Vimalā, and Śivā" (10.1220);
and for the *nirodhinī* as well—
"Rundhanī, Rodhinī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā"— (10.1221)—

thus is the pentad of *kalās*. Regarding the "three locations," this is a classification based on the intention that the piercing of the subsequent knot occurs precisely through the piercing of the first knot.
The same applies hereafter.
Thus, in this manner— whichever place the vital breath (prāṇa) occupies as it moves there [in the body]— || 4-379 ||
The self (ātman) becomes of that very form and attains each respective state (gati).
"Therein" means while moving within those three locations presided over by the principle of Īśvara;
[this refers to] the vital breath (prāṇa), disregarding the moving breath and emphasizing consciousness (saṃvit) as the primary factor.

The meaning is that, having made the vital plane subordinate, in whatever place that qualified self resides, by experiencing the nature of each respective state, it attains identity with that very state.
Then,
having pierced through the *nirodhinī*, the wise one should proceed from there to the *nāda*.
A sound equal to the sound of a bamboo flute arises there subtly;
this subtlety is relative to what precedes it, and that is the principle of Īśvara.
From there as well—one should pierce the abode of nāda, the aperture of Brahmā, which is very difficult to subdue. (4.381)
As the *brahmarandhra* is being pierced, the sound becomes increasingly resonant (*śumaśumāyate*).

That which is the perfect locus of the *nāda* and its place of rest is the station of the *nāda* (*nādasaṃsthāna*), the *brahmarandhra*, which is exceedingly difficult to pierce; it is that very same station at the end of the *nāda*, the aperture of the upper door of the *brahmarandhra*.
It is very difficult to break; it can be broken only by those with extraordinary discernment.
Thus, having pierced the locus of sound and its end, presided over by Sadāśiva— the vital breath situated in the center of Śakti, resembling the resonance at the end of a bamboo flute— 4.382.
Due to the contact with a differentiation of power (śakti), it becomes like the end of the sound of a flute, but not due to a difference in the location of the power;
it becomes similar to that subtle resonance which constitutes the end of the flute's sound in the form of a sweet melody. || 382 ||
Then, one should indeed pierce that power (*śakti*), which is difficult for all yogins to pierce;
and when that power is pierced, then [the state of] Śānta is both auspicious and inauspicious.

And its state of being difficult to pierce is due to the fact that the bliss of experiencing it is so supremely desirable that it cannot be abandoned. Regarding the term "tranquil" (*śānta*): in other cases, the function of sound ceases simply from the impact of the place of articulation and the vocal organs; here, however, the meaning is that having become tranquil, it attains the nature of the touch of bliss.
Furthermore:
"O Goddess, having pierced through Śakti, that which remains thereafter becomes Vyāpinī;
there, the experience (anubhāva) occurs like the touch of an ant. (4.384)
Immediately after the division of the powers (*śakti*), that remaining entity which consists of the constituent parts of the mantra—that which is left over—would be the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*).

Because it pervades all the paths up to the end of the powers, that constituent part of the mantra is called the Pervasive One. The reading, however, is clearly: "In its remainder, there would be the Pervasive One."
And therein, experience takes the form of the manifestation of touch because it is pervaded by a tranquil sound;
the meaning is "like ants" (*pipīlikā*), as if of ants moving along. In the word *pipīlikā*, the elision of the vowel *ā* is due to the Lord (*īśvara*). || 384 ||
Regarding this as well, he states the division of the *kalās*:
"O Goddess, these three locations are endowed with five *kalās* each.
Among them, in the location of *nāda*, presided over by Śrī Sadāśiva..."
The five *kalās* to be mentioned [later]— namely, Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and likewise Ūrdhvagā— [reside] in the *śaktitattva* and in the station of Vyāpinī.
In the lineage presided over by Śrī Śivanātha, in due order:
Śūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Amitā, and Vyāpinī. (10.2142)
Thus there are five *kalās*:
"Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantānāthā, and Anāśritā" (10.1252).
We shall explain all of these in their own proper context.
Since this is so, therefore:
"Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) moves, it shall assume that very form. (4.385)

The meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the individual soul (*jīva*), attains various experiences. However, through the excellence of the practice of those experiences— wherever it may abide, it shall attain that very state.
The meaning is that one becomes the very self of each respective [state].
And thus:
"O fair-hipped lady, the infinite web of bonds extends up to the end of tranquility. (4.432)
Thus, all this which is about to be described—therefore, indeed, by means of great effort, having pierced through [the body], one goes to the supreme goal. (4.386)
Excellent effort consists in ascending the stream of divine instruments. || 386 ||
Regarding this, he states the sequence:
"O Goddess, having indeed pierced through Vyāpinī, one should abandon the mind in Samanā;
by abandoning the mind with the mind, the individual soul (jīva) attains isolation (kevalatā). (4.387)

"Manas" is non-conceptual consciousness (*cetas*). "By means of the mind" (*manasā*) refers to the state where the objects of thought—extending up to tactile sensation (*sparśa*)—have been exhausted; thus, by means of the mind itself, which consists solely of non-conceptual reflection, one abandons that very same mind through the intensification of one-pointedness, [abandoning] its own nature characterized by the contraction of the desire to grasp the appearance of an object of cognition.
The meaning is that, having stilled sensation, the living self (jīva) attains isolation (kevalatva); it becomes pure, consisting solely of the nature of a knower. || 387 ||

Thus, having concluded the discussion begun with the words, "And the differentiation of categories occurs by virtue of the attainment of their respective natures," he states the pervasion of the Self as it follows in sequence:
"In that [state], the individual soul (jīva) alone is endowed with the activity of self-knowledge."
Completely liberated from all bonds, his essential nature is pure existence alone.
Transcending all stages of the paths, being pure consciousness alone (śuddhavijñānakevala),
he perceives neither any other state nor even the supreme state whose nature is Śiva.
The Self is established within its own nature, liberated from both the higher and the lower.

That which is the individual soul (*jīva*), whose essence is vital breath (*prāṇana*), is situated there above *samāna*; for, having transcended every stage of the paths, it is therefore entirely free from the bondage consisting of the three impurities (*mala*).

Thus, liberated completely down to the very limit of latent impressions (vāsanā), the Self— which is by nature pure existence and whose essence is manifestation alone without any counter-correlate (apratiyogin) to objective phenomena— possesses its own appropriate powers of knowledge and action, and not those belonging to Paramaśiva.
He is endowed with and pervaded by the true nature of the state of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium), and not in the manner of liberation according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems.
Furthermore, he is "pure" because of his distinction from the *vijñānakevalas*, who still possess the *āṇavamala* while situated above *māyā*;
and he is "distinguished" because he makes the entire *adhvan* (path) an object of knowledge, and not otherwise.
By means of that very knowledge which takes the form of the object of the illusory person (māyāpuṃviṣaya),

[the soul] is alone and not even conjoined with an object of cognition as is the case with Mantras and Mantreśvaras; for this very reason, it does not assume the lower Śiva-nature consisting of Sadāśiva, nor the higher nature consisting of Paramaśiva.

It is a mass of pure, free, conscious bliss; therefore, this [individual soul], though liberated from the previously explained higher and lower forms and having abandoned the lower form, has not yet attained its supreme nature, but remains established within itself in the mere state of being a cognizer.
And indicating by way of conclusion that one should not yet be satisfied with this, he says, wishing to introduce another point:
"This is the pervasion of the Self; beyond this is the pervasion of Śiva. (4.390)
By virtue of the complete destruction of bondage, she is free from all temporal limitations (*upādhi*) of the three paths;
thus, she resides within *Samanā*, and is not that [nature] described by the Sāṃkhyas, Pātañjalas, and others.

For it is through the ascent to the state of *Unmanā* of this very Self that there occurs the pervasion by Śiva, which consists in the pervasion by the supreme reality that is a mass of consciousness and bliss.
"He is called the substratum of stains because of the complete pacification of all bonds, beginning with māyā and ending with *samanā*. (7.229).
According to this forthcoming principle, all those previously mentioned forms of the sacrifice (*adhvarūpa*) [are contained] within the expansion ending at *samanā*.
The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are the delimiters; even by means of them, [the Self] is devoid of the nature of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the cessation of all bonds,
even when there is the cessation of all bonds up to *Samanā* within the state of pure, isolated consciousness (*śuddhavijñānakevalatā*).

Because it is delimited by the state of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that cessation, it possesses limiting adjuncts (*sopādhitva*); however, the state of Supreme Śiva is indeed undelimited, being a dense mass of autonomous consciousness and bliss that transcends the universe while simultaneously comprising the universe.
Since such is the pervasion of Śiva, therefore: "By those who, without knowing the supreme reality, have merely imagined the state of being Śiva... (4.391).
Those who worship the self do not reach the supreme Śiva;
for by them— namely, the various proponents of the doctrine of the self such as the Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Lākulas, and others— the state of being Śiva has been imputed to the selves.

Although all [these systems] are of the single nature of Śiva due to their equality in infinite attributes such as pervasiveness, eternity, incorporeality, consciousness, and creatorship, some— by means of mere, irrational conceptualization—
assert that they possess a distinct form of Śiva; all of them are to be understood as worshippers of the Self whose pervasive nature has been explained.

In this non-dual Śaiva system, those such as the proponents of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta do not reach Supreme Śiva—whose nature has been explained—and do not become one with Him; for they remain established only in the lower state, so how could there even be a possibility for them to attain such a state? Moreover, all these [others] are merely worshippers of the individual self (ātman) according to the Śaiva view.

The locative case in the seventh position should be construed with the instrumental case in the third, according to the principle of *tantra* (elliptical extension), as in: "They go to Supreme Śiva by means of the knowledge taught in the non-dual Pārameśvara system. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛtyuñjaya*: "Those who say [it is not so] do not find anyone other than Supreme Śiva."
"Those who worship the self do not go to the supreme state in Śaivism" (Netratantra 8.30). For here they speak of another [deity] as Paramaśiva; they do not find Him alone, nor indeed—
The meaning is that they obtain [it] by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are able to establish it.
But all of them, colored by the reality of the Self, attain the realization of the reality of the Self. || 4-392 ||

Regarding the nature of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*): "reality" (*tattva*) here refers to the contraction (*saṅkoca*) consisting in the non-manifestation of identity with Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*).

Those who are colored by that [contraction]—namely, the Pāśupatas and others who take refuge in it—attain the state of the self's reality, which consists in being a *vijñānakevalin* (an isolated soul of pure consciousness), but they do not attain ultimate liberation (*tāttvikī mukti*).
"Because of not abandoning difference. || 392 ||

By one who desires to completely avoid the transmigratory existence of Śiva, the self must therefore be abandoned if one wishes for one's own Śiva-nature. Here, "self" refers to the state of being a liberated individual soul (*aṇu*), while "Śiva" refers to oneness with the supreme Śiva as manifested in liberation.
Thus, in this manner—one should abandon the principle of the self (ātmatattva) and apply it to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). (4.393)
The word "himself" (ātmānam) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 393 ||
"What is the knowledge (vidyā) here?"—to this he says:
"That, however, is to be known as Unmanā.
He explains that [as follows]:
..................the mind is called *saṅkalpa* (volition).
*Saṅkalpa* is knowledge arising sequentially; *unmana* (the state beyond mind) exists simultaneously. (4-394)

*Saṅkalpa* is intention; because it consists of the threading together (*sūtraṇa*) of the sequence of the universe that is to be willed, it is said to be "knowledge" (*jñāna*) by way of succession. *Unmana* is that state where the mind has transcended (*utkrānta*), gone beyond, and reached its highest excellence (*utkarṣa*).
"Simultaneously" (*yugapat*) refers to the beginningless and endless [process] of the threading together, manifestation, and creation of the universe.

For even though it is divided into hundreds of branches, it persists here as the self-nature of the manifestation of the power of absolute freedom, which is a mass of eternally arisen bliss. || 394 ||
Since such a state of *unmanā* is indeed knowledge, it is the power of *unmanā*;
therefore, she is the supreme *vidyā*.
She pervades the path beginning from the *ātmatattva*, which extends up to the limit of *māyā*, and continuing upward through the levels of *śuddhavidyā* and ending with the *śakti*.
Vidyā is indeed something other than the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva) and so forth.
Because there exists nothing else such as this;
for, by implication, it is through this alone that the entirety of the universe is encompassed.
Regarding this, it is said: "For in this state, one simultaneously attains the supreme qualities such as omniscience and the rest. (4.395)

Since the best of yogis simultaneously attains here, in *unmanā*, supreme qualities such as omniscience— which are of the nature of differentiation— this [state] is *parā-vidyā* (supreme knowledge), following the etymological meaning of the root *vidl* in the sense of "attainment.
Furthermore—

Because it brings about the realization that the nature of phenomena such as sensation is the supreme self, and because it leads to the relinquishing of what is not the supreme self, it is therefore called "knowledge" (vidyā). || 4-396 ||

The primordial reality (*svabhāva*) is beginningless, consisting of the power of absolute sovereignty; its "perception" (*vedanā*) is its investigation, and it is the cause for the awakening to—that is, the realization of—the Self’s state as the Supreme Self, which is the nature of Śiva. For this very reason, regarding that which is not the Supreme Self—that is, regarding what is other than that—this avoidance occurs.
Therefore, because it conforms to the meanings of the verbal roots "vida vicāraṇe" (to investigate) and "vida jñāne" (to know), this is called *vidyā* (knowledge). || 396 ||
And thus, abiding therein, one should manifest that supreme splendor which is the ultimate cause;
when that supreme splendor is manifested, one who abides therein attains the state of Śiva. || 397 ||

In that context—within the knowledge known as *unmanā*—one should manifest, i.e., unveil and recognize one's own self. "Luminosity" (*tejaḥ*) is the light of consciousness, the supreme cause which is utterly contracted and whose nature is that of Supreme Śiva;
therefore, one should attain the state of Śiva, meaning one should reach identity with it. || 397 ||

He establishes this by means of an illustration: "Just as a flame is seen in the sky when a fire is well-kindled, so indeed the Self, residing in the body and vital breath, merges into that state. (4.398)
By virtue of the appropriateness of the stages of body, mantra, vital breath, self, and Śiva,
the examples are wood, the fire-drill, fire, its flame, and the sky. Thus,
when the fire has become well-kindled and blazing through the method of rubbing the fire-drill, just as the flame [arises]—

Just as a flame, having consumed its fuel, is seen in the sky because it is perceived there as having attained the nature of that [sky] through dissolution; likewise, by the friction of the divine instruments and the fire-sticks of mantra, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body becomes intensely ignited and assumes the state of a forest fire—both internal and external. That which resides in the body...

The Self is said to be of the nature of pure, absolute consciousness, resembling a flame of fire; having burnt the entire wooden fuel of the body up to the level of *samanā*, it dissolves into that state, meaning it attains identity with the supreme Śiva who is free from all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). || 398 ||
By the reasoning thus stated, when [the disciple] has dissolved into the supreme reality,
the best of teachers should likewise maintain that very sense of identification;
just as in that state, so too should the identification with the supreme state— the full reflective awareness of "I"— be cultivated and embraced.
But this should not be understood as referring to the animal-like state of egoity regarding the body and so forth; for this very purpose, the word "supreme" (uttama) is used.
He clarifies that conceit:
"I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause. (4-399)
The meaning of this has already been established by the previous explanations. || 399 ||
And therefore:
"That soul of the bound creature (paśu), having become one with me in flavor (samarasī-gata), is merged within my vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus, within my vital breath, which consists of the pervasion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) as previously described," [it remains].
Having brought that [consciousness] into a state of equal flavor (samarasīkṛta) through the reasoning previously stated,
I unite it with the supreme Śiva by means of the yoga of the ritual action of mantra.

The mantra is partless; the instrument is divine; and the yoga of action consists of the blocking of the gates, the upward flow [of breath], the abandonment of the lower state, the piercing of the knots, and so forth. || 400 ||
And this does not hold by mere words;
rather— "He who thus knows it in its true essence as being like fire within the center of the body, is joined to the Supreme, just as [the flame] transcends the crest of the fire. (401)
He who, through the firm establishment of experience in reality, knows "thus" the non-difference from Śiva, burns away the fetters within the body— which is like fuel— like fire;
remaining in the form of pure, blazing, radiant light, he establishes the self of the disciple in the supreme Śiva.

When one joins [the breath] in this way, then one attains oneness. How? Just as a flame of fire, having gone upward with great intensity and dissolved into the sky, attains identity with it—so too [is it here]. || 401 ||
And therefore:
"O Goddess, when one is united with that supreme reality, endowed with qualities such as omniscience, one becomes the one Śiva, undivided from him in every respect. (402)
"Yukta" means yoga, which is oneness; as it has been said:
"They desire yoga to be oneness" (Māṇḍūkya-vivaraṇa 4.4).

The word "one" (*eka*) signifies non-differentiation, and by the phrase "from all," he suggests the reality of the doctrine of non-dual Śiva (*abhinna-śivavāda*). Here, omniscience and other such qualities should be understood as having non-duality as their essence, and not as pertaining to duality in the manner of mantras and the like. (402)
Regarding what he will state in the context of initiation into the threefold reality—
namely, "Having known [the disciple], one should unite him with the reality" (4.404)— he says that this very same principle should be understood there as well:
The three principles are known as supreme, as well as inferior when situated within the path;
they consist of the differentiation of categories and their conjunction through abandonment and experience.
Having understood all this as previously stated, one should apply oneself to reality (*tattva*).
This refers to the threefold reality that has been revealed— the supreme, which is the nature of Śiva beyond the *unmanā* state and the pure self—
and the other, which is gross and situated within the path (*adhvan*).
In the midst of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) concerning the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) within the reality (*tattva*) cultivated in the fifth chapter,
the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva— which pervades [the levels] from Māyā up to Sadāśiva and Śiva—
was previously determined even during the purification through expiation (*prāyaścitta-śuddhi*); this same [triad] is [now treated] in the initiation of the three principles (*trittattva-dīkṣā*).

The meaning is that, having understood the nature of the *pradhāna*, as well as the previously mentioned piercing (*bhedana*) and so forth—and by the use of "and" (*ca*), the movement (*cāra*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—one should unite the disciple with the supreme reality primarily through this very knowledge. And it should be understood that this also pertains to other types of initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 403 ||
Now, while determining the nature of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) here,

[the author] speaks in order to indicate, as a secondary point (*prasaṅgena*), the initiation into the single reality (*ekatattvadīkṣā*), even though it was not included among the fourfold types of initiation into reality that will follow:
But listen briefly, O Goddess of the Gods, to the pervasiveness of reality.
O Sovereign, you who are the form of the power of supreme autonomy, the cause of the gods beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śiva. || 404 ||

Having bound himself to the locus of the principle of Vidyā and remaining seated upon the throne of the principle of Bindu, he possesses the body of Nāda and Śakti and is endowed with the pervasive operation (vyāpinī-karaṇa). || 405 ||

Having established a firm station— meaning a state of abiding— within the principle of *vidyā*, namely within *śuddhavidyā*, by means of the expansion of the center attained through the support of the aforementioned instruments; and furthermore, having established a station within the principle of *mātṛkā-vidyā* or within the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Being attentive to its utterance, one stands— that is, ascends— upon the *āsana*, which is the principle of the *bindu* (the point), whose nature is light in which the object of knowledge is non-differentiated, and which is the locus where the entire universe comes to rest; meanwhile, the *nāda* (the resonance), whose nature is pure self-reflection (*vimarśa*), consists of the experience of bliss.

The teacher whose body extends to the end of power (śaktyanta), and whose internal instrument—the means of perception—is pervasive, extending through the path to the end of power, having known everything, should establish [the disciple] in reality; this is the connection with what was stated previously. || 405 ||
The meaning is that she who is the pervasive form of his instrument— Samanā, which is characterized by the awakening to omniscience— is indeed that very [power].
"But she moves within";
the meaning is that she alone is its internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Thus, upon such a seat of reality (tattvāsana), this body—both its internal and external instruments—is filled by that which is declared to be the supreme triad of principles (tritattva). || 4-406 ||
The meaning is: by means of that which consists of the three supreme powers (parā-ādi-śakti-traya), as if it were one's own self. || 406 ||

And because these three principles (tattvas) transcend the path—existing beyond the limit of Samanā—they are the Supreme Principle (para-tattva). However, that which consists of the pervasion of Māyā, Sadāśiva, and Śiva is the Non-supreme (apara), because it lies within the path;
for this very reason, [the universe] from Earth onwards is [governed] by the other triad of principles beginning with Ātman.
Because that which ends with Śiva has been internalized,
the gross body (*tanu*) initiated by it— the *aparā*— is composed of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). This one, however—
And that which is the supreme triad of principles, which encompasses all the paths of the principles.
And by that, her body— which is intent upon the path of reality (tattvādhvan)— is filled without remainder.

Having made complete by means of the true nature of those three principles beginning with the pure self (śuddhātman), which transcend the entire path, it is pervaded by the manifestation of the state of being the Self of all.
That body which has proceeded forth, consisting of the power of sound (nāda), is superior—that is, more excellent—than the path of the principles (tattvādhvan). || 407 ||
Thus, he states that only one who consists of such reflective awareness of non-difference from Śiva is a teacher in the true sense:
"But he who practices in this way the conduct whose essence is Śiva... (4.408).

Because he moves in conjunction with Śiva, he is called the Ācārya (Teacher). "Conduct" (ācāra) is said to be the entry into the expansion [of consciousness], and "conjunction" (sahacāritva) is the ultimate reality of the non-dual reflective awareness of that. 408.
He states its greatness:
"From seeing him, conversing with him, touching him, or even from remembering him... (4.409).
The pervasion of Īśvara certainly occurs; there can be no downward movement from that state.

Since his instruments (karaṇas) consist of the pervasions of Vyāpinī and Samanā as previously described, therefore, through association with them, the pervasion of the Lord—the Śiva-tattva—certainly occurs at the end of the body, and not otherwise.

From Śiva downward, there is never any activity whatsoever. Even he who beholds Him in His true form with devotion becomes like that; therefore, the genitive case is used for both the agent and the object [in the phrase] "of him" (tena tasya). || 409 ||
But the person who is united with [the Guru] by virtue of the descent of the unsurpassed *śakti*— even a slayer of a Brahmin shall become Śiva. (4.410)
It is indeed Paramaśiva himself. || 410 ||
Thus it is:
consequently, there is no one equal to him in this world of the moving and the unmoving. Who is equal to that teacher, whose very self is Śiva? For he is one with Him.
And therefore:
Śiva, in the form of the Ācārya, effects grace for the worlds. (4.411)
For Paramaśiva, intent on bestowing grace, assumes the body of a teacher and severs the bonds of bound souls.

Since this is so—therefore, one should not entertain a sense of pride toward the teacher (*deśaka*). One who imparts instruction is a "teacher" (*deśaka*), that is, an instructor; toward him, one should not harbor a mind of arrogance due to wickedness.
The meaning is that one should cause him who is acting [wrongly] to desist.
For even those who dwell above Māyā, beginning with the venerable Lord Ananta and the rest—they too [are subordinate] to the Teacher, the Mantra, Śiva-knowledge, and Śiva himself. (4.412)

The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), who are the leaders of the wheel (Cakranāyakas)— that is, the leaders and masters of the wheel which is the group of mantras, and the revealers of one's own true nature— are not at all differentiated [in their function] within the supreme teaching of Śiva-knowledge; for in this scripture, the mantra of the Teacher, the instructor, is expressive of Śiva himself.

They do not create a distinction between the partless [Śiva] and so forth, and Śiva who is denoted by them; the meaning is that they do not perceive this as separate, because through the teacher alone there is the realization of Śiva, the scripture, the mantra, and Śiva.
And since even the Vidyeśvaras consider such non-duality in this way, how then could those favored by them [perceive otherwise]?

The cognition of difference must be brought about. And thus, those who perceive the mantras of Ācārya Śiva as non-different from Him are the Vidyeśvaras; they enter precisely into the expansion of the Mantreśvaras. || 412 ||
And this is logical, because:
"O you who are honored by heroes, there are indeed Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (4.413)
All those who are appointed to the office of teacher are remembered as Śivas;
indeed, only a Śiva-ācārya is a fit teacher. || 413 ||
"But those who do not regard the Teacher in this way are subject to transgression"—thus he says:
"Otherwise, those lowest of men who perceive [him] according to his former nature... (414).
They are cooked in hell for three years known as Sādākhya,
because even those who have received initiation fall into a state of inferiority due to hatred toward their guru and being tainted by the power of dissolution (vilaya-śakti).
The measurement of the year Sādākhya will be explained in the eleventh chapter.
"Even association with a sinner leads to sin"—thus he says: "But those who seek the welfare of Śiva must not engage in conversation with him. (4.415)
Having engaged in conversation with him, he too goes to hell.
Since this is so—therefore, all should be viewed as equal to Śiva by one who desires liberation. (4.416)
Because,
by his command alone, the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation surely occurs;
and such is his power that he—
The teacher [destroys] thousands of family lineages of his own kinsmen. (4.417)
Through the thorough knowledge of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, he will deliver all [beings]. His own people— those connected to him through learning, namely his disciples— and,
by the word "and" (*ca*), himself, [will deliver] thousands of family lineages (*kulakoṭi*) of knowledge.
Thus, preceded by the intention to bestow grace upon those to be graced,

[there occurs] the thorough and universal attainment— both non-conceptual and conceptual— of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), which is the object of knowledge to be adopted and which takes the form of a means for entering into the expansion of the supreme power (*paraśakti*).

Through knowledge that consists in resting in the supreme reality and which extends through infinite time by way of the succession of disciples, grand-disciples, and so forth, he will cause [others] to cross over—
that is, he will rescue them from— the ocean of saṃsāra. Indeed, the thorough comprehension of both knowledge and the object of knowledge is the primary form of the Guru.
As was stated previously: "Expert in knowledge and the object of knowledge" (1.13). || 417 ||
Concluding this, he states the subject at hand: "Thus, the teacher who knows the aforementioned method and also knows the nature of reality... (4.418).
By means of that single *pūrṇāhuti* alone, he unites the bound souls (*paśu*) with the Supreme.
The procedure for the movement of the vital breaths and so forth has been explained; "state" (*bhāva*) consists of the contemplation of the supreme reality.
Desiring to know the procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti*, Devala replied:
"I shall now describe to you the procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti*. (4.419)
He states the application of the oblation for the sake of fulfillment:
With the upper body erect and the neck straight, standing with feet even, the base of the *sruva* ladle is placed at the level of the navel, its tip facing upward and held level. (4.420)
O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* spoon upon the *sruc* ladle with its bowl facing downwards,
and having offered a flower at the tip of the *sruc*, one should join both hands together with a *darbha* blade.
Having grasped it with effort using both hands as if with a fist,
O beloved, the right hand should be in front and the left hand indeed behind.
Having grasped [the vessel] with both hands using the upward-facing hand-position,
one should then douse it with ghee and perform the consecration of self-conceit (abhimāna).
I alone am the supreme reality through the division of the higher and the lower.

My upper body is raised; my face is situated with its opening upward, like a lotus on a pedestal, and it remains level and straight. Upon the *sruc* [ladle] is the *sruva* [smaller ladle], representing the pervaders Śiva and Śakti.

Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles facing each other, for that very reason flowers are offered; and thus, one should contemplate that the disciple’s power, having abandoned its downward flow, is turned toward Śiva and consumed by the face-to-face Śiva. In the phrase "the two hands," the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

By means of the fists formed respectively by the right and left hands positioned above and below; for this very reason, the expression "by the two fists" is used. "With effort" means without pride. "In front" is said in relation to the left [hand] located at the base of the *sruva* ladle. "The right" refers to...

With the right hand facing downward like a *sruva* ladle through the pervasion of Śiva, and the left hand facing upward like a *sruc* spoon through the pervasion of Śakti; as it is said: "The union which is with the upturned hand" implies that the right hand is downward-facing while the left is [upward-facing]. "Having sprinkled" means having caused the *sruc* to be filled completely.

One should cause [the disciple] to form the conviction—that is, to achieve a certain realization—[that] "I alone am the supreme reality," which exists as the supreme, the intermediate, and the inferior, as previously described, in the form of the supreme, the subtle, and the gross. || 423 ||
And this is not mere conceit, because:
"For the Reality is indeed one everywhere...
for everything that is an object of cognition has as its ultimate reality nothing but consciousness alone."
And therefore:
"One should not cause another state of being to arise. (4.424)

"One should cause [it] to be done" is as before; the meaning is that one should abandon the conceit of duality, which is easily obtained through the state of being an illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛtā). || 424 ||
Furthermore:
O fair-faced one, that sixfold path which has been deposited here in the jar, within the mandala, in the fire, and inside the disciple, is conceived as common [to all]. (4.425)
Having placed that path within the *sruc*— situated in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and located in the midst of the channels (*nāḍī*)—
and having balanced it upon the flow of the breath, one should discharge the stream by means of the *sruc*.
Having projected the sixfold path— residing in the pitcher (kumbha), the maṇḍala, fire, and the child (śiśu)— into the sacrificial ladle in the form of clarified butter,

which serves as a reflection of the central channel (madhyamā nāḍī), and having likewise established that [path] within the breath according to the previously mentioned method so that it resides in the central channel, one should [offer] that very central breath as a stream.

Having equalized the ghee associated with the *sruc* ladle and having meditated upon it as being the essence of the six sacrificial paths melted by the fire of the mantra, he asks: "How and where should one cast that stream?"— and answers as follows:
By means of the *vasudhārā-prayoga*, one should cast [the offering] into the fire;

that is to say, with an uninterrupted continuity, one should offer the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the stream of clarified butter (*ājya-dhārā*) into the auspicious fire located at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), both internally and externally, through the contemplation of non-differentiation.
By means of the application of a very high stream for the sake of Vasu, who grants desired fruits.
Regarding this, he states the procedure:
"One should lead the base of the *sruk* ladle to the region of the navel, reaching as far as the tip of the nose. (4.427)
In whatever manner one should release the stream [of breath], in that same manner one should exhale the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One should cause that which is situated at the base of the sacrificial ladle in the region of the navel to reach the tip of the nose;
by means of the properly practiced movement of the central breath (*madhyaprāṇa*), it should be directed upward in accordance with the descent of the stream.
One should move it; one should cause it to rest at the *dvādaśānta*. || 427 ||
This being so, not only does the stream consisting of the sixfold path flow rapidly, but even the vital breath (prāṇa) attains the state of phonemes, for it consists of the sixfold path. || 4.428 ||
That vital breath (prāṇa) which consists of the six paths also attains the state of phonemes (varṇatā), that is, the state of reflective awareness of mantra. || 428 ||
And this being the case:
"In the sixfold path, there exists no object of knowledge (*prameya*) other than this;
whatever object of knowledge exists within the sixfold path, it is [included] in this context. The word "from this" (*ataḥ*) refers to the Mantra [tradition].

Because of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). There is nothing else anywhere; for in all cases, such as waking and so forth, everything is rendered residual within the reflective awareness of mantra.
Since this is so—therefore, in the contemplation of the mantra, [beings] remain fixed in terms of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. (4-429)
Those categories of reality that exist as things to be abandoned, ending with Samanā, and those that exist as things to be accepted—
namely the Pure Self, Unmanā, and Supreme Śiva— reside within the mantra itself as its denotator, because the denoted is non-different from it. || 429 ||

Since the previously mentioned group of six causes, which consists of the presiding deities of their respective *tattvas*, is pervaded by the mantras in the form of sounds beginning with 'a'— that is, by the phonemes (*varṇas*)— it is therefore [known] precisely through that pervasion.
The entire universe has been taken possession of by these.
And therefore—.................. dissolution occurs in the seventh through the abandonment of six; "it should be performed" is the ellipsis.
He shows that the group of six causes, which extends as far as it is pervaded by so many mantra-sounds, is to be abandoned:
"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu* itself. (4.430)
The Half-moon, the Obstructress, the Sound, and the Upward-moving; then the Power, the Pervasive One, and beyond that, the Equal One (Samanā). (4.431)
O lady of excellent limbs, the infinite web of bonds,
which is characterized by that which is to be abandoned, resides within the mantra and is pervaded by the six causes up to the limit of the Samanā.

This has already been explained previously. The state of the end of *nāda* is upward-moving. Regarding this elevenfold object of knowledge (*prameya*) belonging to the mantra, its nature as consisting of conceptual differentiation (*bhedakalpanā*) makes it something to be abandoned, whereas its nature as the self of non-dual awareness (*abhedavimarśa*) makes it something to be accepted; this has indeed been distinguished earlier. || 432 ||
Having stated what is to be abandoned regarding that which resides in the mantra, he introduces what is to be accepted:
"Here, above the fetters (pāśa), the Self is like the sky—[pure] consciousness—stainless; through the fragrance of the qualities of the Śiva-principle, it beholds the attributes of Śiva. (4.433)

Immediately upon transcending the bonds that limit one's identity, consciousness becomes perfectly stainless, arising from the joy produced by the desired qualities— such as non-duality and omniscience— belonging to Sadāśiva, who is of the nature of Śiva.
Out of sheer joy alone, one perceives the fivefold sovereignty of Śiva’s activity as something yet to be attained, rather than having already attained that very nature. || 433 ||
For:
"Indeed, that which consists in abandoning the observation of fetters and observing one's own true nature—
this is the pervasion of the Self."
The observation of the bonds ending with *samanā* as one's own self is the conceit of identity;
its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is pure consciousness transcending the bonds, which is the pervasion of the Self up to this limit.
...is the pervasion by Śiva; otherwise, it is different. || 4-434 ||
He explains that [attainment]:

"When one meditates upon those objects which are all-pervasive, such as the qualities of omniscience and so forth, this pervasion by Śiva occurs within consciousness, taking the form of its cause. (4.435)

When one meditates within oneself upon those qualities (*dharmas*)— namely, omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth— which are to be described hereafter, which are "objects" (*arthas*) because they are sought as the supreme goal to be attained, and which are "pervasive" (*vyāpakas*) insofar as they encompass everything without exception through their internal subdivisions; at that time:

The perfection of that cultivation is the pervasion of the Self by Śiva. And that [perfection] exists in the conscious subject as the causal and instrumental factor, for it is solely through its grace that the cultivation of that [state] takes root in the pure Self. (435)
Since he is thus endowed with qualities such as omniscience,
Śiva is therefore recited as being both the nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*) and tranquil;
because the universe manifests as if fixed to a wall, he is the "imagined substrate" (*dharmin-kalpa*) of that which is imagined as a phenomenon (*dharma-kalpa*).

It is "peaceful" (śānta) because all distinctions have ceased without remainder; it is "auspicious" (śiva) because it is the nature of the supreme good through its union with non-duality, omniscience, and so forth; thus it is recited in the scriptures.
Even though it is recited in this way, he says that in reality it is not within the scope of words:
"And the Transmental (unmanā) is graspable by the mind...
Because the Transmental consists in non-difference from Śakti, it lacks the status of being an object; therefore, in reality, it is not expressible by words.
This is the meaning. Not only is Śiva such, but furthermore—[he is] one whose mind has transcended (unmanā) while abiding in self-awareness. || 4.436 ||

Like Śiva, the Self also, having transcended the mind and abandoned the plane of the mind, abides in awakening—which is pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra) and whose nature consists of fullness, omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. The compound [unmanā] is to be understood as "one who is thus abiding and is beyond the mind" (unmanāḥ). || 436 ||
Since both the self and Śiva are not within the range of the mind, therefore—having abandoned mental activity—one should unite [the self] with the nature of pure consciousness.
Then, the bound soul attains the state of Śiva and is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. (4.437)

"Because of the realization of identity through the form of that [supreme] consciousness" (Spandakārikā 2.3). Thus, according to the perspective of the *Spanda*, having first made the disciple’s self one in flavor with one's own self,
and having transcended up to the level of *Samanā* and established a firm state in the pure Self, [one acts] "in the form of consciousness."
By the very touch of non-conceptual consciousness, one should unite [the self] with Śiva, beginning with the entry into the power of supreme mentation (praunmanāśakti).
And at this juncture:
"Furthermore, for one who is engaged [in the rite], he should fill the *sruva* ladle again;
that substance is offered into the fire through the cavity of the *sruk* until it is exhausted. (4.438)
One should contemplate the external *kumbhaka* within the supreme reality;
"external" here refers to the end of the upward *recaka*, namely the *dvādaśānta*.
And thus,
that which is the state of aesthetic identity with Śiva through the condition of external cessation— || 4-439 ||
And from the word, by its power as well. || 439 ||
"Otherwise it would not be so, O Goddess"—
the meaning is that this can never be a cause for becoming inauspicious.
Here is an illustration:
like the force of a river [entering] the ocean.
This is clarified as follows:
If he were to stand upon the waters of the ocean, the sea would become as level as a sacrificial altar.
Likewise, the Self does not undergo further division in the ocean of Śiva;
"with waters" refers to those joined with the ocean, and *sindhu* means a river.
He states the limit for the meditation on the external kumbhaka:
"One should prescribe [the duration] for as long as it takes to fill the sacrificial ladle (sruca). (4.441)

From the *sruk* ladle, with clarified butter until it is full—meaning, as long as the *pūrṇāhuti* (full oblation) occurs in the fire—one should direct or cause the *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) to reach (*samantād diśet*) or pervade the outside. || 441 ||
Thus, in the *pūrṇāhuti*:
"By this very time, through the external practice of *kumbhaka*, the all-pervading Self becomes Śiva by virtue of its state of essential identity (*samarasatva*). (4.442)
Thus, immediately after the disciple has been made into Śiva,
one should subsequently bestow the six qualities—
namely, omniscience and the others that will be described hereafter.

Of what kind? ... "having the number of limbs as their measure. By "limbs" (aṅgaiḥ), it is meant by the primary mantras (naikalaiḥ) which are themselves the limb-mantras (aṅgamantraiḥ); thus, "having the number of limbs as their measure" means having a count equal to that of the limbs.
Those for whom there are exactly six oblations.
Although all the qualities (guṇas) are attained when Śiva-hood is attained because they are non-different from Him, nevertheless,
they must be made manifest by means of the arousal of His own resonance preceded by a clear reflective awareness;
this he demonstrates by way of an illustration:
Just as when one has attained the status of a king, one is consecrated with water-pitchers.
And those virtues of his are proclaimed by bards upon the surface of the earth;
likewise, once the state of Śiva has been attained, the wise man should bring forth virtues.

Regarding the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) in the case of the illustrated [subject], he will state: "Then one should bestow the consecration" (4.448). The limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) are equal to the salutation.
He states the ritual application for the attainment of qualities:
"Become indeed omniscient, Svāhā! And likewise, become completely satisfied; become one whose awakening is beginningless, and thereafter, one possessed of the power of sovereignty. (4.445)
Likewise, [He is] one whose power is undiminished and who possesses infinite power;
furthermore, in this context, the six mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra, preceded by the *praṇava*, should first be applied in their proper order.
Even Kapila and others are omniscient.

Some, however, lack satisfaction in the form of the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) because they consist of mere consciousness devoid of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa-cinmātra*). Others, although endowed with the power of bliss, have attained that state through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), but they do not possess primordial awakening (*anādibodha*). In the case of the candidate for initiation (*dīkṣya*), however, the state of primordial awakening already exists and is merely manifested by this [initiation].

But nothing new is produced. However, some maintain that even though Brahmā and others possess primordial awakening due to their eternal omniscience, they are devoid of independence because they lack the power of emanation; for although they are independent in acts such as creation, they do not possess eternally undiminished power, owing to their state of delusion during their own nights.

However, even though the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and others are free from delusion, they do not possess infinite power; for, in relation to them, the universe is distinct and thus lacks the nature of being their power. Therefore, the six attributes—such as omniscience and the rest—of the one Lord Śiva must be explained in this way through the distinctions of his various manifestations.

In order to clarify that the essence of the qualities (*guṇa*) is their resting within the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), he says that one should first offer six oblations with the root mantra itself, preceded by the resting in the root:
"Having brought all those qualities [to rest], one should recollect the root mantra" (4.446).

One should offer oblations using the syllable *oṃ hūṃ* joined with the word for the self (*ātmapada*), followed by "to the Omniscient One" (*sarvajñāya*) at the end, and employing the utterance *svāhā*. || 4-447 ||
Because the word for oneself (*ātmapada*) is preceded by the name [of the person] in the dative case:
"Whatever is performed with an unexpressed designation, it remains as such;
an action performed directed toward that [person] bears fruit—of this there is no doubt."
"‘To the Omniscient One’ is an elliptical expression; by it, ‘to the Satisfied One,’ and so forth, are also included.
Having first uttered that [formula] up to the words ‘and this is not the last,’ one should offer oblations with the utterance of *svāhā*. (4.447)
And these [offerings] follow the determination of what is possible—
whether they be three, five, ten,
or one— and even when there is absolute impossibility, there is no fault even in a single oblation.
He states that even regarding the material substance here, there is indeed an option:
"either with sesame seeds or with ghee.
He now describes the student's ritual bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) at the conclusion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*):
Then, O lady of excellent vows, one should bestow the consecration with the root mantra.
The meaning is: by means of the *śivakumbha* consecrated with the root mantra, or by the utterance of the root mantra.
How so?—having agitated the supreme nectar of power (*śaktyamṛta*), one should cause it to fall upon the crown of the disciple's head.
One should enter that fourth door; indeed, one should contemplate it as being both external and internal.

The meaning is as follows: having rested at the *dvādaśānta*, which is that supreme state consisting of the touch of bliss, one should stir the supreme nectar of Śakti and, while contemplating it as having fallen from the *dvādaśānta* of the disciple into his body, one should cause the stream [of nectar] to fall from the jar. It is the "door of the fourth" (*turyadvāra*), characterized primarily by the experience of the fourth state (*turya*).
The aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 449 ||
He states the purpose of the consecration (abhiṣeka):
"By means of the fierce powers of the mantras, such as drying up and burning, the body is withered; for that purpose, there is the consecration. (4.450)

"By those aforementioned powers of mantra" (tābhiḥ pūrvoktābhir mantrashaktibhiḥ). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), meaning "by means of" drying, burning, and so forth. "For that purpose" (tadartham) means for the sake of the cessation of drying. || 450 ||
Then— prior to the completion of the initiation— one should cause a flower to be placed in the hand;
and having released the *darbha* grass...

Having instructed the disciple, saying, "Release the *darbha* grass previously given for the conceptualization of the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*)," he should place a flower as a reward in his hand. Alternatively, if the causative sense (*ṇic*) is intended,
the Guru should cause [the disciple] to place it in his own hand, instructing the disciple, "Take it."

This is said with the intention that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) should not be deficient in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). By speaking thus, he indicates the teacher’s state of desirelessness (*niḥspṛhatva*). The meaning is: at that time, the disciple should give whatever he offers without stinginess regarding wealth; however, the teacher must remain entirely free from desire.
Then the disciple— [should offer] into the fire of Śiva, into the jar, and into the Guru. || 4-451 ||
Having performed three circumambulations for each [deity], one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Śiva, who possesses four bases, is preeminently favorable and well-disposed toward me.
Circumambulating three times with the intention that [the deity] may abide in all states and at the beginning, middle, and end,
one prostrates like a staff in order to achieve absorption into Śiva by making the body and other faculties subordinate.
Therefore indeed—having accomplished what was to be done, with a joyful soul, having crossed over existence, and being perfectly pure. (4.452)
With eyes wide open and tranquil, one should contemplate oneself as satisfied; for he whose task—

the manifestation of the state of Śiva through the destruction of the bonds— has been accomplished, is therefore delighted in soul, possesses the experience of full consciousness and bliss, and has thus transcended worldly existence.

Being perfectly stainless through the manifestation of his supreme Śiva-nature, even while in such a state, he should— at times of emergence from samādhi and during occasions such as receiving the Guru’s instruction—
contemplate his own self as one who has previously experienced the mass of full bliss, so that [he may remain] always [in that state].
One becomes absorbed in that (*tanmayībhavati*). To reveal the means for this, he states the reason by way of a qualification: "with eyes wide open and tranquil.
[As it is said: "Liberation (*kaivalya*) arises immediately when the eyes are merely fixed in a steady gaze" (*Viṣṇubhaisajya* 113).
Thus, according to the secret vision, one whose gaze is fixed without a focal point becomes tranquil,
with all longing dissolved and the entire web of conceptual constructions exhausted.
He concludes: "This initiation leading to Nirvāṇa is either seedless (nirbījā) or with seed (sabījikā). (4.453)
Having begun with, "Now, for the purpose of purifying the path of initiation" (4-79), [it continues]:
