"Taking up the cord of bonds, one should suspend it upon the body of the disciple" (4-91).

From this point until the end of the passage "he should fall upon the ground like a staff" (4.452), whatever initiation has been described— whether seedless (*nirbījā*) or with seed (*sabījā*)— both of these are included.
It has liberation as its purpose. By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), he says this:

the procedure consisting of the destruction of bonds and the union with Śiva, which is taught for both types of initiation, is identical; the only difference is that in the *nirbīja* initiation, it occurs at the time of contemplating the purification of the bonds pertaining to *māyā*.
One should also contemplate the bond of the observances (*samayapāśa*) as being internally pure; however, there is no other procedure for their purification. For it was stated previously:
"One should purify the bond of the conduct of tranquility (*śamayācāra-pāśa*) within the seedless [state]. (4.147)
Having said only this much:
"In this way, according to the disposition of the disciples, the Guru should always bring about various kinds of results through a perfect initiation. (4.150)
Thus it has been said:
"These are remembered as the primary bonds;
one should include the many subtle bonds within them. (4.158)

Thus it has also been said. Therefore, in the seedless [initiation], the bonds of the *samaya* (conventional rules) must be conceived as being included within the bonds of *māyā* alone, since they are to be purified;
for it is taught that their bestowal of the enjoyment of the "flesh-eaters" (the lower deities) implies their inclusion specifically within the bonds of *māyā*. For this very reason...

In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated that the purification of the *samaya*-bond occurs immediately after the purification of the bonds pertaining to *māyā* have reached the throat; by this much alone, there is a distinction between the tantras.
Thus, because the two types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) have been summarized as having a single form, that which was previously...
The statement that the surrender of the components of the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) has as its sole object the seedless [samādhi] (nirbīja) is to be considered entirely incorrect.
Having thus described the initiation for the *samayin* and the *putraka*, he proceeds to that of the *ācārya* and the *sādhaka*:
"For them, one should perform the initiation with seed (*sabījikā*) and their consecration (*abhiṣecana*).
For those who are capable of enduring the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), it is 'with seed' (*sabīja*). (4.88)
Because it has been stated thus, the meaning is that one should consecrate those very persons in the office of teacher or in the capacity of an adept.
In that regard—one should appoint those who possess learning, ethical conduct, and proper behavior to the role of teacher. (4.454)

The *deśaka* (instructor) is one who points out those in whom these qualities exist: learning, which consists of the thorough comprehension of the ultimate meaning from a guru according to the *Pārameśvara-saṃhitā*;

conduct, which consists of the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) pertaining to speech, mind, and body; and right behavior, which consists of the practice of the scriptures. He is called a *deśaka* because he instructs those who possess these.

The "instructor" (upadeṣṭā) is the teacher (ācārya); the meaning is that one should appoint someone who possesses that very nature. Now, regarding the consecration (abhiṣeka): it occurs after the yoga with Śiva (śivayoga). Yoga with Śiva culminates in union (yojanā), and the consecration follows that rite of initiation (dīkṣā).
By what means should it be performed? To this he says: "O auspicious lady, by means of five jars smeared with white sandalwood. (4.455)
Having worshipped [the vessel] like the auspicious jar (śivakumbha), filled with water containing gems,
purified by prosperity, growth, and other [auspicious factors], and filled with medicinal herbs and unbroken grains (akṣata).

"With the emissions from the mouths of white lotuses joined with mango sprouts"—*ṛddhi* and *vṛddhi* are two medicinal herbs well-known in Āyurveda. The word "herb" (*oṣadhī*) is used separately in the case of *sahadevī* and others. The "mouths" are the white lotuses themselves; the "emission" (*udgāra*) is their blossoming.
And for those who possess the discernment of the fortune of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, there are mango sprouts and the like,
serving as indicators of excellent shade, leaves, and so forth.
Now, among these—[one] should place the five principles beginning with earth (pṛthivī) into the five [elements]. || 457 ||
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, one should place the *kalā* within the jars; those five *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti, should be deposited therein. (4.458)
"In them" means in [the elements] such as earth and so forth, by way of pervasion; the word "ca" (and) indicates a simultaneous sequence. Regarding the position that they are indeed the seats:
"For within each individual jar, [the deity] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva is indeed pervasive."
The mass of the Lord of the World.
And there— one should worship the god Bhairava in due order with all the ritual requisites. || 4-459 ||
It is endowed with the six limbs and the enclosure (āvaraṇa), and joined with the union of mantras.
The sequence [of the ritual] begins with the Nivṛtti-kalaśa and so forth; some say that the enclosures exclude the cremation grounds (śmaśāna).
Having worshipped in this manner, O Dear One, one should consecrate each individual jar with the Bhairava-mantra. (4.460)

Recalling the Supreme Reality with exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], he describes their directional positions according to their respective digits (kalās): "In the west, in the north and south, in the east, and likewise in the northeast. (4.461)
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Therein—the wise man should prepare a pedestal in the northeast corner of the sacrificial hall. (4-462)
The seat is the pedestal. || 462 ||
How so?
Having prepared a mandala there, adorned with svastikas and other such designs, covered above by a canopy, and beautifully decorated with banners— || 4-463 ||
There, O Goddess, one should place a seat made from *śrīparṇī* and sandalwood;
*śrīparṇī* and sandalwood are characterized by their auspicious nature.
Having placed the Anantāsana there, one should place the child who has become embodied.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, [the teacher] stands facing the northeast;
"there" means on a seat made of śrīparṇī wood or similar materials, where the disciple is intended by the teacher to be initiated.
Then,
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should be reproached with sour gruel and boiled rice.
With lumps of earth, ashes, and cow dung, accompanied by sprouts of dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, curd, and water, and together with the rite of lustration (nīrājana).

The meaning is that the child, having been honored with a lamp-offering (*nīrājana*) consisting of a vessel filled with substances such as *kāñcika* and so forth— representing the nature of the King who has completely departed— and having thus been driven away, should be rendered free from obstacles.
Then, having thus rebuked [the disciple] according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be bestowed;
or, recollecting the Abode (dhāman), one should sprinkle [him] with the mouths of the jars [representing] Earth and the other elements. || 4.467 ||

One should sprinkle with the faces—the mouths—of the jars representing earth and the other elements, ending with Īśāna. Here, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not intended; the same applies elsewhere. The reading "ghaṭādyaiḥ" (with jars, etc. is a corruption. || 467 ||
Furthermore:
"Having meditated in sequence upon the jars...
means having contemplated them according to the sequence of pervasion beginning with Nivṛtti and the others.
Who?
— The teacher who is well-composed;
that is to say, one who possesses the immersion (āveśa) of Śiva.
Then, according to his respective rank, he should be consecrated; having been dressed in other garments, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Through the pervasive casting off of the illusory veil, there is the abandonment of the previous garment; through the pervasive envelopment by the light of Supreme Śiva, one should don another robe. 468.
Having caused the disciple to sip water and enter the southern door...
there, his form as the infinite seat (anantāsana) should be explained through its pervasiveness.
...one should fashion the yogapīṭha.
Therein, as follows:
having established [it] and performed the sakalīkaraṇa...
For him, one should assign the authority to... || 4-469 ||
How so? He says:
"The turban, the crown and so forth, the parasol, the sandals, the throne, as well as the elephant, horse, palanquin, and so on—all these royal insignia without exception. (4-470)
Having given the ritual instrument (karaṇī), the scissors (kartarī), chalk (khaṭikā), the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva), a bundle of darbha grass, a book, a rosary, and so forth,
as well as a turban for binding upon the head, a cloth, and the collection of ornaments such as a crown;
For the sake of ornamentation: a palanquin (*śivikā*) is a vehicle drawn by yokes (*yugya*). Royal insignia include musical instruments such as cymbals (*tūrya*) and drums (*bherī*), etc.

Items useful for the teacher’s duties include the *karaṇī* and so forth; by the inclusion of the word “etc. (*ādi*), messengers, vessels for the guest-offering (*arghapātra*), and other such items are intended.
He explains the section:
".........those established in the four stages of life (āśramas). || 4-471 ||

"By the command of Śiva, you have the authority to always perform the exposition of initiation according to the path of grace for those to be initiated; this must be done from this day forward. (4.472)

For those who abide in any of the four stages of life (āśramas), you must perform initiation (dīkṣā) and provide instruction; this should be done with the desire to show grace through the path of favor toward those fit for initiation— because the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred in them— not out of affection, greed, or similar motives.

"Always" means that one must never remain without acting for the benefit of others; this is the office that has now come to you, and no one else has the power over this—this is the command that is being given. || 472 ||
Then, having raised him up and grasped his hands, one should cause him to enter the mandala.
Furthermore—
Then, having gone to the ground on his knees, he should worship Bhairava.
Having made his request... what [is it], O Blessed One? Thus consecrated by your command...
By me, established in the station of the teacher, who is performing the rite of authorization for you. || 4-474 ||
By your command alone, I stand thus upon the path of the Teacher.
Having informed him, "By your very command, he has been consecrated," [the disciple] should then perform whatever duty has arisen for the instructor;
standing before Śiva, he should expound the meaning of the Śiva-tattva. (4.475)
This is a specific statement: "That explanation of the meaning of the reality of Śiva (śivatattva), which has come down through the lineage of the Gurus, must necessarily be performed;

therefore, standing here before you, who are Śiva himself, I shall perform it. [The question remains: what kind of person is qualified [to receive this], by what means is one graced, and how does one become identical with your own form? || 475 ||
Then, having emerged from the dwelling, one should offer the path of the digits (*kalādhvan*) into the fire;
there, first, according to the sequence of the root mantra—
Having performed the satiation of the mantra,
[one should offer] five oblations for each of the kalās. || 4-476 ||
One should give. || 476 ||
Thus,
having offered five [oblations] into each of the five [fires], the Guru should then offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra.
Then, having performed the worship with the *argha* offering and so forth, and having prostrated, one should announce it to the Lord. || 477 ||
The meaning is that this matter must be declared: "For what purpose was the master consecrated by me? For that purpose, the satiation of the mantra was performed in the fire."
Then,
with his five limbs beginning with the heart, he should mark the disciple's right hand.
Because the eye possesses a pervasiveness that is non-different from its root, it is likewise [pervasive] through its own powers.
How so?
Having placed the *darbha*-grass and firewood into the Śiva-fire...
having performed [this].
With that very [fire],
one should mark the little finger and the others.
One should touch the little finger and the other fingers in sequence with the *darbha*-brand, using the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra.
By means of this, his mantras—being of the nature of instruments—become instantly capable of their respective effects;
the meaning is that through the touch of this hand, the fetters (pāśas) become like burnt seeds and pass away.
Thinking, "This is the fruit of the ritual for one who has thus received initiation," he should place a flower in his hand as a reward;
and that—
...one should cause [the disciple] to drink in the fire of the maṇḍala. || 4-479 ||
For the purpose of prostrating like a staff before the disciple,
he—
having bowed down like a staff to Bhairava, the ritual jar, and the fire— [should proceed].
Having obtained authority, his soul is joyful, endowed with both seen and unseen fruits. || 4-480 ||
That Guru is indeed equal to Śiva and bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva.

The intended meaning in the passage beginning with "prostrating like a staff" has already been stated: the visible fruit is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), whereas the invisible fruit is the state of Supreme Śiva.
Having thus completed the procedure concerning the disciple and the teacher, he now begins that which concerns the practitioner:
"At the conclusion of the rite of pacification (śānti), there is the initiation for prosperity (bhūti-dīkṣā), which consists of the state of Sadāśiva. (4.481)

The *bhūtidīkṣā* is the initiation for the enjoyment of powers such as *aṇimā*, ending with Sadāśiva; the phrase "ending with *śānti*" means at the conclusion of the stage of *śāntyanta*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it also includes the form of the *śivayojanikā* initiation, since it is said:
"One should perform the consecration for those whose initiation is *sabījikā*. (4.454)

Thus it was introduced. And that which possesses the seed (*sabījikā*) has been described as consisting precisely of the union with Śiva (*śivayojanikā*). For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere:
"Success may arise from [the guru's] lack of grace, but the state of Śaṅkara arises from his grace."

If he should become intoxicated by the objects of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), then, for the purpose of ensuring that no obstacle arise for him regarding the state of Śiva, one should perform the union with Sadāśiva after first performing the initiation into Śiva for the practitioner. || 481 ||
Thus,

it should be understood that this is the "initiation of the practitioner" (sādhakadīkṣā), which belongs to the Śiva-dharma; the remainder [of the definition] is that wherein there is union with the principle of Sadāśiva.
And that [attainment] is otherwise than the worldly dharmas,
because it consists in the exhaustion of exclusively unwholesome states and the application to the state of a Lord of those respective worlds and so forth.
And therefore:
"She is proclaimed as belonging to the Śiva-dharma of those practitioners (sādhakas). (4.482)
Having performed their consecration in the manner that will be described hereafter,
those very [persons]—
...one should employ [the disciple] in the state of being a practitioner (*sādhaka*).
In that regard—this is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the practitioner, which follows after the initiation into the Vidyā. (4.483)

Vidyā is the entire mantra; the initiation (dīkṣā) that follows immediately after the union with the state of Sadāśiva—which is of the nature of Vidyā and is brought about by it—is for the practitioner (sādhaka). This consecration (abhiṣeka), whose procedure will now be described, is to be performed as something subsequent to that. || 483 ||

Although the entire mantra also serves as a cause for attaining the supreme state, nevertheless—initiation by means of the *vidyā* exists according to the distinction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For it has been said: "The oblation (*homa*) of mantras, mudrās, paths, and substances is common [to all]. (4.82)
And so forth.
Therefore, indeed—no distinction of action exists, as it abides everywhere throughout the path. (4-484)
The destruction of the fetters of karma. || 484 ||
And therefore:
"All those actions that have been performed and have passed away, having purified them according to the rule, they remain situated within the five *kalās*. (4.485)
At the occasion of the *yojanī*, however, there is a distinction regarding the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the practitioner.

Previously, the persistence of the *kārmamala* was described as being coarse within the first three *kalās*; here, however, it is described as subtle even within the five *kalās*. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. The first word "tu" (however) has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
One also accumulates future actions.
In this regard, he recalls the previously stated rule:
"One should not contemplate that a later commenced action and [an earlier one] reside in the same place. (4.486)

One should not contemplate that the karma already commenced—such as the propitiation of mantras—in this present body, along with that which is yet to come, exists as something to be exhausted all at once; the meaning is that even this karma of propitiating mantras and so forth should not be exhausted by him. || 486 ||
And this has been determined:
"But for the sake of the practitioner's prosperity, one should first purify a single past action.
The meaning is that one should contemplate past and future actions as being unified in a single locus.
And for this reason:
"Having uttered the entire *dhāman*, one should place it within the body of Sadāśiva. (4.487)
The entire [mantra] consists of thirty-two syllables.
How so?— Having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva in the form of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha),
[one attains him] endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) through the application of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 4-488 ||
The body of knowledge is the eighteen-armed Sakalabhaṭṭāraka.
Then,
for the attainment of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, having offered eight oblations with the root mantra using its own specific name, one should consecrate the practitioner. (4.489)

Just as the attainment of those qualities was performed immediately after the Niṣkala-yojanā, so too, immediately after the Sakala-yojanā, the practitioner must effect the attainment of the nature of the qualities such as aṇimā and the rest. Here, preceded by the entire mantra, one should utter for the practitioners: "Let there be aṇimā," and then again—
The ritual application begins with "Svāhā to the Self of Initiation, who possesses the qualities such as *aṇimā* preceded by the utterance of all [mantras].
The phrase "in the attainment of the qualities such as *aṇimā*" indicates that this is for the purpose of that attainment. || 489 ||
One should perform that consecration with five jars as before...
To explain how this is done, he says:
One should place Nivṛtti and the others in the first three [cakras];
Śāntyatītā in the fifth, and then Śānti in the fourth.
"In the three" refers to the five [vessels] located in the southern, northern, and western directions, as well as those facing east and full [of water];

"the fifth" refers to the northeast. "Afterwards" means immediately following the installation of the *śāntyatītā* [kalaśa]. "The fourth" refers to the eastern vessel. And the intention here is that of the practitioner.
Having said, "May there be unimpeded attainment of the state of Sadāśiva, preceded by rest in the state of Śiva," [he adds], "May this person become Śiva through enjoyments. || 490 ||
Thus,
having encapsulated [the ritual] with Peace (śānti) ...
because of the placement of the vessel of Peace (śāntā-kalaśa) immediately after the vessel of Transcending Peace (śāntyatīta-kalaśa), by means of Peace (śāntyā).
It becomes a "sealed" (saṃpuṭīkāra) state, because it contains within it both Śāntyatītā and Śānti by means of the triad of their constituent parts.
Furthermore—...

with the five [elements] beginning with earth, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the water-pots (*kalaśa*) according to the sequence of the *kalās*; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Here, "beginning with earth" refers to...
It encompasses the expansive Lord of all principles and realities, whose ultimate essence is the fivefold Brahman; it does not consist of mere gross elements.
Then, one should subsequently place the mantra of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) into each individual jar. || 4.491 ||
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the limbs of the Vidyā...

the Sādhya-mantra is the primary [deity] here as the Sakalabhaṭṭāraka, or alternatively, whichever [deity] falls according to the casting of flowers; "with the limbs of the Vidyā" means with all the limbs.
Or by means of the various limbs of the mantras to be accomplished, which take the form of omniscience and so forth.
After that,
one should place the enclosure of the limbs of the Vidyā;
for the limbs of the Vidyā possess forms such as omniscience and so forth.
The placement of other veils has not been mentioned, as it is not conducive to the accomplishment of spiritual attainments (*siddhi*).
Then, having consecrated each individual jar one hundred and eight times with the very mantra of the deity to be accomplished (sādhya-mantra), [one should proceed]. || 4.492 ||
Having placed the seat within the outer mandala with the syllable *praṇava*,
one should establish the practitioner there and then perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
Having rebuked [the obstacle] as before, one should sprinkle [it] with all the vessels using the *sādhya-mantra*.

The consecration of each individual vessel, beginning with the *nivṛtti*-kalaśa, is performed with the *sādhya-mantra*, [reciting]: "By the grace of this mantra, may all the stages (*bhūmayaḥ*) grant him success. "Outside" means outside the sacrificial mandala.

The form [of the seat] is that of a svastika and so forth; the seat is made of *śrīparṇī* wood and so forth. Regarding "the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa," the ellipsis is "one should perform it for that. "With all" refers to the previously mentioned substances such as *kāñcika* and others.
There, one should bathe [the deity] facing the eastern direction with the three jars beginning with Nivṛtti.
Afterwards, having taken the jar of the Śāntyatīta [kalā], one should sprinkle the disciple;
thereafter, one should take the Śānti [jar]...
"Śānti" refers to the jar of Śānti.
Therefore, in this manner—.................. one should consecrate [the disciple] with the *sampuṭa* [mudrā]. || 4-495 ||
The meaning of the *saṃpuṭa* and its underlying intention have indeed been explained.
Thus,
this is the initiation of the practitioner according to the direct and reverse orders:
the direct order (*ānulomya*) pertains to the triad beginning with Nivṛtti, while the reverse order (*prātilomya*) pertains to Śānti and Śāntyatīta.
Furthermore:
"Having consecrated him and led him inside, he should cause him to stand upon the southern mound. (4.496)
The meaning is that he has changed his garment; taking recourse to the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is for the sake of quelling obstacles.
In that regard,
having offered him a seat with the *praṇava*, the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the infusion of the limbs) should take place.
Now, his equipment for success (*siddhi*)—
One should prepare the rosary and other implements for the sake of the practitioner’s qualification.
One should present what is appropriate. || 497 ||
Having fashioned these—
the ritual manual for the mantra, a rosary, chalk, a parasol, and sandals—
and having given them along with a turban...
The ritual manual (*kalpa*) is the book of the mantra to be accomplished; the *uṣṇīṣa* must be given to the preceptor alone.
Then, having entered into the presence of Śiva... [4.498]
"O Supreme Lord, having informed You, this practitioner has been prepared by me; by Your command, may he attain the threefold accomplishment through his devotion. (4.499)
Afterwards, one should give the *sādhya-mantra* accompanied by water and flowers.

For the purpose of bringing about the presence of Śiva, having entered [the inner space] and become inward-turned, one should request the deity by means of that very support, saying, "This is the practitioner," and so forth; it is after such a request that one should give the *sādhya-mantra*.
The essential nature [of the rite] is as follows: after the ritual cognition (*vijñapti*), it is appropriate that permission be obtained as previously described;
and specifically in the presence of Śiva, one should offer a flower with the intention of producing fruit, and water for the sake of accomplishing nourishment—thus he says:
It should be placed in his hand for the sake of the practitioner's accomplishment.
The handing over from hand to hand is performed with the intention that "this has arisen from the supreme power (paraśakti) and has become manifest as that very power."
The practitioner, however, having prostrated to both and received the mantra, should place it within his heart.
"Both" refers to both the Guru and the mantra; "within the heart" means that he should make his own self consist of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of each.
Thus, because both have attained a suitable connection, the disciple has a joyful countenance and the teacher, too, is filled with joy. (4.501)
And having both gone out—
[the sense is that] they should remain attentive in the fire-sanctuary.
Then the Guru should satisfy the collection of mantras in the fire;
thereafter, as far as possible—
The propitiation of the Sādhya mantra should be performed either a thousand or even a hundred times.
One should perform [it].
Having thus satisfied [the deity], the Guru should cause the disciple to offer a flower into his hand, as before; by that, the meaning is for himself.
Then the practitioner, having worshipped the God residing in the three [loci], should prostrate like a staff before the sacrificial ground, the fire, and the Guru.
Then, one should also circumambulate it three times to the right. || 503 ||
Having performed.
Having bowed with a mind endowed with devotion, one shall obtain the fruits beginning with *aṇiman* and attain fitness for them.
The Guru, having raised the practitioner up, should say: "Guard the commitments with effort. || 4-504 ||
They will be foremost.
Furthermore, he instructs that— with the exception of those initiated through the seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*)— all disciples should be made to hear the rules of conduct (*samaya*),
and so forth: "O Goddess, at the conclusion of the initiation, they should be made to hear [the rules] by the wise one."
By one who knows the pledge.
Introducing another topic, he says:
"But having thus performed the initiation at all times, O fair-faced one... (4.505).

Listen to how the sacrifice of the self (ātmayāga) is to be performed for those who have received initiation (dīkṣā), such as the initiates of the covenant (samayin) and others. This sacrifice of the self consists in the union with the Supreme Reality (paratattva),
intended to pacify any doubt regarding the possibility of deficiency in the procedure for severing contact with the fetters (pāśa).
It must be performed.
Thus, in this manner—
whether by the teacher's scientific knowledge, natural disposition, or by chance— 4-506.

Initiation occurs [in two forms]: that which is based on higher knowledge (*vaijñānikī*) has consciousness as its cause; that which is natural (*prākṛtī*) has oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter as its cause. || 506 ||
Therein—one should perform the extremely subtle scientific [practice] by means of this method.
"Extremely subtle" means that which is accomplished through complete knowledge. "By this" refers to what is about to be described.
In that regard, he first describes the *prākṛtī* [form], which differs slightly from the previously mentioned type:
"The conceptualization of the Path and Vāgīśī is joined with sesame, clarified butter, and so forth. (4.507)
The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the remainder in the context of the *prakṛti* (archetype). || 507 ||
And there—
one should simultaneously deposit the path pervaded by the five *kalās*,
but not as before.
And he reveals that sequence step by step:
"Having performed the worship, fire-oblation, ritual services, and so forth, one should apply oneself [to the practice]. (4.508)
Just as in the consciousness of a disciple...
[one] should, preceded by invocation, worship, and so forth, unite the self— consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*— with Vāgīśī, whose body simultaneously pervades all arts (*kalā*).
From that as well—...
by means of yoga, one should deposit the path all at once.
Immediately after the union with the womb, one should deposit the path for the candidate for initiation all at once.
And having placed it— and having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings—
right there...
...three oblations for the sake of the yoga. || 4-509 ||
The application here is as follows: "I simultaneously unite the Self, preceded by the *praṇava* and the *haṃsa*-seed-syllable, which pervades all paths, within the womb of Vāgīśī; svāhā! (509)

Then, O Goddess, for the sake of conceiving, giving birth, acquiring, and the dissolution of enjoyments, one who is firm in his vows should simultaneously perform the fire-oblation with the root mantra.
The oblation is performed three times with the meditation on the pervasion of all time-paths, [contemplating] each [deity] both individually and simultaneously. || 510 ||
Thus he says:
"O fair-faced one, three oblations are to be offered for each ritual act.
Because of the preeminence of the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), he speaks of the oblation separately:
The oblations should be offered with the *niṣkṛti* mantras into the five locations within the self. (4.511)
One hundred, or half of that,
[beings]— those parts which have the five locations beginning with earth as their essence and whose domain is those [elements]—
may there be atonement for my consciousness through them in the cessation [of bondage], during the fivefold rites beginning with conception.
The application is "svāhā"; likewise elsewhere.
And this expiation has been fully described;
it was already determined previously.
Then—[upon] the severing of the bonds of separation and so forth—the manifestation occurs simultaneously by means of the very abode itself. || 4.512 ||

And when the extraction [of the soul] is established in the reality of the Self— by the word "etcetera" [in the source text], this refers to the fulfillment of the injunctions and the burning of the fetters— the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) is performed simultaneously. And here, [the sequence involves] striking, cutting, seizing, contemplating the single consciousness, the cause, the invocation, and the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).

The offering of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka) is to be understood as occurring first, because it has been determined that the offering of the parts of the eightfold city occurs even in the state of possessing seeds (sabījā).
Then, [the officiant] should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation;
and by that very [offering], he should—
One should unite the self with the reality of Śiva, the supreme cause.
Then, having likewise attained the qualities as before... by means of the final ablution (*avabhṛthasnāna*).
Make those very [beings] immortal as before—
immortal meaning imperishable.
This is the natural self-initiation for those to be initiated, such as the spiritual sons (putraka) and others.
But upon its completion, for the sake of the cessation of the need for expiation. || 4-514 ||
The meaning is: for the purpose of pacifying doubts regarding the possibility of rules concerning the deficiency or excess in the association with sacrificial animals.
Now, if one who assumes purity for an impure self through initiation is himself impure,

then that is like a blind man grasping the hand of another blind man. But if he is recognized as pure because he is distinct from the vital breaths and other such factors, then everything [is accomplished] simply through the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [purity].
"What is the use of an ordinary initiation (dīkṣā) when [the goal] is already accomplished? This is true;

however, if firm establishment [in the state] were to occur solely through the descent of power (śaktipāta), then an ordinary initiation would certainly not be required. In that case, he describes the initiation of consciousness (vijñānadīkṣā), which is to be accomplished exclusively by one who is skillful:

Then, initiation occurs through the simultaneous utterance in the form of consciousness. That very simultaneous utterance of the root mantra— which consists of the reflective awareness of one's own perfect "I" (pūrṇāhaṃparāmarśa)— is [initiation] itself by means of entering into the central abode (madhyadhāma).
That [initiation of consciousness] is that which has this characteristic.
For it is said:
"But by Bhairava, the snares of both what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted are [severed] simultaneously. (4.515)

By the utterance once of the partless Bhairava, there occurs the simultaneous purification of those things up to Māyā which are to be abandoned because they consist solely of the essence of duality; and likewise of those things up to Samanā which are to be accepted because they have the nature of both difference and non-difference; nevertheless, due to their connection with the aspect of duality, they are designated as "fetters" (pāśa).
The remainder [is as follows]. And it was stated previously:
"O Goddess, when uttered even once, it destroys all sins" (1.44).
Not only is the simultaneous destruction of the fetters (pāśa) performed by means of mantra, but furthermore, there is an eternal abiding in the state of Paramaśiva thereafter— this and...
[this is] also...
Thus the subtle initiation (sūkṣmadīkṣā) has been described.
At the conclusion of the self-initiation (ātmadīkṣā) in this manner, one should perform special worship and fire-offerings (homa) according to one's capacity. (4.516)
One should worship Hara with instrumental music, song, fine dance, and other offerings, as well as with hymns of praise;
then, one should perform three circumambulations around the mandala consisting of the water-pot, the fire, and the maṇḍala.
Having performed a prostration with eight limbs, one should address the Supreme Lord,
having circumambulated the God who is the basis of the three times.
What should he request? To this he says:
"O Blessed One, you have been invoked by me for the sake of the sacrificial victim. (4.518)
Therefore, O Lord, you must always forgive me, who abide by the prescribed rule;
"rule" refers to the ritual of initiation, and "mine" refers to one to whom authority has been granted by you alone.
Even that deficiency in the injunction for one who lacks desire...
the meaning is that even a deficiency in the injunction due to negligence should be forgiven.
Because—..................the worship is declared in the scripture as follows: || 4-519 ||
It should not be performed with an excessive abundance of ordinary material offerings;

rather, as the worship described in the scriptures is most extensive and set forth in a detailed sequence, it should not be done with limited materials consisting merely of the transformations of nature— this is the statement intended for those devoted to discipline (*vinaya*).
Otherwise, since the substances have been consecrated with drops from the arghya-vessel and thus transformed into the nature of Śiva, how could they be considered "ordinary"?
Furthermore, their being measured is intended to prevent stinginess regarding wealth.
Since this is so, therefore: whatever ritual procedure has been performed by me, having relied solely upon devotion. (4.520)
O All-pervading Lord, may all that be fruitful for me while You are well-pleased.
"Well-pleased" means the manifestation as consisting of the essence of pure consciousness through the subsiding of the turbidity of *māyā*. Immediately after this petition—
With a serene face and joyful, one should contemplate the boon that has been granted. || 4-521 ||
Then, having sat down, O Dear One, one should perform the sacrifice in sequence;
therein, first—
Having prayed for the foremost [attainment], one should take it and place it under the protection of the weapon-mantra.

The *agravatī* is the foremost among the *caru* offerings and so forth, because it has been stated elsewhere: "The food offering (*naivedya*) of the God of gods is equal to hundreds of *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts and more. May no one who is uninitiated, such as a *bhūta*, partake of this supreme purifier.
"By saying 'He has brought,' one provides protection for him through the weapon-mantra."
Having done this—
then [perform] the special worship, the *argha* offering, and prostration; thereafter,
taking the *nirodhārgha*, one offers the *argha* from the left and the right.
Having offered [the final offering], one should dismiss the deity while recollecting the mantra of the abode.
Regarding the *argha*: "Thereafter, the *argha* should be presented with wine. (2.136)
Having spoken thus and performed prostration, the *argha* intended for the purpose of cessation is offered;

once the ritual is completed, one should dismiss [the deity] by offering [the *argha*] with the right and left hands— meaning through the pervasion of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*)— for the sake of resting in one's own true nature (*svarūpa-viśrānti*).
He demonstrates the very procedure for dismissal:
"Having performed exhalation (recaka) upon oneself, one should cast the flower toward the deity. (4.524)
By the partless one; this is the implied meaning. || 524 ||
Having gathered the mantras situated at the sides by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā],
and having visualized them as flickering like lightning, one should deposit them into the body of the *dhāma*.
The *saṃhāriṇī* mudrā consists of the contraction of the fingers of the right hand in the sequence beginning with the little finger.
One should place [the deities] within the body of the abode—that is, within the Blessed Lord who possesses all parts—and contemplate them as merged into that very [body]. || 525 ||
One should contemplate even that body of knowledge of Bhairava as dissolved within the partless [Bhairava].
...dissolved within the form of the *bindu*.
That undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) form is dissolved into the *bindu*, which is the self consisting of pure light, by means of the method of the pacification of [the phonemes] beginning with *a*.
One should cause that very *bindu*—which resides within the power of *nāda* and has the nature of *śakti*—to be grasped. || 4.526 ||

By means of the method of pacifying the obstructing half-moon, one should bring about the form of the Power (śakti), which consists primarily of the touch of bliss, having been led to the state of the nature of sound and the end of sound, where discernment (vimarśa) is predominant. || 526 ||
That too—
existing in its own nature— is of the form of power (śakti), pervading, and encapsulated on both sides by the Praṇava.
The *praṇava* is that which is praised (*nūyate*) and extolled (*stūyate*) by all in an eminent manner; it is the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*).
Being "enclosed on both sides" (*ubhayataḥ sampuṭitam*) by it means it is "placed within" (*antaḥkṛtam*), which signifies being pervaded on all sides.
Likewise, having cultivated it—having gathered it by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should join it at the *dvādaśānta*. (4-527)
Then, having placed [the deity] in the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should contemplate it as residing in its own place;
that "own place" is indeed a mass of bliss and light, free from all limiting conditions.
The form is both with parts and without parts, as well as both with and without parts.
O Dear One, one should remember that within the mantras, it exists in distinct states: as residing in the heart;

as *sakala* (with parts), consisting of thirty-two syllables; as *niṣkala* (without parts), which at the conclusion of the mantra is the reality of pure light and awareness (*prakāśa-vimarśa-mātra*); and as *sakala-niṣkala* (both with and without parts), which consists of the nature of the Lord of the Four Kalās.

One should meditate upon this very single mantra-form residing in the heart, which— though one, having manifested in three ways out of a desire to bestow grace, and being further differentiated in states such as the faces and limbs— is thus all-pervasive.
He summarizes: "The procedure for dismissal is indeed thus...
and as it is in the mandala, so it is elsewhere too, he says:
......in Agni thus......
there, at the beginning, one should worship Agni first. || 4-529 ||
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, one should cast the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
And that—
Having offered the water for honor (argha) and the water for sipping (ācamana), one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
In this sense, "one should forgive," this is the reading of Īśvara.
How should one endure [the pain]? To this he says:
"By means of the practice situated in the maṇḍala, through exhalation and inhalation, having gathered the collection of mantras, one should arrange them in their proper places. (4-531)

Immediately after the utterance of the mantra of one's own self, having emerged through the nasal exhalation (*nāsikya-recaka*), one should fill [the space] up to the abode (*dhāman*) by means of the sequence beginning with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and then, having performed the exhalation, one should fill one's own self alone. In that regard, the Bhairavas belong to the mantras of the world-protectors; their limbs (*aṅga*) and faces (*vaktra*); and to those, the *sakala*.
For that [state] as well, there is the Sakalaniṣkala; for that too, the Niṣkalanātha whose form has been explained is the locus—this indeed is the sequence here. || 531 ||
Having thus dismissed the deity residing in the fire,
one should then awaken that fire for the purpose of the daily obligatory rites;
the intention is that there should not be a formal consecration performed every single day.
Then, O Dear One, one should perform the removal of the floral remains and sweep away the dust. (4.532)
Then, having entered, one should sprinkle that ground with auspicious water.

The term *nirmālya* refers to the garland that has been removed [from the deity], and not by virtue of it being assigned to Caṇḍeśa, because such an assignment is not enjoined here in these specific ritual methods.
Then,
having gone outside, one should perform the offering of bali to the spirits as before.
The rite should be performed with the very same mantra as previously stated. || 533 ||
Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), one should thereafter offer libations to the *liṅgins*.
"Liṅgins" refers to those endowed with matted hair, ashes, and so forth. And it has been said:
"What indeed can be done by men for Śiva, who is already perfectly complete? Whatever is done for the devotees of Śiva, that is truly done for Śiva himself.
Thus [it is said].
In the Śiva-dharmas (i.e., among those devoted to Śiva).
Immediately thereafter, the disciple should worship the Guru with extensive offerings according to his means. (4.534)
Then, in order to discharge his debt to himself for him— the provincial governor (deśādhyakṣa) should give a hundred villages, the lord of a district (maṇḍaleśa) half of that;
one who enjoys a hundred [villages] should indeed give five, and likewise one who enjoys twenty should give one village. (4-535)
The village-tenant, however, shall give a field; but the tenant of a field shall give a twentieth part.
This means a twentieth portion. And this is merely an illustration.
In reality, however—one should offer everything by which the guru may be pleased. (4.536)
Then, one who is free from stinginess regarding wealth attains freedom from debt;
however, when there is stinginess regarding wealth, for one possessed by greed and other such traits, the state of being a knower of the body and so forth remains obscured even slightly,
and thus the purificatory rite of initiation does not properly take effect for him.

Thus it is inferred. And where the conduct of the disciple is such as this, there the teacher is established as being free from greed by the very logic of the "stick and the cake" maxim (*daṇḍāpūpika*). For this very reason, it was stated previously:
"One should cause him to offer a flower into his hand" (4.503).
Thus it has been said.
Once the disciple has thus been recognized as being fit,
he should then be made to hear the rules (samayas) in the tantra that has emerged from Bhairava.
And they shall be foremost.
And then— the kisser (cumbaka), with speech restrained and mind serene, seated separately in his own vessel, should afterwards consume the *caru* together with the practitioners. || 4.538 ||
*Caruka* refers to the sacrificial offering (*naivedya*) presented at the outset. The term "by the practitioners" (*sādhakaiḥ*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

According to its etymological derivation—where a *cumbaka* is a Guru who, through the mouth of the lineage-descended Guru, unites [the disciple] with [the deity] and causes the disciple to unite [with it]—the *cumbaka* is the Guru. Furthermore, during the consumption of the supremely pure *caru*, there is the restraint of speech (*vāṅniruddhatva*).
For the sake of one-pointedness of mind, and for that very reason, his self is serene.
And he says that this sacrificial pap (caru) should be given to the practitioners and others according to the sequence of seniority and so forth:
"It should be given in due order... for when this is done, each one becomes a consumer of that sacrificial pap."
...thereafter one shall attain perfection.
And he says that this procedure for initiation is of an extraordinary nature:
"O fair-faced one, those who have been initiated by this very rite... (4.539).
O beloved, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others,
all of them possess equal dharma when they are engaged in the Śiva-dharma.
All are said to wear matted hair and have their bodies smeared with ashes.

Here, unlike in other systems, there is no prior caste-based consecration for those who have received initiation; the distinction exists solely due to differences in the rules of conduct (*samaya*) and so forth.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, all those who observe the pledge (samayins) shall eat in a single row. (4.541)
"All" refers to the Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as those of mixed caste. || 541 ||
Furthermore:
"There shall be one for the sons, likewise there shall be one for the practitioners (sādhakas), and there shall be one for the kissers; it is not [determined] by distinctions of prior caste. (4.542)
The meaning is "a row."
For:
"That single, auspicious, and imperishable lineage of Bhairava is traditionally taught.
Indeed, it was stated previously:
"Engaged in that supreme reality, endowed with qualities such as omniscience,
O Goddess, one becomes the one Śiva, undivided from all things" (4.402).
Since this is the nature belonging to Bhairava, for that very reason it is of the form of the highest good (*śreyas*).
And it is eternal.
Regarding this, he states that this very scripture is the authority:
"Relying upon this tantra, one should not indeed proclaim a previous birth. (4.543)

This applies to the spiritual sons (*putraka*), the practitioners (*sādhaka*), and likewise to those bound by the observances (*samayin*); how much more so for the teachers (*ācārya*) who have taken refuge in this very tantra? This rule does not apply to worldly people; the phrase "having taken refuge in this tantra" is to be applied repeatedly [to each category]. And therefore:
O Goddess, a man who has been initiated into this Tantra becomes liable for penance from the moment he utters his former caste.
The term "nara" refers to one who has grasped a body and so forth.
And for this reason: "He who [commits such an act] is cooked in hell for three days for Rudra, five days for Keśava, and for one fortnight for Pitāmaha. (4.545)
Since this is so—
one would therefore become undiscriminating— if one desires the supreme goal;
[one should remain] undiscriminating, perceiving the initiated as identical with Śiva, just as one perceives one's own self.
For this reason, O Goddess of Gods, through non-discrimination, both spiritual perfection and liberation will certainly be attained. (4.546)
The firm realization of oneness with Śiva alone is the means for attaining all that is most auspicious; may there be well-being.

May the Gurus who uphold the command of the venerable Śaṅkara examine this initiation rite which has been revealed by me here in this *Uddyota*, through my constant vigilance over the meaning of the Tantra, my demonstration at every step of the true pervasion [of reality], and my method of correct synthesis.
He was about to bestow initiation upon those seeking it, which grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation and Consecration," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*,
which demonstrates initiation, the consecration of initiation, and various means of manifestation.
Victory to the Supreme Lord, who rests solely in his exclusive grace!

Then, establishing the connection between the chapters, the venerable Goddess spoke in order to introduce the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*), following a restatement of the previously mentioned initiation into the levels of manifestation (*kalādīkṣā*):
"O Supreme Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, the initiation into the levels of manifestation has been described."
Out of your grace, please explain the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) in brief.

Sureśāna is the lord of Brahmā and the other [gods]. However, Parameśvara [is so called] because of his penetration into the existence of supreme Bhairava. "In brief" means concisely, because the expansion of the ritual procedure has already been stated in the *Kalādīkṣā*. || 1 ||
Thus addressed, the illustrious Bhairava said:

"O fair-faced one, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall briefly describe the initiation into reality (*tattvadīkṣā*) which was previously introduced by your question and which is divided into various categories."
In that regard—O Pārvatī, as for how the principal thirty-six principles (tattvas) are to be purified: || 5-2 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now explain to you how all things from the earth up to Śiva are purified, along with their respective pervasions and corresponding qualities.

In the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*), pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists precisely in the predominance of the principles with respect to the internal paths (*adhvan*) that are included within them, while the other paths remain subordinate. This is the case elsewhere as well. In whatever manner the objects of purification are to be purified, and in whatever way they become pure, [the procedure] pertains to both the purifier and the object of purification.
"I shall describe the manner of you who are solely intent upon showing favor"—this is the promise. (3)
In that regard—
those syllables of the King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) which are characterized by the number nine are the designators of the principles (tattvas).
Of those who are presented as objects to be purified.
Just as they are, so shall I explain them to you in due order. || 5-4 ||
In that regard—
the letter *mū* is traditionally taught as the designator for everything from the Earth principle up to Pradhāna;
and the letter *ya* belongs to the Puruṣa who is endowed with the principle of Rāga.

This is recorded by the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha. Therefore, with that very same phoneme, preceded by the utterance of the ninefold *praṇava*, one should establish each respective *tattva* as if establishing a ritual vessel (*kala*).
Then, as before, everything from the joining of the paths (*adhvasaṃdhāna*) up to the contemplation of the pure and impure *tattvas* should be performed.
This must be done; thus it is in all cases. It is said [to be] "endowed with the principle of passion" because the person consists of longing. || 5 ||
One should know the Niyāmikā to be endowed with the Vidyātattva by means of the letter *va*;
O fair-faced one, one should conceive of Kāla and Kalā by means of the letter *la*.
Because a portion of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*), which consists of limited sensation,

enters into the sphere of necessity, it is mentioned together with Necessity (*niyati*); whereas Kalā, which consists of limited agency and is characterized by action, [is mentioned together with Time].
Because the penetration of time is inevitable, it is mentioned together with time.
This mention together is for the purpose of demonstrating the relationship between the signified and the signifier; however, purification is indeed distinct.
Furthermore:
the principle of Māyā is represented by the letter *ma*; the principle of Vidyā by the letter *kṣa*;
the principle of Īśvara by the letter *ra*; and Sadāśiva by the letter *ha*. (5.7)
Likewise, O fair-faced one, the Śakti should be deposited by means of the Praṇava;
that is, by means of the Praṇava and the Bindu. "Śakti" refers to the Śakti-tattva, which is indeed the very nature of Paramaśiva. || 7 ||
For this very reason—one should purify the pervasive *samanā* right there above. (5.8)
"In that very [place]" means in the Śiva-tattva, by means of the *praṇava* alone.
And having purified all this in due order by means of the entire procedure previously described, O observer of good vows,
the self should be joined with the supreme reality, which transcends the *unmanā* state and pervades all. (5.9)

In the supreme, signless, peaceful, sovereign, imperishable, and unborn [state], within the body of the disciple: from the base of the feet to the ankles is Earth; from the ankles to the navel are the twenty-three principles beginning with Water and ending with Pradhāna; and from there to the palate are those beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā.

Having thus assigned the principles (tattvas)— the seven [from Earth to Śiva], then the triad from the vicinity of the Brahma-aperture up to Sadāśiva (comprising Vidyā and the rest), and above that the Śiva-principle together with the Śakti-tattva ending at Samanā—
one should, according to the previously mentioned procedure, sequentially [assign] all those [principles] to the disciple by means of the parts of the aforementioned Navātman.

Having purified himself, one should unite the self with the supreme Śiva—the ultimate reality—by means of the root mantra; that is, by means of the entire nine-fold mantra, taking into account its individual components. Of what nature is he? He is beyond the state of *unmanā*, attainable immediately after entering that state, the omnipresent and all-pervading Self who possesses power (*śaktimat*).

In that which has emerged from slight manifestation, in that which gives rise to all appearances, in the supreme peace where all differentiation has ceased, in the Sovereign Lord of the universe, and in the imperishable and unborn—thus, in the eternal. || 9 ||
Thus, each one [of these] is to be purified;
therefore, the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) have been declared.
Due to the rule beginning with *pātra* and so forth, there is an absence of the feminine suffix in the collective compound.
Now, we shall explain the nine principles (tattvas). 5-10.
In that regard:
"Nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), as well as necessity (niyati) and time (kāla);
likewise illusion (māyā), knowledge (vidyā), the Lord (īśa), Sadāśiva, and Śiva. (5.11)

Having purified these nine primary principles by means of the ninefold [mantras] in reverse order according to the previously stated rule, one should duly unite the Self with the pervasive reality (vyāpti).
Of the disciple;
but primarily,
when the fivefold reality (pañcatattvī) is to be purified...
Then—................the mantras of the speaker are indeed the denoters. || 5-12 ||
And by means of those [mantras], following the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta, one should purify the elements from Earth up to Space according to that same order.
He now describes the pervasion of the *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti, which is conducive to the purification of all the paths (*adhvan*) within the five *tattvas*:
Indeed, as far as the pervasion of the kalās extends, so far does that of the tattvas.

Speaking thus, it is said that here the entire procedure is as declared in the *Kalādīkṣā*; the only difference is that at the occasion of the installation of the *kalās* and so forth, the installation of the principles (*tattvas*) such as Earth and the rest must be performed with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. And for this reason, these five principles constitute the essence of the expansion of the mantras of the Lord’s faces.
He teaches that since everything consists of Supreme Bhairava, the pervasive realization of non-difference from Him is the supreme means for attaining purity. || 13 ||
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the three principles (tritattva) as they are to be purified:
those known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, which consist of the forms of the object of knowledge (meyam), the means of knowledge (mānam), and the knower (mātṛ).
He states the pervasion of its designator:
"The letter *a* is proclaimed to be the designator of the reality of the Self. (5.14)
One should know that it ends with Māyā...

the letter *a* belongs to the Praṇava (is situated within the Praṇava). One should avoid [the sequence] ending with Māyā by means of thirty-one principles; the Self is the object of knowledge for Śiva and Śakti, and its pervasion extends only that far.
...the generator even of that which is called Vidyā;
that should be known as extending up to Sakala.
Vidyā is the power whose nature is knowledge and action, pervading Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The All-encompassing One is Sadāśiva.
Above that is the letter *ma*, which belongs to Śiva, the pervader of the powers Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā. || 5-15 ||
But that drop which goes beyond that, whose true nature is the pervasion of the Unmanā state—
being the sound of space (khasvara),
it causes the void (kha) to resound and articulate; thus, it is of the nature of the supreme void (parākāśa).
Therefore,
[the mantra] is the designator of the Śiva-tattva, whose nature is the void (kha).
Having thus reflected upon this, and having first established the paths (adhvan) as before—
Having purified the disciple’s own self in due order, one should unite him with the supreme reality. 5-16 ||
By means of the Praṇava, according to the essence of the pervasiveness taught by Khasvaroka. || 16 ||
Thus, in this regard:
"The initiation into the principles (tattvadīkṣā) has been fully described as established in four divisions;
however, it was already shown that the initiation into a single principle (ekatattvadīkṣā) was also mentioned previously at the end of the section on 'Joining' (yojanikā)."

Having thus explained the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) as it was requested, the Lord, desiring to favor [the Goddess] and wishing to satisfy her intention, spoke as follows, intending to describe even the initiation of the levels (padadīkṣā) and so forth, though it had not been requested:
I shall explain the initiation of the feet (padadīkṣā) correctly and in its proper sequence.

He will briefly explain the initiation of the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), which has the same procedure as the initiations of caste (*varṇa*) and mantra, at this very juncture; however, it will be explained in detail in the tenth chapter. Following that, he first describes the initiation of the words (*padadīkṣā*). || 17 ||
In that regard—
since the syllables of the King of Vidyās are characterized by the number nine,
I shall describe to you their arrangement according to their individual distinctions. (5.18)
Therein—
having constructed a city with nine naves, characterized by nine lotuses— how so?
A wise man should draw the house measuring nine cubits and increased by eight finger-joints.

The "house" (*veśma*) is the field of the maṇḍala. When increased by eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—that is, by eight units—this entire field becomes two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths (224), which constitutes the reflection of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). Within that, on all sides...
By calculating it in seven parts, each part becomes thirty-two finger-breadths; therefore, for that purpose, an addition of eight finger-breadths is provided. || 19 ||
Then,
having divided that [circle] into seven parts, one should perform [the following].
Having done what? ...
having first divided the square, which is partitioned into southern and northern sections, and marked therein with fish-diagrams (matsyas). || 5-20 ||
Having marked the eastern and western directions from the Brahma-point using the *bhāvinī* [line], one should, with a cord measuring slightly less than a fourth part of the field's dimensions,
hold the end of the cord in the left hand at the two eastern and western marks and, with the tip held in the right hand, [draw the line].
Having produced two lines on the two sides in the shape of a fish-catcher's hook, and having divided the field into south and north by stretching a thread between them,
one should [mark] the corners with a thread measuring half the field, attached to the central marks situated on the sides.
The summary meaning here is: having produced the four fish-catches and divided them into a square by stretching out the threads therein. || 20 ||
Thus, when the square field is divided into seven parts by threads extending from east to west— one should draw forty-nine squares with a thread;
and by means of six threads extending from south to north through the center, [one obtains] forty-nine.
One should cause the storehouses to be raised up.
Having done thus—[place] a thread measuring thirty-two finger-breadths in the middle square. (5.21)
"Having drawn [the mandala], O Great Goddess, divided into four parts—
meaning that once it has been divided by four equal circular rotations starting from the Brahma-position, the space for the outer boundary line (vyomarekhā) is determined."
There, from among the four sections—
one should form the pericarp in the first [section] and the filaments in the second.
In the third [circle], one should draw the junctions of the petals, and in the fourth, the tips of the petals;
where the petals meet at their tips, those are the petal-junctions (dalasaṃdhi).
He describes the method for drawing the circles within the four previously mentioned divisions:
"Having drawn eight lines in the cardinal directions and likewise in the intermediate directions... (5.23).
One should rotate [the cord] four times to form four circles, each measuring four finger-breadths.
Having laid down eight cords in the eight directions and eight in their center, one should make four rotations from the Brahma-position toward the marks of the eastern divisions.
Then, having placed a thread between the two lines facing each other in every direction, [one should proceed as follows]. || 5-24 ||
Then, one should rotate the tip of the thread according to the method for drawing a half-moon;
for the purpose of forming two half-moons at each petal-junction, one should hold the thread with the left hand over the center of the two [points] marked by the side-lines of the eastern line.

Having fixed [the compass], one should rotate the tip of the string to the right from the two side-lines toward the center-line; here, each individual side-line becomes a petal joined at its length by being divided from the center. || 24 ||
In order to grasp the center between the two pairs of lines situated in each direction— which serve as the causes for the arising of the two half-moons—
and for the sake of establishing the filaments, the wise one should draw a central thread passing through the pericarp. (5.25)
They remain for that purpose within the *kiñjalka* (filaments) and *kesara* (anthers).

Therefore, in order to produce two filaments on both sides of the *kiñjalka*— which has arisen from the central line following the middle of each half-moon petal— and for the sake of producing two half-moons:
In the case of obtaining the middle [result], the first two sūtras should be given at the very beginning. Thus, in their entirety, these constitute thirty-two sūtras. || 25 ||
Concluding this and extending it to other cases as well, he says: "Having thus established the first leaf, one should establish the others in exactly the same way."
And there,
having drawn twenty-four filaments— || 5-26 ||
One should place a very beautiful circular line at the tip of each petal;
there are three filaments on every petal. "At the tip of each petal" means outside the petals once they have been produced, [and] "very beautiful" means complete. || 26 ||
Furthermore:
its end should be made square, according to that same measurement. || 5-27 ||
"Of that" refers to the lotus ending with the line of the square; "according to its measure" means a line having the same measure as the circular line. || 27 ||
To state the primary rule that serves as the foundation for this entire procedure, he says:
"First, Brahma must be established by means of the sun situated at the equinox.
Brahma is the central position; *heli* is the sun.
In that regard, first, O Dear One, one should establish the thread extending from east to west by means of a peg. (5.28)
A peg or stake measuring twelve finger-breadths in length. || 28 ||
How so?—
having fixed a gnomon in the center, one should rotate a line measuring sixteen finger-breadths around its side. (5.29)
From the point of the peg, one should draw a circle of sixteen finger-breadths for the sake of the twelve-finger lotus; this is intended as an illustration for the field one wishes to grasp. || 29 ||
And there—
O Dear One, in the forenoon one should mark the shadow situated in the west with clear indicators;
with the sun situated in the west, one should mark the eastern shadow.
Having thus marked the east and west directions on the back of the shadow-line at the point of the circle,

one should mark the north and south positions by means of the *dhruva*— that is, by means of the gnomon (*śaṅku*) acting as the cause— O fair-faced lady, according to the previously determined directions.
One should mark the circular line situated between the north and south using the thread placed between the two fixed fish-marks; or alternatively, in a sacrifice that must be performed at night,
one should first [mark it] by means of the *dhruva*— the immovable star named *Dhruva*, whose body is composed of fourteen stars.
One should establish the determination of the northern and southern directions. In this regard, they prescribe the following:

having fixed one's aim at the polar star situated in the north through the opening of the hollow tube, and having marked the northern direction according to that tube, [one proceeds] by means of the polar star in the tube.
One should mark the center, and following the star at its tail, mark the south.
Then, following the central aperture, one should also mark the east and west. For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere:
"Or [one may determine] the north by piercing the pole star."
Thus it has been said. As for what was stated there—
"either toward the east or by means of the pole star (dhruvatārā)"— in that case, having determined the center by means of its alignment with the pole star, one should proceed accordingly.

It should be understood that, having taken the eastern line, one should establish the other lines accordingly. Having fixed the pole star and performed the squaring of the site by means of taking the position of the pole star, one should construct a lotus in the middle portion of the forty-nine divisions according to the sequence previously described.
He concludes: "Then one should draw an eight-petaled lotus together with its pericarp. (5.31)
Then, having taken the squares of the directions characterized by the number eight,
the remaining ones are to be deleted, O lady of beautiful hips, by joining every other one.

For the purpose of the four gates in the four directions, one should omit the outer row of squares and, following the central lotus, take eight squares— separated by an intervening square— in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions for the sake of the eight lotuses. And thus, of the central path...
The acceptance of both the field of the eight lotuses and the gateway-passage is stated by means of a single [concluding] verse.
And thus, in the eight compartments,
one should then place eight lotuses in the cardinal directions.
Then, [one should] draw the outer doors.
How so?
O Goddess, one should likewise fashion the *śobhā* measuring half the width of the street (*vīthi*).
One should draw the ornamentation of that same measurement at the edge of the cheeks;
likewise, the neck should be of that same measurement—this is proclaimed as the door.

Having laid a thread along the length through the middle of the outer path (bāhyavīthī), and having formed the path in the first half, one should form the *śobhā* in the second half— measuring half the height of the designated path-area— as well as the *upashobhā*, which is a broad member arising from the sides of the neck of the doorway.
One should conceive of that subtle portion situated below it as the *kapola*. The *kapola* is the broad section at the front of the door.

The *kaṇṭha*, however, is the section preceding the *kapola*; one should conceive of its measurement as being equal to the measure of half the *vīthī* (procession path) previously determined, both in length and in width. Herein, regarding the *kapola*—

Although the measurement of the *māna* (the central hall) has not been explicitly stated because it is established by implication, nevertheless, it is understood from another *saṃhitā* that the measurement of the *vīthi* (the path) is equal to its length, while the measurement of the [outer] enclosure is half of that due to its width; the meaning is that the door is completed through the completion of these respective parts. || 34 ||
Thus,
it is taught that the city has nine naves through the division of eight gates;
since a gate is prescribed for each intermediate direction, there are two gates within the space between every three lotuses in every cardinal direction.

One should construct it thus: this maṇḍala of the city has nine naves, divided by eight doors, with nine lotuses situated in the positions of the nine naves. And here, two doors facing the deity should be kept closed. As it is stated in the Lakṣmīkaulārṇava:
"The three doors should be closed, but one should not close the western one;
and that [door] should be known as being in front of the Goddess and the God."
The east should be known as the west, and the west designated as the east;
the north should be known as the south, and likewise the south as the north.
"This sequence, spoken by Śiva, is common to all mantras;
it must be guarded with great effort from disciples of evil intent.
Thus [it is said].
This, however, has come down through the lineage of the Gurus. It is as follows:

"I bow to the one whose splendor is like that of a sky-lotus, with a radiant light blossoming from the threefold nature of the triad beginning with Ghorā, rising upward through the eight doors of the body perceived by the supreme eye starting from the base (mūlādhāra)."

"I salute my own Bhairava, the Lord of the Ninefold Self, the essence of the secret mandala of nine centers, whose manifestation consists of the divisions of the principles (tattvas), worlds (bhuvanas), and sacred nodes (parvas) beginning with the Root.
Thus [it is said].
The systematic presentation of its meaning here is as follows:

since it was previously stated, "But the falling of the *rajas* [particles] by means of the *dhāman*, beginning with the white [color], is taught in the Āgama" (4.35), the division mentioned in other Āgamas should be followed. And that is as follows:
In this case, a white line made from rice-flour should first be drawn;
the pericarp, mixed with the color of turmeric, should be yellowish-orange.
There should be three filaments on each petal, colored white, yellow, and red.
One may make those [filaments] white, or green in their interiors.
The corners are red, the pedestal is white, and the border line is one finger-breadth wide and white.
Thus it is said:
"The thumb is Śaktimān; the four fingers are the digits (kalās) of the Bindu."
Having made *rajas* the support for that, and through the touch of *śakti* with the *bindu*, [the process occurs].
"One should cause that mandala of power (śakti-maṇḍala) to fall by means of that which contains power (śakti-garbha). Thus it is stated in the venerable *Parā*. Alternatively:
"One should know the lotus to be white, and one should contemplate its filaments."
White, yellow, and likewise red, in sequence from the base, the middle, and the tip.
"The pericarp is like gold, and the lotuses are known to be green.
Here, the scattering of colored powders (rajaḥpāta) should be performed according to the meditation described for the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Then, O Goddess, having bathed according to the rule...
having performed the worship of the door...
The preceptor should enter the residence. || 5-35 ||
Then—
by means of the previously mentioned procedure— one should perform the ritualization of the body (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and so forth.
Then one should worship the god Bhairava, the Supreme Lord.
By what?
By the *praṇava*.
The meaning is: by means of the true essence of the all-pervading upward extension, characterized by the ninefold self (*navātman*), the six (*satka*), and the bindu.
Having done what? He says:
"O lady of excellent complexion, having offered a seat ending with Śiva.
Here, the word "with the *praṇava*" (the syllable *oṃ*) is to be applied as in the case of the crow's eye (applying to both preceding and following elements); therefore—

The meaning here is that one should worship Bhairava with the *praṇava*, which—as previously stated—possesses an infinite pervasion from the beginningless to the endless, the middleless, and the endless; and with that very same [syllable], which possesses a pervasion up to the *unmanā* state and expresses the Supreme Śiva who is non-different from *unmanā*. It describes the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*), the most excellent and sublime.
She who reflects upon that [truth] and possesses such a nature is called "Varavaṇīnī."
Where, what, and how should one worship? To this he says:
"In the center, one should worship the god Svacchanda, the Supreme Lord. (5.37)
According to the previously mentioned procedure, it is endowed with the six limbs (*aṅga*).
"In the center" means upon the pericarp of the lotus. The entire procedure, from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of water for the mouth (*argha*) to the deities, is complete.

Here, the limbs are also [worshipped] by means of the *praṇava* alone, ending with the respective name and the class-suffix (*jāti*), according to the ninefold division of the self's constituent parts.

Because there is no room for other mantras [to intervene], one should understand that in the same way, within the other lotuses as well, there is the worship of Bhairavas such as Kapālīśa and their respective limbs (aṅgas), which will be described hereafter. || 37 ||
Thus, the placement of the phonemes and their corresponding deities within the pericarp of the central lotus has been described; he now speaks also regarding its petals:
"One should place the phonemes on the eight petals, starting from the east and proceeding in order up to the northeast. (5.38)

In that regard—“One should know Sadāśiva by the letter *ha*, and so forth, O fair-faced one; [one should know] everything up to Prakṛti, with the conceptualization of the Lord of the Seat in the middle. (5.39)
Having placed Pīṭheśa Svacchandhanātha, the presiding deity of the Śiva-tattva, in the central pericarp,
[one should worship] according to the sequence of emanation with the syllables ha-ra-kṣa-ma-la-va-ya-ū associated with the Navātman mantra.
In the eight petals starting from the east and ending with the northeast, [one should worship] Kapālīśa, Śikhivāhana-krodharāja, Vikarāla, Manmatha,
Meghanāda, Somarāja, and Vidyārāja,
who preside over the principles (tattvas) of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidya, Māyā, Kalā, Niyati, Puruṣa, and Prakṛti.
The meaning is that one should worship after having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa). || 39 ||
Having explained the procedure for the central lotus, he now describes it concisely for the lotuses in the cardinal directions:

"One should worship the eight deities situated upon the pericarp of the lotuses of the directions. In the petals of the central lotus, starting from the east, those very deities such as Kapālīśa and the others [are worshipped] by means of the letters beginning with *ha*."
One should worship those very Bhairavas with those same syllables in the pericarp of the lotuses of the eastern and other directions.
[40] Regarding the station of Svacchandanātha in the eastern and other lotuses, he says:
"In that place, Bhairava is to be worshipped..."

By means of the *praṇava* as previously mentioned: in the center of the eastern lotus is Kapālīśa with the letter *ha*, while on the eastern petal is Svacchanda with the *praṇava*. In the center of the southeastern lotus is Śikhivāhana with the letter *ra*, and in the southeastern petal, in the place of Śikhivāhana, is Svacchandanātha with the *praṇava*.

The same applies to the others. And thus, because Svacchandanaatha is sequentially deposited in the place of each individual Bhairava, the essence of all Bhairavas and all the *tattvas* presided over by them consists precisely in their pervasion by the *śivatattva*, through the realization of non-duality with Him.
Thus, by virtue of its being composed of supreme non-duality, the essential nature of this great secret of the practice has been revealed;
