and therefore, through the specific form [of the mantra] "from all, from everyone" (*śarvataḥ sarvebhyaḥ*), the meaning of the mantra-word has become manifest— enough said.

Regarding the petals starting from the east, it is stated that for the petals other than those occupied by the lords of their respective seats (pīṭheśvara) beginning with Kapālīśa, the procedure for ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth is exactly as prescribed for the petals of the central lotus:
"The remaining [petals] are [filled] with the phonemes in due order. (5.40)

Furthermore, this arrangement of phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) has already been demonstrated by us previously through a grid (*prastāra*). Here, there are ten divine abodes (*devagṛha*) produced: nine by virtue of their individual residence in lotuses, and one by virtue of their totality. This is because the Blessed One, the King of Knowledge (*vidyārāja*), is the true essence of the *bindu*, and thus his constituent parts are also [of that nature].

At the time of worship, the yoga of the *bindu* (the point) is necessarily present. Furthermore, even each individual phoneme, through the pervasion of the sequence already demonstrated, is the very expansion of the complete King of Vidyās. As he will state:
"Since the God is all-pervading, he is remembered as being contained within all things."
"He is the bestower of that accomplishment and liberation; in the ultimate sense, it is not the letters. (8.25)
Having thus explained the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), he speaks of initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the order of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*):
"And one should purify [the sequence] from *prakṛti* up to Śiva, O beautiful goddess!
One should purify that collection of words whose beginning is *prakṛti*, which consists of the denotable form (*vācyarūpa*), and whose end is Śiva."
How so?
One should purify the central seat, beginning from the northeast direction. (5.41)

Having uttered the nine words beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the syllable *ū*, starting from the northeast petal of the lotus situated in the northeast direction and proceeding in order through the east and north directions,
preceded by the recitation of the *Praṇavavidyārāja*, [one should worship] the *prakṛti-tattva*.

Having contemplated the inclusion within this very [system] of the entire collection of principles beginning with Earth and ending with Guṇatattva— as well as the expansion of the other paths contained therein— just as before,
one should perform all the previously mentioned rites, such as the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), by means of the mantra ending with "Obeisance to the Nine Padas."

One should perform the rite. In this manner, by this sequence, one should purify the steps (padāni) as many as there are, up to the nine steps situated within the central lotus, which pervade the Śiva-tattva and begin with the letter *m* and end with the *praṇava*. As for the [formula] "Obeisance to the nine steps consisting of the form of the Prakṛti-tattva," used by some...

The sequence [of the mantra] has been stated; however, that is not correct, because it would result in the repetition of the well-known sequence of words taught in the *Kalādīkṣā* and the reverse-order pronunciation of the phonemes belonging to the *Navātman*, while neglecting the previously mentioned sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). In this regard, concerning the *Padadīkṣā*:

As in the initiation of the nine principles (navatattva-dīkṣā), the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the eighty-one syllables situated within the nine lotuses—from the center of the navel up to the end of Anāśrita—must be performed. || 41 ||
Having thus purified the path of the worlds (padādhvan), one should unite [the soul] with the supreme reality, Śiva, the ultimate cause.
He also extends [this procedure] by analogy to the initiation of the phonemes (varṇa) and so forth:
In this way, one should purify the castes, as well as the mantras and the worlds.
To what limit? He says:
"From Kālāgni up to Śiva. How should one perform the initiation (dīkṣā) regarding phonemes, mantras, and worlds? He says:
"...by relying on the procedure for the *kalās*.

The meaning is that one should divide each [element], such as the phonemes (*varṇas*), in accordance with the five sections previously described concerning the initiation by *kalās* (*kalādīkṣā*). Herein, mantras are authorized in the same manner as the initiation by *kalās*. And here..."

According to the principle stated in *Spanda* 3.15, "of that which arises from the mass of sounds," phonemes (*varṇas*) possess the quality of bondage; however, this is not the case for words (*padāni*) and mantras.

This is by virtue of denoting realities that are both distinct and non-distinct from one another. Just as mantras possess the quality of being purifiers even while they themselves are objects to be purified, that has already been determined; therefore, it should be recalled here. Thus, in this context, initiation into the categories of reality (*tattvadīkṣā*) is of four kinds, according to the divisions of three, five, nine, and thirty-eight.

The initiations pertaining to the *pada*, mantras, phonemes (*varṇa*), and worlds (*bhuvana*) have been described. Among them, regarding the initiation of the five [categories], there is the extension [of the rule] from the statement, "As far as the pervasion of the *kalās* extends" (5.13); and for the initiations of the phonemes, mantras, and worlds, there is the reference to "by resorting to the procedure of the *kalās*" (5.43).

Because this has been stated, one must consider the inclusion of the five paths (*adhvan-pañcaka*) within the *kalās*. However, in the initiation by words (*pada-dīkṣā*), which is divided into nine parts: in the first, the natural (*prākṛta*) section, within the group of nine words beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *ū*, reside the two *kalās* of *nivṛtti* and *pratiṣṭhā*; [and therein] are the elements from earth up to primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

The twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), the one hundred and sixty-four worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with the group of eight [starting] from Yoga, the twenty-four letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *ṭa*,
and the five mantras— Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Hṛdaya, Śiras, and Śikhā— are all included herein. 1.

In the *pauruṣa* [category], within the group of nine beginning with *ū* and ending with *ya*, there is the *vidyā-kalā*; in the principles (*tattva*), there are *puruṣa* and *rāga*; in the worlds (*bhuvana*), there are *tuṣṭi* and *siddhi*;
and [therein reside] *aṇimā* and so forth, the three rows of teacher and disciple, the channels (*nāḍī*), the eightfold body (*vigraha*), and the adventitious bonds of the body (*dehapāśa*).
The ten worlds of Gaṇeśa and Vidyeśa; the world of the ten Rudras beginning with Suhṛṣṭa;
and the world of the ten [beings] beginning with Kalyāṇī consisting of teacher and disciple—these are the fourteen worlds.
The two phonemes are Ña and Jha; the two mantras are Aghora and Kavaca. || 2 ||

Within the group of nine beginning with the vowel *ū* and ending with *va*, the two *kalā* mantras are assigned as before. Likewise, in the subsequent [groups], namely the principles (*tattva*) of Niyati and Vidya, there are the nine worlds of Vāmadeva and so forth, and the nine worlds of Vāmā and so forth;
the two phonemes are *ja* and *cha*. (3)
Within the ninefold Kālīya [group] beginning with the vowel *ū* and ending with the letter *l*, there is the principle (*tattva*) of Kālakalā;
therein are the ten worlds beginning with Śuddha and the triad of worlds beginning with Mahādeva, as well as the two phonemes *caṅ*. || 4 ||

In the group of nine belonging to Māyā, beginning with the vowel ū and ending with the letter ma, there is the principle (tattva) of Māyā; there are seven worlds (bhuvana), beginning with Gopatya and ending with Ananta; and the phoneme gha. || 5 ||
In the nine-word section of the Vidyā-mantra beginning with the letter *ū* and ending with *kṣa*, there is the principle of Vidyā (*vidyātattva*);
one world-sphere belonging to the Queen of Vidyās (*vidyārājñī*) who possesses the three qualities (*triguṇā*); the *kalā* of Śāntā; the two mantras of Tatpuruṣa and Astra;
and the phoneme *ga*. (6)
From the vowel *ū* to the end of *repha* (the letter *r*), there are nine [entities] belonging to Īśvara; their *kalā*-mantras are as before.

The *tattva* is Īśvara, and the fifteen worlds (*bhuvana*) range from the world of Īśvara up to the worlds of Jñāna and Kriyā. The phoneme *kha* [is associated with] the nine [entities] belonging to Sadāśiva, from the vowel *ū* to the end of *ha*; the *tattva* is Sadāśiva, which is indeed Sadāśiva itself.
The single world that pervades the infinite worlds beginning with Suśiva is the letter Ka. 8.

In the group of nine belonging to Śiva, beginning with the vowel *ū* and ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), there is the *kalā* Śāntyatītā; the *tattva* of Śiva, which is non-different from the *tattva* of Śakti; the sixteen worlds beginning with the world of Śāntyatītā and ending with the world of Śiva; the mantra of Īśāna, whose forms are non-different from [the faces of] Netra; and [the phonemes] beginning with the *visarga* and ending with the letter *ha*.
There are sixteen phonemes. || 9 ||

The initiation of the nine principles (navatattvadīkṣā) is like the initiation of the words (padadīkṣā). The distinction is that in that [initiation], the principles beginning with Prakṛti are to be established in the place of the words, whereas the words are to be included within the place of the principles. However, in the initiation of the three principles (tritattvadīkṣā), [they are included] within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).

The thirty-one principles beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā; the [five] kalās—nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, and kalā; and the one hundred and ninety-one worlds beginning from Kālāgni up to Ananta, starting from the Praṇava located in the direction of the hair-pores within the Prakṛti-square.
From the first *padma* to the end of the syllable *kṣa* in the southern [section], there are sixty-nine *padas*;
there are seven mantras—Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Hṛdaya, Śiras, Śikhā, and Kavaca;
and there are thirty-one phonemes from *kṣa* to *gha*. || 1 ||
In the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva), the Śāntā-kalā resides; the principles (tattvas) are Vidyeśvara and Sadāśiva;

there are seventeen worlds (bhuvanas), beginning with Vidyārājñī and ending with the world of Sadāśiva; the word-syllables (padāni) are three, namely *ra*, *oṃ*, and *ha* from the eastern lotus, and from the central lotus, those beginning with the vowel *ū* and ending with the consonant *ha*.
Eight and eleven; these are the two mantras for the *tatpuruṣa* weapon, consisting of the letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*. || 2 ||
In the Śiva-tattva, Śakti and Śiva are the two principles (tattvas); the word is the Praṇava; the worlds and so forth are as previously described. || 3 ||
1. In the initiation into the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), within the earth-principle (*pṛthivī*) lies the *nivṛtti* kalā;

there are one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*). There are nine lotuses starting from the lotus of *prakṛti*, because they are assigned up to the end of *prakṛti*. The two mantras are in the heart of Sadyojāta, and the phoneme is *kṣa*.
2. In the Water [element], the *kalā* is *Pratiṣṭhā*; the three mantras are *Vāmadeva*, *Śiras*, and *Śikhā*;

and the *padas* are the nine previously mentioned. These mantra-*kalā*-and-*pada*s extend as far as *Prakṛti*. In the same way, the letter *ha* consists of the eight worlds beginning with Lakulīśa and ending with Amara.
3. In fire, the letter *sa* is the seed-syllable; there are eight worlds beginning with Bhairava and ending with Hariścandra.
4. In air, the letter *ṣa* is the seed-syllable; there are eight worlds beginning with Bhīma and ending with Gayā.
5. In space, the letter *śa* is the seed-syllable; there are eight worlds beginning with Sthāṇu and ending with Vastrāpada.

6. In smell (gandha) is the letter *va*; the world belongs to Śarva. 7. In taste (rasa) is the letter *la*; the world belongs to Bhava. 8. In form (rūpa) is the letter *ra*; the world belongs to Paśupati.
9. In touch, the letter ya; the world of Īśāna. 10. In sound, the letter ma; the world of Bhīma. 11. In the generative organ, the letter bha; the world of Kaśyapa.
12. The letter *ba* is in the anus; it is the world of Mitra. 13. The letter *pha* is in the foot; it is the world of Viṣṇu. 14. The letter *pa* is in the hand; it is the world of Indra.
15. The letter *va* is in speech; it is the world of Agni. 16. The letter *dha* is in the sense of smell; it is the world of Earth. 17. The letter *da* is in the tongue; it is the world of Varuṇa.
18. The letter *tha* is in the eye; its world is the Sun. 19. The letter *ta* is in the skin; its world is Wind. 20. The letter *ṇa* is in the ear; its world is the Quarters.
21. In the mind (manas) is the letter *ḍha*; [it rules] the world of Candra.
22. In the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is the letter *ḍa*; [it rules] the eight worlds beginning with Sthaleśvara and ending with Ichagalāṇḍa.
23. In the intellect (buddhi) is the letter ṭha; there are four worlds: Devayoni, Krodha, Tejas, and Yogāṣṭaka.
24. In Pradhāna, which contains the qualities (guṇas) within it as its principle (tattva), is the letter ṭa.

From the first three lines of the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*), there are three worlds belonging to Śiva, Śakti, and the Uniter (*yoktṛ*); together with the world of the eight Lords of Wrath (*krodheśvara*) and the world of Prakṛti, there are five worlds.
Up to this point, the *kalās*, mantras, and words (*padāni*) are as previously described.

25. In the male [deity], there is the *vidyā* and the *kalā*; the two mantras are *aghora* and *kavaca*. At the end of the group of six ending with *māyā*, there are likewise the *kalā* and the mantra. In this same manner, from the letter *ū* to the letter *ya*, there is the group of nine *padas* situated on the lotus of the northern direction; the phoneme *ña*; and the body consisting of the three rows of *tuṣṭi*, *siddhi*, *guru*, and *śiṣya*, as well as the eight channels (*nāḍī*).
The twelve [worlds] of Pāśa, Āgantuka, Gāṇeśa, Vaidyeśa, and Pāśabhuvana.

26. In Niyati, there is a group of nine words beginning with the syllable *ū* and ending with *va*, located in the Vāyavya and Padma [sections], the letter *jha*, and the eight worlds beginning with Vāmadeva.

27. In the *kālatattva*, there is a group of nine worlds beginning with the letter *ū* and ending with *lā*, situated within the lotus of Varuṇa; the phoneme *ja* corresponds to the ten worlds of Śiva, beginning with Śuddha and ending with Śambhurāj.
28. In the *rāga-tattva*, there is the same group of nine worlds belonging to Puruṣa; the phoneme *cha* corresponds to the ten worlds of Rudra, beginning with Suhṛṣṭa.

The world of Kalyāṇādi and the worlds of the ten [groups] of teacher and disciple; 29. in Aśuddhavidyā, there is a fixed group of nine levels, the letter *ca*, and the nine worlds beginning with Vāmā and ending with Manonmanā.

30. In *kalā*, there is a group of nine words beginning with *kālīya*; the letter *ṅa*; and the three worlds of Mahādeva, Mahātejas, and Mahājyotis. 31. In *māyā*, there is a group of nine words beginning with *ū* and ending with *ma* from the *nivṛtti*-lotus; the letter *gha*.
The seven worlds, beginning with Gopatya and ending with Ananta.
32. In Śuddhavidyā, there is a set of nine words beginning with the southern lotus [and] starting with the vowel Ū and ending with KṢA;
the remainder is like the initiation by words (padadīkṣā).
33. In the Īśvara-tattva, there is a group of nine words beginning with ūkāra and ending with repha from the Āgneya-padmaka; the remainder is as in the Padadīkṣā.
34. In the Sadāśiva-tattva, there is a group of nine words beginning with ūkāra and ending with hā from the Prāk-padmaka; the remainder is as before.
Like the initiation by words (padadīkṣā).

35. In the Śiva-principle, which is non-different from Śakti, there is a group of nine words beginning with the letter Ū and ending with the Praṇava (OṂ), starting from the central lotus; the remainder is like the initiation by words (padadīkṣā). This pervasion of the paths (adhvavyāpti) is [described] in the text.
It has been indicated but not fully elucidated; let the wise apply their intellect here to the procedures for the correct initiation.

O Dear One, after a disciple has been initiated in one of these ways— excluding those initiated by means of the seedless initiation— one should subsequently cause them to hear the rules of conduct (*samaya*) arising from the tradition of the Tantras.

By the phrase "arisen from the tradition beginning with the form of Tantra," he indicates that, according to this division of lineages (*srotas*), the forms of the commitments (*samayas*) are indeed both distinct and non-distinct. || 43 ||
He said to them:
"One should not revile the god Bhairava, nor the scripture originating from another;
having abandoned the worldly latent impression (*vāsanā*) that perceives duality, one should likewise abandon all others arising therefrom."

The meaning is that one should regard even those various practices, the Bhairava scriptures, the specific forms of worship taught therein, and each particular deity as being worthy of veneration exactly like Parabhairava himself.
Furthermore: One should not revile Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, nor indeed the Vedas. (5.44)

The meaning is that one should not employ [the word] in censuring that [person], by means of an instigating action consisting in pointing out the impossibility of what was seen in that person's view. || 44 ||
The reason for this is as follows: since all [these paths] originate from Śiva and bestow the fruit of liberation,
they bring about the respective liberation appropriate to each, for those who rest solely in that [particular state], through the unity of their statements.
Even for those who possess complete knowledge of pervasion, [the initiation] grants immediate liberation—
from Śiva, who possesses manifold forms, according to the future teaching: "from the peaceful one whose form is unseen" (8.27).
Because all scriptures have arisen [from that source], they possess an inseparable pervasion with it.
With this very intention, it is said:
"Since everything originates from Śiva, it bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva."
Some here read the text as it is seen in ancient manuscripts:
"But with the intention of [showing] complete pervasiveness and unknowability—'Indeed, Māyā causes all to wander, through the desire for liberation in that which is not liberation. (10.1141)
He will state this and more in the following [verse]. || 45 ||
Furthermore:
One should not revile the Dharma taught in the Smṛtis, which shows the path of right conduct. (5.45)
The meaning is that one should not cause a disturbance in the minds of those who are devoted to that conduct.
The deities beginning with Brahmā, the Mothers, Cumbaka, Giri, the Vīras, the sisters, the cows, and likewise the hosts of spirits.

Even causes such as Brahmā and others are to be transcended; the "mothers" are Brāhmī and the rest according to worldly convention; he is the Guru who awakens the disciple to the secret meaning by kissing him through the lineage of oral transmission (*vaktra-pāramparya*); and he is like a mountain (*giri*), being immovable in the propitiation of mantras and other such practices.
The practitioner, the heroes who are devoted to the secret conduct, the sisters who are devoted to their mothers and are yoginīs,
the cows whose sanctity is established by the Paśu scriptures,
the spirits such as piśācas and apasmāras, and the hosts of Pramathas— one should not revile any of these.
The connection. || 46 ||
Furthermore:
"One must not damage property belonging to the deity, which is established in the Siddhānta.
That which is established in the Siddhānta—in the sense of the final determination—is that this substance is intended solely for the sake of the deity; therefore, one must not harm it.
One should not harm.
Furthermore:
O Supreme Goddess, one should not eat the food of a guru that has not been given.
One should not eat even that food belonging to the Guru which has not been graciously bestowed by him. || 47 ||

O fair-faced one, one should not despise liquor, meat, fish, or other such things; nor should one despise those who follow proper conduct, those who are without such conduct, or those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin).

"Other things" refers to the substances of heroes (*vīradravya*); "those without conventional conduct" (*nirācāra*) refers to those perfected ones (*siddha*) whose true nature is concealed by such [external] forms; therefore, one should not feel disgust toward them. || 48 ||
One should always consume the *caru* offered to one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
...one should always worship the Guru;
otherwise, due to the lack of qualification for the daily worship (nityārcā), [the rite would be invalid].
O Great Goddess, one should not touch household utensils with one's foot.
The household implements, such as the grinding stone, mortar, pestle, and so forth—
these being traditionally taught in the Mataṅgaśāstras as the sites for the symbolic representation of deities within the ritual procedure of the ninefold sacrifice (navayāga).
One should constantly contemplate the *saṃhitā*—
the *Saṃhitā*, which is the Śaiva scripture.
...one should always cause the devotees to hear it.
Whether it be the Guru or another authorized by him, this commitment (samaya) belongs primarily to the Guru alone.
One should not neglect one's daily rites nor the twilight worship, O fair-faced lady. (5.50)
Āhnika refers to the daily obligatory rites such as worship; saṃdhyā refers to the ritual service of mantras to be performed at the time of the twilights. || 50 ||
One should not recite the manual of the scripture in the presence of those who have not been initiated;
"the manual of the scripture" refers to the methodological system of the Supreme Lord’s teachings. (50)
He speaks regarding the subject of the practitioner:
"One should always worship the deity three times a day, remaining devoted to recitation and meditation. (5.51)
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening. || 51 ||
Therefore, a spiritual son or other [initiate], desiring the fruit of both goals, should always observe these commitments (samayas) as appropriate;
"both goals" refers to the fruits of this world and the next, namely enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus explained the ritual initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*) ending with the hearing of the traditional precepts (*samaya*), he speaks in order to define the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*):
"Therefore, I shall now proclaim the initiation of higher consciousness (*vijñānadīkṣā*) in its proper sequence. (5.52)
By means of the internal movement alone for the sake of purification; that is,
by the internal course within the self through knowledge,
which is the ascent upon the path of Suṣumnā, and by that which is "alone," meaning devoid of the *hotṛ* and other officiating priests.
Therein—having grasped the disciple's self, one should unite it with one's own vital breath. (5.53)
Having likewise uttered the *abhimāna*, one should then perform [the rite] as before.
Regarding *abhimāna*: "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*" (4.399).
Of the form thus described. || 53 ||
Having restated all of this that was previously mentioned, he states the specific detail:
"Then, by means of the *uddhātas*, one should purify the path of the disciple. (5.54)
Then, O virtuous lady, while properly uttering the reality (tattva) beginning with earth—

which is the partless nature (niṣkalasvarūpa) as previously described— one should purify the path beginning with earth, which has been deposited through meditative visualization, by means of the application of the previously mentioned binding of mudrās. || 54 ||
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Each one, however, respectively by way of a nature that is both different and non-different. (5.55)
Indeed, it is characterized by the utterance of syllables accompanied by sound (*sasvara*) and endowed with the deities;

through the pervasion of the *mantra*-kalās, it is distinguished as being both divided [from them] and undivided from its own essential nature due to its identity with non-conceptual reflective awareness (*avikalpa-vimarśa*). For that very reason, it is associated with the deities, such as Brāhmī and the others.

It is endowed with the correct, non-differentiated pervasion; each individual syllable, such as *a*, *u*, *m*, and so forth, is accompanied by its respective tone (*sasvara*), meaning it possesses internal resonance and is primarily characterized by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the *paśyantī* level of speech.
Therefore, the implied sense is that one performs the utterance of these syllables in the form of the unswerving sound of mantra. || 55 ||
In this regard:
"From the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā, there are five knots beginning with Earth;
together with their causes, by piercing these, Śiva is attained."
In accordance with the position stated in other scriptural traditions,
the Lord indicates the piercing of the five knots of the subtle elements— earth and so forth— situated at locations such as the center of the eyebrows, by means of the method of *udghāta*.
The first *udghāta* is said to arise from the conjunction of the *bindu* with *śakti*. (5.56)
Freed from the three deities...
as before, having caused the consciousness of the disciple to merge into his own vital breath (prāṇa),
preceded by the previously mentioned binding of the instruments (karaṇabandha).
Uttering the mantra, which is the essence of uncreated reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through the method of the emission of the central power (*madhya-śakti*) from the heart,

[one should contemplate] by means of the light of the *bindu* meditated upon in the center of the yellow, four-cornered, earth-element mandala marked with a thunderbolt (*vajra*) between the eyebrows— [this being] due to the union of that power, whose primary nature is the reflective awareness of the mantra, with the lunar point (*bīndu*).
"Correctly" means through the yoga of the upward-ascending sequence; because of that experience, this first *uddhāta* is liberated from the triad of deities known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra,
and consists of the absorption (*samāpatti*) into the mantra-deity known as Īśvara.
The meaning is that it consists of the purification of the primary quality called "odor" (gandha), which resides within the earth-element (pṛthvītattva) characterized by five qualities.
He states the second [syllable] for the purpose of purifying the quality called "taste" (rasa):
"Endowed with the fourth vowel at its end."
O Goddess of the gods, that is proclaimed as the second, the *uddhāta*.
The end of the fourth point-location is the half-moon (ardhacandra); by that, it is properly conjoined as before, meaning it consists of the immersion into the experience of that [half-moon].
He states the third [exhalation] for the sake of purifying the qualities of form:
"The complete utterance of the syllable *haṃ*, very long and joined with the *bindu*, is the third *udghāta* from the half-moon up to the *nirodhinī*. (5.58)

The correct pronunciation of the syllable that is the path of the *haṃsa* and the form of the *haṃsa*, which is the partless mantra, is according to the previously stated method; it is very long—as in:
"short, long, protracted, and subtle" (6.4).

Thus, according to the method of the future [state], there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*) at the end of the letter *M*; furthermore, it is properly joined with and rests upon the *bindu*—the subtle form—which serves as the limit for the first *udghāta*. Likewise, the third [vibration] is that which, proceeding from the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) up to the limit of the station of *nīrodhikā*—the limit of the rest of the second *udghāta*—is the expansion.
The meaning is that it effects the purification of the qualities of the form of the earth. || 58 ||
For the sake of purifying the quality of touch, he says:
"O Goddess, when the *udghāta* is broken, then there occurs the end of *nāda*.
That *udghāta*, O Mistress of the Gods, is proclaimed as the fourth. (5.59)
The "divided" (*bhinnā*) [utterances] are said to be the three places of *udghāta* (expulsion) by means of which the mantra is uttered;

furthermore, when that [utterance] reaches the end of *nāda* and comes to rest in the experience of *nāda*, then it is called *udghāta* for the sake of purification through the fourth quality (*guṇa*). At that time, the word "then" (*tadā*) would occur immediately after the word [in question].
It is applied. || 59 ||

He states the fifth [udghāta] for the sake of purifying the quality of sound: "That very same utterance of syllables, established at the end of the Vyāpinī, is the udghāta; O Goddess of the Gods, it is proclaimed as the fifth. (5–60)

"And that very [one]" refers to the partless (niṣkala). "Up to the pervasive" means having ascended to rest within that. "The fifth" is for the sake of purifying the fifth quality, which is sound (śabda). || 60 ||
Thus, in this manner—having then performed five expulsions (*udghāta*), the wise one should purify the earth.
"Then" (*tataḥ*) means because earth possesses five qualities; "wise one" (*budhaḥ*) means a knower. Here:
In all five upward movements (udghātas), having maintained the earth-dhāraṇā individually at the location of the *bindu*,
and resting in accordance with the upward movements at the ends of the *bindu*, half-moon (*ardhacandra*), obstructress (*nirodhinī*), sound (*nāda*), and pervasive one (*vyāpinī*),
[the teacher effects] the state of being the enjoyed and the enjoyer within the five qualities— beginning with smell and ending with sound— within the disciple’s own self.
One should purify.

And thus, even when resorting to the pervasive [state] as the ultimate support, he states that through subtle pervasion, the locus of experience for the principles (tattvas) beginning with water is purified only within the abode of the Bindu, and not otherwise:
"Thus, [the sequence] ending with the letters A, U, and M is purified; not otherwise. (5.61)
The end of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* is the locus of the *bindu*. "In this way" means:

through the purification of the earth-tattva by means of the logic of the purification of the five qualities inherent in sound—[achieved] from the fivefold *udghāta* consisting of the penetration up to the *vyāpinī*.

"It is not otherwise" means that purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) occurs precisely through the initiation by oblation (*huti-dīkṣā*); therefore, one should not have any doubt regarding this initiation by knowledge (*jñāna-dīkṣā*), as it has been determined that even in the initiation by oblation, knowledge alone is primary. And it is stated in the venerable *Matanga-pārameśvara* as well:
"For one who does not attain [the goal] through knowledge, ritual action is prescribed.
Thus [it is said]. || 61 ||
Thus, in this manner—
yogis should then contemplate the pure earthly element (pārthiva-tattva) as having become water, together with the self, through yoga. (5.62)
The word *atha* indicates the sequence:

first, the extraction of the disciple’s consciousness from the pure principle (*śuddhatattva*); then, its stabilization therein; then, the union of the mantra, the vital breath, the disciple’s self, and one’s own self within the [disciple’s] own vital breath.
The form [of the practice] consists of the contemplation of *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) and so forth. "That very [element]" refers to the principle (*tattva*) of earth.

By the statement "having become water," the contemplation of both pure and impure principles is indicated. By the phrase "by yogis through yoga," it is shown that those who are not yogis have no qualification for this at any time. "Together with this as one's self" [means...]
The disciple should also contemplate himself as having attained a state of oneness with that water-element for the sake of its yoga.
At this juncture, in the place of the half-moon,
one should visualize [the deity] in the form of a drop of water situated in the center of a white-colored half-moon mandala marked by a lotus.
One should perform the concentration (dhāraṇā) on the water-element; such is the traditional teaching (āmnāya).
Then, when the earthly element and the disciple’s own self have become water through the aforementioned meditation, the practitioner of mantra should again utter that same [seed-syllable] four times,
ending with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and joined with *dhāraṇā*.
"That very" refers to the partless essential nature (*niṣkalasvarūpa*); "the practitioner of mantra" (*mantrī*) refers to one who has attained *sāmarasya*;

"up to the point of the *bindu*" refers to the location of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); thus has *dhāraṇā* been explained. "In four" means, according to the reasoning previously stated, sequentially in the stages of the half-moon, the *nirodhinī*, the *nāda*, and the *vyāpinī*.

The meaning is that one should impart the four upward thrusts (udghātas) which consist of the nature of rest. Regarding the reading "one should utter again," the number four should be applied to the sense of the object and so forth. || 63 ||

Having thus purified the water-principle (jala-tattva) and having resorted to the previously mentioned sequence ending in *sāmarasya*, one should contemplate [the disciple] within oneself, drawing him from that water-principle— ... || 5–63 ||
And for this reason:
"Once the mass of water has been purified, one should contemplate it as having become fire;
by implication, that very water [is merged] with the self of the disciple," and so forth, as before.
And here, in the station of *nirodhikā*,

one should perform the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the principle of fire (*tejastattva*), which takes the form of a red triangular mandala marked with the power (*śakti*), and then, in the stations of *nirodhin*, *nāda*, and *vyāpinī*, [one should maintain] the state of resting in mantra.
Among them, those three consisting of the element of fire remain in a state of cessation. || 5-64 ||
The reading "tejodghātāt" belongs to the Īśa school; the meaning is: having performed the suppression [of the breath], one should fix the concentration on the fire (*tejodhāraṇā*) therein. || 64 ||
Thus, when the fire element has been purified through three upward strokes (*udghāta*)— with the other five paths having been absorbed within it as before—
there is no longer fire; thereafter, the air is purified by two upward strokes.
As before, having performed the [contemplation] of its abiding in that and its abiding in the self, and having visualized the fire as extinguished,
one should bind the wind-dhāraṇā in the place of the *nāda* in the form of a blue-colored maṇḍala marked with a hexagon and a dot (*bindu*).

By means of the two types of *udghāta*, which consist of the resting in mantra at the locations of *nāda* and *vyāpinī*, one should purify the *vāyu-tattva*, the locus of experience for the disciple's self.
Then, one should contemplate that [breath], as it dissolves into space, by means of the upward expulsion (udghāta). || 5.65 ||
That wind. || 65 ||
This clarifies the following:
"When the wind has perished, one should then unite with the void by means of a single *udghāta*.
'Perished' (*naṣṭa*) means that because it has become a mere residue of space (*ākāśaśeṣībhūtatvāt*), it has ceased from being a binder of the disciple's self. From that...
Thus, the extremely subtle principle of space (*ākāśatattva*), within which the other five paths (*adhvan*) are contained, is [traversed] by a single *udghāta*,
because space possesses only one quality.
And that which is this most subtle emptiness—she should be known as the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), established at the end of the fifth [tattva]. || 5-66 ||
In the fifth [stage], situated at the end within the nature of the *vyoma-tattva*,

the Guru— being proficient in the utterance of mantras— should perform the *vyoma-dhāraṇā* (the concentration on space), which has the form of a circular mandala marked by the extremely subtle power of sound (*śabda-śakti*) that is internally void.
Resting right here together with the self of the disciple, one should contemplate the state of being composed of supreme splendor.

And thus, in this case, by means of the greatness of the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), because the disciple’s purpose has been fulfilled, there is no longer any capacity to bestow further experience; consequently, since it is no longer binding, the entire sphere of objects of experience becomes purified for the disciple. This is because [the state is characterized by] the pentad of powers known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action—

The venerable Lord Svacchanda, whose true nature is the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*), who is preeminent in the powers of consciousness and the rest, [is] the Great Māyā, which consists of the concealment of his own nature as the five knots beginning with Vyāpinī and ending with Bindu— [the knots] that manifest as the five principles known as Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidya.

Veiling [the self] by means of his power (śakti), he sequentially projected the thirty principles— from Māyā down to Earth— which involve progressively greater degrees of contraction, through six pentads of categories that mutually participate in a relationship of pervader and pervaded consisting of both power and manifestation.

Regarding the phrase "on the level of the contracted subject": having become one with the disciple’s self through the teacher— the yogi who has attained that very nature by means of [the disciple's] grace— and having dissolved the entire ground of experience (*bhogabhūmi*) of the disciple’s consciousness according to the method of the aforementioned pervasion of the *udghāta*, by means of the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).
One must indeed bring about the state of consisting of the fivefold powers beginning with *cit*.
Therefore, even after thus purifying the extremely subtle elements such as earth— which are the essence of the pervasion of the thirty-five *tattvas*—
he speaks in order to purify even the stage of *samanā*, which consists of their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).

The meaning is that the disciple’s self (ātman) must then be joined by the Guru to the power of *samanā*, which consists solely of the contemplation (*manana*) of the expansion of the most subtle reality (*susūkṣmatamatattvaprapañca*), for the sake of removing even those residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of duality that remain.
And thus—
..................he is said to pervade that reality.
That reality called *samanā*, which consists of the initial outlining of all realities without exception, is what he pervades.
This is the meaning.
And when this entire collection of principles ending with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) has been purified, one attains the state of the pure Self; thus he says:
"Then, extending through the Self, upwards..."
The word "it becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Thus, although the disciple’s self has attained the nature of the supremely pure Self, it nevertheless proceeds from that state to the state of Supreme Bhairava— which consists essentially in non-difference from the supreme powers of consciousness (cit) and the rest—
by means of the process of conjunction (*yojanikā*) to be described immediately hereafter; thus he says:
...all-pervading; then again, [5.67] ||
The word "becomes" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 67 ||
In this context, he states a reasoning in the form of a single summary (udghāta) to indicate the method of union (yojanikā):

"For the knower of yoga, the Self established at the end of the principles (tattvas), by means of a single summary, should unite [it] with the Supreme Reality, which transcends the Unmanifest (unmanā) and is all-pervading. (5.68)
The state beyond the principles (tattvas) is above Samanā; it is called "beyond Unmanā.
By entering into the experience of that, one attains the essential nature of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat). || 68 ||
He clarifies the statement "one should effect the union" [with the following]: "Listen, O Goddess, as I speak of the union in the supreme reality.
By this statement, he shows that the meaning of this matter is to be understood through attentive concentration.
O Goddess, one should recite the mantra in its short, long, and protracted forms, and the supreme [mantra]. (5–69)
Having reached the supreme reality through the division of the higher and the lower—

namely, as short, long, protracted, subtle, and extremely subtle— immediately thereafter, in the section on the five *praṇavas*, [the text treats] each of the measures (*mātrā*) of the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.

Even for those that constitute a single part of the *praṇava*, he will state that they possess the nature of the *praṇava* according to the established principle: "Even a single portion of Brahman does not transcend its universal form. Therefore, one should recite the short mantra, and so forth.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed appropriate. "By way of the division into higher and lower" means by way of the distinction between the subtle and the extremely subtle. "The supreme" refers to that which has gone to, or attained, the state beyond the *unmanā* [state].
In this regard:
the three deities joined with the bindu, the half-moon, and the nirodhikā. (5.70)

One should know the *nāda* as conjoined with *śakti*, along with *vyāpinī*, *samanā*, and *unmanā*; this is the implied meaning. That [state] wherein there is the collection of the three gods, Brahmā and the others, within the three *kalās* whose nature consists of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*—that is so described. || 70 ||
Furthermore:
"And Unmanā, as well as Para, the all-pervading, auspicious, and immutable Śiva. (5.71)
The word "to be known" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, how and of what nature that knowledge is—all of this has already been determined in detail previously. || 71 ||

Thus, having understood the entire procedure for these [mantras] in its entirety and in the proper sequence, the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) should then apply them; otherwise, he should not apply them at all. (5.72)

"Everything" refers to the complete performance—meaning the correct pronunciation—of these objects of mantra, as refined by the previously mentioned measures of recitation (*cāra*) and so forth, through the stages of certainty, firm establishment, and direct experience. For this very reason, he is a "mantrin," one who knows the true essence of mantra correctly. (72)
He clarifies that very procedure:
"The triad residing in the *bindu* is in sound...
That triad of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) belonging to the mantras which ends with the letter *ma* resides in the *bindu*.
Having been brought to the state of being the very essence of the experience of the wise, it should produce within the word— which is itself bliss— the quality of being identical with that [bliss].
Since the fourth is indeed the *bindu* itself,
therefore the triad ending with the letter *ma*— resting in *nāda* and preceded by rest in that [bindu]— [is established].
One should perform [it].
These three—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Rudra—
are [designated as such] due to the distinction of their designata (vācya).
And this—consisting of three measures—is called a phoneme (varṇa). || 5.73 ||
These three measures (mātrās), by virtue of being the nature of the act of utterance and having the form of phonemes (varṇa), are "gross" (sthūla) in meaning. || 73 ||
The fourth, however,
is the Lord Bindudeva;
the meaning is that he consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [Bindu].
Thus, for one who performs the utterance of mantra in this manner— ................the sound proceeds in the throat;
for him, the sound whose true nature is the mantra consisting of the digit of resonance (nādakalā), arising from the heart, [proceeds] in the throat.
It exists in a state of excellence; the meaning is that from that point onward, it attains the state of being uttered according to the method to be described in the section on the five *praṇavas*.
And that—
therein, the word is situated within the act of [utterance]...
it is the form of the word consisting of Paśyantī, included within the act of pronunciation, and not [the other].
The meaning is that it is manifested by the intermediate and the manifest speech.
For this very reason, she is remembered as the power of action (kriyāśakti). || 5.74 ||
Thus, that sound, which resides in the effort of articulation, O Goddess, is said to proceed from the palate;
[this refers to] that [sound] of the speaker [proceeding] in the palate (meaning: in the palate of the speaker).
Having gone even a little further from there, the sound proceeds to the end of the nose. (5.75)
The end of the nose is the middle of the eyebrows; this much is the extent of the pervasion of the power of action (kriyāśakti) belonging to the Mantra level.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) should be understood with effort:
the sound situated in the region of the head extends as far as the forehead. (5.76)

When that very sound, through the aforementioned effort consisting of the practice of the nostrils and so forth, ascends from the cranial site (*mūrdhasthāna*) to the sites beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) by means of the previously described method of *udghāta*, it comes to abide as far as the forehead (*lalāṭānta*).
The meaning is that, by withdrawing into a subtle form at that time, having reached the pinnacle of experience, it attains the nature of knowledge.
Thus, having attained the form of the *bindu* and so forth, the phoneme (*varṇa*) consisting of the letters A, U, and M— which resides within sound—
has entered the state of resonance (*nāda*) and has assumed that very nature.
And being thus—...
"the eradication of those has been proclaimed.
"Of those" refers to [the powers] ending with Bindu; that very sound consists of the experience of the digit of Nāda.
The *udghāta* previously mentioned is distinguished by divisions such as the fivefold and so forth; it is not anything else at all.
Even having resorted to such an extensive level of the Mantra-system,
those who remain there turn back— those who, without ascending the series of steps beginning with Śakti and the rest, find contentment in that very place.
...are utterly devoid of the knowledge of Śiva. || 77 ||

Those who are not content do not even enter the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which is the most effective means for realizing the mantra-based knowledge of Śiva consisting of supreme bliss; how much less, then, Śiva himself? Therefore, the meaning is that one must exert effort to ascend to each successive stage. || 77 ||
Now, in order to demonstrate the internal distinction that will arise— which is accessible only to the subtlest experience— within these very stages beginning with the *bindu*,
he says: "The *bindu* is established in five ways, as are the *ardhacandra* and the *nirodhikā*."
Regarding the description of the enclosure of the *bindu* on the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), he will state:
"O lady of excellent vows, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti are recorded as the retinue of that Śāntyatīta."
"In its northern direction, Śāntyatītā is situated. (10.1217–18).
Likewise:
"Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, Vimalā,
and Śivā— these, O lady of excellent vows, are remembered as being located in the crescent moon within the portion to be restrained."
"Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā. (10-1220-21).
Thus, these [powers] exist in a fivefold state.
Now,
"his sound would have transcended"—
"his" refers to the Lord Bindu, whose pervasion extends up to the experience of cessation; [the sound] has transcended that Lord Bindu.

That phoneme (*varṇa*) becomes sound (*nāda*), and it attains the nature of the awareness of sound (*nādāmarśarūpatā*). Although one should have said "it" (*tam*), the use of the genitive "its" (*tasya*) is intended to show that this attainment of the form of sound belongs specifically to the *bindu*; likewise in what follows, the genitive is to be understood with the intention that each preceding state reaches a further excellence in each subsequent stage.
He states the reasoning for this experience: "But this [consciousness] would be delimited by... (5.78).
When the mouth is slightly opened, it attains a state of being delimited by the previously mentioned divine hand-gesture (*divyakaraṇabandha*); this is the meaning.
And this is the God of gods, Sadāśiva.
He is the "God" (deva) even of the Bindu, which is the essence of luminosity (dyotana); he is the Lord (deva), supremely radiant and sovereign.
And this [breath], which is of the nature of sound—sound is traditionally said to be fourfold, which carries a great velocity. (5.79)
Regarding the obstruction of sound (*nādāvaraṇa*), he will say:
"Indrikā, Dīpikā, Rodhikā, and likewise Mocikā. (10.1226). By means of these powers (*śakti*), its fourfold nature is established. || 79 ||

But surely it will be said: "The fifth *kalā* among them is declared to be upward-moving" (10.1229). How then can there be a fourfold division for this? True; however, that [fifth *kalā*] does not [belong to the fourfold division].
He states that there is no pervasion by sound:
"The fifth does not carry sound..."—
the meaning is that whatever is of the fifth kind does not proceed in the form of sound.
How, then, does it come to be? He says:
"It is traditionally held to be upward-moving;
for that which is established in the state of pervasion through the desire for the upward movement of the *nāda* is precisely non-different from the contact with the Power (*śakti*)."
The meaning is that it is called "nādānta" (the end of sound) and "avyaktadhvani" (unmanifest sound).
Now,
"his power would be past"—
the meaning is that it does not even cause him to sound.
And that [wisdom], established in five ways, is as follows: || 5-80 ||
He will state this later, beginning with: "But the power (śakti) situated above has the form of a sleeping serpent" (10.1241).
She is indeed Subtle, and most subtle, as well as Immortal and Immeasurable.
Since the pervasion of sound has here come to an end, he states what kind of experience there is:
"O Goddess, there touch would be..."— the remainder being "of the nature of bliss."
Furthermore:
"In that regard, the knower of the Self is as before.
In that state of Śakti, the one who knows the Self and is satisfied by the experience of Śakti is "as before," meaning he reaches the state of Śiva.
This means "he attains"; in this way, it should be applied to what follows as well.
Now, therefore—pervasive and extending beyond, she is established in five ways. || 5.81 ||
He too, touching [the state] and desiring to ascend to the upper station, becomes pervasive in form for the yogin who consists of pervasion.
And therein:
"Vyāpinī is of the nature of space, infinite, the Mistress, and also Anāśritā. (10.1252)
Thus, there is the experience of the five most subtle powers that are about to be described. 5.81.
And here—
[the question is] whether one perceives the tactile sensation residing in the tip of a hair at some time or not.
"At some time" means that on the occasion of ascending to that state, one either perceives the tactile sensation in its entirety or does not.
The meaning is that at the height of its ascent, one experiences only pervasion (*vyāpti*) and not a distinct tactile sensation (*sparśa*).
Thus it is said:
"O Supreme Goddess, she is perceived as all-pervasive, not as [ordinary] cognition. (5.82)

Regarding that which was stated—whether it perceives touch or does not perceive it—it was concluded that this is "pervasive" (vyāpinī) and not "cognition" (jñāna); the meaning is that this is not the power of cognition, but rather the power of will (icchā-śakti). || 82 ||
Now,
"even beyond that" means that she remains having transcended even that all-pervasive knowledge (*vyāpinījñāna*).
Because it has been stated that "Śamana is sequential cognition, while Unmanā is simultaneous," one who desires to enter into the experience of Unmanā should not allow the mind to function there.
The meaning is that one should not be satisfied with that alone;
thus, it should be understood that this much is the pervasion of the power of will belonging to mantra.
Since the manifold diversity of existence, consisting of both being and non-being, is not yet fully delineated within the *samanā* state, it remains subject to rejection; therefore,
having transcended that state and ascending to the plane of *unmanā*—
He says that in the middle one experiences the state of the absolute self alone: "But from that, one becomes the pure self. (5.83)

Thus, having attained a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the nature of pure consciousness, the excellent Guru should unite the disciple’s self within *unmanī*; the compound [should be understood as] "at the end of *unmanī*. This occurs within the essence of the aesthetic identity with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*).
The meaning is that one who is proficient in that immersion should cause [the mind] to rest in the experience of the independent Lord.
And thus—engaged therein in that supreme peace, one shall attain great tranquility. (5.84)
Being thus joined, he has attained oneness; through the melting away of every stain of duality, there is supreme peace.
Thus, in this manner,
the tradition transmitted through the lineage of gurus has been revealed.
"Paramparā" (the lineage) indeed means "pāramparam" (transmission from one to another), [referring to] the gurus such as Śakti, Sadāśiva, Śrīkaṇṭha, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: this has been known by me through the lineage (*pāramparya*), which is the sequence of the transmission of secret experience; it is called *sampradāya* because it is bestowed upon those who have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) following proper initiation and other rites;
it has been illuminated, and it has been told by me to you as well, preceded by the logic of its transmission.
Thus, even though the tradition has been received from one's own guru, it is transmitted to disciples by other gurus according to their respective established lineages.
In that regard—[the method] for uniting with the supreme reality has been explained to you. (5.85)
The meaning is that this is stated in the fourth chapter itself, beginning with the verse: "Having known the measure of the movement, as well as the movement of the vital breath" (4.231). || 85 ||
Thus, having understood this most excellent tradition in this way— O lady of beautiful hips— one should perform all ritual actions;
that is to say, one should remain established in the very majesty of the measure (parimāṇa) throughout all states of worldly activity.

The meaning is that one should employ the teacher, the practitioner, and others in their respective appropriate activities only after being preceded by this knowledge. "O lady of excellent hips" (*varārohe*) is as before.

Thus, having discussed the initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*), he gives instruction by way of suggesting that this initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) must also be performed in other initiations pertaining to the paths (*adhvadīkṣā*):
"The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the path of limited powers (*kalādhvan*), and likewise the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). (5.86)
O Dear One, having thus purified the path of phonemes, mantras, and words, one becomes pure;

just as the five other paths are internalized within the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*), so too, having performed this by means of the upward movement (*udghāta*) and having joined [the self] to the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), one becomes pure and attains the state of Supreme Bhairava.
The meaning is that the Guru, together with the disciple's self, as well as any other path, becomes purified by performing exactly in this same manner.
He concludes: "This indeed is the initiation of concentration (*dhāraṇādīkṣā*)...
because, although it begins with the "initiation of consciousness" (*vijñānadīkṣā*), it is performed according to the aforementioned sequence of concentration.
There is no fault even if the term "initiation by means of retention" (dhāraṇādīkṣā) is used in the concluding summary.
Stating that "this [practice] should not be performed by everyone who is a guru," and wishing to introduce the subsequent chapter as well, he establishes the thematic connection of the section:
"But here, it must be performed by the yogin. (5.87)
Or, O Goddess, by a mantra-adept—

a yogi who possesses the higher knowledge of supreme penetration— or else by one who has attained mastery of the mantra through the sequence of practice to be described immediately hereafter in this tantra; by such a person it should be performed.

Because there is no difference in the capacity of both [the teacher and the disciple] in this matter, and because no one other than these two is authorized; thus, this [initiation], when performed in this manner, becomes truly well-performed. (5.88)
One indeed attains perfect cessation.

Thus, in the fourth chapter, the initiation into the *kalās* was taught, as well as the initiation into a single *tattva* according to our own system. Here, however, there are four types of initiation into the *tattvas*— namely those divided into three, five, nine, and thirty-six— as well as the initiation into the *padas*.
Like the initiation of the nine principles (*navatattvadīkṣā*), there are three initiations—of phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and worlds (*bhuvana*)—which are like the initiation of the *kalās*.

And in the tenth [chapter], the extensive initiation of the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*) will occur; thus, these are the eleven initiations according to the variety of the paths (*adhvan*). And the twelfth is the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) by means of the method of emission (*uddhāta-yukti*).

These [initiations] amount to thirty-six in the case of the *putraka* (spiritual son), due to the distinction between those with seed (*sabīja*), those without seed (*nirbīja*), and immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*). In the case of the *ācārya* (teacher), there is only the initiation with seed, which has twelve varieties.

In the case of the *sādhaka*, who is of two types—according to the distinction between the *śivadharmī* and the *lokadharmī*—there are twenty-four varieties as before. [In the case of the] *samayin*...

However, since the *adhvan-āsana* (seating on the paths) has not been mentioned, [the initiation] is twofold by way of piercing the knots of the heart and other centers through knowledge and action; thus, there are seventy-four varieties of initiation here in brief. Even therein, for the practitioner of worldly dharma (*lokadharmī-sādhaka*), there are further distinctions based on the performance of rites such as those of the *sakala-niṣkala-aghoreśvarī*.

Furthermore, they become manifold due to internal diversities and the distinctions between those who follow the material path (*bhautika*), those committed to lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika*), and teachers (*ācārya*). In this regard, the Buddhists raise an objection specifically concerning initiation (*dīkṣā*): "In this context, what is being refined by initiation—the self (*ātman*) or the intellect (*buddhi*)?"
Of what [are we speaking]: of impurities such as the grasping at a self, or of karmas?

Is it for a self upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, or for another? Does the descent of power apply to one whose impurities are not yet exhausted, or to someone else? And what is this "purification" (*saṃskāra*) of the self? Is it the cessation of karma?

Is it the cessation of the experience of pleasure and pain, the vision of discrimination from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth, the knowledge of one’s own true nature, or the vision of non-duality? And what is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the intellect (*buddhi*)?
Is it the capacity to impel the sense organs, the instilling of the abandonment of passion and the like, or its total uprooting?

Is it that the impurities themselves lack the capacity to produce their effects at that very moment, or is their refinement dependent upon death? And what of the same regarding karmas? Furthermore, is that [grace] based solely on scripture as its authority, or is it also established through reasoning?

In this regard, the destruction of impurities such as the misconception of self occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and from the destruction of impurities, the descent of power follows.

Thus, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) were to occur for one whose impurity (*mala*) has not been exhausted, it would happen for everyone; and if the exhaustion of impurity were to come from some other source, then the purification of the self (*ātman*) would result from that very source—so what is the use of the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*) caused by the descent of power? Furthermore, regarding the self...

What kind of refinement (*saṃskāra*) can there be for that which is eternal and of a single nature, remaining unchanged whether it undergoes the cessation or non-cessation of karma and its fruit? If it were to undergo change, its eternity would be lost. Furthermore, when karma and its fruit—which are distinct from it—are destroyed, what happens to that [self]? If you say that its inherence (*samavāya*) in them has ceased, then that inherence itself, like karma and the rest, must also be impermanent.

If [agency and enjoyment] were restricted to the Self alone, then the Self would possess neither the state of being an enjoyer nor the state of being an agent, nor would liberation—which consists in the cessation of those two—be possible. Furthermore, the two positions regarding the nature of the vision of discrimination from *prakṛti* and so forth bring about a distinction between this [Self] and that [nature], because it was previously not of that nature. [This applies to] the vision of the Self and the vision of "mine" and so forth, which are rooted in that [vision of the Self].

Furthermore, since it is the cause of passion and the like, there would be bondage for him [the Self] because of that. In the view of non-duality (advaita), since there is no other whatsoever, and thus action— whether enjoyment or cognition— is untenable,
there would be the dissolution of agency, knowership, and essential sovereignty for liberated souls.
If it were established that the intellect lacks the capacity to impel the senses, there would be a deficiency of instruments for the initiated person;

furthermore, defects such as passion and the like, along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), would not cease for the initiated person. If the uprooting of the intellect were intended, the consequence would be the falling away of the body immediately after initiation. [This is so] because the impurities (*mala*) would have been rendered powerless at that very moment.
The continuity of worldly existence would be severed. The path of flight consists in the induction of incapacity with respect to death.

Furthermore, at the moment of death, the initiate’s grasping of the self and so forth is perceived just as before. The same should be stated regarding karmas; for there is no [need for] initiation in the purification of karmas whose effects have already begun.

If it is argued that [the Buddha] possesses such capacity, then what assurance can there be regarding others? If it is claimed that this is established by the authority of scripture (*āgama*), then what prevents that scripture from having that very same purpose? Just as a seed does not produce a sprout due to the obstructive power of a mantra, so too the seeds of karma do not produce cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

By the statement regarding the perfect accomplishment [of the soul] through seeds and so forth, let it be understood that for one who has been initiated, even such things as oil massages, burning, and the like—which, like seeds and so forth, are causes for the production of incapacity—should be performed. Since actions are formless, oil massages and the like do not exist [in them]; therefore, initiation alone destroys those [actions]. And thus:

If it is argued that even lightness is perceived in one who has been initiated by the *ghaṭadīkṣā*, [we reply: this is not so for formless things such as sin (*pāpa*), because they lack the property of weight (*gurutva*). Therefore, liberation is simply the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadṛṣṭi*) preceded by the cultivation of momentariness and other [doctrines]. To this, it is said: here, it is indeed the purification of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) [that is meant].

Initiation (*dīkṣā*). For instance: this self, by means of the *āṇava* impurity—which consists of the desire for objects denoted by the word "longing" and whose nature is the sense of being incomplete due to the appearance of contraction; and by the *kārmika* [impurity], which consists of various pure and impure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and bestows various births, lifespans, and experiences;...

And by its power, he is enveloped by the impurity called *māyā*, which consists of the sheaths (*kañcuka*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the gross elements; which possesses the threefold bodies of birth; and which experiences the manifold worlds that serve as their substratum, along with the entire multitude of objects to be enjoyed. For this reason, [it applies] to everyone indeed...

This matter is indeed established by such cognitions as "I am contracted," "consisting of attachment and so forth," "filled with hundreds of internal mental representations," "having a form that is thin, fair, and so on," and "I know this in this place.
Thus, even for one who possesses such latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— the result of practice over thousands of endless births— a sudden [encounter with] a Guru...
"Initiation (dīkṣā), which is performed in accordance with the descent of power (śaktipāta) brought forth by the desire to go [to the Lord], devotion, and so forth, is thus defined here:
'Knowledge is bestowed and the latent impressions of the bound soul (paśu) are destroyed;
because it is joined with bestowing and destroying, it is called initiation (dīkṣā).'"

Thus, according to the state established by the sacred tradition (āmnāya), a refinement (saṃskāra) is performed which consists of the capacity for the manifestation of Śiva-nature and the pacification of the bonds (pāśa) such as the individual (āṇava).
And the pacification of these bonds occurs through the power of inconceivable mantras, just as [the germination of] seeds [is prevented].
The incapacity for producing growth. As for the statement: "Ritual injunction is not sufficient for the accomplishment of seeds and the like, nor for the non-birth of persons."
"Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of liberation even through oil massages, exposure to fire, and so forth"— thus they have said;
yet this only reveals their own ridiculousness,
because [liberation] consists in the quelling of the power of a poison— whether of a stationary, moving, or artificial nature— to perform its own function.

Whatever is performed by means of mantras, as in the case of a seed, it follows that this same [principle] applies there as well. Now, if it is argued that in the case of anointing with oil and so forth, the power of the mantra merely suppresses the potentiality of the seed and does not produce any specific transformation, then [we reply]: because their power is inconceivable.

Why is his capacity even for the pacification of the bonds not tolerated? Or, if it is argued that defects persist even in one who has been initiated because they remain within the continuum of their seeds, what then have the mantras accomplished for him? To this, it is replied here: the mantras effect the obstruction of the power of the aforementioned bonds.

This is performed for him, but not for the pacification of passion, hatred, and so forth. For example, just as the enchantment of a transcendentally beautiful woman by means of mantras is performed even though the ugliness of an ugly person cannot be reversed, so too, because the karma that initiated the present body has not been purified, within this current body—

Even if passion and the like have not ceased, what has happened to the mantras that obstruct the future growth of the fetters (pāśas)? Furthermore, it is observed hundreds of times that for those purified by the most intense descent of power (tīvratama-śaktipāta), passion, hatred, and so forth are pacified immediately after initiation.

And in the initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), because of the purification of the bonds (*pāśa*) pertaining to the three times, there occurs at that very moment the dissolution of the body and so forth, as well as the manifestation of Śiva-nature. If it is asked, "What is the proof here for the manifestation of Śiva-nature?"
The inference arising from the pacification of the immediate manifestation of the body effected by the power of a mantra—
just as pacifying, nourishing, subjugating, burning, expelling, withering, killing, and so forth,
occur precisely through the efficacy of the mantra— likewise, the fruit of initiation also certainly occurs; such is the thought [in the mind].

Let it be established. If it is asked, "Why does the manifestation of Śiva-nature not occur at that very moment through initiation?", [the answer is: even this [manifestation] is indeed observed to occur thousands of times when performed by those possessing superior knowledge. Now, it might be argued: "From initiation, [what happens to] the eternal self?"

If it is argued that there would be a distinction [between cognitions] due to the distinction between being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in the arising of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), we say no.

Even though there is a distinction in the respective appearances, the unity of this [consciousness] is established through its identity with the single, non-artificial self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*), because of the unity of that reflection, just as in the case of a temple or similar object seen from far or near. And it is precisely by virtue of this reflection that...
That "all determinations" belong to it has been established in the *Pratyabhijñā*. By this, its status as enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth, is also proven;
for even when there is a difference between various objects, it manifests without departing from the Self. As for that which...

It has been stated that the vision of the self is not liberation, but rather bondage; this applies likewise to the body, the vital breaths, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void—all of which are non-self. However, in the case of the conscious self, whose nature is reality, wherein the ultimate essence of all knowledge and action is accepted as the supreme reality of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃvimarśa*):

In that regard, the very perception of the Self is liberation in truth. And it is not only the perception of the Self in what is not the Self—consisting of false knowledge—that constitutes bondage; rather, [bondage exists] even with respect to the Self, which consists of the supreme reality of the "I-consciousness" of full light and the entire universe, and also with respect to the universe itself.

Even that cognition which perceives things as non-self within the supreme reality of the identity of consciousness and the Self is indeed bondage. Therefore, liberation is solely the manifestation of Śiva-nature, which consists of the universal oneness of a single mass of consciousness whose contractions have entirely dissolved. And since everything culminates in the realization of this essence of non-duality, it is for the sake of attaining that very state [that one must strive].

The commencement of initiation (*dīkṣāpravṛtti*). Thus, since the impurities (*mala*) have been demonstrated through their differentiation according to the aforementioned method, there is no separate category for their purification; rather, it is the Self itself that undergoes the aforementioned purification by means of initiation. Its true nature is indeed non-dual (*advaya*).
There is no difference between the two positions regarding the vision of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) and the vision of non-duality (*advaya*).
However, it has been established that in the *sadyonirvāṇa* initiation, the cessation of the consciousness of karma, pleasure, and so forth, is also effected;
whereas this is not the case in the *asadyonirvāṇa* initiations.
The purification of the karma that initiates the body is not performed because of the Lord’s command, and not due to incapacity.
Therefore, in this case as well, it has been said:
"The substratum is the cause of both movement and cognition; these [causes] cease through the destruction of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)."

As for the statement, "The destination belongs to the initiated one," that too is not a valid objection; for the two positions regarding the purification of the intellect through the discernment of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth are refuted by their own non-acceptance. Therefore, as it has been said:
"Therefore, retention, propulsion, agitation,
and restraint would not be possible for them [the senses] in the absence of its capacity immediately following initiation (*dīkṣā*)," etc.—
this is not a refutation at all. As for what was said regarding the absence of gravity in sin, because it possesses conviction (*pratyaya*)...
The claim that "initiation by the scales (*tulādīkṣā*) is not tenable" is incorrect because its underlying intention is misunderstood;

for the heaviness in the body, which is caused by the veil of sin consisting of darkness (*tamas*), is removed through initiation by the scales—just like the purification of a jar—by means of the cessation of its cause. And so says the author of the Smṛti:

"From unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is darkness (*tamas*), there arises heaviness in the body; however, through the destruction of that [unrighteousness] by means of righteousness (*dharma*), lightness is produced, as is perceived through direct observation.
Thus it is said.

It is exactly so. As for what was further stated—that because one who has not received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) lacks the status of being a candidate for initiation (*dīkṣya*), initiation belongs only to one who possesses the descent of power; and that the descent of power results from the destruction of impurity (*mala*), while that [destruction] results from the descent of power, thus forming a circular dependency; [the response is: if the descent of power occurs even for one whose impurity is undestroyed, then it would apply to everyone.

It might be argued: "If there is some cause for the destruction of impurity other than the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then let that alone be the cause of the descent of power; what is the use of the destruction of impurity? This is true; however, we maintain that the state of being fit for initiation (*dīkṣyatva*) belongs to one who possesses the unimpeded and manifold descent of the Supreme Lord's power, and not otherwise.
For one who is endowed with the ripening of impurities and so forth, there is no contact whatsoever with the refuse-dump of the objections previously stated;

thus, the purification of the self through initiation is indeed logical. Moreover, it is established by the undisputed and well-known consensus of all beings, which is the very life-breath of all worldly transactions.

In the Pārameśvara [scripture], whose authority is established by its being composed by the omniscient Maheśvara, and which has attained corroboration through the attainment of various fruits— such as the nourishment of all things including nirvāṇa— as manifested by the performance of practices carried out in succession by a lineage of teachers acting with circumspection;

In the scripture, whatever is stated is exactly so. Consequently, as it has been said: "For those who do not perceive the basis for the existence of the scripture in that way, claiming liberation through the path of scripture serves only to satisfy their own speech."
That is indeed non-existent. As for the following:
"Therefore, O seekers of liberation, uproot the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi), which has its seeds of a similar kind in a beginningless continuum."

By saying this, it was claimed that the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) is rooted in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual construction of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā-vikalpa*); however, that is merely a deception, because [the self] consists of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*), which is produced by the indication of the head [as the locus of the "I"], just as one points to oneself with a finger.

The state of being like a conceptual designation (*nirdeśaprakhyāsāṅketika*) regarding objects is indeed perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), as if it were something to be reflected upon; otherwise, the initial grasping of a linguistic convention would not be possible for anyone.
Now, it was stated that the cognition of "I" is rooted in the latent impressions of conceptualization (*vikalpavāsanāmūla*); how is that so? For whatever conceptualization...

One conceives of the continuum of cognition (*jñānasaṃtāna*) as "I. Does one determine it as such through a distinction from one's own self, or rather without distinction from one's own self? In the case of the position of distinction, there would be a determination of the continuum of cognition as "this," but not as "I. However, in the case of non-distinction, [there is no room for] conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

It has been stated that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is also [itself] self-natured; however, that is not tenable, because conceptual constructions lack non-conceptuality (*avikalpakatva*) with respect to their own nature. Now, if it is argued that conceptual construction does not determine a difference between itself and other cognitions, but rather that it does not determine non-difference—then in that case...
The prohibition [of the self] would fall upon determination (*adhyavasāya*); thus, this would be an operation of non-determination.
Now, if one does not determine the difference of the self from other cognitions, but determines its internal states as non-different, then with which self...

If the distinction between those cognitions has not been determined, then by determining their non-distinction, the determination of the non-distinction of that self also follows; or else, like the self, their [distinction] would not be established.
Otherwise, what would be the distinction between them and the self? It is not a matter of mere determination; rather, it is the determination of distinction.
