For it is only in this way that this could be so. Furthermore, even by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) that experiences the variety of forms of the self arising from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience, previous experiences that have already ceased can be determined; in that case, for this [cognition]...

Because it is equivalent to being an inhabitant of the Coconut Island (Nārikela-dvīpa). Nor does this [consciousness] have any other operation distinct from its manifestation, even in the sense intended by terms such as "determination" (*adhyavasāya*), "superimposition" (*samāropa*), "conceit" (*abhimāna*), or "ascertainment" (*niścaya*).

That the establishing [agent] is consistent with the systems of other schools—let this matter rest, for it is exceedingly profound; it has been elaborated upon in the *Pratyabhijñā*, but were it to be expanded here, it would weary those of tender heart. Thus, this much remains established.
"Even amidst the diversity of various appearances, this Self is the ultimate reality whose essential nature is established as the non-artificial *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (the reflective awareness of 'I').

Now, one might object: "But the venerable teacher Kheṭapāla has accepted that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is caused by the ripening of impurity (*mala*), and he has refuted the position that the descent of power is independent; so how [is it otherwise]?"
Is this resolved by resorting to the position of the independent descent of power (*svatantra-śaktipāta*)? To this it is said:
if there is a desire to know the truth of this matter, then even this shall be determined. Listen:
"Now, the beginningless impurity (*mala*) of persons is declared to be their state of bondage (*paśutva*)."
"It should be known as being like the husk and the chaff for the sprout born of Māyā.

Thus, in the *Śrīsvāyaṃbhuvasūtra*, by reflecting on the statements "impurity" (*mala*) and "of men" (*puṃsām*), it follows that although this [impurity] is one, it possesses many powers; otherwise, its quality of being a manifold obscuration would not be possible, since [if it were one], upon the liberation of one [individual], [all would be liberated].
And all [souls] would be liberated; furthermore, it would transform together with their *karmas*, because transformation is impossible for that which is unmixed.

And as it transforms, at a particular time, for a certain person, and in a certain manner—through distinctions such as intense, moderate, and so forth—when it reaches full maturation, then, depending upon the ripening of the *karma* of individuals, [it effects] the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

Maheśvara acts such that, as long as the ripening of impurity (*mala*) has not occurred, He transforms it solely as a bond for that individual soul (*puruṣa*). But when He perceives within Himself that the task is accomplished and the [impurity] is ripe, He restrains the power of impurity by means of His own descent of power (*śaktipāta*). And just as...

According to the position of those who maintain that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is independent, the Lord ripens only a certain portion of the karma of each individual at a specific time, making it an object of experience; He does not, however, present everything to everyone simultaneously.
Furthermore, He manifests the principles (*tattvas*), such as *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and so forth, as possessing fixed relations of cause and effect.

And because He brings about the transformation [of states] according to the propriety of sleep and awakening, His agency is not indiscriminate in all cases; likewise, even in the view that the ripening of impurity is the cause, the Supreme Lord effects restraint and grace for individuals in dependence upon the diverse ripening of karma and impurity, and not otherwise.
"It is exactly so, because that would entail the consequence of his acting without prior reflection";
such is the view of the venerable teacher Kheṭapāla. As he says in the *Bhogakārikās*:
"Impurity (*mala*), which is beginningless, eternally connected [to the soul], common [to all], and imperishable..."
"Each person is determined [by their own karma], with their power operative at its respective time" (verse 128).
Likewise:
"Apart from the obstructing powers, no other attribute of this [individual] exists."
"And [it] serves as the cause for one who is joined with the latent impressions of karma in the ocean of existence" (Śloka 140).

Thus, in this context, if impurity (*mala*) were the binder by its own autonomy, it would bind even those souls already liberated by Śiva. If, on the other hand, it is by the will of Śiva, then because Śiva is free from passion and hatred, [that will] would apply even to liberated souls.

[Objection: It may be that [the Self] is the impeller of the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*). [Response: If it is argued that this is not so because those [impurities] manifest their own nature, [we reply] no, because the nature of others [the selves] is likewise [subject to manifestation]. [Objection: It is not so because of the obstruction of beginningless impurity (*anādi-mala-nirodha*). [Response: This is incorrect, because it is precisely that obstruction which has been undertaken for investigation. If...

And [if you argue that] there is no beginning to this cessation, [then] it has been accomplished by the presiding power of Śiva. If that too is beginningless, what is the use of both? Since the cessation brought about by the power of impurity (*mala*) is itself beginningless, let it be stated—by that alone—that its restriction to specific individual souls (*puruṣa*) is easily established. If you say, "Let it be so," [we reply]: No, because of Śiva’s...

There would be the state of being the presiding controller everywhere; and consequently— "Because of contact with impurity, their subjugation by Śiva remains unaccomplished, just like that [impurity]; however, these [powers] are to be restrained by the Lord... (Tantrāloka-nirṇaya, Kārikā 9).

Why was this said? If it is argued that for this very reason Śiva’s status as the presiding agent over the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) is also accepted—this is true, it is indeed accepted—but it is not established [as a logical necessity], because since both are beginningless, there is an absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because the determination of the existence of things cannot be based solely on the presence of a purpose. Let it be so; nevertheless, even in that case...

Those against whom Śiva employs *mala* for the sake of their suppression would, on the contrary, employ it against Śiva himself, because they are equal to Śiva and because they are numerous; for when many act with reference to a single one, their power is superior. Furthermore, if the power of *mala* were an obstructer by its mere presence, [it would affect everyone equally].
That [bondage] would apply even to the souls liberated by Śiva. Now,
if it is argued that it is called "obstructive" (*nirodhikā*) because it veils the essential nature consisting of knowledge and agency (*jñātṛtva-kartṛtva*),

then it follows that the selves are subject to modification (*vikāritā*), or else their very nature is destroyed, since for them there exists no attribute-form (*dharmarūpa*) distinct from that [essential nature].

This is because [the Śaivas] do not accept [the existence of *mala*] as the Vaiśeṣikas do; furthermore, it is not possible for the covering of the souls—which are of the nature of formless consciousness—by a material *mala*.

However, in the case of the rays of the eyes, the sun, and so forth, such [obstruction] is indeed possible because they are composed of material elements (*bhautika*), as in the case of cataracts and the like.

Furthermore, although intoxicants, poisons, and the like act as veils toward the living soul (*jīva*), they do so toward that which consists of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—once it has already undergone contraction—and not toward the pure conscious self (*śuddhacidātman*). Indeed, this primordial contraction caused by impurity (*mala*) alone is what must be investigated; how, then, could that [impurity] be a veil for the pure conscious self?

On the contrary, if it were argued that impurity must be perceivable by one who has entered the battle [of liberation], then everyone would become omniscient. Furthermore, if impurity were non-pervasive, it could not function as an obscuration of its pervasive self;
yet if it were pervasive, it would obscure even Śiva, the liberated souls, and those living beings.

Because there is no distinction in the pervasiveness of the Self— which consists in its occupying all locations— and because that [Self] is covered in every part by the pervasive impurity (*mala*), there can be no *saṃyoga* (conjunction) as a relation between the Self and the impurity,
since conjunction subsists only in what is pervaded (*vyāpyavṛtti*) while both of these are pervasive. Nor can there be *samavāya* (inherence), because that is impossible for two eternal substances.

For this very reason, there is no relation of cause and effect, nor is there identity, because they are distinct. Furthermore, even the relationship between the veiled and the veiler in the case of objects such as a jar and a cloth cannot be anything other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Moreover, [the author asserts] that impurity (*mala*) is eternal, all-pervasive, unitary, and possesses manifold powers.

Śiva’s sovereignty consists in the cessation and the ripening of this [impurity] through the obstruction of the vision and action that constitute the self-nature of Śiva; furthermore, Śiva is distinct from both the liberated Śivas and the individual souls (aṇu), and for this very reason, He does not pervade them and does not possess their powers, because He depends on the ripening of karma, impurity (mala), and so forth.

Furthermore, the statement beginning with "and dependence" (*pāratantryam*) is an excellent exposition by the proponents of duality (*bhedavādins*), which demonstrates the perverted nature of Śiva and *mala*. Moreover, as for their assertion that *mala* is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), how could this be possible for something that is unmixed [with anything else], except when it is conjoined with *karman*?

If it is argued that [the impurity] will exist [in the future], then since those [impurities] bring about the end of the stain (*mala*), how could there be any commingling of this [individual soul] with them?
Even though—
“In conjunction with the transformations of *māyā*, the impurity (*mala*) joined with karma is the cause of existence for living beings” (Tantrāloka-niṣkāya-kārikā).

Thus it has been stated by your venerable selves; nevertheless, since those who are *vijñānakevalins* lack the association of karma with impurity (*mala*), transformation would be impossible, and thus there would be an absence of liberation.
Furthermore, as for this bond of office (*adhikārabandha*) belonging to the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth, it is not...

If it is argued that because innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*) does not exist above *māyā*, another kind of impurity must be admitted for that purpose, and that the state of bondage for those [souls] is due to that specific portion of the power of Mahāmāyā belonging to Maheśvarī,
rather than through some other distinct impurity— then the same would apply to the *aṇus* (individual souls) as well.

Let it be that bondage is the manifestation of contraction through the power of *māyā*; what is the point of postulating an additional, logically untenable impurity (*mala*)? If there were no such consequence, then one would have to postulate a similar separate impurity for mantras and other such things as well. Furthermore, this impurity does not exist on the path (*adhvan*).

Since it has entered somewhere [else], how can its purification be effected by including it within the initiation of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvadīkṣā*)? If it is argued that, like karma, it is included within the *puruṣatattva*, this is not so; for it is logical that karmas are included within the *puruṣa*—the self as agent—in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), because they reside in the agent.
But how can impurity (*mala*), being distinct [from the soul], be included within those [categories of] actions?
Furthermore, an obscuring agent such as a cloth does not modify the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a jar or similar object;
rather, it obstructs the knower's cognition regarding that object. In the same way, that impurity belongs only to Śiva and the liberated souls (*muktāṇu*).

It might be argued that because of the impurity (*mala*) of those [souls], there is the obscuration of the knowledge of objects by the person; thus, first of all, the obscuring nature of *mala* is untenable. Furthermore, as for what is called the "ripening" (*paripāka*) of *mala*, does it mean the destruction of that [impurity] or its power, or rather the obstruction of its suppression? In the first case, in one instance...

If that [single power] were to reach maturation, all things would become pure; for even if one were to admit that there are multiple powers, this same undesirable consequence follows because they are similar and non-different from the possessor of the power.
For the wise maintain that power is indeed the very nature of the entity, its differentiation being merely superimposed due to the difference in results. It is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, the destruction of a beginningless, substantial obstruction of the power of impurity (*mala-śakti-nirodha*) is not logical; however, since a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is a non-entity, let it be so. Moreover, an obstruction to the obstruction of that power would, like an obstruction to the potency of poison or fire, apply to everyone alike. And just as in that case...
Upon the removal of the obstacle, its cessation might recur; furthermore,

if its maturation were causeless, it would occur from the very beginning, or else the powers of the impurities (mala) would mature all at once or in immediate succession, like the fruits of a tree in autumn.
Not by an extremely long interval of time. Now— "Indeed, by obstructing the power of the individual soul (*pums*), he perceives the efficacy of his own power;
and having perceived it, he employs the instrument suitable for its cessation for the sake of the liberation of the person. (Tattvārthasāra-nirṇaya)

According to the principle stated [in Kārikā 21], once the impurity (*mala*) has performed its own function, it undergoes maturation; that [maturation] should occur immediately after the cessation of merit (*puṇya*).

Now, for the sake of that [maturation], during the experience (*bhoga*) which consists in the emergence of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*), [the following occurs].

When there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), it is digested; if that enjoyment here were general, then because the enjoyment which is its effect would be fully accomplished within a single body composed of the principles from *kalā* down to *kṣiti*, the ripening of impurity (*mala*) would occur immediately thereafter. If, however, it were specific, that [ripening] would never occur, because of the nature of the future *kalā*.

Because the specific variety of experiences born of karma arises from that [mala]. Now, if the ripening of mala occurs through the will of the Lord, it has already been stated that if His will were unrestricted, it would be the cause for all individual souls. Or, if it occurs by way of the turn of experience; suppose at some time two opposing karmas of equal strength [confront one another].
Even when [the karma] is ripe, it remains indifferent due to opposition; furthermore, other karmas do not become oriented toward fruition because they are not yet ripe.

Thus, with regard to that time, the Blessed One obstructs the impurity (*mala*), and that time—being devoid of both suffering and pleasure—is considered a "favorable" period (*pakṣa*) since it may even be perceived by some on its own.

To this we reply: how can actions that are performed sequentially and possess sequential fruits become inclined toward yielding their fruits simultaneously? Or, at the time when those [fruits] are obstructed, why would another action not yield its fruit? For it is only at its own proper time that an action becomes inclined toward yielding its fruit.

If it is argued that this does not occur at that time, then it would likewise be illogical for those two [the soul and the Lord] to exist at the same time. If it is argued that it is solely due to the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*), then if that will were independent, it would grant liberation by simultaneously bringing about the maturation of all actions for everyone and thereby bestowing their fruition; or else, regardless of karma, it would remove the impurity (*mala*) of everyone.

[If it is argued that the karma] obstructs [the other], then since it is not independent, another cause for this must also be stated here. Furthermore, for one whose two karmas of equal strength are both oriented toward fruition and yet obstructed, there would have to be a falling away of the body at that very moment. Now, if it is argued that there is no obstruction of the karmas that bestow birth and lifespan, but rather only of those that bestow experience—[we reply: But surely...

Even if the Lord were to obstruct impurity (*mala*) while the karma that bestows birth and lifespan remains unobstructed, why would he fear that which bestows experience, such that he must necessarily depend upon its obstruction? Furthermore, if he were to obstruct impurity only at the stage when karma has its power obstructed, then [that would occur] in the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).

One should act in the same manner toward all of them. If it is argued that even in those cases there exists an attachment to karma that yields such enjoyment, then why can it not be said that when two contradictory karmas are present, there is a karma that grants such enjoyment? Furthermore,

If it were the case that Īśvara simultaneously blocks the impurity (*mala*) of those *vijñānākala*s who are devoid of *kārmamala*, then the fixed numerical limit [of eight] found in the scriptures would be untenable.
Alternatively, even when there is an equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), it might be argued that Īśvara’s will blocks only that impurity which has reached full maturity.

If one were to rely on the view of the commentators on the *Kiraṇa*, then the recurrence of the aforementioned refutation would be untenable, and the fault of admitting an equivalence with futile action (*vyarthakarma*) would ensue. By this, that which some have said is also answered: [text missing].
Dispassion, distaste for enjoyments, a certain spiritual virtue, discernment,
association with the virtuous, and constancy in the practice of worshiping the Supreme Lord and other such disciplines.
The occurrence of a crisis, the observation thereof, certain signs in the body,
devotion to the scriptures, the fulfillment of the multitude of enjoyments, and divine knowledge.
If it is argued that the will, having such causes as these, forcibly obstructs impurity (*mala*), [we reply:
since even upon the arising of this [will], the very cause is the Will of the Lord (*īśecchā*), there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, it is impossible to posit another cause, because that too would lack a restrictive principle (*niyama*). Nor are all these [causes]...
They are not causes, because it is observed that such a state occurs for those upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has come through the will of the Lord;

nor does each [cause] individually have the will of the Lord as its cause, since detachment and so forth are seen to deviate [from the result] in hundreds of instances, and because worship of the Supreme Lord, knowledge, and the like are preceded by the ripening of impurity (*mala*). It is not...

It is logical that the Lord’s will acts as an impeller. Furthermore, regarding what was stated otherwise— that having observed the sequential nature of the liberation of souls, one infers that the Lord’s will also possesses a sequential causality for the ripening of impurities (mala),
just as the sequence of experience [infers] its causality for the ripening of karma— this is also consistent.

As for the claim that [liberation] is gradual, that is incorrect. It is true that the sequence of liberation arises from the sequence of the ripening of impurity (*mala*), and that sequence itself arises from the sequence of ripening effected by the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*). However, no cause for the sequence in which the power of the Lord effects the ripening of impurity can be found; for if it possesses absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*), it has no need for dependence upon the ripening of impurity. Therefore, it is not...
In no way can proponents of dualism establish the distinctness of impurity (*mala*), its power of obstruction, its transformation, its maturation, the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), and so forth;
therefore, what has been stated is indeed correct. Even though it is said in the fourth chapter:

Although the occasion for an investigation into the nature of *mala* arose here in the verse, "But *mala* in this context is [mere] desire" (4.105), nevertheless, that investigation was conducted later in a single continuous section, lest those intent on examining the *Dīkṣātantra* be distracted there.

This is a delusion for those of tender hearts. Furthermore, even if there were an infinity of individual souls (*jīva*) according to the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), because no others would arise thereafter and because they would be delimited by the Lord (*īśvara*) as being finite in number, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) would possess a fixed limit and thus could not be beginningless; consequently, if only one atom (*aṇu*) were liberated per age, [the world would eventually come to an end].

In that case, the total cessation of saṃsāra would necessarily follow. Alternatively, if the souls possess such infinity that even the Lord cannot delimit them, then the Lord would be rendered non-omniscient. As it was stated by the Sage in the Śārīraka [Bhāṣya]:
"[Otherwise] there would be either finitude or non-omniscience" (2-2-41).
Let this matter rest; however, as for that which was raised by them against the doctrine of the independent descent of power (*svatantra-śaktipāta*) regarding the Lord:
In the absence of a cause, there would arise, according to the scriptures, the state of acting without foresight in inflicting punishment and the like;
the simultaneous creation of all principles; the simultaneous bestowal of the fruits of all actions upon everyone;
and the destruction of the essential nature of living beings upon liberation, as well as their reappearance in rebirth.

Furthermore, the claim that it is impossible to describe *mala* as a real entity (*vastu*) is a statement made by those who have not reflected upon the true nature of that doctrine; for in that system,
nothing whatsoever is established apart from the light of the Supreme Lord’s consciousness, and thus it is that very [consciousness] which [is the reality].

Out of His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), desiring to manifest His own nature as the infinite universe consisting of all things from Śiva down to the earth, He appears in various ways; thus, there is no person whatsoever who is the recipient of grace or punishment, nor anyone who is enveloped by impurity. And yet...

He alone, manifesting upon his own ground the various subjects— both restrained and favored— as well as the entire range of objects of knowledge, like a city in a mirror, and manifesting the performance of the five cosmic acts (*pañcakṛtya*), does not exceed [his nature] in the slightest,
or rather, he exceeds it just like a mirror; thus, he alone is the Supreme.
The one who acts with foresight, because the universe consists of manifold wonders,

manifests it in such a way that wherever he extends even a sequence of fixed temporal succession, there, by virtue of the necessity of the causal relationship, [it appears] through the variety of karma, its fruits, and so forth.
By way of being closed and, through its withdrawal, by way of being opened—thus, in that respect, there is the state of being bound or liberated;

yet in reality, it is that very [consciousness] alone which flashes forth as the self of the universe, so that there is no other whatsoever who is bound or liberated. And this is not the case regarding liberation, which consists in the attainment of one's own true nature.

There is indeed the destruction of [limited] form; however, the destruction of contraction is precisely what is desired. Furthermore, for one who has attained non-difference from Śiva—who manifests everywhere and at all times as the self-nature of all—there is no rebirth.
This is because the very essence of Paramaśiva is manifested through His own vast essential nature, extending from Śiva down to the level of Sakala.
From the perspective of limited experience (*saṃsāra*), let it be said that he possesses various forms to that extent;
however, in reality, he is the Supreme Lord himself, the full expansion of the universe. Therefore, the objection raised—that there would be the consequence of rebirth—is indeed untenable.
"There is no other state of existence because of being devoid of beginningless impurity"—

regarding such scriptural statements (*āgama*), there is no disagreement whatsoever. Furthermore, since this [Self] attains the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is no room for the objections raised against the proponents of the doctrine of *pariṇāma-brahma* (the Brahman of transformation).

Because it consists of the unfolding of its own essential nature as the universal self, neither the theory of illusory transformation (*vivarta*) nor that of real transformation (*pariṇāma*) is accepted. Thus it is said:
"By that which possesses contraction and expansion, by that which is endowed with both, and by that which is free from them."
And with his entire being, he constantly flashes forth as the mass of consciousness, acting according to his own will. || 1 ||
Whatever manifests, such as the earth and other elements, is exactly like that;
and by virtue of the fixed order of priority and posteriority among the principles, their sequential nature is also entirely logical. || 2 ||
That [consciousness], which manifests as the contracted form of the individual soul (jīva), experiencing various karmas, their resulting egos, and their fruits,
illuminates them both gradually and, at the time of initiation, even instantaneously.

Thus, even that desire which is of the nature of contraction and is called *laulika*, because it flashes forth as suchness (*tathātva*), must be considered a reality—the impurity (*mala*)—in the scriptures. (4)
Even when impurity is destroyed through initiation, yoga, and knowledge, there is no destruction of the Self;
for liberation is simply the manifestation of the state of being a dense mass of consciousness, which is pure and autonomous. || 5 ||

Just as water poured into water, or milk mixed with milk that remains undistinguished, so too do those who have been initiated attain oneness through the process of initiation by means of the rite of initiation. Thus it is said.
It is also stated in the Raurava Śāstra that the commentator has for the most part rendered it in vain,
by means of his explanations of the meaning, in which the Lord is thus and so proclaimed.

Therefore, enough with these conceptualizations of duality; liberation, which consists of identity with the autonomous Śiva arising from the unimpeded descent of power (śaktipāta), is accomplished through initiation and other means.
In this way, whatever means of initiation has been prescribed by whomever and in whatever manner, all of that must likewise be understood as being empowered by the descent of grace (śaktipāta). 9.

The doctrine of Dharmakīrti has been shattered here by the weapons of logic; the system exuding defects, though well-expounded, has been utterly destroyed by Kheṭapāla. Furthermore, the true essence of initiation has been proclaimed—that which is skilled in joining together the divisions, wherein impurity has dissolved and the unity consisting of consciousness alone has blossomed forth.
By virtue of the expansion of its own pure and autonomous luminosity, it becomes the form of the universal Self in all things. || 10 ||
Thus, may there be well-being.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation into the Tattvas and Other Principles," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
Indeed, those five groups beginning with the short vowel *a* (the letter *a*), Viriñci (Brahmā), waking, the Earth, and so forth;

I constantly remember that Fivefold Praṇava— the Śakti and the others who, through the full contemplation of the praise of Śaṅkara, have attained the name of Praṇava and whose manifestation as the universe occurs even from a mere fragment of their grace— in order to reach the abode of Svacchanda.

In this book of questions, the essential nature of time and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) remains to be determined. Among these, time will be determined by the immediately following chapter; since that [time] is for the most part an auxiliary to spiritual attainment (*siddhi*), and attainments are preceded by the practice of mantras, [this section is intended] to determine the essential nature of the means of accomplishment.

At the end of the fifth chapter, it was briefly indicated with the words "or by one who has attained success through mantra"; now he explains that in detail: "O fair-faced one, for the practitioner who is endowed with the conduct of the observance (samaya), various accomplishments (siddhi) arise..."
The *samayas* are those previously mentioned. The *ācāra* (conduct) is the method for the propitiation of the mantra, which will be described hereafter.

The "face" (*ānana*) is that which possesses an entrance into the supreme state, which bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), and which consists of the expansion of power (*śāktasphāramaya*). It is the most excellent (*vara*) and sublime.
He clarifies the conduct in its proper sequence: ".........resorting to a mountain cave. (6.1)
On a well-purified patch of ground, entirely free from all thorns and debris,
hidden, secluded, and delightful, one should worship Bhairava there.
It is free from all thorns, devoid of the afflictions of cold, prickly thorns, harsh winds, and the like;
it is hidden and invisible. One should worship it with offerings appropriate to one's desire. || 2 ||
Then,
O lady of virtuous vows, having recited one hundred thousand syllables of Bahurūpa,
success is certainly attained for one who recites while joined with the five *praṇavas*.

Having recited thirty-two hundred thousand times—measured by the thirty-two syllables of Bahurūpa, whose ultimate reality has been previously determined—for the sake of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), the practitioner certainly attains accomplishment; that is, he surely achieves his desired *siddhi*. How so?

"Having recited [the mantra]?"—to this he says: "By means of the recitation joined with the five *praṇavas*. That by which the supreme nature of the Lord is praised (*nūyate*) intensely—that is, extolled and contemplated as the ultimate reality of non-duality—and which is filled with the entirety of the universe, is the *praṇava*, the Lord Niṣkala.

The syllable *oṃ* is likewise characterized by non-difference from that [reality]. Its constituent parts—such as the forms *ā*, *u*, and *m*—are like a tiny fragment of musk-paste from a single portion of a musk-pouch;
its denoted deities are Brahmā and the others; and its presiding principles are the *tattvas* such as Earth, Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), and Illusion (*māyā*).

The phonemic units (*kalā*) consisting of the pronunciation of letters, such as the short vowels and so forth, and the states of the one who pronounces them, such as waking and so forth, are each fivefold and gross;
these consist of the *kalās* such as Śakti and Vyāpinī, as well as the forms of the phonemic units of their denotations and pronunciations.

The subtle states (*sūkṣmadaśāḥ*), by virtue of the principle that "even a single point of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization," are denoted by the word *praṇava* because they are filled with perfect wonder. Therefore...
Thus, because they are situated within the body of the mantra, these vowels beginning with 'a' are the specific piṇḍas and bījas denoted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śakti, Śiva, and Praṇava;
considering them to be diverse expansions, all five aforementioned praṇavas exist here.

In that [state] where the fivefold praṇava exists as the partless (niṣkala) and the oṃkāra whose pervasion is non-different from it— by means of correct yoga with those five praṇavas, because of being conjoined with the state of the haṃsa-pada manifested through its utterance, there arises the contemplation of the secret meaning of all mantras, whose true nature is non-different from the pervasion of the previously determined partless [reality].
And that recitation which is "embodied" (rūpa)—the meaning is that it comes from such recitation, and not merely from the mechanical reading of syllables. || 3 ||
Success is achieved not only through recitation in this manner, but rather—one is liberated without a doubt by the piercing (*bhedana*) of the *praṇava*;
as it has been said: "By means of reciting [the mantra] joined with the five *praṇavas*."
That [state] characterized by pervasion does not occur without the piercing (*bhedana*) that effects the separation of the phonemes, kalās, and so forth, which will be described hereafter.
Since piercing bestows immersion into the supreme reality (*paratattva*), it is stated that there is no doubt for one who is liberated.

In that regard, for the purpose of entering the state beyond time—preceded by the knowledge of the divisions of time (*kālakalā*) which constitute a limb of the utterance of mantra—the Lord first instructs on piercing [the centers]:
"Short, long, protracted, subtle, extremely subtle, and the supreme Śiva. (6.4)
Having known the *praṇava* in its fivefold nature and having pierced through it, there is liberation without a doubt; that is,

having pierced through the expansion of the temporal divisions (*kalā*) of the sequential utterances— beginning with the short vowel and ending with the extremely subtle— of the *praṇava* as the syllables *a*, *u*, *ma*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.

The meaning is that by entering into the experience of each respective state (*daśā*) in sequence, one superimposes the supreme state (*paraṃ bhāvam*); then, through the attainment of the stage of *unmanā*, having realized [the truth], one certainly attains liberation. And in this context, the vowels beginning with the short ones and ending with the nasal sound (*nāda*) are to be pronounced as mutually interconnected.
Above the extremely subtle *bindu* and *nāda*,
one must also follow the ten stages beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and ending with *nādānta*, which possess a gradation of intensity,
as was stated previously:
"O Dear One, one should abandon [the levels] in this very manner through states that are increasingly subtle and most subtle" (4-267).

Just as the nature of the *praṇava* has been determined for the short vowels and so forth, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed appropriate. This is stated by the words "there is no doubt."
He demonstrates that this is established through one's own direct experience. || 4 ||

Thus, through the sequence of temporal units beginning with the short vowel and so forth, and through the sequence of the denotators (vācaka) to be described hereafter, this single Great Mantra-essence—
the Praṇava— exists in five states.
Previously,

based on the established principle that "even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its universal form," it was stated that there are five *praṇavas* such as the short vowel (*hrasva*) and so forth; however, now it is said that there is only one.

The statement that "the mantra, whose essence is great deliberation (*mahāvimarśa*), thus abides in five ways" is merely a difference in expression, because from the perspective of definitive insight, there is oneness in the reality of the thing itself.
Is this [Self] merely of the nature of these fivefold states? No, he says:
"It is conjoined with the *haṃsa*. (6.5)
Previously [it was stated]: "Now the utterance of *haṃsa* is being described:
the letter *ha* is traditionally held to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), well-functioning and having the form of a *ha*-stroke. (4.257)

By this passage, it is established that the *haṃsa* is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*). Therefore, because it is self-activated, it exists in the form of the vibration of the uncreated *madhyama-prāṇa*,
which— according to the principle about to be explained immediately hereafter— is coextensive with the expansion of the entire range of speech.
This *praṇava*, which is of the nature of the Great Mantra, is here the ultimate reality consisting of the repose of reflection upon that [union]. || 5 ||
Whatever verbal expression exists in the world is established in the knowledge of Śiva,
and the knowledge of Śiva resides therein... whatever exists in the world within the midst of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), all that is the knowledge of Śiva and Śiva himself.

"Śivajñāna" (the knowledge of Śiva) is that by which [Śiva] is known; it is established without distinction and resides within the *praṇava*— which consists of the expansion of knowledge, is the essence of the pervasion taught by the Supreme Lord, and is described by the perspective already stated and to be stated hereafter— because that [knowledge] is composed of speech, being the very form of the unfolding of *parāvāk*.

As it is said in the *Śrīsārasvata-stotra*: "O Goddess who, through the three letters beginning with 'na', express the triple Veda, the three modes of conduct, the three worlds, and likewise the three musical notes— transcending all modification;..."
"The fourth state of yours, which conforms to subtle sounds both collectively and individually—the word *Om* praises You, O Giver of Refuge. (Mokṣopāya-stotra 27).
Although one should have said "in the *praṇava*," by saying "in the knowledge of Śiva," the intended meaning is this: that...

Although there is a similarity in form between the *praṇava* and [mantras] such as the *vedagaruda* and *vaiṣṇava*, its superiority in the *Pārameśvara* [Tantra] is due to its essence being the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the knowledge that has been taught and will be taught hereafter. For this very reason,
in accordance with the knowledge of this pervasion, it is everywhere characterized by the nature of full expansion (*pūrṇasphāramayatva*).
He is the bestower of supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*). As it has been said:
"Since everything originates from Śiva, it bestows the fruit that is the abode of Śiva" (Svacchanda Tantra 5.45).
However, according to the respective limited extent of its pervasion, He alone is the bestower of limited accomplishment (*mitasiddhi*).
With this intention, he will say: "Indeed, Māyā causes them to wander, for they desire liberation where there is no liberation" (10.1141);
let this matter rest for now. And as for this knowledge of Śiva, which consists of such a Praṇava—
That too remains there, within the *haṃsa* whose true nature has been thus defined.

Thus, in this Niṣkalanātha, who is the fivefold Praṇava and whose nature is the eternally uttered Nāda, the *ahaṃsa* joined with the Praṇava is of the nature of reflective awareness (amarśa). || 6-6 ||

Being properly joined with the *praṇava* whose true nature has been declared, he abides in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, precisely because of his connection with the *haṃsa* which encompasses the entire universe,
this [state] possesses the pervasive non-duality of the *praṇavas* of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śakti, and Śiva as taught in other scriptures.
It has already been stated that this is the "Great Mantra. Therefore, regarding what was said—
"By reciting [it] in conjunction with the five *praṇavas*, one certainly attains success" (6.3)—
therein lies the true essence of resting in the unstruck (*anāhata*).

The ultimate conclusion is that recitation (japa) should be performed by means of being absorbed in the central abode, which has been rendered fit through the utterance of the partless (niṣkala). || 6 ||
Now, raising the doubt as to what this [state] is like without the conjunction with the *praṇava*, he says:
"Without the conjunction with the *praṇava*, the *jīva* alone remains established;
the *jīva* is the life-force of the universe, having the very form of the letter *ha*. As it has been said:
"The letter *ha*, however, is remembered as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), well-functioning and having the form of a plow (*halākṛti*)" (4.257).

Here, "the vital breath" means that which exists without connection to the *praṇava* consisting of the digits (*kalā*) beginning with the letter *a*; "one" means non-dual; it is established within the potency of all mantras.

Thus, because its nature is immovable, it is not to be uttered; yet, being unestablished, it does not abide in any fixed form—this is the meaning of "unrestrained expansion. By employing the word *jīva*, it is implied that this very Self, whose nature is great radiance (*mahāsphurattā*), is to be understood. However, some [hold a different view].

In this treatise, which is intent upon defining the true nature of mantra, setting aside the primary literal meaning, the term *haṃsa* refers to the path of the *haṃsa*, and by the term *prāṇa*, it is that very same thing; or else, because of the identity of the *praṇava* and *prāṇa*, [it denotes] the individual soul (*jīva*) or the person (*puruṣa*) without the yoga of *prāṇa*. It is one.
Thus he explains: "its nature consists of unmanifest knowledge and action. Whether this is correct or incorrect, those with intelligence will discern for themselves.

Since this individual soul (jīva) exists merely in its own nature without being joined with the Praṇava, it therefore remains neither conjoined with its primordial nature (prakṛti) nor does it abide in isolation. || 7 ||

Likewise, the individual soul (jīva) functions within the body as conjoined with the sixth [element]. The soul is the *haṃsa*, joined by not overstepping its nature— that is, by not transgressing its inherent character— and by this non-transgression of its own nature, it [proceeds].
According to the principle stated in [the verse] "There is no distinction between these two" (4-350), he remains conjoined with the letter *a* alone; thus, he is united with the vowel *a*.
He does not abide in a single form—the non-dual nature whose essence is the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*)—but rather in something slightly different.

Just as it undergoes an increase in vibration (*spanda*), so too, conjoined and mixed with the sixth vowel *ū*, it functions within the body; indeed, it is perceived as flowing through the entire natural course of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In view of the word "tathā" (so), the word "yathā" (just as) should also be supplied here.
When impelled by that [breath] according to the previously mentioned configuration of the channels, it then proceeds upwards. (6.8)

"By that" means by the sixth vowel, *ū*, which by implication is joined with the *bindu* (dot) and so forth. "And then" means at that very moment. "Above" refers to the places of articulation such as the palate. The meaning is that without this impulsion (*codanā*), even for this [vowel] joined with the letter *a*, there is no upward movement. || 8 ||
Thus, even though that reality is directly perceived, those who are deluded by the great māyā do not recognize it, unless there is the instruction of the scripture. (6.9)
This very essence of the mantra-principle, whose core is the reflective awareness of the primordial sound (nāda), is the nature of every subject;

for it is self-luminous because its form is eternally resonant, and thus it is described by the scripture through the words of the tradition as being [the source] even of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the others, despite the presence of the Great Māyā.

They are deluded by that which is called "incompleteness," whose ultimate nature is non-recognition; for, because its essence is consciousness, it specifically causes the manifestation of the self-nature as the infinite Self throughout the universe, while simultaneously manifesting a sense of selfhood in the non-self, such as the body and so forth, thereby inducing a state of contraction.

Regarding the word *codanām*: without the awakening of that power (*śakti*) which dispels the great illusion (*mahāmāyā*) and bestows the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśa*), people do not "know" (*abhijānanti*)—that is, they do not know by facing toward [it] (*abhimukhyena*) with a firm state of confidence (*āśvāsa*).
Therefore, the essential meaning is that the thorough knowledge of this very reality (*tattva*) is in every way the supreme thing to be adopted. And it has been said:
In the *Jñānagarbha*:
"O Mother, this supreme syllable (*paramākṣarī*) of yours becomes this form externally;
within the hollow of the heart, it attains the state of the twenty-fold *praṇava*."
"O Mother, whose nature consists of *bindu* and *nāda*, that which is unknowable by those of unrefined self they perceive with ease through the constant remembrance of You. (9)
To explain that, he says:
"And the sixth should be known as the upward-moving, abiding in the face of its own nature.
The sixth is the vowel *ū*; it is that which is referred to as "the upward-moving" in the verse, "But when impelled by that" (6.8).

The upward-moving [current] has been described; its nature is the Middle Path (*madhyamārga*), which vitalizes the universe. That alone is the "mouth," the means for attaining the state of Śiva; it should be understood as arising therein according to the previously explained sequence of binding the instruments (*karaṇabandha*).
And therefore:
"Unmanifest, residing within its own body, it functions as a subordinate quality. (6.10)

This Anāhatanātha, who—because he is self-manifesting—is impossible to reveal and exists in the form of a secret, abides within one's own body, which is the nature of the central channel (*madhyadhāman*) in its accumulated form;
being eternally present there, he has attained the state of the various qualities (*guṇaprakāra*). By that [attainment]...
Being disciplined, he proceeds; that is to say, he ascends upward. || 10 ||
Otherwise:
"But when the God is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), solitary, and has conquered time, there would be nothing to be known; he is indeed absolute (kevala) and partless (niṣkala). (6.11)

The Lord is the expansion of autonomous consciousness; He is solitary because there exists nothing apart from Him; He has conquered time because He is eternal. Such is the Unstruck Lord (*anāhatanātha*). There is nothing whatsoever to be known of Him, nor can He be known by any means, for His nature is solely that of the Knower; therefore, He is absolute (*kevala*).

Thus, he is without a second (*advitīya*). He has emerged from the *kalās*, that is, from the phonemes beginning with 'a', from the temporal divisions such as short vowels, and from the limitations consisting of the state of being an object of knowledge; and since he is that from which those *kalās* have emerged, he alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). It is precisely because of this essential nature that—
And even the Lord of the four kalās is called "partless" (niṣkala). || 11 ||
And for this reason: "He has neither form nor body, nor color, nor likewise action.
Form refers to such qualities as resembling pure crystal; body refers to the five faces and so forth, which pertain to the object of expression.

*Varṇa* (color/letter) refers to the form of the signifier, such as the letter *a* and so forth; *kriyā* (action) refers to the form of pronunciation and so forth. Alternatively, some take *varṇa* to mean caste, such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, and *kriyā* to mean the activity appropriate to that [caste].
Thus, having transcended the side of the knowable—how can he be grasped, being subtle, ungraspable, eternal, and immutable? (6.12)

Subtle, the cause of the universe, ungraspable, beyond the range of the senses, imperishable, and characterized by the absence of transformation— because it is such as this, O Goddess, the sixth seed-syllable has been employed.
By this [process], he has attained the state of being the King of Mantras by means of the Supreme Lord; the phrase "for the sake of favoring men" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And because of that application:
"Endowed with five pentads, he is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala) within the body. (6.13)

The first [set] consists of the five units of time required for the pronunciation of the short vowel and so forth; the second consists of the five expressive units known as the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the bindu, and the nāda; and the third consists of the five deities signified by those [letters]: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, and Sadāśiva.
The fourth [category] consists of the principles (tattvas) such as Earth, Nature (prakṛti), Māyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, which are governed by that [consciousness];

and the fifth consists of the states of the one who utters phonemes—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). Thus, through these five pentads, both already mentioned and to be described hereafter, [the reality] exists in its supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā) forms.

When he is joined with the body while stationed in the fields such as the heart and throat, then the Lord Anāhata, although partless (*niṣkala*), is called "both with parts and partless" (*sakalaniṣkala*) due to his association with various powers of vision; this is the meaning. || 13 ||
Therefore, he says that even during the utterance of this [mantra], one must focus exclusively on resting in the partless reality (*niṣkalatattva*):
"But when the yogi, who contemplates yoga, takes hold of that [mantra]—even though it has been brought forth by yoga—he should contemplate it as mere being (*bhāvamātra*). (6.14)

In this verse, the word "icchati" (he desires) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Thus, when that yogi contemplates the yoga consisting of the aforementioned fivefold pentads— which is of the nature of non-conceptual reflective awareness preceded by conceptualization— then, for him...
If he desires both the grasping and the utterance [of the mantra], then by means of yoga—

consisting of the previously mentioned divine instruments (*karaṇas*), bindings (*bandhas*), and so forth— he brings about the mere state (*bhāvamātra*) of that which has been carried all around through the central path (*madhyadhāman*) and brought to the desired state.

One should contemplate the full radiance of the ultimate reality of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*), as determined by the *yojanikā* text in the verse "the supreme, peaceful mere capacity" (4-293),
preceded by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the desire to utter the mantra according to the aforementioned pervasion, and by means of its very apprehension.

The meaning is that, having ascended to the level of mantra (*mantrabhūmi*) and resting at its further limit, one should cultivate the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*). This has been stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The reality of the body of knowledge (*vidyāśarīrasattā*) is the secret of mantra" (2.3).
Thus, it is said:
"Through the contemplation of the Great Lake, there is entry into the potency of mantra" (1.22).
The existence and radiance of the Great Lake—the body of Vidyā, which is the expansion of supreme consciousness—is [the means].

The secret power of mantras consists in entering into them by following the pervasion of the mantra— preceded by the desire to utter it and the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that follows the central path of the great lake.
The meaning is: through reconnection, by ascending to the repose within the mantra. || 14 ||
Having thus explained the method for entering the potency of mantra, he describes the sequence of that entry as appropriate for the practitioner:
"When one performs emanation, the *bindu* proceeds upward."

When the practitioner (ārādhaka) desires accomplishment (siddhi), then, by the very logic already stated, the mantra— having attained rest in the upper plane (ūrdhvapada)— is one whose Śākta power has blossomed in accordance with the consciousness of that practitioner, at the "upper" point, which is the summit of all paths.

He proceeds as the undivided form of light, consisting of the weaving together of the universe—from Śiva, who is the nature of both existence and non-existence in its totality, down to the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
From that point onward, through the process of emanation, He fills it up to the Heart; the meaning is that He fulfills it by completing the desired state.
For one who desires liberation, however, the recitation of mantras is not performed primarily by relying on the *bindu* as previously described;
rather— "And that which is beyond the *bindu* is the Peaceful Śiva, the supreme cause. (6.15)
Therein, the *bindu* dissolves;
thus, its distinction from Paramaśiva is stated by virtue of its being the supreme cause. || 15 ||
Since this is so,
therefore that state is difficult for the gods to attain;
"by the gods" means by the deities and by all the senses— that [state] whose activity consists of the subtle mind, which is primarily characterized by mere mental reflection.

Because it transcends the state of equilibrium with objective domains (*viṣaya-sāmarasya*). It is called "the abode" (*sthāna*) based on the etymological derivation: that in which the universe abides non-differently.
Even such a state as this—one shall obtain without delay through practice and by union with the sixth vowel. (6.16)

The phrase "intent on union" (samavadhānodyata) is to be supplied [to the previous verse]. It has already been stated that the sixth vowel is intended as an indicator for the bindu and so forth. || 16 ||
Therefore—O Goddess, the sixth and the fifth [vowels] are remembered as the qualities of that;
"of that" refers to the supreme reality whose nature is great reflective awareness (*mahāvimarśa*). The sixth is the vowel *ū*, while the fifth is...

The letter *u* is indeed included within that; "those two alone [are] below and above, consisting of the external power (*bahiḥ-śakti*) of this"—thus, by the very words *ca* (and) and *eva* (only), the previously mentioned object of knowledge (*meyārtha*) is established as the fixed sequence of objects of knowledge beginning with the letter *m* and the *bindu*, whose forms have been described. The qualities (*guṇas*) are the causes for the downward and upward expansion.

The meaning is that the *dharmas* are of the nature of power (*śakti*). "Recalled" (*smṛta*) means by the unbroken lineage of gurus beginning with Śiva and ending with Śrīkaṇṭha. However, some, failing to perceive the particle *ca* and the word *eva*, [interpret] the plural number in *guṇāḥ* as being in reference to the repetition of the recitation (*japa*).
He has explained.
Since this is so, therefore:
the qualified is to be known as the manifest (sakala), while Śiva is the unqualified and partless (niṣkala). || 6.17 ||

According to the principle thus stated, even Niṣkalanātha becomes possessed of parts (*sakala*). As for that which was previously designated as Anāhatanātha in the passage, "The letter *ha*, however, is remembered as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), active by its own nature" (4.257), he alone is in reality partless (*niṣkala*) because of his being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). || 17 ||
Therefore:
"The *sakala* (with parts) is conjoined with the *graha* (seizer), while the *niṣkala* (without parts) rests in *bhāva*.
Here, *graha* is the utterance (*uccāra*), and *bhāva* is the great vibration (*mahāsphurattā*) whose nature is the well-functioning vibration (*sphurattā*).

And since, according to the perspective previously stated, this Lord of Four Kalās— who was previously designated by the term "sakalaniṣkala"— is in essence nothing other than the awareness of the ultimate partless (niṣkala), therefore, when this "sakala" [mantra] is recited, the "niṣkala" is indeed recited. || 18 ||

If this is so, then let this very subtle form of the Lord consisting of four syllables be resorted to through practices such as recitation (*japa*) for the sake of resting in the ultimate, partless reality (*niṣkala-tattva*) that transcends all [dualities]; why [resort to] the gross [form] consisting of thirty-two syllables?
Having raised the doubt: "Is Sakala described as one who has been worshipped according to such statements as 'having recited a hundred thousand syllables of Bahurūpa' (6.3)? he says:
By the God, for the sake of providing the means of sacrifice for the Suras and Asuras,
his entire form was manifested in two states.

By the Lord Svacchandabhaṭṭāraka, whose essential nature is determined by the opening statement and who is the supreme reality of consciousness and bliss— for the sake of the gods, whose hearts are comforted by the path of knowledge,
and for the sake of the asuras, who are unqualified for knowledge and whose hearts are comforted by the path of ignorance, [He acts] for the purpose of liberation and so forth.
As a means for sacrifice (*yāga*). "Of that" refers to the nature of one's own essential form, which is the unstruck self (*anāhatātman*), existing in two states.

"The whole" (*sakala*) means it is manifested as consisting of four parts and many forms, suited for bestowing grace upon various recipients of grace. This is what is meant: this single supreme reality of the Lord is one alone.
It remains as it is, manifesting according to the need for grace toward those who are to be graced; however, there is no real distinction whatsoever here.
As it has been said:
"For the sake of gracing individual souls, even the Supreme has assumed a non-supreme state."
Thus, for this very reason, with the intention of [instructing] qualified individuals,
the procedure for practice (*sādhana*) based solely upon the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka Niṣkala will follow hereafter.
However, that which is the ultimate Niṣkalanātha never takes the form of an object of meditation, recitation, or the like.

It has been stated that this is because [the Lord] is the single, dense mass of the flashing forth of the supreme subject who is the self of the entire universe without remainder. As for the statement that "the Sakala [state] exists in two conditions" and is thus revealed as both Sakala and Niṣkala to the gods and the Daityas respectively—
having explained this, [one might object that] such a revelation is inappropriate for the Daityas because of their tamasic nature.

Someone might raise the objection that it is contradictory to mention the former birth of the Asuras by referring to them as "possessing acquired power" (*āyāta-śaktitvena*); this has been resolved by stating that this is merely a description of their previous state.
Whether this is correct or incorrect is for those with discernment to judge; enough of this point-by-point discussion with our predecessors.
By means of persistence. || 19 ||
Now, regarding this root mantra:
first is its natural form (*prākṛta-rūpa*), and second is its modified form (*vikṛta*).
It is called "first" because it serves as the foundational wall for the manifestation of the universe; thus, it is primary, being the *prakṛti*.

That which has come forth from its own nature is the form that sounds by itself; however, its first manifestation is the form consisting of the letter *A*, and it should not be explained otherwise, for "the *haṃsa* sounds by itself. (7.59)
Thus:
"Therefore, the phonemes arise from the vital breath and return to dissolution... (4.248).
Thus, [this would lead] to the contradiction of such statements as: "The entire scripture consists of sound; sound is proclaimed to be the *haṃsa*" (4.341).
Thus, even within a single mantra, both the original form (prakṛti) and the modified form (vikṛti) are simultaneously joined with the sixth vowel. (6.20)

This is indeed clearly stated: just as in the mantra, within the form of the *ha* which is the original nature (*prakṛti*), there exists the portion of the letter *a* (the *akārakalā*)—which is the modification (*vikṛti*) denoted by the word "head" (*śirorekhā*)—such that both the original nature and the modification are simultaneously endowed with the sixth digit (*ṣaṣṭhakalā*). || 20 ||
Therefore—among those categories previously mentioned, he repeatedly breathes forth therein;
by this [breathing forth] he proceeds, and by that [breathing back] he returns again. (6.21)
He who was immediately thereafter described by the statement, "But when the Lord is devoid of qualities" (6.11), is this very Niṣkalanātha.
Exhaling while merging the *kalā* of the vowels *A* and *U*, it ascends upward;

"therein" means into the previously mentioned categories of objects ending with the *unmanā*; by that same aforementioned sequence, it proceeds and ascends to the *dvādaśānta*. Again, by that same [process], it returns in reverse order to the end of the heart.
It attains clarity of color and enters precisely the unstruck sound (anāhata-dhvani). "Again and again" means repeatedly at the time of recitation. || 21 ||
Thus, this *praṇava*, performing ascent and descent among the categories of existence (*padārtha*), exists in five states;
it manifests its fivefold nature through the sequence of the expressive phonemes (*vācaka-kalā*) and the sequence of the expressed meanings (*vācya*).
The Praṇava is recited as having three phonemes and three deities, and as being joined with the Bindu and the Nāda. (6.22)
Without the fusion of *bindu* and *nāda*, there is merely the form of a combination of phonemes (*varṇa-saṅghaṭṭana*),
but it does not possess the nature of the *praṇava* in the sense that "by this the supreme reality is excellently praised.
Thus, due to the distinctions of *a*, *u*, *m*, *bindu*, and *nāda*, there are five forms of the signifier (*vācaka*) as previously described.
The Praṇavas, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the two yet-to-be-described Lords, Īśvara and Sadāśiva, constitute the five in the form of the objects denoted. || 22 ||
Thus it is said:
"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the third, the letter *m*—these three phonemes are proclaimed to be the three deities beginning with Brahmā. (6.23)
Through the union of Bindu and Nāda, there are Īśvara and Sadāśiva;
these indeed are the five Praṇavas...
[connected with] the three deities beginning with Brahmā—this is the relationship. The meaning is that they exist in the form of the signified and the signifier.
And these very ones...
the *haṃsa* is always joined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (6.24)
"The letter *ha*, however, is remembered as the vital breath" (4-257).
Thus, that which was previously described as the *haṃsa*-breath—the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*)—is always joined with it, attached to it; [she] is that.
The meaning is that nothing whatsoever can manifest without the wall of great reflective awareness (mahāvimarśa). || 24 ||
Therefore, in this context:
"The Supreme Self is Śiva, while the Haṃsa is conjoined with the other;
that which is the Haṃsa is the form that arises by itself through the function of the signifier (vācaka), whereas through the function of the signified (vācya), it is the Supreme Self."
He is the animator of all beings, beginning with Brahmā;

he is Śiva because he bestows the supreme good which consists of ultimate liberation. Because the signified and the signifier flash forth here as an undivided mass of light and bliss, such is this Haṃsa. [The phrase] "by another" refers to...
It is endowed with, or connected to, the fivefold *praṇava* in the form of the previously mentioned signified (*vācya*) and signifier (*vācaka*).

Here, within the *praṇavas* consisting of the letter *A* and so forth, there are the states of waking and the rest, which are the subtle measures (*kalā*) of pronunciation such as the short vowel, as well as [the principles] beginning with Earth and ending with Nature (*prakṛti*), Māyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

The principles presided over by Brahmā and the others— these five groups— are to be understood as being included within [the preceding categories] and, according to the established view, are to be followed as having the nature of the *praṇava*.
Not only do five other forms of the *praṇava* reside in this mantra in this manner, but furthermore, I shall speak again of five subsequent *praṇavas*. (6.25)
The meaning is: by way of its distinction from the established tenets of other tantras. || 25 ||
He said to them: "O Goddess, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, Niṣkala, and likewise Unmanā—these are declared to be the five Praṇavas. (6.26)

Here too, by the previously stated reasoning, the nature of the *praṇava* belongs to the powers of the denotators (*vācaka-kalā*), the denoted (*vācya*), and the coverings (*āvaraṇa*)— such as the states, powers, and principles (*tattva*) of the utterer and the extremely subtle mode of pronunciation (*uccāra-kalā*) which are contained within them. || 26 ||
This supreme *haṃsa*, which serves as the foundation for this entire universe, remains pervading everything beyond the beyond.
That supreme *haṃsa* who has been definitively established is "beyond" (*parataḥ*) by virtue of its excellence.
The pentad of *praṇavas*, divided by the distinctions of the higher and the lower, exists pervading the universe through that very gateway;

therefore, it alone is the supreme object of attainment. And because it consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of non-duality with that [pentad], the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka is also partless (*niṣkala*).
Therefore, in this regard: "These indeed are the five Praṇavas, according to the division of the higher and the lower. (6.27)
They are perpetually bowed down by the Parāpara Haṃsa.

The Haṃsa, whose form is the plow (halākṛti), having attained a four-syllable state through its union with the Parāpara Praṇava beginning with the letter 'A' and its own powers, is called Parāpara. By that [Haṃsa] in its dual form, they are bowed down.

They have been brought to a state of prostration, made inclined toward their own self-reflection; "praṇāmitāḥ" is the reading belonging to the Lord (Īśvara). For this very reason, we stated at the very beginning that they are called *praṇavas* because by them the supreme reality is praised (*nūyate*) intensely (*pra-*) [or, they themselves are bowed down]. || 27 ||
And therefore these [mantras]—indeed, they operate everywhere, bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. (6.28)
"Everywhere" refers to the context of the spiritual practitioners (sādhaka), their sons (putraka), and so forth. || 28 ||
Therefore, this is the root mantra:
joined with these five, it consists of five *praṇavas*.

It is that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), [pervading] everywhere precisely by means of the manifestation of the distinction between the supreme (*para*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*) *praṇavas*.
That the Lord of the Four Kalās is the cause—this has indeed been definitively established.
Furthermore: "Abiding therein, he is indeed of a single form; in reality, he is remembered as being partless (niṣkala). (6.29)
"Therein" means in that abode of repose in the previously mentioned *praṇava*, which is the Lord of the four *kalās*.
"He who remains" refers to the Lord Anāhata-Bhaṭṭāraka, whose nature is as described as being of a single form;
the meaning is that he alone is, in reality, partless (*niṣkala*). || 29 ||

Not only is he [the Lord] so, but even the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is likewise; because it is connected with that [Lord], and because of its relation to the aforementioned *niṣkala* (partless) state, the seed-syllable is also called *niṣkala*. Thus, even the Lord of the four *kalās* is called *niṣkala*.
This is the meaning.
Furthermore:
...the sprout of all seeds;
that is, of all seeds—namely, the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, as well as the mantras of the limbs and the Brahmās, etc.
It is the cause of growth and the bestower of capacity precisely through that conjunction.
The reason for this is: "Because from this [place] proceeds the abode of the gods and asuras. (6.30)
It is called *aya* because it goes (*eti*), moves, and rises up by itself, vibrating as non-different from the light of consciousness;

it is shaped like a plow (*hala*). Therefore, because—according to the principle previously established—it serves as the abode (*niketana*) or place of worship for the gods and asuras, the two mantras consisting of four parts and many forms proceed [from it] for the sake of grace and other purposes.

It spreads forth; therefore, it is rightly said: "Because of its connection with that, its seed causes all seeds to sprout" (6.30). Some maintain that the gods and asuras are the senses, and their abode is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 30 ||

And therefore, according to the pervasion determined in the first chapter, because the universe is accepted by means of the four-fold and the multi-formed [energies], and because those two rest in the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*) whose essence is mutual vibration—
therein the mantras and phonemes find their foundation, and not otherwise.

Mantras are the seed-syllables of the *piṇḍas*. All phonemes (*varṇas*)—those belonging to the *mālā-mantras* as well as those consisting of the *mātṛkās*—are established in the *anāhata* alone. Indeed, without the supreme vibration (*sphurattā*), the manifestation of anything whatsoever is not possible. And it has been said in the *Śrī Spanda*:
"The mantras, having seized that power...
(2.10), and so forth.
And therefore, O Beloved, through the awakening to that [Self], they are liberated like a snake from its slough. (6.31)
The word "initiated" (dīkṣitāḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 31 ||
This is clarified as follows:
"One wanders in saṃsāra for as long as one does not find reality;
but once the supreme reality is known, one is never born again anywhere. (6.32)
Just as a snake, once it has cast off its slough, does not cling to it again, so the knower of reality, having abandoned the bondage of the ego-sense, is no longer touched by it. || 32 ||

Showing that reality is indeed the form of the *haṃsa*, he clarifies this very point further: "A man remains one who has not accomplished his purpose as long as he does not find the *haṃsa*; he finds it—that is, he attains it by way of his own nature and recognizes it."
He applies this, along with its method, to the present subject by means of showing the contrast:
"One should point out that [the mantra] joined with the *praṇava* has accomplished its purpose. (6.33)

The meaning is that a person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (kṛtārtha) because he rests in the supreme, partless (niṣkala) nature— which is precisely the means for the utterance and the knowledge of the utterance of that [Oṃ] which was determined above as being properly joined with the four-part Praṇava. || 33 ||
And therefore:
"Having understood that utterance (*uccāra*) from that [source], one should utter it, O fair-faced one.
"One should utter" means one should cause it to be uttered; "that" refers to the four-syllabled [mantra] which serves as the means for resting in the Supreme (*paraviśrānti*).
In that regard—O Goddess, the utterance of the Haṃsa is declared to be threefold. (6.34)

Due to the presiding presence of the aforementioned higher and lower *praṇavas*, the *haṃsa* also possesses a threefold utterance: as the "higher-lower" (*parāpara*) by virtue of being established in its own essential nature, and as the "higher-than-the-higher" (*parātpara*).
This has been declared: "These indeed are the five *praṇavas*, according to the division of the higher and the lower, [along with] the higher-lower *haṃsa*" (6.27).
Thus, it was stated immediately prior [in verse 6.27] by such expressions as: "The supreme *haṃsa* stands pervading everything from beyond. || 34 ||
He clarifies that very utterance:
"The third [syllable] is at the end of the bindu, conjoined with the letter *ha* and the letter *u*;
by its placement within the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), it is called the utterance of the yoga of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). (6.35)

The syllable *ha* here is used with its case-ending elided for the purpose of revealing the nature of the Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*). Thus, that *Haṃsa* which is self-manifesting in form becomes joined with the phonemes *a* and *u*, and above them, at the end of the *bindu* (the nasal dot), there is the third [element], which is of the nature of the *anusvāra*.

The letter *ma* is indeed connected to this; such is the utterance that concludes it. Regarding "of emanation" (*sṛṣṭeḥ*), by means of the deposition (*nyāsa*)—that is, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as distinct designators—of the emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal performed by the differentiated Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who preside over the three states beginning with waking, [it is not so].

The meaning is "by way of non-differentiation. However, for these three which consist of differentiation, the "method of withdrawal" (saṃhārayoga) is said to consist of the unification with the state of the *bindu*, which is characterized by contact with the initial limit of the fourth state (*turya*); there is no pervasion through the utterance of phonemes (*varṇoccāra*) here. || 35 ||
Just as it was previously divided by him—in this very sequence beginning with "thus" (*evam*), the wise one should recite the mantra.
"The wise one" means the knower; "thus" refers to the form already described; "beginning with" refers to the sequence starting with the letter *a*.
One should utter the *haṃsa*, which has attained the nature of a mantra precisely through its connection with this [mantra].
Repeating this, he now states another procedure to be followed when uttering the mantra from this point forward:
"Having placed the triad within the *bindu*, one should then open the mouth. (6.36)

The triad ending in *m*—having placed it within the *bindu*, that is, having accomplished its essence as the pervasion of non-differentiation—one should open the mouth, the face, for the purpose of uttering the *nāda*; this means that at the time of this utterance, one should bind the divine instrument (*divyaṃ karaṇam*). || 36 ||
And then— when the mouth is slightly opened, one should recognize the sound (nāda) by means of this procedure,
being attentive to the utterance of the mantra.
The meaning is that the manifestation of the sound (nāda) occurs at the end of the non-sound (anāda).
Furthermore: "That which resides in Nāda is fivefold, and that which resides in Śakti is likewise fivefold. (6.37)
The connection is: "knowing the form of the mantra in five ways within the Pervasive One. And as for its fivefold nature, it is stated:
"that which is the pentad beginning with Brahmā" (6.41).

Having begun with this, one should understand it according to the state about to be described immediately thereafter: "They are established everywhere through the division of the supreme and the non-supreme" (6.41). Therefore, in the *Yojanikā* text, [this applies] to the *nāda*.

The state of being eightfold that was previously mentioned was established through the reasoning of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) on the nature of the signifiers; however, this state of being fivefold is established through the reasoning of the reflective awareness on the nature of the causes which are the signified objects mounted upon those [eight] levels. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever between the preceding and the following.
Furthermore—

[the phrase] "one who knows the form previously determined" is to be supplied [to the verse concerning] the two, the *sakala* (with parts) and the *niṣkala* (without parts), which abide higher and higher.
Now, above this—Unmanā is the supreme reality, established pervading everything. (6.38)
The meaning is: "Know the form previously determined. || 38 ||
He concludes: "Knowing thus, people who know the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) are liberated.
That is to say, by knowing in the manner described—having experienced the stages ending with the Transmental (unmanā)—those who [know] the principle of Śiva...
Those who know—that is, recognize—the Self as Paramaśiva are liberated specifically by way of the Siddhānta's distinction [from other systems]. For therein it is said:
"The letters A, Va, Ra, Ma, Ka, A, Bindu, and Nāda are its excellent mantras."
Thus has the pervasion of the mantra been shown by the teachers.
In this regard, he states the dissimilarity:
"Otherwise, those who remain fixed at the end of the drops are not liberated at all. (6.39)

Those who are established in and have found rest within the Bindu, at its end, and in the stages beginning with Nāda, are not liberated at all; rather, they enjoy only the specific sovereign power (vibhūti) appropriate to each of those stages. || 39 ||
For it is said:
"The form of light resides in the *bindu*; the form of sound resides in the *nāda*;
that which resides in *śakti* is the realm of touch; and above that is the form of emptiness. (6.40)

Regarding what was stated—that "the triad resides in the *bindu*" and "the pentad resides in the *nāda*"—that which resides in the *bindu* is of the nature of light (*jyotis*), meaning it is of the nature of the manifestation of the non-differentiation of the object of knowledge. That which resides in the *nāda*, however, is of the nature of power (*śakti*), meaning it consists of the power of emission (*visarga*). As for that which is situated in the plane of power (*śaktipada*)...
It has the true nature of the bliss of the touch of sparśagamana; beyond that, in the Vyāpinī, it takes the form of the manifestation of emptiness (śūnyatā). || 40 ||

Because the pervasive abode is that which consists of the pentad beginning with Brahmā, as well as their void— that state— and by the use of the word "ca" (and), it is also [the state] void of those principles (tattvas) which are to be presided over by Brahmā and the others; thus, it is "void of them."

When it is said that "they are empty," he shows by means of the genitive case that they all abide therein as the very nature of that appropriate, supreme consciousness, and have not gone anywhere else;
for this very reason, it was previously stated that "the non-empty is empty," and so forth.
One might object: "Since Brahmā and the others are established in locations ranging from the heart to the forehead, how have they reached such a high level? To this he says:
