"By means of the division into the higher and the lower, they are established everywhere. (6.41)

For the powers of the Supreme Lord— known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action— which possess the pervasion of the cosmic manifestation appropriate to His state, have manifested [the universe] down to the level of Brahmā;
thus, Brahmā and the others, whose essence is that pervasion, abide everywhere through their pervasion of the gross, subtle, and other levels.

And this will become clear in the eleventh [chapter]. Alternatively, these [mantras] bestow those various supernatural powers (siddhis) according to the suitability of their respective words. || 41 ||
Now,
Śūnyātītā is indeed Samanā, and likewise Tūnmanā is the Pure Self;
the meaning is that they are, in sequence, the forms of consciousness appropriate to themselves.
Then—[the state] beyond all, the supreme reality, abiding pervading everything. (6.42)
Even though it transcends all things, its pervasiveness of everything arises from its beauty as pure, autonomous consciousness-bliss;
and because this supreme reality remains established by pervading all,
therefore even those [phonemes] denoted by *ā*, *u*, and *m*— though exceedingly gross— [are likewise pervasive].

The deities are to be understood as having the form of mantra because of their nature as *bindu*; the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only. They are to be known as being exclusively of the nature of mantra, through non-separation, by virtue of the essence of their non-dual pervasion.
For thus—those situated there accomplish all rites; of this there is no doubt. (6.43)
In that context, "abiding" means established or ascended within the mantra whose true nature is the pervasion to be explained. || 43 ||
Having thus described the utterance of the mantra that constitutes the limb of liberation (*muktyaṅga*) from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the process of upward expansion (*ullāsakrama*),
he now indicates that same [utterance] as the limb of accomplishment (*siddhyaṅga*) in reverse order:
"The reality (*tattva*) is indeed the *unmanā*, while the *samanā* is the void (*śūnya*)."
And likewise touch, as well as sound, and form immediately after that. || 6-44 ||
All these must be known by the teacher as abiding within the nature of mantra.
"Form" refers to the splendor of the *bindu*. "Immediately following that" refers to the essential nature of the phonemes consisting of the letters *ma*, *u*, and *ā*.
All these objects of cognition (*prameya*) are established within the partless (*niṣkala*) nature of the essence of mantra.

The meaning is that without reflecting on the sequence of entry into the state of *ullāsa*, they are perceived at the very moment of the mantra as being the very limbs for the accomplishment of liberation (*mukti-siddhi*). The phrase "by the teacher" (*daiśikena*) is used because of his preeminence;
however, through his instruction, it may also be attained by another. || 44 ||
O fair-faced one, these not only accomplish all rites while situated in the mantras, but furthermore, while situated therein, they bestow the yoga of knowledge.
Knowledge is the experience of the reality of each respective object of knowledge; yoga is the attainment of identity with that.
Regarding what was stated— that all rites are accomplished— therein he describes the meditation on the mantra-deities in accordance with the specific rite:
"But at the time of the rite, one should [meditate on] all [the deities] as being endowed with heads, hands, and so forth."
Ritual action consists of worship, fire oblations, and so forth.
O Goddess, one should gradually recite all [the mantras] conjoined with the partless (niṣkala). || 6-46 ||

The word "one should meditate" (dhyāyet) from the immediately preceding verse is supplied here. [One should meditate on those] who are perfectly endowed with the partless [reality], which is the ultimate truth of the density of consciousness, and whose essence consists in resting therein. 46.

But when one desires the accomplishment (siddhi) consisting of omniscience and so forth, then one should meditate upon all [the deities] as composed of light, whose true nature is repose in the Bindu.
For it has been said:
Regarding the statement, "But the form of light resides in the Bindu" (6.40),
it is understood from the context that this is stated here for the purpose of defining the fruit [of the practice], and thus it is not a redundant repetition.
Now, regarding the state of the upward-sounding resonance (ūrdhvanāda) which follows the repose of the point (bindu):
the meaning is that those [mantras] which bestow the accomplishment of sound grant that very accomplishment to the meditator by virtue of consisting in the repose of the resonance (nādaviśrānti).
In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, these [mantras] grant their respective accomplishments through meditation on the forms appropriate to them.
As it has been said:
"Those situated in Śakti are declared to be the givers of power; those situated in Śūnya are remembered as the pervasive ones.
O fair-faced one, those situated in Samanā indeed bestow knowledge in due order. (6.47)
Beyond that, they bestow liberation; and in the stage of unmanā, they are all-knowing.

*Śakti* is the capacity for all instruments of action. *Śūnya* is the pervasive one (*vyāpinī*). The term "pervasive ones" (*vyāpakāḥ*) refers to those who bestow pervasion upon the worshiper. Knowledge (*jñāna*) arises in succession, encompassing all objects from Śiva down to the earth. *Kaivalya* is the state of being an isolated one (*kevalin*) through pure consciousness.
That which is the supreme goal to be attained by the dualistic Śaivas; "above" means in the state of the pure self (*śuddhātmapada*).
"Omniscient" means those who bestow the manifestation of the non-differentiation of the entire universe without succession. As was stated previously:
"Śamanā is the knowledge of succession, while Unmanā is without succession" (4.394).
And these experiences of the constituent parts of mantra—all those which have been described by me—are "pierced" (vedhitāḥ) in their true essence;
that is, they are pierced by Paraśiva and pervaded by him in his entirety as the universal self. The term "pierced" (vedhitāḥ) is used here in the sense of [divine] sovereignty (aiśa).
The reading is this very usage of the root "vidha," meaning "to ordain" or "to arrange."
Therefore—having known that, all [mantras] bestow both supernatural powers and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (6.49)

The word "tat" refers to reality (*tattva*). For it has been determined in the *Yojanikā* treatise that even for practitioners, this [attainment] culminates in success and liberation through the sequence of mantras; this is so because the Lord (*Īśvara*) is the authoritative source, even though there is a difference in the authors [of the respective texts]. (49)
He concludes: "I have explained to you the reality conjoined with the five *praṇavas*;
the reality attained through the means of the utterance of the five *praṇavas*."
The nature of the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), which is identical with Paramaśiva, has been told by me to you alone, who are a worthy Śakti, and not to anyone else whatsoever.
Having understood this—
preceded by the five *praṇavas* and beginning with ten thousand *oṃkāras*— || 6-50 ||
O you of excellent vows, by reciting it in its many forms ending with the salutations,
one attains perfection through one hundred thousand repetitions according to the count of syllables.

The word "sādhaka" (the practitioner) is to be understood as the ellipsis. [He is] one by whom [the mantra] preceded by the four-part *pañcapraṇava* has been recited; who, having first performed the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the differentiation, pervasion, and non-pervasion already explained, rests upon the middle path opened by that recitation, and who, being absorbed in that, possesses manifold forms.

The connection is that "therefore, one attains success through recitation (*japa*). By the phrase "joined with the *oṃkāra* and so forth," he says this: although the pervasive application of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) was employed at the beginning of the section starting from "the Lord of the Four Kalās" up to "from the forms of Bahurūpa, Aghora, and the rest," nevertheless, regarding the worship and recitation of all mantras—
It is the established convention of the scriptures that a "lamp" (dīpaka) should be formed by connecting the *praṇava* and the salutation (*namaskāra*) at the beginning and the end.
Therefore, those very same *praṇava* and salutation mentioned previously for the thirty-two-syllable mantra should be applied to the one preceded by the four *kalās*. For it is said:
It has been stated: "Those situated there accomplish all rites" (6.43). By the count of syllables, "by a hundred thousand" (*lakṣa*) means by thirty-two hundred thousand.
He completes this very point by adding further detail:
"One should always recite the mantra joined with the *praṇava* at its beginning.
That is to say, one should always recite the mantra properly joined with that which has the *praṇava* as its first part—the Lord of the Four Kalās.

This means "up to that point. First of all, the recitation (japa) of this [mantra] must be performed with uninterrupted one-pointedness; this is the meaning. The word *sadā* (always) is an addition here.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should again perform a fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part [of the total number].
Having begun with the passage, "Having recited a hundred thousand syllables of Bahurūpa" (6.3),
and having determined the nature of the five *praṇavas*, [the text concludes]: "One should always recite the mantra joined with the *praṇava* at its beginning" (6.52).
Having thus concluded, it was stated:

"But at the end of the recitation, there is again an oblation" (6.52). Therefore, the ancillary oblation has been performed by means of the commencement of the recitation; as for the recitation itself—

The meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is as follows: once the self-realization through the manifestation of the mantra-deity has been accomplished, for the purpose of its satiation (*tarpaṇa*), a fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed with the mantra ending in *svāhā* at a tenth part of the number of recitations; thus, if [the recitation] was three hundred thousand, the oblation should consist of thirty-two thousand. || 52 ||
Regarding this fire-offering (homa), he states the appropriate substance: "Human flesh combined with wine and thoroughly saturated with ghee;
from that, one attains accomplishment—whether inferior, middling, or superior. (6.53)

Pura is guggulu resin. Having offered these three substances simultaneously, one attains all the supreme and other forms of accomplishments, such as mastery over the principles (tattveśvaratva), soaring through the sky, and reaching the netherworld (pātāla);
however, this is not according to their respective numerical order, because that would not accord with the meaning of the words and would contradict other scriptures. 53
But when, through three times the number of recitations, one becomes equal to Svachanda,
one attains the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas, Daityas, and lords of the Uragas. (6.54)
He may become a giver of fear and a taker away, one who inflicts curses or bestows grace;
he can take away the pride of Time itself and even cause the mountains to fall.
One may shatter the *bilva* diagrams and even cause the elephants of the quarters to tremble;
[one may likewise overcome] Brahma-rākṣasas, vetālas, cruel grahas, and vināyakas.

O Goddess, by mere remembrance, he destroys [all obstacles], being invincible even to the gods; because he bestows both curses and favors, he is the giver and the remover of fear. The meaning of "by remembrance" (smaraṇāt) is that he destroys them as soon as he is remembered. || 56 ||
And by means of this mantra, even ordinary rites are accomplished through one hundred thousand recitations. (6.57)
The rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others, which are accomplished through the application of substances produced from nature, are "natural" (*prākṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "from a hundred thousand recitations," this refers to the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*), which should be completed along with a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that number.
At the time of the ritual application (*prayoga*), there is the consecration of the materials appropriate for the rite by means of the specific mantra.

It is already established that the substances mentioned in the ritual applications to be described hereafter, as well as those belonging to the scope of ritual applications in other kalpas, are likewise valid; as he will conclude:
"In this way, there are hundreds of thousands [of mantras], and those arising from other kalpas."
"This Lord of the Sovereigns of the Kings of Mantras performs the ritual applications. (6.94) || 57 ||

Thus, I shall correctly explain, in due order and as it truly is, those [practices] which, for one who has previously propitiated a mantra, are to be employed at certain occasions as constituent parts of the primary siddhis.

"Samyak" (correctly) means so that they will not be inconsistent; "yathāvat" (accordingly) means as they are joined with the proper procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Regarding this, the interpretation that "one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra should be performed, ending with the insertion 'May such-and-such a person be under my control'" is incorrect.

Because the nature of the mantra has already been specifically established previously by the statement: "With ten thousand [repetitions] beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with a salutation" (6.51). To this extent, according to the explanation provided, it is for one who generally intends the attainment of minor supernatural powers (*kṣudrasiddhi*).

Having performed the recitation and fire-oblation for the sake of preliminary service, at the time of application, the ritual employment of the mantra— beginning with the specific caste-appellation appropriate to the rite— should be carried out.
In that regard, he first states the applications for subjugation:
"Mohanā, Sahadevā, Bhūdhātrī, and Cakralāñchanā. (6.58)
One should grind it together with *rāmavallī* using one's own seed (semen) as the liquid;
this should be given in food and drink as a supreme means of subjugation. (6.59)

*Mohanā* is *balāmoṭā*; *bhūdhātrī* is *bhūmyāmalakī*; *cakralāñchanā* is *cakrāṅkā*; and *rāmavallī*, known as *rāmataraṇi*, is a well-known medicinal herb. *Ātmabīja* refers to one's own semen. It should be administered after being consecrated with mantras; for in this way, it becomes unfailing.
Furthermore, one should cause [the practitioner] to grasp the root of the *utpala* plant under the asterism of Puṣya;
when combined with the faculty of the self, this is the supreme means of subjugation.

The *uttarāvaraṇī* is extensive. Regarding the phrase "by the Puṣya asterism," it means by the Puṣya nakṣatra when conjoined with a benefic planet. It is stated in the *Oṣadhikalpa* that the collection of medicinal herbs should be performed during the night in the bright fortnight. "Self-faculty" (*ātmandriya*) refers to one's own semen (*śukra*). As it has been said:
"The seed-syllable *ṅṛ* has Indra as its presiding deity; therefore it is called *indriya*.
Its superiority arises from its association with a single medicinal herb (*ekauṣadhi*). It is established that [this applies] both to what is eaten and what is drunk. (60)
The impurities of the ears and eyes, saliva, blood,
along with the sense organs and earth-cadamba (bhūkadamba), should be offered with milk at night.
The five [impurities] are the two ears, the two eyes, and saliva;

blood is associated with the left ring finger; semen is the organ; these constitute the seven personal [impurities], and *bhūkadamba* (or *bhūtīka*) is the eighth. Having combined these together, one should drink water consecrated by mantras during the night.
It should be given for the sake of subjugation. || 61 ||
And this—
[the gift] should be given when not away from home...
having given it, one must not depart on a journey.
Otherwise,
she would perish from the pain of separation;
such is the power of this practice— this is the meaning.
Sixty seeds of gold and sixteen moon-like jewels.
O beautiful woman, you should offer these [substances] joined with human and cow dung;
this Kāpālika yoga follows after one who is departing.
The word "him" (*tam*) is to be supplied as the object. *Kanaka* is *dhattūra* (thorn-apple). *Maṇicandrikā* is *raktikā*.

There is no fixed rule regarding the number [of grains] of human or cow bone here. This powder is to be administered with food or drink, as previously stated. A *kāpālika* is one who is surrounded by skulls, that is, bones. || 63 ||
The root of white Arka, Mañjiṣṭhā, the head of a sparrow, Kuṣṭha grown in a house, along with one's own blood and [the juice of] the Indrī plant; (6.64)
This supreme means of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa) should be given in food and drink.
The whiteness of the arka tree is due to its white flowers. The house-sparrow and the mouse [are also used]. One's own blood and semen are used as before. 64.
And Mohanā, as well as Kāntārī, joined with Mayūraśikhā. || 6-65 ||
The supreme subjugation [mantra] is joined with *ātmalā* and the sense organs (*indriya*).
*Kāntārī* is *priyaṅgu*. *Mayūraśikhā* is a medicinal herb shaped like that [peacock's crest].
Because of the plural number in "with *ātmalā* and the sense organs," both types of substances arising from the sense organs are intended.
It is supreme and non-deceptive. || 65 ||
Lajjālukā, Gorambhā, and likewise Caṇḍālīkarmakā. || 6-66 ||
"O lady of excellent vows, this divine and supreme yoga, consisting of the feet of the Lord of Nagas combined with its own seed-syllable, is bestowed upon whomever it may be."
Combined with a sweet substance, it brings mastery for as long as one lives.
*Lajjāluka* is *laṅguḍā*; *gorambhā* is *chatrā*. The primary root is the medicinal plant known as *caṇḍālī*. [It is combined] with a sweet poison, and of that—
Through conjunction with another substance, the power of killing is obstructed. || 67 ||
Chickpeas, black gram, and mung beans have emerged through the lower opening.
Vomited matter, ghee, semen, female menses, as well as the impurities of the heart, urine, blood, hair, and saliva, O fair-faced one. (6.69)
Putrajānī, Kṛtāhvā, and Nāgendrapada joined together;
Mohanā, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Dhātrī likewise stand on one side.
O fair-faced one, under the Puṣya asterism, one should employ this yoga, which is honored by the thirty gods, when giving food and drink to cows. (6.71)

Excreted through the downward breath (*apāna*), they have become feces; "vomit" refers to ghee and the like. One's own impurities of the heart and the impurities of the navel. *Putrajani* is a specific medicinal herb.
*Kṛtāhvā* means one who has joined the palms in reverence. *Viṣṇukrāntā* is well known [as a plant]. *Dhātrī* is the *āmalaka* fruit.
"Worshipped by the thirty-three [gods]" is non-contradictory. Thus, the eight applications for subjugation have been explained.
Now,
I shall explain the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) for enemies who are arrogant in spirit.
In that regard—
The feathers of a crow and an owl, as well as the urine of a donkey and a camel, and earth.
Having fashioned an image with these substances, the wise man should smear it with the blood of a crow.
Now, another [method]—
And one should insert the feathers of a crow and an owl into her anus.
Then,
one should bury her at a crossroads;
having dug there, she is to be placed and covered over.
Then, having kindled the cremation fire above, one should perform the oblation there with crow feathers, O lady of excellent vows.
Having prepared [the substances] together with wandering birds and infused them with donkey urine,
one should recite the name of the person targeted, beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *ra*.
At the conclusion of the mantra, one should recite that which ends with the *visarga*, having been placed [therein].
"That" (*tam*) is the understood subject. "Whirling leaves" (*udbhrāntapatrāṇi*) refers to leaves situated amidst the shafts of dust stirred up by the wind from the *arjuna* trees.
"At the conclusion of the mantra" means at the end of the propitiation of Bahurūpa. "Ending with the *visarga*"...

The practitioner who, having uttered with anger the name of whichever enemy is to be exorcised— enclosed and encapsulated by the syllable *ya* applied at the beginning and the end, such as "May Devadatta be exorcised"— and while still possessed by wrath, offers one hundred and eight feathers of a crow's wing according to the method to be described, he...
The connection is that one should cause him to be eradicated. || 75 ||
Thus expelled, that enemy wanders like a crow upon the earth, tormented by disease. (6.76)
He states the application for causing enmity: "Having made an image of the enemy out of oil-cake, neem leaves, clay, fermenting agent, and husks, and having wrapped it with *akṣa* flowers... (6.77).
One should bury that [image] in a cremation ground after kindling a fire upon it;
then, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with flowers from the *vibhīta* tree while uttering the name of the person [against whom the rite is directed].
"Even one who is equal to Kāmadeva shall indeed become a hated enemy.

*Piṇyāka* is a paste made from the seeds of *guggulu*. *Kiṇva* is the substance used for fermenting liquor. "With *akṣapuṣpas*" means with *vibhītaka* flowers. "Enveloped" (*veṣṭitām*) means encircled by a garland of those [flowers]. "By name" (*nāmneti*).
"May he become hostile"—by means of this [mantra] endowed with the class of incantations for creating enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), which, by implication, possesses many forms;
the oblation (*homa*) consists of one hundred and eight counts. || 78 ||
Now he describes the method for making oneself beloved by another who is hostile, or by anyone else:
"Guggulu mixed with *priyaṅgu* creepers and pierced with clarified butter. (6.79)
O Goddess, by performing one hundred and eight oblations, one becomes fortunate.
*Priyaṅgulatikā* is the fragrant *priyaṅgu*. Here too, having invoked Bahurūpa, one should employ a gentle mantra at the end, saying: "May so-and-so become fortunate."
By offering oblations of sesame seeds mixed with *jātī* buds and soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*). || 6.80 ||

Even a man devoid of beauty attains good fortune by [offering] the "three sweets" (trimadhu), milk, sugar, and ghee. Here too, as before, the mantra is used and the oblation (homa) is performed one hundred and eight times. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
The fire-oblation (homa), performed according to the ritual requirements for the end of birth, is exactly one hundred and eight in number. || 80 ||
By offering beloved sesame seeds mixed with salt and anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu), [one attains the desired result].
Within seven days, even a woman renowned for her beauty comes under one's control.
Regarding the method of attraction:
mustard seeds and salt, soaked in honey, milk, and ghee. (6.82)
One should offer oblations mixed with *rājikā* (black mustard) and *āsurī* (datura); by this, one shall swiftly attract that person. (82)

Previously, eight methods of subjugation were taught in the sequence of food and drink, and one by means of fire-oblation; now he speaks again according to the sequence of substances to be employed for bathing and other purposes:
"Having taken the *rocanā* of a man and the ichor of an elephant... (6.83).
Having meditated upon it and empowered it with this mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times;
then, whether it is given for bathing, as an unguent, or with wine or perfume, [the desired result follows] for whomever it is bestowed.
He quickly becomes submissive, a bestower of wealth and likewise a giver of life.
Having taken human bezoar (nararocanā) and smeared it with elephant ichor (gajamada), one should [use] the mantra known as Bahurūpa.

The connection is as follows: having consecrated this substance by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the previously mentioned application of the *ūha* and *jāti* methods, whoever is given it for bathing and so forth becomes submissive (*vaśya*). || 84 ||
Regarding killing, he says:
"Alternatively, one should certainly kill one's own enemy swiftly. (6.85)
One who is burdened with hundreds of injuries, ungrateful, and evil-minded—not, however, one whose offense is slight. (85)
There, having taken two skull-halves, one should write the name of the enemy. (6.86)
That [substance], placed within a hollowed skull-cup, processed with charcoal from a poison-tree, combined with blood, and made terrifying by the utterance of *huṃ phaṭ*, [is employed]. (6.87)
Having gone to the great forest of pretas...
having made ink with charcoal from a corpse, charcoal from a cremation ground, and blood mixed together,
[one should write] the name of the enemy in the dative case (dvitīyāntam) and the word "vidabhītam" within two skull-bowls right there in the cremation ground.
"First there should be the object to be designated, then the mantra occurs once;

this becomes [the mantra] beginning with *vidabhīta*... because it is thus handed down in scripture, one should correctly [recite] that which ends with the *huṃ phaṭ* syllables placed at the end, ending with "I kill, *huṃ phaṭ*."
One should write [the mantra] by means of the continuous contemplation of the identification with one's own self, whose form is restrained Bhairava. || 87 ||
Then, [the practitioner],
having [performed the preliminary rites] at will, should thereafter worship with offerings of black garlands and the like.
In the cremation ground itself, during the dark night; that is to say, it should be situated within the enclosure of the cremation ground.
...then one should commence the ritual action. || 6-88 ||
"Having informed the god Bhairava, 'Strike down my enemy,' and then,
permitted by the god, he took those two heads. (6.89)
Having gone there, O Great Goddess, he sat upon a skull-seat;
remaining there, filled with wrath, he stood facing the south.
Having perceived his own form as Bhairava— terrible and most fearsome—
the practitioner, filled with wrath, should utter the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.
O illustrious lady, then, in reverse order, one should utter the name of the enemy at the end, followed by the two syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, and strike it violently with the *kādya* [thunderbolt].
As it is ground into pieces, so the enemy perishes;
within seven nights, O Goddess of Gods, this application is irreversible.
"Permitted" means by way of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "Two heads" refers to a pair of skulls.
"Skull-throne" means a seat made of severed heads. "Anger" arises from the recollection of intense injury.
"Then" means immediately after the recitation of the mantra in reverse order (*viloma*). "Irreversible" means that one does not turn back; it cannot be otherwise.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 93 ||
He brings them together—
thus, this Lord of the Lords of the Kings of Mantras performs hundreds of thousands of applications arising from other kalpas. (6.94)
In this way, he acts without contradiction and brings [the practice] to completion. || 94 ||
If, out of compassion for one who is thus sealed by this sequence of practice, either that person himself or another desires the peace of someone else, then—
[one should visualize] the deity situated in the *anuloma* order, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Having uttered the phrase "of so-and-so," substituting the appropriate name as required.
O Goddess, one should offer milk as an oblation for the sake of peace; it is beneficial.
Now, he states the appropriate applications for the castes regarding rites both mentioned and unmentioned:
"The word *vaṣaṭ* is recommended for nourishment; *svāhā* at the end is for the rite of subjugation;
and [the word *namaḥ*] is for the purpose of satiating the mantras."
The word "end" (anta) is connected to both [sides].
Furthermore, regarding the essential nature of mantra:
it is traditionally held that [the mantra] should be recited with extreme devotion during worship. (6.96)
The word "namas" means salutation; by the use of the word "ca" (and), it also applies to recitation (*japa*). || 96 ||
Concluding this, he establishes the connection with the upcoming chapter:
"O Goddess, this has indeed been taught for the wise practitioner who is endowed with the proper time and portion of ritual action; it brings happiness without any hardship. (6.97)

For one who is wise, whose intellect is brought under control through the observances (*yama*) and restraints (*niyama*), and for that very reason who does not undertake minor rites in any way whatsoever, but rather who is fit to accept [the higher path] as an auxiliary to the primary accomplishment (*mukhyasiddhi*), [there remains only] the expulsion (*uccāṭana*) and so forth, which are obstacles to the means of achieving accomplishments such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

For one who acts at the proper time through ritual action— consisting of the observance of the times for bathing and worship— and who is endowed with the portion of time to be determined in the eighth chapter, having understood that;

For one who follows the prescribed application without effort, this practice— performed preceded by the propitiation and consecration with these mantras— is indeed conducive to happiness and bestows the desired fruit; may there be auspiciousness!

Remembering again and again the inexplicable and supreme mantra-power manifested here by me through the flashing radiance of the pair of feet of my excellent Guru— bow within that power, O Gurus, for it is the sole essence of the wheel of mantras.
Cross the ocean of saṃsāra with speed; attain the state of Bhairavī!

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Section on the Five Praṇavas," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
"The Radiance of Self-Will" (Svacchandodyota): That which is the inner self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose nature is the vibration of contracted consciousness, is manifested by that [Self].
The unborn one, who sustains the universe as time and space for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, is victorious.
Having restated the nature of action (*kriyā*) as summarized in the verse, "of that which is joined with the parts of time" (6.97), the Goddess spoke in order to understand the portion of time:
"O God, O Maheśvara, by your grace, action has been understood by me."
O Lord of Gods, please explain the divisions of time in detail.

*Ritual action* (*kriyā*) refers to everything from worship (*pūjana*) up to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). *Time* (*kāla*) refers to the appropriate occasion for achieving each respective *siddhi*.

*Aṃśaka* refers to the divisions such as the portion of Brahmā (*brahmāṃśaka*) or the portion of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇvaṃśaka*), and so forth. By the phrase "according to its expansion" (*prasārataḥ*), explain it through its pervasive extension both externally and internally. For this very reason, [it was stated] previously—
Although the nature of time was indicated by the statement, "and also time in brief" (1.9), it was questioned again because its true essence had not been understood.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O beloved, time is to be understood here as twofold: solar and internal.

Time is that which, being of the nature of the vibration of the Supreme Lord’s power of action (*pārameśa-kriyā-śakti*), impels and delimits the universe through the sixfold modifications such as birth, persistence, and so forth. Although it is of a single form, it is said to be "twofold."

Existing as both external and internal, he is to be known here by the worshippers as a constituent part (*aṅga*) in all rites—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*). That which exists in the sun (*saura*) is the gross [body] consisting of day and night and so forth; yet that very same [sun] is said to be "in the self" (*ātmani*), meaning in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) presided over by it.

That which exists within is "internal" (*ādhyātmika*), referring here to subtle form (*sūkṣmarūpa*). In that regard, auspicious ritual action (*śubhakarma*) should be performed on such occasions as the *suvāra* and *sudina*. Furthermore, for the sake of attaining results both in this world and the next, the nature of the southern and northern solstices (*dakṣiṇāyana-uttarāyaṇa*) and so forth must necessarily be known.
He says that all of this is known precisely from external time:
"O beloved, when the hour is auspicious, the conjunction is favorable, and the day is excellent. (7.2)
But in a heap where there is a decrease of *tejas* (fiery energy),

even if the day is auspicious, and the lunar date, the planets, and the *nakṣatra* are favorable, and the *karaṇa*— such as *vava*, *vālava*, *kaulava*, *taitila*, and so on— is present provided it is free from *viṣṭi*, and it is a good day with a non-empty lunar date (*ariktatithi*) and a favorable conjunction (*yoga*).
Thus, for one who is established in the yoga of Ānanda and so forth, which is favorable starting from one's own natal asterism and depends on the movement of the sun,

there occurs daily, according to the regulation of *ghaṭikās*, the rising of the zodiac signs beginning with Pisces; therein, during the transit of Capricorn— which is the sign of the waning of light— and in Cancer, which is characterized by that [transit] and is the sign of its increase.

The distant connection is as follows: that time which must necessarily be known regarding the commencement of actions pertaining to the next world and this world is the *saura* (solar) [day]. Furthermore, the nominative reading "suvarakaraṇam" and so forth is clear;
moreover—
The southern course and the northern course, the eclipses of the moon and the sun, as well as time and the seasons. (7.3)
The fortnight, the month, the time, the equinox, and likewise the transition between zodiacal signs;
the arising of merit and demerit, O Goddess...
[and] the eclipse characterized by the moon and the sun.

This refers to actions whose fruits pertain to this world or the next, such as the southern and northern solstices. Time is that which is designated as the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*). The seasons are spring and so forth. The fortnights are the bright and the dark.
The months begin with Caitra. The specific times (*velā*) are those based on the movements of the planets and other celestial bodies.

The division of day and night is clearly distinguished. The *viṣuvat* day is the time of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) into Aries and Libra, characterized by the equality of day and night. The other transits are those into the intervening zodiacal signs.

The auspicious time (*puṇyakāla*) begins with the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and so forth. The inauspicious time (*apuṇyakāla*) includes the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) and similar periods. 3.
Thus, all such [factors] as these, which are employed as constituent parts of their respective rites—that is time; this is proclaimed as the solar ( saura ) [time]. || 7.4 ||
The word "external" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 4 ||
Furthermore, O Goddess, I shall speak of the internal; understand this from me.
The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction. By the statement "understand this from me," he intimates that this is of supreme importance to be adopted.
In that regard:
"But the body consisting of the six sheaths is joined with the elements and the subtle elements. (7.5)
His body was presided over by the mind, intellect, ego, the organs of perception and action, the qualities (guṇas),
all the principles (tattvas), and likewise by the gods.

In that context, the self (*ātman*) and the power of the Lord (*prabhu-śakti*), as well as the vital air (*vāyu*) moving through the channels (*nāḍī*), remain present—this is the ellipsis. The six sheaths (*ṣaṭkośa*) are skin, flesh, blood, marrow, bone, and semen.
That which is the body consists of the twenty-three [principles] consisting of the organs of action and perception, along with the qualities such as *sattva* and all the *tattvas*.

The Self (ātman) is that whose form (vigraha)— its essential nature— is presided over and established through its state of being correctly pervaded by the principles beginning with Niyati and ending with Śivatattva, as well as by the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, in the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader.

He who is the performer of various actions and the enjoyer of their fruits, whose nature is consciousness contracted [by limitations], is the power (*śakti*)— consisting of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)— of the Lord Svacchandabhairava, manifesting during moments of mental clarity;
and he is also the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the wind that flows through the path of the nostrils.
Moving through and abiding within the channels that will be described hereafter— this is the intended meaning: here,
the independent Lord (Bhaṭṭāraka), beautiful with the bliss of consciousness which transcends the universe yet comprises the universe, by means of His power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti)—

"By the principle stated in [the verse], 'He alone exists established in both gross and subtle forms' (4.295), one should first manifest the universe— from Sadāśiva down to the earth— within the mirror of one's own self upon the ground of the Void-beyond-the-Void (*śūnyātiśūnyabhūmi*), which is the foundational wall for that manifestation. And therein:

Because the void (śūnya) becomes secondary through the predominance of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa), that which gives rise to the expansion of the contraction of the pure subjects— beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the mantras— is called Mahāmāyā. However, when the light of consciousness becomes secondary...

It demonstrates primarily that [the world] is indeed empty; thus, this power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) is called that which displays the expansion of contraction (*saṅkoca-prapañca*) regarding all the Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, Sakala subjects, and their objects of cognition. And that very contraction which is displayed by it—[is as follows:]...

The subject as emptiness (*śūnyapramātā*) is one whose power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is submerged. When he becomes oriented toward the apprehension of an object (*meyagrahaṇa*) that is distinct [from himself], he then manifests in the form of vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Even while manifesting in this way, like a grain of musk, he remains present within that very state to that same extent.

It manifests as the self-nature of the entire contracted universe; and with that very intention, it was previously stated that the sixfold division of the paths (adhvan), consisting of a variety of extremely expanded forms, resides within the vital breath (prāṇa). And here, within a single utterance of the vital breath, starting from the tube (nālikā)...

Up until the end of the emergence of the sixty-year cycle, and as stated in the eleventh chapter, the measure of the lifespan of the universe— beginning from the lifespan of human beings up to that of Anāśrita—
is of the nature of an exceedingly vast and expanded variety of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Thus it is.

This will be demonstrated. And although it has been established that even in the state of being identified with a body that is extremely contracted— just as in the stage of the vital breath (prāṇabhūmikā)— the Supreme Lord remains in his very nature as the expansion of the full thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), [nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, according to the principle that "prior [to manifestation], consciousness is transformed into prāṇa," the form of prāṇa is the internal locus of the supreme power, because through the process of descending from it, there occurs the descent into the elements,
states of being, and bodies.

By the process of ascending the plane of the *madhyamaprāṇa* (the central breath), which serves as the foundation for the expansion of the entire vital force (*prāṇa*), and preceded by the firm support of entering the state of Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), great yogis attain the state of the autonomous Bhairava (*svacchandabhairavatā*); and limited yogis [attain it] preceded by resting in those respective internal temporal segments.
That perfection is attained without obstacle by those who perform the prescribed rite;
therefore, every sequence of worship— whether taught in this scripture, whether already explained or yet to be explained, or even taught in other compendiums— is [to be followed].

It is precisely by means of the mantra arising on the path of the central breath that one becomes the bestower of fruit; with this intention, there is great effort here in this chapter to establish the nature of time as the supreme self of the Supreme Lord.
Thus, enough of this further elaboration for now. || 6 ||

Although the powers of the self, the lord, and the vital breaths (ātma-prabhu-śakti-vāyavaḥ) are situated everywhere within the body, nevertheless, with reference to their predominance, they are situated respectively— in the navel, below the navel, in the genitals, and in the kanda.
The pervasion of the *prakṛti-tattva* extends as far as the navel;

thus, the Self resides primarily within the network of residual channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) located at the navel, whereas the Central Power (*madhya-śakti*) resides below the perineum (and the vital air resides in the *kanda*). And of these, here—
One's true nature (*svarūpa*) is correctly perceived only by those whose wealth is attentive concentration, and not by the ignorant (*paśu*).
This being the case, from the state of rest in the Self—from the center of the navel... || 7-7 ||
From that, O beloved, the channels (nāḍīs) emerge sideways, upwards, and downwards.
For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere:
"Knowledge of the array of the body is in the navel-cakra. (Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra 3.29)
Thus [it is said].

However, some, having applied the reading "nābhicakrataḥ" (from the navel-wheel) to the preceding [passage] itself, have referred back to the word *kanda* by means of the term "tasmāt" (therefore). || 7 ||
From among them, ten principal channels are situated there, arranged like a wheel. (7–8)
There, "there" means in the lotus at the navel; he will state by name the ten channels. || 8 ||
From those ten,
however, seventy-two thousand channels have emerged;
from them others have emerged again, and from these yet others, repeatedly.
"Have gone forth" means they have spread upwards, downwards, and across. || 9 ||
To what extent have they emerged? He says:
"As many as there are millions of pores of the body, so many nāḍīs are recorded;
[specifically] three and a half crores."
And therefore:
"Just as the leaf of the Palāśa tree is pervaded everywhere by its fibers. (7.10)
In the same way, the body of all living beings is pervaded by the channels (nāḍīs).

Here, according to the established principle that "consciousness previously transformed into the vital breath (prāṇa)," consciousness, having illumined the plane of the void (śūnyabhūmikā), has taken recourse to the plane of the vital breath; and therein as well—

Having assumed the form of the central vital breath (*prāṇa*) residing in the central channel— following the analogy of the middle branch of a *palāśa* leaf— and having established itself there in its initial sequence, it further assumes the form of the primary winds, such as *prāṇa*, which reside in the ten principal channels.

There are thirty-six thousand days possible within a human lifespan for the prāṇa-nāḍīs that flow outward, and exactly as many for the apāna-nāḍīs that flow inward; thus, both together amount to seventy-two thousand.
She has illuminated those things which constitute the primary essence. For it being so, even if the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—
such as the contemplation of the Lord’s true nature— which are prescribed for the initiated as duties to be performed throughout their entire lives,
are performed by one who knows the reality of the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) only once, they are all indeed considered to have been fully accomplished.
It is so. As it is said in the *Kakṣyāstotra*:

"The seventy-two thousand oblations of the Agnihotra that would occur throughout a human lifespan—those you, knowing the path, accomplish by offering them all at once through the application of the divisions of the channels."
Thus it is said. Furthermore:

"The vital breaths (prāṇas) that have issued from the *haṃsa* situated in the central breath and take refuge in the pores of the skin—possessing bodies characterized by subtle discernment (*vimarśa*) and numbering three and a half crores—"

"He who reverses those [energies] through their nature as mantras within the body, which is the locus of all principles without exception— he is here the supreme Svacchandanaṭha, whose form is Nādabhairava.
Thus [ends verse 10].
And these channels—filled with vital air, they are all constantly moved by the power of the Self. (7.11)

The Self (ātman) is the subject, whose nature is contracted consciousness; Śakti is the sovereign power, whose essence is the supreme radiance of the entire universe without exception. By virtue of these two causes, they move—that is, they expand—with manifold variety. || 11 ||
And these—
divided by the distinctions of their respective functions and by the distinctions of their movements—
the functions (*vṛtti*) are the operations caused by the distinctions of movement consisting of the subtle flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, O fair-faced one, there is a distinction in terminology based on the different modes of movement. (7.12)
It comes to be. || 12 ||
And therefore, due to the difference in designations— the distinction between the channels (*nāḍīs*) and the winds (*vāyūs*) should be known to exist by the thousands;
that is to say, up to three and a half million.
In that regard—O fair-faced one—the ten principal channels that have been described are as follows: [7.13]
O Goddess of the Gods, among those [channels], the winds which are situated in the middle—“in the middle” means within. (13)
Learn from me the names, functions, and activities of those channels and vital airs.
The functions, that is, the activities. || 14 ||
In that regard, Saṃjñā said: "Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī. (7.15)
Ālambusā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
Regarding their function, it is said: "These ten principal channels are declared to be the carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa). (7.16)

He states the distinction in the names of the winds, which carry in their respective order the tenfold vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is of the nature of the general life-force (*prāṇana*) and is divided into the specific designations of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth, as will be described hereafter: ... [The text continues with the list of the ten winds] ...
Thus he has stated the distinction in the names of the winds.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. (7.17)
Regarding the differentiation of their functions:
"Speech, laughter, singing, dancing, the movements of battle, the arts, craftsmanship, and all actions—this is the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (7.306)
He will explain this in detail at the end of the chapter with the words beginning "ityādi. || 17 ||
And these winds and channels, O Dear One, are situated like a wheel;
that is to say, they revolve around the center of the navel.
O fair-faced one, for one who moves among them, there is success and indeed yoga. (7.18)
Because it moves about, it is called "sañcara"; presiding over that wind, one may attain various appropriate supernatural powers (siddhis) and yoga through one-pointedness of mind.
And for one who recites [the mantra], O lady of excellent hips, he shall attain the perfection of recitation (*japa-siddhi*).
"Of one moving among them" is understood from the previous context. "From recitation" means *japataḥ*.
Of these ten as well, O Goddess, three channels are declared to be supreme. (7.19)
Indeed, the two [channels] consisting of *bindu* and *nāda* are situated in the middle; they are considered to be of the nature of *śakti*.
*Bindu* is primarily the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the *prāṇa* which is of that nature is *piṅgalā*, the right channel.
*Nāda* is primarily the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the *apāna* which is of that nature is *iḍā*, the left channel.
Between those two is the one called Suṣumnā, which is the manifestation of the supreme power of will (icchā-śakti). || 19 ||
These three are declared to be in the heart-cakra, bringing benefit to practitioners. (7.20)
By entering perfectly and completely into the pericarp in the center of the heart-lotus, these truths are renowned for bestowing the threefold accomplishments upon practitioners. || 20 ||
This being the case—prāṇa indeed moves within them according to the division of day and night.
Prāṇa is that whose nature is breathing; it is the universal form. The word "day and night" [refers to this].
It indicates the fortnight, the month, and the year.
Just as it is— so shall I explain to you, having analyzed it clearly.
Here, he first establishes the introductory framework:
Drawn forth by the power of the Lord, these three—wind, vital breath, and the self—residing within one another, circulate everywhere without distinction. (7.22)

The *marut* is the universal self (*ātman*) of vital breath; the *prāṇa*, however, is that which flows through the right, left, middle, and other channels, distinguished by the names of prāṇa, apāna, udāna, and so forth; and the *ātman* is the contracted conscious self.
These three entities exist in the form of the power (*śakti*) of the Lord Śiva.

"Drawn together" means that, preceded by the manifestation of the state of emptiness (*śūnyapada*), having caused the ground of vital breath (*prāṇanā*) to blossom forth and having delineated the specific paths of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so on, they proceed toward the face-to-face encounter with enjoyment;
they move without division and take recourse in various bodily grounds. || 22 ||
Among these three, that which is spoken of as gentle is as follows:
because it flows upward and downward, setting all the channels in motion,
therefore for this [practitioner]—
Through the various distinctions of phonetic behavior and nomenclature, the forms of letters are manifold. (7.23)
Function (*vṛtti*) refers to the operations of outward-flowing, inward-flowing, and so forth; by means of that, there arise the various designations such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna*.
Furthermore, these consist of the twelve, sixteen, and other varieties of vowels, which incorporate within themselves the nature of the consonants.

The phonemes (*varṇa*) and their corresponding forms, which consist of various respective experiences, exist in manifold ways. In this context, according to the teachings of other scriptures, there is the emergence of phonemes (*varṇodaya*), which consists of the arising of the fifty phonemes—or the nature of the arising of the eight groups—having the vowels as its primary manifestation while the consonants are implicitly included within them. That...
But here it has not been explicitly stated; it is merely indicated by the word "caste" (varṇa). || 23 ||
In this regard— O Dear One, from the seventy-two thousand [channels], ten indeed arise;
those ten, beginning with Prāṇa, [arise] from the seventy-two thousand for the sake of the seventy-two thousand.
They are born; the meaning is that they take recourse in the pervasion of that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
He states that even beyond that, the vital breath (prāṇa) assumes the nature of three and a half crores:
"O Varārohā, that one [breath] is established as ten-fold crores. (7.24)
And that vital breath, consisting of prāṇa and apāna, is directed toward emission and inhalation;
for it is said: "The letter *ha* is remembered as prāṇa" (4.257).

Thus, that very life-force (*prāṇa*), which was previously described as having the form of a plow (*halākṛti*) and consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the undivided relationship between the signified and the signifier, possesses its current form through a determined process of descent (*avaroha*), preceded by the manifestation of contraction (*saṅkoca*) projected by its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
Abiding in the universal vital breath (*sāmānyaprāṇa*), he perceives emission and inhalation; thus,
through the method of entry preceded by that manifestation, for the sake of emission— which consists of the creation of the manifestation of various objects externally from the hollow channels—
and for the sake of internal filling by means of taking [them] in, he breathes intensely.

The meaning is that "vital breath" (prāṇa) refers to the reflective awareness (vimarśa) appropriate for the stages of resonance, the desire to grasp the object, the grasping itself, and the state of rest.
He clarifies this very point:
"Constantly filling [the body], it remains in the chest of living beings. (7.25)
Because it performs the act of breathing (*prāṇana*), it is therefore celebrated as *prāṇa*.

Although it pervades the entire body, it remains clearly perceived in the chest of living beings, constantly filling them; that is to say, it fills the living beings and their objects through its inhalation and exhalation.
It performs the act of living, which consists of the vital breath (*prāṇana*) and is composed of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); therefore, it is called *prāṇa*.
(25) Connecting that very point for the sake of which this introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) was constructed, he says:
"Now I shall describe to you the movement of day and night within the *prāṇa*. (7.26)
The movement, the manifestation, and the expansion.
In that regard—sixteen *tuṭis* in the vital breath have indeed been previously described by me; by external time alone, they are proclaimed to be *lavas*. (7.27)
Those sixteen *tuṭis* which were previously mentioned in the fourth chapter as having a measure of two and a quarter finger-breadths [of rising] are as follows:
"A *kṣaṇa* is said to be one-eighth of a human blink of an eye."

"Two *kṣaṇas* should be known as a *tuṭi*, and two of those are recorded as a *lava*" (11.201). Thus, by means of the external time described in the eleventh chapter, those *lavas*—the divisions of time designated by the word *lava*—are established. And in this way, the *tuṭi* pertaining to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed distinct from the external *tuṭi*; it is not [the same].

One should not be confused here by the similarity of the terms. An external *lava* is an internal *tuṭi*, and an external *tuṭi* results in half an internal *tuṭi*. Thus, it should be understood that an external moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the fourth part of an internal *tuṭi*. And by this very sequence...

The day-and-night (*ahorātra*) consisting of thirty *tuṭis*, which occurs without the time of the junctions (*saṃdhyākāla*) and takes the form of the internal arising of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, is itself— as follows:
"Two *lavas* should be known as a *nimeṣa* according to the sequence of calculation."
"Fifteen *nimeṣas* are declared to be a *kāṣṭhā*" (11.202).
Thus, the division of time called a *kāṣṭhā* is defined according to the arrangement of the eleventh chapter.
This will be stated further on in this very [chapter]:
"By means of an internal day-and-night, an external *kāṣṭhā* is established," [as stated in verse 7-50]. || 27 ||
But here, O Goddess, by means of those four [tuṭis], a *yāma* is ordained within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By "by means of those" is meant by the *tuṭis*; just as externally, so too internally, a *yāma*—that is, a *prahara*—consists of a fourth part of the day.
O Goddess, by those very four watches, a day comes to be. || 7-28 ||
Just as in the sequence of exit, so too in the sequence of entry it is exactly the same—
the night is to be known by four seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Thus, having synthesized it in this way:
... "A day and night [of the breath] consists of eight [such moments].

Just as there is an external division of day and night based on the state of the sun's rising and so forth as regulated by the power of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara), so too for the yogin, there is an internal [division] based on the state of the rising of the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa)."
This has already been largely explained by the intention to describe tasks that must be accomplished daily and so forth.
He establishes how this vital breath (prāṇa) lacks any fixed regularity in its outward or inward flow:
"By means of dharma it is Śiva; the haṃsa is the sun; the haṃsa is endowed with radiance. (7.29)
The Self (ātman) is indeed called *haṃsa*; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is endowed with the nature of *haṃsa*.

That which was previously described as Śiva, a mass of consciousness and bliss, by virtue of His own freedom—the essential nature of His being—becomes *haṃsa*, characterized by the qualities of abandoning and assuming, and the agent of the creation and dissolution of the universe.

Precisely because He is Śiva, He performs the fivefold activity whose true nature consists of relinquishing and assuming. And just as He is so, the Sun, who is composed of His power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), is likewise the *haṃsa*— possessing the qualities of relinquishing and assuming through the sequence of emitting and taking up the essence (*rasa*) by means of its radiance and light.

And since, according to the established principle, Śiva alone is the Self whose nature as consciousness appears contracted through His own sovereignty, He too is called *haṃsa* because He possesses the qualities of abandoning and taking up [objects] through the sequence of opening and closing the instruments [of perception].

In the *Yojanikā* commentary on the verse "By this very yoga, the *haṃsa* is the *puruṣa*" (4.260), it is stated as follows: that same *prāṇa*, although resting upon the level of *prāṇa*, is indeed the *haṃsa* because it performs the acts of abandoning and taking up both externally and internally; for it is this very one who is the Sun.

The Self (*ātman*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are perfectly united with the Lord who is the unstruck (*anāhata*), partless (*niṣkala*) essence of the *haṃsa*, whose nature is Śiva. Indeed, by descending through the process of emanation and taking recourse in the state that culminates in the vital breath, performing the inward and outward movements of coming and going, He is the agent of creation and dissolution. Therefore...
Thus, by the very practice of repeatedly studying these words, great yogis suddenly enter the state of Supreme Śiva. In this context, the secret meaning has been indicated incidentally. (29)
But as for the subject at hand:
"From its arising, [there is] time, [which is] kalā...
From the arising of that *prāṇa*, beginning from birth and proceeding through the sequence of the six modifications (*vikāra*), there is *kāla*.
Flowing through the distinctions of past, present, and so forth, he impels the entire universe; "kalayet" is the reading belonging to the Lord (Īśa).
And here, within this movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) consisting of the stated day-and-night (ahorātra), the rising of the planets occurs. || 7-30 ||
And that will become manifest before long.
Furthermore:
"The constellations, the zodiac signs, the stars, and likewise the degrees—all these indeed rise within the vital breath during a single day and night, O lady of virtuous vows. (7.31)

Having established the sequence according to the external stars of the day, within the measure of the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna* divided twenty-sevenfold, [one should know] the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī and their presiding deities.

Just as in the external world, there is also the rising of the zodiacal signs and their degrees within the human body, according to the calculation of the third and ninth parts of the birth-star and other stars that are favorable or unfavorable to the signs beginning with Aries. || 31 ||
Now, O beloved, I shall explain to you the division of the very rising of day and night: it is that which flows from above the heart down to below the throat. (7.32)
When [the distance] is deficient by one finger-breadth, it is known as the first watch (*prahara*).

As for what was stated previously—that "a *yāma* consists of four *tuṭis*"—that refers to the duration of time required for the flow of those four *tuṭis*; however, this [present case] refers to spatial distance, and thus [they do not coincide].
This is a redundancy. From the heart to the throat, the previous measurement of ten finger-breadths becomes nine finger-breadths by a reduction of one finger-breadth. || 32 ||
Beyond that as well—[the second] should be known as the upward [breath], [occurring at] midday from the center of the palate. || 7-33 ||
Here too, it is exactly nine finger-breadths; that which is the second is the midday at the center of the palate. || 33 ||
Regarding this, he states the fruit of practice for one who has found rest here: "In this state, fire-offerings, recitation, and meditation, when performed, truly become bestowers of liberation.
Now—
O lady of virtuous vows, it extends upward from the tip of the nose for three finger-breadths.
O lady of excellent complexion, this shall indeed be the third watch:
from the tip of the nose to the middle of the eyebrows, four finger-breadths above is the forehead;
from the palate to the throat is four finger-breadths, and from there the middle of the eyebrows is two finger-breadths—thus, three finger-breadths are said to be above that.
Above that—
up to the end of Śakti— is the fourth watch;
"at the end of Śakti" means at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta).
Up to this point, the *ahaḥ* (day) has been fully described. (7.35)
Internal. || 35 ||
And therein:
"O Goddess, at the end of the fourth [watch], the sun of the vital breath (prāṇasūrya) is always set.
By "always" it is meant that whenever the end of the fourth watch occurs, then the vital breath itself—
The sun sets because it is the cause for the division of day and night.
Moreover:
"From that, O Dear One, the twilight of sunset here shall consist of half a *tuṭi*. (7.36)
Then, relying on that [word] ending in the fourth case,

[the state consists of] resting in the immersion into the light of the Power (śakti) and its Possessor (śaktimān) as they emerge, by virtue of their becoming subordinate to the flow [of consciousness] through the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) arising from the desire of the prāṇa to withdraw and the apāna to surge upward.
The *tuṭi*-kalā is the twilight of setting. || 36 ||
And here, at the junction (sandhyā), the sun of the vital breath (prāṇasūrya)—
having paused for that duration— proceeds downward once again;
for that duration is half a *tuṭi*, having come to rest in the state of union (*saṃghaṭṭapada*), and thus, by the very same process of ascent.
And again—meaning repeatedly—it proceeds downward; having become the moon of the *apāna*, it descends as far as the heart.
Thus it is said: "And that, O Goddess, is ordained as the rising of the moon and the night. (7.37)
Those who know time say that the sun itself is the moon by way of its transition into radiance. || 37 ||
He extends the analogy by stating that even at night, the sequence of watches proceeds as before, with a duration of nine finger-breadths according to the order of the movement of the lunar apāna:
"By means of the previously described sequence, it moves in this way during the watches."
In this context, after resting during the twilight, the first watch consists of the period ending with the emergence of the fourth watch of the day.
Then—at the palate, at midnight—this [rite] is performed once again in this manner. || 7-38 ||

"Again in this way" means by the sequence of descent, specifically by remaining at nine finger-breadths; here, it is implied that the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth grant success. Furthermore, "is again prescribed in this way" means that once more, by remaining at nine finger-breadths, the third watch of the night extends from the throat down to the end of the fingers.
From there also—
when he has reached the heart-lotus at the time of dawn,
even there—
O lady of excellent hips, the morning twilight then lasts for half a tuṭi.
This is to be explained as before. Its "prior" nature here is because the day—consisting of the rising of the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa)—begins immediately after that junction (saṃdhyā).
As it has been said:
"Therefore, that indeed becomes the rising of the sun;
the sun is the vital breath (prāṇa)."
And having arisen—as before—by means of the sequential yoga, one should always practice, O auspicious lady. (7.40)
"O auspicious one!"—this is the address. || 40 ||

In this very day, the sun moves in the [upper] stream and the moon moves in the [lower] stream; the prāṇa is indeed the sun, while the apāna is the moon. Furthermore, the sun is the group of sense organs during the day.

At the rising of the *prāṇa*, it moves, surging forth and illuminating the external world. At night, during the flow [of consciousness] upon the rising of the *apāna*, the Moon—consisting of the forms of the objects of knowledge—moves; having entered the illumination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it attains identity with the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Thus, within the course of a day and night, this rising of the moon and the sun has been described by me to you. (7.41)
In order to achieve the peaceful and other types of accomplishments for practitioners, he shows here in the center the sequence of the rising of the five planets, as described in the *Sūryodaya*:
"Indeed, the planets beginning with Mars move in this manner according to their respective divisions."

Just as the sun and the moon always move externally and internally during both day and night, so too do the five [planets] beginning with Mars and ending with Saturn always move through those two [spheres], which are divided fivefold and fivefold respectively,
according to the sequence of their divisions; and by that, they become the limbs for the accomplishment of the cruel and the gentle.

Now, following the sequence of the external tides during the day and at night, he demonstrates the rising of the seven planets even within [the body], according to the logic seen in the *Garuḍatantra* and other scriptures:
"O Dear One, these also rise in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during every watch (*prahara*). (7.42)
Whichever *velā* (time-period) or *vāra* (day/planet) it may be, that one should move for two *praharas*.

Whichever planet has its day (*vāra*) on the outside, that [planet] rises both inside and as if on the outside during the first *prahara*. Then, during the day, by way of a sixfold rotation, the others [move] in each successive half-*prahara*, until the end.

On that day, at the half-watch [of the first period], it is that very same [planet]; on the subsequent occasions, in sequence, others [arise] according to the order of five revolutions, until finally, at the half-watch of its night, it is that very same one again. Thus, for each individual planet, there is a rising for a half-watch during the day and a half-watch during the night.

Since it is established that those who possess the day (vārabhāgin) have double [the duration], by combining the day and night, the portion of the day belongs to them for two watches (prahara), whereas for others, the rising occurs for one watch. As it is said in the Śrītotula:
"They all move through the day and night, each enjoying half a watch."
In the *Saṃhitāsāra* as well:
"Those who enjoy [the day] during the two watches of night and day, and during the afternoon of the householder— his day and his turn pass away like nights without food."
By the revolution of desire they experience day and night, through the revolution of arrows.
Thus [ends the section]. 42.
Right here in the middle, Rāhu moves with the Moon, and Ketu moves with the Sun.
The meaning is "not so. Therefore, the movement of those two is simply their own movement; it is not something separate, as is the case with other grahas. || 43 ||
Furthermore: those who are the planets are indeed the Nāgas, and they are the eight guardians of the world;
they are the eight forms, and they are the eight lords of the Gaṇas.
And those five groups of eight Rudras, as well as the other eight Yogas,
and those eight Vidyeśvaras beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
All the principles (tattvas), beginning with Sakala, are situated here beyond [the previous levels];
and all those eight Bhairavas mentioned previously are likewise established here.

The planets, beginning with the Sun and ending with Saturn, correspond respectively to the nāgas Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kārkoṭa, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Kulika; Rāhu, however, is Kulika. As it has been said: "The Sun is called Ananta, and the Moon is called Vāsuki."
Takṣaka is said to be Kuja, and Kārkoṭa shall be born from Soma.
Saroja is declared to be Jupiter; Mahābja is said to be Venus;
Śaṅkha is to be known as Saturn; these are the seven serpents corresponding to the planets in order.
"The eighth is named Kulika; Rāhu is a cruel planet. And as it says in the Śrītotula:
From the center of Ravi, sixteen; from the end of Bhārgava, four;
two caṣakas for Budha at the beginning; and eight for Soma from the middle.
"He consumes sixty-four [caṣakas] from the end of the Sun, thirty-two from the middle of Jupiter, and [thirty-two] from the end of Mars, revolving six times.
Thus, the time of Kulika is stated by way of the number of *caṣakas*; that [time] here refers to the extremely subtle movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*).

"It is indeed difficult to perceive" means it is not to be deliberated upon. Thus, for the planets presiding over half-days and *praharas* for the sake of male enjoyment (*puṃbhoga*), there is their being presided over by the *nāgas*;

and for the *nāgas*, there is their being presided over by the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) such as Indra and others, who abide according to the sequence already stated. [The world-protectors] beginning with Indra...
"By the forms" (mūrtibhiḥ) means by the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras), such as Śarva, Rudra, Bhava, and others, who are the presiding deities over the forms beginning with Earth;
and these [are accompanied] by the previously mentioned Gaṇeśas, such as Caṇḍa, Nandin, and so forth; and these too are the most secret and pure [deities].
These [principles] are presided over in sequence by the five groups of eight, beginning with Sthāṇu and the others;

they too are pervaded by the eightfold yoga beginning with Akṛta. Furthermore, they are pervaded by those who are beyond even the eightfold yoga—namely, Krodha and the others who abide in Prakṛti, and Maṇḍalin and the others who abide in Māyā.

They [the Vidyeśvaras] are also [accompanied] by Ananta and others who have attained the level of Vidyātattva; and the Vidyeśvaras themselves are accompanied by Sakala and others—those who constitute the retinue of Sadāśiva—[namely] the Sakala, Niṣkala, Śūnya, Kalāḍhya, and so forth. (10.1194)

Thus, by means of the eight [deities] to be mentioned hereafter— or else, by the "principles" (tattvas) consisting of Sadāśiva as a whole who is the first among those [eight], namely Ūrdhvatī, Bindu, Īśa, Brahmā, Vyāpin, Vyoman, Ananta, Anātha, and Anāśrita—
[the Lord is worshipped] by these deities who are ultimate because they touch the ground of non-duality.

They too are presided over by the Bhairavas, such as Kapālīśa and others, who are themselves presided over by Śrī Svacchandanātha, who abides in the state of pervasion of the plane beyond the mind (aunmanasa). Thus it is said:
"All these [deities] are established within those [periods] consisting of the breath, day-and-night, half-periods, and watches. Herein—
According to the sequence of the first half-watch and so forth, the rising of Indra and the others occurs for two *tuṭis* during both day and night;
it does not occur according to the six-fold rotation or the fixed positions of the planets, because there is no possibility of conjunction between the seven planets and the [eight] *lokapālas*.
Their established state is pervaded by non-differentiation; for this very reason, the expression here is made through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

And thus, the state of being composed of the expansion of Supreme Bhairava culminates precisely in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, that demonstration of pervasion which we have presented in the stage of the vital breath according to the sequence of day and night—
What was previously established should not be considered contrary to the sūtras; and thus,

since all this is non-dual with the Supreme Lord, for the knowers [of reality], liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is as if held in the palm of the hand through knowledge alone, whereas for practitioners...

It is thus demonstrated that even by following the specific planes (padas) pervaded by the respective lords of the worlds and so forth, the arising of those respective accomplishments occurs precisely through the unimpeded contemplation of the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti). || 46 ||
It reiterates that very same point:
"Presiding over the planets and so forth, they are the causes of the rising of all [planets]—
all these [deities], from the world-protectors (lokapāla) down to Bhairava, throughout all days, nights, and watches."

They bring about the rising [of the planets]. How? By presiding over, without distinction, the planets such as the Sun and others—whose days have arrived in rotation during their respective half-praharas—as well as the Nāgas such as Ananta and others, indicated by the word "and so forth" (ādi).
Furthermore: "Together with the zodiacal signs, those lunar mansions rise day and night. (7.47)

Starting from the heart up to the *dvādaśānta*, there is a zodiac sign (*rāśi*) for every six finger-breadths (*praty-aṅgula*). According to this arrangement, the six signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) and ending with Gemini (*mithuna*), as well as the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) presiding over them, rise there at every degree in accordance with that very sequence; and likewise...
From the *dvādaśānta* down to the heart are the months beginning with Cancer and ending with Sagittarius.
Right here he states the rising of Abhijit:
"The rising of Abhijit occurs at midday and at midnight;
the meaning is 'in the palate. It is called Abhijit because it conquers (abhijayati) all obstacles; it is a specific lunar mansion (nakṣatra)."
And for this reason, the desired fruit shall be attained here by the practitioners in that [state]. (7.48)

Regarding the word "here" (*iha*), it refers to the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*). That fruit known as enjoyment and liberation, which is desired by practitioners, certainly occurs at midday, at midnight, or during the *abhijit* asterism. || 48 ||
Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says:
"In this manner, I have described to you this division of day and night;
now I shall tell you of the fortnights, months, and years. (7.49)
Therein, he applies the determined internal day and night to external time:
by means of the internal day and night, an external *kāṣṭhā* is established.
Here, *kāṣṭhā* does not mean a *ghaṭikā*, but rather consists of fifteen *nimeṣas*.
That it is a specific division of time has already been explained.
Furthermore:
"By means of the internal month alone, there shall be a digit (kalā) in the external as well. (7.50)
In that regard, O lady of excellent complexion, thirty days and nights constitute a month;

this is the internal month. Those thirty days and nights consist of the movements of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*), while externally they correspond to thirty *kāṣṭhā*s. By means of such an internal month, [there is] that which is called the external *kalā*.
Such is the time;
and he will state in the eleventh [chapter]: "Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are to be known as a *kalā*" (11.203).

The word *eva* is to be construed immediately after the word *kalā*. She is called *varavarṇinī* because she describes (*varṇayati*) what is excellent (*vara*) and refers to the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*), which is the most exalted.
Furthermore,
with twelve internal months, there shall be one external ghaṭikā.
He clarifies that very point:
"Three hundred days and nights, plus sixty more—this is declared to be one year externally, and it is indeed a ghaṭikā. (7.52)
An external *ghaṭikā* consists of three hundred and sixty movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. For it is said:
"Since that [day] consists of sixty *caṣakas*, and one *caṣaka* consists of six movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. (52)
Thus, sixty *ghaṭikās*—measured by the internal years of the aforementioned form—indeed flow externally as one day and night;
those same sixty, through their internal movement, are known as years. (7.53)

The external ghaṭikā is indeed divided as being an internal year; therefore, those sixty [ghaṭikās] are likewise internal years according to the subtle movement of time. For this very reason, the arising of sixty years occurs within a single movement of the breath (prāṇacāra); this supreme state of time will become clear further on.
Now, regarding those years consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās*, I shall further tell you the number of breaths (*prāṇas*) within them:
twenty-one thousand and six hundred, O lady of noble limbs. (7.54)
By an external day and night,
there are three hundred and sixty breath-movements in one *ghaṭikā* within the Lord of the Gods (the Sun); by this calculation,
based on that [external] support, there are sixty *ghaṭikās* in the external day and night, which correspond internally to the Self.
This very number applies to the movements of the vital breaths.
Thus, such a number of breaths has been fully described; it must be understood by the practitioner. (7.55)
Thus, by means of the true nature of the pervasion (vyāpti) already described and to be described—
[the practitioner] who is always absorbed in the *haṃsa* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)... [is] absorbed,
meaning resting through contemplative observation (*nibhālanā*).
Likewise, by means of the immersion into the plane of Śakti through the downward orientation of the vital breath and the earth element,
he becomes a knower of the supreme reality (paratattvavit). And at that time—
This recitation of it is prescribed as bestowing the fruits of both spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
In this context, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called "Haṃsa" because it is the support for the *haṃsa* which has become the realized potency of all mantras.
