That which is dissolved therein becomes perpetually engaged in this much recitation by means of the very count of the vital breaths.
As it is said in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava*:
"Twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations of the Goddess are prescribed for each day and night; this is extremely difficult to achieve at the end of a single breath. (Verse 156) || 56 ||
Regarding what was stated—that [the breath] bestows both accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti)—he analyzes that as follows:
"Accomplishment occurs when it flows downward as far as it has reached the heart-lotus; and liberation indeed occurs when it moves upward into the Supreme Reality, O lady of excellent vows. (7.57)
And this has been determined in detail in such passages as, "When he performs creation... (6.15). || 57 ||

Thus, having stated that for the yogi who knows the supreme reality (paratattva) through the prior knowledge of the aforementioned pervasion (vyāpti), all time— by virtue of being dissolved in the *prāṇahaṃsa* and due to the excellence of its sprouting— becomes composed solely of such an experience, he says:
Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eyes are cast elsewhere,
the vital breath continues to function at all times without any effort whatsoever.

The word "tathā" (so it is) is to be supplied in the middle [of the sentence]. Therefore, although internal and external mental constructs have issued forth into one's own intellect, nevertheless, for one who knows the pervasion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by virtue of being intent upon resting in the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the vital breath [is established] in that very same manner which bestows rest in the supreme.
The middle [channel], whose essence is the *haṃsa*, flows and carries [the breath] at all times, effortlessly and by its own natural impulse.
This very point is further confirmed: "There is no one who utters it, nor is there anyone who obstructs it;
the *haṃsa* situated in the chest of living beings utters itself. (7-59)

The *haṃsa* is the Supreme Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*), partless (*niṣkala*) and of the nature of the Absolute (*paratattva*) as previously described; because it presides over it, the central vital breath (*prāṇa*)— the essence of which is the established pervasion (*vyāpti*)—
also rises up by itself, transcending the entire sequence of the signified and the signifier.

It vibrates by its very nature as the potency of the Great Mantra, whose essence is supreme non-duality; for there is no one to utter or obstruct it, since it alone, as the agent of all, is the form of the Supreme Mother. For this very reason, it is proclaimed to be "unstruck" (*anāhata*), unlike other phonemes.
Because it is not manifested by the impact of the vocal organs and places of articulation, and because it has never set,
this [sound] remains in the chest and heart of living beings as the very life of life itself;
yet only those whose wealth is attentive concentration enter into its existence.
Thus, with the intention of accomplishing the recitation (*japa*) of the practitioner who is intent upon the supreme reality—this number of months and years has been told by me to you;
the remainder is that it is "spiritual" (*ādhyātmikī*). Thirty movements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) constitute one spiritual month.
Three hundred and sixty years constitute a *vatsara*; this is indeed firmly established.
Now, right here in this movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), I shall thereafter describe the eclipses of the moon and the sun. (7.60)
It is established that this bestows upon the practitioner the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 60 ||
In that regard, first—
O beautiful goddess, that which has been described as a day and night within this vital breath (prāṇa),
I shall now explain to you as two fortnights and a month. (7.61)
The word "without division" is to be supplied as the remainder. There are thirty movements of the vital breath. 61.
In that regard, he first defines the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) by demonstrating the junction of the fortnights:
"Half a *tuṭi* below and half above are declared to be the rest (*viśrama*).
Those fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) which are said to be in the middle are proclaimed [as the days]. (7.62)

Furthermore, that half-tuṭi which was previously described as occurring at the rising of day and night in the form of the preceding and following twilights (saṃdhyā) is here designated as the "rest" (viśrama) by way of being the junction of the fortnights (pakṣasaṃdhi).
As for those fifteen tuṭis in between, they alone are the lunar days (tithis), beginning with the first (pratipad). || 62 ||
And here, having set aside the half-tuṭi at the junction of the two phases, he describes the division of day and night for each individual tuṭi:
"But at the first rising, from the heart-lotus, the first half-tuṭi shall be the day;
and when [the breath] moves during the second half-tuṭi, that is the night. (7.63)

The mention of the "heart-lotus" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). By this, it is meant that for each individual *tuṭi*, the first half—measuring one and a half finger-breadths—is the day, whose nature is light;
the latter half, however, is the night, whose essence is repose. For this divine Consciousness consists of both light and darkness.

Therefore, wherever and to whatever extent this manifestation of light (*prakāśa*) and bliss (*ānanda*), which consist in the repose of the known and the knower, is projected, there day and night are of precisely those same forms.

Thus, it is entirely logical that for a mosquito and the like, as well as for Sadāśiva and the like, the duration of these two [day and night] is respectively extremely brief or exceedingly vast. In this way...
And at every half-moment, according to the sequence to be described, even within the subdivisions of those parts,
these two appear as such to the subject, manifesting the appropriate distinction between day and night;
sometimes there is an excess of light, sometimes of rest, and sometimes of both.

Considering them equal, there is indeed a disparity between day and night both internally and externally. Following the portion of the aphorism, "When he moves," the word "then" (tadā) is to be supplied. 63.
And here, regarding the distinction between day and night—
the zodiac signs, planets, and lunar mansions rise in their proper sequence. For by the supreme Lord’s consciousness, whatever arrangement of day and so forth is established, that [is what occurs].
All the planets and other celestial bodies follow its course.
Thus, O fair-faced one, in this very day and night, as before— || 7-64 ||

A fortnight is prescribed by means of fifteen *tuṭis*. "In this" refers to the internal [process]. "Thus" means by the calculation of half-and-half *tuṭis*. "As before" means with a very subtle vision. "Fortnight" implies the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Now, within this very context, desiring to determine a solar eclipse by demonstrating the conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) and the degree of the sign (prātipada), he shows the decrease and increase of the lunar day:
"In the case of the decrease of the lunar day, it should be known as a debt (ṛṇa); and in the case of its increase, it becomes wealth (dhana). (7.65)
Debt indeed becomes cough, while exhalation is called wealth.

Debt belongs to the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāha*); due to the short duration [of the cough], it occurs by virtue of the cough. This being so, by running suddenly, the portion of the new moon (*āmāvāsya*) spreads to the position of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). And this—

This is useful for the solar eclipse that is about to be shown. However, due to the force of the exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*), there is a slight prolongation of time for the moon of the downward breath (*apāna*); this being so, the rising of the full moon becomes useful for the lunar eclipse.
But its natural [process]—through the upward movement during the dark fortnight—becomes dissolution, that is, destruction. (7.66)

The meaning is this: the withdrawal of the aforementioned *prāṇa* by means of the upward movement in the form of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is precisely the gradual depletion of the fifteen digits (*kalā*), ending with the new moon (*amāvasyā*), occurring digit by digit at every *tuṭi*, of the immovable moon that was previously established within the *prāṇa* during its entry. As it has been said:
In the Śrīkāmikā:
"The nectar, in the form of the moon, is twofold and again sixteenfold;
all the gods drink the fifteen supreme digits."
"She who dwells within the entire cave [of the heart] as the New Moon (amāvasyā), she who offers up the universe.
Thus,
"in two ways" means by virtue of her extremely pure nature, which serves as the foundation for the fifteen lunar digits (kalās).
The meaning is that [the moon] consists of the fifteen digits (kalās) of its visible white fortnight. || 66 ||
Since the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is of such a nature, therefore—performing indeed cruel deeds therein, one may attain success;
but auspicious deeds, O lady of excellent vows, do not succeed during the dark fortnight. (7.67)

The two *ca*s have the sense of the words *tu* and *eva*. Here, according to the principle that "whatever is internal is also external," whatever fruit has been stated regarding the internal [states]—such as day, night, their junctions (*saṃdhyā*), fortnights, months, and so forth—it should be understood that it exists in exactly the same way externally as well. || 67 ||

Then he shows this new-moon day: "O fair-faced one, that *tuṭi* which is prescribed as entering into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *śakti* should be known as the new moon in the dark fortnight. (7.68)

Śakti is the location situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); "tuṭi" refers to the fifteenth [lunar day] when the moon has waned away. Therefore, because she dwells in the sixteenth tuṭi known as Amā, and because she relies upon that very foundation, she is to be known as Amāvāsyā. || 68 ||

Now, he clarifies the junction of the fortnights (pakṣasaṃdhi) which was previously indicated in outline: "That half-tuṭi which is proclaimed to be in the middle and upper part of the Śakti is to be known as the junction of the fortnights..."
The midpoint of the power (śakti) that has arisen from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is the location of the skin; the remainder of the skin is the location of the hair.
That which is the single half-tuṭi above is the junction of the two fortnights, the dark and the bright. For that very same final half-tuṭi of the prāṇa is the initial [half-tuṭi] of the apāna.
That which "comes to be" consists of both [halves] and is spatially one, being composed of half a *tuṭi*; it is the "junction-word" (*saṃdhipada*) that carries the duration of two such half-*tuṭis*.
Now, he shows the solar eclipse therein: "The new moon [at the end] of the half-[month] and the first day of the lunar fortnight. (7.69)

Indeed, by the cutting off of the lunar day (tithi) there, an eclipse of the sun occurs. Due to the previously mentioned coughing, when there is a cutting off of the lunar day— that is, the new moon (amāvāsyā)— the time of the half-moment of the junction between the fortnights, being connected to that,
[occurs] within its own portion of the twilight-tuṭi together with the time of the first lunar day (pratipat).
When that occurs, then a solar eclipse takes place.
For this reason: "O Goddess, at that time, the lunar disc will be within the solar disc. (7.70)
In that interval, O fair-faced one, Rāhu appears seeking the nectar;
the moon pours forth the nectar, and Rāhu swallows it. (7.71)

Having drunk [the nectar], he abandons that lunar orb; then he is said to be liberated. "Then" means at the conjunction of the portion of the new moon (*amāvāsya*) on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*); within the solar orb, that is, in the center of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the lunar orb—the downward breath (*apāna*)—should enter. And by the method previously described, Rāhu is the companion of the Moon.

Having drunk the lunar nectar melted by the touch of the sun and having savored it for some time, [the yogi] releases the lunar orb—which is of the nature of the *apāna*—due to its connection with himself. This is the underlying reality here:
the lunar nectar, when melted by the forceful friction of the solar *prāṇa*, becomes eager for the essence of that [melted] nectar.
Svarbhānu indeed obscures the sun; however, one who knows how to strike the three [planets] should taste the essence here during this auspicious planetary conjunction.
In this way, just as it is within, so too it would be without by means of this very same reasoning.
And in the world, that very eclipse of the sun is taught.
Then, according to the method taught in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
"When these three planets—Rāhu, the Sun, and the Moon—are seen together in conjunction, that shall be a great planetary eclipse. (7.73)
It manifests its very greatness: "That time shall be the most meritorious of all times for all the worlds.
And likewise:
In that regard, bathing, giving gifts, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth [should be performed]. (7.74)
O Goddess, whatever is performed by practitioners shall have infinite fruit—
that is, its fruit is called liberation (*mokṣa*), which is infinite and undivided— as he will state: "And liberation itself, O auspicious lady" (7.86).
And so forth.
Having thus demonstrated the dark fortnight and the solar eclipse, the Lord sequentially indicates the light fortnight and the lunar eclipse:
"And by abandoning that very half-tuṭi, the rising of the light fortnight occurs. (7.75)

Regarding the word "tām" (that): it refers to where a solar eclipse is indicated; the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) consists of the form of the rising of the moon through the downward breath (apāna). || 75 ||
Thus it is said: "From the womb of power (śakti), emanation (sṛṣṭi) occurs below; from that, growth is produced.
The womb of power is its coiled form (kuṇḍalākāratā); for that, by way of being like a pod (śimbikārūpatayā), contains everything within itself."
Having woven the entire universe, it emits that very same [universe] downward, as far as the heart. For this reason, growth occurs progressively through the gradual nourishment of the lunar apāna;
likewise, growth arises in the form of wealth consisting of exhalation. In this regard, by way of the sequence of coughing:
Because there is no interruption of the lunar day (tithi).
Since this is so, therefore:
"And from that time forward, he performed auspicious deeds leading to worldly prosperity. (7.76)
For one who is engaged in meditation, mantras, and so forth, these are accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.

"Starting from that" means having grasped the essential nature of the womb of power (śaktigarbha), [one performs] auspicious rites such as nourishment (āpyāyana) and so on, as well as those leading to worldly prosperity and their fruits.
Here, he demonstrates the division of day and night during the bright fortnight: "When the swan of the vital breath has reached the first *tuṭi* below... (7.77).
The first half of the day is said to be the day (*ahaḥ*), and the other half of the *tuṭi* is the night (*niśā*).

"Prāṇa-haṃsa" is as before. "Below" refers to the first *tuṭi* following the half-*tuṭi* of the junction, which takes the form of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa-pratipad*). Because of the hearing of the word "when" (*yadā*), the word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied.
The division of day and night is exactly as before; this should be understood likewise for the second lunar day and the others as well.
Furthermore, in this regard:
the zodiac signs, the planets, the asterisms, the yogas, and the karaṇas. || 7-78 ||
In the same manner as before, through the sequential application of yoga, those [lights] rise day and night;
this has already been explained.
And this first *tuṭi*—
that should be known as the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
Here—
And the moon shall become single-rayed. || 7-79 ||
Furthermore:
"In the second, the second indeed increases in due order.
The phrase "in the second" refers to the *tuṭi*; "the second" refers to the *kalā*.
These very *tuṭis* are the lunar days (*tithis*), beginning thus up to the fifteenth *tuṭi*. (7–80)
It comes to be. || 80 ||
And that fifteenth day—
the full moon (paurṇamāsī)— must indeed be recognized as the lunar day (tithi) by the practitioner;
for it is so called because the moon (māḥ) is full therein, and for this very reason, it accomplishes worldly success (aihikasiddhi).
Therefore, this [reality] should be understood by practitioners as having the essence of the pervasion (vyāpti) that has been stated and will be stated.
And therefore:
"In that [state], worship, recitation, and meditation become complete and fruitful. (7-81)
The meaning is that it has results pertaining to this world. || 81 ||
For this reason: "O lovely-eyed one, the moon indeed becomes full within her.
The word "ca" (indeed) has the sense of "hi" (for). "Candra" refers to the *apāna* wind.
Now, that half-tuṭi of hers is known as the junction of the fortnights (pakṣasaṃdhyā). || 7.82 ||
It is just as before. In the word *tasyāḥ*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).

Regarding the junction of the lunar fortnight (*pakṣasandhi*), which is denoted by the term "twilight of the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣasaṃdhyā*): as before, its half consists of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) joined with half of the first day of the lunar phase (*pratipad*).
The word "with" (*saha*) in the instrumental case (*pratipado 'rdhena*) is used in the sense of accompaniment.
And thus, by the very pervasion previously stated: "The grasping of the moon occurs in the center of the junction of the heart-lotus. (7.83)

The "junction of the center" (*saṃdhimadhya*) is the locus where the *prāṇa* and *apāna* meet. The essential point here is as follows: "When Rāhu seizes the full moon by means of the flow of the nectar-essence poured forth by Śakti, he obscures it during this auspicious 'great eclipse' (*mahāgraha*), and the great sage drinks that which has been liquefied."
Thus, this [reality] exists both within and without. || 83 ||
In this world, the lunar eclipse (somagrahaṇa) is said to occur even in the absence of the sun;
for although the moon is touched by the sun while standing at a distance due to its conjunction with the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), there is no sun present during the night.
In a solar eclipse (sūryagrahaṇa), however, the sun is indeed touched by a digit of the full moon (pārvaṇendu).
Moreover: And in that very place, there is great merit through meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth. (7.84)

Just as the eclipse of the sun in the upper station is of great merit because it bestows liberation, so too is the eclipse of the moon in that very same place— namely, in the heart attained through the process of entering the middle abode— of great merit because it bestows the supreme siddhis of this world. 84.
And it is not only during the central channel that there is an eclipse of the moon and sun;
rather, O Mistress of the Gods, there is an eclipse of the moon and sun even during both fortnights.
For this indeed bestows various accomplishments upon the diligent practitioner. (7–85)

On both sides, the right and the left, there are two graspings just as in the middle. "Various" means it bestows the accomplishments of both the fierce and the gentle [deities] upon the practitioner who is diligently engaged. 85.
But for one who desires liberation— liberation itself, O auspicious lady, is free from both sides;
the word "and" (*ca*), together with the word "only" (*eva*), has a restricted scope.

It gathers together the supreme enjoyment consisting of the attainment of the state of the Lord of Reality (Tattveśvara) and so forth. By that, there is liberation on the middle path which avoids both extremes; above that, during a solar eclipse, there is liberation alone, whereas in the heart, during a lunar eclipse, there is both enjoyment and liberation.
And therefore, he who seeks liberation—
having abandoned both sides by means of the previously mentioned practice (7.86)—
Those who always rely on the transformation of others consider themselves superior;
however, having abandoned everything below, one should remain established in meditation and apply oneself [to the practice]. (7-87)
For him there is liberation, of this there is no doubt; otherwise, he would become a possessor of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

The divine instrument (*karaṇa*) has been previously described. The supreme state (*parā vṛttiḥ*) has been taught and is now being characterized: having abandoned everything below up to the *unmanā* state and having brought that into a state of equal flavor (*samarasīkṛtya*), one should practice meditation.
The investigation of the supreme reality (*paratattva-vimarśa*). "Otherwise" means situated above the paths of the right and left [channels] (86–87).
And he says that this grasping of the Middle Path is difficult to attain, whereas the other is indeed easy:
"Grasping would indeed occur for all embodied beings even in both positions. (7.88)
By the phrase "of embodied beings" (dehinām), he shows that limited yogis possess an absolute identification with the body as the subject; he concludes:
"Thus has this been fully explained, O fair-faced one, for as long as life lasts."
"Etad" (this) refers to the grasping [of the object] after it has been clearly perceived with full attention.
In this very context, the arising of the internal day-and-night and the year is now described. (7-89)
He said to him:
"The six zodiac signs are situated from the heart-lotus up to the top; the signs beginning with Capricorn."
In this movement of thirty-six finger-breadths,
each [stage] consists of six finger-breadths, starting from the heart-lotus up to the Śakti.
"Each one" refers to a heap.

Thus, in this [cycle] of thirty-six finger-breadths, which arises over six months—here, in every single finger-breadth, five lunar days (tithis) are established. Of that [day], the first half is day and the latter half is night. (7–91)
Of that [measurement], the limit is at five finger-breadths.
Therefore:
"Those six pentads of lunar days (tithis) constitute the monthly days and nights;
by thirty such days and nights, a month is said to consist of two fortnights. (7.92)

The meaning is that at the point of the rising of the zodiacal sign (rāśyudaya) spanning six finger-breadths, the completion of a month consisting of thirty days and nights occurs. By the phrase "two fortnights" (dvipakṣa), he says this:
that even beyond this, for the sake of accomplishing the various cruel and gentle rites to be performed in each respective month, one must rely upon the dark and bright fortnights.

It must be pursued by the yogin with a most subtle vision. For this very reason, regarding a ritual to be accomplished over a year, the yogin should perform the specific rites for each month after first following the method of unifying the external and internal months; such is the intended meaning regarding the "arising of the year" (varṣodaya). || 92 ||
Thus, in this manner—when the sign (rāśi) of the month arises during the upward or downward movement of the breath;
even when the breath moves downward as it does upward, this same sequence and so forth is to be understood. This is the meaning.
Now, the rising of the zodiacal signs is indicated in its divisions with the intention of showing the distinctions of the months:
"From the heart, which is the place of arising, the transition (saṃkrānti) resides in Capricorn. (7.93)
Having abandoned six finger-breadths below, it again enters the water-pot (Kumbha);
having abandoned two finger-breadths above the neck, it again enters the fish (Mīna).
Having abandoned [the breath] from the throat upwards as far as the palate, one should then transition into Aries;
the transition extends as far as the end of the nose, which is exactly six finger-breadths.

This indeed is the equinoctial transit (viṣu-saṃkrānti) established in the north, from the place of rising—that is, from the ground of mantra recitation. By implication, "transit" refers to the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa); for this very reason, the sequence of months beginning with Māgha is established here.
"Six finger-breadths" is like the eye of a crow [seen from both sides]. "Equinoctial transit" means the transit at the equinox. "In the north" means during the northern course [of the sun].
And this should be understood as being, as before, for the sake of accomplishing success in the other world and so forth. Thus it is said:
"Through recitation, fire-oblation, worship, and meditation, she brings about great prosperity. (7.96)

This means that this is the equinoctial transit (viṣuvatsaṃkrānti). Here too, as before, it should be remembered that even in the external transits, each respective fruit is bestowed, just as in the internal ones. || 96 ||
Then,
having avoided the tip of the nose, the swan of the vital breath (prāṇahaṃsa) should move into Taurus;
having abandoned six finger-breadths, it should then transition into Gemini.
The transition through the path as far as the Śakti is said to occur in the Mithuna [cakra].
"Six finger-breadths" is like the eye of a crow [which moves between two objects]; "as far as the Śakti" means up to the Dvādaśānta.
By restating this, he shows the culmination of the fruit:
"O lady of excellent vows, beginning from Capricorn and ending with Gemini. (7.98)
This is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), which is free from obstacles to success in this life;
it is called the "northern course" by way of etymology, as one crosses over [to liberation] by means of it.
And therefore:
bathing, meditation, as well as giving, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth. (7.99)
Whatever has been performed by practitioners and others in many thousands of ways, one does not obtain its fruit in this life; it manifests only in the next world.

By performing rites such as ritual bathing here for practitioners (sādhakas) and their spiritual sons (putrakas), their desired enjoyment and liberation are attained at the end of that body. || 99-100 ||
Regarding the statement "one does not attain [liberation] in this birth," he states the reason for it: "From Capricorn until the end of Gemini, the days increase there;
at that time, one should withdraw the vital energy (*vīrya*) from this world, both moving and unmoving. (7.101)
The Haṃsa, having drawn [the breath] with its rays, should cause that which resides within the womb to be performed;

therein, during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), there is an increase of days through the practice of grasping the object of measurement, due to disregard for the parts of the three-fold exhaustion. The "vīrya" is the essence that effects the nourishment of the universe. The Haṃsa.
The unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) is within; externally, it is the sun.

Internally, by means of the goddesses of the senses who consist of reflective awareness and whose rays are turned inward; externally, by means of its splendors. He explains [the phrase] "one should withdraw": that which is situated in the womb, contained within power (*śakti*).
One should cause [the ritual] to be performed; for one who performs it, [the mantra] binds the rays.
Having performed that—[he attains] that ancient form which was previously assumed while dwelling in the womb in many ways. (7.102)
Starting from Cancer and so forth, all that [rain] falls again;
"from Cancer and so forth" means from the place where the rising of the apāna occurs; "that" refers to the vital energy (vīrya).
Since the arising of the vital breath (prāṇa) in this way effects the gathering of vigor (vīrya),
one should therefore begin the practices of meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth, starting from Capricorn (makara).
For the sake of the next world, its fruit shall be boundless;
this is a restatement of what was previously mentioned.

In this very context, during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*), for the sake of the practitioner’s service to the mantra, he prescribes the initial recitation by relying on specific times characterized by particular internal locations, beginning with:
"The vow for grasping the mantra (*mantragrahavrata*) which is for the purpose of the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*). (7.104)
One should begin everything for the sake of one's own mantra-siddhi starting from the sign of Pisces (mīna).
First is the *puraścaryā*, which is the observance (*vrata*) preceded by the reception of the mantra, consisting of the performance of fixed recitations (*japa*) and so forth.
Having left two finger-breadths above the region of the throat, which measures eight finger-breadths, [the area] extending upward to the palate—

The position of the Fish (mīna) is six finger-breadths; this begins from the limit of Śakti and ends at the position of the Twins (mithuna). From this point onward, due to the conjunction of the vowels *ū* and *a*, there is the state of being a mantra for the subsequent Niṣkala [state], as was previously stated:
"By means of the union with the turning of the Fish, she is established in the cavity of the palate."

And because this has been established in the *Śrītrikasāra*, it is stated here as follows: by the snapping of the mouth and tail like a fish, the power (*śakti*) ascends from the palate to the *uḍḍiyāna* (the uvula);

through the tasting of the essence (*rasa*) residing there, the consciousness of the practitioner is rendered full of flavor (*sarasatva*), thereby causing the sprouting of the fruit yet to come. Thus it is said.
And this is logical, because here—in the external world as well—trees [bear fruit] impelled by the six seasons. (7.105)

The trees, such as the *kuravaka* and others, attain the joy of the blossoming of flowers— the illuminator of the flower-armed god (Kāmadeva)— beginning from the springtime characterized by the movement of fish. And that [joy] is proclaimed among the six seasons.
Because flowers bloom not only in spring but also in other seasons,

the phrase "the lamp for the flower-armed god" (Kusumāyudhadīpaka) denotes its nature as a cause for inflaming desire; through this similarity, it suggests that even other springs serve as effective means for [awakening] desires.
For this very reason, just as externally a flower alone is the material cause of the fruit, so too internally, in the case of [the practice involving] fish and the like,
the commencement of the ritual action is like a flower; it brings face-to-face the fruit that is necessarily desired by the practitioners— this is the intended meaning of the word "flower."
Therefore:
"The mantras, impelled by the practice of vows and other rites in accordance with the time," (7.106).
And [these yogis] are illuminated by the awakening to the knowable and are the achievers of accomplishment and liberation.

"Time" refers to the rising of the signs beginning with Pisces. "Vow" (vrata) refers to the rules for propitiation. "Conduct" (caryā) refers to the customary behavior of the practitioner according to the observances; by the word "etcetera," the means of utterance such as the binding of the instruments (karaṇabandha) and so forth are included.
"Excited" means stimulated. "Cognition of the object of knowledge" is the knowledge of the pervasion of the deity expressed by the mantra;
"blazing" with that means having as their essence the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is non-different from its illumination.
Since the state of all mantras is thus, therefore this mantra belonging to this [context] is for the purpose of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*):
"Consisting of the nature of internal sound and form, impelled by the tasting of the six flavors. (7–107)
The flaming swan of awakening, however, is situated in the throat as the fish;
the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*) of the inner self (*adhyātma*) is its ultimate reality. "Śiva is the swan by virtue of his nature" (7.29).
In this context, [the deity] is inflamed by the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the awakening of the *haṃsa* as determined therein;

he has reached the transit through the zodiac sign of Pisces (*mīnarāśi*) at the throat by means of the pervasion of the power of the explained Fish; furthermore, the sixth seed-syllable itself, consisting of the upper and lower *kalās*, acts as the snapping of the mouth and tail.
Having assumed the form of a leaping fish, he has ascended; and from that very moment,

impelled— that is, urged— for the sake of tasting the essence [of the nectar] by the Self mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the support of all the senses, he has attained the state of a mantra, meaning he is to be uttered.
He indicates this very point by way of a concluding summary:
"Because, in that state, the perception of sound becomes clear for him. (7.108)
From that point on, O Goddess of Gods, everything proceeds for him through recitation up to the end of the couple; from that, perfection is born.
Of that internal sound (*adhyātma-śabda*): the clear perception of sound is the experience of the reality of mantra (*mantra-tattva*).

"Therein" means in the locus of the Fish (*mīna*). "Of him" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "Everything" refers to the preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*), such as recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth. [One should attain] rest in the state of Śakti at the end of the Couple (*mithuna*).
The meaning is "having performed [this]. Accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises; that is, the propitiation of the mantra is perfected.

In this context, it is stated that during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) of the breath (*prāṇa*), the breath itself takes on the form of Capricorn (*makara*) and so forth; they explain that externally, it follows that same pattern. For instance, when the breath has its mouth opened from the heart—
From its spreading [outward], it attains the state of a *makara*; from its abiding like a jar (*kumbha*) in the throat, the state of a *kumbha*;

then, from leaping upward by snapping the front and back, the state of a *mīna*; thereafter, from piercing the space between the eyebrows like a ram-fight (*huḍayuddha*), the state of a *meṣa*; and following that, from the raining down of the two fluids (*rasa*), the state of a *vṛṣa*.
Immediately following that, because it consists of both Śiva and Śakti, there is the state of being a couple (mithunatva). || 109 ||

Having thus determined the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), ending with the union in the *prāṇa*, he speaks in order to determine the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), beginning with Cancer and ending with Sagittarius,
in the *apāna*: "The Haṃsa, situated within the power of the Bindu, faces downward through the gateways of accomplishment (*siddhidvāra*)."
From Cancer onwards, that [wind] blows until the end of Libra within the space of the palate.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) which exists together with the *haṃsa* is situated within the power of the *bindu*— according to the perspective stated in [verse] 6.15, "When he performs creation, the *bindu* proceeds upwards"— it resides in the station of *Samanā* by means of those [channels], because it bestows spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

With four movements of six finger-breadths each, facing downwards and having entered within by way of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should rain [the nectar] upon the throat, which measures six finger-breadths, reaching as far as the palate— that is, into the middle of the palate.
Now, as long as [the breath] proceeds from below the throat, the embodied soul should go everywhere from the heart-lotus;
"everywhere" means throughout the entire body. It is called a "lotus" because it is expanded by the filling of the *apāna* wind within the heart.
"From the heart-lotus" means depending upon that.
Since it is thus, therefore one should accomplish [the practice] here for the sake of establishing the self and for the sake of nourishment. (7.111)

Here, the accomplishment of the self (ātman) consists in the manifestation of powers such as atomization (aṇimā) within this very body; nourishment (puṣṭi) is the absence of wrinkles, grey hair, and other signs of decay. || 111 ||
Furthermore, as before, even externally:
because at the time born of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) creation is produced;
for the south is favorable, bringing nourishment to the body and the world, [replenishing] those dried up by the heat of summer.
Since the sprouting of grass, creepers, shrubs, and so forth occurs again during the rainy season,

the connection [of the verse] is that one should accomplish the previously mentioned siddhis through recitation (japa) and other means by unifying this external and internal time. Now, in the section on recitation—
Those desiring liberation should perform the recitation (japa) while standing during the day, equalizing it with their breath;
that indeed should be known as the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra), which bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva.

"When the sound, having reached the void, returns once more, that is to be known as the night, until it has returned to the heart-lotus. This is declared to be the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), which brings about the fruit of all accomplishments. (2.140–142)

Thus, the previous division has been stated; however, here it is taught that for the sake of a practitioner’s mantra-siddhi, recitation (japa) and so forth are prescribed starting from the sunrise at the commencement of Pisces, and likewise, that one should accomplish [the goal] starting from Cancer and so on for the sake of self-perfection (ātma-siddhi). How is this so? It is said:
While the classification of recitation (*japa*) set forth in the second chapter remains established, a specific distinction is stated here:

practitioners should accomplish the mantras through preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) by resting in the signs beginning with Pisces and ending with Gemini, according to the sequence of recitation and so forth prescribed in the *Kalpa*. When thus accomplished, they are for the sake of success at the time of practical application (*prayoga*).
There is no doubt here that these [mantras] should be employed primarily with a rest in the period beginning from Cancer and ending with Libra.
Now he defines the sixfold [period] beginning with Karkaṭa by means of the division of finger-breadths:
"O Dear One, the Haṃsa should transition below Śakti into the heart during Karkaṭa. (7.112)
Having abandoned six finger-breadths, it indeed enters Leo;
again, when another six finger-breadths have been abandoned, it enters Virgo.
Having abandoned [the flow] from the tip of the nose up to the palate in this manner, it becomes the equinox;
this is declared to be the transition of Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti), and it becomes the southern equinox.

Below the power (*śakti*) that takes the form of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the pervasive power (*vyāpinīśakti*). At the station of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and so forth, it is like a crab, a *haṃsa* with its face turned downward; thereafter, at the station of Sadāśiva, it is a lion because of its predominance in sounding and its capacity for traversing the entire universe. Then—

Because of the predominance of the light of the *bindu* at the center of the eyebrows and so forth, due to its connection with radiance and beauty, and because of its movement in the form of a universal diffusion, it is denoted by the word "maiden" (*kanyā*). Furthermore, because it abides in equilibrium within the middle of the palate, it takes the form of the "balance" (*tulā*); and precisely because of this equilibrium, it is the "equinox" (*viṣuva*).

Because it deserves to be all-pervasive (*vyāpti*), it is designated by the term *viṣuvat*. Furthermore, the word *viṣuvat* signifies that this is a time of equinox distinct from the previously mentioned northern equinox; such is the meaning. || 114 ||
And precisely because of its otherness—
that which was established as a means of accomplishment [in a previous life] grants desires here in this birth;
that is the meaning.
And for this reason—one should undertake from it victory over death, as well as peace and nourishment. (7.115)
Therefore, that food consisting of the six tastes, once it has passed below the throat, nourishes the body.

This threefold accomplishment here consists of the superior (uttama) and other forms. "That" refers to the time situated in the southern equinox (*dakṣiṇaviṣuvat*), which is equal; for this very reason, cruel rites performed in this world do not bear fruit here.

Thus, it follows here by implication that this [practice] must be performed through resting in the movement of the vital breath (dhānvicāra), which presides over the month of Pauṣa and withdraws all aesthetic flavors (sarvarasa).
Then,
having left behind six finger-breadths, it moves forward again in Scorpio.
Having left two finger-breadths above the throat and four finger-breadths below the throat;
having left eight finger-breadths from the surface of the palate and six finger-breadths from the throat—
two finger-breadths above in consideration of entry, but two finger-breadths below in consideration of the arousal of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having abandoned [the previous position], in the field six finger-breadths below the throat, one first remains for four finger-breadths; there,
remaining as motionless as a scorpion for six finger-breadths including the preceding two, one is called a "scorpion" (*vṛścika*) due to moving forward very slowly.
Then, having left Scorpio, the transit into Sagittarius is said to occur. || 7-117 ||
Six finger-breadths below [the navel], however, situated in the bow, it moves within the heart. "Below" means resting in the six-finger space located beneath; there it moves and finds repose.
And in that state, this *haṃsa* is called a "bowman" (*dhanvin*) because its aim is fixed.
Thus, in this manner—the *haṃsa*, having moved as far as the heart-lotus, rises upward. (7.118)
The meaning is that it again resorts to the function of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 118 ||
He summarizes:
"In this manner, one should always perform [the ritual] twelve times during the transits through Capricorn and the other signs.
By this very sequence described, [one determines] the lifespan of all embodied beings. (7.119)
Regarding the phrase "at the transition" (*saṃkrāntau*), because the singular is used for the genus, it refers to those transitions occurring in Capricorn and the other signs;

in these, according to the sequence thus described, there are twelve. Thus, the *haṃsa* (the vital breath) always moves through the months beginning with Māgha during every movement of the individual life-force. To what limit? He says: "The lifespan of all embodied beings."
The meaning is "for as long as one lives. || 119 ||
Now, for one who is awakened, because they constantly obtain auspicious times such as the transits of the sun (*saṃkrānti*) and the southern and northern solstices (*dakṣiṇāyana* and *uttarāyaṇa*),
the attainment of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) occurs without effort. This very point he states:
Success pertaining to this world and the next— whether inferior, middling, or superior—
accrues to practitioners who remain in this state.
He summarizes: "The two paths have been described...
and herein, within the twelve [months] beginning with Capricorn, there is the state of being an embryo and the state of being about to emerge for the effect."
The desire to arise, the state of being about to arise, the commencement of arising, the state of arising, birth, existence,
transformation, growth, decline, and decay occur in succession. Therefore,
the teachers have declared that ritual actions such as recitation (*japa*) produce a result of precisely this nature.
But when rest is achieved in the heart and at the end of the twelve [fingers] by means of abandoning the coming and going of the prāṇa and apāna, then—
..................the perfection of liberation, free from duality. (7.120)
The meaning is that, by means of the abandonment of duality through differentiation, she who consists of non-duality becomes [the consort] of the great adept (*mahāsādhaka*).
For this reason, that great adept—
abiding eternally at the end of the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*) within the state of *unmanī*— is [as described].
Whenever it resorts to the two courses (of the breath), at those times it is called "ending in Unmanā.
Thus, in the state of the cessation of prāṇa and apāna, it rests in the experience of the Supreme Reality at the End of the Twelve and in the heart.
Although the state of ending in Unmanā was previously stated to be only at the End of the Twelve, [it is here understood to apply to both].

Nevertheless, by stating that the state of *unmanā* extends up to the limit of the two *ayana*s, he demonstrates that there is a pervasive presence (*vyāpti*) within the heart that is undivided from the *dvādaśānta*.
For this very reason—
And it has been stated elsewhere: "In the dvādaśānta and in the heart," and so forth.
And therefore:
"Abiding there, indeed, one shall attain the perfection of liberation through recitation and meditation. (121)
The meaning is that he who, through recitation and meditation as his primary practice, abides and finds rest in that very Supreme Reality, is liberated. || 121 ||
Therefore, by this very nature—having attained liberation, one shall not return; such is the vow of Bhairava.
It is the vow of Bhairava, and not that of Śrīkaṇṭha, Umāpati, and the others; thus it is in every respect.
"Restraint [of the breath] should be performed between the twelve-finger space and the heart," and so forth, has been thus instructed.

Likewise, instructing the practitioner that even a task requiring twelve years to accomplish can be achieved without effort by perceiving the pervasion of those twelve years within the vital breath (prāṇa) through its most subtle state, the Lord ordains the arising of the twelve-year cycle as follows:
In this emergence of the year, listen again to the emergence of the twelve years.
Therein, the twelve months beginning with Caitra are designated by the names of the year, the month, and the equal [period].
Since the rising of the months occurs in the year of Caitra,
therefore the practitioners of mantra should begin their mantra-sādhana from that point.
"Starting from that" means taking the year named Caitra as the beginning. || 123 ||
The time of the arising of the year beginning with Caitra here is precisely the same as the previously mentioned time of the arising of the month of Caitra and so forth;
thus he says:
"O fair-faced one, that [year] consisting of twelve months is to be understood as beginning from the month of Caitra."
Leaving two fingers below the eight-finger-thick neck, that six-finger space which was previously described as the location for the month of Caitra is indeed the location for the year of Caitra.
Now,
I shall describe its characteristics according to their specific divisions within this vital breath.
In that regard, O lady of good vows, according to what has been stated, a day and night as described there consists of twelve parts of a year, O beloved. (7.125)

Indeed, those twelve days and nights constitute one year within the internal year of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This refers to a twelfth part of that internal day and night, which measures five-fifths of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).

In the arising of twelve years, one day-and-night (ahorātra) is obtained; thus, this becomes the sixtieth part of an aṅgula. In this way, twelve day-and-nights constitute one day-and-night [of the breath]; and so, sixty day-and-nights are produced within a true aṅgula.
Multiplying those by five, twelve years shall constitute one season (ṛtu).
The meaning is "for two months. || 126 ||
By doubling that same period,
the time known as the four-month season is prescribed.
By this threefold movement...
through the three fingers multiplied by three, that is, by the three-fold season, the first is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa); other than that triad, it is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
Thus, in this manner—..................a year [is calculated] by means of sixfold multiplication. || 7-127 ||
Thus,
just as twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) are proclaimed here in a year,
so those years are proclaimed in the vital breath (prāṇa) at the rising of the twelve-year cycle. (7.128)
"Just as" refers to the calculation of six finger-breadths. || 128 ||
Now, those [days and nights] which occur in twelve years...
they come into being.
...Learn from me their number: four thousand, three hundred, and twenty. (7.129)
"O Goddess, the arising of twelve years in this vital breath has been described by me"—
here, the two locative case endings (*dvādaśābdodaye* and *prāṇe*) are in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), meaning "in the vital breath at the time of the arising of twelve years."
Now, by means of an exceedingly subtle arrangement, I shall explain to you once again the emergence of the sixty-year cycle within this very [system]. (7.130)
O fair-faced one, those sixty years beginning with Ānanda should be known to occur within this very single movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra).
Thus it is said:
"And those two, O beautiful goddess, [occur] when the vital breath (prāṇa) moves both downward and upward within that one [channel]. (7.131)
I shall explain to you how they proceed according to their specific divisions.
Therefore, he who desires the accomplishment (siddhi) that is to be achieved in sixty years should commence the propitiation of the mantra from the intermediate year known as Ānanda onwards.
Thus he said:
"O Goddess, whoever would worship the mantra beginning with Ānanda... (7.132).
O Goddess of the Gods, bliss indeed arises for him together with the mantra.

Because the mantra, by virtue of its nature as the supreme *niṣkala* (partless), is filled with the entirety of the universe and is thus of the nature of supreme bliss, one who knows the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇoccāra*) consisting of the reflective awareness of non-difference from that [mantra] becomes composed of bliss itself.

Thus it is. Consequently, by means of the established emergence and duration of the sixty-year cycle mentioned here, for the knower who understands the pervasion (*vyāpti*), whatever lifelong obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) must necessarily be performed—all that is accomplished once and for all within a single movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*). However, for one who desires supernatural powers (*siddhi*):

It is to be accomplished over sixty years; however, for one who performs the respective rites to be accomplished within each of those years preceded by the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) pertaining to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is no contradiction.
With this intention, nothing beyond the arising of the sixty-year cycle has been stated here in the section on the practitioner (*sādhaka*). But in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*, it says:

With the intention of explaining the pervasion of consciousness (*jñāna-vyāpti*), the arising of one hundred and twenty [breaths] has also been mentioned. And thus, for those yogins of knowledge, everything is accomplished without effort simply through the knowledge of the pervasion within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
As it was said by the venerable Utpaladeva:

"O Lord, since everything within the entire universe is directly composed of You, what place is not a field for those possessed of devotion? For them, what mantra does not attain accomplishment? (Stotrāvalī 1.4).
Furthermore:
"In the twelfth year, one should divide that day and night into five parts. (7.133)
Those days and nights are said to be exactly five during the emergence of sixty years;

it has been stated that when twelve years emerge, one day and night is the sixtieth part of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). Now, however, one should divide even that fivefold. Thus, during the emergence of sixty years, [the calculation applies] to the breath-finger (*prāṇāṅgula*).
One three-hundredth part constitutes a day and night.
By this extremely subtle state—those [moments] multiplied sixfold there are proclaimed as one month. (7.134)
And by those twelve [days], O Goddess, one year is constituted.
"Those" refers to the days and nights that arise from the twelve-year cycle; "by those" refers to the months consisting of such [days].
And thus:
"This measurement is proclaimed as being one finger plus a fifth part. (7.135)

Since ten months correspond to three hundred days and nights within one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and two months correspond to two-fifths of a finger-breadth within sixty days and nights, it follows that this [measurement] applies to a finger-breadth plus one-fifth; thus, the measure of a year has been stated in relation to the emergence of the sixty-year cycle. || 135 ||
Thus, in this manner— five years arise from six finger-breadths, and those [fifty] years arise from sixty;
by means of the twelve-year cycle of arising, five [years] here arise through six finger-breadths which serve as the basis for the arising of the year.
The years consist of [the following]: one *aṅgula* consists of ten months of rising;
by those six [units], there is the accomplishment of sixty months, which initiates the five-year cycle.
And by this calculation—from the heart-lotus up to the level of Śakti—the emergence [of consciousness] occurs over thirty years. (7.136)
Furthermore—
down from the *śakti* as far as the heart-lotus, there occurs the arising of thirty years.
Moreover—
I shall now state the number of those days and nights that occur within a sixty-year period.
O fair-faced one, in a period of sixty years, the number of days and nights is said to be twenty-one thousand six hundred.
The number of breath-movements occurring during an external day and night. || 138 ||
He concludes:
"The arising of sixty years has been explained by me to you as being within a single breath.
Here, he states the purpose at the end of the arising of the sixty-year cycle:
And during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and during the fortnights, months, and solstices. || 7-139 ||
O fair-faced one, [this occurs] at the beginnings of the ages, at the ends of the ages, as well as during the year, during twelve years,
and also during a sixty-year cycle.
Whatever has been performed during the external time through bathing, giving, sacrifices, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, as well as through the yoga of knowledge and so forth— (7.141)
O fair-limbed lady, when this has been spoken by him, one obtains that great fruit.

Whether externally during a lunar eclipse and so forth, or at the end of sixty years, when [the teaching] has been spoken by him through this internal method, whatever is performed at that very time according to the sequence of bathing, giving, and so on, its fruit is great; it is the means for accomplishing the infinite.

He attains [success]. (In this way, by means of the duration established at the commencement of the yugas, for the sake of accomplishing Caitra, Āṣāḍha, Āśvayuja, and Pauṣa... he calculates the remaining four.
— Having understood the movement of the breath-goose (*prāṇahaṃsa*) in its course, one should apply that to a single [unit]. (7.142)

The nature of the *haṃsa* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is as previously described. Regarding "in the movement" (*cāre*), it refers to the flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* which extends over the duration of sixty years. "That" (*tat*) refers to the lunar mansions, planets, and so forth. 142.

Now, one might ask: "In that case, how does the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses such pervasion come within the range of intuitive perception according to the actual state of things? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The movement [of consciousness] becomes clearly self-evident through mastery over the movement within the channels (nāḍī)."

Through mastery over the movement and flow within the channels (*nāḍīs*), and by attaining independence in their circulation through practice, all vital pervasion (*prāṇīyā vyāpti*) becomes manifest in the central path (*madhyamārga*); therefore, the essential point is that one must exert effort in the practice of yoga.
When there is proficiency in the practice of yoga— or else, when [the Self] has been thus exceedingly nourished by recitation alone— 7.143.
The practitioner of mantra (mantrī) understands yoga; having understood it, he attains omniscience.
"From recitation" means from the number of recitations as stated in the section on the five *praṇavas*.
"Strengthened" means having attained excellence. "The practitioner of mantra" means one who knows the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mantra as described. "Yoga" is according to his inclination.

[He attains] mastery over the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), omniscience— which is the capacity for direct realization of the aforementioned all-pervasiveness of the vital breath— and supreme sovereignty. For it has been said:
"But by reciting [the mantra] three hundred times, one becomes equal to Svacchanda. (6.54)
Having concluded this, he introduces another [topic]:
"I shall explain once more according to the division of the three channels. (7.144)
During the southern and northern solstices, as well as during the equinoxes, that *haṃsa* moves through this world of the moving and the unmoving in such a manner. (7.145)
Abiding within in the form of Time, fashioning the universe through its constituent parts (kalās),

the state of movement is said to be established by resorting to the middle path. Now, regarding the right, the left, and that which consists of both— the equinox— as well as the Haṃsa within the world consisting of the moving and the stationary:

He moves among moving beings, and by means of the extension of his senses, he touches even stationary things; for this very reason, he is "dwelling within" (antaḥstha) in all subjects. Fixing his station through the forms of time—past, present, and so forth—he fashions the entire universe by means of its temporal parts, such as moments, tuṭis, and lavas.

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: I shall explain how the *haṃsa* moves while creating and withdrawing [the world] in the form of the sixfold modifications beginning with birth (*janmādi-vikāra-ṣaṭka*). Furthermore, even though it is immobile, the *haṃsa* brings about the nourishment of flowers and fruits through the application of vital essence (*rasa*) within the right, left, and middle channels of the sentient being who possesses internal consciousness.
Those who possess knowledge of the Ayurveda of trees.
To explain what kind of movement this [breath] performs, he says:
"Having made its support in the three channels, it is established in the three paths. (7.146)
Pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas), established in the three states,
overcome by the six causes, and endowed with the triad of powers.
"Pierced by will, knowledge, and action, situated in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire"—this he explains through the sequence beginning with the three channels:
"In the right nostril, the channel is indeed known as Piṅgalā. (7.148)
The *iḍā* is indeed on the left, while the *suṣumnā* is situated in the middle.
He says that these three channels alone constitute the three paths:
"The path of the gods (*devamārga*) is on the right, and likewise the path of the ancestors (*pitṛmārga*) is on the left. (7.149)
The middle path, however, is the path of Śiva.
But what is its "Śiva-nature"? To this he says:
"Having gone there, one is not born again."
"Having gone" means having come to rest through the perception [of that state].
Right here he demonstrates the three qualities (guṇas) and the three states (avasthās): "In the right [channel] is the waking state born of sattva; in the left is the dreaming state of rajas. (7.150)
Tamas is to be understood as being in the middle, specifically in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti).

Sattva exists in the form of knowledge due to the predominance of cognition; Rajas is on the left because it consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti); whereas Tamas is in the middle, consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti), because its nature is the path of withdrawing differentiation—hence it is called "middle."
Here, the state of flowing equally through both channels is due to their balanced pervasion (*samānavyāpti*), and not because of an upward flow through the middle channel;
for that [middle channel] consists of the light of the fourth state (*turya*), and thus lacks any connection with the darkness of deep sleep (*sauṣuptatamas*).
Regarding this very point, he states the reasons:
"Brahmā and Īśvara reside on the right, while Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva reside on the left. (7.151)
In the middle, Rudra and Śiva are proclaimed; the Supreme Śiva is beyond all.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as Parameśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva, abide as the presiding deities over the right, left, and middle [channels] for the sake of supreme pervasion. Therefore, indeed—

It should be understood that even within the triad beginning with waking (jāgarādi), there is also the pervasion of the fourth state (turya) due to the presiding presence of Īśvara and the others; however, by the term "transcending all" (sarvātīta), the nature of the supreme cause is expressed.

He describes the abiding of the three powers through the distinction between cause and its effects, as well as their mutual succession: "Jyeṣṭhā resides in knowledge, Dakṣā in action, and Vāmā likewise in the north. (7.152)
Raudrī and Icchā are situated in the middle;
Jñānā and the others are the lower (aparā), while Jyeṣṭhā and the others are the higher (parā).
In accordance with the [preceding] reasoning, he also describes the nature of the supreme power (*paraśakti*), which is like the nature of the supreme cause:
"The supreme power is both supreme and non-supreme;
it exists pervading everything, both the supreme and the non-supreme"—this is the meaning.
In this very context, he speaks of the Moon, Sun, and Fire:
"The Sun is situated on the right, while the Moon shines resplendent on the left. (7.153)
In the acts of cooking and illuminating, fire (*pāvaka*) stands as the mediator;
thus, fire is the instrumental cause for both cooking and illuminating. As for the moon and the sun:
"The sun blows [and heats], and the moon rains down nectar" (7.157).
Thus he will explain the task to be performed.
He explains *pāka* and *prakāśa* by way of their objects:
"For one should cook all that is to be cooked, which arises from the qualities of Soma and the rest. (7.154)
One should reveal the stainless supreme reality through one's own power.

Regarding the phrase "through one's own power": by virtue of having emerged as the nature of consciousness through the subordination of the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the stability of the planets and other celestial bodies was previously described in accordance with the rising of the day on the middle path.
Now, however, he speaks also by means of the right, the left, and both [channels]:
"All the zodiac signs, the planets, and whatever asterisms, yogas, and so forth [exist]. (7.155)
They move in succession precisely along the path of the moon and sun;
and all of them, O beloved, enjoy the sun and moon in due order.

"All those" refers to the group ending with the eight Bhairavas; "the Moon and Sun" means they preside over them either separately when the flows are distinct, or simultaneously when the flow is unified. || 156 ||
And thus:
"They indeed consist of the Moon and the Sun, established in the three paths;
on the right they consist of the Prāṇa and the Sun, on the left they consist of the Apāna and the Moon, and in the middle—"
They possess both natures. And this has already been analyzed in the second chapter, precisely at the occasion of the division of the three paths of the clarified butter (ājya).
And since they possess the nature of both Soma and Sūrya, they too bestow that fruit; thus he says:
"The Sun blows and the Sun burns; the Moon rains down nectar. (7.157)
Since the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of Soma and Sūrya;

because, through the aforementioned pervasion, the entire world is connected to the carriers of Sūrya and Soma, it is composed of Sūrya and Soma—[as it is said]: "Even snow burns, and even fire nourishes by its touch."

By this principle— that is, by the principle of each respective subject, place, and time— the universe is perceived as being both gladdening and distressing; therefore, the "Sun" (sūrya) is the rightward flow which blows,
dries up (*ovai* means "to dry up"), and heats, while the "Moon" (soma) is the leftward flow, which is nectar.
It rains and nourishes; therefore, the ultimate truth is that one should act with propriety toward those intent on achieving cruel, gentle, or virtuous ends.
Furthermore:
The solar southern path is designated as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa). || 7.158 ||
That which is called the left, gentle [channel] is indeed the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
the equinox (viṣuvat), consisting of the nature of both Moon and Sun, issues forth from the two nostrils.
The meaning is that, just as there is an upward and downward flow [of breath], here too there exists a division such as the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and so forth. || 159 ||
Here he demonstrates the division of the transits (saṃkrānti):
"There are five transits in the north and indeed five in the southward course;
between the south and the north, there are two equinoxes by virtue of the transit. (7.160)

According to the principle that will be stated [later] in the verse, "Twelve are said to occur in a day" (7.168), externally, during the day, there are twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) through the left, right, and middle channels,
consisting of nine hundred flows of prāṇa and apāna. || 160 ||
Here he shows the result:
"The solar southern path grants success in malevolent rites (abhicāra); likewise, for nourishment and prosperity, the lunar northern path is used for pacifying rites. (7.161)
Now he teaches the sequence regarding the ten transits (saṃkrānti):
"When it goes from the south to the north, or from the north to the south, that is the southern and northern transit, and it is established in this very way. (7.162)

Externally, on the day of the southern equinox, according to what will be explained, having remained in the internal state of the southern equinox time through equal flow (*samavāha*), it rises from the southern path and goes to the northern path; when it again goes from the north to the south, then that—

The southern transit and the northern transit are thus described. In this very sequence, it is further established—that is, determined—that [the breath] goes again from the north to the south. Therefore, the meaning is that it carries five transits within the southern, northern, southern, northern, and southern [cycles]. || 162 ||
Now he describes the sixth [transit], the northern equinoxal transit (uttaraviṣuvatsaṃkrānti):
"When it transits into the northern channel from the southern one, for as long as it remains there, it flows through the middle toward the north. (7.163)
That is declared to be the northern equinox during the northern course.
When, having remained in the southern channel consisting of five transits, it moves toward the northern path, then,
by passing through the middle between both, the northern equinox occurs.
"Uttarāyaṇa" (northern course) is so called because it takes its support from the northern course consisting of the downward flow (*dakṣiṇavāha*). To the question "How so?", he says:

"Therein. The meaning is that, having made the southern half belong to the *prāṇa*, it flows through both nostrils (*puṭa*). And as for the phrase "as far as the north," there remains something yet to be explained.
This is its meaning: immediately after that, it flows from the north (uttara) starting from the northern [node] as far as the fifth northern transit (*saṃkrānti*).
Therefore, the intended sense is that one should flow through the five transits—northern, southern, northern, southern, and northern.

The word "uttare" (in the north) from the Sūtra should be repeated twice. However, since the commentators explain the passage beginning with "dakṣiṇottaram" and ending with "uttarāyaṇe" as referring exclusively to the northern equinox (*uttara-viṣuva*), they have not shown the division of the *saṃkrāntis*, which results in a redundancy of the text.
And it is dependent upon this.
Now he speaks of the southern equinox: "O fair-faced one, moving from the north toward the south... (7.164).
O Dear One, as long as it flows there for half [the duration], for half it flows to the south;
that is the southern equinox, born of the southern solstice.
From the northern path, which consists of the nature of the five transits, as it moves into the southern channel, half of the vital breath (prāṇa) is there in the north, and half is in the south,
as long as it flows equally through both nostrils (puṭas).
The meaning is that this occurs during the southern solstice, which takes place at the time of the sun’s southern course. || 165 ||
Regarding this, he states the fruit of the two equinoxes:
whatever worship, recitation, or fire-offering is performed therein becomes a bestower of liberation.
That [is the result].
Furthermore:
"By means of the yoga of meditation during initiation, the Guru, established therein, shall indeed grant liberation. (7.166)
In this context, meditation has the supreme reality as its object.
Thus, O fair-faced one, while there are twenty-four external transitions of day and night, the swan of the vital breath undergoes twenty-four transitions internally. (7.167)
Those who know the pervasive extension (*vyāpti*) say that it is thus simply by touching the three principal channels of the eight petals of the heart-lotus;
"the swan of breath" (*prāṇahaṃsa*) is as explained previously.
In this regard, the following is the distinction: twelve [transits] are declared for the day, and twelve indeed are recorded for the night.
Here too, he states the distinction regarding the equinoxes and solstices:
One [should be performed] in the forenoon at the equinox, and the second at midday.
The third occurs in the afternoon, and the fourth at midnight;
thus the Viṣuvat is said to be fourfold, bestowing liberation through a single day and night.

Therefore, on the external equinoctial day (*viṣuvaddin*), there is one and a quarter *ghaṭikās* remaining from the end of the night and one and a quarter *ghaṭikās* from the sunrise; this constitutes one equinox. Following that, there are five transits (*saṃkrānti*) in succession, each consisting of exactly two and a half *ghaṭikās*; thus, starting from the beginning of the day, they are less than three [full *ghaṭikās*].

These constitute fourteen ghaṭikās. Then, the second equinox consists of two and a half ghaṭikās. After that, there are likewise five transits; thus, up to this point, there are twenty-nine nālikās less a quarter.

From that remaining portion of the day, one and a quarter *ghaṭikās* [pass], and one and a quarter *ghaṭikās* mark the commencement of the night; thus, by this sequence, there is the third equinox (*viṣuvat*), and at midnight occurs the fourth equinox. In whatever manner there is a decrease or increase in the duration of day and night, [the same applies].
Thus, it should be understood that this [same principle] applies to the transits (*saṃkrānti*) as well; such is the collective meaning.
As was stated by our own teacher in the *Tantrāloka*, the illumination of the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all scriptures:
"On the day of the equinox (*viṣuvat*), at dawn, he, situated in the middle, [traverses] a nāḍī along with its parts."
By means of the left, the other [right], the upward, and the downward paths, for as long as five transits [of the breath].
Thus, when thirteen and three-quarter *nāḍīs* have elapsed,
at midday, one should carry nine hundred breaths during the southern equinox (*dakṣiṇaviṣuvat*).
From the south to the north, and from the north to the south, there are five transits (saṃkrānti) again;
each consists of one hundred and nine breaths, after which follows the northern equinox (viṣuvad-uttara).
Just as there is an external equinox at the transition after every five [transits],
so too is there an internal transition consisting of nine hundred breaths.

"In this same way, [the calculation applies] even at night; thus, starting from the equinoctial day, this [movement] proceeds through the solstices, characterized by the increase and decrease of day and night. (6.201–205), and so forth, in the sixth chapter of the *Kālatattvaprakāśana*. As for that which [occurs] there at midday...

It was stated that [the equinox] belongs to Dakṣa; this was said with the intention that on the day of the external northern solstice equinox (*bāhyottarāyaṇaviṣuvaddina*), the northern equinox occurs in the morning. However, here it is stated otherwise with the intention that on the day of the external southern solstice equinox (*bāhyadakṣiṇāyanaviṣuvaddina*), the southern equinox occurs in the morning. || 169 ||
Now he teaches the external duration of time corresponding to the internal transits:
"The *haṃsa* always carries twenty-four transits, by its very nature, for one whose constituent elements (*dhātu*) are balanced; it carries each one constantly nine hundred times. (7.170)

This refers to one whose bodily elements are in equilibrium and who is not afflicted by phlegm or other humors. In this regard, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, for the first three days the *haṃsa* (vital breath) flows through the left channel for the first two and a half *ghaṭikās*;
thereafter, for another three days it flows through the right; then again for another [three] days through the left, and so forth is the sequence.
It should be remembered for the purpose of knowing the emergence [of the breath] as taught in the *Śrīkālottara* and other scriptures. As it is said in the *Kālāvalī*:
"In that regard, first, having reached the new moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight, the wind..."
In the ritual procedure, first of all, there arises a period of three lunar days.
Then, as the sun transits there, it likewise rises for three days;
having transited these three from that point, it returns again to the moon.
And so forth.
He summarizes:
"This measure has been fully explained..."—
the remainder [of the sentence] being "of the transits" (saṃkrāntīnām).
He states that a contrary movement indicates both the desired and the undesired: "When it flows in a contrary manner, then it portends both what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. (7.171)
[The word] "of the element of concentration" alone [is used].
Since it is thus—whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others—the yogi should investigate.
He should investigate for his own sake by examining with his own self; he should investigate for the sake of others.

However, in the context of detailed examination (*nirūpaṇā*) or investigation (*parīkṣā*), one should employ [the term]; here, in the expression "one should examine" (*nirūpayet*), there are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*).
Then, he states the time for examination here:
"But when the first rising of the sun has arrived, O fair-faced one," (7.172).
From that point onward, one should investigate both life and death;

since the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is bound up with life, the investigation of that [life] alone is undertaken here first as being primary. "Of the Sun" refers to the right breath (*prāṇa*). "At the eastern rising" means—

One should begin the investigation from the moment the dawn occurs immediately after the time of the morning equinox (viṣuvat), which consists of the flow of both [currents] as previously described; and in this case, during the external northern course (uttarāyaṇa),
one should examine it starting from the morning time of the day of the equinox— so says the author of the Kālāvalī.
"The teachers maintain that at all times, it begins from the right flow following the *kālottara* [period] ending with the dawn-uttered *viṣuvat*."
Therein—
the yogi, a hero with a well-restrained mind, established in the yogic posture— || 7.173 ||

O beloved, recollecting his own life-force (prāṇa) situated within the *suṣumnā*, the hero—one-pointed in observing the vehicle of the vital breath—attains perfect restraint of the mind and freedom from the defilement of sense objects. Yoga-posture refers to the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others; [he recollects] his own life-force.
Thus, having explained [the process] according to the sequence of descent, he correctly remembers [it as having arisen from the very nature of consciousness],
contemplating it through the sequence of binding the divine instruments by means of the previously mentioned method of penetration.
And therefore:
"Then, being perfectly tranquil, one should remain with the mind focused solely on the vital breath. (7.174)
By focusing on the flow of the central breath, other mental modifications are stilled, and thus [the mind] becomes perfectly tranquil. || 174 ||
Thus, for the yogin who has perceived the path of the Suṣumṇā as the foundation for all expansions,

when the time for the transition of the vital breath arrives— O Goddess, once one knows that the flow is situated solely in the Piṅgalā during the equinox (viṣuvat), one should determine the [auspicious] time.
After the word "having known" (*jñātvā*), the word "then" (*tadā*) must be supplied; therefore, the meaning is as follows:

having observed the time of dawn—which consists of both flows—while simultaneously observing the middle path, immediately thereafter, [one should practice] in the *piṅgalā* alone, which is the southern path.

Having observed that the flow has remained in such a state for a long time by transgressing the previously described sequence of movement through the right and left [nāḍīs], one should predict the death— either of oneself or of another— at such a current of the breath. || 175 ||
He analyzes this as follows:
"O lady of excellent vows, life for one year is to be known [as corresponding] to a single day and night;
he shall live for two years by means of two days and nights. (7.176)
In this case, three years are completed by three [days], four years by four, five years by five days, and six years likewise by six. (7.177)
With seven [lines], one shall live for seven years; with eight, for eight years;
with nine, for nine years; and with ten, for exactly ten years.
O beloved, by means of eleven days alone, one lives for eleven years;
by twelve days, the yogi shall live for twelve years. (7.179)
If [the breath] flows for seven watches (yāma), he lives for six months;
if one can sustain it for six watches, he lives for three months.
If it flows for five watches, his life lasts exactly two and a half months;
O Goddess, with four watches, he lives for one month.
If it flows for three watches, one lives for half a month;
he whose [wind] flows for two watches lives for eight days. (7.182)
If one should carry [the breath] for one watch (prahara), he would live for four watches;
