if one carries it for half a watch, he would live for two watches. (7.183)

In this regard, if— beyond the flow of the ninety-six breaths mentioned here— the vital breath of one with balanced humors should flow for twelve days up to one year, remaining solely in the *piṅgalā* without touching the left path, then his lifespan shall be exactly that many years.

It occurs as follows: when the flow [of breath] exceeds its own natural flow during the period from seven *praharas* down to half a *prahara*, the lifespan becomes six months, three months, two months, one month, half a month, eight days, four days, one day, or half a day respectively. However, some say:

Following the flow of nine hundred [breaths], there is the division of days by means of the duration of the internal day consisting of the flow of prāṇa and apāna; furthermore, for the purpose of examining oneself and others,
there is the division of watches (prahara) by means of the duration of the internal circulation consisting of four *tuṭis*.
He has explained this solely for the purpose of self-examination, and he has stated that the flow of the breath during the external days and so forth contradicts actual experience;

however, the flow of seven *praharas* and so on, while accepting it as external, is to be disregarded. For if the breath of one whose death has arrived were to flow through all twelve external days, [it would be impossible].
What sublation by experience could there be in this case? It cannot be said, without undue haste or lack of attention, that such an apprehension does not exist;
for for the other [the opponent], such an apprehension certainly does occur.
Furthermore, a flow of seven or more *praharas* based on the duration of a *prahara* consisting of four *tuṭis* is entirely untenable;

for the flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* never, for anyone at any time, flows by abandoning its natural measure of seventy-two finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), especially when the flow consists of four *praharas*.

If the apāna does not enter within thirty-six finger-breadths [from the heart], there would be the consequence of death at that very moment. Furthermore, such a flow of the parts and sub-parts, accomplished by the yogi through great effort, bestows various supernatural powers (siddhis); likewise, when produced through effort during the new moon (amāvasyā), it indeed bestows success.
However, it would not indicate the end of one's life; furthermore, the phrase "Piṅgala stationed alone" here is unconnected [to the context].

If, however, yogis place their weight of authority on this interpretation, then even though it has a figurative meaning, it is indeed correct; we have no objection to that either, yet that too is merely a day’s discourse for the sake of our own examination.
However, there is no scriptural statement whatsoever to the effect that the movement of the watches (*yāma*) is for the purpose of examining oneself and others;

furthermore, since the regulation of the movement of hours (*prahara*) and so forth is accepted even as something external, this [claim] is clearly a mere fabrication of one's own imagination— so enough of this insistence with those who came before.
This was said with the intention that a distorted understanding of the meaning of the scriptures—which is a cause for error in practice—should not occur. (7-183)
Furthermore:
"Immediate death shall befall him for whom the *haṃsa* [breath] moves through the three paths.
"Immediate" (*sadyas*) means within that very same half-watch (*ardhaprahara*). The three paths are the two nostrils and the mouth.

And one should calculate that life, beginning from the time of its examination; thus he says: "From the moment it is determined, one should indeed perceive Time as the Lord within the vital breath. (7.184)
O beloved, having carefully observed the month, the fortnight, the day, the year, that very day, and so forth, one should reach a certain conclusion at that time through diligent effort. (7.185)

One should investigate and examine the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as *kāla* (time), because it initiates the arrangement of all time starting from external time; and one should examine it as *īśvara* (the Lord), because it pervades the universe through its sovereign power. One should do so by means of the effort of intense contemplation according to the reasoning thus stated; and from that point onward—
The connection is as follows: having correctly observed the months, fortnights, days, years, and so forth, there will necessarily arise at that time a certainty regarding one's lifespan.
He concludes:
"Thus have I described [the practice] for the time born of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
Here, the 'northern course' refers to the flow through the right nostril, because it is primarily characterized by withdrawal (saṃhāra)."
In this context, he promises another method for the sake of knowing the time of death:
"Learn from me the knowledge of death even for one who is not disciplined regarding the vital breath. (7.186)
Regarding this, it is said: "O Goddess of Gods, when one who has placed his thumb in the opening of the ear no longer hears sound, one should declare his death to occur within six months. (7.187)

He does not hear the sound that imitates the noise of a rushing river; rather, he certainly hears the sound residing within it, which is like the "ciñciṇī" sound produced by living beings such as monkeys and is known as the speech of Cīra. || 187 ||
But when even that supreme sound amidst the roar— the sound of rustling bark garments and the *ciñciṇī*—
is not heard for one month, O Dear One, he shall live for only one more month. (7.188)
The phrase "having placed the thumb in the ear-canal" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. || 188 ||
In this context, he says something else as well:
"Hear from me about the *utpāṭa*, the *kāṇa*, and the *mṛtyuyoga*.
Regarding these—"
When the vital breath flows through the opening of the mouth during the five transits, [it is as follows].
One should call that "uprooting" (utpāṭa) yoga;
because the vital breath (prāṇa) is uprooted from its own place via the nasal path, this is called "uprooting. || 189 ||
As it is said:
"He would go from one place to another;
therefore, even one endowed with such signs of imminent death (*ariṣṭa*) wanders from place to place like a bird that has lost its way."
"It wanders"—this is also the meaning here.
Furthermore, for one who possesses such a sudden upheaval—loss of wealth, as well as agitation and an increase in disease, arise. (7-190)
The destruction of a friend's house and a loss of splendor occur;
as Kaṇa said: "When one of the two right nostrils is active during the southern solstice... (7.191).

Indeed, that Kāṇa-yoga occurs through the flow of the eight transits (saṃkrānti). It occurs during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) by the flow through the left nostril, and during the northern solstice (vajīta) by the flow through the middle [channel], which is devoid of those two. Thus he declares.

The phrase "thirty [breaths] are the arising of the destruction of life" (7-202) will describe the nature of the *saṃkrānti* in the context of the *mṛtyuyoga*; he indicates that this should also be connected here, because since there is no occurrence [of it] during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), its exclusion would be untenable. And therefore:
By closing the left eye while the right remains open, one is like a one-eyed man; thus he is "one-eyed."
And for this reason:
fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, eye disease, and jaundice. (7.192)

Painful piercing (śūla), eruptive boils (visphoṭikā), suffering, and chest ailments (urodoṣa) occur; as do fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara) and anal diseases, dysentery accompanied by colic (anugrantha-saśūla-atīsāra), eye disease, and the affliction of cataracts (timira). Eruptive boils are pustules; chest ailments include chest wounds and the like.
Having spoken of the left eye, he speaks of the right eye:
"By means of the left nostril alone, one performs thirteen transits. (7.193)
If the vital breath were to flow [only] there, then this [eye] would also be one-eyed due to the closing of the right vehicle. || 193 ||
Therefore— fever, headache, pain, hemorrhoids, stiffness, dysuria, urinary disorders, and anemia arise. (7.194)
Prameha is the discharge of white and other [colored] urine. || 194 ||
Thus, O lady of excellent vows, the *prāṇa* residing in the *iḍā* provokes disease by means of phlegm (*śleṣman*);
"disease" here refers to everything from fever up to anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).

He determines the time of onset for this arisen disease: "On whichever day of the movement [of the breath] it is diagnosed, on that same day in the following [period], [the disease will arise]. (7-195)

One is afflicted by all diseases— whether on the left, on the right, or on both sides alternately. If, at the time of riding [the horse], a "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*) configuration is seen on the left or its opposite, the right, or elsewhere on the face, then on the following day at that very same time, one will suffer from the aforementioned diseases.
The meaning is that it is afflicted. || 195 ||

Having thus determined the two [types of] *utpātaka* and *kāṇa*, and without yet explaining the yoga of death (*mṛtyuyoga*), he describes—in connection with the topic—the touching of the parts of the nostrils, which indicates auspiciousness and so forth:
"Now, another cognition of touch [occurs] below the nose, and likewise above. (7-196)
The word "I shall speak" is the ellipsis. || 196 ||

In that regard—[the phrase] "and by the upward [breath]" means that the aforementioned defects of disease (*rug-doṣa*) would occur; this is the ellipsis. "By the upward" means by the *prāṇa* that flows upward. "Upward" means...
Of the nose; and here, that which is situated on the north is connected with the south.
Having spoken above, he speaks below: "When one carries [the breath] to the right, it overcomes verbal abuse. (7.197)
In the reading "one should touch with the right hand," it should be explained as forming a single syntactical unit together with the preceding [passage].
Furthermore:
"In the middle, touching the middle chamber, one attains the state of overcoming others.
Regarding "in the middle": this means excluding contact with all the sides; "the middle chamber" refers to the central beam (*vaṃśa*), and "touching it" means making contact with that.
and ||
Furthermore:
when that single [channel] flows by transferring in many ways here and there, || 7.198 ||
Then there will be worship, great honor, and gain for him.
When nine hundred breaths have passed during the transit (saṃkrānti),
if the vital breath (prāṇa) should flow repeatedly back and forth through the left and right channels in alternation, then there is worship and so forth.

It occurs. As for the fact that someone, having read "tadā" in place of "yadā," has connected the half-verse with the preceding result of overcoming others, and the half-verse beginning with "pūjanam bahu" with the following verse—that should be disregarded because it lacks substance. || 198 ||
Furthermore:
When the swan of the vital breath flows slowly through the Suṣumnā, || 7-199 ||
"There shall be gain of land, dharma, sovereignty, and the arrival of beloved ones here"—
this [verse] must be explained as referring to when [the breath] flows spontaneously through the *suṣumnā*, that is, the central path; it is not, however,
as the author of the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* has explained it, namely, "in the middle of the nostrils."
Having thus spoken incidentally, he says the following in order to determine the remaining yoga of death:
"One should carry exactly twelve transits on one side of the equinox. (7.200)
Then, one should predict death in exactly one year;
when each transit (saṃkrānti) shortens by one, then one month shall be shortened accordingly.

Regarding the term *viṣuvate*, since the usage "from the heights to the depths" (*udvato nivataḥ*) is observed, and because the word ending in the suffix *-arha* is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the third case is employed. Thus,
if there are twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*) due to the simultaneous presence [of the sun] in the left and right [sides].

By means of the calculation of a single transit (*saṃkrānti*), which consists of thirty breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) as will be explained immediately hereafter, one should exclude the nine hundred natural flows consisting of three hundred and sixty movements; if then [the breath] should flow in a single mass (*ekataḥ*) as one continuous unit, that indicates death within a month. Each [transit]...
If the transition [of the breath] should decrease, then when one carries the transitions of eleven, ten, and so forth,
death occurs after that many months; provided that, upon exceeding the flow of the natural nine-hundred equinoxes,
one carries a single transition consisting of thirty movements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then [death occurs] in one month.

Death is certain. Previously, that which was stated as the measure of the transit— “The *haṃsa* always carries nine hundred [breaths] for each and every one” (7.170)— that very same [measure] applies to the transits of *utpāṭa*, *kāṇa*, and *yoga*.
This has been determined on the basis of the statement: "It is like the southern solstice" (7.191). || 201 ||
But in the case of the *mṛtyuyoga*, it is otherwise; thus he says:
"O Varārohā, a single transit (*saṃkrānti*) is the arising of the destruction of thirty breaths (*prāṇa*).
This is because the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* has been stated to constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*), and here [the transit] occurs by means of thirty such units.
The transition is to be understood; this is the meaning.
If, in this manner, there is only this single transference after setting aside the natural equinoctial flow, then instead of that: "It should flow externally day by day for thirty days. (7.202)
Then—
at the end of that month, O fair-faced one, death shall occur instantly.
Thus it is:
O lady of excellent complexion, the yoga of death has been fully explained by me to you.
Regarding this as well, it is said that one should perform the calculation of time— beginning from the time of examination— as previously described to indicate inauspicious signs:
"When one practices for a year, a month, likewise a fortnight, a lunar day, or a specific hour..."
From whatever time one begins, from that very same time one should assign it.

The meaning is that from whatever time one begins to practice, and from whatever time one starts to investigate, beginning from that very time, one should gradually announce to oneself or to another the duration of years, months, and so forth, as indicators of death and the like. || 204 ||
Such is this very [movement], which indicates various kinds of auspicious and inauspicious events—the wise know the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the channels of *iḍā* and *suṣumnā*.
The meaning is that only yogins who are truly attentive shall know it, and no others. [Regarding] *iḍā* and *suṣumnā*:
They perceive both Piṅgalā and the equinox.
He concludes: "Thus has this auspicious [teaching] been told to you regarding the time born of the sun's southern course. (7.205)
The time arising from the southern course is the flow through the left nostril;
this too is intended as a mere illustration, just as before. || 205 ||
He introduces the purpose for which all this has been said:
"Thus, having understood the death and the inauspicious [omens] that arise from the body in time, the yogi shall conquer death and all inauspicious things without exception. (7.206)
Of oneself or of another. || 206 ||
To the question "How? he says:

having meditated upon Kāleśasvacchanda, or the Haṃsa who is the Lord of all (sakaleśvara)—the Lord of all time, which possesses distinctions such as gross and subtle, and consists of external, internal, and other forms.

Having meditated upon the illustrious Svacchanda— the swan that manifests according to one's inclination, whose nature as the supreme partless (niṣkala) has been explained, and who is the Lord of the entire universe— and having made him manifest through the method of penetration, the yogi shall conquer death; such is the connection with what precedes.
"Where situated and of what nature is he who is to be meditated upon? To this he says:
"Situated in the path of the nostril-aperture, he creates and withdraws the world. (7.207)
Established in the Tantra, one who abides within all beings should contemplate everything:
"That which is called *Nāda*, the supreme seed-syllable, resides within all beings in the form of both the immobile and the mobile" (Kālacakratantra 1.5).
Thus, abiding according to the state described in other Tantras, the *nāsikā*— so called because it "does not move" (*na sate*) but proceeds with a certain crookedness (*kauṭilyena*)—
is the central power (*madhyaśakti*). Abiding in the path of its aperture, the *sauṣumna* abode,
and having resorted to the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the aforementioned process of descent, [it resides] in the nose within the paths of the apertures.

And abiding within the cavities of the eyes and other sense organs, he creates and withdraws the world of external and internal forms through the process of opening and closing the eyes; for, remaining there,
he can conceive everything situated within and cast it outside, and cast what has appeared outside back within.
And yet, one should "kalay" (conceive)— that is, count, establish through variety, know, and reflect upon it—
since the root *kal* has the meanings of casting, numbering, moving, and sound.
Having meditated upon such Svacchandanaatha, the Lord of Time, as residing therein, one shall conquer death—
[him] who stands pervading all the apertures starting from the central channel.

Having meditated upon— that is, having recognized as one's own essential nature— that which consists of the reflective awareness of the consciousness of others and is untouched by time, and remaining established through its support, one certainly conquers death.
For:
"The Lord [acts] upon that which is not situated in time. (7.208)

If one should abide at the wrong time within the Supreme Lord, who transcends time, as non-different from Him, the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, would not perceive him [as such], because of the obstruction of His own creative activity within Himself. || 208 ||
And if the lord of yogis remains constantly attentive to this very state, then for him who is engaged in meditation, omniscience arises after six months.
The knower of yoga, joined with time, perceives the three periods of time. (7.209)
Through the stimulation of the continuum of consciousness by the savor of immersion into the nature of one's own supreme will, after six months,

one knows everything from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to Śiva; however, when one becomes attentive and engaged in the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra) at a time permeated by that very savor of immersion, then [one knows] the past, present, and future.
The best of yogis knows everything. || 209 ||
Moreover,
O Maheśvarī, by reciting or even meditating upon the Kālahaṃsa mantra,
one indeed becomes the very form of Time; autonomous, he moves like Time itself.
Having slain death and abandoned old age, freed from all diseases and all fears,
that very *haṃsa*— the supreme, partless Lord whose nature was previously determined—
is here called *Kālahaṃsa*, as he fashions the universe by means of the determined qualities of relinquishment and acquisition.
Reciting that [mantra] or meditating upon it,

one proceeds by means of contemplating the pervasive extension taught in the *Pañcapraṇavādhikārayojanikā* (the treatise on the application of the five praṇavas), with the aim of repeatedly resting within that [reality].
By reciting and repeating the mantra of the venerable Lord Catuṣkala, he should perform his *japa*;

for he whose form is time—possessing the auspicious nature of time which consists of the manifestation of the entire universe—is indeed that venerable Lord Svacchanda himself. And in that very manner, he should always conduct himself.
He should proceed by performing the fivefold activity; he is abandoned by that fear which is produced by the causes of disease.
Furthermore, his—[his] consciousness [is such that] hearing is from afar, as is reflection and vision. (7.211)
Through the conquest of time, there shall always be the attainment of all sovereign qualities.
The word "from afar" (dūrāt) is to be applied everywhere. Vijñāna is the function of the intellect (buddhi); manana is the activity of the mind (manas);
and avalokana is that of the eye. And this—

This is intended as a characterization of the activity of all internal and external organs. Thus, when there is the pervasive realization of one's own nature as the *haṃsa*— which is the essence of Svacchandabhairava, transcending space and time and pervading all apertures— there follows the crossing over the ground of the body, senses, and so forth.

It has been stated that, because of the non-manifestation [of the world] through the savor of the supreme reality (paratattva), the absence of old age, death, disease, objects of knowledge, lack of sovereignty, and so forth, is established as a matter of course.
Now, regarding the meditation on the *haṃsa* in the successive flows of the right, left, and middle channels, he teaches the conquest of death appropriate thereto:
"Having meditated upon it in the right nostril, one shall attain the sovereignty of Brahmā. (7.212)
Therefore, he knows that lifespan, its corresponding vigor, and the past;
thus, he becomes a knower of the future and possesses strength equal to Viṣṇu on the left [side]. (7.213)
Equal to that is his sovereignty; he becomes a king of yogins with such a lifespan.
From the midst of it, he knows all—past, present, and future. (7.214)
By means of constant yoga of meditation, one shall attain equality with Rudra;
in lifespan, strength, vigor, form, and sovereignty, one becomes his equal.
Through the supreme state of Brahmā, one shall attain the station of Īśvara;
through the supreme state of Viṣṇu, one shall obtain the sovereignty of Sadāśiva. (7.216)
By meditating upon that which is the supreme state of Rudra, one becomes Śiva.
Here—
Brahmā and Īśvara are situated on the right, while Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva are on the left.
"In the middle, Rudra and Śiva are proclaimed... (7.151).
Thus, it was previously stated that the abiding of the six causes within the three channels (*nāḍī*) occurs through the distinction between the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*).
Therefore, if one [perceives] the *haṃsa*—which takes the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—within the right and left channels by means of the non-supreme [state]...

Meditating with pervasiveness, he reflects; then, he becomes endowed with their power, vigor, and sovereignty. He knows the universe throughout the three times—past, future, and present. And herein, having meditated upon Brahmā and the others in this manner of pervasion as being the forms of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva, [he attains this state].
It acquires that very nature.
He concludes: "Thus, the conquest of death is proclaimed...
Now—"
...victory belongs to one who meditates on the deceased. || 7-217 ||
The word "from death alone" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 217 ||
He asks "How? and replies:
"Having meditated upon the sixteen-petaled heart-lotus, white, fully blossomed, endowed with the sixteen digits, situated within the hollows of the petals divided by the channels (nāḍīs). (7.218)
One should contemplate oneself in the center of that [lotus], as pure as clear crystal, with limbs complete and having a form shaped like a pericarp, resembling the full moon. (7.219)
Above, in the great ocean of the nectar of Śakti, is a second lotus filled with the nectar of waves situated within the ocean of milk and ambrosia.
And that downward-facing lotus has a full moon as its pericarp;
in its center, one should contemplate a swan, with a drop at its crest facing downwards.
One should contemplate divine nectar raining down from all sides; one should contemplate that [nectar] having entered through the aperture at the top of one's own body. (7.222)
One should contemplate oneself being flooded and filled by that white, abundant, and thick nectar which destroys death. (7.223)
One should constantly contemplate the entire body as being filled with nectar through the openings of the channels connected by lotus stalks. (7.224)
Thus, one whose self is ever-disciplined becomes equal to Amṛteśa;
having abandoned diseases, death, and old age, he sports with the powers such as aṇimā.
Thus, from that meditation on nectar (amṛta-dhyāna), victory over time and death occurs.
[The syllable] beginning with 'A', which is situated above and below the heart-lotus and is denoted by the deities such as Śrīpūrvā and others who are associated with nectar and so forth—
It resides in the center of a white lotus that has blossomed with as many petals as there are sixteen phonemes;
it is fixed upon the full moon-disk within the pericarp of the lower lotus,
and [it consists of] a downward-facing white dot of four *kalās* situated in the center of the full moon within the pericarp of the upper lotus.

Having meditated upon oneself as having the luster of crystal, situated in the midst of a mass of nectar, and flooded by the surging waves emanating from the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) which is filled with a stream of nectar flowing forth from that light; [one should contemplate] that nectar [descending] through the openings of the various channels located at the base of the white lotus-stalk below it.

The summary meaning is this: he who constantly meditates for six months upon that which rises up and pervades the entire body becomes free from disease, old age, and death; attaining the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, he becomes equal to Amṛteśabhairava. Those [channels] which are differentiated by their tubular form manifest in various shapes.

"Through the holes of the stalk"—meaning those situated below in the lotus—refers to that which is located there; "connected by them" means joined with those situated at the place of the knots. Here, the "stalk" (nāla) takes the form of the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī). "Milk" refers to the nectar (amṛta) produced from the Ocean of Milk and so forth; thus, the connection is that it is an ocean consisting of that [nectar]. [The word] "amṛta" [means] nectar.
And here, the essence is the bliss of the supreme power (paraśakti).

Having thus explained the conquest of death through the meditation on the *haṃsa* and the meditation on the nectar, which are based upon the three paths of all the channels, he begins to teach the ultimate reality, the essence of the unsurpassed:
"Alternatively, one who abides in the supreme reality is not afflicted by any times. (226)
By the word "or" (*athavā*), this is what is implied:

this method for conquering death—which is entirely distinct from other methods such as maintaining the stability of the body for a limited period of time—is exceedingly rare and reaches the very heart of the great lords of yogins; it is that method wherein [the practitioner] remains within the body itself.
A certain person who is in their final birth enters the state of the illustrious Svacchandabhairava at all times. || 226 ||
Regarding that, he speaks in order to point out what the supreme reality (tattva) is like and how one becomes absorbed in it:
"One should contemplate the supreme reality, which is free from the movement of time, liberated from the stain of the kalās, partless, and the highest state. (7.227)

One should contemplate—that is, reflect—upon the supreme reality as non-different from oneself; it is the essence of the mass of consciousness and bliss, manifesting at the heart and the *dvādaśānta*, devoid of the movement of time both externally and internally, and empty of the stain of parts (*kalā*) and the impurity of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); for this very reason:
Because it lacks the association with the kalās such as *a* and the others—unlike that which possesses four kalās—it is partless (*niṣkala*), the supreme state, the unsurpassed abode. || 227 ||
Not only is it the supreme light, but even so:
"The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is indeed partless (niṣkala)...
the reality of the Self is above *samanā*, the Pure Self; 'partless' means having abandoned all conceptualization of distinctions ending with *samanā*."
For it is said:
"The body is called *kalaṅka*;
it is joined with the six causes and endowed with all the principles (*tattva*). (7.228)

The phoneme (varṇa), the point (bindu), as well as the sound (nāda) conjoined with the pervasive power (vyāpinīśakti), extending up to the limit of the level of the Equal One (samanā), is called the support of the digit (kalaṅkādhāra). (7.229)

This is what is meant: just as this gross body, consisting of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, is a stain, so too is this [body] a stain within the Self by way of the supreme pervasion (*paravyāpti*), being of the nature of the causal *aparabhairava*. Just as the body, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth are stains for him from the perspective of the gross view, so they are from the perspective of the supreme view.
The entire series of objects of knowledge (*prameyamālā*) ending with *samanā* is indeed a stain (*kalaṅka*). The phonemes are *a*, *u*, and *m*.

The compound is to be understood as "that which has the nature of a stain and is the substratum. Its status as a stain consists in the fact that it does not manifest the non-difference of all this from Paraśiva. || 229 ||
And he for whom this is the substratum is the supreme Self to be supported—
the one previously described by the proponents of duality as the ground of liberation, consisting solely of pure consciousness.
Now, that which is beyond even that is remembered as Unmanā; at the end of this is the supreme reality, which is free from both the manifest and the unmanifest. (7.230)
It is all-pervasive, auspicious on all sides, within everything, and facing in every direction;
it abides in the reality of the five pentads and is endowed with eighteen qualities.

The *sakala* (with parts) extends up to the level of *samanā*, while the *akala* (without parts) is the pure self (*śuddhātmā*). That which is devoid of these two is [the Supreme], because those two are contracted through mutual limitation; it is all-pervasive, uncontracted by space and time, auspicious in every respect, a mass of consciousness and bliss, and the innermost core of everything.

It exists as the very life-force, situated within the beginning, the end, and the middle. It is, in every respect and in every way, like a face—a face that serves as the means for the recognition of one's own Self. Furthermore, it will itself explain the five groups of five principles (*tattvas*) as well as the eighteen qualities (*guṇas*).

It abides within the five pentads and within the principles (tattvas), possessing a form non-different from them, and is likewise associated with the qualities (guṇas) by way of being pervasively present within them. || 231 ||
This is how it is: if one knows that which is supreme within this [body], then one would be liberated from bondage;
for it was introduced [in the previous verse] with the words, "The stain is said to be the body" (7.228). In this [context]:
If one, while remaining within the body, vital breath, and so forth, knows the supreme reality in the manner described,
then one is indeed liberated from bondage; the meaning is that even while living, one enters into the state of Supreme Bhairava through one's own direct experience.
Now he shows the group of five fives: "The causes, the mantras, as well as the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti. (7.232)

The Bindu, the Half-moon, the Obstructer (Nirodhī), the Sound (Nāda) ascending upwards, the Power (Śakti), the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), the Self of the Equal (Samanā), and likewise the Transmental (Unmanā). (7.233)
O fair-faced one, this which has been told to you is indeed the "five-fives" (pañcapañcaka).
The causes are six, beginning with Brahmā. As for the "mantras," these are the three—A, U, and M—which denote Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

Because the Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti— which denote Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva— are mentioned among the ten objects of knowledge beginning with Bindu and ending with Unmanā that are common to all mantras; therefore,
by the word "mantra," only the three uncommon [principles] remaining after the common ten objects of knowledge are intended.

These have been stated. Likewise, there is the group of eleven mantras consisting of the faces and limbs; these ten, along with the five levels (kalās) beginning with Nivṛtti which are presided over by the causal deities starting with Brahmā and were previously explained, and the category of reality (tattva) consisting of the ten objects of knowledge beginning with Bindu—this constitutes the five pentads.
He states the principles (tattvas): "The principles themselves are indeed thirty-six...
The thirty-six [principles], beginning with earth, have already been mentioned previously. In all these cases...
The connection with the preceding [phrase] is that the supreme reality exists as non-differentiation.
Now, furthermore, learn from me also the qualities [of these]. || 7-234 ||

The *guṇas* are the powers (*śaktis*), which are the attributes of Supreme Bhairava abiding in the state of the subject who has assumed *māyā*, existing in accordance with the propriety of the intermediate (*parāpara*) state. (234)
He said to them:
"Ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (dhī), mind (manas), and likewise the objects of the senses;
grasping (grahaṇa), contact (sparśa), the substratum (ādhāra), and power (śakti) is remembered as the eighth. (7.235)
And these eight qualities are as follows:

the three internal organs; the fourth category being the group of objects together with their corresponding sense organs; "grasping" (grahaṇa) is the cognition of those objects; "contact" (sparśa) is the perception of internal pleasure and so forth; and the "substratum" (ādhāra) is the body.

Power (*śakti*), which consists of knowledge and action, as well as effort (*prayatna*), are the eight powers that are the attributes of the Self, whose nature is not other [than these]. For whatever appears—whether it be an object, the body, or anything else—that is non-different from consciousness, whose nature is luminosity; otherwise, its manifestation would be impossible. This is his [the author's] view.
Everything is indeed of the nature of Dharma.
Of this very [reality] that has entered into supreme pervasion (paravyāpti)—
the eight Bhairavas constitute the Bhairavāṣṭaka.
Those eight Bhairavas previously mentioned, beginning with Kapālīśa, are essentially identical with it through supreme pervasion.
The meaning is that there is an octad of qualities belonging to Bhairava.
Furthermore, its [attributes]—
the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *haṃsa*, as well as the power (*śakti*)—
are the qualities that arise sequentially from the non-supreme and supreme states, just as it is with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

Thus, by virtue of its own autonomy, [the Self] assumes a state of being an individual soul (ātmabhūmika), and likewise, its power (śakti)— which is essentially its own autonomy— shining forth in a contracted form is what has been described as "vital breath" (prāṇa).
Thus, in this manner—these eighteen qualities [are as follows]. (7.236)
And therefore:
"In these [practices], that supreme reality exists apart from utterance (uccāra) and support (ālambana).
Utterance is the sounding of mantras preceded by the binding of the organs (karaṇabandha) and so forth; support is..."
The reliance upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth; the implication is that, without those, [the reality] remains undifferentiated within all these various distinctions.
This is because even those things considered to be means (*upāya*) are manifested as one with the wall of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidbhitti*).
As it has been said by our venerable masters:
"The web of skillful means does not reveal the auspicious [reality]; for what could a jar illuminate the thousand-rayed sun?
Reflecting thus, he of noble vision—
"One should enter Śiva, who is self-luminous, in an instant. (Tantrāloka-sāra, Chapter 2).
He specifies that very [reality]:
"The supreme reality is beyond syllables, being devoid of both the imperishable and the perishable. (7.237)

The meaning is that it is liberated from the impure syllable, from the individual self (jīvātman) as its form, and from all beings that flow away on every side; or alternatively, it is liberated from the syllables that are signifiers and from the [phonetic] letters.

The meaning is that it is devoid of those forms associated with [the phonemes] to be expressed— namely, the portions of mantras that express *a*, *ā*, *u*, and so forth— and thus it does not possess the nature of what is expressed by them.
And this is logical, because:
"How can there be liberation in syllables? How can there be a flower in the sky?
This is absolutely impossible, since [liberation] is to be articulated through places of articulation and efforts, and thus remains associated with limiting conditions (*sopādhi*)."
When the syllables, which constitute the components of the mantra, are being uttered,

liberation occurs as the immersion into the reality of the unconditioned mass of consciousness (*nirupādhicidghanatattva*), because the supreme reality lacks the nature of being either the phonemes or their denotable objects. And this has been stated previously:

"His form and body do not exist, nor do his color or action" (6.12). Furthermore, if many liberated selves distinct from one another were admitted among the imperishable ones, how could there be liberation?
Because it has been stated [in the verse], "They are worshippers of the Self" (4.392).
For this very reason:
"As long as it is uttered by speech, and as long as it remains even in writing... (7.238).
To that extent, it should be known as "with parts" (sakala); when free from parts (niṣkala), it is devoid of differentiation.

Even while being uttered by the speech-sounds culminating in Paśyantī, the mantra becomes "with parts" due to its connection with the various kalās such as the letter 'A' and so forth; likewise, even in the process of meditating on the phonemes, although it performs functions such as nourishment and the like, [it remains essentially partless].

Even through the union with the phonemic energies known as Ambā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Vāmā, one remains *sakala* (with parts). However, that which consists of the self-luminous, unstruck (*anāhata*) supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*), due to the complete subsidence of all differentiation, is *niṣkala* (without parts).
This has been determined in detail at the beginning of the section on the five *praṇavas* and elsewhere. And it is said:
In the *Śrī-Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
"Supremacy does not arise through a distinction of phonemes or a distinction of bodies;
it exists as being partless (*niṣkala*), and it would not exist in a state of having parts (*sakala*). (Verse 6)
Thus.
Therefore, this [Self] is—freed from creation and dissolution, and devoid of action and time. (7.239)
This [mantra] is not created or withdrawn like other mantras, nor does it have a time for activities such as recitation or meditation. Thus it has been said:
"There is no one whatsoever who recites it" (7.59).
And so forth. || 239 ||
This clarifies the following:
"In the downward movement there is emanation; in the upward [movement], withdrawal is said to occur.
Born by means of the downward movement, one indeed becomes dead by the upward [movement]. (7.240)
Having abandoned both birth (sūtaka) and death (mṛtaka), one should indeed abide according to the conduct of reality (tattva).

The downward-moving is the apāna; the upward-moving is the prāṇa. This pertains to the threefold embodied subject characterized by emanation and withdrawal. "This one" refers to the embodied subject. Thus, repeatedly...
It consists of the impurities of birth and death. However, when one pacifies the conceit of being a limited embodied subject and takes recourse in the true state of being the conscious subject,

then— even while abiding within the body, vital breaths, and other such factors that are like petals— this person remains established in the reality of the essential nature, beautiful with the fragrance of consciousness.
The phrase "thus" implies that there is no possibility even of the impurity of death or birth; this is how it should be explained.

It does not mean, however, that one must remain constantly in the state of the cessation of inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*), because for yogis, since the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) is possible, remaining constantly in that [cessation] is impossible.

For this would result in a contradiction with the text already stated— “In these [states], that supreme reality exists apart from the support of vocalization” (7.237)— and with the text yet to be spoken. Furthermore,
if the observation of the state where the expansion of the vital breath is stilled were the means for experiencing the operation of reality at the outset, [it would follow that...].

Nevertheless, preceded by the means thereto, the constant knowledge— across all states and everywhere— that one is composed of the supreme state of Śiva, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss, is itself the state of abiding in the true nature of reality.
As he will say:
"One should remember everything as consisting of Śiva," and so forth. (7.244)
Thus, this true state (tattvavṛtti), which is free from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of all the paths (adhvan), has been explained. || 7-241 ||
Because even the sixfold path is fully known through its ultimate reality as consciousness,
it lacks the nature of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), due to the absence of any distinction [between them]. This has been specifically declared in various scriptures.

This is because it is designated by such terms as "beyond conduct" (*nirācāra*), "shaken off" (*avadhūta*), "transcending boundaries" (*nirmaryāda*), "the throbbing of great being" (*sphurattā-mahāsattā*), "attainment" (*samāpatti*), and "immersion" (*samāveśa*). || 241 ||
And therefore:

"The yogi, liberated from the dharmas of the path of the principles (tattva) and free from the causal deities, abides in the state of the reality of the principles, having abandoned all undertakings. (7.242)
Freed from passion and hatred, and having overcome both dejection and joy, one should never desire sense objects nor ever disparage them. (7-243)
He should be equal toward enemy and friend, and equal toward a Brahmin and a dog-cooker; he should always maintain an even vision and remember everything as being composed of Śiva.
The meaning is that his sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) is not delimited by the body or by the principles (tattva) and so forth residing within it. For this very reason,

because he has attained identity with consciousness (cit), he is free from all undertakings— activities concerning objects to be rejected or accepted— which consist essentially in specific forms of attachment.

Because he is free from the defects of attachment and aversion, which are the causes for its [the mind's] engagement; his freedom from these is due to his absence of both dejection and joy produced by attachment to sense objects. For this very reason, he lacks desire and so forth, because he merely passes the time by experiencing whatever comes to him. Not his...
Regarding enemies, friends, Brahmins, and outcastes, as well as those who cause harm and those who offer service, his mind perceives them with purity and so forth through their essential equality;
he sees everything solely as such, yet while situated in the world, he does not cause the disruption of the world's order. However, his primary form is that which perceives everything as Śiva.
One should reflect on this, as it is said in the Śrīvijñānabhairava:
"O Dear One, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—therein lies the state of Śiva; because of its all-pervasiveness, where could it go? (116)
Thus:
"One should indeed contemplate the entire body, or the world, as consisting of consciousness. || 244 ||

It has been stated that one should remember everything as consisting of Śiva. In that regard, although the Self is included within all things, he says [the following] so that the error of a dualist perspective— that this Self is distinct from the beginningless Śiva— may not arise:
And one should always remember oneself in that very same way;
"in that very same way" and "in this manner" means through identity with Paramaśiva, who is the self of the universe.
And therefore:
"All the principles (tattvas), the elements (bhūtas), the phonemes (varṇas), and those which are remembered as mantras," || 7-245 ||
By means of this contemplation on Śiva, they indeed become eternally subject to his will;
for he perceives all things as non-different from his own self through their identity with Śiva, including the fourteen elements and the phonemes residing within the body of the mass of sounds.
Precisely because he is established in such conduct according to reality, O lady of noble vows, he performs neither merit nor sin. (7.246)
He does not perform any action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, preceded by conscious intent. || 246 ||

Since he is one who has accomplished his task (kṛtakṛtya) and whose self is serene— meaning one for whom the "task" (kṛtya), consisting of the attainment of identity with the Supreme Lord’s own Self, has been performed and perfected.
He is serene and unstained by the blemish of impurity.
"And for him, no task exists. Here, the particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only/just) and is displaced in its order. Since no task whatsoever exists for him, how [could there be one]?
One may perform either merit or evil.
He says that even while living, he is liberated: "In this world and in the next, he is indeed always completely fulfilled. (7.247)
The word "here" (iha) means in the state intended for emergence from meditative absorption.
If one does not intentionally practice virtue and so forth, is that which is accompanied by negligence—such as helping others and the like—an obstacle for him? No, he says:
"He is liberated from both dharma and adharma..."
Because an action lacks the quality of being binding in the absence of intention (*abhisandhi*).
He states that even the merit and so forth acquired prior to the body do not act as an obscuration for him:
"He is free from merit and demerit.
The meaning is that these two have been reduced to ashes by the fire of the aforementioned knowledge.
Therefore, for such a yogin who is a mass of knowledge—there is indeed neither edible nor inedible, and likewise neither drinkable nor undrinkable. (7.248)
For him there is nothing impure, nor indeed anything pure, O lady of good vows;
for he is eternally independent, having abandoned all dependence.
Because everything is perceived as one with Śiva. As it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*: "That purity which is taught by those of limited knowledge is impurity in the vision of Śambhu;
for there is neither pure nor impure—therefore, one should always be free from conceptual construction. (123)
In the Śrīmaducchuṣmabhairava it is also said:
"O Dear One, as long as these [perceptions] are not knowers, how could they be objects of knowledge?
Since the knower and the known are one, there is no such thing as impurity."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 249 ||
And for one such as this—there is no sacred field (*kṣetra*) for him, no place of pilgrimage (*tīrtha*), nor even any observance (*niyama*) or restraint (*yama*).
Observance refers to the adoption of matted hair, ashes, and so forth; for one whose nature is the expansive manifestation of Supreme Bhairava, there is nothing whatsoever [that must be observed].
The meaning is "contraction. This has been stated in the eighteenth chapter of the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, which elucidates the secret [teachings]:
"In this, there is neither purity nor impurity" (18.74).
By such a lengthy passage as this.
He describes the supramundane field and so forth belonging to such a yogin:
"His field is the supreme power (parā śakti), from which everything is produced. (7.250)
O Goddess, since all the paths proceed while remaining established therein, it is indeed the supreme, peaceful sacred site (tīrtha), eternal, and pervading the bliss of the universe. (7.251)
That by which this entire universe is pervaded through its infinite powers, and through which there is constant detachment from worldly existence—this is proclaimed as Yama. (7.252)
"Discipline (niyama) is constant meditation, being single-mindedly intent upon the supreme reality.
That is called the 'field' (kṣetra) wherein, situated in the midst of the circle of deities,
one attains whatever is desired..."

Therefore, for this supreme yogin, the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) alone— situated within the wheel of the deities of the path which consists of supreme non-duality— is the field (*kṣetra*), the ground of the birth of all things, and the sacred site (*tīrtha*) that effects the destruction of all impurities.
And that [field] of his is the supreme, tranquil state, pervading the universe, consisting of the essence of bliss, and free from the waves of the agitation of duality.

The state of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat), which is filled with all powers without exception, consists of total absorption in the Supreme Reality (Paratattva) and is composed of the reflective awareness of non-duality with It; this is His observance (niyama) and His vow (vrata).
And this yogi should not contemplate his own birth, nor his lineage, nor his kinsmen. (7.253)
For the connection with the stains of birth and so forth belongs to the body-self, not to the consciousness-self. || 253 ||
And even though he is such—
*he should practice the state of all castes*;
that is, he should practice the condition (*bhāva*) of all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, according to what is appropriate for each.
Either his true nature or his conduct alone would praise that very thing.
And he says that one should not adopt the restrictions of caste and stage of life regarding the Self: "Nor should one abide within the castes;
rather—"
One should always conduct oneself according to the nature of others and through the qualities of others. || 7-254 ||
The meaning is that it should proceed. || 254 ||
He shows that very same mode of activity belonging to another by means of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with this [subject]:
"Omniscient and completely satisfied, he is perfect by his very nature;
independent, with unimpaired power, and resting in that which is without beginning or end. (7.255)
For primordial awakening is indeed incomparable, free from the divisions of time and duration;
it is liberated from movement and exhalation, and devoid of day and night. (7.256)

He is fully perfected and possesses infinite power. These six qualities, beginning with omniscience, have already been explained by us in the *Yojanikā* treatise. He is "incomparable" (*atula*) because he manifests as one with Śiva, owing to the absence of a second. He is "free from the divisions of time and occasion" (*kālavelāvivajīta*), unlike those of limited yoga.
Because there is no utility in observing the portions and sub-portions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for this very reason,
even that "utterance" (*uccāra*) consisting of the upward impelling of the flow of the vital breath is useless for him.
And therefore, because he is constantly permeated by the contemplation of identity with Śiva alone, for him—
Just as for one desiring liberation and one desiring enjoyment, there is some application [of the self] throughout day and night.
Nor even does he possess any differentiation of that; thus he says:
"One should not keep watch by day, nor should one sleep at night at any time.
One should abide in one's own nature alone, transcending day and night. (7.257)

Just as an ordinary person, wandering about during the day, habitually pursues only the conventional practice of differentiation, and at night sleeps within illusion without attaining awakening, so it is not with this [Yogin]; rather, being established in non-duality, he is not overcome by illusion. For him, there is neither waking nor dreaming, whether he is awake or even while sleeping.
They exist, because they are never separated from the light of the fourth state (*turīya*). As it has been said:
"The perception of that [light] is constant, never deviating from the three states; it is eternally present for one who is perfectly awakened. (1.17)

Thus, in the *Śrī Spanda*: "The perception belonging to that supreme reality is the light consisting of that [reality] for the well-awakened one. This occurs "constantly" and so forth—in the middle and at the end—within the three states beginning with waking.
It exists eternally, without interruption. I myself have explained this in such a manner in the *Spandanirṇaya*.
The yogi who indeed conducts himself in this manner— he [is...]— he is...
...he shall attain equality with the Supreme;
and Time shall not reckon him, even in hundreds of millions of eons. (7.258)
Because it is of the singular nature of the Supreme Lord, who is not limited by time. || 258 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"He who always maintains this contemplation is liberated even while living;
for Śiva is constantly contemplated..."
And therefore, [one should worship] him—... [so that] Time shall not seize Śiva. (7.259)
How could Time overcome Śiva, who is of the singular nature of auspiciousness and the Great Yogin? || 259 ||

Now, he demonstrates that this knowledge of the Great Pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) is the very essence of the teachings of all the Upaniṣads, by first showing the qualifying epithets of the deities to be worshipped in this Tantra:
"The Yogin, through the yoga of his own will, moving with a gait of his own will..."
Engaged in the state of Svacchanda, he shall attain equality with Svacchanda. || 7-260 ||

He who necessarily moves with autonomous movement, established in his own self through the state of abiding in the function of the principles (tattvas) as they have been taught— this Great Yoga (mahāyoga), which is denoted by the word *Svacchanda* because it consists of the realization of identity with the Supreme Reality— is joined to, that is, intent upon, the station, the abode, of the venerable Svacchandabhairava.
He attains equality with that. || 260 ||
But through the excellence of yoga—
being truly independent, he moves about independently at all times;
for he remains as the radiant Śrī Svacchandabhairava himself, manifest throughout the beginning, middle, and end.
...up to ...
The practitioner becomes clearly visible through mastery over the movement of the channels;
or else, he becomes so by means of recitation (japa) when it is exceedingly augmented.
"The practitioner of mantra knows the yoga; having known it, he shall attain omniscience" (7.143–144).

Regarding that which was thus introduced, [the text] discusses in its midst the description of the flow through the three channels, the knowledge of ill omens arising from their abnormal flow, the conquest of death, and so forth.
Thus, an immeasurable interval has occurred. Therefore, concluding this, he reiterates what was previously stated:
"In this way, indeed, these are the signs of death, as well as other portents (riṣṭas). (7.261)
Through yoga, the lord of yogis knows those [states] contained within the *nāda*;
having mastered these by means of yoga according to the sequence thus described. (7.262)

The word "thus" (*evam*) refers to those [signs] which are of a nature contrary to what has been stated, as well as others— the portents (*riṣṭa*) such as "one whose finger is placed in the ear-cavity does not hear sound" (7.187), which were mentioned as being included within the category of those born from *nāda*— by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*).

The yogi knows the piercing of the eye-vein (*kāṇotpāṭa*) and so forth solely through yoga— meaning through the aforementioned form of practice and focused attention— and having known them, he conquers death once again by means of the yoga that overcomes death (*mṛtyujit*), which consists of the states of the *haṃsa-dhyāna*, the *amṛta-dhyāna*, and the reality of the mental functions (*tattvavṛttyavasthāna*), and which is the supreme, the intermediate, and the non-supreme self.
The connection is as follows: through the practice of mastering the movement of the channels (nāḍī), the yogi comes to know; and having known, he shall attain omniscience. || 262 ||

Now then, O lady of good vows, listen to me regarding those external signs which an unyoked person, whether disciplined or undisciplined, perceives here as portents of death: athedānīm ---- ayogī yāni jānāti ayukto vāpi suvrate | bahilīṅgāni tānyatra aṅgāriṣṭāni me śṛṇu || 7-263 ||
"One who is not a yogi" means one who has not attained yoga. "One who is unyoked" means either one who is not applying himself to yoga or one who is merely worldly;
he describes them as follows:
"If his palate, lips, and throat are parched, and his complexion suddenly becomes ashen..."
And if both shoulders undergo a collapse, one shall meet death within six months. || 7-264 ||
"Accidentally" means without a known cause; and this [term] is to be applied everywhere. || 264 ||
He who day after day sees a blue,
white, green, or black circle in the sky shall die within half a year.
"Accidentally" (akasmāt) means precisely that. "Mandala" refers to the outer halo of the solar disc. || 265 ||
One who sees the sun devoid of rays, or the moon bereft of its mark,
or sees the stars and the moonlight as black, has but six months to live.
The sun situated within the orb, the [solar] disc. || 266 ||
He who indeed sees in a dream a golden-colored person, or one that is tawny or even black, lives for six months.
It is established that this is because there is no sudden provocation of the *pitta* humor and so forth. || 267 ||
For one who sees the shadow of one's own headless body has six months of life remaining;
this is the meaning in the context of the examination of the shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*).
Anointing with oil, as well as drinking it, wearing red garlands, and anointing oneself with [red] unguents. || 7-268 ||
When one indeed sees red and black garments in a dream, along with ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, dogs, jackals, and boars; || 7-269 ||
One who is surrounded by vultures and crows, buffaloes, camels, and donkeys;
one whose limbs are being devoured, one who is being carried away, one who is naked, and one who is utterly distraught. (7.270)
He who indeed sees [this] in a dream lives for one year.
Here, the phrase "the self by the self" should be applied according to the context. "Carried away by vultures and the like" means being led away by them in the form of vehicles. 270.
In the Śaṅkhāvarta, in the middle of the arms, in the ankles, and in the vital joints. || 7-271 ||
He for whom this throbbing does not occur will certainly meet his death.

The *śaṅkhāvarta* (conch-whorl) marks are located at the junctions of the frontal bones near the corners of the eyes. The region between the arms is known as the *matsyasthāna* (fish-place). The vital joints (*marmasandhi*) refer to the arteries and other vessels. || 271 ||
Furthermore:
"The orbs of the moon and sun within the body, as well as Dhruva and Arundhatī," (7.272).
That man who does not perceive the Mahāyāna will inevitably go to hell.
He explains these [verses] in reverse order:
"The smoke that has reached the cavity of the palate—that is called the Mahāyāna. (7.273)
The tongue is called Arundhatī, and the tip of the nose is called Dhruva.

The cavity of the palate is the Brahmabila; one who has turned the sun behind [the head] does not see the streak of smoke arising from that in the shadow. The tip of the nose is the edge of the three-fold junction (tripuṭikā). || 273 ||
Furthermore: When the corners of the eyes are pressed by the fingertips, the mandalas of the moon and the sun [appear]. (7.274)
When the corners of the left and right eyes are pressed with the fingernail, the light that is then seen is the mandala of the Moon and the Sun.
All this—should a man not behold even this in the sky, he will certainly go to hell.
Immediately after the period of the seasons (ṛtu), there is the outward journey along the path of the celestial Gaṅgā; [there one sees] Arundhatī.
The Seven Sages (the Great Bear) are situated in the middle; Dhruva has a body composed of fourteen stars;
and the orbs of the Moon and Sun refer to the halo surrounding their disks.
He would suddenly become fat, and he would indeed suddenly become thin. (7.275)
Extremely enraged and extremely terrified, he lives for one year.
Again, he speaks regarding the subject of dreams: [he sees] a black man wearing black garments, with a rod of iron raised in his hand. (7.276)
And having seen a man facing him in a dream, one should determine that his life span is three months. || 276 ||
The heart of one who has just bathed dries up at that very moment. (7.277)
If his body is not even slightly warm, he lives for only one season; likewise, if a meteor falls at night or during the day, or if lightning is seen in a cloudless sky, [he will die]. (7.278)
Even in a region not scorched by fire, he lives for one month if there is a "fire in the quarters" (digdāha).

Regarding the "bow of Indra": even in a region not scorched—that is, where no other people perceive a fire in the quarters—if a fire in the quarters appears to him, he lives for a month; likewise, if a meteor is seen during the night or by day.
If one's eyes are flowing with tears, one will not clearly hear sounds. || 7-279 ||
"He does not smell a fragrance...
he smells" is this reading.
And for whomsoever there is— [omitted]—
stupidity of speech;
the word "suddenly" (akasmāt) is to be connected with every instance.
For him—
whose life span has reached one month—
the connection is that his life [is at its end].
And all of a sudden—his face becomes like a red lotus, and his tongue indeed turns black. (7.280)
He whose limbs possess various colors and whose heart weeps,
and who experiences a trembling of the palate and the navel, lives for only half a month.
He weeps repeatedly for no apparent cause and perspires; others say he experiences weeping. || 281 ||
And he who,
like a leader of crows before his very eyes, does not smell the smoke of a lamp,
nor recognizes what was seen before— he lives for four months. (7.282)
By whom even the crows, vultures, and herons, though not present, are seen directly before one's eyes as if they were at the head of the army. || 282 ||
He who does not see the beneficial drop (bindu) constantly following the mouth,
yet constantly suffers from hiccups, lives for only one year.

Even after performing the sixfold practice (*ṣaḍaṅgakaraṇa*), he who does not perceive the *bindu*—which follows the mouth and resides between the eyebrows—[overcomes] hiccup (*hikkā*) and asthma (*hidhmā*). || 283 ||
He summarizes:
"And these external signs, as well as those [internal] signs of death that have been mentioned"— this is the ellipsis.
Now, O Dear One, these [mantras] are to be honored through recitation, burnt offerings, meditation, and concentration. (7.284)
By performing the ritual of protection (*rakṣāvidhāna*), [the obstacles] are conquered; there is no doubt in this matter.
[The sequence] beginning with worship and ending with meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) has the Blessed One as its object; the ritual of protection will be described hereafter.
Thus, having performed this pacification of obstacles, one should engage in the practice of yoga itself;

and since that [practice] proceeds from the conquest of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) preceded by the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*), with the intention of elucidating that, the venerable Goddess said:
"And how is the purification of the channels and the conquest of the vital airs accomplished? (7.285)
"O Lord, tell me the location, form, sound, and function of those winds previously divided.
Desiring to resolve these six questions, Śrī Bhairava said:
O Dear One, this is the supreme essence of yoga, more secret than the secret.
Listen to that Yoga in its true essence, which has not been declared to anyone;
for that secret of Yoga which you have asked about cannot be attained without the practice of Yoga.
In that regard, first of all:
on a highly auspicious portion of ground, not near fire or water. (7.287)
In a place devoid of sand and gravel, free from withered trees, silent and without insects or anthills, and avoided by calamities. || 7-288 ||

One should practice yoga in a meritorious place where righteous people dwell; "calamities" refers to excessive rain and the like. "Meritorious" means endowed with sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth; "where righteous people dwell" means a refuge of merit.
Then he,
having worshipped the God of gods, Bhairava, together with Vināyaka— || 7-289 ||
The connection is as follows: having paid homage to the former teachers, being disciplined and devoted to meditation,

and having first performed the worship of Gaṇapati for the pacification of obstacles, and having worshipped the Gurus to receive their command, one should worship Bhairava and become disciplined and devoted to meditation.
To the question "How?", he says:
"Having assumed the svastika posture, or the padmaka, or indeed the bhadraka. (7.290)

Having performed the burning and purification of the meditation belt (yogapaṭṭa), which is supported by a base and shaped like a half-moon, according to one's ease, one should then flood it with nectar.
Then, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of the limbs) is performed with both the external and internal [mantras];
thereafter, the inner sacrifice (antaryāga) is to be recited as before, and likewise the supreme [mantra].

One should practice the *haṃsasvacchanda* in ten ways through the path of yoga. That which consists of the soles of the feet placed upward upon the thighs is called *padmāsana*; *svastika* is formed by crossing the shanks while seated in a cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*); *bhadra* is by standing with the feet even; [and] from leaning against a wall...
This "half-moon" (ardhacandra) posture is characterized by its support:
it is the half-moon in which one foot remains on the ground while the second foot is placed with the sole upward upon the thigh;
having assumed one of these postures—or another—for the purpose of yoga and for tying the cloth belt around the waist, [one should proceed].
Whatever pleasure does not cause affliction to the body— as it has been said:
"Posture is that which is steady and pleasant" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.46)—
then, having performed the previously mentioned rites from the burning [of the body] up to the utterance [of the mantra], one proceeds tenfold by way of yoga.

By means of the future [practices] consisting of the sixfold external and internal exhalations (*recaṇa*) and so forth, the peaceful breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*), and furthermore, preceded by the mastery of the ten vital winds such as *prāṇa* and others that are yet to come, one should practice and enter into the aforementioned supreme, partless Lord (*niṣkalabhaṭṭāraka*), who is the pure *Haṃsa*.
He clarifies the entry into that [state] by means of the previously mentioned method:
"But the mantra, which transcends the *bindu*, has the form of the light at the end of the *nāda*. (7.293)
Having formed a mental resolve upon the object of conceptualization, one should indeed meditate through that [resolve] upon the all-pervading [reality].
[One should meditate on] the mantra, preceded by the utterance of the vowels beginning with 'A' and the four lords of the *kalās*, as that which transcends the *bindu*.
By transcending that, having opened the stages of the *ardhacandra* and *nirodhikā*, [one proceeds] through the sequence of *nāda* and *nādānta*.

Having first conceptualized the form of light as consisting of the manifestation of power (*śakti*) and so forth, and having attained it through non-conceptualization, one should meditate upon that which is unperceivable by mental constructs, the mass of self-luminous consciousness-bliss, all-pervading, the *haṃsa*, and autonomous.
Having dissolved everything up to the limit of the *samanā*, one should enter [the state] through the arising of uncreated discernment (*akṛtakavimarśa*). || 293 ||

With the intention that this [practice] would be easily accomplished by means of the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*) preceded by the conquest of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he first describes the mastery of the channels:
"One should fill [the right channel] with the *apasavya* [nostril] and expel [the air] through the *savya* [nostril] alone. (7.294)
This is the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*) and of the path of the way to liberation.

"By the left" means through the right nostril one should exhale—that is, perform exhalation (*recaka*); "by the right" means by the left, one should fill—that is, perform the filling of air (*pūraṇa*). Thus, it should be done continuously.
This purification of the channels, or of the path of the way to liberation, and of the central abode, being performed,
results in the pacification of the vital breaths.
He begins to explain the mastery of the vital breath (prāṇajaya):
"Prāṇāyāma is traditionally said to be threefold: through exhalation (recana), inhalation (pūraṇa), and retention (rodha). (7.295)
The "restraining of the vital breath" (prāṇāyāma) is the bringing [of it] under one's own control by means of conquering its movement as it naturally occurs. || 295 ||
These three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), when performed by the common method of the nasal path, are said to be "common" and "external"— as it is said:
"But these common ones are external..."
By those who apply these internally preceded by practice—
...furthermore, there are three within;
he states them as follows:
One should exhale by means of the internal [wind], and one should fill [the body] by means of the internal [wind].
Having performed a motionless *kumbhaka*, three internal [breaths] should be practiced.

Here, by means of the internal middle path, there is exhalation at the *dvādaśānta*, filling at the heart, and a motionless *kumbhaka*; "motionless" means a *kumbhaka* that is effortless and perfectly tranquil. These should be performed.
Thus, they become subject to cessation. || 296 ||
Then—[from] the navel, through the movement into the heart, and from the range of the mind and the senses. (7.297)

The fourth [stage] is breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is known as "well-peaceful" (supraśānta). Following the motionless kumbhaka, by means of moving [the breath] gradually from the heart downward— specifically, by restraining the vital breath at the navel itself through the technique of moving it from the heart— this is the intended meaning.

Likewise, by means of the method of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), having restrained the mind from the sphere of the senses right at the navel, for one who restrains the vital breath (prāṇa) in the navel preceded by the restraint of the mind, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) becomes perfectly tranquil. || 297 ||
Thus, when the restraint of the vital breath is complete, one should lead it to the navel while breathing out. || 298 ||
Immediately thereafter—
one should slowly release the breath through the left nostril in order to remove the agitation caused by the restrained breath.
Having thus described breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), ending with the conquest of the *arājas* [element], he defines concentration (*dhāraṇā*):
"The aerial [concentration] is on the big toe; the fiery is in the middle of the navel. (7-299)
The earth-element concentration is in the region of the throat, while the water-element concentration resides at the uvula;
the space-element concentration at the crown of the head is remembered as that which brings about all accomplishments.
Because of the presence of the horizontal movement [of air] at the region of the feet, of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) at the navel,

of the earth (*dharaṇī*) at the station of the throat, of the fluid (*rasa*) at the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*), and of space (*vyoman*) at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the respective meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) are taught. And here, regarding the upward stroke (*udghāta*):
The nature of the letters as consisting of the castes (*varṇa*), the maṇḍalas, the marks (*lāñchana*), and the phonemes, as determined in the introduction to initiation,
is to be meditated upon through concentration (*dhāraṇā*). In that regard, having first performed the concentration on earth (*pārthivī*) at the throat,
one should pierce the fivefold earthly principle (*tattva*) from the heart by means of five upward thrusts (*uddhāta*).
Then, by this very sequence, from the heart itself, with four *uddhātas*, one draws out the water-element (*aptattva*) which possesses four qualities;

then, from the heart itself, with three *uddhātas* into the field of the navel, the fire-element (*agni*) possessing three qualities; immediately after, from the heart itself, with two [uddhātas], the wind-element (*vāyu*) located in the big toes, possessing two qualities.
Then, by means of the technique of contraction from that very thumb, one awakens the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) upward;

and by means of a single forceful impulse (ekodghāta) starting precisely from the heart, like an arrow, one pierces the single-knotted knot of Vyoma situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), whereby all the supernatural powers (siddhis) belonging to that which resides at the "End of the Twelve" (dvādaśānta) come to be.
The meaning of the sentence. || 300 ||
He says this very thing: "It is accomplished by means of one, two, three, four, or five expulsions (*udghāta*).
He defines the expulsion (*udghāta*) as follows:
But when the vital breath is completely restrained, having gone to the crown of the head, it turns back.

This is declared to be the *udghāta* (upward stroke), which should always be known by yogins. The mention of "in the head" (*mūrdhni*) is intended as an illustration for the cranial centers (*kṣetra*), such as the throat and others. "Should be known" means that this [experience] consists of an experience corresponding to each respective location. For this very reason:
Previously, this was stated as being primarily characterized by experience. || 301 ||
Now, he indicates the fruit of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the other practices:
"Attachment and aversion are abandoned through well-maintained breath controls. (7.302)
One should burn away evil through the *dhāraṇās*; in *pratyāhāra*, there is the restraint of the senses.

The phrase "one should burn away evil" refers to the piercing of the knots of the earth element and others that act as obstructions, thereby severing the bondage of both auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Now, regarding that which was asked concerning the objects of the vital breaths and so forth— "Tell me their location, form, sound, and action" (7.286)— he speaks in order to determine them sequentially:
"In the heart, the anus, the navel, the throat, and likewise in all the joints" (7.303).
For these five, beginning with prāṇa and ending with vyāna, are established there as a matter of course.
And of these—
[omission]— hear from me their form and sound;
therein—
It is red like molten gold and resembles the indragopaka insect. || 304 ||
The characteristics of the five [kinds of silver] are that it has the luster of milk and the luster of crystal; it is quick to melt and flows when liquefied. || 304 ||
The roar of the elephant was a great sound, as sweet as a bell, bronze, or thundercloud.
This sound is said to belong to the five [breaths], beginning with prāṇa:
it is like the sound of a bell-metal vessel (kaṃsa), a cloud (megha), or a great roar resembling the rushing noise of a river. || 305 ||
He instructs them in their respective activities, which therein consist of: speech, laughter, singing, dancing, the movements of combat, and the arts (kalās). || 7-306 ||
Crafts and all actions are likewise the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The "arts" include painting and so forth; "all actions" refers to these very same things. 306.
One should cause food and drink to enter [the body] and cause that waste to flow downward.
The *apāna* wind will cause blindness and diseases of the ear;
by the word "and," [diseases of] the sense of touch, smell, and so forth are included. || 307 ||
The *samāna* [vital breath] brings to equilibrium that which has been eaten, licked, and drunk.
One should cause [the breath] to circulate through the channels. || 308 ||
Agitation, hiccups, and likewise sneezing are the functions of udāna;
"sneezing" (chikkā) refers to the act of coughing (kṣuta).
Perspiration, horripilation, pain, burning sensation, and breaking pain in the limbs. (7.309)
These are the functions of the vyāna; it perceives touch, and it alone experiences it. || 309 ||
He indicates the locations of the nāgas and others:
"They are situated in the thumbs, the knees, the heart, the eyes, and the head. (7.310)
The meaning is that the Nāgas and the others [are worshipped] in sequence. || 310 ||
He states that the variegated nature (*śabalarūpatā*) and the variegated terminology (*śabalaśabdatā*) of all these are equal:
"And it is multiform (*bahurūpaśca*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that there are many words (*bahuśabdāḥ*).
...Now learn from me their functions.
In that state of non-modification, they proceed in sequence as follows:
[the wind] produces exhilaration and agitation, as well as desiccation and terror. (7.311)
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, and Devadatta as the fifth; then Atinidrākara, and another, Yojaka, and Dhanañjaya. (7.312)
Excessive sleep is lethargy; the "connector" (yojaka) is that which effects the connection with another body. || 312 ||

In their state of transformation at the time of death, the following are the movements of the five [winds] beginning with Nāga: the contraction and cutting off of the breath, and likewise the gurgling sound as it departs. (7.313)
Utkramaṇa is the departure from the body. || 313 ||
This, however, is the distinction between Dhanañjaya and the tortoise:
Dhanañjaya does not depart at the time of death after abandoning the body;
for some time, he does not leave the corpse.
One should indeed contract [the limbs] like a tortoise and dry up the body.
Contraction is the closing of the joints; drying up occurs in the locations such as the palate and so forth. || 314 ||
Thus, established in these ten ways:
"One should first conquer the vital breath (prāṇa); when the vital breath is conquered, the mind is conquered.
When the mind is conquered, for one who is at peace, the supreme reality shines forth. (7.315)
Therein—one should meditate on prāṇa and apāna at the anus; prāṇa and samāna at the navel; prāṇa and udāna at the throat; and prāṇa and vyāna as pervading the whole body. (7.316)
