In this context, the word *prāṇa* denotes the general vital breath (*sāmānya-prāṇa*), being used in grammatical apposition with its specific forms such as *apāna* and so forth. However, one should meditate upon that specific form of *prāṇa*, which consists of outward movement, in the previously mentioned location, namely the heart.
And these meditators, whose natures consist of the colors, sounds, and so forth as previously described, become mastered. || 316 ||
And in this very way—
the Nāgas and the others, being conjoined with the vital breaths, are connected to the universal vital breath (sāmānyaprāṇa).
One should restrain these, which have the form described above, in the previously mentioned locations.
That duration of time by which the mastery of this group of ten through their restraint is achieved— during that time...
To speak of this, he says:
"And as for the time of that which has been restrained, I shall explain it; listen to me. (7.317)
One should meditate upon that from the moment of the sound *tāl* until five hundred [breaths] have passed;
then the vital wind (*anila*) is surely conquered for the practice of transference and egress.

A *tāla* is the duration of time required for a finger to circle the knee. When five hundred of these have elapsed, if the unwavering meditation on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is accomplished, then they are conquered.
Consequently, one gains the capacity for entering another body and for the upward departure (*utkrānti*).
And this is the superknowledge regarding its mastery:
his divine luster, auspicious fragrance, and wisdom increase;
divine vision, divine hearing, and divine speech arise. (7.319)
One may move through the worlds like the wind and behold the Siddhas and the gods;
the attainment of whatever is conceived by the mind proceeds, and the eightfold qualities manifest.
With all desires fully satisfied and free from all dualities, he becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra and is equal to Śiva. (7.321)

The eight qualities, beginning with *aṇimā* [and so forth]. By this much of the text, that which was introduced in the verse, "One should practice the *Haṃsa-svacchanda* through the tenfold path of yoga" (7.293), has been brought to completion. || 321 ||

Now, demonstrating the states such as waking that are appropriate for yoga by means of the "pregnant" meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) belonging to living beings, he instructs the yogis in the knowledge of the nature of the penetration (*samāveśa*) described in other systems: [The verse: The waking state is the manifestation of the object; dreaming is its dissolution; deep sleep is the cessation of both; and the fourth is the cessation of that [cessation]. This is the fourfold state of consciousness. [The commentary: Waking is the manifestation of the object; dreaming is the dissolution of that [manifestation]; deep sleep is the cessation of both [manifestation and dissolution]; and the fourth is the cessation of that [cessation]. This is the fourfold state of consciousness. By this, the state of the Fourth (*turya*) is indicated. It is called "the Fourth" because it transcends the three states. It is called "consciousness" because it is the essence of the Self. It is "fourfold" because it consists of these four states. It is "the state of consciousness" because it is the substratum of all states. It is "this" because it is directly perceived. Now, he explains the nature of the penetration (*samāveśa*) taught in other systems: [The verse: The penetration (*samāveśa*) is the absorption into the Self, which is the cessation of the activity of the mind. It is of two kinds: with support (*sālambana*) and without support (*nirālambana*). [The commentary: Penetration (*samāveśa*) is the absorption into the Self. What is that? It is the cessation of the activity of the mind. It is of two kinds: with support and without support. With support is that which relies on an external object; without support is that which does not rely on anything. Of these, the one with support is for beginners, while the one without support is for those who have attained stability. Now, he describes the method for attaining the penetration with support: [The verse: One should contemplate the object of meditation, whether it be a deity, a mantra, or a form, until the mind becomes one with it. Then, the penetration occurs spontaneously. [The commentary: One should contemplate the object of meditation—be it a deity, a mantra, or a form—until the mind becomes one with it. Then, the penetration occurs spontaneously, without effort. Now, he describes the penetration without support: [The verse: Or else, by the grace of the Guru, one may attain the penetration without support through the sudden destruction of the veil of ignorance. [The commentary: Alternatively, by the grace of the Guru, one may attain the penetration without support through the sudden destruction of the veil of ignorance. This is the supreme method. Thus ends the instruction on the nature of penetration. Now, he shows how the yogi, having attained this penetration, experiences the fruits of yoga: [The verse: Having entered into this state, the yogi perceives the truth of all things, just as a lamp illuminates objects in the darkness. He is no longer bound by the cycle of birth and death. [The commentary: Having entered into this state of penetration, the yogi perceives the truth of all things, just as a lamp illuminates objects in the darkness. He is no longer bound by the cycle of birth and death, for he has realized his identity with the Supreme Reality. Thus, the fruit of yoga is liberation. This concludes the chapter on the states of consciousness and the nature of penetration.
When the lord of yogins, having joined the prāṇa and apāna breaths together with ten million short [syllables], remains in the foundation of the navel,
then for him—
...perspiration and trembling arise. || 7-322 ||
When, following the rest in the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) where all waves have subsided within the heart,

there arises the unfolding of the increase of mantra, then the *prāṇa* and *apāna*— abiding in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) within the heart— are joined with the downward movement through the contemplation of the digit (*kalā*) in the form of the short vowel-limit.
Having joined [the breath] at the navel through the process of expansion, perspiration and trembling occur for one who remains for the prescribed duration. || 322 ||
Then he—once again, indeed, should restrain the prāṇa and apāna residing within the heart;
through the union with the long-pointed [state], he shall fall to the ground at that very moment. (7.323)
Immediately after resting at the navel-center, having ascended upwards and brought [the breath] to reside in the heart,
one intent on the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the second digit (*kalā*) of the mantra consisting of the long vowel should restrain it for the prescribed duration at the throat-end,
which is the place of utterance (*uccāra-sthāna*) at that time.
He may remain [in that state], but due to the intensity of his one-pointed concentration, he might fall to the ground. || 7-323 ||
Furthermore,
if he likewise restrains the vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the throat,
then through the union with ten million pluta [vowels], the state of dreaming arises. (7.324)
When there is *ullāsa* (exaltation), because of the cessation of drinking [the flow], it is here called *prāṇa*; its duration is ten million *plutas*.

According to the previously stated method, it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the digit of the letter *M*, articulated as far as the palate. Here, *svapna* (dream) is appropriate, consisting of the manifestation of the object sought to be known. By commanding in this manner, [there arise] trembling, perspiration, and falling.
Thus, it has been explained that this is the awakening of the yogi. || 324 ||
But when one causes the restraint of the vital breath through the application of the *bindu* between the eyebrows, deep sleep arises there, and one awakens in an instant. (7.325)

Because the palate has been pierced by the *pluta* [vowel] alone, for one who remains in the middle of the eyebrows for the prescribed duration through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the pervasion of the *māntra*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*) arises with the mental fluctuations stilled;
and awakening occurs in an instant, so that one is not overcome by the veil of darkness as is the case with ordinary people.
Thus it has been said: "But elsewhere, he consists of consciousness" (Spandakārikā 2.2). || 325 ||
Then, having resorted to the door of the crown of the head, one should begin the meditation on the partless (niṣkala).
As he practices in this way, a sign of attainment will then arise for him. (7.326)

The "piercing by the ant's thorn" (*pipīlakaṇṭakāvedha*) consists of the experience of touch resulting from the piercing of the upper door (*mūrdhvadvāra*) by means of the pervasion of the resonance of the light of the phonemes (*varṇajyotis*), which is "partless" (*niṣkala*). It is called "piercing by the ant's thorn" because it is like the touch of a moving ant and like the touch of a thorn.
The meaning is "contact. || 326 ||
Furthermore:
having sequentially pierced all those [channels] up to the *unmanī* state... (327)

"O Goddess, by the previously mentioned characteristics..."—the ellipsis "by the characteristics" refers to the experiences described in the section on the *praṇava*; the remainder of the sentence is that [the practitioner] is joined with these. That much is the state of the Fourth (*turya*) here.
Then, having abandoned all this— [the body, senses, and objects]— one should proceed to absolute freedom (*svacchandatā*),
by virtue of the excellence of resting in the state of the intensely firm *unmanā* stage, through the attainment of the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*).
The meaning is that the lord of yogis experiences immersion into the Supreme Bhairava, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss.
Not only does his supreme immersion (*parasamāveśa*) occur in a state transcending the body, but rather:
"Indeed, even with this very body, the state of *unmanatva* arises for the practitioner. (7-328)

The meaning is that even during the state of the body and upon emergence from absorption, the practitioner experiences a state of reeling due to the excellence of his immersion and the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the essence of that bliss. || 328 ||

Moreover, through the unfolding of the power of his autonomy, he may enter into the bodies of others; he is not afflicted by hunger or thirst, and he perceives whatever has occurred or will occur throughout the three worlds. (7.329)
That [object] becomes directly perceived by him, and his omniscience arises.
Whatever proceeds—that is, whatever exists in the present—all of that becomes directly perceived by him. This is what is meant by "omniscience."
The meaning is that, through the gradual intensification of practice, one becomes equal to the Mantras, the Mantreśas, and so forth. || 329 ||
Concluding the subject matter of this chapter, he demonstrates the connection with the subsequent chapter:
"In this context, the knowledge and the realization of the inner time (adhyātmakāla)... (7.330).
All this has been fully explained; now learn from me regarding the *aṃśas* (subdivisions),
as well as knowledge in its true nature concerning the exposition of the internal self (*adhyātma*) and time—
including the piercing (*vedha*) and other forms consisting of the state of awakening for the yogi who has conquered death.

This consciousness has been described, even that which was not explicitly mentioned, out of a desire to favor [the seeker]. Therefore, regarding what was asked— "O Lord of Gods, please graciously explain the division of time"— the nature of time has been explained, and along with it, knowledge as well.

Consciousness has also been taught; however, the essential nature of its constituent parts remains to be determined. Therefore, understand—know—the constituent parts that will be determined by the forthcoming chapter. This is the thematic connection of the chapter. May there be auspiciousness! 330.
"Having correctly understood the universe as situated within the vital breath through the expansive pervasion of consciousness,
one should attain the state of fullness by means of the partial knowledge of those various supernatural powers (siddhis).
Thus it is said in the Śrī Svacchandatantra.

The seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Time" (*Kālādhikāra*), together with the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
From that great ocean of consciousness, Brahmā and the other lords of the worlds [arise].
We praise that Supreme Bhairava, whose portions are limited like bubbles.
Regarding that which was introduced at the end of the chapter with the words, "And learn from me the *aṃśakas*," Śrī Bhairava spoke in order to explain it:
"O Goddess, I shall describe the sixfold *aṃśaka* in its proper sequence."

The partial manifestations (*aṃśas*) are those presided over by the powers (*śaktis*) of the supreme Bodhabhairava—namely Brahmā and the others—and thus illuminated as such; therefore, even those who are to be graced by Him are called His "partial manifestations. Consequently, he [the teacher] proclaims these partial manifestations who abide as objects of worship. This...

That which will be described in the sequence beginning with "this is a portion of Brahmā" or "this is a portion of Viṣṇu," such as the nature of one's disposition (*bhāvasvabhāva*) and so forth, is called an *aṃśaka*. And because it is favorable toward the practitioner’s attainment (*siddhi*), that small portion is designated as an *aṃśaka*.
He points this out: "The portion of dispositions, the portion of inherent nature, and the very portion of the casting of flowers. (8-1)
Another [aspect] is known as the *mantrāṃśaka* (the portion of the mantra), and the attainment of that portion is twofold:
the disposition (*bhāva*) is the innate inclination endowed with devotion to each [deity]; the nature (*svabhāva*) is the activity consistent therewith;
and that which is determined according to the falling of flowers by one whose eyes are bound through the previously mentioned method—
That portion of the mantra is for the practitioner to perform as the very self of the deity expressed by that mantra.

The "attainment of the portion" (aṃśakāpādana) is performed for the worshipper—whether the mantra's portion has not yet been specifically determined—either through the oblation of *vīradravya* and other substances, or through the sequence of the practitioner’s initiation; thus, it is of two forms.
The sixteenth [chapter].
He states the definition of the first of these:
"The state of being is the recollection of the gods; one who knows that [state] is born with it. (8.2)

Even for one who does not practice [the prescribed rites], that innate recollection of this or that specific deity which arises by virtue of the ripening of impressions from previous births—that is the aspect of being (bhāvāṃśa). || 2 ||
He states the second [point]:
"And its nature would be activity...
in this very way, the activity consisting of the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth conforms precisely to the previously mentioned state."
And that I shall relate to you in due order:
[the portion] of Brahmā who is devoted to the Vedas; now learn from me the portion of Rudra as well. (8.3)
He was a devotee of Rudra, possessed of excellent character, and always delighted in the scriptures of Śiva;
he was a portion of Viṣṇu and a devotee of Viṣṇu, while being a portion of the Moon and of pleasing appearance.

One who delights in all the gods is known as Śānta; one who is a portion of a Yakṣa is a hoarder of wealth; one who is greedy and eats what is savory is known as the portion of a Gava; and one who is fickle is known as the portion of Vāta. || 8-5 ||

He moves with the confidence of a serpent, possesses the nature of a nāga, and sleeps for long periods; he harbors long-standing resentment, has a foul-smelling mouth, and always has a craving for the milk of elephants.
O fair-faced one, he is known as a celestial musician (gandharva) who constantly sings and is a devotee of Śiva;
he is a living being with the nature of a Vidyādhara, while his portion of hatred is said to be that of a Daitya.
He possesses a portion of Kāma and is handsome, fortunate, and beloved by courtesans;
he possesses a portion of Rākṣasa and is cruel, merciless, hostile toward the gods, and [hostile] toward the twice-born.
Having a portion of a Piśāca, he seeks out deceptions; by day he is fearful and timid;
having a portion of Fire, he is harsh, intense, a consumer of hot food, and tawny. (8–9)
And he was a son of Savitṛ, radiant and always devoted to the dharma of public works;
compassionate and imbued with the spirit of Śiva, he constantly performed sacrifices. || 8-10 ||

With a putrid mouth and foul-smelling saliva; he was a devotee of Śiva who possessed a portion of a Vidyādhara, having attained mastery over medicinal pills, collyrium, and other such powers according to the prescriptions of the Śiva scriptures;
cruel, with a harsh heart; merciless in his actions; and rough in speech.
"Tīvra" refers to action. "Pūrta" is the construction of ponds, wells, and so forth. "Iṣṭa" is sacrifice.
The rest is clear. || 10 ||
And those who are their respective portions— namely these [deities] beginning with Brahmā—
all of them bestow the fruits of their own accomplishments through meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings.
To whatever extent a particular deity possesses sovereignty, to that same extent it grants [its powers] to practitioners when propitiated.

Speaking thus, he said this: that for a limited portion [of the path], the arising of the mantra alone is the means for attaining those respective stages; and for those for whom [such specific mantras] do not exist in the scriptures, the *praṇava* itself, joined with their name and salutation, [serves as the mantra].
But when—
“Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is directed to that very place;
he becomes a possessor of accomplishment through the power of mantra...”

According to the principle stated thus, for a practitioner who has received initiation through the mantras belonging to this [system], those specific deities are propitiated by means of the worship of these mantras; at that time, they are all indeed of the nature of Bhairava, and are therefore the accomplishers of all siddhis— so he says:
O fair-faced one, all the gods were anointed with the limbs of Bhairava.
"All the Bhairavas are traditionally held to bestow the fruit of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
By the statement 'endowed with the limbs of Bhairava,' he says this [regarding] those mantras beginning with Kapālīśa for whom the faces have not been mentioned."
Their worshippers should employ the limbs of the Naiṣkala [mantra] as the faces. Here, someone,
unable to accept the application of the word *sarva*, which occurs twice, to two separate sentences— namely,
in the phrase *sarve devāḥ* and in the phrase *sarvasiddhiphalapradāḥ*— [interprets them differently].

Having read "sarvakāmasamanvitāḥ," he explained that practitioners initiated by this mantra become Bhairavas themselves through its propitiation and thus become vessels for complete accomplishment (*siddhi*). However, in ancient manuscripts, the first reading is seen without dispute.
Thus has the aspect of intrinsic nature been fully explained for the benefit of practitioners indeed. (8.12)
By the term "aspirant" (sādhaka), he indicates that for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), this restriction does not apply, and so forth. || 12 ||
She indicates the portion for the casting of the flower:
"O beautiful goddess, the name must be assigned according to the falling of the flower,
for one whose disposition and nature are undecided, who desires enjoyment, and whose eyes are bound, after all obstructions have been worshipped."

In the mandala of the Blessed One, according to the previously stated procedure, one should cast a single flower; wherever it falls, the name should be assigned in accordance with the deity designated by that mantra.
And therefore, for one who has been instructed in each respective reality by a teacher who knows that portion [of it], that mantra is accomplished, provided he worships that very [reality]. (8.13)
This means "according to the procedure prescribed in the treatises," by implication. || 13 ||
Having omitted for now the section on mantras— which follows in sequence— because it requires further explanation,
he introduces the calculation of the *aṃśaka* (division):
"O Goddess, I shall describe the calculation of the *aṃśaka* in brief."
To the question "How so?", he says:
"The practitioner who should offer as a burnt oblation a banner suspended in the air... (8.14).
O you of excellent vows, even that mantra which ends with the word *ārya* will be accomplished for him;

indeed, according to the procedure to be described, even a mantra ending in *ārya* is for the very purpose of propitiation. "Vaihāyasa" refers to human flesh from a man who has hanged himself, and "dhvaja" refers to human flesh from a man impaled on a stake—one hundred and eight [offerings] of each.
Whether a thousand times or according to the capacity and resolve of the practitioner— be he an *ārādhaka* (a worshiper),
an *ācārya* (teacher), one commissioned by him, or any other practitioner— he should perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*,
i.e., *juhuyāt*). For him, [the deity], being thus propitiated, becomes perfected and becomes conducive to his spiritual practice (*sādhana*).

However, if someone desires to propitiate a certain mantra— because they have heard of its extraordinary power— even though they have not analyzed its constituent parts according to the prescribed sequence, and they lack the fitness for the sequence of heroic substances (*vīradravya*),
then, at the outset, they should satisfy that mantra they wish to propitiate through worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth.

Stating that the attainment of the status of being a constituent part of that mantra must be performed by means of the very procedure for the initiation and consecration of the practitioner (sādhaka) previously described, he characterizes the second attainment of the constituent part as follows:
"O fair-faced one, even a mantra that lacks a constituent part [is made complete] by means of the signs of knowledge. (8.15)
Then, having first performed the sacrifice (yāga), one should cause the oblation (homa) to be offered into the fire according to the prescribed methods.
An "anaṃśaka" disciple is one whose portion (aṃśaka) has not been determined by the aforementioned procedures; for such a disciple, the sacrifice and the oblation [are performed].
For the purpose of bringing the mantra face-to-face.
Then— having performed the ritual for the disciple as before, according to the prescribed rule— 8.16.
One should unite [the disciple] in the eternal state by means of the application of the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation).

"Ritual" (*karman*) refers to that which begins with the worship of the Lord and ends with the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "One should unite" means that very disciple, together with the mantra, in the eternal—that is, in the state of Paramaśiva—or in the state desired by the practitioner.
In the abode of Sadāśiva and others, which bestows eternal enjoyment, this [individual soul], by virtue of being joined to the eternal state,
abandons its state of being partless and attains the state of possessing parts.
Having thus attained this portion, he, meditating upon the supreme reality (paratattva), shall accomplish whatever is desired by his mind. (8.17)
Having thus explained the division into parts in two ways, he states the division of the mantra:
"But having counted the portion of the mantra, one should take it after careful deliberation;
that is, the mantra which has been made into parts according to the sequence of the differentiation of syllables, forming the portions of the mantra's form."
Since it also takes the form of portions corresponding to the practitioner, I shall briefly describe [the initiation] as inferior, middling, and superior according to those portions. (8.18)
In that regard—
one should recognize the inferior as the enemy, the middling as one who is capable of being won over,
and the accomplished and the well-accomplished as the supreme. (8.19)
How so? To this he says:
"Having separated the syllable of the mantra, provided with its vowel-measure (mātrā) and bindu, one should likewise join the syllable of one's own name beneath it. (8.20)

In the mantra beginning with "oṃ śivāya namaḥ," one should analyze the mantra-syllables such as *oṃ* as being endowed with the vowels *a*, *u*, and so forth, along with the nasal drop (*bindu*); and having thus separated the vowels *a*, *u*, etc., and the *bindu*, one should conceive of them as the constituent parts (*mātrā*) of the syllable *ma*.
Having separated [the components], one should thus disjoin the vowel *i* from the consonants *ś* and *k*, and the vowel *ā* from the consonant *r*.

However, the mere vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; one should not disjoin it from anything, but rather, from whichever syllable another mantra has been disjoined, one should assign the vowel *a* to that for the sake of pronunciation.

Otherwise, it would be impossible to pronounce [the mantra]. Thus, one should separate each individual syllable of the disciple’s name—such as Viṣṇumitra and so forth—which belongs to oneself, according to the aforementioned division of *mātrās*, and join them below the analyzed mantra. By means of that, [the mantra becomes]: *aumaśaivāayanama*.
Thus, one should place the syllables of the name Viṣṇumitra, distributed below the ten syllables.
Where there are many mantra-syllables, one should join the name-syllables again and again, continuing until the completion of the mantra-syllables. || 20 ||
This being the case:
"O Goddess, starting from the letter of one's own name up to the letter of the mantra that has been reached, one should determine that [deity] upon which it falls. (7.21)
Taking each single syllable of the disciple’s name as a limit, by counting according to the sequence of recitation of the *mātṛkā* letters,

one reaches a certain number of mantra-syllables situated above each syllable of the name; then, according to the calculation of the divisions into *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* to be described hereafter, when [the name] falls into any one of these—
That name-syllable might fall or be joined; one should determine it as "this is the arrival," indicating good or bad fortune.
As it is said in the *Mayasaṃgraha*:
"Arrivals occur for the sake of desired or undesired objects; therefore, they are called 'arrivals' (āyas). || 21 ||
In this context, having first demonstrated the method of calculation, he indicates the nature of *āya*: "I shall explain briefly that which resides in lines and fingers;
that *āya* which is indicated by lines and resides in the fingers is explained as being within the lines of the fingers."
And he is perfected on the first lunar day, and likewise, he is to be accomplished on the second. || 8-22 ||
In the third [case], however, he will be well-accomplished; in the fourth, he should be known as an enemy.
Having counted the syllables of the name up to the attainment of the syllables of the mantra according to this sequence, one should examine the *āya*.
In that regard—having abandoned those that are hostile and difficult to accomplish, the [mantra] should be bestowed by the Cumbaka. || 8-23 ||
The *siddha* and *susiddha* [planets] bestow the fruits of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

There is a rejection of the *ari* (enemy) and *sādhya* planets when they are situated at the beginning and end or when they are strong; however, there is acceptance of the *siddha* and *susiddha*, because they grant enjoyment and liberation respectively. As it has been said:
"In the *siddha* position, success is certain; in the *sādhya* position, it is achieved with great effort;
in the *susiddha* position, it is already accomplished; but in the *ari* position, it does not succeed at all.
Thus it is said. Furthermore—

"If, when purity has been thus established, the practitioner is highly perfected and superior, he does not find what is to be grasped even in the case of a [lesser] goal, provided that the goal is also superior.
Thus, "when purity has been established" means when it has been determined regarding the specific portion; and "even in the case of a goal" means when that goal is also superior.

The meaning here is that when [the mantra] has arrived three or four times, its mantric forms (mantramūrti) should be accepted as the object of worship. Furthermore, this examination of the *aṃśaka* (division/portion) is not to be performed for single-syllable mantras or for garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*).
As it has been said:

"O beautiful lady, in the case of single-syllable *kūṭas*, garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*s), and other mantras, one should not examine the *aṃśakas*; however, one should examine those belonging to other mantras.
Here, "in *kūṭas*" refers to the non-dual principles (*advaitatattva*). For this very reason—
"O Goddess of the Gods, [this applies] to Māyā, the two eyes, and likewise to the thirty-two syllables;
there, no fear of enemies shall exist," so it is also stated elsewhere.
Therefore, through such investigation—O fair-faced one, he whose portions have been purified here becomes Bhairava. (8.24)
Having worshipped that one situated in the center, one should place the central [deity] in its location.

"Ya" refers to any one of the [deities] beginning with Kapālīśa. "Situated in the center" means because it has become the primary element in the rite of propitiation. "In its location" means in the position belonging to that [deity] within the circle of the enclosure.

Regarding the station of Kapālīśa and the others: it is taught that one should examine the "middle" state—which consists of the venerable Svacchanda—as having the nature of the fourth state (*turya*) and so forth.
Now, how is there an assignment (*nyāsa*) of the retinue of the venerable Lord Svacchandana as a retinue [unto him]?
To quell this doubt, he says:
"Because the God is omnipresent, he is remembered as being contained within all. (8.25)
In the ultimate sense, it is He who bestows both worldly attainment and liberation, not the letters; for He is the all-pervading, omnipresent Lord, whose nature is play and the like,
a mass of consciousness and bliss— the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Svacchanda— within all [the deities] beginning with Kapālīśa.

Since the ultimate reality (paramārtharūpa) is included within those things that exist through the pervasion of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca), for that reason, it alone is remembered as having various forms such as Kapālīśa and others; from the perspective of ultimate truth, it bestows accomplishment (siddhi) upon the practitioner through the purification of their constituent parts (aṃśaka-śuddhi) and liberation (mukti) through non-dual pervasion (abheda-vyāpti), and not otherwise.
Letters devoid of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) accomplish nothing. For it was stated previously: "How can there be liberation in mere syllables? (7.238).
Therefore, even if one conceives of the differentiation of one's own obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) otherwise, there is no impairment whatsoever of the ground of reality (*tattvabhūmi*).

This matter, which has arisen incidentally at the conclusion of the investigation into the "parts" (aṃśaka), has been told to you along with its secret: it is the supreme reality, more hidden than the hidden. (8.26)

Now, in order to authenticate what has been stated as "that which was spoken," he demonstrates the sixfold relationship—beginning with Parā and ending with Divya—showing how this secret Tantra descended through the lineage of gurus starting from Paramaśiva: 1. *Parā-sambandha* (The Supreme Relationship): The relationship between Śiva and Śakti. 2. *Pārameśvara-sambandha* (The Supreme Lord’s Relationship): The relationship between Śakti and Sadāśiva. 3. *Sādākhya-sambandha* (The Sadāśiva Relationship): The relationship between Sadāśiva and Īśvara. 4. *Māyīya-sambandha* (The Māyā Relationship): The relationship between Īśvara and Vidyeśvara. 5. *Anugraha-sambandha* (The Grace Relationship): The relationship between Vidyeśvara and Mantra. 6. *Divya-sambandha* (The Divine Relationship): The relationship between Mantra and the human Guru. Thus, he illustrates that this secret Tantra has descended through the succession of gurus from Paramaśiva onwards.
Therefore, for the purpose of introducing the Tantra, I shall speak in brief:
therein [is that which] has come from Śiva, the supreme cause, whose form is unperceived. (8.27)
That very [reality], which is of the nature of sound, extremely subtle, perfectly pure, and endowed with radiant luster, exists in another form as Śiva, the Supreme Self. (8.28)
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, he who is the great soul of the five mantras quickly deliberated upon human goals and their respective means of accomplishment.
From the worldly level up to the state of Śiva, [these stages exist] for the sake of higher and lower manifestations,
within their respective spheres of objects, for those who are fit to receive his grace.
Bound by the *anuṣṭubh* meter, it consists of thousands of millions of billions [of verses].

It proceeds from Śiva—the supreme cause whose nature is the manifestation of non-duality and the form of ultimate well-being—who, as the ultimate source, causes all causes ending with Śiva to appear within his own self-limitation; for this very reason, he is unseen.

From that whose very nature is a body whose form is non-dual with the Supreme Seer— this word [“tasmāt”] being distinct [from the preceding compound] due to the Vedic substitution of the ablative case ending [for the genitive]— and moreover,
from that in which there has arisen an expansion and vibration of that very same form, [which is] the nature of resonance (dhvani), consisting of the reflective awareness of sound (nādāmarśātmaka).

That which is extremely subtle, immeasurable, and all-pervasive; which is perfectly pure because it is devoid of being delimited by the *kalās* such as the letter 'A' and so forth; and which is endowed with supreme radiance and consists of the form of Great Knowledge—that very same [reality] is, in its other form, Śiva known as the Lord Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka.

Having deliberated upon the practices and ritual performances— ranging from worldly matters up to Śiva— for the sake of attaining their respective accomplishments, [one proceeds] by means of the gross form itself, which is other than [the subtle], and whose body consists of the five great mantras of Sadyojāta arranged in the sequence of the Daṇḍavaktra-bhaṅgī. This is done according to the specific recipients of grace for each individual case.

It is composed as a collection of various scriptures arising from the diverse streams of tradition, beginning with the Vedas and ending with the secret tantras, consisting of an infinite array of excellent texts. By this very statement— that [the scripture] was compiled by the Lord of three and a half crores of mantras seated upon the throne of mantras— room has been provided for the infinity of the scriptures.
By the phrase "O Great-Souled One of the Five Mantras," the various divisions of the scriptural streams (*srotas*) as taught in the *Śrīkaṇṭhīya-saṃhitā* and other texts are indicated. Among them:
"From Śiva, the supreme cause, who is peaceful and whose form is unseen..."
Having defined the nature of *nāda* with the passage beginning, "The great form of knowledge has emerged, which is beyond words," [it continues]:
"From that, this entire universe was born, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life."
Having said this, the emergence of the manifold elaborations of various scriptures through their different streams has been demonstrated.

From the words "That very [Self]" up to "is bound," it is shown that although the scriptures have distinct fruits according to the dispositions of those to be graced, they are in reality a single syntactical unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*).
It suggests that these [states] are vast, consisting of a full and undivided reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), in which the entire manifold of difference and non-difference has been woven together;
thus, it intimates that they are indeed the ultimate reality— the repose within the essence of the single, dense mass of consciousness and bliss— for one who knows such pervasion and knows the truth.
As it has been said:
"Since everything originates from Śiva and bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva."

Having thus demonstrated that the expansion of this treatise is rooted in a relationship with another, [the author] says the following with the intention of showing that it is also within the scope of other types of relationships:
"This was also raised in this manner by Paramaśiva himself."
Abiding in the roles of both teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself [manifests].
Through sentences consisting of preceding and following words, according to the distinction of their respective bases,
that knowledge was imparted to Īśvara by Śiva, through the will of the Lord.

This Vidyā was previously taught with due reverence by the Lord Śivabhaṭṭāraka—who consists of the supreme power of speech—to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). He is Sadāśiva himself, assuming various respective roles; thus, he stands in the position of both teacher and disciple within the realm of intuitive insight.

He bestowed upon the Lord that knowledge— which consists of the entire collection of scriptures characterized by *tantras* composed of sentences whose preceding and succeeding words are manifested by the supreme *mahāpaśyantī* power of speech through the subtle indication of the relationship between questioner and respondent.
He transmitted [it]. Regarding the phrase "by way of a difference in the substratum" (*ādhārabhedataḥ*), the meaning is:

having himself remained as that very self by relying on the difference in the substratum which consists of the Lord (*īśvara*). As for the reading "that knowledge was given to the Lord," this should be construed as having been indicated at the end of the previous verse, and then connected with the word "and" (*ca*) through ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).

It is to be explained. By this much, the great connection has been shown. By the phrase "by the will of Śiva," meaning by the will of Sadāśiva, he suggests that one upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has not occurred is not to be instructed. Regarding the word "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*)—

"Furthermore, that Vidyā, divided into eight groups, is indeed the Mātṛkā" (10.1144). This is because the Goddess, who is expressed by the term *mātṛkā*, is primarily characterized by such knowledge (*vidyā*); and thus, for the entire collection of mantras denoted by the word *vidyā*, as well as for [the teachings] beginning with Ananta-bhaṭṭāraka.
The Lord has taught that Tantra and its knowledge to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), who are the sovereigns of the wheel of mantras, by means of the method of transmission;
this has been brought to the state of reflective awareness (vimarśapada). "With devotion" means through the excellence of the outpouring of fervent love.
This is so even though the Mātṛkā belongs to the Blessed One and the mantras arise from it.

In the abode of the *vidyā-tattva*, the pervasion of the non-difference of the entire universe remains as if submerged, since it manifests there as non-different from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Therefore, in order to cause that [pervasion] to emerge, the transmission of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃkrānti*) occurs here by the Lord, out of a desire to favor the universe.
The agent is indeed appropriate [here]. From this point onward, the connection with the intervening material will continue until the end of the aphorism:
"O Goddess of the Gods, I too have fully drunk that which possesses authority" (8.36).
Having thus described the state of the scripture as extending up to the expansion of the *paśyantī* level, he speaks of it through the expansion of the *madhyamā* level:
"Therefore, that [state] is also attained by the Rudras, beginning with Māyā and ending with Niyati. (8.33)
"Therefore" means from Ananta Bhaṭṭāraka, the sovereign of the wheel of the principles of knowledge (vidyātattva).

"By those ending with Māyā and Niyati" refers to the Rudras who dwell within the coverings (kañcukas), beginning with the Maṇḍala; [the soul] reaches them by the very logic of transmigration. || 33 ||
Immediately thereafter, that very same knowledge— indeed,
that most difficult knowledge obtained by Śrīkaṇṭha from Īśvara—
is as follows: "For I am the disciple of the Lord Śiva, whose nature is Īśvara."

The disciples in the mandala and so forth are infinite. Here, in the center, the Rudras who preside over the principle of the individual (puruṣatattva) have been established as the cause of bondage; therefore, the transmission of this knowledge-power has not been bestowed upon them.
From that as well, in the same manner—by the will of the Lord (Īśvara), that [world] below was proclaimed by him for the Rudras. (8.34)
Having initiated [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule from Pradhāna up to the end of the Śatarudra,
my own initiation as well as my consecration was likewise performed in the past.
The Tantra that accomplishes all aims was given of old by Śrīkaṇṭha;

for although Lord Śrīkaṇṭha resides in the principle of *guṇa*, he nevertheless possesses an extraordinary power due to being a disciple of Śiva, and thus [the Tantra] belongs to those situated above him, who possess *prakṛti*.

He is the bestower of grace upon Krodha and the other [eight Rudras], as well as upon the Rudras beginning from Svādhāra-tattva and ending with Śatarudra. "Myself also"—this is the statement of the Blessed Lord Umāpati, the dweller of Kailāsa and the proclaimer of the Tantra. Thus, Ananta and the others [are likewise graced].
Śrīkaṇṭha is a disciple of Śiva, whose nature is that of the venerable Lord Īśvara;

the Maṇḍalins, however, are disciples of Ananta; and Krodha and the others, ending with the hundred Rudras, as well as Umāpati, are disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha—this was taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, that which [was stated] by Kheṭakanandana—

It has been stated [in the *Tantrasadbhāva* 30]: "The lords of the maṇḍalas are Śrīkaṇṭha, Krodha and the others, the hundred Bhavas, and the Vīreśas; these have had their vision and action manifested by the Supreme Lord through the conjunction with Kalā and the other [categories].
This occurs, as described, either directly or through a lineage.

This must be explained, and not without distinction. Regarding the phrases "having initiated" and "having performed the consecration," these refer first to the application of the immersion of Śambhu (śāmbhava-samāveśa), and subsequently to the application of the immersion of Śakti (śākta-samāveśa).
Thus, there is no [right] for one who has not been initiated to receive knowledge, nor for one who has not been consecrated.
Thus, it is taught that one has the qualification for giving that [gift].
Now, O Mistress of the Gods, this tantra and that knowledge have been drunk up by me along with you, through the very method of transmission, together with their authoritative power.
From this point onward is the expansion of Vaikharī speech. || 36 ||

Having thus revealed the relationship known as the "intermediate," he prescribes the end of the divine [offering]: "You too, having first performed the ritual, should give [the offering] to Skanda and Rudra, and to the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, as well as to the Vasus, the Mothers, and the Sun. (8.37)
O Supreme Goddess, having gathered the Nāgas and Yakṣas in the world,
the ritual consists of initiation and consecration.
He speaks of the relationship between the divine and the non-divine:
"Tell [me] of the sages...
And thus, by the Goddess's entrustment of the office of bestowing grace upon the universe, the Blessed One’s great compassion is demonstrated.
Fully nourished.
He states the extraordinary relationship: ".........to the sages, and even among men. (8.38)

"Speak," [the Lord] remained standing. For it is the Goddess herself, whose nature is that of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), the presiding ground of the universe, and whose heart is overflowing with the essence of the desire to bestow grace, who effects this grace by entering the bodies of various teachers.
And thus, everywhere, the supreme relationship alone—extending even to the divine relationship—is what prevails.
This has been stated. As it was said:
"All [of these] consist of the portions of the Supreme;
they are the Great, the Intermediate, the Divine, the Mixed, and the Non-divine, which follows that."
Thus, in the Trikahṛdaya. || 38 ||
He concludes:
"Thus, this supreme, divine tantra, a casket containing the jewels of accomplishment, must be kept strictly secret by you; it should not be given to just anyone. (8.39)

Although you have been granted authority over all the previously mentioned tantras, nevertheless, because it is filled with the secret meanings contained within these chapters that have already been determined and those yet to be determined,
this is the most excellent and superior among the collection of Bhairava tantras arising from the Southern Stream.

This supreme, divine Tantra, which bestows all enjoyments and liberation, must be concealed by you; it should be revealed only to those who have received the descent of the power of the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti, and not to others. May there be auspiciousness!
From the gods down to the end of the Krama, this entire [teaching] consists of the form of instruction and protection.

May this entire universe, from the state of Supreme Śiva down to the end of the worlds, which is established as a single unified sentence within the scripture— having attained rest through the dissolution of duality and being intent upon the manifestation of its own pure and autonomous abode— be for the benefit of every living being.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Section on Aṃśakas," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
Having delineated the state of the manifest (*sakala*) upon the sublime foundation of the venerable unmanifest (*niṣkala*), [the author proceeds].
I take refuge in that Bhairava, in whom one finds rest within the reality that is beyond time.

Following the description of the five *praṇavas* to be propitiated for the sake of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the true nature of time—which contains many objects of knowledge useful for that purpose—has been stated, and the reality of the *aṃśakas* has been explained.
Incidentally, the descent of the *tantra* has also been shown. Now, [the text proceeds] with the destruction of the multitude of obstacles.

Desiring to bestow grace, Śrī Bhairava spoke, wishing to explain the procedure for the venerable Koṭarākṣa— which instantly accomplishes one’s desired goals and constitutes an expansion of the protective wheel— even though it had not been asked about: Śrī Bhairava said:

Henceforth, I shall proclaim this supreme secret. The word "henceforth" (ataḥ) serves to indicate the sequence already explained. I shall speak with excellence—that is, with great care and a desire to favor [the disciples]. It is the "supreme secret," which pacifies all obstacles.
And it bestows the desired accomplishment instantaneously.
Therefore,
O lady of excellent vows, I shall tell you that which has not been declared to anyone.

By the address "O you whose vow is beautiful"—meaning whose state is one of focused attention upon the supreme reality—it is intimated that this practice is intended for the most capable and diligent disciples. For this reason, it has not been taught to anyone other than a worthy Goddess. || 1 ||
This is revealed: "O beautiful lady, as the god Mahābhairava was sporting, [the mantra] that effects creation and destruction emerged from his heart. (9.2)
The Lord Mahābhairava is Svacchandanātha according to the definition established in the tenth chapter of the first book;

he is one who habitually performs the play (*krīḍā*) consisting of the desire to favor [beings] by pacifying all obstacles without exception and accomplishing all supernatural powers (*siddhi*), [proceeding] from his heart, which consists of the power of his own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
The creator of both emanation and reabsorption is the deity named Śrīkoṭarākṣa, who is about to be described;
he has "emerged swiftly," meaning he has surged forth. For this very reason, the Lord is called Aghorahṛdaya (the One Whose Heart is Not Terrible). || 2 ||
To show that Blessed One, he said:

[He is] one whose body is like the fire at the end of an aeon, whose roar is like the clouds at the time of dissolution, whose fangs resemble a mass of lightning, and whose radiance is equal to the flames of matted hair. (9.3)
His eyes were the moon, the sun, and fire; he had deep-set, terrifying eyes, a broad expanse of chest, and wore a serpent as his sacred thread.
Wearing a crown of shimmering rubies, adorned with serpent earrings,
displaying the majesty of a necklace of snakes, and possessing bracelets and anklets made of serpents.
Clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with a girdle of serpents,
his garment covered by an elephant hide, and having the moon as his crest-ornament.
Five-faced, mounted upon a corpse, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
adorned with a garland of skulls and bearing a sword and a shield.
The god holds a noose and a goad, is equipped with an arrow and a bow,
carries a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and has hands that grant boons and fearlessness.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, radiant with its throbbing lower lip,
it is bowed to by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and is difficult even for the gods to attain.

All of this has its true nature explained by the commentaries previously cited. He whose two fangs have risen like a mass of lightning, whose matted locks and flames possess an incomparable radiance and brilliance, and whose eyes are shaped like hollows— by this, his state of being perceived from within is indicated.
He displays an outward gaze, and his extreme ferocity is expressed by his very name.
In the word *mekhala*, however, the vowel is short; he is the Lord (*īśvara*). He has three eyes in each face. His arms are extended and formed into a circle. His lower lip is quivering.
By virtue of being intent upon devouring all obstacles without exception. || 9 ||
He states that this form is to be worshipped by those who are to be favored: "In this way, one should contemplate that god Bhairava as Svacchanda;
for Svacchandanātha himself, due to his manifold forms, appears in this most terrifying guise for the purpose of striking fear into obstacles."
The meaning is that one should contemplate by means of the form.
And therefore:
"By remembering [him], the Lord destroys the most formidable mass of sins. (9.10)

It was precisely for the sake of pacifying the great sins of meditators that caused the arising of diseases and the like that he assumed such a form by his own will. Therefore, through mere remembrance, it indeed destroys the mass of sins that has become ready to yield the intense experience of suffering. For this very reason:

It is understood that from the Four-faced One [Brahmā] there arose another deity, such as the venerable Śrī Vyādhibhakṣa-bhaṭṭāraka, who consumes the great sins that serve as the cause of diseases. 10.
Furthermore, his mantra, previously described as consisting of thirty-two syllables,
should be recited while being absorbed therein— preceded and followed by five *praṇavas*— in accordance with its terrifying form.

One should recite this great mantra at the conclusion of worship during the occasion of *japa*, [a mantra] whose beginning and end consist of five *praṇavas* whose true nature has been previously explained, which is dissolved and resting within that very form of the five *praṇavas*, and which is both based upon and permeated by them for the sake of breaking through that [limitation]. And thus:
Because it is radiant through the sequence of the signified and the signifier, because it is spoken by Aghorīśvarī,
and because it is surrounded by a specific future retinue of deities—
distinct from others— this is indeed a separate ritual practice [consisting of] thirty-two syllables. || 11 ||
I shall now declare the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for such a person as this, in brief and not in detail.
It is called *kalpa* because by means of it one is fashioned (*kalpyate*) or propitiated (*ārādhyate*); thus, it is a rule (*vidhāna*).
He said to him: "And on that previously mentioned plot of ground, which is purified and possesses auspicious characteristics... (9.12)
Having drawn the mandala there with the auspicious pigments previously mentioned, in a place strewn with heaps of flowers and perfumed with incense and fragrances; (9.13)
Having made it well-measured with a cord, equal on all sides, and square, measuring one cubit, two cubits, four cubits, or eight cubits; || 9-14 ||
Having established [the mandala] as before, O fair-faced one, [one should mark] the directions and sub-directions with the previously mentioned [mantras]:
"The falling of the colored powders is done with the *dhāman*. (4.35)
By this statement, it is indicated that [the decoration] is with pigments such as vermilion and the like; the rest is already explained.

He says that this mandala is superior to the previous one: "Having drawn a lotus in the center, provided with eight petals, a pericarp, and endowed with four gates, it is distinguished by its filaments. (9.15)
Having drawn a beautiful wheel of thirty-two syllables on the outside,
and having thus properly laid out the lines, one should likewise draw a circle on the exterior.
One should fashion a square adjacent to that, with a pathway on the outside;
the gate should be fashioned according to the measurement of the central lotus, as before.

Thus, according to the measurement of the circle, having drawn a well-executed circular rotation and having made a square adjacent to it, one should fashion the pathway (vīthī). Outside of that, [one should fashion] the inner lotus-field measurement, enriched with the beauty of the neck, the cheeks, the ornaments, and the secondary ornaments.
One should arrange four doors in the four directions. || 17 ||
Then, once the mandala has been completed, the practitioner— his body smeared with ashes, adorned with mudrās and ornaments,
wearing his hair as a sacred thread, naked, and with his senses restrained— [should proceed]. (9.18)
O Dear One, with a conch and arghya vessel in hand, having consecrated his body through the sakalīkaraṇa rite and having assigned the weapon-mantra (astra) all around, one should worship Bhairava.
Seated upon the seat of the *praṇava*,

[the practitioner]— by virtue of being smeared with ashes and so forth— is said to possess the status of one who has undertaken the Great Vow (*mahāvratin*) at the time of the practitioner’s mantra-worship; for this very reason, obstacles arise against those who identify with him on account of his imitation of Supreme Bhairava.

They perish. Regarding what is to be cultivated here, bathing in water and so forth are not mentioned; he is "clothed in the directions" (*digvāsas*), because for anyone other than him, the wearing of a loincloth (*kaupīna*) occurs precisely through the destruction of his bonds. Here, by the force of the context, the "conch" (*śaṅkha*) refers to the *mahāśaṅkha*. "On all sides" (*paritaḥ*) means a rampart of weapons (*astraprākāra*) everywhere.
The state of being seated upon the *praṇava* is as before.
How one should worship, and who that Bhairava is, he says:
"...with the syllable *Haṃsa*, [one worships] that very same manifest god, Svacchanda, the Supreme Lord. (9.20)

"By the *mūrti* [mantra] with the syllable *haṃsa*" refers to the previously mentioned *cinmūrti* mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables, which takes the form of the complete *mūrti*. "That very one" refers to what was mentioned before. || 20 ||
What is undifferentiated? He says, "No"—that which is supremely radiant, stainless, and formless;
with that, O Goddess, one should invoke...

One should invoke [the deity] with the *āvāhana-mudrā*, accompanied by that which was previously described as the partless (*niṣkala*) reality— possessing a supreme (*parama*) and most excellent radiance (*nirbhāsa*), free from affliction (*anāmaya*) because it removes the connection with illusion (*māyā*), and formless (*arūpaka*) because it is without shape (*anākṛti*)— which, according to the method stated, abides without beginning or end.
One should bring [the deity] face-to-face for the purpose of worship.
Furthermore:
...and likewise the head of Ṛcīka and the topknot (śikhā). || 9-21 ||
One should likewise fashion the armor (*varma*), the eyes (*netra*), and the weapon (*astra*) with that very same [mantra].
"With that very same" means with the *hṛdaya* and other limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in their unmanifest form (*naiṣkala*), and not, as before, with the manifest form (*sakala*).
However, for the five Brahma-mantras, there is no division into manifest and so forth; thus, it is as previously stated.
Immediately after that assignment (nyāsa), the placement of the partless limbs (niṣkalāṅganyāsa) is performed upon the form of the Blessed One.

And thus, when at the very time of invoking the Blessed One who is of a single nature consisting of both the partless (*niṣkala*) and the with-parts (*sakala*), one has performed the utterance of the partless and with-parts mantras, applied the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*) prescribed for the partless state, and completed the placement of the faces and the partless limbs—
Installation, placement, and the worship consisting of the offering of cessation, the water for honor, and so forth. || 9-22 ||
O fair-faced one, everything—both that which has been stated and that which has not been stated—must be performed by him alone.

All [rites] beginning with the installation (sthāpana) should be performed as previously demonstrated, preceded by the binding of mudrās. "By him alone" means by the manifest (sakala) form encapsulated within the unmanifest (niṣkala). "That which has been stated" refers to the installation and so forth; however, "that which has not been stated" is as follows:
The sequence beginning with the welcome, water for the feet, water for sipping, and bathing, and ending with the offering of oneself.
And thus:
"One should worship Bhairava, who stands in the center, accompanied by the six limbs. (9.23)
"Situated in the middle" means located in the center; "Bhairava" means the splendor of Bhairava—this is the meaning. || 23 ||
Furthermore, here in the wheel with thirty-two spokes outside the lotus— one should place the goddesses residing on the petals by means of the thirty-two syllables,
beginning from the eastern spoke until they are established at the end. (9.24)

"Situated on the petals" means that since an eight-petaled lotus has been mentioned, one should arrange [the deities] within the wheel consisting of the four spokes situated along each petal in every direction.
"By thirty-two syllables" refers to the Lord (Īśvara) with the letter *ta* elided; by that [mantra], one [worships] the thirty-two goddesses.
One should arrange it by dividing [the mantra] into thirty-two syllables, meaning those consisting of thirty-two syllables. || 24 ||
I shall state their names, numbering thirty-two.
He now defines them as being in the form of the initial syllables of names that correspond to the essence of the expansion of the syllables situated within the mantra:
Aruṇā, Ghoṣā, and the goddess Revatī, the bestower of enjoyments. || 9-25 ||
Sthāpanī, Ghorasaṃjñā, Rakṣā, Bhārabharā, Ghorarūpā, Ravā, Ghoṇā, Rati, Tārā, and Rūpiṇī. || 9-26 ||
Bhayahāni, Caṇḍā, Sarvadā, Varā, Takṣakī, Śārvī, Barbarā, and Sarvagā likewise [are the goddesses]. (9.27)
Raudrī, Bhrāmaṇī, Nāginī, Manoharā, Stambhanī, Roṣaṇī, Drāvā, Rudrā, and Praśāsinī. (9.28)
"The Goddess who removes fear is to be known as thirty-two [syllables] according to that sequence.

By "according to that sequence," it is meant following the order of the syllables contained within the mantra. By stating this, he indicates that the pervasion of the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra is not merely in the form of the previously determined sentences.
The Lord indicates that these goddesses also possess a pervasive nature corresponding to the previously described wheel of deities according to their respective colors, and so forth;
he then states the mantra for the invocation and other rites of these goddesses: "First the Praṇava, then the syllable, then the name of the goddess, and likewise the word 'namas'. (9.29)
This procedure, however, must be performed for all [mantras] by one who knows the ritual rules.

"Syllable" (varṇa) means each individual [syllable] in sequence, pertaining to the thirty-two syllables. "Name" (nāma) means [the name] ending in the dative case, as is implied by the context. "Procedure" (vidhi) refers to the manner of reciting the mantra concerning the worship and other rites.

By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure," it is implied that one should understand that the name is used with the vocative case-ending for the invocation and so forth, and that the application of the caste-designation should likewise follow the specific requirements of the rite.

Now, he indicates the visualization for these four goddesses in each direction, according to the previously mentioned method, following the principles of the pervasion of the Bhairava-expansion (*bhairavīya-prapañca-vyāpti*), the principles (*tattva*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and the Bhairavas themselves: [The visualization follows...]
The first group of four is golden-hued, possessing a radiance equal to that of a rainbow.
One should meditate upon him as having four faces and four arms, holding a vajra in his hand, well-adorned, decorated with a garland of skulls, and smiling. (9.31)

The "first four" refers to the group of four beginning with Aruṇa, situated upon the four petals of the lotus in the eastern direction; because they correspond to the guardians of those directions, they possess a golden luster and hold vajras in their hands, and are described as having a splendor equal to Indra’s bow, meaning they are radiant with various shimmering colors within.
Because the upward-facing face is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it lacks suitability for the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*);

therefore, even though the circle of deities is presided over by the five-faced Śaktimat, it is shown to assume forms such as four faces and four arms in accordance with the practitioner’s attainment of powers. In one [instance], in the right hand...

Since the *vajra* has already been mentioned, even though it is not explicitly stated, his bearing of the skull-bowl (*kapāla*) and the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), as well as his hand displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-hasta*), are understood to be present in part because he imitates the form of Bhairava; for this reason, his being adorned with a garland of skulls is also entirely consistent, and accordingly, one should understand that he possesses three eyes in each face.
The state of having a beautiful voice and the state of being smiling are intended to show that this entity is of such a nature as to be conducive to granting unimpeded success;
thus, everything from the four-facedness up to the state of being smiling should be understood to apply to every group of four.
Likewise, [the description of] holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga in the hands, and so forth. || 9-31 ||

One should always remember the deity of the southeast as having the luster of red color and holding a spear in his hand; one should remember the deity of the south as black-colored, extremely terrifying, and holding a staff in his hand.
One should visualize the deity of the Nairṛta direction as blue, with the luster of a blue lotus, holding a sword in his hand;
one should contemplate the deity of the western quarter as dark-green, holding a noose in his hand.
In the northwestern direction, one should know [the deity] to be smoky-colored, holding a banner in his hand, and very restless; in the north, he is white and holds a mace and a shield.
Likewise, in the northeast, [the deity] has the luster of crystal and holds a trident as a weapon in his hand.

Regarding the four goddesses in the north, since it was stated by his own throat that they hold shields, they should not be visualized as holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). [The same applies to] the four-facedness and so forth.
Everything else is as before.
Regarding this meditation, he states the result: "He who, devoted to such meditation, should constantly practice this wheel... (9.35).
O lady of excellent hips, within half a year, his success shall become threefold,
consisting of the superior, the middling, and the inferior forms.
Having thus described the perfection of meditative absorption (dhyāna), he now indicates the appropriate field for the perfection of recitation (japa) for that very [practitioner]:
"On Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Pāriyātra, and likewise Arbuda. (9.36)
O beloved, these eight mountain sites— namely Vindhya, Śrīparvata, and likewise Kolagiri— are conducive to the attainment of siddhi.
Furthermore:
"In the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā..."—the term *sambādha* means a crowded or narrow space; it refers to the extent of the riverbed where those two [rivers] are mixed together.
...in Kurukṣetra, O fair-faced one. || 9-37 ||
Established at Gaṅgādvāra and Prayāga,
the region situated between the Sarasvatī and Carmaṇvatī rivers is Brahmāvarta.
Likewise, on the highly meritorious Antarvedī and on the Narmadā river.
Antarvedī is the region between the flows of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; it is also on the bank of the Narmadā. || 38 ||
Furthermore:
"In a very moist region of the earth, delightful with clusters of lotuses"—the construction is: "in that region of the earth which is a very moist place, delightful with clusters of lotuses."
Furthermore: "In whichever places the Blessed Lord Śiva, the Self-Existent One [dwells]," || 9.39 ||
In those places, O Goddess of the Gods, one who is established in restraint, has conquered the senses, whose speech is controlled,
and whose mind is serene, should be devoted to the recitation of a hundred thousand syllables.
Subsisting on vegetables, eating fruits, and devoted to consuming wild rice and similar grains;
intent upon worship at the three times of day, he was dedicated to the fire-sacrifice.
The mantra of that great being who has cultivated his own self and knows the ritual procedures for protection shall indeed be successful.
And he shall accomplish the moving and the unmoving world. 9-42.

Because that field has descended [into this world] solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon the self-existent ones (Svayambhūs), it possesses an extraordinary capacity for granting spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). "Established in the observances" (niyamastha) means one who is devoted to purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and surrender to the Lord (Īśvara-praṇidhāna). And as for speech...
By whom [the breath] has been completely restrained and made single-mindedly intent upon recitation (*japa*);

whose self—that is, the mind—has become serene and free from the latent impressions of attachment; and who is devoted to the recitation of thirty-two hundred thousand syllables along with the ten-fold sacrificial offerings (*homāḥ*), as previously described, and not like others—[who merely recite] a single syllable.
"The mantra for him [is recited] one hundred thousand times," because the word *akṣara* does not denote a mantra,

and because this statement appears no different from the previous statement, "by a hundred thousand [recitations] according to the number of syllables" (6.51). Nor [does it apply] to that which lasts six months.

There is no inconsistency in the aforementioned meditation on the wheel (*cakradhyāna*), because it is the very purity of that [meditation], even without the rule for the number of recitations (*japa*), that serves as the cause for the stated result. Nor should it be said that accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not arise from meditation alone, for that is established hundreds of times in the *Āgamas*; however, in the case of recitation (*japa*), such appropriate meditation is not [required].

We respond: if the aforementioned meditation on the wheel were an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the mantra recitation, it would also have to prescribe a rule for the recitation of the goddesses of that wheel; so enough of this. "One whose self is cultivated" means one whose heart is confident; for that very reason, he is a "great being" (*mahāsattva*), steadfast and possessed of an utterly pure mind.

"Of protection"—meaning in the form of the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), the protective wall (*prākāra*), and so forth; by the word "and" (*ca*), the offering to the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla-bali*) and the like are included; "one who knows the procedure" means one who knows the ritual requirements (*itikartavyatā*). || 42 ||
To briefly demonstrate what was stated— that one should accomplish all that is moving and unmoving— the author casts a glance toward the subject matter of the forthcoming chapter:
"The Fire of Time, the hells, the netherworlds, and Hāṭakeśvara."
Beyond that are the seven worlds together with the Brahmāṇḍa, consisting of five groups of eight.
And the eightfold divine womb (devayoni), ending with Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
as well as Niyati, the principle of Time (kāla-tattva), Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā. (9.44)
The principles of Māyā, Vidyeśvara, Sādākhya, and that which is within the sphere of Śakti—all these are accomplished without effort through the power of the King of Mantras. (9.45)

Everything up to the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva), which is to be determined in the chapter immediately following this one, comes under the control of the practitioner; therefore, the practitioner becomes one whose very form is Śiva—this is the meaning. || 45 ||

And since this entire universe exists within it, the principle of the "stick and the cake" (the simultaneous attainment of both) remains established for those who have achieved limited results; thus he says:
"The previously mentioned action is indeed swift, whether it be inferior, middling, or superior."
One shall accomplish it; of this there is no doubt, according to the word of Bhairava.

The inferior and other rites are as previously described. Furthermore, this King of Mantras— when propitiated through one hundred thousand recitations along with burnt offerings according to the previously stated method, and assisted by the combination of substances as previously specified— accomplishes all those inferior and other rites previously mentioned, such as killing, driving away, subjugation, summoning, pacification, and nourishment.

Since it accomplishes [the goal], this [teaching] is indeed established. One should have confidence here exactly as are the words of Bhairava; for confidence that is unshakable is the sign of accomplishment. || 46 ||
Now, in order to describe this very same vision as the "Solitary Hero" (ekavīra)— without the retinue of the circle of thirty-two deities— as the subject for the most capable practitioner,
he says: "Now, relying upon the Solitary Hero, [the practice] is endowed with the six limbs."
Having joined it with the *jāti* [mantra], one should place it upon an eight-petaled lotus of *kuśa* grass.
One should worship, according to the previously mentioned procedure,

the Supreme Lord alone— the Hero who is intent on accomplishing those various supernatural powers (siddhis) that culminate in liberation for practitioners— surrounded by the retinue of goddesses and others, accompanied only by the six faces and limbs.

"By the previously mentioned method" means by the entire sequence stated in the passage beginning with "one whose body is smeared with ashes" (9.18), for the purpose of worship in that very same field mentioned before.
One should worship according to the ritual procedure ending with the oblation (homa). || 47 ||

Then, having pledged to perform the recitation and the fire-oblation according to the stated number, and being intent upon the recitation, the oblation, and the worship for their successful completion— O Great Goddess— he meditated solely upon the Supreme Lord Svacchanda. (9.48)
"O Goddess, one obtains all desired objects; there is no doubt in this.
Having thus described the modes of worship according to the specific requirements for the practitioner's success, he speaks in order to introduce the ritual for protection:
Now, one should apply the Aghora mantra in the protective rites as follows: || 9.49 ||
I shall speak thus; listen with a one-pointed mind.
O beautiful lady, having drawn the wheel endowed with thirty-two spokes therein— || 9.50 ||
O fair-faced one, it should be perfectly level and joined with the filaments of the navel;
having taken yellow pigment (gorocanā) combined with prepared lac-dye.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should draw it with a green blade of *dūrvā* grass.
Having mixed *gorocanā* with *siddha-siddhārthaka* seeds and lac,
one should write that wheel— meaning on birch bark— with a dark-blue blade of *dūrvā*.
Others say that "siddhālaktaka" is a specific kind of lac-dye. However, the claim that it refers to saffron taken from the feet of the blessed goddess Caṇḍikā is incorrect.
Then, at the hub of this wheel, one should place the King of Vidyās, accompanied by the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (9.52)

O Goddess of gods, one should draw the object to be accomplished (sādhya) at the end of the power (śakti); O lady of excellent hips, it should be placed within the eyes and so forth in the middle of the *kaṣa*.
Having encircled it with the letter *ī*,
one should place the King of Vidyās, the nine-syllable mantra, within the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*).
This means it is situated in the pericarp of the lotus located at the hub of the thirty-two-spoked wheel.
The *bindu*, *nāda*, and *śakti* are to be written here according to the sequence of the script. "Sādhya" refers to the name [of the person to be accomplished];
by stating it thus, he indicates that the non-difference between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) is produced by the will of the Lord (*īśa*).
"In the middle of *ka* and *ṣa*" refers to the *ka* and *ṣa* sounds belonging to the letter *kṣa*, which is associated with the ninefold self (*navātman*).

"Between those two" means in the first part of the *ṣa* that follows the *ka*. "Obstructed" means encapsulated by the previously mentioned three-syllable eye-mantra (*netramantra*). Furthermore, regarding the syllables of that eye-mantra, there is first the forward order (*anulomakrama*) and subsequently the reverse order (*pratilomakrama*).

The tradition: "Having encircled with the letter *ī*" means that one should write the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*), and within it, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished, enclosed by the Netra-mantra and surrounded three times by that letter *ī*, in the middle of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*. This is the meaning.
Having written thus in the pericarp,
O Goddess, one should place [the mantra] within the enclosure of the rampart for the previously mentioned deities.

The tradition here is that the previously mentioned [deities] beginning with Aruṇā, who consist of the individual syllables of the aforementioned mantras, should be situated at the end of the object of accomplishment (sādhya) facing the Blessed One, and not turned away from him.
Then, [in the center of that], one should write the object to be accomplished within its interior. || 9-54 ||
Its name is "the probandum" (sādhya). || 54 ||
How so?—Having performed that within the womb of existence (*bhavagarbha*), one should envelop it with that which is called the letter *ī*;
three times, O lady of excellent limbs, while relying upon the yoga of meditation. (9.55)
Let there be the *praṇava* (oṃ) here; since the mantra of the Goddess preceding it has already been stated, [place the name] within its womb—that is, in its middle.

Having thus formed the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should subsequently encircle it from above with the letter *i*, which is the first half of the *māyābīja*, as before. Such is the name of the person to be accomplished, characterized by this specific procedure.

The meaning is that one should write [the syllable] in the middle of each individual mantra-syllable of the Goddess. In this way, for the sound *gho*, the sound *re*, and any other, this should be written in the middle of the first curved portion. And each such individual mantra-syllable of the Goddess is thus constituted.
One should place [the deities] upon the spokes in the sequence starting from the east, facing the King of Mantras located in the pericarp.

"Relying on meditative yoga" means that one should write [the diagram] after having meditated upon the essential form of the Blessed One and the deities according to their described forms suitable for the attainment of siddhi, and having contemplated their pervasive presence.

Thus, this entire wheel has been described as follows: "And having fixed [the syllable] *kroṃ* above, O fair-faced one, eight *kroṃ*s should be placed outside its eight directions; such is the meaning."
Then, having sprinkled this with wine, one should worship it thoroughly with flowers and incense. || 9-56 ||

Indu is camphor. The worship, beginning from the central mantra with all the mantras, is accomplished according to their respective places and according to the drawing, as well as the rite of *utpuṃsana*. || 56 ||
Then,
O fair-faced one, one should wrap that flawless and even birch-bark [manuscript] without gaps;
having wrapped it with a five-colored thread— (9.57)
One should subsequently seal it with *siktha* and place it in the midst of honey (*kṣaudra*).
*Siktha* refers to beeswax; *kṛṣaudra* refers to honey, which is the essence of the sap of all medicinal herbs. Placing [the object] therein serves to nourish the one to be accomplished.
He states the fruit of this protective rite:
"O beloved, when one is seized by Time and has come under the sway of death... (9.58).
"Having recognized one who is marked by the signs of death, one should inscribe this protection;
for such a person, death shall not occur—thus spoke Bhairava. (9.59)
