The word *yadā* is displaced in order and should be joined at the beginning of the phrase *samālikhet*; after this, the word *tadā* is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). Thus, [the subject] is marked by other ill omens (*ariṣṭa*) mentioned in the section on time or by others;
and for that very reason—
"One hundred and one deaths are established within this body;

among them, one is the death of time (kālamṛtyu), while the remaining are known as adventitious (āgantuka). According to this principle, that which is afflicted by the hundred adventitious [deaths] and seized by the single death of time is curable.

The Blessed One has declared that when a Guru, having understood this protection (*rakṣā*), inscribes it, then for him there shall be no death whatsoever; one should not have any doubt in this matter. How does this come about from mere writing? Because, according to the principle established in the *Śrīsarvavīra* and the *Śrībhargaśikhā*:
Even the script is of the very nature of the expansion of the Supreme Power; therefore, since this has been thus promised by the Lord Himself, this must be considered as truly so. || 59 ||
He states another method for protecting against death:
"O lady of excellent hips, one should write the name of whoever [is to be protected] within the womb of Kapālīśa on a birch-bark leaf with the juice of *rocanā*. (9.60)
Situated in the middle of a cavity formed by the syllable Oṃ, and constricted by the letters of the eyes, through the application of the Vauṣaṭ-suffix, death does not occur for him. (9.61)
Kapālīśa is as previously mentioned; his "womb" (garbha) is, as before, in the middle of *kaṣa*. Of what kind is the name?

It stands in the middle of a cavity formed by the syllable *oṃ*, being encapsulated by the syllable *oṃ* at both the beginning and the end. And having been thus made, it is characterized by the previously mentioned "eye-syllables" (*nayana-akṣara*) through the application of the *auṣaṭ*-class suffixes placed afterwards.
"Enclosed" (*rodhitam*) means that, as before, it has been encapsulated at the beginning and end by means of the forward and reverse sequences;

"in all directions" refers to the eight directions because no specific direction was mentioned. And here, as before, [the procedure] extends from the drawing with stalks of *dūrvā* grass and worship, up to the placing of honey in the center.
Everything should be followed accordingly. || 61 ||

Having thus described the victory over death through this protective rite based on the eight Bhairavas situated in the enclosure and the King of Vidyās, Kapālīśa, located at the beginning and end, the Lord also incidentally prescribes the accomplishment of other rites by means of the sequence of yantras:
O Goddess of the gods, one should interlace the name of the target with the word "śikhya";
one should then apply the syllable of fire both below and above the syllables of the target. (9.62)

By means of the mantra of the one whose vehicle is the peacock (Śikhivāhana), which was previously mentioned and is called Śikhyāhva; "one should interlace" (vidarbhayet) means that one should form the mantra by interspersing it according to the rule stated in another scripture: "The object of expression (abhidheya) should come first, and then the mantra should follow once. [In this case], the "syllable of fire" (analārṇa) is the letter *ra*.

In each instance, one should join the syllables of the name to be accomplished (sādhya) above and below [the seed-syllable]. In this manner, one should fashion this [diagram] as described, situated within a wind-mandala inside a fire-mandala;
the fire-mandala is triangular, and outside of that, the wind-mandala is hexagonal and circular.
And for whomever this is written, a burning indeed arises...
because it is fanned by the wind and kindled by fire, and because its syllables are situated in the midst of the color of fire.
And because he was terrified by the one whose vehicle is the peacock (Śiva).
Is the fire-mandala (āgneyamaṇḍala) to be entered merely by the mere fear of Śikhivāhana? It is not merely that; rather—..................
[it is] raised within by the utterance of *phaṭ* and other [mantras].
The interpretation that "it is not feared by one who knows the seed-syllable of the fire-vehicled [deity] ending with the sound *phaṭ*" is incorrect,
because such a meaning of the sentence does not exist.
And immediately after this writing, having worshipped the Lord of Mantras, one should contemplate the person to be accomplished as blazing right in the center of this wheel for seven days.
Then, for him—
according to the word of Bhairava— a burning sensation arises at that very moment.
He now describes the killing by means of the application of the King of Wrath (Krodharāja):
But [the deity] Krodharāja, restrained and situated in the center of the charnel ground cloth, || 9-64 ||

O beautiful lady, one should write [the mantra] with a pen from a cremation ground, using ink mixed with poison and blood; the name of the person [to be targeted] should be included, accompanied by the terrifying utterances of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Through the application of the mantra "māraya," one who is endowed with the cruel class [of mantras] causes death within seven nights, even if he is well protected by various safeguards.

The word "he too" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Taking charcoal from a cremation ground—that is, *śmaśānāṅgāra*—and having made ink with it mixed with the blood and poison of a *preta*, one should write the name of the person upon a fragment of a *preta*-cloth, placing the syllables *huṃ phaṭ* at the end as a terrifying threat; then, having uttered *huṃ phaṭ*, afterwards...

It is written as being obstructed by the previously mentioned King of Wrath (*krodharāja*), and so forth, as internally enjoined; furthermore, it is joined with the word "slay" (*māraya*); and moreover, it is inscribed together with the fierce seed-syllable *huṃ phaṭ*.
Even if he is protected by guardians, he dies within seven nights. Herein is the form of the glorious King of Wrath.
One should contemplate that which is fierce and suited for the destruction of enemies. 66.
Now, he describes the terrifying application for the purpose of terrifying an enemy:
"O Great Goddess, O Mistress of the Gods, the *vikarāla* [mantra] is established with the noose above and below;
it is conjoined with the name of the victim and the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*. (9.67)
Without effort, he does not endure [the enemy]...
for that person whose name is to be accomplished, the specific mantra called Vikarāla— accompanied by *huṃ* and *phaṭ* and terrifying— is written in the four directions using the aforementioned ink.
He does not tolerate that [offense] of his with ease or without effort; thus reads the manuscript from Aiśa (the Vedic/epic dialect).
He asks: "What is not endurable for this [practitioner]? and answers: ".........there shall be fear of that enemy.
And here, the form of the venerable Vikarāla is situated in the four directions around the target who stands in the center.
It should be contemplated as having arisen through its nature of causing terror.
Now he describes the application of Manmatha for the purpose of subjugation:
"O fair-faced one, having joined the name of the person to be acted upon with Manmatha... (9.68).
Beginning with *dhruva* and ending with *svāhā*, accompanied by red visualization—O lady of excellent hips, [the practitioner] named so-and-so stands here facing that direction. (9.69)

One should perform recitation and fire-offerings so that [the person] may come under the control of such-and-such a one; they come under control within seven days—this is the certainty of the scripture. (9.70)

One should divide that very name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), which is joined with the "Manmatha" (the seed-syllable *hvūauṃ*)— consisting of the aggregate of the syllables *hvūauṃ* as previously described and accompanied by the nasal bindu— by appending the word *svāhā* at the end; that is, having joined it with the internal word ending in "O so-and-so, may he come under the control of so-and-so."
With such a mantra preceded by the *praṇava*,

the practitioner— visualizing the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) as red and facing the direction in which that person resides— if performs recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*) for seven days using substances appropriate for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), then that object of accomplishment [will be subdued].

The meaning here is that [the target] indeed comes under one's control. Furthermore, from the context concerning the yantra, it is certain that one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) after having written and worshipped such a mantra. (70)
He states the application of Meghanāda for eradication:
"At the end of Meghanāda, one should write the name of the person;
it should be enclosed between the letters *ya* at the beginning and end, and the mantra should be accompanied by two *phaṭ*s. (9.71)
Having placed this [image] in the abode of the *preta*s, one should worship that *Bhairava* there with *akṣa* flowers, O lady of excellent hips, while standing facing that direction.
O Goddess, it swiftly banishes him; there is no doubt in this matter.
Meghanāda consists of the collection of the syllables *ha*, *ri*, and *ū* with the *bindu*.
According to the tradition (*āmnāya*), it is enclosed by the letter *ya* together with the *visarga*. This very [mantra] is written upon birch bark (*bhūrja*).

"Having caused it to be deposited" means having placed it inside the ground of a cremation ground; "therein" refers to such a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrja*). "Akṣāḥ" means *vibhītaka* seeds. "That" means facing the direction of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). "After seven days" remains as it stands.
The rest is clear.
He speaks of the practice of *somarāja* for the sake of prosperity and for the sake of subjugation:
"O Goddess of the Gods, [this practice] with *somarāja* is joined with the beginning, middle, and end. (9.73)
O beautiful goddess, having written his name accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* syllable and the [appropriate] caste-mantra (*jāti*), one should place it nearby and set it in the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
By practicing for seven nights with three hundred and eight recitations at each of the three times of day, one quickly accomplishes even the impossible and shall obtain vast wealth. (9.75)
The Moon-King is the syllable *huṃ*. Having joined the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with it at the beginning, middle, and end— meaning,
having written the Moon-King three times at the beginning, middle, and end of the name— then having placed *vaṣaṭ* at the end, one should set up that yantra, worship it, and enclose it in beeswax.

Having placed [the substance] inside a pair of vessels filled with milk, honey, and sugar, whoever recites [the mantra] in that same manner at the three junctions of the day for seven days accomplishes even that which is impossible to accomplish and brings it under control;
he also attains prosperity. || 75 ||
Furthermore, he explains the ritual application for the purpose of causing insanity through the recitation and fire-offering (*homa*) of the aforementioned King of Wrath:
"O Goddess, one should utter the name of the Piśāca ending with the King of Wrath, along with its five limbs, conjoined with the cruel class. (9.76)
The one to be cured becomes insane through *homa* and *japa*.
The five limbs of the *piśāca*— the root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit of the *vibhītaka* tree—
should be ground together for seven days with [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *krodharāja huṃ phaṭ*.
Having uttered the name of the person to be accomplished, whoever offers one hundred and eight oblations at the three junctions of the day, that enemy to be accomplished becomes insane.
Furthermore, out of a desire to bestow favor, he speaks the ritual for the Conqueror of Death:
"I shall proclaim the Mṛtyuñjaya [rite]; listen with a one-pointed mind. (9.77)
Having taken a birch bark leaf that is smooth, without holes, and free from blemishes,
one should draw upon it an eight-petalled lotus together with its pericarp.
O Goddess, O slender-waisted one, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center of that very *kaṇīkā*, surrounding it with the eight directions according to one's own will.
Having encircled [the name] with the *praṇava*,

[one should do so] with "by one's own will," with "bestower of success," and with the entire [mantra]; having encircled the eight directions of the name to be accomplished in the manner of a wheel according to the sequence of the enclosures, and then having encircled it again with the *praṇava*.
The construction is: "one should write in the center of the *kaṇīkā*."
He says that one should write it upon each leaf like a central seed-vessel (kaṇīkā):
"In this manner, one should write it upon all eight leaves."
Furthermore:
On the eight petals, one should also write the name of Aghora beneath each. (9.80)
The meaning is that, by means of the sequence of coverings external to the petals, one reaches the line of space (*vyomarekhā*).

Having written thus and filled it with camphor and other substances as before, and having worshipped it, one should speak for the sake of the petition: "O Lord, protect me! I have come to you for refuge"—by implication, "protect me, the one to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). Then, this protection [the amulet] should be wrapped in beeswax or similar material and placed in water.
It should be cast. Having written that "as soon as it is thrown into water— that is, milk—
it instantly destroys the death of the one to be protected," one should write exactly the same on the eight petals joined to that [central] part.
Now he speaks of the rite for pacification:
"First, the arrangement of the three syllables, and immediately after that, the Svachanda [mantra]. (9.81)
One should write the birth-name of the person to be accomplished, interspersed with other syllables;
then one should again apply the arrangement of three syllables ending with *vaṣaṭ*.

Having written the three syllables of the Netra-mantra and the four-part [syllable], one should intersperse them with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as it was at the time of birth; that is to say, they should be separated by the syllables belonging to Aghora, each [name-syllable] being intervened by one of those [Aghora-syllables], such as: *a devadattaḥ gho*.
Having written [the names] in the sequence beginning with "Devadatta," one should again write them ending with *vaṣaṭ* as before.
Having worshipped this protection,
one should seal it with beeswax and cast it into milk.
And thus, for one who has accomplished this, supreme peace arises...
moreover—
...hear from me yet another [matter]. (9.83)

How so?— O lady of excellent hips, having placed the name in the middle of a *sampuṭa* (enclosed) formation and joined it with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at both ends, one should cast it into the three sweets (*madhuratra*).
The meaning is that one should enclose the name with "juṃ sa" as before—first in direct order (anuloma) and then in reverse order (pratiloma)—and subsequently enclose it with the *praṇava* (oṃ).
The "three sweets" (*madhuratraya*) are as previously described. || 84 ||
And thus:
"He attains supreme peace and is not afflicted by death or disease"—
the meaning is that he is one who is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
He states another method for conquering repeated death: "O fair-faced one, having taken a birch-bark leaf [and] yellow pigment (rocanā)... (9.85).
One should draw what is called the "Matrix-interlaced" (mātṛkāntarita) with a blade of dūrvā grass;
within its inner core, however, one should make it interlaced with the vowels.

Furthermore, O fair-faced one, having written the name of the person to be accomplished within the womb, one should subsequently encircle it with the *dhruva* mantra and then with the letter *va*, O beloved. (9.87)
One should write the letter *sa* and the letter *kṣa* immediately thereafter;
then, O virtuous lady, one should encircle it again with the letter *ṭha* and the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*).
O Goddess, one should restrain with the goad the protection that destroys death—
[the protection] joined with Svacchandā and preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and other offerings that [bead] which is endowed with the Vaṣaṭ-syllable class and smeared with camphor powder, one should cast it into the three sweets.

Having placed the name of the one to be protected within the womb [of the mantra], joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and likewise enclosed within the *praṇava* at the end, and having performed the protection accompanied by the *svacchanda* and endowed with the *vaṣaṭ*-class [mantra],
one should surround the *praṇava*— in which the name has been thus enclosed— with the *aghora* mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*.
One should draw that [diagram], and within its innermost core, one should intersperse it with the vowels.
On the outside, it should be made pervaded by the Mātṛkā alphabet arranged from *ka* to *kṣa*, which has been internally formed by sixteen vowels written in a circular fashion. As it is said:

"Interposed by the *mātṛkā*": all of this, being further encircled by the *dhruva*, should be encircled in sequence by the letters *va*, *sa*, *kṣa*, and *ṭha*. Thereafter, one should encircle it three times with the *māyābīja* and the syllable *satke*. Afterwards, in the eight directions, [one should encircle it] with the syllable *kroṃ*.
This wheel is shown in accordance with the connection of the syntactical meaning, following the [phrase] "one should obstruct."

Having worshipped this [image] and sealed it with beeswax, if it is placed within the "three sweets" (madhuratrika), for whomever it is offered, supreme peace arises; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
When employed by one of certain mind, this certainly accomplishes the desired goal.
Alternatively, having made it into a pill, one should wear it on the neck or on the arm.
"Bhairava declared that for such a person, no disease shall arise.
Having thus prepared a pill, bound with lac and adorned with gold and other materials, one should place it around the neck or on the arm."
Or one should maintain [it]. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "or."
He describes the procedure for conquering death through the constant practice of consuming food and drink consecrated with a specific mantra, even without the use of a pill:
"The three-syllabled root mantra, endowed with the *vaṣaṭ* suffix. (9.92)
For one who always eats food, water, and drink after having consecrated them with mantras, death does not occur; such is the word of Bhairava.
For one who constantly consumes both food and drink with the two mantras of the Netra and Catuṣkala lords ending in *vaṣaṭ*, death does not occur. || 93 ||
Now, he instructs even that practitioner for whom death does not occur due to poison and other such causes:
"Then, O Great Goddess, when the practitioner has been afflicted by a snake,
then— "
One should employ the Aghora mantra there, accompanied by the root mantra.

The root mantra is the illustrious *catuṣkala*; [the ritual] is endowed with that, meaning it is encapsulated by it. "Therein" means for the purpose of pacifying the affliction caused by snakes. At the end of this [mantra], the modification ending in the cruel class [of syllables]—"O Blessed One, pacify, pacify the poison! Hūṃ Phaṭ"—should be employed; such is the implied meaning. || 94 ||
And at the time of the ritual application:
"Having assumed for oneself a most terrible form of Bhairava—fierce with protruding fangs, formidable, and adorned with a garland of flames. (9.95)
With [many] swords hanging down from his waist, he was most terrifying with sword in hand;
endowed with his former form, he possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns.
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate that which has been stepped upon as being bitten;
one should contemplate the poison as being consumed by its intensely blazing flames. (9.97)

O Goddess of the lords of gods, at that very moment he becomes free from poison. Having performed [the ritual] and meditated thus—[meditating on him] as characterized by serpents, such as those forming necklaces, bracelets, and so forth; his former form belonging to the venerable Koṭarākṣa; and "being defiled by snakes" being intended as an illustration for being defiled by poison.
Furthermore—
whoever should perform such meditation upon the planets... he...
...shall liberate [them] in an instant. || 9-98 ||

The meaning is that [the practitioner] should pacify those afflictions such as apasmāra and other grahas; and here, the person to be treated (sādhya) should be [sprinkled] with water, flowers, and so forth, consecrated by the previously mentioned mantra ending with: "O Blessed One, pacify, pacify the graha of this person to be treated, hūṃ phaṭ."
One should strike [him], as is implied by the sense. || 98 ||
Out of compassion, Śambhu also prescribes the application of medicinal herbs for the neutralization of poison for one who is incapable of meditative concentration:
"Now, when some man should be unskilled in meditation..."
Then, O Great Goddess, by means of those medicines, he renders [the victim] poisonless in an instant.
"Daṣṭam" means bitten, and "bhakṣita-viṣam" means having consumed poison. || 99 ||
He spoke of the remedy:
"Taking the two *kumāri* plants together with a female *nāginī*, [one should take] the root of *gokaṇīkāsitam* combined with the root of the plant called *soma*. (9-100)
One should eat [the powder] ground with raw cow's milk and become free from poison.
The medicinal plant called *kumārī* exists in two forms: one with fruit and the other barren;
this constitutes one formulation, along with *nāginī* and that known as *mahāgonasā*, ground with cow's milk.

Gokaṇīkā and girikaṇīkā— also known as somāhvā and somarājī— their white roots ground with cow’s milk constitute the second [preparation]; this, when ground with milk, should also be administered for drinking or as a nasal drop (nasya) along with clarified butter (ghṛta).
As he will say:
"One should drink medicines mixed with ghee," and so forth (9.108).
Furthermore:
By means of the root of *gonimba*, freedom from poison is produced. (9.101)
*Gonimba* is *bhūmyāmalakī*. In some places, however, the reading is "with the root of *eraṇḍa*"; even here, the state of being ground with raw cow's milk remains the same. || 101 ||
One should grind the root of *aśvamāra* with water; when administered as a drink or as nasal drops (*nasya*), one then becomes free from poison. (9–102)
Aśvamāra is karavīraka. || 102 ||
One should grind the root of *āragvadha* with water; when administered as a drink or as nasal drops (*nasya*), one then becomes free from poison. (9–103)
Āragvadha is commonly known as *ārocaka*. || 103 ||
One should employ the essence of madhuka as an errhine or for drinking;
thus one shall become free from poison, according to the word of Bhairava.

The *sāra* of *madhuka*—the inner portion of the *madhūka* tree—one should grind that with water or milk, as is the established practice for these two [substances], and administer it as nasal drops (*nasya*) or for drinking. Others say that *madhuka* is *madhuyaṣṭi*. 104.
One should employ the root of Jambulāsika in a drink or as a nasal drop; O Goddess, one shall become free from poison—of this there is no doubt. (9-105)

*Jambulāsikamūla* means the root of the *jambu* tree. Here too, it remains established that [the powder] should be ground with cow’s milk. Now, he describes the application of medicinal pills (*agadaguṭikā*) for the purpose of preventing the onset of poison:
"One should prepare a fine powder of *ṣaḍbindu*, *paṭa*, and dates."
O beloved, one should prepare pills combined with peacock bile.
Having encased it with the three metals, one should place it on the hand or around the neck;
poison does not take effect upon him, even if he has been bitten by great serpents.

The *ṣaḍbindu* is a specific kind of insect; the *paṭakharjūra* is a centipede. After the phrase "one should have [them] made into a pill," the word "and that" (*tām ca*) is to be supplied; after the phrase "one should cause it to be deposited," the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) is also to be supplied. "Three metals" (*triloha*) refers to gold, silver, and copper. || 107 ||
Regarding the application of antidotes, he states the remaining rule:
"One who has been afflicted by poison should indeed drink the antidotes mixed with clarified butter;
poison does not take effect upon him—this is the certainty of the scripture. (9-108)

Demonstrating that there is no contradiction when these aforementioned remedies or others— such as the individual roots of *kuṇḍalīya*, *gāruḍya*, *ekavīra*, *abalā*, *moṭā*, and so forth— are employed with unwavering conviction, he concludes the chapter:
In this way, there are other yogas as well, composed according to one's own will;
likewise, Kālāgni, the hells, the netherworlds (pātālas), and Hāṭakeśvara.
One whose self is purified should bestow [this]; they will attain success, there is no doubt in this.
All of this was indeed set forth by the Supreme Lord according to His own will, as it is stated in the venerable *Śrīkaṇṭhī*:
Everything proceeds from Īśvara, and likewise everything ceases from Īśvara;
the entire world, both stationary and moving, is presided over by Īśvara.
"There is nothing higher than Mahādeva; this is the truth and not otherwise.

Here, the word *ca* has the sense of *eva*; thus, the meaning is that only one whose self is purified (*bhāvitātman*) should employ [this]. The topical connection (*pāṭalika-saṅgati*) follows immediately thereafter.

By means of the text beginning with "Kālāgni, the hells, the netherworlds, and Hāṭakeśvara" (9.109) and extending to the end of the chapter, [the procedure] has been performed; may there be auspiciousness!
We worship Mahādeva, the divine medicine for diseases, the eradicator of mental afflictions, and the crusher of calamities.

Thus ends the ninth chapter in the illustrious Svacchanda Tantra, accompanied by the commentary named Uddyota composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
This entire path, which extends from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) up to the supreme city of Śiva, is all...

Victorious is that Lord Mahābhairava, the illustrious Svatantra, whose wave of manifestation flashes forth as a radiant form, who proclaims the entire universe as an object of knowledge, and who reveals the supreme state of subjectivity to those possessed of devotion.
At the end of the ninth chapter, for the purpose of understanding the nature of the paths (adhvan) hinted at by the words "Kālāgni" and so forth, the venerable Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, this path has indeed been indicated, but not described in detail."
Please speak of that out of your grace for the benefit of practitioners.

This path, consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*), which was introduced at the beginning of the ninth chapter as the means for attaining the abode of the Supreme Lord and as that which is to be consumed by the awakened ones, belongs to the practitioners (*sādhaka*)— that is, to the teachers (*ācārya*) and others who seek to accomplish both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). || 1 ||
Śrī Bhairava spoke this resolution of the question:
"I shall indeed fully proclaim the Path for the benefit of practitioners.
'The Path' (adhvā) refers to the form of the worlds (bhuvana), [to be explained] correctly according to the sequence presided over by the respective lords of those worlds."
I shall explain in detail and with full expansion.
He introduces that [topic]: "Now, below the Rudra of the Fire of Time (Kālāgnirudra), the cauldron (kaṭāha) is situated. (10.2)
[The Egg] is ten million yojanas in thickness...

because the earth is enveloped by all the principles (tattvas), first [is situated] within that Brahmāṇḍa the world of Kālāgnirudra; below that is the Kaṭāha, the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa, the "cauldron."
And where one sinks and emerges with difficulty, as it were; "bāhulya" means density.
Furthermore:
Above that are the worlds;
there are nine hundred and ninety million and one thousand cosmic eggs.
Seventy million, one hundred thousand, ten thousand, as well as arbudas, vṛndas, and kharvas. (10.4)
"There are also countless lotuses," and so on, in many such ways;
indeed, the leader of them here is the Supreme Lord Ananta. || 10-5 ||

"On the upper surface of that cauldron" means on the exterior of its shell. By the words "nine hundred and ninety million," etc., the infinity of the worlds and cosmic eggs situated outside of it is expressed. As it has been stated in the *Śrī Mālinīvijaya*: "The cosmic egg..."
And with reference to the primordial egg (*prakṛtyaṇḍa*), it is said:
"The two are distinct and innumerable" (2.50).
Also, in the *Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā*:
It has been stated that "the cosmic egg is ten million [yojanas] in extent. As for what the commentators [said]:
"Now, below Kālāgnirudra... (10.2).

In this context, because of its proximity to the world of Kālāgnirudra, the first world, that of Earth (pāthīva), is said to be the infinite world (ananta-bhuvana); and in the passage beginning with "of the cosmic eggs" (aṇḍānām), the word "egg" (aṇḍa) refers to worlds, and it has been explained that these worlds are situated between the two panels of the shell of the cosmic egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa-kavāṭa). That [explanation] is not based on scripture (anāgamika).

The notion that it is "self-imagined" (svayaṃkalpita) should be disregarded; for even though it is the first of the infinite worlds, it is seen in the Āgamas as being situated in the lower region outside the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), specifically within the midst of the hundred Rudras.
As it is stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
Having begun with, "Outside of that are the separate worlds of the hundred Rudras" (5.12), [the text continues] with,
"Ananta is the first among them" (5.13).
In this [text] as well, it will appear in the eleventh [chapter]: "The Lord, who exists as the sustainer on the path, abides in infinite forms" (11.22).
Likewise:
"And Hūhuka, the support of Śakti, is situated at the summit of the waters. (11.24)
This will become clear immediately thereafter. Furthermore, it is not well-known for the word *aṇḍa* to denote a world (*bhuvana*). Even so, the word *bhuvana* would have to be mentioned separately.
And as for what is about to be said...
Regarding the non-specification of the measurement of the infinite worlds (*ananta-bhuvana*) among the measurements of the worlds contained within the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*):
the world of Ananta is situated between the worlds of Karparikā and Kālāgni;
moreover, it is located below, on the outer back surface of Karparikā, amidst the ten groups of hundred Rudras situated below. Enough of this. 5.
Thus, by pervading the manifold of phenomena (*prapañca*), the earth rests upon infinite cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*). Therefore,
through the purification of that Blessed One who is denoted by the word "infinite," there occurs the purification of the countless worlds situated below all the cosmic eggs, known as the *ūhakas*.
He says that [the disciple] becomes one with this initiation into the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*) together with the worlds of Rudra:
"By that which is purified, the pure cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) along with the *ūhakas* are purified here.
They are called *ūhakas* because they 'infer' (*ūhante*), that is, they deliberate upon and delimit the universe."
He asks, "By what kinds of inferences? and replies:
"Precisely by those which have the support of power as their basis...
Power itself is the Supreme Lord's sovereignty; because it constitutes the foundation of the universe, it is the support.
The meaning is that it is the support, just like [the body], by means of those very [faculties] which rest upon it as its powers.
As for how many those hooded snakes are, what they are like, and who they are—he says:
"By a count of thirty-two. (10.6)
Surrounded by retinues of millions upon millions, they were endowed with incomparable virtues;
they were thronged by floods of celestial women whose eyes were made lovely by the play of their arched brows.
Resplendent like ten thousand suns and adorned with arches and watchtowers;
moreover—therein no one was suffering, except for the pain born of the bodiless god [Kāma]. (10.8)
There indeed the heroes sport with women in playful delight,
situated within various worlds that are shaped like wombs.
By this, the predominance of enjoyment by women in these worlds is indeed reinforced. || 9 ||
Thus,
in this manner, the worlds have been described as they exist for those dwelling within other worlds—
those which were introduced with the words, "Above that are the worlds" (10.3).
These are stated to be the abodes for those thinkers who dwell in specific worlds situated within the midst of the infinite worlds here.
And thus, in initiation—when Ananta has been purified—all these things attain purification. (10.10)

The meaning is that when the Lord Ananta-bhaṭṭāraka has bestowed initiation upon a candidate, because he bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*), the *ūhakas* presided over by him and his infinite worlds are purified; they do not become causes of bondage by way of granting enjoyment. It is exactly the same in the subsequent cases as well.

The purification of the worlds (bhuvana-śuddhi) is to be understood by means of the purification of each respective lord of the world (bhuvaneśa). Regarding the procedure for purification, he will explain the ritual preceded by the ritual attendance (upasthāna) and so forth later on. Thus, outside the skull-bowl (karparikā) is the world of Ananta.
Then, however—thereafter, Kālāgni was stationed above by Śrīkaṇṭha; acting in accordance with his command, he exercises his authority. (10–11)
O Dear One, he remains accompanied by many millions of Rudras;
"above" refers to the top of the cauldron (*kaṭāha*). Kāla is the fire that performs the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Although, according to the principle previously stated, the entire universe consists of the independent Lord (*svatantra-bhaṭṭāraka*), there exists a division into upper and lower [realms].
Although it does not exist [in reality],

nevertheless, by His will alone, this sequence has appeared in such a manner to those who desire to ascend, as well as to the teachers and the taught. And although Kālāgni and the others are all-pervasive because they consist of Supreme Bhairava, they too appear [as such] solely by His will.
Thus illuminated, it is situated there in each respective place accordingly.
Having thus described the two worlds above and below the cauldron (kaṭāha), he begins with the desire to determine the measurement of the city:
"Now I shall fully declare the measurement established by Śiva. (10–12)
O lady of excellent hips,
listen to how that [occurs] from the very beginning of its commencement.
In that regard:
"The Great Principle (mahat) is perceived as ten times more gross than the Unmanifest. (10.13)
The "Great One" (Mahat) and the subsequent principles constitute two-fifths of the gross [evolutionary series] and are called "gross.

In this system, for the yogi, the entire universe is the object of knowledge (*meyam*). However, for the non-yogi, the determination of the objects of knowledge begins from the principle of *prakṛti* onwards, because *māyā* conceals the *puruṣa*, as do the principles beginning with *kalā*.

Because it consists of the power of the subject (*grāhaka-śakti*) in the form of a bodice (*kañcuka*), the *prakṛti-tattva*— which is the universal form of the object (*vedya-sāmānya*)— indeed appears at the moment of death as if being remembered, like something situated in the throat. For the throat is the abode of Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of *prakṛti*, and the locus of maintenance (*sthiti*).

Thus, in this manner, the grossness of the Great Principle (mahat), which is the intellect (buddhi), is ten times greater than that of the unmanifest (avyakta) in its nature as an object of cognition.

For the intellect, whose function consists of ascertainment (adhyavasāya), is cognized through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). And its grossness, compared to the aforementioned object of cognition consisting of primordial matter (prakṛti), is indeed attested by direct experience.

"Two-fifths of such a Great One (mahat)" means precisely tenfold; the "origin of the elements" (bhūtādi) is the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is gross, and not the *ahaṅkāra* (ego), for that [ego] cannot be conceived as exceeding the Great One. However, the nature of the subtle element is as follows:

Abiding within in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*), it indeed flashes forth as the mere form of a woman who has become an object of longing for an old man; and flashing forth as a mental mode (*ākāra*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is determinative (*adhyavasāya*), it certainly assumes grossness. Thus, he says that this [object] is to be delimited solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*):
And the dimension of the *bhūtādi* is perceivable by the internal sense (*bhāva*), not by the eye. || 10-14 ||
From such a [subtle] element as that— namely, the dust seen as ten times more minute than the former, when the sun shines through a lattice opening— that is called an atom (*paramāṇu*). (10.15)

It is subtler (*aṇīyaḥ*), meaning much smaller; yet, in comparison to the primordial elements (*bhūtādi*), it is ten times grosser because it is perceptible to the eye. Furthermore, this atom (*paramāṇu*) is distinct from the atoms accepted by the Tārkikas (logicians).
And such is this:
"The conjunction of eight atoms which occurs is known as a *trasareṇu*; that is called a 'lotus-dust' (*padmarajas*). (10.16)
*Samavāya* means conjunction; its two names are *trasareṇu* and *padmarajas*.
Eight *trasareṇus* are prescribed as one hair-tip (*bālāgra*);
likewise, eight hair-tips are declared to be one nit (*likṣā*).
They know that eight *likṣās* make one *yūkā*, and eight *yūkās* become one *yava*.
O beautiful lady, eight *yavas* make one joint (*parva*), which is then an *aṅguṣṭha* or a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
A span (vitasti) is said to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure;
two spans make a cubit (hasta), which consists of twenty-four finger-breadths. || 19 ||

The terms beginning with *bālāgra* (the tip of a hair) are designations for specific measures of length. *Parvan*, *aṅguṣṭha*, and *aṅgula* are synonyms; likewise, *vitasti* and *tāla* are synonyms. || 19 ||
The bow-staff is four cubits long, as are the nālikā and the sacrificial post (yūpa);
thus, the names "bow," "staff," "nālikā," and "sacrificial post" refer to the same object.
Two full thousand bow-lengths are designated as one *krośa*. || 10-20 ||
Two *krośas* make one *gavyūti*, and two *gavyūtis* make one *yojana*.
He applies this to the present context:
"O illustrious lady, by this measurement of *yojanas*... (10.21).
The lion-throne is greatly radiant, two thousand [yojanas] in width and one thousand [yojanas] in height;
"of that" refers to that Kālāgni.
...in the great sacred seats (mahāpīṭha), O observer of good vows. || 10-22 ||
Therein abides the Lord of Gods, Kāla, the twelve-eyed one;
he stands and shines forth.
He has four faces—white, red, yellow, and black—facing west, north, east, and south; he is possessed of great strength. (10.23)
The upper face of this [fire] was not opened by the Blessed One; it was restrained so that there might not be a burning of the worlds, beginning with the earth. || 23 ||
Moreover:
"Then Raktāṅga and Karāla, with tawny eyebrows, bearded eyes, and blazing flames from their mouths, matted hair, and body hairs, were intensely aflame. (10.24)
The extremely intense flames of his weapons blaze within the palms of his hands;
thus he is—resplendent like a burning mountain, adorned with blazing tongues of fire. (10.25)
The great-souled one indeed has ten arms; he carries a sword and a shield, holds arrows and a bow, and likewise bears a noose and a goad.
He holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, bearing hands that grant boons and fearlessness;
he is both handless and possessed of distinguished hands.
Moreover:
his body shines brilliantly, extending for a million yojanas. (10.27)

This is the measure of the beloved Bhāvasvarā’s radiance, not of her physical body; otherwise, the previously mentioned measurement of her seat would be inconsistent. Indeed, her bodily measurement is not stated here. Furthermore, her world blazes forth with a measurement of ten million yojanas.
And that was gathered together by the daughters of Rudra and by the Rudras bearing flaming tridents. || 10-28 ||
It was surrounded by various celestial palaces blazing with light;
moreover—ten million flames issued forth from it upwards. (10.29)
"Of that" refers to the world. || 29 ||
Above that, O Goddess of gods, O lady of beautiful countenance, there are five crores [of yojanas];
no one dwells here, as it is enveloped in smoke and heat.

Thus, the cauldron (kaṭāha) is ten million [yojanas], above it the world of Kālāgni is ten million, the flames of that world are one hundred million, and the void is fifty million; thus, there are seventeen [crores]. Furthermore, since the measurement of the world of Ananta in the middle has not been stated here, it has already been said that postulating it in the middle is incorrect.
Beyond this, O lady of excellent hips, the hells have been fully described;
fifty crores of them, O Goddess, have indeed been recounted in their proper sequence.

In the Mahāsaṃhitās, it is stated that they are called "hells" (narakāḥ) because, by virtue of the causative sense being inherent [in the root], they cause men to experience suffering, thereby making them cry out. 31.
But here,
O fair-faced one, I shall proclaim the principal [mantra], which consists of one hundred and forty syllables as has been taught.
Now hear that which is in the Mahāsaṃhitās, according to its name. || 10-32 ||
Avīci, Raurava, and Mahāraurava;
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Sañjīvana, and Sujīvana. (10.33)
Thus, these [verses]:
"Avīci is covered with waves consisting of mire of pus, blood, and so forth;
Raurava is where crying living beings are cast down."

"Tāmisra is mixed with darkness, grey with the gloom of night; and Andhatāmisra is of such a nature that the cardinal directions are not distinguished. Thus they are defined in the Śrīparā. Mahāraurava is simply Raurava intensified.

Those two, Sañjīvana and Sujīvana, are so called because they provide perfect life—indeed, excellent life again and again—for those who are as if dead due to the torments of hell, for the purpose of further tormenting them. || 33 ||
Padma, Mahāpadma, and likewise Kālasūtra—these are in Śrīparā. Regarding Padma: "Padma is shaped like a lotus, perfectly cool, and filled with frost and mud."
The Mahāpadma [continent] is of such a nature, but it is further characterized by cold and snow.
"The black thread is a dark noose, a firm triple-thonged binding"—
thus they are etymologically explained.
The needle-mouthed [wind]...
this too is the needle-mouthed [wind], which pierces like a needle with an extremely sharp point.
Thus it is stated in that very place.
...of great body... where there is a vast body that is difficult to bear.
...the mountain of swords with edges as sharp as razors. || 34 ||

"It is said: 'The razor's edge shaves the limb, being continuous with the razor's edge. The sword is the *asi-khaḍga*, and the mountain consisting of that [sword] causes suffering to those who travel upon it. (34)
Asitāla, Druma, Drumamastaka,
and the renowned Drumārāma—
these are known by the name Asita.

"A sword, when grasped by its blade, cuts the limbs"—thus it is explained in the *Parā-nirukti*. The *tāla* also [is described]: "The *tāla*, like a palm tree, tears at the body with its bark-like [limbs]."
Thus it is etymologically explained. *Druma* refers to a tree-like form that is immovable due to its body being overcome by a fierce wind;
where there is a *druma* at the head, that is a *drumamastaka*. Likewise, where there is a grove (*ārāma*)—that is, a collection—of trees among the limbs, that is a *drumārama*.
............and likewise Kumbhīpāka. || 10-35 ||
"The Kumbhīpāka [hell] is vast and terrible, with a mouth like a jar and blazing crests of flame"—thus it is defined. || 35 ||
"Ambareṣa is a heap of glowing coals...
'Ambareṣa is so called because from him [the cloud] rains down extremely sharp arrows;
he is like heated coals, resembling fire, and his abode consists of iron coals.'"
Thus, these two are explained in the Nirukta.
...and likewise the Sharp-beaked,
and the Vajra-beaked bird—
by such birds as these, people are struck where [they dwell].
...ṃīnodara and Kharodara. || 10-36 ||
In the bellies of fish and wild beasts, where people are tormented by great suffering. || 36 ||
Sandaṃśa...
Sandaṃśa is that [hell] where people are tormented with red-hot tongs.
And the adamantine body (*vajrakāya*):
that which is an adamantine body for those who undergo great torments.
And Medaka, O fair-faced one,
where there is great torment and the state of having a body composed of fat.
Camel-necked, large-bodied, a Vetāla with the face of a mare. || 10-37 ||

The neck is so excessively long that food can only be reached with great difficulty, as if it were that of a camel; the body is massive and requires a vast amount of food to sustain; there are terrifying Vetālas with flaming mouths;
and there is a fierce, scorching fire shaped like the mouth of a submarine mare. || 37 ||
And the lake of blood and pus...
namely, the lake of blood and the lake of pus.
...the bee and likewise the mosquito;
where there are bees and mosquitoes that are harmful and act as stingers.
And Saṃghāta is that place where people are gathered together and boiled like heated water.
And the Kapāla [hell]...
where people are baked like cakes upon skull-bones.
And also Taptakavaca. || 10-38 ||
Where the limbs are tormented by those who have entered within heated armor;

where people are oppressed by elephant-footed beings, by those with great mouths, by those called tortoises, and likewise by mongooses; where [they are oppressed] by elephant-footed creatures and by beings with great mouths.
Devouring: where people are devoured and terrified by tortoises and mongooses.
And *pīḍana* (oppression) is where people are oppressed by means of large stones.
...the Kumbhīra...
terrifying with that name as a great aquatic creature.
...the saw and the trident as well. || 10-39 ||
Where there is the cutting of limbs with saws, and where there is impalement upon stakes. || 39 ||
And Anaṅga is a vomit of burning coals,
wherein the limbs melt away from the heat, and wherein there is torment through the great fumes of the vomited coals.
...blazing, with three faces,
as well as five faces and a hundred faces; blazing elsewhere...
It is said: "Causing internal torment and heat, with its belly and throat dried up," where five hundred and thirty creatures bite.
......the leech, and the smoke from a burrow. || 10-40 ||
Where there is harassment by creatures known as leeches, and where birth occurs in burrows filled with thick smoke.

"Heat-tormented" refers to being scorched by glowing lac-paste; it is said that when the fire alone is blazing, it causes torment. "Lac-paste" refers to one whose body is singed by the application of burning lac.
Thus it is explained in the Śrīparā.
...of ghastly form and exceedingly terrible;
because those of ghastly form cause terror therein, it is for this very reason exceedingly terrible.
"Broken bones" and "putrid flesh"...
where there is a breaking of the bones, and where the body consists of putrid flesh.
And you are indeed a substance that is impure. || 10-41 ||
That substance in which there is dwelling amidst much urine and amidst impurities. || 41 ||
The owl, the axe, the staff, and likewise the one called the crow;
where there is devouring by owls, cutting with an axe, beating with staffs, and devouring by crows of the people.
"With breath and without breath...
With breath (*socchvāsaḥ*) means characterized by frequent breathing, being motionless while feigning a support;
without breath (*nirucchvāsaḥ*) means characterized by the absence of breathing due to the obstruction of the senses."
...and likewise Vṛkāsya as well. || 42 ||
Aśvāsya and Gopalāda...

[are names of hells] where people are cast into the mouths of great wolves, jackals, and horses for the purpose of devouring them; where cows, beasts, and flesh-eaters consume meat. As it has been said:
"The flesh-eater is that which extracts all the flesh situated within the entire body.
Thus [it is said].
"...the world is likewise a conflagration, wherein no other world exists; and that which is the conflagration is described as:
'Hot, initiating a most intense fever, and causing a burning sensation throughout all the limbs.'"
Thus, elsewhere it is declared that [it] is hot.
Then Śvavaktra and Davāgni...
Śvavaktra is one who possesses a dog's face; [it is so called] because his birth was in the midst of a forest fire.
.........the Pit of Alkali, likewise.........
where people are cast into a pit consisting of caustic lye.
"Tamas is so named, and Mahāmoha is that which deludes the quality of consciousness"—thus it is etymologically defined. || 43 ||
And there was a heap of snakes,
consisting of terrifying black serpents.
"And [the hell] Ṭaptapāṣāṇa is filled with glowing stones and iron rocks that cause intense burning; thus it is defined."
He is both the deformed and the beautiful;
he alone is the bestower of deformity.
Through the sight and conversation of those who possess beauty—beauty that is rare and desirable—...
The second is the one who provides a miserable existence.
Citrī and likewise Citradhara. || 10-44 ||

*Citra* is that which, like *śvitri*, has a variegated form where one thing after another repeatedly arises in great abundance as an object of loathing; whereas *citradhara* is that living being whose single form is itself variegated.
[One with] a face that is black, tawny, and red... 44.
Where there was one who was black, tawny, and red-faced, exceedingly terrifying.
...and likewise the Rākṣasa Mahiṣa;
there, they are terrified by fearsome buffaloes and Rākṣasas.
Kubja:
A place where only hunchbacks are born.
......called Utaptataila (Boiling Oil)......
where boiling oil is poured over the limbs.
Śani, Vṛṣṭi, and Mudgara. || 10-45 ||
Where rain, thunderbolts, and lightning fall from above. || 45 ||
Musala...
a rain of pestles.
"...and 'anātapa' as well... 'Anātapa' is said to mean cold. And so it is stated in the Śrīparā:
'Cold is the onset of a cold fever, which produces a pervasive burning sensation throughout the body.'"
"...and likewise Yamalādri.
'Yugmādri, Karkaśāśmādri, and Sandaṃśaparipīḍita'— thus it has been said."
*Krimikūṭa*... as it is said: "A *krimikūṭa* is declared to be a heap of worms, a mere accumulation of worms. The meaning is: where [the soul] takes birth in the midst of that.
...the many-branched śālmali tree and likewise the phaḍi tree. || 10-46 ||
The iron chain, the iron rope, and the iron cage:
the *phaḍi* is a foot-shackle; the *nigaḍa* is a binding with chains, single bars, and so forth;
the iron rope is for binding in all respects; likewise, the iron cage is for producing immobility of all limbs.
The divisions of the body are the serpent, the scorpion, and Time itself.
Where there is the breaking and pulverizing of bodies; where people are tormented by serpents; where they are stung by scorpions; that is Time, filled with the Person who destroys. || 47 ||
Vajrakaṇa and Kaṭāha...
where people fall upon heated vajra-grains and fall into cauldrons.
.........the iron band (paṭṭa)......... where men are bound with heated iron bands; and this is also called the iron pillar elsewhere, as it has been said:
"A pillar of iron, its body scorched by flaming iron plates.
Thus [it is said].
...and indeed in a crowded place;
where, in a crowded location, there is bodily distress due to lack of movement.
Ghora and Ajagara,
where terrible pythons swallow [their prey].
...and likewise the great Vaitaraṇī. || 10-48 ||
"In the Vaitaraṇī, living beings are tossed about, filled with pus;
therefore, that terrible river always flows with a foul stench.
Thus [it is said].
It provides crossing for those afflicted by thirst and creates the illusion of water. || 10-48 ||
The vulture, the osprey, the cock, and the *pramardaka*—
these four are swarms of predatory birds such as vultures and others.
Kardama...
where those submerged in the midst of mud are born.
...and Durdura, Lamboṣṭha, and Vajranāsika. || 10-49 ||
The *cipiṭa* and the *khañjarīṭa*,

as well as the *durdura* which abounds in frogs— these hells are filled with many such terrifying creatures, including those with hanging lips (*lamboṣṭha*). The *khañjarīṭa* is a predatory bird of that name.
...Śabala and Nīla as well;
Śabala means variegated, and Nīla refers to the nest where [he dwells].
The crow... is filled with uneven crows.
And also the Kaṅkamukha...
Kaṅka refers to a pair of tongs; it is made from a bird whose mouth has that [tongs-like] shape.
...and after that, the howling of jackals. || 10-50 ||
Where people are terrified by the howling cries of jackals. || 50 ||
Gajanāda, Mahānāda, and likewise Siṃhanāda—
these three have clear meanings.
Likewise, there are great crocodiles, sea-monsters, mice, insects, and the ocean.

"Grāhas" refers to extremely cruel creatures other than the specific aquatic animals known as *nakras*; that which contains such large ones is "Mahāgrāha. Similarly, "Nakra" refers to the "Mahānakra" (the great crocodile). "Mūṣikāmaya-sāgara" is an ocean consisting of rats. "Kīṭa-sāgara" is an impure ocean abounding in minute worms.
As for that which is stated in the *Śrīparā*: "One who [eats] feces and urine, and whose mouth is filled with the powder of crushed human excrement and stones... || 51 ||
"Head-downwards" (avākśirāḥ) means having the head below, while the feet are directed upwards.
"...trirāvartaḥ... [means] that where [the winds] revolve three times, they circulate all around. As it is said in the Śrīparā:
"The triple abode, its belly tormented by thirst and hunger."
............and likewise the Cakrapīḍanaka [hell],
where people are crushed by a wheel like sesame seeds.
*Trapulepastrapukūpa*:
A place where the limbs are smeared with molten, heated tin, and where there is likewise a pit [filled with it].
The sugarcane press...
wherein people are crushed like sugarcane.
...the creeper of the mountain. || 10-52 ||
Where people are struck by creepers that grow on the mountains and are as thick as clubs.
And Kaṭaṅkaṭa is renowned...
this is an extremely perilous well, resembling a great cauldron (mahākaṭāha) of that name.
And also the Taptavāluka [Hell],
where the most wicked are made to walk upon sands that are intensely heated.
Thus, these forty-one hundred in number—these most terrible hells are described as being triangular. (10.53)
The meaning is that, in terms of their configuration, the regions of the hells are triangular.
And these [are for] the downfall of those living beings who delight in improper actions;
"improper" refers to that which will be described in the eleventh chapter, consisting of both general and specific [forms], from one's own [nature].
Excluded from the treatise.
But specifically for those who perform cruel deeds, for the deceitful, and likewise for the sinful— (10.54)
He says that [this applies] to sinners whose actions are cruel, such as the killing of others—
specifically those who do not desist even when restrained— and who, for that very reason, possess the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of sin acquired previously, and thus commit evil once again.
And thus,
for these people of the most base and pitiless caste, whose very souls delight in harming others—
likewise:
And for those who take pleasure in the wives of others,
and especially for those who revile the Śiva scriptures. || 10-55 ||
For those who steal the property of the gods, for killers of Brahmins and fathers, for killers of cows, for ungrateful people, and for those who betray the trust of friends— || 10.56 ||

Those who destroy a benefit received are "ungrateful" (*kṛtaghnāḥ*). Those whose character is to destroy a friend through intimacy—that is, through trust—are "those who betray the confidence of a friend" (*mitravisrambhaghātinaḥ*). || 56 ||

Furthermore: "For those who seize the land of gold, who have abandoned purity and right conduct, who are devoid of compassion and generosity, and whose minds are intent on malice and falsehood... (10.57)
The hells, however, have been described for those who do not follow the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Purity and conduct are as prescribed in their respective scriptures; otherwise—“That purification which is taught by those of limited knowledge is impurity in the vision of Śambhu.”
Since purity does not exist in that which is impure, a person should therefore be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*);
such is the teaching of the Śruti. Thus, [the text] would be subject to the rule:
"by means of a crooked sacred thread" (3.2).

And such [statements] as previously mentioned would be inexpressible. In this context, the status of being an object of body, mind, and speech should be applied as appropriate. This very thing—acting in contradiction to one's own scriptures—is what constitutes the state of not being on a path of action (*akarmapatha*). Furthermore, due to the connection with degrees of intensity or lack thereof, these sins...
That is the connection with the hell appropriate to that [action].
But those who are the opposite of this—people devoted to auspicious deeds—do not indeed fall into hell. (10.58)
And whatever auspicious (*śubha*) karma belongs to them—
that I shall explain in brief, exactly as it is, in proper sequence.
"In proper sequence" means—
Because it has been stated that "all denotable objects are fixed, rooted in speech, and bound by speech," [the sequence follows] the order beginning with the vocal.
And that— truthfulness, patience, and non-violence—
these actions of speech, mind, and body are sources of happiness.
Furthermore—purity, bathing, and freedom from guile. (10.59)
He who possesses compassion and lack of greed does not go to the hells.

Purity is as previously described; bathing may even be performed with ashes and the like. Absence of guile is the state of having pure intentions. Lack of greed is the absence of restlessness in the senses.
Peaceful, self-controlled, joyful in soul, free from egoism, and equanimous. || 10-60 ||

One who is free from malice, free from envy, and devoid of longing for the prosperity of others does not go to hell; this is certain. He is peaceful, having conquered his mind; he is self-controlled, having mastered his senses.
And because of the absence of subjection to sense objects, his soul is well-joyful and he is free from egoism. He is equanimous.
Beholding enemies, friends, and others with equanimity, he is free from desire for the prosperity of others and remains contented.
Furthermore:
freedom from envy, absence of pride, devotion to Śiva, and lack of fickleness. (10.61)
Delight in recitation and meditation, steadfastness, the avoidance of miserliness, religious observances, restraints, self-study, and the practice of the three daily junctions. (10.62)
Faith in all things, straightforwardness, modesty, self-respect, vigor, tranquility, contentment, and the avoidance of unpleasant speech— (10.63).
Constant acting with circumspection, restraint of the mind and ego, freedom from hypocrisy, absence of deceit, lack of guile, and the nature of wisdom; 10.64.

Devotion to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, seeking refuge with cows and Brahmins, offering oblations into the fire, giving gifts to the guru, and attending upon those possessed of knowledge. || 10.65 ||
Delight in solitude, meditation, and contentment with the Self alone;
non-interference in the affairs of others, and indifference toward those who are innocent. (10.66)
Freedom from anger and freedom from indolence—these qualities have been proclaimed.

Devotion to Śiva is the primary duty. Freedom from fickleness is steadfastness regarding one's obligations, particularly in the cessation of recitation and meditation. Splendor is the state of being invincible by others. Tranquility...
Having a gentle appearance; avoiding involvement with the mind and ego wherever they arise;
absence of hypocrisy, which is false conduct; absence of deceit, which is the cheating of others; being free from guile, meaning having a mind devoid of evil;
non-interference regarding the affairs and wealth of others, meaning not even thinking of them in the mind; this is called equanimity.
Regarding the domain of conventional practice: "being blameless" means being free from negligence toward the commands of one's guru and so forth;
"freedom from indolence" means exertion in the performance of what is to be adopted. These are virtuous qualities and auspicious conducts.
And therefore:
"But he who devotes himself to these states is fit for immortality. (10.67)
O Śivā, is devotion to Śiva alone the bestower of liberation, or is it [liberation] accompanied by other dharmas? (67)
For this reason— indeed,
even those infinite bonds of human nature that have been proclaimed perish for embodied beings who are devoted to the conduct of Śiva and who possess the quality of righteousness. (10.68)
Therefore, having understood this, one should apply the mind to *dharma*.

Regarding the bonds of the individual (*pauruṣāḥ pāśāḥ*) which will be described in the section on the reality of the person (*puruṣatattva*) and the worlds (*bhuvana*), even those perish for those who possess devotion to Śiva. *Dharma* is that which has been described in its proper form.
Moreover:
"He whose mind is undisturbed, free from conceptual construction, and stainless... (10.69)
He goes to the supreme worlds and does not see the hells;
because he is stainless and free from evil, having rendered himself free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and being fully confident in the ultimate reality (*tattvika-artha*).
Since it is said that "he does not see," he lacks even mere perception; what possibility, then, could there be for his experiencing [those worlds]?
He whose intellect is undeluded and who is free from sin toward all beings—|| 10.70 ||
One who is free from guile and possesses true being does not see the hells;
one who is undeluded has turned away from ignorance. Being free from guile means having a pure intention, and for that very reason, being established in the conduct of true being.
He by whom the senses have been conquered and whose mind remains under control.
By his victory, all the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, have been conquered;
the meaning is that the ground of all enjoyment has been easily attained by him.
He praises this very point:
"Whether it be one's own task or the task of another, he whose intellect remains steadfast [is truly wise]. (10.72)
This alone is true wisdom; all others are merely readers of books.
One's own duty is steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self, while the duty toward others is to engage them in that same knowledge of the Self. He concludes:
Thus, this tantric principle has been explained in brief. || 10.73 ||
There is no fixed enumeration of others who are non-tantric.
A "tantric" is one renowned in the compendia of the Supreme Lord; "non-tantric" refers to those renowned among the authors of the *Dharma-sūtras* and others.
By means of uncommon practices—those who are devoted to the Śiva scriptures and intent upon devotion to the Guru. || 10-74 ||
But for those who know the supreme reality, no evil shall occur;
the meaning is that their birth—which is a miserable arrival—is not [evil].
Having spoken thus by way of digression, he states the subject at hand:
"Learn from me the principal ones among these hells. (10.75)
There are thirty-five hells;
for these very [hells] are proclaimed to be of four distinct types.
The meaning is that thirty-five multiplied by four results in one hundred and forty.
Thus it is said: "This [number] of one hundred and forty has indeed been proclaimed in brief. (10.76)
Because—by those very [deities], who are pure, those fifty crores are purified. "By those" refers to those numbering one hundred and forty; "those" refers to the ones previously introduced.
Or alternatively—when these thirty-five, or thirty-two, have been purified. || 10-77 ||
O fair-faced one, these together constitute one hundred and forty pure [hells];
excluding Avīci, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava, there are thirty-two whose names will be mentioned hereafter.
Or rather:
"By means of the three pure [spheres], the thirty-two indeed become pure. (10.78)
Since there is no generality devoid of particulars, the purity of the particular arises through the purity of the general;
or, the purity of the general arises through the purity of the particulars that have internalized the general.
In this regard, the intention of the Gurus is as follows: for whichever initiate there is an abundance of sin...

It is certain that for him [the initiate], purification from hell must be performed in detail, whereas for another it is done in brief; thus, purification is taught here through four sections (*praghaṭṭaka*), but in the *Kiraṇa* through three sections. As it has been said:
"That which has been proclaimed for these [kings] is forty-four;
among them, thirty-two are kings and three are lords of the kings of kings.
Thus it is said.

In the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, it is stated that the purification of those [deities] occurs precisely through the purification of Kūṣmāṇḍarudra; thus, there is a difference in the methodological system (*prakriyā*). || 78 ||
Now, I shall declare the names of those three most excellent hells: the one renowned as Avīci and the terrible Kumbhīpāka. (10.79)
And Mahāraurava-rāja... now,
listen to me regarding their place of residence.
They are situated in the lower, middle, and upper parts respectively.
Furthermore:
"I shall explain their pervasion correctly and in due order;
that is to say, just as the thirty-two hells are pervaded by the three through internal containment."
In this regard, O Dear One, one should purify Avīci, which is the eleventh destination among the hells. (10.81)
O Goddess, one should purify the twelfth hell, Kumbhīpāka, by means of the self;
and likewise the one named Mahāraurava—of this there is no doubt. (10.82)
I shall describe these thirty-five in brief, O fair-faced one:
Avīci, Kriminicaya, and likewise the river Vaitaraṇī.
Loha, Śālmali, and Asiparvata; Socchvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, Pūtimāṃsa, and Paratathā.
The Taptatrapu (Heated Tin), Kṣārakūpa (Alkali Pit), and likewise Jatulepa (Bitumen Smearing) are included within Avīci; however,
this [Avīci] is specifically distinguished by the phrase "a mass of worms," and it is not distinct from that previously mentioned.
It would be distinct [from them], because it would follow that there is an excess in the number.
Now, hear concerning Kumbhīpāka. || 10-85 ||
The Asthibhaṅga, the Krakacaccheda, the Kūpa, the Kaṭaṅkaṭa, the Vasāmiśra, the Ayastuṇḍa, and the Trapulepa are proclaimed [as the hells]. 86.
Kumbhīpāka is to be known, as well as Tīkṣṇāsika;
Taptaloha is to be known, and likewise Kṣuradhārapatha. || 10.87 ||
Aśani and Sutapta—these twelve are proclaimed;
they are known as the eleven final seeds of the terrible Kumbhīpāka hell.
And after Mahāraurava, learn from me [the names of] Kālasūtra, Mahāpadma, Kumbha, Sañjīvana, and Ikṣuka. (10.89)
The noose, the ambarēṣaka, and likewise the iron band;
the staff-machine, the impure one, and another of terrible form. (10.90)

Mahāraurava is situated above these; what was previously called Medaka is here Vasāmiśra. Ayastuṇḍa means "sharp-beaked," tīkṣṇāsira means "sharp-edged," kumbha means "crocodile" (kumbhīra), and aśani means "thunderbolt."
It was previously stated that "vṛṣṭi" and "mudgara" [are synonyms], that the noose (pāśa) is also the serpent (uraga), and that the staff-mechanism (daṇḍayantra) is the staff (daṇḍa).
When, at the outset, only the triad beginning with Avīci is being purified, then: "In Avīci, the worms of hell; in Kumbhīpāka, those most terrible... (10.91).
One should contemplate those who have fallen into the impurities within Mahāraurava.
Now, listen to me regarding the extent of these thirty-two hells that are pervaded by these three. (10.92)
In that regard, the height of each [of these] is recorded as ninety-nine lakhs of yojanas.
And these—
They should be known to be separated by intervals of one hundred thousand [yojanas], numbering thirty-two in sequence.
Thus, this region of hell extends for thirty-two koṭis of mānas. || 93 ||
Then, O fair-faced one, above these, he stands as their sovereign,
endowed with the qualities of yogic mastery, the lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
And this [is stated]:
"Where is the earth designated? Upon it, following the sequence of heat (ūṣman), there is that egg (aṇḍa); just as it is difficult to behold, so too is Kūṣmāṇḍa formidable."

Thus it is explained in the *Śrīparā*. Furthermore, because this [deity] instructs people who commit evil deeds, its fierce form and its manifestation from a fierce form are described in the *Śrīparā*;
therefore, after effecting the purification of all hells, this proclamation should be performed. The same applies elsewhere. (94)
Furthermore—
his city is proclaimed to have nine million nine hundred thousand [inhabitants].
Now—
Above that, I shall describe the netherworlds (pātālas) in brief.
Ābhāsa, Varatāla, Śarkara, Gabhastimat,
Mahātala, Sutala, and beyond that, Rasātala.
The eighth is to be known as golden, endowed with all objects of desire.
This qualification is common to all [the levels]. It is so called because it shines on all sides (*samantāt*) with all kinds of jewels and other things;
because it possesses excellent enjoyments; because its qualities are desirable like sugar (*śarkarāvat*); and because of its luminosity.

These are their names because they possess great splendor (*mahābhoga*), because their surfaces are beautiful (*śobhanatala*), because they possess the quality of relishing flavor (*rasāsvādavattva*), and because they are composed of gold (*suvarṇamaya*). As it is said in the *Śrīparā*:
"Because the luster of all jewels shines forth intensely from them on every side..."
"And because of that appearance of those [male] dharmīs and their women, it is remembered as such," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is stated therein that the level called Śarkara is the ground of the complete attainment of enjoyments and the like.
Now,
I shall describe to you the measurement starting from the *ābhāsa* up to the golden one.
Each of these excellent cities has a height of nine thousand [yojanas];
"height" (utsedha) refers to vertical elevation.
Likewise, the interval between each one should be known to be numbered at a thousand [yojanas]. || 10.98 ||
In this way, there are eighty thousand [yojanas] down to the netherworld (pātāla). || 98 ||
Moreover: "All their worlds are indeed shaped like umbrellas; they are endowed with all objects of desire and possessed of all excellent qualities. (10.99)
[The city was] adorned with golden ramparts topped with parasols and banners,
resonant with networks of small bells, and embellished with archways and watchtowers.
With exits and windows adorned with divine garments,
and filled with the sounds of singing and musical instruments such as lutes and drums.
With multitudes of rows of various celestial abodes, resplendent with every kind of jewel, and with lofty-pitched palaces possessing a radiance equal to the light of moonbeams; || 10.102 ||
With excellent gardens along the streets and roads, always endowed with flowers and fruits, sweet with the cries of cuckoos, and frequented by peacocks and bees; || 10.103 ||
[The lakes] were crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by ruddy geese,
and graced by clusters of lotus ponds resounding with the cries of cranes.
They were filled with ponds abounding in clear water and endowed with long lotus stalks,
and they were guarded by men of massive stature, great strength, and heroic prowess.
They were enriched with the nature of all sovereignty, endowed with all auspicious marks,
and provided with divine garments, excellent betel, and celestial fragrant ointments.
"Endowed with divine ornaments and crowns adorned with jewels"—this is the meaning of "yuktāni. By the word "mukuṭaiḥ," it is meant that they are characterized by crowns.
Furthermore:
"Those practitioners who are intent on the worship of Śiva, by his grace," || 10.107 ||
O Great Goddess, they enter Pātāla, which is frequented by the Siddhas;
this is to be understood as occurring "by her grace," like the eye of a crow (which serves both purposes simultaneously).
Having entered, they obtain the divine elixir of taste, a perfected substance.

*Rasa* is the means for alchemical gold; *rasāyana* is the cause for the stability of the body; and *siddhadravya* refers to enchanted articles such as magical sandals (*pādukā*). The meaning is that, having obtained these for the sake of the appropriate supernatural powers (*siddhi*), they wander through the worlds according to their pleasure. || 108 ||
But those who do not depart from there—
others [among them] constantly sport with hosts of divine women, who are full of passion (or capable of assuming forms at will) and walk with the gait of rutting elephants. (10.109)
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments, highly skilled in the arts of love as taught in the Kama-shastra, dressed in divine garments, and bent by the weight of their breasts. || 10-110 ||
With waists slender and firm, with serene faces and tremulous, long eyes,
their hips were adorned with small bells, and they were beautified by necklaces and armlets.
With their limbs smeared with fragrant perfumes and adorned with waistbands and girdles—
thus, O Goddess, have those who dwell within the netherworlds been described to you.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, it is said that the three classes— the Asuras, Nāgas, and Rākṣasas— dwell separately, one by one, in each of the Pātālas.
Śrī Bhairava reminds Śrī Devī of that which has been stated in other scriptures with the words "It has been told. And so it is said in the *Śrī Parā*:
"In the manifestation [of the world], the Lord is known as Śaṅkukarṇa; he is crooked and incomplete."
In Varatāla, there are also Prahlāda, Vāsuki, and Lohitānana.
(vi)1 On the first level is the one named Śiśupāla, Kambala, and Yamadaṃṣṭraka;
on the level called Gabhasti are Sakarkandhu, Karkaṭa, and Vikaṭānana.
In Mahātala there are those named Hiraṇya, Kālāṅga, and Karāṅgaka;
in Rasātala there are Bṛhadbhoga, Durdarśa, and Bhīmaniḥsvana.
"These six triple-sections are to be enjoyed by these great-souled ones; Bali, Takṣaka, and Piṅgala are situated below in Sutala," so it is said. (113)
Furthermore:
"In the seven netherworlds (pātāla), other lords of the worlds are to be known: Bala, Atibala, Balavān, and Balavikrama. (10.114)
Subala, Balabhadra, and Balādhyakṣa are proclaimed;
since these Rudras are stationed respectively in the seven netherworlds (pātālas), therefore—by means of these pure ones, these inhabitants of the seven netherworlds are purified. (10–115)

The meaning is that these specific enjoyments, which consist of various objects of experience acquired through their own karma and which they dwell upon extensively within the seven netherworlds (pātālas), are what are here said to be purified. || 115 ||
Therefore— above that, indeed, is what is celebrated as the golden Pātāla;
there dwells that god Hāṭaka, the Supreme Lord.
Surrounded on all sides by thousands of millions of cities,
he was attended by Siddhas, divine hosts of Rudras, and by his sisters and mothers.

"By the Siddhas and Rudras" means by those who have attained the forms of Rudra as specific Siddhas; the "Sisters" are the goddesses born from the treasury of the limbs of Brāhmī and the others; the "Mothers," however, are Brāhmī and the rest, for they abide almost everywhere through their pervasion of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in both higher and lower states. || 117 ||
Furthermore: "By the Yoginīs, the Yogakanyās, and the Rudras together with their daughters—
the Yoginīs are those perfected through yoga, while the Yogakanyās are those who, upon being born, have their yoga immediately recalled."
Furthermore:
"By means of mantras equal to perfected substances, and by wish-fulfilling gems and elixirs," || 10-118 ||

The meaning is that the attainment of equality with accomplished substances (siddhadravya) consists in the granting of desired objects merely upon being received, [just as] by means of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) and elixirs (rasāyana). || 118 ||
Thus, in this manner—
the temple of Hāṭakeśa is indeed enriched by perfected vidyās;
and this [description] is intended as an illustration for the previously mentioned Rudras and others.
He provides the etymological explanation of the term *hāṭaka*:
"One should forcibly cause those people, whose minds have become absorbed in that state, to enter [it]. (10.119)
Therefore, that Maheśvara is called Hāṭaka;

he is the God of the gods (devadeva), meaning the God of the gods such as Bala and others. He is Maheśvara because he exists in this form as the bestower of enjoyment (bhoga) specifically for the Blessed Śrīkaṇṭha.

And thus, within the seven subterranean realms (pātāla) that have been included [in the mandala], once those cities have been purified, one should perform the entire range of ritual procedures— from the preliminary installation of Hāṭaka Rudra up to the conclusion of the proclamation— consisting of the reconnection of the paths (adhvasandhāna) and so forth, as described in the fourth chapter.

One should perform [the rite]. In this same manner, this very [measurement] should be remembered for each lord of the worlds (*pratibhuvaneśa*). Thus, the shell of the earth (*bhūkaṭāha*) is ten million [yojanas]; the city of Kālāgnirudra is ten million; its flames are one hundred million; its smoke is fifty million; the hells are three hundred and twenty million; and the city of the Kūṣmāṇḍas is...
Ninety-nine lakhs and eighty thousand [yojanas] in Pātāla; thus, there are fifty crores minus twenty thousand. The extent of the path is exactly fifty crores, while the remainder is as follows:
Above that, however, there are twenty thousand yojanas.
O fair-faced one, the "earth-pot" (bhūkaṭāha) is designated as being on all sides;
the earth-pot is the support for human beings. Thus, up to this point, it constitutes half of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Therefore, the blessed earth is filled with various provinces. || 10-121 ||
In its center, O lady of beautiful countenance, is the great Meru, made of gold;
I shall describe to you the extent of that mountain from top to bottom.
A country (janapada) is the dwelling place of people. || 122 ||
Therein—its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
it is planted sixteen thousand yojanas deep beneath the surface. (10.123)
He states its extensiveness:
"Those very [elements] are the expansion of the root...
'Those' refers to exactly sixteen."
