The width of the head is double [that of the base];
the meaning is that the width of its head is thirty-two [units].
"And that liṅga belongs to Bhairava, and the earth is its pedestal" (Tantrāloka 8.45).
Thus say the teachers; and this is described in the Śrīparā as having the form of a pericarp at its summit.
Now,
above that, there is a divine assembly hall named Manovatī.
It measures fourteen thousand yojanas in extent;
it is richly adorned with all kinds of jewels and is accompanied by thousands of women.
Endowed with all multitudes of enjoyments, it is the abode of the Great-souled Brahmā;
for it is the seat of the descent of a portion of Brahmā residing in Satyaloka, and therefore the station of Brahmā is called the center everywhere.
And it was crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and surrounded by ṛṣis. || 10.126 ||
In its northeastern direction, the Jyotiṣka peak is recorded;
Jyotiṣka means made of crystal.
And that [palace]—
resembling ten million suns and served by the foremost of the Gaṇas— || 10.127 ||
It was endowed with flowers of every season, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
crowded with thousands of women, and possessed of all sovereign powers.
The foremost of the hosts are the principal groups. || 128 ||
There dwells the Blessed Lord, the three-eyed Supreme Ishvara,
who is indeed surrounded by the world-protectors and is the leader of Brahma, Vishnu, and Indra.
"You should know that portion of mine which is saluted by gods and siddhas"—
this is the speech of Umāpati, the dweller of Kailāsa.
And there, impelled by the will of another, he exercises his authority. (10.130)

By speaking thus, the opponent himself indicates that I am Śrī Sadāśiva, existing as Īśāna, Ananta, and Śrīkaṇṭha; that I abide through the pervasion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as Rudra situated above the realm of Viṣṇu and as Tryambaka on the peak of Mount Meru, but that there is no separate existence for these [deities]. [He thus establishes] his authority.

This indeed refers to the state of being presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra; and this is mentioned here because the peaks are predominant, but it is not the case that only these [three] exist, for in the *Śrīcandragarbha* and other texts it is said:
"The abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are endowed with three peaks."
However, in the *Śrīkiraṇa*, it is established as follows: "It is endowed with three peaks made of silver, gold, and jewels. || 130 ||
And of this Meru,
fourteen thousand yojanas below the assembly hall of Brahmā, there is a circular wall (cakravāṭa) on all sides. (10.131)
A circular enclosure is a collection of cities. || 131 ||
And this very [set] is designated as the "Eight Heavens" (svargāṣṭaka),
because:
There dwell the world-protectors,
Indra and the others.
There,
to the east, is the renowned city of Indra named Amarāvatī.
The city of Tejovatī is proclaimed as belonging to Citrabhānu in the southeast;
to the south belongs the city of Yamarāja, named Saṃyamanī.
Kṛṣṇāṅgārā is said to belong to the Lord of the Rākṣasas in the southwest;
to the west, that of the Lord of Waters is known by the name Śuddhavatī.
In the northwest, O beloved, is the city of Vāyu named Gandhavahā;
and to the north is the city of Soma named Mahodayā.
In the northeast is the city of the Lord of Ishana, named Yashovati.
Likewise,
O Goddess, hear now of the twenty-six cities to the north of these.
To the south of Amarāvatī is the city of the Apsarases called Kāmavatī;
it is golden, belonging to the hosts of Siddhas, and indeed situated to the south of that [city].
To its south is another auspicious city of the Ādityas, adorned with rubies, renowned by the name Aṃśumatī.
The divine city of the Sādhyas, renowned as Kusumāvatī,
is indeed to the south; it is incorrect to say that Kāmavatī is the city of the Revatīs, for its two names are Kāmavatī and Sauvarṇī.
In the western quarter of the Fire-god lies the city of Viśveṣāṃ Revatī.
It is called Revatī, where the Viśvedevas reside. || 139 ||
To the west of that, O Goddess, is the divine [abode] of Viśvakarman,
known by the name Divyā.
To the west of Dharmarāja, the city of Mātṛnandā is remembered.
There the Mothers sport, reeling from their drinking of honeyed wine.
To the west of that [river] belongs to the Rudras; it is golden and named Rohitā.
There, the Rudras bearing tridents are the attendants of Yama;
to the west of that [city] is to be known the city named Guṇavatī.
To the east of Nirṛti is the city named Piṅgalā, which possesses a gateway and a vajra-fortification wall for the eleven Rudras. (10.143)
O Queen of the Gods, the Piśācas dwelling there have names derived from their own actions;
they are so called because of their own act of devouring flesh, which serves as their defining characteristic.
Near the northwestern direction, the city known as Kṛṣṇāvatī is remembered.
In that very place dwell the Rākṣasas known as Nistriṃśas;
[it is] there, in the vicinity—that is, near—the north of the direction of Nirṛti.
To the north of that city as well is the golden city Sukhāvatī.
Mitra dwells right there, surrounded by many servants, in the place known by the name Sukhāvatī.
To the north of that as well is the famous golden mountain named Gāndharvī.
Gandharvas, surrounded by divine maidens, dwell there;
their number is proclaimed to be ten thousand crores.
The army of the Siddhas belongs to the Bhūtas, while that of Varuṇa is to the south;
the one called Hema belongs to the Vasus, and that of Varuṇa is also to the north.
"Of Varuṇa" refers to that city. || 148 ||
To the north of that, O Goddess, is the city named Siddhavatī;
that city is celebrated as belonging to all the Vidyādharas.
To the south of Vāyu, O Goddess, is remembered the city named Siddhā;
there dwell the Kinnaras in cities possessing the splendor of gold and the sun.
To the east of Vāyu is the city of Gāndharvī, made of gold, belonging to Citraratha,
the chief of the Gandharva kings, which resounds with the divine songs of the Gandharvas.
The Blessed Lady herself resides there, adorned with the seven musical notes,
clothed in the three scales (grāmas), and embellished by the girdle of the musical modes (jātis).
Her limbs are variegated with melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) and melodic expansions (*tāna*); she arises through the emergence of various rhythmic cycles (*tāla*);
she is endowed with primary and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); and she is veiled by the middle [register]. (10.153)
There, that goddess Sarasvatī was being sung of by Gandharvas,
and she was attended by sages such as Nārada, as well as by Nāgas and Kinnaras.

The villages (*grāma*) are the six, beginning with Madhyama and Gāndhāra. The eighteen *jātis*, such as Ṣāḍjī and Nandayantī, are the girdles (*mekhalā*). The melodic sequences (*mūrcchanā*), such as Uttara-mandrā and others, are those by which the notes (*svara*) "faint" (*mūrchanti*)—that is, they are raised through their interweaving.
"The seven notes arranged in sequence are designated as *mūrcchanās*. (28–34).

Thus, twenty-one *mūrcchanās* are defined in Bharata’s *Nāṭyaśāstra*. Those by which [the notes] are stretched (*tāyante*) or expanded are called *tānas*; there are forty-nine and thirty-five of them. As it is stated in that very same work:
Beginning with "The *tānas* consist of six and five notes" (28–34), [it continues]:
"In that regard, there are eighty-four *tānas* based on the *mūrcchanās* that consist of five notes, and forty-nine that consist of six notes."

"Fifty-five vowels" (28–35). The *tālas* are those such as *cañcatpuṭa* and others, which consist of rhythmic measures (*yati*). The *kalās*, however, are the long and short prosodic units (*mātrā*) that constitute the syllables of the *tāla*. The defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) are as follows—

"Bhūṣaṇa, akṣarasaṅghāta, śobhā, udāharaṇa," and so forth—these are the thirty-six [types]. "Vyañjanā" means that which is endowed with those specific songs (*gītaka*) by which [the meanings] are manifested (*vyajyante*). "By the middle" refers to the tone (*svara*) known as the middle [register].
On account of its connection with an excellence of audibility, it is veiled; in the case of the heroine, the shadow of the puns upon the metaphors is clear. (154)
To the east of that city is Citrā, belonging to Tumburu and Nārada;
to the west of Soma is the city of the Guhyakas, known as Pramadā.
To the east, however, is the city of Soma named Citravatī;
and belonging to the high-souled Kubera is the variegated city made of all kinds of precious minerals.
For there,
surrounded by twenty-six thousand koṭis,
that glorious and supreme among yakṣas dwells with unsurpassed enjoyments. (10.157)
It is appropriate. || 157 ||
To its east is a city named Śubhā, made of Jāmbūnada gold;
there indeed dwell the Karmadevas,
and they...
...have attained divinity through their actions. || 10-158 ||
By means of the Vājapeya and other [sacrifices]. || 158 ||
To the west of the Lord of the Mountains lies the glorious city of Viṣṇu;
there dwells the illustrious Lord of Śrī, who resembles the flax flower.
Janārdana, holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and clad in yellow garments, resides there;
to the south of Īśa is the city named Padmavatī.
Of Brahmā, who is seated upon a great lotus, who wears a garland of lotuses,
whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, and who was born from a lotus.
Of the incarnation who is a portion of Brahmā residing in Satyaloka. || 161 ||
To its south, O Goddess, is the city named Kāmasukhāvatī;
there, O Queen of the Gods, dwell the two Aśvins,
the physicians of the gods.
...and likewise Dhanvantari stands there. || 10-162 ||
The physician for cows. || 162 ||
To the north of Amarāvatī, there is the one renowned as Mahāmedhā;
that divine dwelling place of the Vināyakas has been established there. (10.163)
For they were formerly ten thousand times ten million valiant ones, [known as] the Kubhas, as well as the Vināyakas, greatly radiant, with splendor blazing like fire. || 10.164 ||
For the sake of slaying the Asuras, they were created by me from my thumb;
because they were fashioned from the thumb, which is the locus of the fire of time (kālāgni), they possess this brilliance.
He summarizes: "In this manner, Meru is surrounded below and above by such excellent cities. (10.165)
Above the assembly hall of Brahmā, [it is reached] by means of the city of Tryambaka situated among the luminous realms. || 165 ||
And these cities— which have been fully described as being all around Meru— are all filled with thousands of millions of cities, O beloved. (10.166)
Completely filled with all forms of sovereignty, resplendent with every kind of jewel,
crowded with divine women, and teeming with divine men.
There, O Goddess, in every city of the gods, there is constant bliss, with celestial palaces, cities, groves, and the pavilions of the four gardens. (10.168)
With parasols, banners, and flags, crowded with elephants and horses,
and with the sounds of drums and cymbals, and the resonant blasts of conchs and trumpets.
The temple of the gods was always filled with songs and dances;
"filled" (ākīrṇa) means crowded or bustling.
And therefore—
O Goddess, those men in the meritorious land of Bhārata who are devoted to sacrifices and charitable works, || 10.170 ||
Those men who worship Tryambaka even once go to Meru.
Those people who are devoted to *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and works of public utility) in the land of Bhārata— which is the refuge of the virtuous and will be described hereafter—
and who worship Maheśvara, known as Tryambaka, even once, that is, for a single moment, as if in sport, they go to Meru.
Those who have received initiation, however, being constantly devoted to its worship, are indeed liberated.
Even those who have been thoroughly sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā... they too will be there.
...the best of gods sport. || 10-171 ||
Having attained the state of being preeminent gods. || 171 ||
Thus, having heard of the power of Gaṅgā, the venerable Goddess, desiring to know it, said:
"O best of gods, please tell me in brief by your grace: how did Gaṅgā, who is saluted by gods and siddhas, come into being? (10.172)
The illustrious Bhairava said: "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall describe the origin of the Gaṅgā;
he now begins to speak of it."
For in the past, that Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, was indeed my wife.

By my supreme pervasion, my wife—the power called Kṣayā—abides through the very same supreme pervasion of the Cause of the Universe; for this reason, she is the Mother of the World from of old, the cause of the expansion of the universe at the primordial creation.
Because he has voluntarily assumed the form of Rudra as the presiding deity of the world of Rudra, this— namely,
my "eye-water"—
means tears of bliss.
O Mother of the World, because in the past, under the influence of amorous play with you who possess form, my eyes were sometimes covered by your fingernails and then opened again by you. (10.174)
"O beloved, water flowed from the mouths of the leaders of the attendants by means of your fingers.

Speaking thus, the Lord of Umā (Umāpati) indicates that his own self is non-different from Rudrabhaṭṭāraka, who possesses the world of Rudra situated above, and that the Goddess residing therein is non-different from Umābhaṭṭārikā, and so forth.
And that water which has flowed out by means of the fingers, that alone [is to be used].
The Gaṅgā has issued forth in ten streams...
from among them... [is] within my skull-covering. (10.175)

"Seven indeed are established there... [referring to] which Prajāpatis he protects; "Kapāla" is Rudra; "in his enclosure" means in the world of Rudra, which is characterized by the upper skull of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). As he will state later:
Vareṇyā, Varadā, Variṣṭhā, Varavarṇinī,
Vasiṣṭhā, Varāhā, and Varārohā as the seventh.
"For these are declared to be the Gaṅgās that always carry one to the world of Rudra.
(10.550.551) Thus [it is said].
Of these three,
however— one resides in the city of Viṣṇu,
and the second is situated above the world of Brahmā.
Regarding that which is above the world of Brahmā, the world of truth (satyaloka):
"O Dear One, at a distance of ten million yojanas above the world of truth, there is the place known as the Seat of Brahmā (brahmāsana), possessing the luster of hibiscus and vermilion. (10.534)
Thus, where that abode of Brahmā is, there.
The third [state] goes to Satyaloka. || 10-176 ||
It is indeed the third [state], by virtue of the power of irresistible will (prākāmya)—
both in heaven and...
moreover—
...she indeed remained once more in the lunar orb,
in the world of Soma.
This very [power], having issued forth from Soma, was established in the sky of old. || 10.177 ||
From Soma, from the world of Soma. || 177 ||
Then, O Goddess, being praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, I [descended] to the highly meritorious river Gaṅgā out of a desire for the welfare of mortals. (10.178)
Having brought him down, O Mahādeva, release him into the mortal world—
from the sky, that is to say.
Then, O Mistress of the Gods, that Aparājitā was addressed by me:
"O beautiful goddess, come for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
Then she,
having arrived, [placed her hand] upon my head...
"Mine! [was the thought] of him who had gone to the peak of Jyotiṣka.
...returned once more to the summit of Meru. || 10-180 ||
Emerging from that, O Goddess of gods, she flows toward the oceans in the four directions;
she is designated as the Sītā in the east, while the Suvahā is in the south.
Sunandā is in the western part, and likewise Bhadrasomā is in the north;
it should be understood that the Gaṅgā reaches the oceans situated in the four directions, though separated by many mountains and so forth, through its power of sovereign will (*prākāmya*).
Having spoken of the majesty of the Gaṅgā as an incidental digression, he states the subject at hand:
"But Mandara, O Great Goddess, is known by the name Gandhamādana. (10.182)
Vipula, Supārśva, and the others ending with Uttara are declared to be the *viṣkambhas*—
meaning they are the supporting pillars— as stated in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"By these [mountains] supporting the earth, Mount Meru stands motionless," thus [it is said]. (8.60)
Learn from me also the colors of these mountains. || 183 ||
White, yellow like turmeric, blue, and having the luster of a pomegranate—these are equal to crystal, gold, sapphire, and ruby, respectively; such is the meaning.
And since a separate measurement for these has not been stated, it should be understood that they are merely parts of the nine thousand Ilāvṛtas that are to come.
Thus, it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
Since it has been stated, "The Meru-peak is square and joined by nine thousand [yojanas]," it follows by implication that the trees and mountains occupy a portion of that space.
Furthermore:
"Near the Prāgviṣkambha, there is a forest named Citraratha. (10.184)
There is a lake named Aruṇodaka adorned with lotuses,
and near Gandhamādana is the great forest called Nandana.
In its center is the Mānasa lake, covered with lotuses;
near Vipula, however, is the great Vaibhrāja forest.
In its center was a pond of pure water called Sitoda;
near its own flank was a forest named Pitṛvana.
Within it, however, is the great and beautiful Bhadra lake;
right here, I shall describe the four Kalpa trees—learn of them. (10.188)
Then, on Mount Mandara, there is a Kadamba tree situated upon its summit,
extending for a thousand yojanas in length and rising five hundred yojanas in height.
That well-flowered *kadamba* tree shines with flowers the size of water-jars;
it stands together with its branches at a height of one thousand five hundred *yojanas*.
The Jambū tree on the summit of Gandhamādana is remembered as being of that same measurement.
The juice arising from the mass of its fruits should be known as being like nectar;
by that, O beloved, the river Jambū was produced, flowing with great force.
"By that" means by means of the aesthetic flavor (rasa). || 191 ||
And he, having circumambulated Meru, shall enter his own Jambū tree at its root;
from contact with that [tree], gold is produced which serves as an ornament for the gods.
Therefore, it is known in the world as Jāmbūnada, the supreme ornament;
there, the trees, creepers, shrubs, birds, beasts of prey, and so forth [are golden]. (10.193)
All those who dwell there are made of Jāmbūnada gold;
furthermore,
even within that vast [region], there is a tree known as Ketumāla, which is like a great Aśvattha.
"So be it"; thus, that is the authoritative means of knowledge. || 194 ||
He explains the designation "Ketumāla":
"After Indra had conquered the asuras there, a garland of jewels was suspended;
therefore, that region, frequented by the Siddhas, is known as Ketumāla. (10.195)
Furthermore:
"The Nyagrodha tree on Supārśva is said to be equal to that [Meru] in both size and magnitude."
Thus, in brief, Mount Meru is renowned as being endowed with manifold virtues. || 196 ||
Now, as this has been stated in brief— I shall describe, in summary, the regions situated at its side, my dear; first of all:
From the center of Meru, in the four directions, it extends for half a lakh [yojanas], in brief.
Jambudvīpa extends all around up to the salt ocean;
from the base of Meru to its center it measures fifty thousand [yojanas], and by calculating both sides of that, it becomes one hundred thousand.
Indeed, there are nine divisions there, separated by mountains.
"Therein" means in Jambudvīpa; "parts" means sections.
For it is thus:
"In the southern direction, three mountain ranges are to be known;
those three are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat. (10.199)

"Where indeed Tārkṣya was forbidden when he was intent on killing the serpent Śeṣa," and, "Likewise, that mountain Hemakūṭa where a great peak of gold was given by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) to Prajāpati for the sake of sacrifice."
"...[He is] Himavat, possessing peaks of snow; though rich in jewels, he is full of snow, and for that reason this mountain is Himavat. Thus it is described in the Śrīparā. || 199 ||
Furthermore:
"To the north of Meru are the mountains Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān.
There, the planet Śani was born with a deep blue luster; therefore, that mountain is called Nīla."
And there is a white mountain, blue in hue, where the great sage Śveta resides.
"Though being swallowed by Death, he was protected by the Moon-crested Lord.
And: "The three-peaked mountain Śveta is like the crushing of a thunderbolt;
indeed, the three gods are stationed upon those three peaks."
Thus it is also stated in that very same place.
He states their measurement:
"For these six mountain ranges indeed extend from east to west. (10.200)
They have reached the western ocean from the eastern ocean. || 200 ||
There too—
Nīla and Niṣadha are both proclaimed to be one hundred thousand yojanas in extent,
because they are situated in the middle.
Following the circular shape of the continent, Śveta and Hemakūṭa are recorded as being ninety thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Himavat and Śṛṅgavat, as well as the eighty thousand [other mountains]—
these [mountains], extending as far as the salt ocean...
But from the measurement of the sides, they are two thousand [yojanas] in width. || 10-202 ||
Furthermore:
"Himavat is joined with Kailāsa, and Triśṛṅga together with Jārudhi.
Kailāsa is in the middle of Himavat and has the form of a peak. As it is stated in the Devīyāmala:
Beginning with, "In its center is Mahāśṛṅga, extending for a hundred yojanas," and continuing,
"There the wielder of the trident dwells forever together with the immortals."
But Jārudhi is attached to Śṛṅgavat.
He describes their color in reverse order:
"The Śṛṅgavan [mountain] shines white, bright like the moon. (10.203)
Niṣadha is blue, composed of sapphire; Hemakūṭa has the luster of rubies;
and Himavat is like snow, made of gold.
Regarding the two mountains to the east and west of Meru, he says:
"To the east of Meru, the mountain Mālyavat shines forth, O Goddess of the Gods, extending for thirty-four thousand yojanas. (10.205)
Extending from south to north, its width shines at one thousand [yojanas];
likewise, on the western side, there is the Gandhamādana mountain, equal to that.
In terms of length and breadth. And this is distinct from the Gandhamādana support-mountain located to the south. Regarding these two, it is said in the Śrīparā:
"Having seen divine garlands by those who have come for the sake of serving Brahmā..."
"Because the *mālya* [garlands] were gathered there by the perfected ones (*siddhas*), it is therefore called Mālyavat.
And likewise:
"In former times, a Vidyādhara woman named Mālyā was seen indeed intoxicated with passion."
In this [place], it was smelled by the seer Nārada and became permeated with joy.
"In the Nirukta it is said: 'The fragrance that intoxicates the wise is called Gandhamādana. || 206 ||
He states the height of all these [mountains]:
"Nīla, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana are forty thousand yojanas in height. (10.207)
The blue mountains and the others stand as if occupying the positions of the various walls of Meru, having such dimensions.
As for the Hemakūṭa and Himavat mountains situated to the south and north, their height is ten thousand *yojanas*, like that of the Śveta peak. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendrottara*:
"Two thousand [yojanas] in width and ten in height, with nine internal [divisions]" (13.65).
Thus, Jambudvīpa is divided into nine parts by eight mountains—three each situated in the south and north, and one each in the east and west. || 207 ||
Furthermore:
On the four sides of Mount Meru, there are two boundary mountains each,
facing the directions starting with the east, extending as far as the ocean.
Therein—Jaṭhara and Hemakūṭa are situated on the eastern side. (10.208)
Kailāsa and Himavat are situated on the southern side,
while Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are the two mountains on the western side.
Jārudhi and Śṛṅgavān are situated to the north.
These Hemakūṭas and others are indeed different from the previously mentioned ones of the same names; these eight constitute the ninefold division of Jambudvīpa because they are insurmountable.
They are the causes for the interval between the nine parts.
Regarding the division of regions by name within this area divided into nine parts by the previously mentioned mountains, he says:
"Surrounding Meru on all sides, Ilāvṛta is declared to be delightful. (10.210)
Beneath the Cakravāḍa mountain range, it extends for nine thousand yojanas,
square in shape on all four sides.

Therefore, having calculated that each of the two sides of Mount Meru— which stands in the middle and measures sixteen thousand [yojanas]— is nine thousand [yojanas], this [distance] becomes thirty-four thousand [yojanas] in the direction of length.
For this very reason, Mālyavat and Gandhamādana, situated in the east and west, are thirty-four thousand [yojanas].
It is rightly said that this refers to length. And its etymological explanation is as follows:
"A divine Apsaras named Ilā, endowed with beauty and youth, was seen wandering about, captivating the mind with her nectar-like form."
"Because it is covered by those two arms out of passion, it is called Ilāvṛta.
Thus it is stated in the Śrīparā. || 211 ||
And here, because it is surrounded by the Cakravāḍa mountain range—
neither the heat of the sun nor the rays of the moon prevail there over the worlds.
But this—.........is illuminated by the light of Meru. || 212 ||
For this very reason—people there possess the luster of fresh lotus petals and are exceedingly delicate;
subsisting on the juice of jambū fruits, they are entirely free from old age and death. (213)
Their lifespan is proclaimed to be thirteen thousand years;
therefore, it is said that they are free from untimely death.
Furthermore: "The gods, gandharvas, siddhas, rishis, and vināyakas... (10.214)
And this Ilāvṛta is surrounded by the Gaṇas, Mātṛs, sisters, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and others of this kind, in incalculable numbers.
Now,
to the east of the ocean and south of Gandhamādana,
there is a region known as Ketumāla, which possesses the highest of all qualities. (10.216)
That which is the western [direction] of Gandhamādana, situated behind Meru, becomes the very eastern direction of the western ocean.
And it is said in the Śrīparā:
"When the terrible conflict between the gods and the asuras has arisen..."
Suddenly, a garland of comets rose up there all at once.
Seeing her, the gods were terrified; therefore, Ketumāla is so called. Thus ends the section on the region (varṣa) as a populated district (janapada). || 216 ||
The people there are exceedingly beautiful, dark as the petals of the blue lotus;
having drunk the juice of the jackfruit tree, they live for ten thousand years.
Ten thousands are an ayuta.
Furthermore:
Jayanta, Vardhamāna, Aśoka, Hariparvata, Viśāla, Kambala, and Kṛṣṇa—these are the seven principal mountain ranges there. (10.218)
At the summit of Meru, on the eastern side of Mālyavat and to the west of the ocean,
lies the region known as Bhadrāśva; there too, the lifespan is ten thousand years.
The people resemble the moon and subsist on the fruit of the black mango (*kālāmra*).
And it is said in the *Śrīparā*:
"Uccaiḥśravas and Bhadrāśva emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk."
Because he moved there, the horse [was called] Bhadrāśva, and thus that region came to be known by that name.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore: the kaurañja, the śvetaparṇa, the nīla, and likewise the mālāgraka. || 10-220 ||
And Padma is likewise declared; there are five mountain ranges of the *kula* type.
These [ranges] in Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva are recorded as extending thirty-two thousand [yojanas] from east to west.
Thirty-four thousand [yojanas] extend from south to north;
likewise, Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva extend thirty-two thousand each from east to west;
and Gandhamādana and Mālyavat are each one thousand [yojanas].
Ilāvṛta occupies eighteen [lakṣas] on both sides, while Meru occupies sixteen; thus Jambudvīpa extends for one hundred thousand yojanas from east to west.
This includes the measurement of the boundary mountains such as Jaṭhara and others, as well as the measurement of the principal mountain ranges such as Jayanta and others.
In that very context, because it is already included as a single part, it should not be counted separately.
Having thus described the location of the two regions in the east and west, he speaks of it in the north as well: "Two regions indeed are declared...
The term "are declared" (*samākhyāte*) should be applied to both the conclusion and the beginning, like the eye of a crow (which moves between two sockets).
In the east and west are the two regions known as Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva.

But those who dwell in the region of Kuru and Hiraṇmaya—which will be described in their respective divisions to the north of Meru—[reside] from the middle of those two: [they are] the inhabitants of the Kuru-varṣa. || 222 ||
Those worlds are called the Kurus,
because [the inhabitants] eat the fruits of the kuru-tree.
And for this reason: thirteen thousand live with perpetual youth. || 10-223 ||
They give birth in pairs, free from the fear of separation;

they are born at the same time and likewise pass away at the same time—this is the implication. And for this reason, it is possible that women who follow their husbands [into the next life] are born after them.
Furthermore, in this regard: men and women who resemble the *śyāmā* flower, being glossy and handsome. (10.224)
The meaning is "and women. || 224 ||
Likewise:
the ground consists entirely of jewels and is strewn with Himalayan sand.
And this Kuru-varṣa is [measured] from its side—
It is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a bow. || 225 ||

In the expression "dhanvākāram," the elision of the letter *s* is a Vedic (chāndasa) anomaly. Because of its length, this measurement is like that of a horn; however, due to its proximity to the northern ocean situated in the form of a circle, it assumes the very shape of a bow (*dhanurākāra*) through proportional calculation (*anupāta*).
And there are two mountain ranges there, Sūryakānta and Indukānta;
and right there is the Kalpavṛkṣa tree named Kuru, radiant with flowers.
That most beautiful region should be known as Kuruvarṣa after his name. In the Śrīmatparā, it is said:
"Upamanyu was [established] by Hara in the region called Ramyavatkuruvarṣa."
"But do this; drink the milk, and do whatever was told by him. Thus it is explained. || 226 ||
Then, having entered the salt ocean from its northern direction— || 10-227 ||
The Moon Island is proclaimed to be five thousand yojanas in extent;
likewise, having entered the salt ocean in the northwestern direction. (10.228)
O fair-faced one, it is exactly four thousand yojanas;
the auspicious island is proclaimed to be ten thousand yojanas [in circumference]. (10.229)
It should be known as having an auspicious form, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
By the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in "only four," it is understood that this [number] applies even to the previous entry into the ocean. || 229 ||
Furthermore:
"There, people with a lifespan of ten thousand years subsist on divine nectar and fruits. (10.230)
In this very manner—
even in the region called Candra— the lifespan is ten thousand years, and those who enjoy the fruits [of their karma] live thus long.
Having thus described Kuru-varṣa as being like a horn in the interval between the north and the interior, he speaks of the Hiraṇmaya-varṣa.
And between Śveta and Śṛṅgavān, it should be known that there is a golden region. || 10-231 ||
It is described here in this way because it consists of gold; however, regarding the *parā* [kalā], it is said:
"Where the principal Gandharva forcibly took his pleasure with Ramaṇā, that supreme region is called Ramaṇa..."
Thus it was stated by another name: the Apsaras named Ramaṇā [was wedded] by Citraratha, the chief of the Gandharvas. || 231 ||
Having consumed the fruit of the *lakuca*, people there, resembling the moon, live for thirteen and a half thousand years by that measure. (10.232)
Now,
to the north of Nīla and likewise to the south of Śveta,
there is a region named Ramyaka.
This is also stated in the *Parā*: "The auspicious Apsaras Urvaśī, having been seen by Candramas, was indeed addressed as 'Ramya'; from that word, this [place] received the name Ramya."
Thus it is explained in the Nirukta.
And there—... subsisting on the fruit of the nyagrodha tree. || 10-233 ||
Dark as the petals of the blue lotus and free from old age and disease,
their lifespan is proclaimed to be twelve thousand years. (10.234)
And although this has already been stated in terms of length, it is now described from the side:
"Ramya and Hiraṇmaya have an extent of nine thousand [yojanas]";
that is to say, both Ramyaka and Hiraṇmaya.
Having described the location of the regions to the north of Meru, he now speaks in order regarding those to the south:
"To the north of Hemakūṭa and to the south of Niṣadha. (10.235)
Harivarṣa is thus described; the beings there have the luster of silver, live for twelve thousand years, and subsist on sugarcane juice.
And that [place] is exceedingly beautiful and extends for nine thousand [yojanas];
and this is where Hari was propitiated by the serpent Śeṣa.
Thus ends the etymological explanation in the Śrīparā.
Now,
to the south of Hemakūṭa and to the north of Himavat— || 10-237 ||
The region named Kiṃpuruṣa is there; its people have complexions like gold, live for nine thousand years, and subsist on the fruit of the Plakṣa tree.
Its width is said there to be exactly nine thousand [yojanas].
Regarding Kiṃpuruṣa:
this too [is described]—where a beautiful Vidyādharī, released from the hand of a Vidyādhara, [descends].
"Was a man abandoned by you?"—thus she was addressed; this is explained in the *Parā-nirukta*.
Now,
[it is located] to the south of the lord of the Himālayas and to the north of the salt ocean.
The region known as Bhārata is indeed small, and its happiness is considered slight;
for—people there are terrified by the fear of disease, suffering, and possessing meager prosperity. (10.240)
Some are handsome and others are ugly; some are fortunate and others are unfortunate;
some possess enjoyments while others have meager enjoyments, and likewise others are utterly miserable. (10.241)
Fair-complexioned, dark, black, tawny, and white-brown—according to the distinctions of color and caste, and in accordance with their various respective duties. (10.242)
The four castes (*caturvarṇa*) and even the outcaste tribes (*antya-jā*) are born in the land called Bhārata.

"Caste" (*varṇa*) refers to the Brāhmaṇa and the others; "birth" (*jāti*) refers to the lineages (*gotra*) such as Pulastya, Pulaha, and so forth. Furthermore, this region [is called Bhārata] because "suffering was borne (*bhṛtam duḥkham*) here by Bharata through his sons who had gone astray."

Thus it is stated in the *Śrīparā*. In this way, these nine regions (*varṣa*) are explained in the *Śrīparā*; however, [the author] will state here that they are presided over by lords whose names begin with Ilāvṛta.
And here—[he described] the islands and the intermediate islands, together with their own local languages. (10.243)
The wise and likewise the foolish, those skilled in arts and sciences, as well as yogis and men of knowledge, the most virtuous and others who are sinful—[all these are equal]. (10.244)
O beloved, some are born as beggars while others are born as givers; likewise, many men are born as messengers and slaves throughout their lives. (10.245)
Within the continents are the intermediate islands; these are the "other islands. Servants are those who are to be employed, even though they may not be slaves. (245)
Thus, although it is possessed of faults, there remains therein one virtue: the acquisition of both auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
Both of these are possible here; however, for those with discernment, by avoiding the inauspicious, they may strive for the acquisition of the auspicious.
They exert themselves. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"If even a single quality were to be fully exerted, nothing desired would remain unaccomplished" (13.92).
Furthermore, in the other continents—excluding Bhārata—none of the conditions consisting of the three ages (yugas) exist. || 10.246 ||
Apart from the Kṛta Yuga, it consists of the Tretā and the other ages.
Therefore,
O fair-faced one, it should be known that [the land] called Bhārata possesses four yugas;
and thus—
In that very place, whatever action is performed, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
By means of that, the worlds from Śiva down to Avīci abide [in it].
He states that right here there is the abundance of self-manifested holy fords and great rivers, which are the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
Mahākāla, likewise Ekāmra, and so forth, O fair-faced one. (10.248)
Ten million sacred fords (tīrtha) are said to exist there, yielding the fruit of great merit;
and five hundred rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, are also located there.

By the word "evamādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the five groups of eight [shrines] beginning with Śrī Amareśa, as well as the sixty-eight forms of Śrī Mahādeva located in Vārāṇasī and other places.
By the term "tīrthānām" (of the sacred sites), there is the inclusion of Prabhāsa and others, as it is stated in the *Śrī Deviyāmala*:
"O fair-faced one, there is one crore of sacred fords beginning with Prabhāsa;
and right there is the group of five octads (pañcāṣṭaka), which always bestows grace upon the worlds. (249)
And know that Kuru-varṣa is nine thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a bow;
and as for Bhārata-varṣa—
Nine divisions are recorded there, separated by oceans, O beloved.
Separated by the ocean waters brought down from the Himalayas in their length, there lies here the eighth region of water known as Bindusaras. As he will say:
"Beginning from Bindusaras, [the land] called Kumārī... (10.254). || 250 ||
In this regard, one thousand *yojanas* each are proclaimed for every single continent;
the meaning is that this measurement includes the water as well.
As it is said:
"Five hundred [yojanas] are to be known as the land, and likewise five hundred as the water. (10.251)

This is the measurement of the side; as for the length, it is like that of the Himavat mountain according to the proportional sequence, because it is separated by water measuring five hundred [yojanas]. || 251 ||
And thus—
those [regions] are mutually inaccessible;
"those" refers to the specific continents.
.........hear from me their names: Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimat. (10.252)
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Vāruṇa;
and the island named Kumārikā is proclaimed as the ninth. (10.253)

It has been stated that there are seven oceans acting as separators for the eight continents. Regarding the ninth, however, he describes the separator by defining its boundary: "Starting from Bindusaras itself, it is proclaimed as the one called Kumārī."
This is its distinction from the previous ones: namely,
that this [distance] is one thousand yojanas—
not five hundred like the others— but rather the division of this [region] which consists of a thousand.
It was created by Bindusaras, situated within the sphere of Varuṇa.
And this—[is] endowed with various castes and stages of life. (10.254)
The castes are those beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. || 254 ||
Moreover:
"O beloved of excellent complexion, those qualities previously mentioned that exist in the world of Bhārata reside right there in the world known as Kumārī. (10.255)

The qualities—consisting of the acquisition of auspiciousness, self-manifestation, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), holy rivers, and sanctuaries—are located in Kumārīdvīpa alone. As it is stated in the venerable *Śrīkaṇṭhī*:
"In the center of that [world] is a great island known as Kumārīdvīpa."
"In that place, a full hundred Rudras have descended, bringing about auspiciousness;
they are the cause of liberation for bound souls (paśus) and destroy sins through mere remembrance.
As for Indradvīpa and other such lands, they are the dwelling places of those who are mostly Mlecchas and similar [non-Aryans].
And [the place] is not presided over by deities, sacred fords (tīrtha), and so forth. As it has been stated elsewhere:

"The conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) exists in the region called Kumārī; of this there is no doubt. Others are designated as Mlecchas, being excluded from the conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭa). || 255 ||
And furthermore:
"The seven mountain ranges are to be known as being situated right there, most beautiful:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śaktimān, and the Ṛkṣa mountain. (10.256)

The Vindhya and Pāriyātra mountains shine as these principal mountain ranges (*kulaparvata*), beautiful and conducive to the accomplishment of spiritual attainments (*siddhi*). The Pāriyātra range mentioned here is distinct from the one located in Ketumāla;
so it is elsewhere as well.
Now, O Dear One, there are six sub-islands situated in the midst of the Southern Ocean. (10.257)
He states them as follows:
Aṅgadvīpa, that called Yava, Malaya, the one named Śaṅkha, Kumuda, and Varāha—thus they are celebrated. (10.258)
From among these—on the island of Malaya, it is said, there is a mountain named Malaya;
at its foot is indeed Trikūṭa, and Laṅkā is situated upon it. (10.259)
At the end of the foot [of the verse]. || 259 ||
And that city was made of gold, radiant, adorned with crossroads and gardens—
with crossroads established by Śiva that grant liberation, and with gardens.
Adorned with places of enjoyment.
Likewise:
"Adorned with variegated walls, it is embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli. (10.260)
There, Rākṣasas of infinite wealth and great strength and prowess, devoted to young maidens, take their pleasure with celestial nymphs. || 10.261 ||
Parākrama means enthusiasm. || 261 ||
And furthermore:
"There, on that best of mountains, Malaya, is the peak of Agastya;
there is the most meritorious hermitage of Agastya, radiant as crystal. (10.262)
There, beings who are otherwise mutually hostile play together without fear; there no pestilence arises, nor does untimely death occur. (10.263)

There is neither old age nor sorrow, nor is there fear of calamities anywhere. "Mārī" refers to excessive mortality; "unseasonable time" refers to the reversal of rain and heat; and "upasargas" refers to diseases.
Furthermore: No one speaks untruth, nor is there any passion or hatred anywhere. (10.264)
By the power of Agastya, your ignorance has been cast far away;
there indeed dwell heroic sages who have exerted themselves in the yoga of knowledge. (10.265)
O Great Goddess, they are devoted to recitation, study, fire-oblations, worship, and praise, and are constantly intent upon the propitiation of Tryambaka, the Great God.
Accompanied by Agastya, all those who proclaim liberation and worldly prosperity remain there with purified souls, capable of both inflicting curses and bestowing grace.
Those whose character is such say that liberation itself is the highest prosperity; by them, the self has been cultivated and brought to the state of Śiva.
He summarizes: Jambudvīpa extends for one hundred thousand yojanas all around;
it is ten thousand [yojanas] from east to west, and it is said to be the same from south to north.

The six regions—Kuru, Hiraṇmaya, Ramyaka, Hari, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata—are each nine thousand [yojanas], making fifty-four. Each of the mountain ranges—Śṛṅgavat, Śveta, Nīla, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, and Himavat—is two thousand [yojanas] wide, making twelve. [These surround] Meru.
Including the eighteen regions situated to the left and right, such as Ilāvṛta, and the sixteen thousand [yojanas] of Meru, Jambūdvīpa thus consists of one hundred thousand yojanas.
And outside of this, the salt water stands, extending for one hundred thousand yojanas. (10.268)
The salt-water ocean is the Kṣārasamudra. || 268 ||
And that—
consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), existing in a circular form by way of its circumference—
is indeed stated in the Śrīmalaya:
"In all cases, the circumference is three times the diameter... thus [it is said].
Furthermore: "Terrified by the fear of Vṛtra’s enemy, the mountains entered there. (10.269)
There are exactly twelve of great prowess; I shall name them in brief: Vṛtrāri, Indra, and so forth.
He said to them:
"The bull, the drum, and the smoke-colored one have entered from the eastern side. (10.270)
Candra, Kaṅka, and Droṇa entered by the north;
then Aśoka, Varāha, and Nandana as the third.
Other mountains there entered the salt ocean:
Cakra, the one named Maināka, and the third was Balāhaka.
O lady of excellent hips, the mountains have entered from the south;
and here,
between Cakra and Maināka, indeed stands the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha).
Thus, Jambūdvīpa, surrounded by the oceans, has been described...
Now, these [regions] exist solely through the presiding authority of their respective lords, named Ilāvṛta and so forth.
Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): he begins by demonstrating the form and the source that serve as the cause for the arising of perceptions of deities—
.........whereas the source is now being explained.
Among them, the first king was named Svāyambhuva Manu.
His son was Priyavrata. || 10-274 ||
Then ten sons were born to him, preeminent in heroism and strength:
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vapu. (10.275)
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana,
and Satra— among these, Medhā, Satra, and Agnibāhu are the three who have gone forth as renunciants. || 10-276 ||
Those remaining great powerful consecrated [kings] throughout the seven continents— among them,
in Jambudvīpa, was Agnīdhra...
Having said "So be it," he was consecrated.
His nine sons are recorded. || 10-277 ||
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Hari, Ilāvṛta, Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Ramyaka, and Hiraṇmaya. || 10-278 ||
The ninth is named Kuru...
these are remembered as the lords of the nine regions (varṣas).
Those born from Agnīdhra were indeed heroes, exceedingly powerful and fierce.
O Pārvatī, the nine regions here are marked with their names;
among them, the first region was Bhārata-varṣa, which was marked with the name of Nābhi.
Afterwards, however, there was the son of Nābhi, the greatly heroic Vṛṣabha, who was devoted to dharma. || 10-280 ||
His son was the powerful Bharata;
it is after his name alone that this most excellent region should be known as Bhārata-varṣa.
Then, O beloved, eight sons were born to him once more, with a daughter as the last;
from among them—
In this Bhārata consisting of eight islands, eight sons were established.
The ninth, however, is called "the maiden" (kumāryāhva), because it is dedicated to the maiden;
it is termed "the maiden" precisely because of the dedication to a maiden.
And therefore: "Those islands were proclaimed by Bharata after their names. (10.283)
Those who were previously mentioned as "Indra and Kaśeru" (10.252). || 283 ||
Thus, having first described Jambudvīpa as divided into seventeen parts, he speaks of the other continents:
"O Pārvatī, Jambudvīpa, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomeda, and Puṣkara—these are the seven continents. (10.284)
O lady of virtuous vows, I shall now describe to you those oceans by which the continents are encircled:
salt water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and likewise sugarcane juice. (10.285)
And the seven oceans are declared to be Madyoda, Svādūda, and so forth;

these are situated according to the sequence of the aforementioned continents, for it is stated exactly thus in all the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara). Therefore, they consist of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sweet water.
Thus, the sequence that is observed in the *Pātañjala* [Yogaśāstra] should be understood as being inverted due to a scribe’s error.
Now, by way of restating the measurement of Jambūdvīpa as previously described, he states the measurement of these islands and oceans:
"Jambūdvīpa is recorded as being one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) yojanas in extent. (10.286)
It should be known as circular; outside, it is like alkaline water.
"Circular" means in terms of its breadth.
In this manner, the oceans situated between the continents increase twofold here.

The word *saṃsthitāḥ* (situated) contains the prefix *sam-* in the sense of "together with. Thus, the oceans of milk and so forth are situated together with the continents of Śāka and the rest, increasing respectively by double [the size of the preceding one].
For example, Śāka-dvīpa is two hundred thousand [yojanas], and likewise the Ocean of Milk; Kuśa-dvīpa is [two] hundred thousand [yojanas]...
Four [lakṣas], likewise the ocean of curd and Krauñca [dvīpa] eight; likewise the ocean of clarified butter.
Śālmali [dvīpa] sixteen, and similarly the ocean of sugarcane juice. Gomedaka thirty-two, and likewise the ocean of wine. Puṣkara sixty-four, and similarly the ocean of sweet water. And this—
He will conclude the similarity between the continents and the oceans with the statement:
"The ocean of sweet water (svādūda) is situated at the end, multiplied by Puṣkaradvīpa" (10.327). And thus, from the half of Meru to the end of the svādūda, there are twenty million [yojanas].
There are fifty-three lakhs and fifty thousand [yojanas]. As he will say:
"Fifty thousand, and likewise fifty-three lakhs, as well as two crores of yojanas."
"The measurement is proclaimed to extend from Meru and Arbuda as far as Svādūdaka.
And likewise:
"O fair-faced one, he is known as Agnīdhra in Jambudvīpa.
And so forth.
In the Śāka [continent], there is one named Medhātithi; in the one called Kuśa, there is Vapuṣmān.
Then Jyotiṣmān is the king on Krauñca, and Dyutimān is remembered as the king on Śālmalī;
Havya is the name on Gomeda, and likewise Savana on Puṣkara.
Furthermore:
"The time for those dwelling in Śāka and Gomedha is equal to the Tretā Yuga;
likewise, the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramācāra) of the inhabitants there should be understood [in the same way]. (10.290)
"So be it"—thus [the periods] correspond to the Tretā Yuga; since no specific distinction is stated elsewhere, it is possible that they are equal to the four Yugas. || 290 ||
He describes the internal divisions of Śākadvīpa and the other islands:
"Medhātithi had seven sons who were consecrated as rulers in Śākadvīpa:
Śānta, Abhaya, Aśiśira, Sukhada, Nandaka, and Śiva. (10.291)
And Kṣemaka and Dhruva—these are marked by the names of the regions (varṣa);
the meaning is that their names follow the well-known names of the regions.
The seven regions are well known... learn from me the mountains that serve as the causes for their divisions. (10.292)
Gomeda, Candrasaṃjña, Nārada, Dundubhi, Somaka, Ṛṣabha, and Vaibhrāja are the principal mountain ranges. (10.293)
And these, situated according to the lateral divisions of Śākadvīpa, constitute its seven constituent elements (dhātu).
It is the same elsewhere. || 293 ||
Furthermore: Sukṛtā, Anasūyā, and Sumukhī as the third;
Vipāśā, Tridivā, Kumbhī, and likewise Amṛtanālikā. (10.294)
These very great rivers have issued forth from these mountains;
the meaning is that, being established [there], they have emerged from them.
And these, having emerged starting from the east, entered the ocean of milk. || 10.295 ||
And here— those people in Śākadvīpa who subsist on milk and eat fruit;
and for this reason—
All are as beautiful as moonstones, handsome, and pleasing to behold. || 10-296 ||
Endowed with all sovereign powers, they sport with celestial women.
Thus, in this manner—seven sons were formerly established by Vapuṣmān in Kuśa. (10.297)
Śvetalohitajīmūta, Harita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suvrata are likewise marked by the very names of their rain-clouds.
And here are the causes of the divisions—the seven boundary mountains: Kumuda, Aśvavadana, Vārāha, Droṇakaṅkata, Mahiṣa, and Kusuma. || 299 ||
And here— Śvetatoyā, as well as Kṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, Locanī, Vīvṛtā, and Vivṛndā— these seven are the best of rivers. || 10.300 ||
Those rivers of purifying waters entered the curdled milk;
meanwhile, the people there lived happily, consuming curds and fruits that tasted like nectar.
All of them, devoted to divine enjoyments, sport together with their consorts;
they eat fruits consisting of nectar along with curd. Thus it continues further on.
Seven sons were established by Jyotiṣmān in Krauñcadvīpa.
Udbhijja is also proclaimed, as well as Veṇu, Maṇḍala, Rathakāra, Lavaṇa, Dhṛtimān, and Suprabhākara. || 10-303 ||
And Kapila—these are the kings, marked by the names of their respective regions.
Here too, the causes for the division are: Vaidruma, Hemanābha, Dyutimān, and Puṣpadantaka. (10.304)
Kuśala and Harimarda— these seven are the Kulaparvatas (boundary mountains).
From them [proceeds] the earth, which is the sustainer, auspicious, sinless, pure, and of unceasing luster.
And Dambhā—these seven rivers are thus declared; O beloved, all these sin-removing streams flow into the Ghṛtoda ocean.
All the people dwelling there were handsome and intense in their splendor;
subsisting on food consisting of ghee and ambrosial fruits, they were well-satisfied yet tormented by love.
Accompanied by women whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, they sport; their state is one of being tormented by love and being solely intent upon sensual enjoyment.
Likewise—seven sons of Dyutimān were consecrated as kings over Śālmalī. || 10.308 ||
Manonuga, Uṣṇa, Pāvana, Andhakāraka, Muni, Dundubhi, and Kuśala—these are remembered as [the names of the winds]. (10.309)
The names of those seven [mountains] are indeed, in order, the names of the seven regions:
Krauñca, Vāmana, Andhakāra, and Divākṛti.
Dvibindu, Puṇḍarīka, Dundubhi, and the Kulādris;
Pauṇḍarīkā, Kauśikī, Gaurī, Siddhā, and Kumudvatī. (10.311)
Sandhyā and Rātrī are thus renowned; these rivers, which flow forth from the mountains, have been described in brief as they proceed toward the Ikṣurasārṇava ocean.
The people dwelling there who drink the sugarcane juice are endowed with divine splendor, peaceful, handsome, and pleasant of speech.
Crowded with various women and yielding all pleasures of the senses—
thus did Havyarāja consecrate his seven sons in Gomoda.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Marīcaka, Kumuda, Unnata, and Mahābhadra are thus remembered. || 10.315 ||
The regions (varṣas) are marked by their names; they are named after themselves: Udaya, Kesara, Jaṭhara, and Surāvata. (10.316)
Śyāma, Ambikeya, and Meru—these are the mountains situated at the boundaries;
as are Gabhasti, Sukumārī, Kumārī, and likewise Nalinī.
The Veṇukā, the Ikṣu, and the Dhenukā—these excellent rivers carry intoxicating liquor;
they are holy, bearing sacred waters.
O fair-faced one, the inhabitants of that world eat delicious fruits comparable to nectar and drink the nectar of wine. (10.319)
Regarding the term *madirodam*, [it is governed by] the rule: "Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), the destination (*gantavya*), and the path (*adhvan*) are designated as the object (*karman*). || 319 ||
And they—
having all their desires fulfilled, handsome, and free from disease—
are accompanied by various throngs of young women, who are themselves endowed with beauty and youth.
O beloved, they always delight in drinking bouts with those languid from intoxication;
therefore, in the place called Puṣkara, Savana is the leader there.
Two sons, renowned by him, were established in the place called Puṣkara; they are to be known by the names that will be mentioned hereafter.
And there, moreover, is the mountain named Mānasottara, which is circular in shape. (10.322)
O lady of excellent hips, its height is fifty yojanas and its width is twenty-five;
and that—
...endowed with all kinds of jewels. || 323 ||
When the land has been divided into two parts by him— Dhātakī is the king in the middle, and Mahāvīta is the king on the outside—
"middle" is said with reference to the terrestrial globe.
And here—free from envy, from the thirst of passion, and from fears. (10.324)
Calamities (īti) are the causes of suffering pertaining to the divine sphere (ādhidaivika). || 324 ||
For this very reason—
during those two years, all the people there were happy;
and that mountain—
But it should be understood as wheel-shaped in the mind, O fair-faced one. (10.325)
Now,
I shall describe to you here on this mountain the cities of the four world-protectors.
There, in order starting from the east—Hara’s city is called Vasvekasarā, and the southern city is Saṃyamanī. (10.326)
Sukhāhvā and Vāruṇī are the two forms of Soma; the term "Vibhāvarī" serves as a reminder that its nature and measure are exactly as previously described under the name Svādūdaka.
Multiplied by Puṣkaradvīpa, the Svādūdaka ocean is situated at the end.
"Multiplied" means that, by doubling the number in successive stages, it reaches the count of six million four hundred thousand; it was previously divided in that same manner.
Thus, he summarizes the measurement from the center of Meru down to the Svādūdaka ocean as follows:
"Two hundred million, five hundred and fifty-three thousand yojanas. (10.328)
The measurement from Mount Meru up to the Svādūdaka ocean has been fully described;
this has already been explained previously.
Beyond that, O fair-faced one, is a ground made of gold extending for ten crores [of yojanas].
Beyond this is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in extent, circular in shape like a bracelet, existing for the sake of the gods' recreation.
O fair-faced one, its height is exactly one hundred thousand yojanas—
that is, ten thousand times ten thousand.
And he is proclaimed as being endowed with all jewels and having a golden complexion. || 10-331 ||
Furthermore:
O celestial beauty, the sun does not illuminate that [world] externally;
rather, it is the illumination of the worlds consisting of the fourteen types of beings situated within, wherein there is light. Or else:

That which has both light (loka) and darkness (aloka) within and without is called Lokāloka; because Mount Meru is equal in height to the Lokāloka range and stands between them, it does not illuminate what lies beyond that range.
And furthermore:
"The world-protectors are stationed there, as are the Rudras of unfailing power. (10.332)
The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only). It is the venerable Rudras alone, together with the pregnant world-protectors (*antarvatī-samagra-lokapāla*), who are stationed there;
for Indra and the others do not possess the capacity to guard those paths. Therefore, the appointment here belongs to the Rudras alone.
Indra and the others, however, [are governed] by the unfailing power consisting of the Lord’s own power.
It is precisely because they are presided over by portions of Rudra that they are called world-protectors; for this very reason, they are to be worshipped as the retinue of the Blessed One.
He enumerates them by name:
Viraja, Vasudhāmā, Śaṅkhapāt, and likewise Kardama;
Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and likewise Bhājana. (10.333)
These [are situated] in the radiant abode of the Siddhas and immortals made of Jāmbūnada gold,
starting from the east and proceeding in order as far as the domain of Īśāna.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) indeed stand there, protecting these subjects;

they reside in the abode where half of the dwellings of the Siddhas, Yogins, and immortals are situated. "These" refers to the fourteenfold creation of beings consisting of the islands within [the cosmic ocean].
Thus it is said: "In its center, O lady of beautiful hips, there are fourteen yonis. (10.335)
They act in various forms, colored by their own karma;
as it has been said:
"The sun should shine within that. (10.332)
Thus, by means of the variety of its movements manifested through proximity to and distance from the Lokāloka mountain,
[the text] indicates the state of the sun's southern and northern courses:
"But above the Lokāloka mountain is the sun’s southern course" (10.336).
Likewise, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is proclaimed there as being to the north.
Here, moving incessantly through the middle of the path in the sky situated between Meru and Lokāloka, [the sun] revolves around Meru, which stands as a pillar fixed upon the surface of the earth.

The leader of the planets, moving among the planets that traverse the stellar sphere bound to the navel of the Pole Star, circumambulates by means of external time consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās* regulated by the destiny (*niyati*) of the Supreme Lord; and according to his movement through the respective zodiac signs, he bestows various states of association.

The variety of luminosity—ranging from intense, moderate, and dull—is of a different nature [from the sun], and it causes the manifold course of the elemental creation to proceed. For this reason, He is all-pervasive (*vibhu*). Regarding the phrase "above Lokāloka," that is because [the light] revolves in close proximity [to it]. As for the word "there," it refers to the region situated between Lokāloka and Meru.

By remaining [in its orbit] and gradually moving outward from the vicinity of Meru through its revolution, there occurs the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*), which consists of the movement through the six zodiac signs beginning with Cancer; and by entering further and further inward toward Meru through proximity to the Lokāloka mountain, there occurs the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*).
The northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), however, consists of the movement [of the sun] through the form of the passage of the crocodile and other signs; for he will say:
"Mount Meru is to the north of all [the worlds], while the Lokāloka mountain is to the south.
Thus, this must be explained solely according to the system established by the concordant scriptures (*āgama*), and not otherwise.
By way of following the doctrines of the various schools of astrology, which are mutually contradictory.
Having thus described the state of the southern and northern solstices, he speaks of the distinction between sunrise and sunset:
"It is midnight in Amarāvatī when it sets in the city of Yama. (10.337)
It is recorded that at midday it is in the western direction (Vāruṇī), and sunrise occurs in the north (Saumya);
and at the very moment its rising is seen in Amarāvatī.

Then, according to the established rule for the sun circling Mount Meru from left to right, when its rising occurs in the northern region of Meru—known as Saumya—and its setting is seen in the western direction (Vāruṇī), that is the coming and going of the sun. At that time, it sets in Vāruṇī. Thus ends the description of the sun's movement.
When the sun, circling Meru clockwise, rises in the northern part of Meru called Saumya, and is seen setting in the west (Vāruṇī) as it moves there, then [it is said to set].
Due to the shadow of the Meru mountain and the aforementioned mountains situated at its sides, the sun sets in the direction of Yama (the south);

the meaning is that its light is no longer visible. At that very time, it is midday in the western direction (Vāruṇī), because the sun has moved from its point of rising in the east toward the southern direction.

Since the passage of time up to the limit of fifteen *ghaṭikās* has been completed, at that very moment it is midnight in Amarāvatī, because the sunrise will occur there after fifteen *ghaṭikās*. And thus, at the very moment his [the sun's] rising occurs in Amarāvatī, at that same moment...

Since the solar [wind] that flows for thirty ghaṭikās arises within those [channels] belonging to Vāruṇī, the sun sets in Vāruṇī and the end of the day occurs; in this manner, the coming and going of the Sun should be understood even in the intermediate directions (vidiś), because the sequence already explained serves as an illustration.
And here:
"The Suvīthī is to its north, and the Ajavīthī is to its south. (10.339)
He explains this as follows: "For this path of the ancestors and the gods has indeed been described by me to you;
it is a beautiful thoroughfare, the path of the gods. It has not [yet] arisen at its place of origin now."
The term *ajāḥ* refers to those who have attained something [specific]; they are the *pitaraḥ* (fathers). Their *vīthī* is their path;
this should be construed according to the context. Because the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) is the cause for divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*), it is the "path of the gods" (*devamārga*);
whereas because the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) fulfills worldly accomplishments (*aihikasiddhi*), it is the "path of the fathers" (*pitṛmārga*). And this—
According to the principle stated in the section on Time (*kālādhikāra*), this should be understood to apply both internally and externally. As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal.
By one of these, one goes to non-return; by the other, one returns" (8.26).

Even within [the body], Meru is precisely the pericarp of the heart-lotus; attached above that is the Sun of Prāṇa, which has the form of the Self as mere consciousness-light (cit-jyotis), fixed (dhruva), and followed by the entire stellar sphere, planets, and so forth, described as having the nature of time.
By touching the openings of the principal channels located at the root of the ears,
he remains constantly revolving clockwise,
following the sequence of the respective transits of Capricorn and so forth, according to the divisions of north, south, and so on.

It has already been largely stated that [the sun] causes [things] to be seen; and because the sun constantly circumambulates Meru through the middle of the path of space situated between Meru and Lokāloka, for that very reason, [this applies] to those facing the eastern direction, which consists of its place of rising.
For all people residing in the eight regions— excluding Ilāvṛta— as well as in the other continents and intermediate spaces,

Mount Meru is to the north and the Lokāloka mountain is to the south. Indeed, for those dwelling in Ketumāla and the other regions, the sun rises to the south of Meru as it revolves clockwise around that mountain.
According to the established position that for those dwelling in Uttarakuru and other regions situated to its north it is to the west;

for those dwelling in Pūrvabhadrāśva and other regions to its east it is to the north; and for those residing in Harivarṣa and other regions to its south it is to the east—for all of them [the sun rises in the same direction].
Even for those residing in other continents, Meru remains the divider between the worlds of light and darkness, situated to the north and south respectively,
with the exception of Ilāvṛta; in that case as well, it should be understood that some state of existence follows the solar illumination merely by way of shadow.
Having thus established, by way of incidental discussion, the southern and northern solstices as well as the positions of sunrise and sunset, he states the subject at hand:
"Outside of this is a terrible darkness, difficult to behold, inhabited by living beings. (10.340)
Thirty-five crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand yojanas are recorded, O fair-faced one. (10.341)

The Lokāloka mountain is said to be ten thousand [yojanas] in extent; together with those, Merv and the regions below it up to Jambudvīpa amount to fifty [thousand]. By this figure of fifty, when added to the previously calculated total, there are forty-seven crores, along with two crores and ten crores of golden ground.
Now—
[the measurement] of the seven oceans is such that the Garbhoda [ocean] is known to be equal to them.
Within the Garbha [ocean], extending as far as the Lokāloka mountain, it is characterized by the waters belonging to the seven oceans.
That which contains the universe is the Garbhoda [ocean]. "Equal to that" means it is like the salt ocean in its essence. As it is said in the Parātantra:
"Those seven oceans that have been described are situated here within this Garbha."
"Therefore, it is celebrated as Garbhoda, the bearer of the essence of all the oceans.

And that [ocean] has a measurement equal to one crore and twenty-seven lakhs, which is the extent reached by doubling the measure starting from one lakh for each of the seven oceans, beginning with the salt ocean (Kṣāra). Thus far.
Together with the previous measurement, there are forty-nine crores;
and since the shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍakarparikā*) is one crore, there are thus fifty crores from the center of Meru to the edge of the shell.
Regarding this, it is said: "Indeed, [the worlds] are joined with the shell of Brahmā’s egg at the center of Meru. (10.342)
Fifty *koṭis* are to be known [as existing] all around in the ten directions; by calculating both sides together, this great earthly realm (*pārthiva*) is to be known as one hundred *koṭis*. (10.343)
"Pāthīvam" means the vastness existing on the earth. || 343 ||
Thus the measurement for the earth’s lower and middle regions has been stated; now, however—O lady of excellent complexion—I shall declare the measurement from above.
"From above" refers to that which pertains to the Bhuvarloka.

Let this be; however, with the intention that the disciple being instructed should not forget the previously mentioned sequence of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the purification of the worlds situated in the *bhūrloka*, [the author] says, in order to remind him of that very sequence:
"Or else, O Great Goddess, here [in this world], in its entirety and according to the proper order... (10.344).
Now, regarding the purificatory rites that must be performed at the time of initiation,
learn from me their sequence.

Although the very same purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that were prescribed for the initiation by means of the *kalās*— preceded by the installation of the *kalās*— are performed here preceded by the installation of the worlds (*bhuvana*), nevertheless, for the benefit of the disciple,
the Supreme Lord causes them to be recalled and supplements them with what remains to be said.
One should likewise install the power (śakti), the principle (tattva), the world-sphere (bhuvana), and the womb (yoni).

In the consecrated fire (saṃskṛtāgni), after first observing the junction of the beginning and end of the path, establishing that [junction], and bringing it into proximity, one deposits power in the form of the support; from that, the principle (tattva) which has the worlds as its locus; and from that as well—

One should cause the world together with Bhuvaneśa to enter [the self] and intend it as that which is to be purified. Then, moreover, one should install Vāgīśī, who pervades all wombs (yoni), by means of the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya). || 345 ||
Then—
having performed the ritual service with fragrances for them in due order;
"for them" refers to the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the principles (tattva), the worlds (bhuvana), and so forth.
And here, he shows the worlds to be purified, together with Bhuvaneśa, in their proper order:
"Ananta, Kālāgni, and the hells, in due sequence. (10.346)

Then one should purify the subterranean realms (pātāla) and those above them in successive order. Regarding the purification according to whichever one of the aforementioned sections is intended— here, the procedure for the initiation into the *kalās* (kalādīkṣā), ending with the hearing of the Lord of the Worlds (bhuvaneśa-śrāvaṇa), must be followed in its entirety.
Having purified up to this point,
O fair-faced one, one should then perform the worship of the Bhuvarloka.

By means of the previously mentioned mantra beginning with "dhāmādiḥ praṇavādiśca" (4-101), there is merely the non-insertion of the worlds in the place of the *kalās*; and [there is also] the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the six substrates beginning with the water-pot (kalaśa) and ending with fire (agni). || 347 ||
Having done thus—then the goddess Vāgīśvarī is to be worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
Thereafter, the bound soul (paśu) is to be sprinkled, struck, and separated [from his bonds]. (10.348)
Then for him—[there is] cutting, as well as drawing out, grasping, and then joining; likewise, there is the authority over the holding of the embryo and its birth. || 10-349 ||
One should perform yoga, enjoyment, dissolution, and then the purification of the source (yoniviśodhana). All of this has already been explained previously.
Regarding that which was called "the purification of the wombs," I shall describe there those wombs—in brief, fourteen of them—in their proper sequence. (10.350)
They know the Paiśāca, the Rākṣasa, the Yākṣa, the Gāndharva, and the Aindra; likewise the Saumya, the Prājāpatya, and the Brāhma as the eighth.
And this has already been stated. || 351 ||

By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), [the levels] are to be purified in the path of Śiva. By the phrase "by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal," this is what he says: having purified the fivefold group of tamasic beings beginning with the immobile and ending with the bound soul (paśu), one should purify the human state; thereafter, [one purifies] from the state of the Piśācas up to that of Brahmā.
And this very sequence known as the "Eightfold Divine Womb" will become clear further on.
Having thus explained the eightfold womb, he also speaks of the sixfold womb:
"Beasts, birds, and wild animals, as well as others who are reptiles. (10.352)
The fifth is the stationary state, and the sixth is the human womb.
This very cycle of existence (saṃsāramaṇḍala), joined with the divine wombs, has thus been described. (10.353)
And indeed, this fourteen-fold [purity]...
and this...
shall purify one in the world of Bhūr.
The intention is that on the earthly plane (bhūrloka), all this is to be purified through specific analysis according to one's karma, whereas elsewhere it may be purified even in a general manner.
And why is this the circle of saṃsāra? To this he says: "For it is the self that transmigrates here within the domain of the earth, beginning with Māyā. (10.354)
Therefore, it is called *saṃsāra* (wandering), because one wanders here and there within it.
And this *saṃsāra*—being situated in the midst of the path—one experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion. (10.355)
Endowed with the three bonds and presided over by the power of Vāmā,
it proceeds along the path of creation and withdrawal through the instrumental cause that is Īśvara.

Either directly or through the mouth of the Great Lords of Mantra (Mantramaheshvaras) and others, he is presided over by the Lord’s own power Vāmā— which consists of the emission of transmigratory existence— and is thereby rendered dependent; for that very reason, he is fully possessed, overwhelmed, and bound by the three fetters beginning with the atomic (āṇava).
Experiencing the triad beginning with pleasure. || 356 ||
Again and again, in the midst of the path, he is joined with the auspicious and the inauspicious.
And for this reason:
"Those bonds within the midst of the path should be known to be infinite crores. (10.357)
Up to the state that is without support, according to the distinction between primary and secondary qualities, it has been said:
"O fair-limbed one, the infinite web of fetters extends up to the end of tranquility. (4.410)
And since this is so—
therefore one should understand it thus...
moreover—
...is the cause of bondage. || 10-358 ||
Thus, he states that in this cycle of saṃsāra, karma alone is the cause:
"The cycle of saṃsāra has been declared to be of fourteen kinds;
its divisions, indeed, are infinite..."
Those which are differentiated by the distinction of karma—[these are] yours. || 10-359 ||
Thus, these infinite creepers of karma, which have become the cause of the circle of saṃsāra, along with the agents such as the Lord of Karma (Karmeśa) and others,
exist for the sake of the individual soul’s own experience— this soul whose greatness has been obscured by the power of beginningless māyā.
Exerting itself, it is bound by infinite successions of karma.
And this [bondage] has not come to him from anywhere else, but rather arises solely through the sense of incompleteness; thus he says:
"For the self is bound by the self...
and it is bound by the power of darkness."
...one should not release oneself by means of oneself. || 10-360 ||
[This occurs] without the grace of the Supreme Lord; this is the implied meaning. The reading "one should release oneself" (muñcedātmānam) is not appropriate.
He clarifies this by means of the following illustration:
"Just as the silkworm-creature firmly envelops itself..."
And he is not able to cause himself to recoil, just as [before]. || 10-361 ||
In the same way, all transmigrating beings are bound by their own fetters;
like animals caught in snares, they are not able to liberate themselves.
Śiva himself does not perceive his own self by means of his power of grace (anugraha-śakti) until [the disciple is ready].
For: "By the descent of Śiva's power, they are indeed liberated from the bondage of the fetters. (10.363)
Otherwise, they do not know their own nature, which is utterly stainless, innate, pure, incomparable, and free from affliction. (10.364)

It is perfectly pure and of the singular nature of Supreme Śiva; therefore, due to the absence of a second, it is beyond comparison. Likewise, its own self (*ātman*) alone is its lineage (*abhijana*) and cause; the meaning is that it has no other effect and is an independent reality. Because it is pure and a single mass of consciousness, it is also free from affliction (*anāmaya*).
That which is empty of illusory contact is the supramundane. || 364 ||
To the question "Why do they not know this true nature? he says:
"Deluded by the delusion of impurity (mala) and bound by karma, kalā, and the rest, they remain hidden therein, just as fire is within wood. (10.365)

Regarding the statement, "But here, desire is the impurity" (4.105), that very impurity previously described as consisting of the sense of being incomplete and having the nature of the non-manifestation of one's true self (*svarūpākhyāti*)—that is precisely delusion (*moha*), which is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Those who are deluded by it are rendered ignorant; and for this reason, they remain within that very bondage of fetters (*pāśabandha*).

They remain hidden, their own true nature submerged and unspoken, just as fire exists within wood; yet, when that fire hidden in the wood is drawn forth by means of friction-sticks, it becomes clearly manifest.
One should perceive one's own true nature, which is luminous and perfectly stainless.
For other living beings as well, whose eyes are overcome by darkness, it illuminates objects by destroying the gloom with its rays. (10.367)
In that same way, O Goddess, the Self recognizes its own beginningless nature through the power of the churner (manthaka), and not otherwise by any means whatsoever. (10.368)
He analyzes the statement "by the power of Manthaka" as follows:
"But here, O Goddess, Manthaka is Sadāśiva himself;
having assumed the body of an Ācārya, he is ever established in bestowing grace. (10.369)
And "ca" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed). || 369 ||
The mantras are to be known as being like the friction-sticks, and the path here is like the fire-drill;
Vāgīśī, situated in the womb, is to be known as the smoke, like impurities and the like. (10.370)
