The Self (ātman) is indeed to be known as fire; the supreme Śiva is the awakener.

The churning-stick (manthāna) is the cause of churning, namely the Vaiśākha [mudrā], and likewise the mantras; the path ending at Samanā is the fire-drill (araṇi), for when enveloped by these, the Self becomes fire.

By means of the vision of the previously determined pervasion (*vyāpti*), the removal of the worthless impurity consisting of non-recognition— which stands in the place of smoke— is awakened by Paramaśiva through the agency of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva residing in the form of the Guru, within the womb of Vāgīśī.
And therefore:
"Just as fire, when kindled, becomes stainless and exceedingly radiant. (10.371)
Having been extracted from the path of the self, he shall not enter the wood again;
liberated from impurities, karma, kalās, and so forth, he is free from all fatigue.
Even while remaining there, he would not be bound, because he is exceedingly pure;
having cast off impurities and the like, he is free from the exhaustion of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
Even though situated therein, his sole purpose is merely to pass through the enjoyments that have arrived, even while dwelling in their midst.

One who possesses the conceit of "I-ness" would be bound; however, he does not become such, but rather remains at all times thoroughly permeated by the nature of the pure, dense mass of consciousness.
Furthermore:
Just as copper, through contact with mercury and fire, is freed from its blackness, || 10.373 ||
But once separated by those who know reality, gold attains its true nature and never again returns to the state of copper; so it is with the Self, which never [returns to its former state]. (10.374)
The meaning is that the Self, once separated by the Guru through the power of *akhyāti* (non-apprehension) which is temporal, is not joined again.
And in this regard:
"But the power of the mantra is to be known as action like fluidity, while [the power of] fire is like fire itself."
And Śiva, who knows that [reality], should be known as the one whose body and form are the teacher. || 10-375 ||
The self is indeed to be known as gold, while impurity is to be known as tarnish.
Ritual action is initiation; one who knows that is a knower of the true nature of initiation, which consists of knowledge, yoga, and ritual action, like the application of mercury and fire.
And for this reason: "O Dear One, through the union of mantra, substance, and ritual action, [the deity resides] upon the support of fire. (10.376)
Indeed, when the self has been purified by a Guru who is learned in the Tantras, it no longer undergoes impurity; being stainless, it attains the state of Śiva. (10.377)

"So be it"—this refers to the sequence for application according to the method taught in the fourth chapter. By the phrase "by one who knows the Tantra," he teaches that here, the knowledge of the Tantra is the supreme means (*upāya*). For it has been said:
"And there should be no contempt at the time of ritual action regarding the liberation from *saṃsāra*."
"One who obstructs a disciple regarding the instruction on mantras, gifts, or vows shall become a denizen of hell. Thus [it is said].
"Impurity" (malatām) refers to non-recognition (akhyāti), which consists of the feeling of being incomplete; "Śiva-nature" (śivatvam) is identity with the Supreme Śiva.
He concludes [the section]:
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, initiation should be performed as before, according to the sequence stated in the fourth chapter; for he will say:
"There is no liberation equal to initiation" (11.199).
And in that initiation,
one should purify the primary bonds which were previously described by me.
"But impure action is the cause, while that which follows from it is the effect," so it is said in another Tantra. || 378 ||
And for this reason:
"But those fetters which have become subordinate qualities are also purified by virtue of that.
"Subordinate qualities" refers to pride, delusion, and so forth; "by virtue of that" means by virtue of the purification of the *āṇava*, *kārmika*, and *māyīya* [impurities].
But even this, which consists of qualities and was previously described by me as being of fourteen kinds— || 10-379 ||
"O Goddess, that maṇḍala of saṃsāra on the surface of the earth is to be purified.
The meaning is that it is to be purified as something distinct.
And therefore—I shall explain all of that in due order, as it is to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva. (10.380)
Not far at all. || 380 ||
And as for that which begins with Brahmā and ends with a blade of grass, one should purify it primarily;
however, it has been stated that this is not by way of its being included [within the self].
He indicates that sequence in order:
"The Brāhma, the Prājeśa, the Saumya, and likewise the Aindra. (10.381)
Furthermore, the Gāndharva, the Yākṣa, and likewise the Rākṣasa;
the Paiśāca should be purified in sequence, as well as the Sthāvara and the Mānuṣa.
The fivefold immobile [beings] are indicative of the animal realm; "in sequence" means by way of the order of dissolution. || 382 ||
As it was said:
"And they are to be purified by means of the sequence of withdrawal" (10.352),
purification occurs through the sequence of withdrawal.
He introduces them one by one, according to the order of the principal beings within each respective class of stationary things and so forth:
"Of stationary things, the Saptacchada tree; likewise, Vāsuki of serpents;
Garuḍa of birds; and indeed, the lion of wild beasts. (10.383)
And for animals, [one should offer] to the cow-source...

and here, one should perform the modification [of the mantra] as follows: "I purify the *saptacchada* tree, which was the primary cause of birth in the species of stationary beings and so forth acquired through prior karma for the self of Devadatta; svāhā," and so on.
Having thus purified the fivefold animal realm in reverse order,
one should purify the human beings as well,
in that same reverse order.
One should purify the outcastes, as well as the Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, O Goddess, among all these births, one should purify one's offices by means of the five Brahmans;
"offices" refers to the associations with various specific births that are brought about by the power of prior karma.
How—by the application of ten oblations—from the lowest castes up to the Brahmins? || 10.385 ||
Regarding the statement, "Three, fifteen, or one" (4-448),

this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously stated. In that context, within the pentad beginning with immobile beings and ending with animals, and within the pentad beginning with the lowest castes and ending with Brahmins, the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta are applied in reverse order (*prātilomyena*).
The mantras, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Īśāna, are to be meditated upon. || 385 ||
Since a Brāhmaṇa is entitled to the six duties (*ṣaṭkarman*), he states a specific rule regarding his purification:
"One should purify the Brāhmaṇa’s forty-eight entitlements. Thus it is said.
He states them in order:
the conception rite (garbha), the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and the birth rite (jātakarman). || 10-386 ||

Naming, the rite of departure from the womb, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony—O lady of excellent hips, these eight are declared to be purified by this very [mantra]. (10.387)
The *sīmanta* is the perfection of the division of the limbs and sub-limbs; the *niṣkramaṇa* is the first sighting of the sun;
and the *cūḍaka* is the fashioning of the top-knot. "By this very [rite]" means by the application of ten oblations, which follows the stated sequence and has the venerable Lord Īśāna as its cause.
And therefore—
O Goddess, by means of these aforementioned [factors], he is then born as a twice-born (dvija) from two unviolated Brahmins,
through Vedic mantras and purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
The second birth of the twice-born, which is accomplished— that is both of these— is performed by means of the very mantras belonging to this [Vedic] tradition.
Thus, for this twice-born man,
the ninth sacrament is indeed the investiture with the sacred thread (*vratibandha*).
And this is declared to be the possessor of the limbs [of the path]. || 388 ||
Since [it was taught] by him,
I shall explain its limbs correctly and in their proper sequence.
He states them as follows:
The girdle, the tooth-stick, the deerskin, and likewise the *tryāyuṣa* [formula]. || 10-389 ||

They know that the meditation on the fire, the worship [of the fire], and alms-gathering are indeed the seventh; the triple-aging ash-mark (tripuṇḍra) is the eighth. These seven are the vows of the girdle; the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should practice these.
And they were seen as the controllers at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.

At the time of initiation (dīkṣā)—that is, at the future occasion of the Godāna ceremony marked by the mandala—these restraints remain unfulfilled; therefore, they must necessarily be practiced so that there may be no lapse in the maintenance of the first stage of life (āśrama).
Furthermore:
Bhauteśa, Pāśupatya, Gāṇa, Gāṇeśvara, Unmattaka, Asidhāra, and they know Ghṛteśa as the seventh. (10.391)
These seven vows of the *brahmacārins* are indeed observed;

"observed" means they are found in the *Pārameśvara* scripture, whereas in the Veda they belong to the category of lost branches (*ucchinna-śākhā*), as they are not to be practiced in the present day.
And these—
the observances of conduct (caryāvratas)—
are to be understood as those to be practiced at the time of the binding of the vow (vratibandha).
And these have been proclaimed as being auxiliary to the Kīrti [sacrifice]. || 10-392 ||
These other vows are constituent parts of the sacrament known as the *vratibandha*, which possesses fruit by virtue of its own result. || 392 ||
And therefore:
"Indeed, this ninth binding of the vow is one that is accompanied by these [others];
it has been stated that this sevenfold set of vows is actually contained within it. (10.393)
Thus, having established that there are seven [vows] beginning with Mekhalā and seven beginning with Bhauteśa,
[it is said]: "O fair-faced one, these fourteen vows must be offered in this manner individually, and not merely by being included within the Vratibandha ceremony"— this is the intended meaning.
Then, the four Vedic vows must undoubtedly be offered as oblations. || 10-394 ||
These are to be accomplished by means of the oblation. || 394 ||
He states them as follows:
"The *aiṣṭika*, the *pāvīka*, the *bhautika*, and likewise the *saumika*.

By the recitation of Vedic texts that expound the sacrifices of the *iṣṭi*, the seasonal festivals (*parvan*), the elements (*bhūta*), and the *soma* sacrifice, the duties pertaining to time are fulfilled.
The vows are described in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord using terms such as *aiṣṭika* and others. However, in the *Yajñasūtra*, it is stated:
"The three Vedas, the four *hotṛ*-priests, the gift of a cow, and likewise the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)."
"The four Vedic vows..."—thus they have been described. But here, the Godāna ceremony shall indeed be performed separately.

And because these four lords of vows (*vrata-īśvara*), which govern the student (*brahmacārin*), are primary in comparison to other vows by virtue of conferring the qualification for Vedic study— "Thus, there are four lords of vows who are the regulators of the religious student. (10.395)
They are the regulators of those practicing the holy life (brahmacārin) and the bringers about of suchness. || 395 ||
One should understand these preparatory rites (*saṃskāras*) to be as many as this;
indeed, one who has performed these is entitled to the Vedas— thus he says:
...therefore, indeed, one becomes a vessel for the Vedas.
Moreover: "From that, O beloved, there arises the gift of a cow, which consists of fourteen [parts]. (10.396)
At the conclusion of the study of the Vedas, the *godāna* ceremony consists of the shaving of one's own hair and so forth, characterized by the gift of a pair of cattle to the preceptor. || 396 ||
Then, having been authorized for the householder’s life by his gurus— one who has attained knowledge and perfection should marry a maiden;
he is called a *snāta* (one who has bathed) because he has obtained purification through the study of the Vedas, for at the conclusion of that study—
The ritual bath is prescribed with this very intention; therefore, it is perfected and complete by means of the knowledge whose nature is the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas.
Alternatively, because it is enjoined that "one should go forth from the very state of brahmacarya," desiring to enter the life of renunciation immediately—
having fashioned a wife made of darbha grass, he should perform sacrifices with her. (10.397)
This rite, consisting of the performance of the sacrament of marriage in the form of obligatory and occasional duties prescribed for the householder stage of life—
this is to be known as the fifteenth [duty].
And by this very [text]:
"The satiation of the ancestors, gods, humans, and living beings,
as well as the study of the Veda— these indeed are the five great sacrifices."

Thus, the obligatory sacrifices (*nityayajña*) as set forth in the *Yajñasūtra* have been summarized. As it has been said: "The householder has five slaughter-houses (*sūnā*): the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar; he who employs them is bound [by sin]."
For the sake of expiating all those [sins] in due order,
the high-souled ones have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.

"Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); the libation (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña); the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
The intention [of this verse] is that these daily sacrifices are thus included within marriage itself. || 397 ||
The Naimittikas said:
"Thereafter, the Pākayajñas [occur] in succession;
we shall declare those occasional rites (naimittika) in their proper order. (10.398)
The Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrāyaṇī,
as well as the Caitrī and the Āśvayujī— these are the seven cooked sacrifices (pākamakhas) in their proper order.

The *aṣṭakās* beginning with the dark fortnight of Pauṣa consist of vegetables and other offerings. The *pārvaṇī* occurs on the first day of both the bright and dark fortnights; the sacrifice performed then is likewise so designated. The *śrāddha* is the rite prescribed for the days dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). The sacrifice performed on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa is the *śrāvaṇī*; [the sacrifice on the full moon of Āśvina is] the *āgrayaṇī*.

The *navānnayāga* (sacrifice of new grain). In this same manner, the sacrifice beginning in the month of Caitra and so forth should also be understood. Others, however, reading "the two *āgrayaṇas*," explain that there are two *navānnayāgas* in autumn and spring;
they describe the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* as being only one. And these—

In the Veda, the *pākayajñas* are said to be performed with sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like; however, the *haviryajñas* to be described later are performed with parched grain flour (*saktu*) and so forth. But here, since no specific material is mentioned, it should be understood that they are to be performed with the very sesame seeds under discussion. || 399 ||
Thus,
one should understand these together with those [seven] as twenty-two in number;
that is, together with these seven, the fifteen previously mentioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
Then—
[he performed] the Āgneya and the Agnihotra, and after that, the Darśa.
The full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) is to be known likewise, as is the four-monthly sacrifice (cāturmāsya);
the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) is specified next, and after that, the sautrāmaṇi.
O beloved, these seven are declared to be the Havis-yajñas, which are purifying.
The Āgneya is the bringing of the fire by means of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*). The Agnihotra is the oblation performed in the evening and in the morning.
The Darśa is, by way of figurative indication (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*), the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*) performed when the moon is not visible.

The *cāturmāsya* is a distinguished sacrifice occurring on the full moon at the end of a four-month period, beginning from either Phālguna or Caitra. By the word "full moon" (*paurṇamāsī*), however, the general sacrifice pertaining to all full-moon days is indicated. The *paśubandha* is a specific sacrifice in which—
The flesh, fat, and so forth of the sacrificial animal are offered. The Sautrāmaṇī is a sacrifice of surā liquor dedicated to the deity Sutrāman;
one should understand that these too are included—along with these, one should recognize the twenty-nine purificatory rites (saṃskāras). || 10.402 ||
Now— Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra-Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, as well as Vājapeya, Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma is the seventh. || 10-403 ||
These specific sacrifices are designated as *somasaṃsthās* (Soma-terminuses).
The *somasaṃsthās* are ritual actions in the form of a sacrifice (*yajña*) characterized by the drinking of Soma using the *graha* vessels.
One should perform these formative factors (saṃskāras), ending with this many—
specifically thirty-six in number—
in accordance with the sequence of mantra-offerings; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
Now,
Hiraṇyapāda was the first, as well as Guhyahiraṇyadhṛt.
Hiraṇyameḍhra, Hiraṇyanābhi, and Hiraṇyagarbha;
likewise Hiraṇyaśrotra, Hiraṇyatvak, and Hiraṇyākṣa. || 10-405 ||
The ten sacrifices are proclaimed as having golden tongues and horns.
The embryo is the heart. These are specific types of fire-altar constructions (agnicityā) in the form of birds and other creatures, for whose positions such as the feet and so forth gold is offered.
For those [beings], due to the distinctions in their various forms such as those belonging to specific factions and so forth—
one hundred [seeds] produce one [offspring] here, and each one is born with clarified butter.
Regarding the specific requirement for the *homa* (fire-offering) for the sake of attaining this perfection, he says:
"All these are purified by a thousand [offerings]...
That very *cityayajña* (altar-sacrifice), beginning with the *hiraṇyapāda*, is to be accomplished by means of a thousand *homas*.
...the thirty-seventh [chapter].
Furthermore:
thereafter, one should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) according to the proper sequence. || 10.407 ||
Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has attained the status of a sovereign emperor through the power of his karma, this Aśvamedha sacrifice must indeed be performed. || 407 ||
Thus, from marriage onwards,
through these many rites— when all of them have been performed in this manner— one then becomes a householder, established in the second stage of life (āśrama).

The meaning is that one should know that thirty-eighth [initiation] to be the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) called the Horse Sacrifice (aśvamedha). ... thereafter, one becomes a forest-dweller (vānaprastha). || 10-408 ||
Thereafter, through renunciation (*pārivrājya*) and the funeral rites (*anteṣṭi*), one attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Renunciation and forest-dwelling (*vānaprastha*) constitute two forms of stages of life (*āśrama*), which are two types of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
The funeral rites are for the purpose of purification through expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for any possible failure in performing those prescribed rites.

This [practice] is to be performed by one established in the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), but not by a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or one who has resorted to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*); therefore, he is not counted separately. "In this manner" means according to the sequence of the *pārameśvara* mantra-homa;

however, even though there exists a ritual procedure belonging to the bound state (*pāśava*), because of the presence of defects such as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the *āhara*, true Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) is not fully realized.
This, however, is the characteristic of wandering mendicancy; one understands this fortieth saṃskāra along with these [others], meaning that it is counted together with them.
Therefore, I shall briefly describe the eight qualities of the self. || 10-409 ||
Compassion toward all beings, patience, and freedom from envy;
purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness—these are further [qualities] beyond this.
Freedom from miserliness and freedom from longing—these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*).

Compassion is sympathy for others; forbearance is the absence of retaliation even when one has the power to do so against those who cause harm; lack of envy is the tolerance of the virtues of others; and purity is the cleanliness of mind, speech, and body.

Effortlessness is the performance of actions that do not bring about affliction; auspiciousness consists in the sight, touch, or contemplation of auspicious objects; lack of miserliness is the practice of giving according to one's ability;
and contentment is the absence of craving—these belong to the self.

The qualities belong to that which is closely associated with the self, such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and speech, but not to the self itself, because the self consists solely of consciousness (*cidekarūpatva*). In this regard, first [one performs] the *garbhādhāna* for the sake of the Brahminhood of the self to be initiated, by means of the mantra preceded by the utterance of the *īśāna* [face] together with the *praṇava*: "I perform the *garbhādhāna* for the sake of the Brahminhood of the self to be initiated; *svāhā*."

Having offered five times, one should offer again five times with the words ending in "may the re-conception (*garbhādhāna*) be perfected. In this very manner, having established the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*), and preceded by the arousal of the eight qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*) according to the sequence of mantras to be described hereafter—
Having first established his entitlement and enjoyment through Īśāna, his status as a Brāhmaṇa must be purified by means of that very Brāhmaṇya.
In this very way, there are forty-eight formations in brief. || 10-411 ||
O observer of excellent vows, by these pure [practices], even those innumerable [impurities] are purified—
the forty pertaining to the body and the eight residing in the *puryaṣṭaka*. "Innumerable" refers to the various forms of conduct described in the Chapter on Conduct (*Ācārādhyāya*).

Since these forty qualities of the self have been described immediately following the purification of the body, one should therefore, after performing the funeral rite, indeed instill these qualities in the child. (10.412)
Here too, since the application of the Īśāna-mantra for the purification of the Brahman-portion would follow from the general statement, he states an exception:
"Having offered five oblations with each of the five Brahma-mantras in due order..."
The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only); [they are to be practiced] by the Brahmins alone, and because of the word *api*, they are joined with those who are endowed with [the other qualities].

This is the meaning of the word *anukrama* (sequence): according to the previously stated order, by means of the four [qualities] beginning with *sadyas*, the group of four known as compassion (*dayā*), forbearance (*kṣānti*), freedom from envy (*anasūyā*), and purity (*śauca*) is [to be practiced] fivefold according to the stated method.
Having become fivefold, one should likewise accomplish the fourfold set known as Īśāna, Ayāsa, Maṅgala, and Akārpaṇyāspṛhā with oblations.
He states the instrument for the oblations:
"Having given those [oblations] with sesame seeds or with ghee"—this is the connection. Sesame seeds consist of oily seeds, while clarified butter (ājya) is solidified oil.

Thus, these forms which are the counterparts of the seeds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the craving and attachment for latent impressions must be offered as oblations in the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists in the burning away of the oil of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Having done thus—..................one should then apply it above. || 10-413 ||
To the question "What is above?", he says:
By the word "above" (ūrdhva), that karma which is called impure is meant;
for karma that bestows human birth has already been purified in the world of Bhūr.
That karma which bestows a divine birth above that [level] is called "upward."
And for the sake of its purification, the initiation of the candidate must be performed; the union [of the deity] should be effected within that [candidate],
and not by abandoning him for another— thus he says:
...and it is not prescribed elsewhere. || 10-414 ||
This clarifies [the following]:
"Therefore, no extraction should be performed, nor should there be any leading anywhere;
rather, one should apply the ritual action there according to the prescribed sequence. (10.415)

"Extraction" (uddharaṇa) means transcending [the state]. "Leading" (nayana) refers to the purification of this [state] by placing another in its stead. "One should appoint" refers to the candidate for initiation (dīkṣya). || 415 ||

Having thus purified the various classes of human beings through the sequence beginning with the immobile beings, he speaks in order to purify the divine births: "Then, by means of the Brahma-mantras, [the powers] beginning with *aṇimā* are to be attained in due order."
And thus, by means of the application of the five oblations, for the sake of one's own enjoyment.

As before, following the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava* and *sadyojāta*, he offers five oblations with the mantra: "I cause Devadatta to attain the *aiśācī* powers such as *aṇimā*, svāhā.
Having contemplated the attainment of those enjoyments for him, [he should offer] with that same mantra: "his *paiśāca* enjoyment..."

One should offer five oblations with the mantra "śodhayāmi svāhā. Following this sequence, having purified the Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas by means of Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Tatpuruṣa, one should purify the fourfold group beginning with Indra and ending with Brahmā— predominantly characterized by *sattva*— by means of the venerable Lord Īśāna alone.
One should purify. || 416 ||
One should not think that the higher celestial births immediately following the human state are what must be purified;
rather, one should purify those [realms] belonging to the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).
Furthermore, by the word "higher" (*ūrdhva*), that which is to be known as resting upon the *bhūrloka* is intended.
One who is engaged in that [practice] should never perform any other duty whatsoever. || 10-417 ||

Whatever karma, based on the *bhūrloka*, results in birth among the divine classes (*devayoni*) within the *bhūrloka*, that is to be understood here as being "above" [the *bhūrloka*]. For one who is joined there for the sake of experience—meaning one who has been engaged by means of mantras—the purification must be performed; however, this does not apply to the *buddhitattva*, because therein...
This is because purification will be described by means of the specific utterance of names such as Sunanda and Karāla;
and this is logical, for otherwise, if the place of purification were not extracted from the disciple’s self according to the established sequence, how could there be union?
And it is not appropriate to extract [the soul] from there at that time—
[that is,] by means of the power of initiation through the initiate— as long as the karma has not been exhausted; this is the remainder of the sense.

Since this [individual] must necessarily experience the fruit of his karma, the Teacher therefore effects through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) a state for him consisting of one-pointed concentration upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those respective karmas; thus he says:
"Therefore, by the word 'yoga,' there is the singular contemplation of those respective karmas. (10.418)
O Great Goddess, it is turned back;
then,
one should perform the expiation by means of oblations.
"By Śiva" means by means of the partless (niṣkala) [form]; this has been determined in the fourth chapter itself,
as well as that which will be stated hereafter.
As it is said:
"From that [he attains] the lords of the worlds. (10.419)

Having purified the dwellings within the worlds and the worlds themselves in their proper sequence by means of the fire-oblation alone, one should likewise perform the rites of disjunction and severance.

The ellipsis [of the sentence] is that one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti*, the extraction (*samuddhāra*), and abiding within that (*tatsthatva*) in due order. While the purification of the worlds (*bhuvana*) is under discussion, [one should purify] the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśa*) beginning with Kālāgni, who are the primary [beings], as well as others dwelling within the worlds.
Having summoned those who constitute its limbs, one should dismiss them after first causing them to hear the recollection [of the mantras] through oblations (*āhuti*).

Having performed their purification, there is the separation—meaning the disjunction—of the initiate from the enjoyments already experienced; furthermore, there is the cutting of the bond (*pāśa*) consisting of the world-syllables (*bhuvana*), which is like a thread, and then the extraction (*samuddhāra*) from that.
The state of abiding in the world (*bhuvana*), the entry into the heart of the disciple, and so forth, have already been determined previously.

By saying "in due order," he refers to the very sequence mentioned before: immediately after the extraction (*uddhāra*) comes the making [of the deity] abide in oneself (*ātmasthīkaraṇa*); from that, the making [of it] abide in that [world] (*tatsthīkaraṇa*); and from that, the invocation of the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśāhvāna*).
"The Blessed Lord Śarva, the sovereign lord of the worlds, will remember [this] first," he said.
Furthermore:
"Then, having performed an expiation (prāyaścitta) on account of any deficiency or excess [in the ritual], [one should proceed]. (10.421)
The remainder is that the subsequent rite is to be performed. || 421 ||
This entire description of the *bhūrloka* is extended by analogy (*atidiśati*) to the purification of the other worlds as well:
"In this very sequence, one should purify [the realms] up to the *dhāman*.
The *dhāman* is that which consists of the *śivatattva*, having the *samanā* as its limit; it is the end of that. As it has been said:
"O fair-limbed one, [this] infinite web of fetters ends with *śamana*. (4-410).

"By the sequence beginning with *vam*" means that, preceded by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, the soul of the disciple is there further refined by the previously mentioned other purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

The meaning is that one should perform the consecrations (*saṃskāra*)— namely, birth, qualification, enjoyment, repose, expiation, separation, severance of bonds, the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and abiding in the Self and abiding therein— by means of the procedure beginning with the invocation, libation, proclamation, and dismissal of the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśa*).
Having thus spoken this incidental matter, he resumes the subject at hand:
"The world of Bhūḥ has been fully described; now learn from me about the world of Bhuvaḥ. (10.422)
From the surface of the earth up to the sun, the measurement is one hundred thousand [yojanas].
And therein—there are ten paths of wind in the middle, numbering ten thousand each. (10.423)
An *ayuta* is ten thousand; in the reading "an *ayutāyuta* interval," it should be explained as meaning that their dwelling place is at an interval of an *ayutāyuta*. || 423 ||
Therein—
first, I shall describe the clouds as they exist upon the paths of the wind.
The "paths of the wind" are the regions for the enjoyment of the movement of the winds, which are spread out and regulated by the will of the Supreme Lord.
There—fifty yojanas above—is the wind named Ṛtadhīḥ. || 10-424 ||
He who increases the nourishment and strength of the herbs likewise causes the entire earth to flourish and, being imperishable, brings it to fullness.
"Imperishable" means that even while constantly performing acts such as nourishing others, he does not diminish. || 425 ||
Furthermore:
By day he is the *haṃsa*; indeed, he is the wind that brings happiness to human beings.
He himself—
Because he supports the vultures, he is known as Gṛdhradhara. || 10-426 ||
The meaning is that this [Self] is indeed one, though it possesses various designations and various functions. || 426 ||
Above that is the wind named Prācetasa, which was fashioned by Pracetas;
it indeed destroys trees and sometimes sets them in motion again. (10.427)
Produced by Varuṇa Pracetas, it destroys—that is, it burns—and it causes [seeds] to sprout, that is, it brings about the emergence of shoots. || 427 ||
He explains how wind possesses the quality of burning:
"The fire named Prācetasa dwells together with that very [wind]; through association with it, this [wind]—”
When he burns down houses, then he is so designated. || 10-428 ||
The meaning is that this is indeed its name. || 428 ||
And he says that this fire is the nature of the *vaḍavā* (the submarine mare): "Happy it dwells in the ocean, its food and drink consisting of various waters obtained without effort."
And while dwelling here—
[the fire] is not extinguished by water or food;
on the contrary, it blazes up.
Now, beyond a hundred yojanas, the wind is called Senānī. || 10-429 ||
Some read, "It is known as the low wind (ṅīcavāyu).
Regarding the phrase "beyond a hundred [yojanas]," the intention is as follows:
fifty yojanas above the surface of the earth, at the fiftieth yojana, are Ṛtadhī and Pracetas.
In fifty [years]. || 429 ||
And when this wind blows, silent clouds accompanied by lightning abide;
for *ca* has the sense of "and" (*hi*).
Standing at a distance of one krośa from the earth, they discharge the waters. || 10.430 ||
Beyond a hundred yojanas, clouds that carry sentient beings are recorded;
these rain down fish, frogs, and tortoises during an ill-fated time.
Since they are such as these, the meaning is that they carry forth sentient beings (sattva). || 431 ||
Beyond this hundred yojanas, which is pervaded by the *sattvavaha* wind, the mass of winds known as *vāyurodha* is proclaimed.
In that [region], however, disease-inflicting clouds rain down poisonous water. (10.432)
From that, the prefixes arise;
*ca* is used in the sense of "and."
And by those afflictions, such as suffering and the like,
the Mārakas of all embodied beings proceed.
Then—thereafter, O Goddess, the wind Amogha remained for that long above it. 10-433.
In that [place], those clouds of Māra are established in the Amogha [region].
"Tāvat" means up to fifty [yojanas]; the word "tāvat" refers to the fifty yojanas mentioned earlier.
Now, the wind named Vajrāṅga is indeed situated at a distance of fifty yojanas. || 10-434 ||
In that [region] are clouds named Tūpala, which rain down tūpala;
above that, at exactly the same number of yojanas, is the Vaidyuta wind.
And the clouds belonging to lightning dwell in that Vaidyuta region;
they number fifty times as many as those [previously mentioned].
He states that their nature is electrical because lightning is their cause:
"Indeed, by the agitation of the wind, that great thunderbolt is produced within them. (10.436)
Lightning and thunderbolts: [occur] within those clouds. || 436 ||
Fifty yojanas above that, the mountain Raivata is said to be located;
there, the one named Puṣṭivaha rains down nourishment upon embodied beings.
"Raivata" is its name; "Puṣṭivaha" is the name of a cloud. || 437 ||
Situated above that are the Saṃvarta clouds, which bestow disease; raining down waters of sickness,
those clouds indeed remain at a distance of fifty yojanas from there.
Beyond that, the wind named Viṣāvarta is situated fifty [yojanas] above;
in it are established the clouds named Krodhodaka. (10.439)
They will be full of anger and passion, as well as full of strife;
they will cause the destruction of kings and likewise bring about the ruin of the subjects. || 10-440 ||
And here they cause rain whenever those clouds rain;
those clouds [occur] at intervals of fifty [yojanas] above the Saṃvarta [wind], and fifty [yojanas] above that.
The measurement of the Viṣāvarta [wind], however, will be stated later. Passion accompanied by anger is "anger-passion" (krodharāga); by that [passion].
"Abundant" means full; that is to say, it brings that about.
He distinguishes the seven winds, beginning with Ogha, by their similarity to phenomena:
Ogha, Amegha, Vajrāṅga, Vaidyuta, and likewise Raivata. (10.441)
And the winds Samvarta and Viṣāvarta, possessing terrible velocity;
"possessing terrible velocity" means those in whom a terrible speed exists in abundance.
He describes those for whom this group of seven is the abode, in due order:
"The divine Piśācas, born from the body of Skanda, indeed dwell in the Ogha. (10.442)
Thirty thousand crores are recorded as the followers of Skanda;
they indeed worship the son of Hara with divine flowers.
Above that,
in the Amogha [wind], there are the terrible Vināyakas born from Mahādeva;
thirty thousand koṭis of them are established in that wind.
Those who take away the performed karma of men who have not disciplined themselves— those of undisciplined self and lacking self-restraint.
Likewise, in the Vajra-limb and in the wind [element], there are Mātaṅgas who perform cruel deeds. || 10-445 ||
Resembling crushed collyrium, they are known as the terrible Tāpanas;
those who mount them are the lowest of the Vidyādharas, traveling with the speed of thought and the wind.
Those of such a character travel by means of their mind alone, like riders on elephants moving through the air; for this very reason, they are considered base.
The superior ones, however, attain those various regions solely through the power of their knowledge and other such qualities. 446.
Moreover:

Those who, through their knowledge and manly effort, have mastered the Vetālas and other spirits from the cremation grounds, once they have attained perfection, they are established in this wind. || 10.447 ||

Regarding "knowledge and manliness" (*vidyāpauruṣe*), this refers to those who became famous for competing in sciences, learning, and so forth, or who died after having accomplished [the rites of] *vetālas* and the like; such is the meaning. || 447 ||
In that Vaidyuta region, the Apsarases dispatched by Vāsava always remain there for the protection of the city of the earth.

And this is the protection of the city of the earth for them: that the inhabitants of that region, through their virtuous conduct, attain their own celestial realms by means of aerial chariots. || 448 ||
Thus it is said:
"Whether on a mountain, in fire, or even in water, those supreme men who do not retreat in battles—whether in the seizure of cattle or in the liberation of prisoners—are reborn as gods. (10.449)
Then they proceed upwards in celestial chariots marked with jewels,
strewn with long banners and the like, and resounding with the sound of divine bells.

"Non-returners" (*anivartaka*) means those who do not turn back; the meaning is that they die right in front [of the enemy]. "The seizing of cows" refers to being attacked by lions and other predators. "Captives" refers to the wives of others who have been seized by force and are being led away against their will. And these, having died in battle or similar circumstances, are the best of men because of their virtuous conduct.
But it was not said previously— "Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self" (Īśā Upaniṣad 3).
Because they are described as being unsurpassed in the Śruti; "thence" means from their own level. || 450 ||
He explains how they go:
"Those [apsarases] lead them away with palaces surrounded by thousands of women.
The word "yataḥ" (from where) is to be supplied; "tāḥ" refers to the apsarases.
On Raivata, however, the great-souled Siddhas are indeed firmly established.
Having mastered the gorocanā collyrium, the ashes, the sandals, the deerskin, and so forth, those great-souled ones became perfected beings capable of assuming any form at will. || 10-452 ||
The perfected ones have attained completion. || 452 ||
And then, in this regard:
those high-souled ones dwell there, established in divine perfection;
because they abide in the state of the Vajrāṅga and possess its nature, they are called the lowest of the Vidyādharas.
Even during the great wind of universal dissolution (saṃvarta), the hosts of Vidyādharas are said to remain.
Those forty million [beings] were adorned with divine ornaments;
they were anointed with divine perfumes and graced with the splendor of divine garlands.

The meaning here is that the ten groups which exist in brief are, in detail, thirty crores. Furthermore, these Vidyādharas are indeed specific types of divine beings (*devayoni*), and not humans who have become perfected through the attainment of powers such as the magical sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*).
Now, regarding this:
"The smoke-born clouds of fire are known to grant coolness and relief from distress;
mingled with the wind, they move like a boat upon the whirlpool of poison. (10.455)
There, skilled in the Gandharva arts and sharing the nature of the Gandharvas, were birds capable of assuming any form at will, who were experts in the methods of the flute and the lute. || 10.456 ||
Through the Gandharva rite, performed in accordance with the dharma of the Gandharvas, [one attains] the state of being a worshiper of Maheśvara. || 456 ||
The clouds named Brahmajā, born from the breath of Brahmā, are situated a hundred yojanas above Durjaya. || 10-457 ||
Above the hundred yojanas pervaded by the wind called Viṣāvarta, there is the wind named Durjaya; it is logical that the clouds born of Brahmā are situated above that. || 457 ||
Furthermore:
"In that place, indeed, there are the guardians of Indra named Durjayas;
they remain stationed there, taking refuge in the wind called Parāvaha. (10.458)
Ten koṭis are proclaimed as being endowed with the power of great heroism;
the connection here is that they do so by relying on the wind named Parāvaha in the vicinity of Durjaya.
Beyond this, moreover,
there are clouds named Puṣkarāvartakas, which indeed originate from Padmaja.
Likewise—
those wings of the great-souled mountains that were severed by Śakra,
Parāvaha carries them away just as an elephant carries off men. (10.460)
The wind named Parāvaha carries those Puṣkarāvartakas as well as the mountains that possess wings.
Furthermore:
In that [region], there are Gandharvas named Vāyugamas who dwell in the sky;
eleven crores of them are said to exist. || 10.461 ||
Likewise:
"Those clouds named Jīmūta, which arise from the life-force of the gods, rest upon the second wind, Āvaha. (10.462)
In that [wind], there are ten classes of Vidyādharas named Jīmūtakas;
they are called "born from life" (jīvasamudbhava) because "life" (jīva) means breath, and they arise from that.
The second is the Āvaha wind, which refers to the Parāvaha wind that has the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds as its support, and not otherwise.
First is the basis of the Durjayas.
Then the wind Āvaha blew from there to where the Droṇas had taken refuge.
In that [region], the Droṇas are renowned as the protectors of the clouds;
the Droṇas are a specific class of clouds that guard the lower-flowing clouds against their failure to act according to their nature.
For this reason:
"Indeed, they were created by me in the past for the welfare of all beings. (10.464)
"May it be so" refers to one residing on Kailāsa; this is the statement of the speaker therein. "Beneficial" means protection from calamities against clouds that bring down rain. 464.
Now, above these—rising from the skull-caps—are the clouds named Saṃvarta;
the wind named Mahāparivaha is their support. (10.465)
"Born from the skull" means "belonging to me alone," by implication. || 465 ||
He summarizes: "In the first path of the wind, indeed, the clouds together with the winds, as well as the Siddhas and the Lords who move within the clouds, have been described in this way. (10.466)

This first path of the wind, which measures ten thousand [yojanas], has fifty yojanas of empty space above its surface; above that are the winds Ṛtadhī, Prācetasa, Senānī, Sattvavaha, Ogha, Amogha, Vajrāṅga, Vaidyuta, Raivata, and Saṃvarta.

Regarding the term *viṣāvarta*: among these eleven winds, the two known as Senānī and Sattvavaha are situated at intervals of one hundred *yojanas* each from the center; the remaining [nine] are each situated at intervals of fifty *yojanas*. By this calculation, [the distance] from the surface of the earth to the end of Viṣāvarta is reached.
Seven hundred yojanas above that, at a height of nine thousand three hundred [yojanas],
there abide five winds known as Durjaya, Parāvaha, Vyāvaha, Āvaha, and Mahāparivaha. || 466 ||
Having first elaborated upon the path of the wind, he now classifies the others in brief:
"In the second path of the wind, the daughters of Agni and the Mothers (mātaraḥ) are to be known;
endowed with virtues, they dwell there, presided over by the power of Rudra. (10.467)
The Mothers, such as Brāhmī and others, exist in another form; they are endowed with qualities such as omniscience because they are presided over by the power (śakti) of Rudra. || 467 ||
Then, in the third path of the wind, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas dwell;
perfected through the enjoyment of their own karma, they are presided over by all the Siddhas. || 10.468 ||

One's own prior auspicious karma is the cause; "enjoyment" consists of the pleasure appropriate to each respective station. "Perfected by its power" means having attained those stations. They are "presided over"—that is, reached—by all other perfected beings (*siddhas*) who have likewise attained perfection through yoga suited to their particular stations. || 468 ||
Above that— on the fourth path here— dwell the deities of the weapons:
the iron arrow, the discus, the bow, the sword, the trident, the spear, the shaft, and the mallet.

The *ṛṣṭi* is a specific type of weapon; these [terms] also imply the sword (*khaḍga*), the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and so forth. Furthermore, they refer to the names of those deities who possess such weapons. || 469 ||
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, on the fifth path dwell Airāvata and the others: Airāvata, Añjana, and the great elephant Vāmana. (10.470)
Supratīka, Gajendra, and likewise Puṣpadanta;
Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and Sārvabhauma as the eighth.
The epithet for Vāmana is "Great Elephant," and likewise, that for Supratīka is "Lord of Elephants."
These very ones are renowned as the "Elephants of the Quarters" (Diggajas), established in their respective directions;
that is, they are situated in the sky itself according to the sequence starting from the East.
Beyond that, O Goddess, on the sixth path of the wind dwells the king of birds, possessed of great strength. || 10.472 ||
He is renowned as Garuḍa, exceedingly invincible and possessed of great heroism;
meanwhile, in the seventh [heaven], the celestial Gaṅgā flows, followed by various aquatic creatures.
That meritorious river is proclaimed to be threefold,
possessing divine water equal to nectar (amṛta). It is "threefold" by virtue of its presence in Satyaloka, Svarloka, and Bhuvarloka.
That [light], whirling in the midst of the sky, was perfectly circular on all sides.
The celestial Gaṅgā, renowned as the constant festival of the gods,
shines like a garland of flowers resting upon the head of the sky.
There, O fortunate one, [he was honored] by the Siddhas, by the hosts of Vidyādharas, by Gandharvas and Apsarases, by the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts.
Together with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Pitṛs, gods,
and great sages, as well as with the Rākṣasas and Guhyakas who were intent upon divine hymns of praise.
By high-souled beings praising, muttering prayers, and singing;
by those dancing and leaping, amidst the sounds of divine drums.
With the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums, the resonances of lutes, and the notes of flutes, all impelled by the vital breaths of the mind; || 10.479 ||

In that context, "by the Siddhas" indicates those characterized as Siddhas and so forth. "By the Pitṛs and Devas" is an epithet for the three beginning with Rudra. The preceding [terms], such as "praising," etc., are to be construed as appropriate qualifiers for the [respective] subjects. "With the sounds of divine drums," and so forth, refers to dancing and leaping.

And the third case endings [in the words] *prati* and *hetu* [are used]. In the phrase "by the wind presided over by the mind," it should be construed as "impelled" and "filled" by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 479 ||
Furthermore:
with fragrant lotuses having stalks of beryl and petals of gold, and with filaments as large as great wheels made of rubies. || 10.480 ||
The great river, the support of dharma, adorned with hundreds of celestial palaces and graced by divine forests, seems as if it were dancing, O best of rivers. (10.481)
"With filaments of ruby" (kesaraiḥ padmarāgaiḥ) means with lotuses possessing filaments made of rubies.
It is that by which Dharma is maintained (dhāryate) or accomplished on all sides (ā) through seeing, touching, and so forth. || 481 ||
And this is logical, because:
"That supreme power of action (kriyā-śakti) indeed issued forth from my eye";
this has already been determined previously.
This very one is the goddess Mahāmandākinī, who is attended by the gods of the three worlds.
Adorned by billions of great celestial palaces situated without any gaps,
this blessed goddess always dwells in the expanse of the sky.
Its greatness arises from its preeminent power; "by those who abide" is an epithet qualifying the gods (tridaśa).
There, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, this [teaching] fell from my head onto the summit of Mount Meru and descended upon the surface of the earth. (10.484)

This Gaṅgā, having been summoned and released by me— who was entreated by the gods according to the reasoning previously described— for the sake of purifying the mortal world, reached my head as I stood upon the summit of Meru; falling from there, she remained upon the peak of Meru, and subsequently upon the surface of the earth.
The connection is that [the breath] "fell. And it was said previously:
"Having come to my head, O Mistress of the Gods, it went again to the summit of Meru; having emerged from there, it went to the oceans in the four directions. (10.181)
Thus [ends the verse]. || 484 ||
Furthermore, due to the constraint of my power of destiny—
that very Gaṅgā remains unagitated,
held by the wind; otherwise, how could she not be disturbed by the wind, or how could she be carried along?
Its width is proclaimed to be a full hundred yojanas. || 10.485 ||
"The circumference from there is millions..."—the word "from there" (tataḥ) means in that space; the word "millions" (koṭyaḥ) means many millions.
And here in this case—
this auspicious [mandala], possessing great velocity, should stand as if revolving, perfectly circular on all sides. (10.486)
"Perfectly circular" because the space within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is likewise. || 486 ||

Having filled the Dhruva, that goddess remains in an exceedingly wonderful state. "Dhruva" means the circle of stars bound to its navel; "goddess" (devī) means the shining one; she remains having performed something most marvelous.
Furthermore:
"The divine river that carries nectar is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins. (10.487)
It carries the celestial, supramundane, immortal water that exists in heaven. || 487 ||
Now, in the eighth [chapter], the King of Bulls (Nandin), together with his wife and accompanied by Sanandana,
dwells there; he is unimpeded, and he is Dharma himself made manifest.
The "King of Bulls" (Vṛṣarāja) is the vehicle of Maheśvara; he is unobstructed and moves according to his own will. Regarding "Dharma":
"Dharma is the Bull; it is the attribute of the Lord, consisting of knowledge and action."
Because he sustains both the conscious and the unconscious, he is called *dharma* by the wise;
such is the true nature as stated in the venerable *Mayasaṃgraha*. || 488 ||
And here, on the ninth path, resides the Prajāpati named Dakṣa;
he is Brahman himself manifest, presided over by the power of Brahman.
The power of Brahman has the form of the creator. || 489 ||
O Goddess, on the tenth path of Vāyu dwell Vasu, Rudra, and Divākara;
these were previously drawn down from here for the purpose of serving the Gaṅgā.
Therein, because of their preeminence, he first shows the Rudras by name:
"And here [are] Aṅgāraka, Sapī, Nairṛta, and Sadasatpati" (10.490).
Budha, Dhūmaketu, the renowned Jvara, Aja, Bhuvaneśa, Mṛtyu, and likewise Kāpālika. || 10-491 ||
The eleven Rudras are remembered as the source from which the fruits of all desires arise.

He who is sometimes called Sadasaspati is known as Jvara, famous throughout the three worlds. The compound [sarvakāmaphalodayāḥ] is analyzed as "those from whom there is the arising (udaya) of the fruits of all desires."
Thus it is:
Dhātṛ, Dhruva, Soma, Varuṇa, Anila, and Anala. || 10-492 ||
Pratyūṣa and Pradoṣa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. Thus, these Vasus have been described; now learn from me about the Ādityas. (10.493)
Āryamā, Indra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu who holds the bow, and Mitra are likewise proclaimed; among them, Ajaghanya is the youngest. (10.494)
Vivasvat, Parjanya, and Dhātṛ are indeed remembered as the twelfth;
they know these to be the Kāśyapeyas—
meaning these are the offspring of Kaśyapa, the descendants of Kaśyapa.
...of those [beings], and then of that treasury of splendor (tejonidhi). || 10-495 ||
The divine chariot born of nectar is attended by all the gods;

among those Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, it belongs to Āditya, the treasury of splendor, for his chariot is born from the Ocean of Milk, as he alone, mounted upon it, is appointed to illuminate the world.

It has also been indicated by the previously mentioned perspective that the chariot— which consists of all the gods and takes the form of the vital breath (prāṇa)— has arisen from the nectar of the supreme power of the sun of consciousness, which is a treasury of splendor.
By this, he analyzes what was stated [in verse 495], namely that [the chariot] consists of all the gods:
"The sacrifice is the wheel in that chariot, and the pole consists of all knowledge. (10.496)
The seven horses are the seven musical notes, resounding with the *hūṃ* of the Vedas;
the serpents are their yokes, and Aruṇa is indeed the charioteer.
Truth is its couch, and the force of the wind is that of its chariot.

Sacrifice, whose essence is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), is the deity; it is the wheel of this chariot, for by its power the movement of all worlds situated above and below is accomplished. As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"Therefore, the omnipresent Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice" (3.15).
Because it is traditionally taught that "he sacrifices all," the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgīśvarī*), who consists of the knowledge of all scriptures, is his yoke-pole;
upon which the horses are hitched and draw [the chariot]. And they...

The seven musical notes, beginning with *ṣaḍja*, are manifested by the sound of neighing in the form of the syllable *hūṃ*, which constitutes the primary essence of the Veda as the denoter of all things. Thus, they arise from the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of the resounding *nāda*;

furthermore, because they consist of the sections pertaining to knowledge (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*), action (*kriyā-kāṇḍa*), and the deities, they embody both the supreme (*parā*), the intermediate (*aparā*), and their union.

Through the connection between the upward and downward powers (*ūrdhvādhara-śakti*), he shows that the Vedas function as the place for the mudrās of each mantra. *Yoktrāṇi* means binding ropes. *Nāgāḥ* refers to Ananta and the others; [the text says] "of those," meaning of the six notes (*ṣaḍja*) and so forth. *Na agāḥ* means those whose nature is constant movement—namely, the volitions (*saṅkalpa*) which are the directors.
Aruṇa, Anūru, Dīpta, and Ahaṅkāra; Satya and Ṛta; Mañcaka as the seat;

the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), which consists of the quality of purity (sattva) and stands as the excellent support throughout all that is manifest; the speed of the chariot, the deity named Vāyu; and [the power] of the inner self consisting of vital breath (prāṇa).
And the speed of the chariot is indeed of the nature of air, consisting of the vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna.
Thus, for one mounted upon such a chariot,
the body of the Sun-god is nine thousand yojanas in extent.

His mandala, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), shines brilliantly throughout the three worlds. The physical form of the Sun of Life (jīvāditya) is nine tālas in height; and the mandala is luminous in nature, endowed with the three qualities beginning with sattva.
And he says that this [power] is indeed extraordinary:
"For this supreme power of consciousness blazes forth, having the form of the sun. (10.499)
The meaning is that the cognitive power (*jñānaśakti*) of the omnipotent Maheśvara, which illuminates the universe, exists in the form of both the individual soul-sun and the external sun.

Thus, the twelve Ādityas, whose nature consists of the power of the Supreme Lord’s knowledge, move by the will of Śiva through the application of the lunar months and the days of the week. A day of the week [is assigned] to each month; that very application is the regulation (niyoga). This is the division of the months and so forth for the Jīvāditya.

This has already been determined previously. Its state as the twelve elements is due to a differentiation of cognition. By the phrase "by the will of Śiva," the meaning is that no other's will has power here.
And for this reason:
"These [planets] revolve day and night all around the Bhuvarloka. (10.500)
And this should be applied according to what was stated [in the verse]: "The rising [of the sun] which is Amarāvatī" (10.338). As for that which—

How can it be that Paṭañjali stated that knowledge of the worlds arises from *saṃyama* on the sun, given that the Great Commentator Rājānaka Bhullaka [asserts] that the sun’s pervasion in illuminating the entire world does not extend [that far]? To this, [the answer is]: the sun [pervades] from the netherworld (*pātāla*) up to the end of Satyaloka.
The claim that "it is the state of being an illuminator" is explained according to one's own whim; because it lacks substance, it should be disregarded. || 500 ||

Now, he describes the division of the positions of the moon and the other [planets] above the sun: "Then the moon is situated one hundred thousand [yojanas] above the sun, nourishing the entire world by raining down streams of nectar. (10.501)
And thus:
"The power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva indeed shines in the form of the moon;
above the moon, at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas], stands the circle of the constellations. (10.502)
The circle of constellations is the wheel of stars. || 502 ||
Two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that is situated the son of Earth (Mars);
two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that is situated the son of Soma (Mercury).
Surācārya is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above him;
and two hundred thousand above him dwells Bhṛgunandana.
Two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that, Saturn moves with ease;
"moves" means it traverses the zodiacal signs; "with ease" means very slowly, since this is Śanaiścara (the Slow-Mover).
Two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that—
But I shall describe the sages in brief, by means of a mere hundred thousand.
He states them according to the order of their establishment:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha,
Kratu, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci.
Śṛṅga is one and the same person according to both his lineage and his name.
These seven are celebrated as the ṛṣis. || 10.506 ||
For it is through the observance of the restraints (yama) and the observances (niyama) that these [mantras] become capable of bestowing curses or favors.
Non-violence and the others are the restraints; purity and the others are the observances. (506)
Furthermore—
being afraid of causing pain to others...
they do not even inflict punishment upon those who have committed transgressions, because they are under the sway of compassion.
Likewise—those who are heroes in the investigation of the scriptures. || 10-507 ||
The brave are sharp-witted. || 507 ||
For this very reason, regarding those to be graced:
"All [the teachers], with the sword of knowledge raised, remove the veil of ignorance. Ignorance itself is called a "veil" because it obscures the light of consciousness; they destroy that [veil].
And for that very purpose:
"The practices of mantra, yoga, ritual action, and conduct are difficult to transcend when undertaken with full commitment. (10.508)

Endowed with the qualities of the power of yoga (yogaiśvarya) and intent upon the worship of Śiva, [they are characterized by] mantras whose essence is contemplation (manana), yoga consisting of meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and so forth, ritual action (kriyā) as the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, and conduct (caryā) in the form of vows (vrata) and the like; [these are the means] through these mantras and other such practices.

They are armored and adorned; for this very reason, they are difficult to overcome and are never subdued by ignorance. Furthermore, they are endowed with the qualities of yogic sovereignty, such as the supernatural powers (siddhis) beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Nevertheless, they are constantly devoted and intent upon the primary practice of worshipping Śiva.
Then, O Goddess, from those [stars] at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas], there is Dhruva; and the stars are fourteen.
Being indeed one alone. || 509 ||
Therefore, O woman of excellent complexion, his body was constructed from fourteen stars by those [stars] of Dhruva;
and thus it is said:
Uttānapāda, Makha, Hanu, Śuci, Dharma, Mūrdhan, Nārāyaṇa, Aśvin, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Hṛt, Pada, Uru, Saṃvatsara, Prajanana, and Mitra residing in the hips.
"The tail consists of Vahni, Indra, Kaśyapa, Marīci, and Abhaya. Thus, in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), the commencement of his limbs, beginning with the jaw and head,
is described as being presided over by deities such as Yajña, Dharma, and others.
And this one—Brahmā himself in another form—has been appointed to the position of Brahmā. (10.510)
Abiding in Satyaloka, Brahmā is stationed within the Bhuvarloka by means of the cosmic egg as his other form. || 510 ||
In this way, O Goddess, the multitude of lights belonging to him who is situated in the center like the hub of a wheel revolves constantly;
yet he should be known as immovable, for he is presided over by the power of Śiva. (10.511)
The meaning is that he is thus established by Śiva-Śakti alone. And this very Self of Consciousness (cidātman), remaining immovable within,
is surrounded by the wheel of the stars of the thirteen internal senses.

It should be understood that [the Pole Star] is the initiator of the movements of the sun and moon, as well as the prāṇa and apāna breaths, which depend upon all the planets, asterisms, and so forth, according to the stability described in the section on time. For this very reason, regarding the Pole Star (dhruva), who is the representative of the Self:
"Whatever sin one commits by day, one is released from it upon seeing [the Pole Star] at night."
"And the lifespan increases year by year for those ending with Dhruva"—this is heard in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and other such works. As for that which is mentioned there:
the revolution of the sphere of the earth situated outside the wheel of planets and constellations, which is fixed to the navel of Dhruva, [and] of the sun and others...
Furthermore, the specific locations, dimensions, and other details of the earth and so forth are heard [in scripture]. Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as a lamp reveals objects in the darkness, this scripture reveals the sequence of that accumulated merit and demerit from previous births. (Sūtrajāti 1.3)

Thus, according to the very process described therein, it is so in relation to deities such as the Sun, who preside over the spheres of light (tejo-golaka) in accordance with prior karma, and likewise in relation to the earth situated at the place where karma is acquired; however, this—
In relation to the deities such as the Sun who preside over the fiery globes and so forth,

the positions, configurations, revolutions, and so on of the Sun and others, as well as the dimensions of the netherworlds (pātāla), the earth, and so forth, are real according to the very process already described.
Since this very [teaching] has been perceived by the Great Lord, the omniscient of all, one need not engage in discussions regarding its agreement or disagreement with it. Therefore:
"That which is not seen in other scriptures is seen in the scripture of the Supreme Lord."
"Where else is speech seen [to range] from Niyati up to Śiva?
Thus, this very process is the correct one. || 511 ||
From the terrestrial sphere up to the Pole Star (Dhruva), there are fifteen hundred thousand [yojanas].
The spheres of Bhuḥ, Sūrya, Indu, and the Nakṣatras are each separated by one hundred thousand;
the five planets beginning with Mars are each separated by two hundred thousand; the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) are separated by one hundred thousand; and Dhruva is separated by one hundred thousand.
Thus, up to the end of Dhruva, it amounts to exactly fifteen lakhs.
Furthermore:
I shall describe here, in brief, the masses of wind that abide therein. || 10-512 ||
Here, within these two Svar-lokas, which together measure one hundred and fifty thousand yojanas,
I shall describe the layers of wind (vāyuskandhas), consisting of worlds and other structures situated by means of winds regulated by the power of the Lord (Īśvara). || 512 ||
He describes the division of their enclosures (kakṣyā):

"From the sun to the clouds, from the moon to the lunar mansions, from the circle of the planets to the designation of the seven sages, and up to the Pole Star (dhruva)—this is the seventh [enclosure]. (10.513)

"From the clouds," it is said; thus, from the clouds situated in the path of the wind up to the Pole Star (Dhruva), seven layers of wind are established across seven concentric zones. As it is stated in the Purāṇas: "The first layer on the earth, extending up to the clouds, is the Āvaha wind."
And the second is the Pravaha wind, which extends from the clouds up to the sun.
That which is known as Udvaha is situated above Sūrya and likewise above Soma;
and Saṃvaha is the fourth, situated above Soma and the constellations (ṛkṣas).
The fifth wind, Vivaha, extends from the stars up to the planets;
the sixth, Parāvaha, extends from the planets up to the sages (Ṛṣis).
"Likewise, above the seven sages, up to Dhruva, the seventh is known as the Vātaskandha wind-layer, called Parivaha. Thus [it is said].
And in that very place, seven intermediate subdivisions for each are mentioned, with names such as Śukrajyotis, Satyajyotis, Citrajyotis, Jyotiṣmat, and so forth. || 513 ||
Thus, this celestial world (svarloka), extending from the Sun to Dhruva, has been fully described.
Here indeed resides King Mahendra, honored by the gods. (10.514)
Surrounded by ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, and hosts of apsarases,
the Bhuvarloka extends from the surface of the earth up to the sun for one hundred thousand yojanas. Beyond that, extending up to Dhruva, the Svargaloka spans fourteen hundred thousand yojanas.
And having performed such a rite as this—the Agnihotra or even other sacrifices—those devoid of knowledge [fall]. (10.515)
Men go to the heavenly world (svarloka) and return again to the human realm.
The *agnihotra* is the oblation performed by one who is constantly devoted to the sacred fire; the sacrifices (*kratu*) include the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others.
Because they are devoid of [true] knowledge, they go to the heavenly world at the end of the body. There, they experience the fruit accumulated through their own actions.

Having enjoyed [the fruits], they return again to the human state and so forth; however, the intention is that the wise, even while performing sacrifices and other rites, are liberated because of their lack of desire.
In this very way, above such a world of the gods (Svarloka), there are two crores of yojanas.
And eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas], O fair-faced one, is Maharloka.
Thus, according to the system of this world, Bhuvarloka extends up to the sun; Svarloka extends up to Dhruva;
and above that is Maharloka, consisting of two koṭis and eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas].
In the *Śrīparāmṛgendra* and other texts, however, Bhuvarloka extends up to Dhruva;
above that— "Svarloka, the abode of heaven, measures eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas];
Maharloka, where the Great Ones (Mahāntaḥ) reside, measures two koṭis. Thus it is said.
"Bhuvarloka extends from the surface of the earth to the limit of Dhruva for ten million yojanas; Svarloka is one-tenth of that [nine million]... (13.114).
Thus, a difference in the system is observed. This...
This is because it was not compiled in that manner by the authors of those [other] texts.
However, this was stated directly by the Supreme Lord:
"From Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar up to Dhruva, there are one hundred thousand [yojanas]... and so forth.
"...the Mahāloka would be two koṭis.
Thus, this very sequence is logical here in Mahāloka, in accordance with the dialogue between the Lord and Saṃvarta as stated in the *Kiraṇa* and other scriptures.
Indeed, the ṛṣis and the siddhas, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others, dwell there.
Now,
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, Janaloka is situated above Maharloka at a distance of eighty million yojanas. (10.518)
Furthermore:
Ekapāda, Jahnu, Kapila, Āsuri, Bhautika, and Vāḍvali are the inhabitants of Janaloka. (10.519)
Then,
O Dear One, twelve crores above Janaloka is declared to be Tapoloka, which is filled with sages and lords of yoga. (10.520)
He spoke to them: "Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatkumāra, Sanandana, Śaṅku, and Triśaṅku—these are the inhabitants of the world of Tapas. (10.521)
Now, as an incidental digression, he states the number of worlds from the earth (bhūrloka) up to the world of truth (satyaloka):
"O fair-faced one, starting from the end of the earth-world up to the world of truth, there are fifty-six and five hundred crores, and twenty lakhs. (10.522)
This number of worlds has been fully declared by the Supreme Lord in the *Bṛhattantra*—this is the implied sense, O fair-faced one. The "lotus-number" will be explained in the eleventh chapter.
He now states the subject at hand:
O beloved, Tapoloka is sixteen crores [of yojanas] in measurement above [Brahmaloka].
Satyaloka is fully described as the place where Brahmā himself resides;
there the blessed Lord sports, surrounded by those born from his own self who are equal to him.
Because they there—
perfected through the knowledge of action, firmly established in non-duality,
having attained the state of bliss, they have reached the state of bliss. || 10-525 ||

They are perfectly perfected through the combined practice of obligatory and occasional rituals (*nityanaimittika*) as well as the knowledge taught in the Vedānta; for this very reason, they are firmly established in the state of non-duality described as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28), and thus their meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) has become fully rooted. And therefore—

They have reached and ascended to this state of bliss known as Satyaloka, a place of great enjoyment; even here, having arrived at the station of bliss, they remain solely delighted in their own Self—this is the meaning. || 525 ||
Furthermore:
The Ṛgveda is embodied; within it resides Indra, equal in splendor to him, his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments. (10.526)
Established to its east, blazing with his own splendor,
is the Yajurveda to its north, resembling pure crystal.
Wearing divine earrings, with a massive body and great arms,
the eternal Sāmaveda stands in the western quarter.
Clad in red garments, glorious, with a radiance like that of a ruby,
he wears a garland of flowers and is adorned with various ornamental necklaces.
Then Atharvan stood to the south, dark as collyrium,
with tawny eyes, a red neck, golden hair, and a massive body.
The *Ṛgveda* is dark because its performance lacks clarity, as it is devoted solely to ritual acts and the praise of deities;
the *Yajurveda* is white because of the clarity of that [performance]; and the *Sāmaveda* is red because of its captivating nature due to the predominance of chanting. As for the *Atharvaveda*...
Blackness and variegatedness arise from being intent upon worldly activities such as malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the like.
Furthermore, in this regard: the six auxiliary sciences, the Itihāsas, all the Purāṇas, the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, as well as the Mīmāṃsā and the Āraṇyakas. (10.531)
The utterances of Svāhā and Vaṣaṭ, as well as the secret doctrines,
and the Gāyatrī itself abide there where the four-faced god resides.

The "limbs" (*aṅga*) of the Veda are the sciences of phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual procedure (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
"History" (*itihāsa*) refers to works such as the *Mahābhārata*. The "ancient lore" (*purāṇa*) consists of the treatises spoken by Vyāsa and others.
The "Vedāntas" are the Upaniṣads of the Veda. "Mīmāṃsā" is the science of inquiry into the Veda. The "Āraṇyaka" is...

The *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* is also mentioned separately among the Vedāntas because it is recited in the forest (*araṇya*). The two mantras concerning radiance and nourishment are the *svāhākāra* and *vaṣaṭkāra*. The *rahasyas* (secrets) are specific portions of the Vedānta such as the *Taittirīya*; they are mentioned separately precisely because of their secret nature. The *Gāyatrī*...
The Mother of the Vedas; all these deities possess anthropomorphic forms. || 532 ||
This is that Satyaloka—
the abode of enjoyment for Brahmā—
where he, having completed his office, dwells.
...one should then go to the Supreme Brahman;
the meaning is that it is what has been described as "Brahman is without form, consciousness, and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).
Then,
O Dear One, at a distance of ten million yojanas above Satyaloka—
Known as the Brahmāsana, it has the luster of hibiscus and vermilion;
it is called an "āsana" because one sits (*āsate*) upon it, and it is the world situated above Satyaloka.
There he is—situated in the center of a red lotus, with a radiance equal to a ruby. || 10-534 ||
Four-faced, the knower of the four Vedas, following the course of the four ages, Brahmā is surrounded by those who know Brahman and attended by sages. (10.535)
Endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, he is the creator of the sixfold emanation and the bestower of the connection between dharma and its fruits in age after age.
Of animals, hell-beings, and sentient beings, as well as gods and humans;
he is the creator of all beings among the worlds of gods, asuras, and men. (10.537)
The phrase "he whose [powers] are the four ages (yugas) and the four masteries (vaśās)" involves an inversion of the rule for prior placement (pūrvanipāta).
The eightfold sovereignty consists of *aṇimā* and the rest. Regarding the term "sixfold":
the *tāmasī* [creation], consisting of hell-beings, stationary beings, reptiles, and ending with domestic animals, is threefold; that which consists of both *rajas* and *tamas* is sixfold.

She will be human, consisting of the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*, silent, characterized by *sattva*, and divine—thus she will exist in the eleventh [age]. The phrase "in age after age" refers to the bestower of the fruits of dharma and so forth. He is the creator of all fourteen classes of beings, including animals and others, within this world of gods, asuras, and humans.
Then, O fair-faced one, two crores of yojanas above that is [the realm] resembling the blue water-lily and possessing a luster like sapphire. (10.538)
The city of Viṣṇu is remembered as being beyond the world of Brahmā;
it is endowed with all objects of desire and resplendent with every kind of jewel.
With stairways and pillars of emerald, crowded with blue banners, extensive with canopies of bells, and adorned with beautiful yak-tail whisks. || 10-540 ||
She was surrounded by groups of maidens who resembled the petals of blue lotuses,
their deer-like eyes startled by the sound of Cupid’s bow.
Resounding with the tinkling of anklets, stumbling with soft, languid movements,
they were shattered by hundreds of falling shafts from the bow of the God of Love.
That Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like lotuses, is served by those whose white eyes roll with the intoxication of well-drunk wine.
Having a form like sapphire and the luster of blue lotus petals,
four-armed and large-bodied, with a broad chest, he holds a mace.
Wearing a crown, earrings, and a conch, and intent upon protecting his subjects,
that Blessed One is served by hosts who possess his own prowess.

(Kirīṭī =) He whose crown is a diadem; he is also characterized by the mace, conch, discus, and the Śārṅga bow. "By his own prowess" means by those hosts—that is, by the multitudes of his attendants—whose valor is like his own, he is served. || 545 ||
Moreover:
"And those who are constant devotees of Viṣṇu, devoted to meditation, worship, and recitation—they, possessing immeasurable prowess, go to that abode of Viṣṇu. (10.546)
"Devotees of Viṣṇu" refers to those intent on meditating upon Him in that form. || 546 ||
Then—seven crores above that, the world of Rudra is situated;
it resembles pure crystal and is adorned with courtyards and gardens. (10.547)
It was adorned with rows of palatial mansions consisting of a thousand stories,
and joined by celestial chariots (*vimāna*) like the *puṣpaka*, as pure as swans, jasmine, and the moon.
With groves and garden thickets radiant with flowers of every season, there were terraces (*bhūmikā*) consisting of charming wooden structures arranged one above another like staircases.
There were flower-carts (*puṣpaka*) that moved by mere thought. But in Śrīparāyaṇa—
"That Brahman is above, and Viṣṇu is [situated] beyond four crores;
that god Śaṅkara, Hara, is established [there] at six crores. However, in the Kiraṇa [Tantra]:
"Sixty million [yojanas] is the Truth...
having said this—
"Above that, Brahmā resides, measuring three crores [of yojanas]."
"Viṣṇu stands with three crores, while Hara stands with four.
