This difference in procedure is not contradictory, because for this triad of deities who remain established [in the body], there is no loss of their status as occupying ten crores when taken together.
And here—
the breezes are pleasant to the touch and carry the fragrance of lotuses and camphor.
And this—
abounding with rivers, streams, and lakes, and adorned with clusters of lotus ponds;
and likewise—
She is the most excellent, the giver of boons, the supreme, and she of the most beautiful complexion.
Vasiṣṭhā, Varāhā, and Varārohā as the seventh—
these are indeed declared to be the Gaṅgās that always carry one to the world of Rudra.
And these [lakes] were adorned with white lotuses rich with a hundred thousand petals,
possessing stalks resembling sapphire and emitting fragrance for a yojana.
The petals (*dalāni*) are the principal leaves; the meaning is that there are one hundred thousand leaves for each. The meaning [of the instrumental] is "characterized by" those [petals]. || 552 ||
Moreover, here in the world of Rudra— women who are as delicate as fresh butter, resembling the autumnal moon, grey with heaps of flowers, and enriched by throngs of thousands of women. (10.553)
With beautiful brows, foreheads, and faces, slender waists, and languid with passion;
with hair resembling a swarm of bees and fragrant with the scent of musk.
Their ears had long lobes, and their eyes were as broad as lotus petals;
their lips, resembling the pomegranate flower, possessed the fragrance of blue lotuses.
With shanks resembling plantain stalks, with arms as tender as lotus fibers, with feet shaped like the shoots of the *aśoka* tree, and with soles comparable to lotus petals. (10.556)
With claws resembling *ketakī* flowers and teeth brilliant as pearls,
she was naturally rich in exquisite fragrance, as if distilling nectar.
She is always adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; with clusters of crest-jewels, girdles, and upper-arm bands, as well as with intensely red flowers.
The noble women were enriched by their retinues in the form of thousands of female attendants. *Mṛgāmoda* refers to musk;

*śravaṇādhāra* refers to the earlobe. The sprouts of the *aśoka* tree serve as a comparison for redness, while lotus petals serve as a comparison for delicacy. The *ketakī* flowers possess reddish streaks.
And they are transparent. || 558 ||
Furthermore:
With breasts that are elevated, shaped like water-jars, well-rounded, with full sides, and resting upon thick necks; (10.559)
Bowed under the weight of their heavy hips, adorned with strings of pearls,
they possessed the grace of intoxicated elephants while rivaling the gait of royal swans.
Their gentle strides were faltering and made resonant by the tinkling of their anklets;
their eyes were tremulous with playful arches of the brows, enriched by the charms of laughter and dance.
As if gladdening the limbs of the Rudras dwelling there,
with breasts that take refuge upon full throats— those breasts which have silver as their bright [ornament]— there was a delicate dance (*lāsya*) and graceful gestures (*vilāsa*).
The compound is a descriptive determinative (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) consisting of [the words] "rich in laughter and so forth" and "with eyes flickering due to the knitting of eyebrows."
Moreover:
"Possessed by the demon of desire, reeling and overwhelmed by intoxication," (10.562)

Gladdening the lords of the Gaṇas by the mere act of embracing them, [they cause] attachment—that is, intense clinging—to sensual desire and sexual enjoyment; this very attachment is to be understood as a "graha" (seizing spirit) that has become manifest.
These women, endowed with such beauty and charm—
even though such women are [as described]—
nevertheless...
...afflicted by fear of their own husbands. || 10-563 ||
The meaning is that they are not independent. || 563 ||
And therefore— women with eyes like those of startled deer, having come into the embrace of their husbands,
and such as these—
And having embraced him with all their limbs, they drank from his face with their mouths. || 10-564 ||
In the abode of Rudra, the daughters of Rudra sport together with the Rudras.
Moreover, in this place—the Rudras themselves possess such forms as these, being preeminent through the power of knowledge and yoga. (10.565)
The meaning is that even those whose aim is desire do not fall away from the yoga of knowledge. || 565 ||
And these [beings]—with crowns and variegated earrings blazing with great jewels; with armlets, bracelets, girdles, and ornaments of flowers and garments. (10.566)
Being distinguished by necklaces of pearl strings and upper garments with Brahma-threads.
They have massive bodies, broad chests, three eyes, and hold tridents in their hands. || 10-567 ||
Resembling ten thousand moons, grey with the powder of camphor,
all were praised by gods and siddhas, exceedingly gracious, and bestowers of boons.
Having obtained boons by force, they were satisfied; they possessed ten arms and the moon as their crest-jewel.
And for them—therein there is neither death, nor old age, nor sorrow born of separation. (10.569)
And for this reason, these [beings]— playing together with maidens...—
do not transmigrate again once the karma that grants those enjoyments is exhausted; thus he says:
...who have abandoned the fear of saṃsāra;
these alone—upon the exhaustion of their office—are Rudras, surrounded by the daughters of Rudra. (10.570)
By the will of Śrīkaṇṭha, all go to Śiva upon the dissolution of their bodies;
having gone there, they are not born again even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (10.571)
"Desire" here means the wish to favor; the meaning is that without that [desire], they would not be emitted upward at all. || 571 ||
Thus,
in this manner— by those who travel in such countless celestial chariots,
mounted upon great bulls and elephants, and possessing excellent vehicles such as lions and horses. || 10-572 ||
It was surrounded by hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Rudras;
in its center was the Sarvatobhadra [palace], with lion-gates and excellent archways.
It was surrounded by rampart walls resembling clear pearls,
and it was attended by the hosts of gatekeepers Nandīśvara and Mahākāla.
Resounding with networks of small bells, crowded with banners and flags,
and adorned with clusters of canopies and parasols from which pearl necklaces hung down.
Abundantly adorned with bells and fly-whisks, and further beautified by mirrors,
as well as by water-pots placed at the doors and joined with jeweled sprouts.
The courtyard of the world was adorned with auspicious svastikas and leafy creepers, fashioned by experts in the science of painting and made radiant with powdered gems. (10.577)
It was strewn with hundreds of lion-thrones, adorned with jeweled altars,
and featured gate-towers, watchtowers, chariot-paths, streets, and circular corridors.
It is exceedingly beautiful, adorned with various and rich ornaments of all kinds of jewels, secured with doorways,
and featuring well-fashioned balconies, windows, and cornices with the luster of crystal.
With pillars joined by staircases, radiant with the luster of diamonds and lapis lazuli, and adorned with turrets shaped like the full moon; || 10.580 ||
With thousands of grounds radiant with the luster of pearls, and with theaters for dramatic performance, richly adorned and filled with the sounds of dance and song. || 10.581 ||
With pavilions richly adorned with various jewels and filled with circular assembly halls,
[the place was] occupied by throngs of Rudras and multitudes of Rudra-maidens.
It was adorned with delightful artificial elephants and beautifully decorated with moon-chambers;
it was perfumed with incense sticks and sprinkled with saffron water.
It was covered with variegated cloths and strewn with heaps of flowers,
resounding with the sound of musical instruments, the roar of victory, and the blaring of trumpets.
With flutes, lutes, and clay drums; with gomukhas and mouth-organs;
with small drums, cymbals, and the sound of conchs and kettledrums. || 10.585 ||
With the sound of kettledrums, the beating of hand-drums, the great noise of the snapping of fingers, and the resounding lion’s roars; || 10.586 ||
With the shouting of the hosts of attendants, with sounds like the thundering of clouds, with the hymns of the bards, and with the resonance of the Sāmaveda; || 10.587 ||

With the sounds of *huḍuṅkāra* and boisterous laughter joined by the rhythmic clanging of songs, with the sound of the bull’s joyful bellowing, and with the noise of elephants and horses; || 10.588 ||

The great city resounds as if with the sound of waist-bands and anklets; this is a compound meaning "the hosts of gatekeepers, headed by Nandīśvara and Mahākāla. The phrase beginning with "resounding with networks of small bells" is an adjective qualifying the cluster of canopies and umbrellas.

The inversion of the prior compound in *muktāhārapralambitaiḥ* [is for metrical reasons]. It was wonderful because of the *svastika* designs there in Rudra’s abode, which were fashioned with powdered gems by craftsmen skilled in the various arts (*citraśāstra*) and adorned with leafy creepers (*patravallī*), richly decorated with patterns of foliage.

"Bhuvanājiram" and "bhuvanāṅganam" should be understood as referring to the courtyard of the world. It was adorned with altars (*vedikābhiḥ*), which are square platforms, and with jewels set within the walls. "Gopurāṇi" refers to the main gateways;
"aṭṭālāḥ" refers to the battlements of the city walls; "rathakāḥ" refers to specific types of chariot-like structures; and "vīthyaḥ" refers to the streets.
The grounds for the movement of celestial chariots (*vimāna*); with rotating pipes that serve as conduits for the flow of water;

and because they are variegated with all kinds of jewels, they are splendid, opulent, and beautiful, with [ornaments] placed at the ends of the doorways. *Nirgama* refers to the paths or exits. *Gavākṣa* refers to the lattice-work locations for looking out. *Viṭaṅka* refers to the decorative niches or cornices.
It was adorned with pillar-capitals; it possessed egg-shaped temples (*aṇḍas*) of circular form;
it was enriched by the wonderful artistry of inlaid jewels; and likewise, it was joined with pavilions filled with circular mandalas fashioned from powdered gems in the assembly halls.
*Tūrya* is a double-sectioned wind instrument made of copper or other metals; *kāhalās*, however, consist of three sections.

*Gomukha* is a *taṭṭarī*. A *paṇava* is a small drum. A *ḍhakkā* resounds with the jangling of internal strings and rings. *Tālavādya* refers to the sound of clapping; *dundubhi* is the sound of bronze cymbals; and *phanatkāriṇī* is a whistling sound.

*Ḍhakkā* is a kettledrum. *Garjana* is a roar produced by the strength of all one's vital breaths. *Huḍuṅkāra* is an internal sound uttered through the intensity of devotion. *Nandita* is the sound arising from the joy born of the bull’s identification with being the vehicle of the Supreme Lord; [the term refers to the drum] by means of that sound.
The sound of waist-bands and anklets belongs to the dancing daughters of Rudra; thus, by such sounds as these, it is known that the city itself resounds directly.
Thus, in this manner—the glorious temple of Śaṅkara, which bestows all prosperity. (10.589)
This means "of those residing therein. || 589 ||
There, the Blessed Lord Rudra, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra,
is constantly bathed by the Gaṅgā and is clothed in divine garments.
His limbs were anointed with the fragrance of the earth, he was beautifully honored by Śrī with flowers,
and he was praised by Sarasvatī and the foremost of the seven musical notes.

The earth has fragrance as its quality; Śrī is dependent upon flowers. And likewise, the deities of the Gaṅgā and others, having descended by their own power (prākāmya) from the worlds to be described above this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), perform their appropriate bathing and other rites, constituting the inner retinue. || 591 ||
Moreover, for this god—
his full moon and parasol are established of their own accord.
But in that case—
The Gaṅgā, however, is superior to Uttarikā;
the Gaṅgā stands having resorted to sovereignty through her power of irresistible will.
And furthermore, for him—.........and all the Ādityas are his lamps. || 10-592 ||
Likewise—
his seat is covered by Puṣpadanta, Gaṇeśa, and others;
and upon that seat—
Kapila, Karkaṭa, Vimarda, and likewise Kaṅkaṭa. || 10-593 ||
Vikrama, Dṛḍha, Niṣkampa, and likewise Niṣkala—these eight are declared to be the tawny ones (Haras), three-eyed and of immense prowess. (10.594)

Having the forms of lions, possessing great splendor, and radiant with formidable manes— with such mantras, which bear the form of Śakti and are endowed with the sovereignty of yoga— [they were filled]. 595.
The seat was disclosed by those of great enthusiasm and overwhelming power, considering that even for this Blessed One who dwells within the cosmic egg, there is supreme majesty;
thus [it is said]: "O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the mantras consisting of Śiva and Śakti are to be deposited. (2.63)
Thus, as in the previously mentioned Bhairava-seat, the lions are indeed the ultimate reality of Śiva and Śakti.
There, Rudra is seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana), adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Complete with all the primary marks, adorned with all ornaments,
the three-eyed, ten-armed deity is decorated with a crown of matted hair.
With a full chest and thighs, broad shoulders and mighty arms,
he sat in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), grey with the powder of camphor.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, and likewise bearing all weapons;

"bhadram" means praiseworthy. The two primary hands are those granting boons and fearlessness. All weapons refer to those previously mentioned, such as the sword (khaḍga), shield (kheṭaka), and so forth.
Furthermore:
"With hands and feet marked by lotuses and exceedingly tender. (10.599)
With fingers adorned by the luster of moon-like nails, with well-knit knees and ankles, and with feet that were perfectly elevated; || 10.600 ||

By means of being worshipped by the Gaṇas and Rudras, and being saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, as well as by such divine characteristics as having hands and feet marked with the hundred-petaled lotus and so forth, His possession of divine marks is declared. The plural "with feet" (*pādaiḥ*) is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), or it may be due to the power of creative will (*prākāmyataḥ*), as in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3.3): "(He is) the one whose feet are everywhere."
Even though he possesses many feet by virtue of his stability, these third-case endings are used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Moreover:
"On all sides, Rudra’s wives raised yak-tail whisks as fans. (10.601)
He is eternally fanned by glory, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
his soul is thoroughly satiated with the nectar of knowledge, and he is the bestower of the sovereignty of yoga.
Meditated upon constantly by yogis with serene faces and eyes, he appears as if smiling through the rays of his stainless wisdom. (10.603)
Having destroyed the darkness of ignorance, he shall reveal his supreme form;
surrounded by Rudra and the hosts of Mothers, he is the bestower of all happiness.
When meditated upon, it shines as if laughing with rays of knowledge through its entry into the supreme nature;
therefore, having destroyed ignorance, it reveals the supreme nature itself. || 604 ||
Moreover:
Seated upon his lap was the goddess, possessing the beautiful luster of gold;
she was worshipped by hosts of yoginīs, by practitioners, and by gods and kinnaras. (10.605)
Complete with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she eternally bestows the perfection of yoga and grants both liberation and worldly prosperity.
Umā, however, with her beautiful eyes, is eternally facing the Lord.

He states that these two— the Power of Supreme Penetration (parāveśa-śakti) and its Possessor (tadvat)— having assumed this other form, perform the creation and dissolution within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
And Śakti exists in another form, and likewise, the possessor of Śakti is Hara.
In the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), Brahmā and Śiva perform creation and destruction by the will of Śiva.

Here, the two *ca*s indicate equal coordination (*tulyayoga*). Likewise, the second *ca* functions as an alternative form (*apararūpeṇa*). Furthermore, the *ca* conjoins maintenance, dissolution, and grace. In this context, Śiva is the Supreme.
Furthermore, this is as follows:
those who are devoid of initiation and knowledge, yet are intent upon the worship of the Liṅga. || 10-608 ||
They proceed to the abode of Hara, which brings all sovereignty and happiness;
the meaning is that by this sequence as well, he possesses the quality of being a bestower of grace.
They are liberated from old age and death, and are entirely free from disease and sorrow.
And they, O Goddess, do not go back down again into the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra; rather—
Then, beheld by Śrīkaṇṭha, they proceed upward to Śiva.

"Tataḥ" means from the abode of Hara. "Properly beheld" means graced by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). This is the majesty of this city, because it is presided over by the Blessed Lord: those who have attained it do not go downwards, but rather are properly beheld by Śrīkaṇṭhanātha with the gaze of grace.
They are liberated; otherwise, however, they are projected for the sake of experience, proceeding higher and higher in succession. || 610 ||
Thus, O Umā, the world of Rudra has been fully described; now hear of what lies above it,
where each successive world is situated in a state of progressive increase.
Increase occurs through both measure and power; this will be explained later. || 611 ||
But now—
below even the Brahmāṇḍa and above the world of Rudra,
the city of Daṇḍapāṇi is to be known, surrounded by various hosts of Rudras. (10.612)
But the Blessed Lord Daṇḍapāṇi, endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty, held the staff in the very palm of his hand by the will of Śiva. (10.613)
Lord Rudra himself remains in this very body. || 613 ||

And he reveals the path to liberation, which is very difficult to master, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, having been propitiated according to the prescribed rites through meditation by the will of Śiva. (10.614)

Having been propitiated through the prescribed method of meditation, worship, recitation, and so forth, he reveals— that is, renders free from obstruction— the path to liberation within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is extremely difficult to pierce and can only be penetrated by yogis with great effort, employing the technique of splitting the shell of the cosmic egg.

He makes it straight, but does not obstruct it. Furthermore, the Lord Rudra, whose self is the expansion of the consciousness of another, by means of the application of the staff of vital breath (prāṇadaṇḍa) made perfectly clear through his own power,
[acts] upon that which is called the "heart-knot" (hṛdgranthi)— the nature of which is the non-recognition of one's own Self residing in the region of the heart within the body.

In the Brahmāṇḍa [Tantra], he prepares the path to liberation by means of the pacification of the knots described in the sacred tradition, such as: "The knot which resides in the heart is the regulator of above and below. Thus, he reaches the plane of Śakti situated on the central path.

The inner meaning is that [the verse] clarifies the cause for attaining the state of Śiva, according to the established tradition stated in the *Vijñānabhairava* (20): "The Śaivī [power] is said here to be the mouth.
It is not, however, to be explained as the pervasion of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) ending at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*). For, in this way...
The pervasion of the coverings such as water and the rest does not depend upon the body; rather,
Nāda, whose support is the nāḍī, having pierced through this entire universe and emerged by means of the downward power (adhaḥśakti), reaches as far as Brahmā above.
"The unmanifest, imperishable sound, dissolved in the *brahmabila* through the channel (*nāḍī*), resounds within all beings, presided over by the power of Śiva. (10.234–36).
Such future passages would otherwise be rendered objectless due to the cessation of the pervasion of duality. As for that which—
"In the path of deep sleep, having set [the sun] and abandoned the sphere of the cosmic egg" (SpK 2.8)—
thus it was stated by the venerable Guru in the *Śrīspanda*.
That [path] is characterized by the five Brahmās who will be described as presiding over the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*).

The path extends as far as the Egg of Śakti; with this intention it is established that even by way of error, the pervasion of the Brahmāṇḍa should not be explained as ending at the Muṇḍa. Thus, as it has been explained, all is auspicious. (614) In this way, within the world of Rudra at the end of the Daṇḍa, he remains established in two forms because of his sovereignty over the universe.
Among the Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśas), he who is Paśupati is the presiding deity over Rudra;
whereas the other seven Lords of the Embodiments, beginning with Śarva, are the sovereigns over the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr and ending with Satya— thus he instructs.
Those Rudras who are the sovereign lords in the seven worlds...
I shall describe them in brief. He said to them:
Śarva, Rudra, as well as Bhīma, Bhava, and likewise Ugra.
Mahādeva, as well as Īśāna and these lords of the worlds of Rudra, are the presiding deities of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, respectively. With this very intention—[it is said]:
"Within Nivṛtti is the Earth, extending for a hundred crores [of yojanas]."

And within that [egg], there are one hundred and eight worlds. In this commentary, it is stated that in the lower part of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) there are three: Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Hāṭaka; Śarva is in the *bhūrloka*; and Brahmā is at the end of the *satyaloka*.

It has been explained that there are seven worlds within, ending with Viṣṇu and Rudra in their own respective realms, one hundred Rudras outside, and above them, Vīrabhadra, the presiding lord of all.

If these Rudras are to be purified individually within the initiation of the worlds from the earthly realm up to Satyaloka, then what is their status above that? To this he says: "Brahmā resides in the world of Brahmā, and Viṣṇu indeed in the city of Viṣṇu. (616)
The world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), which was previously described as the "seat of Brahmā" (brahmāsana).
Likewise, regarding this:

Rudra, abiding in the world of Rudra, is remembered as the leader of all—meaning the leader of the triad beginning with Kālāgni, the group of seven beginning with Śarva, and of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. This...
Because he is the sovereign lord of the universe, he is designated by the name Paśupati among the lords of the [eight] forms (*mūrtīśvara*). And thus it is said:
"One should purify, in due order and succession, Ananta, Kālāgni, the hells, and then the netherworlds (*pātāla*) above them. (10.347)
Having purified according to the sequence thus stated, one should purify the seven worlds from Bhūr to Satya in order; then, having purified Śarva and the others up to Īśa,
one should purify Brahmā and Viṣṇu for the purification of the worlds of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

In this *Bhuvanadīkṣā*, the division of the purification of the worlds (*bhuvaneśa-śuddhi-vibhāga*) remains established exactly as it is set forth in the text. Therefore, that which Śrī Bhullaka [states]— that from the world of Ananta onwards,
up to the end of all the islands, oceans, earths, and worlds, [the presiding deity is] Śarva in the worlds of Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahas— [is thus accounted for].

He has stated according to his own imagination that Rudra, Bhīma, and Bhava [are to be purified] in the Janas, Tapas, and Satya worlds respectively; that Ugra is in the Viṣṇu world; and that Mahādeva is the sovereign lord (adhipa) in the Rudra world as Īśāna—this must certainly be disregarded.
To summarize this, he says: "From Kālāgni up to Daṇḍapāṇi, there are ninety-eight crores. (10.617)
O lady of excellent hips, this path of yojanas has been described;
O fair-faced one, the Kaṭāha is both below and above the Brahmāṇḍa.
It stands in a solid form with a measurement of ten million *yojanas*;
O fair-faced one, it extends fifty million [yojanas] upward from the surface of the earth.
And fifty [yojanas] should be known below on all sides;
thus, one hundred crores should be known as the reality of the earth element (pārthiva-tattva). || 10-620 ||

Just as it was stated that from the bottom of the vessel (the earth's core) to the surface of the earth is fifty [lakṣas], so too from the surface of the earth to the Pole Star (Dhruva) is fifteen lakṣas;
above that is Maharloka, consisting of eighty-five lakṣas and two koṭis;
Janoloka is eight koṭis; and Tapoloka...

Twelve crores [make up] Satyaloka; Brahmabhuvana is one crore; Viṣṇuloka is two crores; Rudraloka is seven crores; and the upper shell (ūrdhvakaṭāha) is one crore—thus, including the upper regions, the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) consists of fifty crores. Within that, there is a gross expansion, but not...

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reality extends only this far; for even up to the point of the *bindu* in the initiation of extraction (*uddhātadīkṣā*), its pervasion has been shown by means of subtle vision. It is called "that which is to be known" (*jñeya*) because it is that which must be understood by the teacher, the practitioner, and others during the performance of initiation, the wearing of the thread, and so forth.
The meaning is "by the Blessed One. || 620 ||
This very [disc], extending as far as the Śatarudra [mantra], should be known to be golden and circular;
its essence is superior even to that of the diamond (vajra), and it is impenetrable even by the gods.
That which has an essence superior to the essence of a diamond.
And he says that this must be pierced by the application of the mantra, nāda, and weapon for the one to be initiated:
"O fair-faced one, one should pierce it by the application of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*;
thus, indeed, by the penetration of the expansion of the splendor of the mantra."

If the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which extends from the tip of the big toe up to the heart, were to split apart, then it is said by the Blessed One that even that which is external to it would likewise be shattered in its wake.
Regarding what was stated, "one should recite the Śatarudra," he speaks to explain that in detail:
"O slender-waisted one, I shall hereafter describe the Śatarudras in brief. (10.622)
Regarding this, he says that they are called the "Hundred Rudras" because:
"Ten by ten, in due order, throughout the ten directions on all sides,
according to the sequence beginning with the East..."
The ellipsis is that because they are situated there, these are called the "Hundred Rudras."
And I shall describe them to you in due order. || 10-623 ||
Kapālīśa, Aja, Bradhna, Vajradeha, Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa. || 10-624 ||
And these great gods, having surpassed the power of Indra and being endowed with sovereign might, roam about, highly honored by Indra. (10.625)

"Having stepped upon" means having presided over; the reason for this is that they have been made to grasp such a field of authority—one in which the powers of vision and action are unfolded—having been presided over by the power of the Lord Parabhairava, whose nature is autonomy; thus they move about.
Performing creation and other acts, they sport; for this very reason, they are worshipped by Indra with excellent and intense devotion. The same should be applied to what follows as well. || 625 ||
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka. || 10-626 ||
Having overcome the power of Agni,
those great gods, endowed with sovereign power and highly honored by the King of Fire, wander about.
Agnirāja is the lord of the southeastern direction (āgneyī); the same applies to the others.
He is Yāmya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and he who is designated as the Creator; he is the uniter and the disuniter, as well as Dharma and the Lord of Dharma.
Having overcome the power of Yama, those great gods, endowed with sovereign might and highly honored by King Yama, wander about.
The slayer Nairṛta, the son of the Wind, is cruel-eyed and terrifying;
he has hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored, reddish fangs.
Having overcome the host of Nairṛta,
those great gods, endowed with sovereign power and highly honored by the lord of the Nairṛtas, roam about.
Bala, Atibala, Pāśahasta, Mahābala, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka. (10.632)
Meghanādī and Sunādī have been briefly described;
endowed with sovereign power, they overcome the strength of Varuṇa.
The great gods, highly honored by Varuṇa and Indra, roam about;
[the wind] is swift, light, possessing the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, and terrifying.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana—
having overcome the power of Vāyu, they are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods wander about, well-honored by the king of the winds;
he is the lord of treasures, handsome, fortunate, gentle of body, and wears matted locks.
Lakṣmī, Ratnadhara, Kāmī, Prasāda, and Prabhāsaka, having seized the power of Soma, were endowed with sovereign might. || 10-637 ||
The great gods, highly honored by Soma as their king, wander about;
then there is the omniscient Lord of Knowledge, whose vision is wisdom and who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Śarva is the lord of the gods, the eldest, the protector of beings, and one who delights in offerings;
the gods, honored by the immortals, act with the approval of Īśāna.
The great gods, presided over by the power of Īśa, move about:
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and the one named Māruta. (10.640)
Grasana, Ḍambareśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭraka,
endowed with the power of the Lord, having overcome the strength of Viṣṇu— || 10-641 ||
The great gods wander about, well-worshipped by Ananta;

they whose lord is Īśāna, the guardian of the quarter, who is approved and esteemed as the guardian of the quarters by all the gods because he bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). [This applies] to Viṣṇu, who is situated in the downward direction; [and] by Ananta.
By the presiding deity of the entire lower direction.
In the upward direction, however, are Śambhu, Vīrabhadra, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Tridaśeśvara. || 10-642 ||
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nala, and Trilocana, endowed with sovereign power, having overpowered the strength of Brahmā, were desirous of seizing [it]. || 10-643 ||
The great gods, well-honored by Brahmā himself, move about;
from among all of these, the retinue of each one is said to be a thousand. (10.644)
In the extensive tantras. || 644 ||
And these,
known as the hundred Rudras, remain pervading the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*);
"pervading" means surrounding it.
And these—innumerable thousands—are those who reside in the directions beginning with the zenith. || 10-645 ||
The gods are self-willed and all-pervading even throughout the kalpas and manvantaras;

they are impossible to number even by the count of thousands. Because they are endowed with the aforementioned power of lordship, they are self-willed—meaning independent in bestowing grace and other such acts—and all-pervading despite possessing fixed bodies.
And the pervasive deities shine even at the beginning of the eons.
And he says that these are situated within the arrangement of the ten directions, one for each direction:
"The Rudras of the ten directions, beginning with the East, are established ten by ten. (10.646)
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the individual lord of each group of ten:
situated to the east of the cosmic egg is the one known by the name Śveta.
Endowed with hundreds of Rudras, he possessed great heroism and prowess,
like the sun with its blazing and most intense rays.
In the southeast is the one resembling fire, renowned by the name Vaidyuta;
he too is surrounded by hundreds of Rudras with the brilliance of lightning.
To the south of the Egg is Mahākāla, resembling the fire at the end of an eon;
O Goddess, he stands there surrounded by the hundred Rudras of immeasurable prowess.
In the southwest stands the one named Vikaṭa, surrounded by a hundred followers;
possessed of great splendor, he is like a second sun.
"By a hundred" refers to the primary [number]; likewise elsewhere. || 651 ||
In the western part of the Egg, he who is known as Rudra Mahāvīrya,
possessed of immeasurable prowess, dwells surrounded by the hundred Rudras.
In the northwestern direction of the cosmic egg, the illustrious and mighty Vāyuvega stands here, surrounded by a hundred [attendants]. || 10.653 ||
Surrounded by a retinue of one hundred named Subhadra,
the mighty one, endowed with great heroism and strength, dwells here.
Surrounded by rays of light, the valiant one remains there;
the Rudra named Vidyādhara is indeed established in the northeast.
Surrounded by the hundred Rudras, like the moon-king encircled by stars,
he stands there endowed with great heroism and strength, possessing infinite prowess.
He was served by rays of light and surrounded by them. || 656 ||
Below, another Kālāgnirudra stands here as the second;
he is surrounded by hundreds of Rudras stationed here, O fair-faced one. (10.657)
The second [Kālāgni] is other than the Kālāgni located within the semi-vowels (antastha). || 657 ||
Surrounded by hundreds [of attendants], Rudra was like the sun with its rays;
he was celebrated above all by the name "Rudra."
Thus,
Vīrabhadra, surrounded by the Rudras, was stationed above the Egg.

The eleventh [Vīrabhadra] is surrounded by those of great body born from the wrath of Rudra—namely, these [deities] beginning with Śveta who preside over the hundred Rudras situated in the directions starting from the east.
Thus, Vīrabhadra in the center is the eleventh. And by these [deities], there is the driving away of all diseases.
[They were] produced from the wrath of the Blessed Lord Rudra, who causes terror to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

The reading *krodhasamudbhavaḥ* (produced from wrath) refers specifically to Vīrabhadra; for it is precisely because these [beings], Śveta and the others, constitute the retinue of Vīrabhadra that it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
Ananta is the first among them, and Kapālīśa is another;
likewise Agnirudra, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala.
"Śīghra, Nidhīśvara, and another, Sarvavidyādhipa; and Śambhu... (Mānavadharma-vidhi 5.13–14).
Thus, having mentioned one Rudra from among the ten Rudras situated in each direction, [he mentions] Vīrabhadra and—
The eleventh is said to be Vidhūmajvalanaprabha; however, Śveta and the others are not counted as primary because they constitute his retinue.
He summarizes: "In this way, those great-souled ones here [protect] each one with a hundred. (10.659)
O Goddess of good vows, these ten are surrounded by the hundred Rudras;
each is further encircled by a retinue of one hundred, and surrounded by the ten inner [deities] beginning with Kapālīśa. Thus, when this [wheel] is expanded—

In the initiation pertaining to the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), all these lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) contained within the cosmic egg of the earth are to be purified as previously described; however, one should not misinterpret this on the basis of the intention that "only the one hundred and eight [worlds] mentioned in the brief initiation" are to be purified, for there is a specific injunction stated for each individual step.

This is because [the system] is more authoritative due to the excellence of its scriptural evidence (*śruti*). As for what was postulated by Śrī Bhūllaka—that there are ninety-seven [continents] along with the infinite Śrī... and so forth, including the islands (*dvīpa*) and others, plus eleven outside—that is simply incorrect.
Regarding these ten, beginning with Śveta, who are surrounded by the hundred Rudras—though it was said that each is surrounded by a hundred—that was intended as a summary; for in detail:
"The retinue of these great-souled ones is beyond counting. (10.660)
And therefore, all these—
having surrounded the cosmic egg, they remain there just as honey-bees surround the honey,
or as a kadamba flower is encircled by its filaments. (10.661)
For thus was the egg surrounded by Rudras of immeasurable prowess;
"madhuvratāḥ" means honey-bees.
Likewise—[he saw] houses adorned with various jewels, featuring archways and watchtowers. || 10-662 ||
It was adorned on all sides with variegated objects made of Jāmbūnada gold,
crowded with celestial women, and endowed with everything that fulfills every desire.
This universe has been described as being cast down by the snare of bonds, submerged in the great ocean of birth, disease, old age, and death. (10.664)
Covered by the impurity of the three qualities (guṇas), crowded with various castes, overcome by the ignorance of the bound soul (paśu), and agitated by the three states of existence. || 10-665 ||

The "houses" are the worlds (*bhuvana*). They are said to be "descended," "covered" by the net of bonds such as those of *āṇava* and so forth, and "overflowing with birth" and so on, with reference to the people who inhabit them. The "three qualities" (*guṇatraya*) are *sattva* and the others; that itself is the impurity (*mala*). The "classes" (*jāti*) are the fourteenfold creation of beings (*bhūtasarga*). By the knowledge of the bound soul (*paśu*).
"Completely pervaded on all sides by the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, and so forth" means that it is abundant with the confidence derived from the knowledge of those [scriptures].
"The three states of existence" refers to the forms of gods, humans, and animals. || 665 ||
And in this regard:
"The destinies of all disputants are indeed impermanent;
the destinies are the occurrences among gods, humans, and animals."
"In this way, those who have resorted to the dharma of the three Vedas and desire objects of desire obtain the state of going and returning. (Bhagavad Gītā).

According to this principle, they are impermanent and limited in duration. "Of the disputants" refers to those adhering to the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Saugata (Buddhist), Ārhata (Jaina), and so forth.
For these [beings], being deluded, do not know the distinction between the higher and the lower at all. (10.666)

Because they have been deluded by *māyā*, they do not know that the state characterized by duality is the lower, while non-duality (*advaita*) is the higher; therefore, within the very state of duality, they consider the states of gods, humans, and animals as attainable through the distinction between the higher and the lower. || 666 ||
And therefore:
"In the past, the golden egg was created, having the form of the world and the nature of destruction, for the welfare of the group of selves permeated by the Māyā of the Lord. (10.667)

Although everything up to the level of *samanā* is subject to destruction, nevertheless, what has been described as its nature of destruction is intended to demonstrate its insignificance due to its extremely limited duration. "Of the one who is entered" means of the one who has been embraced [by that state]. "For the sake of prosperity" means for the purpose of accomplishing the experience of karma. || 667 ||
This has been concluded.
Now, hereafter, the principles (tattvas) beginning with water and ending with Śiva are stated; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In that regard, by means of the calculation of pride, these—
arranged in an ascending sequence— are established as tenfold.

The water-element is ten times the size of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which extends for a hundred crores [of yojanas]. From that, fire is ten times larger; from that, air; from that, space; and even beyond that is the Guṇa, which contains within itself the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the sense organs. || 668 ||
From the *ahaṅkāra* of such measured dimensions...
above that, however, the intellect (*buddhi*) is situated in a hundredfold manner.
Beyond that,
O lady of excellent complexion, the Pradhāna should be known as extending upwards a thousandfold.
The meaning is that the magnitude of the principle of *prakṛti* is together with the principle of the *guṇas*. || 669 ||
Above that—
ten thousand *pauruṣa*s...
even beyond that—
...niyati is said to consist of one hundred thousand [units].
Above that, O virtuous lady, it extends for ten hundred thousand units up to kalā. (10.670)
Thus, even from such a measurement of the *kalā*-tattva,
Māyā is ten millionfold;
and that—
...pervading and abiding in all that is moving and unmoving.
"All" refers to everything from the *kalā* principle down to the earth (*kṣiti*). This is intended as an illustration for all the *tattvas*;
therefore, the *tattvas* beginning with earth are pervaded by the subsequent *tattvas* such as water and so forth. And thus:

That which is said to be ten times the extent of the Brahmāṇḍa, which measures one hundred koṭis, includes everything contained within it along with the Brahmāṇḍa itself. By that calculation, there are one hundred koṭis for the Brahmāṇḍa in the middle,
four [koṭis] for the layer of water below, and all together one hundred koṭis for the watery covering.

The measure of the internal Brahmāṇḍas, together with the already-explained [external] Brahmāṇḍa, is indeed one hundred crores on all sides; and according to the established rule that the water-enclosure within the surrounding Brahmāṇḍas measures ten thousand crores,
the principles beginning with fire (tejas) are also measured by the dimensions of the internal water-principle and so forth.
Together with each subsequent one, they should be explained as being multiplied tenfold and so forth.
Thus, from such a measure of Māyā,
Vidyā is ten times ten millionfold (daśakoṭiguṇā). According to the perspective already explained, that [Vidyā] also has a measure of nine upper and lower units (koṭi), starting from the center.
From a measure of parts multiplied by ten million.
...pervading the māyā, she remains established. || 10-671 ||
Then, even beyond that— this [universe] is pervaded by Īśvara with a power a hundred times ten millionfold;
"by Īśvara" means by the principle of Īśvara (Īśvara-tattva).
Beyond that as well, it remains pervading [the universe]:
the Sādākhya [level] consists of a thousand million, and above that are Bindu and Nāda.

The reality known as Sādākhya, which measures one thousand million [yojanas], is itself "above"; thus, in that very path, in its upper portion, it exists as the supreme Sādākhya through the pervasion of Parā, abiding in the form of the coverings consisting of Bindu and Nāda, which will be described hereafter.

Form (*rūpa*) [is indicated] by the *bindu* in the covering of the half-moon and the *nirodhikā*; and by the *nāda*, the covering of the end of sound (*nādānta*) is implied. This will become clear further on. || 672 ||
Even further above this, a multitude of *yojanas* is pervaded and occupied by Śakti. "A multitude" refers to hundreds of thousands of crores; "Śakti" refers to the Śakti-tattva.
And right here, in the upper portion related to Śakti—O Goddess, Vyāpinī is established, pervading the entire path. (10.673)

Śakti alone, through her supreme pervasion, is of the nature of the Paraśiva-tattva and exists in the form of Vyāpinī; she stands pervading the entire upper path (ūrdhvādhvan), which consists of the levels from Śakti and Sadāśiva downwards, including the level of Samanā. The essential nature of all these tattvas has already been explained previously.
Up to the level of Māyā, there exists the abiding of various individual souls (kṣetrajñas) appropriate for their respective levels;

however, from Vidyā up to Vyāpinī, there is the abiding of Rudras who are differentiated by the rotation of Mantras, Mantreśvaras, Mantramaheśvaras, and so forth— this being said with reference to those respective levels.
In the same way, the enjoyment of the worlds and so forth is indeed appropriate; the Blessed One will clarify this point further ahead.
Having thus described the measurement of the path ending with the principle of Apara-Śiva, he states that there is no measurement for the supreme Śiva-principle which pervades the universe:
"Therefore, O fair-faced one, the Śiva-principle is to be known as immeasurable."

Beyond that path, from Vyāpinī up to Samanā, there is the reality which is the form of the supreme good (*śreyas*), the ultimate, consisting of a mass of autonomous light and bliss, whose nature is Paramaśiva;
that is immeasurable and has the singular form of the supreme subject— thus it is to be known and ascertained, and not otherwise.
The other [levels] should be understood as being progressively greater in their degree of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the preceding principles (*tattva*).

By stating this, he indicates the following: while making the entire universe up to the level of *Samanā* an object of knowledge (*prameya*) through the aforementioned process, one remains within the nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), which is a dense mass of self-luminous consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*).
One should enter into the state of Paramaśiva.
Having thus spoken by way of digression, he says in order to reveal the arrangement of the worlds (*bhuvana*) within the water-principle (*aptattva*) and the others:
"I shall proclaim the worlds in their proper sequence, beginning with the water-principle. (10.674)

Likewise—its form (*ākāra*) and its power (*vibhava*), as well as the manifold extension of the worlds (*bhuvana*). "Form" refers to the configuration (*saṃsthāna*); "power" refers to sovereign majesty (*vibhūti*). Of the many worlds...
The expansion of the multitude of worlds, which is attached to each respective primary world, is a vastness measured by the number ten.
And he says that this is not seen anywhere other than in the Supreme Lord:
"That which is not seen by the cognitions of bound souls (paśu), whose vision is deluded by false paths. (10.675)
Because they are bound by the fetter of the non-recognition of their own essential nature as the Supreme Bhairava— which consists of autonomous, dense consciousness and bliss—

their power of vision is contracted; thus, by means of those "treatises for the bound" (paśuśāstra) through which the desired objects of knowledge are known by the bound (paśus), that which is not truly known is [perceived] through such a wrong path.

Those whose vision— having attained a semblance of true illumination— is deluded by a presentation of means that effects only the pacification of limited afflictions, rather than bestowing the attainment of the perfect state, and who thus conceive of knowledge as something to be realized [merely through such means].
By such [means]. || 675 ||
To show these animal-like cognitions even in brief,
he says: "That which is not [attained] by the Sāṃkhyas, nor by the Yogins, nor indeed by the Pāñcarātrikas—
[namely,] that saṃsāra arises merely from the non-discrimination of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, while liberation arises from their discrimination— such is their knowledge."

By the Sāṃkhyas; and by those established in the Yoga-śāstras who maintain that liberation consists in the abiding in the true nature of the Seer, which is attained through the immersion in the yoga of one-pointedness of mind;
and [by those who maintain] the Supreme Nature known as Vāsudeva, whose essence is the great majesty consisting of the twenty-six principles.
The connection is that this was not seen by the Pāñcarātrikas, who maintain doctrines such as that the world originates from primordial matter (prakṛti) characterized by transformation.
Likewise—neither by those who propound intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor by those who propound karma (*karman*). (10.676)
Nor [is it established] by those who propound doubt, such as the naked ascetics (Jainas) and others— namely,

the proponents of inherent nature (svabhāvavādins)— who assert that earth and the other elements proceed by their own nature for the sake of effects such as bodies, organs, and worlds, and that there is no Lord (īśvara) acting as an instigator therein.

By those who proclaim that karma alone is the cause of the universe and nothing else—the proponents of karma; by those who assert that either destiny or human effort is the cause of the universe—the proponents of doubt; and [by those who state]:
"The soul, the non-soul, influx, as well as restraint and shedding..."

"Bondage and liberation—these seven are variegated by the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī). According to this formulation of the statement, bondage and liberation are established as beginningless. The soul (jīva) is threefold; the non-soul (ajīva), however, consists of the immobile (sthāvara); matter (pudgala) is the body; and merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) are the substrata such as the world, namely, the space of the universe (lokākāśa).
The sixfold conceptual activity regarding objects such as sound— consisting of the location of liberated persons and non-luminous space— is permeated by pleasure, pain, and so forth;
it is called an *āsrava* because it flows (*āsravati*) and spreads incessantly in every direction (*samantāt*), having the nature of pacifying conceptualization.

Saṃvara is the correct adoption of meditation on the form of the stainless *pudgala* by means of first restraining the activity of the senses through the observances (*yama*) and restraints (*niyama*),
which results in the experience of all forms of suffering, such as the plucking out of hair, leaping onto heated stones, and the bearing of weights.
It is a breach that destroys, like a waterfall, the previously accumulated store of inauspicious karma;

it is a binding that obstructs individuals, causing them to sink like gourds into an iron cage of greed, delusion, grief, and the like; [it is so called] because upon the removal of that obscuration...

For those who maintain the doctrine of the seven categories of existence, such as the living being (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*), liberation (*mokṣa*) consists of the emergence of a person (*pudgala*) whose nature is the consciousness of the face, and the unconditioned space (*alokākāśa*). These are expressed through the following [sevenfold predication]: 1. *syād asti* (it may be that it exists), 2. *syān nāsti* (it may be that it does not exist), 3.

*syād asti ca syān nāsti ca* (it may be that it both exists and does not exist), 4. *syād avaktavyam* (it may be inexpressible), 5. *syād asti ca avaktavyam* (it may be that it exists and is inexpressible). 6.

The connection is as follows: that which has not been seen by the naked ascetics (Jainas) and others—who assert that everything is indeterminate through these very seven modes, namely: "it may be," "it may not be," "it may be inexpressible," and "it may be, it may not be, and it may be inexpressible."
Likewise:
"Nor by those who speak of the elements...
there exists only the fourfold collection of elements—earth, water, fire, and air—as perceived through direct observation."
By the Cārvākas as they speak.
Nor would it even be [perceived] by worldly people. || 10-677 ||
By those who are devoted solely to the arts of livelihood and the science of statecraft.
Nor even by those who contemplate the Self— namely,
the followers of the Vedas who reflect on such [passages] as: "The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be" (Ṛg Veda 10.90.2).
And it is not [established] by those who propound mere reasoning (*tarka*):
"Reasoning (*tarka*) is an inquiry for the sake of knowing the truth regarding an object whose true nature is unknown, based on the logical possibility of the causes" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.40).
by those establishing a systematic arrangement through reasoning in the form of such substitutions.
Nor even by the Vaiśeṣikas, who are devoted to the six categories of existence. || 10-678 ||
By the disciples of Kaṇāda, who assert that reality consists solely of the six categories known as substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence.
Nor [is it established] by those who speak according to logic (nyāya),
the Naiyāyikas, who assert that the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) results from the knowledge of the sixteen categories (padārtha), beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
...by those who assert [the necessity of] reasons and examples.
And it is already established that "that which is observed" [is not required].
For, regarding one who does not know it, the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause are [established] by means of an example.
"...only the reason (*hetu*) is indeed to be stated by the learned," as proclaimed by the Buddhists in [Pramāṇavārttika 3.27].

Nor [is it established] by those who maintain the doctrine of a single birth— those who assert that this present life alone is the only birth, and that there was no other birth in the past nor will there be one in the future— nor by those who maintain the doctrine of oneness. (10.679)

[This is] by those who maintain doctrines such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth, which are distinct from the non-dual doctrine of self-luminous, autonomous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-svatantra-cit*) as propounded in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśa-śāstra*). || 679 ||

The Lord is not well understood by people who speak like rogues—that is, those devoted to scriptures composed by rogues such as the Mlecchas and others—nor by those who claim to know Him. Rather, it is that which was proclaimed by the Lord Śivabhaṭṭāraka himself:
the detailed expansion of the forms and manifestations of the worlds, beginning with the six principles (ṣaṭ-tattva).
It has not been fully understood by anyone, from the Sāṃkhyas and others down to the common rogues;
therefore, the connection [of the verse] is established simply by the statement, "I shall explain that."
And these are not the only disputants; rather, there are three hundred such doctrines held by those who speak in this manner. (10.680)
Furthermore, there are sixty-three others who are disputants with deluded minds;
this [work] is the supreme means for opening the eyes of those blinded by the cataracts of ignorance. (10.681)
It is the supreme means of rescue, like a boat, for those submerged in the mire of saṃsāra;
it is the supreme dispeller of darkness for those blinded by the gloom of great delusion. (10.682)
This divine nectar of knowledge, which has issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, has been obtained by me; it encompasses the expansion of various worlds.
"Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess, to this wonderful and diverse form.
The word *iti* signifies "manner"; thus, it refers to those arguments belonging to the disputants who speak in such a manner. Among these—
By demonstrating the process of making known each respective path (adhvan), beginning with the element of water and ending with Śiva,

this nectar of knowledge bestows immersion into the state of the Great Subject, who is the Supreme Bhairava, consisting of both the object and the subject of cognition. [Those] blinded by the darkness of ignorance— the obscurity that prevents the realization of reality— [are thus illuminated].
Those whose power of vision has not yet opened, and for that very reason whose minds are deluded—for them, [the teaching] is obtained through the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*);

it effects an opening, causing the unfolding of one's own true nature. Likewise, for those submerged in the mire of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it is like a boat, providing a supreme crossing that leads to the further shore. Great delusion (*mahāmoha*)...

Self-identification with objects such as ornaments, clothing, women, and so forth is *tamas*; self-identification with the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) is *moha*. By these two, *mohatāmisra* and *andhatāmisra* are indicated.
Thus, for those blinded by these [afflictions], [the Lord] is "the dispeller of darkness," meaning the destroyer of ignorance.
"Born from the mouth of the Supreme Lord" means that it has come forth from Parabhairava himself through the sequence of Śakti, Sadāśiva, and so on;
"that which was obtained by me," meaning it was acquired by one who, as a resident of Kailāsa, received initiation from the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha. It is marvelous when being contemplated.

By means of entering into the seal of wondrous amazement (*sadvismayamudrā*), it manifests the essential nature of Supreme Bhairava; for this very reason, it is divine (*divya*). It is that in which there is the expansion—the manifold manifestation of power (*vibhava*) and so forth—of the various worlds being expounded. This scripture alone is the expounder of the nectar of knowledge (*jñānāmṛta*).
"The nectar of knowledge. By saying "listen with a one-pointed mind," he indicates its supreme worthiness of being adopted.
The wondrous nature of the worlds is clarified: "The infinite multitude of worlds remains established due to its lack of interruption. (10.684)
The dense covering is like the network of honeycombs;
that is, it is an uninterrupted and continuous enclosure. In a honeycomb—the globular-shaped dwelling of honey-bees—there are networks situated one above the other in a circular form.
"An extensive covering of masses" means they exist in a state of mutual concealment and being concealed by one another through their vastness.
Furthermore:
it resembles the nest of a fish or a conch, and is situated like the seed of a pomegranate. (10.685)
The mass of ancient [seeds] resembles the filaments of the Kadamba flower; "kulāya" means a nest. It is situated with an extremely dense interior, like the seeds of a pomegranate.
Furthermore: "Like a great military camp in a forest, like a grove of trees. (10.686)
O fair-faced one, there are endless worlds, continuous and infinite,
of various forms and wonderful, and composed entirely of all kinds of jewels.
It is a "great army" (mahāsenā) because it is both great and an army; its "encampment" (āvāsaka) is its camp, and it is like that.
"Form" (ākāra) means configuration. "Variegated" (vicitrāṇi) means possessing various kinds of beauty. || 687 ||
Likewise—
circular, long, crescent-shaped, human-shaped, and others shaped like the *nandyāvarta* [swastika]. (10.688)
Forms shaped like mountains and those shaped like herds of elephants;
others shaped like shallow bowls and those shaped like flames. || 10.689 ||
The forms of the great celestial palaces (vimānas) are shaped like tridents,
others have the form of drums, and there are ancient cities with triangular shapes.
O fair-faced one, there are forms of great beings shaped like hundred-peaked mountains, as well as others with a thousand peaks and whirlpools. 10-691.
There were other peaks numbering ten million and countless summits,
some circular, some square, and others triangular.

There are those that are circular and those that are long; thus, while they are circular at the back, they are long at the front, and for this very reason, there is no tautology with the term "spherical" (*vṛtta*). A *nandyāvarta* is a particular type of configuration. Among the worlds shaped like drums (*muraja*), those shaped like triangles—
"Purāṇi gṛhā yeṣām" is a qualifying phrase; by this, [the description] as "triangular" is not redundant.
The Mahāpuruṣa is described as:
"broad-chested, with long arms and thighs."
Such is the form [of the description]. The phrase "having the shape of a person," however, is a general statement. || 692 ||
Furthermore:
divine multicolored banners and divine bells and flags, enriched by the sounds of kettledrums and the resonance of divine songs. || 10.693 ||
The sounds of divine drums and the resonances of great flutes,
the noises of various musical instruments, and all the worlds at all times.

Having thus described their manifestations (*vibhūti*), he speaks of their color: "White, resembling crystal, shaped like rubies, having the hue of moonstones, and resembling strings of pearls. (10.695)
Some excellent garments have a color like lac juice;
others have the hue of indragopaka insects, and some resemble sapphire.
They have the color of blue lotuses and resemble masses of lightning;
they have the color of the morning sun and resemble the interior of a lotus. || 10-697 ||
Others have the luster of the moon, resembling ten million moons;
some have the color of the midday sun, resembling ten million suns. || 10-698 ||
Resembling clusters of *aśoka* flowers, resembling yellow orpiment,
having the color of Indra’s bow, and white as cow’s milk.
They have the luster of vermilion and saffron, resemble yellow orpiment,
possess the color of molten gold, and are like smokeless fire.
Some worlds are white like a conch shell, while others are of various colors and possess diverse forms and shapes. || 10.701 ||
The *indragopaka* is the firefly. These [entities] have been described as such, beginning from the water-principle (*jala-tattva*) up to the unconditioned Śiva-principle (*anāśrita-śiva-tattva*).
For this reason, O Goddess, beyond these is the all-pervading supreme state,
which is immeasurable, incalculable, and inaccessible to all disputants. (10.702)

This is immeasurable (*aprameya*), because it cannot be delimited as "this much," since it is impossible even to describe it by means of number. Consequently, it is inaccessible and unattainable for all the aforementioned disputants, with the sole exception of those who know the Śaiva scriptures. (702)
Thus it is said: "Without the grace of the Lord, this knowledge is not obtained;
nor does spiritual transformation occur for embodied beings without having received initiation. (10.703)
The meaning is that this knowledge, once obtained, takes root only for those who have received the initiation of Maheśvara through the descent of power (śaktipāta), and not otherwise. || 703 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"But when, through a cause, the power that brings about liberation arises, one should, by the will of Śiva, attain the auspicious initiation consisting of knowledge. (10.704)

The divine [power] consisting of mantra-yoga... [this is to be explained in the middle as "then"]. From the cause, which is Paramaśiva, the power that effects liberation arises; then, for the one who is to be graced, that power emerges, and that person to be graced attains initiation (dīkṣā).

By the phrase "initiation consisting of knowledge" (*jñānamayīṃ dīkṣām*), he indicates that this [initiation] bestows the manifestation of entry into the state of the supreme subject, which is attained through the realization of the entire path (*adhvan*)—both what has been taught and what will be taught—as the object of measurement (*meyīkaraṇa*). He describes it as "auspicious" (*śubhām*), meaning it takes the form of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
Furthermore, by the term "consisting of knowledge," he teaches that even ritual initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*) has knowledge as its very essence.
In this initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is a union—that is, identity—with that which has the nature of protecting through contemplation by means of mantra;
for through the propitiation of the mantra, one attains identity with it. It is called "divine" because its power exceeds that of initiations such as those of the Vaiṣṇavas and others.
Having thus obtained initiation consisting of knowledge—.........the bound soul (paśu) thereafter proceeds to liberation;
he attains liberation while living. The term "bound soul" is a restatement of his previous state.
But if one does not ascend from this much knowledge of all that is to be known to the supreme state of the Knower, then one is not liberated; thus he says:
"Otherwise, one does not attain liberation, even through hundreds of knowledges. (10.705)
By means of the forms previously indicated. || 705 ||
And therefore:
"He alone attains liberation for whom everything has been revealed by Śiva, who possesses infinite forms..."

By the word "revealed" (prakāśita), it is meant that [the teaching] has been brought to manifestation through the knowledge of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvajñāna) by means of His infinite forms, which constitute His entire body.
"What is his attainment of liberation? To this he says:
"Śiva, the Great Lord of All. (10.706)

"Śiva" refers to that whose nature is the supreme good (*śreya*), which is a mass of non-dual light and bliss; for that very reason, because he is the presiding lord over all beings from Brahmā down to Anāśrita, he is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of all.
Furthermore—
"Therefore, this primary knowledge was previously taught by me to you"—
by "by me" is meant by me, who am the Supreme Essence whose nature consists of all the Great Lords (Maheśvaras) and who dwells on Kailāsa;
and by "previously taught to you," it is meant to the Goddess, who is the form of the Supreme Power (Paraśakti).
By means of making known the true nature of the other (the Self), the Goddess causes [the soul] to awaken to its own natural state;

thus, by expanding this [consciousness], the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Umā, becomes liberated through the initiation of the aforementioned knowledge, and [He and the soul] constitute a single reality (*tattva*). Therefore, it is precisely the essence of the supreme relationship described in the chapter on the descent of the *tantra* that is intended here.
"In all cases" means it is so taught.
And this is the supreme means of deliverance, like a boat for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. (10.707)
Since this—
transcending the collyrium of Mahāmāyā—
is the Mahāmāyā above Māyā, she is that which eternally arouses the appropriate contraction even in Sadāśiva and the others.
Power (Śakti) has the nature of the void and the supreme void; the ointment produced by it, which is the obscuration, has also passed away.
For this very reason— ..................'It is known within the sphere of the bound souls (paśu); because the bound souls have not conquered Māyā.'
And what is this?—the infinite, the ultimate, the unshakeable, the easily understood Supreme Lord. (10.708)
"Endless" (*ananta*) means unconditioned by space, time, or form. "Having a limit" (*pāra*) means having the nature of the boundary of *māyā*.
Because its form is a single, dense mass of autonomous consciousness, it cannot be agitated by anything;
rather, through the process of manifestation and withdrawal, it is the agitator of the universe. This is easily understood.

"When [the Self] remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand by oneself. (4.13) According to this principle established in the venerable *Spanda*, [this state] is easily attained through the universalization of all objects of knowledge.

Because its very nature consists of self-luminous consciousness; furthermore, this scripture of the Supreme Lord, being expanded across hundreds of millions of verses, is infinite and boundless, and cannot be disturbed by other disputants. || 708 ||
Such is this wondrous [teaching] which was emitted from the mouth of the Supreme Lord and obtained by me—
that...
I shall speak this nectar of knowledge; listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved.
"Listen!"— by this address, which again calls for attentiveness, he makes [the listener] face toward the subject with interest and proclaims the supreme worthiness of this knowledge to be acquired.
In that regard:
Indeed, above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there exists a group of eleven,
belonging to the eleven Rudras whose splendor is equal to the fire at the end of an eon.

"Above" means having transcended the city of the hundred Rudras; for these eleven previously mentioned [deities], beginning with Śveta and ending with Vīrabhadra, possess a splendor equal to the fire at the end of an eon due to their extreme brilliance. || 710 ||
Having thus described the worlds of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the hundred Rudras, together with his retinue, he speaks of the city of Śrī Bhadrakālī above that:
"Now, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the world of the Goddess situated above."
Divine, made of sapphire, and perfectly circular on all sides. || 10-711 ||
In that place resides the Blessed Goddess Bhadrakālī; she dwells there,
dark as a blue lotus, with a luster like smooth saffron.
Adorned with two earrings in the form of solar discs,
she shines like the twilight on the full moon day, radiant with both the moon and the sun.
Kaṅkuṣṭha is a specific type of coloring substance. || 713 ||
And of her—
there shines a great necklace situated between her two breasts,
like a river between two mountains of black collyrium. (10.714)
In the phrases "with the breasts" (stanābhyām) and "with the two rocks" (śailābhyām), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment. || 714 ||
Furthermore,
her seat— a throne— is supported by four lions of immeasurable prowess.
"Pīṭha" means a seat.
And there— in that divine realm consisting entirely of vajras, adorned with divine jewels— || 10-715 ||
On her radiant seat, the goddess possesses a luster like that of pure collyrium;
she stands upon a white peak of the Himalayas like a dark blue cloud.
Furthermore—
her divine girdle, composed of every kind of jewel, shines resplendently;
and this queen—
Clad in yellow garlands and garments, she was like the night at the rising of the dawn.
The night is dark, yet at the time of the dawn of Aruṇa, it becomes suffused with the color of twilight because of the Goddess’s nature as the power of Rudra;
her third eye, situated on her forehead, shines forth.
Like the sun standing at its rising, adorned with a network of rays. || 10-718 ||
Moreover—
she shines with that white umbrella held aloft,
like the night illuminated by the moon situated above a dark cloud. (10.719)
And she, in the form of a goddess, was surrounded by thousands of millions upon millions of women,
like the crescent moon in the vault of heaven encircled by the stars.
And these women— some with the hue of the white water-lily or the blue lotus, some dark as gold, some dark as the Priyaṅgu bud, and others fair as the moon, all in the prime of youth. (10.721)
They possessed forms as pure as lotuses, with full hips and breasts;
they were experts in the rules of amorous gestures and expressions, and highly skilled in dance and song.
There, those women, seated near that single goddess, take their delight with the sounds of lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and other wind instruments.
Hāva is characterized by physical gestures, whereas bhāva is a sattvic quality arising from those various gestures and so forth. || 723 ||
This very thing belongs to the Goddess— know thus, O fair-faced one, that it is the world named Jaya;
and she is that Goddess.
She who is known in the world as Durgā dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg.
Having previously propitiated the Supreme Lord through austerity, Viṣṇu brought her down for the purpose of slaying the great-souled Mahiṣa.
Of the Great-Souled One who possesses a vast body. || 725 ||
It reveals the majesty of Mahisha:
"By that single horn alone, the Lord Himavat mountain was cast aside like a withered leaf..."
The Blessed One is the self of the deity.
Thus, this very Mahiṣāsura, such as he was, has been destroyed by the Blessed Lady. || 10-726 ||
He asks, "How so? and says:
"That Goddess would destroy him, just as the risen sun destroys darkness.
Moreover—"
That Goddess exists through the names and forms of all goddesses.
"Concealed by yogamāyā":

that *māyā* which arises from *yoga*—that is, from identity with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*)—is the concealment of one's own true nature; she is "concealed" by that, meaning her supreme nature is veiled. [She is so] by means of the manifold expansion of names and forms belonging to all the goddesses.
The meaning is "established."
Furthermore, having descended into the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
she is the maiden who brings forth the worlds;
this power of the Lord (bhagavat-śakti) remains assuming the state of a maiden because she is not to be enjoyed by others.
And such as she is, she brings the worlds to fulfillment by making them fruitful through their desired results.
Even though she possesses such a form, in the investigation of reality, she is recited elsewhere as being inconceivable and immeasurable. (10.728)
"In another" refers to various treatises that are concerned with reality and intent upon defining its essential nature.
Moreover,
this goddess, together with Viṣṇu, appears again and again in every kalpa in the form of a sister, through various changes of name and form. || 10.729 ||
In every Manvantara and likewise in every Yuga,
she acts for the protection of the worlds, bestowing benefit like a mother.

The true nature of the cosmic cycles (*kalpa*) and so forth will become manifest in the eleventh [chapter]. The phrase "by the reversals of name and form" refers to the various experiences of names and forms. (730)
He summarizes:
"Thus, O fair-faced one, the world-sphere named Jaya has been described. And from this—"
Devotees who have received initiation into her mandala go there.
By the word "maṇḍala" is meant the world that serves as its locus, for the purpose of attaining it. || 731 ||
Thus, this [state] is to be attained through the sequence of devotion preceded by initiation, and not otherwise; so he says:
"Nor is this attainable through austerity, nor by sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, nor even by various kinds of gifts, O fair-faced one. (10.732)
But—
by the grace of the God of gods, whose crest is marked by the moon,
having received initiation, they attain...
The word "victory" (jaya) is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule].
And they have not been initiated merely for the sake of attaining this knowledge; rather— [the mandala] of the universal monarchs. (10.733)
Even those such as the Mantras and Mantreśvaras obtain this maṇḍala through initiation (dīkṣā).
In the reading where "maṇḍale" is in the locative case, the construction should be understood as "attainment occurs within the maṇḍala. || 733 ||
And it is not only to those who have undergone initiation that the Goddess grants the attainment of her own mandala and the station of a Vidyeśvara;
rather, she indeed grants liberation to embodied beings through initiation without seed (nirbījadīkṣā).
He grants liberation through initiation without seed; how much more so, then, through that with seed?
For it is said:
"That initiation for liberation has been fully described according to the supreme rule. (10.734)
"According to rule" means by the procedure ending with the purification of the bond of the pledge (samayapāśa). || 734 ||
Furthermore:
"O fair-faced one, whatever initiation is performed for men within the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), they attain a corresponding state within this world. (10.735)

"To whatever extent and of whatever kind [the initiation] brings about enjoyments—by implication, the initiated one attains them. However, "yāvatīṃ kurute" (to whatever extent he performs) is the clear reading. "Here" means in the world of Śrī Bhadrakālī. || 735 ||
Now, above this world of Bhadrakālī—[I shall describe] all the worlds, their lords, and their locations in due order; listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved. (10.736)
Structures are the arrangements of the worlds. || 736 ||

O Goddess of the gods, the supreme deity of Bhadrakālī is born from the wrath of Rudra; he possesses the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon and is present in the measure of ten million [forms]. (10.737)
His roar was like the thundering sound of a multitude of clouds at the end of an eon;
he possessed a hundred arms, great splendor, and was adorned with divine ornaments.
Bearing the moon upon his head, he is dark with a luster like blue collyrium;
resembling the neck of a peacock, he is somewhat pale and reddish.
It has the color of a blue jay or a cloud, resembling the flax flower;
it resembles sapphire and has a form somewhat like that of a bumblebee.
Its form resembles natural collyrium, and it is accompanied by the eleven Rudras.
Regarding the eleven Rudras:
"And here, Aṅgāraka is with Sapīr Nairṛta" (10.490).
That which was previously described by such passages as these stands here in the form of the other.
Moreover:
"Accompanied by a thousand times ten million high-souled Rudras. (10.741)
The world of that god is renowned by the name Vijaya;
it is divine, resembling sapphire, like all vajras, and vast.
The state of being like a diamond is due to the excellence of its essential core.
And here—
ten thousand times ten million Rudras of excellent complexion stand as the principal ones.
And this world is surrounded by other collections of intermediate worlds. || 10-743 ||
Dark like the petals of a blue lotus and resembling the throat of a peacock;
furthermore,
it was surrounded on all sides by Rudras who were fierce, blazing, and possessed of great heroism.
The meaning is: "even by those who are the foremost among the foremost. || 744 ||
Furthermore:
with hymns of praise, auspicious rites, songs, and the playing of dances and musical instruments—with drums, flutes, lutes, kettledrums, cymbals, and gomukhas. || 10.745 ||
With kettledrums and trumpets, with conchs, dundubhis, and pīlukas; with clay drums, taṭṭarīs, cymbals, and murajas likewise.
With the sounds of *maunda*, *kāhala*, and *ṭaṅka* drums, with Tamil *draghata* drums and others, with dancing musical instruments, rhythmic beats, shouts, and cymbals for the mouth. || 10.747 ||
By the spirits and hosts of spirits, by the Rudras, through their mutterings and recitations, as well as by those meditating, chanting, running, and performing various actions. || 10-748 ||
And by other high-souled beings who were emitting the cries of peacocks and cuckoos, and who were manifesting various playful modulations of sound.
Enveloped by them, the one of great splendor was like the sun with its rays—
by those with elephant faces, lion faces, horse faces, and auspicious countenances.
The Blessed One is attended by those with the faces of cows, those with the faces of oxen, others with the faces of leopards and bears, as well as those with the faces of tigers and monkeys.
Vīrabhadra, of great splendor, possesses a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
Here, specific musical instruments such as the *pīluka*, *mṛdaṅga*, *tala*, *dragaṭa*, and others are well known.

And these [instruments] are used with the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) according to their application, in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*), as an agent (*kartṛ*), as an instrument (*karaṇa*), or as a cause (*hetu*).
They are to be applied.
Furthermore: "The great seat of that god consists entirely of adamant. (10.752)
Ten yojanas in extent, square-shaped, and possessing the brilliance of fire,
it shines there, surrounded by eight lions of terrifying prowess.
"Caturasrānalaprabham" is a *karmadhāraya* compound. "Here" refers to the city named Vijaya. (753)
He shows those for whom this is the place according to their attainment:
"In this [place], those of meritorious deeds are born..."
Those who remember Maheśvara—
whether they die in water, among the winds, or in fire, or even by decapitation— [attain liberation]. (10.754)
