And those who attain the divine awakening of the greatly resplendent Vīrabhadra—
whether they remember Maheśvara among the Maruts or in great whirlwinds (if the reading is *maruṣu*, then "on great paths")—
or those who have died for the sake of worshipping the feet of the Blessed One, or those who have died by the severing of their own heads.

Those who die in battle with their heads severed, having remembered Maheśvara at the time of death, attain this station. However, those who die in water or other such places without the remembrance of Maheśvara follow the previously mentioned path of lightning or the path of the wind; such is the distinction.
Then,
O Goddess of gods, there is indeed a great enclosure above this world.
But the mother was thick and dense, standing like a rainbow;
that auspicious one was situated in the midst like a canopy. || 10-756 ||
"Extremely dense" means very solid. "Auspicious" means beautiful. "In between" refers to the worlds of Jaya, Vijaya, and so forth, as well as the element of fire (tejas-tattva).
And there dwells that Great Soul, the Blessed Lord Rudra, measuring only the size of a thumb-tip; having assumed a subtle form for the meditation of those who meditate,
he remains there, endowed with preeminent power.
And just as the upper shell of the Brahmāṇḍa is ten million *yojanas*, so too is the shell of the Āpya enclosure; thus he says:
"In that regard, ten million *yojanas* are indeed stated to be its diameter from above. (10.757)
"In that place" refers to the region of the *āvaraṇakarparikā* (the shell-like covering). It is called "above" because of its width and density;
thus, by implication, it means the *āvaraṇakarparikā*.
And therefore:
"O Dear One, the watery covering has a width of three times that [of the previous layer] across;
since the watery covering is ten times greater than the Brahmāṇḍa, which has a width of one hundred koṭis."

It has been stated that the measurement is one thousand crores; according to the principle that "all of that should be multiplied by three," the meaning is that its dimension is three thousand crores. However, one should not apply a threefold expansion based on the thickness of the skull-cup (karparikā), as that would result in inconsistency.
And therefore:
"All that is covered by it, which spreads across the great ocean. (10.758)
"By that" means by the obscuration. || 758 ||
"What is it that covers [it]?"—to this he says:

"O Dear One, it is renowned as the *rudrāṇḍa* and as the world of Rudra (*rudraloka*). It is called the *rudrāṇḍa* and the world of Rudra in the scriptures because it is the abode of heroes such as Vīrabhadra."
The meaning is that what is known as "born of the city" (purajāta) is covered by an obstruction (āvaraṇa).
He analyzes this very point:
"And the abode of Vīrabhadra, as well as the temple of Bhadrakālī. (10.759)
It is adorned with thirteen other worlds;
that is, together with the eleven previously mentioned Rudra-worlds— such as the abode of Vīrabhadra and the residence of Bhadrakālī—
and with thirteen others.
Shining with the worlds beginning with the Earth (Dharitrī), which are to be described hereafter.
And this [place] is adorned without interruption by various groups of radiant Rudras. (10.760)
"O beloved, the egg of Vīrabhadra is indeed like the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

It is called 'the egg of Vīrabhadra' because of his preeminence; and it is like the cosmic egg because it is adorned with various worlds that serve as the substratum for the creation of the fourteen kinds of beings."
Regarding what was stated by others as "and by other worlds," he clarifies that: "Henceforth, I shall describe the great world of the Earth. (10.761)
The Goddess Dhātrī is eternal in this world of the earth;
she is called Dhātrī because she sustains everything—she is the embodied power of the Lord.
For she has indeed obtained incomparable gold, upon which this foundation is established. || 10-762 ||
The "support" (ādhāra) is the world (bhuvana). || 762 ||
Of what sort was it?
It was surrounded by many celestial palaces of the Cakravartin kings, and filled with hosts of beings and teachers who were devoted to that [path]. (10.763)
He was surrounded by hosts of Rudras within the multitude of worlds, amidst the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments enriched by the resonance of divine songs.

Here, the Cakravartins, the gods, and others are possessors of great merit; [this is said] by means of these fourteen classes of beings (*bhūtasaṅgha*). "By the teachers who are devoted to that" means by those who have attained the power of sustaining the earth, appearing in the form of yogis. This is the supreme form of the Lord.
Having thus made this world surrounded by the worlds of Rudra.
In the midst of this world, he is like the rising sun;
divine, resembling a red lotus, with the luster of an *aśoka* flower cluster.
A divine palace made of ruby, possessing many stories.
A "palace" (prāsāda) is a celestial abode; "possessing many stories" means it is endowed with various levels extending upward from the base to the pinnacle.
In its center is the Blessed Lady Dharitrī, the sustainer of the world.
She is eternally adorned with a hanging garland of red flowers,
and her cheeks are beautified by the circular forms of the sun and moon.
Clad in yellow golden raiment and adorned with great necklaces,
she stands upon the back of a tortoise extending for a hundred yojanas.
She has four faces and eight arms, adorned with divine ornaments;
her upper garment is made of yellow gold, and she wears excellent cloth.
Furthermore: "Endowed with beauty and youth, they are experts in dance and song. (10.769)
Divine women born of the mind attend upon her, surrounding her;
they have arisen from her own mind.
Who are they? And how many are they? To this he says:
"There are indeed thirty crores of them, adorned with divine ornaments. (10.770)

The meaning is that these were created by Śarva, the Lord who has the earth as his form, out of his own mind for the sake of the welfare of his own manifestation, the Earth, and for his diversion— Śarva desiring her well-being.
Moreover, these women—resembling molten gold and adorned with divine ornaments—[are seen]. (10.771)
They were graced by held-up, upturned parasols;
moreover—standing before them was that very Meru, the great mountain of immense splendor. (10.772)
Sitting there, that lord of mountains remained gazing at her;
the meaning is that he possessed a form with a head, hands, and other limbs.
Likewise:
"Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, resembling a dark rain cloud. (10.773)
The great mountain named Nīla was clothed in yellow garments and possessed of great splendor;
with his exceedingly beautiful form, he was like another enemy of Kaiṭabha.
Being worshipped by divine cities, the Lord of Mountains,
resembling the moon and adorned with various ornaments, was situated to his north.
The great mountain named Śveta is radiant and possesses a white parasol;
to its north is [the mountain] resembling the sun, adorned with a crown and other ornaments.
Clad in yellow garments, glorious, and renowned as Śṛṅgavān,
he was like another god of love with his exceedingly beautiful form.

The word "its" refers to the first [mountain]; it should be understood that Nīla is to the north of Meru, and Śveta is to the north of that as well—just like the eye of a crow [which moves between two sockets].
Furthermore, O beloved, listen attentively as I describe those mountains possessing distinct forms situated to the south of this Meru— this is the remainder of the sense.
He describes them in sequence:
"Possessing a splendor as bright as the moon, adorned with divine ornaments. (10.778)
Clad in white garments, glorious and renowned by the name Niṣadha,
he resembled molten gold and was adorned with divine ornaments.
With an exceedingly radiant body, like a second Grandfather (Brahmā),
the glorious one wore yellow garments and was adorned with yellow garlands and unguents.
The blessed Hemakūṭa mountain, possessed of great splendor and like a collection of all radiant energies,
shines like the sun enveloped by the twilight.
Resembling a pale white cloud, like a conch shell or cow’s milk,
wearing white garments, glorious, and adorned with divine earrings.
With a great parasol being held over his head, he was renowned as Himavat, appearing like a second sun. || 10.783 ||
Furthermore:
Gandhamādana, resembling an *indragopaka* insect, is situated in the west;
glorious and wearing red garments, he stands like the sun upon the Asta mountain. (10.784)
Resembling pure crystal, wearing white garments, and auspicious,
there is the glorious mountain named Mālyavat, adorned with a crown and earrings.
It is thus surrounded by these and other mountains,
ending with the Lokāloka range, as well as by other principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
The meaning is that the Goddess, possessing a divine form, is indeed the supreme body of the Lord;
those such as Meru and other mountains in the world of earth are merely her presiding forms.
By the term "supreme" (pārameśvarī), it is indicated that—
"That one [reality] is established through its divisions into gross and subtle" (4.295);
thus, what was stated previously is made the authoritative basis.
Since this is so, therefore:
"The yogi, having abandoned the vital breaths in the subtle element of smell, [attains] concentration (dhāraṇā). (10.787)
Those yogis attain such a form, the supreme body of the earth;

having performed concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), they reach this supreme, embodied form of the earth through the distinctions of union (*sāyujya*), proximity (*sāmīpya*), and residence in the same world (*sālokya*).
And thus, that which was previously stated by the Teachers—that [the Goddess] is being worshipped—is now made clear.
Beyond this, O Goddess, lies the great world-ocean.
It is divine, consisting entirely of vajra, endowed with hundreds of various wonders;
it is called "sāmudra" because it is the locus of the presiding deity of the ocean.
And that [body] has a luster like a blue lotus and is perfectly circular in every respect. || 10-789 ||
In the center of this world, however, is a mandala resembling the moon,
measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in circumference all around.
In its center, however, was a person of golden complexion and great splendor,
wearing a crown, earrings, and garlands, adorned with divine ornaments.
He is the supreme body of the Lord Varuṇa, the ocean;
he is the Puruṣa, the very soul of the deity of the sea.
But having surrounded that high-souled god on all sides, || 10-792 ||
The goddesses, endowed with beauty and youth, constantly attend upon him.
In their midst, however,
was the goddess clad in white garments, anointed with white perfumes and unguents.
She was adorned with a white sacred thread and beautified by white garments;
a white parasol was being held over her head.
To his north stands indeed the Gaṅgā, his supreme body—
the goddess clad in blue garments, anointed with blue perfumes.
And the Yamunā, with a blue garland around her neck, is on his right;
thus these and other great rivers surround him of great splendor.
And the eight oceans, O Goddess of gods, surrounded by their own rivers,
always worship with devotion that supreme form of Varuṇa.
"The supreme body" refers to the form of the presiding deity. || 797 ||
And here, there are indeed those possessing forms— the various lakes and sacred fords—
and likewise:
And those devoted to it are also established there;
having properly performed meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) right here upon the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra). || 10-798 ||
Having reached the supreme source of the waters, [they reach] this very [earth].
Because of this,
that [Vāruṇī] is the supreme body of the Great Lord who possesses eight forms; this [other form] is his second body, appearing as the presiding deity of the waters.
The nature of *dhāraṇā* was previously shown on the occasion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) concerning *dhāraṇā*.
Henceforth, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall describe the world-realm.
The meaning is that it is known as "Śrīniketa" and heard of as "Padmagarbha"; it is recognized by these two names in the Āgamas.
And that [place] was filled without any gaps by hundreds of assemblies of celestial palaces standing closely together.
It was adorned by the lords of the worlds, by the Rudras, and likewise by the hosts of Rudras;
it was beautified by divine lakes such as Mānasa and Dīrghikā.
And with lotuses the size of chariot wheels, adorned with jewels and collyrium, having stalks of beryl and fragrant with divine scents. || 10.802 ||
It was beautifully adorned with various peacock feathers that were soft, radiant, and resembling the orb of the moon, as well as with diamond-like filaments.
It was adorned on all sides with various gardens resounding with the songs of diverse birds and with trees that grant every desire.
With divine pleasure-mountains made of various jewels, and with celestial women possessing the loveliness of youth, [he was filled]. || 10.805 ||
It was adorned by divine women rich in gestures, emotions, and amorous charms,
and with variegated jewel-lotuses and white petals, O lady of virtuous vows.
It was adorned with those mounted upon lordly elephants, who uttered hymns of praise and auspicious benedictions;
it was filled with celestial women singing and dancing.

"By mental [powers]" means by those accomplished through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*). By their very nature, the lotuses are adorned with jewels and gold, and possess stalks made of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
By the phrase "resembling the orb of the moon," the whiteness of the lotuses is expressed. *Vajram*...
"Heraka": by trees that grant various desires; the meaning is "wish-fulfilling trees" (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
"Mānasībhiḥ": agreeable to the mind. "Straiṇam": a collection of women. || 807 ||
In such a divine world, possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus,
there appeared a divine mandala resembling the autumnal moon, filled with rays of light.
The maṇḍala is the primary world. || 808 ||
In its center is the Blessed Lady Śrī herself, the creator of the world, whose splendor surpasses that of thousands of millions of moons. || 10-809 ||
He brings the worlds to manifestation and accomplishes them as endowed with emergent splendor. || 809 ||
And that—
[the splendor] of lights shines simultaneously in one place;
the light belonging to all lights becomes, as it were, gathered into a single mass in one location.
And yet, because of his gentle appearance, she is as tranquil as nirvāṇa, captivating with all forms of bliss. (10.810)
Possessing form... having a physical shape.
In reality, however—
this supreme goddess, the non-deviating form of the Supreme,
the very Goddess who shines as the Supreme, has assumed this particular form; such is the meaning.
The Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha is said to be eternally bound to this very glory of liberation;
and she—[residing] in [the city] extending for a hundred yojanas, possessing the radiance of the rising sun. (10.811)
Upon a lotus made of moonstone, with a vajra as its filaments and pericarp, possessing ten million petals, most divine, and endowed with the qualities of fragrance and flowers. || 10-812 ||
Seated here eternally upon the lotus throne, the Blessed Lady possesses a radiance equal to the interior of a lotus, endowed with supreme majesty.
Bearing upon her chest a beautiful, hanging garland made of great jewels,
she shone like the moonlight upon the path of the triple-streamed river.
The sky is the path of the triple-streamed Ganges. || 814 ||
Moreover—
she wore earrings that resembled the orb of the sun, shimmering as they moved upon the surface of her cheeks. || 10.815 ||
Furthermore— she,
possessing a girdle that shone with a mass of flickering rays,
golden-hued, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with a magnificent necklace; || 10.816 ||
She shone with a moon-like parasol being held over her,
and was accompanied by songs sung by Gandharvas born of Rudra’s mind.
The Blessed Lady, that subtle form of the Supreme Lord,
was surrounded by the mental [beings] born of Rudra— those who were created by the Blessed Lord Rudra himself for the very purpose of her worship.
Moreover: "She who was obtained by the powerful Viṣṇu after propitiating her through ascetic penance. (10.818)
And precisely because of his propitiation,
Rudra, being pleased, granted him a river to flow upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
yet not with his entire self, but rather—
With one half, that Blessed Lady is established upon the body of Viṣṇu.
By one quarter she resides in the heaven of the god Indra;
by half a quarter, O Goddess, she is established among the gods; and by another quarter, she is situated among human beings on earth.
Half of that [is] among humans...

[meaning] in the mouth of the god who dwells there in heaven. Regarding "among those belonging to the earth," this refers to all universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) due to their connection with portions and sub-portions. Among humans refers to ministers and so forth.
Thus, it is stated that Śrī resides in all [beings] as a portion of a portion of Viṣṇu, but in her entirety, she resides in the Blessed One Śrīkaṇṭha alone.
In this way, she alone pervades and abides throughout this entire world with her embodied forms;
she is proclaimed to be twofold: as the one whose nature is the Absolute (Svarūpā) and as the one who assumes forms at will (Kāmarūpā). || 10-821 ||

She whose own ultimate, perfect form is manifested through partial incarnations such as Mūrti, Abhinīja, and Aṃśāṃśika; she whose form, by mere will (*kāma*), bestows upon Viṣṇu, Indra, and others their respective greatness—she is Kāmarūpā. || 821 ||
In that regard, the essence of its own nature is as follows:
that subtle body is immovable and remains there unshakable.
It is subtle, pervading all its own manifestations; it is unshakable, being unsurpassed. "Therein" refers to what has been described.
She remains immovable in her own city.
He instructs on how this Śrīpura shall be attained:
"O lady of excellent vows, in the sacred sites such as Prayāga, which are the playful incarnations of Rudra... (10.822).
And one who dies especially on Śrīparvata shall go to that world of Rudra.

Those places such as Devadāruvana and others, where there are incarnations through the sport (*krīḍā*) of Rudra— and not through a desire to favor [beings]— are called "incarnations of Rudra’s sport."
And therefore:
"Even though other enjoyments exist, this is declared to be the [highest] goal. (10.823)
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "as that which is to be attained by those desiring enjoyment. || 823 ||

Because those desiring enjoyment—whether through death at Śrīgirya and other such places or through the propitiation of this [goddess]—attain her, the goddess who is of such a nature; the ellipsis is "they obtain sovereignty, such as the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth. The phrase "having attained her" implies, by context, that they have reached her world.
Not only this, moreover: having become eightfold and divine, she abides even among the gods. (10.824)
"In eight ways" means by way of the forms beginning with *aṇimā*.
Likewise, among those who have attained perfection through birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption—
that Goddess is said to be the supreme accomplishment.
Moreover:
For whose sake the battle was fought by Tāraka and the other lords of the gods.
Together with the terrible and innumerable [powers] that have been performed...
likewise, [the power] whose form consists of the aforementioned parts and sub-parts.
By those desiring to attain that glory,
indeed, countless battles were waged by the Cakravartin queens.
Thus, this has been described:
"This is declared to be the supreme bondage for those who are thus described—
the ignorant, such as the Tārakas and others, who [possess] a longing for perishable enjoyments."

For those engaged in battle and the like, this prosperity is indeed bondage; yet for the liberated ones—those who have recognized their true nature and partake in liberation while living—that very same prosperity is bondage.
They do not strive for it, but rather bestow upon seekers that prosperity which they have already attained. Those...

This should be explained by repeating the word "those" (*teṣām*) and eliding the vowel *a* (through *praśleṣa*), such that it means: "that [state] is desired as the supreme goal to be attained by those very same ignorant ones."
This very thing has been correctly described as Śrīpura, O fair-faced one. (10.827)
Now, from this point forward, I shall proclaim; learn from me the world-system.
It is known as Sārasvata and is also remembered as Gāndharva. (10.828)

"Ūrdhvam" means situated above. "Sārasvatam" belongs to Sarasvatī. And since Sarasvatī is the expansive form of all scriptures and the form of the science of music (gāndharvavidyā), the name of this city is "Gāndharva. || 828 ||
Furthermore,
O observer of excellent vows, this city within the lotus-womb is said to measure one crore yojanas in circumference.
The meaning is that it has the form of the interior of a lotus, being delicate and radiant.
Furthermore:
"It is divine, consisting of all kinds of jewels, endowed with every sovereignty, and possesses various auspicious celestial chariots (vimānas) made of many gems and taking diverse forms. (10.830)
With Gandharvas and Mānasas singing in many ways,
and with others dancing, as well as with various attendants standing by his side.
It was crowded with beautiful women and Gandharvas;
by those celestial chariots of the Gandharvas belonging to the Gandharvas, which were mental— that is, accomplished by mere volition— and by the Gaṇas, the attendants of the Supreme Lord.
In the midst of such a [place], O Goddess of Gods, there is an auspicious [spot] resembling the autumnal moon. (10.832)
A divine, circular mandala, filled with garlands of rays, exists;
in its center stands the Blessed Lady, Sarasvatī herself. (10.833)
The Goddess, clad in yellow garments and possessing eyes as long as lotus petals, surpasses the splendor of a thousand autumn moons.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing a golden sash as her lower garment, and bearing divine earrings.
Bearing upon her breast a great necklace with the luster of the moon, she was adorned with a pair of earrings from which clusters of shimmering rays radiated.
The maṇḍala is the primary abode; *kānti* is radiance, while *śyāmatva* is the complexion. *Ambaram* is the inner garment, whereas *parīdhānam* is the outer garment. || 836 ||
He states that her body consists of the complete totality of music:

"The auspicious Goddess has the three scales (*grāma*) as the folds of her waist, the seven notes (*svara*) as her limbs, the melodic phrases (*tāna*) as her hair, and she bears the melodic modulations (*mūrchanā*) as the hairs on her body. (10.837)
She whose feet are like the seats of lutes (*tālapāda*), who possesses the power of the syllables of song,
and whose waist is adorned with three folds— namely the three scales (*grāma*) called *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *gāndhāra*—
she has a body consisting of the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*, and likewise she is stretched out and expanded.
She whose hair-locks are the *tāna* scales, which consist of the weaving together of musical notes (*svaragumphanāmaya*);
she who bears the horripilation of the *mūrcchanā*s themselves; she whose seat consists of the *pada*s—metrical songs;
and she whose spreading causes are the *tāla*s such as *cañcupuṭa*.
She whose feet are her two feet; she whose splendor is radiant with the phonemes of song, which are sung as musical notes consisting of two or three *śrutis* and which constitute parts of words.
Moreover, O fair-faced one, her fingers and even her joints are auspicious marks. (10.838)
The joints are the vital points (*marmāṇi*). The characteristics are as follows:
"That which is adorned with many ornaments and poetic qualities (*guṇas*), like [a body] with various meaningful decorations, is known as *bhūṣaṇa* (the Ornamented). (16.6)

Thus, thirty-six [ornaments]—beginning with *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) and *akṣarasaṅghāta* (concatenation of syllables)—have been characterized by the sage Bharata through such definitions. Therefore, this Sarasvatī herself, having thus become one whose body is composed of vowels and so forth, is here declared to be the presiding deity in her supreme form (*pararūpa*). Previously, however, in the city of the Gandharvas situated on Mount Meru—
"By such statements as: 'The Blessed Lady herself resides, adorned with the seven musical notes, clothed in the three scales (*grāma*)... (10.152).
The distinction is that, while her nature consists of speech adorned with vowels and other elements, she exists in another form as the form presided over by this deity. || 838 ||
Thus, here on this supreme, divine seat, surrounded by the lords of the hosts of beings,
she stands resplendent like the very Fortune of the entire world. (10.839)
According to the principle that "all objects of speech are deposited therein, rooted in speech, and bound by speech," this Goddess alone is indeed the cause of the world's order.
Furthermore—
she was surrounded by mind-born women and mind-born Gandharvas;
and likewise—
Hāhā, Hūhū, Citraratha, Tumburu, and likewise Nārada.
Viśvāvasu, Viśvaratha,
and so forth—
these [gandharvas] are experts in celestial song.
Having united the self with the mind and abandoned desire for the fruits of action.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having indeed reached that station of Sarasvatī, they—
established with one-pointed minds upon the stages of Madhyamā and Paśyantī through the sequence of abiding on the ground of Svarā and Vaikharī— are those who worship this very Goddess.
The leaders of the Gandharvas have reached this city.
Not only have these reached this city, but also those embodied beings who, having meditated upon the retention of speech, release their vital breaths. || 10-842 ||
Those best of men indeed attain the world of Sarasvatī;
this retention of speech will be explained in the twelfth chapter on the attainment of the principles (tattvasiddhi).
And this is logical, because:
"This goddess Sarasvatī is indeed the supreme form of the Lord. (10.843)
How is it that she remains by means of her other aspect within the interior of the cosmic egg? He says: "And that Goddess stands upon one foot in the world of Brahmā. (10.844)
And in the world of Śakra, it is half of that;
in the world of Śakra, it is one-eighth [of that].
Among the Gandharvas, it is half of that;
[among the others], by a sixteenth part.
And among the Siddhas, [the measure] is half of that...
by a thirty-second part.
Among the kinnaras, it is half of that. || 10-845 ||
By a sixty-fourth part. || 845 ||
And half of that [is] among the Nāgas...
by the one hundred and twenty-eighth part.
Furthermore, among the yakṣas, it is indeed by half;
[and] by a two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth part.
Among the Piśācas, it is half of that [measure],
namely one part in five hundred and twelve.
Thus, in this manner—she indeed remains divided into parts. 10.846.
Furthermore—
she exists among humans as a thousandth part of what she is among the Piśācas;
yet this Goddess has not descended through such a minute fraction of a fraction, but rather—
Having performed severe austerities and having propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow, they...
That goddess, however, was brought down, possessing form and adorned with her own splendor;
"possessing form" means having a physical manifestation.

Thus, when the wielder of the Pināka bow had been propitiated by his asceticism, it was by his very command that, at the beginning of the kalpa, the Vedas first appeared to Brahmā as he remembered them.

She is Sarasvatī because she has emerged from the vowels (*svara*); for, by entering into the awareness of the emergent resonance (*nāda*) stirred up through the reflective awareness of the vowels, she has arisen and attained manifestation as if from the vowels of Brahmā. Therefore, due to her similarity in form to the syllables (*akṣara*), she is [Sarasvatī].

It is called Sarasvatī. However, when the reading is "of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest," then it should be explained as follows: that Supreme Brahmā residing in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), whose birth is from the unmanifest—the primordial nature (prakṛti) to be described hereafter—has attained manifestation through the grace of Pinākin (Śiva).
Thus, having entered in this manner—she, who is established in all the scriptures, has taken her place within the poetry of poets. (10.849)
The meaning is that she remains having taken up her station. || 849 ||
Moreover:
"That Goddess who resides eternally in Vālmīki and in Vyāsa, and who increases the memory and intelligence of all the sages. (10.850)
Medhā is the flash of insight free from conceptual construction; buddhi is the intellect characterized by ascertainment. || 850 ||
For she is indeed the bearer of all knowledge; she is omniscient and worshipped by the gods.
And [she is the one] who has gradually descended into the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
In the northwestern direction from Meru, her city is proclaimed.
Another [method]—
but this supreme one of the Goddess has been fully described by me to you.
He concludes this as follows:
The world of Sarasvatī is proclaimed as Bhuvana,
where the blessed goddess Sarasvatī resides.
...the supreme body. || 852 ||
The meaning is that the supreme form belonging to the Supreme Lord remains present.
Now,
listen here indeed to the supreme world within this very [realm] that is not yet attained;
the eightfold world which is superior even to the worlds already mentioned, according to the perspective to be described.
Listen.
And he shows that by means of the gateway of Bhuvaneśa: "Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, and likewise Naimiṣa. (10.853)
Āṣāḍhin, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍin, Bhārabhūti, and Lākula— these,
O Dear One, are known as the "Eight Secrets" (Guhyāṣṭaka) residing within the enclosure of water. (10.854)

Their secrecy is due to their superiority even over the Śatarudra and other such [mantras]. These are the Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras), who have descended for the sake of bestowing grace in the form of various self-manifested holy sites (svayambhūtīrtha) and so forth located in different directions, within this world that bears their very name.
These are well-known. In this same way, others that will be mentioned hereafter should also be understood. || 854 ||
Now,
therefore, I shall briefly describe the principle of fire (tejas-tattva) above this;
O fair-faced one, I shall there describe the world of Agni.
And that [place]—
bearing a brilliance everywhere from clusters of *aśoka* blossoms,
possessing the hue of full-blown *kiṃśuka* flowers, and resembling the *japā* flower— 10.856.
The meaning is "excessively red. || 856 ||
In the midst of this world, however, there is said to be a circular mandala of fire, possessing a radiance equal to the risen sun. (10.857)
The mandala, which is triangular in shape on all sides and perfectly circular, is the mandala of fire;
it consists of fire and is the primary world. || 857 ||
In its center, however, is the Lord Śivāgni, the supreme cause.
Śivāgni is the Supreme Lord Śiva himself who has assumed a fiery form. He is the supreme cause of all the various fires within the cosmic egg.
As it is said: "He who, having descended into the midst of the cosmic egg, remains eternally in a threefold and threefold manner. (10.858)
By way of being the terrestrial, the atmospheric, and the digestive fire. || 858 ||
Moreover:
"In the mouth of that Rudra, the Supreme Self, Svayambhū Nīlalohita resides in the form of the tongue. (10.859)

"Of him" refers to Rudra in the form of the Śiva-fire. He who is Nīlalohita, whose essence is the flaming liṅga, and who is renowned as self-manifested at Śrīparvata and other sites—he exists in the form of a tongue in the right face; the meaning is that he has descended from that right face for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world. || 859 ||
Furthermore:
"O Great Goddess, he alone is the Supreme Lord Kālāgni, who has been established upon the surface of Karparikā and above the Egg of Brahmā. Thus it is said.
Nīlalohita, whose right tongue is the fire of time (kālāgni) consisting of the measure of the self, is the universal self (niḥsāmānyātman); such is the meaning.
I shall describe the form of this Śiva-fire, which is useful for those who practice meditation; listen attentively, O beloved. (10.860)
Having the luster of the petals of a red lotus and a brilliance equal to rubies,
he is glorious, wearing red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
His auspicious face was adorned with two earrings radiant as the sun,
and he shone brilliantly with a great, glowing necklace resting upon his chest.
"By means of that which consists of ruby," is the implied meaning. || 862 ||
Furthermore:
"The radiant one, wearing a crown and earrings, is called the mouth of the gods.
It is called the "mouth" because by means of this, which has the form of the auspicious fire and consumes the universe, the oblation is cast forth.
And here in this world, the Lord himself is seated upon a pedestal composed entirely of vajras. (10.863)
Like a forest fire ignited by the friction of bamboos on a mountain peak,
moreover— there are ten thousand times ten million Āgneya lords of the Gaṇas.
From the southern mouth of this self-existent Svayambhū as he breathed forth,
there emerged the Rudras, possessing the splendor of the sun, for the welfare of all the worlds.
Therefore, those high-souled Rudras, who are the lords of their respective hosts and retinues, constantly attend upon Agni for the welfare of all beings;
they do so by presiding over the sun’s rays and other such elements, as well as by presiding over Agni.
In order to accomplish the grace that takes the form of both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), it is likewise stated in the Purāṇas:
"Those who are situated between the moon and the sun, those who are within the rays of the moon and the sun,
those who have gone to the subterranean realm (*rasātala*), and those who have gone beyond that."
Salutations to them, salutations to them, let there be salutations to them forever—
those whose number, measure, or even form is not known.
"Salutations always be to those Rudras who are in incalculable hosts"—
this is the statement of praise found in the Vāma-purāṇa (26.159–161).
Furthermore—there were various noble women, divine, and experts in celestial song. || 10.866 ||
The connection [of the words] is: the Gaṇas, the Rudras, the hosts of spirits, and the Kiṅkaras by the thousands, waited upon him.
Moreover:
"He is indeed recited as the auspicious fire (śivāgni), the supreme lord of all oblations. (10.867)
In the scriptures of the Supreme Lord, within the Śiva-sacrifice which consists of initiation (dīkṣā).
Furthermore, he is always offered as an oblation in the rites of fire-offerings by those who know that [method].
In this context, "those who know that" (*tadvidāḥ*) refers to those who possess knowledge (*vidā* = *jñānam*) of it; by them.
Furthermore:
"Having performed the fire-retention (dhāraṇā), they go to that Agni, who is the Lord. (10.868)
"At the end of the body" is the meaning [of the word "iti"]. || 868 ||
And this is the majesty of this Śivāgni:
that—pervading everything, it remains both as one and as many. "As one" means in the form of Śivāgni; "as many" means in the fifty forms that will be described hereafter.
Furthermore—
He is the source of all luminous bodies;
for...
From him was born Divākara. || 10-869 ||
He was born; that is, he was manifested. And it has been said:
"This power of knowledge of the Supreme One shines forth, assuming the form of the sun" (10.499).
For it is stated that his origin here is from the fire of Śiva. || 869 ||
Furthermore:
"And he is manifested in many ways during the kalpas, manvantaras, and so forth.
During the kalpas and other periods to be described hereafter, he is manifested in many ways, that is, in various modes.
He descends through a minute fraction of a fraction of another cosmic egg.
Furthermore,
this one is divided by various births and by fifty [divisions] upon the earth.

And these [fires] are described in detail in the Vāyu Purāṇa and other texts as being distinguished by their origins from the fire-drill, the sun-gem, and so forth— being designated as Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci— and further distinguished by their sons, grandsons, and others, such as Bharata, Vaiśvānara, Atharvabhṛt, Ṛg, and so on.

Fifty [fires] have been specified, some worldly and some Vedic, serving as the substrates for obligatory, occasional, and optional rites. However, the liberator is indeed only one: Śivāgni, consecrated by the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of the Supreme Lord’s mantra; he alone has descended directly, and thus he is "one."
That which has been pointed out immediately preceding. || 870 ||
He concludes:
"Thus, in this way, the great world of Agni has been correctly described.
Right here—"
And hereafter, I shall describe to you the lords of the worlds within the world-system.
Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpa, Āmrātakeśvara, Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
When that is mentioned, the Rudrāṣṭaka is superior to the previously mentioned Guhyāṣṭaka—
it is declared to be "extremely secret" (atiguhya), because it is more excellent than the [other] secrets. The same applies hereafter.
"How is this situated here?"— to this he says:
"In sequence from the east to the northeast," meaning it is situated starting from the eastern direction and extending to the northeastern direction.
The meaning is that this group of eight Rudras is the primary one.
This also indicates that other groups of eight, both those already mentioned and those yet to be described, exist in this same manner and possess this same primacy.
Then above is the enclosure of wind; the imperishable wind resides there. (10.873)
O lady of excellent complexion, the world of the vital breath (prāṇa) belongs there to Vāyu;
it is as white as a conch shell or cow's milk, and possesses the luster of the autumnal kunda flower and the moon. (10.874)
Of the wind known as *prāṇa*, the primary breath—
in that divine world, endowed with hundreds of divine wonders,
there is in the center a divine mandala with a radiance equal to the autumnal moon. (10.875)
The divine mandala, filled with garlands of rays and illuminating the ten directions, is indeed the preeminent city.
But in its center, O Goddess of gods, is the supreme body of Vāyu.
The meaning is that the presiding deity of wind is situated there. || 876 ||
And he— wearing a crown and earrings, radiant, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
his limbs variegated by various ornaments, and decorated with wonderful garlands and unguents. || 877 ||
Wearing variegated garments, glorious, and adorned with great necklaces—
[and] those [who followed him], indeed, were the gods named Māruta, numbering one hundred crores and possessed of great strength.
They worship the Great-Souled One, whose form is wind and who possesses great splendor.
Who is he? He says: "He who, being all-pervasive, pervades bodies in a single way or in five ways. (10.879)

In one way, it is as the universal self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); but in five ways, through the distinction of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. "One should pervade" means that one should employ the winds which, by their very nature of pervading, constitute the pervasion of one's own manifold expansion. || 879 ||
Not only does he pervade all bodies with subtle winds in the form of his own manifold expansion, but even externally—
[he is] the all-pervasive Lord, moving transversely in seven ways and again seven ways, doubling [his reach] at each step.

According to the principle stated in the passage beginning with "from the clouds to the sun" (10.513), those seven [winds], each being sevenfold according to the well-known tradition of the Purāṇas, constitute the forty-ninefold wind moving horizontally outside;
it is "twofold," meaning it is endowed with the two qualities known as sound and touch.
Thus, for that which is divided by such distinctions, she—the self of the presiding deity of her own maṇḍala—shines as the one supreme, divine body. (10.880)
Furthermore:

"The yogis, having meditated upon this very one—the single self consisting of the ten vital breaths—and having performed concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon it, indeed abandon their vital breaths. (10.881)
The great-souled ones enter it, having become like the wind and taking on the form of space.

"It" refers to that single entity in the form of the universal vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Tenfold" is due to the distinctions of the [five] vital breaths such as *prāṇa* and others, as well as the distinctions of the [five] secondary winds such as *nāga* and *kūrma*. "They enter it" means this.
Because they have reached the covering of the wind, they attain union with the deity of the wind.
He concludes:
"Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, the world of the vital breath has been described to you. (10.882)
Now, I shall describe the Rudras who are the lords of those worlds in their proper sequence:
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākala, and likewise Kanakhala.

Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Māhendra, and Bhīma as the eighth—just as before, the world has descended [into these]. Indeed, this which is more secret than the secret must be understood with diligent effort. (10.884)
It should be understood that, in the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the body] is to be purified, preceded by attendance and other such rites. || 884 ||
Then, above—in the sky, as vast as space, pure like clear crystal. "Sky" refers to its covering; "as vast as space" means all-pervasive; "pure" means transparent.
The meaning is "the world."
Likewise, in this regard—subtle in form, imperishable, and eternal, it is situated in the middle region. (10.885)
The Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa) is, by implication, none other than that which is called space, having the form of the body of the Supreme Lord. || 885 ||
Furthermore:
A yogi engaged in the concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā) shall be united with that state in this very body.
Now,
in this very space, I shall proclaim those Rudras who are duly stationed here.
To them. || 886 ||
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as the eighth.
This eightfold purification has indeed been proclaimed in brief;
for, by virtue of being established in the state of the unconditioned (*nirāvaraṇapada*), it is superior even to the preceding [stages].
Then— outside of this is the *ahaṅkāra*...
the *ahaṅkāra* situated outside of this enclosure of space (*ākāśāvaraṇa*), pervading it on all sides.

The meaning is that this is the covering of the *ahaṃkāra*, which contains within itself its own sixteenfold transformation consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*).
And therefore—learn from me concerning the Rudras therein. (10.888)
Chagalāṇḍa, Duraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara,
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara.
The group of eight is known as *sthāṇvaṣṭaka*.
It is called by the term *sthāṇu* because all the perfections of enjoyment abide within it by means of its presiding over the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*).
This is that group of eight denoted by the word *sthāṇu*.
This group of eight is as before— [it is] situated from the east up to the domain of Īśāna; this is the meaning by implication.
And precisely because of this presiding over the eight [sites], the Lord Rudra, the master of the ego (ahaṅkāreśvara), is situated in the Middle Country. || 10.890 ||

The self of the presiding deity of ego (ahaṅkāra) possesses a form inseparable from this very principle; for this very reason, in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra) [5.21–22], it is stated that the eightfold group which constitutes the primary [evolutes] is to be purified (*śodhya*), but not the Lord of Ego (*ahaṅkāreśvara*) who is presided over by them. 890.
Now, he prescribes in sequence the forms useful for meditation during the initiation of the eightfold pentad beginning with the secret [center] of the Lord of the Water-principle (jalatattva):
white, red, yellow, black, and having the luster of crystal.
Thus, in this manner—those phonemes which have been briefly described to you in the five groups of eight (pañcāṣṭaka). || 10-891 ||

He now describes the classification of colors for the hundred Rudras according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east: they are to be known as white, red, black, blue, dark-green, cloud-colored (grey), yellow, and white.
But those above are tawny, while those below have the luster of smoke.
These are their descriptions: they are known as the hundred Rudras, three-eyed and holding tridents;
all have the crescent moon upon their crests and are accompanied by their Rudrāṇīs. (10.893)
"All" refers even to the five and eight Rudras, who possess forms such as the three-eyed one and others. || 893 ||

Having thus described the form of the gods, he also speaks of their worlds: "The worlds of the hundred Rudras should be known as being shaped like lotuses, endowed with various jewels, and possessed of enjoyments and sovereignty. (10.894)
In the Pañcāṣṭaka, there are cities shaped like tortoises on all sides.
Having thus described the Rudras within the covering of the ego (ahaṅkāra),
he now begins to delineate the worlds according to the sequence of the sixteen principles, beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātras), contained therein:
O Dear One, above the obstruction of space and below the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), [is the region]. || 10-895 ||
I shall proclaim the worlds; listen again with a one-pointed mind.
Therein, first of all, is the great and expansive mandala of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra).
O Goddess, it stands like a canopy for many tens of millions of *yojanas*.

From the *maṇḍala* world, which measures one hundred million, up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is a gradual increase tenfold at each stage; thus, the covering of the ego (*ahaṅkārāvaraṇa*) is a billion times larger. This applies to those situated within it.
The veils beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) indeed become infinite crores in number.
And that is white, red, black, yellow, green, and has the luster of crystal. || 10.897 ||
O Goddess of the gods, it is circular on all sides like a canopy;
as it is in the world of beings (bhūloka), so it is also in the cause of the elements (bhūtattva).
For Śarva alone is the sovereign there, O fair-faced one. (10.898)
And this is logical, because:
"Therefore, the earth is born, impelled by Śarveśa;
otherwise, how could an insentient *tanmātra* possess causality? The same applies elsewhere as well.
It should be understood.
Then—therefore, above that maṇḍala is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra). || 10-899 ||
O beloved, O fair-faced one, that which is green, dark like an emerald, or resembling the wing of a blue jay—there, indeed, Bhava alone is the sovereign lord. (10.90)
Therefore, the waters emerged, impelled by Bhava;
then,
above that mandala, is the mandala of the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra).
Resplendent with the brilliance of shimmering sunbeams and possessing a luster like that of rubies,
Rudra Paśupati alone resides there.
Therefore, that splendor emerged by the will of Paśupati;
O Supreme Goddess, that splendor pervades all the worlds.

Rudra is known as Paśupati. "Pervading the worlds" means that he exists both internally and externally in the form of fire, such as the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) and the terrestrial fire (*bhauma*). || 903 ||
Then, O Dear One, above this mandala is the mandala of the subtle element of touch; it is the mandala of air, with a luster like the dawn-red. (10.904)
At twilight, the quality of rajas becomes slightly mixed with tamas, appearing variegated and greyish. || 904 ||
And this very [mandala], resembling the shape of a canopy and circular on all sides—
in that very mandala, O Goddess, Īśāna is firmly established. (10.905)
The sovereign lord. || 905 ||
And therefore:
"O Dear One, impelled by the will of the Lord, the wind has emerged from that [place];
it is what was previously described as having the nature of the wind-principle."
Furthermore:
"Therefore, the five beginning with breath...
The word "therefore" refers to air (vāyu).
Then he [becomes] the supreme pervader of that wind. || 10-906 ||
He, though being one, has become manifold, divided sevenfold and again sevenfold;
this has already been determined previously.
Then—therefore, above that maṇḍala is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). || 10.907 ||
Dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with a radiance equal to clear water,
its form is like a canopy, perfectly circular on all sides.
Bhīma alone remains there as its sovereign;
therefore, the great sky issues forth, impelled by the will of Bhīma.
O Dear One, it pervades all worlds and extends to both the higher and the lower;
the higher is the locus of the principles (tattvas) beginning with water, while the lower is that which is within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Now, above that mandala, the solar mandala is spoken of. (10.910)
Resembling a thousand suns, it blazed forth on all sides;
radiant with rays like a canopy, it was perfectly circular in every direction.
For Rudra alone remains there as the presiding lord;
from him, O fair-faced one, the suns emerge in every kalpa.
Those who are presiding over other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas). Thus it is further on. 912.
Now, above that maṇḍala, the moon maṇḍala is described; its orb is equal in brilliance to thousands of millions of moons. (10.913)
And "equal" means a circle, that is to say, a mandala. || 913 ||
And here—Mahādeva alone remains as the sovereign lord; therefore, the moons and others, impelled by Mahādeva, become moons. (10.914)
Countless thousands have emerged in every eon.
Now, above that maṇḍala, the Vedamaṇḍala is described. (10.915)
With a luster equal to ten million moons, perfectly circular on all sides,
it stands like a celestial canopy, presided over by the fierce Lord Ugra.

"That [Vedic maṇḍala] is obstructed by Vāmā" means that the circle of the Vedas is obstructed— covered— by the power (śakti) named Vāmā belonging to the Rudra named Ugra; the meaning is that its nature as the supreme non-duality remains unmanifested.

And therefore, because the nature of the non-dual Self— which is the subject matter of the Vedānta— is veiled by the power of Māyā (vāma-śakti), those [scriptures] that prioritize the performance of ritual action are indeed characterized by duality;
for they have indeed emerged from that [non-dual reality].
For indeed, thousands of sacrificers remain established in every single kalpa.
From that Brahmā,
who was in the form of the circle of the Vedas and was impelled by Ugreśa, those [beings] emerged,
characterized by fierce austerity; they did not emerge without the impulsion of Īśvara, but rather through that fierce austerity.
The cosmic egg descended for the performance of sacrifices.
And at that very same time—the various Vedas and sacrifices of Brahmā, whose path is infinite. (10.918)
Therefore, these sacrifices and the fruits of sacrifice proceed, together with austerity, charity, and the like, being governed by the power of *vāmā*. (10.919)

The *veda-yajñas* are the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices; the term "sacrifices" (*yajñāḥ*) here also includes the sacrifice of self-study (*svādhyāya*), the sacrifice of recitation (*japa*), and so forth. And this is stated [in the scripture]:
"This cosmic egg has been described as having brought down the net of bonds" (10.664).
According to the view thus stated,
and by the principle that "he impels the individual soul (aṇu) from below via the Vāmā [power]," this is accomplished by Ugradeva alone through the sequence of presiding over the power of Vāmā.
For even Brahmā’s conceit of being their creator was bestowed by Him alone.
He concludes:
"Thus, these eight bodies are proclaimed as supreme"—
that is to say, belonging to the Supreme Lord.
He also speaks of those which are inferior in comparison to these: "The inferior [energies], indeed, remain pervading the entire egg of Brahmā. (10.920)

The meaning is that they exist both externally and internally as the forms of stationary beings (*sthāvara-bhūta*). By stating this, he maintains the theme already introduced: that all this is essentially the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), thereby sustaining the non-dual vision (*advaya-dṛṣṭi*).

Thus, the division of the worlds (*bhuvana-vibhāga*) pertaining to the tenfold category of effects (*kārya-tattva*) consisting of the elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*) has been described.
In connection with that, the group of eight Lords of the Forms (*mūrtīśvarāṣṭaka*) who preside over the eight forms has been mentioned.

Among those presiding over the aforementioned eight forms, the form pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamānī mūrtiḥ*) is declared to be the most preeminent and primary; of this [form], the pentad of forms consisting of the effects (*kāryātmaka*) is the object of experience (*bhogya*).
And the two forms consisting of the sun and the moon exist as the cause. || 920 ||
Having thus described the fivefold veil of the objective (kāryāvaraṇa) as being included within the ego (ahaṅkāra),
he speaks in order to reveal the elevenfold veil of the instruments (karaṇāvaraṇa):
"And beyond these is also the mandala consisting of the instruments."
*Karaṇa* is the locus for the emergence of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which are the means for the activity of uttering sounds and so forth.

*Maṇḍala* refers to the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) divided, according to the perspective to be explained, into the five principles (*tattva*) consisting of speech and the other organs of action. This is the meaning.
And that, in sequence, is white, red, black, yellow, and green by color. || 10-921 ||

And therein— five presiding lords reside in the mandala consisting of the instruments; and they, according to the method to be explained in the chapter on the substratum (ādhāra), are Vahni, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Kaśyapa.
Furthermore: "The gods of action (karmadevas) proceed from that [state] for all embodied beings. (10.922)
The "action-deities" (karmadevas) are the organs of action (karmendriyas), which manifest their own functions such as speech and so forth;
from that circle of instruments, they proceed for embodied beings and arise in distinct forms for every atom [of the body].
And these—

Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth; among these, speech is the instrument for the internal functions of grasping and releasing. However, external grasping and releasing—this pair—is accomplished by the hands, the anus, and the feet.

The function of the organ of generation (*upastha*) is the repose in one’s own nature, which consists of bliss, through the pacification of agitation regarding the taking up and discarding of all things.
There is no activity other than this; thus, there are exactly five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
And although these pervade the entire body, their specific seats of location are the hands and so forth. Therefore...
Even that apprehension which occurs through the mouth and so forth is indeed the effect of the tactile sense organ alone.
He speaks of the sense organs:
"Beyond these is that which is called the illuminator, resembling the sun. (10.923)

Based on the established principle that "the function of the five [senses] with respect to form and the rest is held to be mere perception" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 28), since the ears and other senses illuminate sound and the other objects, their place of origin is called the illuminating *maṇḍala*; for this very reason, it is said to be "resembling the sun. || 923 ||
And this circle of instruments (karaṇamaṇḍala) likewise consists of exactly five [faculties]. As it is said: "From that, indeed, the five sense-faculties of cognition (buddhīndriya) proceed forth.
The meaning is that they exist as distinct forms for every individual atom.
And those are—the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose, respectively. (10.924)
The meaning is: by way of the sequential expansion of the principles (tattva) beginning with space and air.
And of these—
the function [of the senses] is the perception of objects—
since:
They are eternally established within the circle of light;
as lords of their own respective families, they are the constant instigators therein.

The sense-faculties (buddhideva), impelled by their respective presiding deities known as Bhāvinī, Ākāśa, Vāyu, Sūrya, Varuṇa, and Aśvin, engage in the perception of form and other objects according to their specific impulses; thus, the meaning is that the function (vṛtti) of these [intellective faculties] is the perception of their respective objects. And this applies to the organs of action (karmendriya) as well.
The purification of the worlds should be performed in reverse order. || 925 ||
Now,
beyond these, there exists a circle of rays resembling the lunar disc, equal in extent and circumference in every direction. (10.926)
From that indeed proceed the five objects for all embodied beings:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. || 10-927 ||

From that [Prakṛti], all objects such as form and so forth arise, which serve as the objects of enjoyment for each individual Puruṣa and bring about their various experiences. For this very reason, because it causes the manifestation of the moon consisting of all things,
its resemblance to the lunar orb is described both in terms of its magnitude and its appearance.
And because this circle of rays exists, for that very reason these elemental objects are of the nature of these rays;
by virtue of their being manifest, they have the nature of self-luminosity. As it is said in the venerable *Ucchuṣmabhairava*:
"As long as these are not knowers, how can they be objects of knowledge, O beloved?
Since the reality of the knower and the known is one, there is therefore no impurity.
Although earth and the other elements have arisen as nothing but qualities such as form and so forth, nevertheless, with respect to each individual person—
The forms and other objects that produce various enjoyments are entirely different from those [previously mentioned]. || 927 ||
Furthermore:
"And beyond these, O gentle one, is the orb of Soma.
By "beyond these" is meant beyond these orbs of instruments, light, and rays.
Therefore, the mind has issued forth with fifteen rays.

Considering that it is the unifying form of the fifteen rays— known as the objects of the cognitive and active senses and consisting of the nature of the grasper and the grasped— it has been stated that it is joined with those very [rays].
And that—
being thus described as "citta," "cetas," and "manas"— is...
...which impels the senses toward sound and the other objects;
and because this [individual soul], being thus impelled, has its body filled by the cluster of fifteen rays, it is therefore sixteen-fold (ṣoḍaśakala) together with its own nectar-ray. Thus—
Its lord is the Moon, possessed of great splendor and gentle radiance.
He possesses great splendor because his form is eternally complete with the sixteen digits and so forth, never diminished;

and because he serves as a representative for the conscious Puruṣa— who, being endowed with the sixteen transformations and so forth, will be determined in its own context through the process of descent— by way of a gradual downward progression.
"It is proclaimed: 'In the person consisting of sixteen parts, they call that one part immortal. (929)
Then— above that mandala, however, further beyond, there is a great mandala,
resembling the hibiscus flower and like the rising sun in its ruddy hue.
"And as before, it is circular all around according to its measure. "As before" means the measurement of the lunar disc mentioned previously.
Furthermore:
"Therefore, O Goddess, [he emerges] from that mandala with a luster equal to the dawn-red. (10.931)

This ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) indeed proceeds like fire accompanied by smoke; the meaning is that the ego-senses residing in all subjects arise. The singular number in "ego-sense" is used to denote the class.
Because it presides over all objects and the senses ending with the mind, and because its nature consists in the conceptualization thereof,
this [element], which takes the form of the taijasa-bhūta and so forth, is said to be like fire accompanied by smoke. And thus,
these are the causes of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the mind (manas), the objects, and the sense organs (buddhīndriya).

The principle of ego (ahaṅkāratattva) exists pervading the five solar and lunar light-producing spheres as well as the five subtle element spheres; thus, the group of sixteen beginning with the mind is said to be derived from ego. For this very reason, from the perspective of the causal aggregate:

The external principles (*tattva*s) are uniform in nature; however, from the perspective of the aggregate of instruments (*karaṇaskandha*), they possess distinct natures for each individual. Thus, the emergence of the group of sixteen does not arise from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) in the form of the aggregate of instruments, but rather from the solar-like orb in the form of the aggregate of causes (*kāraṇaskandha*).

It should be understood that the origin of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which consists of the group of instruments and forms and is distinct for each individual subject, as well as the origin of the sixteenfold group beginning with the mind (manas), occurs in this manner.
And this egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of the aggregate of instruments (*karaṇaskandha*),
is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) residing within the Self;
it is the innermost [aspect] of the Self, meaning it is the cause that serves as the means for the perception of all things, beginning with the earth.
Moreover:
...by which this world is colored. || 10-932 ||
The meaning is that by him the world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, was colored—that is, made to enter into its respective appropriate forms of self-identification. || 932 ||
And this— blind as it were, like a rutting elephant, approaches like a forest fire.
Just as a rutting elephant and a forest fire approach for the destruction of various trees, living beings, and so forth, [so does this].
Likewise, this blind one, without investigating what is logical or illogical, becomes the destroyer of the entire world through the sequence of taking up pride in that [delusion].
Is this nature of his, which causes harm to others, produced from himself? No; it says:
"Rudra is indeed his presiding deity (adhideva), by whom he is always impelled. (10.933)

Regarding Rudra, who was previously mentioned— wherein it was stated: "Rudra, the Lord and Master of the ego-sense, resides in the Middle Country"— he is impelled for the sake of protecting the cycle of existence, being set to work upon his own task within the nature of the ego-sense (*abhimāna*).
Those who stand surrounding this, they too—
Chagalāṇḍa and the others, O Goddess, were previously described by me.
This [section] is concluded.
Above the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the veil of the intellect (buddhyāvaraṇa) is then described. || 10-934 ||
Possessing a splendor equal to the radiance of thousands of millions of suns;
"varcas" means brilliance or light.
Furthermore—listen now to the world of the eight classes of divine beings right here [on this earth]. (10.935)

The intention of the word "eva" (only) is that the eight worlds exist right here, within this very principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), which is endowed with the eight qualities such as *dharma* and exists in its supreme form; these are the eight divine births, beginning from the *paiśāca* and ending with the *brahma*, which were previously described as being in the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and which abide through the variety of their *sāttvika* and other mental dispositions.
Therein is a world named Kakubha, possessing a luster equal to the dawn-red of twilight,
and it is filled with joyful women who are his mental emanations.
Mental [pleasures] are those conformable to the mind. || 936 ||
Furthermore—
there dwell Piśācas, possessing a luster equal to the dawn-red twilight,
numbering ten thousand crores...
Furthermore:
[the merit] of those inhabitants dwelling there. || 10-937 ||
In the middle—
there is one named Svananda, valiant...
and he is among those very ones—
...among the Piśācas, the Great Lord is like the twilight-red in hue, with the appearance of a Bandhūka flower. || 10.938 ||
Adorned with earrings, decorated with necklaces and armlets, wearing a crown and bracelets, with a diadem and beautiful golden garments. || 10.939 ||
He was surrounded by a vast multitude of spirits, as well as by those attending at his side,
who assumed various forms, sported playfully, and were adorned with divine ornaments.
With divine garlands and ointments, endowed with divine sovereignty;

*mauli* is a crest-jewel. Divine sovereignty consists precisely of the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā*, which are appropriate for a *piśāca*; likewise, in what follows, "divinity" refers to that which is appropriate to each respective being.
It must be considered.
And he, possessed of great splendor, was surrounded by these [beings], like a great host by its attendants. || 10.941 ||
He whose hosts are great is Mahāgaṇa, the Great God.
Now, hereafter, I shall describe the great realm of the Rākṣasas,
which resembles the throat of a cuckoo and is like a dark blue cloud. (10.942)
In that divine world, endowed with celestial sovereignty,
there was indeed the great Karāla, lord of the Rākṣasas, resembling natural collyrium in appearance.
Wearing a crown and earrings, radiant and of great splendor, he shone like a majestic mountain fire, resembling pure black collyrium. || 10.944 ||
He whose splendor is known as Śrī (Glorious Radiance) is for that very reason compared to a forest fire abounding in smoke. || 944 ||
And its retinue consists of ten thousand koṭis of rākṣasas named Muditās;
possessing the hue of bumblebees and clouds, these beings of great splendor dwell here. (10.945)
Now,
from this point forward, I shall describe the great world of the Yakṣas,
which is entirely made of Jāmbūnada gold and resplendent with divine jewels.
In that auspicious world, which is completely surrounded by enjoyments arising from sovereignty, there dwells the king of the yakṣas named Subhadra.
Shining with the color of molten gold, adorned with a crown and other ornaments,
he was accompanied by thousands of tens of millions of yakṣas of immeasurable prowess.
Surrounded by all of them, Śarva shines like Śarva with all his hosts. Now,
from this point forward, I shall describe the great world of the Gandharvas.
It resembles the yellow *kauśītakī* flower and has a luster equal to that of the *campaka*;
*kauśītakī* is a specific type of flower.
In that divine world, O beloved, there was indeed one named Surūpa.
He is like Gandhamādana, the lord of the Gandharva gods,
because of his immovability.
Likewise:
"Resembling molten gold, with a radiance like that of the young sun. || 10-951 ||
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, he was adorned with divine ornaments,
and he was surrounded by ten thousand times ten million gandharvas.
The Gandharvas named Svakāntas, adorned with variegated garlands and ointments, resemble fragments of realgar as well as yellow orpiment.
All of them wear variegated garments and are adorned with colorful ornaments.
Now,
O Pārvatī, I shall describe that which is even higher than that, the station of Indra.
Above that is the region known as Bṛhadbhoga, which grants all desires;
it is white like a conch shell or cow’s milk, resembling the autumnal kunda flower and the moon. (10.955)
"Bṛhadbhoga" is a name according to its literal meaning; "ūrdhva" means excellent. || 955 ||
In that divine world, endowed with hundreds of celestial wonders,
dwells the Lord named Vibhūti, the great Indra and sovereign of the world.
Resembling the orb of the moon, adorned with strings of pearls, wearing white garments, glorious, and anointed with white garlands and unguents. || 10-957 ||
With his crown blazing and adorned with two radiant earrings,
wearing necklaces and armlets, he was white and decorated with a white turban.
The gods known as the Bhūtijas are indeed endowed with supreme prosperity;
they wear crowns and earrings, and are adorned with divine garlands.
Ten thousand times ten million gods, including Indras, are proclaimed;
by them the one of great splendor is surrounded, like the moon by the stars.
They are called "born of prosperity" (bhūtijāḥ) because they are born together with prosperity. || 960 ||
Beyond this, however,
is the auspicious world named Manoja, resembling the autumnal moon;
it is radiant like a white cloud, possessing the brilliant luster of a pearl necklace.
There indeed resides the supreme Moon, named Amṛta;
he resembles pure crystal, is glorious, and wears white garments.
Adorned with earrings that resemble blazing light, he shines resplendent;
his limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and he is decorated with celestial ornaments.
There, indeed, are the gods named Raśmis, who possess a splendor equal to the array of rays.
Those who are divine and gentle should be known as having arisen from the splendor of Soma.
There are indeed ten thousand times ten million of those of gentle splendor.
Now,
O Goddess of the Gods, beyond this is the great world of Prajeśa.
In that divine world, you shall be the lord of subjects, possessed of immeasurable luster, universal in form, universal in color, and adorned with all ornaments.
Surrounded by gods who possess universal forms, the Supreme Self,
whose splendor is immeasurable, has this name.
And of them—
ten thousand times ten million Viśvas of immense splendor.
Surrounding the Great-Souled One, they wait upon him in a beautiful manner.
The word *viśvānām* is a designation [of the worlds]; for this very reason, because it is not a pronominal (*asarvanāman*), there is no application of the *suṭ* augment.
The word *śobhane* is an adjective qualifying the worlds (*bhuvana*).
Now, from this [it should be known that] the Brahma [mantra] is likewise to be understood as resembling a conch shell or cow’s milk. || 10-968 ||
There the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) resides, gentle of aspect, seated upon a white lotus,
wearing white garments, glorious, and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
Wearing a white sacred thread and adorned with great necklaces,
he was accompanied by ten thousand times ten million [beings] possessing a radiance equal to the orb of the moon.
Surrounded by the Brahma-deities like the sun by autumnal clouds—thus it was:
[he beheld] the Piśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra [realms]. (10.971)
Likewise, O beloved, the Saumya, Prājeśa, and Brāhma worlds are said to have presiding deities; this is the meaning.
These indeed are the cities that serve as the abodes for those born of the divine race.
These cities are indeed the primary abodes and the principal seats of residence for those born of the divine race.
And from these places, descending and meditating upon their own births, they indeed come into existence, impelled by the command of the Supreme Lord and urged on by Māyā. (10.973)
And constrained by the destiny of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
they are manifested at the beginning of creation in manifold ways through names and forms.
O lady of excellent hips, [it occurs] by a mere portion...

clearly manifesting as a vast physical body; this refers to the daily task at the beginning of creation and so forth, pertaining to that Brahmā who is the sovereign of Satyaloka within the cosmic egg.

At the beginning of creation, those who possess forms appropriate to their respective stations manifest; meditating upon Brahmā, the self-born who resides within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), they are born within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) by the command of the Supreme Lord and through the power of *māyā* and other factors. They—
They are manifested by a mere fraction alone.
Furthermore, these [elements] do not abandon their own abode in every respect—
that is, they do not leave the "abode" which is their own place situated within the intellect (buddhi).
Having thus explained the eightfold divine birth-states situated within the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*),
he says— with the intention that one should not forget what is relevant to the initiation (*bhuvana-dīkṣā*) currently under discussion—
"The self should be purified by means of mantras, together with the *puryaṣṭaka* and the senses. (10.975)
When the world-born collection, extending up to the intellect (*buddhi*), has been purified,

that Self which remains together with the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)— consisting of the subtle elements, mind, ego, and intellect— and along with the external instruments of the senses, is [the one] who [is purified] by means of the mantras; that is the meaning.

In the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā), one should purify [the site] by means of the Mūla-mantra, Vāmadeva, and the others, which are free from the divisions according to the ritual action, following the previously established arrangement; "is being purified" (viśodhyate) is the clear reading. || 975 ||

Concluding this and introducing another topic, he says: "Having thus purified the five groups of eight and the eight forms, as well as the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) in due order through diligent effort, [one proceeds] thereafter to the group of eight Krodhas. (10.976)
The word "should purify" (*viśodhayet*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. By the mention of "in due order," the following intention is expressed:

having purified the four groups of eight, beginning with the secret (*guhya*) and ending with the principles (*tattva*) from water up to space, one then purifies the eight forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Śarva, which reside within the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the moon, the sun, and the altar-circle (*vedyamaṇḍala*).
They are to be purified; then,

having purified the eleven presiding deities of the organs of action and perception, beginning with Agni and ending with Soma, one purifies the fifth group of eight, the *sthāṇvaṣṭaka*, which resides in the *ahaṃkāra*, and after that, those residing in the *buddhi*.
"And let there be no contempt at the time of action regarding the deliverance from saṃsāra.
Having thus purified up to this point, he indicates that group of eight Krodheśvaras residing within the principle of *buddhi* which is to be purified:
Saṃvarta, Ekavīra, Kṛtānta, Jananāśaka, ... [and so forth].
The slayer of death, Raktākṣa, the one of great wrath, and the invincible. || 10-977 ||

This group of eight wrathful deities (*krodhāṣṭaka*) is so called because it is characterized by Rudra, who presides over wrath under the name Mahākrodha. And these [are listed] in the *Rurusaṃgraha*:
"Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, and Sūraka..."
"Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikhī, Deśa, Hita, and Īśvara"—thus they are also recited under these alternative names. (4.17) || 977 ||
Their worlds indeed have the luster of blue lotus petals;
the retinue for each one consists of one hundred and ten million.
Now, in this very reality—above the eight Lords of Wrath (Krodheśvaras) stands the great group of eight Splendors (Tejoṣṭaka):
Balādhyakṣa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tridaśa, and Tripurāntaka; || 10.979 ||
He is all forms and yet tranquil; "nimeṣonmeṣa" means the opening [of the eyes] together with the closing.
And their retinue is said to consist of fifteen thousand [attendants]. || 10-980 ||
He states the reason for the designation "Tejoṣṭaka" (the group of eight consisting of fire):
"For these are remembered as Agni-Rudras; by their splendor they are black-colored.
Because they are radiant like fire, they are Agni-Rudras, characterized by splendor consisting of the radiance of knowledge; for this very reason..."
Furthermore, this is called the "eightfold light" because it presides over the eightfold light whose nature is the radiance residing within the intellect (buddhi).
Their worlds, indeed, are variegated and shaped like tortoises.
Now,
therefore, the unsurpassed eightfold yoga is fully described for those established in both samprajñāta and asamprajñāta yoga.

Because it is the presiding authority over yogins, it is the "Eightfold Yoga"; for this very reason, it is "unsurpassed" (anuttama) due to its superiority in comparison to the preceding eightfold sets.
And that is—both the uncreated and the created, as well as the Raibhava and the Brāhma. || 10-982 ||
Then there is the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Auma, and the Śraikaṇṭha;
this [is] the Raibhava of the Ribhus, the gods. In this same manner, "the Brāhma world" and so forth are to be applied.
Therefore, the explanation that it means "that which exists there in the *rā* (wealth)" and so on is incorrect. And this is the eightfold yoga.
In the *Śrīmālinīvijaya* (5.24–25),

it is stated that for those established in yoga with qualities (*saguṇa-yoga*), the intellect characterized by the quality of pure *sattva*, or *pradhāna*, is the state of attainment; thus, there is no difference whatsoever in the underlying reality.
And for this reason: "There the yogins sport with worlds that have the luster of crystal. (10.983)

Among them, those established in the yoga of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya-yoga) abide in the unconditioned state (akṛta-pada); those established in the yoga of action (karma-yoga) abide in the conditioned state (kṛta-pada);

those who have attained the yoga of emanation (nirmāṇa-yoga) abide in the state of sovereignty (īśvara-pada); those who practice the yoga of non-dual puruṣa abide in the state of Brahman (brahma-pada);
those who practice the yoga taught in the Vaiṣṇava scriptures abide in the state of Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇava-pada); and those who have perfected the yoga of celibacy (brahmacarya).
In the station of Kumāra, they sport, characterized by worlds that are transparent with the luster of crystal.
Above that is the abode of Umā and Śrīkaṇṭha,
wherein the relationship of power and the possessor of power is taught according to the Śaiva Siddhānta.
This is the state of attainment for those who have perfected the cessation of mental fluctuations through the prior practice of the worship of the Lord.
Regarding that, he describes the world of the blessed goddess Umā, the Śivayoginī, who abides in a supreme form beyond the eightfold yoga:
"Beyond that, the blessed Mother of the World is directly established."
O Umā, you are immeasurable, the source of the universe, and self-existent.
By the use of the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*), he states that among the eight yogas, there is an incarnation of a portion (*aṃśāvataraṇa*) of the Blessed Lady;
this should likewise be understood regarding the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭha who is about to be described.
[She is called] "Self-born" (*svayambhū*) because, by virtue of her sovereignty (*svātantrya*), she remains there for the sake of bestowing grace upon others.
She has not attained this state through the power of yoga like other yogis.
And she—
