resembling molten gold, possessing the radiance of the rising sun—
is seated upon a beautiful, great jewel throne endowed with eight lions.
The ellipsis "is situated" is to be supplied; [she is] on that [island] which is one hundred yojanas in extent and adorned with divine garlands and pure ornaments.
Furthermore:
The divine goddess Kuṇḍalinī is adorned with a great necklace. || 10-986 ||
Moreover—
before Vijaya stood the highly fortunate Jayā, possessing a form as excellent as Śrī herself,
with a radiance like the interior of a lotus and adorned with every ornament. (10.987)
And Nandā, with eyes like lotus petals, adorned with necklaces and armlets, her limbs variegated by all manner of ornaments; and Sunandā, who is captivating to the mind.
The female doorkeepers stood surrounding her on all sides;
"like Śrī" means like the form of Śrī mentioned previously. "On all sides" means in the four directions.
Furthermore: thirty thousand crores and three hundred crores. (10.989)
Those various divine and noble women always attend upon him;
"those" refers to the supramundane ones. In the reading "triṃśatkoṭī," the transposition of vowels is a Vedic (chāndasa) anomaly.
Furthermore:
"And there is one celestial chariot for each of the Rudras of immense splendor."
There it exists. || 990 ||
And since those Rudras, residing in their celestial palaces (vimānas), were solely intent upon his propitiation,
they were designated as "Aumā.
Furthermore—

"Vaimānas" means they are otherwise. She from whom pride (*māna*)—the conceit regarding objects such as the body and the senses—has departed is the Blessed Lady *Vimānā*; those who belong to her are the *Vaimānas*.
For these indeed worship that one Goddess as sons do their mother. || 991 ||
And she did not remain there solely intent on bestowing grace;
rather, O fair-faced one, having descended into the midst of the cosmic egg together with me,
that eternal one manifested for the sake of favoring the worlds.

The meaning is that she, who is eternal and constant, has manifested— having assumed various names, forms, and appearances through her pervasion of the phenomenal world— for the sake of bestowing grace upon men;
that is to say, she has become manifest along with me, as will be described later in the incarnation of Śrīkaṇṭha who dwells on Kailāsa.
The meaning is "together with. || 992 ||
He says that she has appeared in every kalpa under various different names:
"In the first kalpa she was Jaganmātā; in the second, Jagadyoni; in the third, she was named Śāmbhavī; and in the fourth, Viśvarūpiṇī. (10.993)
In the fifth [kalpa] she was named Nandinī, and in the sixth she was Gaṇāmbikā;
in the seventh kalpa she was Vibhūti, and likewise Subhūti in the eighth.
Ānandā was in the ninth kalpa, Vāmalocanā in the tenth, Varārohā in the eleventh, and Sumaṅgalā in the twelfth. (10.995)
In the thirteenth kalpa, O Goddess, she is proclaimed as Mahātanu;
and in the fourteenth kalpa, she is celebrated by the name Anantā.
Bhūtamātā is remembered as being on the fifteenth and the sixteenth [day];
Sahasradhārā is on the seventeenth, and Satī was formerly on the eighteenth.

A kalpa, consisting of fourteen intermediate periods (manvantaras), is a single day of Brahmā; at its conclusion, the fire of time (kālāgni) consumes the world. Within that [cycle], she has descended in succession through the first, second, and subsequent kalpas under these various names and forms for the sake of favoring the worlds.
Or let it be; enough with this innumerable recounting of those various incarnations belonging to countless past kalpas.
Rather, in this very present Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, there was the auspicious daughter of Dakṣa.

Because he was created by Brahmā with his own eyes (cakṣus), he is Cākṣuṣa; the *kalpa* belonging to that Manu Prajāpati—meaning, during this *kalpa* connected to him, which constitutes the first Manvantara—you descended for the sake of favoring the worlds in the form of the daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati. This is the meaning.
And having descended—
due to the insult from Dakṣa, you formerly cast off your own body.
This is indeed well-known in the Purāṇas. || 998 ||
Then that very [power],
out of affection for Maheśvara, remained filling up again that digit of the moon called Amā, which resides upon his head and nourishes the universe.
"Having filled the digit of the moon"—even so, the Goddess has as her sole purpose the grace of the world.
Then the Supreme Goddess, impelled by a desire to show grace,
once again worshipped Himavān and made him her own daughter.
O Goddess, you,
having assumed such a form... having performed a most wondrous penance that is exceedingly difficult to practice...
"O beloved, having regained me as your husband once more, you have become one whose lotuses are in full bloom."
"Me"—that is, the Supreme Lord Himself, who by His absolute sovereignty has assumed the form of a resident of Kailāsa;
"climbing onto the lap" means she who has ascended to the position of the left half of His body. 1000.
Thus it is:
"O fair-faced one, I, whose abode is Kailāsa, together with you— and by the sight of me for my devotee— "
You are the body of the left half...
and therefore, just as when the reality is perceived, even in the state of [manifested] form, you are never separated from me. 10.1001.
Not only in this present kalpa have you existed as half of my body, but furthermore—
you were born again at Dakṣa’s sacrifice under the name Bhadrakālī; "again" means in another sacrifice of Dakṣa.
The meaning is that, due to the excellence of the worship performed by Dakṣa Prajāpati, you became incarnated as Bhadrakālī for the sake of bestowing grace upon him.
Thus, you are indeed of another form—Satī, the supreme embodiment of Ekānaṃśā, who has emerged from Śiva. || 10.1002 ||

"Being one, undivided, and of non-dual form"— thus, you are the other supreme form that has emerged from Īśāna, appearing in the various ways described as the manifold other forms; this occurs solely through the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord.
The meaning is that she remains thus desiring to show grace to the world;
furthermore, the meaning is that she has also descended as the deity named Ekānaṃśā. || 1002 ||
Furthermore:
Having reached this cycle of four ages (caturyuga), during the Dvāpara [Yuga], she was born as Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā together with Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying Mahiṣa.

In the Dvāpara age of the current cycle of four yugas, having been propitiated by Viṣṇu according to the method prescribed in the Śrī-Bhadrakālī-purāṇa, she descended along with him— who was her brother—
for the sake of slaying the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Furthermore:
Known by various synonymous names such as Kātyāyanī and Durgā,
she is affectionate toward her devotees and grants boons to those humans who are devoted to her.

"You have already descended upon the summit of the Vindhya mountain under various synonymous names," such as Vindhyavāsinī, Bhramaravāsinī, and other distinct appellations. [The word] *kātya* refers to the offspring of Kāta, who was born among the Vṛṣṇis. His...

Kātyāyanī is the sister of Viṣṇu, the progeny of the Primordial Person who took the incarnation as Kṛṣṇa. She is called Durgā because she is difficult to reach—even by sages through the hardships of recitation, sacrifice, charity, and austerity—and is attained only by those possessed of devotion; and she resides upon the summit of the Vindhya mountains.
"Already descended"— this means that at the very beginning of this kalpa,
you descended upon the peak of the Vindhya mountain in Jambūdvīpa for the sake of bestowing grace upon your devotees;
now, however—
Henceforth, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall describe the world-system.
It is renowned as Sucāvī, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns;
it has the form of a peak of Kailāsa and the luster of pure crystal.
It was surrounded by millions of great celestial palaces belonging to the Cakravartins.
These lords of mantras, the Cakravartins, have descended here for the sake of bestowing grace by assuming physical forms.
In that divine realm, [the Lord] possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns.
He has a thousand arms and feet, a thousand faces and eyes;
he is the Lord of Umā, the Master of the World, the supreme bestower of grace upon all.
And for that Blessed One Viśvabhoṭḥu,
the entire place of enjoyment is indeed situated there on the left side;
resting upon the left half of the body from the left side, everything remains right there.

The left half is the locus of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*), consisting of the nature of all objects to be enjoyed (*bhogya*) without exception, while the right half is indeed the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Thus, this Blessed Lord has the entire universe as his body, consisting of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed; for this very reason, he possesses a form with a thousand arms, feet, and so forth.
Furthermore,
this [place]— extending for a hundred yojanas and adorned with various jewels— || 10.1009 ||
Upon a supreme, divine seat, covered with celestial rugs, radiant as a hundred suns, and variegated with jeweled lotuses.
The one of great splendor sat down, surrounded by eight bulls;
he wore golden and Chinese garments and was adorned with necklaces and armlets.
He wore two earrings that were brilliantly shining like the orb of the sun, throbbing with a mass of rays and crowded with beams of light.
*Mayūkhāḥ* are subtle rays of light, whereas *raśmayaḥ* are coarse rays.
Furthermore:
Wearing upon his head a crown variegated with divine jewels, which was exceedingly brilliant, most fierce, and resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa. || 10.1013 ||
His great necklace, Pralamba, was thick with radiating rays,
like a mountain torrent falling from a peak of the Himalayas into the Ganges.
Moreover:
with thirty thousand crores and likewise three hundred crores [of beings], all bearing tridents, wearing matted hair, possessing three eyes, and adorned with celestial ornaments. || 10.1015 ||
He was surrounded by Rudras assuming various forms as well as hosts of spirits,
and was encircled by divine and mind-born women.
Indeed, he was entirely surrounded by hundreds of millions of celestial palaces;
furthermore— The seven Mothers, possessing form, adorned with various ornaments. (10.1017)

Surrounding the Great-Souled One, they stood encircling him on all sides; he spoke to them according to their respective directions: "The goddess Brāhmī, with the luster of a lotus petal, adorned with divine ornaments... (10.1018)
O Goddess of gods, she stands in the southeastern direction like another Śrī;
O fair-faced one, she resembles a conch shell or cow’s milk in the northeastern direction.
The highly resplendent Māheśvarī stands there, honored by the gods;
and Kaumārī, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, is adorned with necklaces and armlets.
In the northern direction, O Goddess of the Gods, she is attended by Kāminī;
she resembles a glossy blue lotus and is adorned with necklaces and earrings.
In the southern direction, she worships the Supreme Lord;
she is renowned as Vaiṣṇavī by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
This [Goddess] is meditated upon as being presided over by Śiva alone, and not by Viṣṇu;
on the contrary, it is precisely because she is presided over by a portion of his power that he possesses the nature of Viṣṇu. || 1022 ||
Resembling a dark blue cloud and adorned with all ornaments,
O Goddess of gods, Vārāhī stands present in the western quarter.
White as a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and adorned with necklaces and earrings,
that goddess Indrāṇī stood present in the eastern direction.
Terror-inspiring with her face aflame, adorned with all ornaments,
Cāmuṇḍā worships the Supreme Lord in the south-western direction.
These seven are her attendants; however, the goddess Umā, who occupies half of the Lord’s body, is the eighth. She alone is Yogeśvarī, of whom these are the manifestation (*prapañca*).
As he will say:
"Becoming sevenfold from being one" (10.1029).
For this very reason, previously—
"One should worship the god Mātṛkābhairava with the *avarga*;
Bhairavī is to be worshipped with the *kādi* [vowels], and one should worship the Mothers with the [consonant] groups.
(1.34) Thus it is said.
On the occasion of this explanation, the arrangement has been shown in accordance with the temple located here. || 1025 ||
And these goddesses do not indeed abandon that God, who is endowed with all states of being; they remain with their entire being,
perceiving everything internally and externally through their all-encompassing vision.
Endowed with non-dual pervasion, it is the presiding substratum.
Thus, although these [energies] are constantly followed by the Supreme Lord, they have been brought down to the human world in part by Brahmā. || 10.1026 ||
For the sake of slaying the Asuras and for the benefit of human beings;
"benefit" (hita) means favor (anugraha). The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but/rather).
"How was she brought down?"—to this he says:
"After performing most terrible asceticism by Brahmā, the sustainer of the world. (10.1027)
By one who acts for the welfare of living beings. || 1027 ||
Furthermore:
"For the sake of slaying Ruru, they were also brought down by me.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this was done by me as a sovereign lord, and not by performing austerities like Brahmā.
And this embodied form of theirs is not their ultimate reality; rather, these [energies]—autonomous, supreme, and distinct—are established in the supreme void. (10.1028)

"Attending upon the Svacchanda [Lord] according to the distinction between the higher and the lower"—the word "always remaining" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The "higher" Svacchanda is the Bhairava of Consciousness (*cid-bhairava*) in His supreme form, which is non-different from that [consciousness]; the "lower" is the form of Umāpati. By this which has been thus stated...
And by this very analysis, this Lord of Umā is indeed the very essence of the expansion of Supreme Bhairava.

With this very intention, we have rightly explained the term "Supreme Bhairava" in the opening sūtra; for it is said that the Lord of Umā is Bhairava because his essence is the existence of Supreme Bhairava.
And he says that these Mothers consist of the pervasive expansion of the supreme power (paraśakti):
"Uma herself, having become sevenfold through various changes of name and form... (10.1029).
Thus that Blessed Lord, surrounded by his Mothers,
dwells there with supreme splendor, illuminating the world.

Umā is the supreme goddess, consisting of the radiance of knowledge; together with her, Maheśvara is the eightfold power, for Umā herself, abiding in seven ways, is non-different from the body of the Lord of Umā.
For this very reason, these [verses] consist solely of the essence of pervasion (vyāpti): "And likewise, above him, the wise one, there are eight forms;
above this beautiful world, of that wise one"—this refers to Him who is non-different from Umāpati.
The eight forms belonging to the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha— who is established in the reality of the qualities (guṇas) and principles (tattvas) to be described hereafter—
are the Lords of Form (mūrtīśvaras). "And in that same way" means they exist in that very manner which is non-different from Śrīkaṇṭha himself.
She said to them: "Śarva, Bhava, the Blessed Rudra, and likewise Paśupati."
Īśāna, Bhīma, and Mahādeva-Ugra;
according to the perspective that will be explained later, Rudra should be recited immediately after Īśāna.
The compound [Mahādeva-Ugra] is to be understood as "Ugra together with Mahādeva."
With these aforementioned mantras, Śarva performs the most excellent creation. (10.1032)
The Lord, the Sovereign of Umā, by means of these eight forms— by this group of eight Mūrtīśvaras distinguished as supreme (parā), non-supreme (aparā), and so forth—
presides over the entire upper and lower plane as the very self of his own wheel of powers (*nija-śakti-cakra*).
"Creation" refers to the creation consisting of the gross and subtle forms, the elements and their subtle counterparts (*tanmātras*), and the *kalās* and so forth to be described hereafter;
"supreme" means that this aforementioned subtle and gross creation has emerged and is situated above.
The Blessed One, who is indeed the Lord of Speech (Umāpati), abides in various places according to the distinctions of higher and lower as will be described hereafter, and acts [therein]. || 1032 ||
"What is that creation?"—to this he says:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the sun, as well as the moon and the sacrificer; these eight are remembered as this creation. (10.1033)
This group of eight should be understood as existing here and there through the divisions of gross, subtle, and supreme.

And among those, in the initiation by means of the *uddhāta*, the nature of the earth and the other elements was previously shown by means of the stages beginning with the *bindu*; furthermore, the sun and moon are also of the nature of the power of the instruments (*karaṇa-śakti*).
And because he is their substratum, the sacrificer is the knower; this is indeed established throughout the entire path.
Thus, these are the Mūrteśvaras: "But they abide in him with their whole being, whereas elsewhere they abide only partially."

"In that" refers to the enclosure of the Lords of Form (mūrtīśāvaraṇa) situated within the principle of intellect (buddhitattva). "Elsewhere" refers to the enclosure of the subtle elements (tanmātrāvaraṇa) and within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
By way of this concluding summary, he demonstrates the extent of the Lord Umāpati’s pervasion of the phenomenal world:
"Thus the God resides in this [world], and likewise above the Brahma-world. (10.1034)
And on the summit of Meru resides Īśāna; furthermore, he is sought after as the eightfold yoga, known by the name Śrīkaṇṭha and dwelling in Kailāsa.
He remains pervading [the universe] through his eight forms beginning with Śarva.

"In this" refers to the most beautiful world; "above the world of Brahmā" refers to the world of Rudra; and "on the peak of Meru" refers to the summit of Jyotiṣka. Immediately thereafter, it is this very Lord who is intended by the "eightfold yoga," and not anything else.
That is something else entirely. Likewise, he who is known by the name Śrīkaṇṭha,
this very Lord of Umā residing on Kailāsa, pervades the universe— whether gross, subtle, or otherwise— in various places through these forms of the Lord, such as Śarva and the rest.

Therefore, because [all things] abide in identity with Him, this very one remains; thus, this pervasion of the phenomenal world (prapañca) belongs at all times to the One alone—that is to say, to the Supreme Lord. And this will become even more clearly evident in the eleventh [chapter].
He states that this world of Umāpati is their place of origin: "But those who fully practice the qualified yoga of Maheśvara... (10.1036).
Through devotion, celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint, those wise ones, having perceived the Self residing within the body, proceed to that state here.

But those who worship— that is, serve— with long-term, uninterrupted, and respectful practice the *parayoga* defined in the scriptures of Maheśvara as being "with qualities" (*saguṇa*) because it consists in abiding in the state of pure being (*sattva*), yet not as the form of immersion into the expansion of the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-ādi-śakti-sphāra-samāveśa-rūpa*), do not [perceive] that which resides in the body.

Having known the Self as having an unconditioned form and having directly realized their own nature as the agent, they go "here," meaning they attain the state of Umāpati through union (*sāyujya*) and other forms of liberation.
And in this regard, devotion is the primary cause, being the most essential among truth, celibacy, and self-restraint (*dama*). Self-restraint—
It is the conquest of the senses. And in this way, the fact that this yoga possesses attributes (saguṇatva) has been made manifest. || 1037 ||
And this state is not to be attained through the Śāmbhava yoga characterized by qualities (saguṇa);
rather— "Having beheld his mandala with supreme devotion, the wise ones who have abandoned duality and restrained their selves go there. (10.1038)

"Of him"—that is, of Umāpati; "the mandala"—meaning the sacrificial rite which is its locus; "having seen"—meaning that by seeing it, one obtains the initiation of the covenant (samayadīkṣā); and "by devotion to him"—meaning having become free from duality through the certainty that Umāpati alone is the one ultimate deity—for the sake of serving him.
With disciplined minds, as before, the wise—whose intellects are confident in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord—attain this state through union (sāyujya) and other means. || 1038 ||
Then, above them indeed, twelve Suśivas are situated;
they are "excellent Śivas" because, despite possessing individual forms, they have attained oneness with Śiva.
They consist of the forms of Pūrṇa, Sarvajña, and so forth. And they are: Vāma, Bhīma, Īśa, Śiva, and likewise Śarva. (10.1039)
The Lord of the Vidyās, the Sole Hero, the Holder of the Fierce [Power], Īśāna, the Consort of Umā, Ajeśa, and Ananta as well. (10.1040)
Likewise, Ekaśiva and the twelve Suśivas are remembered;
for their meditation—[they are described as] all resembling saffron in hue, with a radiance equal to ten million suns. || 10-1041 ||
Since the forms of the Lords of the Embodiments (Mūrtīśvaras), who reside within the various conch-shaped worlds,
consist of the very nature appropriate to the earth and other elements they preside over, this has not been mentioned here.
Now, from this point forward, Vīrabhadra is the sovereign lord of the maṇḍala. || 10-1042 ||

He is the sovereign of the eight lords of the mandalas, beginning with Mahādeva, who will be described hereafter. Furthermore, he is that supreme form of this very [deity] which was previously mentioned in the center of the Śveta and others, and above them; for this reason, he is called the Lord (prabhu). || 1042 ||
Now, he who is fully established in this meditation and so forth, having attained union with that [Brahman], rejoices together with it. Now—
Beyond this, O Great Goddess, they know the group of eight Mahādevas.
Mahādeva, Mahātejas, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Udbhava,
Ekapiṅga, Ekeṣaṇa, Īśāna, Bhuvaneśa, and Purahsara.
The eight Mahādevas, together with Aṅguṣṭhamātra, are the Śivas;
these, being liberated from the collyrium of Māyā, are esteemed by the Supreme Lord. (10.1045)
According to the principle set forth in the tenth chapter on the "Introduction to the Tantra" (*Tantrāvatāra-paṭala*), they are "approved by the Supreme Lord";
thus, through the lineage, they have been graced by the Supreme Lord in the form of the venerable Ananta.
Consequently, because they have attained the excellence of awakening, even while holding the office of the *māyāgarbha* (the womb of *māyā*).

It has been stated that they are "freed from the ointment of illusion. These lords of the mandala (maṇḍaleśvara) have been described here in one form; however, in another form, they will appear within the principle of Time (kālatattva). Regarding them, it is said in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:
"Mahātejas and the others, known as the lords of the maṇḍalas, reside in the principle of Māyā... (5-28). Thus have been stated these variations in the system. || 1045 ||
He concludes: "In brief, the lords of the worlds within the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) have been declared by me;
[namely] the five groups of eight—the divine origins, the wrathful ones, the splendors, and the forms—making forty."

Furthermore, above the eight worlds of Yoga are the worlds of Aum and Śrīkaṇṭha; then follow the twelve worlds of Suśiva and the eight of Mahādeva— thus, sixty-two worlds are said to be here, all of which must be purified in this extensive initiation into the worlds (bhuvanadīkṣā).
As for the method of purification in the abbreviated [version], it has been determined in the fifth chapter.
Now, above that is the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*).

It is entirely distinct from the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitattva*), which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities; for it consists of the predominance of the quality of *sattva*. Precisely because of this distinction, it is designated by the specific term "intellect" (*buddhi*).

How can an effect, such as a sprout from a seed, arise until it reaches a state of swelling characterized by some degree of differentiation? With this intention, the *guṇatattva* is mentioned here, which arises from the *prakṛtitattva* and is designated as not being significantly distinct from it.
It is taught as being a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*). However, in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya* and other texts,

because the designation of the "qualities" (*guṇa*) does not cease— just as the name "seed" persists even when it has slightly changed state or is about to sprout— the "principle of qualities" (*guṇatattva*) is described as being non-different from the "principle of primordial matter" (*prakṛtitattva*).

This is intended as a concise presentation of initiation regarding the world (*bhuvana*). However, since the detailed exposition of the ritual procedure for the worlds (*bhauvanavidhi*) is what is currently under discussion here, the *guṇatattva* is shown as distinct from the *prakṛtitattva*; therefore, one should not suspect any contradiction with the scriptures.
And this reality of the qualities (guṇatattva) is established within that very [pradhāna]. || 10.1046 ||
The three divine lineages of gurus...
"Divine" is said because of their possession of an extraordinary degree of power.
And that [Self] remains concealed by the qualities (guṇas);
the meaning is that it is seated upon the ground of sattva and the other [qualities].
Therein—the first row of darkness is situated above. (10.1047)
The meaning is that she has ascended above the quality of darkness (tamas). || 1047 ||
Therefore, in this regard—
their names are stated here correctly and in proper sequence.
"Theirs" refers to those gurus who stand at the end of the lineage.
Śiva, the Lord Vāmadeva, and the powerful Caṇḍa. || 10-1048 ||
Prahlāda, Uttama, Bhīma, Karāla, and likewise Piṅgala;
Mahendra, Dinakṛt, Pratoda, and Dakṣa as well.
Kalevara is renowned, as well as Kaṭaṅkaṭa;
Ambuhartā, Nārīśa, Śveta, and indeed the Ṛgveda. || 10.1050 ||
The Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and likewise the very auspicious Atharvaveda;
Virūpākṣa, Jyeṣṭha, Vipra, and likewise Nārāyaṇa.
Gaṇḍa, Nara, Yama, Mālī, Gahaneśa, and Pīḍana—
this is declared to be the first row, remembered as consisting of thirty-two Rudras.
Now, above Rajas, the second row is described:
Śukla, Dāsa, Sudāsa, Lokākṣa, and Sūrya. (10.1053)
Suhotra, Ekapāda, Gṛdhra, Śiveśvara,
Gautama, Yogīśa, and another, Dadhibāhu.
Ṛṣabha, Gokarṇa, and the god Maheśvara; Guhyeśāna, Śikhaṇḍin, Jaṭin, Mālin, and likewise Ugraka. || 10-1055 ||
Bhṛgu, Śikhin, Śūlin, Sugati, Supālana, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, Lāṅgalin, and Atidaṇḍaka. || 10-1056 ||
Bhavana, Tathābhavya, and Lakuleśa—these are declared to be the thirty Rudras; this is the second, most excellent row.
Now, above the Sattva [element], the third row is described:
the god Aruṇa, Dīrghabāhu, Atibhūti, and Sthāṇuka. (10.1058)
Sadyojāta, Jhiṇṭhī, Ṣaṇmukha, Caturānana, Cakrapāṇi, the one named Kūrma, and likewise Ardhanārīśvara. (10.1059)
Kapālī, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and likewise Vaṣaṭkāra;
Vauṣaṭkāra, as well as Svāhā and Svadhā, are thus proclaimed.
Saṃvartaka, Bhasmeśa, and Kāmanāśana—these are the twenty-one Rudras; this is the third row.

Thus, these eighty-three gurus should be known as supreme lords (*parameśvara*) who, desiring for those who wish to attain the enjoyment of the *guṇatattva*, bestow upon them the appropriate knowledge and yoga; having been appointed there for a certain period of time, they sport therein. As it has been said:
Endowed with the power of the yoga of knowledge, these supreme teachers sport;

even though they abide in the *guṇatattva* by means of the highest state (*uttamapada*), they are not colored by it. Thus he says: for this very reason they sport, and are not bound by the *guṇas* like others.
For: "Those liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra...
means those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), being free from the impurities of the individual self (āṇava), karma, and māyā.
Furthermore:
...completely free from great delusion. || 10-1062 ||
Great delusion (*mahāmoha*) here consists of the nature of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), which is *māyā*; they are free from that, and for this very reason, they are pure.
Due to the dawning of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), all these gurus are three-eyed and as stainless as pure crystal.
They are all-knowing and all-pervading, acting for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.
Omniscience is their attainment through the yoga of all-encompassing knowledge.

As for the claim made by some—following the views of the Sāṅkhya and Pātañjala—that this [omniscience] arises from delusion regarding the locus of the qualities (*sattva-guṇa*) and the principles (*tattva*), that is simply not the case; for these [systems] are merely motivated by the desire for worldly enjoyment.
Those who have attained those stages abide there through union with the Supreme Lord. || 1063 ||
And for this reason, the divine worlds of all these [beings] are shaped like elephants;
previously—
By the passage beginning with "And the abode of Vīrabhadra, as well as the temple of Bhadrakālī;
[these] with thirteen...
(10.759), the eleven worlds beginning with Śveta are indicated.

Together with the worlds of Bhadrakālī and Vīrabhadra, thirteen [worlds] are thus enumerated. As for what was further stated: "...adorned by other worlds as well" (10.759), those other worlds are situated above the world of Vīrabhadra.
Now, in order to enumerate the Rudras from the world of Rudra—measuring only a thumb's breadth—up to the end of the *guṇatattva*, which were previously not enumerated, he says:
"Learn from me those Rudras who exist from the intellect (*buddhi*) up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (10.1064)
"Of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*) means: understand those [principles] which remain to be enumerated prior to the intellect. To what limit? He says: "ending with primordial nature" (*prakṛtiparyante*).

That in which primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is at the end is "ending with primordial nature"; that is, the principle of the *guṇas* (*guṇatattva*); the meaning is "having that as the limit. || 1064 ||
He enumerates those Rudras by way of the compendium of the worlds:
"O fair-faced one, there are two hundred and seven worlds.
Among them [are the worlds] of the Lord of the Water-enclosure (who is) the size of a thumb, of Earth, of the Ocean, and of Śrī."
There are thirteen worlds: those of Sarasvatī and the Guhyāṣṭaka;
then those of Śivāgni and the Atiguhyāṣṭaka; those of Vāyvīśa and the Guhyātiguhyāṣṭaka;
those of Ākāśeśa and the Pavitrādyaṣṭaka; and thereafter those presided over by the Mūrtīśas beginning with Śarva.
There are eight mandalas consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sun, the moon, and the Vedas;
beyond those, there are five mandalas of the instruments (karaṇa), illumination (prakāśa), rays (raśmi), the sun, and the moon, belonging to the Lord of Ego (ahaṅkāreśa);
and then eight belonging to the group of eight Sthāṇus—thus, up to the second tooth, there are sixty-two worlds.

Even in the case of the Buddha, according to the previously stated method, there are sixty-two; and in the principle of Guṇatattva, there are eighty-three; thus, these two hundreds amount to two hundred and seven.
Moreover, in this very context— O fair-faced one, those others who exist included herein have not been mentioned.

Those lords of the worlds who are described in the *Bṛhattantras* as Rudras—such as those residing in the realms of error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*)—are not mentioned here separately, because they are already included within this very [system]. || 1065 ||
Now, beyond the qualities (guṇas), the Pradhāna is proclaimed.
It is called Pradhāna because the entire universe, ending with the qualities, is deposited within it.
Therein, those Rudras who are established—
I shall describe them to you in brief. || 10-1066 ||
Krodheśvara, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, Krūradṛk, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikheda, Sahita, and Īśvara. (10.1067)
These eight, including Śikhidhva, are the lords residing within the primary principle (pradhānatattva); this is the meaning. || 1067 ||
These aforementioned Rudras, who possess great heroism, are proclaimed to belong to the primordial nature (*prākṛta-tattva*);
the meaning is that they are difficult to overcome.
Regarding the essential nature of this primary principle (pradhānatattva), he says:
"That which is the ultimate limit of the qualities (guṇas) is here called pradhāna. (10.1068)
The ultimate limit is the state of non-differentiation. || 1068 ||
Now, therefore—listen to me regarding the worlds within the principle of the Puruṣa.
"Therefore" means above Prakṛti; [this occurs] due to the concealment of the essential nature of the Supreme Lord.

The principle of the Puruṣa has the nature of a contracted manifestation of consciousness; whereas the worlds therein depend upon the aspect of contraction, they [ultimately] depend upon pure consciousness alone, because that [consciousness] is devoid of modification.
In that regard, first of all:
Ambā, Salilā, Oghā, Vṛṣṭi, and together with Tārayā. (10.1069)
Sutārā, Sunetrā, and Kumārī after her;
and likewise Uttamāmbhasikā—these nine are proclaimed as the Tuṣṭis. || 10-1070 ||
Likewise:
Tārā, Sutārā, Tārayantī, Pramodikā, Pramoditā, Modamānā, and Ramyakā beyond that. (10.1071)
And Sadāpramuditā— these are declared to be the eight attainments (siddhis).

As for the nine contentments (tuṣṭis) and the eight attainments that are enumerated in the Sāṃkhya treatise as objects to be cultivated by means of the intellect (buddhi), because they are qualities of the intellect, they are here [included] within the nature of the contracted consciousness.
The sheaths (kañcuka) beginning with *kalā* serve as a veil for the *puruṣa*, who is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because he is incapable of discernment;

however, no enjoyment whatsoever can possibly arise in the *puruṣa*, whose nature is pure consciousness (*dṛśimātra*) and who is not an enjoyer, through the influence of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties.
For it is not the case that when snow is reflected within Devadatta, [Devadatta becomes cold].

Experience characterized by the perception of cold can occur even in a figurative sense. Therefore, since all this experience is possible only when there exists a supreme enjoyer in the form of the Puruṣa as previously described, it is logical that the presence of notions such as contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and so forth resides in Him alone; thus it has been stated. In that regard—

"The four internal [sources of suffering] are called nature, acquisition, time, and fortune; the five [external ones] arise from the cessation of sense-objects due to the hardships of acquisition, preservation, attachment, destruction, and misfortune. (Sāṅkhyakārikā).
Likewise:
"Reasoning, oral instruction, study, the three-fold destruction of suffering, acquisition of friends,
and charity— these are the eight perfections (siddhis) according to the Sāṃkhyas. Thus [it is said].
"The contentment that arises from perceiving what is not reality as reality is 'tuṣṭi' (satisfaction) here;
the notion of something worth accepting even toward what is to be rejected is 'siddhi' (accomplishment). Thus have the satisfactions and accomplishments been defined by the Teachers.
Their presiding deities, beginning with Ambā and Tārā, are established here as being situated in the worlds corresponding to these names.

Furthermore, he states that even the sovereignty consisting of the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā*, which is to be accomplished through the stages of yoga according to the Pārameśvara doctrine, is presided over by these very eight deities and exists right here within the *puruṣa-tattva* as a veil, in accordance with the previously explained principle: He says: [the following verse]...
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and likewise prāpti; || 10-1072 ||

Likewise, there is irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and that which is called mastery (vaśitva); and the power of determining things according to one's desire (yatrakāmāvasāyitva)—these are remembered as the eightfold [powers] beginning with atomization (aṇimā). || 10-1073 ||

Aṇimā is the capacity to make the body subtle; laghimā is the power to produce lightness like that of cotton wool; mahimā is the power to produce greatness; prāpti is the attainment of any desired place by mere volition; and prākāmya is the state of being one's own master.

The power to produce various bodies simultaneously is *īśitva*, which is sovereignty; *vaśitva* is the subjugation of the elements; and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva* is the determination of objects—separated by space, time, or nature—by mere volition.

Because the Person (puṃs) is the enjoyer of the three qualities which constitute the objects of enjoyment, he too possesses qualities through connection with the reflection of those three qualities. || 1073 ||
Now, listen to the three rows of gurus and disciples that follow;
"thereafter" (ataḥ) means above the previously mentioned group of eight, beginning with *aṇimā*.
Therein—Maskarī, Pūraṇa, Kṛtsna, Kapila, and Kāśa as well. || 10-1074 ||
Sanatkumāra, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, and others were likewise portions [of him]; as were Kaśyapa, Nāsiketu, Gālava, and Bhautika. || 10.1075 ||
And Śākalya is celebrated, as is Durvāsas, the supreme ṛṣi;
and Vālmīki, the best of gurus, along with Parāśara and Gālava. (10.1076)
Pippalāda, the son of Sumitrā (Sautrāmaṇi), Vāyuputra, and Bhadantaka;
two Gālavas are mentioned here.
The disputants range from Maskarī to Bhadanta, concerning both the seen and the unseen. || 10-1077 ||
The first row is considered to consist of twenty-two excellent gurus.
And these were established by the will of the Lord in these positions as the cause for those to be graced to attain that very state, just as before. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"This was also previously taught by me to the high-souled Kapila" (16.24).

They say that this [practice] consisting of worship suitable for attaining the state is the "seen" (dṛṣṭa), while that which consists of the attainment of the state itself is the "unseen" (adṛṣṭa). And these twenty-two are indeed the gurus.
Beyond this, in order to set forth the sages in the form of disciples belonging to the lineage primarily characterized by the contact with *rajas*, he says:
"And Jahnu, Tṛṇabindu, Muni, and likewise Tārkṣya. (10.1078)
Dhyānāśraya, Dīrgha, Hotṛ, Jāgara, Agastya, Vasubhauma, and Upādhyāya are proclaimed as the preceptors. (10.1079)
Śukra, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Adhvaga, Sthūlaśiras, Bālakhilya, and Manu are thus proclaimed. (10.1080)

Vajrātreyas, Viśuddha, Śiva, and Arurathānuga; Bhauma together with Vasu—these two; Aṅgiras together with Bhṛgu—these also two; Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, alone; and Upādhyāya, whose name is this. These are the teachers (upādhyāyas).
This, however, is incorrect, because it would result in the contradiction of the number that is about to be stated.
Thus, in this manner—the lineage beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru—is intended as the second row. || 1081 ||
Then, regarding even the stage characterized by the contact with sentient beings (*sattvasaṃsparśavatī*), it is said:
Hara, Jhiṇṭhī, Pratoda, and Amareśa as the fourth;
Kṛṣṇapiṅgeśa-Rudra, Indrajit, Vṛṣaka, and Śiva. (10.1082)
Yama, the renowned Krūra, Gaṅgādhara, Umāpati,
Bhūteśvara, Kapālīśa, and likewise Śaṅkara.
Ardhanārīśvara, and likewise Piṅgala as another; Mahākāla, Saṃvarta, Maṇḍalī, and Ekavīraka. || 10-1084 ||
Likewise, another renowned one is the eternal Bhārabhūteśvara;
Kṛṣṇapiṅgeśa and Rudra are indeed one and the same. Vṛṣaka, Śiva, and Śreyorūpa are also one and the same.
"Yama" is his epithet; "krūraḥ vikhyātaḥ" means he is famous for his ferocity, that is, he is well-known for his cruelty.
"Gaṅgādhara" is the epithet of Umāpati; "Bhūteśvara" is the epithet of Kapālīśa. "Another is renowned" means that another has a famous name.
Thus, there are twenty-five sages, beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru. (10.1085)

The meaning is that they have reached the end of the third row. Here, the sages, who do not employ the sophisticated speech of a guru, indicate that these very disciples have attained this stage through the excellence of their practice of the principle of the individual soul (*puruṣatattva*) and so forth.
Just as those situated in the first row, so too those situated in the third row are indeed *gurus*. As it is said:
"From Hara down to Dhruva, twenty are remembered as *gurus*;
and all these, though residing here, have descended into the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) by way of a partial manifestation."
It should be understood that, having transcended their respective appropriate spheres of authority, they enter into that very state.
He summarizes: "The three lineages of sages, as well as those of the teacher and the disciple, have been fully explained. (10.1086)
The meaning is that, according to the previously stated rule, this constitutes the three rows of sages in the form of teacher and disciple. || 1086 ||
Now, O Goddess, I shall describe to you thereafter the eightfold science of the channels (nāḍīvidyāṣṭaka),
which consists of the group of eight channels that are connected to the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka) and will be described hereafter.
I shall speak of the increase of bondage.
And they are as follows: Iḍā, Candriṇī, Gaurī, Śānti, and likewise Śāntikarī. || 10.1087 ||
Mālā, Mālinī, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā—
these are the eight channels of this [system].
Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, the group of eight forms (vigrahāṣṭaka) is described hereafter.

The group of eight that arouses the subtle body (*vigraha*) serves the purpose of the veil of the *puruṣa-tattva*, which consists of the deities of ego-identification (*abhimāna*) to be described hereafter. || 1088 ||
And that—both effect and instrument, as well as that which produces pleasure and pain;
it is renowned as knowledge, the goal to be accomplished, and likewise the means and the cause. (10.1089)

The "object" (*kārya*) is that which arouses the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) that constitute the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), which is the essence of the object. The "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is that which arouses the ten external organs, which reside within the subtle body and are for the most part unmanifest;
their names are themselves the ten deities. It is that which produces pleasure and pain.

The two deities who accomplish the experience of pleasure and pain— consisting of the five cognitive faculties and the five active faculties— are that which accomplishes both knowledge and the goal to be realized; they are renowned and understood as being merely knowledge and merely activity, respectively, while remaining unmanifest.

That which was described here as the form of the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*) means the triad of deities pervading the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), referred to as the "means" (*sādhana*). "The cause" (*kāraṇa*) means the form of the deity that arouses the *pradhāna-tattva*, which is the nature of the cause. And although—

In the context of the discourse on the *prāgraśmikaraṇa* and the *tejo-maṇḍala*, the cause for the arising of effects, instruments, and so forth was explained; nevertheless, that very same [cause] exists here in the form of the deity within the *puṃs-tattva* as well, in a subtle form, precisely because it is the purpose of bondage.
Because of this conclusion; for he will state that in Māyā, this entire web of bonds exists in its supreme form (pararūpa). || 1089 ||
Now,
[the author] will describe the bonds of the body (dehapāśas)—
that is to say, those which consist of the specific presiding deities who initiate the gross body (sthūladeha).
In that regard—...and the dharma taught in ten ways.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only/precisely). I shall first speak of the tenfold primary bondage, which is indeed dharma itself.
And that is: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile. || 10.1090 ||
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness—this is the tenfold dharma by which a man becomes a performer of dharma. || 10-1091 ||

"Uprightness (*akalkatā*) is clarity, equanimity, and affection that does not waver even through hundreds of injuries; it is said that this is the state where one is unable to endure becoming turbid—this is what is called uprightness. (Viśeṣastava 17.39)
Thus, in the venerable Mataṅgapārameśvara, [the initiation] is thus characterized. 1091.
Having thus described the primary bondage of the body known as "dharma," he speaks of the secondary:
"I shall describe the sixteen modifications existing in a subordinate state.
This means they exist in a subordinate state—that is, in a subtle form—relative to the gross forms previously mentioned.
The meaning is that they abide [there], yet they will exist within Māyā by way of another form.
He said to them: "Taste, smell, form, touch, and likewise sound. (10.1092)
The five subtle elements have been declared; now learn from me the sense organs:
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ, which are designated as the organs of action. (10.1093)
The meaning is the pentad of the sense faculties. || 1093 ||
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose is recorded as the fifth;
these,
O Goddess of Gods, are the organs of perception.
the mind is traditionally taught as being sixteenfold. || 10-1094 ||
These are declared to be the bonds of the body.
Furthermore—
"...those who know the principles (tattvavidaḥ) know [them] as the qualities of the intellect (buddhiguṇān),
existing in the person (puṃsi) in a subtle form as fetters (pāśakatvena); thus they know them through an uninterrupted tradition."
And those are—dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and thereafter sovereignty. (10.1095)

Non-dharma, as well as ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery, are distinct from this dharma previously described as non-violence and so forth; this [other] dharma is characterized by sacrificial rites (iṣṭa) and public works (pūrta).
Furthermore: "And I shall explain the threefold ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) in due order. (10.1096)
The meaning is that they are, respectively, the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*,
which correspond to the *rājasa*, *sāttvika*, and *tāmasa* [aspects].

Thus, these— the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the external organs, and the internal organs— which have been described here as the binders (*bandhaka*) abiding within the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) in their subtle form, are precisely these that are presented here as the internal wheels (*cakra*) of Bhūcarī, Dikcarī, and Gocarī. It is in accordance with this very [principle] that it is said here:
The statement "the forms of others" was made at the very outset; however, the Khecarī-cakra will be internal, consisting of the nature of the deities of the sheaths (kañcuka).
He recalls the very procedure for initiation that was commenced in reverse order: "Learn from me how their purification occurs at the time of initiation. (10.1097)
The meaning is: of these bonds of the *ahaṃkāra*—namely *taijasa* and the others—which have entered into the principle of *puruṣa*.
The meaning of "yathā" is: by which sequence. || 1097 ||
He states that very sequence:
"One should purify tamas, rajas, and likewise sattva in successive order.
This is intended as an illustration; the meaning is that one should purify all the bonds (pāśas) in reverse order.
Furthermore: sound, touch, as well as form, taste, and smell as the fifth. (10.1098)
And the objects (*viṣaya*) have been fully described; they must be purified with great effort.
Specifically, they are called "objects" because they bind (*sinvanti*) the experiencing subject, the *puruṣa*.
They exist in the form of subtle objects of enjoyment within the *puruṣa*, but they do not consist of the previously mentioned subtle elements (*tanmātra*); this is the meaning.
The intention behind the statement that "they must be purified with effort" is as follows:
unlike in the case of the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣiptadīkṣā*) concerning the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth, one should contemplate the subtle and infinite [forms of the deities]. (4-158)

According to the principle thus stated, one might consider their inclusion [within other categories]; however, all of these must be purified individually here in this extensive initiation of the universe (bhuvanadīkṣā). The same applies elsewhere.
Furthermore: desire, anger, greed, delusion, and indeed malice. || 10.1099 ||
Birth, death, old age, disease, hunger, thirst, and likewise craving;
as well as despondency, fear, intoxication, and even exhilaration. (10.1100)
Passion, hatred, and mental instability; anger, falsehood, and malice; deceit, the quality of envy, unrighteousness, and lack of self-mastery. || 10-1101 ||

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is longing; the state of one who is angry, untruthful, and malicious is "angry-untruthful-maliciousness" (*kupitānṛtadrohitā*); anger (*krodha*) is an intense outburst of wrath devoid of reflection on what precedes or follows; pride (*mada*) is arrogance;
and the quality of envy (*mātsaryadharma*) is a disposition characterized by intolerance of the virtues of others. And these—
In the Śrīmataṅgapārameśvara, these have been explained in detail. || 1101 ||
These twenty-seven snares in number should be understood as adventitious;
they are so called because they come from elsewhere, being distinct from the innate ones previously mentioned, and possess that same nature.

Precisely because they are introduced [in this context] as occurring after the attainment of a body, detachment (*vairāgya*) and the other qualities manifest for persons and are therefore adventitious (*āgantuka*); for this very reason, they are also innate (*sahaja*).
The implication is that another [kind of] passion (*rāga*), which is gross and adventitious, must be purified with effort.
The same applies hereafter.
Furthermore—
learn from me the snares of the Gaṇas,
and what they are:
The Goddess, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the Bull.
Bhṛṅgī, Caṇḍīśvara, and Kārttikeya is remembered as the eighth.
These are called "fetters" (pāśas) because they veil the self, which is the very nature of the Supreme Lord consisting of non-dual transcendence.
As it was said by our Master in the *Tantrāloka*:
Whatever is other than the Supreme Śiva— whose nature has been described as beautiful with the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness— is called a *pāśa* (bond).

Thus, even though the Supreme Lord has attained masculinity and is complete, individual persons remain established in a state of wonder due to their lack of recognition of His true nature. (8.292–293)
Furthermore:
Ananta, Tritanu, Sūkṣma, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śivottama. || 10.1103 ||
Śikhaṇḍin, Ekanetra, and another, Ekarudra—
one should purify the bonds consisting of the Vidyeśvaras at the time of initiation.

According to the principle stated in another tradition, "In the pure path Śiva is the agent; in the impure, Ananta is the Lord," regarding that venerable Lord Ananta— who, surrounded by the three principles (tattvas) and others, is the cause of the impure path— his state of being the veiler of the *puruṣa*-principle [is as follows].
Because the state of being the creator of the path purified by truth bears fruit, [the Lord] will remain there in a subtle form.
Thus, there are nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*), eight perfections (*siddhi*), and the group of eight beginning with *aṇimā*;
these twenty-two, arranged in three rows, together with the twenty-five [principles], constitute the total.

There are sixty-seven guru-disciple pairs; the eight channels (nāḍīs); the eightfold body (vigraha), consisting of the ten [virtues] beginning with non-violence (ahiṃsā); the sixteen transformations (vikāras); the eight qualities of the intellect (buddhi-dharmas); the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra);
and the five objects of sense, beginning with sound and ending with the five objects of the virtues such as non-violence.

There are forty-two innate bodily bonds (pāśa), such as desire and the rest; thirty-seven adventitious bonds that are dependent on what is not independent; eight Gaṇeśas; and eight Vidyeśas as bonds—thus, there are one hundred and ninety-three worlds of bonds.
It has been stated that purification is to be performed in the principle of the male (puṃstattva). || 1104 ||
Furthermore:

"Those [impurities] mentioned here, as well as those not mentioned, which are characterized in other tantras—all these must be purified in the *pauruṣeya* [tantra]; through that, the individual (*pudgala*) shall be liberated. (10.1105)

Those one hundred and ninety-three bonds (pāśas) mentioned here, as well as others not mentioned here— such as pleasure, laughter, sorrow, effort, and so forth, as well as despondency, exhaustion, and so on, whose natures are described in other systems such as those of Bharata— all of these are to be purified within the principle of Puruṣa. This being the case:
Then the *pudgala* is liberated from the fetters;

for the *pudgala*—the subject of illusion (*māyā-pramātṛ*)—is one whose "swallowing" (*gilana*), characterized by the object of enjoyment, consists of violence (*hiṃsā*) in the form of the arousal of internal latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from doubt and affliction (*antaḥ-śaṅkā-taṅka*). || 1105 ||
This has been explained.
Now, one should know that beyond the Artha-tattva lies Niyati; learn from me regarding the Rudras within it.
He speaks of them:
Vāmadeva, as well as Śarva, and likewise Bhava and Udbhava.
Vajradeha, Prabhu, Dhātṛ, Krama, Vikrama, and Suprabheda as the tenth—these are remembered as the Śaṅkaras within Niyati. || 10-1107 ||
The meaning is that they are situated in the ten directions. || 1107 ||

To demonstrate that the person (puruṣa), constrained by the principle of necessity (niyati-tattva), assumes the state of the cognizing subject (buddhi-pramātṛ) and, consisting of egoity (ahaṅkāra), resides within the heart-lotus of the body, [the author] says: "That lotus which is situated in the heart— therein the Self (ātman) is established."

"Although it remains pervading this entire body with its full extent, its supreme abode is nevertheless the casket of the heart-lotus. According to this principle, the heart-lotus is the place of rest for the Self; therefore, it is here that [the Self] resides.
By virtue of its nature as the *padmāsana*, according to the stated sequence, it performs the creation consisting of the manifestation of various objects and so forth;
and that lotus is such that:
"Fate is its petal, the ego is its filament, and the intellect is its pericarp. (10.1108)

It should be explained as that whose petals—which consist of the forms of mind, intellect, action, and the objects of the senses—have arisen by the power of necessity (*niyati*), and whose movement-places are these; however, it should not be explained as that of which necessity itself is the petals, because necessity lacks the downward pervasion of the filaments of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*). For it is egoity alone that is the coloring agent.

Wherein the form of the filaments exists, the intellect (*buddhi*)—because it accomplishes the enjoyment of objects up to the limit of determination—is situated above in the form of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). And here, for this self, [it is said]:
"Having entered the primary receptacle, it is permeated by the three qualities" (2.41).
Thus, the nature previously described should be kept in mind, for otherwise the status of the cognizer as an agent of cognition would be impossible. || 1108 ||

And this state of being regulated by necessity (niyati) is possible only for that which is affected by time, but not for that whose nature transcends time. Therefore, regarding that which is the cause of such temporalization—
in that reality of Time (kālatattva), Śivā is to be known...
The word "as that which is to be purified" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And those—I shall describe them in brief:
the Pure, the Awakened, the Fully Awakened, the Tranquil, and the Supreme Immutable. || 10-1109 ||
Śiva, Suśiva, Dhruva, Akṣara,
and Śambhurāṭ— these ten, O fair-faced one, should be known as the Śivas within the principle of Time (kālatattva).
"Akṣararāṭ" and "Śambhurāṭ"—these two [are the names]. 1110.
In that regard:
"The Śaṅkaras are said to have the luster of gold; the Śivas resemble crystal.
The Śaṅkaras abide in Niyati, while the Śivas abide in Kāla."
Moreover,
O illustrious lady, the retinue assigned to each one has been specified.
There is one crore and sixteen thousand others;
for all of them, the worlds are said to be shaped like tortoises.
Now,
therefore, understand from me hereafter [the nature of] Hari and Hara within the principle of attachment (rāga-tattva).
For the person whose essence is consciousness, the process of temporalization (kālya-kalana) is not possible without a connection to an object of knowledge (vedya).
With the thought "may something be mine," by way of a general desire for objects of knowledge (*vedya*),

this [Self] is necessarily colored by the *rāgatattva* (the principle of passion), which is distinct from the gross passion consisting of the mental states directed toward objects such as women and the like. Therefore, Hari and Hara reside within the *rāgatattva*, which colors the person (*puruṣa*).
The two primary Lords of the World are [Suhṛṣṭa and Suprahṛṣṭa]. He mentions others as well: Surūpa and Rūpavardhana. (10.1113)
Manonmana, Mahādhīra—
these, together with the two previously mentioned, constitute the eight Vīreśas who have been fully described.

Just as the Rudras, Śaṅkaras, and Śivas are said to have reached their destined time, so too are these Vīreśas called by those names; they are spoken of in this way because they are difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, I shall also declare the other Rudras who are established within the principle of passion (rāga-tattva). || 10-1114 ||
The word "them" (tān) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 1114 ||
Kalyāṇa, Piṅgala, Babhru, Vīra, Prabhava, Medhātithi, Chandaka, Dāhaka, and Śāstrakārin; || 10-1115 ||

Regarding the term "śāstrakāriṇaḥ," although there is only one person named Śāstrakārin, the plural is used here to demonstrate that there are five teachers, as he alone possesses the status of a guru. || 1115 ||
As it is said:
"Five are the disciples and likewise ten are the teachers; these are thus established.
The former are the disciples, the latter are the teachers."
The principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*), which consists in the manifestation of objects of knowledge that are common [to all], is established through the illumination of those objects.
To explain its illumination, he says that the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), which bestows limited omniscience (*kiñcijjñatva*), is connected to it:
"Therefore, above that is the principle of knowledge; hear now of the world (*bhuvana*) within it. (10.1116)
"Bhuvanam" means "bhuvanāni" (worlds). || 1116 ||
He presents those [powers] by way of their respective lords:
"Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, and Raudra; Kala and Vikaraṇa likewise; Balavikaraṇa and Balapramathana. (10.11–17)
Sarvabhūtadamana, as well as Manonmana;
and Kalavikaraṇa—meaning *kala* (power) and *vikaraṇa* (transformation)—is thus *kalavikaraṇa*. In some places, these [deities] beginning with Vāmā are seen in the feminine gender.
Since even the connection with *vidyā*, which consists in limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), is not possible for one who is not an agent, there exists the principle of *kalā*;
for this [Self], whose full power of knowledge and action is concealed by *māyā*, the manifestation of a slight degree of agency occurs. Therefore, therein—
O Great Goddess, the triad of great deities resides within the principle of Kalā.
Mahādeva is of great splendor and great light, possessing majesty.
The triad of deities characterized by the word "great" (mahat) is the "Triad of Great Deities" (Mahādevatraya). Possessing majesty means being exceedingly radiant;
thus it is said:
The principle of *kalā* has been fully explained in brief, O fair-faced one.
By the statement "in brief," the intention is that there are others here as well, namely those known as Vāmadeva, Bhavodbhava, Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, Bhuvaneśa, and Aṅguṣṭhamātra.
For these eight Maṅgaleśvaras were previously mentioned in their unmanifest form within the *buddhitattva*; [they are now mentioned] here.
However, it is [described] by way of its external form. And therein, only three are mentioned because of their predominance.

Thus, this pentad of principles (tattvas) called Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā, which has been described, is indeed common to the external world as the locus for the aforementioned arrangement of the worlds (bhuvanas). Beyond that, however—

For each individual, this pentad of principles denoted by the term "sheaths" (kañcuka) is indeed distinct and diverse for every person, just like the internal organs and so forth; and this serves as the supreme veil for the Person, like the husk of a grain of rice, whereas [the series] beginning with Prakṛti and ending with the subtle elements (tanmātra) is...

The subtle body, which is its constituent cause, is subtle like the husk; whereas the five gross elements, which are the constituents of the gross body, are indeed gross like the awn. All of this is to be purified in reverse order according to the previously described division of the worlds. || 1119 ||
All these Rudras, O Great Goddess, have been mentioned by name; they are three-eyed and have the moon as their crest-jewel,
adorned with the extraordinary super-knowledge of Maheśvara.
And those whose retinues were not previously enumerated—they too are surrounded on all sides by thousands of crores of Rudras. || 10-1120 ||
Resembling pure crystal...
all of them indeed... endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty.
He states their distinction:
"Those who are attached to passion (rāga) should be known as those whose power of knowledge and yoga is predominant. (10.1121)
Their houses are indeed shaped like parasols and adorned with various jewels;
for others, however, they are said to be shaped like tortoises.
This has been explained. Now, regarding these—above them would be Māyā;
and those... her.
...I shall explain in brief. || 10-1122 ||
Having pervaded the lower path through its manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpyeṇa*),
it remains established by having pervaded everything excessively— from *Ākala* down to the earth— according to this etymological derivation; and here,
the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is not one of difference, but rather of non-difference, with the intention that it has "pervaded the universe" (*viśvaṃ vyāpya*) in this sense.
It has been stated that [the Goddess] is "established. The phrase "in brief" is intended to indicate a concise presentation of Bhuvaneśī.
Regarding that, it is said: "There, the highly fortunate Rudras are exactly twelve, possessed of great strength. (10.1123)
They remain as the primary [obstacles]; "possessing great power" means they are difficult to avoid without the knowledge of the Supreme Lord. || 1123 ||
He shows these very ones through the division of the *puṭas*:
"The Gahana and the Asādhya, likewise the Lord Hariharaprabhu;
Daśeśāna, O Queen of the Gods, Trigala, and likewise Gopati. (10.1124)
O fair-faced one, these six are to be understood as being in the Māyātattva within the lower vessel; such is the meaning.
Kṣemeśa is the lord of Brahmā, and likewise Vidyeśāna as well.
Vidyeśa, Śiva, and Ananta is said to be the sixth;
these Rudras are proclaimed as residing above, within the enclosure of Māyā. (10–1126)
Among these, however, the Blessed One Ananteśa is the Lord of the World.
Furthermore, in the Śrīmeṅgaśāstra, it is stated regarding the central chamber:
"Therein resides that Vigraheśāna, who is supremely invincible. (1.8.83)
By the passage, "Wherein Śarva, Bhava, Ugra, the powerful Bhīma, Bhasmāntaka, Dundubhi, and the mighty Śrīvatsa [reside]," the group of eight is mentioned. However, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (5.28–29):
The eight lords of the mandalas, each the size of a thumb, beginning with Mahādeva, are said to reside within Māyā;
this constitutes the distinction in the tantric methodology. And this Anantanātha—having brought forth the emergence (udbhava), the Lord acts according to his own will. (10.1127)

Having contemplated— that is, having reflected upon— that particular arising consisting of stationary objects and so forth which is appropriate for someone according to the ripening of their own karma, the Supreme Lord performs it by His mere will, as impelled by His own volition; He does not depend on auxiliary causes like a potter, because He is the Sovereign over this entire path.
One whose nature is to manifest. || 1127 ||
Furthermore,
this [Lord] is omniscient and the creator of all, intent upon both restraint and grace;
He knows and creates everything from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*), as stated in that very [text].
He bestows grace and exercises restraint upon those who have received the descent of power, as well as upon others.
Thus, in this manner—by the first division, the twelve Rudras are proclaimed. (10.1128)

In this context, Māyā is the power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*), according to the view that will be stated hereafter: "Beyond this is Māyā, which deludes all living beings" (10.1138). She exists as the nature of the *tattva* (ontological principle).
And it manifests in two ways by way of being a knot (*granthi*). Among these, as for that which consists of *tattva*:
"Māyā, having pervaded everything mobile and immobile, exists in ten million ways" (10.671);
and likewise—

Regarding that which was stated: "She who, indeed, pervading the upward and downward paths, abides in her universal form" (10.1123), she possesses the nature of a section (*kāṇḍa*) consisting of two cavities (*puṭa*), upper and lower. Within those two cavities, by means of the first division according to the nature of the *tattvas* of Māyā, there are twelve Rudras.
They have been explained as being established through their distinct classifications. || 1128 ||

That which is the cause for the emergence of the stream of the succession of principles (tattvas) beginning from *kalā* and ending with *pṛthivī*, which is divided into countless internal distinctions, and which is traditionally taught as being like a slight swelling of this power (*śakti*), is this [seed] whose nature is a knot (*granthi*) and whose character is gross.

It exists in three ways, according to the division of the upper, middle, and lower knots (*granthi*), by way of the nature of the most subtle *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, having a form similar to the knot of the palate (*tālu*). As it was stated previously:
"One should designate the white [knot] as the covering below and the red [knot] as above."
"One should know that darkness (*tamas*) is in the middle; these qualities (*guṇas*) are thus established. (2.66).
In that regard, he describes the existence of the Rudras in their distinct divisions within the threefold form consisting of the *granthi*:
"But as for those Rudras who are established in this Māyā-tattva..."
In that manner, I shall explain it according to the division of the three types of distinctions.

In this [reality], which is the cause for the production of the continuous flow of the stream of principles (tattva) beginning with Kalā as previously described, and which consists of the nature of Māyā in the form of knots— therein reside Gopatya and the others, as well as Ananta and the others, in whatever order they are situated;
"according to the division of the threefold differentiation" means by way of the distinction consisting of the knots of Sattva and the other [guṇas].
I shall describe it. || 1129 ||
Therein—
O Goddess, Gopati is situated above the lower knot (adhogranthi). "Therein" refers to that which is above the worlds of Rudras, such as Mahādeva and others, as established in the Kalātattva.
The illusory lower knot is situated there as Gopati, who exists in his supreme form, just as was previously described.
Likewise:
situated above the knot are Viśva, Trikalā, and Kṣema. || 10-1130 ||
"Brahmā, Adhipati, and Śiva as the fifth"—the phrase "above the knot" (granthi-ūrdhvam) means "in the upper knot. "He" refers to the very one previously mentioned;
the meaning is that this Rudra, named Viśva, exists here in his lower form (apararūpa), and not as someone else.
Furthermore:
"Below and above, Ananta..."—
the meaning is that Ananta resides at the knot above the lower knot.
And this duality of Māyā, by virtue of its nature as the reality of the knots, is described in the *Śrīśivatanu*:
"This is called the 'hole of Māyā,' but beyond that is the 'cave,' the womb of the universe;
for within these [knots], she is produced in accordance with the agitation of the power of the Lord."

"The designation *bhaga* refers to the openings of the womb (*yonivivara*) which abound with various objects of desire"—this and other passages were shown by the Gurus. Having abandoned this method of explanation, however, Śrī Bhullaka has explained it as follows: that the Supreme Lord [bestowed] knowledge upon Lakuleśa through differentiation (*bheda*).

He has revealed [this] according to the established position shown in the *Śrīlakulasvacchanda*; thus, the supreme Lord’s knowledge consists of two sections, and here the division of the worlds within Māyā is shown in two ways.
Whether this is correct or incorrect, those with discernment know.
And as for this middle knot which has been described as having the venerable Ananta as its locus— ............ the fetters (pāśas) themselves are situated here. (10–1131)
And those—O Goddess, as was previously stated...
the word "vai" has the sense of "eva" (indeed). Precisely as before, at the occasion of the determination of the principle of Puruṣa...

By the verse beginning with "The mother and the floods of water" (10.1069), those bonds (*pāśas*) that were described— starting from contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*) up to the bonds of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa-pāśa*)—
are here meant to exist in their supreme form (*pararūpa*). For *māyā* is [the source] of all of them.

It is the place of origin of the fetters (*pāśas*). By means of these—possessing the nature of specific deities impelled by Ananta, or existing in subtle forms presided over by the power of Vāmā—the individual souls (*aṇavas*) are bound. In the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), however, certain fetters such as contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and accomplishment (*siddhi*) exist in gross form; such is their [nature].
The state of non-existence has already been explained in essence.
Furthermore—...
"therein would be the Ṛṣikula.
Regarding that which was previously called the Ṛṣikula, consisting of three rows of gurus and disciples situated within the noose (pāśa):
Therefore, it stands here above the nooses.
Furthermore, in this regard:
"The source is indeed Vāgīśvarī; one who is born from her is not born again. (10.1132)

According to the principle that "Speech alone gave birth to all beings," the womb (yonih) is the universal cause, namely the Sovereign Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī), who exists here in a subtle form; for she will be established as the Supreme (parā) in the context of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), while she is described as the Lower (aparā) in the world of Sarasvatī. Indeed, everything...

Divided into three forms—the gross, the subtle, and the supreme—consisting of the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, and abiding in various ways in various places, He will explain this in the eleventh [chapter]. Of what nature is Vāgīśvarī? To this he says: "In whom," that is, in her, according to the state previously determined.
Born in a form that is gross, subtle,
or supreme, produced through the purificatory rites such as *garbhādhāna* accomplished by the refinement of mantra,
he is created in various distinct wombs for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those respective actions previously performed within each respective *tattva*. He is not [created otherwise].
The meaning is that he is liberated by attaining oneness with Paraśiva, because the purification of bonds (*pāśa-śuddhi*) and the unification (*yojanikā*) have been accomplished. || 1132 ||
Furthermore, regarding this Māyā—
Oṃkāra, Sādhyadhātṛ, and Damaneśa after that;
they say that Dhyāna is indeed Bhasmeśa.

Some say that the five Rudras, beginning with Sādhya, are designated by the syllable Oṃ; others, however, have explained that the very group of seers (ṛṣikulam) mentioned immediately prior is divided into six by means of the names Oṃ, Sādhya, and so forth.
Furthermore:
...the means of valid cognition [are established] beyond that. || 10-1133 ||

Because they establish all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding everything to be abandoned and everything to be accepted, the eight Rudras, who are denoted by the term "means of valid cognition," reside above the enclosure of the five Rudras known as the Praṇava. || 1133 ||
He enumerates those authorities:
"The Fivefold Object, the Secret, and then the Rudrāṅkuśa;
as well as the Heart, the Characteristics, the Array, and the Attraction. (10.1134)
And likewise, the eighth is proclaimed here as Ādarśa.

These are the Rudras, the introducers of the Pāśupata scriptures bearing those names. And therein, whatever authority (pramāṇa) called Hṛdaya has been mentioned, those [scriptures] which are included within it—

The six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which are primarily concerned with ritual action and known as the "Golden Hall of Ancient Kalpas" and the "Unsurpassed Universal Manifestation," and which are distinct from the eight means of valid cognition primarily concerned with the aforementioned knowledge—
these have been extracted by Musulendra, the disciple of Lakula, from the means of valid cognition called the *Hṛdaya*.
These were first shown for those desiring to ascend [the path], but they are not counted here separately. Thus, regarding the statement:

"The *tantra* is proclaimed to be twofold: *Lākula* and *Mausula*" (11.71), that which is the *Pāśupata* exists here as being subordinate to the interior of *māyā*, whereas the supreme state [is beyond it].

He will state that "the reality of these [Pāśupatas] is Īśvara. For this very reason, it has been said that there is a great difference between the Pāśupatas and the Śaivas, according to the principle that will be stated later: "But for the Śaivas, the supreme state is entirely free from both the [categories of] Śarva and the paths" (11.74).
Those Rudras who have been described as being equal in measure to the Praṇava—
these, O Goddess, are surrounded by thousands of crores of Rudras.
Variegated with various colors and adorned with diverse ornaments,
they take delight with thousands of women according to their husband's wish.
Of the husband Ananta; and for this reason, he alone is the teacher of Lakuleśa and the others. || 1136 ||
Moreover:

All [of them] have three eyes and carry tridents; they possess matted hair, the moon, and crowns; their power and majesty are undiminished; and they hold authority over the principle of Māyā. (10.1137)
Established within the various worlds that exist in the form of wombs,
those who thus worship this [deity] become partakers of the attainment of that state; it follows by implication that, upon the completion of their office, they are liberated together with it.
Having thus determined that Māyā is both the nature of reality (tattva) and the nature of the knot (granthi), he speaks in order to explain its nature as power (śakti):
"Beyond this, Māyā exists as the deluder of all living beings. (10.1138)

It deludes all living beings as they are being born and created, making them possessors of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality) whose true nature is the non-manifestation of their own essential form. By stating this, he declares that the impurity (*mala*) is unreal; and this has already been determined by us previously.
Furthermore:
"With their intellects deluded by that [ignorance] which is without enmity yet obstructive, disputants here contend, 'This is reality; this is not. (10.1139)

They dispute, meaning they speak in mutual contradiction; for this very reason, these proponents are limited to mere debate and do not possess knowledge of reality. The use of the *parasmaipada* ending for the verb *vad*, which is normally *ātmanepadin* when used with the prefix *vi-*, is due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
And for this reason,
he— having abandoned the true path— leads them swiftly onto a wrong path;
the true path consists of the scriptures of the Supreme Lord, while the other is the wrong path.
This very point he clarifies:
"Those lowest of men who are not devoted to the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, and the Scripture... (10.1140).
Those who know the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic—
Māyā indeed causes them to wander, for they desire liberation while remaining in non-liberation.

False reasoning is that logic which stands outside the supreme non-dual scriptures of the Supreme Lord; it is non-liberation, for everything other than the pervasion of oneness with the Supreme Lord—who is a dense mass of supreme non-dual consciousness and bliss—is precisely that. 1141.
"How might this [impurity] be avoided?"— to this he says: "Severed by the sword of Śiva-initiation, it shall not sprout again—
that [initiation] which was proclaimed by Śaṅkara, who is Śiva, the mass of pure, autonomous consciousness and bliss."

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of various types, primarily characterized by knowledge, yoga, and ritual action; its nature was previously defined as that in which "the true essence of knowledge is bestowed. That very initiation is like a sword because it severs the fetters (*pāśa*); thus, for whomever [it] has been severed—

The meaning is that [the seed of Māyā] has been uprooted by the recognition of one's own true nature, which consists of the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), and thus it never sprouts again with respect to that person. In this way, the threefold form of Māyā—consisting of the reality-knot (tattva-granthi) and the power (śakti)—has been described. Among these:

It consists of reality (*tattva*), pervades the entire universe, and resembles a massive pillar; it is threefold in nature as knots (*granthi*). The *śākta* [knot], however, has the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) as its very essence.
Because it is not recognized for what it truly is, it is called *māyā* with respect to those who are deluded.

Thus, this [power] directed by Īśvara, through its own principles (tattva) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *niyati*, causes the individual souls— whose true nature is concealed and who possess the forms of knower and agent—
