to experience limited agency, limited knowledge, desire, conceptualization, regulation, and the enjoyment of objects of experience.

Having made those who are bound by the hundreds of previously mentioned bonds into recipients, He deposits them into the substrate of Pradhāna— which consists of the common nature that is to be enjoyed as a portion—
so that they become bound by the gross bonds beginning with the qualities (guṇas) produced from that [Pradhāna] and ending with the earth.
These [individuals] follow from one womb to another; therefore, they must be utterly eradicated through initiation into the Supreme Lord (pārameśadīkṣā).

Furthermore, although this [Māyā], which is known as non-recognition (akhyāti), pervades the entire universe, it shines forth only upon the wall of the Supreme Lord’s Light. It is by means of this [Light] that...
The illuminator of all things, the wall of the light of the Supreme Lord—that is called Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā). Thereupon, he defines it:
"Now, above that is Mahāvidyā, the source of the arising of all vidyās. (10.1142)
The imperishable [power] is the treasury of the dissolution, origination, and manifestation of the universe.

Because it is stated that "Vidyā, possessing ten times ten million qualities, exists pervading Māyā" (10.671), she is called Vidyā because she is distinct from impure Vidyā (aśuddhavidyā) and because her nature consists of the knowledge of all things in their entirety; thus, she is Great (mahatī).
She is the source and the radiance of all mantras— beginning with the Vidyārājñīs and other divine beings, as well as all worldly existences— which are characterized by the *praṇava* (Oṃ);
she is the origin of the universe, which consists of the principles (*tattvas*) such as *māyā*, the various subjects (*pramātṛs*), the worlds (*bhuvanās*), and so forth.
Regarding the manifestations at the time of dissolution and origination:
"The manifestations of the kings of the vidyā-maṇḍalas and of the maṇḍalas themselves,
as well as those of the mantras and their respective selves, cannot be fully enumerated."
Thus, by remaining as such, the treasure-trove (nidhi) is the support for the perfection of the self's enjoyment;

the meaning is that it effects the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the universe, whereas it is otherwise [in its own nature] due to being of the nature of light. As for the fact that withdrawal and so forth will be described here even in the eleventh [chapter], [it refers to the state of manifestation].
In relation to its contraction.
Furthermore—she alone is proclaimed as the supreme goddess Vāgīśī. || 10-1143 ||

The term *paramā* refers to that which has been described as *māyā*, the arouser of the manifestation of duality; this other [power], which serves as the first step for the unfolding of the manifestation of non-duality, is designated as *vāgīśī*—the speech-lordess of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), whose nature is the supreme self-reflection (*paraparāmarśa*). || 1143 ||
Therefore—
though divided into eight groups, that Vidyā is indeed the Mātṛkā itself;
it is not divided by the eight groups beginning with a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa.

One should unfold the mantras, which, by virtue of consisting of the non-differentiated awareness of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), possess the manifestation of the entire universe in its differentiated state; for this very reason, although this *Mātṛkā* is the cause of the entire universe in both its denoted and denoting aspects, she is called the "Mother" because she is not recognized as such by bound souls (*paśus*).
Now, in this regard,
I shall describe the worlds here in their proper order and according to the truth.
Therein— Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī, Kālī, Vikaraṇī,
as well as Balavikaraṇī and Balapramathanī. || 10-1145 ||
Damanī is the [power] of all beings, and likewise Manonmanī.
Regarding these, it is said in the venerable Ānandabhairava:
"One should emit everything by means of Vāmā, and again protect it by means of Jyeṣṭhā."
The Lord, by his own will, effects the destruction of the world through Raudrī.
With one [power], Kālī impels all beings; with Vikaraṇī, she scatters the constituent parts (kalās).
With another, she [bestows] all strength, and with yet another, she churns away all power.

"Having subdued the mind, which consists of volitional constructs (*saṅkalpa*), by means of *damana* (subduing), Maheśvara leads [the soul] to the supreme station by means of *unmanī*. Thus they are etymologically explained. Regarding *vikaraṇyā*: by means of *kalavikaraṇī*, one should scatter all the *kalās* (powers).

She makes [the soul] abide by its own power. By another, the *balavikaraṇī*, she disperses power—the capacity for performing one's own functions—everywhere. By another, the *balapramathanī*, she crushes the power of all Rudras and *kṣetrajñas*. "Having subdued" refers to [the powers] ending with *samanā*.

The connection here is thus: "having entered the plane" (*bhūmim āviśya*). As for those nine deities, Vāmā and the others, who were previously mentioned as belonging to impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*)—or, because they are listed with feminine endings, as the nine powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā (10.11–17–18)—they should be understood as the gross forms that are descents from these [subtle] portions.
And these [goddesses] have the appearance of molten gold; they have five faces and three eyes. || 10.1146 ||
Possessing unfailing vigor, they are omniscient and abide everywhere at all times;
endowed with all-knowledge, they are all adorned with every ornament. || 10-1147 ||
Endowed with all the marks and possessed of all sovereign powers, having the appearance of molten gold and exceedingly radiant; the marks consist of the forms of wisdom and yoga;
they abide everywhere, in all places, and at all times—nothing exists that is not presided over by this.

The meaning is that there exists something of this kind. Even such [beings] follow the omniscient Maheśvara and are presided over by Him, the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). All ornaments indeed are adorned by Him.
Furthermore, there are seventy million principal mantras that are established. (10–1148)
From among them—
each one has a retinue numbering in the hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and thousands.
"Each one" refers to each mantra.
Moreover—those [gods] sport in divine worlds that are shaped like lotuses. (10.1149)
By the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group), the term "they" refers to the powers beginning with Vāmā as well as the mantras.
Right here—Triguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā, Rūpiṇī, Madinī, and Jvālā; these are the seven [goddesses], and their lords are as follows. (10–1150)
They are declared to be the Vidyārājñīs (Queen-Consorts of Knowledge).
They are the sovereigns and sources of power for those mantras and vidyās; therefore, they are called the Queens of the vidyās and mantras.
Therefore,
one should purify these at the time of initiation;
for when these are purified, there is the attainment of the purification of the seven crores of mantras presided over by them.

Thus, that pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) which has been described as the substratum for all mantras— comprising the entire manifold universe up to the level of Māyā— is also, by virtue of being like its own limb, grounded in the principle of Īśvara; this principle consists of the manifestation of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "I" and "this," wherein the distinctness of "this" and the "I" shine forth as one.

Existence shines; for even omniscience in its differentiated aspect is not possible without the manifestation of both difference and non-difference. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the principle of Īśvara, he says:
"In the external world, his principle is that of Īśvara..."
"Of that" refers to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). "External" means that very same [principle] which exists as it stands, having been encompassed by pervasion (vyāpti).
And therefore—listen now to my worlds here. || 10-1151 ||
Regarding that, he first states the essential nature of the Lord (Īśvara) who resides in the primary world:

"Endowed with the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), free from Māyā, and stainless, he is indeed the agent of maintenance and withdrawal, and the bestower of liberation and sovereignty. (10.1152)

He is "engaged" (yukta) in the manner that will be described hereafter and is "surrounded. He is "one from whom illusion has departed" (vītāmāya), because he has emerged from the impurity called *māyā*, which consists of the manifestation of objects as distinct [from consciousness].
For he does not know everything indistinctly like a mantra; rather, he knows it through the nature of both difference and non-difference. Therefore:

Because it touches upon the aspect of differentiation (*bhedāṃśa*), its being surrounded by the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the arrangement of the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth, as they are described, are not illogical. Thus, since differentiation exists in a subtle form, even down to the limit of the Śiva-tattva, the arrangement of the worlds and so forth also [exists].

It is indeed appropriate that [the subject] will be described as something to be purified. Through the mention of maintenance (*sthiti*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is also implied. And regarding this triad beginning with emanation:
"On the pure path, Śiva is the agent."

According to this principle, it should be understood that his [domain] consists precisely of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), such as the mantras and the maṇḍala. And so it is stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"Desiring to emit the world, at the very beginning of creation, by his own will..."
"He awakened eight individuals who were solitary in their consciousness" (1.19);
likewise, "in the same way,
he created seventy million mantras together with their maṇḍalas" (1.21).

Thus, it is not only from mantras that liberation and sovereignty—consisting of supramundane enjoyments—are bestowed; rather, they are also granted to those who have reached the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) through the application of mantras and other means, even if they remain within the womb of *māyā*.
This is intended as an illustration; by it, [liberation is also granted] to those people devoted to the gods, the guru, and so forth, even if they are practitioners of *māyā* through hypocrisy.
It also brings about dissolution. In this way, its performance of the fivefold activity is thus described.
The description of his seat, suitable for meditation, is taught as follows:
"His seat, however, is vast, measuring a thousand petals"—
the meaning is that it has innumerable petals.
For here,
thirty-five million mantras abide upon her seat.
Although there are seventy million mantras, nevertheless:
"Even when the world has just come into being, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
three and a half crores of mantras have been assigned by Śiva."
"Having graced the multitude of individual souls, they have gone to the state free from affliction. (1.40.41).
According to the principle stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, it is thus said that three and a half crores [of deities] abide for the sake of the office of grace (*anugrahādhikāra*). || 1153 ||
Thus, he who is to be employed [in ritual] is mounted upon the lotus-seat of the mantra;
seated there, the Lord God is the bestower of boons, facing in all directions.
"God" (deva) means one whose ultimate nature is luminosity and so forth; "facing in all directions" means that his primary form is omnipresent.
Also by way of his form: he has five faces, is possessed of great splendor, has ten arms, and three eyes. || 10-1154 ||
The gentle god was white as cow’s milk, wearing a sacred thread made of serpents;
he was clothed in divine garments and anointed with divine perfumes.
Complete with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
holding a trident in his hand, with the moon upon his crest, and graced by a crown of matted locks.
With a serene countenance, lovely, and the bestower of the sovereignty of yoga, his hands granting boons and fearlessness—he is to be meditated upon by the masters of yoga. (10.1157)

In the form [of the deity] with five faces and so forth, the true nature previously described should be understood. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "with hands granting boons and fearlessness," there is the inclusion of the sword, shield, and other implements. It is "gentle" (*saumya*) because of the predominance of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), due to the predominance of the Lord’s power of action (*kriyāśakti*); for this very reason...
When meditated upon according to the manner described in the twelfth chapter, he bestows the sovereignty of yoga upon the lords among yogins. || 1157 ||

And just as the Supreme Lord assumes the form of an Īśvara in order to bestow grace upon the Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas) through meditation, worship, and so forth, so too does His inherent power (śakti) assume a corresponding form; thus he says:
Seated upon his lap was Vidyā, the support of all sciences,
clothed in divine garments and adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
Adorned with divine garlands of flowers and strings of pearls,
resembling pearls in appearance, she has five faces and three eyes.

"Vidyā" refers to Mātṛkā in the form of the Lord of the letters belonging to Māyā; even so, because duality has not been entirely removed due to a partial [residue] according to the reasoning previously stated, she is said to be "on the lap" (utsaṅgagatā), as is further explained below. She is the field of origin for all Vidyās and all the hosts of Mantras and Vidyās.
"Resting correctly without distinction" means being firmly established; "resembling a pearl" means it is gentle because it is inclined toward bestowing grace. || 1159 ||
And she, when propitiated according to the prescribed rite, always makes the wise perceive [the truth];
when propitiated by means of the internal distinction of the rite through the power of [her] grace, she is brought to a state of favor.
Being present, she causes those possessed of knowledge to experience [it], that is, she brings about the manifestation of their own true nature.
Furthermore—she appears as if smiling because of her gazing upon the face of Maheśvara. || 10-1160 ||
The face (vadana) is so called in relation to its form, while as the supreme power (parā śakti) it is in relation to its essential nature;
the gaze (īkṣaṇa), however, is both vision and knowledge. || 1160 ||
Therefore, I shall describe from this point the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), who are the forms of the Blessed One’s retinue, proceeding in order from the East to the North-East;
although they belong to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), they abide here in their supreme form.
Ananta, Sūkṣma, and likewise Śivottama; || 10-1161 ||
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and Trinetra are proclaimed;
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are to be known as the Vidyeśvaras in their respective order.
And these [principles], beginning with Ananta, have been described by the Teachers in the *Śivatanu* as follows:
"The Lord, seated upon the throne at the summit of the cave pierced by hundreds of apertures, joined with eight powers,
creates [the worlds] from Gahana down to Niraya and appoints the Rudras."
By means of *manonmanī*, she uplifts those men; among them, he becomes the mediator.
With their consciousness thus uplifted by him, they apply themselves to the contemplation of the Supreme Reality.
Furthermore, Śiva, having completed his assignment as Lord over those atoms belonging to the lower path,
[remains] together with many millions of mantras that possess multiple forms.

The Infinite Lord (Anantanātha) attains liberation and enters that abode; however, the subtle Rudra, having bestowed grace upon the individual soul (aṇu), establishes him as a new [deity] in the station of Śikhaṇḍin.
Thus, while the single Guru proceeds through the eight stages in succession until he reaches the ultimate abodes,
he brings about the liberation of countless living beings.
All eight of them, seated upon pure lotuses joined with the eight powers,
contemplate the Lord, the supreme cause who resides within the heart.
"Meditating upon the infinite Blessed One as the peaceful cause within their own hearts,
they likewise meditate seven times upon ten million pure mantras.
Thus it is said.

The cave is Māyā; its summit is Śuddhavidyā, which is the very seat. Seated upon that stainless lotus, where there is union with the eight powers beginning with Vāmā, they abide. "The supreme Ananta" refers to the attained form of the Lord. 1162.
In this very context of the principle of Īśvara, he speaks of other worlds:
"Therefore, the form, the abode...
The meaning is that above the enclosure of the Vidyeśas is the world named Rūpāvaraṇa (the Enclosure of Form). The same applies to what follows.
...In that regard, learn from me concerning the Rudras: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya as the fourth. (10.1163)

By virtue of which [power], the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) possess the quality of being the substratum for the lower path, omniscience, complete freedom from desire, and the capacity to bestow great sovereignty. These Rudras, beginning with Dharma, are the retinue of Īśvara. || 1163 ||
And right here, within this very principle of Īśvara—
above this subtle veil,
and thus above the veil of form.
In that regard, they know there to be three powers (śakti).
And these are proclaimed as the powers: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. (10–1164)
They are the primary elements. || 1164 ||
For Kālī and the others previously mentioned are indeed the manifestation (*prapañca*) of these very [energies]. Therefore, it is said:
"Their retinue, moreover, consists of many millions in number," because these [energies] themselves constitute the entire manifold expansion of power (*śakti*).
And those who stand as their retinue—all these mantras are omnipresent, omniscient, and granters of all desires. || 10-1165 ||
Resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, with tridents in their hands,
they were endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
They were fully endowed with all sovereign splendors and bore beautiful crescent moons as their crests;
moreover,
they possessed the appearance of hundred-petaled lotuses and the pure rays of the moon and pearls.
Accompanied by the Lord, they all remain in those worlds, which are filled with variegated ramparts blazing with various jewels and crowded with arched gateways.

The connection is as follows: in those worlds characterized by other brilliantly shining enclosures whose forms possess a luster like that of hundred-petaled lotuses, [the deities] play, accompanied by the mantras of the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka.
For this very reason, these [deities] are worshipped in all rites by those seeking to propitiate Him, the God, in order to worship Him:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give..."

According to the principle stated in the *Bhagavad Gītā* (9.27): "Whatever austerity you perform, O Kaunteya, do that as an offering unto Me," these mantras, which constitute His retinue, are worshipped in order to propitiate that Lord regarding the sphere of action;
and for those who worship them and thus know this pervasion (*vyāpti*), [the fruit is attained] through their medium.
The meaning is that the attainment of the Lord occurs.
Furthermore:
"Those who, having conquered their senses, practice the divine Pāśupata vow," || 10.1169 ||
Those who are devoted to the ash, whose practice consists of recitation and meditation, go to the state of the Lord;
those for whom devotion to the ash takes the form of ritual bathing and the performance of religious rites.
Having spoken incidentally, he states the subject at hand:
"In that regard, the Lord is the Blessed One, the God of gods, the stainless one. (10.1170)
Impelled by the ordinance of Śiva’s will, he exercises his authority therein.

In that *īśvara-tattva*, the Lord [exercises authority] over the gods beginning with Ananta. "Authority" (*adhikāra*) refers to their appointment in tasks such as bestowing grace (*anugraha*). "Will" (*vidhi*) means that Śiva’s will alone ordains everything.

Impelled by that [desire], Paramaśiva himself—whose nature is primarily characterized by will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*)—manifests the stages (*bhūmikā*) of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara. As it is said in the *Śrīmataṅgapārameśvara*:
"Through the contemplation (*vimarśana*) of the teaching on the three principles (*tattva*) called dissolution (*laya*), authority (*adhikāra*), and experience (*bhoga*)."
"This category, named Pati, is proclaimed as the first. (1.2.14).
And here, the forms already mentioned and those yet to be described—
Fifteen and ten worlds are to be purified in sequence within Īśvara.
In that regard, there are four [levels]: (1) the world of Īśvara; (2) the world of the enclosure of the eight Vidyeśvaras;
(3) the world of the enclosure consisting of the substratum of the fourfold [powers] beginning with Dharma;
and (4) the world of the subtle enclosure consisting of the substratum of the three powers beginning with Vāmā. Thus, there are four.

Thus far have been described; however, the seven coverings (āvaraṇas) to be discussed hereafter are known as the covering of purity (śuddhāvaraṇa), the covering of knowledge (vidyāvaraṇa), the covering of valid cognition (pramāṇāvaraṇa), the covering of pride (mānāvaraṇa), the covering of illusion (māyāvaraṇa), the covering of pure Śiva (śuddhaśivāvaraṇa), and the covering of liberation (mokṣāvaraṇa). Beyond those is the eternal world (dhruvabhuvana), and beyond that...

The world of the power of will (icchā-śakti), which rests upon the triad of powers beginning with Vāmā; then the enclosure of the awakened (prabuddhāvaraṇa); and then the enclosure of the convention (samayāvaraṇa)—these eleven, together with the four [previously mentioned], become fifteen. || 1171 ||
O fair-faced one, at the time of initiation, one should know that these fifteen worlds are situated in sequence within the upper palate;
specifically, above the knot of the palate which consists of the *māyā*-tattva, and above the pericarp of the lotus of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) located there.

If the reality of Īśvara is situated above the palate, one should know that one must purify it by means of the previously mentioned sequence of mantras, preceded by resting therein; this is the meaning.
This is also an illustration, by which the worlds contained within the cosmic egg [are purified] through resting in the heart.

The worlds situated from the element water up to primordial nature (prakṛti) are to be purified by resting at the throat; those from primordial nature up to Māyā by resting at the palate; and the worlds belonging to the principle of Śuddhavidyā by resting in the state above that. Thus, [the purification proceeds] to the forehead and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
By resting in the state of the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), the worlds to be purified— which belong to the principles of Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva, and which will be described below— must be cleansed.
Now, he shows the eleven worlds beginning with Śuddhāvaraṇa in sequence:
"Above Śuddhāvaraṇa, however, two powers (śakti) are recorded within it. (10.1172)
Knowledge and action are renowned...
[as] "that world" (tadbhuvana) means in the form of the two worlds consisting of the powers of knowledge and action; likewise in what follows.
Now—
Beyond these two, there are also two further sciences;
within that pair of powers, they are known as the one termed "existence" and the one termed "non-existence."

Within that aforementioned pair of powers called knowledge and action, there exist two others termed existence and non-existence as objects; these are established as *vidyā* because their ultimate reality consists in cognition. Therein, according to the reasoning previously stated, one power is the cognition of existence characterized by the nature of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

The meaning is that this "veil of knowledge" (vidyāvaraṇa) consists of the nature of this world-duality, which is characterized by the power of perceiving the non-existence of the Self through the ignorance known as the fear of rising from this state. || 1173 ||
And therefore:
Tejeśa and Dhruveśa are the supreme state of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas);
and above that, in the obscuration of the means of valid knowledge...
This supreme state, the place of attainment for the five objects and other means of knowledge previously mentioned which depend upon the *māyātattva*, belongs to Tejeśa and Dhruveśa;
and since they reside above the *vidyāvaraṇa* in the *pramāṇāvaraṇa*, this [level] is also the *pramāṇāvaraṇa*.
He who is joined with the two worlds.
Now, ... I shall speak out of respect. || 10-1174 ||
Regarding the conceit within conceit, concerning the obscuration that has ascended above the obscuration of valid cognition and is named "conceit," I shall describe those Rudras to you:
Brahmā, Rudra, Pratoda, and Ananta as the fourth.
Therefore, the meaning is that this world of the veil of māyā is adorned by the four worlds of the Rudra-realms.
Then, above that, is the perfectly pure enclosure; therein, they know there are three Rudras.
The one-eyed, tawny-colored Haṃsa has thus been described in brief;
it will be stated that their retinue is innumerable. Now—
Above the enclosure of Śiva, there is one [world] known as Dhruva.
Established in the presence of Rudrarāja... then...
the covering of liberation above.
And therein—I shall describe the eleven Rudras in brief. || 10-1177 ||
He said to them:
"Brahmadanki, Diṇḍimuṇḍa, and likewise Saurabha;
Janmamṛtyuhara and Praṇīta, who bestows both happiness and suffering. (10.1178)
Vijṛmbhitaḥ... the remover of birth, the remover of death. He gives pleasure by cutting it away, thus he is "Sukhada" (the giver of happiness); likewise, he is "Duḥkhada" (the giver of suffering).
These eleven— ...— are thus declared to be situated above the palate.
By the phrase "above the palate," he reminds us that the previously mentioned Īśvara-tattva is their locus.
Then, furthermore, above that, the auspicious stainless state known as Dhruva is to be understood. || 10-1179 ||

The meaning of the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is that Rudra, known as Dhruva, is mentioned three times here— once in the *pramāṇāvaraṇa*, once in the *śivāvaraṇa*, and once in the *dhruvāvaraṇa*— due to his division into gross,
subtle, and supreme forms. Now, regarding this *dhruvāvaraṇa*:
The three powers of the Lord are situated upon the crown of the head.
And that has been explained in due order:
as for the triad of powers previously mentioned in the subtle enclosure (sūkṣmāvaraṇa) as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—
The meaning is that this very [reality] exists here in the form of the other.
Furthermore, this is the city of that very power which is the primary [principle] here, designated as the power of will (icchā-śakti).
And those [goddesses] beginning with Vāmā are proclaimed to be included within this one. || 10-1180 ||
Therefore, the meaning is that this world of Will (icchābhuvana) is surrounded by the three worlds beginning with Vāmā. || 1180 ||
Then—
the veil of awakening above...
and there the Rudras—
...I shall explain in brief:
Prīta, Pramudita, Pramoda, and Pralambaka. || 10-1181 ||
Viṣṇu, Madana, Gahana, and likewise Prathita—
this is declared here as the Rudrāṣṭaka, which should be understood [as situated] in order from the eastern direction onwards.
Beyond that— [the veil of the convention (samayāvaraṇa) above]...
here [are] the Rudras...
...I shall explain in brief:
Prabhava, Samaya, Kṣudra, Vimala, and likewise Śiva. || 10-1183 ||
Then Ghana is proclaimed, and after that Nirañjana;
Rudra and Oṃkāra— these five are the qualifiers of the convention (samaya) called Prabhava, [the first being] Kṣudra, and [the last] Vimala Śiva.
He is known by the name Vimalaśiva.
And these—one should know them above the palate. 10-1184.
The plural form "vijānataḥ" (those who know) is used due to the distinction between the disciples and grand-disciples to be instructed, and so it is elsewhere.
The phrase "above the palate" is intended as a reminder that this point marks the limit of the locus of the Īśvara-tattva. || 1184 ||
Thus, having first enumerated the number of worlds contained within the fifteen worlds [of the lower sphere], he concludes this as follows:
"The fifty-nine worlds, beginning with Jñānaśakti, are in successive order."
One should purify this [mantra] ending with Rudra and the syllable Oṃ at the time of initiation.

From the worlds situated within the subtle coverings of Īśvara and Vidyeśvara— which are the first manifestations of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti)— down to Rudra and ending with Oṃkāra, there are fifty-nine intermediate worlds within the Īśvara-tattva.
In that [system], there is one for Īśvara, eight for the Vidyeśas, four in the Rūpa-āvaraṇa,
three in the Sūkṣma-āvṛti, two in the Śuddha-āvṛti, two in the Vidyā-āvṛti, two in the Pramāṇa-āvṛti, four in the Māna-āvṛti, three in the Suśuddha-āvṛti, and one in the Śiva-āvṛti.

This Īśvara-tattva is endowed with fifty-nine intermediate worlds: eleven in the Mokṣāvṛti, one in the Dhruvāvṛti, four in the world of Icchā-śakti together with the triad of powers beginning with Vāmā, eight in the Prabuddhāvṛti, and five in the Samayāvṛti.
Thus, this Īśvara-tattva is joined with these fifty-nine intermediate worlds.
One should purify it in brief, but not in detail. || 1185 ||
And for each of these, there is an entourage of many thousands of millions;
and they—
All three-eyed, bestowing boons, they possess bodies of pure power.
Resembling pure crystal, with ten arms and the moon as their crest-jewel, they all hold tridents in their hands and are adorned with crowns of matted hair. || 10.1187 ||
All were endowed with every virtue, omniscient, and lords of all;
they were complete with all the primary marks and adorned with every ornament.
Crowded with Rudra-maidens of divine and captivating forms,
they sport with the foremost of cities, impelled by the ordinances of Śiva’s will.
That very capacity, which is pure— unpolluted by the impurity of *māyā*— and has knowledge and action as its object,

is the "body" (*vigraha*) or essential nature of those [deities]. Although all [beings] are essentially the manifestation of the entire universe, which is like their own limbs, in the sense of "I am all this," nevertheless, by the will of the Lord...
Even though they are of various forms; likewise in what follows as well. || 1189 ||
Now, [above] Īśvara and likewise below Sadāśiva is the enclosure of Suśiva; within that, Sadāśiva is to be known. (10–1190)

This single principle of Īśvara, which has been described as the manifestation of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the clearly manifest "thisness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*) regarding all objects, is not possible without the intermediate principle of Sadāśiva, which consists in the manifestation of an "I-ness" that veils the clearly manifest "thisness."
Since the arising of external manifestation does not occur without internal manifestation,
there must be the *sadāśiva-tattva*, which serves as the foundational wall for the *īśvara-tattva*; with this intention, [the text speaks] above *īśvara*.

It has been stated that below the world of Sadāśiva—which belongs to the Sadāśiva-tattva and will be described as the primary [world]—there exists the enclosure of Suśiva, which rests upon the Sadāśiva-tattva. And here, Suśiva is indeed the venerable Lord Sadāśiva himself. As it is said: "In that [enclosure], Sadāśiva is to be known."
The meaning is that this is the "lower form" (apara-rūpa), distinct from Sadāśiva, who will be described as the "higher form" (para-rūpa). || 1190 ||
And he— the god with fifteen eyes, adorned with the crescent moon as his crest, endowed with five faces, possessing ten arms, and of great strength— [is seen]. (10.1191)
Resembling pure crystal, shimmering indeed with blazing splendor,
he was seated upon a lion-throne,
and above that—
...seated upon a white lotus throne. || 1192 ||
Accompanied by the five limbs of Brahmā, endowed with the Sakalādya [mantras], joined with the ten Śivas, and possessed of the eighteen Rudras. || 10-1193 ||
The five Brahmans are Sadyojāta and the others; the limbs are the heart and the others. || 1193 ||
He divides [the mantras] beginning with Sakala:
"Sakala, Niṣkala, Śūnya, Kalāḍhya, Khamalaṅkṛta, Kṣapaṇa, Kṣayāntastha, and Kaṇṭhyauṣṭhya is remembered as the eighth. (10)
He states its location according to the internal sequence: "The God of gods, Sadāśiva, should be known to be between the eyebrows;
the Lord is surrounded by [the principles] beginning with Sakala."
"Deva" means one who shines.
Furthermore: ... by Oṃkāreśa and the others, in sequence. || 10-1195 ||
The word "vṛta" (surrounded) is understood [to carry over]. || 1195 ||
He speaks of the ten Śivas beginning with Oṃkāreśa:
"Oṃkāreśa, Śiva, Dīpta, Kāraṇeśa, Daśeśaka, Suśiva, Kāleśa, Sūkṣmarūpa, and Sutejas. (10.1196)
And Śarva is declared as the tenth;
these [deities] are situated in order, beginning from the eastern direction and ending with the zenith.
Outside of Sadāśiva’s Brahmā-enclosure and the enclosures beginning with Sakala.
Of these also— namely,
"the eighteen Rudras are situated outside"— it is exactly thus.
... hear indeed their names. || 10-1197 ||
Then Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Svayambhū, Agnivīrarāja, Raurava, Mukuṭa, Visara, Candra, and Bimba sang forth. || 10.1198 ||
Lalita, Siddharudra, Santāna, and Śarva; Para, Kiraṇa, and Pārameśvara as well. || 10-1199 ||
"Agnisahita" and "Vīrarāṭ"—these two are the incarnations (avatāras) of liberation for one who bears this name;
they remain bestowing grace upon the Lord through the descent of the scriptures.
For this very reason, it is said that there are ten and eighteen divisions. || 1199 ||
Thus, surrounded by the four enclosures of Brahmā’s limbs, the Sakalas, and the Śiva-Rudras, he is known as Sādākhya— the manifest one whose body consists of mantra,
the presiding witness over all causes, and the agent of creation and dissolution. (10.1200)
And he is the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon practitioners who perform the rites.

Because the designation "the Existent" (sat) has been in use from the time of the manifestation [of the universe] onwards, the Lord Bhava resides in the Sadāśiva-tattva known as "the Existent" (sādākhya); and he, being possessed of parts (sakala), is the embodiment of mantra.

In relation to the partless form (niṣkalamūrti) which will be described later, he is the presiding lord (adhyakṣa), the supervisor of all, and the all-seeing. He makes his status as the cause of all perfectly clear with the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi):
"creation" and "destruction" (saṃhāra) also imply maintenance (sthiti) and dissolution (vilaya).
For practitioners— that is, for those who worship and seek liberation—
She accomplishes liberation; indeed, for those devoted to ritual performance, She brings about liberation preceded by worldly enjoyment.
Furthermore:
seventy million mantras are established upon his seat.
The meaning is that all seven crores of mantras— consisting of three and a half crores whose office has ceased and three and a half crores whose office is active— are presided over by him; however,
according to the venerable Lord Īśvara, it is the three and a half [crores] whose office is active.
Thus it is presided over by him, because his enjoyment is gross; this is the implied meaning. For this very reason, the thousand-petaled lotus-seat of Īśvara was previously mentioned. || 1201 ||
He states that her seat is even more distinguished than that:
"The seat is rich with a hundred thousand petals and possesses the luster of ten million moons.
This means it has more petals even than the lotus of the Lord (Īśvara).
And that lotus [is presided over] by the five faces, beginning with the left and ending with the lord (the eastern face), each possessing three eyes. || 10.1202 ||
It is surrounded in the eastern direction by the various powers (śakti-bheda) beginning with Tārā;

Vāmā and the others previously mentioned are present here in their supreme form, while those beginning with Vibhu were stated earlier as follows: "Vibhu, Jñānī, Kriyā, Icchā, Vāgīśī, and likewise Jvālinī."

"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—all [these] have the radiance of the fire of time. Thus they are taught in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra). As for the powers beginning with Tārā, they consist of the thirty-eight *kalās* previously mentioned. Among them, Vāmā and the others are situated according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east.
The [powers] beginning with Vidyā are on the petals from the middle to the end, whereas those beginning with Vidyā are in reverse order, from the middle to the eastern petal.
As it is stated in the *Śrīpūrva*: "Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā... (8.33).
Having begun thus, [it continues]: "One should place [the deities] along the path of the sun;
one should arrange the other nine, beginning with Vibhu, in reverse order. (8.65)
Tārā and the others, however, should be visualized as being placed in the sequence starting from the east and so forth.
And of this god,
the power of knowledge and the power of action are situated on the left and the right, respectively.

According to the principle that the sequence of meaning is stronger than the sequence of recitation, it should be understood that the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) resides in the right [hand] and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in the left.
Furthermore:
"O Goddess, the supreme power of will (icchā-śakti) is that by which everything is presided over: [the powers of] emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. (10.1204)
That [power] by which the Lord of Gods always performs everything on every path—
she indeed always rests upon his lap, being as one with his own self.
"Pervades" (*paraiti*) refers to [the Lord's] dependence upon knowledge and action. "Presided over" (*adhiṣṭhitam*) means pervaded.
"All" (*sarvam*) is a qualification of the fivefold process beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*). "At all times" (*sarvadā*)—as it is said:
"Thus, even in worldly transaction, the Lord enters the body and so forth."
"By his own will, he may manifest externally that very mass of objects which is already shining within.

According to this principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, the conscious self (*cidātman*), who is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) presiding over the body and so forth, [performs] the manifestation of those objects, their persistence, the relishing of them, and the establishment of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
By bringing about the state of being composed of that light, it performs the five cosmic acts (pañcakṛtyāni) for the world at every moment.
Regarding the phrase "resting on the lap": this refers to the embodied form of Ātmaśiva. || 1205 ||
How then is it said to belong to Sadāśiva? He states its number:
"And that will of Śiva, the God of gods, the Supreme Self, is indeed he himself in another form, having the five mantras as his great body. (10.1206)
The glorious Sadāśiva, the God of gods, assumes forms according to his will;

since Śiva himself exists as Sadāśiva in another form, the meaning is that his power is said to be Will (icchā). By means of the five mantras beginning with Īśāna, she is "great," that is, pervasive throughout the universe.

And because his body possesses great majesty, he states that this assumption of another form by Śiva for the sake of bestowing grace occurs through his own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), saying: "the one who assumes a form by will. For this very reason, because he is like Śiva in both assuming and not assuming a formal appearance at all times, he is called Sadāśiva.
The glorious one, endowed with an excellence of the radiance of knowledge.
And here— those powers of his which have been described, beginning with Vāmā... ||
...and likewise indeed are the leaders of mantras. || 10-1207 ||
Those who abide in the fourfold obscuration. || 1207 ||
All these,
O Goddess, each one surrounded by hundreds of millions of *arbuda* lotuses,
as well as by *kharva*, *nikharva*, and other similarly powerful manifestations.
[They were] endowed with the forms of knowledge, rich in their own nature, possessed of immeasurable qualities,
complete with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament.
Rich with laughter, dance, and amorous play, with the intoxicating movements of raised eyebrows,
they resembled hundreds of millions of moons and seemed to pour forth nectar.

The meaning is "surrounded. "Each one" (*ekaikam*) is an adverbial modifier. "Lotus-germ" (*padmārbuda*) and so forth refer to specific numerical categories that will be described later. "With counterparts" (*pratirūpaiḥ*) means with those resembling the principal [deities].
"Power" (*balam*) refers to the capacity for knowledge and action. "Form" (*rūpam*) refers to the beauty of appearance as well as essential nature.

The qualities (*guṇas*) are omniscience and so forth; the characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) are knowledge, yoga, and sovereignty. Being adorned with every ornament, they are the self of the entire universe without exception. Due to their inclination toward the grace of others and their state of eternal joy, they are endowed with laughter, dance, and the like. For this very reason, [they act] by mere playfulness (*helāmātreṇa*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: she was surrounded by hosts of celestial nymphs who possessed such amorous gestures (*vibhrama*) and playful charms (*vilāsa*) that their intoxication arose even from a mere movement of the eyebrows due to their perfection in bestowing grace upon others. || 1210 ||
And therefore, here—
along with them, the Rudras always sport at will with the Lord in excellent cities that are auspicious on all sides and possess a radiance equal to ten million moons. || 10.1211 ||
They sport with those vidyās solely for the sake of favoring others, dwelling there distinguished by magnificent cities. || 1211 ||

All these [Bodhisattvas], being completely liberated from the phenomena of *māyā*, are stainless and free from the fever [of affliction]; possessing all-knowing and unfailing powers, they exercise their authority. || 10-1212 ||

The nature of *māyā* is the veiling of the essence of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*); they are liberated from that. Although, in relation to Paramaśiva, their state of contraction is the effect of *mahāmāyā* and constitutes a bond (*pāśa*), nevertheless, unlike the subjects of *māyā*, they do not consist of contraction. For this very reason, they are stainless (*nirmala*).
They are not veiled by *māyā*. For it has already been stated that contraction alone is the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality) for persons.

Therefore, these [beings] are free from fever—that is, devoid of all torment. Nevertheless, for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who are to be graced, they have been established by Śiva as being bound by the authority of *niyati* (fate) and *kāla* (time). And they are omniscient.
And the compound is "those whose powers are unfailing" (amoghaśaktayaḥ).
Furthermore:
"Upon the exhaustion of their office, they become peaceful, all-pervading, and auspicious (śiva).
'Peaceful' means those from whom the expansion produced by Great Māyā has ceased; likewise,"
The meaning is that they become one with the all-pervading Śiva.
And thus:
"Those who are impelled by another shall never again come into existence. (10.1213)

Those who have not realized the true reality (tattva) attain the state of the Void beyond the Void throughout the entire universe, from the great cycle of transmigration down to Sadāśiva; they are created again in the Great Emanation, as will be shown in the eleventh [chapter]. However, these venerable ones are indeed liberated—this is the meaning of the word "again" (punaḥ).
He concludes: "O fair-faced one, this is known as the enclosure of Suśiva, containing the essence of mantras;
that which has mantras situated within its seat and within its enclosure is this [enclosure] of Suśiva."
The meaning is that the *āvaraṇa* (veil) belongs to the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, and it refers to the *bhuvana* (world). Furthermore,
they are called *āvaraṇas* precisely because, for all others except those possessing perfect knowledge, they act as obstructions to the supreme state (*parapada*).
Then,
above this, is the enclosure of the Bindu, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
The veil whose nature is the pervasion of the locus of the reality of the *bindu* is the *bindu*-veil. || 1214 ||
There, a lotus greatly radiant, endowed with ten koṭis, exists;
there, seated upon that lotus, is the deity Śāntyatīta, of great splendor.
Five-faced, large-eyed, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
possessing the brilliance of a mass of a thousand lightning flashes, he is adorned with shimmering rubies.
That which is the entire universe, because it is here distinguished by its union with the brilliance of the great expansion attained, is the ruby (māṇikya). || 1216 ||
Furthermore:
"O lady of excellent vows, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti are known as the retinue of that Śāntyatīta. (10.1217)

The fourfold *kalās* previously mentioned, which contain within them the entire path of the universe and abide as the form of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), constitute the retinue (*parivāra*) of this deity.
Furthermore:
on its left side, Śāntyatītā is situated.
And these—
All of them are remembered as having five faces, ten arms, and the moon as their crest-jewel.
Thus, in this way—
the *bindu-tattva* has been fully described as being surrounded by hundreds of millions of *pura*s,
associated with the mantras, the lords of mantras (*mantreśas*), and their respective masters (*tadīśas*). And this is the *śāntyatīta*.
It consists of the supreme pervasion (*paravyāpti*) of the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka. As he will state:
"The Bindu, the Lord, conjoined with these *kalās*, is to be meditated upon" (12.157).
It is also said in the *Yojanikāgrantha*:

Regarding the statement, "And the *bindu* is indeed the Lord himself" (4.264), it has already been explained that on this path, the mantra-deities and so forth abide through the distinctions of gross, subtle, and so on.
Having described this enclosure of the Bindu, he also speaks of the enclosures beginning with the Half-moon:
"Above that is the Half-moon, and above that is the Nirodhikā. (10.1219)
Regarding this, he speaks of the worlds:
"These two, however, are great stations endowed with five pentads of kalās. The kalās are the deities."
Therein:
Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, Vimalā, and Śivā. || 10-1220 ||
These indeed reside in the Half-Moon; listen, O Dear One, regarding their presence in the Nirodhinī:
Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā. (10.1221)

The qualification of Vimalā is "Śivā. Because of the excellence of illumination and bliss inherent in the state of the Half-Moon (ardhacandra), the powers associated with it possess names appropriate to that state. Furthermore, because they are the cause of obstruction, the three powers associated with the state of Nirodhinī are Rundhanī, Rodhanī, and Raudrī.

Regarding the powers (*śakti*): for those who are awakened, when the obstruction has ceased, there is the pair of powers known as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "awakening" (*bodha*), which dispel darkness; they are designated thus because they grant entry into the upward path. || 1221 ||
In this context, he recalls the previously mentioned division of measures:
"The *bindu* is said to be half a measure, and its form as the vowel [A] consists of four measures;
half of that is the *ardhacandra*, and the *nirodhikā* is one-eighth. (10.12–22)

Regarding the passage, "short, long, protracted, subtle, and extremely subtle" (6.4), this was already determined at the very point of resolving that text: to the extent that the utterance of the mantra ascends higher and higher toward the supreme state, to that same extent the gross form residing in the relationship between the signifier and the signified [diminishes].

It returns, and as its states of being increasingly subtle and most subtle are manifested, they grant an excellence of rest until, at the ultimate limit within the Self of the supreme reality of Unmanā, there occurs an immersion into the nature of Svacchandabhairava— a mass of consciousness and bliss— through the cessation of all limiting adjuncts.

That very point has been reminded here by the Supreme Lord; likewise, on the occasion of the purification of the worlds (*bhuvana-śuddhi*), the teachers must follow the mantra-based pervasion (*māntrī vyāpti*) in its forms ranging from the subtlest to the most subtle.
In the same way, it should be followed by oneself in what follows as well. || 1222 ||
He explains the essential nature of Nirodhinī:
"O fair-faced one, she brings about the cessation of even the gods, beginning with Brahmā;
what need is there to mention ordinary beings?"
Since this is so, therefore she is renowned as "the Extinction-bringer" (*nirodhinī*).
And thus, by means of the application of mantra-recitation preceded by the pursuit of the pervasion of the previously mentioned bond of instruments (*karaṇabandha*)—
But having pierced that [arrow], O fair-faced one, || 10.1223 ||

The remainder of the sentence is "is obtained" (*labhyate*). The meaning is "the deity Sādākhya. By the phrase "by means of the supreme state" (*parabhāvena*), it is meant that he is the very one previously mentioned, but now in this subtle form.
He describes its location and form:
"Above that, Nāda is said to exist; it has the luster of the pollen of a lotus filament. (10.1224)
It is pervaded by great beings possessing the splendor of ten million times ten thousand suns.
"Of that" refers to the veil that obstructs.
"Nāda" is the supreme form, which is Śrī Sadāśiva himself, whose true nature consists of the non-dual reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that encompasses all denotators.

"Having the luster of the pollen of a lotus filament" means being endowed with an excellence of radiance. "By great persons" refers to those situated at progressively higher levels of excellence, beginning from the stage of the Great Lords of Mantras (mantramaheśvara).
Moreover, in this regard—I shall declare their presiding goddesses, five in number, within the world. (10.1225)
Among those great beings, the *nāyikās* are the presiding deities.
"In the world" (*bhuvane*) means when the veil of sound (*nādāvaraṇa*) has passed away; that is to say, within the fivefold world (*bhuvanapañcaka*). || 1225 ||
She said:
"Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā;
this fifth digit (kalā) is declared to be Ūrdhvagā. (10.1226)
These names are due to their excellence in brilliance; among these, Pañcamī is the most preeminent.
Furthermore:

"In that [place], a very extensive lotus..."—the phrase "in that" refers to the abode of the upward-moving power (*ūrdhvaga-śakti*). It is described as "very extensive" in comparison to what has been previously mentioned.
And there—
................the Lord, the Master of the Upward-Moving (Ūrdhvaga), resides;
he is the presiding sovereign over the power known as the Upward-Moving (Ūrdhvagā), whose nature is the End of Sound (Nādānta).
And he—resembling the moon and the arbuda [tumor], five-faced, and three-eyed. || 10-1227 ||
Crowned with the crescent moon, peaceful, ten-armed, and of great body,
the god holds a trident in his hand, wears matted locks, and is surrounded by Indhikā and the others.
"He is peaceful" because of the cessation of the entire universe up to the limit of sound; his wearing of matted hair and so forth are as previously described.
Furthermore:
"But his upward-moving *kalā* always moves upon his lap.
Such is the extent of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *sādāśiva-tattva*. Thus it is here in the *sādāśiva-tattva*.
The five coverings (*pañcāvaraṇa*) consist of Suśiva, Bindu, Ardhacandra, Nirodhikā, and the forms of Nāda and Nādānta.

Among these, in the covering of Suśiva, there is Sadāśiva, the eleven faces and limbs (*vaktrāṅgaikādaśikā*), the eight beginning with Sakala, the ten Śivas beginning with Oṃkāra, and the eighteen Rudras beginning with Vijaya— thus [it is said] by the venerable Sadāśiva.

Including the presiding deities, there are forty-eight. Those seated upon the lotuses of the thrones are fifty-six: nine beginning with Vāmā, nine beginning with Viśvā, and thirty-eight beginning with Tārā; then Jñāna and Kriyā situated at the sides, and Icchā on the lap—thus, there are one hundred and seven deities here.

In the Bindu-enclosure (bindvāvaraṇa) there are six deities: Śāntyatīteśa, Śāntyatītā, and the four beginning with Nivṛtti. In the Ardhacandra-enclosure, however, there is the pentad of powers beginning with Jyotsnā. In the Nirodhinī [enclosure], there is the pentad of powers beginning with Rundhanī. After that is the venerable Lord Nāda (nādabhaṭṭāraka). After that...
In the state of Nādānta, there are four beginning with Indhikā; and in the state of Ūrdhvageśvara, there is Ūrdhvagā—thus making six.
In this way, there are one hundred and thirty deities here in the Sadāśiva-tattva.
Now, regarding the Śakti-tattva, he instructs on the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas) and so forth: "Thereafter is the world of Suṣumṇā; Suṣumṇā is established therein. (1229)
The deity named Suṣumṇā, by whose presiding the central channel is called Suṣumṇā.
And it is not she alone who resides there, but rather her lord—
the Lord of Suṣumṇā— who stands there with the luster of ten million and ten thousand moons,
possessing ten arms and three eyes, seated upon a white lotus. (10.1230)
The glorious one, whose crest is the moon, has five faces and a massive body.
Furthermore:
the *iḍā* and the *piṅgalā* are situated on the left and the right. (10.1231)
But Suṣumṇā, O lady of excellent hips, is grey like a particle of frost;
the goddess holds a white lotus in her hand and is adorned with a garland of lotuses. (10.1232)
The goddess, who has five faces, is richly adorned, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident; she should be meditated upon by practitioners and others as seated upon his lap.

Regarding the phrase "tuṣāradhūsarā tviti," by the word "tu" (but/and), it should be understood from another tantra that [the other two channels] are iḍā and piṅgalā, which are dark-blue and reddish-brown respectively. || 1233 ||
He says that this Suṣumṇā is all-pervasive: "By her, this entire path extending below and above is strung together. "Strung together" means bound, filled, and pervaded;
"below" refers to the limit of Ananta, and "above" refers to the limit of the Śiva-tattva. "The entire path" refers to the path within the body (śārīra).
And the external [is also included].

And therefore, the *nāda*, resting upon the foundation of the powers such as Suṣumṇā which pervade the universe, having pierced through the entire lower path— which is presided over by the downward-flowing channel— by means of its upward movement, and having ascended to the plane of the *nādānta*, [attains its goal].
"It dissolves into the *śakti-tattva* within the *brahmabila*-self"—thus he says: "The *nāda*, which is indeed the support of the *nāḍīs*, having pierced through this entire world... (1234).
Having emerged downward through the lower power as far as the head of Brahmā above,
it merges into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) via the channel as the unmanifest, imperishable sound.
Residing within all beings, he resounds, presided over by the power of Śiva;

his support is the *suṣumṇā* channel. Regarding the word "having pierced" (*bhittvā*), this refers to the instrument: the Power (*śakti*), having arisen from the place of emergence below, ascends gradually. Upwards...

Thus, by means of the upward-pointing power (*ūrdhva-śakti*) which has become manifest through the previously mentioned practice, [the practitioner], having emerged as far as the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*), becomes merged and united with that very channel (*nāḍī*). For that channel also terminates there; thus, it is joined right there, and from the union of the two powers, the vowelless resonance (*anacka-nāda*) arises.

Because it has the form of two *kubjas* (hunchbacks). And that *nāda*—according to the principle stated in another tradition, "That supreme seed called *nāda* resides within all beings" (*Kālikā-kula*, 1.5)—is in the form of an unmanifest sound within all beings; therefore...

Thus, this imperishable [syllable], whose nature is unchanging, exists as the resonance of the sound and other qualities to be described hereafter. Although it is said to be "dissolved in the aperture of Brahma" (brahmabila), its dissolution nevertheless consists in its abiding in an extremely subtle form as the very vibration of Śakti; for this reason, it is [identical with] Śiva-Śakti.
It has been stated that [the soul] is presided over by Him, but since there is no absolute destruction, the description as "imperishable" (akṣara) is entirely appropriate.
Since the pervasion of the Nāda is of such a nature, therefore—having understood this, O lady of excellent hips—one should purify that [path] within the Śiva-path. (10.1236)
Beyond that, one should know the Brahmabila, which is filled with billions of Rudras;
there, the supreme Brahmā is to be known, possessing the splendor of a hundred moons.
He has ten arms and three eyes; he has five faces with the moon as his crest-jewel;
the Blessed One holds a trident in his hand and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
The enclosure named Brahmabila exists both internally and externally as the support for the worlds.
Although three and a half crores of mantras have been mentioned, nevertheless,
because their retinue is innumerable, they are here also [treated] in their most subtle form.

Because he abides in form (*rūpa*), it is said that he is accompanied by tens of millions and hundreds of billions of Rudras. He is "supreme" (*para*) because he is superior to the previously mentioned gross [form] residing within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and to the subtle [form] residing within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*); for this very reason, due to his nature as Śakti, he is white and possesses ten arms and so forth.
Furthermore: "Brahmāṇī is indeed the supreme power (parā śakti) who stands upon the path to liberation;
she remains having blocked the gateway to the path of liberation. (10.1239)
And she is the bestower of the path to liberation, seated upon the lap of Brahman— meaning, in the highest sense, on the path to liberation:
"The power of Śiva is said here to be the mouth" (Viṣṇubhagavatītantra 20).

Thus, she abides on the path of the power directed upward from the state of persistence (*sthiti*). Therefore, for those who are ignorant, she remains obstructing that very door to liberation consisting of the path of power by the will of the Lord;
yet for those who possess knowledge, she is disposed to grant them the path to liberation.
Since Brahmāṇī is of such a nature, therefore, by means of the sequence of reciting the prescribed mantra—having pierced her here, O fair-faced one, one must proceed upwards, O beloved. (10.1240)
The meaning here is: "in this," that is, within the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva), [referring to] that which is above, namely the abodes of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
Now, therefore, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe that power which stands above [the earth], coiled like a sleeping serpent, and which is the support of all the worlds. 10.1241.

"Power" (śakti) refers to the veil of power residing within the principle of power (śaktitattva). By the phrase "whose form is like that of a slumbering serpent," [it is meant] that because its nature has blossomed throughout the entirety of the internal space up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmabila), it has rendered [the world] like one overcome by the stupor of poison.

Abiding in the form of a motionless coil, she is situated within, having entered the layer of skin above the *brahmarandhra* by means of a gradual progression. This very one is the support (*ādhāra*), for it is she who, pervading both below and above, sustains the universe; thus, she is called the "Supporting Power" (*ādhāraśakti*). I shall now describe her.
The meaning is: "I shall describe the worlds situated therein by way of their presiding deities. || 1241 ||
In that regard—
[there are] Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtāmitā;
because of their connection with subtlety, exhilaration, and boundlessness, these belong to the deities of the plane of Śakti.
The names are indeed of that very same kind.
And of these,
Vyāpinī is to be known as being in the middle...
these indeed are—
The remaining [deities] follow in order from the east onwards. || 10-1242 ||
And all these—
five-faced, three-eyed, highly resplendent, and possessed of great strength.
Thus it is:
The principle of Śakti has been fully described...
And here, in the enclosure of Suṣumṇā, there are Suṣumṇā and her Lord; in [the enclosure of] Iḍā and Piṅgalā, there are four deities;
in the enclosure of Brahmabila, there are two, namely Brahmā and Brahmāṇī; and in the enclosure of Śakti...
The five deities beginning with Sūkṣma constitute the eleven deities within the Śakti-tattva.

Furthermore, that which was previously described as the *sadāśiva-tattva*, characterized primarily by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), on account of the manifestation of the non-distinct co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "this" and "I," would not be possible without the *śakti-tattva*, which is characterized primarily by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). For indeed...
Without the threading of some internal form of slight swelling, nothing can arise;

thus, the Śakti-tattva is said to be the foundational wall for the Sadāśiva-tattva. Since that too, being of the nature of power (śakti), requires its own substratum, [the following discussion concerns] this entire universe up to the end of the Śakti-tattva.

That which is its substratum is called the Śiva-tattva; and since it transcends the path ending with Śakti, it is to be attained only by ascending that very sequence, and thus its perception does not exceed this [process]. Therefore, in order to describe the arrangement of the worlds within that [tattva] as well, with extreme subtlety, he says:
.........Listen to the Śiva-tattva, O beloved. || 10-1243 ||
It was surrounded on all sides by many excellent cities,
constructed with golden walls and adorned with jewels and rubies.

"Even here, within the Śiva-tattva that has ascended to the highest peak—endowed with the perfection of all enjoyments and the arising of all qualities of desire—the arrangement of golden ramparts and so forth exists; oh, how great is the power of the teaching! Thus, by speaking in this way, [the author] indicates that even at the limit of such extreme subtlety, there remains a state of existence.

The pervasion of earth and the other elements consists precisely of the fivefold power known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, appearing in the form of the manifestation of the thirty-five principles through the variety of appearances such as the predominance or subordination of the qualities (guṇas).
It manifests in the form of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) through an ever-increasing intensification of its solidification;
and even those five elements, in their progressively more subtle and most subtle appearances,
manifest in their full form as the aforementioned five powers (*śakti*), whose nature is the dissolution of solidification.

"It blooms"—thus, by the logic stated in [the verse]: "That single reality, consisting of the equilibrium of the five powers, exists in this manner as both gross and subtle forms" (4.295), it abides as the very self of the universe. Therefore, in each respective state, it exists in the form of Śiva.

The Supreme Lord teaches that even though [the self] possesses the nature of illuminating everything, the removal of the bondage consisting of the non-illumination of that [nature] is accomplished through the sequence of initiation and knowledge;
thus, "the arising of all desirable qualities" refers to all desires in the form of the most excellent enjoyments.
And it should be understood that "wherein" and "whence" refer to the arising of qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
Furthermore:
I shall describe the worlds situated right there. || 1245 ||
And he states those [powers] by way of their presiding deities:
"Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, without master, and without support;
this pentad of causes is established within the Śiva-principle. (10.1246)
"Ananta" is the collective term for the triad. || 1246 ||
Furthermore:
therein is a lotus, vast and extensive, arising from the infinite and the infinite; "vast and extensive" means in comparison to all the lotuses previously mentioned.
Because from this very obstruction of the infinite sun just mentioned onwards, there arises the manifestation of the infinite universe— without end, middle, or limit—
it was therefore previously called the "Infinite Seat" (*anantāsana*), which is itself infinite and so forth.
We consider it logical that we have explained the seat as "the end of the infinite" (adhyānantānta) and thus "the infinite seat" (anantāsana);
and this deity situated in the center of that lotus is Anāśrita.
The Goddess is of the nature of illumination and so forth; she does not reside within any particular path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), but rather is resorted to by all the lords of the worlds.
And he is the bearer of five faces, peaceful, omniscient, the Supreme Lord;
ten-armed, greatly radiant, the agent of creation and destruction. (10.1248)
He is the benefactor of all, the destroyer of those who bow down to him,
the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and possesses a radiance equal to ten million billion suns.
With the ruby of his crown shimmering, he was adorned on all sides;
the god wore divine garments and was anointed with divine perfumes.
With his chest raised in the lotus posture, having made the moon his crest-ornament,
seated upon a jeweled couch, and fanned by the waving of chowries.
He is adorned on all sides by hosts of tens of millions and billions of Rudras.
He is "Peaceful" (*śānta*) because even the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of duality have been stilled, extending as far as the enclosure of Power (*śakti*).
His possession of five faces and so forth is as before. [His nature comprises] emanation and withdrawal.

One should also observe [the signs of] stability and dissolution. The word "all" implies that for whomever grace descends, from that very moment comes the destruction of the fetters (*pāśa*). This is as before, according to the intention of the practitioner.
This very point is made explicit by the statement "enjoyment and liberation. [The practitioner] is one with a lofty chest and great enthusiasm.
And what more is there here?—She is all-pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, without a protector, and without support. (10.1252)
They have five faces, great heroism, ten arms, and the moon as their crest;
they possess three eyes, hold tridents in their hands, and are endowed with their respective causal origins.
These [energies], beginning with Pūrvā and ending with Uttarā, are established in this very way;
by these causes alone—namely Vyāpinī and the others—they are perfectly endowed, meaning they are non-different from them. "These" refers to the four ending with Anāthā.
He states the state of the fifth [stage]: "But the immutable Lord, established as the middle, remains unattached. (10.1254)
The goddess Anāśritakalā is seated upon his lap.

The intention of one who speaks thus is this: it is solely through their connection with Śakti that all things possessing power (śaktimant) accomplish their respective effects; and for this reason, even the state of Paramaśiva [is so].
Only that which possesses the expansive flavor of the throbbing power (*śakti*) is to be sought here, and not that in which all powers have become quiescent.
As for the designation "quiescent" used here, it refers to the subsiding of duality.
He concludes: "Thus indeed, O beautiful one, has the Śiva-principle been explained to you. (10.1255)
Having purified this very [reality], that which is above it is known as the Supreme Śakti;
she is to be understood by the name Samanā.
Then, above the Śiva-tattva,

she is to be understood as resting in that state in relation to the venerable Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka, who abides in the station of Vyāpinī where only the skin remains; and she is together with the mind, which is most extremely subtle.
It functions through *saṃvedana* (perceptive awareness), but because it has not yet attained the three levels within pure consciousness (*saṃvit*), it is called *samanā*.
As was stated previously:
"Conceptualization [leads] to knowledge in due order" (4.394).
He states that beyond this point there is no further activity of thinking: "And the mind is not born again thereafter. (10.1256)
And this Samanā is established as the agent of all causes, from the earth up to Śiva, for those who abide in the sequential order. (10.1257)
"Of all" refers to those beginning with Ananta and ending with Anāśrita. || 1257 ||
And for this reason, she—presided over by Śiva—bears many cosmic eggs:
"A separate pair, innumerable; each one, a separate pair" (2.50).
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*,
the two spheres consisting of the *brahmāṇḍa* and the *prakṛtyaṇḍa* are innumerable; however,
considering that the pair of the *māyāṇḍa* and the *śaktyaṇḍa* each exists as a single form, this [is the case].
The doctrine of that scripture— that Śakti remains with many other cosmic eggs contained within her— is indeed accepted here as well.

And regarding what was stated—that this [power] is presided over by Śiva through a perfect non-dual pervasion precisely because it is power—it is clarified here by means of the logic of unifying with the subject matter of the forthcoming chapter:
"Established therein, Śiva, the supreme cause, acts. (10.1258)

The meaning is: having ascended to his own stage of power— which consists of mere reflection, serving as a wall for the weaving of all phenomenal existents— by unfolding [the powers of] emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.
The supreme cause is Paramaśiva.
For he is the Great Lord, the causal agent, the cause of all causes. (10.1259)

The meaning is that He is the cause of all causes—from Brahmā down to Anāśrita, and from Earth down to Bīja—which, having been manifested by Him alone through His own sovereignty, are grasped as their respective levels; thus, He is the Great Lord who brings them forth within His own screen. Likewise, He is the Great Īśvara of those [causes].

The "agent" (kartṛ) is the independent one who excels all others by bestowing the respective appropriate powers; the "cause" (hetu) is the instrumental motive that impels and directs those very powers toward their respective functions. || 1259 ||
Furthermore:
That power called Samanā is known as His instrument;
the meaning is that She manifests the entire universe by means of Her own power alone.
For this reason: "By means of that, the Lord of Gods indeed presides over the five lower causes. (10.1260)

By means of that power of her own thought, she should preside over the five causes—beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Vyāpin—because she is the cause of all [principles] beginning with Sadāśiva; she should render them endowed with the capacity for their respective effects by means of vitalizing them. And thus, Śiva alone...
The supreme form assumes the nature of the unmanifested (anāśrita) and other forms; likewise, its supreme power also manifests as the nature of the powers of the unmanifested and so forth. || 1260 ||
Among those five causes, that which is the primary cause of the Supportless Lord (Anāśrita Deva) is this Supported [cause].
The venerable Anāśrita and the others are manifested by the Supreme Lord through His own power.
They appear together with their respective powers of grasping; therefore, those very goddesses assume the state of being the causes and effects of Anāśrita and the others.
And he, endowed with this power,
impels once again the Lord of the world, who is indeed without a protector.
The intention of the word "furthermore" (bhūyaḥ) is this: that Paramaśiva himself, having assumed the state of the Anāśrita [Bhuvana], issues this second impulsion. || 1261 ||
And in this very way:
Ananta, who is himself without a protector, shall awaken the Lord Vyomavyāpin—the Great God, whose form is space and who is all-pervading—unto the Infinite Lord (Ananteśa). || 10.1262 ||
And these, together with their respective powers as previously described, are both the impellers and the impelled.
Furthermore:
"The pervasive [power] is his instrument; the Lord is indeed the agent who is to be pervaded.
This agency of his is manifested through the demonstration of action.
Māyā, which exists in the form of karma, is situated below Śaktikuṇḍalī.
The Śakti that contains the entire universe within her, by virtue of the previously mentioned coiled form, is Śaktikuṇḍalinī.
She is Mahāmāyā because she is the "māyā" (the thread) of all things through her act of weaving them together, and because she serves as the foundational wall for their emergence up to this limit;
the term "kuṇḍalī" is used here due to Vedic usage. This is because she pervades the creative power (*kriyā-śakti*) of this [universe].
The Blessed One, being the agent by virtue of manifesting these [entities] which abide as the forms of karma, has himself become the object of that karma. As it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"Therefore, this [Self], existing in a state of separation, would make itself an object of knowledge."
"The object of knowledge is not [separate], yet its sovereignty is not fragmented by the orientation toward that [object].
(1.5.15). Likewise:
"Therefore, the nature of cause and effect is precisely the essence of the agent and the object. (2.4.2).
Even in the case of vibration—[it is said]:
"And here, the pair of states is designated as 'the state of being the agent' and 'the state of being the effect'" (1.4). || 1263 ||
He is not only the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā) whose nature is power, existing as his object; rather,
he is also that which is contained within it and that which is manifested by it—
the effect consisting of sound (nāda) and the point (bindu).
And this will be made manifest in due order in the immediately following chapter.
And therefore, from this all-pervading Lord Paramaśiva, who is the presiding authority, arises the manifestation of the universe—

beginning with [the aforementioned] and extending to the entire range from Mahāmāyā down to the Earth, consisting of the supreme, subtle, and gross levels, and comprising both the signified and the signifier.
The source of the universe (*viśvodbhava*). The meaning is that this very Lord then flashes forth as the self of that manifestation.
Since the Supreme Lord, by resorting to the level of *samanā*, manifests the universe in its supreme, subtle, and gross forms, for that very reason, that which is being manifested—
O lady of virtuous vows, that which begins with the earthly element and extends up to Sadāśiva—
All that is to be known as *prākṛta* (the phenomenal), characterized by destruction and origination.

Here, Sadāśiva is the supreme form, the venerable Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka. From the perspective of subtle vision, that which has descended from *Samanā*—the cause of the universe—is *prākṛta*; however, from the perspective of gross vision, it is...

The expansion of the principles (tattva) consists of thirty-four, beginning from the Sadāśiva-tattva down to the Earth (kṣiti). This [expansion] proceeds from Prakṛti—that is, from the Śakti-tattva—which partakes in non-difference from the Śiva-tattva.
In this regard, two methods of interpretation are well known; of these, the former alone is superior.
For it is stated in the forthcoming chapter that even the Unconditioned (*anāśrita*) is subject to emanation and withdrawal;
and this [Unconditioned] is to be known as possessing destruction and origination, yet it must not come to rest here at the level of the Support (*ādhāra-pada*), but rather,
by the very fact of being an object of knowledge, it attains identity with the Supreme Knowledge through the process of ascending into consciousness.

The meaning is "to be dissolved. Although one should have said "origination and destruction," the reversed order of the terms is intended to demonstrate that the succession of creation and dissolution is beginningless.
Having thus described the path up to the level of Samanā, he recalls the very procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) previously introduced:
"That power which was previously mentioned as being at the summit of the path, namely Samanā... (10.1265).
Having meditated upon her as infinitely radiant with rays like a thousand shimmering suns, the knower of the ritual, having invoked her, should establish her.
Then, having performed the ritual service (upacāra), as well as the invocation of Vāgīśī,
her installation, her worship, and likewise the sacrifice of the victim (paśuyāga).
Likewise, [he teaches] the authority regarding the conception and birth [of the embryo],
as well as yoga, enjoyment, dissolution, and immediately thereafter, expiation.

O fair-faced one, having performed the oblation for the lords of the worlds and for those dwelling in the worlds, as well as the oblation for the worlds themselves according to their respective order; 10.1269.

One should then purify the three principles (tritattva) and their constituent parts in due order. By the words beginning with "sphurat," he says this: that the universe, though appearing as if woven here [in this world], consists essentially of power (śakti) whose nature is nothing other than pure radiance. In the phrase "yā sā," the term "māyā" is used.
Some read: "This [one]" refers to the venerable Śiva (*śivabhaṭṭāraka*), who is the presiding deity of the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*).

The invocation and so forth follow the previously stated sequence. "Ritual service" (*upacāra*) means worship. Here, the invocation of Vāgīśī is that of her in her supreme form (*parasvarūpa*). Following the installation and worship of Vāgīśī—

The union of that consciousness within the womb of Vāgīśī is preceded by the sprinkling and striking of the disciple, the entry of that [consciousness] into his heart, the extraction of his consciousness, and its grasping;
this state of being conceived in the womb is due to the fitness of being composed of the Great Mantra appropriate for this stage. As for those of the worlds...

Having performed the oblation for those who are the lords of the worlds and constitute the primary [entities], one should also perform it for those other Rudras who, in relation to those primary worlds, dwell in other worlds and reside in the intermediate worlds contained within those respective *tattvas*.
