"According to what is appropriate" means that in the case of the *saṃkṣiptadīkṣā* (abbreviated initiation), it is by means of the reasoning that [the other rites] are included within it; however, in other cases, one should perform the *homa* separately and then carry out the proclamation (*śrāvaṇa*) and so forth.
Even though there are other worlds (*bhuvana*) within the level of Vyāpinī, which is included within Samanā, that exceed the pentad beginning with Vyāpya.
Although they do not exist [in that way], it is stated thus because this ritual is the remainder of all [others]. Afterwards, one should purify the triad of principles known as Ātmavidyā and Śiva;
for the sake of purifying the bodily, vocal, and mental [faculties], it is purified according to the previously mentioned sequence of oblations.

One should accomplish [this]. For thus the teacher, being engaged in the bodily and other activities within this Śiva-sacrifice (śivayāga), becomes composed of the pure principles (śuddhatattva) alone;
by the words "and the limbs," he indicates that these include everything from Māyā up to Sadāśiva, as they are contained within those three principles.
One should purify the principles (*tattva*) themselves, which are the constituent parts, by means of the rite of oblation (*homakarma*) through the very logic of their internal inclusion.
As it was stated previously:
"One should indeed offer a hundred [oblations] according to the division of the *ātmatattva* by means of the *dhāman*."
By means of the application of vocal utterance, one should offer oblations into the reality of the Self (ātmatattva);
this is to be understood by the teacher in the sacrifice of Śiva as extending up to the reality of Māyā (māyātattva).
"For the sake of the rite when there is a deficiency in the procedure, and for purification through expiation," and so forth (4.210–212).

And here, in the midst of this, after the rite of atonement (niṣkṛti), having performed the severance and the cutting of the bonds (pāśa), one should indeed cast the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 10-1270 ||
This was stated previously:
"Separation [from bondage] occurs through expiation and experience," and so forth (4.126).
And here, following the severance of the fetters (*pāśa*), preceded by the contemplation of the oneness of that [sacrificial] fire with consciousness, [the process continues].
The final oblation is performed with the word "Śiva. || 1270 ||
Then, having performed the extraction of that consciousness, its stabilization within oneself, and its stabilization [within the deity],

and having performed the invocation of the Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras) such as Vyāpin and others, their worship, the offering of portions of the eight cities (puryaṣṭaka), the announcement, the dismissal (visarjana), and so forth, the expiatory fire-oblation (prāyaścitta-homa) should be performed according to the method of the three principles (tritattva).
He reminds us briefly of such a sequence:
"Then, having performed the expiation...
He then states what should be done after that: "Then..."
...one should consecrate the razor with mantras;
and with it—
having cut the topknot...
According to the previously mentioned sequence of meditations, mantras, and so forth—having offered this to someone’s hand... [insert name]... may it be accepted.
The Guru should bathe the child. || 10-1271 ||

One should prescribe [the ritual] for bathing. Likewise here as well, since there is no specific injunction regarding the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*), that which was previously explained by the commentators as being the subject matter of the "seedless initiation" (*nirbījadīkṣā*) must be considered entirely incorrect. || 1271 ||
Then the teacher, having become purified and performed the rites such as the sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual of empowering the limbs),...
Having formed the *śikhā* (topknot) at the tip of the *sruva* ladle and offered the oblation, one should immediately bathe thereafter.
Then,
O fair-faced one, having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor,
having also performed the ritual for the disciple...
It consists of the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and so forth, as previously described.
One should worship the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha).
Likewise—Bhairava, who resides in the central region...
[is the object] of the sacrifice; this is the meaning.
Furthermore—.................. one should worship the Bhairava-fire;
the preceptor should perform the worship.
Then, having informed the Blessed One, for the purpose of the *yojanikā* according to the previously stated method— having duly completed the *pūrṇā* while recollecting the left-hand mantra.
One should recite that mantra with effort, precisely according to the previously stated characteristics.

The "previously stated characteristic" refers to the form of the ritual application of the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), preceded by the contemplation of all the objects of knowledge as described in the section on initiation (*yojanikā*). That [mantra].
Therefore, on this occasion of the utterance of the mantra, O fair-faced one, one should exhale while casting down the path of that which is to be abandoned. (10.1275)

As long as that power of *samanā* exists... because everything up to *samanā* is a fetter (*pāśa*), it belongs to the path to be abandoned (*heyādhvatva*). "One should expel" means upwards; this is the sense.
Then he describes the *yojanikā* (the process of unification), which consists of resting in the supreme reality (*paratattva*), beginning with the entry into the path of what is to be adopted:
"And above that, the *unmanā* state is said to exist.
Even *manas*, whose nature is mere cogitation, does not proceed there, nor is it possible; rather—"
The meaning is that this [reality] is indeed the nature of mantra as tenfold. For this very reason, it was stated previously here:

"Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with the nature of pure consciousness. Then the fettered soul attains the principle of Śiva and is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. (4.437)
Thus it has been said.
And because mental reflection does not proceed here, for that very reason:
"Here there is no time, no divisions of time, no movement, no category of reality (tattva), and no deities. (10.1276)
Time (*kāla*) extends from a moment (*kṣaṇa*) up to the highest limit (*parārdha*). The digits (*kalā*) range from *nivṛtti* up to *śāntyatītā*.

Movement (*cāra*) is the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Reality (*tattva*), according to its etymological derivation as "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*), consists of the manifestation of various universals (*sāmānya*) that pervade the respective worlds, perceivers, and so forth. The deity (*devatā*)...
From Brahmā down to Anāśrita. || 1276 ||
What then is this?
It is called the "well-extinguished," the supreme purity, which is the mouth of the Guru.
The "mouth" of the Guru, who is Paramaśiva, is the means for attainment. As it is said in the *Triśirobhairava*:
"The power of the Guru is even greater [than that of the Lord]."
And therefore:
"O fair-limbed one, that which transcends these is the supreme, stainless reality. (10.1277)

That [state] also is the transcended form of his ultimate repose; however, it is not something to be surpassed like the *samanā* state, because it is designated as "perfect nirvāṇa. "O fair-limbed one" (*varārohe*) is as before. It is supreme (*para*) because it transcends the universe, and full (*pūrṇa*) because it consists of the universe. Of that...

The *tattva*—the ultimate, essential nature—is the fact that everything from the earth (*kṣiti*) up to the *Unmanā* state has as its inherent nature the light of consciousness (*citprakāśamaya*), according to this etymological derivation; it is not, like the earth-principle (*pṛthvītattva*) and others, a form consisting of the manifestation of objects such as hardness. It is "without affliction" (*anāmaya*), meaning that wherein no affliction—in the form of non-recognition (*akhyāti*)—exists.
And it is said in the *Trikasāra*:
"By means of bodies consisting of bindu and nāda, which are peaceful and born of Śiva, the Lord transcends them;
he is the stainless, supreme Śiva."
Thus [ends the verse]. || 1277 ||

Therefore, for this reason: one should be joined to that eternal, unwavering state—which transcends causes, is stainless, pure, and auspicious—by means of the application of the Guru’s oral instruction. (10.1278)
In the omniscient, supreme reality, which is beyond the sky and indeed beyond the senses—in the mouth of the Guru, in the state of *unmanā*, that which is the preeminent yoga is identity with That.
Regarding this, [it is said]: "Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite [the mind] with the nature of pure consciousness" (4.437).

In the manner thus described—consisting of entry into that [reality] and its stabilization—the disciple’s self should be joined with one’s own self; that is, it should attain identity (*sāmarasya*) with it. As it has been said:
"Joined to that supreme reality, he becomes endowed with qualities such as omniscience."

"Śiva alone should eternally exist, undivided in every respect" (4.402). [He exists] in that which is eternal and perpetually manifest; for this very reason, in that which is unwavering and always of a single form consisting of the mass of pure consciousness, even during the states of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). He has transcended the causes, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Anāśrita.

The meaning is that it consists of the manifestation of the entire universe, which is distinct from the experience of that [limited] object. Furthermore, although this [consciousness] is the light of the entire universe, it is not in the slightest degree affected by that universe, because that universe has as its sole nature the light of that [consciousness]; therefore, it is "stainless" (*virajaska*) due to its purity, and consequently "auspicious" (*śubha*).
In that which has the nature of supreme bliss; in that supreme reality which is omniscient—being both "all" and "knowing"—and whose form is the non-dual light of the universe;
in that [reality] where there is the cessation and tranquility that transcends even the state of the "void beyond the void," and which is beyond the reach of the senses.
Thus, at all times and in all places, for everyone, there is only the single ultimate reality that is self-luminous.
He concludes:
"Thus, O sinless one, this path has indeed been declared by me in brief. (10.1279)
By the word "and" (ca), its purification and preparatory rites are also included. "This" refers to the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), which pervades the other paths.
And this [initiation] was not described in this way merely for the sake of purification;
rather, it reveals even the penetration into the supreme subject (parapramātṛ) within the entire range of objects of knowledge to those possessed of wisdom. Thus he says:
Having realized this, O Great Goddess, one attains the supreme state. Whoever discerns this path, described in such a manner, as an object of knowledge, enters into the state of the supreme subject.

Furthermore, O lady of excellent hips, having understood this regarding the body, the deity, the disciple, and the water-pot, as well as within the midst of the fire, the teacher is liberated and also liberates others. (10.1280)

Having stated, "I am manifest, residing within my own body, the agent of acts of grace" (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 9.49), one should first recognize that the entire path (*adhvan*) resides within the body; by means of this, one becomes possessed by Supreme Bhairava, whose body consists of the entirety of the paths. Then...
By knowing the manifestation of non-difference from one's own "I-consciousness" (svāhaṃbhāva) within the fourfold substrates beginning with the deity, in that very manner,

one is liberated and attains the state of Supreme Bhairava, who is the self of all; and by perceiving even those to be graced through non-difference from such a self of one's own, one liberates them as well.
"Having attained equality with Me, the living being is said to be liberated" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 9.53).
According to this established principle, [the Guru] brings about the very state of Supreme Bhairava; may there be auspiciousness. || 1280 ||
The unraveling of the knots of the text, the examination of each word in light of what precedes and follows,
the application of unbroken, essential reasoning, the perception of the unity of internal and external reality,
the correct synthesis of matters concerning the Lord of the City, and the full non-dual contemplation— these constitute [the true study].
Thus, in this path of the worlds according to my own free will, that which pertains to it has been briefly illuminated by me here.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Initiation into the Path of the Worlds" (*bhuvanādhvadīkṣāvidhi*), in the illustrious *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. || 10 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
"The Radiance of Self-Will":
Creating the universe as non-different from Himself by means of the power that is His own essential nature.
And withdrawing [the universe], the solitary, autonomous Bhairava of Consciousness triumphs.
As it has been said:
"Mounted upon this, Śiva, the supreme cause, performs creation... (10.1258).
And so forth. Desiring to determine that [matter] and establishing the connection between the chapters, the venerable Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace this path has been understood by me.
O God, the creation of the world was indicated by you, but not described. (11.1)

"This" refers to the Self of the universe (*bhuvanātman*). "The world" (*jagat*) is precisely the form of the sacrificial ritual (*adhvara*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*), both those residing within the body and those existing externally. It is "indicated" [in the passage]:
"The emergence of the world begins with the effect, such as *nāda*, *bindu*, and so forth" (10.1264).
Thus [it is said].
And therefore, you— O Mahādeva, tell [me] the creation of the paths by your grace.
O Mahādeva, Lord of the entire universe, whose true nature is luminosity and so forth, [reveal it] from yourself, your own self.

Tell of the creation— the origination— of the path (*adhvan*), because it has attained internal purity through grace (*prasāda*) and because it does not conceal the ultimate reality (*tāttvikārtha*). The term "creation" is intended as an illustration,
since maintenance (*sthiti*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) will also be described.
To resolve this, the illustrious Bhairava said:
"He who is that subtle, supreme deity, the all-pervading Śiva, the cause of all. (11.2)
O virtuous one, he has been described here as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) for you;

he who is established as the mass of extraordinary consciousness and bliss, the supreme and subtle, beyond even the reach of the internal organ (antakaraṇa), the deity whose true nature consists of luminosity and the like, and who acts by means of his own power.

The meaning is that because everything is manifested within this [consciousness], it is the cause; therefore, as the independent agent, he manifests everything within his own screen by means of his own power alone. As he will state:
"By his own splendor, O fair-faced one" (11.4).
And so forth. He says that what it causes to appear is not distinct from it: "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*).
It goes to, attains, and assumes the nature of all things; and yet, it goes to them, causes them to appear, and presides over them.

To that extent, because it is all-pervasive and its self-luminosity is never obscured, no miserable means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is required for the establishment of this self-luminous reality; on the contrary, the establishment of entities such as the means of knowledge themselves depends upon it. And therefore, Śiva remains so even in states such as the opening and closing of the eyes.

That which is of such a nature—namely, having the very essence of the supreme good (*śreyas*)—is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for what is to be done in this world. O lady of excellent vows, you who are the cause of attaining that non-duality have been described as such;
however, not merely by virtue of being all-pervasive and eternal, qualities shared in common with space, time, and so forth.

Nor has he been described in the manner common to potters and others—namely, as a producer of effects in dependence upon materials and so forth—for that would result in the Lord being no different from those others who are unfit for the teaching of non-duality. As it has been said by others: [text follows]
"But those who designate the Lord as the efficient cause— here, a handful of sesame seeds has been offered by them to that Controller,
who has been brought under subjection by resorting to another's wife."
"Alas, these [fools] proclaim the state of being a lord of desire! Thus [it is said].
Therefore, exactly what has been stated is correct.

Now, one might object: "The activity of those who act with foresight is never without purpose; yet we perceive no purpose whatsoever in this creation, which brings such exhaustion to the wheel of living beings.
To dispel this doubt, he says:
Without desire, he would create the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. || 11-3 ||
O lady of excellent hips, having effortlessly agitated the sky by her own splendor,

she creates the entire world— both stationary and moving, consisting of individual souls— not out of desire, but through her state of perfection and without longing for fruits, but solely through her independent play (*līlā*); yet there are no such things as "individual souls" [inherently existing].

Some [souls] are eternal; for if this were not so, then even though the souls in this beginningless saṃsāra are infinite, if one by one were liberated in each age, there would surely be an end to saṃsāra itself. Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone [is the source], whose forms consist of pure and autonomous consciousness alone.

In accordance with the position stated in the *Śivasūtra*, "The universe is the accumulation of His own power" (3.30), the world— which consists of the expansion of the object and subject based on the concealment of one’s own nature (*svarūpagopanā*)— manifests as if it were distinct, though it is not distinct from Him, like a city in a mirror. And thus, it is not...

If there were some distinct entity called the "soul" (jīva), then the Lord’s action would be subject to deliberation due to that [soul's] exertion. However, He does not manifest such a world through any external cause, but rather by His own splendor.

"In accordance with the principle stated in the venerable *Kālikākula*: 'The supreme power is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that God of gods, whose nature is supreme consciousness; by this [power] the Lord is never separated,' the void (*vyoma*), which is the enclosure of the Transmental (*unmanā*), is indeed one's own essential nature."
Having agitated [the breath],
one acts as Śiva, the supreme cause, according to the perspective stated in [verse] 10.1258: "But having ascended here, Śiva acts as the supreme cause."

The essential meaning is this: having taken recourse to the ground of the power of *samanā*, which serves as the foundational wall for one's own powers consisting of the existence and non-existence of states such as *vyāpinī* and *sadāśiva*, the universe is manifested by the Supreme Lord through His own power alone upon that wall of His own power which is the nature of *samanā*.

And therefore, that which was previously explained as the threefold meaning of the word "cause" (kāraṇa) has here become manifest; for this very reason, there is no separate material cause (upādāna) here at all, but rather it is that very [consciousness] itself which is space (vyoman)— thus he says:
But that [state] is declared to be "clinging" (upādāna) when it is agitated through its coming together. || 11-4 ||

That very space (*vyoma*), which is the essential nature of the pervasive obscuration, becomes agitated through its connection with the supreme power (*parā-śakti*)— which consists of eternal, inseparable awareness (*vimarśa*)— by virtue of *samavāya* (inherent relation),
thereby manifesting a state of agitation and displaying the stage of suitable contact.
It appears as if surging upward by manifesting itself as the foundational wall for the flash of the semblance of ideation (*idantā*),

which is slightly mobile; for in reality, it is the Supreme Lord’s power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), known as *unmanā*, consisting of supreme self-reflection (*vimarśa*), whose sole essence is the I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*), and whose play consists in the concealment of its own nature.

It manifests as being identical in nature to the wall-like thread that projects all existents, whose essence consists of the states of Sadāśiva and Anāśrita. In this way, it is established that everything—consisting of the instruments, the locus, and the material cause—is indeed non-different from the Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe. || 4 ||

And just as the world, although non-different from the Lord himself, is manifested by him as if it were distinct due to his state of being manifest, so too, upon the plane of the power of Great Māyā and in the realm of Māyā, does the manifold relationship of cause and effect appear, characterized by a manifestation of a fixed temporal sequence within that [world].
It is demonstrated as follows, as stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"By means of the diversity of forms, this Lord causes the succession of space to appear;
and by means of the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He causes the succession of time to appear as well. (2.1.5)
Thus [ends section] 4.
To establish this, he says:
"Therefore, that which is empty has arisen; from the empty, the emergence of touch occurs;
from that, sound has arisen—this was indeed previously told to you. (11.5)
Therefore, from that space (*vyoman*) whose nature is the power of equality (*samanā-śakti*),

there has arisen the station of Vyāpinī, which consists of the manifestation of the non-existence of the cessation of the manifestation of the entire universe, ending with the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka Śūnyamanāśrita. From that too—
Touch is the essence of the *tattva* of power (*śakti*), which has the form of a serpent asleep in the manner already described.

Thus, the single power of the Supreme Lord’s will (*icchā-śakti*)—consisting of the threading together of the manifestations of the objects of knowledge through its forms as supreme, subtle, and gross—is called both the *samanā* and the *vyāpinī* power. This is because of that very same will.

Because of the triadic nature arising from the differentiation of the powers of subtle form, knowledge, and action; and because of that very touch which is the essence of power, from the midst of the universe—which consists of both the void-form and the signifier-signified—the *nāda* (the primordial sound), composed of the undifferentiated totality of all signifiers, first arose. By the word "saṃ" (in the phrase *saṃśabdena*), [there is the indication] of that which is being produced.

It is stated that every effect is connected to a causal substratum whose nature is power (*śakti*). The word "previously" refers to the occasion of the manifestation of the veil of sound (*nādāvaraṇa*) and so forth.
And as for this resonance (*nāda*) that has been mentioned: "O Goddess of Gods, it is manifested in eight ways through the differentiation of sound;
although its nature is inherently unmanifest sound, it attains a manifest form through the eightfold divisions that are about to be described."
It has been attained.
Namely: resonance (ghoṣa), sound (rāva), noise (svana), word (śabda), that which is called a burst (sphoṭa), and indeed vibration (dhvani). || 11-6 ||
The sounds *jhāṅkāra* and *dhvaṅkṛta*—these eight sounds are proclaimed.
And regarding these, Dharmaśivācārya states in his own *Paddhati*: "We shall state their characteristics as they have been transmitted through the lineage of gurus."
Having begun thus, they are explained as follows:
"The sound that arises from the contact of the ear with a finger,
appearing like the roar of a blazing fire— that sound is called *ghoṣa*."
That sound which ends with it, being harsh like cracked bell-metal, slightly spreading to the vital points (marmas), and having experience at its conclusion, is known as *tadantaga*.
Then that sound, resembling the resonance of a bamboo flute, like a gentle rain in a windless place, is called "Svana"; indeed, that which follows it is described as "Asau."
That fourth sound, however, is the source of all sounds;
it is a resonance that makes itself heard in space, like the humming of bees.
Therefore, the fifth [element], the resonance (nāda) which manifests the distinction between phonemes and bestows clarity upon the sentence, is called "Sphoṭa" by the teachers.
Then, because it transcends all other sounds, there arose a resonance that brought delight to the ear,
produced by striking the fifth string of the lute with intense effort.
Likewise, it manifested in space along with the sixth, known as *dhvani*,
which is as excellent as the sound produced by the striking of all the strings of a lute.
This seventh [type] is soft yet firm and resounds with a "jhāṅkāra" sound;
it sometimes imitates the ringing of a bell, or at other times manifests differently.
That eighth sound, resembling the roar of a towering cloud, is known as *dhvaṅkṛta*.
Of these eight, the ninth is known as the Great Sound (*mahāśabda*), which pervades them all. (11.7)
Because he always resounds while abiding within all beings—
"The *nāda* situated in the midst of the *śakti* is like the resonance at the end of a bamboo flute"—
that *nāda* which has been thus explained is the Great Sound (*mahāśabda*).
He resides within all beings, from those with internal consciousness and external consciousness down to the immobile and ending with the divine wombs. For this very reason:
"That supreme seed called *nāda* which resides within all beings" (Kālacakra-tantra 1.5).
Thus, by means of the reality of reflective awareness (vimarśa) called Nāda, which is established through such statements, all things possess existence.
Since this is so, therefore:
"Hence, the Lord Sadāśiva is indeed manifest, consisting of the nature of vision and action. (11.8)
The meaning is that this very *nāda* is the essential reality (*satattva*) for the manifestation of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, who is the union of knowledge and action. || 8 ||
Then,
from this *nāda*, the *bindu* was produced, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the *nāda* in which the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is predominant within, and it is undivided from all that is knowable.
The Bindu is the light whose essence is the power of action; because its manifestation is undivided from all that is to be known, it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
It should be known as tenfold, bestowing the fruits of the ten principles. (11.9)
In ten ways, it manifests through ten colors and is conjoined with ten deities.

Predominant in the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the Bindu contains within itself the two powers of will (icchā) and knowledge (jñāna). Since each individual power is a convergence of all powers, there are nine powers; the primary [Bindu] consists of the equilibrium of these.
"The tenth is its own-nature (svabhāva)," thus it has ten elements. And these are: "White, red, yellow, black, green, and tawny;
blue, variegated in color, and crystal-like and beautiful. (12.154)
Thus, there are ten ways [of meditation] according to the distinctions of color and form to be described in the twelfth chapter. In that very same [text]:
"One should meditate upon Nāreśa, who has the luster of saffron, three eyes, and matted hair;
facing east, one obtains the fruit that belongs to one who subsists on air."
"He obtains that fruit of merit... (12.125–126).
Thus, [the text] will set forth the meditation on the five deities beginning with Tatpuruṣa, as well as the fivefold fruits thereof. Likewise...

In that very context, with reference to the manifestation of the *bindu* whose form has emerged from the internal resonance (*nāda*): "Through meditation on the resonance of the bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*), accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall occur within six months;
indeed, whatever he desires in the mortal world, that accomplishment arises for him."
But he who performs meditation on the *liṅga* conjoined with the primordial seed-syllable (*pūrvabīja*) shall,
within one month, behold the subtle *liṅga* above his body.
"Having seen that which resembles pure crystal, one is liberated;

indeed, perfection arises in the world of men within six months. (12.157) Thus ends the meditation on the sixth deity, whose nature is the light of consciousness differentiated as the internal *nāda*, and its fruit.
And he will explain it as follows:
"The Bindu, the Lord, should be meditated upon as endowed with the four digits (kalās): nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, and likewise śānti. (12.157)

He will state this and more. Thus, it should be explained that [the mantra], conjoined with the ten deities and together with the kalās such as Nivṛtti and the rest, bestows the fruits of the ten tattvas.
However, the commentators, having failed to reflect upon what precedes and follows this, [have stated otherwise].

The passage beginning with "And that very [reality] is tenfold" (11.9) concerns the principle of Vidyā; therein, excluding the neuter vowels and the *bindu* and *visarga*, there is the possession of the ten vowels starting with *a*.
The claim that there are ten levels of reality (*daśatattva*) here due to the union with the deities of each individual consonant beginning with *ka* as differentiated by those [vowels],
and that the fruit consisting of the nature of all speech is tenfold because it is manifested by this group of ten phonemes—
this which has been explained through one's own imagination is to be disregarded. The text, however, concerns the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
"The [state of] knowledge arises from that, and from that, illusion" (11.54)—this will appear later. This too has not been considered by them; so, enough of this insistence with those of the past.
Now, from this very *bindu*, Sadāśiva is to be known; he is endowed with eightfold divisions and limbs. (11.10)
He is joined with the five Brahma-kalās and the powers that are limbs of knowledge;
he is endowed with the five great knowledges and accompanied by the mūrtis.

He is Sadāśiva, who was previously described as having a gross form below the enclosure of the Bindu on the path of Bhuvana; for he is indeed [accompanied] by his eight divisions beginning with Sakala, by his limbs, by his five retinues beginning with Īśāna, and by the five Brahmās beginning with Īśāna, whose nature consists of omniscience and so forth, and who are primarily characterized by knowledge.
By means of the six limbs, the powers beginning with Vāmā and those beginning with Vidyā, the thirty-eight digits beginning with Tārā,
and the great scriptures of knowledge consisting of the five streams arising from the five faces.

It was previously stated that manifestation [of the Bindu] occurs through the ten [vowels] beginning with Oṃkāra and the eighteen Mūrtis beginning with Vīja. Therefore, as for the reading by others that "Bindu is Sadāśiva," it means that the Bindu is the form of Sadāśiva known as Nāda, which is endowed with the eight limbs beginning with Ghoṣa.
It has been explained by way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), but that is incorrect.
Furthermore—
He alone is the immutable Śiva in another form;
he who was previously described as the immutable Śiva in the form of the supreme cause is indeed [Śiva] in another form.
The meaning is that [he is] Lord Sadāśiva, and not something distinct from him.
Therefore—He should be known to exist in two states: that which is accompanied by utterance and that which is free from utterance. || 11-12 ||
And that very [reality] is again twofold by way of the nature of mudrā and mantra;
it is also twofold by way of the nature of action and knowledge, and by way of the nature of will. || 11-13 ||
That which is called Śiva, the imperishable, should be known as existing in two ways through its pervasiveness.

How so? To this he says: He exists by means of "simultaneous utterance" (sahoccāra), which consists of the nature of the supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, in the form of upward utterance (*ūrdhvoccāra*).
The innate nature (*svabhāva*) is the Supreme Śiva-self, free from excrement and pervading the entire universe without exception;

it is twofold even as the means for attaining this essential nature, in the form of *mudrā* and *mantra*. For *mudrā* is the reflection of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), which bestows joy (*mudaṃ rāti*) by sealing the wealth of internal consciousness.
Acting as the liberator from bonds, the shatterer, and the dissolver, she emulates the supreme expansion by assuming various specific configurations; likewise,
the mantra too possesses its true essence as the nature of supreme reflective awareness, consisting of internal, secret speech.

That which possesses the nature of both reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), the means for attaining the supreme reality, is indeed the Supreme Lord himself. For the Supreme Lord alone manifests in the form of the means, just as he does in the state of the goal (*upeya*). Furthermore, [he manifests] through the nature of the venerable Lord Īśvara, in whom the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) predominates, and through that in whom the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) predominates.

He alone has manifested as the venerable Sadāśiva; likewise, He has manifested as the nature of the power of will (icchā-śakti), as the form of Anāśrita, and as His own essential nature in the form of Paramaśiva, who possesses all powers. || 13 ||

The Lord does not manifest in this way solely through the diversity of powers as the means (*upāya*) for attaining the goal (*upeya*); rather, He manifests as the self of all denotative words (*vācaka*) pertaining to all worldly and scriptural conventions, and as the self of all denoted objects (*vācya*). Thus he says:

The meaning is: "as the full conscious Self" (pūrṇacidātmanā) by way of the nature of the thing as the form of verbal cognition, by way of the form of the word, likewise by way of the form of that [word's] cognition, and by way of its own essential nature (svarūpeṇa) as the thing denoted by the word. By the use of the term "by way of its own essential nature" (svarūpeṇa), this is the underlying intention: [The text continues: ...by way of its own essential nature. By stating "by way of its own essential nature," this is the intended implication: [the Self is not limited by these forms, but exists as their ground].

Since the Supreme Lord, even while manifesting in the form of the thought of all word-meanings without exception, remains a dense mass of undiminished consciousness and bliss, all this is indeed of the nature of the non-duality of Supreme Bhairava. As I have stated myself:

Some consider this external world to be abandoned; others [hold it] to reside within the body; still others [place it] within the locus of measurement (*meyānta*); and yet others [say it] resides in another, supreme body.
However, since this [world] never appears as something separate from the light of the sun of consciousness (*cidbhānu*), [it is not truly distinct].
I, Bhairava, the soul of the universe, shine everywhere with these my own splendors.
Thus [it is said]. However, for those who, due to being veiled by the power of illusion (*māyā*) of the Supreme Lord, lack the fitness for this manifestation, with reference to them it is said:
"O fair lady, the infinite web of bonds extends up to the end of *śamana*. (4.432)
Since this and more has been stated, there is no inconsistency whatsoever between what precedes and what follows.
Thus it is:
gross, subtle, supreme, and beyond the supreme, stainless. (11-14)
O Goddess of gods, Śiva is to be known in the Śivāgama as being of the nature of space, as Samana and Unmanā, and as transcending even Unmanā. (11–15)

He who has understood the sequence of the Transmental (unmanā), having attained it with excellence as described, and who has ascended the stream of that [power]— that Śaktimat-ātman is called "Śiva" in the Śiva-āgama, whose nature is supreme bliss (śreyas). He is gross in the form of the elements beginning with earth and ending with primordial matter (prakṛti), and subtle...

From the principle of *puṃs* up to *māyā*, and from the supreme *śuddhavidyā* up to the *śakti-tattva*, [the Lord] has thus manifested; likewise, by way of His own nature as the unconditioned (*anāśrita*) self in the form of space (*vyoma*). Furthermore, He possesses the powers of *samana* and *unmanā*; the meaning is that He is of the nature of that which has these two powers, namely the Supreme Lord Himself as the self of the entire universe without exception.
It means "it throbs" (sphurati).

Having thus stated, from the perspective of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), that the entire universe—from the gross level up to *unmanā*—is nothing but the Supreme Lord, he now instructs that, by way of its outward expansion (*prasara*), He alone vibrates as each respective causal principle and so forth:

... [the text continues] ... Thus, having shown that the universe from the gross level up to *unmanā* is identical with the Supreme Lord through the perspective of withdrawal, he indicates that He alone shines forth even in the process of emanation as the essence of each respective cause.
The state of Unmanā and Samanā is presided over by Śiva;
below that, he exists again in the form of the five causes.
That in which the universe abides is the "place" (*sthāna*), whose form is *unmanā*, consisting of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*).

And that place, whose form is *samanā*— consisting of the complete threading together of all things in the form of existence and non-existence— manifested by that very freedom, is perfectly presided over by Śiva upon his own foundation.
The meaning is that it manifests as non-different from itself. Below that *samanā*— in the state of *śūnyātiśūnya*, which is the pervasive self— is the *anāśrita* (the Unsupported),
which is primarily characterized by the five powers known as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).
That very Śiva exists once again in the form of the five causes, beginning with Divya; however, there are no others, such as Anāśrita and so forth, that exist apart from him. || 16 ||
And what is this? O Goddess, having presided over the pentad of causes from below,
[it arises] from the form consisting of the pentad of causes beginning with Anāśrita, which is situated beneath that.
Having presided over the stages of Śakti, Brahmarandhra, Suṣumṇā, Nāda, Nādānta, and Bindu by means of non-duality,
and having illumined those planes, this pentad of causes remains— this is the syntactic connection.
He analyzes this as follows:
"The pervasive one, situated at the summit of power, is the unconditioned [Anāśrita] at the door of the cavity. (11.17)
Ananta, Suṣumneśa, Anātha, and likewise Ūrdhvaga;
O Great Goddess, Vyomarūpī is proclaimed as Bindvīśa. (11–18)

"Pervasive" means the venerable Lord who pervades the manifest universe (*prapañca*) by his pervasion; "situated at the summit of power" means situated upon—that is, located within—that summit which consists of the enclosure of power (*śaktyāvaraṇa*).
"Gross and subtle" (11–14).

Thus, he manifests as the nature of the five causes previously mentioned; likewise, the venerable Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka is the "cave-door," being the form of Brahmā who presides over it; similarly, Ananta is the form of Suṣumneśa, the presiding deity of the Suṣumnā-enclosure; and Anātha is the "one who goes upward."

The Lord of Sound (Nāda), who presides over the End (Anta) and has the form of the Lord of the Upper Path (Ūrdhvageśa), as well as the Lord of Space (Vyomabhaṭṭāraka), possess the forms of the Bindvīśas known as Śāntyatīta, which reside within the enclosure of the Bindu. Now, as for those previously mentioned— the Anāhata, Anātha, Ananta, and Vyomavyāpin— if they are indeed the subsequent ones...

The levels (bhūmis) should be approached in direct order (ānulomyena), for it must be according to such statements as: "One who does not rely on them stands at the summit of power (śaktimūrdhastha). Alternatively, in reverse order (prātilomyena), it is likewise stated:
"But the pervasive one (vyāpī) stands at the summit of power; he whose nature is the letter Kha is the door of the cavity (biladvāraṃ kharūpakaḥ)."

Such things should be observed; what, then, is the sequence here? The Supreme Lord alone, through the state of equilibrium of the five powers (*pañcaśakti-sāmarasya*), assumes—by virtue of His absolute freedom—the nature of the five causes beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Vyāpin, and abides therein by pervading the manifest universe (*prapañca*).
He also manifests as the various forms of the Lords (Īśas) residing within the coverings (āvaraṇas) of Śakti and the rest;

however, there is no such thing here as either direct order (anulomya) or reverse order (prātilomya). Rather, the intention is that there is only non-succession (akrama) here, because in reality all things consist solely of the Lord, and thus succession is [merely] a conventional mode of being. It is with this in mind that he speaks in this manner.
The sequence here has been demonstrated; it should be remembered in the same way in what follows. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"And this intuition (*pratibhā*), which is colored by the sequence of various objects..."
"The subject, whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness, is that Great Lord.
He demonstrates this very pervasion of phenomenal expansion, whose essence is non-differentiation, in a verse and a half:
"Anāśrita himself, having presided over [the universe], remains established;
Anātha is said to be Viṣṇu, and Ananta is indeed Rudra. (11.19)
The Lord whose form is space (vyomarūpīśvara) is proclaimed as the pervasive Sadāśiva; indeed,
the venerable Anāśrita himself remains directly presiding over [the universe], from the earth up to the world of Brahmā— this is the implied meaning.
Furthermore,
O Goddess, the Supreme Lord Hāṭaka is all-pervasive.
Endowed with hosts of vidyās and mantras, he is the lord of the seven netherworlds;
O Goddess of gods, he is Ananta himself, Rudra, whose form is the fire of time.
The Lord Hūhuka, O Great Goddess, remains as the sustainer on the path in an infinite form; he is the one who abides without support. || 11-22 ||
"By way of Ananta's form" means by way of the Lord Ananta who has descended into the skull-bowl (karparikā). "On the path" means at the edge of the skull-bowl.

"Hūhuka" refers to the one residing within the previously mentioned infinite worlds. Thus, in this manner, he is indeed one and the same, [manifesting] through the pentad of the gross, such as Hūhuka and others, and the subtle, such as Brahmā and others.
The Supreme Lord, Svacchandanaatha, who consists of the five powers previously mentioned, has manifested through the pervasion of the phenomenal world; with this intention as well, [it is said]:
"He is the gross, the subtle, the supreme, the one beyond the supreme, and the stainless" (11.14).

Thus, this half-verse is to be connected. Having thus demonstrated the pervasion of the five [deities] beginning with Anāśrita by the *prapañca*, as well as the fact that Sarva, the Lord Anāśritanātha,
takes the form of Hūhukanātha at the end of all, [the author shows that] all this—

It teaches that [the Self] is indeed the very reality of the stainless (nirañjana), because in truth the venerable Lord Anāśrita is non-different from the nature of the supreme Bhairava who is stainless. || 22 ||
As it has been said:
"That Blessed Lord is described as 'un-supported' because He rests upon His own power;
for that supreme power of the Lord, which is the source of the universe, does not depend on any specific [external] substratum."

The Supreme Lord, resting upon that power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), manifests directly upon its foundation as an expansion inseparable from it. For the Bhaṭṭāraka Anāśrita, whose nature is the power of will (icchā-śakti), is essentially identical with His own essential nature (svarūpa). As the venerable author of the Pratyabhijñā has said:
"Śiva-nature is indeed nothing other than this second [state]."
And therefore, O fair-faced one, the entire universe, from Unmanī downwards, is supported by her. (11.23)

The power *unmanī* is at the end of that world which has *samanā* as its limit; the meaning is that it is "supported by that," namely supported by the *śivatattva* in the form of the Lord Anāśrita-bhaṭṭāraka. || 23 ||
And just as Anāśritanātha relies upon the supreme, all-sustaining power of absolute freedom belonging to the Supreme Lord (Pārameśī),
so too does the venerable Hūhuka remain relying upon that very same power; thus he says:
And Hūhuka, the support of Śakti, is situated at the summit of Ambhas;
"support of Śakti" means resting upon the other Śakti. By the phrase "at the summit of Ambhas," its location is specified. As for what Śrī Bhullaka says regarding the "support of Śakti":
He has also explained here that [the universe] rests upon the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) whose form is the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-karparikā);
however, since this is merely an attempt to justify what has been forgotten, it should be disregarded.
Furthermore:
"The water-principle (aptattva) is indeed below that, and immediately after that is the fire-principle (āgneya). || 11-24 ||
The subtle elements of air and ether, the sense organs, the objects of the senses, the mind, and the ego-principle follow in this sequence. (11.25)

O Goddess of gods, [these are] the Buddhist, the secondary (gauna), the natural (prakrta), and likewise the personal (paurusha); as well as necessity (niyati), time (kala), passion (raga), knowledge (vidya), and likewise limited agency (kala). || 11-26 ||
The principle of Māyā, as well as Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
then Bindu, Ardhendu, Nirodhī, Nāda, and beyond that, the Nāḍī. (11.27)
Below that, O Goddess, is the Brahmabilam; beyond that is the Śaktitattva;
and beyond that is Vyāpinī, conjoined with the five causes.
O Dear One, the *samanā* and *unmanā* [levels] are joined with the *prakriyā-aṇḍas*.

Those which were previously called "objects" (*viṣaya*) and situated within the enclosure of the rays (*raśmy-āvaraṇa*), they exist here in the form of objects. And therefore, as the venerable Bhullaka said: "The objects are of the nature of the great elements."
The claim that these [objects] perceivable by the senses were mentioned incidentally in connection with the mention of the senses is incorrect.

In the passage beginning with "the Buddhist" (*bauddha*), the word "reality" (*tattva*) should be supplied. Regarding the term "channel" (*nāḍī*), it refers specifically to the Suṣumṇā situated within its enclosure. Having set aside the phrase "the Brahma-aperture below," one should read "the Brahma-aperture above."
The reading of the commentator is not correct, because the path ending at the *suṣumnā* extends upward as well as downward, reaching up to the *brahmabila*,
since the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Earth exist in a state of successive internal and external pervasion.
Because it has already been established. The qualification of *unmanā* is "joined with the cosmic eggs" (*prakriyāṇḍairyutā*);

by the aforementioned process (*prakriyā*), she is joined with—that is, connected to—the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*), which are the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*), the Egg of Prakṛti, the Egg of Māyā, and the Egg of Śakti. For these indeed...
All have that as their single basis.
This summarizes it: "In this way, indeed, the egg of the process (prakriyāṇḍa) is situated above and below. (11.29)

By the process previously described, that which exists as the "Egg" (*aṇḍa*)— indicated by the singular number— is the Egg of Māyā and the Egg of Śakti as a single form; it is situated specifically below and above, encompassing within itself the various respective *tattvas*, and is perfectly established through a pervasive extension both externally and internally.
Is it that only the two eggs—the Śakti-egg and the Māyā-egg—exist, situated through the pervasion of various principles (tattvas) in upper and lower positions? No; he says:
"Such as these indeed [exist] below, above, and all around.
Regarding the plural form "such as these," it refers to the Egg of Prakṛti (prakṛtyaṇḍa), the Egg of Māyā (māyāṇḍa), and the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), because of their multiplicity.
This has been stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"Two separate [groups], each innumerable; one, and one again two, separately.
The expression "of such a kind" is used in reference to the phrase "below and below, above and above, and on all sides."
It has been explained.
He clarifies the multiplicity indicated by the plural number:
"Just as, O Goddess, the individual souls (ātman-aṇavaḥ) are established as being innumerable. (11.30)

Thus, indeed, the *prakṛty-aṇḍas* (cosmic eggs of primordial nature) are innumerable and manifold; they are "established" in this way by means of the sovereign power of *māyā*, through the manifestation [of things] in a state of contraction—this is the meaning. This is indicated by the use of the plural form "*prakṛty-aṇḍāni*" (plural of *prakṛty-aṇḍa*).
It has already been stated that they take the form of the primordial egg and the cosmic egg.
Why then are those [other paths] not described separately?
For it is said:
"O beloved, by describing one path here, the entire course is described. (11.31)
For just as it is with one, so it is with all; the manifest egg (prakriyāṇḍa) exists in its own essential nature within all manifest eggs, O beloved, O lady of excellent vows. (11.32)
Śiva, however, is all-pervasive, subtle, and situated both outside and within;
he is free from all excellence and devoid of all causal agency. (11.33)
Freed from creation and dissolution, his sphere of experience transcends the phenomenal world (prapañca);

by his own essential nature, which is the imperishable and eternal light of consciousness, he is Śiva— the subtle one for all— and the venerable Paramaśiva, who pervades both the external and the internal.

The meaning is that, since the existence of anything whatsoever cannot be established apart from the nature of Supreme Śiva, who consists of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśātmaka*), the entire universe is indeed composed of Śiva (*śivamaya*).

While there is a progressive excellence (*atiśaya*) in the emergence of Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the others relative to each preceding lower level, [this excellence does not apply to the ultimate state].

Paramaśiva, however, being essentially the nature of the light of consciousness, consists of Great Being (*mahāsattā*) and has the form of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*); since there is no other limit for excellence beyond him, he is free from all degrees of excellence, the cause of all, transcending all causes, and eternally arisen as the singular embodiment of consciousness— this is to be explained by way of *tantra* (concise aphoristic expression), because:

He is liberated from both creation and withdrawal. For this very Lord alone is the creator and the destroyer of the entire universe, possessing a single nature of pure and autonomous consciousness; there is no other creator or destroyer even for Him, because even that which is postulated as such would be impossible without having this [Lord] as its essence of light. Furthermore, this...

The object of whose [vision] is the entire world, which transcends conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and diversity (*vaicitrya*), appearing solely as the light of its own consciousness (*svacitprakāśaikamayatva*). As it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"But for the Immeasurable One, all objects appear as full within Himself, by means of Himself, just like His own Self" (2.1.7).
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, this—stainless, pure, and peaceful—is established both below and above. || 34 ||

Since the impurities such as *āṇava* have departed from him, he is thus "stainless" (*vimala*), having the singular nature of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). And because all dualities have subsided, he is "peaceful" (*śānta*). Nevertheless, he alone is "below" in the form of *māyā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*), and "above" in the form of *śuddhavidyā* up to *Śiva*.
It exists in various forms, for it has been stated that there is never, for anyone, any existence whatsoever apart from its manifestation. || 34 ||
This is illustrated by means of the following example:
"Just as space has no top, no middle, and no bottom anywhere, so too is the omnipresent Lord Śiva, the supreme cause. (11.35)
O Goddess, having pervaded the entire universe, You abide like space within spaces;

just as space remains as a single, undifferentiated reality within the regions of space delimited by houses, jars, and so forth, so too does the entire universe exist [as one with You] because it is manifest.

Śiva, whose nature is the light of consciousness, abides pervading all things as the essence of luminosity through non-duality; therefore, for him, there is no distinction whatsoever such as "above," "middle," or "below" produced by space, time, and so forth.
He states that this very non-dual knowledge is the supreme thing to be adopted:
"O lady of excellent hips, having known it thus, one shall not again be subject to birth. (11.36)

Having thus demonstrated the pervasive non-difference of the entire universe from the Lord Śiva, who consists of self-luminosity, he now also demonstrates the extent of the pervasion of Brahmā and the others, who are of the nature of His manifestation:

Furthermore, I shall briefly explain the pervasion of the causal principles (*kāraṇas*). Previously, the relationship of pervaded and pervader was shown for the five supreme causes beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Hūhuka; now, however, it is presented in its other form.
The pervasion of the fivefold form beginning with Brahmā is demonstrated by way of their presiding over the principles (tattvas) and so forth:
"But regarding the principle of earth, Brahmā is established as the presiding deity. (11.37)
Viṣṇu resides in the principle of water, Rudra is established in fire;
Īśvara resides in the principle of air, while Sadāśiva resides in space.

It was previously established— because it was stated [in the scripture], "The extent of the pervasion of the kalās is indeed the same as that of the tattvas"— that the nature of the tattvas, such as āp and others, follows the pervasion of the tattvas by the kalās, beginning with Pratiṣṭhā.
It must be considered. || 38 ||
O lady of virtuous vows, Āditya is remembered as Brahmā, and Soma as Viṣṇu;
Rudra is the lord of the planets, and likewise the sovereign of the lunar mansions.
O Goddess of the gods, the sacrificer is himself the god Sadāśiva.

Here, the five elements beginning with earth, along with the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer—these eight are the forms of Maheśvara; from them arises the true nature of the pervasion of the *kalās*, which is of the form of the object of knowledge (*meyarūpa*).

It has been stated that the pentad of elements beginning with earth is presided over by the causal agents beginning with Brahmā. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the fifth element, which belongs to the sacrificer, is included within the category of the instruments (*karaṇa*), there too it was stated that it is presided over by Brahmā and the others. "Āditya" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rightward current (*dakṣiṇasrotas*).

Soma is apāna and the left channel; the external Soma and Sūrya, as lords of the planets and constellations, are employed for the illumination of objects of cognition (*prameya*). Sadāśiva possesses the status of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) because he consists of the supreme subject (*paramātṛ*), who presides over all objects of cognition and means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Even those such as Brahmā and others, who are the presiding deities over the entire form of Maheśvara, are themselves composed of the divine mantras beginning with Sadyojāta; thus, he teaches that the universe is likewise non-dual with the Supreme Lord.
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā, while Vāmadeva is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu.
Aghora is said to be Rudra, and likewise Puruṣa is Īśvara;
but Īśāna, O lady of beautiful hips, is the Lord Sadāśiva himself. (11.41)

And that pentad of mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, which is the form of the Lord’s power acting as the presiding deity over Brahmā and the others, is itself the manifestation of the entire expanse of scriptures such as the Vedas; thus he says:
"Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda."
Aghora is the Sāmaveda, while Puruṣa is said to be the Atharvaveda.
And Īśāna, the best of the gods, is remembered as being composed of all knowledge (*sarvavidyātmaka*).
Each of the Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, should be understood as consisting of the sections on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), the deities (*devatākāṇḍa*), and knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*).
By the statement "composed of all knowledge," even the aforementioned division is declared to be the manifestation (*prapañca*) of this very Lord.
Thus, even according to the sequence of the scriptures, the world consists solely of the non-dual Lord.
He states that non-duality is also attained through the sequence of knowledge:
"O Goddess, worldly consciousness has emerged from Sadyojāta. (11.43)
O fair-faced one, the Vaidika [knowledge] emerged from Vāmadeva, the Ādhyātmika from Aghora, and that which is called Atimārga emerged from Puruṣa.

The great knowledge known as mantra has indeed emerged from Īśāna. It consists of worldly knowledge—comprising agriculture, policy, ethics, medicine, archery, dramaturgy, and so forth—as well as the knowledge expounded by the Vedas, such as ritual, phonology, grammar, etymology, metrics, and astronomy; and it includes the sciences of livelihood, governance, and medical treatment. This is the Vedic [knowledge].
The nature of obligatory, occasional, and optional sacrifices and so forth;

the spiritual [knowledge], such as the discernment between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) taught in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the knowledge of the cessation of all mental fluctuations; and the supernatural [powers].

What is intended here by "knowledge" (vijñāna) is not the specific fourfold [knowledge], but rather that which transcends the well-known paths consisting of the Vedic, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and other forms of worship; it is, in general, the means consisting of various mudrās, maṇḍalas, rituals, and so forth, as set forth in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara). It is called "that which is termed mantra."
In those very scriptures of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśa), according to the principle established in the section on the five Praṇavas,

there is a great gnosis (*mahājñāna*) which bestows the vitality of mantra (*mantravīryada*), characterized by being "manifested" (*ākhyāna*)— that is, fully revealed (*ā samantāt*)— within the mantras.
It proclaims that the essence of mantras lies in direct experience, distinguished from the self-knowledge found in the Kriyā and other tantras taught by Jñānapāda.

The state of being the presiding lord of the universe has been described by means of the presiding over the five principles (*pañcatattva*) of the five causes beginning with Brahmā; however, in order to explain this in detail, he says:
"In that manner, O lady of good vows, listen again to [the account] according to the division of the principles. (11.45)
O Goddess of the gods, Brahmā is established pervading the twenty-four principles up to Pradhāna; Janārdana, however, pervades the principle of Puruṣa.
Since the *guṇatattva* is not intended to be mentioned separately, [the Goddess] pervades the twenty-four *tattvas*,

presiding over them non-differently as before; for this very reason, she is Brāhmī, who effects the creation consisting of perception and so forth, which has the Heart previously explained as its object.
"It is pervasion" is stated here and there.
Then Rudra stands pervading everything up to Niyati and Māyā;
likewise, the principle of Vidyā is pervaded by Īśvara.
Above, the Lord Sadāśiva remains pervading everything. "Above" refers to the triad of principles known as Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva. "Sadāśiva" here means the supreme pervasion of Anāśrita [Śiva].
And by means of the division of the three principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, he declares that the causes are presided over by the universe:
"Furthermore, O lady of excellent vows, I shall explain [this] again according to the division of the three principles" (11.48).
The remainder [of the sentence] is "the pervasion by the cause. || 48 ||
In that regard:
"Brahmā is established in the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) up to the end of Māyā;
likewise Viṣṇu [is established] in the reality of Knowledge (vidyātattva) as far as the sphere of the Sādākhya. (11.49)
Likewise, O fair-faced one, Rudra is to be known within the Śiva-tattva;
he stands pervading the entire path above the Sādākhya [tattva]. (11.50)

"The sphere of Sādākhya" refers to the principle of Sadāśiva. "Everything" means that the pervasion of Brahmā extends up to the principle of Śiva—specifically ending with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; that of Viṣṇu extends up to Īśvara and Sadāśiva;
and that of Rudra consists of the form of Śiva itself. Thus, by this method, there is indeed non-duality even among the five causal deities.
Ten times [that]. || 50 ||

Not only is the reality of the pervasion of these three causes limited to these five causes, but even those three causes have as their ultimate reality the triad of powers beginning with Raudrī of the Supreme Lord; thus he says:
"He whose self is presided over by Raudrī is indeed proclaimed to be Rudra."
Viṣṇu is pervaded by Vāmā, and Pitāmaha by Jyeṣṭhā.
Because they dissolve all diseases, vomit forth the universe, and because of their predominance, excellence, and intensity in [the aspects of] non-duality, sovereignty, and pre-eminence,
there is a transposition of the sequence in the presiding over those powers known as Raudrī, Vāmā, and Jyeṣṭhā, in order to demonstrate the reality of the ultimate non-dual sequence. 51.
Furthermore:
Brahmā is known as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), Janārdana as the power of action (kriyā-śakti),
and the supreme Rudra as the power of will (icchā-śakti).
The word "para" (supreme) is connected to all three [terms]. Here too, the intended meaning when the sequence is otherwise has already been stated:
"And this supreme Rudra... he is celebrated as Śiva. (11.52)
Viṣṇu, the god Sadāśiva, and likewise Brahmā and Īśvara—
thus it is stated that, by means of these three powers, the supreme triad of causes, which pervades them, presides over the other triad of causes as well.
Thus, by means of the statement regarding the identity of the means and the goal,
through the pervasion of the entire path via the relationship of the presiding subject and the presided object within the cause,
or through the principle of being presided over by the eight forms, and by means of the expressive word through the vision of that knowledge;
By means of explaining the distinctions between the thirty-six or thirty-five principles (tattvas) denoted by that [text],

and through the sequence of defining the presiding presence of the three powers (śakti), he demonstrates the ultimate Upaniṣadic meaning— that the universe is non-dual with Supreme Bhairava— by revealing the true nature of the pervaded and the pervader.

With reference to the creation of the world that has entered into manifold conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it follows that there is indeed a diversity in the distinction between cause and effect:
"O Goddess, from Śiva was born Sadāśiva, the Lord Īśvara. (11.53)
Although it was previously proposed that "Sadāśiva is to be known from the bindu" (11.10), nevertheless...

The intended meaning here is that, according to the ultimate vision (*paramārthadṛśā*) which establishes the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, [the Lord] has extended Himself as far as the *bindu*; thus, through the pervasion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the venerable Śiva himself becomes the Lord Sadāśiva and Īśvara. 53.

Therefore, from that [arises] Māyā; "from that" means from the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva). Furthermore, the reasoning regarding the order of origin of these principles has already been demonstrated previously.
Furthermore:
Moreover, by his own will, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of Knowledge, [acts] with the tip of the hand of his power of cognition. (11.54)
"He creates seven crores of mantras whose nature consists of knowledge and action.
That supreme Vidyā, Mātṛkā, is divided into eight groups"—from this Vidyā, whose essential nature was previously described, [the Parameśvara [emanates]). Thus it is said.

The venerable Lord Īśvara, whose essential nature is that of Paramaśiva, for the sake of manifesting the activity known as grace (anugraha) by his mere will, creates with his very hand-tip— which is indeed the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti)— the seven crores of mantras, whose true essence consists of contemplation (manana) and protection (trāṇa).

Because they possess the instruments of the power of knowledge and because they are being emanated, these [powers] consist of knowledge and action in accordance with their cause; thus, having the true nature of perfect knowledge and action, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By the qualification "Supreme Lord" (parameśvara), the nature of the Lord as Supreme Śiva is stated; for that very reason,
he declares that the mantras created by him exist everywhere for the sake of bestowing grace, because they belong to the category of the individual soul (aṇu), power (śakti), and Śambhu.
And those [elements], O virtuous one, beginning with the earthly and ending with that which is called the "Inexpressible" (sādākhyam), [are established].
Abiding in the worlds, they bestow grace upon embodied beings.

Remaining within those worlds beginning with Earth and ending with Anāśrita, they continuously and preeminently perform the grace that consists of worldly enjoyment and liberation for embodied beings.
And these—pervaded by Śiva and Śakti, three-eyed, with the moon upon their crests. (11.56)
Precisely because they are permeated by Śiva and Śakti, these possess the capacity to bestow grace. || 56 ||
And this is logical, because:
"This one Śiva, the supreme cause, the wielder of the trident, exists as the possessor of Māyā, pervading the world in manifold ways through the forms of Rudra. (11.57)

The Rudras are the mantras that dispel all diseases. Although he is one, he remains pervading the universe in manifold ways through the forms of Rudra; the reason for this is indicated by the epithet "the Illusionist" (māyī), referring to his power of great illusion (mahāmāyā-śakti) which consists in the concealment of his own true nature.
Yesterday, for the sake of accomplishing the activity known as grace (*anugraha*),

the Supreme Lord— beautiful with the splendor of self-manifesting, pure, and autonomous consciousness-bliss— manifested through various forms of Rudra by means of His power of *māyā* alone, which takes the form of the universe to be described hereafter, out of His own sovereignty.

It has been stated more than once that, like a city in a mirror, there is no form whatsoever that does not exist as something exceeding its own [nature], even if it appears as if exceeding it; therefore, as the venerable Sadyojyotis said:
"Śiva is one and changeless, and so too is His Power; therefore, those two are not [mutually] distinct."
Or [the claim that] it exists in many ways because it is subject to modification when deprived of consciousness (Tattvasaṃgraha 45)—
that must be disregarded, for it contradicts both the previously cited scriptures and reasonings, and thus its true nature as non-duality has not been properly considered. || 57 ||
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, having again beheld the infinite forms of the Lord who is his support through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*),
he is pervaded by the power of will (*icchāśakti*) and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), O lady of excellent vows. (11.58)
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, eternal and all-pervasive by its nature; having placed the group of souls within it, the Lord simultaneously agitates them. (11.59)

The seed—that is, the cause—of the entire universe, from *kalā* down to *kṣiti*, is the *māyā-tattva*; it is eternal because its power has been operative since time immemorial (*anidamprathamika*), and for that very reason it is imperishable (*avyaya*). However, it is not eternal or indestructible in the sense of being the essence of a *tattva*, as it is stated [in the scripture]: "From that, *māyā*."
Because its withdrawal will be explained later; having thus made the group of selves— whose knowledge and action are concealed by the power of that *māyātattva* which is situated in such a manner—
manifest upon its own screen, and then having again illuminated that same [group] with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
"One should simultaneously and without succession cause agitation"—
this refers to the transition from the state characterized by the attributes of being the agent of all, omniscience, self-sufficiency, being unconditioned by time, and universal identity,
to a state consisting of non-reflection, which is marked by limited agency, limited knowledge, dependence on others, and limitation by time.

The Supreme Lord, preceded by the manifestation of the coverings (*kañcuka*) consisting of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*—which are the factors that determine [the soul's state] and necessarily give rise to [limited agency]—renders [the soul] subject to the primary cause (*pradhāna*), its effects, and [the cycle of] bondage.
Of what nature is He? To this he says: He is pervaded by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

"When [the subject] thinks, 'Let this object become thus,' and it immediately becomes so, that very act of making it so is here called *kriyā* (action). (3.8). According to the principle taught in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*, immediately after mere will (*icchāmātra*), [the object arises].
The meaning is that [the Lord] causes [it] to appear through His power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 59 ||
He illustrates the statement "one should agitate simultaneously" with a simile:
"The fruits of a jujube tree struck by a staff with ease emerge, in brief, sideways, upwards, and downwards. (11.60)

The word *vā* has the sense of *iva* (like). Like the fruits of the jujube tree (*badarī*), the selves (*ātman*) of Māyā go to the levels (*bhūmi*)—to be described immediately hereafter—which are horizontal, upward, and downward. || 60 ||
In that regard—those here who are meditated upon by Śiva become vessels for liberation;
they all go upward to Śiva, who is supremely stainless. (11.61)
"Anudhyātāḥ" means those upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has been bestowed. As it is said in the *Śrīśrīkaṇṭhī*:
"That by which Śiva is not omniscient [without it] is the Sovereign Power (*aiśvarī śakti*).
When impelled by Śiva, she then liberates the bound souls (*paśu*)."
"When there is a continuous application toward initiation, initiation characterized by knowledge and so forth [occurs].
Thus, "upward" means that their upward movement is precisely the attainment of oneness with Śiva. || 61 ||
Likewise:
"Those who are vessels for knowledge indeed become the form of mantras among the animals.
This has been stated elsewhere:
"But the state of being a Lord of Knowledge and Vidyeśas is the lower liberation... (Tantrāloka-saṃgraha 51).
Furthermore: "But those who possess the vessel of saṃsāra, endowed with impurity (mala), action (karman), and limited agency (kalā)... (11.62).
Below them, they proceed along this terrible path that is exceedingly harsh.

Impurity (*mala*) consists of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), which is of the nature of *āṇava*; action (*karman*) consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as those for auspicious deeds and so forth; while that which begins with *kalā* is of the nature of *māyīya*.
"Terrible" means consisting of duality; "exceedingly harsh" means abounding in suffering. (62)
Having thus, as a digression, established the nature of mantras—both bound and liberated—he now demonstrates the very creation under discussion:
"From that, Kalā was produced, as well as Vidyā and Rāga. (11.63)
Time, the principle of necessity (niyatitattva), the principle of the person (puṃstattva), and likewise the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti)—

this alone is said [to constitute the five coverings]. Enveloped by these five sheaths, persons are the enjoyers, while primordial nature, which is the common form of all objects of enjoyment, arises simultaneously from Māyā.

Because the enjoyer and the enjoyed are mutually dependent, it is stated here that the emergence of *kalā* and the other categories occurs simultaneously from that, namely from the *māyā-tattva*. However, in the *Śrī Mālinīvijaya*, the fourfold group beginning with *vidyā* as well as *prakṛti* emerge from *kalā*; whereas in the *Śrī Raurava* and other texts, *rāga* and *vidyā* emerge from *kalā*.

Regarding the sequence stated in the scriptures, such as "having given birth" (*prasūya*), meaning she gave birth to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and likewise the variation in number where sometimes a tetrad of coverings (*kañcuka*) is mentioned and sometimes a triad— no confusion should be entertained therein.
"Like the fibers within the core of a plantain tree, like the flavors of sweetmeats and the like,
or like the variegated globes of the *kadamba* flower, the diverse cognitions are but various coverings.
According to this principle established in the *Śrītrikasāra*, one person perceives while another is impassioned.
The sequence of "sheaths" (kañcukas), beginning with "he who knows desires," follows the diverse order of perception among men and is conceived in various ways,
because the sequence of the principles (tattvas) starting from *kalā* has been taught for each individual; therefore, it is presented in that manner by the founders of those respective scriptures.

Thus, this has been presented merely to demonstrate a difference in sequence; furthermore, a numerical distinction is shown based on whether [the categories] are included or not included. In reality, however, [the subjects] are enveloped by the fivefold sheaths (kañcuka) consisting of the five principles (tattva) implied by the fivefold cognition beginning with "I am doing something."

The souls (*pumāṃsaḥ*) are the enjoyers, while *prakṛti*— which consists of certain portions and has the nature of the common object of enjoyment— is produced simultaneously from *māyā*; this very view stated in the *Tantra* appears to be the most excellent.
Now, sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are indeed the three qualities of Prakṛti. || 11-64 ||
The meaning is that the *guṇatattva* has arisen with its three forms. || 64 ||
He analyzes these according to their distinct functions:
"Sattva is that which produces illumination; rajas is that which produces activity; tamas is declared to be that which causes obstruction—these three qualities (guṇas) are to be known. (11.65)
It is that which supports and that which conceals; the proof for all these cases has already been demonstrated previously (in verse 2.66).
Regarding the presiding deities of the three qualities (guṇas), it is said: "Sattva is Brahmā, Rajas is Viṣṇu, and Tamas is proclaimed as Rudra.
By the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the non-difference between the presiding deities is indeed indicated.
The presiding deities are also three due to the difference in their respective functions; however, in reality, there is only one Supreme Lord who manifests through those various functions.

He expands upon the very subject previously introduced by means of an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya): "In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Viṣṇu he is the cause of their maintenance. (11.66)
In his capacity as Rudra, he should withdraw this entire world of moving and non-moving beings;
and in accordance with this, there are also the three states pertaining to him: waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (11.67)
"Directed toward that" means arisen by the power of qualities such as goodness (*sattva*) and so forth.
Then,
from the qualities (guṇas), Dhiṣaṇā was born;
Dhiṣaṇā is intellect (buddhi).
And that [Prakṛti] is endowed with various states (bhāva) and distinctions (bheda).
"States" refers to dharma and the rest; "distinctions" refers to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the sense organs (indriya), and so forth, which will be described later.
Furthermore: Brahmā is established there in the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) by virtue of his sovereignty. || 11.68 ||
The followers of the Āgamas declare that very one to be omniscient and the supreme state of the Buddhists;
they say that he alone is the omniscient Brahmā, but not the creator of all, and that he is the supreme state and the abode of liberation for the Buddhists. "Śarva himself says that very thing."
The entire reading must be explained as follows: "The followers of Āgama say that the reality of the intellect (buddhitattva) is the supreme state for the Buddhists."
Thus, in the context of explaining its origination,

for the Buddhists— who maintain that the ultimate goal consists in the cultivation of a momentary stream of cognitions in the form of joy, sorrow, and so forth, which are essentially modifications of the intellect (buddhi)— the attainment of the principle of the intellect itself is [the result].

Having established that [this] is liberation (*mokṣa*), and having demonstrated the pseudo-liberations consisting of the states to be attained as conceived by other disputants, he clarifies that the Śaivas are the recipients of the supreme, true liberation.
As was stated previously:
Thus, there are three hundred such doctrines of those who speak in this manner.
"And there are sixty-three others, proponents whose minds are deluded;
this [work] is the supreme opener for those blinded by the cataracts of ignorance. (10.680–681), and so forth. In that regard—
And among those who speak from the Vedas, the primary [authority] is that which is established upon the qualities (guṇa). || 11-69 ||

The connection is "the supreme state" (*paramaṃ padam*); the same applies hereafter.
