For the Ārhats, liberation consists in the immersion of the *pudgala*—which is of the nature of the experience of bliss—into the tranquility resulting from the power of asceticism (such as climbing heated stones), which removes the veils of sorrow, delusion, and so forth that constitute the cage of the world; and this bliss is...
"The form of the qualities of the *sattva*," thus they abide within the qualities. || 69 ||
For they [cite]:

"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—the one unborn male lies beside her, delighting in her; another unborn male abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5).
Saying such things, they generally declare that *prakṛti* alone is the supreme state (*parama-pada*). As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"The Vedas have as their subject matter the three *guṇas*" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.45).

And for the Sāṃkhyas, human effort consists precisely in the avoidance of pleasure, pain, and so forth; for them, liberation is the attainment of one's own true nature, which is the mere power of consciousness, distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) that is composed of pleasure, pain, and the like.
And the twenty-sixth, O Goddess of gods, is the supreme state in the Yogaśāstra.

Although the attainment of the distinct nature of the Puruṣa— expressed by the statement, "Then there is the abiding of the seer in his own nature" (Yogasūtra 1.3)— is declared by those established in Yoga to be liberation, which is indeed the twenty-sixth principle itself; nevertheless—
"In the commentary on this sūtra— *kleśakarmavipākāśayairaparāmṛṣṭaḥ puruṣaviśeṣa īśvaraḥ* (Yoga Sūtra)—

the venerable sage Vyāsa [states] that the distinction of the Lord (*īśvara*), consisting in his being eternally liberated and endowed with eternal sovereignty, exists even as compared to those liberated persons who were previously bound for countless aeons."

Having set aside the twenty-fifth principle, that which is taught in the Yoga-śāstra as the supreme state—the form of the Lord (Īśvara) consisting of the twenty-sixth, which bestows grace upon it—is thus described. || 70 ||
"In the Pāśupata vow, the supreme state of Īśvara is proclaimed.
Thus, since the Pāśupata is said to be twofold— namely, the Lākula and the Mausula—
and because it is the Mausula that will be determined [hereafter], [the following applies].

In this context, it is precisely the Pāśupata vow propounded by Lakulīśa that is being described. And therein, the attainment of the principle of Īśvara (the Lord) alone is the supreme state. As was previously stated:
"Those who, having conquered their senses, practice the divine Pāśupata vow..."
"Those who are devoted to ashes, to recitation, and to meditation, go to the state of the Lord.
Thus it is said. (10.1170)
But within the Pāśupata division itself, which is primarily concerned with ritual action—in both the Mausula and the Kārūka—the Māyā-tattva is proclaimed. (11.71)

By another disciple of Śrī Lakuleśa, the Muslim lord who descended at the site of Kārohaṇa, various specific vows were taught in their respective scriptures for the purpose of attaining Kṣemeśa-Brahmasvāmin, who resides within the principle of Māyā; thus, in that system, the principle of Māyā alone is the supreme state. (71)
And likewise, Kṣemeśa, the lord of Brahmā, is established in the principle of Māyā; that is their supreme state,
according to the respective order.

Regarding those known as the Vaimalas, who are divisions of the Pāśupatas, as well as others devoted to the worship taught in the *Pañcārtha* and the *Pramāṇāṣṭaka*, he states that for them, Tejeśa and Dhruveśa within the principle of Īśvara constitute the supreme state:
He says: "For them, Tejeśa and Dhruveśa, situated in the principle of Īśvara, are the supreme state."
Tejeśa is the lord of the Vaimānikas, and his station is fixed in the Pramāṇa heaven.
For one who is firmly established in the stainless scriptures of valid cognition, whose self is purified by initiation and knowledge, and who, until the end of the body,
abides in the practice while undertaking the vow of the skull, goes to his own respective state. (11.73)

By the phrase "the self purified by initiation and knowledge," a distinction is shown here from the Mausulas and Kārukas, who are devoted solely to the vows where ritual action (*kriyā*) is predominant. Each [of these] has its own form as the aforementioned Tejeśa and Dhruveśa, as was stated previously: [The text continues: "O Lord of the World, you are the supreme *sādhaka* of all *sādhakas*, the supreme *siddha* of all *siddhas*, and the supreme *guru* of all *gurus*. You are the supreme *mantra* of all mantras, the supreme *mudrā* of all mudrās, the supreme *tattva* of all *tattvas*, the supreme *kalā* of all *kalās*, the supreme *padārtha* of all *padārthas*, the supreme *liṅga* of all *liṅgas*, the supreme *sthāna* of all *sthānas*, the supreme *maṇḍala* of all maṇḍalas, the supreme *pīṭha* of all pīṭhas, the supreme *yāga* of all *yāgas*, the supreme *dīkṣā* of all initiations, the supreme *japa* of all recitations, the supreme *homa* of all fire-offerings, the supreme *tarpaṇa* of all libations, the supreme *arcana* of all worship, the supreme *nyāsa* of all placements, the supreme *dhyāna* of all meditations, the supreme *samādhi* of all absorptions, the supreme *bhoga* of all enjoyments, the supreme *mokṣa* of all liberations, the supreme *vibhava* of all manifestations, the supreme *aiśvarya* of all sovereignties, the supreme *vīrya* of all potencies, the supreme *tejas* of all splendors, the supreme *bala* of all strengths, the supreme *kāla* of all times, the supreme *karma* of all actions, the supreme *bhāva* of all dispositions, the supreme *śakti* of all powers, the supreme *nāda* of all sounds, the supreme *bindu* of all points, the persistence, the supreme *sarvopasaṃhārakartṛ* of all agents of withdrawal, the supreme *sarvaprakāśaka* of all illuminators, the supreme *sarvavilakṣaṇa* of all that is distinct, the supreme *sarvātmaka* of all that constitutes the self, the supreme *sarvottīrṇa* of all that transcends, the supreme *sarvānugrāhaka* of all benefactors, the supreme *sarvānugrahya* of all those to be favored, the supreme *sarvādhāra* of all supports, the supreme *sarvādheya* of all that is supported, the supreme *sarvābhinna* of all non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhinna* of all dualities, the supreme *sarvābhinnābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvabhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dual-non-dualities, the supreme *sarvābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhedābhinna* of all non-dual-non-d
"Tejeśa and Dhruveśa are the supreme state of all means of valid knowledge" (10.1174). || 73 ||

As for those who bear the ascetic observances of carrying skull-bowls and other bones, [they do so] according to the previously mentioned *Lākula* tradition and the injunctions of the *Pāśupata* scriptures, such as "one should sleep on ashes" (1.3).
Those who are devoted to the practice of recitation (*japa*) and the application of sacred ash (*bhasma*) proceed to the state of Īśvara.
Here, in the midst of this, having transcended the state of the *māyātattva* pertaining to regions such as Mausulā—[it is said]:
"In the Pāśupata vow, the supreme state of Īśvara is proclaimed" (11.71).
Thus, that which was stated out of sequence was for the purpose of demonstrating the various divisions of the Pāśupata school, such as the Mausula and others.

Thus, from the Buddhists up to the Lākulas, these [practitioners] partake in the enjoyment of the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), but they are not liberated. However, for those who are established in the Śaiva scripture, which is divided into the six currents (*ṣaṭsrotas*)—for them:
"But for the Śaivas, the supreme state transcends the entire path. (11.74)
And it is said elsewhere:
"The Śaiva [scripture] is superior to the Vedas and so forth...
As for that which—
When it is said: "From the Śaiva [path] comes the Vāma, and from that the Dakṣiṇa;
beyond the Dakṣiṇa is the Kaula, and there is nothing higher than the Kaula," that—
This is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the internal diversity among the scriptures proclaimed by Śiva.

For in the phrase "from the Śaiva [comes] the Vāma," the word *śaiva* refers to the Siddhānta scriptures, such as the Kairaṇa and others, which lead to the attainment of the state of Śiva that has not yet transcended [the lower levels]. || 74 ||
Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"From the principle of the intellect (buddhi-tattva), O Dear One, ego (ahaṅkāra) is born again in three ways;
it is proclaimed as being sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. (11.75)
As for the distinction of technical designations, according to the reverse order: it exists in three ways—as the *bhūtādi*, the *vaikṛta*, and the *taijasa*. Among these—
Then, from the source of the elements (bhūtādi), it produced the subtle elements (tanmātras), and from those, it generated the gross elements (bhūtas).

The word "Parameśvara" (the Supreme Lord) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Furthermore, he is called "Bhūtādi" (the Origin of Beings) based on the etymological derivation that he is the "ādi" (origin/cause) of "bhūtānām" (beings), both gross and subtle.
He states the subtle elements (tanmātras):
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
these five are known as the subtle elements.
Among these, in due order: || 11-77 ||
From sound, space (vyoma) was produced; likewise, from touch, wind (vāyu);
from form, fire (tejas) was produced; and from taste, water (āpas) was born. (11.78)
From fragrance, however, earth is born...

it should be understood from the *Samānatantya* (the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*) that for air and the other elements, which possess two and more qualities respectively, each subsequent quality— beginning with touch— is the cause, accompanied only by each preceding quality in turn.
Thus, this birth from the subtle elements and the gross elements has been described to you in brief.
Furthermore—
Then, from that Vaikārika [ego], the organs of action were born.

That which has as its purpose *vikāra*—meaning restlessness characterized by assuming various different forms—is here intended to be the *vaikārika*, which is of the nature of *rajas*. The word "atha" is for the sake of completing the meter. || 79 ||
He states which they are:
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth.
Likewise—
Furthermore, the five sense organs arise from the taijasa [element].
The word "atha" (now/then) is as explained previously. That which has light (*tejas*)—meaning illumination—as its purpose is here intended to be *taijasa*, that is, *sāttvika*.
He states them as follows:
"The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
[these are the senses] because of their restlessness and because they illuminate all objects."
The mind is said to possess the nature of both; it pervades all the sense organs.
The suffix *tṛn* is used in the word *vyāptṛ*; for this very reason, there is an absence of the genitive case in the phrase "all the senses" (*sarvendriyāṇi*).
However, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it says:
"From that [element] *taijasa*, the mind, the lord of the senses, was born."
"From that, the vaikārika [ego] produces the sense organs... (1.31);
thus, there is merely a difference in the method of exposition. || 81 ||
Thus, all these principles whose order of production has been explained in this manner are said to be truly for the benefit of the Self alone, according to their actual nature,
for the sake of the Self whose divisions will be described hereafter.

By means of giving mundane and supramundane enjoyments, their instruments, and their bases, and by accomplishing each respective purpose according to its true nature, these [gifts] are indeed beneficial.
And for this reason, he says that the Self, having created various ornaments, possesses a manifold form:
"The Self, O beautiful one, is indeed the inner self and the outer self as well. (11.82)
I shall explain these—the non-self and the supreme self—in brief:
namely, the ignorant, the wise, and likewise the one who is becoming wise. (11.83)
The awakened and the well-awakened—I shall tell you about them once more;
these indeed are they.
In that state—relying on the equilibrium of the primary constituents (pradhāna)—one is free from pleasure and pain. (11.84)
O Goddess, when one is established in that, then he is called the Self; that is,

by relying upon the equilibrium of the primary matter (pradhāna), which consists of the nature of the constituents (prakṛti), wherein the qualities (guṇas) abide in a state of harmony due to the absence of mutual suppression and so forth.
"In that" refers to *pradhāna* alone. [The soul] is deluded because it is merged in *prakṛti*, being devoid of pleasure and the other [qualities].
As he will say:
"The equilibrium of the *guṇas* is indefinable, inconceivable, and incomparable."
"In that [state], the entire world remains as if fast asleep. (11.287).
Thus, this Self is said to be dissolved in *prakṛti*, having as its body nothing more than the *kañcuka*s (sheaths).
And this very [self], through its conjunction with the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), wanders through all wombs. || 11-85 ||

That [individual] is to be known as the inner self (antarātman), bound indeed by good and evil deeds. The "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) consists of the five subtle elements (tanmātra) that originate the internal subtle body, along with the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṅkāra). Due to its connection with this, it is bound by good and evil actions in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Moving from womb to womb, it should be known as the inner self (antarātmā) because it abides in the middle, between the self and the non-self.
But this very [self],
joined with the organs of perception and action, and enveloped by the gross elements— || 11-86 ||
But the outer self, O Goddess, always enjoys sense objects;
that is to say, it possesses a gross body.
But when this [person] is liberated from the states of past existence and abandoned by even a fraction of the reality of dharmas, || 11-87 ||
The self should always be known as devoid of impure qualities, obscured by the nature of illusion, and indeed without a self;
it is liberated from gross and subtle elements, as well as from all states consisting of the attributes of the intellect.

He is abandoned by the *tattva* of the person (*puṃstattva*), which consists of the nature of form characterized by *kalā* as its covering; he is joined solely with the single impurity of the nature of *āṇavamala*, which consists of the sense of incompleteness and is defined by the property of impurity alone.

He is of a contracted nature, because he has been obscured— rendered into a state of limited manifestation— by the attribute of *māyā*, which consists of the previously mentioned powers, but not by the essence of reality (*tattva*); being thus characterized by the nature of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), he is "without self" (*nirātmā*) in relation to the true Self (*ātman*).

The meaning is as follows: having emerged from the nature characterized by the *puruṣa-tattva*, which is entwined with the hundreds of previously mentioned bonds (*pāśa*), and having cultivated, through the vision of the Supreme Lord’s scripture, the knowledge that discriminates between *māyā* and the *puruṣa-tattva*, one is a *vijñānākala*.
As it is said in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:
"...therein, the *vijñānakevala* [is] joined with *mala* alone... (1.23). Thus, the reading "the self joined with *mala* and *karman* alone" (*malakarmaikayuktātmā*) is a corrupt reading.
When this [consciousness] shines forth in its fullness through the most intense grace, then it is called the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 11-88 ||
But it is not, as before, in the form of a sacrificial animal. || 88 ||
For it is said:
"O Dear One, when he is liberated from impurity (mala), karma, kalā, and the rest;
when he has transcended all paths (adhvan); and when he is freed from the delusion of Māyā. (11.89)
O Goddess, when it attains stainlessness—that supreme, imperishable state—then the Lord is called the imperishable Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 11-90 ||

Precisely because he is completely liberated from the three impurities beginning with *āṇava*— in their entirety and up to the very limit of transmigratory existence— he has, by means of the method of dissolving them, correctly transcended the entire path ending at *Samanā*, and thus he no longer maintains the conceit of a self (*ātmābhimāna*) anywhere along that path; and for this reason:
Regarding the phrase "by the delusion of Māyā":
as previously stated [in verse 10.1263], "Māyā, which exists in the form of karma, is the Kuṇḍalinī power situated below," by the delusion produced by that Māyā, even though it is extremely subtle.

When, having abandoned— that is, being devoid of— the contraction of Mahāmāyā, he attains a state of stainlessness in the form of union with Supreme Śiva, which is the supreme state, then this imperishable and undecaying Lord, the sovereign everywhere, is called the Paramātman (Supreme Self).
Now he begins to explain the distinctions starting with the ignorant (abudha): "And furthermore, O Goddess, I shall describe the ignorant in brief;
and likewise—"
In the withdrawal of the self into its true essence, which has as its range everything from the *kalās* down to the earth (*kṣiti*).
Having indeed withdrawn [the world] during the night of equality with Māyā, the Supreme Lord remains without activity until its emergence once again. (11.92)

The connection is with what will be stated [later] in the verse, "the ignorant one remains there" (11.95). [This refers to] the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*),
as well as the fourteen [levels of existence] beginning with the immobile beings and ending with Brahmā, which have those [principles] as their substratum.

The Supreme Lord, engaged in the withdrawal of that which is the self—the intrinsic nature—of all beings, [attains] the equilibrium of Māyā, which consists in the pacification of all modifications. That very state is the "night" due to the universal sleep; during that night, the entire manifold expanse of the paths belonging to Māyā, headed by the infinite Bhaṭṭārakas, [is withdrawn].

Having withdrawn [the world], he remains inactive, with no inclination toward the creation of differentiation, for as long as the emergence of the night of Māyā—which will be described later—consisting of its subsidence has not occurred; that is, for as long as this [state] has not proceeded into bliss. For when that proceeds, he again creates the universe by means of his inward-turned [consciousness].
It is indeed possessed of activity. || 92 ||
And at this time,

there is indeed the absence of pleasure, pain, and so forth for the group of selves; that is, for the entire group of selves who have been made to manifest through their connection with bodies ranging from *kalā* down to the earth, which are the effects of their own karma.
The meaning is that for all living beings, there is an absence of pleasure, pain, body, and so forth; they attain a state of profound stupor.
For then this group of selves—its soul deluded by the sleep of impurity, its consciousness, vision, and action obstructed—[remains as such]. (11.93)
O fair-faced one, it does not perceive sounds and the like, nor does it know itself;
O beloved, it does not know its cause, nor its own place. (11.94)
Since his faculties of sight and action have been withdrawn, he, being ignorant, does not perceive any of this;
he remains there until the dawn of Māyā.

The Self (ātman) is specifically deluded— that is, rendered inert— by sleep, which is produced by the nature of "non-apprehension" (akhyāti); consequently, its full powers of perception and action, which consist of consciousness, are obstructed,
and its sensory-related powers of perception and action are lost due to the force of withdrawal.

Being thus constituted, for this very reason, he does not cognize sounds and other objects, nor the self in its nature as a perceiver; nor does he determine through the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) that "I am such. Furthermore, he does not recognize the Supreme Lord as the cause who brings about this state of delusion and so forth, nor his own nature as consisting of Māyā.

He does not know the place or the support. Because he does not know all this, he is called "unawakened" (*abudha*) due to his lack of awakening. Therein, in *māyā*, he remains for as long as the dawn of *māyā* lasts. The term "*māyā-aharmukham*" is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) for the absence of the intermediate case-ending (*sandhi*).

Since [the word] "dependent on sound" (*śabdāpekṣam*) follows, the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) must be supplied. Thus, this one who is merged in *māyā* is called a "non-cognizant one in dissolution" (*pralayākala*). As for the one previously mentioned [in the verse]: "Having resorted to the equilibrium of *pradhāna*" (11.84).
Thus the Self has been described by this passage; the distinction is that it is "merged in primordial nature" (prakṛtilīna). || 11-95 ||
Thus, in this manner—
the ignorant one has been fully described... now—
...and understand from me the state of being a Buddha as well:
there, when karma has reached full maturity and is impelled by the will of the Lord (Īśvara), [the awakening occurs]. (11.96)
Just as the sun favors the visual light,
so too does the Lord favor the instruments of the individual selves.

From among his own manifold karmas, when a certain karma has reached maturity through the force of its predominance and is ready to yield its fruit, that very will of the Lord— who possesses infinite forms— expressed as "Let such a fruit arise for this atom from this karma"— that indeed is the hand [of the Lord].

When [the Self] has been extracted from the midst of the infinite stream of karma and joined to each respective Self for the sake of experience, [the Lord] favors— that is, unfolds— the instruments such as *kalā* belonging to those very Selves, by which those Selves come to possess the perception of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and so forth. In this regard:
The illustration is as follows: just as the sun does not grasp the light of the eye,

and without its favor that [light] cannot illuminate objects, so too, the *kalās* and other powers, when not unfolded by the Lord, do not bring about for the self the experience of agency and the like.
In all cases, it is solely the divine will of the Lord that prevails. || 97 ||

For it is solely through His grace that the Self— whose consciousness has been unfolded by *kalā* and whose range of perception is illuminated by *vidyā*— [attains this state]. This has already been explained previously.
Furthermore: "Its passion, by virtue of its coloring nature, is characterized by the bliss of sense objects. (11.98)
Attachment, whose nature consists of clinging to general objects, exists as passion (*rāga*) within this person by virtue of its coloring power.
Likewise—
Time indeed impels him, from the *tuṭi* moment up to the final dissolution.
One should also apply destiny, which is certain and eternal, to both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
This also has already been determined previously. || 99 ||
And having combined that fruit of his—
neither less nor more than a thousandth part of an atom—
it is thus encircled by the five [principles] beginning with *kalā*.
Having attained the state of masculinity within the reality known as Puruṣa.
The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Since it is stated that "the words *ākhyā* and *āhvaya* are to be understood as synonyms for *nāman*," the term *āhvaya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a name. Thus, [it refers to] that which has "Puruṣa" as its name (*āhvaya*).
That which is called Puruṣa. || 100 ||
He provides an etymological derivation of the word *puruṣa* based on the similarity of syllables:
"The city (*pura*) is said to be Pradhāna, which is crowded with many manifestations;
because he nourishes (*puṣayet*) that city, he is indeed remembered as *puruṣa*. (11.101)

The meaning is that because the *pradhāna*— which is crowded and pervaded by a manifold expansion beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*), and which consists of an abundance of transformations— is nourished by this [entity], thereby being rendered conscious through its attachment to the light of the Self, therefore this is called "Puruṣa."
In the compound *prapañcāneka*, the reversal of the prior member is a Vedic (chāndasa) anomaly. || 101 ||

Thus, having reached this state of primary intentionality— since the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, by means of necessity (niyati) and karma, would improperly envelop the bound soul (paśu) with the net of the bonds of primary matter (pradhāna)— 11.102.

The Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who presides over the path ending with Pradhāna, [binds] the Puruṣa— who is fettered by the noose of the individual soul (paśumāṇava), enveloped by the coverings (kañcuka) beginning with Kalā, and has fallen into the state of Pradhāna—
with an inconsistent web of bonds related to Pradhāna, according to the sequence of karma arising from the power of Niyati.
One should clothe oneself in that which is entirely inconsistent with the insistence upon a non-self. || 102 ||
He clarifies the binding by the noose of primordial matter (pradhāna):

"Bound by the bond of the three qualities, by the intellect (buddhi), and by the modified ego (vaikārika); firmly bound by the bond of the subtle elements and the senses, and enveloped by the gross elements. (11.103)

First, it is enveloped by the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; then, through the process of their transformation, by the intellect (*buddhi*) whose nature is determination (*adhyavasāya*); then, for the purpose of the difficult-to-overcome modification consisting of egoity (*abhimāna*), by the *ahaṅkāra* in the form of the *vaikārika* and so forth. The mention of the *vaikārika* is intended as an illustration.

Beyond that, it is further enveloped and bound by the group of subtle elements (tanmātras) and sense organs derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra); and beyond that, it is firmly and tightly encased by the gross elements, which are the effects of the subtle elements and have issued forth in the sequence of semen and blood arising from the influence of food and other factors. || 103 ||
Of what nature is this?
Indeed, being bound, it thus wanders within the realm of Māyā and the lower worlds;
thus bound, from the ground of Māyā down to the end of the earth, it wanders from one womb to another.
And for this reason:
"Therefore, he is called a transmigrator (saṃsārī), because he migrates again and again. (11.104)
Thus, for this person who transmigrates as defined by etymology— since objects such as sound and so forth exist for him, he is therefore the "possessor of objects" (viṣayin);
this is the meaning of "this very one."
And for this reason,
he says: "Objects are supreme"—
meaning that those objects such as women and so forth, he declares to be the supreme, most excellent reality.
What kind of objects [are they]? — ...
drunk by various means. || 11-105 ||

They are characterized by various distinctions through the diverse ripenings of karma (*nānākarmavipāka*). "Overwhelmed" means they have been overtaken; that is to say, together with the various ripenings of karma, such as the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Thus, this [individual] experiences these objects, being permeated by their state— that is,
his inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is perfumed and conditioned by the state, the very existence, of those objects.
Because he indeed eats in this manner, he is therefore called the "eater."
"He" refers to the subject. || 106 ||
Furthermore:
"In that [field], O lady of excellent limbs, he who knows it is like a farmer in a field.
The phrase "in that" refers to the field at the limit of the elements. "He who knows it" is called the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). "Like a farmer" means...
The word "yathā" (as) refers to the category of examples; in this context, "kṣetra" means a field or a plot of land.
He clarifies the illustration through the shadow of a pun:
"Having observed a great desire, one should plow it with the plows of greed. (11.107)
Just as a farmer, observing such a great desire that there might be no rest for the turbid water and the dust, examines that field and plows and turns it over with ploughs and harrows; so too—

In accordance with the established principle stated in [Svacchandatantra] 4.105, "But desire is the impurity here," the expression is made through the shadow of a metaphorical pun (*rūpakaśleṣa*): having contemplated desire in its form as impurity, one plows the field consisting of the body with great greed, thereby making it fit for the sowing of the seeds of karma.
And yet—
through a state of delusion, one always sows the seeds consisting of merit and demerit, pertaining to mind, speech, and body, scattering them everywhere. (11.108)
"By way of delusion" means without investigating that "this [practice] gives great fatigue. "One should sow" means one should bring it to completion in the field.
And at a time subsequent to that:
"From that indeed arises the sprout" (tasmādvai aṅkurotpattiḥ)
— from that very seed, the sprout, which consists of various bodies and sense-faculties, comes into being.
He asks, "Of what nature is it? and says:
"...the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain.
This refers to that wherein there occurs the arising of the fruit of suffering from that which is of the nature of pleasure.
And that sprout of birth grows, being thoroughly watered by the water of passion and nourished by desire and anger. (11.109)
And therefore:
"In whatever place and at whatever time, and by whatever age, a virtuous or non-virtuous action was sown, its fruit is obtained at that very time. (11.110)
"At that time" means at the period of youth and so forth occurring in a future birth. || 110 ||
And having obtained that,
the wise one (*budha*)— he who was previously introduced as the one to be defined— enjoys it in various forms according to the power of his past karma.
Thus, this one is such a field; because he knows it in this way, he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 11-111 ||

Thus, because he perceives objects, he is celebrated as "Budha" (the Wise). In this way, this person is called *saṃsārī* (one who wanders in transmigratory existence), *viṣayī* (the subject of objects), *bhoktā* (the enjoyer), and *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).
It is expressed by means of designations that correspond to their respective objects.
He characterizes that which is being awakened:
"When a person contemplates that very [object] in an undesirable form... (11.112).
But when he is then becoming awakened,
[he perceives] that very same thing, such as the enjoyment of sense objects.
He analyzes this very point:
"Now I shall tell you;
likewise—"
When one feels aversion toward enjoyments, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious, || 11.113 ||
Relying on supreme detachment, one should consider these very things to be artificial;
for one understands that everything from Māyā down to the earth is but a magical illusion.

By the passage beginning with "māyā" and so forth, his detachment even toward the various enjoyments of the principles (tattva) and worlds (bhuvana), which are composed of duality, has been demonstrated;
furthermore:
"Sons, friends, wives, well-wishers, kinsmen, and relatives..."
Whatever wealth has been acquired by me, whether through auspicious or inauspicious means, || 11-115 ||
But all these [others] shall enjoy it, free from fear and free from distress;
and I alone shall go to the abode of Yama.

Therefore, these are indeed not auspicious, for they are enemies who cause harm. A friend is affectionate by virtue of mutual assistance; the very cause of friendship is a beautiful heart. One's own kin refers to servants and the like. "Sādana" means simply a dwelling place.
He does not feel revulsion toward his son and others alone; rather, he feels a constant revulsion even toward this body of his own. (11.117)
Born from semen and blood, corrupted by the serpents of the sense objects, filled with various diseases, and agitated by the fear of old age and death. || 11-118 ||
And for this reason: "How can I, who am that very Self, take delight here in that which is strewn with impurity?
By means of scripture and other sources, I come to realize the true nature of the Self as "I am That. Impurity refers to unclean substances.
Thus, having manifested dispassion in this way, one whose mind is constantly agitated should indeed reflect again and again: || 11.119 ||
"How may liberation from this saṃsāra, so difficult to transcend, be attained?"—thus awakened, O Goddess of Gods, he becomes absorbed in That and devoted to That. (11–120)
Then, being liberated from all undertakings, one is said to be "released"; such a person is declared to be "awakened. Now hear from me concerning the "thoroughly awakened. || 11-121 ||
O you of excellent vows, when one has reached the supreme state, which transcends the path and is free from all affliction, through initiation, knowledge, yoga, and conduct— || 11-122 ||
Stainless, immaculate, peaceful, its sphere of experience transcending conceptual proliferation, unmoving, beyond causes, omniscient, and facing in all directions. || 11-123 ||
Indeed, he is perfectly satisfied, the primordial awakened one, independent and eternal; his power and majesty are never lost, he is perfectly enlightened and everlasting. || 11-124 ||
One who is indeed joined to that [state], whose self is absorbed in it, and who is endowed with its qualities,
is called "thoroughly awakened" (suprabuddha), according to the word of Bhairava.
Furthermore, there is no eligibility for the yoga of Śiva without initiation.

Here, the Self (ātman) is said to be the inner self (antarātman), the "consciousness-only" (vijñānākala) is called "without self" (nirātman), the "dissolution-consciousness" (pralayākala) is called "unawakened" (abudha), and the "embodied" (sakala) is called "awakened" (buddha) due to his cognition of external objects.

One whose descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred is "becoming awakened" (buddhyamāna); one initiated into the sacrifice of Śiva who has attained knowledge is "awakened" (prabuddha); but one whose knowledge is well-practiced, who has attained identity with Śiva, whose realization is unshakable, and who is liberated while living, is "fully awakened" (suprabuddha)—thus, the pure self is "becoming awakened."
He is said to be of four kinds: the awakened, the well-awakened, and the supreme self.

Thus, following the description of the creation of the principles for the sake of the Self's own utility, and having described the specific states of the Self in order to demonstrate what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted for the sake of the knower-yogi, [the author says]: "From the qualities (guṇas), the intellect (dhiṣaṇā) is born, endowed with various modifications of existence (bhāvabheda). (11.68)
Thus, in order to define the various types of emotional states (bhāva) introduced above—[the author says]:
"Now I shall describe the various types of emotional states, O fair-faced one. (11.126)
They are called *bhāvas* because they cultivate and perfume the internal organ; these are the eight [qualities], beginning with *dharma*. 126.
Therein, he first states the divisions:
"O Dear One, there are ten causes, three effects, and the objects of being are also tenfold.
He further states the states of being:
There are eleven obstructions of the sense organs, while egoism (ahaṅkāra) is indeed threefold.
Intellect is indeed eightfold, while error is fivefold;
herein, the threefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is to be counted among the divisions.
Now, I shall describe the names of the others in their proper order through their classification. || 11-128 ||

In this context, the causes have the effects as their domain, and the effects—being gross—are the means for the cognition of the subtle; with this intention, he states their names in a sequence contrary to the order of enumeration: "Earth, water, fire, air, and space. (11.129)
Smell, taste, and the subtle element of form, as well as touch and sound— these five are indeed declared to be the subtle elements (tanmātras).
They have been uttered and proclaimed. || 130 ||
This has been declared to you as tenfold action, according to the enumeration of names.
Now—speech, hands, feet, the anus, and likewise the generative organ, so they know. (11.131)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose—
thus it is declared, O Goddess— that the external instrument is established in ten ways.
The internal organ is traditionally said to be threefold, consisting of mind (manas), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi).

Having thus described the twenty-three effects and causes, he now elucidates, in their proper order, the conditions known as the "deaths of the senses" (indriyavadha), which consist in the incapacity of the sense organs.
Muteness, lameness, crippledness, as well as the inability to discharge [semen]. || 11-133 ||
One should know that there is also lack of joy, as well as deafness;
likewise, the decay of the limbs and even blindness. (11.134)
Lack of relish, lack of scent, instability of the mind—these are known as the eleven impairments of the faculties (indriyavadha) in their respective order. (11.135)
"By that sequence" means by the sequence beginning with speech, hands, and so forth, as previously stated.
And even before that—
O lady of excellent complexion, I have described to you the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra): that called Vaikṛta, Bhūtādi, and the third.
Now—dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth;
likewise adharma, ignorance, non-dispassion, and lack of sovereignty. (11.137)
These eight qualities of the intellect (buddhi), beginning with dharma, have been fully described.
Furthermore: darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and the other, perversity (viparyaya). [11.138]

They call these the five misconceptions, beginning with "blind darkness" (andhatāmisra). [These occur] regarding the subtle body—consisting of the intellect, ego, and the subtle elements; regarding the gross body—composed of the senses and the elements; and regarding the fivefold objects such as sound, which are desirable through both direct perception and scripture.

Self-conceit is, in its sequence, called *tamas*, *moha*, and *mahāmoha*. That hatred toward external objects which cause harm to the body is *tāmisra*. The terror arising from the fear of separation from those objects is *andhatāmisra*.
Thus, in this manner, those fifty varieties of states (bhāva) have been fully described in their proper order. (11–139)
Now, while establishing the subdivisions of virtue (*dharma*) and the other qualities, he begins to show those such as contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and perfection (*siddhi*) mentioned by the Sāṃkhyas:
"Furthermore, there are eight subdivisions of the intellect (*buddhi*), beginning with virtue (*dharma*) and so forth."
I shall describe to you their various divisions exactly as they are differentiated.
The word "punaḥ" (again) is to be joined immediately after the words "I shall tell."
That intellect which consists of the eight forms beginning with dharma binds the person in seven ways on the path of saṃsāra, excluding the specific state called knowledge (jñāna);
but by the eighth—
One should liberate those men devoted to the knowledge of Sāṃkhya by means of the nature of gnosis.
From the statement beginning with "Sāṃkhya," it will become clear later that their liberation occurs only within the Sāṃkhya view, and not here [in this system]. || 141 ||
Among these—dharma and the rest—knowledge is declared to be sāttvika; the other three are remembered as rājasa;
and the four beginning with adharma are indeed tāmasa, O fair-faced one. (11.142)
The three are the qualities of sovereignty, dispassion, and virtue. (142)
Furthermore: "Dharma is said to be tenfold, and knowledge is traditionally held to be eightfold;
dispassion is ninefold, and they know sovereignty to be eightfold. (11.143)
These very same [qualities], when reversed, are proclaimed as non-dharma and so forth;
the meaning is that these are precisely those qualities such as dharma, with the numerical divisions as previously stated.
In that regard, he first states the tenfold dharma:
"Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (11.144)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile—thus, O fair-faced one, has the tenfold Dharma been described. (11.145)
Freedom from guile is the state of being free from an evil mind. || 145 ||
He states the divisions of knowledge:
Tāra, Sutāra, Taraṇa, Tāraka, Pramodaka, Pramudita, Ramyaka, and likewise Sadāpramudita. (11.146)
O Supreme Goddess, this knowledge has been fully explained in brief,
which was previously [stated] during the determination of the worlds of the *puruṣa*-principle:
"Tārā and Sutārā" (10.107).
The above and so forth are stated using the feminine reading with reference to *siddhi*;

this is intended to mean that the eightfold *siddhi*—consisting of *ūha* and the rest as described by the Sāṃkhyas—is a specific type of knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣa*). Here, because it is expressed in the neuter gender in grammatical coordination with "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it refers only to what was previously [stated].
Regarding what was recited as *modamāne*, in this context the reading is *taraṇe*; this is merely a difference in wording, and there is no difference whatsoever in the underlying reality.
He states that even the previously mentioned ninefold contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is a form of the divisions of detachment (*vairāgya*):
"Ambhā, Salilā, Oghā, and another known as Vṛṣṭi. (11.147)
Sutārā, Supārā, and Sunetrā are remembered as the next;
the eighth is Kumārī, and likewise Uttamāmbhasikā.
Thus, in this manner— dispassion has indeed been described by me to you as ninefold;
this, along with the seventeen forms of contentment regarding accomplishments, constitutes [the thirty-six topics] here.
It has already been stated previously that this was said precisely because [the lineage] is presided over by deities such as Tārā.
Now he shows [these powers] by way of their division according to sovereignty: Aṇimā, laghimā, and indeed mahimā, as well as prāpti. (11.149)

Likewise, there is irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and supreme control (vaśitva); the eighth is proclaimed as the power of determining the course of things according to one's desire (yatrakāmāvasāyitva). || 11-150 ||
O fair-faced one, the eightfold sovereignty has thus been described.
Now he speaks of the divisions of unrighteousness (*adharma*), such as anger and so forth, which are the opposites of non-anger and the rest:
"Anger, lack of service to the guru, and impurity after that. (11.151)
Lack of contentment, lack of straightforwardness, violence, untruthfulness, theft, unchastity, and likewise crookedness. (11.152)
Thus, this collection of ten types of unrighteousness has been fully explained.
He now states the divisions of ignorance: "The non-crossing, the difficult crossing, and also the failure to cause others to cross," (11.153).
And the Atāraka, O Queen of the Gods, is proclaimed as the fourth;
then there is the Apramoda, the Apramudita, and also the Aramyaka. (11.154)
Thus, that ignorance is eightfold, including lack of faith and lack of joy;
these very same eight are described by the Sāṃkhyas as the incapacities of the intellect (buddhi), being the opposites of the perfections beginning with *ūha*.
He states the divisions of non-detachment:
"The waterless, the water-free, and likewise the rainless cloud. (11.155)
Beyond this, one should know the Asutārā, the Asupārā, and the Asunetrā; likewise, the Akumārī and the Anuttamāmbhasikā. || 11-156 ||
Thus it is:
"O Maheśvarī, [the powers] are indeed aṇimā, laghimā, and mahimā;
as well as aprāpti, aprākāmya, and likewise anīśitva. (11.157)
Lack of mastery, as well as the inability to resolve things according to one's will—
thus,
O Goddess of the gods, lack of sovereignty is proclaimed to be eightfold.

Thus, having described the creation of objective entities (bhāva-sarga) as being separated from the creation of principles (tattva-sarga), he speaks in order to demonstrate where and how that [creation] is situated:
"And these [entities], such as the Piśācas and others, are presided over by those [principles] beginning with non-sovereignty. (11.158)
They are presided over and pervaded. || 158 ||
And therefore—[I shall] tell you how those eight [powers] are established in them in their respective order;
"in them" means in those [beings] such as the Piśācas and others; "the eight" refers to the lack of sovereignty and so forth.
In that regard:
"Indeed, lack of sovereignty is found in the Piśāca [state], and lack of dispassion in the Rākṣasa. (11.159)
In the Yakṣa [element] there is ignorance, and in the Gāndharva there is indeed unrighteousness;
in the Aindra [element] there is righteousness, and in the Saumya knowledge is established.
In the realm of Prajāpati, however, dispassion and sovereignty reside in Brahman;
the word "predominantly" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And as for this sovereignty that has been described—it consists of sixty-four qualities and is established in the state of Brahmā. (11.161)
That merit is established as sixty-fold in the Prājāpatya rite,
and it is proclaimed as forty-eight-fold in the Saumya.
The sovereignty of Mahendra is said to possess forty qualities;
O Goddess, the sovereignty of the Gandharvas is said to possess thirty-two qualities.
The Yakṣa [power] is known to have twenty-four qualities, the Rākṣasa sixteen; sovereignty is eightfold, and the Paiśāca is proclaimed [to have four]. (11.164)
Thus, O observer of excellent vows, that sovereignty remains established among the divine classes of beings (*devayoni*).

By stating "among the divine classes of beings," which is already implied by the context, the underlying intention is this: whatever sovereignty belongs to a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*), the sovereignty of the *piśācas* is eight times greater than that.

Beyond that, the power increases eightfold for each successive class, beginning with the Rākṣasas; otherwise, in the absence of a limit, in relation to what would there be this eightfold increase? Thus, the lack of sovereignty among Piśācas is more intense when compared to the sovereignty of Brahmā, just as it is when compared to that of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The eightfold sovereignty is thus described.
But those [entities] such as Dharma and the rest, which are devoid of such manifestations of sovereignty, abide in other ways—sevenfold in nature—within the divine wombs. (11.165)
Although all the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) exist [simultaneously],

it has been stated that, according to the sequence beginning with the Piśācas, there is an intensification of each one— such as lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*)— and a corresponding diminution of the others. || 165 ||

Not only do these exist in such a manner among the divine classes through the predominance or subordination of their qualities, but furthermore—these very same [qualities], when thoroughly intermingled, are established among human beings.
"Thoroughly intermingled" means that their distinctions are no longer perceptible; for this very reason, the human state is of a single uniform nature.
Regarding the question of what the situation is for the various divisions of the animal realm, he says:
"Established as far down as the stationary beings (plants) according to the state of being primary or subordinate qualities. (11.166)

Animals and the like, due to their state of darkness (tamas), consist of the fourfold [qualities] beginning with unrighteousness (adharma); and even therein, unrighteousness and the others increase progressively in each subsequent stage. || 166 ||
Now, regarding the differentiation of states within this very same subject matter as it has been divided, I shall explain the pervasion of the three qualities (guṇas) exactly as it exists.
In that regard—
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Indra, are presided over by Sattva. || 11-167 ||
The four [classes of gods], beginning with Brahmā and ending with Indra, are dominated by the quality of sattva.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and humans are of the rājasa nature, while daityas,
yātudhānas, and piśācas are declared to be tāmasa.
The Daityas are essentially of the same nature as the Yakṣas. || 168 ||

The sages of firm vows are to be known as those in whom *rajas* and *sattva* predominate. "Firm" (*saṃśita*) means very sharp; they are those whose vow—a rule consisting of the practice of the means for knowledge and realization—is firm.
Because they mostly occupy an intermediate state between gods and humans, they are predominant in *rajas* and *sattva*.
And those various classes of beings, from the gods down to the sages, who mutually overcome one another, are all established upon the earth. (11.169)
It should be explained that although those beginning with the *yātudhānas* overwhelm those beginning with the gods and sages in the world of mortals through wicked conduct,

the latter likewise overcome them through the power of their heroism, austerity, mantras, and so forth; however, this does not mean that the *guṇas* themselves mutually overcome one another on earth, for such mutual subjugation is merely a figurative description of their nature.
Because there is no distinction [in the rule] regarding all [substances], the specific injunction "on earth" would be untenable. || 169 ||
Furthermore: "Immersed in absolute darkness are the immobile beings and the crawling reptiles—
trees and the like, as well as snakes and so forth— for they are characterized by intense tamas due to being composed of delusion and anger."
Furthermore:
"And those who are devoid of even a single foot are proclaimed to be tāmasa. (11.170)
"Crawling creatures and so forth" (sarīsṛpādyāḥ) should be understood as follows:
those beginning with crawling creatures—in reverse order, including birds and the rest—down to animals, are all entirely characterized by tamas; however, they are devoid of feet.

Thus, among reptiles, birds possess less darkness (*tamas*) than those [reptiles] because they lack feet; even less than birds do wild animals (*mṛga*); and even less than those do domestic cattle (*paśu*). Such a pervasion by the qualities (*guṇa*) has been shown here by the Blessed One through differentiation, whereas by the followers of Sāṃkhya—
"The creation is expansive with *sattva* at the top, expansive with *tamas* at the root,
and expansive with *rajas* in the middle, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 54).
Thus, without distinction, gods, animals, humans, and others are composed of *sattva*, *tamas*, and *rajas*.
It has been explained.
Thus, O lady of good vows, those fourteen distinct classes of birth, beginning from the gods down to the stationary beings, have been shown through the diversity of their qualities.
And included within these are other infinite wombs as well. || 11-171 ||
Likewise, among human beings, those infinite varieties cannot be fully described due to their endless classification, arising from the infinite distinctions of karma. (11.172)

By the specific mention "among humans," he indicates that these [lineages] have infinite branches due to the diversity of directions, locations, times, customs, and so forth. The phrase "due to the infinite differentiation connected with karma" provides the reason for the infinity of wombs (*yoni*). || 172 ||
Furthermore— virtues, however, abide in the world of humans like dharma and the other [puruṣārthas],
as follows:

The meaning is that just as dharma and the other qualities are said to be "thoroughly intermingled" among humans— as in the verse, "These very [qualities], thoroughly intermingled, are established among humans" (11.166)— so too are the *guṇas* (the constituent qualities), whose specific distinctions are not perceived.

O lady of excellent vows, those humans who are mixed with qualities such as unrighteousness (*adharma*)—for them, there are these teachings concerning dharma and the rest, which consist of the various forms of knowledge that have been codified. (11.173)
I shall explain to you those [qualities] which exist in the case of unrighteousness and so forth;
"in the case of righteousness and so forth" means with respect to that subject, by extension meaning with respect to its verbal expression. These are the cognitions and the scriptures.
In that regard—the treatise on logic (*hetuśāstra*) which, in the world, mocks [the concepts of] permanence and impermanence. || 11-174 ||

It "mocks" or deceives the person being instructed regarding the two properties to be proven—eternality and non-eternality—because it is impossible to ascertain them in reality; thus, it is called "the mocker of the eternal and the non-eternal. This is an expression where the abstract quality (bhāva) is the primary referent. 174.
Furthermore—through debate (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)...

as it has been stated: "It consists of the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's] by means of valid cognition and reasoning, and is not contrary to established tenets."

*Vāda* (debate) is the adoption of a position and its counter-position in the form of a discourse on one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). That same [discourse], when joined with quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), for the purpose of testing a person's capability, is *jalpa* (wrangling).
However, *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is that same [wrangling] when it is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position.

Such a treatise on logic (*hetuśāstra*), which is a treatise on reasoning (*tarkaśāstra*) standing outside the authentic scriptures (*sadāgama*), by means of that—[those who] dispute, being uncertain.
Those for whom there exists no certain determination of the true nature of reality (*vastusattva-niścaya*) dispute thus: "This..."
"This is the truth; it is not so"—thus they cry out, contradicting one another.
Because their statements are grounded in logical reasoning (*hetu*), and not in the form of an investigation into the meaning of scripture (*āgama*).
And for this reason,
O lady of excellent vows, they are entirely devoid of any real entity.
But those [scriptures] which are devoid of the yoga of knowledge and lack a presiding deity—
for that reason, no certainty regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa arises from them. (11.176)
Therefore,
these are bound by ignorance, with unrighteousness serving as the instrumental cause.
And it was said previously:
Those lowest of men who are not devoted to the Guru, the Deity, the Fire, and the Scripture;
"Māyā indeed deludes those who know the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic, for they desire liberation in what is not liberation. (10.1140–1141).
Likewise—
"But having abandoned the right path, it leads one swiftly onto a wrong path. (10.1140)
Because the treatises on logic are of such a nature, therefore—those men who take delight therein go to hell. (11.177)
Furthermore, regarding dry reasoning (śuṣkatarka) consisting of ignorance caused by unrighteousness (adharma):
"Due to a lack of dispassion (avairāgya), they constantly experience a lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya) in hell.
Therefore, the attributes of the intellect (buddhidharmāḥ) are those known as unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya).
O lady of excellent limbs, these four always cause suffering for you in hell.
Since they cause delusion for all living beings, they are known as *tāmasa*.

Having thus described the dry logical treatises consisting of the fourfold group beginning with unrighteousness (*adharma*), he speaks of the scriptures bound by righteousness (*dharma*) and the others:
O Goddess of the Gods, worldly knowledge is indeed bound by a single dharma.
Worldly [knowledge] consists of livelihood, the science of government, and so forth. || 179 ||

But the Vedic Pāñcarātra is bound to the knowledge of Dharma; through the practices of approach (*abhigamana*), material collection (*upādāna*), worship (*ijyā*), and so forth, as prescribed by the Pāñcarātras,
one indeed becomes that very [Brahman] oneself.
Thus, knowledge is also taught [in the Vedic tradition], just like the performance of rituals;
for instance, in the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) and elsewhere, knowledge is expressed as: "The Person alone is all this" (*Ṛgveda* 10.90.2).
Both the Buddhist and the Māhārata [scriptures] are indeed [established], O lady of excellent vows, solely through dispassion.
It is simply bound. || 180 ||
O Pārvatī, Sāṃkhya-knowledge is indeed connected with wisdom and dispassion;
knowledge is the realization of the distinction between the Puruṣa and Prakṛti.
Knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established upon the knowledge of yoga.
Because even sovereignty has been mentioned in the Vibhūtipāda of the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra] and other such works. || 181 ||

Thus, the scriptures beginning with the worldly ones and ending with Yoga are grounded in the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of attributes such as *dharma* and so forth; but beyond those is the scripture of the Supreme Lord—
transcending the states of the intellect and proclaimed as the path beyond the paths.
But that knowledge which transcends the world is known as the "superior path. || 11-182 ||

The word "atīta" (transcended) is used with a genitive case by way of transposition in place of the accusative for all the states of the intellect—the aforementioned manifestations such as *dharma* and so forth. This scripture is called *atimārga* because it transcends the path—that is, the world of bound souls (*paśu*). || 182 ||
This is clarified as follows:
"The worlds are said to be the fettered souls (paśus) on the path of creation and dissolution;
those who are established on the Transcendental Path (atimārga) should be known as having transcended them. (11.183)

Those bound souls (*paśu*) on the path of emanation and withdrawal who do not know the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which consists of the self that emanates and withdraws its own creation—they, being thus created and withdrawn, are all called "worlds" (*loka*) here. Those who have transcended them abide on the Path Beyond (*atimārga*). || 183 ||
For this reason: "Those who observe the vow of the skull, as well as those who are Pāśupatas—
for them, no creation exists..."

The word "also" (*api*) is placed out of its logical order; for even those who observe the *kapāla* vow and the Pāśupatas have no [independent] creation, let alone the Śaivas who have transcended the entire path (*sarvādhvottīrṇa*). This is the implied meaning.
What, then, is their state? To this he says:
"And they abide in the eternal Lord. (11.184)
And it was said previously: "One whose self is purified by initiation and knowledge, through the Śaiva practice at the end of the body,
and having undertaken the vow of the skull (kapālavrata), goes to his own respective state."
"Those who are devoted to the practice of recitation and the application of sacred ash attain the state of the Lord.

Now, since every path is subject to creation and dissolution, must not even those situated in the principle of Īśvara be subject to these two? It is said: for them, the dissolution of that portion consisting of the non-recognition of the limited measure [of duality] results in the attainment of the nature of Supreme Bhairava; however, they do not have their essential nature dissolved again like bound souls (paśus).
They are created. Regarding this, it is said:
"Since they will attain liberation, which is the cause of no further rebirth, therefore it is rightly stated that for them there is no creation"—this is the connection.
But for those who do not abide on the supreme path—namely, the worldly ones—there is only repeated creation and repeated dissolution. (11.185)
And for this reason, they— having mounted the wheel of saṃsāra— wander like a water-wheel (*ghaṭayantra*);
*ghaṭayantra* means a water-lifting machine (*araghaṭṭa*).
He establishes this very point:
"O Dear One, there is an eight-spoked wheel joined with the protective rims of Dharma and the other [virtues]. (11.186)
O Goddess, presided over by Īśvara and struck by the rod of Niyati, pierced by impurity (mala), karma, and kalā, it revolves with the force of time. || 11-187 ||
Those factors such as *dharma* and so forth which constitute the causes of *saṃsāra* are themselves like spokes (*āraka*), being the causes of wandering;
as they say:
"By means of *dharma*, there is upward movement" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 44), and so forth.

A *cakraka* is a contemptible wheel; a *daṇḍaka* is a stick that revolves as destiny itself. By that [wheel], one is struck—that is, impelled—by *mala*, namely the *āṇava* [impurity], by *karman*, and by that which is characterized by *kalā*, namely the *māyīya* [impurity].
Impelled by knowledge and so forth, it revolves with speed, driven by the force produced by the principle of time (kālatattva), which consists of mental construction (kalanāmaya).
Since this wheel is thus exceedingly difficult to traverse,
therefore— O Dear One, those who are devoted to worldly and other such forms of knowledge, those who are intent upon the treatises on logic, and others who are performers of evil deeds; || 11.188 ||
And all of them, being deluded, do not see the end of this wheel.

Regarding the phrase "among them," which refers to those described by the aforementioned forms: by the words "but those who," the author suggests that those devoted to dry logic are even more afflicted than those devoted to worldly matters; they are "deluded" by *māyā*.
Their own true nature is concealed.

And this is the distinction of the Śiva-scripture among all scriptures, namely: "Those goals which are to be accomplished in the worldly [spheres] and so forth, up to the domain of the Atimārga... (11.189).

One should effortlessly accomplish all those specific supernatural powers (*siddhi*) to be attained in worldly matters and the like, within the Great Awakening (*mahodaya*) of the knowledge of Śiva; that which is characterized by the Supreme Path (*atimārga*),
the ultimate locus of mastery over all scriptures, and which has that [knowledge] as its sphere and object, being the cause of the Great Awakening.
In the knowledge of Śiva, the practitioner accomplishes [all things] with ease.
And that which is accomplished through Śaiva knowledge is not indeed accomplished by all [means],
such as worldly ones and the like.
The reason for this is: ... because it is exceedingly pure. (11.190)
The word "knowledge of Śiva" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 190 ||
He clarifies this very state of utter purity: "O Goddess, because [the mind] is joined to the supreme state of non-existence,
where objects do not exist in the form of various distinct entities."
This clarifies [the following]:
"Non-existence that transcends conceptualization, a domain beyond the sphere of discursive proliferation. (11.191)
It is free from mind, intellect, and the like; it is devoid of causal discourse; it transcends the means of valid cognition such as direct perception; and it is the sovereign and imperishable.
Beyond all logic and scripture, free from fetters and mantras, omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, stainless, and untroubled. || 11-193 ||

That supreme state is one in which no entities exist; it transcends all mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Since it is beyond the manifold world (*prapañca*), its nature cannot be conceived as an object within the sphere of sensory or cognitive experience.
For this very reason, it is free from the mind, intellect, and so forth; and for this same reason, it is devoid of causal discourse.
The meaning is that it cannot be investigated because it serves as the foundational ground for all investigation.

Likewise, it is not an object of means of knowledge such as perception, because even those means of knowledge are manifested by virtue of its own self-luminous nature as their ground, and because it is the source of the manifestation of all appearances. It is the "Lord" (prabhu), whose nature is to bring forth.

It is independent (*svatantra*). Furthermore, because there is not even the slightest alteration in it upon the destruction of the *ullāsa*, as there might be in another thing, it is called "immutable" (*avyaya*). It has transcended even those specific scriptures of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-āgama*) by which everything is reasoned and investigated, for it is those very scriptures that possess the capacity to investigate all things.

This too is beyond their scope, because it is enveloped by the bonds (*pāśas*) consisting of *māyā* and the rest belonging to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), as well as by the mantras residing in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). He knows all and perceives all without distinction;
he goes everywhere and pervades all. Nevertheless, he is not tainted by that even in the slightest degree.
It is quiescent and of the singular nature of consciousness; nevertheless, it is such that the impurities of *āṇava* and the rest have emerged and arisen from it.

Even so, because it is untouched by them, it is free from affliction (*niruplava*), free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), and is of the singular nature of autonomous consciousness, which is eternally luminous and the illuminator of all things. || 193 ||
Furthermore:
"For it is one, consisting of all powers, independent, without beginning, and without a master; it is free from all excellence and is the primordial seed of beginningless existence. (194)
The supreme Śaiva knowledge is traditionally held to transcend the sphere of all [empirical] cognition.

According to the principle that "His powers are the entire universe," its essential nature consists of all powers whose very self is the universe. It is one and without a second. One’s own... [svam ātmīyam].

That which has form itself as its tantra—that is, its fivefold creative activity, its functions, and its instruments—is independent (*svatantra*). Likewise, that which has no other lord is "lordless" (*anātha*), meaning it is the Lord of the Universe (*viśveśvara*). Furthermore, it is "without beginning" (*anādimat*), being the primordial source of all things. It is unbound by any objects of knowledge, action, and so forth.
The meaning is that its nature is pure consciousness alone, which transcends all things and is unsurpassed.

It is untouched by *bhava*—the beginningless cycle of existence driven by the egoistic impulse (*ahaṃprathamikā*). It is the "state" (*pada*) which is the respective locus of rest for all forms of knowledge, such as those of the Buddhists, the Sāṃkhyas, the Lākulas, and others.

It stands even transcending that. Such is the supreme, unsurpassed knowledge of Śiva; it is remembered as being of the nature of direct experience, meaning it is unimpeded through an uninterrupted lineage of transmission.

Having thus established the emanations of the distinctions between reality, the elements, and the categories of existence, [the author] describes the mundane and other forms of knowledge bound by dharma, jñāna, and so forth, followed by the majesty of Śaiva knowledge.
Having determined and described the creation of the principles (tattvas) and so forth by way of restatement, he concludes by further elaborating upon the very greatness of the knowledge of Śiva:
"In this manner, O fair-faced one, the principles and the knowledges have been created. (11.195)
By these principles, the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, was emitted;
it was specifically created and expanded through the fourteenfold creation consisting of the elements.
Moreover: "The worlds are manifold, by the hundreds and by the thousands. (11.196)
Those worlds which are situated within the principles (tattvas) and which are mentioned in the context of the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), they too are created by the principles themselves.
Likewise, there are various scriptures whose nature consists of the aforementioned knowledge—
neither merely the worlds nor the scriptures alone, but all those which are internal to the principles (tattva). Furthermore:
Consciousness is the deceptive art, characterized by a multitude of supernatural powers.
All of this should be understood within the principles (*tattva*):

namely, the various forms of knowledge concerning mantras, maṇḍalas, mudrās, and so forth; as well as deceptive arts that cause amazement and produce conviction in limited minds, which are mostly like magical illusions (*indrajāla*); and craftsmanship.

It should be understood that all that knowledge which characterizes and demonstrates the collection— the multitude— of magical powers such as painting, puppetry, dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as those consisting of subjugation, attraction, and the like, exists within the *tattvas*.
For this reason:
[it] is seen in all the principles (tattvas);
it is perceived through the direct realization of those very principles and other means, according to the suitability of each respective principle.
Not only is there that which is to be known useful for the practitioner within the principles (tattvas), but furthermore:
"The ritual process (prakriyā) and initiation into Śiva (śivadīkṣā) are obtained through these very principles. (11.198)

The procedure, which consists of the demonstration of the previously mentioned principles (tattvas) and so forth, is useful for practitioners endowed with knowledge; likewise, it brings about the cessation of the fetters— such as birth in various wombs appropriate for the experience of the diverse worlds within each respective principle, as well as karma and its requitals— and effects union with Śiva.
This is attained through these aforementioned principles and not otherwise;
therefore, the nature of the principles as described must necessarily be known. 198.
And this is logical, because:
"There is no liberation equal to initiation...
Initiation alone liberates and leads one even to the supreme abode of Śiva."
For this has indeed been established elsewhere.
And initiation is that which is performed by means of those mantras; it consists of their potency—[the supreme Vidyā Mātṛkā].
For she is indeed the Blessed Lady.
The ultimate reality of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), which consists of the wonder of non-difference from the entire universe— comprising all that is signified and all that signifies—
is pointed out in various scriptures as the source of all mantras (*sarvamantrāraṇi*). And this very [mass of sounds],
through the reflective awareness of the universe, bestows supreme knowledge.
And since that [knowledge] consists precisely of the process of the paths already explained, he says:
"There is no knowledge higher than the process...
Knowledge other than that which is supreme through the process is indeed utterly trivial.
According to the principle previously established— that knowledge makes known the object of knowledge—
the limited yoga (*mitayoga*), which is distinct from that yoga whose nature is the supreme reality (*paratattva*) characterized by the known, is indeed to be abandoned; thus he says:
...there is no yoga, however, that is without a focal point. || 11-199 ||

There is no yoga for one whose supreme goal—the abode of rest—is non-existent; even if it exists, "limited yoga" (mitayoga) is effectively "non-yoga" (ayoga) in this discourse on the Unsurpassed (Anuttara), as stated in the *Yojanikā*. Therefore, only "supreme yoga" (*parayoga*) is true yoga here. || 199 ||

Thus, he demonstrates that this entire matter—the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which brings about the supreme human goal (*parapuruṣārtha*), the knowledge of the procedure of the *mātṛkā* which is its requisite, and the nature of yoga characterized by the unmanifest (*alakṣya*)—is taught with its preeminent excellence only in the teaching of the Supreme Lord; therefore, that alone is the best of all scriptures: "Thus, this entire matter—the initiation which brings about the supreme human goal, the knowledge of the procedure of the *mātṛkā* which is its requisite, and the nature of yoga characterized by the unmanifest—is taught with its preeminent excellence only in the teaching of the Supreme Lord; therefore, he establishes that that alone is the best of all scriptures."

All of that, O Goddess, has been told in the *Śivajñānamahodadhi*. Indeed, the *Śivajñāna* is called a "great ocean" because of its unfathomable depth, because it is the resting place where all the various rivers of knowledge converge, and because it is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity.
Concluding the current topic and introducing another, he says:
"Thus the creation has been fully described; now its maintenance and dissolution are being told. (11.200)
The meaning is "and dissolution. In that context, persistence consists in remaining for a fixed duration of time, and at its conclusion, dissolution occurs in the same manner. || 200 ||
He speaks in order to instruct on everything— starting from when [the practice] began, what it is like, and the time for both that which is to be established and that which is to be withdrawn:
"A moment (kṣaṇa) is said to be one-eighth of a human blink of an eye."
Two kṣaṇas should be known as a tuṭi, and two of those are recorded as a lava.
Two lava-s are to be known as one nimeṣa according to the sequence of calculation;
fifteen nimeṣas are declared to be one kāṣṭhā.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are to be known as one *kalā*, and thirty of those [kalās] constitute one *muhūrta*.
Furthermore, thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a human day and night (*ahorātra*). (11.203)

The *kṣaṇa* is that most minute division of time, which is one-eighth part of the closing of the eyelids— the blinking of the eyes— which is established by the self-experience of those humans whom the treatise intends to instruct; it is conceived in dependence upon the very duration of a blink of the eye.
A *lava* is that period of time within a breath (*prāṇa*) known as a *tuṭi*. As was stated previously:
"The sixteen *tuṭis* in a breath were indeed explained by me before; by external time alone, they are designated as *lavas*" (7.27).
Thus: two *lava*s constitute a *nimeṣa*, which consists of eight *kṣaṇas*; a *muhūrta* consists of two *ghaṭikās*. || 203 ||
Furthermore,
O beloved lotus-eyed one, three hundred and sixty days and nights are to be known as a human year. (11.204)
A full hundred years is to be known as the human lifespan;
indeed, it is well known that the maximum lifespan is one hundred and twenty years.
Regarding what was stated—that a year consists of three hundred and sixty days and nights—that very point is now clarified through the division into fortnights, months, and so forth:
"Fifteen days and nights are declared to be a fortnight. (11.205)
Two fortnights constitute a month, and two such months constitute a season (*ṛtu*).
Two seasons make a period of time (*kāla*), and three of those make a solstice (*ayana*). (11.206)
O lady of excellent hips, by those two [movements] a year is proclaimed;
time is known as consisting of four months, comprising the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
He states that the year of humans, which consists of these two solstices (ayanas), is itself a day and night of the ancestors (pitrya):
"The southern solstice is the night, and the northern solstice is the day. (11.207)
That is a day and night for the ancestors; by this measure, a year is as previously described.
Likewise, that is a day and night for the gods; there too, the year and so forth are as previously described.

By the word "etcetera," [periods such as] fortnights and months are included. Thus, the calculation of day and night is equal for both the ancestors (pitṛs) and the gods; this is seen in the Purāṇa manuscripts. However, by contemporary [authorities], it is stated:
"That [year] is indeed double the length of a season" (11.206).
Immediately following this:
"The dark fortnight is indeed the day, while the bright fortnight becomes the night;
that too constitutes a day and night for the ancestors, and by this measure, the year is as before."
Having thus reversed the reading and explained that a human month is a day and night of the ancestors (pitṛs),
the worldly convention regarding the annual calculation of ancestral days has also become established.
Thus, based on that divine year, which consists of three hundred and sixty human years— [it is said]:
