"The four yugas should be known to consist of twelve thousand [divine] years."
Twelve thousand years are to be known as a cycle of four ages (caturyuga).
And here is the division: O Goddess, [the worlds] were created by four thousand [years] each, in due order. (11.209)
O Goddess, Tretā is to be known by three [hundred years], and Dvāpara is remembered as being by two; O Beloved, Kali is to be understood as lasting for one thousand years.
Thus, for ten thousand years. || 210 ||
As for the two thousand that remain,
from them I shall state the measure of the two twilights (sandhyā) belonging to the beginning and the end in each respective age (yuga).
In that regard—four hundred [are mentioned]; and for the Kṛta age, the beginning and the end are proclaimed. (11.211)

Three hundred years are to be known as the duration of the Tretā age, two hundred for the Dvāpara, and one hundred for the Kali; this is remembered as the measure of the transitional periods (saṃdhyā).

And thus, at the end of the Kali age there are one hundred [years], and at the beginning of the Kṛta age there are four hundred; so the twilight (*sandhyā*) between the Kali and Kṛta ages consists of five hundred years. Similarly, the twilight between the Kṛta and Tretā ages consists of seven hundred years, that between the Tretā and Dvāpara ages consists of five hundred years, and that between the Dvāpara and Kali ages consists of three hundred years.

Having calculated two thousand [years], this four-yuga period consists of twelve thousand years when combined with the previously mentioned ten thousand. But as for the duration of the junctions (*saṃdhi*) and the portions of the junctions (*saṃdhyāṃśa*), I shall now explain.

If this is the reading, then, because both have been stated [previously], one should know that each hundred [verses] including the junctions is the measure of the junctional portion (sandhyaṃśa). || 212 ||
And this very point—
I shall tell you again according to worldly measurement,
as many as there may be.
Forty-three hundred thousand and twenty thousand.
But according to worldly calculation, this number refers to years within a cycle of four yugas; this is the remainder [of the statement].
Furthermore,
O Goddess, I shall describe to you each individual age in detail.
The number of years according to the worldly reckoning. || 214 ||
One million seven hundred twenty-eight thousand— this is the measure of the Kṛta [Yuga],
including the four hundred transitional periods (saṃdhyāṃśas) at its beginning and end, but not the pure [yuga] alone. The same applies hereafter.
...of the Tretā age, I shall tell you.
The measure of the Tretā Yuga is twelve hundred thousand and ninety-six thousand years; now learn from me the measure of the Dvāpara Yuga.
O you of virtuous vows, sixty-four thousand and eight hundred thousand [years] constitute the measure of the Dvāpara age; now I shall tell you of the Kali age.
O lady of virtuous vows, the measure of the Kali age has been declared to you in brief as four hundred and thirty-two thousand years.
Thus,
O Goddess, this measurement in human years occurs age after age;
according to the measurement of divine and worldly years as thus described—
Furthermore, seventy-one cycles of the four yugas constitute a manvantara.

And this [measure] of his—devoid of the *sandhyā* and *sandhyāṃśa* periods—is proclaimed as the measure of the *yugas*. By this material measure, the measure within a *manvantara* is remembered. (11.220)
One should calculate twelve thousand years as one hundred four-yuga cycles multiplied by seventy-one. || 220 ||
And this very measurement—I shall tell you again in terms of worldly years, O fair-faced one: seventy-six lakhs and thirty koṭis. (11.221)
O beloved, the measure of a *manvantara* should be known as twenty thousand [years];
and by calculating three hundred and sixty [such years], the duration of a *manvantara* is indeed the period of Indra's tenure.
In this very manner, O Goddess of the gods, a kalpa occurs within a manvantara through these fourteen [periods]. (11.222)
He states the measurement of the *sandhyā* (twilight period) at the transition between *manvantaras*:
"When one *manvantara* has passed and another has arrived, there is always a *sandhyā* in the middle lasting five thousand years. (11.223)
This means "divine," by implication. || 223 ||
However, this is the distinction:
that at the beginning of all [ages] there is a thousand, and likewise again at the end;
"at the beginning and at the end" refers to the beginning and the end of the first *manvantara*, in view of the *manvantaras* contained within a day of Brahmā.
At the end of the final manvantara, it is one thousand and one [years].

Thus, the period consisting of fourteen manvantaras along with the transitional periods (saṃdhyākāla) is called a kalpa; a thousand cycles of the four yugas is declared to be a day of Brahmā. (11.224)

It is called a *kalpa* because the universe is fashioned (*kalpate*) within it; and by means of seventy-one sets of four ages (*caturyuga*) multiplied by the number of *manvantaras*, there are one thousand four-ages minus six.
According to the stated method, the period of the junctions (*sandhyākāla*) during the *manvantaras* amounts to seventy-two thousand [years], which corresponds to six of their own sets of four ages.
This has been stated as measuring one thousand. || 224 ||
And this—
measured by divine years— I shall tell you again; the word "calculated" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus it is said:
"One crore and twenty lakhs of years. (11.225)
By the divine measure alone, a day of Brahmā occurs;
it consists of twelve thousand [years] multiplied by a thousand in this very manner.
Of such a Brahma-day as this, the period of the twilight (sandhyā) is proclaimed to be ninety-six thousand [years]. (11.226)

Eight *caturyugas* consist of ninety-six thousand years. Therein, the division is such that there are four hundred-year *caturyugas* at the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*) and four at the evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*). Those occurring at the beginning and end of the night are likewise; thus, the morning [period] consists of eight *yugas*.
And evening is the time of twilight. || 226 ||
And this—
I shall now tell you by means of worldly measurement; the word "calculated" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus it is said: "Four groups of varṣas and exactly three arbudas. (11.227)
O Goddess of the Gods, two crores are remembered as a day of Brahmā;
three crores and five hundred thousand are declared to be the twilights.
Likewise, forty and sixty thousand, as well as ninety-six thousand increased by three hundred and sixty; thus they become exactly so. And therefore, that which Śrī Bhullaka [states]—
As for what was recited, beginning with "three crores and seventy-four lakhs of sandhyās," that should be disregarded.
And just as this last junction is thus, so indeed is the junction,
the time of the junction.
Likewise, the morning twilight is also equal to that. 11-229.
Thus, O Dear One, this duration of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) together with the hells, as well as that of the seven worlds, ending with the day of Brahmā, has been described. (11.230)
Of the worlds, that is, of their places of residence such as the earth and so forth.
Likewise, O Goddess, listen as I describe to you their dissolution;
at the end of Brahmā’s own day, that is indeed called the Kalpa-dissolution.

"At the end of the *svādina*" means during that night. "Kalpa" is so called because it is conceived (*kalpyate*) as that in which the universe is cut away (*cchidyate*). "Saṃhāra" refers to the time of dissolution. || 231 ||
Therein—
within a single day of Brahmā, fourteen Indras,
having ruled in succession according to the arrangement of the Manvantaras, pass away. (11.232)
Having ruled for the duration of each Manvantara, each Indra departs according to the fitness of his own karma.
Then he withdraws the universe, extending as far as the end of the seven worlds;
O Goddess, when the Grandfather is asleep, the Fire of Time gazes upward.

The word "tataḥ" (then) refers to the end of the fourteen Indras. While Brahmā, filled with wonder, remains as if asleep like a bound soul (paśu), and gazes upward toward the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), he withdraws the entire range of objects within the seven worlds. || 233 ||
Then, at the time of gazing—
his southern face indeed emits a great flame.
And therefore—
From that mouth, a great flame issued forth, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Blazing upward with intense speed and difficult to endure, it ascends;
and at this moment, those worlds situated in the seven [worlds] and those inhabitants who dwell in the nether regions— || 11-235 ||
When pleasure, pain, and their combination have been exhausted and delusion has largely subsided,
they all become mere existence in the realm of Brahman.
And by the word "ca" (and), those who have gone to realms such as the hells are included; in the Brahmaviṣṭapa, which is situated above Satyaloka, in the world of Brahmā. || 236 ||
To what extent does their delusion last? To this he says:
"As long as there is no further arising of the karma of pleasure, pain, and so forth, so long do those deluded ones remain, until Brahmā awakens. (11.237)

The "arising" (udaya) refers to the maturation (vipāka) of those karmas which, by means of pleasure and pain—and by implication, through the word "and so forth," birth and lifespan—serve as the causes for them. || 237 ||
But those who are the lords of the world of Rudra and the lords of the netherworlds,
such as the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakas, and others— they remain exceedingly pure.
But they do not wither even in the slightest degree. || 238 ||
But—
those [deities] remain devoid of activity until creation occurs again;
that is, their activities such as bestowing grace have ceased.
Then,
when the worlds have become empty, an irresistible flame burns.
O Goddess, she would burn the hells and the netherworlds on all sides;
she burns even the three worlds, as far as the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
"In worlds that have become empty" refers to the cause for that; it burns everything from the hells up to the world of the gods (svarloka). || 240 ||
But those others,
O fair-faced one, by smoke the three worlds— Mahar, Jana, and Tapa— are destroyed.
But the seventh,
O lady of virtuous vows, is even Satyaloka.
And all those who were previously standing there, their minds deluded by sleep, became like the dead;
then—
Having thus burned the entire world, the flame enters the mouth once again.
To the south of Kālāgni alone. || 242 ||
Then great winds arise, born from the breath of Brahmā;
and they,
O beloved, destroy that ash produced by the burning of the world.
Then,
O Goddess, the water born from the perspiration of Brahmā shall again inundate that world;
by that very water, the world shall become a single ocean.
His perspiration is born from the heat of the fire of time. || 244 ||
Then, at the end of the night, having again stood by as the fruits of pleasure and pain arise for all the world through karma, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted]. (11.245)
Having perceived that [the world] has become void, the Lord, the Blessed One, by his own will,
effects a sixfold creation according to its previous arrangement.

At the end of the night— characterized by the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain from various actions according to the sequence of the ripening of karma— one remains with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of sleep entirely unsubsided; then,
through the mere force of desire resulting from the ripening of karma, [one perceives] the sixfold [world].

The *tāmasī* [nature]—consisting of hell-beings, immobile beings, reptiles, and so forth, ending with domestic animals—is threefold, becoming progressively diminished in degree; the *mānavī* is pervaded by *tamas* and *rajas*; the *maunī* (human) is pervaded by *rajas* and *sattva*; and the *daivī* is *sāttvikī*. "By way of arrangement" means according to the boundaries of the worlds and so forth. || 246 ||
Therein,
he first creates a Tāmasī creation consisting of various forms of hells, which are dominated by darkness.
Then, through the gradual diminishing of the intensity of *tamas* part by part,
[he binds] the fettered souls (*paśu*) down to the level of immobile beings.
"Beasts" means reptiles, birds, wild animals, and domestic cattle.
From that [state] as well,
he would again create human beings through the immersion in *tamas* and *rajas*;
and, permeated by *rajas* and *sattva*, he would create the lords of the best of sages.
Thus, up to this point, there is a progressive increase in the intensity of the latent impression of sleep within Brahman.
Then,
having cast off sleep and awakened, the Lord of the World, who is established in sattva,
creates the gods and their worlds according to the previous arrangement.

Those who exist together with the worlds—that is, along with their respective places of residence. And this qualification is also connected to what precedes it by way of the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokita) maxim. The prior arrangement consists of the [gods] beginning with the Piśācas and ending with Brahmā. 249.
Thus, when the sixfold creation has been accomplished—
then Rudra, Indra, Sūrya, Indu, the lunar mansions, and the lords of the planets exercise their authority within their respective spheres of activity. (11.250)
By the command of the Supreme Lord,
Brahmā thus creates day after day.
But the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) ... shall withdraw [all] at the end of the day;
and of this Brahmā—
And the measure of the day that has been declared, the number of nights is exactly that much.
Thus, by this day and night, a year is traditionally reckoned as before,
consisting of three hundred and sixty [days].
When a full hundred of those years has passed, that is called a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
O Goddess, listen to my divine years within a hundred Brahma-years: they are ninety-one crores and twenty lakhs. (11.253)
Likewise, there are seven *kharvas* and eight *nikharvas*;
this should be known as one hundred years of Brahmā by one who understands time. (11.254)

It is stated that a single day of Brahmā, excluding the time of the twilights (saṃdhyākāla), measures one hundred twenty million divine years; his night is of the same duration, thus totaling two hundred forty million. When this is multiplied by three hundred and sixty such days, it results in eight *vṛnda*s.

There are six hundred million and four crore. As for the period of twilight, which was stated to consist of ninety-six thousand [breaths], when calculated by three hundred and sixty, it becomes three crore,
forty-five lakh, and sixty thousand.
That [number], being doubled by the distinction between evening and morning,
becomes sixty million, nine hundred and twenty-one thousand. Both together [form] eight *vṛndas*, seventy billion, nine hundred and twenty-one lakhs, and twenty [thousand].

There are eight hundred and seventy-nine billion, one hundred and twenty million [years] (8,709,120,000,000). This number of years, multiplied by a hundred, results in eight nikharvas, seven kharvas, a zero in the place of vṛnda, ninety-one crores, and two million (8,709,120,000,000). Thus, this number is exactly as previously stated.
It occurs; "eighty-nine crores" is a corrupt reading.
Thus, in this manner—
the measurement according to the divine standard is proclaimed as follows.
Now, this very same—
But now, learn from me again concerning worldly pride (laukika-māna). || 11-255 ||
Namely:
thirty-two koṭis of years, O Dear One, as well as eight kharvas;
two kharvas, O Goddess of Gods, and exactly five nikharvas. (11.256)
Three *śaṅkus*, one *padma*, and three *sāgaras*—
this very number is arrived at by calculating the aforementioned ninety-one *koṭis* of divine years, which constitute a hundred Brahma-years,
according to the measure of a worldly year, using the calculation of three hundred and sixty [days per year].
As for that which Śrī Bhūllaka stated: "............ eighty kharvas and five nikharvas, O beloved, as well as one arbuda and ten koṭis."
And he recited: "The four stakes and thirty oceans"; however, because that is inconsistent, it should simply be disregarded.
Thus, according to the measurement of the worldly year—this has been fully explained, O Goddess, and it should be known by those seeking liberation. (11.257)
Even the state of Brahmā, which grants existence until the end of a great kalpa, is ultimately devoid of essence because it is subject to withdrawal;
likewise, by the method to be described, even that which extends up to Anāśrita is so.
Thus, considering that all enjoyments are like dreams, one should wish for well-being in every respect.

The essential meaning is that those seeking liberation must take refuge solely in the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) into the nature of Supreme Bhairava, which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) unconditioned by space, time, or form. || 257 ||
He concludes:
"By this worldly measure, it is recorded as a hundred years of Brahmā;
[this refers] to the number beginning with one and ending with the highest unit (parārdha), which is necessary for the measurements already stated and those yet to be stated."
He defines the sequence of units as follows:
ten times the preceding unit is one [next]; ten times that is a hundred. (11.258)
One hundred multiplied by ten is declared to be a thousand;
a thousand multiplied by ten is indeed called ten thousand (ayuta). (11.259)
Ten tens of thousands (ayuta) make a hundred thousand (lakṣa), and ten of those make a million (niyuta).
Ten of those make ten million (koṭi), and ten koṭis likewise make an arbuda.
Ten *arbudas* make a *vṛnda*; ten times that indeed is a *kharva*;
ten times that is a *nikharva*, while ten of those constitute a *śaṅku*. (11.261)
Ten *śaṅkus* make one *padma*; ten *padmas* make one *sāgara*.
Ten *sāgaras* make one *madhya*, and ten of those are said to make the final [unit].
Having multiplied the last [place] by ten, the *parārdha* is proclaimed.
He concludes: "Thus, these eighteen are the places of calculation. (11.263)
The word "they become" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 263 ||
Having thus demonstrated the nature of number as a digression, he states the subject at hand:

"At the end of the great kalpa, Brahmā goes to dissolution in the *para*; [he who has] not experienced the descent of the supreme power (*para-śaktipāta*) [goes] to the *para*. Here, "in the *para*" means in the preeminent [state], which is immediate [to the preceding].

It dissolves into its cause; however, regarding the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) upon one whose conduct is excellent, the intention of the preceding text—namely, "he shall go to the Supreme Brahman, the Paramaśiva" (10.533)—is precisely this. This same principle should be followed in the subsequent passages as well.
And this great kalpa which has thus been described—that is declared to be one day of Viṣṇu, and his night is indeed equal to that. (11.264)
Of one who dwells in the worlds that correspond to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 264 ||
Furthermore:
by this measure, his year is ordained as consisting of exactly three hundred and sixty days.
And when a full hundred years have passed, he too goes to dissolution in the Supreme.
In this manner,
that which has been stated as the lifespan of Viṣṇu constitutes a single day for Rudra who resides in the world of Rudra.
And he,
day by day, creates two others, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the lords of creatures.
The meaning is that, after creating another Viṣṇu from the Supreme Brahman— which had dissolved at the two previous creations— the Lord, having entered that form, creates another Brahmā as well.
And this is logical, because:
"The power of Brahmā and the power of Viṣṇu, having attained a position of authority, whatever self they preside over, that [self] acquires their respective designation. (11.267)

The word order is inverted. The meaning is that when the power of the Supreme Lord—whether Brāhmī or Vaiṣṇavī—presides over, that is, exercises authority over, a certain individual soul (pudgala), that soul attains the designation corresponding to her; in other words, it attains the state of Brahmā or Viṣṇu. || 267 ||
And having attained that very nature,
he exercises his authority by the will of the Supreme Self—
that is, of Paramaśiva, whose essential nature has been determined, and not [of any other].
[This occurs] by the will of that which has a successive cause presided over by another's desire.

And just as Brahmā and Viṣṇu are, in ultimate reality, the power of the Supreme Lord—whether it be the Brāhmī or the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti—so too this entire universe consists solely of the power of the Supreme Lord; thus he says:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra, as well as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and Īśvara. (11.268)
And the lords of the worlds, O Goddess of the gods, as well as the lords of the realms, the planets and other mothers, the Rudras, the yogas, the lunar mansions, and the zodiac signs. || 11-269 ||
All of them, presided over by him, become endowed with power;
possessing his prowess and heroism, they remain established in their own positions.

The lords of the worlds are Indra and the others; the world-protectors (lokapālas) are the planets and so forth; and the "mothers" (mātaraḥ)—namely Brāhmī and the others—form a copulative compound. The "yogas" are the *sunaphā* and others well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
All these, being presided over by that will of the Supreme Lord as previously described, are endowed with power (*śakti*).
They each possess their own respective capacities. || 270 ||

Previously, it was stated that [the body] is presided over by Brahmā and Viṣṇu through their respective powers; now, however, it is shown that all [beings], even including Brahmā and the others, are presided over by the Supreme Power (paraśakti), and therefore this entire universe—
Śiva has one great power, and Śiva is indeed one and without beginning;
yet that power, O Goddess, is divided by distinctions arising from infinity. (11.271)

The great power is called Sovereignty (svātantrya). Śiva is the mass of light and bliss, whose nature is supreme well-being. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that Power (Śakti) also—being one, non-dual, and beginningless—is divided by various diversities of distinctions; she manifests as the appearance of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth.
Having incidentally described the state of non-duality between Śiva and Śakti, he states the subject at hand:
"In this very way, Rudra indeed performs creation day after day,
and at the end of the day, he performs withdrawal."
And that [time] would be equal to a night of the one whose form is saṃsāra. || 272 ||

The view of the commentator—that the equality of day and night occurs due to the movement of the sun and moon by the will of Īśvara—is incorrect; for it is nowhere heard that the sun and other luminaries serve as illuminators in the worlds of Brahmā and others, which shine with the splendor of their respective lords and realms. || 272 ||
In this manner, by means of this measure of day and night, there is a year for him;
"for him" refers to Rudra.
When a full hundred years have passed, due to the destruction of the day and night of the hundred Rudras.
He too goes to the supreme abode, having gone to which he becomes partless;
a hundred years of the Raudras is one day for the Śatarudras, and its exhaustion marks the end.
And at its end—in that very place—there shall again be another lord equal to him. (11.274)
Through union with the power of Rudra, he becomes the leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra. Thus,
by means of the calculation of days and nights and so forth— O Goddess of the gods, the hundred Rudras [pass away] at the end of a hundred of their own years.
They proceed to the supreme reality, and thereafter the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) perishes;
this means that the duration of the Brahmāṇḍa's existence lasts for the lifespan of a hundred Rudras.
As to what kind of cheek it is, he says:
"The support for the qualities of all beings, the abode of the abode of all principles. (11.276)
Adorned with mountains, forests, gardens, islands, and oceans;
crowded with rows of celestial palaces and graced by the planets and constellations.
By the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and uragas;
by the ṛṣis, humans, and others who dwell in the seven worlds.
It is joined with the hells and the netherworlds (pātālas), and it is the ornament of the universe;
it is the locus of all beings, such as the earth and other elements, of qualities such as sound and the rest, and of the qualities of beings such as wisdom and heroism. And likewise—
It is the abode, in the sense of a dwelling place, for all the abodes of reality— namely, the various bodies composed of the thirty-six principles.
And such is this mandala, the support of all worlds without exception, which dissolves into the waters. (11.279)
And thus, according to their order of emergence, the principles dissolve back into their own causes, as he will state:
"Water dissolves into fire," and so forth. || 279 ||
Thus, when the state ending with the Śatarudra has been dissolved, he who exists above the upper and lower shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) in the form of the Destroyer—
then Kālāgnirudra shall go to dissolution into the *kāla-tattva*.

Because he effects the manifestation of the entire universe without exception, he is both Time and Reality; thus, the Supreme Lord is "one who has been fashioned by the reality of time" (kālatattvakālakalita).
If this is so, who performs the withdrawal of the principles beginning with water? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Starting from the principle of water up to the sphere ending with Māyā" (11.280).
Time itself shall withdraw all that, both moving and unmoving.
Time— meaning the Supreme Lord who fashions the entire universe without exception—
having entered the forms of the lords of each successive world above, effects the gradual withdrawal of the principles (tattvas) from the lowest to the highest.
The meaning is "he performs"; this will become clear later on.
"Who is the destroyer in the pure path? To this he says:
"Above that, the pure path extends as far as the range of the End of Power (śaktyanta). (11.281)
The non-terrible (Aghora) [deity], the destroyer of the terrible, should withdraw all that which is terrible.

By the qualification "terrible" applied to the path ending with Śakti, it is understood by implication that everything from Māyā down to the earth is even more terrible. There exists no form here that is terrible or associated with duality.
The meaning of "he whose [nature] is non-terrible" (*aghora*) has been explained by the term "the destroyer of the terrible" (*ghoranāśana*). Here too,

the intended meaning is that the venerable Lord Aghora, having entered the forms of the Lords of the principles (*tattveśvara-mūrti*) such as Īśvara and Sadāśiva in ascending order, withdraws each lower principle.
This should be understood in accordance with the connection of the text to be explained hereafter.
He concludes the incidental investigation into the Destroyer:
"In this way, Rudra, the Great Lord in the form of Time, is established within these three. (11.282)
In the three levels ending with the earth, the power of *māyā*, and the power (*śakti*): "thus" means by way of being the withdrawer. "Rudra" refers to Kālāgnirudra on the earth;
the venerable Ananta, in the form of Time, presides over the level up to the end of *māyā*; and Maheśvara presides over those ending with the power (*śakti*). Alternatively, there is one...

Maheśvara is Rudra because he causes weeping and fleeing; the meaning is that, in his form as Time (Kāla), he exists as the destroyer throughout the three stages, manifesting in various forms such as Kālāgnirudra and others. || 282 ||
Having thus concluded this incidental matter, he returns to the subject at hand: "Then,
when a hundred [cycles] of the lords of the immortals have passed,
Rudra, presiding over the principle of fire (tejastattva), withdraws the water."

The meaning is that at the end of the number of days counted as a hundred years related to Amareśa, he withdraws the water, which is the *jala-tattva*. Furthermore, a day for Amareśa is measured by the duration of the lifespan of the hundred Rudras;
according to that [calculation], a year is as previously stated, and his lifespan is a hundred such years, and that too...
The sequence beginning with "the [deity] of the lord of the fire-principle (tejastattvādhipati) is Dīna" and so forth should be followed in successive order.

The reading "Amareśa [is the lord] at the end of a hundred" is a corrupt reading; for it is impossible for him to be the destroyer at the end of his own hundred-year cycle, as this would also apply to the end of the Taruḍra-cycle of Tadadhara-vatīśa.
Because there is no withdrawal of the water-tattva.
He points that very thing out:
"In this way, the lords of the coverings beginning with Bhūta [also perish] after a hundred [kalpas] have passed. (11.283)
And they, O Goddess of gods, withdraw and create one another;

the lords of the coverings beginning with the gross elements and subtle elements, possessing sovereignty in ascending order, withdraw at the end of their own day— which consists of a hundred years according to the calculation of the lord of each respective lower principle— the lower principles along with their associated lords.

Furthermore, at the end of the night of Kālasvara, they create others once again. In some places, however, it is said: "O Śāṅkarī, when a hundred years have thus elapsed for the Lords of Beings (Bhūtapatis), those who have passed away go to the station of Niṣkala; thereafter, the beings [are created anew]."

"And they withdraw and create one another, O Goddess of Gods"—this is the reading. Here too, it should be explained that the principles (tattvas) situated in each lower level [are withdrawn] into the one immediately above;
this clarifies the withdrawal consisting of the mutual dissolution of the principles.
The waters dissolve into fire, and that fire, in turn, dissolves into wind.
Likewise, the wind, having reached space, dissolves into it;
and the subtle elements dissolve in their respective order into the [subsequent] tanmātras, just as they were produced.

The subtle elements, together with the sense organs, dissolve in turn into the ego; that [ego] dissolves into the intellect, and that [intellect] dissolves into the profound state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya).
In that state where the qualities are in equilibrium—indefinable, inconceivable, and beyond comparison—the entire universe remains as if fast asleep. (11.287)

"It dissolves along with that very [element]" means that space (vyoma) dissolves together with that wind (vāyu), which has internally contained the three principles (tattva) of earth, water, and fire. To the question "Where does it dissolve?", he says: "Into the subtle elements" (tanmātreṣu).
The intention behind the plural number and the prefix *pra-* in "they dissolve" (*pralīyante*) is that space is dissolved into them.

The principles of earth, water, fire, and air dissolve completely into their respective causes, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and become identical with them. Just as they were produced—in the sequence beginning with the one [subtle element] and so forth—so too do they dissolve. Thus, earth dissolves into the five subtle elements, water into four, and fire into three.

Air [is dissolved] in that pair; space in the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Smell [is dissolved] in the subtle element of taste; likewise, the sequence should be followed such that the organ of generation [is dissolved] in the anus, the anus in the hand, and so forth. "The Impenetrable" (*gahana*) refers to the principle of primordial nature (*pradhāna*).

"Aupama" means simply comparison (*upamā*). Thus, when [the elements] beginning with earth and ending with the intellect have come to rest in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), [the dissolution is complete].
Meanwhile, the entire world remains immersed in a deep sleep without exception. || 287 ||
In this way, when the primary nature (prakṛti) has been dissolved at its end, the world remains merged in the form of atoms—
atoms that are extremely minute, exceedingly subtle, and beyond the range of the senses and other faculties.
The entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, remains dissolved.

And that which is the lifespan of the Rudras residing in the principle of Prakṛti, according to the previously mentioned calculation, is remembered here as a single day for the twenty-sixth Rudra. (11.288)

The Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, who is the master of all the Rudras residing within the twenty-five principles— from the principle of Guṇa down to Pradhāna— situated in twenty-five sections, is intended here as the twenty-sixth. || 288 ||
His progeny are the lords of creatures, the Pitṛs together with the Mānavas—
those who have attained perfection through the knowledge of Sāṅkhya and those who discourse on Brahman according to the Veda. (11.289)
O Dear One, the *chandas*, the *sāmans*, the syllable *oṃ*, the intellect, and their respective deities—all these abide during the day within the wise Supreme Lord. (11.290)
"Subjects" refers to the fourteen kinds of beings being born; "lords" refers to the rulers of the worlds;

"others" refers to those beginning with the *anva*. Although humans are already included within the term "subjects," they are mentioned again because of their predominance in *saṃsāra* due to their performance of actions that give rise to diversity.
The knowledge of Sāṅkhya is the cognition of the discrimination between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*). Regarding the phrase "by the Veda, the proponents of Brahman":

those who know the Vedānta and proclaim Brahman—saying, "All this is indeed the Person" (*puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam*, Ṛgveda 10.90.2)—are the ones referred to. Their deity is that which resides within the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).

The divine origins beginning with Brahmā belong to the Supreme Lord, whose majesty has been described in the Path of the Worlds (bhuvanādhvan); they "abide by day," meaning they are manifested at the commencement of the day. || 290 ||
Furthermore,
at the end of the day they dissolve into it...
and once again...

At the end of the night, Viśvasambhava [arises]. Now, because it is impossible to calculate by means of either the human or divine measurement of years the duration of the day belonging to Rudra, who resides in the principle of the Unmanifest (avyakta-tattva), [the calculation is made] by means of the dissolutions and creations associated with Brahmā, who resides in the principle of the intellect (buddhi-tattva).
He speaks in order to provide a summary:
"But thirty-six thousand Brahmās undergo dissolution and rebirth. (11.291)
And for the Rudras who dwell there, a day in the Unmanifest (avyakta) is said to be equal to that [year].

According to the previously stated principle, Brahmā, residing in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), is withdrawn at the end of the day of the Rudra situated in the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), and another is emitted at the beginning of that day; thus, within his own year—
There are three hundred and sixty dissolutions and manifestations for the Brahmās residing in the intellect (dhī).
That same duration is the limit of life for the Rudras dwelling in the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva).
And that is a single day for the Rudras whose abode is the Unmanifest (avyakta). This is as follows:
If such a day of the Rudras residing in the unmanifest (avyakta) has been described, its internal division is now stated:

that diverse dissolution which was mentioned as pertaining to the principles (tattvas) beginning with water and ending with the qualities (guṇas), occurring between the dissolution of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and the primary dissolution (pradhāna-pralaya), is to be understood as the intermediate dissolution (avāntara-pralaya).
He states who is the agent of that dissolution and of the creation at its end:
"In that [state], when the day of Pradhāna has ended, he withdraws everything. (11.292)

And at the end of the night, Śrīkaṇṭha, the leader of the universe, emits [the world] once again. How he possesses the status of the leader of the universe, even though he is situated at the summit of the qualities (guṇa), has been explained in detail in the tenth chapter.
Now, by this same principle, the stability of its measure would also be established. (11.293)
Since, by this same principle, thousands of millions of dissolutions have already passed,

the duration of the persistence [of each tattva]— limited to three hundred and sixty days and one hundred years— is likewise followed by millions of dissolutions that have elapsed for the lords of the respective principles (tattvas) below.
And at the end of this [section], it says: "Then Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and likewise Kalā. (11.294)
All [the coverings] gradually merge into one another according to their own measure;

"tataḥ" (then) marks the conclusion of the section on Śrī Śrīkaṇṭha; "kramāt" (gradually) refers to that pentad of coverings (*kañcuka*) which exists through the diversity of space, following the sequence of *kalā* and so forth in direct order.
In the reverse order beginning with *niyati* and so forth, they dissolve into one another like powder, stone, and water.

"At its own measure" means at the end of a hundred years for all the Rudras residing in the *kañcukas*. By this it is indicated that for all those residing in the *kañcukas*, including the Rudras together with the *puruṣa-tattva*, [the same duration applies].
And the dissolution occurs simultaneously. Thus it was previously stated regarding them:
"From that [Māyā], Kalā was produced, as well as Vidyā and Rāga; likewise Kāla, the principle of Niyati, Puruṣa, and Prakṛti. (11.64)
Thus, even though emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) was taught as occurring simultaneously, the arrangement of the locations beginning with the worlds (*bhuvana*) is distinct;
with that intention, it is stated here that "all [occur] in sequence."
Thus, at the end of the day of Gahaneśa, [the dissolution] extends from Kalā down to the earth. (11.295)
Adorned with the arrangement and design of various worlds,
it is crowded with the Rudras who are the support of the qualities (guṇas) up to the limit, as well as the individual souls (kṣetrajñas).
Gahaneśa merges into the Mūlaprakṛti, which is the cause.
Gahaneśa is the primordial Rudra residing in the principle of Māyā. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "creation and so forth," manifestation (*vibhava*) is also included.
One should contemplate the covering below and the [covering] above as red and white respectively.

"One should understand that darkness (tamas) is in the middle; these qualities (guṇas) are thus established. (2.66) According to the principle stated previously, Māyā is the substratum (ādhāra); that which has this as its limit at the end is "ending with the substratum of the qualities," referring to the Kalā-tattva and those [principles] ending with the substratum of the qualities.
It is crowded with those Rudras and Kṣetrajñas. "Gahaneśa" refers to him whose lord (īśa) or master is Gahana;
in that Gahaneśa, which is the Māyā-tattva, the cause even of the Mūlaprakṛti or Pradhāna.
And that, having thus become dissolved, is born again at the end of the night through the impulsion of Gahaneśa. || 11-297 ||
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, this has been declared as the natural day-and-night (*ahorātra*);
for here, "nature" (*prakṛti*)— because it is not specified otherwise— is the cause of the entire universe, from *kalā* down to the earth.
It is called illusion; this belongs to that [illusion], being natural and illusory.
And that period of night which has gone toward it—that alone, O Supreme Goddess, is said to be the dissolution of all beings. (11.298)
Since it is impossible to calculate all the durations from *kalā* down to *tattva*— as they are exceedingly long compared to lower time units—
he states the following, taking the time of *pradhāna* as the limit for calculation:
By means of ten times the supreme half of Pradhāna,
Māyā withdraws everything and likewise creates the world again.

This is the time of Pradhāna, consisting of ten times its aforementioned specific number (parārdha). The meaning is that a day of Māyā consists of ten times the time of Pradhāna, and its night is of equal duration.

This is what is meant: the lifespan of Rudra, the presiding lord of Pradhāna, which constitutes one day for those dwelling within the *kañcukas*, is three hundred and sixty *kalās*; a hundred such [days] constitute a year, and a hundred such years constitute his lifespan. However, no such calculation is made here; rather, it is that very lifespan consisting of the days of the dwellers in the *kañcukas* [that is intended].
The time of the Pradhāna, multiplied by ten parārdhas, is the lifespan of those who dwell in the *kañcukas*;

and that [lifespan] constitutes a single day for the Gāhinikas—this distinction from what precedes has been shown here. And thus, the hundredth part of that time of the Pradhāna which is multiplied by ten parārdhas [is the duration of the Gāhinikas].
A year for those dwelling in the Kañcuka [worlds] is a day here when divided by three hundred and sixty;
in this manner, the arrangement of years, days, and so forth should be established here. || 299 ||

The day of Gahaneśa is ten times a *parārdha* as thus described; a year is calculated by that [day]; and the period of Gahaneśa’s abiding, which consists of one hundred such years, is precisely the duration of the *māyātattva*, which is its substratum. Taking that as the limit...
Having established the Lord as the presiding authority over the principle of Īśvara, he speaks in order to demonstrate the measurement of His day:
"Īśvara creates the world from a hundredfold multiplication of the *parārdha* of Māyā’s time, and He likewise withdraws it again. (11.300)

In this context as well, the period of the duration of Māyā is multiplied by one hundred; that is, it consists of a number equal to one hundred *parārdhas*. For that length of time, Īśvara maintains the creation during his day and performs the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) during his night, [governing] the entire universe up to the level of the *tattva* of Śuddhavidyā.
The meaning is that he performs [this]. Regarding the statement "multiplied by a hundred," the intention is as follows:
the period of time up to the limit of Māyā, multiplied by ten *parārdhas*, constitutes the period of authority for Anantanātha, the lord of the Vidya-tattva; and even within that...

The division of the days of the year is to be understood through the calculation of parts as before. Thus, this period of authority belonging to Anantanātha, when multiplied by ten *parārdhas*, constitutes a day of Īśvara. Here too, the period of Īśvara’s authority consists of one hundred years according to the aforementioned sequence.

That [period] as well, multiplied by a hundred parārdhas according to the method previously introduced, constitutes a day of Sadāśivanātha; at its conclusion, he descends and withdraws the universe, as it is said:
"Then the god Sadāśiva shall withdraw [the universe] according to his own measure."
And again, at the break of day, he creates his own [world] once more.
This has already been explained in the introductory commentary itself: *punarbhūyaḥ* means "again and again. || 301 ||
Thus, it is said that this very [dissolution] is the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), occurring at the end of the day of Sādākhya;
compared to the previously mentioned dissolution pertaining to Māyā, this is "great," as it also involves the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan).
Because of its withdrawal.
And by this measure, at the end of his own hundred years, he too— possessing the great body of the five mantras— dissolves into the principle of the Bindu (bindutattva).

Because it is designated as the "principle of the Bindu" (bindutattva), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) situated below that is indicated; here, the gross Sadāśiva is intended. He goes to dissolution in the principle of the Bindu and enters into the state of being the Lord of the Bindu (bindvīśvara). || 302 ||
And such is he:
having pierced the Bindu and the Half-Moon, as well as the Nirodhikā, he attains dissolution in the principle of Nāda, having grasped all that is moving and unmoving. (11.303)
Having entered sequentially the stages of Bindu, Ardhacandra, and Nirodhikā—
each established with a duration calculated by multiplying the preceding measure by a hundred parārdhas—
the gross Lord Sadāśiva dissolves into the subtle state of Sadāśiva, which is the nature of Nāda.
The meaning is that its self is born. || 303 ||
And that sound also, O Dear One, having pierced the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) by way of the suṣumnā path,
goes to dissolution in the Śakti-tattva at the end of the day of the Śakti-tattva.
Lord Sadāśiva, whose nature is sound (*nāda*) and who is subtle,

having assumed that very form at the end of the day of Suṣumneśa— which is calculated by the previously mentioned reckoning of kalās— and likewise at the end of the day of Brahmeśa, which is calculated by the reckoning of time up to that limit, [attains] the nature of Brahman situated in the *brahmarandhra*.

Having resorted to that [state] at the time of its persistence, when it is calculated in the same manner, the deity and so forth situated within the *śakti-tattva*—at the end of that [period], one becomes identical with it; such is the meaning. || 304 ||
Now, how long is the period of time extending up to the Śakti-tattva? To this he says: "O beautiful one, that time should be known as a Parārdha," as previously stated.
"By a parārdha of Pradhāna multiplied tenfold," (11.299), and likewise:
"And by a parārdha of Māyā multiplied a hundredfold" (11.300).

Because it has been stated thus, Time—whose self consists of [the principles] from Śakti down to Earth, whose essence comprises a parārdha after a parārdha, and whose number is exceedingly vast—is to be understood as such; it is not, however, merely of the form of a single parārdha, for that would result in a contradiction with what was previously stated. To explain:

The purport of this text is as follows: just as in the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) an increase in spatial magnitude is stated for each successive level of the principles (*tattva*), so too here the duration of time for stability (*sthiti*) and so forth increases progressively.
Thus, a day of Śakti measures two *parārdhas*, and her night is of the same length.

A night measured by this calculation consists of one hundred years; at its conclusion, there is the completion of the authority of the subtle deity presiding over the principle of Śakti (Śaktitattva).
And that [state] is the dawn even for Vyāpīśa, who abides in the Śiva-tattva.
Therein he— then,
being all-pervasive, he should again emanate within that whose nature is space;
he too dissolves into Ananteśa, he into Anātha, and he into Anāśrita.
Upon the completion of its own office, it dissolves. || 306 ||
Now, how much would be the gift for him, who is the refuge of all without refuge and whose own refuge is none? To this he says:
"Of a parārdha of the power of time multiplied ten millionfold..."
This day is proclaimed as belonging to the God who is without support. || 11-307 ||

The day of Him who is not dependent on that time which—by virtue of the context—is said to be the power-time (*śakti-kāla*) consisting of a parārdha multiplied by a parārdha, and further multiplied by ten million (*koṭi*) parārdhas, is [the day of Anāśrita]. || 307 ||
Then, by this measure multiplied by a parārdha,
he too goes to the supreme station, the cause which is self-supported and without external locus.

The time of power (*śaktikāla*), which consists of a parārdha-parārdha and is composed of the days of Anāśrita multiplied by ten million parārdhas, is itself multiplied by a parārdha— that is, by a parārdha-parārdha—
to constitute the period of authority (*adhikārakāla*) of Anāśrita.
By extracting one-sixtieth of that [period] and three-hundred-and-sixtieth of that [sixtieth], the arrangement of the days of the year for this [cycle] should be followed as previously described.
Thus, when the period of his own authority, which extends over a path of exceedingly vast time, comes to its conclusion, [there arises] Anāśritanātha.
[He is] his own support, the cause—[as it is said]:
"Seated here, Śiva, the supreme cause, performs creation... (10.1258).

According to the principle stated in such passages, [the individual soul] reaches Paramaśiva himself; by the etymological derivation that "the universe abides in this," it is called the *sthāna* (abode), and [the soul] goes there, becoming one with its essence. || 308 ||
And this time, which has ascended the stream of the path that is so exceedingly vast and extended— that time known as *sāmya*—
is like the *pradhāna*, which is the equilibrium of the *guṇas*; so too is it for all things.

That which is the equilibrium of the appearances of the operations of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal— a form devoid of increase or decrease— that equilibrium is to be known. Because it is the locus of equality and because it is itself being fashioned through that very equality, it is designated by the word "Time" (kāla).
And precisely because it consists of equanimity (*sāmya*), which is the cessation of inequality (*vaiṣamya*),
this [state] removes the fear of birth and death for one who has attained it— this is the meaning.
Then, beyond even that, the time would be immeasurable; this is the ultimate limit.
O Goddess, he is eternal and eternally risen; he is not unwell, nor is he made well.

Time, designated as "equilibrium" (sāmya), is being rendered well because of its nature as the complete pacification of all imbalance; thus it is an object of cognition, whereas this [Reality] is not. For this very reason, it is the supreme limit.

The meaning is that [He] is the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), whose nature consists of the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with the supreme reality (*paratattva*)—the *unmanā* state which is the foundation for all objects of knowledge, subjects, and so forth.
The particle *ca* has the sense of "for" (*hi*); because He is not conceived (*na kalpyate*), He is therefore inconceivable (*akalya*).
How, then, is the word "time" (kāla) employed here? To this he says: "And that [power] would project everything below, from the pervasive [Prakṛti] down to the earth. (11.310)
By means of the divisions beginning with the *tuṭi* and the *kalās*, [the Goddess] internalizes the path of the goddess— which consists of the mobile and immobile,
is known as "equilibrium" (*sāmya*), and serves as the foundational limit— taking as its basis that time which has arisen therefrom;
for she impels within her the entire path, from the *vyāpinī* down to the earth.
The meaning is that [the Lord], abiding as the singular essence of light, projects hundreds of external diversities [into consciousness],
draws back what has appeared externally into within, and enumerates them as manifold; because he thus encompasses everything, he is called "Time" (kāla).
Reiterating this very point by adding further elaboration, he concludes:
"And that which is above the Unmanā [state], there time does not exist. (11.311)
No one who is possessed of parts is awakened; he who is partless has conquered time.
He who transcends Śaṅkara and the Unmanā state is eternal, all-pervasive, and immutable. (11.312)

In that state which belongs to the *unmanas*— the higher state consisting of the supreme reality (*paratattva*)— there is no time (*kāla*) as a cause of differentiation (*kalanā*), because nothing whatsoever fit for differentiation (*kalya*) or capable of being differentiated (*kalanārha*) is differentiated there; for everything exists therein in the state of absolute identity with Paramaśiva.

And because this [Lord] has emerged from the divisions of time—such as *tuṭi* and so forth—which consist of temporal parts due to His being immeasurable, He is therefore free from time, which consists of the manifestation of succession; He does not possess that nature. Nevertheless, because He effects the "calculation" (*kalana*) of the universe according to the true principle of the aforementioned explanation, He is called "Time" (*kāla*). He is imperishable (*avyaya*).
Thus, their forms are never exhausted. And it is said in the *Yojanikā*:
"At all times, the supreme, imperishable [Lord] pervades time; he is to be joined with the Supreme at the end of *unmanā*. Time does not exist there. (4-287)
Thus [ends the section]. || 312 ||
Because—
its form at the beginning is exactly the same as it is at the end of the eon;
"at the beginning" means at the time of creation.
Furthermore:
"Formless and free from form, he is beginningless and devoid of existence. (11.313)

He is omniscient and the creator of all, endowed with virtues such as generosity. "Rūpas" (forms) are so called because they are manifested; he for whom there is no restriction of place, time, or form—therefore, he is liberated from forms, that is, from the operations of form such as "this is such-and-such. Precisely because he is beginningless, therefore...
He is "unfrightened" by birth from existence, being untouched [by it]. "Omniscient" is as explained previously.

He is the agent in every form, independent in his very essence. The word "and" (*ca*) expresses the perfect integration (*sāmarasya*) of omniscience and agency. And he who is the knower and the agent with respect to objects of knowledge and effects that are distinct [from himself],...
This [universe] is joined with qualities that are illusory in nature and exist as a beginningless, eternally flowing stream;
however, this [Self], because its essence consists of non-differentiation, omniscience, and being the agent of all existence, remains untouched by them.
Even so, there is nothing whatsoever other than it, but rather—
That very same [reality], though flashing forth through its own sovereignty in another form...
is situated at the crown of the *unmanī*. (11.314)
Therefore, this— God of gods, Lord of the world, the Supreme Self, Śiva, the imperishable—
by means of the sequence of prior [causes], creates the universe without desire. (11.315)
He is the Lord of the World (*jagannātha*) because he is entreated by the world, from Kālāgni up to Śiva.

"By means of the sequence of the preceding [stages]" means having ascended to the plane of *Samanā* by taking recourse to the respective forms of the causal deities. "Without desire" means: "In this way, I [shall act] thus."
"Without the resolve (saṅkalpa) that 'I am doing [this]'; the remainder has already been mostly explained. 315.
Challenging [the Lord] with the words "without desire," the illustrious Goddess said:
"For one without desire there is no action; and how could one who is inactive create?
Tell me this excellent and secret question by your grace. (11.316)

All actions, such as going or cooking, are preceded by volition (*saṅkalpa*), and volition is not admitted in the Blessed Lord, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss; therefore, how can there be creatorship for one who is actionless?
Moreover, there is no existence whatsoever of anything other than the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, which consists of the light of consciousness.
How much more so, then, agency? Therefore, among these questions, this is the best and most excellent;
for by its resolution, all doubt is eradicated.
By your grace, through the unfolding of the true reality, please tell me—declare this resolution. (316)
Thus questioned, the illustrious Bhairava said:
"Just as fire is produced from a sun-gem when it is heated by the rays of the sun, so too [fire] arises from that sun; in that case, there is no longing for the sun itself. (11.317)

Just as a jewel lacks the quality of being a desirer, so too is the activity of the Lord. For if one, such as a potter, produces some effect distinct from his own manifestation with a specific purpose in mind, let it be that he does not possess agency, since without his volition (*saṅkalpa*), the actions preceded by it would not arise.

This alone is the supreme lordship of the Supreme Lord, the independent Bhaṭṭāraka, namely that— according to the principle stated in [Tantrāloka 1.3], "He who is the agent of emission and withdrawal"— by the power of His sovereignty, upon the wall of His own consciousness, [He manifests everything] like a city in a mirror.

Manifesting everything from Śiva down to the earth— including even that which is not distinct from Himself as if it were distinct, and variegated by infinite internal diversity— He remains, for that very duration, essentially a mass of full bliss consisting of total wonder; thus,
by virtue of the identity of their fundamental nature alone, He is here like the fire produced from a sun-crystal when touched by the sun.
The illustration.
Thus it is said: "Śiva is to be known as being like the sun, while Śakti stands like a gem. (11.318)

However, one should not suspect that dullness and difference exist in the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika), because it is impossible for there to be complete similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
Furthermore:
"Just as time, derived from the seasonal period of a tree, is the ordainer of the sprout, so too, through union with Śiva, is the persistence of the world due to Śakti. (11.319)
Just as it is the very nature of a tree that experiences the seasons to possess the diversity of sprouts and so forth,

so too it is the essential nature of Śiva and Śakti— the two whose self consists of eternal, inseparable consciousness and bliss— that they manifest as the expansion of the fivefold cosmic activities (*pañcakṛtya*). As it has been said in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The universe is the accumulation of His own power" (3.30).
And thus,
[He is] the ground of His own consciousness, which consists of Supreme Śiva— the essence of the wonder of this entire universe in its suchness.

With the intention that "deliberation upon all scriptures is said to be the supreme means to be adopted and bestows liberation while living," the secret has been declared in this interrogative statement; may there be auspiciousness! || 319 ||

"I contemplate this own complete deity, who is the Goddess whose nature is the single essence of the triad of goddesses, surging forth as the external manifestation of Śambhu— the mass of jewels of consciousness and perfect bliss. Thus [it is said] in the *Śrī Svacchandatantra* by the venerable and most excellent Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya...
The eleventh chapter, accompanied by the commentary titled Uddyota composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 11 ||
The Twelfth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
Within one's own self, by one's own will, there arises the vivid manifestation of various respective principles (*tattva*).
Manifesting accomplishments that are non-different from Himself, the Lord Svacchanda is victorious.
Repeating what was stated for the sake of the connection between the chapters, the venerable Goddess, desiring to know the establishment of reality,
said: "Creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the principles have been described by you,
as well as the cause of the world's origin..."
Paramaśiva is the cause, the supreme cause, of the world in its forms as the principles (tattva), the elements (bhūta), the states of being (bhāva), the worlds (bhuvana), and so forth.
And this—
[having been heard by me through your grace]— || 12-1 ||
The [procedure for] the consecration and so forth is as before. || 1 ||

Now, however—explain the knowledge of reality (tattva-vijñāna) so that accomplishment (siddhi) may arise with respect to them. "Knowledge" refers to direct realization through the sequence beginning with concentration (dhāraṇā); "with respect to them" means having those [realities] as its object.
So that there may be accomplishment.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Bhairava said:
"I shall explain, in brief, that which begins with earth and ends with Śiva. (12.2)
Just as it exists within the body and just as it exists externally—in brief, that is, in summary;
however, in detail, it will be explained later during the section on *dhāraṇā*. || 2 ||
In that regard—
listen to how the earth exists in the body in the form of solidity; "how" (yathā) means by which manner, such as flesh and so forth.
Thus it is said: "In the flesh, as well as in the bones, and likewise in the sinews, hair, and nails... (12.3).
And within the marrow and intestines, the earth element is to be known as predominant with its five qualities;
this will become clear further on.
In phlegm, blood, raw matter, and urine, as well as in lymph, sweat, and muscle fat.

The waters, possessing four qualities, abide in both semen (*śukra*) and cohesion (*saṃgraha*) within the body. Thus it is said. *Rasa* is the primary constituent (*dhātu*) that sustains the body, arising from the transformation of food and drink.
*Saṃgraha* is the binding together of the earthy and other elements that have been transformed into the state of flesh and so forth.
It is established in the act of cooking, in burning, in brilliance, and in heat. || 5 ||

The fire-element resides in the body for the purpose of digesting food and other substances, for the burning that consists in the production of great alkalinity, for an intense heat that is difficult to withstand, and for the attainment of perceptible warmth. || 5 ||
O Goddess, fire (tejas) exists in this way, characterized by three qualities within luminosity (prakāśa).

"Within luminosity" means for the purpose of manifesting objects through the gateway of the ocular rays. Its three characteristics are form (rūpa), touch (sparśa), and sound (śabda). And this [fire], by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), has its form and touch unmanifested within the body.
This is clear.
Wind is characterized by inhalation, exhalation, and tactile sensation. || 12-6 ||

In the discharge of urine and feces, in the taking in of food and drink, in touching— meaning the grasping of external and internal sensations— and in arrangement, which is structural formation; "excretion" (uccāra) is the transformation of waste matter, and "emission" (visarga) is its expulsion.
Thus, in this manner—the wind residing in the body through these [channels] should be understood as having two characteristics. || 12-7 ||

It is characterized by these activities. That which has two characteristics—namely, sound and touch—as its defining marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or causes of cognition (*jñapti-hetu*) is "possessing two characteristics" (*dvilakṣaṇa*), that is, possessing two qualities (*dviguṇa*). || 7 ||

I shall describe space as it exists, characterized by a single mark. That which has sound as its sole characteristic: therein, the mark of earth is the sound *khaṭ-khaṭ*, that of water is the sound *cchala-cchala*, that of fire is the form of the sound *dhaga-dhaga*, and [that] of wind...

The nature of sound is that of a parrot’s cry; it is the sound known as an echo belonging to space (*ākāśa*). Touch (*sparśa*) is also [of four kinds]: that produced by heating (*pākaja*) in earth, which is neither hot nor cold; in water, it is cold; in fire, it is hot; and in air, it is not produced by heating and is neither hot nor cold. The color of earth is manifold, such as white and so forth; that of water—
Whiteness belongs to fire, as does its luminosity; the sixfold taste, beginning with sweet, belongs to earth, while sweetness alone belongs to water;
and fragrance in the form of fragrance belongs to earth alone. Thus, the elements such as earth and the rest within the body are to be characterized by these specific qualities.
He clarifies what was stated as "as it exists":
"It should be known as being hollow in nature, characterized by nine types of apertures. (12.8)

It is characterized by nine apertures or gates located at the aperture of Brahma (the crown of the head), the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, the nipples, the navel, the penis, and the anus. || 8 ||
"Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, this [element] characterized by nine gates has been described to you as having sound as its quality.
Having thus demonstrated the five elements within the body, [I shall now describe] those which establish them and those which illuminate them."

Having illuminated the organs of action, the intellect, and the mind, he will establish the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which are of the nature of non-distinctive form and so forth, as being inferable by virtue of the perception of the gross forms of the elements— which are the material causes of the sense organs— such as color-form and the rest. In that regard, first of all:
The organ of speech utters speech, and that speech is of four kinds.
"Refined (saṃskṛtā), natural (prākṛtī), corrupted (apabhraṣṭā), and nasalized (anunāsikā)—
that which is called refined is the divine speech as described by the great seers.
This is the intended meaning stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari regarding that which is refined (*saṃskṛtā*), being the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Prakrit has arisen through a sequence such as the elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*) and their alteration (*anyathābhāva*). As they say:
"The threefold system of Prakrit consists of *tadbhava*, *tatsama*, and *deśī*.
Apabhraṃśa refers to the various regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*). Anunāsika means that which follows after the nose (*nāsikāmanugata*).
She whose form consists of the syllables being sung is well known as Varṇāṅgī.
Cutting, splitting, piercing, boring, and the application of craftsmanship. || 12-10 ||
Seizing and victory are both situated in the organ of the hand.

Cutting refers to [the action] upon ropes and the like. Piercing (*bhedana*) is the splitting (*bheda*) produced by arrows and such, directed toward a target. Victory (*vijaya*) is battle; or alternatively, the reading is *vijayī* (the victor).
And [the ground] was made level, free from depressions and elevations, as well as from clods of earth, thorns, and gravel.
Muddy places, water-fortresses, streets, watchtowers,
and mountains are traversed by means of the organ of the feet during travel to and from other regions.
The places that are level, sloping, and so forth, which serve as the basis for going to and coming from other lands, are perceived by the foot-faculty (*pādendriya*).

Regarding "excretion" (*utsarga*) and "the sound *padīta*": the anus (*pāyu*) is always active; "excretion" is the release of waste, while "*padīta*" is the foul sound produced through the anal opening.
The generative organ is the producer of bliss and the impeller toward those who may or may not be approached for sexual union. || 12-13 ||
Because its very nature is to produce bliss, its inherent disposition is to engage in all things, whether prescribed or prohibited;
for this very reason, its restraint is established by the scripture. || 13 ||
Thus, these function in actions; therefore, they are indeed the organs of action (karmendriyas).
And just as these are such, so too—
O Goddess of the gods, the sense organs function through the connection with the intellect.
The "yoga" of the intellect—that is, its connection with knowledge—occurs therein; they proceed with that as their cause. || 14 ||
In this regard, after first defining the various divisions of the objects known as sound, he explains that the sense organ of hearing is the means for their perception:
"O Beloved, [the notes] named Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and Pañcama..."
Dhaivata and Niṣadha—these are proclaimed as the seven notes.
Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and Ṣaḍja—these are the three *grāmas*, O Pārvatī.
Thus:
there are seven notes (*svaras*), three *grāmas*, and twenty-one *mūrchanās*. (12–16)
These forty-nine constitute the circle of the gods (*suramaṇḍala*).
Thus it is said:
"For these subtle sounds are known to abide as the sounds of all moving and non-moving beings. (12.17)
They consist solely of subtle sound; for this very reason, they exist everywhere—in all moving and stationary things—in the form of resonance as mere sound. || 17 ||
Now, I shall describe the gross [sounds] as they truly are; listen to them from me.
They arise from the *bherī*, *paṭaha*, and *śaṅkha* drums, and originate from the *mṛdaṅga* and *paṇava* drums. (12.18)
There was the sound of flutes and horns, the deep resonance of drums, various stringed instruments, and those played with the hands.
Arising from conjunction and disjunction, produced from wood, stone, and water, the sounds are Apabhraṃśa, nasalized, Saṃskṛta, and Prākṛta. (12-20)
Those born of conjunction arise from the contact of hands, such as the sound of a drum; those born of disjunction, however, arise from the separation of petals and the like. || 20 ||

Thus, in this manner— by means of the faculty of hearing, it perceives those things established in the seven notes, whether manifest or unmanifest, and whether already mentioned or yet to be mentioned. (12.21)
A person perceives with the sense of hearing all forms of sound— whether produced by musical instruments or otherwise— which are characterized by the resonance of the seven notes (saptasvara).
And from that—
Sound is indeed its object, by which a person (pudgala) may perceive it.
This sound, in the form described, is the entire object of this faculty of hearing. To whom does "its" belong? He says: that by which a person—a human being—might perceive or know it.
In this manner, the connection should be established in the subsequent cases as well.
Soft and hard, as well as rough and cold. || 12-22 ||
Hot, slimy clods of earth, mud, and likewise sands;
as well as blows from arrows, spears, and swords, and likewise beatings and cuttings. (12-23)
One indeed knows these: touch and the sense-organ of the skin.
"Knows touch" means that one perceives it through the process of touching.
Thus, in this way—this touch is indeed its object, by which the person (pudgala) would perceive. || 12-24 ||
Now, listen as I describe the functions of the faculty of sight:
white, red, yellow, black, green, and smoky-grey. (12.25)
Tawny, reddish-brown, and dark-brown— these and other forms in particular.
Likewise—men, women, domestic animals, wild beasts, luminaries, and all things stationary and moving. (12.26)
Thus, in this manner—the eye always perceives things devoid of color and shape;
"color" refers to white and so forth, while "shape" refers to configuration; [the objects] are devoid of these two, meaning they are distinct from them.
The statement "the eye sees objects" is a metaphorical attribution of agency.
Thus it is:
"For its object is that which is called form, by which the self is awakened. (12.27)
The tongue perceives the taste as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and that which is mixed with astringent or sweet. (12.28)
In this way—this [smell] is indeed its object, by which a person perceives it; it is fragrant, divine, foul-smelling, and of many other kinds. (12.29)
Both smell at the tip of the nose;
the nose is the instrument, and both, standing at the tip, smell.
Therefore,
this is its object, designated as "odor," by which that field-knower, deluded by egoism, perceives it. (12.30)
Precisely because of the firmly established identification with the body and so forth, one perceives objects as distinct [from oneself];
and this [point] should also be connected to what precedes.
It runs toward the ten sense organs in both conceptualization and discrimination;
its doubt is unimpeded and it is unconquerable by all embodied beings.

And this mind has indeed been described as that which binds one to dharma and adharma. It is that which, regarding the objects of the organs of cognition and action, forms the resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—"this I shall resort to, this I shall take"—and the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) consisting of the determination "it is such and so"; it runs toward these and proceeds in whatever manner.

For this very reason, this [mind] is everywhere accompanied by doubt, its uncertainty being unavoidable; it cannot be conquered by anyone without the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga); it is "binding" because it binds through dharma and adharma—that is, it causes attachment to them.
Now, in order to demonstrate the existence of the subtle elements (tanmātras) within the body by means of the perception of their effects, such as the sense organs, form, and so forth, he says:
"I shall describe the essential nature and attributes of the subtle elements according to reality. (12.32)

"Artha" means purpose; in accordance with that, I shall state the nature (dharma) or essential character (svabhāva) of those subtle elements (tanmātras), which consists in their abiding in a fixed substratum once they have attained their own form.
Regarding that— [verse 32] —therein:
He smells the fragrance, which is the subtle element of smell, with the tip of his nose;
he perceives the taste, which is the subtle element of taste, as it abides upon the tongue. (12.33)
The eye perceives the subtle element of form as form when it has come into contact;
the skin perceives the subtle element of touch as touch when it has come into contact. (12.34)

And it perceives sound as the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) by means of the sense of hearing. Furthermore, residing in the field of the nose and other organs—the seats of the olfactory and other senses which are the instruments for the cognition of smell and so forth—there exists, by the power of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), the manifested subtle element of smell and the rest; by that very [subtle element], the olfactory and other senses [perceive their respective objects].

The connection [of the senses] is that they grasp qualities such as odor; and here the underlying intention is this: although the senses are all-pervasive because they are derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), their locus of manifestation is restricted to specific sites such as the nose, which are determined by the presence of the subtle elements (tanmātra) of odor and so forth.
Therefore, the perception of odor occurs as it is regulated by the odor-tanmātra from which its function has arisen; thus,
the sense organs are of the nature of ego (ahaṅkārika) colored by their respective specific tanmātras, otherwise they would be like those of the Sāṅkhya school.

If it were purely of the nature of ego (āhaṅkārika), its connection with fixed objects would not be possible; or, if it were purely material (bhautika) like that of the Naiyāyikas, there would be no continuity of the cognition "I."
He summarizes this as follows: "This subtle property of the tanmātras [arises] from the sequence of the natures (prakṛti) of the elements. (12.35)
Since the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are the primordial natures (*prakṛtis*) of the gross elements (*bhūtas*), it is precisely from those respective subtle elements—

acting as the causes for the respective sense organs— that the perception of qualities such as odor, residing in the gross elements like earth which are presided over by those respective sense organs, occurs; this [is the function] of the subtle elements residing in the sense organs.
There exists a subtle dharma that is not perceived by all people. || 35 ||

He shows the abiding of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) within the body: "From that, the Vaikārika [ego] arises by which the person (pudgala) perceives: 'I am learned,' 'I am an enjoyer,' and 'I am born into a noble family. (12.36)
I am the giver and the enjoyer; I am radiant and powerful. I am the warrior in battle, and my enemies have been conquered by me.
"I am indeed virtuous in character, endowed with qualities, and a bringer of supreme welfare;
yet I am also a sinner, ill-behaved, foolish, and ugly in form. (12.38)

"Nothing has been given by me, nothing has been enjoyed by me; there is no one as miserable as I"—thus for those whose minds are possessed by egoism and who are under the sway of the sense of "mine. (12.39)
Egoism binds people in the cycle of worldly existence with firm fetters.

Egoism binds individuals through firm bonds that cause transmigration, appearing in the form of notions such as "I am learned," "I am a knower," or "I am a sinner"— notions characterized by the qualities of goodness (sattva) and the others.
The word "above" (ūrdhvam) refers to [the state] by virtue of pervading all the principles (tattvas) up to that limit.
Thus, in this manner, this threefold nature of the ego (ahaṅkāra) has been fully described. (12.40)
As for what was stated [in verse 12.36], "From that, the vaikārika [arises] above," that was for the purpose of showing the predominance of the rājasa nature of the ego (ahaṅkāra). || 40 ||
Now, by way of its attributes (*dharma*), he states the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is of the nature of *dharma*, within the body:
"Therefore, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe the attributes of the intellect—*dharma* and the rest—to you.
These four are: *dharma*, knowledge (*jñāna*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). (12.41)
Non-dharma, as well as ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery—
among these,
that [māyā] binds in seven ways and deludes through the state of knowledge.
"Established by the Sāṅkhya," that is to say, by implication. || 42 ||
And he says that this [buddhi] is characterized here primarily as follows:
"The intellect (buddhi) performs both determination (adhyavasāya) and [cognition] with respect to various objects."
Now listen, O beloved, to the characteristics of the eight [principles], beginning with Dharma.
In that regard:
fasting, recitation, silence, freedom from anger, abstention from theft, straightforwardness, truthfulness, purity, generosity, compassion, and forbearance should always be practiced. (12.44)
The study of knowledge, modesty, restraint of the senses, the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility, pilgrimage to sacred fords, and the libations offered to the ancestors. (12.45)
Granting fearlessness to all beings and protecting their lives—
this is indeed the first quality of wisdom, and it is designated as "Dharma."
In this regard, that which was previously stated:
"Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, straightforwardness,
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile" (11.145).

Thus, the tenfold Dharma has been described; this is its exposition through various detailed methods. Accordingly, the restraint of the senses is the elaboration of celibacy (*brahmacarya*): namely, modesty, fasting, recitation (*japa*), silence, charity, and compassion.

Patience is the manifestation of the triad of *iṣṭa*, *pūrta*, and so forth, as well as freedom from malice. The practice of knowledge and the preservation of life are the fruits of service to the guru.
Non-violence consists in granting fearlessness to all sentient beings. The avoidance of theft and patience take the form of contentment and uprightness.
Thus,
for those bound by the karma of their actions and following the cycle of existence,
there is repeatedly birth as a mortal, repeatedly birth in heaven, and repeatedly the state of an animal. (12.47)
