The word "becomes" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 47 ||
Thus the nature of phenomena has been fully explained;
now—
...and hear from me the nature of knowledge;
that is the state which is the quality of the intellect.
He clarifies that very point:
"The aggregate consists of twenty-four principles, conjoined with the organs of action. (12.48)
That [self] should be understood as the ordinary one, which sets in motion dharma and adharma;
through the activities of mind, speech, and body, it is the acquirer of dharma and the rest.
I am neither an agent nor possessed of qualities; therefore, for one who is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti), there is no natural bondage for me. || 12-49 ||
I consider all this to have been brought about solely by primordial nature (prakṛti);
I am certain that it proceeds by means of the intellect (buddhi) and the other faculties.

From that very latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from such discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), one is liberated. *Vāsana* means a residual trace (*saṃskāra*). "Is liberated" refers to the Sāṅkhya mendicant.
This very knowledge of Sāṅkhya has been declared by me, by which one is liberated from Prakṛti. (12.50)
For some time, it remains separate. || 50 ||
Now,
if the Lord were to bind again that one who has been liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*, then he would be...
Bound, he transmigrates further as long as he does not find the Divine.

Since the agency of insentient *prakṛti* is untenable, and since that [agency] cannot be attributed to the *puruṣa*, even upon their conjunction the emergence of the world would not occur; therefore, one must accept an *Īśvara* as the creator of the universe, the binder of all beings, and the ordainer of bondage and liberation for those two. As long as such an *Īśvara* is not accepted...
Even one liberated through Sāṅkhya attains only that much [result] and returns again, because true knowledge has not arisen.
To define dispassion (*vairāgya*), he says: "Through dispassion, one should renounce sons, wives, and beloved, highly esteemed [possessions]. (12.52)
Elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; friends, enjoyments, and wealth; and those who are highly esteemed and well-disposed.
Furthermore: fasting, recitation, visiting sacred fords, maintaining the five fires, and sleeping in water; (12.53)
Having meditated upon these formidable [fires], one abandons the body in an instant.

This is the penance known as "the five fires" (*pañcāgnitapas*), performed in the summer season, consisting of abiding amidst the five fires named Dakṣiṇāgni, Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, Aupasada, and Sāvitra. The word "these" (*etāni*) refers to these austerities.
How does one abandon [the body]? To this he says: "By means of blows from mountains, trees, water, and fire, or by hanging, and starvation. (12.54)

The meaning is "having resorted to mountains and so forth. A tree refers to a banyan tree situated at Prayāga or similar locations. "Āśana" is the usage of the root *aś* (to eat) preceded by the prefix *ā*.
Other similar instances of this kind are as follows:
"But relying upon dispassion, one may even perform reckless acts;
having attained a state of sovereignty, one finds no satisfaction in material objects. (12.55)
One should not accomplish penance, vows, or mantras for the sake of sovereignty by means of wives, wealth, enjoyments, attendants, or vehicles. (12.56)
Furthermore:
"War, gambling, as well as deceit, theft, falsehood, and violence—these and other improper acts, such as treachery and the betrayal of trust. (12.57)
Having attained a state of sovereignty, he performs many acts:

those of a sattvic nature such as asceticism and vows; those of a rajasic nature such as warfare; and those of a tamasic nature such as intimidation and slaughter, which serve as the means for seizing wealth.
Having demonstrated the fourfold set beginning with dharma, he now shows, in sequence, those who possess adharma and so forth:
"One who is constantly devoted to the injury of living beings, and who possesses theft, falsehood, and deceit. (12.58)
The beggar and the giver of suffering would be those whose conduct is unrighteous (*adharmaceṣṭita*).
Theft, robbery, being intent on harming living beings, and so forth— this is the meaning of "the conduct of unrighteousness" (*adharmasya ceṣṭitam*).
There is neither dharma nor adharma; who has ever gone to heaven or liberation?
Having fallen into a state of ignorance, he declares everything to be false;
he is perpetually miserable, a servant to others, and even while carrying a burden or a vehicle. (12.60)
And one who lives in constant hardship does not become weary as long as there is no dispassion; this is the meaning of "being."
Having ruled as a provincial governor, he shall become a village lord by virtue of that governorship. || 12-61 ||
Fallen from his kingdom, he subsists on half of that [income];
though lacking sovereignty, he neither grieves nor is distressed, but plays as if in his former reign. (12.62)

Thus has this state of lack of sovereignty been described to you. Now I shall speak of that which resides in the body—the unmanifest, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), which sets the cycle of transmigration in motion. || 12-63 ||
"By the will of the Lord," that is to say, by implication. || 63 ||
Precisely for this reason— and because the world originates from it— it is called *prakṛti* (nature);
for it is this very [nature] that is produced and expanded forth extensively, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the earth (*kṣmā*).
"Everything in this [world] is by means of the Lord"—this is the primordial nature (prakṛti).
Furthermore, I shall declare its nature—which is designated as rajas, sattva, and tamas—serving as the cause for the perception of the body's continued existence. (12.64)
In that regard—luminosity and being (*sattva*) are qualities (*dharma*) dependent upon *sattva*.
Luminosity is the cognition of the form of the object; *sattva* is the state of pure consciousness by which [the aforementioned]...
Dharma.
And he who, solely out of concern for sentient beings, constantly and perpetually shares with others wealth, food, and so forth, is one who always benefits sentient beings. (12.65)
One who is endowed with forgiveness and compassion, and has reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment—he is the one characterized by *sattva*.
This means he is a benefactor of living beings; even without giving material gifts, he assists sentient beings through speech and other means.
Furthermore: joy, generosity, fortitude, intelligence, austerity, purity, and likewise self-restraint. (12.66)
Truthful speech, impartial vision, and the awakening of divine intelligence—these qualities always reside in that Supreme Person. (12.67)
He is to be known as one of sattvic nature...
whose vision is equal toward all, who perceives others as he does himself, and whose intuition is divine.
Now, listen to me regarding the characteristics of a king:
he is cruel, excessively greedy, hateful, and likewise prone to anger. (12.68)
The lustful man, overwhelmed by joy, wanders constantly afflicted by suffering;
the proud man, joined with hypocrisy, remains established in egoism.
Constantly devoted to battle, he is a hero; though full of desire and joy, he does not possess the happiness of contentment.
For one who is of such a kind,
this quality of ruthlessness and so forth is the characteristic mark of the *rājasa* (passionate) quality.
Now—
Being overcome by desire and anger, and being possessed by greed. || 12-70 ||
Envy, hypocrisy, despondency, intoxication, and madness; sleep, laziness, cowardice, as well as impurity and ignorance. (12.71)
The state of possessing a mind contrary to the nature of reality, nihilism, and a deceitful mind—
all this is darkness.
It has the nature of the quality of darkness (tamas).
And for this reason:
"Furthermore, these marks are seen upon that man [in whom the signs appear]. (12.72)
That person should be known as *tāmasa*, one whose disposition is turbid.
Thus it is said: "This unmanifest (*avyakta*) consists of the three qualities; it is declared to be composed of the three qualities. (12.73)
Because it is endowed with these three qualities, it is called "triguṇa" (possessing the three qualities). || 73 ||
Having correctly understood this, however, one is liberated from the primal qualities (*guṇas*).
Having understood [it] as an object of knowledge and having discerned it, one is released from the attributes of *prakṛti* and attains the state of being distinct from *prakṛti*.
In reality, however, he is not liberated, because his perception extends only this far:
"I am not the qualities or their attributes, nor am I the intellect or the ego, for I am not a quality. (12.74)
Devoid of the organs of action, transcending the elements and the subtle constituents (tanmātras), I am remembered as the Puruṣa—non-doing, devoid of qualities, and pure consciousness alone. (12.75)
"He is considered equal to the presiding deity of the instruments and the external senses," as recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas and other texts.
And for this reason, "I am the non-doer. (75)
Therefore—
whatever action has been performed, whether mental, vocal, or physical— all that—
I consider it to have been caused by nature;
I understand that it was performed by the mind and other faculties impelled by nature.
And thus, since the person possesses neither the status of an instigator nor primary agency, it is said:
"The person is traditionally regarded as the agent. (12.76)
Having thus renounced all actions, such a person continues to act without doing so constantly;
that man who understands, "I am not the doer, nor is there any bondage for me," [is liberated]. (12.77)
"He would be liberated from primordial nature as long as the Lord does not create";
by this statement, the connection is made with the phrase "having renounced actions."

Thinking that the self is merely distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti), and out of delusion failing to discern the truth, he considers for some time that agency belongs to the insentient prakṛti— which is actually non-agent— while the presiding Lord, the agent of bondage and so forth, is non-agent.
Even one whose connection with *prakṛti* has ceased is not, in reality, liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*.
Thus it is said: "One who is utterly deluded by Sāṅkhya knowledge fancies that liberation has been attained. (12.78)
For him, there would not be liberation consisting of the state of being bodiless for any length of time;
since that state of being bodiless which lasts only for a certain period is not liberation, he who is deluded by Sāṅkhya knowledge falsely believes that it is liberation.
By this much knowledge alone, he remains liberated from primordial nature (prakṛti), free from the cycle of creation and dissolution. || 12-79 ||

To whatever extent this Lord, the Supreme Lord, performs creation—this very thing constitutes his state of being liberated from *prakṛti*: namely, his freedom from the creation and dissolution of bodies and other effects of *prakṛti*. And thus, as long as the Lord...

It is said that as long as he does not again undertake creation for the enjoyment of men, he remains essentially merged in *prakṛti*. Moreover, his sovereignty does not consist merely in this much power of creation; rather—
With the intention that [His] object is the entire path, both pure and impure, it has been stated that the Supreme Lord is the master of the universe, from Anāśrita down to the end.
Then, for the sake of bestowing experiences upon persons according to the ripening of their karma, the Lord resorts to a state of being oriented toward creation; thus says the Sāṅkhya-yogin.
To that extent, one is again cast into saṃsāra by the bondage of prakṛti.
Cast into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, he wanders further still, bound by dharma and adharma and deluded by the knowledge of Sāṅkhya. (12.81)

First, by that "bondage of nature" (*prakṛti-bandha*) which is not distinct from nature itself; it is "terrible" (*ghora*) because it produces hundreds of terrors, and it is like the "ocean" (*sāgara*) because of its fathomless depth. And although it has been concluded that "I am not the agent, but nature alone is the agent," nevertheless, because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*), that [nature]...

This is not tenable; for if consciousness is attributed to the intellect (*buddhi*) through its association with the reflection of the conscious self (*cicchāyā*), how could agency—which is [otherwise] primary—be [merely] figurative?
Furthermore, since *prakṛti* lacks an abundance of the quality of goodness (*sattva*), it is incapable of receiving the reflection of consciousness;
thus, even figuratively, it possesses no state of being conscious. How then [could it act]?
There is a connection with karma; or else, how could the attainment of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action) arise from knowledge?

Therefore, it must necessarily be that the human being’s limited agency—which has as its cause the connection with the *kalās* and other factors produced under the influence of the Lord’s will—is bound by the merit and demerit accumulated throughout beginningless existence.
We consider it logical that [the notion] "it exists" belongs to one who is deluded by the knowledge of Sāṃkhya. || 81 ||
Thus, through the will of the Lord, this one becomes engaged in the battle of saṃsāra, thinking:
"I am the doer and the enjoyer; I am the powerful lord."
Deluded by the very sense of "mine," one wanders like a waterwheel.
Because the sense of "mine" (*mamakāra*) is preceded by the sense of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*). It is said [to be] "deluded" by the Lord (*īśvara*). As it is stated in the *Gītā*:
"O Arjuna, this Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings."
"Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of Māyā. (18.69)
He concludes this as follows: "The knowledge of Sāṅkhya has been proclaimed by me...
that which was previously asked about here."
"In order to explain the knowledge of reality so that success (*siddhi*) may arise within them," it was stated [in verse 12.2].

To determine that, the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*), which have the body as their locus, were expounded. Now, for the sake of attaining those respective successes through the sequence of utterance (*uccāraṇa*) and so forth—

Having demonstrated this nature of the reality of the effects as something to be directly realized through the gross vision, [the author now shows] that for the sake of accomplishment, there are meditations on other principles— beginning with Niyati and so forth, and extending from Śuddhavidyā up to Śiva— which are all based upon the Self, according to the subtle vision and the supreme vision.
Demonstrating this, he begins: "Listen to the presiding deity of meditation;
[I shall describe] the meditation on the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth."

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Listen to the nature of the presiding deity of those respective realities (tattvas) which are to be expressed, and which bestow the various siddhis that will be described hereafter. And herein, at the outset:
"O fair-faced one, for the practitioner who is endowed with the conduct of tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*yama*)."
Various accomplishments arise for one who has taken refuge in the mountain caves.
"On a well-purified plot of ground...
(6-1-2), and so forth; following this sequence, one should begin the meditation on the principles (*tattva*) starting with Earth, preceded by the aforementioned worship of Bhairava.
In that regard, first of all: [He beheld] the earth, girdled by the four oceans, in its distinct and solid form. (12.83)
[One should meditate on the earth] strewn with mountains and forests, teeming with beasts and birds,
perfectly stable, possessing a yellowish luster, and endowed with the seed-syllable ŪM.
Having meditated upon this, one attains its accomplishment:

that earth which was previously described as having the four oceans for its girdle— [one should contemplate it] as being very firm, hard, and yellowish in luster, consisting of the various deities established within the path of the worlds.

Having meditated upon her as pervading the entire body, the practitioner becomes one with her and attains that perfection. And according to the previously mentioned procedure concerning the nature of the *rasa* (flavor/essence):
"The letter *mū* is traditionally held to be the designator of everything from the earth up to *pradhāna*" (5.5).

Having stated this, it is said that [the syllable] is denoted by the seed-syllable *oṃ*. By the expression "having meditated," concentration (*dhāraṇā*) prior to meditation is implied. And that [concentration is described as]:
"One's own body, resembling gold, square, and marked with a thunderbolt" (Mā.vi. 12.12).
Thus, one should practice the meditation on the earth preceded by such concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
...one should ward off poisonous beings.
"Poison" refers to the stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama) types, and "beings" refers to piśācas, apasmāras, and so forth;
he destroys them with ease, by means of the sequence of paralyzing their power and so on.
But he, having attained the meditation on the earth-element, becomes unshakable by all beings, just as the earth itself is. || 12-85 ||

This is a clarification of what was previously stated in the verse, "He attains its perfection" (12.84). It is just as [the attainment of] the Earth-element is achieved through the conquest of the Earth.
Like its presiding deity, one attains sovereignty therein; this should be applied in the same way for what follows as well. || 85 ||
He describes the meditation on water:
"With all his limbs filled with water, he should fill [them] by means of the meditation on water.
Practicing in this way, he shall destroy poisonous beings. (12.86)
Freed from the burning heat of craving and devoid of calamities,
the perfected one, endowed with the primordial seed-syllable, shall fill the world.

"One should fill [the universe] through meditation on water" means that one should contemplate the entire universe as being filled by means of the sequential expansion of the limbs and sub-limbs. By practicing in this way, "one destroys poison and the like"—that is, through the method of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), one nourishes the object to be treated and renders the defects of poison and spirits pacified; and one does so oneself as well.

At every occasion of distress and the like, being free from all calamities such as thirst and other afflictions, he gradually becomes perfected (*siddha*); thus, with his meditation on the state of a perfected being accomplished, he nourishes the entire world just like water.
The original seed-syllable is indeed the letter *M*, for it has been stated that this alone is the designator (*vācaka*) up to the level of Pradhāna.
Here too,

according to the principle stated in the venerable *Pūrva* [Tantra]: "One should meditate on the body as consisting of water, white, cool, and perfectly round" (*Mālinīvijaya*, 13.2), [the practitioner should meditate on the body] as being of the nature of a white half-moon mandala marked by a lotus.

Having performed the concentration on water (jaladhāraṇā), preceded by the contemplation of the syllable *ū*, one should meditate upon one's own body as consisting of water, presided over by the deity previously indicated. || 87 ||
"The fire arising from one's own body, blazing and indeed burning everything, should contemplate the body as a triangle enveloped by rows of red flames. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 13.21).
Having thus meditated upon one's own body through the fire-concentration (*vahnidhāraṇā*) described in the venerable *Pūrva* [Tantra]—
"One who has been sown with his own seed (svabīja) may perform thousands of rites.

"Sown" (bījita) means joined through the method of reflective awareness (parāmarśa-yukti). Here, it is incorrect to take "one's own seed" (svabīja) as the letter *ra* (*repha*), because there is no such context. Having thus described the principles (tattva) residing in the body up to the level of Pradhāna...

This is precisely the intention behind the exposition of the meditation on reality (tattvadhyāna): that its accomplishment should occur through the process of the ninefold self, preceded by the reflective awareness of the denotative [phonemes] beginning with the letter *ū*.
The wind, consisting of black particles, should be meditated upon as conjoined with the seed-syllable.
One should indeed fill the bodies of the world... here too—
one should contemplate one's own body as Kṛṣṇa, circular and marked with six dots.
"...moving and making a whistling sound... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 13.34).
Thus, by means of meditation preceded by the aforementioned Vāyavīyadhāraṇā, one should fill and nourish the bodies existing in the world with a mere breath. || 88 ||
But through the excellence of meditation, he becomes a perfected being who performs wonders;
the meaning is: what cannot he accomplish by the power of the presiding deity of the wind-element?
One's own body is hollow by nature, and the world is likewise hollow by nature.
One should meditate [on her] with the seed-syllable of Prakṛti, namely the letter E (or Ū).
And thus—
one should have various paintings executed.
As it is said in the Śrīpūrva:
Within six months, he will take on the form of the sky and pass even through subtle apertures;
after three and a half years, he will become the very void itself.
By his mere will he may assume a massive body, and likewise by his will, a subtle body.
"And it is indeed uncuttable and also indivisible... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 13.46–47), and so forth.

Having first established [the foundation], he describes in sequence the meditations on the organs of action, the organs of perception, and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Among those, when fire is meditated upon in the organ of speech, it bestows the perfection of speech. (12.90)
"So be it"—
just as it was previously stated, "blazing, he is indeed the burner of all," that [fire] resides within all bodies, but this one...
The distinction is that [the deity] has its locus in the body, from the heart and so forth up to the head, following the tongue as the organ of speech.
Indra was meditated upon in the hand... [and thus] drunk, by implication.
By which he is that one who is possessed of great learning and is unconquerable;
the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of "possessing" (*svārthe*).
Viṣṇu, when meditated upon, bestows the power to travel great distances on foot.
Mitra, white in color, should be meditated upon at the anus; he is the destroyer of diseases of the anus.
One should meditate with a concentrated mind on Prajāpati, who is dark blue, at the penis. (12.92)

He becomes one who has conquered his senses and enjoys for a hundred years according to his will. The previously mentioned seed-syllable, though not explicitly stated here, is to be applied; [it is] Viṣṇu, who is dark-complexioned, by implication.
One should meditate on the various directions within the sense organ of hearing as being conjoined with the seed-syllable.
The presiding deities of the directions are variegated, meaning they possess diverse forms. The seed-syllable is as before.
And he who is such as this—one who grasps what is spoken even once—[is liberated].
"Even a vast composition of words," that is to say, by implication.
And by the mere intention toward this,
the journey to the [desired] direction is accomplished;
even the reaching of a very distant quarter occurs.
One should meditate upon the wind situated in the skin, in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
He who is impenetrable by fangs and the like,
and for whom [there is this]— no pain whatsoever arises.
That is to say, he is born with a vajra-body.
One should meditate on Āditya in the eye, and likewise on Varuṇa in the tongue.
In the nose, one should meditate on the earth element as yellow, and likewise the moon in the mind;
the subtle element of smell is yellow, and the subtle element of taste is white.
The red is the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra), while the black is designated as the subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra);
the formless is the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and it should be meditated upon in the form of a drop (bindu).

One knows the desired accomplishment regarding the objects of the senses as it was contemplated. Furthermore, the locations of the subtle elements (tanmātras), such as the tip of the nose and so forth, as well as their square and other forms,
should be understood from the *Śrīpūrva* [Tantra] as follows:

"One should meditate upon the yellow [element], the subtle essence of smell, which is square, measured by five, situated at the tip of the nostril, and marked with the insignia of a vajra. (14.2), and so forth;
likewise—

One should contemplate the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra), which resembles a water bubble and is situated at the tip of the tongue, as the support for one's own self located at the tip of the tongue.
"It is very cool, possesses the six tastes, and is unctuous; with the inner self absorbed therein," (14.12.13),
and, "When the yogi, staying in solitude, has his eyes closed..."
One perceives that which resembles an autumnal twilight cloud, appearing as something indistinct.
Having fixed the mind there, as long as one remains for ten days,
one perceives therein even the most subtle drops.
Some there are white, red, blue, and others yellow;
having seen them there, one should fix the mind upon them with an entirely undistracted intellect.
"Within six months, one sees very many forms within them. (14.20.23) Likewise:
"One should contemplate oneself situated within a hexagonal mandala."
Rough, resembling collyrium, each part quivering and agitated.
Then, O Goddess, after ten days, the sensation of an ant’s touch will arise everywhere upon his skin; thereafter, reflecting upon that, he should continue.
"Having attained the state of the Vajra-body, one should obtain what was previously mentioned, as before," (14.29–31), and likewise:
"Having closed his ears with effort and with eyes closed..."

"Whatever great sound one hears, one should direct the mind toward it; then the digestive fire blazes up, and from that, within ten days, the power of understanding speech from a distance arises after six months. (14.33-35)
Thus [it is said]. "And having the form of the *bindu*" should be applied accordingly to the objects of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

Regarding "the desired accomplishment in the objects": since the senses are presided over by the subtle elements according to the aforementioned view, [this refers] to the objects of the subtle elements, such as form and so forth, within the domains of the eyes and other senses.
He knows the perception and so forth regarding things remote in space, time, or nature;
and he knows what has been contemplated—meaning he knows the accomplishment of the mental resolve (saṅkalpa-siddhi) belonging to anyone at all.
This is the accomplishment of mental meditation (mano-dhyāna-siddhi).
He states the meditation on the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra):
"Likewise, Rudra is to be meditated upon within the Vaikārika [ego] by one desiring success. (12.98)
And therefore—
from meditation— one attains perfection characterized by liberation from the bondage of egoism;
that [perfection] which has the bondage of egoism released.

The meaning is that [the practice] culminates in the attainment of identity with the supreme subject. Here too: "With a mind focused on nothing else, one should meditate upon the sixteen-spoked wheel within oneself, contemplating 'I am this,' surrounded by its own functions."
"The yogin shall become invincible... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 16.2.3);
such passages from the venerable *Pūrva* [Tantra] should be considered here.
Then,
with a disciplined mind, one should meditate upon Brahmā as abiding within the intellect.

"Indeed, by remembering with the former seed-syllable..."—by "the former seed-syllable" is meant the syllable *ū*. This should also be understood as applying to what precedes. Recollection is the cause for meditation (*dhyāna*). Here too—
"One should visualize in the heart a lotus resembling the orb of the rising sun,
possessing eight petals and a pericarp, and endowed with the factors such as Dharma.
This and other passages from the *Māyāvajrīkalpa* (16.8) are to be followed accordingly.
Thus, for one possessed of meditative absorption—..................a flood of knowledge proceeds;
and a divine intellect arises, which brings about the destruction of doubt. (12.100)
The past, the present, the becoming, and the future become directly perceived;
it should be understood that here, the flood of knowledge and so forth takes the form of the deity named Brahman, who is the object of meditation.
Now, the primordial nature (prakṛti) is indeed black in color, yet it shines forth as red and white. || 12-101 ||
This presiding deity of Prakṛti, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas), is said to possess many colors.
And thus, regarding her who possesses three colors: "Her heart is red...
the remainder of her body, above and below, is white and black," which means:
And she—
whose face has the appearance of a serpent’s hood—
should be meditated upon with the seed-syllable of reality (tattvabīja) if one desires one's own accomplishment. 12.102

Because she bestows the arising and persistence of diverse manifestations toward all persons, she possesses many faces and so forth. Since her seed-syllable is the letter *ū*, according to the method previously introduced, which belongs precisely to the reality known as *prakṛti*, she should be meditated upon as the presiding deity of that reality.

The intention of one who speaks thus is this: in the system of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*), all principles (*tattvas*) are indeed presided over by their respective deities; they do not possess such insentience (*jaḍatva*).

Therefore, in this context, meditation on the principles is said to have the deity as its primary focus. The perfection of the self (*ātman*) consists in its being distinguished from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Apprehension. || 102 ||

For thus the Self, having been liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*, becomes perfected (*siddha*), independent (*svatantra*), and possessed of divine vision. It is "perfected" because it is perceived through the discernment of *prakṛti*; for that very reason it is independent, and not subject to *prakṛti*.
And thus, he becomes one who possesses such a divine, supramundane vision regarding himself and others— a correct realization.
Regarding the time required for this accomplishment of his, he says for the sake of instruction:
"By the practice of yoga for six months, divine vision arises. (12.103)
And this time for practice should be understood as having all principles (tattva) as its object. || 103 ||
Thus, when divine vision has arisen, whatever occurs in the three worlds becomes directly perceptible to him.
That is to say, whatever exists within the three realms consisting of gods, humans, and animals—
Whatever exists— whether subtle, concealed, or remote— that proceeds from or is born of primordial nature (prakṛti),
all of that becomes directly perceptible to him.
He concludes: "This ordinary yoga has been taught to you...
thus, within the body ending with the material nature (prakṛti), the abiding of the principles (tattvas) [is established] through the sequence of concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth."

Having stated that each of these is a cause for specific supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the Lord teaches the transcendence of the direct realization of *māyā* over the direct realization of *prakṛti*, in order to introduce the meditations on other principles:
"...the supreme [realization] which brings about liberation. (12.104)

The "Beyond" (para) is called Māyā; it is said to be "beyond" even because of the direct realization of Prakṛti. And that [realization] brings about liberation, for only from the moment one has crossed over Māyā does the ascent of the steps upon the path to liberation begin for those who possess the knowledge of the discrimination between Puruṣa and Prakṛti.
Because it has already been stated that the manifestation of re-bondage occurs [only] for that very reason. || 104 ||

Having established the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) preceded by meditation upon the principles beginning with the body and ending with *prakṛti*, he says the following in order to establish the powers arising from meditation on the principle of the Puruṣa who presides over these:
"Beyond this, however, is the Puruṣa..."
The word "to be meditated upon" (dhyeya) is the ellipsis.
And he—
standing in the midst of the lotus—
although he remains pervading this entire body directly.
"Nevertheless, his supreme abode is the casket of the heart-lotus.
Thus, [he] resides within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
What is its essential nature? To this he says: "And its nature is consciousness...
it is indeed pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). As it has been stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"Consciousness is the self" (1.1).
Therefore, he says that for this very reason, there is no real difference whatsoever as admitted by the proponent of difference:
"He remains, having filled the body in all [beings]. (12.105)

The Supreme Lord abides within all living beings, whose distinctions are manifested through the power of His māyā-śakti; therefore, although He appears as if divided due to the differences of those limiting adjuncts (upādhi), He is not so in reality. This is the intended meaning of the use of both the plural and singular numbers in the words "in all" and "abides. || 105 ||
Thus, precisely through the manifestation of the contraction of the *puryaṣṭaka*,
that [pure consciousness] is renowned as the "living being" (*jīva*), by which that city lives; "city" (*pura*) means the body.
He shows this very point by way of contrast: "By that which has departed, one is dead; without consciousness, the body perishes. (12.106)
And thus, having assumed ego-identification with the *puryaṣṭaka* and so forth through the power of *māyā*,
this [individual] is bound—
even though he shines as the nature of perfectly full consciousness, which is the foundation of the universe.
To that extent, by means of its own nature as a manifestation of contraction, it binds itself; as was stated previously:
"For the self is indeed bound by the self" (10.360).
But when that appearance of contraction, which serves as its wall, is dissolved by the power of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā),
then he is indeed liberated...
And liberation does not come for him upon the fall of the body, but rather even while he is living; thus it is said:
"He experiences pleasures and pains.
And it was stated previously:
"He is liberated even while living, for whom this contemplation is established" (7.259).
But as for the falling away of the body, he is simply Paramaśiva himself; thus it has already been stated that for whom could there be liberation, and from what?
For that which consists of such a nature of pure consciousness alone—neither its form nor its color, nor its measure, is seen anywhere. (12.107)

"Caste" refers to the Brahmin and so forth; "form" refers to white and so forth; "measure" refers to height, largeness, and so forth—[all of which are absent] because of the absence of any indication by means of "this-ness" (idantā). And this [absence] indicates that difference is indeed unreal. Nevertheless, because its nature is consciousness, it is eternally manifest in form.

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) known as perception, inference, and so forth—which consists of the appearance of the nine categories—is never observed anywhere, nor is it logically tenable. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"But when the cognizer, whose form is always manifest, is the means of valid cognition..."
"What is the means of knowledge? It is the ninefold manifestation within that which partakes in all cognition.
(2-3-16). Also, in other Vedic scriptures:
"By what, my dear, should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
In this way, the Blessed One has indicated in certain places that this matter is simply inconceivable through words. 107.

And because this [reality] is not made an object of cognition in any way whatsoever, for that very reason— it cannot even be described; by the force of the word "even" (api), it implies that it cannot even be conceptualized.
And therefore,
this one— ......... subtle and possessing infinite forms—
for this very reason, he manifests—
Of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts; || 12-108 ||
His individual soul (*jīva*) is even more subtle, and it is capable of attaining infinity.
[It is subtler] than the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, which has itself been divided into a hundred parts;
because it is conceived as being so subtle, one disregards it as having fallen into the state of an object of knowledge (*vedya*).

The supreme, subtle living soul (jīva) is knowable by some means or another; precisely because it consists of the singular nature of the knower whose essence is consciousness (cit), it is fit for infinity— due to being undivided by space, time, and form— and for the state of absolute oneness with all things, by virtue of having that as its very nature.

It flashes forth by its own freedom; it is not, however, imagined as such by anyone. Being "imagined" means being brought forth by an act of imagination, whereas "being established" (kḷpti) is simply its abiding in that state by itself.

Thus, because that which is to be meditated upon is non-conceptualized (*akalpita*), he describes meditation as a limb for the accomplishment of visualization (*utprekṣā*), which is not far removed from the aforementioned state when it is invested with the *kañcukas*:
"Having the color of the sun, shining like gold, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf. (12.109)

Yogins behold it with their divine eye like a star. By the phrase "having the color of the sun," it is stated that its nature is merely luminosity—meaning its radiance is like that of gold or refined metal—but not that it possesses a physical form; this is further illustrated by the comparison "like a drop of water on a lotus."
The phrase "not touching the levels of the body and so forth" indicates that its essence is vibration (*sphurattā*).

By the words "with the divine eye," it means by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, here, following the context, the second phoneme associated with the *navātman* should be applied as the signifier (*vācaka*) in reverse order. By the word "tāraka" (the savior),...

Furthermore, it has been stated that the meditation on that [Supreme Reality] possesses the very quality of delivering one from the bondage of innate dispositions (*prakṛtibandha*); thus, its attainment (*siddhi*) is also indicated.

By the phrase "with divine vision" (*divyacakṣuṣā*), the indication of attainment is made by showing that through that meditation, a divine eye that illuminates everything without exception manifests for the yogi. Thus, in this way...

This meditation belongs to one who is under the sway of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka); however, in reality, he is meditated upon in his true nature as pure consciousness alone, and is not an object of meditation. With the intention that the Self alone is the presiding deity of all, [the text] here [negates] the idea of the Self being presided over by another deity.
It has not been stated.

And this Puruṣa, who has been described as being devoid of color, form, and so forth because his essential nature is consciousness—this one, when joined with passion (rāga), ignorance (avidyā), and the kalās, and bound by time, indeed possesses form. (12.110)

Previously, the Self, enveloped by the fivefold sheaths (*kañcuka*) whose nature as form, power, and so forth has been determined, was described as "possessing form," meaning it has the form to be meditated upon as having the color of the sun and so on. || 110 ||
Now,
by means of the ninefold system of the self as previously taught in the passage beginning with "Nature and the Person" (5.11), he describes the meditation on destiny:
The deity residing in the vital breath (jīva) is to be known by her dark complexion;
she has a white body on the right side and a black form on the left.

With the intention that the living state of the individual soul (*jīva*) exists solely through the vital breath constrained by destiny (*niyati*), she is called the "Deity" (*devatā*). And because she is the regulator, she is "Dark" (*śyāmā*). Furthermore, although her complexion is dark, the fact that her right and left sides are respectively white and black indicates that she brings forth both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). || 111 ||
And of this [goddess]—
her faces have those colors, and her mandalas especially;
the four faces are white on the right and black on the left, such that even the four faces are white from the right side.
To the left is the black [one]. "Mandalas" refers to the circles of light radiating from the faces and limbs.
And because this [nature] possesses both white and black forms,
it binds the person through the bondage of karma... and of this—
.........bestows pleasure and pain. || 12-112 ||
Therefore, one should recognize this destiny as such— irresistible even by gods and asuras—
for everyone is indeed constrained by it.
In this way, she—possessing the meditation together with the previous seed-syllable—is endowed with two forms. || 12-113 ||

She whose meditation consists of contemplation accompanied by the awareness of that [seed-syllable] together with the letter *va*, which is the previously mentioned seed-syllable belonging to the ninefold self;
she is thus endowed with the two forms described as white and black. 113.
And from that meditation one attains perfection. What is this perfection? To this he says:
And he is liberated from necessity;
the meaning is that he is no longer constrained by necessity.
Now he describes the meditation on the reality of Time (kālatattva):
"Three-eyed, four-faced, black in color, and four-armed. (12.114)
[He saw] the Lord, who was withdrawing [the universe], who is invincible, and infinite;
"invincible" meaning incapable of being overcome by anyone other than the supreme yogi;
"infinite" meaning immeasurable by another; and "Lord" meaning the one empowered with the creation and destruction of the universe.
One should meditate on time as being of such a nature.
And therefore, for him—[who knows the nature of his own seed and meditation]—it is not brought about by time. || 12-115 ||
Its own seed-syllable is the letter *la*, which is connected to the ninefold self. || 115 ||
But those who do not strive to deceive Time— they, deprived of meditation on Time, revolve like a wheel.
As it was said by the venerable Hari:
"By means of activities resembling the operation of a water-wheel,
that Lord, fashioning all things, receives the name 'Time'. (3.9.14)
Since this is so, therefore one should always meditate upon the form of the aforementioned deity in this manner;
for in this way, for the meditator, [there occurs] the form of the deception of time as previously described.
...and the accomplishment of what is to be meditated upon arises. || 12-116 ||
The meaning is that mastery over time is achieved not only through the method of Mṛtyuñjaya described in the section on Time, but also from meditating upon the aforementioned times. || 116 ||

Having thus described the meditation on the *siddhyaṅga* (auxiliary to accomplishment) of the Person (*pums*), Necessity (*niyati*), and Time (*kāla*)— which are denoted by the letters *ya*, *va*, and *la*— immediately following the meditation on the ultimate reality of the discerned primordial nature (*prakṛti*),
[the author proceeds] by means of the ninefold process of the self (*navātmaprakriyā*) through the three principles beginning with the Person, arranged respectively in pairs.

For this very reason, he also describes the meditation on attachment (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), and limited agency (kalā), which have been defined and are to be contemplated according to their respective colors:
"Attachment is indeed red in color; Knowledge is dark-complexioned with beautiful eyes."
One should meditate upon that digit (kalā) which is white in color and which awakens consciousness.

The term *sulocanām* (the fair-eyed one) is used here like the "crow's eye" [idiom, applying to both]. Here too, the four faces and four arms are to be understood as previously described. Furthermore, this is an epithet of *kalā* (the digit), meaning "that which unfolds consciousness," as was stated before:
[As it was said previously...]
Regarding the phrase "one whose consciousness has been opened by *kala*" (11.98),
this refers to the statement:
"the domain of the state of *vidyā*" (11.98).

The above is intended as an illustration; furthermore, those principles (tattvas) should be made known through the direct realization of the sequence of meditation within the heart, which is one's own self. 117.
He describes the meditation on Māyā for the purpose of pacifying delusion:
"She is black in color, with red eyes, long teeth, and beautiful eyes;
her hair is brown and stands upright, and she has a stout body and a large belly. (12.118)
Because she deludes all living beings, her meditative visualization (*dhyāna*) is described as having such a form.

"With tawny hair rising upward" means she whose hair is tawny and stands erect. Although in this context the meditative visualization of some principles is described merely by their essential nature (*svarūpa*), while for others it is described as having the form of an anthropomorphic deity (*ākṛtimad-devatārūpatva*).

Although that [state] is presided over by those respective deities, nevertheless, since in every case the principles (tattvas) take the form of the appearance of those respective [deities], it is correct that they are indeed presided over by those respective deities;
thus, all the principles should be meditated upon as forms presided over by their respective deities. || 118 ||
It clarifies her very nature as that which deludes all living beings:
"She who causes beings, beginning with Brahmā, to fall again and again;
she causes them to fall by first veiling their true nature and subjects them to the cycle of transmigration."
And therefore, by them—
because it stands as an adversary without enmity— the knot of māyā is difficult to cross.

Without enmity and for no other reason, Māyā—which is the very form of the power of the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty—is an adversary; by concealing His full nature, She brings about the state of the limited individual soul (*kṣetrajña*).
Precisely because it has that nature, Māyā is called the "knot" that binds the person. || 119 ||
And for this reason, he says that without the grace of the Supreme Lord, no one can cross over [this ocean of existence]:
"Those who know the Sāṅkhya, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas, as well as those who are learned in other scriptures, and others who propound liberation—they are not capable of crossing over it. (12.120)
Other scriptures belong to Maheśvara. || 120 ||
For all of them are indeed afflicted by delusion, wandering through illusion with a desire for liberation where there is no liberation;
for what other [liberation] exists than that which consists in the attainment of identity with the Supreme Bhairava, who is the mass of pure and autonomous consciousness?

A certain state is called liberation; however, even when one has transcended one path, because one has not yet transcended other paths, there is an appearance of liberation where there is no liberation, due to the yoga of meditating on its own seed-syllable according to the nature of the previous meditation. (12.121)
Having severed that [bond] with the sword of initiation (dīkṣā), they enter the imperishable Śiva.

His own seed-syllable is the letter *ma*, which is connected to the ninefold self (navātman); its meditation is the reflective awareness (parāmarśa), accompanied by that which was previously described as being dominated by it.

The meditation beginning with "dark-complexioned and red-eyed" (12.118) and so forth— by means of that very sword, which is the initiation previously described and defined according to its essential nature and cause, they cut through that *māyā* and enter into Śiva.
Then they attain oneness.
He states the meditation on Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā):
"Knowledge (vidyā) consists of four phonemes; she is remembered as pervading those phonemes. (12.122)
She, whose nature is the void, should be meditated upon as white, red, yellow, and black;
she is mounted upon space and wind, and is endowed with beauty and youth.
"In this [system], there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the 'Being-knowledge' (*sadvidyā*) and the 'I-this' (*ahamidantayoḥ*)," as stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*.

In the manner previously indicated, the Supreme Lord thus prescribes the all-pervasive form of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), which consists of the manifestation of the undivided distinction between all denotators and the denoted;
for indeed, by means of the four [energies]— Ambā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Vāmā— ...

She whose description— the manifestation of her own nature— is through the forms prescribed in the Āgamas, namely the arrangements of the *bindu*, the *sṛṣṭirekhā*, the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and the *ardhacandra*; and who, for that reason,
pervades the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* according to the sequence of the four aforementioned powers.
By the phrase "remembered as the arouser of the essential nature consisting of the fifty venerable phonemes," her form as pervading all denotators (*vācaka*) is stated;

however, by the words "white" and so forth, [her form] is described according to the principle established in the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the five principles (*pañcatattva*) of all denoted (*vācya*) and denotator (*vācaka*).

Because he himself consists of the five principles (tattvas) beginning with earth— being composed of yellow, white, red, black, and the void— the Goddess who pervades him is said to possess that same nature.
Furthermore, since she pervades all denoters (vācaka) according to the reasoning already established, therefore...
This very [power], having ascended to the state of *sauṣumna*— the space and wind that is the locus for the arising of all phonemes—

is, according to the previously stated principle, the vehicle for the *varṇakuṇḍalinī* because it is the *prāṇakuṇḍalinī*, and precisely because it is completely filled with all that is signified (*vācya*).

She is described as being endowed with beauty and youth. The reading beginning with "caturvaktra" is a corruption; for, having introduced the passage "That Vidyā, however, is divided into eight groups" (10.1144) in the section on the governance of the worlds (*bhuvanādhikāra*), [it describes] even the powers such as Vāmā and the others who are presided over by the Vidyās.
This is because of the description of the visualization [of the deities] beginning with: "Having the appearance of molten gold, five-faced... (10.1146). || 123 ||
Thus,
she should be meditated upon by means of her own seed-syllable— that is,
by the letter *kṣa* associated with the ninefold self (*navātman*), through the method of combining the letters *ka*, *sa*, and *a*.
She should be touched by means of the seed-syllable (bīja) which is the essence of the universe and has been internalized.
And thus, for the practitioner, there arises that very accomplishment which consists in the manifestation of the entire universe...;
by the word "and" (ca), the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth is included according to the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikānyāya*).

Thus, by means of the method of manifesting the nature of the entire universe without exception, this divine and unfailing accomplishment culminates in the supreme fruit, which consists in the expansion of the unsurpassed abode.
And therefore, this practitioner becomes one whose knowledge is perfected. || 12.124 ||
He possesses seven crores of perfected vidyās that are under his control. || 124 ||
Furthermore:
"He [knows] all the worlds from that..."—
the "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) are the Rudras and the individual souls (*kṣetrajñas*), for they are called "worlds" because they perceive (*lokayanti*) or because they are perceived (*lokyante*).

The categories of Māyā, beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with the earth (kṣiti), consist of infinite principles; he knows them all as resting upon his own support, perceiving them through his own grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Not only is he omniscient, but furthermore— ................he goes assuming any form at will; that is to say, like Śiva, he becomes a creator of various forms by his mere will.
Now, he describes the meditation on the faces of Īśvara, the Lord of the Principle of Īśvara, beginning with the eastern face:
"One should meditate on the Lord of Nārā [the East] as having the luster of saffron, three-eyed, and bearing matted locks. (12.125)
One should meditate upon the one whose face is turned toward the east...
this [is] Nareśa, belonging to the venerable Tatpuruṣa, the lord of men and the performer of grace and other [acts]. "Ardhanārīśa" is a corrupt reading. On the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan)—
Since it has been stated, "His knowledge resides in his lap" (10.1158), how can this [knowledge] be consistent with [the Lord's] being Ardhanārīśvara?
That which was his former face— by meditating upon that [face] of one who is established in supreme austerity, subsisting on air alone,
he attains the fruit of that merit.
Since the scripture has stated that this face [of Śiva] is pervaded by Vāyu, the fruit for the meditator of this [face] manifests right here at the commencement of its meditation.
But gradually... [and] of ten thousand horse-sacrifices. || 126 ||
One obtains the fruit. || 126 ||
And through the excellence of his meditative concentration,
the world comes under his control,
because [he is] everywhere throughout the three worlds.
...he proceeds and attains perfection;
he becomes powerful like the lords of those respective worlds and possesses the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
And this for him—
“without doubt in six months” means that through meditation for six months, it becomes certain.
He begins to describe the meditation of the right [hand]—the right [hand] is likewise indeed thus. (12.127)
"Of the Lord": "one should meditate on the three-eyed one"—this is the meaning of the phrase "in that very manner. || 127 ||
He states the specific details:
"Resembling a dark blue cloud, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes;
his face is formidable with a frown, and he is adorned with skulls and snakes. (12.128)
One should contemplate his right face as possessing many forms and matted locks;
the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "iti" (thus), serving to indicate a specific distinction. The second occurrence of the word "dakṣiṇa" (right) expresses favorability toward the practitioner.
And this is so:
for the destruction of pleasure and pain, there is the destruction of calamities and fever. (12.129)
The specific distinction, however, is this:
everything such as poison, planetary afflictions, and so forth, is destroyed in an instant through meditation.
Furthermore—
The yogi, freed from old age and death, blazes like fire. || 12-130 ||

He indeed traverses all worlds and the perfected one (siddha) attains equality. "The perfected one" [is so called] as before due to meditation for six months. "Traverses" means he presides over them as their lord. "Attains equality" means he reaches a state of identity with the Supreme Lord.
He describes the meditation on the western face:
"O Goddess, it is white, three-eyed, and holds a rosary and a water-pot. (12.131)
One should meditate upon the western face,
which bestows divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*), such as the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest.
Such is the greatness of this meditation, that—having slain thousands of living beings and hundreds of others' wives— [one attains liberation]. (12.132)

The pure-souled *alepaka*, having attained perfection (*siddhi*), becomes Śiva. Here, the root *han* has the meaning of "killing" as well as "going" in successive order. Not only does one who has received the initiation of a practitioner (*sādhaka-dīkṣā*) attain perfections such as *aṇimā* through the immediate meditation upon the [five] faces [of Śiva], but he also becomes Śiva.

The meaning is that it applies even to one who has been released from a great sin (*mahāpātaka*). Therefore, it is taught that this meditation should also be determined as being applicable to the subject matter of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
He describes the meditation on the northern face:
"The northern face has three eyes and possesses a luster equal to a red lotus. (12.133)
"By meditating upon whom the entire world comes under his control, there is no doubt"—
this refers to one who meditates for six months; that is the meaning.
Moreover:
"He indeed causes heat, he causes rain, he creates, and he also withdraws. (12.134)
He who meditates for one year attains his desired success;
[this applies] to the middle-voice endings through transposition.
He describes the meditation on the upward-facing [form]: "One should always meditate upon the white one, facing upwards, holding a trident in his hand and wearing matted hair. (12.135)
Clad in a tiger skin, holding a rosary,
a water-pot, a lute, and a hand-drum, and wearing a serpent as his sacred thread.
One should constantly meditate upon Maheśvara as having a linga above his moon-like head.

The term "ūrdhvalinga" (upward-facing linga) means that it has the form of a linga located at the position of the crown of the head. By the word "Maheśvara," one should meditate on Maheśvara as having a single face; the meaning is not that he possesses merely a face [without other features]. The word "constantly" (nityam) [indicates this should be done perpetually].
For a period of six months.
And for this reason: "By this very body, he becomes omniscient and able to assume forms at will. (12.137)
The word "it becomes" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 137 ||
Thus, the meditation on Īśvara, who possesses form and presides over the principle of Īśvara-tattva, has been described.
Now, regarding this very [Īśvara]:
"And Bindu itself is Īśvara" (4.264).

Thus, according to the perspective of the *Yojanikā* text, he describes the state of non-appropriation (*anādhyāna*), which consists of the internal differentiation of the denotative powers of the universe within the form of the *bindu*— the essence of the knowledge of the non-difference of the entire universe expressed as "All this am I, Śarva."
Through meditation on the sound of the bell, accomplishment shall be attained within six months;
indeed, whatever he desires, that accomplishment arises for him in the world of mortals.

Through meditation on the reflective awareness of the *nāda* contained within the *bindu*, which has the form of the resonance of a bell (*ghaṇṭāravākāra*), accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs within six months; that is, within six months, he attains the accomplishment consisting of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reflective awareness of the *nāda*.
And upon the attainment of that accomplishment, the acquisition of whatever object he desires is possible for him while still remaining in his body.

Now, he describes the meditation on that very *liṅga* which was previously mentioned as the "upper *liṅga*"—the meditation on the face of Īśāna—which consists of the light of the *bindu*, whose nature is the knowledge of the non-duality of the entire universe, and which contains within it the *nāda*:
[He says: "The meditation on that [liṅga]..."
But he who performs meditation on the *liṅga* joined with the previously mentioned seed-syllable shall,
within a single month, perceive the subtle *liṅga* above his body.

Upon seeing that [reality], which resembles pure crystal, one is liberated. Its *liṅga* consists of the light of the *bindu*, whose nature is the realization of non-difference from the entire universe; it is the universe itself, which remains latent within it in an unmanifest state.

First, there is only the upper face of Īśāna. The first seed-syllable is the letter *ra*, which belongs to the Navātman; it should also be contemplated as the reflective awareness (*parāmarśaka*) during the meditation on the eastern face.
One should perceive that which is subtle and the object of all the senses; becoming composed of its light, one flashes forth and is liberated.
One attains liberation while living. || 139 ||
But if one who possesses this meditation should have a desire for supernatural powers (*siddhi*), then—supernatural power arises in the world of humans within six months. (12.140)
He demonstrates this:
"The intellect regarding the vision of the three worlds arises as direct perception for him.
A cognition in the form of immediate intuition regarding the vision of the three worlds dawns for that person.
The meaning is that this person becomes one who has directly realized the entire universe.
Likewise—
[he] shall traverse all worlds and bring them under his own control.
Moreover—..................he would become equal to Īśvara. || 12-141 ||
Even while remaining in the body, he becomes equal to the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka. || 141 ||
And this is his equality with the Lord:
"The moon and sun shall be his two eyes; the intellect is indeed the wheel of the chariot.
The subtle elements are its horses, impelled by the mind as the charioteer. (12.142)
Egoity (ahaṅkāra) is the warrior; its great bow is the [three] qualities (guṇa).
The senses are its arrows, and Dharma is declared to be the deer. (12.143)

In this world, one whose discriminative wisdom has not yet dawned, who is bound by the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, and who is entered by the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), becomes bound by merit and demerit while experiencing objects through the senses set in motion by the mind presided over by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). However, he who, through the propitiation of the Lord, has attained identity with Him—

The lord of yogis, although remaining within the body, has mounted the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) as if it were a chariot; this [body], which moves outward by means of the subtle elements consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā), is being properly driven by his discerning intellect in the form of a wheel. Thus, even while the collection of sense-objects is being swallowed [by death], he is not [overcome].

Sometimes he touches [the world] with conceptualizations such as dharma and so forth, which are easily accessible even to common folk; thus, he is beyond the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya) and consists of the fullness of the I-consciousness (pūrṇāhaṃbhāvamaya). The rest is merely poetic embellishment. 143.
And therefore:
"In this way, O Supreme Goddess, that yogi sports within the Supreme Self (abiding in the heart), moving according to his will amidst merit and demerit. (12.144)

Thus, abiding in the Supreme Self situated within the heart according to the previously stated method—[one realizes]: "The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading; I am He alone, whose nature is Śiva. Through such firm conviction, there arises the emergence of Śiva. (109)

Thus, according to the principle taught in the *Vijñānabhairava* and other scriptures, the yogi, consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is non-different from That, plays at will with merits and sins which are essentially mere play; the meaning is that they never touch him at any time. || 144 ||

Now, if this realization of non-duality does not take root in him due to the absence of the most intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then the Lord, out of compassion, instructs him in the means for pacifying the bondage of merit and demerit:
"I am not the agent, nor is there bondage for me; everything has the Lord as its cause."
And having realized the knowledge of the Lord, one should renounce all actions.
The word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied. || 145 ||
And for this reason:
"He who resides in the heart is the impeller of everyone regarding their agency in merit and demerit."
I have gone for refuge to him; for me there is no bondage, nor is there any agency.

Sadāśiva, endowed with the eightfold division and accompanied by the previously mentioned seed-syllable, should be meditated upon in the form described above by one who desires the fruit of that attainment. (12.147)

"By means of the eightfold division" means being joined with the eight forms beginning with Sakala. "The prior seed-syllable" refers to the letter *ha*, which is connected to the Ninefold Self (*navātman*). "In the form previously described" refers to the nature defined as the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).
"The fruit of its accomplishment" is the attainment of equality with that [deity]. || 147 ||
Having thus described his gross meditation, he speaks of the subtle:
"One should indeed meditate upon the pervasive Nāda during the days, nights, and solstices.
It is called "pervasive" precisely because it takes the form of pervading the eightfold sounds previously mentioned, such as Ghoṣa and the rest.

It is the pervader of the prāṇa and apāna forms described in the section on time, as well as the solstices (ayanas) consisting of the rightward and leftward flows, because it consists of sound (dhvani) in all its aspects. For this very reason,
it is distinct from the gross, divine nāda which is like the sound of a bell.
It is the subtle differentiation of sound that pervades all sounds.
And by way of meditation, this [time]—through the solstice occurring at the southern and northern transits—is the bestower of liberation for one who knows the equinox. || 12-148 ||

At the end of the five *caṣakas* of the southern and northern transits, at whichever time of the equinoctial transit flows equally through both channels (*puṭa*), for one who knows— that is, perceives— the *nāda* there,
this [practice] bestows liberation. || 148 ||
He shows its essential nature:
"That which resembles the sound of a bamboo flute is known as the *śāntanāda*;
it should be understood as Sadāśiva."...

Because the specific forms of sound and so forth have subsided, it is called "quiescent" (śānta); it is distinct from the previously mentioned gross Sadāśiva. Now, hear the fruit of perfection resulting from meditation upon this: || 12-149 ||
Within one month he becomes radiant; in the second month, he becomes a master of speech;
in the third, he beholds the Siddhas; and in the fourth, he possesses divine vision.
As for that which consists of the destruction of wrinkles, graying hair, and so forth—that perfection (siddhi) shall be attained in the world of humans within half a year; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore—
Divine perfection is attained in one year, while union is attained in the second.
In the second year, there arises the state known as "oneness with Sadāśiva. || 151 ||
Having described the meditation on the name in the state of Sadāśiva, he now explains the meditation on the *bindu* along with its practical application:
"Having performed the sixfold orientation (*ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa*), one should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva.
The meaning is that one should meditate on the three *bindus*.
The two ears and the two eyes [are touched] by the two thumbs, using the index and middle fingers [to touch the nostrils]. (12.152)
With the remaining two [syllables], one whose mind is firmly fixed should place them upon the nose at the six-faced [center];
and through meditation on that, Sadāśiva is indeed perceived in ten ways in the form of the phonemes. || 12-153 ||
"In the form of a drop," that is to say, by implication. || 153 ||
White, red, yellow, black, greenish-brown, blue, variegated in color, and beautiful like the luster of crystal. || 12-154 ||

It should be as clear as crystal and beautiful; however, that which is described in the upcoming passage beginning with "resembling the lunar disc" (12.156) and so forth is what should be adopted. || 154 ||
As it is said: "Having seen all forms, the wise man should abandon them;
he should grasp only the One alone, for all others are merely forms of qualities. (12.155)

The discerning one is intent upon the knowledge of reality. "One" refers to that which is delightful; "others" refers to specific forms. Those whose nature is merely qualities are not to be grasped. || 155 ||
Regarding that one [point], he says:
"One should perceive the *bindu* as resembling the lunar disc, with eyes like a mass of lightning, and having the appearance of shimmering stars. (12.156)
Whose gaze is like a mass of lightning; whose form is that of the movement of a flickering star—that is to say, resembling a throbbing star—[is he]. || 156 ||
Such is the nature of the *bindu* of Sadāśiva. As for that which resides in the principle (*tattva*) of Īśvara, it is as follows:
"The *nivṛtti*, the *pratiṣṭhā*, the *vidyā*, and likewise the *śānti*—the *bindu* as Īśvara, joined with these *kalās*, is to be meditated upon. (12.157)
Therefore, at the occasion of explaining the nature of the eleven *bindus*,
we [interpreted] the passage, "united with the ten deities" (11.10), as referring to the pentad of deities beginning with Sadyojāta, as well as the resonance of the bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*).
And as for the four kalās beginning with Nivṛtti which have been explained here as objects of meditation, they were explained there with that same intention. || 157 ||
He concludes: "The meditation on the *bindu* has been fully explained...
[this applies] to both types, namely, that of Īśvara and that of Sadāśiva."
"...understand from me the hundred thousand-fold power (śakti-lakṣa). The meaning is: understand that meditation which is characterized by such a hundred thousand-fold power."
Thus,
having gazed at the sky with eyes closed, [he beheld that which was] like the rising sun.
And she beholds that great splendor; thus she is remembered as the Sovereign Power (Śakti).
"Space" (kha) refers to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). She is the Sovereign (prabhvī), whose nature is to manifest at the end of the end of Nāda.
And there she is yellow, red, black, and crystal-like in appearance, beautiful to behold. || 12-159 ||
The supreme power is to be beheld;
it is to be known as manifested through the mastery of gnosis.
And then—
having seen her, one attains the state of Śiva;
she is worthy of that state and is the very form of Paramaśiva.
Then, one should contemplate her as all-pervasive, and thereafter, above that, in five forms.
Endowed with its own causes, such as the pervader and so forth.
And having meditated upon that—
[as described]— one should proceed with freedom by means of the method for attaining the stages beginning with *samanā*; this is the implied meaning.
Then, one should meditate with a disciplined mind upon Samanā and Unmanā, whose forms have been previously determined and described in sequence. (12.161)

And here, in the meditation on [the principles] beginning with Śakti and ending with Śiva, the *praṇava* associated with the ninefold self (*navātman*) is to be considered as the designator. "One should meditate" means that one should reflect by means of the power of one's own self-awareness (*svavimarśa*). || 161 ||
And therefore—
from meditation one attains perfection,
by which he—
.........the pervasive, sovereign, and imperishable Lord.
Through meditative absorption on the *samanā*—[as it is said]:
"But Śiva, mounted there, performs [his work]" (10.1258).
The meaning is that one becomes of the same nature as that Śiva who was previously described as having the form of the all-pervasive one and so forth.
But through meditation on the Unmanā [state]—
and thereafter, Śiva is peaceful (śānta) above that— the meaning is that because of the cessation of the entire universe up to the limit of Samanā, one becomes Supreme Śiva himself, who is peace.
And that—indeed, it was previously explained by me. || 12.162 ||
"In the passage beginning with, 'Above Śiva, Śiva is to be known, where one who is united is not born' (4.197), and likewise:
'That one [reality] exists established through the distinction of gross and subtle' (4.295)."
And in such enumerations as these. || 162 ||
To demonstrate its essential nature here as well, he says:
"That which may be seen by the eye, or that which is within the range of speech;
those things which the mind reflects upon, and those which the intellect determines. (12.163)
Whatever consists of the ego-sense, whatever exists as an object of cognition, and that which does not exist—all that must be diligently sought right there. (12.164)

"He" refers to Paramaśiva, the mass of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśaghana*), who is to be sought and recognized through the identity with the light of consciousness within the three worlds— the universe consisting of existence and non-existence—
just as this Great Lord is the light whose nature is Being-Consciousness (*saccidātman*), by virtue of being non-different from His own light.

This entire universe shines forth, for it is impossible for anything external to light to be manifested; and that self-luminous light which shines as the very essence of the manifestation of the universe— that indeed am I.
And for one whose heart is thus entirely absorbed in the supreme reality, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding place, stage of life (*āśrama*), or other such factors; thus he says:
"Staying in whatever place, engaged in whatever stage of life..."
Seated comfortably, with self-controlled mind, one-pointed, and concentrated.

Having recollected the Svachchanda [Tantra], one should always meditate on non-existence (abhāva), sitting comfortably, free from the exertion of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like, because of having known that which is to be known. He is explained by the term "one-pointed mind" as "one whose self is restrained"; he is "composed" (samāhita) even during emergence from meditation.
Established in the contemplation of the supreme reality, one should "recollect with freedom" (svacchandam samanusritya),
that is, reflect upon it as being the nature of the light of consciousness whose essence is the manifestation of the universe. One should "cultivate non-existence" (abhāvam bhāvayet),
meaning one should recognize through direct recognition (pratyabhijānīyāt) that nothing whatsoever ever exists apart from the light of consciousness.
And therefore:
"From the cultivation of that reality, one who is equal to it is born. (12.166)
"Even in the state of the body"—this is the meaning. || 166 ||
And this is logical,
because those qualities of his which were previously described, O lady of excellent complexion—
namely omniscience and the rest— [are indeed present].
Endowed with those qualities, O beloved, he indeed becomes a yogin.
I have described the meditation on the essential nature and the metaphorical form of the elements:
essential nature refers to hardness and so forth, while metaphorical form refers to yellowness and so forth.
And therefore:
"Having thus known and meditated upon it, one attains perfection and is also liberated. (12.168)
Even the spiritual attainment (siddhi) found here culminates only in liberation; may there be auspiciousness! 168.
Victorious is the Lord, the Master, who is the mass of consciousness and bliss, whose nature is the expansive manifestation filled with the glory of all principles, and who is autonomous.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrī Svacchandatantra, accompanied by the commentary named Uddyota composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 12 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
Augmented by the expansive awakening of the essence of the flow of the nectar of the Supreme (*parāmṛta*).
Victorious is the glorious Lord, who bestows all prosperity and acts according to his own will.
Thus, within this portion of the text at the end of the twelfth chapter, twenty-two varieties of practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) have been shown. They are as follows: Mātṛkābhairava;
and Śrī Svacchandabhaṭṭāraka, surrounded by the eight Bhairavas beginning with Kapālīśa.

"O fair-faced one, whichever [deity] among you is pure in its *aṃśaka*, that Bhairava should be worshipped here as situated in the center; having worshipped him, one should install the central [deity] in his place. (8.25).
According to the perspective of the text mentioned in this discussion on *aṃśakas*, [these are] the Nāthas beginning with Kapālīśa.

The Lord (Koṭarākṣa Bhaṭṭāraka) exists in eight forms according to the diversity of his retinues; he is ninefold as the Nine-Self (Navātmā), distinguished by each of the nine individual stations; he is one in his collective state; or he is surrounded by thirty-two goddesses, or alone. Now, at this point—

Having thoroughly recollected the *Svacchanda*, which is the essence of all philosophical systems (*sakaladarśana*), the twenty-third [Tantra], consisting solely of the undivided Lord (*niṣkalanātha*) and being perfectly free (*svacchanda*). (12.166)
Thus, at the end of the chapter, in order to determine that which was briefly indicated for the sake of connecting the chapters,
the Śrī Devī said: "O Supreme Lord, [tell me] the essence of this tantra, namely the sacrifice."
Tell that in brief, indeed for the benefit of practitioners.
That which is sacrificed to is *yāga*; it is Niṣkalanātha, the essence of all systems.
Sacrifice (*yajana*) is the act of worship; explain that method of propitiation, which is of two kinds. || 1 ||
Thus questioned, the illustrious Bhairava said:
"The root seed-syllable is the leader of mantras, the supreme Lord;
it is mounted upon the seat of the *praṇava* and is endowed with the limbs and faces. (13.2)

One should worship the Supreme Lord with the collections of substances mentioned previously—the Supreme One, whose nature is the root-seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*), the imperishable Bhaṭṭāraka consisting of four parts (*catuṣkala*). "The Lord" refers to Svacchandabhairava in his form as the deity; the "Supreme Lord" is the sovereign of all.

It is the designator (*vācaka*) of all mantras that have entered into obscuration [and] whose names [begin with] *praṇava* (oṃ), as before. "With the limbs" means with the ultimate realities such as omniscience and so forth—
[expressed by] "the peaceful one with the six long vowels" (1.71).
Thus, by the previously mentioned [faces],

and by the [faces] beginning with *ya*— namely, by those very ones previously mentioned in the verse: "The letters from *ya* to *va* joined with [the letters] in the order of withdrawal" (1.45)— and not otherwise.

This should be explained as consisting of the letter *ha*, which is essentially non-different from the pervasive Lord Prāsāda-bhaṭṭāraka as described in the *Śrīkālottara*, and which is permeated by the fivefold group of *buddhi* (intellect) and so forth;
for it is traditionally held that "since the division of Tantras is remembered to arise from the distinctions of action (*kriyā*) and the rest, therefore, in that regard, [it is] as has been stated."
