"That must be performed, not from another tantra," according to the scripture. Therefore, it is "properly" endowed with the aforementioned limb-mantras (*aṅga*) and face-mantras (*vaktra*) precisely through non-duality (*abheda*), and not by way of their remaining as separate enclosures (*āvaraṇa*); for this very reason, it is also endowed with the venerable Aghoreśvarī through non-duality alone.
Although there is a scriptural statement formulated in the scriptures where the expansion of Śakti is predominant— namely, "one should imagine Gaurī as occupying half of his body or in his lap"—
nevertheless, here she is non-different from the very nature of the Possessor of Power (śaktimat), just like the mantras of the limbs and faces.
This mantra of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat) found here contains within itself the expansion of Śakti;
by the phrase "the previously mentioned," everything such as the deposition of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) and the deposition of the parts (kalānyāsa) is included,

with the sole exception that the deposition of the manifest (sakalanyāsa) must be performed by the Lord beyond parts (Niṣkalanātha) alone, who is the pervader of both the manifest and the unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala).
Because this [deity] is mentioned after Bhagavat Koṭarākṣa, some maintain that he has ten arms like him;
however, the Gurus hold that because he is Svacchandabhairava, he must have eighteen arms.
By the phrase "with collections of substances," it is indicated that the worship which is a limb of accomplishment (*siddhi*) must be performed with a great abundance of materials.
For this [deity] who is invariably worshipped—

this very same arrangement of the fire-oblation (homavinyāsa) is performed for the Blessed One when He has been installed in the consecrated fire; [one should offer] a hundred or a thousand [oblations].
The meaning is that a fire sacrifice (homa), beginning with clarified butter (ājya) and ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), should be performed one hundred and eight times;
and this ritual action is to be commenced by one who has been initiated for the practice of Śiva-dharma, or by anyone else.
And for him, that very [initiation] is proclaimed as the initiation. 13-3.
That very same [state] as previously described. || 3 ||

Thus, having performed the worship and libation for the Goddess after being initiated by the previously mentioned Śiva-dharma initiation, he who— single-minded and composed— recites [the mantra] one million times on the bank of a river flowing into the ocean, avoiding companions, [attains success]. (13.4)
One who has conquered the senses and possesses a single-pointed mind, remaining steadfast in celibacy, should offer one hundred thousand oblations of human flesh mixed with guggulu resin. (13.5)
O Goddess, one shall accomplish that which is impossible to achieve; there is no need for deliberation here.

This refers to one whose mind is fixed solely upon the recitation of the Niṣkala-Bhaṭṭāraka alone, and who is therefore concentrated (*samāhita*). The term "river flowing to the ocean" means a great river (*mahānadī*). One should avoid [distractions] along with companions.
The meaning is that just as the deity to be propitiated is a sole hero, so too is the worshiper;
according to the principle that "as is the oblation, so is the recitation," it is appropriate [to practice] with one-pointedness of mind even during the oblation.
Furthermore, whatever rites there may be here, established in the four seats (catuṣpīṭha), [are all contained within this]. || 13-6 ||
Whether they be inferior, middling, or superior, O fair-faced one, they attain success, O Goddess of gods, according to the word of Bhairava. (13.7)
In the scripture of the Supreme Lord, which consists of the four seats (pīṭhas) of the Vidyās and Tantras,
there are certain rites to be performed here in this world—

rites of an inferior nature and so forth— which serve as the cause for the pervasion of the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), the netherworld (pātāla), and the ether (ākāśa).

It should be understood that those [mantras] which have been previously practiced by the yogin become effective; however, it must not be explained as referring to low or middling types such as deceptive spells (*kuhakavādi*) and the like.
For it is said: "Even rites that have been performed [previously] succeed through a hundred thousand recitations" (6.57).

Thus, because these [powers] were previously enjoined as being achievable through limited prior service (*pūrvasevā*), by the phrase "according to the word of Bhairava," he indicates that no doubt— such as that which is easily accessible to an ordinary subject under the influence of *māyā*— should be entertained here. Now, at certain occasions, even for this practitioner who is intent upon the means of attaining the primary accomplishments (*mukhyasiddhi*),...

He speaks in order to instruct on the useful rites for subjugating nature and so forth, which are accomplished through substances, mantras, and proper application, by means of narratives concerning noble beings and others:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme *Kārikā-kośa*."
Knowing which, O Goddess of the gods, practitioners move about here in this world. || 13-8 ||
"A meaning that is expressed by the wise in brief through a very concise designation—that should be followed according to the *sūtra*, which teaches the meaning of the *kārikās*.
This refers to the collection or compendium of those *kārikās* thus defined. "Supreme" (*uttama*) means—

The meaning is that because it is the domain of heroes, its fruit is free from obstacles. For this very reason, the phrase "roaming about" means they sport according to their desire, having attained all accomplishments (siddhis) as if they were in the palm of their hand. || 8 ||
Therein—having taken up the blood that has soaked the head of a hero struck down by a sword held face-to-face;
[one should write] the name joined with the mantra upon the body of the target, marked with red lac. || 13-9 ||
Having placed [the target] in a preta-fire that is intensely heated at night, he who recites [the mantra] one hundred times brings him—
whether he be a universal monarch of the asuras or the preceptor of the asura lords— under his control with the speed of the wind.
The skull-cup, dried and stripped of its flesh, is smeared with lac mixed with the blood of a *preta*; it is inscribed with mantras, as taught in the fifth application.
Because of the statement, "one who knows the mantra is fearless" (13–16), that which has been known should be written on the forehead; as he will state in the seventh application:
"and his name [should be] on the forehead" (13–20).

The name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—ending with the modification (*ūha*) "bring him" (*ānaya*)—is inscribed upon that very substance in the body of the one to be accomplished; having thoroughly heated it at night in the fire of the *preta* while facing the direction of the practitioner for whose sake it was written, he recites [the mantra] a hundred times. Him...
It brings the object to be accomplished with extreme speed, like the force of the wind, according to its specific application. || 10 ||
Drawn with *pretālaktaka* upon a human head and heated by the fire of a *preta*, it brings the subject (*sādhya*) from the world of Yama by force, as before, in no long time. (13.11)
As before, it is understood that one should recite the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) joined with the mantra a hundred times.
"Pretālaktaka" refers to blood derived from the body of a *preta*. "On a human head" means on one belonging to a non-hero.
The word "also" (*api*) indicates a distinction from what precedes. || 11 ||
Having taken the dust from the left foot of a dead woman who was hanged,
one should [draw] the body of the person to be acted upon, joined with the mantra, using blood, lac, and yellow orpiment.
If one recites [the mantra] a hundred times while facing [the deity] for half a night over a well-heated fire of khadira wood,
one brings Śacī or Ahalyā within a hundredth part of a day.

At the end of the word "saṃyuktām," the word "likhitām" (written) should be supplied; at the word "sutaptām" (well-heated), the word "kṛtvā" (having made) should be supplied. Here, "rocanā" refers to yellow pigment (*narasārka*). Others say "pāṃsulī" means the bone of the heel. A "hundredth part of the day" refers to a minute division of time. || 13 ||

Having taken the dust from the foot of a woman whose body is suspended [by her neck], and having drawn the form of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) using that dust as vermilion and one's own blood as yellow pigment; 13–14.

Having prepared a fire of the *preta* class that is intensely heated, over which one has recited the mantra one hundred times and which is joined with the mantra of one's own name, one quickly summons the women of the *yakṣas*, *surās*, *asuras*, and *pannagas*. (13–15)
The distinction is that previously it was the blood of a preta, whereas here it is one's own blood.

The name of the person to be acted upon, written with lac-dye and yellow pigment (rocanā) on one's own left hand, should be empowered by a knower of mantras through a hundred recitations and heated over a fire at night. (13–16)
In a smokeless fire of *khadira* wood, one brings even the preceptor of the Asuras [Vṛhaspati] by the force of the wind at the end of his name;
the application of the mantra has already been explained previously.
The object to be accomplished, written with red ochre upon the surface of the ground. || 13-17 ||

Having stepped upon the [diagram] drawn on the ground with the left hand raised with scents and joined with the seed-syllable of reality (tattvabīja), one should face the target at the time of midnight.
He brings even the lord of the earth, along with his ministers, within a hundredth part of a moment;

having first inscribed [the names] through the medium of their designations by one skilled in mantras who is free from fear, as before— using red ochre and vermilion, indeed with blood arising from a corpse— it is for this very reason that this ground is like a cremation ground.
And here, the application of reciting [the mantra] a hundred times, which is relevant to the context, remains established.
The person to be acted upon (sādhya) should be drawn in the center of a human skull with yellow pigment mixed with red. || 13-19 ||
Having inscribed his name upon the forehead with the mantra, and having taken a second human skull smeared with scented water; || 13-20 ||
Then, having formed a hollow cavity by joining two skull-halves, one should properly wrap it with a cord made from a corpse;
then, having heated it thoroughly with acacia charcoal embers, one should coat it again with beeswax. (13–21)
As long as this wax attached to the skull remains melted,
it attracts even the Lord of the Gods through the application of a hundred recitations in a mere twinkling of an eye.

"With the thread of the dead" means with the sinew of a corpse, according to the method of the *chummakās* to be described hereafter. It is established that the recitation (*japa*) in this context takes place only at night. || 22 ||
Having written the name of the target person on a wall with red ochre, accompanied by the syllables of the mantra,
and facing toward that person at night, one should mutter it while angry and pressing [the name] with the left hand.
By means of the conjunction of the syllable *kroṃ* and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), one swiftly brings forth gods and asuras.
"On a wall" refers to one located in a cremation ground. "Its designation" refers to the name of the desired god or asura whom one wishes to summon.
"By means of the conjunction of the syllable *kroṃ* and the goad" means by virtue of the left hand pressing down upon the syllable *kroṃ* written in the shape of a goad.
The meaning is "the son of Aditi."
One should offer as an oblation human flesh fallen from the blows of weapons in battle, combined with the three sweets.
Having bound the inverted wheel-mudrā, one should place the subject in the center;
having visualized him between the hands with his mouth agape and his palms pressed together in distress. (13.25)
"It brings even a great man, a lord of the earth, within a hundredth part of a day.
By the rotation of the two fingers, the wheel becomes a fierce cutter.
Thus, with the right hand placed upon the upturned left palm with the fingers extended...
By the friction of the palms of the outstretched fingers,
and by the rotation of the right index finger reaching the side of the left little finger—
that *cakramudrā* which is established in the Āgamas— one should perform it in reverse, [starting] from the side of the left little finger.

Having bound [the victim] by entering within the south, and having meditated upon the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) situated in the middle of that [space], overwhelmed by the pressure of the hands, the knower of mantras, reciting the name of the person to be acted upon one hundred times without fear, performs a fire-oblation (*homa*) at night with the aforementioned substances— even against a king.

The meaning is that he brings [them] under his control. At night, in the cremation ground, the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth, which are relevant to the context, remain established right here.
Having seized a hundred thousand banners and human heads, which were free from the falling of cold weapons. || 13-26 ||
Whoever writes down and worships the abode described as possessing the three forms,
for him there are Hari, Pavana, Kamalaja, Dhana-da, and Indra, along with the Siddhas and Gandharvas.
They bring about various excellent types of accomplishments (*siddhi*) and other diverse supernatural powers;
first, for that man who remains uncut by a weapon upon the banner,
one should take the skull of a man impaled on a stake, and there, as before, once it has been dried.

Having written or engraved that deity— who is described as possessing three forms, whose nature consists of both manifest and unmanifest lingas, who is the abode, and who is denoted by the root mantra— one who worships him daily shall bring even the guardians of the world under his control.
He clarifies this very point through two verses:
"The manifest and the unmanifest, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest—thus it has a threefold form. (13.28)
The wise person who properly worships that abode attains the threefold perfection born from the body of the King of Mountains.
Of that very King of Mountains, whose mind was perfectly resolved;

"there" means at the place where the skull of Naraka had been fixed upon the trident; "of the King of Mountains" refers to the sovereign practitioner (sādhakendra) by virtue of the *chummakā* perspective that is about to be described.
In this regard, he states the subjugation accomplished by means of a specific substance offering:
"The powder of red sandalwood, as well as black mustard seeds and salt... (13.30).
Having gathered the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished, one should grind it together while muttering the mantra of the god Svachchanda and rubbing both hands.
One should offer the powder as an oblation into the funeral fire or even into the fire of a *cāṇḍāla*;
facing the person against whom the rite is directed, one should perform this practice. (13.32)
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times until the king is summoned.
The dust from the foot of a man should be taken from the right foot, and that of a woman from the left.
Having uttered the *praṇava*, the name of Niṣkalanātha, and ending with *namaḥ*, one should say: "So-and-so must come under my control."
The mantra ending with "svāhā" should be employed in both recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa).
And once he has been drawn under control by the practitioner, that lord of the earth comes under his sway, both with himself and with his wealth. (13.33)
"There should be no doubt in this matter," he says:
"This application is indeed established; I tell you that it is not otherwise.
Having thus explained the ten applications for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkṛti*) and the application for the sake of attaining the supreme and other accomplishments (*siddhi*), [he continues:]
He describes the application for immobilization:
"Having taken that very same dust and mixed it with iron filings... (13.34).
Having tied [the mantra], over which it has been recited one hundred times, to a rag from a cemetery,
one should bury it eight finger-breadths deep in the earth at a crossroads, together with the name of the enemy.
If one casts it into the name of another, that person will be paralyzed in an instant.
[This should be done] with a piece of a shroud from a cemetery—a fragment of a corpse's garment—having recited the mantra one hundred times with the appropriate modification:
"Paralyze so-and-so! using the prescribed mantra.
He states the application for insanity: "Having collected that very dust combined with the five types of intoxicants... (13.36).
Having tied it with a garment from a corpse, inscribed with the name of the enemy,
and having recited the mantra over it one hundred times, one should quickly bury it in a cremation ground.
The one to be treated may become insane...

the fivefold *dhattūra* (thorn-apple) consists of its five parts known as root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit. Here too, the modification "make so-and-so insane" (*amukam unmādaya*) should be performed.
He states the method for bringing him back:
"But when [the substance] has been extracted, he is released;
his madness ceases."
He asks "How? and says:
"Having taken up the extracted cloth, one should purify it with milk. (13.38)
For this bringing back is indeed already accomplished; there is no doubt.
It has been extracted from the abode of the cremation ground and drawn forth.
Furthermore, he states another application for summoning:
"Then, one should collect the flowers of the red Aśvamāra. (13.39)
One should cause those [mantras] to be recited one hundred and eight times;
then, with a flower over which the mantra has been recited once, one should strike the top of the liṅga.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] day by day for ten days with a well-concentrated mind.
Having taken separately each day the flowers of the red *aśvamāra* and the red *karavīra*— for which the procedure has been prescribed— one should keep them well-protected.
Then, having gathered these eleven flowers, however...
Then, having gone to a great river, the knower of mantras should cause each [syllable] to flow there one by one in succession, having recited them all together just once. (13.42)
The meaning of the sequence is that first there is the offering of the flowers from the first day, and thereafter those from the second day and so forth. || 42 ||
For that last flower of theirs indeed moves against the current;
the meaning is that it flows upwards.
Having taken that [mixture], one should drink it mixed with water, without touching it with the teeth.
One should make the water yellow. || 43 ||
Then, having consecrated red *aśvamāraka* flowers one hundred times with mantras, the wise practitioner should place them at the tip of the index finger and press them with the thumb. (13.44)
To the south. || 44 ||
Then,
the knower of mantras, while reciting the *Svacchanda* mantra at will, should whirl the flower to the left with the name of whomever he intends; he shall swiftly bring that person under his control.
"To the left" means on the right side; here too, the ritual application is "draw [such-and-such] hither. || 45 ||
He states the procedure for the dismissal of one who has been drawn in:
"Having whirled it counter-clockwise, there is again its dismissal;
[the practitioner] whirls that *aśvamāra* flower on the left side, which is the counter-clockwise direction, for the sake of the practitioner."
Having been employed according to its application, it performs the act of dismissal; may there be auspiciousness.
Victorious is the supreme Bhairava, who acts according to his own will, who bestows grace, and who, through his supreme power of sovereignty, displays manifold wonders.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the venerable Svacchandatantra, accompanied by the commentary named Uddyota composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter: *Svacchandodyota*.
It liberates from the net of bonds, dissolves duality, and bestows joy.
It seals the collection of mantra-siddhis by plundering the thieves that are obstacles.

Victorious is the form of Śambhu’s mudrā, which manifests the various expansive expansions of consciousness that are its very nature; it takes the form of a physical gesture and is accomplished through the worship and other rites of the Lord.

Through thirteen chapters, the performance of the constant, occasional, and optional rites to be accomplished by the four classes of initiates, beginning with the *samayin*, is fully described. Among these, the purposes such as protection, the presence [of the deity], and entry [into the mandala] are established.
Regarding the statement, "One should subsequently display the mudrā three times during the ritual action of the three periods of time" (2.102),
the venerable Bhairava, wishing to explain the nature of the mudrās previously described as being accomplished through body, speech, and mind, said:

"I shall explain the characteristics of the mudrās as they exist in this tantra. He thus pledges that he will describe the characteristics— the essential form that establishes their true nature— of those mudrās which have been taught in this tantra for specific purposes and which take the form of imitations of the Lord’s weapons.
Although here the sequence of weapons is stated as "holding a sword and a shield" (2.90), nevertheless—
"One should employ the skull-bowl (*kapāla*) and the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in cases not explicitly mentioned" (14.21). According to this forthcoming principle,
since the skull-bowl and skull-topped staff are common to all deities residing within the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), [this applies] in the case of the venerable Lord Koṭarākṣa.
And because these two are primary, he first states the definition of their mudrās: "Having placed the palms of the hands face upwards, it is proclaimed as the *kapāla* [mudrā]. (14.1)
And this [state] conforms to the nature of consciousness engaged in the withdrawal of the universe. As I myself have stated in the *Śrībhairavānukaraṇastotra*:
"Amidst the fragments of the cosmic egg of Śakti, I always withdraw the very essence of the universe."
"You seem to manifest this very thing within me under the guise of the blood from the skull-bowl in your hand.
Even so—
referring to [the description of him as] "one who carries a shaven head and a khaṭvāṅga staff" (2.91).

Although this was previously recited, nevertheless, because of the mention here of the *kapālamudrā*, he indicates that sometimes a skull (*kapāla*) occurs in place of the severed head (*muṇḍa*), and so forth. The *muṇḍamudrā* also should be displayed by showing the fist, just like the sword (*khaḍga*). || 1 ||
O Goddess, having turned the left hand sideways, one should press down the three fingers beginning with the little finger with the thumb, keeping the index finger straight. (14.2)
Having turned the hand away, one should place it upon the shoulder;
this is indeed called the *khaṭvāṅga*.
Because of the specification "the left," it implies that the *kapāla* mudrā is indicated by the right [hand]. Likewise...
And in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"The right palm, slightly hollowed with its fingers somewhat bent, should be known as the *kapāla* [gesture]... (7.23).

"Three fingers" means they are positioned in the form of a fist; "turned away" means with respect to the shoulder. The true nature of this mudrā is also shown in that very hymn: "The entire world, its essence entirely withdrawn, abides in me alone; therefore, it consists of me."
Thus, under the pretext of carrying the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), you grant your command. Thus [it is said].
Now, listen to me regarding the sword mudrā. || 3 ||
O Goddess, one should press down the little finger and the ring finger with the thumb;
with the middle and index fingers pointing upward, this is proclaimed as the Sword Mudrā (khaḍgamudrā). 14-4.
This [mudrā] is to be displayed with the right hand turned away from the field of the aggregates (*skandha-kṣetra*); the word "having done" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
As it is said in that very same place:
"With the sword of compassion whose power lies within, you manifest the blade that cuts through cyclic existence."
"For the best of heroes have indeed taken possession of the entire universe through the majesty of their own power.
Thus [ends verse 4].
Having formed a fist and extended the little finger, O fair-faced one, and having brought it toward oneself, its throbbing has been described by me. (14.5)
"Having done so" means with the left hand; "sphara" refers to that which is being called "sphara. And it is said in that very same place:
"I am he who removes the fear of worldly existence, I am established as the one named Sphara; do not be afraid."
"Thus, O Master, by the sight of your snapping the bowstring, you grant us [our desires].
O Goddess of the gods, having formed a fist, one should bend the index finger upward;
this is indeed called the *aṅkuśa* (goad) mudrā.
Having turned the right hand [inward], it is said in that very same place:
"I withdraw all this, which consists of differentiation, by means of my own power in order to destroy it"—
thus does the Supreme Bhairava manifest himself to us through the wielding of the goad.
Alternatively, having demonstrated it with the left hand—learn from me the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā). || 14-6 ||
Having made the index finger circular, one should join it at the base of the thumb;
this is indeed called the noose (pāśa), which binds the nets of the wicked. || 7 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the thumb," this refers to that which is connected to the left hand in the form of a fist at its location. "The net of the wicked" means a multitude of obstacles. Its true nature has also been demonstrated in that very same place:
"Mahākāla is rendered auspicious by the ashes of consciousness, which envelops him with the noose of his own power."
Thus, by virtue of wielding the noose, you expand as the Death of Death. || 7 ||
Having formed a fist, O lady of excellent hips, and extending the index finger, it is called the *nārāca* mudrā; thus it has been briefly explained to you, O Bhairavī. (14.8)
"Having drawn [the bow]" means standing at the side like one who has mounted an arrow upon a bow.
The essential nature of this [mudrā], together with the Pināka-mudrā which will be described immediately hereafter, is determined in that very same place:
"By displaying the arrow mounted on the bow, [one attains] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśāna."
"With your power, you simultaneously pierce through Śiva, along with his cause, Hari, and the deer.
Having formed a fist, O beloved, one should extend the index finger and thumb;
if these are slightly bent at the tips, it is proclaimed as the Pināka mudrā.
The *pināka* is the bow. By slightly contracting [the fingers] at the tips, the arrangement takes on the very form of a bow. Its true nature (*satattva*) has already been explained. || 9 ||
O fair-faced one, when the hand is extended forward with the fingers joined together,
and that [gesture] is turned away, it is proclaimed as the Abhaya (Fearlessness) mudrā.
The meaning is that the right hand, with the *patāka* gesture, is raised while turned away from one's own body. And it is said in that very same place:
"By means of the *abhaya* [gesture], fears are constantly revealed as being uprooted."
"Your instrument is that which has the nature of bestowing grace upon all.
Thus [ends verse 10].
Extending the left arm, one should place it upon the knee;
O Goddess, this mudrā, called Prasṛta, should be displayed as the bestower that accomplishes all aims. (14.11)
And it is said there:
"With your boon-granting hand, you gesture toward the bestowing of universal prosperity;
indeed, one who is established in the supreme reality is never touched by the impurities of wealth."
Thus [ends the section]. 14-11.
Having made the left hand into the shape of a bell and turned it face downwards, one should rub it with the index finger of the right hand; this is known as the bell (ghaṇṭā) mudrā.
The true nature of this [deity] along with the vīṇā and ḍamaru mudrās to be described is also shown in that very same place:
"Displaying the vīṇā, bell, and ḍamaru, you grant this [boon] in a most formidable manner."
"Internally contemplating the reflective awareness of the Sound (nāda), which is divided by the threefold distinction of its modes.
Thus [ends verse 12].
With a concentrated mind, one should press the little finger with the thumb;
extending the other three fingers, this is proclaimed as the trident (triśūla) mudrā.

"Concentrated" (*samāhita*) means that one should contemplate the essential nature of the *vīrya* (vital energy), which consists of the expansion of each respective consciousness, within all mudrās; this is what he indicates by this [term]. And his *vīrya* is shown in that very [context]:

"You constantly imitate the gods externally under the pretext of bearing the trident— that beautiful Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) who possesses the triad of powers beginning with will, knowledge, and action.
And this [Power], turned away from the face, emerges from the support of birth in the form of a blazing crest of flame.
The Gurus maintain that she, having reached the state at the *dvādaśānta* by means of the radiance of the three spokes ending in the point (*bindu*), is the one who binds [the soul]. 13.
The staff (daṇḍa) is indeed to be imitated by the clenching of the fist; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. And it is said in the hymn:
"The entire world is subdued by my power and maintains all its established orders."
"Thus, by virtue of wielding the staff (*daṇḍa*), Bhairava of Consciousness reveals Himself to us. So it is said. But the Gurus [state]:
"She is resplendent upon the path of the *suṣumnā* channel, which has been touched by what is called the staff (*daṇḍa*)."
...Learn from me the vajra-mudrā:
having placed the left hand downward and turned it upward with a concentrated mind. || 14 ||
Having turned the right hand downward, and having rubbed together both the thumb and the little finger, one should display the Vajra-mudrā. || 15 ||

"Uttāna" (upturned) means that the right hand— with the index, middle, and ring fingers extended and spaced apart— is placed facing upward over the left hand, which is likewise positioned; the two hands are joined by interlocking the thumbs and little fingers, with the elbows resting at the sides.
This indicates her state of being seated at the side. And her valor is displayed in that very place:

"O Goddess, you carry your own supreme power, which consists of six spokes and is like adamant, whose three lower domains are illuminated by its own innate powers such as will (*icchā*) and the rest."
The teachers also [state]: "When the vajra-mudrā is bound, its firm stability becomes like the svastika. || 14-15 ||
O lady of excellent vows, O fair-faced one, one should display the ḍamaru with the fist of the right hand joined to its hollow opening. 16.
The meaning of "That thou art" has indeed been demonstrated. || 16 ||
I shall now describe the *mudgara* [mudra]: one should extend both hands straight out.
This is indeed called the *mudgara*.
Regarding the phrase "should extend," it means one should extend them facing forward, joined together with one another. Of this...
Furthermore, the reality is shown right there along with the axe-mudrā:
"O Īśāna, bearing a mallet and an axe whose forms imitate the [central] bindu, you demonstrate your intent toward piercing, splitting, and shattering duality."
The Gurus also state: "The bursting of the multitude of tight knots proceeds by means of the mallet.
However, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, the mudrā of the mallet is taught as the three-pronged [mudrā]. And so it is said:
The two hands should be made facing upwards with the fingers interlaced;
the two index fingers should rest upon the middle joints of the ring fingers.
The two middle fingers should be joined at their tips, while the little fingers are kept apart up to the knuckles;
the two index fingers are positioned on the sides of the middle fingers and made slightly separated.
"For this mallet with three prongs is indeed beneficial in an instant. (7-27-29).
Now— ...
"And learn from me concerning the lute. (14-17).
The *vallakī* is a lute (*vīṇā*). || 17 ||
O Goddess, with a concentrated mind, one should extend both hands palms upwards;
having then bent the two ring fingers, this is proclaimed as the vīṇā-mudrā.
The hunchbacked woman has the lute as her object; she is to be shown on the left side. Her true nature has already been explained.
One should extend the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger;
one should press the first [finger] with the thumb—this is declared to be the *paraśu* (axe) mudrā.

This [mudrā] should be displayed at the shoulder region with the right hand turned away from oneself. The *tattvamasi* [mudrā] has already been shown previously. These mudrās should be displayed in secret;
however, in public places and the like, they should be covered with a cloth, or else merely remembered.
Thus say the teachers. Some here read, in place of the description of the *paraśu*-mudrā:

"One should rotate two fingers [around the wrist]; this is the wheel (*cakra*) that cuts down the wicked. Others, however, by way of this context, also provide the definition of the conch (*śaṅkha*) and lotus (*padma*) mudrās.

It has been stated; however, by others, the characteristic of the *paraśu* (axe) is read immediately after this: "O Goddess, the mallet (*mudgara*) and likewise the axe (*paraśu*) resemble *rājāvarta* [stone]. That...

Everything should be disregarded because it is inconsistent with the introduction and the conclusion. And thus, for the most part, this text is seen to have hundreds of branches of interpolation from other works, as well as inversions of the text and inversions of the readings, imagined by those difficult to outwit; these have been [examined] by us.
Let this suffice: he was removed as far as possible through the search for ancient manuscripts. || 19 ||
Concluding this, he applies it to the present context:
"O Great Goddess, one should display these mudrās of Bhairava during invocation, restraint, and likewise during dismissal. (14.20)

Because of the concluding statement "these [are the mudrās]," what other occasion for the *paraśu* (axe) mudrā of Bhairava could there be in the chapter on the [mudrā] manual? And what room is there for the *cakra*, *padma*, and other mudrās in the chapter on meditation (*dhyāna*), since they are not mentioned therein?
Therefore, it is best to accept [the text] exactly as it is recited. This is indicated by the passage beginning with "invocation" (*āvāhana*) and so forth.
"Subsequently, one should display the mudrās three times during the ritual action of the three periods of time. (2-102) Thus, what was previously stated has been fully established. || 20 ||
Now, he demonstrates the common hand-gesture (*mudrābandha*) for those [deities] situated in the enclosures, such as Vaktra-Bhairava and the others:
"One should display the skull-cup (*kapāla*) and the staff with a skull at its top (*khaṭvāṅga*) for those not specifically mentioned."

Having described the arrangement of the mudrās because they consist essentially of the expansion of the powers of knowledge and action for all [beings], he now states their mental form according to what is appropriate:
"The skull is to be known as white, and the khaṭvāṅga is likewise. (14.21)
The trident, the iron arrow, and the sword with the luster of a blue lotus; the spear is red, and the Pināka bow is proclaimed to be black.

The bell is to be known as having the luster of gold; the goad has the luster of emerald; the noose resembles crushed collyrium; and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) is remembered as being like crystal. || 14-23 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, he should be meditated upon with a serene mind as the Supreme Lord, holding a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) resembling gold and a lute (*vīṇā*) of equal radiance. (14.24)
One should know the staff to be red; one should contemplate the vajra as yellow.
O Goddess, the mallet and likewise the axe are like the color of lapis lazuli (rājāvarta).

"By the clarity of the mind" (cittaprasādena) means that clarity is identical to the mind, which is to say, it is of the nature of the manifestation of consciousness free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhisaṃvitprakāśarūpa).
He concludes: "The seat of the mudrā is fully described as that which brings about the fruit of the four aims of life."

Not only is this tantra, according to the principle previously indicated, of the nature of the vidyās, mantras, maṇḍalas, and seats; it is also, here, of the nature of the seats of the mudrās by virtue of being the locus of the mudrās. [This applies] to the fourfold group, namely the four beginning with the *samayin*.
Because this is the cause for entering into the reality of the presence of the protection, from which the arising of the fruit occurs;
this [verse] constitutes the conclusion of the work, namely: "The Great Tantra of the Four Seats, which brings about the arising of the fruits of the four aims" (1.5).
Having thus described the physical and mental forms of the mudrās, he also speaks of their verbal form:
"O fair-faced one, those beginning with the syllable Oṃ are mounted upon the seat of the Praṇava. (14.26)
One should contemplate the true nature of the mudrās, which are forms of the power of the Blessed One, arranged according to their own names and concluding with a salutation.

Thus, O Great Goddess, these [mantras], made manifest through the application of ritual arrangement, visualization, meditation, and mantra-recitation, accomplish various fruits consisting of protection from obstacles, the presence of the Lord's own nature, and entry into that [nature]. (14–27)
By qualifying the Goddess with the term "mahat" (great), he reveals her knowledge of the potency of the mudrās, thereby teaching that the potency of the mudrās alone is their essential core. || 27 ||
He concludes the section on the subject matter concerning the *pāṭalika*:
"O Dear One, the characteristic of the mudrās, which is known for removing obstacles, should be understood with effort and accomplished by one of great soul. (14.28)

Although this characteristic of the mudrās must be known even by initiates (*samayins*) and others for the purpose of dispelling obstacles during the presence of the Blessed One, his entry [into the body], and so forth, it must nevertheless be known specifically by the practitioner (*sādhaka*), because the accomplishment of the goal is achieved only for one who is protected by the binding of the mudrās.
As it was stated in the previous scripture:
"By those [observances] protected, the practitioner of mantra shall attain the perfection of mantra. May there be auspiciousness. || 28 ||

By the power of their own self-confidence, flashing forth through the contemplation of their own great mantras, consisting of the spontaneous vibration of the Self, and streaming with the nectar of the supreme expansion— these sequences of mudrās indeed arise in that state spontaneously and instantaneously.
May that one Śiva protect you, by whom the burden of the elephant of the noose is shattered.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mudrās," in the illustrious Svacchandatantra, accompanied by the commentary named Uddyota composed by the eminent and illustrious Mahāmāheśvara teacher, Śrī Kṣemarāja. || 14 ||
The Fifteenth Chapter:
*Svacchandodyota* ("The Radiance of the Independent One") "He is the creator of the entire world, its sustainer, and its destroyer all at once."
Victorious is the Lord Svacchanda, the foundation for resting in one's own self.

Now, in order to ensure the unimpeded attainment of accomplishment by means of concealing the tantric conduct of the practitioners (*samayins*) among themselves, [the author], beginning this chapter as a supplement to the previously discussed subjects, [explains] the synonyms for *chummakā* and *śarma*:

In order to demonstrate the esoteric nature of this treatise through its profundity— by employing technical terminology (*pāribhāṣika-saṃjñā*) to initiate supramundane discourse— the venerable Bhairava said:
"For one who is engaged in recitation, meditation, and so forth, and who observes the vows of conduct (*caryā-vrata*),"
O fair-faced one, I shall now fully explain the secret kisses for the practitioner.
*Chummakā* is a technical term (*pāribhāṣikī saṃjñā*) based on intentional thought (*sañcityā*) that has entered into those conventions.
The phrase "of the practitioner" (*sādhakasya*) is used by way of its predominance. (1)
In that regard:
Bhairava is known as the Abode (Dhāman), the Guru is known as the Bestower of All;
the Sādhaka is to be understood as the Mountain, and the Putraka is known as Vimala. || 15-2 ||
This statement is made at the outset because the deity to be propitiated is the most supreme object to be attained.

It is called "the Abode" (*dhāma*) because it illuminates even the splendors of the sun, moon, and fire, and because it is the place where the universe comes to rest. "Always" (*sarvadā*) refers to the Guru, who is free from all desire due to being perfectly complete within his own self.
Because his sole purpose is the welfare of others; because he is like a mountain, he is "unshakable" and solely intent on propitiation;
because he has purified the entire inner ground, he is "stainless," meaning free from impurity; and because he is "remembered" through an uninterrupted lineage—so it shall be hereafter. (2)
The initiate possesses a beautiful body, and even sisters are brought under his power.
"Beautiful body" means one whose body has become radiant through the penetration of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
Those women who have become arrogant as a result of attaining success in mantra are like sisters to him.
Thus it is said: "of those who are devoted to the propitiation of the mantra."
He states the *chummakā* (secret code) concerning the specific substances used for sacrifice among all these:
"Wine, however, should be known as 'gladdening' (*harṣaṇa*),
because it gladdens (*harṣayati*)."
But the gods are known as *muditā* (joy). || 15-3 ||
"Sympathetic joy" (muditā) means joy (mudita), because it is the cause of that [joy]. || 3 ||
Likewise—

fishes are to be known as aquatic beings... because, according to the principle established by the Śrīcaryā lineage, they have been initiated through the consumption of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) from among the species of aquatic creatures.
Thus, by means of the *chummakā* (esoteric code), the supreme desirability of the Bhairava-sacrifice is indicated.
And meat increases strength;
for through meat— which is the cause of extraordinary wonder— strength and vigor are increased by the process of nourishing the six constituents (dhātus), such as the rasa (plasma) and the rest.

According to the principle established by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka in the verse, "From the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) produced by the exhilaration of eating and drinking" (72), this designation [of *bala*] is used because of the intensification— that is, the stimulation— of the power (*śakti*) of the yogin, which is the vitality (*vīrya*) consisting of vibration (*spanda*).
And according to the maxim of the cow and the bull, "fish" is stated to be distinct from "meat.
They say that what has been born is "grown," and what is dead is "turned away. (15.4)
Those established in the traditional lineage say that [the soul] has turned away from the face-to-face encounter with the bondage of the body, vital breaths, and so forth.
They say that what is red is nectar; the collection of entrails is the lotus-stalk;
semen is declared to be the moon; and the sinew is proclaimed to be the thread.

The secret conventional names for the blood, heart-lotus, entrails, semen, and sinews— which are employed in various specific secret sacrifices— are "nectar," "lotus-stalk," "moon," and "thread"; these are kept hidden because they serve as causes for supreme nourishment.

The reasons here are to be applied in sequence as follows: because it possesses a pericarp, petals, and so forth; because it has a form that is neither gross nor long; because it is endowed with whiteness and a quality of refreshing delight; and because it is the cause for stringing together various objects being offered.
In the word *padmam*, the term *padma* occurs twice through repetition; by this, the heart [is indicated].
The meaning is that it should be designated as "lotus" (padma). || 5 ||
Furthermore, regarding the place for the practice of heroes (vīracaryā):
the cremation ground is to be known as *ḍāmara*... it is called *ḍāmara* because of its wildness (*uḍḍāmara*) in its capacity to shatter all fear and distress.
Even in certain rites performed there, he is employed as an attendant:
"The *rākṣasa* is terrifying;
the *piśāca* causes hair to grow..."
Because it causes terror in the hearts of the undisciplined and because the hair stands on end due to fear.
In certain secret practices, she who is employed [as such] should be known as *ṛuhā*, that is, a woman in her menses.
It is called *ruhā* because it grows (*rohati*); it is that which serves as the basis for heroic conduct (*vīracaryā*).
Know indeed that night is the "concealer" (chādikā);
it is called chādikā because it conceals—that is, it causes the beasts to reach a state beyond the range of vision—according to the conduct of heroes.
But where the conduct of the secret hero (rahasyavīrācāra) is not visible, that is—
..................— "and the day is manifest" (prakāśa). The meaning is that it is called "manifest" (prakāśa) because of its being openly evident.
Now, he establishes a technical convention regarding specific parts of the body that are employed for particular functions, such as the eyes and the tongue:
"The eyes should be known as flickering; they know the tongue to be the grasper. (15.7)
Because it collects the essence [of the fluids] starting with that of the *lambikā*. || 7 ||
Likewise:
"The two hands should be known as 'wealth-givers' (dhanakara), and the two feet as 'companions' (sahacara);
for each one is the agent of worship, which is the treasury for attaining the state of the Supreme Lord."
And because going and so forth are not possible.
Moreover:
"The male organ (liṅga) generates contentment; the female organ (bhaga) increases delight. (15.8)
In the case of a name whose meaning is clear, [the suffix *cha* is applied]. || 8 ||
In some cases, such as the cutting of a hero’s bonds,
the weapon being employed produces a division;
likewise—
The *kartarī* is that which accomplishes the task;
it accomplishes the task, namely the cutting of the cords of the fetters (*pāśasūtra*) and so forth.
Likewise—
the messenger (dūtī) should be known as the "conveyor" (saṃvāhikā);
she is called a "conveyor" because she conveys or carries out the secret conduct of the hero together with him.

The messenger (dūtī) is called the wife; furthermore, the messenger is the bell, for she carries and brings forth the external by means of the internal sound, and thus she is the "conveyor" (saṃvāhikā).
Likewise—..................incense is said to be refreshing. || 15-9 ||
"Perfume generates contentment...
Here, "perfume" refers to a substance for anointing the body. These two [verses] are for the purpose of clarity.
......The kings are known as the supports (*dhāraka*). Those supports made of flour and other materials, which serve as the bases for the lamps, are called "kings" because they shine and gleam;
however, other kings who are protectors of the earth are so called because they uphold worship.
Having done so, they explained [the term] as "those who uphold."
The "awakener of the bound soul" (paśuvibodhaka) is to be understood as follows:

that which is offered as a sacrifice to the deities—the bound soul—awakens those various deities of consciousness through the process of consuming its fat, blood, and so forth; thus, it is called the "awakener."
But whatever distinguished *caruka* has been prepared by the deities—that *caruka* fulfills all desires. || 15.10 ||
Thinking that one attains all desires [thereby]. || 10 ||
It has been stated that food is the means;
furthermore, that which is food is said to be the means.
...the scum of fat is here called *maṇḍa*.
Because it is common to all people, like the scum [of boiled rice], it is called *maṇḍa*; thus, *ācāma* is [so named].
Now,
the ear is the mouth of the quarters;
because the ear is presided over by the deities of the quarters, it is called the "mouth of the quarters."
And the skin is known as that which experiences sensation. || 15-11 ||
It is so called because by means of it a tangible object is perceived.
The nose is said to be "well-established" because it is comfortably situated in that place where consciousness abides by means of the successive smelling of fragrant substances.
The "face," however, is that which investigates.
"Face" refers to the head of the sacrificial animal; it is called "investigating" because by means of it, objects such as form are investigated through the doors of the eyes and other senses.
The "pasture" (pracāra) is to be understood as the sacrificial animal (paśu),
because it is the cause for the pasture's release from all fuel and salt.
Having thus explained the *chummaka* concerning the objects of the limbs of the animal, he speaks of others as well:
"The mother is called the nurse (*dhātrī*). (15.12)
They know the father to be the creator and the brother to be the protector;
the sister is to be known as the bringer of auspiciousness, and the female friend as the accomplisher of all goals. (15.13)
They know that which produces virtues to be a friend, and that which destroys virtues to be an enemy;
this is clear.
Furthermore, regarding the parts of the body, he spoke of the *chummakās*:
"O Goddess, *chit* refers to the buttocks (*sphijau*)...
[The term] *chit* is so called because it cuts [the ignorance] and reveals the lower part of the body in two ways; thus, it is *chit*.
Vision is proclaimed to be the eye. || 15-14 ||
Vision (*dṛṣṭi*) is the activity of seeing. It is called the eye (*cakṣus*) because it sees—that is, it manifests form (*rūpa*). || 14 ||
The ten teeth are to be known as "khaṇḍakas" (fragments),
because they fragment [their objects].
The abdomen is known as the *ādhāra* (support). It is called the *ādhāra* because it holds (*dhāraṇāt*) from all sides (*samantāt*) that which has been eaten and so forth.
The heart is said to be the secret;
the seat of the heart is called "secret" because it is the locus of the secret self. And that which is secret was previously described as that which increases joy.
...know that the bone is indeed the hard [part]. || 15-15 ||
One should understand that fat (*medas*) is *vasā*... bone is said to be hard (*kaṭhina*). That which is fat, because it causes [the body] to grow fat, is called *vasā*.
Marrow is known as that which promotes nourishment (*puṣṭikara*). It is called "nourishing" because it is the cause of the nourishment of the specific bodily constituent (*dhātu*) known as marrow.
Know that *viṣṭhā* is the *vidūṣikā*,
because it causes disgust (*vidūṣayati*) by producing a state of the body that is loathsome (*vikṛtā*).
...the emission of urine is here called [mūtrasrāva]. || 15-16 ||
*sravaṇam* is *srāvaḥ*. || 16 ||

As for the flower called *kāleyaka*, it is the black lotus (*kṛṣṇapadma*). It is called a "flower" because, like that [black lotus], it produces wonder and serves as the cause for the manifestation of the deity's own essence.
...they know smoke to be "steadying" (dhṛtikara).
Here, the smoke arising from a cremation ground is intended; and because it is dear to the deities, it is called "steadying."
And "melaka" as well as "saṅghāta":
that which is the meeting or gathering belonging to the deities is called "saṅghāta."
By means of this instruction on the union (melaka), he who is the son of the gods—[is] known as Uddyotaka. || 15–17 ||
It is so called because it illuminates the world by removing ignorance. || 17 ||
Furthermore: "The daughter is to be known as the one who gladdens...
because she gladdens the world through the instruction of reality."

They know that which is *kṣubdha* to be "agitated. One who desires to ascend [the path], because of not attaining stability during the initial practice of yoga, is said to be "agitated" (*kṣubdha*) and "moved" (*calita*),
and is called a "corrupter" (*dūṣaka*) or a "paramour" (*jāra*).
He who is a detractor of any sacrifice or similar rite is called a *jāra* (paramour), because he is the cause of the destruction of the *jyā* (bowstring).
...was drunk and indeed honored. || 15-18 ||
They say that what has been consumed is "attained" (*prāpta*); what has been covered is "transformed" (*vikṛtīkṛta*).

Whatever secret substance has been drunk is called "saluted" (*vandita*). In this very same way, whatever has been consumed is said to be "attained. Whatever offering (*naivedya*) has been covered is [so designated].
That which was eaten in great quantity due to the varying degrees of concordant devotion, but then vomited through negligence,
or that which has been transformed into a derivative product, should be mentioned.
In this way—
whatsoever has been defiled, such as *nalaka* and so forth, that should be known as *kaṣīta*; the meaning is that it is to be understood as having been brought [into the ritual] after being defiled.
...the wise know this to be the established convention. || 15-19 ||
The Pārameśa Samaya is called "Sammata" (the agreed-upon) because it must necessarily be practiced. || 19 ||
The *mahalla* is to be known as the protector...
he who is the protector of the conduct of the Supreme Lord is called *mahalla*, because he attains (*lāti*) the great (*maha*), most excellent state of the Supreme Lord.
The goat, however, is the youngest.
That animal which is a goat is called the youngest; this sequence is due to [the order of] eldest and middle.
Discipline (vinaya) would be bodily action;
for that indeed brings about a state of being disciplined.
...but recitation is traditionally taught as the means of accomplishment. || 15-20 ||
It is called a "means" (sādhana) because by means of it, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are accomplished.
That oblation which has been offered, which produces success,
and which has entered into the rite of homa— that oblation generates threefold accomplishment.
Likewise—.................. division is considered to be "delighting" (rocaka).
That which is the division or the act of distributing the sacrificial porridge (caru) and so forth is "delighting," for it causes one to experience supreme delight.
Because it brings [them] forth.
They call a *kadamba* a "group" (*vṛnda*).
That which is a group or collection of deities, heroic substances, and so forth, they call a *kadamba*. A "rare" one is said to be unconnected (*aśliṣṭa*). || 15-21 ||
This means one who has become distinct from the conduct of a hero. || 21 ||
"The disciple is called 'Vimala' (the Stainless)...

means that the disciple who is to be instructed is designated as "Vimala" because he has become free from impurity through the grace of the Guru. Furthermore, "will" is proclaimed to be "Command" (ājñā).
The meaning is that wherever the command (ājñā) related to the Guru and others was received, there the Guru’s grace-bestowing will (anugrāhikecchā) resides.
That which is the vision of the deity is...
[this is] something extraordinary; the meaning is that it has been thus reflected upon.
...is known by the wise as being slain by a weapon. || 15-22 ||
They declare that the animal which has been slain by a weapon is one that has been properly obtained. || 22 ||
The night-walker is the cat...
he who is a wanderer (cara) at night is called a cat (biḍāla). For while a cat seizes mice at night, this one [seizes] the sacrificial animals of the hero.
...and the clawed ones are the renders.

Those who rend heroic sacrificial animals are called "the clawed ones" because of their common characteristic of being renders; it should be understood that what has been brought [to them] is "set in motion."...
When the great caru and other offerings have been brought forth, they are said to be "sārita" (consecrated) because they have become unified in a state of aesthetic-spiritual equilibrium (sāmarasya).
... guarded and likewise concealed. || 15-23 ||
That which is protected should be called "concealed."
Then, on one occasion, when a *melaka* (gathering) had been attained through the power of an intense descent of grace (*tīvra-śaktipāta*),

the Supreme Lord, intent on bestowing grace, commanded that the goddesses should show the path to the direct realization of each respective reality (*tattva*) to the preeminent practitioner (*sādhakendra*).
She who touches the crest-lock (śikhā) should designate Śakti;
she who indicates the head (śiras) should designate Bindu. || 15-24 ||
She who shows her forehead shall designate Īśvara;
she who shows her palate has proclaimed Rudra. (15.25)
But she who displays her tongue should teach that vidyā;
O lady of excellent vows, it should be known that seven crores of mantras belong to her.
She who shows the uvula indicates Ananta;
she who touches the throat points out the principle of Time (Kālatattva).
She who shows the heart-lotus indicates Puruṣa; she who shows the navel indicates Prakṛti. || 15-28 ||
O Dear One, if the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) were situated below that [principle of Śakti],

then there would be no accomplishment whatsoever for practitioners, because it would be the abode of Śiva in which all waves have subsided and which consists of supreme liberation; thus, at the time of the gathering, the Goddesses, intent on bestowing boons upon the practitioners, [state this].

Since they bestow [the fruits] starting precisely from the station of Śakti, which is mounted upon the Ādhāra and constitutes the attainment of success (*siddhi*), the description begins with that very point.
"The Bindu" refers to the abode of Sadāśiva, which is the light of the undifferentiated state between all objects of expression and their expressive words.

"Proclaimed" means "realized by me" or "shown. By the statement "seven crores," it is meant that the attainment of the respective mantra-siddhis occurs from this [deity] for the practitioner. *Tāluka* is the cavity of the palate (*tālu-randhra*). *Ghaṇṭikā* is the power (*śakti*) known as the uvula (*lambikā*), which hangs below that. *Ananta*...

Thus [ends the section on] the presiding deity of the *māyātattva*. Just as in the system of the ninefold self (*navātmaprakriyā*), the principles of *kāla*, *niyati*, and *puruṣa* are included, so too are the principles of *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga* subsumed and shown. "If it were to be" means: if it were directly realized by her.
Furthermore,
O Goddess, when he touches the secret place...
then he—
Ego (ahaṃkāra) is the presiding deity. || 15-29 ||

The meaning is that it indicates what has been directly perceived. It is within this very [perception] that the sixteenfold group consisting of the sense organs and the subtle elements (tanmātras) is included; they are not seen separately.
Furthermore:
She who displays her hips indicates the sky as its presiding deity;
she who displays her thighs, O Goddess, points to the wind. (15.30)
She who shows her knees has proclaimed her splendor;
she who shows her shanks should designate Varuṇa.
Thus, at the time of the meeting, when a *chummakā* (secret sign) has been shown by the goddesses, he states what kind of *pratichummakā* (counter-sign) must be shown by the practitioner:
"O Goddess, O Beloved, one should show the body as consisting of all the gods."
Then, for this practitioner who is engaged in worship, fire-sacrifice, and recitation, and who is devoted to meditation— || 15-32 ||

O Dear One, O Goddess of Gods, for one who is joined with the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), who knows the divisions of time, and who is endowed with ritual action, the Yoginīs bestow boons. (15.33)
O Goddess of the Gods, they show the great path endowed with various enjoyments, by going along which one attains the fruit [of the journey] at the King of Mountains. (15.34)
The ritual action (*kriyā*) is of the form already described. They "show" means they cause one to perceive directly that which resides within one's own body.

For the king of mountains, the lord of practitioners—having "gone" to it, meaning having experienced it directly, since the root *gam* has the sense of "knowing"—he "enjoys the fruit," meaning he becomes an enjoyer of those respective experiences. || 34 ||

Moreover, due to such an excellence of his fitness— O fair-faced one, the powers (śaktis) commanded by Bhairava, as well as various other accomplishments (siddhis), whether inferior, middling, or superior [arise for him]. (15.35)
"And those arisen from other tantras accomplish [their goals] without a doubt.
By this statement—"commanded by Bhairava"—the Supreme Lord himself exerts himself in this way for the sake of granting the practitioner's desired object; thus he says, "without a doubt."
The meaning is that this is indeed certain.
He concludes:
"Thus, O fair-faced one, the *melaka* has been briefly explained. (15.36)
Through the yoga of constant practice,
the state of being most fit has arisen.
To him he gives his own *caru* offering.
This is the usage of the root *dā*, meaning "to give. *Svakam* means for one's own self.
The meaning is that it has been established as being non-common (asāmānya).
Regarding this, it is said:
"O Goddess, by consuming which one becomes like Vīreśa. (15.37)
Consuming it without conceptualization is the act of taking; he is Vīreśa, the Lord Bhairava.

Since this is so—therefore, O fair-complexioned ones, those of purified soul perform fire-offerings, recitation, meditation, and worship; by that means, the practitioners of mantra attain success. || 15.38 ||
The state of having cultivated the self is a very firm confidence. || 38 ||
The Lord, who bestows complete accomplishment upon yogins and practitioners as appropriate, triumphs with sovereign freedom. (1)

Victorious is this Lord, the treasury of all perfections, who is the ocean of consciousness— spontaneous, pure, surging, and beautiful— which constantly flashes forth everywhere as the very self of all things in every way.
Possessing the power of Sarasvatī, which is vast, throbbing, incomparable, and full of the essence of nectar.

By its very name, the *Śrīmat-svatantra-tantra*— which, through the shaking off of the vision of duality (*bhedadṛṣ�ṭi*), is the reality of non-independence— does not tolerate an interpretation based on duality;
for from the beginning, it has been woven together by the continuous threads of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of dualistic perception.
People do not perceive the true nature of their own self, which is the pure and autonomous consciousness.

Having dispelled the darkness [of ignorance] through the explanation of the distinctions taught in the *Gatānugatika*, he has manifested the spontaneous radiance [of consciousness], which is overflowing with the nectar of non-duality (advaita). || 4 ||
Having heard the independent [Tantra] for a long time from the lineage of gurus beginning with the venerable Brahmadeva,
the illustrious [author] has explained it; likewise, there are other gurus who have practiced it.
When they, moreover, do not engage in making a request. || 5 ||
His mind, permeated by the distinctions fully grown through births and deaths that transcend the boundaries [of this world], did not conceive [of anything else],
for it was rooted in the lotus-heart blossomed by his own vital energy (*ojas*).
May the great festival of Svacchandabhairava shine forth within his mouth. || 6 ||

The descent of the supreme non-dual power of Śrī Bhairava, which has taken root and attained fullness within the heart-lotus of the practitioner— [that lotus] having been blossomed by the *ojas*, which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of [the Master] himself, namely Svacchandanaatha.
May the gurus, ever purified and with all other desires dissolved,
eternally attain the reality of the Self— which is transparent, autonomous, and most beautiful— together with those who have received initiation. (7)
Wherein perfect experience, sound reasoning,
and the tradition of noble conduct find their rest, and even the teachers have attained their ultimate goal.

He who, through his instruction in reality, is the moon for the nectar-ocean of knowledge, and by whose compositions—the ornaments of the conduct prescribed in the scriptures—the world is adorned. (9)
Suddenly, this fivefold set of marks, which was taught in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, became clearly visible to people because of his spontaneous knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures.
Having received this scripture from the illustrious teacher Abhinava— who liberated living beings in an instant merely by a glance of compassion—
Kṣemarāja, purified by the dust of his feet, has now expounded it. (11)
This entire existence has been swallowed up; the impurities of karma and māyā have dissolved;

a state of dense bliss has been attained; what more remains? The supreme Light has been gained by us, who have risen through the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the hymn to the venerable Cetana-Bhairava, in this stainless [reality].
One dwells without restraint beneath the sky of the heart. || 12 ||
The independent, pure-souled Śiva, who is consciousness, shines forth eternally;
and this Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), arisen at the very limit of the path of the senses, is his nature.
When she expands, this entire universe flows forth as her sole essence.
I do not know where this sound of saṃsāra will follow after me. || 13 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Chummakās," in the venerable *Svacchandatantra*, accompanied by the commentary named *Uddyota* composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 15.
